```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/debugawrongtag/Step4IntersectionsExample.scala" showLineNumbers
import izumi.reflect.macrortti.LightTypeTag

/**
  * Debug a Wrong Tag or Subtype Check ? Simplify Intersections Before Comparing
  *
  * A tag of Child with Parent built in generic code is not equal to the tag of Child until its tautologies are removed.
  */
object Step4IntersectionsExample {
  def withParent[T: Tag]: LightTypeTag = Tag[T with Parent].tag

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    println(s"withParent[Child]: ${withParent[Child]}")
    println(s"withParent[Child] == Tag[Child].tag: ${withParent[Child] == Tag[Child].tag}")
    println(s"after removeIntersectionTautologies: ${withParent[Child].removeIntersectionTautologies == Tag[Child].tag.removeIntersectionTautologies}")
  }
}
```

</details>

### Inspect the Inheritance Data

If two types print as you expect but `LightTypeTag#<:<` still gives the wrong answer, look at the inheritance data stored in the tag. `LightTypeTag#debug` prints it:

```scala
println(Tag[Child].tag.debug("child"))
// ?? begin child: repl.MdocSession::MdocApp::Child
// ??bases:
//  - repl.MdocSession::MdocApp::Child ->   
//    * repl.MdocSession::MdocApp::Parent
// ??inheritance:
//  - repl.MdocSession::MdocApp::Child ->   
//    * repl.MdocSession::MdocApp::Parent
// ?? end child
```

`LightTypeTag#<:<` only knows the parents listed in this output. The tag of a type contains the parents of every type mentioned in it, as the compiler knows them when it creates the tag at compile time. If a parent is missing, the subtype check can't see the relationship.

</details>

### Check the Known Limitations

Some answers differ from the compiler on purpose, because the model of the type system in `izumi-reflect` is simplified. For example, `Null` is treated as a subtype of every type, and every type as a subtype of `AnyRef`:

```scala
Tag[Null].tag <:< Tag[String].tag
// res8: Boolean = true
Tag[Int].tag <:< Tag[AnyRef].tag
// res9: Boolean = true
```

Before digging deeper, compare your case with the [Limitations](../index.md#limitations) section of the introduction and with the version-specific gaps in [Scala 2 vs Scala 3](../reference/scala-2-vs-scala-3.md#known-version-specific-gaps). F-bounded types, existential types and path-dependent types are the usual suspects.

### Turn On the Debug Log

When the cause is still unclear, ask the library to explain its subtype checks. Set the system property `izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti` to `true` in the JVM that runs the check, for example in the forked test JVM:

```scala
Test / javaOptions += "-Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti=true"
```

Every call to `LightTypeTag#<:<` then prints the steps of the check to standard output: the two types, each parent it tries, and the result of each step. Run only the failing check with the property set, because the log is long.

On Scala 2, the same property also prints how the macro builds each tag during compilation, which helps when a tag is built from the wrong parts. Set it in the sbt JVM:

```bash
sbt -Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti=true compile
```

On Scala 3, the macros have no debug output. See [Debugging and DebugProperties](../reference/debugging.md) for all settings, including `izumi.reflect.rtti.optimized.equals`, which helps when two tags created by different versions of `izumi-reflect` compare as not equal.

### Running the Examples

All runnable code from this guide is in [`izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/debugawrongtag/`](https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect/tree/develop/izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/debugawrongtag). Run any file from that folder with `scala-cli run <File>.scala`, or from the repository root with `sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.debugawrongtag.<ObjectName>"`.

### Going Further

If the result is still wrong and not covered by the limitations, report it in the [izumi-reflect issue tracker](https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect/issues). A good report contains:

- The Scala version and the `izumi-reflect` version.
- The smallest code that shows the wrong result, with the expected and actual values.
- The output of `LightTypeTag#debug` for each tag involved.
- On Scala 2, the compile-time debug log for the tags, if the problem is in how a tag is built.

## Build a Type-Safe Heterogeneous Map

In this guide, we build `TypedMap`, a small immutable map that stores values of different types and finds them again by type, as in `map.get[List[Int]]`. It is the same idea that dependency injection containers and ZIO's environment are built on. We start with lookups by exact type, then make the map work in generic code, and finally add lookups by supertype.

### The Problem

A map from types to values needs a key that identifies a type at runtime. The obvious key on the JVM is a `Class`, but a class doesn't know the type arguments of a generic type: `List[Int]` and `List[String]` share the class `List`, so their values overwrite each other.

For example, consider a registry of settings keyed by class:

```scala
final case class ClassMap(entries: Map[Class[_], Any]) {
  def put[A](value: A)(implicit ct: scala.reflect.ClassTag[A]): ClassMap =
    ClassMap(entries + (ct.runtimeClass -> value))

  def get[A](implicit ct: scala.reflect.ClassTag[A]): Option[A] =
    entries.get(ct.runtimeClass).map(_.asInstanceOf[A])
}

val classMap = ClassMap(Map.empty)
  .put(List(1, 2, 3))
  .put(List("a", "b"))
// classMap: ClassMap = ClassMap(
//   Map(class scala.collection.immutable.List -> List("a", "b"))
// )

classMap.get[List[Int]]
// res0: Option[List[Int]] = Some(List("a", "b"))
```

The lookup for `List[Int]` returns the list of strings: the second call to `ClassMap#put` replaces the first one, and the cast in `ClassMap#get` cannot detect it. The error only shows up later, as a `ClassCastException` far from its cause. A `Tag` from `izumi-reflect` knows the full type, including type arguments, so it makes a safe key.

### Prerequisites

Add `izumi-reflect` to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "izumi-reflect" % "3.0.12-SNAPSHOT"
```

The guide uses `Tag`, described in [Tag and the TagK Family](../reference/tag.md), and its `LightTypeTag`, described in [LightTypeTag](../reference/light-type-tag.md). All examples use these imports:

```scala
import izumi.reflect.{Tag, TagK}
import izumi.reflect.macrortti.LightTypeTag
```

### Storing Values by Exact Type

`TypedMap` keeps its entries in a `Map[LightTypeTag, Any]`. `LightTypeTag` implements `LightTypeTag#equals` and `LightTypeTag#hashCode` as type equality, so it works as a map key directly. The `TypedMap#put` and `TypedMap#get` methods ask for a `Tag` of the value type and use its `tag` field as the key:

```scala
final case class TypedMap(entries: Map[LightTypeTag, Any]) {
  def put[A: Tag](value: A): TypedMap =
    TypedMap(entries + (Tag[A].tag -> value))

  def get[A: Tag]: Option[A] =
    entries.get(Tag[A].tag).map(_.asInstanceOf[A])
}

object TypedMap {
  val empty: TypedMap = TypedMap(Map.empty)
}
```

The cast in `TypedMap#get` is safe: a value is only ever stored under the tag of its own type. Now the two lists get separate keys:

```scala
val settings = TypedMap.empty
  .put(List(1, 2, 3))
  .put(List("a", "b"))
  .put(Map("timeout" -> 30))
// settings: TypedMap = TypedMap(
//   Map(
//     List[+Int] -> List(1, 2, 3),
//     List[+String] -> List("a", "b"),
//     Map[=String,+Int] -> Map("timeout" -> 30)
//   )
// )

settings.get[List[Int]]
// res1: Option[List[Int]] = Some(List(1, 2, 3))
settings.get[List[String]]
// res2: Option[List[String]] = Some(List("a", "b"))
settings.get[Map[String, Int]]
// res3: Option[Map[String, Int]] = Some(Map("timeout" -> 30))
settings.get[Option[Int]]
// res4: Option[Option[Int]] = None
```

Type aliases and different import paths name the same type, so they find the same entry:

```scala
type Ports = List[Int]

settings.get[Ports]
// res5: Option[Ports] = Some(List(1, 2, 3))
settings.get[scala.collection.immutable.List[Int]]
// res6: Option[List[Int]] = Some(List(1, 2, 3))
```

### Using the Map in Generic Code

A `TypedMap` is most useful inside generic code, where values come in as type parameters. Because `TypedMap#put` and `TypedMap#get` only need a `Tag`, a generic method can call them as long as it has a `Tag` context bound for its own type parameter. `izumi-reflect` builds the tag for the full type from the tags in scope:

```scala
def putAll[A: Tag](map: TypedMap, values: List[A]): TypedMap =
  map.put(values).put(values.headOption)
```

Calling it with a concrete type stores the values under `List[A]` and `Option[A]` for that type:

```scala
val withScores = putAll(TypedMap.empty, List(9.5, 7.0))
// withScores: TypedMap = TypedMap(
//   Map(List[+Double] -> List(9.5, 7.0), Option[+Double] -> Some(9.5))
// )

withScores.get[List[Double]]
// res7: Option[List[Double]] = Some(List(9.5, 7.0))
withScores.get[Option[Double]]
// res8: Option[Option[Double]] = Some(Some(9.5))
```

The same works for type constructors. A method generic in `F[_]` asks for a `TagK[F]`, and can then store and read values of types such as `F[String]`:

```scala
def putGreeting[F[_]: TagK](map: TypedMap, greeting: F[String]): TypedMap =
  map.put(greeting)
```

To store an `Option[String]` through the generic method and read it back:

```scala
putGreeting[Option](TypedMap.empty, Some("hello")).get[Option[String]]
// res9: Option[Option[String]] = Some(Some("hello"))
```

If a generic method forgets the context bound, for example `def broken[A](map: TypedMap, a: A) = map.put(a)`, compilation fails with a message that asks for a `Tag` for `A`. The map never stores a value under an incomplete key.

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with the `TypedMap` from "Storing Values by Exact Type": <code>Step4GenericCodeExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/heterogeneousmap/Step4GenericCodeExample.scala" showLineNumbers

//> using file TypedMap.scala

/**
  * Build a Type-Safe Heterogeneous Map ? Using the Map in Generic Code
  *
  * Stores values through generic methods with Tag and TagK context bounds, using the TypedMap from the previous section.
  */
object Step4GenericCodeExample {
  def putAll[A: Tag](map: TypedMap, values: List[A]): TypedMap =
    map.put(values).put(values.headOption)

  def putGreeting[F[_]: TagK](map: TypedMap, greeting: F[String]): TypedMap =
    map.put(greeting)

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val withScores = putAll(TypedMap.empty, List(9.5, 7.0))

    println(s"get[List[Double]]: ${withScores.get[List[Double]]}")
    println(s"get[Option[Double]]: ${withScores.get[Option[Double]]}")
    println(s"get[Option[String]]: ${putGreeting[Option](TypedMap.empty, Some("hello")).get[Option[String]]}")
  }

```

</details>

### Looking Up by Supertype

Exact lookups are not always enough. A plugin registry, for example, stores concrete implementations but is queried by interface. `LightTypeTag#<:<` checks subtyping at runtime, so we can find all values whose type is a subtype of the requested one:

```scala
implicit final class TypedMapSubtypes(private val map: TypedMap) {
  def getAll[A: Tag]: List[A] =
    map.entries.collect {
      case (key, value) if key <:< Tag[A].tag => value.asInstanceOf[A]
    }.toList
}
```

To query the settings stored earlier by the supertype `Seq[Any]`, which matches both lists, and by `Iterable[Int]`, which matches only the list of numbers:

```scala
settings.getAll[Seq[Any]]
// res10: List[Seq[Any]] = List(List(1, 2, 3), List("a", "b"))
settings.getAll[Iterable[Int]]
// res11: List[Iterable[Int]] = List(List(1, 2, 3))
```

The subtype check respects variance: `List[String]` is a subtype of `Seq[Any]` because `List` and `Seq` are covariant, but not of `Iterable[Int]`. A `Map[String, Int]` is an `Iterable[(String, Int)]`, not an `Iterable[Int]`, so it does not match either.

:::note
A subtype lookup tests every entry, so it is slower than an exact lookup. If you query the same supertype often, cache the result per tag, the way ZIO's environment does.
:::

## Migrate from scala-reflect TypeTag

In this guide, we move code that uses `TypeTag` from `scala-reflect` to `Tag` from `izumi-reflect`. By the end, the code compiles on Scala 2 and Scala 3 and runs on the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native. We start with a mapping of the common operations, then convert generic code, higher-kinded code and type-keyed maps, and finish with a way to migrate a large Scala 2 code base gradually.

### The Problem

`TypeTag` is part of `scala-reflect`, which exists only for Scala 2 on the JVM. Scala 3 has no `TypeTag`, so any library or application that uses it can't cross-build for Scala 3 until the `TypeTag` usages are gone.

For example, consider this Scala 2 code, which keeps a registry of handlers by the type they accept:

```scala
// Scala 2 and scala-reflect (not compiled here)
import scala.reflect.runtime.universe._

final class Handlers {
  private var handlers = List.empty[(Type, Any => Unit)]

  def register[A: TypeTag](handler: A => Unit): Unit =
    handlers ::= (typeOf[A] -> handler.asInstanceOf[Any => Unit])

  def handlersFor[A: TypeTag]: List[Any => Unit] =
    handlers.collect { case (tpe, h) if typeOf[A] <:< tpe => h }
}
```

The code does not compile on Scala 3. It also has subtler problems on Scala 2: `Type` values must be compared with `=:=`, not `==`, so they can't be used as `Map` keys, and `scala-reflect` has known thread-safety issues.

### Prerequisites

Add `izumi-reflect` to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "izumi-reflect" % "3.0.12-SNAPSHOT"
```

Use `%%%` for Scala.js and Scala Native projects. During a gradual migration on Scala 2 you keep `scala-reflect` as well; remove it at the end.

All examples on the `izumi-reflect` side use these imports:

```scala
import izumi.reflect.{Tag, TagK}
import izumi.reflect.macrortti.LightTypeTag
```

### Mapping the Common Operations

Most `TypeTag` code uses a handful of operations, and each has a direct counterpart. In this table, `tpe` is a `scala-reflect` `Type` and `tag` is a `LightTypeTag`, obtained with `Tag[A].tag`:

| `scala-reflect`                           | `izumi-reflect`                        |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `A: TypeTag` context bound                | `A: Tag` context bound                 |
| `A: WeakTypeTag` context bound            | `A: Tag` context bound                 |
| `F[_]` with `TypeTag[F[Any]]` workarounds | `F[_]: TagK` context bound             |
| `typeTag[A]`                              | `Tag[A]`                               |
| `typeOf[A]`                               | `Tag[A].tag`                           |
| `tpe1 =:= tpe2`                           | `tag1 =:= tag2`, or `tag1 == tag2`     |
| `tpe1 <:< tpe2`                           | `tag1 <:< tag2`                        |
| `tpe.typeArgs`                            | `tag.typeArgs`                         |
| `tpe.typeConstructor`                     | `TagK[F].tag` for the constructor `F`  |
| `tpe.typeSymbol.name.toString`            | `tag.shortName`                        |
| `tpe.typeSymbol.fullName`                 | `tag.longNameWithPrefix`               |
| `tpe.toString`                            | `tag.toString` (with variance markers) |
| `mirror.runtimeClass(tpe)`                | `Tag[A].closestClass`                  |
| `tpe.decls`, `tpe.members`, annotations   | No counterpart                         |

The last row is the one real gap: `izumi-reflect` does not keep fields, methods or annotations. Code that inspects them needs another approach, such as a type class derived at compile time. See [Comparison with scala-reflect TypeTag](../reference/typetag-comparison.md) for the full comparison.

`WeakTypeTag` maps to `Tag`, not to the weak tags of `izumi-reflect`: a `WeakTypeTag` context bound resolves the caller's type arguments, and so does `Tag`.

### Converting Generic Code

In most code, the migration is a change of context bound and of the call that reads the type. For example, a generic function that describes the type of its argument becomes:

```scala
def describe[A: Tag](value: A): String =
  s"$value: ${Tag[A].tag}"

describe(Map("a" -> List(1, 2)))
// res0: String = "Map(a -> List(1, 2)): Map[=String,+List[+Int]]"
```

The rendering differs from `Type#toString`: `izumi-reflect` prints variance markers (`+`, `-`, `=`) on type arguments. If you compare rendered names with stored strings, use `LightTypeTag#shortName` or `LightTypeTag#longNameWithPrefix`, which contain only the class name. Subtype checks keep the same shape:

```scala
def accepts[A: Tag, B: Tag]: Boolean = Tag[A] <:< Tag[B]

accepts[List[Int], Seq[Any]]
// res1: Boolean = true
accepts[Seq[Any], List[Int]]
// res2: Boolean = false
```

### Converting Higher-Kinded Code

`scala-reflect` has no tag for an unapplied type constructor such as `F[_]`, so code generic in `F` usually asks for a `TypeTag[F[Any]]` or similar and extracts the type constructor at runtime. With `izumi-reflect`, ask for a `TagK[F]` directly. The macro then builds the tag of any type that mentions `F`:

```scala
trait Repository[F[_]]

def repositoryTag[F[_]: TagK]: Tag[Repository[F]] = Tag[Repository[F]]

repositoryTag[Option]
// res3: Tag[Repository[[A >: Nothing <: Any] =>> Option[A]]] = Tag[MdocSession::MdocApp::Repository[=? %0 ? Option[+0]]]
```

To get the type constructor of an applied type, as `Type#typeConstructor` does, summon its `TagK`:

```scala
TagK[List].tag
// res4: LightTypeTag = ? %0 ? List[+0]
```

### Converting Type-Keyed Maps

Code that stores `Type` values as keys usually needs a list and a linear search with `=:=`, because `Type#equals` is not type equality. `LightTypeTag#equals` and `LightTypeTag#hashCode` match type equality, so the handler registry from [The Problem](#the-problem) can use a `Map` for exact lookups and `<:<` for supertype lookups:

```scala
final case class Handlers(handlers: Map[LightTypeTag, Any => Unit]) {
  def register[A: Tag](handler: A => Unit): Handlers =
    Handlers(handlers + (Tag[A].tag -> handler.asInstanceOf[Any => Unit]))

  def handlersFor[A: Tag]: List[Any => Unit] =
    handlers.collect { case (tag, h) if Tag[A].tag <:< tag => h }.toList
}
```

The registry is now an immutable value. To register handlers for two types:

```scala
val handlers = Handlers(Map.empty)
  .register[Seq[Int]](seq => println(s"seq of ${seq.size}"))
  .register[String](s => println(s"string $s"))
```

Only the handler for `Seq[Int]` accepts a `List[Int]`, so only it runs:

```scala
handlers.handlersFor[List[Int]].foreach(_(List(1, 2, 3)))
// seq of 3
```

The [Build a Type-Safe Heterogeneous Map](heterogeneous-map.md) guide develops this pattern further.

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with the registry and the lookup in one program: <code>Step6TypeKeyedMapExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/migratefromtypetag/Step6TypeKeyedMapExample.scala" showLineNumbers
//> using scala 3.3.8
//> using dep dev.zio::izumi-reflect:3.0.11
// Run from this folder:  scala-cli run Step6TypeKeyedMapExample.scala
// Or from the repository root:  sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.migratefromtypetag.Step6TypeKeyedMapExample"

package izumi.reflect.examples.migratefromtypetag

import izumi.reflect.Tag
import izumi.reflect.macrortti.LightTypeTag

/**
  * Migrate from scala-reflect TypeTag ? Converting Type-Keyed Maps
  *
  * A handler registry keyed by LightTypeTag, with lookups by supertype.
  */
object Step6TypeKeyedMapExample {
  final case class Handlers(handlers: Map[LightTypeTag, Any => Unit]) {
    def register[A: Tag](handler: A => Unit): Handlers =
      Handlers(handlers + (Tag[A].tag -> handler.asInstanceOf[Any => Unit]))

    def handlersFor[A: Tag]: List[Any => Unit] =
      handlers.collect { case (tag, h) if Tag[A].tag <:< tag => h }.toList
  }

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val handlers = Handlers(Map.empty)
      .register[Seq[Int]](seq => println(s"seq of ${seq.size}"))
      .register[String](s => println(s"string $s"))

    handlers.handlersFor[List[Int]].foreach(_(List(1, 2, 3)))
  }
}
```

</details>

### Migrating a Large Code Base Gradually

In a large Scala 2 code base, you may not be able to replace every `TypeTag` at once. During the transition, a module that still has a `TypeTag` can produce a `LightTypeTag` from it at runtime with `LightTypeTagImpl.makeLightTypeTag`, so it can talk to modules that already use `izumi-reflect`. This works on Scala 2 on the JVM only, and needs `scala-reflect` on the classpath:

```scala
// Scala 2, JVM only (not compiled here)
import scala.reflect.runtime.universe
import izumi.reflect.Tag
import izumi.reflect.macrortti.{LightTypeTag, LightTypeTagImpl}

def fromTypeTag[A](implicit tt: universe.TypeTag[A]): LightTypeTag =
  LightTypeTagImpl.makeLightTypeTag(universe)(tt.tpe)

fromTypeTag[Map[String, List[Int]]] == Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag // true
```

The tag built at runtime is equal to the one the `Tag` macro creates at compile time, so both kinds of module agree on map keys and subtype checks. Building tags at runtime with `scala-reflect` is slower than summoning a `Tag`, so use this only at module boundaries, and remove it, together with the `scala-reflect` dependency, once the migration is complete.

### Running the Examples

All runnable code from this guide is in [`izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/migratefromtypetag/`](https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect/tree/develop/izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/migratefromtypetag). Run any file from that folder with `scala-cli run <File>.scala`, or from the repository root with `sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.migratefromtypetag.<ObjectName>"`.

### Going Further

After the migration, the code no longer depends on `scala-reflect`. From here:

- Read [Scala 2 vs Scala 3](../reference/scala-2-vs-scala-3.md) for the differences between versions that remain, mostly in how tags for unusual kinds are declared.
- Read the [Limitations](../index.md#limitations) section of the introduction for the places where the subtype checks of `izumi-reflect` are less precise than `scala-reflect`.
- Read [Tag and the TagK Family](../reference/tag.md) for the full list of tag types.

## Store and Exchange Type Tags

In this guide, we save the full type of a value next to the value itself, so that another process, or the same program after a restart, can read it back and check it against the type it expects. We start by turning a type tag into text, then read it back and compare it, and finish with the version check that keeps old readers from misreading tags written by newer code.

### The Problem

Persisted data often needs a record of its type: an event store keeps the type of each event, a message bus labels each message, a cache stores values of different types side by side. The obvious label is the class name, but the JVM class of a value has lost its type arguments, and it is often an implementation class rather than the type the program works with.

For example, consider labelling stored values with their class names:

```scala
def classLabel(value: Any): String = value.getClass.getName

classLabel(List(1, 2, 3))
// res0: String = "scala.collection.immutable.$colon$colon"
classLabel(List("a", "b"))
// res1: String = "scala.collection.immutable.$colon$colon"
classLabel(Map("retries" -> 3))
// res2: String = "scala.collection.immutable.Map$Map1"
```

Both lists get the label of the list cell class, `::`, and the type arguments `Int` and `String` are gone. A reader can't tell a `List[Int]` from a `List[String]`, so a wrong cast only fails later, far from the cause. A `LightTypeTag` describes the full type, and it can be written out and read back.

### Prerequisites

Add `izumi-reflect` to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "izumi-reflect" % "3.0.12-SNAPSHOT"
```

The guide uses `LightTypeTag#serialize` and `LightTypeTag.parse`, described in [LightTypeTag](../reference/light-type-tag.md#serialization). All examples use these imports:

```scala
import izumi.reflect.Tag
import izumi.reflect.macrortti.LightTypeTag

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1
import java.util.Base64
```

### Turning a Tag into Text

`LightTypeTag#serialize` returns a `LightTypeTag.Serialized`, a case class of four fields: a hash code, the structure of the type, the inheritance data used by subtype checks, and the format version. To serialize the tag of a type:

```scala
val serialized: LightTypeTag.Serialized = Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag.serialize()
```

The two strings hold binary data: each character stands for one byte, in the ISO-8859-1 encoding, and many are control characters. Text columns, JSON and log lines can mangle them, so encode each string as Base64 before storing it. We keep the four fields in a small record of our own, which is what the storage layer sees:

```scala
final case class StoredType(hash: Int, ref: String, databases: String, version: Int)

def toBase64(binary: String): String =
  Base64.getEncoder.encodeToString(binary.getBytes(ISO_8859_1))

def store(tag: LightTypeTag): StoredType = {
  val s = tag.serialize()
  StoredType(s.hash, toBase64(s.ref), toBase64(s.databases), s.version)
}
```

The stored record contains only printable text and two numbers. To store the type of a `Map[String, List[Int]]` and look at the result:

```scala
val stored = store(Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag)
// stored: StoredType = StoredType(
//   hash = -472871146,
//   ref = "AQEBHnNjYWxhLmNvbGxlY3Rpb24uaW1tdXRhYmxlLk1hcAIABAABEGphdmEubGFuZy5TdHJpbmcBAQAAAQEBH3NjYWxhLmNvbGxlY3Rpb24uaW1tdXRhYmxlLkxpc3QBAAQAAQlzY2FsYS5JbnQBAQIBAgE=",
//   databases = "...
```

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with the serialization and the stored record in one program: <code>Step3TurningIntoTextExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/storeandexchangetypetags/Step3TurningIntoTextExample.scala" showLineNumbers
  *
  * Serializes a tag and stores it as a record of Base64 text and two numbers.
  */

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val serialized: LightTypeTag.Serialized = Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag.serialize()
    println(s"serialized.version: ${serialized.version}")

    println(s"stored: $stored")
  }
}
```

</details>

### Reading a Tag Back

To read a tag back, decode the two strings and pass the four fields to `LightTypeTag.parse`. The result is a `LightTypeTag` like any other, equal to the tag of the same type created by the compiler:

```scala
def fromBase64(text: String): String =
  new String(Base64.getDecoder.decode(text), ISO_8859_1)

def load(stored: StoredType): LightTypeTag =
  LightTypeTag.parse(LightTypeTag.Serialized(stored.hash, fromBase64(stored.ref), fromBase64(stored.databases), stored.version))
```

To read the stored tag back and compare it with the tag the reader expects:

```scala
val loaded = load(stored)
// loaded: LightTypeTag = Map[=String,+List[+Int]]

loaded
// res3: LightTypeTag = Map[=String,+List[+Int]]
loaded == Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag
// res4: Boolean = true
loaded == Tag[Map[String, List[String]]].tag
// res5: Boolean = false
```

The loaded tag keeps the inheritance data, so subtype checks work too. A reader that accepts any `Map[String, Iterable[Int]]` can check the stored type with `LightTypeTag#<:<`:

```scala
loaded <:< Tag[Map[String, Iterable[Int]]].tag
// res6: Boolean = true
```

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with the record stored in "Turning a Tag into Text": <code>Step4ReadingBackExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/storeandexchangetypetags/Step4ReadingBackExample.scala" showLineNumbers
//> using scala 3.3.8
//> using dep dev.zio::izumi-reflect:3.0.11
//> using file StoredTypes.scala
// Run from this folder:  scala-cli run Step4ReadingBackExample.scala
// Or from the repository root:  sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.storeandexchangetypetags.Step4ReadingBackExample"

package izumi.reflect.examples.storeandexchangetypetags

import izumi.reflect.Tag
import StoredTypes.{load, store}

/**
  * Store and Exchange Type Tags ? Reading a Tag Back
  *
  * Reads the stored record of "Turning a Tag into Text" back into a LightTypeTag and compares it.
  */
object Step4ReadingBackExample {
  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    // Setup from "Turning a Tag into Text": the type of a Map[String, List[Int]], stored as text
    val stored = store(Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag)

    val loaded = load(stored)

    println(s"loaded: $loaded")
    println(s"loaded == Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag: ${loaded == Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag}")
    println(s"loaded == Tag[Map[String, List[String]]].tag: ${loaded == Tag[Map[String, List[String]]].tag}")
    println(s"loaded <:< Tag[Map[String, Iterable[Int]]].tag: ${loaded <:< Tag[Map[String, Iterable[Int]]].tag}")
  }
}
```

</details>

### Checking Stored Values Against an Expected Type

With tags that survive storage, a reader can refuse values whose stored type does not match what it expects, instead of casting blindly. An envelope keeps the value next to its stored type, and the reader compares before it casts:

```scala
final case class Envelope(payload: Any, payloadType: StoredType)

def seal[A: Tag](payload: A): Envelope = Envelope(payload, store(Tag[A].tag))

def open[A: Tag](envelope: Envelope): Either[String, A] = {
  val actual = load(envelope.payloadType)
  if (actual <:< Tag[A].tag) Right(envelope.payload.asInstanceOf[A])
  else Left(s"expected ${Tag[A].tag}, but the envelope holds $actual")
}
```

To seal a `List[Int]` and open it as a matching and as a non-matching type:

```scala
val envelope = seal(List(1, 2, 3))
// envelope: Envelope = Envelope(
//   payload = List(1, 2, 3),
//   payloadType = StoredType(
//     hash = -1818167878,
//     ref = "AQEBH3NjYWxhLmNvbGxlY3Rpb24uaW1tdXRhYmxlLkxpc3QBAAQAAQlzY2FsYS5JbnQBAQIB",
//     databases = "...

open[Seq[Int]](envelope)
// res7: Either[String, Seq[Int]] = Right(List(1, 2, 3))
open[List[String]](envelope)
// res8: Either[String, List[String]] = Left(
//   "expected List[+String], but the envelope holds List[+Int]"
// )
```

In a real system, the payload is serialized too, for example as JSON. The stored type then decides which decoder to use, and the check stops a reader from decoding a payload with the wrong one.

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with `store` and `load` from the previous sections: <code>Step5EnvelopeExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/storeandexchangetypetags/Step5EnvelopeExample.scala" showLineNumbers
//> using scala 3.3.8
//> using dep dev.zio::izumi-reflect:3.0.11
//> using file StoredTypes.scala
// Run from this folder:  scala-cli run Step5EnvelopeExample.scala
// Or from the repository root:  sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.storeandexchangetypetags.Step5EnvelopeExample"

package izumi.reflect.examples.storeandexchangetypetags

import izumi.reflect.Tag
import StoredTypes.{load, store}

/**
  * Store and Exchange Type Tags ? Checking Stored Values Against an Expected Type
  *
  * Seals a value with its stored type and opens it as a matching and a non-matching type, using store and load from the previous sections.
  */
object Step5EnvelopeExample {
  final case class Envelope(payload: Any, payloadType: StoredType)

  def seal[A: Tag](payload: A): Envelope = Envelope(payload, store(Tag[A].tag))

  def open[A: Tag](envelope: Envelope): Either[String, A] = {
    val actual = load(envelope.payloadType)
    if (actual <:< Tag[A].tag) Right(envelope.payload.asInstanceOf[A])
    else Left(s"expected ${Tag[A].tag}, but the envelope holds $actual")
  }

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val envelope = seal(List(1, 2, 3))

    println(s"open[Seq[Int]]: ${open[Seq[Int]](envelope)}")
    println(s"open[List[String]]: ${open[List[String]](envelope)}")
  }
}
```

</details>

### Handling Format Versions

The `version` field is the binary format version of the two strings. `LightTypeTag.parse` reads tags written by the same or an older version of `izumi-reflect`. A tag written by a newer version can't be read: `LightTypeTag.parse` throws a `java.lang.LinkageError` that asks for a newer `izumi-reflect` jar. The version the library on the classpath writes is `LightTypeTag.currentBinaryFormatVersion`.

`LinkageError` counts as a fatal error in Scala, so `scala.util.Try` does not catch it. Catch it explicitly where tags from other processes are read:

```scala
def loadChecked(stored: StoredType): Either[String, LightTypeTag] =
  try Right(load(stored))
  catch {
    case e: LinkageError => Left(s"cannot read type tag: ${e.getMessage.linesIterator.next()}")
  }
```

To see what happens with a tag from a future version, we change the version of the stored record:

```scala
LightTypeTag.currentBinaryFormatVersion
// res9: Int = 30

loadChecked(stored)
// res10: Either[String, LightTypeTag] = Right(Map[=String,+List[+Int]])
loadChecked(stored.copy(version = LightTypeTag.currentBinaryFormatVersion + 1))
// res11: Either[String, LightTypeTag] = Left(
//   "cannot read type tag: Couldn't parse a `LightTypeTag` version=31 generated by a newer version of `izumi-reflect`,"
// )
```

When services of different versions exchange tags, upgrade `izumi-reflect` in the readers before the writers. A reader on a newer version reads every older tag; a reader on an older version fails on tags from a newer one.

:::note
Tags from an older format are read without their stored hash code, so the first comparisons are a little slower. Tags written by the current format compare by their serialized strings first, which is fast.
:::

<details>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/storeandexchangetypetags/Step6FormatVersionsExample.scala" showLineNumbers
  */

    try Right(load(stored))
    catch {
      case e: LinkageError => Left(s"cannot read type tag: ${e.getMessage.linesIterator.next()}")
    }

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    // Setup from "Turning a Tag into Text": the type of a Map[String, List[Int]], stored as text
    val stored = store(Tag[Map[String, List[Int]]].tag)

    println(s"loadChecked(stored): ${loadChecked(stored)}")
    println(s"loadChecked(newer version): ${loadChecked(stored.copy(version = LightTypeTag.currentBinaryFormatVersion + 1))}")
  }
```

</details>

## Understanding Type Tags

Welcome to Understanding Type Tags! This tutorial is for Scala developers who know generics (`List[A]`, `def f[A]`) and context bounds (`def f[A: Ordering]`), but have never used `izumi-reflect` or any other type tag library. You don't need any prior experience with runtime reflection to follow along.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will understand:

- Why the JVM forgets type arguments such as the `Int` in `List[Int]`
- How a `Tag` keeps the full type of a value available at runtime
- How tags travel into generic code through context bounds, and how bigger tags are built from smaller ones
- What a `TagK` is, and how to read a type constructor such as `λ %0 → Option[+0]`
- How to ask questions about types at runtime: equality and subtyping

We'll learn these concepts through:

1. Types Disappear at Runtime
2. Capturing a Type with Tag
3. Passing Tags into Generic Code
4. Building Bigger Tags from Smaller Ones
5. Type Constructors and TagK
6. Asking Questions About Types

We recommend reading from top to bottom — each section builds on the previous one.

### Background

Scala checks types while it compiles your program, and then mostly throws them away. The JVM keeps the class of each object, but not the type arguments of generic classes, a process called type erasure. Most of the time this doesn't matter. It starts to matter when a program has to make decisions based on types at runtime: a dependency injection container finding a service, a map holding values of different types, a message bus routing messages by their type.

A type tag is the fix: a value, created by the compiler, that describes a type completely. Your program carries it around like any other value and asks it questions when it needs to. `izumi-reflect` creates these tags at compile time, on Scala 2 and Scala 3, on the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native.

### 1. Types Disappear at Runtime

Let's start by seeing the problem for ourselves. A list of numbers and a list of strings are different types, but let's ask the JVM what it knows about them:

```scala
val numbers = List(1, 2, 3)
// numbers: List[Int] = List(1, 2, 3)
val words = List("a", "b")
// words: List[String] = List("a", "b")

numbers.getClass == words.getClass
// res0: Boolean = true
numbers.getClass.getName
// res1: String = "scala.collection.immutable.$colon$colon"
```

The code above:

- `numbers` and `words` have the types `List[Int]` and `List[String]`.
- `numbers.getClass == words.getClass` compares the runtime classes of the two values, and it is `true`: at runtime, both are just lists.
- `numbers.getClass.getName` shows the class name, the `::` cell of a list (encoded as `$colon$colon`), with no trace of `Int`.

Notice that nothing in the runtime class says "of `Int`". That information exists only while compiling, and it is gone at runtime.

### 2. Capturing a Type with Tag

A `Tag[T]` is a value that describes the type `T`, including its type arguments. We ask for one with `Tag[...]`, and the compiler builds it from the type it sees in our code:

```scala
import izumi.reflect.Tag

val numbersType = Tag[List[Int]]
// numbersType: Tag[List[Int]] = Tag[List[+Int]]
val wordsType = Tag[List[String]]
// wordsType: Tag[List[String]] = Tag[List[+String]]

numbersType == wordsType
// res2: Boolean = false
```

The code above:

- `import izumi.reflect.Tag` brings the `Tag` type class into scope.
- `Tag[List[Int]]` and `Tag[List[String]]` create two tags at compile time.
- `numbersType == wordsType` is `false`, because the tags remember the type arguments that the runtime classes lack.

The printed form of a tag shows the type with a marker in front of each type argument: `+` means the type parameter is covariant, as in `List[+A]`. You'll also meet `-` for contravariant and `=` for invariant parameters. Try `Tag[Map[String, Int]]` to see an invariant key: it prints as `Map[=String,+Int]`.

### 3. Passing Tags into Generic Code

Tags are most useful in generic code, where the concrete type is only known at the call site. Inside a method `def describe[A]`, the compiler can't build a tag for `A`, because `A` could be anything. Instead, we ask the caller to pass the tag in, with a context bound:

```scala
def describe[A: Tag](value: A): String =
  s"$value has type ${Tag[A].tag}"

describe(42)
// res3: String = "42 has type Int"
describe(List(Some("hello")))
// res4: String = "List(Some(hello)) has type List[+Some[+String]]"
```

The code above:

- `A: Tag` is a context bound: it asks every caller to provide a `Tag[A]`.
- `Tag[A]` inside the method summons the tag the caller passes, and `Tag#tag` gives its `LightTypeTag`, the part that renders and compares types.
- `describe(42)` and `describe(List(Some("hello")))` are ordinary calls: the compiler creates `Tag[Int]` and `Tag[List[Some[String]]]` at each call site and passes them in. Notice that the tag describes the type the compiler inferred, `Some[String]`, which is more specific than `Option[String]`.

Notice that the caller never mentions tags. As long as the caller knows the concrete type, the tag comes for free.

### 4. Building Bigger Tags from Smaller Ones

Here comes the part that makes `izumi-reflect` special. Inside `describe`, we have a tag for `A`. What if we need a tag for a type that contains `A`, such as `Map[String, A]`? The compiler can't build it directly, since it still doesn't know `A`, but `izumi-reflect` can combine the tag of `A` with the rest of the type:

```scala
def settingsOf[A: Tag]: Tag[Map[String, A]] = Tag[Map[String, A]]

settingsOf[Boolean]
// res5: Tag[Map[String, Boolean]] = Tag[Map[=String,+Boolean]]
settingsOf[List[Double]]
// res6: Tag[Map[String, List[Double]]] = Tag[Map[=String,+List[+Double]]]
```

The code above:

- `Tag[Map[String, A]]` asks for a tag of a type that mentions `A`.
- The macro behind `Tag` finds the `Tag[A]` from the context bound and writes code that plugs it into `Map[String, _]` at runtime.
- `settingsOf[Boolean]` and `settingsOf[List[Double]]` show complete types, built from the caller's tag and the method's own type.

This is the key idea of the library: a generic method only needs tags for its type parameters, and it can describe any type built from them.

### 5. Type Constructors and TagK

Some type parameters are not types but type constructors: `F` in `def f[F[_]]` stands for something like `List` or `Option`, which still needs a type argument. A plain `Tag` can't describe those, so `izumi-reflect` has `TagK`, the tag of a type constructor with one parameter:

```scala
import izumi.reflect.TagK

TagK[Option].tag
// res7: LightTypeTag = ? %0 ? Option[+0]
TagK[Option].tag.combine(Tag[Int].tag)
// res8: LightTypeTag = Option[+Int]
```

The code above:

- `import izumi.reflect.TagK` brings the type class for type constructors into scope.
- `TagK[Option].tag` prints as `λ %0 → Option[+0]`. Read it as "a function that takes a type `%0` and returns `Option[+%0]`": a type that is still waiting for its argument.
- `LightTypeTag#combine` with `Tag[Int].tag` gives that function its argument and returns the tag of `Option[Int]`.

With a `TagK` context bound, a generic method can build tags of types that apply `F`, the same way as in section 4:

```scala
def boxOf[F[_]: TagK, A: Tag]: Tag[F[A]] = Tag[F[A]]

boxOf[Vector, String]
// res9: Tag[Vector[String]] = Tag[Vector[+String]]
```

The code above:

- `F[_]: TagK` asks the caller for the tag of the type constructor `F`, and `A: Tag` for the tag of `A`.
- `Tag[F[A]]` is built at runtime by applying the `TagK` of `F` to the `Tag` of `A`, exactly the `LightTypeTag#combine` call we did by hand above.

For type constructors with more parameters, there are `TagKK` (for `F[_, _]`, like `Either`) and more siblings.

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with both examples of this section in one program: <code>Concept5TagKExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/understandingtypetags/Concept5TagKExample.scala" showLineNumbers
//> using scala 3.3.8
//> using dep dev.zio::izumi-reflect:3.0.11
// Run from this folder:  scala-cli run Concept5TagKExample.scala
// Or from the repository root:  sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.understandingtypetags.Concept5TagKExample"

package izumi.reflect.examples.understandingtypetags

import izumi.reflect.{Tag, TagK}

/**
  * Understanding Type Tags ? 5. Type Constructors and TagK
  *
  * Renders the tag of a type constructor, applies it with combine, and builds Tag[F[A]] from TagK[F] and Tag[A].
  */
object Concept5TagKExample {
  def boxOf[F[_]: TagK, A: Tag]: Tag[F[A]] = Tag[F[A]]

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    println(s"TagK[Option].tag: ${TagK[Option].tag}")
    println(s"TagK[Option].tag.combine(Tag[Int].tag): ${TagK[Option].tag.combine(Tag[Int].tag)}")
    println(s"boxOf[Vector, String]: ${boxOf[Vector, String]}")
  }
}
```

</details>

### 6. Asking Questions About Types

Now that types are values, we can ask them questions while the program runs. The two most useful questions are "is this the same type?" (`=:=`) and "is this a subtype?" (`<:<`):

```scala
Tag[List[Int]] =:= Tag[scala.collection.immutable.List[Int]]
// res10: Boolean = true
Tag[List[Int]] <:< Tag[Seq[Int]]
// res11: Boolean = true
Tag[Seq[Int]] <:< Tag[List[Int]]
// res12: Boolean = false
Tag[List[String]] <:< Tag[Seq[Any]]
// res13: Boolean = true
```

The code above:

- The first line is `true`: the two spellings name the same type.
- The second line is `true`, because `List` extends `Seq`.
- The third line is `false`: not every `Seq` is a `List`.
- The last line is `true` because `List` and `Seq` are covariant, so a `List[String]` is also a `Seq[Any]`. The tag knows the variance of each type parameter.

Try changing `Seq[Any]` to `Seq[Int]` in the last line and see the answer flip to `false`.

### Running the Examples

All runnable code from this tutorial is in [`izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/understandingtypetags/`](https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect/tree/develop/izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/understandingtypetags). Run any file from that folder with `scala-cli run <File>.scala`, or from the repository root with `sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.understandingtypetags.<ObjectName>"`.

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned:

- Why the JVM forgets type arguments: `List[Int]` and `List[String]` share one runtime class
- How a `Tag` keeps the full type, type arguments included, as a value at runtime
- How a context bound such as `A: Tag` carries tags into generic code, and how `izumi-reflect` builds tags of bigger types such as `Map[String, A]` from them
- What a `TagK` is, how to read `λ %0 → Option[+0]`, and how `LightTypeTag#combine` applies a type constructor
- How to compare types with `=:=` and check subtyping with `<:<`, variance included

You now have a solid foundation in type tags. The next step is to put them to work in a real program.

- **Ready to use this in practice?** [Build a Type-Safe Heterogeneous Map](heterogeneous-map.md) uses tags as keys of a map of values of different types.

## Use izumi-reflect Tags with the ZIO Environment

In this guide, we write generic ZIO code that reads services from the environment: an accessor for any service type, a layer that provides a service for any type parameters, and a service generic in an effect type. Along the way we see why ZIO asks for a `Tag` in each of these places and how to satisfy it. ZIO 2 uses `izumi-reflect` to identify services, so everything here relies on the tags described in the rest of this documentation.

### The Problem

The environment of a ZIO effect, `R` in `ZIO[R, E, A]`, is a map from service types to service values. To find a service at runtime, ZIO needs a value that describes its type, and in ZIO 2 that value is an `izumi-reflect` tag. For concrete types, the compiler creates the tag automatically, so most ZIO code never mentions it. In generic code, it can't, and an accessor for any service type does not compile:

```scala
import zio._

def serviceOf[A]: URIO[A, A] = ZIO.service[A]
// error:
// A is a type parameter without an implicit Tag!
//   could not find implicit value for izumi.reflect.Tag[A]. Did you forget to put on a Tag, TagK or TagKK context bound on one of the parameters in A? e.g. def x[T: Tag, F[_]: TagK] = ...
// 
// def serviceOf[A]: URIO[A, A] = ZIO.service[A]
//                                             ^
```

The fix is always to pass the tag in from the call site, where the type is known.

### Prerequisites

ZIO 2 depends on `izumi-reflect`, so a project that already uses ZIO 2 needs no extra dependency. The `zio` package re-exports the types you need: `zio.Tag`, a subtype of `izumi.reflect.Tag`, and aliases for `izumi.reflect.TagK`, `TagKK` and the rest of the family, `LightTypeTag`, and `EnvironmentTag`, an alias of `izumi.reflect.Tag`. All examples use one import:

```scala
import zio._
```

To run the effects on this page, we use a small helper that runs a ZIO effect and returns its result:

```scala
def run[A](effect: ZIO[Any, Nothing, A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(effect).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

### Accessing Any Service

To write an accessor that works for any service type, add a `Tag` context bound to its type parameter. The caller's concrete type then carries its tag into the method, and `ZIO.service` uses it to find the service:

```scala
def serviceOf[A: Tag]: URIO[A, A] = ZIO.service[A]

final case class Config(url: String)
```

To provide a `Config` and read it through the generic accessor:

```scala
run(serviceOf[Config].provide(ZLayer.succeed(Config("jdbc:h2:mem"))))
// res1: Config = Config("jdbc:h2:mem")
```

  <summary>Runnable version, with the `run` helper from Prerequisites: <code>Step3AccessAnyServiceExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/zioenvironment/Step3AccessAnyServiceExample.scala" showLineNumbers

import Runner.run

  *
  * A generic service accessor with a Tag context bound, run with the helper from Prerequisites.
  */
object Step3AccessAnyServiceExample {
  def serviceOf[A: Tag]: URIO[A, A] = ZIO.service[A]

  final case class Config(url: String)

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    println(s"serviceOf[Config]: ${run(serviceOf[Config].provide(ZLayer.succeed(Config("jdbc:h2:mem"))))}")
  }

```

</details>

### Writing Generic Layers

A layer that is generic in its type parameters needs a tag for every type parameter that appears in the service it provides. With them, ZIO keeps services that differ only in their type arguments apart, because their tags differ. For example, a generic in-memory cache:

```scala
final case class Cache[K, V](entries: Map[K, V]) {
  def get(key: K): Option[V] = entries.get(key)
}

def cacheLayer[K: Tag, V: Tag](entries: (K, V)*): ULayer[Cache[K, V]] =
  ZLayer.succeed(Cache(entries.toMap))
```

`izumi-reflect` builds `Tag[Cache[K, V]]` from the tags of `K` and `V`. An effect can then require two caches that differ only in their type arguments:

```scala
val lookups: URIO[Cache[String, Int] with Cache[Int, String], (Option[Int], Option[String])] =
  for {
    byName <- ZIO.serviceWith[Cache[String, Int]](_.get("answer"))
    byId   <- ZIO.serviceWith[Cache[Int, String]](_.get(42))
  } yield (byName, byId)
```

To provide both caches and run the effect:

```scala
run(lookups.provide(cacheLayer("answer" -> 42), cacheLayer(42 -> "answer")))
// res2: Tuple2[Option[Int], Option[String]] = (Some(42), Some("answer"))
```

A lookup keyed by the class alone could not keep the two `Cache` services apart, because both have the class `Cache`.

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with the layers, the effect and the `run` helper in one program: <code>Step4GenericLayersExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/zioenvironment/Step4GenericLayersExample.scala" showLineNumbers
//> using scala 3.3.8
//> using dep dev.zio::izumi-reflect:3.0.11
//> using dep dev.zio::zio:2.1.27
//> using file Runner.scala

// Or from the repository root:  sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.zioenvironment.Step4GenericLayersExample"

import Runner.run

  * Use izumi-reflect Tags with the ZIO Environment ? Writing Generic Layers
  *
  * Provides two caches that differ only in their type arguments and reads both.
  */
object Step4GenericLayersExample {
  final case class Cache[K, V](entries: Map[K, V]) {
    def get(key: K): Option[V] = entries.get(key)
  }

  def cacheLayer[K: Tag, V: Tag](entries: (K, V)*): ULayer[Cache[K, V]] =
    ZLayer.succeed(Cache(entries.toMap))

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val lookups: URIO[Cache[String, Int] with Cache[Int, String], (Option[Int], Option[String])] =
      for {
        byName <- ZIO.serviceWith[Cache[String, Int]](_.get("answer"))
        byId <- ZIO.serviceWith[Cache[Int, String]](_.get(42))
      } yield (byName, byId)

    println(s"lookups: ${run(lookups.provide(cacheLayer("answer" -> 42), cacheLayer(42 -> "answer")))}")
  }
}
```

</details>

### Writing Services Generic in an Effect Type

In tagless-final style, a service is generic in an effect type `F[_]`. To put such a service in the ZIO environment, the code that builds or reads it needs a `TagK[F]`, which describes the type constructor `F`. `izumi-reflect` combines it with the rest of the type to build `Tag[Repository[F]]`:

```scala
trait Repository[F[_]] {
  def find(id: Int): F[String]
}

def repositoryLayer[F[_]: TagK](repo: Repository[F]): ULayer[Repository[F]] =
  ZLayer.succeed(repo)

def findWith[F[_]: TagK](id: Int): URIO[Repository[F], F[String]] =
  ZIO.serviceWith[Repository[F]](_.find(id))
```

An `Option`-based repository implements it for one effect type:

```scala
val optionRepo: Repository[Option] = new Repository[Option] {
  def find(id: Int): Option[String] = if (id == 1) Some("Alice") else None
}
```

To provide the repository and call it through the generic accessor:

```scala
run(findWith[Option](1).provide(repositoryLayer(optionRepo)))
// res3: Option[String] = Some("Alice")
```

Without the `TagK` context bound on `findWith`, compilation fails with a message asking for a `Tag`, `TagK` or `TagKK` for `F`.

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with the service, the repository and the `run` helper in one program: <code>Step5EffectTypeExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/zioenvironment/Step5EffectTypeExample.scala" showLineNumbers
//> using scala 3.3.8
//> using dep dev.zio::izumi-reflect:3.0.11
//> using dep dev.zio::zio:2.1.27
//> using file Runner.scala
// Run from this folder:  scala-cli run Step5EffectTypeExample.scala
// Or from the repository root:  sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.zioenvironment.Step5EffectTypeExample"

package izumi.reflect.examples.zioenvironment

import zio._
import Runner.run

/**
  * Use izumi-reflect Tags with the ZIO Environment ? Writing Services Generic in an Effect Type
  *
  * A tagless-final repository in the ZIO environment, read through a generic accessor with a TagK context bound.
  */
object Step5EffectTypeExample {
  trait Repository[F[_]] {
    def find(id: Int): F[String]
  }

  def repositoryLayer[F[_]: TagK](repo: Repository[F]): ULayer[Repository[F]] =
    ZLayer.succeed(repo)

  def findWith[F[_]: TagK](id: Int): URIO[Repository[F], F[String]] =
    ZIO.serviceWith[Repository[F]](_.find(id))

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val optionRepo: Repository[Option] = new Repository[Option] {
      def find(id: Int): Option[String] = if (id == 1) Some("Alice") else None
    }

    println(s"findWith[Option](1): ${run(findWith[Option](1).provide(repositoryLayer(optionRepo)))}")
  }
}
```

</details>

### Looking Up Services by Supertype

ZIO does not need an exact match to find a service. It looks for a service whose type is the requested type or a subtype of it, using `LightTypeTag#<:<`, and caches the result per requested tag. So an effect can ask for an interface while the environment holds an implementation registered under its own type:

```scala
trait Clock2 { def now: Long }
final case class FixedClock(now: Long) extends Clock2
```

To store a `FixedClock` and read it as a `Clock2`:

```scala
val environment: ZEnvironment[FixedClock] = ZEnvironment(FixedClock(1700000000L))
// environment: ZEnvironment[FixedClock] = ZEnvironment(MdocSession::MdocApp::FixedClock -> FixedClock(1700000000))

environment.get[Clock2].now
// res4: Long = 1700000000L
```

When several services match the requested type, ZIO returns the one added most recently. To avoid surprises, register each service under the type its users ask for, as `ZLayer.succeed[Clock2](FixedClock(...))` does.

<details>
  <summary>Runnable version, with the service types and the lookup in one program: <code>Step6SupertypeLookupExample.scala</code></summary>

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/zioenvironment/Step6SupertypeLookupExample.scala" showLineNumbers
//> using scala 3.3.8
//> using dep dev.zio::izumi-reflect:3.0.11
//> using dep dev.zio::zio:2.1.27
// Run from this folder:  scala-cli run Step6SupertypeLookupExample.scala
// Or from the repository root:  sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.zioenvironment.Step6SupertypeLookupExample"

package izumi.reflect.examples.zioenvironment

import zio._

/**
  * Use izumi-reflect Tags with the ZIO Environment ? Looking Up Services by Supertype
  *
  * Stores a FixedClock in a ZEnvironment and reads it back as its supertype Clock2.
  */
object Step6SupertypeLookupExample {
  trait Clock2 { def now: Long }
  final case class FixedClock(now: Long) extends Clock2

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val environment: ZEnvironment[FixedClock] = ZEnvironment(FixedClock(1700000000L))

    println(s"environment.get[Clock2].now: ${environment.get[Clock2].now}")
  }
}
```

</details>

### Common Mistakes

Most problems with tags in ZIO code have one of three causes:

- **A missing context bound.** The compile error names the type that has no tag. Add `A: Tag` for a proper type, or `F[_]: TagK` for a type constructor, to the method that has the type parameter, and to every generic method that calls it.
- **A tag for the wrong type.** When `A` is inferred, the tag describes the inferred type, which may be more specific than you meant, such as `FixedClock` instead of `Clock2`. Write the type argument explicitly in generic calls like `ZLayer.succeed[Clock2](...)`.
- **Abstract type members.** A service type that refers to an abstract type member, such as `x.Out`, needs a tag for that member in scope, like any other type parameter.

To register a `FixedClock` under the type its users ask for, and read it back as that type:

```scala
run(ZIO.serviceWith[Clock2](_.now).provide(ZLayer.succeed[Clock2](FixedClock(1700000000L))))
// res5: Long = 1700000000L
```

To see why a lookup fails at runtime, print the tags involved with `Tag[A].tag` and compare them, or follow [Debug a Wrong Tag or Subtype Check](debug-a-wrong-tag.md).

Run any file from that folder with `scala-cli run <File>.scala`, or from the repository root with `sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.zioenvironment.<ObjectName>"`.

### Going Further

The ZIO environment is a type-indexed map like the one in [Build a Type-Safe Heterogeneous Map](heterogeneous-map.md). [Tag and the TagK Family](../reference/tag.md) lists all tag types and their kinds, and [LightTypeTag](../reference/light-type-tag.md#subtyping) explains how subtype checks work and where they are less precise than the compiler.

## Introduction to izumi-reflect

[![Production Ready](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Production%20Ready-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fizumi-reflect_3%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/izumi-reflect_3/) [![izumi-reflect](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/izumi-reflect?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect)

## izumi-reflect

> @quote: Looks a bit similar to TypeTag

`izumi-reflect` is a fast, lightweight, portable and efficient alternative for `TypeTag` from `scala-reflect`.

`izumi-reflect` is a lightweight model of Scala type system and provides a simulator of the important parts of the Scala typechecker.

### Why `izumi-reflect`

1. `izumi-reflect` compiles faster, runs a lot faster than `scala-reflect` and is fully immutable and [thread-safe](https://github.com/scala/bug/issues/10766),
2. `izumi-reflect` supports Scala 2.12, 2.13 and **Scala 3**,
3. `izumi-reflect` supports Scala.js and Scala Native,
4. `izumi-reflect` works well with [GraalVM Native Image](https://www.graalvm.org/reference-manual/native-image/),
5. `izumi-reflect` allows you to obtain tags for unapplied type constructors (`F[_]`) and combine them at runtime.

### Credits

`izumi-reflect` has been created by [Septimal Mind](https://7mind.io) to power [Izumi Project](https://github.com/7mind/izumi),
as a replacement for `TypeTag` in reaction to a lack of confirmed information about the future of `scala-reflect`/`TypeTag` in Scala 3 ([Motivation](https://blog.7mind.io/lightweight-reflection.html)), and donated to ZIO.

  
  
  

### Limitations

`izumi-reflect` model of the Scala type system is not 100% precise, but "good enough" for the vast majority of the usecases.

Known limitations are:

1. Recursive type bounds (F-bounded types) are not preserved and may produce false positives,
2. Existential types, both written with wildcards and `forSome` may produce unexpected results, the support is limited,
3. Path-Dependent Types are based on variable names and may cause unexpected results when variables with different names have the same type or vice-versa (vs. Scala compiler)
4. This-Types such as `X.this.type` are ignored and identical to `X`
5. `izumi-reflect` is less powerful than `scala-reflect`: it does not preserve fields and methods when it's not necessary for equality and subtype checks, it does not preserve code trees, internal compiler data structures, etc.
6. There are some optimizations in place which reduce correctness, namely: subtype check for `scala.Matchable` will always return true, no distinction is made between `scala.Any` and `scala.AnyRef`,  no distinction is made between `scala.Nothing` and `scala.Null`. In other words, the library does not recognize that `Null` is not a subtype of `AnyVal`s.
7. Lower bounds are not preserved in abstract higher-kinded type members which may produce false comparisons.
8. Type and value members are not preserved in concrete types which may produce false comparisons with refined/structural types. (https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect/issues/481)

### Debugging

Set [`-Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti=true`](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/izumi-reflect_2.13/latest/izumi/reflect/DebugProperties$.html#izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti:String(%22izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti%22)) to enable debug output at runtime when tags are compared and, on Scala 2, during compilation when tags are constructed. (Scala 3 macros have no debug output.)

```shell
sbt -Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti=true
```

To see debug output when compiling in Intellij, add the above flag to `VM options` in [Preferences -> Build, Execution, Deployment -> Compiler -> Scala Compiler -> Scala Compile Server](jetbrains://idea/settings?name=Build%2C+Execution%2C+Deployment--Compiler--Scala+Compiler--Scala+Compile+Server)

You may also set it in `.jvmopts` file during development. (`.jvmopts` properties will not apply to Intellij compile server, only to sbt)

Set `-Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti.assertions=true` to enable additional assertions.

Other useful settings are:

- the system property [`izumi.reflect.rtti.optimized.equals`](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/izumi-reflect_2.13/latest/izumi/reflect/DebugProperties$.html#izumi.reflect.rtti.optimized.equals:String(%22izumi.reflect.rtti.optimized.equals%22))
- the Scala 2 macro setting [`izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.compile`](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/izumi-reflect_2.13/latest/izumi/reflect/DebugProperties$.html#izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.compile:String(%22izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.compile%22)), passed to the compiler as `scalacOptions += "-Xmacro-settings:izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.compile=false"`

## Debugging and DebugProperties

`izumi-reflect` can explain what it does: it can print how each tag is built during compilation, how each subtype check is decided at runtime, and the inheritance data stored inside a tag. This page describes the switches that control this output and the other settings in `izumi.reflect.DebugProperties`. For a step-by-step procedure, see [Debug a Wrong Tag or Subtype Check](../guides/debug-a-wrong-tag.md).

### DebugProperties

`DebugProperties` is an object whose fields hold the names of all supported settings, so you can refer to them from code instead of typing the strings:

```scala
import izumi.reflect.DebugProperties

DebugProperties.`izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti`
// res0: String = "izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti"
```

Most settings are Java system properties, read once when the library first needs them. One is a compiler option for Scala 2 macros. The table lists them all:

| Setting                                     | Kind                  | Default | Scala versions | Effect                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti`            | System property       | `false` | 2 and 3        | Logs subtype checks at runtime; on Scala 2, also logs tag creation during compilation                |
| `izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti.assertions` | System property       | `false` | 2              | Enables extra consistency checks while tags are created                                              |
| `izumi.reflect.rtti.optimized.equals`       | System property       | `true`  | 2 and 3        | Compares serialized tags by their strings first; set to `false` to always compare the full structure |
| `izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.compile`          | Scala 2 macro setting | `true`  | 2              | Caches tags computed during compilation                                                              |
| `izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.runtime`          | System property       | `true`  | 2 (JVM)        | Caches tags built from `scala-reflect` types at runtime                                              |

### Debug Output

The `izumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti` property turns on the library's debug log. It has two parts, which you enable in different places.

#### Runtime Subtype Checks

When the property is set in the JVM that runs your program, every call to `LightTypeTag#<:<` prints each step of the check to standard output: which parents of the left type it visits and which rule decides the result. Set it when you start the program:

```bash
java -Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti=true -jar app.jar
```

In sbt, `run` and `test` usually fork a separate JVM, so pass the property to the forked JVM in `build.sbt`:

```scala
Test / javaOptions += "-Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti=true"
```

The library also enables the log when a shorter prefix of the property name is set to `true`, such as `-Dizumi.reflect=true` or `-Dizumi=true`.

#### Tag Creation During Compilation (Scala 2)

On Scala 2, the same property also makes the macros print how they build each tag, as compiler info messages at the position of the `Tag` in your source. The property must be set in the JVM that runs the compiler, which is sbt itself:

```bash
sbt -Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti=true compile
```

You can also add the flag to the `.jvmopts` file of your project. IntelliJ IDEA compiles with its own Scala compile server, which does not read `.jvmopts`: add the flag to the VM options of the compile server in **Settings → Build, Execution, Deployment → Compiler → Scala Compiler → Scala Compile Server** instead.

On Scala 3, the macros have no debug output: the switch is turned off in the library code, so this property only affects runtime subtype checks.

### Inspecting a Tag

`LightTypeTag#debug` returns a description of a tag together with the inheritance data it carries. This data decides the result of every subtype check, so it is the first thing to look at when a check returns an unexpected result:

```scala
import izumi.reflect.Tag

println(Tag[Some[Int]].tag.debug("someInt"))
// ?? begin someInt: scala.Some[+scala.Int]
// ??bases:
//  - ? %0 ? scala.Some[+0] ->   
//    * ? %0 ? scala.Option[+0]
//    * ? %0 ? scala.collection.IterableOnce[+0]
//    * java.io.Serializable
//    * scala.Equals
//    * scala.Product
//  - scala.Int ->   
//    * scala.AnyVal
//  - scala.Some[+scala.Int] ->   
//    * java.io.Serializable
//    * scala.Equals
//    * scala.Product
//    * scala.Option[+scala.Int]
//    * scala.collection.IterableOnce[+scala.Int]
// ??inheritance:
//  - scala.Int ->   
//    * scala.AnyVal
//  - scala.Some ->   
//    * java.io.Serializable
//    * scala.Equals
//    * scala.Option
//    * scala.Product
//    * scala.collection.IterableOnce
// ?? end someInt
```

The `bases` section maps each type, and each type constructor written as a type lambda, to its known parents. The `inheritance` section maps class names to parent class names, without type arguments. If a parent you expect is missing from both, `LightTypeTag#<:<` can't see the relationship. The output of `LightTypeTag#debug` is also the most useful thing to attach to a bug report.

### Other Settings

The remaining settings change how the library works internally. You rarely need them; they exist to work around suspected bugs.

#### Assertions

`-Dizumi.reflect.debug.macro.rtti.assertions=true` enables extra consistency checks in the Scala 2 code that creates tags. Like the debug log, set it in the sbt JVM to check tag creation during compilation.

#### Optimized Equality

Tags created at compile time are stored in a serialized form. By default, two such tags with the same format version are compared by their serialized strings, and different strings mean different types. If you suspect two tags of the same type compare as not equal, set `-Dizumi.reflect.rtti.optimized.equals=false` in the JVM of your program to compare their full structure instead.

#### Caches

The Scala 2 macros cache tags they compute during compilation. To turn the cache off, pass a macro setting to the compiler, not a system property:

```scala
scalacOptions += "-Xmacro-settings:izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.compile=false"
```

The system property `izumi.reflect.rtti.cache.runtime=false` turns off the cache used by `LightTypeTagImpl.makeLightTypeTag`, which builds tags from `scala-reflect` types at runtime on Scala 2. See [Scala 2 vs Scala 3](scala-2-vs-scala-3.md#interoperating-with-scala-reflect).

All code from this page is available as runnable examples in the `izumi-reflect-examples` project.

Prints the name of the debug property and the inheritance data of a tag:

```scala title="izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/debugging/InspectTagExample.scala" showLineNumbers

  */

```

([source](https://github.com/zio/izumi-reflect/tree/develop/izumi-reflect/izumi-reflect-examples/src/main/scala-3/izumi/reflect/examples/debugging/InspectTagExample.scala)) Run it with `scala-cli run InspectTagExample.scala` from that folder, or with `sbt "izumi-reflect-examples/runMain izumi.reflect.examples.debugging.InspectTagExample"` from the repository root.
