## How to Dead-Letter and Expire Messages

A *dead-letter exchange* receives messages that a queue could not keep: a consumer rejected them with `requeue = false`, they sat in the queue longer than their time-to-live, or the queue was full. This guide shows how to declare the queues for that, how to set a time-to-live, and how to read the dead letters. ZIO AMQP has no dedicated API for it: you pass the broker's `x-` queue arguments through the `arguments` parameter of `Channel#queueDeclare`. The meaning of each argument is in the RabbitMQ guides on [dead letter exchanges](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx) and [time-to-live](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/ttl).

All snippets assume these imports:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.AMQP
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val workQueue     = QueueName("orders")
val deadLetters   = QueueName("orders.dead")
val deadExchange  = ExchangeName("orders.dlx")
```

### Declare the Dead-Letter Topology

First create the exchange that collects dead letters and a queue bound to it. A fanout exchange sends everything to the bound queue whatever the routing key. Then declare the work queue with `x-dead-letter-exchange` naming that exchange:

```scala
def declareTopology(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    _ <- channel.exchangeDeclare(deadExchange, ExchangeType.Fanout, durable = true)
    _ <- channel.queueDeclare(deadLetters, durable = true)
    _ <- channel.queueBind(deadLetters, deadExchange, RoutingKey(""))
    _ <- channel.queueDeclare(
           workQueue,
           durable = true,
           arguments = Map[String, AnyRef]("x-dead-letter-exchange" -> ExchangeName.unwrap(deadExchange))
         )
  } yield ()
```

`ExchangeName.unwrap` turns the newtype into the plain name the argument needs. The dead-letter queue must exist and be bound before messages die, or they are dropped.

A queue's arguments are part of its identity: declaring an existing queue again with different arguments is an error that closes the channel. Delete the queue first when you change them.

### Dead-Letter a Rejected Message

Rejecting a message without requeueing it sends it to the dead-letter exchange:

```scala
def handle(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(workQueue, ConsumerTag("orders-worker"))
    .mapZIO { delivery =>
      val tag = DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)
      ZIO
        .attempt(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8").toInt)
        .foldZIO(_ => channel.nack(tag, requeue = false), _ => channel.ack(tag))
    }
    .runDrain
```

### Expire Messages After a Time

To drop or dead-letter every message of a queue that stays unconsumed for a minute, declare the queue with `x-message-ttl` in milliseconds. The value must be a number, so box it as a `java.lang.Long`:

```scala
def declareExpiring(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, String] =
  channel.queueDeclare(
    QueueName("orders.expiring"),
    durable = true,
    arguments = Map[String, AnyRef](
      "x-dead-letter-exchange" -> ExchangeName.unwrap(deadExchange),
      "x-message-ttl"          -> Long.box(60000L)
    )
  )
```

To give a single message its own time-to-live instead, set the `expiration` property, a string of milliseconds, when publishing:

```scala
def publishExpiring(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.publish(
    ExchangeName(""),
    "short-lived".getBytes("UTF-8"),
    RoutingKey("orders"),
    props = new AMQP.BasicProperties.Builder().expiration("30000").build()
  )
```

### Read the Dead Letters

The dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue. Consume it like any other, for example to inspect or republish failures:

```scala
def inspect(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(deadLetters, ConsumerTag("dead-letter-reader"))
    .mapZIO { delivery =>
      Console.printLine(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8")) *>
        channel.ack(DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag))
    }
    .runDrain
```

The broker adds an `x-death` header to each dead letter, with the reason and the original queue. It is available through `delivery.getProperties.getHeaders`.

---

## How to Limit Prefetch to Apply Back-Pressure

By default, a RabbitMQ broker pushes every message in a queue to a consumer as fast as the network allows. A slow consumer then accumulates an ever-growing backlog in memory, and a fast consumer on the same queue sits idle. This guide shows how to use `Channel#basicQos` to cap the number of unacknowledged messages a consumer holds, and how to pick the cap.

All snippets assume these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val queue = QueueName("jobs")
```

### Set a Prefetch Count Before Consuming

The prefetch count is the number of deliveries the broker sends before it waits for acknowledgements. Call `Channel#basicQos` before `Channel#consume`, because the setting applies to consumers that are started afterwards. With a prefetch of 10, the broker sends ten messages, then one more for each acknowledgement it receives:

```scala
def worker(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.basicQos(10) *>
    channel
      .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("worker"))
      .mapZIO { delivery =>
        Console.printLine(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8")) *>
          channel.ack(DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag))
      }
      .runDrain
```

The limit only works with manual acknowledgements. A consumer started with `autoAck = true` is never limited, because its deliveries count as acknowledged when they are sent.

### Choose the Count

A prefetch of 1 gives the fairest distribution between workers: a worker receives its next message only when it is free, so one slow task never holds up messages that another worker could take. The price is a network round trip between every two messages, which limits the throughput of workers with very fast tasks.

For tasks that take milliseconds, raise the count until the consumer is no longer waiting for the broker. A count of a few tens to a few hundred is common. For tasks that take seconds or longer, a count of 1 costs nothing. The prefetch should also be at least the size of any batch you [acknowledge in one call](./how-to-acknowledge-messages.md#settle-a-batch-with-one-call), otherwise the batch can never fill.

A count of `0` removes the limit, which is the default behavior.

### Apply the Limit to a Whole Channel

With the default `global = false`, the count applies to each consumer that is started on the channel afterwards: two consumers with a prefetch of 5 can hold ten messages together. To share one budget across all consumers of the channel, pass `global = true`:

```scala
def sharedBudget(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.basicQos(10, global = true)
```

Because `Amqp.createChannel` gives each channel its own prefetch setting, the simplest way to give every consumer its own limit is to give every consumer its own channel.

### See the Limit at Work

The count of ready messages on a queue excludes the ones that are delivered but unacknowledged, which makes the effect of the prefetch visible. If a consumer with a prefetch of 5 never acknowledges, a queue of 20 messages shows only 15 as ready:

```scala
def demonstrate(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Long] =
  for {
    _     <- channel.basicQos(5)
    fiber <- channel.consume(queue, ConsumerTag("holder")).runDrain.fork
    _     <- ZIO.sleep(1.second)
    ready <- channel.messageCount(queue)
    _     <- fiber.interrupt
  } yield ready
```

### Running the Example

The file [`PrefetchExample.scala`](https://github.com/zio/zio-amqp/blob/master/zio-amqp-examples/src/main/scala/zio/amqp/examples/howto/PrefetchExample.scala) publishes 20 messages, starts a consumer with a prefetch of 5 that never acknowledges, and prints the number of ready messages. Start RabbitMQ with `docker compose up -d` and run `sbt "zio-amqp-examples/runMain zio.amqp.examples.howto.PrefetchExample"`. The output is:

```text
Ready messages with prefetch 5 and no acks: 15
```

---

## How to Process Messages in Parallel

A consumer made from `Channel#consume` handles one message at a time unless you ask for more. This guide shows how to process several messages at once with one channel, how to set the prefetch count to match, and why batch acknowledgement is unsafe when messages finish out of order.

All snippets assume these imports:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.Delivery
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val queue = QueueName("jobs")

def process(delivery: Delivery): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.sleep(100.millis) *> Console.printLine(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8"))
```

### Process Several Messages at Once

`ZStream#mapZIOPar` and `ZStream#mapZIOParUnordered` run the processing stage for up to `n` messages at the same time. The unordered variant emits each result as soon as it is ready, which is what a consumer wants because it only acknowledges. This worker processes four messages concurrently and acknowledges each one when it is done:

```scala
def worker(channel: Channel, parallelism: Int): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("parallel-worker"))
    .mapZIOParUnordered(parallelism) { delivery =>
      process(delivery) *> channel.ack(DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag))
    }
    .runDrain
```

The processing runs on many fibers, while the `Channel` takes turns between them: each `Channel#ack` waits for the channel's one permit, which is held only for the short call to the broker.

### Match the Prefetch Count

The broker sends at most as many unacknowledged messages as the prefetch count allows, so a count below the parallelism leaves some of the parallel slots idle. Set it to at least the parallelism before consuming:

```scala
def run(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.basicQos(4) *> worker(channel, parallelism = 4)
```

A count equal to the parallelism keeps every slot busy and holds at most that many messages away from other consumers. See [How to Limit Prefetch](./how-to-limit-prefetch.md) for choosing it.

### Settle Failures Individually

With `mapZIOParUnordered`, a failure in one message fails the whole stream and stops the consumer. To keep the other messages running, handle the failure inside the stage and reject only that message:

```scala
def resilientWorker(channel: Channel, parallelism: Int): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("resilient-worker"))
    .mapZIOParUnordered(parallelism) { delivery =>
      val tag = DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)
      process(delivery).foldZIO(
        _ => channel.nack(tag, requeue = true),
        _ => channel.ack(tag)
      )
    }
    .runDrain
```

### Do Not Use Batch Acknowledgement Here

`Channel#ackMany` and `Channel#nackMany` act on the highest tag in the sequence and settle every lower unacknowledged tag with it. When messages finish out of order, a batch that ends at tag 7 also acknowledges tag 5, even if tag 5 is still being processed, and the broker forgets it. If that worker then crashes, message 5 is lost. Acknowledge each message on its own, as above, unless the processing order is guaranteed. See [How to Acknowledge Messages](./how-to-acknowledge-messages.md).

---

## How to Publish Durable Messages

A message survives a broker restart only if two things hold: it sits in a durable queue, and it was published as persistent. This guide shows how to set both from ZIO AMQP, and how to attach other message properties such as a content type, a correlation id and headers.

All snippets assume these imports:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.{ AMQP, MessageProperties }
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._
```

### Declare a Durable Queue

A durable queue is re-created by the broker after a restart, but it comes back empty unless its messages were persistent too. Declare it with `durable = true`:

```scala
def declare(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, String] =
  channel.queueDeclare(QueueName("invoices"), durable = true)
```

The same flag exists on `Channel#exchangeDeclare`. A durable queue bound to a transient exchange loses the binding on restart, so declare exchanges that feed durable queues as durable too.

### Publish a Persistent Message

`Channel#publish` takes the message properties as a RabbitMQ `AMQP.BasicProperties`. A `deliveryMode` of 2 marks the message as persistent, and the broker writes it to disk. The client provides ready-made constants, so for a plain-text payload:

```scala
def publish(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.publish(
    exchange = ExchangeName(""),
    body = "invoice-1".getBytes("UTF-8"),
    routingKey = RoutingKey("invoices"),
    props = MessageProperties.PERSISTENT_TEXT_PLAIN
  )
```

The effect completes once the message has been handed to the client's connection. It does not wait for the broker to confirm that the message reached the disk, and ZIO AMQP has no publisher-confirm API, so a crash in that window can still lose a message.

### Attach a Content Type, an Id and Headers

To describe the payload to consumers, build the properties with the client's `AMQP.BasicProperties.Builder`. The content type tells consumers how to decode the body, the correlation id ties a message to a request, and headers carry free-form key-value pairs:

```scala
def publishJson(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] = {
  val props = new AMQP.BasicProperties.Builder()
    .contentType("application/json")
    .deliveryMode(2)
    .correlationId("order-42")
    .headers(java.util.Collections.singletonMap[String, AnyRef]("source", "checkout"))
    .build()

  channel.publish(ExchangeName(""), """{"id":42}""".getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey("invoices"), props = props)
}
```

Publishing without `props` sends a message with no properties, which the broker treats as transient.

### Read the Properties on the Consumer

Each `Delivery` exposes the properties through `getProperties`. The getters return `null` for a property the publisher did not set, so wrap optional ones in `Option`:

```scala
def consume(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(QueueName("invoices"), ConsumerTag("invoice-worker"))
    .mapZIO { delivery =>
      val props       = delivery.getProperties
      val contentType = Option(props.getContentType)
      val source      = Option(props.getHeaders).flatMap(h => Option(h.get("source")))
      Console.printLine(s"contentType=$contentType source=$source") *>
        channel.ack(DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag))
    }
    .runDrain
```

Header values come back as the RabbitMQ client's own types: a string header is a `LongString`, not a `String`. Call `toString` on it, or use `props.getHeaders.get("source").toString`.

### Running the Example

The file [`DurableMessagesExample.scala`](https://github.com/zio/zio-amqp/blob/master/zio-amqp-examples/src/main/scala/zio/amqp/examples/howto/DurableMessagesExample.scala) publishes a persistent JSON message to a durable queue and prints the properties that the consumer reads back. Start RabbitMQ with `docker compose up -d` and run `sbt "zio-amqp-examples/runMain zio.amqp.examples.howto.DurableMessagesExample"`. The output is:

```text
deliveryMode=2 contentType=application/json correlationId=order-42 source=howto
```

## How to Recover from a Closed Channel

When a broker-side error closes a channel, or the connection drops, a running consumer stream fails and every later call on that `Channel` fails too. This guide shows how to see that happen, how to restart a consumer on a fresh channel, and how to keep the retries bounded. The background is in [Delivery and Failure](./explanation/delivery-and-failure.md#failures-close-channels).

All snippets assume these imports:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.{ Delivery, ShutdownSignalException }
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val queue = QueueName("jobs")

def process(delivery: Delivery): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  Console.printLine(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8"))
```

### See the Failure

`Channel#queueDeclarePassive` fails if the queue does not exist, and the broker closes the channel as a result. Any call after that fails as well, although the connection is still open:

```scala
val demo: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    connection <- Amqp.connect(AMQPConfig.default)
    channel    <- Amqp.createChannel(connection)
    first      <- channel.queueDeclarePassive(QueueName("does-not-exist")).either
    second     <- channel.queueDeclare(QueueName("other")).either
    _          <- Console.printLine(s"first: ${first.isLeft}, second: ${second.isLeft}")
  } yield ()
```

Both calls end in `Left`: the first with the broker's error, the second because the channel is closed. A consumer stream on that channel fails with the client's `ShutdownSignalException`.

### Restart the Consumer on a New Channel

Put everything that depends on the channel, from opening it to the end of the stream, in one scoped effect. If it fails, its scope closes the dead channel, and running the effect again opens a new one:

```scala
def consumeOnce(connection: com.rabbitmq.client.Connection): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    Amqp.createChannel(connection).flatMap { channel =>
      channel.queueDeclare(queue, durable = true) *>
        channel
          .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("recovering-worker"))
          .mapZIO(d => process(d) *> channel.ack(DeliveryTag(d.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)))
          .runDrain
    }
  }
```

Messages that were delivered but not acknowledged when the channel died are redelivered by the broker to the new consumer, so processing must tolerate duplicates.

### Retry with a Bound

Retry on failure with a pause between attempts, and stop after a limit so a permanent fault, such as a wrong password, is reported:

```scala
def resilient(connection: com.rabbitmq.client.Connection): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  consumeOnce(connection).retry(Schedule.spaced(2.seconds) && Schedule.recurs(10))
```

To also reopen the consumer when the broker cancels it, which completes the stream without an error, repeat the effect with `forever` before the retry: `consumeOnce(connection).forever.retry(...)`.

### Recover from a Lost Connection

A lost connection fails every channel on it, so retrying on the same `Connection` cannot help. Move the connection inside the retried effect as well:

```scala
val fullyResilient: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO
    .scoped {
      Amqp.connect(AMQPConfig.default).flatMap(consumeOnce)
    }
    .retry(Schedule.spaced(5.seconds) && Schedule.recurs(10))
```

Retry only errors you expect, for example with `.retry(...)` after `ZIO#refineToOrDie[ShutdownSignalException]`, so that a bug in `process` is not retried ten times.

---

## How to Route Messages with Exchanges

A publisher sends every message to an exchange, never directly to a queue, and the exchange decides which queues receive a copy. This guide shows how to use a direct, a fanout and a topic exchange from ZIO AMQP to deliver one message to the right set of consumers. The semantics of the exchange types are those of RabbitMQ; see [Model Types](./reference/model.md#exchangetype) for the list.

All snippets assume these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._
```

### Send to a Queue by Name

When a message has exactly one destination, use the default exchange, `ExchangeName("")`. RabbitMQ declares it for you, and it routes a message to the queue whose name equals the routing key, without any binding:

```scala
def sendToQueue(channel: Channel, queue: QueueName, body: String): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.publish(ExchangeName(""), body.getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey(QueueName.unwrap(queue)))
```

### Route by Exact Key with a Direct Exchange

To send messages to different queues depending on a label, declare a direct exchange and bind each queue with the label as its routing key. A message goes to every queue whose binding key equals the message's routing key. In the example, only the `errors` queue receives the second message:

```scala
def directRouting(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] = {
  val logs   = ExchangeName("logs")
  val infos  = QueueName("logs.info")
  val errors = QueueName("logs.error")

  for {
    _ <- channel.exchangeDeclare(logs, ExchangeType.Direct)
    _ <- channel.queueDeclare(infos)
    _ <- channel.queueDeclare(errors)
    _ <- channel.queueBind(infos, logs, RoutingKey("info"))
    _ <- channel.queueBind(errors, logs, RoutingKey("error"))
    _ <- channel.publish(logs, "disk is 80% full".getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey("info"))
    _ <- channel.publish(logs, "disk is full".getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey("error"))
  } yield ()
}
```

Binding one queue several times, once per key, delivers to it every message that matches any of them.

### Broadcast with a Fanout Exchange

To deliver every message to every interested consumer, such as a cache-invalidation notice, use a fanout exchange. It ignores routing keys, so the key given to `Channel#queueBind` and `Channel#publish` is arbitrary. Each subscriber declares its own queue, and a server-named exclusive queue disappears with the subscriber:

```scala
def subscribe(channel: Channel, exchange: ExchangeName): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    queue <- channel.queueDeclare(QueueName(""), exclusive = true, autoDelete = true).map(QueueName(_))
    _     <- channel.queueBind(queue, exchange, RoutingKey(""))
    _     <- channel
               .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("subscriber"), autoAck = true)
               .mapZIO(delivery => Console.printLine(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8")))
               .runDrain
               .forkScoped
  } yield ()

def broadcast(channel: Channel, exchange: ExchangeName): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.exchangeDeclare(exchange, ExchangeType.Fanout) *>
    channel.publish(exchange, "cache cleared".getBytes("UTF-8"))
```

A queue only receives messages published after it was bound, so declare and bind the subscriber queues before the first publish.

### Route by Pattern with a Topic Exchange

A topic exchange matches the routing key against patterns made of dot-separated words. In a binding key, `*` stands for exactly one word and `#` for zero or more words. With the keys `orders.created`, `payments.error` and `orders.error`, the queue bound with `orders.*` receives the first and the third, and the queue bound with `*.error` receives the second and the third:

```scala
def topicRouting(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] = {
  val events = ExchangeName("events")
  val orders = QueueName("orders")
  val errors = QueueName("errors")

  for {
    _ <- channel.exchangeDeclare(events, ExchangeType.Topic)
    _ <- channel.queueDeclare(orders)
    _ <- channel.queueDeclare(errors)
    _ <- channel.queueBind(orders, events, RoutingKey("orders.*"))
    _ <- channel.queueBind(errors, events, RoutingKey("*.error"))
    _ <- ZIO.foreachDiscard(List("orders.created", "payments.error", "orders.error")) { key =>
           channel.publish(events, key.getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey(key))
         }
  } yield ()
}
```

A message that matches both bindings, here `orders.error`, is delivered once to each queue.

### Clean Up

Exchanges and queues declared without `durable` or `autoDelete` stay on the broker until they are deleted, or until the broker restarts. Delete the ones that a program or a test created with `Channel#queueDelete` and `Channel#exchangeDelete`. Deleting a queue or an exchange also removes its bindings:

```scala
def cleanUp(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel.queueDelete(QueueName("orders")) *>
    channel.queueDelete(QueueName("errors")) *>
    channel.exchangeDelete(ExchangeName("events"))
```

### Running the Example

The file [`RoutingExample.scala`](https://github.com/zio/zio-amqp/blob/master/zio-amqp-examples/src/main/scala/zio/amqp/examples/howto/RoutingExample.scala) runs the topic exchange scenario above and prints how many messages each queue holds. Start RabbitMQ with `docker compose up -d` and run `sbt "zio-amqp-examples/runMain zio.amqp.examples.howto.RoutingExample"`. The output is:

```text
orders.* queue: 2 messages, *.error queue: 2 messages
```

## How to Stop a Consumer

A stream returned by `Channel#consume` has no end of its own: it waits for the next message until something stops it. This guide shows how to stop a consumer after a number of messages, on a shutdown signal, on a timeout and when the application ends, and what happens to the message that is being processed at that moment.

All snippets assume these imports:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.Delivery
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val queue = QueueName("jobs")

def process(delivery: Delivery): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  Console.printLine(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8"))
```

### What Happens When the Stream Ends

However a consumer stream ends, whether it is completed, fails or is interrupted, `Channel#consume` cancels the consumer on the broker. The broker then stops sending messages to it. Messages that were already delivered but not acknowledged are not returned to the queue by the cancellation: they stay unacknowledged until the channel closes, and the broker then redelivers them.

For that reason, stop consumers with the techniques below and close the channel promptly. Closing happens automatically when the `Scope` that created the channel ends.

### Stop After a Number of Messages

To process a fixed number of messages and stop, use the ordinary stream operators `take` and `takeUntil`. Here the consumer stops after the first ten messages:

```scala
def firstTen(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("first-ten"))
    .take(10)
    .mapZIO(d => process(d) *> channel.ack(DeliveryTag(d.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)))
    .runDrain
```

### Stop When a Signal Arrives

To stop a long-running worker from another fiber, for example when the application receives a termination signal, complete a `Promise` and halt the stream with `ZStream#haltWhen`. Put `ZStream#haltWhen` before the processing stage: the stream then stops asking for new messages, but the message that is already being processed runs to completion and is acknowledged:

```scala
def gracefulWorker(channel: Channel, shutdown: Promise[Throwable, Unit]): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("graceful"))
    .haltWhen(shutdown)
    .mapZIO(d => process(d) *> channel.ack(DeliveryTag(d.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)))
    .runDrain
```

To trigger it, run the worker on a fiber, and later complete the promise and wait for the worker:

```scala
def run(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    shutdown <- Promise.make[Throwable, Unit]
    worker   <- gracefulWorker(channel, shutdown).fork
    _        <- ZIO.sleep(1.minute)
    _        <- shutdown.succeed(())
    _        <- worker.join
  } yield ()
```

Combine this with `channel.basicQos(1)` set before consuming to bound how many messages the broker has already delivered when the signal arrives. With a prefetch of 1, at most one further message, which the broker sends right after the current acknowledgement, is left unacknowledged and returns to the queue when the channel closes. See [Limit Prefetch to Apply Back-Pressure](./how-to-limit-prefetch.md).

:::note[Interrupting stops mid-message]
Interrupting the worker fiber, or using `ZStream#interruptWhen`, cancels the processing stage as well. A message that was being processed is then never acknowledged and is redelivered after the channel closes. Choose that when processing is idempotent and fast shutdown matters more than finishing the current message.
:::

### Stop After a Period of Silence

To stop a consumer that has been idle for too long, use `ZStream#timeout`, which ends the stream if the next element does not arrive in time:

```scala
def untilIdle(channel: Channel): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("until-idle"))
    .timeout(30.seconds)
    .mapZIO(d => process(d) *> channel.ack(DeliveryTag(d.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)))
    .runDrain
```

### Stop When the Application Ends

A worker that should live as long as the application can run on a fiber that is tied to a scope. `forkScoped` interrupts the fiber when the scope closes, which cancels the consumer, and the scope then closes the channel and the connection in reverse order of acquisition:

```scala
val program: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      connection <- Amqp.connect(AMQPConfig.default)
      channel    <- Amqp.createChannel(connection)
      _          <- channel
                      .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("app-worker"))
                      .mapZIO(d => process(d) *> channel.ack(DeliveryTag(d.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)))
                      .runDrain
                      .forkScoped
      _          <- ZIO.never
    } yield ()
  }
```

`ZIO.never` keeps the program alive until it is interrupted, for example by `ZIOAppDefault` when the process receives SIGTERM. The scope then runs the finalizers.

### React When the Broker Stops the Consumer

Two events end the stream without any action by the program. If the broker cancels the consumer, for example because the queue was deleted, the stream completes normally. If the channel or connection is shut down, the stream fails with the RabbitMQ client's `ShutdownSignalException`. To reconnect after a shutdown, wrap the whole acquire-and-consume program in a retry, because a closed channel cannot be reused:

```scala
def resilient(program: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  program.retry(Schedule.exponential(1.second) && Schedule.recurs(5))
```

### Running the Example

The file [`StopConsumerExample.scala`](https://github.com/zio/zio-amqp/blob/master/zio-amqp-examples/src/main/scala/zio/amqp/examples/howto/StopConsumerExample.scala) publishes three tasks of one second each, requests shutdown while the first is being processed, and prints what is left. Start RabbitMQ with `docker compose up -d` and run `sbt "zio-amqp-examples/runMain zio.amqp.examples.howto.StopConsumerExample"`. The output is:

```text
started task-1
shutdown requested
finished task-1
consumers: 0, messages left: 1
```

The consumer finished `task-1` after the shutdown request, started nothing new, and was cancelled. One message is still ready in the queue. The second task was already delivered when the first was acknowledged, so it is unacknowledged on the channel and returns to the queue when the channel closes.

## How to Test with Testcontainers

ZIO AMQP is a thin layer over a real broker, so the most reliable way to test code that uses it is to run against a real RabbitMQ. This guide shows how to start a throwaway RabbitMQ container for a ZIO Test suite with [Testcontainers for Scala](https://github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-scala), the approach the library's own test suite uses, and how to point the same tests at a broker that is already running, as on a CI server.

The test code on this page needs libraries that are not dependencies of ZIO AMQP itself, so the snippets are shown without being compiled by the documentation build. They are taken from the library's own test, [`AmqpClientSpec.scala`](https://github.com/zio/zio-amqp/blob/master/zio-amqp/src/test/scala/zio/amqp/AmqpClientSpec.scala), which compiles and runs in CI. Docker must be running on the machine that runs the tests.

### Add the Test Dependencies

Add ZIO Test and the Testcontainers module for RabbitMQ to the test scope, and register the ZIO Test framework with sbt:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio"      %% "zio-test"                      % "2.1.26" % Test,
  "dev.zio"      %% "zio-test-sbt"                  % "2.1.26" % Test,
  "com.dimafeng" %% "testcontainers-scala-rabbitmq" % "0.44.1"        % Test
)

testFrameworks += new TestFramework("zio.test.sbt.ZTestFramework")
```

The versions above are the ones this repository's build uses at the time of writing. Check Maven Central for newer releases.

### Start a Container as a Layer

A container should start once per test run and stop afterwards, even if a test fails. Model it as a scoped `ZLayer` that acquires the container with `ZIO.acquireRelease`, and expose only what the tests need, the host and the AMQP port:

```scala
import com.dimafeng.testcontainers.RabbitMQContainer
import zio._

final case class ContainerDetails(host: String, amqpPort: Int)

val rabbitContainerDetails: ZLayer[Scope, Throwable, ContainerDetails] =
  ZLayer.fromZIO(
    ZIO
      .acquireRelease(ZIO.attempt(RabbitMQContainer.Def().start()))(c => ZIO.attempt(c.stop()).orDie)
      .map(c => ContainerDetails(c.host, c.amqpPort))
  )
```

`RabbitMQContainer.Def().start()` pulls the module's default RabbitMQ image on first use (at the time of writing `rabbitmq:3.7-management-alpine`; the CI workflow of this repository runs `rabbitmq:3.13`) and waits until the broker accepts connections. Testcontainers maps the AMQP port to a random free host port, which is why the layer reads `amqpPort` instead of assuming 5672.

### Write a Test Against the Broker

A test connects with the container's host and port, using the `ConnectionFactory` overload of `Amqp.connect`, and uses unique queue names so that tests do not interfere with each other. The suite shares one container with `provideSomeShared`:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.ConnectionFactory
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._
import zio.test._

import java.util.UUID

object PublishConsumeSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec: Spec[Scope, Throwable] =
    suite("PublishConsumeSpec")(
      test("a published message is consumed") {
        val queue = QueueName(s"queue-${UUID.randomUUID()}")

        ZIO.service[ContainerDetails].flatMap { container =>
          val factory = new ConnectionFactory()
          factory.setHost(container.host)
          factory.setPort(container.amqpPort)

          Amqp
            .connect(factory)
            .flatMap(Amqp.createChannel)
            .flatMap { channel =>
              for {
                _      <- channel.queueDeclare(queue)
                _      <- channel.publish(ExchangeName(""), "ping".getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey(QueueName.unwrap(queue)))
                bodies <- channel
                            .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("test"))
                            .take(1)
                            .runCollect
                            .map(_.map(d => new String(d.getBody, "UTF-8")))
                _      <- channel.queueDelete(queue)
              } yield assertTrue(bodies == Chunk("ping"))
            }
        }
      } @@ TestAspect.timeout(60.seconds)
    ).provideSomeShared[Scope](rabbitContainerDetails)
}
```

The connection and the channel are scoped, and ZIO Test's `Scope` environment closes them when the test ends. Always put a `TestAspect.timeout` aspect on a test that consumes: a stream that waits for a message that never arrives would otherwise hang the build.

### Wait for Asynchronous Effects

The broker updates some state asynchronously. For example, `Channel#messageCount` right after a publish can still return the old value, and `Channel#consumerCount` right after forking a consumer can return 0. The library's tests delay the assertion by a second, which needs the real clock because ZIO Test runs with a simulated one:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.test._

test("messageCount sees a published message") {
  // ... declare queue, publish ...
  channel.messageCount(queue).delay(1.second).map(count => assertTrue(count == 1L))
} @@ TestAspect.withLiveClock
```

### Use a Broker That Is Already Running

On a CI server, starting a container per job is slow, and the job may not be allowed to use Docker at all. The library's test suite switches on the `CI` environment variable: when it is set, it uses a RabbitMQ at `localhost:5672`, started by the CI workflow with the repository's `docker-compose.yml` (`docker compose up -d`), and otherwise starts a container:

```scala
val rabbitContainerDetails: ZLayer[Scope, Throwable, ContainerDetails] =
  ZLayer.fromZIO(
    zio.System.env("CI").flatMap {
      case Some(_) => ZIO.succeed(ContainerDetails("localhost", 5672))
      case None    =>
        ZIO
          .acquireRelease(ZIO.attempt(RabbitMQContainer.Def().start()))(c => ZIO.attempt(c.stop()).orDie)
          .map(c => ContainerDetails(c.host, c.amqpPort))
    }
  )
```

Because the broker is shared by every test in that run, keep the unique queue names and delete what each test creates.

## Introduction to ZIO AMQP

ZIO AMQP is a ZIO-based wrapper around the [RabbitMQ Java client](https://www.rabbitmq.com/client-libraries/java-api-guide). It exposes queues as `ZStream`s of deliveries and serializes access to the underlying RabbitMQ channel, so concurrent fibers cannot corrupt it. Connections and channels are scoped resources: they are closed automatically when the `Scope` that owns them ends, even if the program fails or is interrupted.

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-amqp/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-amqp_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-amqp_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-amqp_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-amqp_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-amqp_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-amqp_2.13) [![ZIO AMQP](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-amqp?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-amqp)

### Installation

Add the following to your `build.sbt` file. ZIO AMQP is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3, on the JVM only:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // ZIO AMQP: ZIO wrapper around the RabbitMQ Java client (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-amqp" % "1.0.3"
)
```

ZIO AMQP depends on ZIO 2, ZIO Prelude and the RabbitMQ Java client, which sbt resolves automatically.

### Where to Go Next

Start with [Getting Started](./getting-started.md), which connects to a broker, publishes a message and consumes it back. To understand the ideas behind the API, read [AMQP Basics](./explanation/amqp-basics.md). To look up a type or method, use the [reference](./reference/amqp.md).

## Amqp and AMQPConfig

`Amqp` is the entry point of the library. Its four methods acquire the two resources every program needs, a RabbitMQ `Connection` and a ZIO AMQP [`Channel`](./channel.md), and release them through the surrounding `Scope`. `AMQPConfig` describes how to reach the broker. The signatures are:

```scala
object Amqp {
  def connect(factory: ConnectionFactory): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Connection]
  def connect(uri: URI): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Connection]
  def connect(amqpConfig: AMQPConfig): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Connection]
  def createChannel(connection: Connection): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Channel]
}
```

`Connection` and `ConnectionFactory` are the types of the RabbitMQ Java client (`com.rabbitmq.client`). ZIO AMQP does not wrap them.

### Creating a Connection

All three overloads of `Amqp.connect` open a connection on a blocking thread and register a finalizer that closes it when the `Scope` ends. If closing the connection fails, the error is not reported through the error channel: the finalizer dies with it (`orDie`).

The overloads differ in how the broker is described. To connect with a fully configured RabbitMQ `ConnectionFactory`, for example to set TLS options or a custom executor:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.ConnectionFactory
import zio._
import zio.amqp._

val factory = new ConnectionFactory()
factory.setHost("rabbit.internal")
factory.setPort(5672)

val connection: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, com.rabbitmq.client.Connection] =
  Amqp.connect(factory)
```

To connect with an AMQP URI, which carries the host, port, credentials and virtual host in one string:

```scala
import java.net.URI
import zio._
import zio.amqp._

val connection: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, com.rabbitmq.client.Connection] =
  Amqp.connect(URI.create("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/%2F"))
```

`Amqp.connect(uri)` creates a `ConnectionFactory` and calls `ConnectionFactory#setUri`, so any URI the RabbitMQ client accepts works, including the `amqps` scheme for TLS.

To connect from an [`AMQPConfig`](#amqpconfig), which is the typed form of the same information:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val connection: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, com.rabbitmq.client.Connection] =
  Amqp.connect(AMQPConfig.default.copy(host = "rabbit.internal"))
```

`Amqp.connect(amqpConfig)` converts the configuration with `AMQPConfig#toUri` and then behaves like the URI overload. See [Connect to a Broker](../how-to-connect.md) for a task-oriented walkthrough, including loading the configuration from the environment.

### Creating a Channel

`Amqp.createChannel` opens a channel on an existing connection and wraps it in a [`Channel`](./channel.md). The wrapper owns a one-permit `Semaphore`, and every operation on it takes that permit, so the underlying RabbitMQ channel, which is not thread-safe, is used by one fiber at a time.

The channel is closed when the `Scope` ends. The finalizer also takes the permit, so it waits for an operation that is in flight before closing. Like the connection finalizer, it dies if closing fails.

To open a channel and use it in one scoped program:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val program: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      connection <- Amqp.connect(AMQPConfig.default)
      channel    <- Amqp.createChannel(connection)
      _          <- channel.queueDeclare(QueueName("example"))
    } yield ()
  }
```

Because the finalizers run in reverse order of acquisition, the channel is closed before its connection.

A single connection supports many channels. Create one channel per independent unit of work, for example one for a consumer and another for a publisher, so a slow operation on one does not hold the other's permit.

### AMQPConfig

`AMQPConfig` is a case class in `zio.amqp.model` that holds everything needed to build an AMQP URI. It has no ZIO Config or JSON codec of its own, so load the values with the mechanism your application already uses and construct it by hand. Its definition is:

```scala
case class AMQPConfig(
  user: String,
  password: String,
  vhost: String,
  heartbeatInterval: Duration,
  ssl: Boolean,
  host: String,
  port: Short,
  connectionTimeout: Duration
) {
  val encodedVhost: String
  def toUri: AmqpUri
}
```

The fields are:

| Field               | Type       | Meaning                                                                    |
| ------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `user`              | `String`   | User name.                                                                 |
| `password`          | `String`   | Password.                                                                  |
| `vhost`             | `String`   | Virtual host. `"/"` is the default virtual host.                           |
| `heartbeatInterval` | `Duration` | Heartbeat interval. Written to the URI in whole seconds.                   |
| `ssl`               | `Boolean`  | When `true`, the URI scheme is `amqps` instead of `amqp`.                  |
| `host`              | `String`   | Broker host name.                                                          |
| `port`              | `Short`    | Broker port.                                                               |
| `connectionTimeout` | `Duration` | Connection timeout. Written to the URI in milliseconds.                    |

#### Default Configuration

`AMQPConfig.default` points at a local RabbitMQ with its stock credentials. To inspect its values:

```scala
import zio.amqp.model._

AMQPConfig.default
// res4: AMQPConfig = AMQPConfig(
//   user = "guest",
//   password = "guest",
//   vhost = "/",
//   heartbeatInterval = PT10S,
//   ssl = false,
//   host = "localhost",
//   port = 5672,
//   connectionTimeout = PT10S
// )
```

Use `AMQPConfig#copy` to override individual fields. To target a TLS broker on the conventional TLS port:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.amqp.model._

val secure: AMQPConfig =
  AMQPConfig.default.copy(host = "rabbit.example.com", port = 5671, ssl = true, user = "app")
```

#### Converting to a URI

`AMQPConfig#encodedVhost` is the virtual host URL-encoded with UTF-8, so `"/"` becomes `%2F`. `AMQPConfig#toUri` assembles the URI from the other fields. To see the URI for the default configuration:

```scala
println(AMQPConfig.default.encodedVhost)
// %2F
println(AMQPConfig.default.toUri)
// amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/%2F?heartbeat=10&connection_timeout=10000
```

The result has the type `AmqpUri`, a subtype of `java.net.URI`, so it can be passed anywhere a `URI` is expected. See [Model Types](./model.md#amqpuri).

:::warning[Credentials are inserted into the URI as they are]
`AMQPConfig#toUri` writes `user` and `password` into the URI without percent-encoding, and `port` is a `Short`, so it cannot hold values above 32767. If a password contains characters such as `@`, `:` or `/`, or the broker listens on a higher port, build a `ConnectionFactory` and use `Amqp.connect(factory)` instead.
:::

---

## Channel

`Channel` is the handle through which a program talks to the broker: it declares queues and exchanges, publishes messages, consumes them as a `ZStream`, and acknowledges them. It wraps a RabbitMQ Java client channel together with a one-permit `Semaphore`, and every method takes that permit for the duration of its call. The underlying client channel is not thread-safe, so this makes a `Channel` safe to share between fibers.

A `Channel` has no public constructor. Obtain one from [`Amqp.createChannel`](./amqp.md#creating-a-channel), which closes it when the enclosing `Scope` ends.

All the examples on this page assume the following setup, which opens a channel against a local broker and names a queue and an exchange:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.AMQP
import zio._
import zio.amqp._
import zio.amqp.model._

val queue    = QueueName("reference-queue")
val exchange = ExchangeName("reference-exchange")

def withChannel[A](use: Channel => ZIO[Any, Throwable, A]): ZIO[Any, Throwable, A] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    Amqp.connect(AMQPConfig.default).flatMap(Amqp.createChannel).flatMap(use)
  }
```

Every method returns a `ZIO[Any, Throwable, _]` (or a `ZStream[Any, Throwable, _]`): the effects need no environment, and any failure of the RabbitMQ client, including an `IOException` from a closed channel or a protocol error from the broker, appears in the error channel. Methods that call the broker synchronously run on ZIO's blocking thread pool.

:::note[Broker errors close the channel]
In AMQP, most broker-side errors, such as operating on a queue that does not exist or re-declaring a queue with different arguments, close the channel they happened on. After that, every call on that `Channel` fails. Create a new channel with `Amqp.createChannel` to continue.
:::

### Queues

A queue stores messages until a consumer takes them. These methods create, inspect and remove queues.

#### Channel#queueDeclare

`Channel#queueDeclare` creates a queue, or does nothing if a queue with the same name and the same properties already exists. It returns the name of the queue as a `String`:

```scala
class Channel {
  def queueDeclare(
    queue: QueueName,
    durable: Boolean = false,
    exclusive: Boolean = false,
    autoDelete: Boolean = false,
    arguments: Map[String, AnyRef] = Map.empty
  ): ZIO[Any, Throwable, String]
}
```

The parameters are:

| Parameter    | Meaning                                                                                              |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `queue`      | Name of the queue. An empty name asks the broker to generate one.                                    |
| `durable`    | The queue survives a broker restart. This does not make its messages persistent; see [Publish Durable Messages](../how-to-publish-durable-messages.md). |
| `exclusive`  | The queue is used by this connection only and is deleted when the connection closes.                 |
| `autoDelete` | The broker deletes the queue once its last consumer has gone.                                        |
| `arguments`  | Optional queue arguments such as `x-message-ttl` or `x-dead-letter-exchange`.                        |

All flags default to `false`. To declare a durable queue with a message time-to-live of one minute:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  channel.queueDeclare(queue, durable = true, arguments = Map("x-message-ttl" -> Int.box(60000)))
}
```

To let the broker choose a unique name, pass an empty `QueueName` and use the returned `String`. A server-named queue is usually also `exclusive`:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  for {
    name <- channel.queueDeclare(QueueName(""), exclusive = true, autoDelete = true)
    _    <- Console.printLine(s"declared $name")
  } yield ()
}
```

#### Channel#queueDeclarePassive

`Channel#queueDeclarePassive` checks that a queue exists without creating it. It returns the RabbitMQ client's `AMQP.Queue.DeclareOk`, which carries the queue name, the number of ready messages and the number of consumers. If the queue does not exist, the broker answers with an error and closes the channel:

```scala
class Channel {
  def queueDeclarePassive(queue: QueueName): ZIO[Any, Throwable, AMQP.Queue.DeclareOk]
}
```

To read the message count of an existing queue:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  for {
    _  <- channel.queueDeclare(queue)
    ok <- channel.queueDeclarePassive(queue)
    _  <- Console.printLine(s"${ok.getQueue}: ${ok.getMessageCount} ready, ${ok.getConsumerCount} consumers")
  } yield ()
}
```

#### Channel#queueDelete

`Channel#queueDelete` removes a queue and everything in it. With `ifUnused` or `ifEmpty` set, the broker deletes the queue only when it has no consumers or no messages respectively; otherwise it replies with an error that closes the channel:

```scala
class Channel {
  def queueDelete(
    queue: QueueName,
    ifUnused: Boolean = false,
    ifEmpty: Boolean = false
  ): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

To delete a queue unconditionally:

```scala
withChannel(_.queueDelete(queue))
```

#### Channel#purgeQueue

`Channel#purgeQueue` removes all messages that are ready to be delivered from a queue and keeps the queue. It returns the client's `AMQP.Queue.PurgeOk`. Messages that were delivered but are still unacknowledged are not removed:

```scala
class Channel {
  def purgeQueue(queue: QueueName): ZIO[Any, Throwable, AMQP.Queue.PurgeOk]
}
```

To empty a queue and report how many messages were dropped:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  channel.purgeQueue(queue).flatMap(ok => Console.printLine(s"purged ${ok.getMessageCount} messages"))
}
```

#### Channel#messageCount

`Channel#messageCount` returns the number of messages that are ready to be delivered to consumers. The queue must exist: otherwise the broker closes the channel with an error. Messages that have been delivered but not yet acknowledged are not counted:

```scala
class Channel {
  def messageCount(queue: QueueName): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Long]
}
```

#### Channel#consumerCount

`Channel#consumerCount` returns the number of consumers on a queue, with the same requirement that the queue exists:

```scala
class Channel {
  def consumerCount(queue: QueueName): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Long]
}
```

To read both counts of a queue:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  for {
    _         <- channel.queueDeclare(queue)
    messages  <- channel.messageCount(queue)
    consumers <- channel.consumerCount(queue)
    _         <- Console.printLine(s"$messages messages, $consumers consumers")
  } yield ()
}
```

The counts come from the broker at the moment of the call and can be stale as soon as they arrive. Use them for monitoring and tests, not for coordination.

### Exchanges and Bindings

Publishers send messages to an exchange, and the exchange routes them to queues according to its [`ExchangeType`](./model.md#exchangetype) and the bindings between the exchange and the queues.

#### Channel#exchangeDeclare

`Channel#exchangeDeclare` creates an exchange, or does nothing if one with the same name and properties already exists. The `type` parameter is a Scala keyword-quoted name; pass it by position or as `` `type` = ... ``:

```scala
class Channel {
  def exchangeDeclare(
    exchange: ExchangeName,
    `type`: ExchangeType,
    durable: Boolean = false,
    autoDelete: Boolean = false,
    internal: Boolean = false,
    arguments: Map[String, AnyRef] = Map.empty
  ): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

The flags mean:

| Parameter    | Meaning                                                                                        |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `durable`    | The exchange survives a broker restart.                                                        |
| `autoDelete` | The broker deletes the exchange once its last binding is removed.                              |
| `internal`   | Publishers cannot send to the exchange directly; only other exchanges can route messages to it. |
| `arguments`  | Optional exchange arguments, such as `alternate-exchange`.                                     |

To declare a durable topic exchange:

```scala
withChannel(_.exchangeDeclare(exchange, ExchangeType.Topic, durable = true))
```

#### Channel#exchangeDelete

`Channel#exchangeDelete` removes an exchange. With `ifUnused = true`, the broker refuses to delete an exchange that still has bindings:

```scala
class Channel {
  def exchangeDelete(
    exchange: ExchangeName,
    ifUnused: Boolean = false
  ): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

#### Channel#queueBind

`Channel#queueBind` binds a queue to an exchange, so messages that the exchange routes by this binding's `routingKey` end up in the queue. What the key means depends on the exchange type: a direct exchange compares it for equality, a topic exchange treats it as a pattern, and a fanout exchange ignores it. A headers exchange ignores it too and matches on `arguments` instead:

```scala
class Channel {
  def queueBind(
    queue: QueueName,
    exchange: ExchangeName,
    routingKey: RoutingKey,
    arguments: Map[String, AnyRef] = Map.empty
  ): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

To route every message with a key that starts with `orders.` to a queue:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  for {
    _ <- channel.exchangeDeclare(exchange, ExchangeType.Topic)
    _ <- channel.queueDeclare(queue)
    _ <- channel.queueBind(queue, exchange, RoutingKey("orders.#"))
  } yield ()
}
```

The library has no method to remove a binding. Deleting the queue or the exchange removes the bindings that refer to it.

### Publishing

Messages enter the broker through an exchange. One method sends them.

#### Channel#publish

`Channel#publish` sends one message to an exchange. The body is a byte array, so the encoding is up to the caller:

```scala
class Channel {
  def publish(
    exchange: ExchangeName,
    body: Array[Byte],
    routingKey: RoutingKey = RoutingKey(""),
    mandatory: Boolean = false,
    immediate: Boolean = false,
    props: AMQP.BasicProperties = new AMQP.BasicProperties()
  ): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

The parameters are:

| Parameter    | Meaning                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `exchange`   | Target exchange. `ExchangeName("")` is the default exchange, which routes to the queue named by the routing key.                         |
| `body`       | Message payload.                                                                                                                         |
| `routingKey` | Routing key, matched by the exchange's bindings. Defaults to the empty key.                                                              |
| `mandatory`  | Ask the broker to return the message if it cannot be routed to any queue. ZIO AMQP has no API to receive returned messages.              |
| `immediate`  | Ask the broker to return the message if no consumer can take it immediately. RabbitMQ 3.0 and later reject this flag, so leave it `false`. |
| `props`      | Message properties such as `deliveryMode`, `contentType`, `headers` or `correlationId`, from the RabbitMQ client's `AMQP.BasicProperties`. |

The effect completes when the message has been handed to the client's connection. It does not wait for a broker confirmation, so success does not prove that the broker stored the message. A message that no binding matches is silently dropped.

To publish a UTF-8 text message through the default exchange directly to a queue:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  channel.publish(ExchangeName(""), "hello".getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey(QueueName.unwrap(queue)))
}
```

To publish a persistent JSON message with a content type, building the properties with the client's builder:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  val props = new AMQP.BasicProperties.Builder()
    .contentType("application/json")
    .deliveryMode(2)
    .build()

  channel.publish(exchange, """{"id":1}""".getBytes("UTF-8"), RoutingKey("orders.created"), props = props)
}
```

Publishing is safe to call from many fibers at once: calls queue up on the channel's permit and run one at a time.

### Consuming

A consumer receives messages from a queue as a stream. Two methods start it and tune how much the broker sends ahead.

#### Channel#consume

`Channel#consume` registers a consumer on a queue and exposes the deliveries as a `ZStream` of the RabbitMQ client's `com.rabbitmq.client.Delivery`:

```scala
class Channel {
  def consume(
    queue: QueueName,
    consumerTag: ConsumerTag,
    autoAck: Boolean = false
  ): ZStream[Any, Throwable, Delivery]
}
```

The parameters are:

| Parameter     | Meaning                                                                                                                      |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `queue`       | Queue to consume from. It must exist.                                                                                        |
| `consumerTag` | Identifier of this consumer on the channel. It must be unique among the channel's active consumers.                          |
| `autoAck`     | When `true`, the broker treats a message as acknowledged as soon as it sends it. When `false` (the default), the program must call `Channel#ack` or `Channel#nack`. |

The consumer is registered when the stream starts running, not when `Channel#consume` is called. A `Delivery` has `getBody`, `getEnvelope` and `getProperties`: the envelope holds the delivery tag, the exchange, the routing key and the redelivery flag.

The stream behaves as follows:

- It emits one element per delivery and has no end of its own: it keeps waiting for the next message.
- When the stream stops, whether it was completed by an operator such as `take`, failed, or interrupted, the consumer is cancelled on the broker. Errors from the cancellation itself are ignored.
- If the broker cancels the consumer, for example because the queue was deleted, the stream completes.
- If the channel or connection shuts down, the stream fails with the client's `ShutdownSignalException`.

To print five messages from a queue and acknowledge each one after it has been handled:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("reference-consumer"))
    .mapZIO { delivery =>
      Console.printLine(new String(delivery.getBody, "UTF-8")) *>
        channel.ack(DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag))
    }
    .take(5)
    .runDrain
}
```

The delivery tag is a `Long` in the envelope, so it is wrapped in `DeliveryTag` before it is acknowledged. See [Acknowledge Messages](../how-to-acknowledge-messages.md) for the full picture and [Stop a Consumer](../how-to-stop-a-consumer.md) for shutdown patterns.

#### Channel#basicQos

`Channel#basicQos` sets the prefetch count: the maximum number of unacknowledged deliveries the broker sends before it waits for acknowledgements. It is the main tool for bounding how much work a consumer holds at once:

```scala
class Channel {
  def basicQos(count: Int, global: Boolean = false): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

With `global = false`, the limit applies to each consumer started on the channel afterwards. With `global = true`, it is shared by all consumers on the channel. A `count` of `0` means no limit. The setting has no effect on consumers with `autoAck = true`. Call it before `Channel#consume`:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  channel.basicQos(10) *>
    channel
      .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("limited"))
      .mapZIO(delivery => channel.ack(DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)))
      .take(100)
      .runDrain
}
```

See [Limit Prefetch to Apply Back-Pressure](../how-to-limit-prefetch.md).

### Acknowledging

A delivery stays "unacknowledged" on the broker until the consumer settles it. If the channel closes before that, the broker puts the delivery back on the queue and delivers it again. These four methods settle deliveries.

#### Channel#ack

`Channel#ack` acknowledges one delivery, or, with `multiple = true`, every unacknowledged delivery up to and including the given tag on this channel:

```scala
class Channel {
  def ack(deliveryTag: DeliveryTag, multiple: Boolean = false): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

Acknowledging an unknown or already settled tag is a protocol error that closes the channel.

#### Channel#ackMany

`Channel#ackMany` acknowledges several deliveries with a single call to the broker. It sends `Channel#ack` for the highest tag in the sequence with `multiple = true`, so it also acknowledges every lower unacknowledged tag on the channel, including tags that are not in the sequence:

```scala
class Channel {
  def ackMany(deliveryTags: Seq[DeliveryTag]): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

The sequence must not be empty: `Channel#ackMany(Seq.empty)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when called, rather than failing the returned effect. To acknowledge a batch of five deliveries at once:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("batch"))
    .grouped(5)
    .mapZIO { batch =>
      val tags = batch.map(d => DeliveryTag(d.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag))
      channel.ackMany(tags)
    }
    .take(1)
    .runDrain
}
```

#### Channel#nack

`Channel#nack` rejects one delivery, or with `multiple = true` every unacknowledged delivery up to and including the tag. With `requeue = true` the broker puts the message back on its queue; with `requeue = false` (the default) it discards the message, or dead-letters it if the queue has a dead-letter exchange:

```scala
class Channel {
  def nack(
    deliveryTag: DeliveryTag,
    requeue: Boolean = false,
    multiple: Boolean = false
  ): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

To put a message back on the queue after a failed attempt:

```scala
withChannel { channel =>
  channel
    .consume(queue, ConsumerTag("retrying"))
    .mapZIO(delivery => channel.nack(DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag), requeue = true))
    .take(1)
    .runDrain
}
```

`Channel#nack` is a RabbitMQ extension to AMQP 0-9-1, and it can reject several deliveries at once, which the standard `basic.reject` cannot.

#### Channel#nackMany

`Channel#nackMany` rejects several deliveries with a single call. Like `Channel#ackMany`, it uses the highest tag with `multiple = true`, so it affects every lower unacknowledged tag as well, and it throws for an empty sequence:

```scala
class Channel {
  def nackMany(deliveryTags: Seq[DeliveryTag], requeue: Boolean = false): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit]
}
```

---

## Model Types

The `zio.amqp.model` package holds the small types that appear in the signatures of [`Amqp`](./amqp.md) and [`Channel`](./channel.md): five newtypes that keep queue names, exchange names, routing keys, consumer tags and delivery tags from being mixed up, a typed URI, and the `ExchangeType` of an exchange. [`AMQPConfig`](./amqp.md#amqpconfig) lives in the same package. The examples on this page use the following import:

```scala
import zio.amqp.model._
```

### Newtypes

Queue names, exchange names, routing keys and consumer tags are all strings, so passing one where another is expected compiles with plain `String` parameters and fails at run time on the broker. The model package wraps each of them in a [ZIO Prelude](https://zio.dev/zio-prelude/) newtype, which the compiler treats as a distinct type and which has no run-time cost:

```scala
package object model {
  object QueueName    extends Newtype[String]
  object ExchangeName extends Newtype[String]
  object RoutingKey   extends Newtype[String]
  object ConsumerTag  extends Newtype[String]
  object DeliveryTag  extends Subtype[Long]
  object AmqpUri      extends Subtype[URI]
}
```

Each object is both the companion and the type: `QueueName` is the type `QueueName.Type` and the constructor `QueueName.apply`. To create the values and get the underlying strings back with `QueueName.unwrap`:

```scala
val queue    = QueueName("orders")
// queue: QueueName.Type = "orders"
val exchange = ExchangeName("orders-exchange")
// exchange: ExchangeName.Type = "orders-exchange"
val key      = RoutingKey("orders.created")
// key: RoutingKey.Type = "orders.created"
val tag      = ConsumerTag("billing-service")
// tag: ConsumerTag.Type = "billing-service"

QueueName.unwrap(queue)
// res0: String = "orders"
```

Because the newtypes are distinct, a call such as `channel.queueBind(exchange, queue, key)` with the first two arguments swapped does not compile.

#### QueueName

`QueueName` names a queue. [`Channel#queueDeclare`](./channel.md#channelqueuedeclare) accepts an empty name, which asks the broker to generate one, and returns the name it chose as a `String`:

```scala
val serverNamed = QueueName("")
```

#### ExchangeName

`ExchangeName` names an exchange. The empty name, `ExchangeName("")`, is the broker's predefined default exchange: it is a direct exchange that routes a message to the queue whose name equals the routing key.

#### RoutingKey

`RoutingKey` is the label a publisher attaches to a message and a binding matches against. [`Channel#publish`](./channel.md#channelpublish) defaults it to `RoutingKey("")`.

#### ConsumerTag

`ConsumerTag` identifies one consumer on a channel. [`Channel#consume`](./channel.md#channelconsume) requires one and uses it again to cancel the consumer when the stream ends, so two live consumers on the same channel must not share a tag.

#### DeliveryTag

`DeliveryTag` identifies a delivery on a channel so it can be acknowledged. It is declared with `Subtype[Long]` rather than `Newtype[Long]`, so a `DeliveryTag` is also a `Long`: it can be passed where a `Long` is expected and compared with `<`. The broker assigns tags in increasing order, which is what makes [`Channel#ackMany`](./channel.md#channelackmany) possible.

The consumer hands out the raw tag as a `Long` through `Delivery#getEnvelope`, so it has to be wrapped before it is acknowledged:

```scala
import com.rabbitmq.client.Delivery

def tagOf(delivery: Delivery): DeliveryTag =
  DeliveryTag(delivery.getEnvelope.getDeliveryTag)

val asLong: Long = DeliveryTag(42L)
```

A delivery tag is only meaningful on the channel that received the delivery. Acknowledging it on another channel is a protocol error.

#### AmqpUri

`AmqpUri` is a `java.net.URI` that has been produced by [`AMQPConfig#toUri`](./amqp.md#converting-to-a-uri). Because it is a subtype, it can be passed to `Amqp.connect(uri: URI)` directly. To build one by hand:

```scala
import java.net.URI

val uri: AmqpUri = AmqpUri(new URI("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/%2F"))
```

### ExchangeType

An exchange decides how a published message is routed to queues, and its type fixes the rule. `ExchangeType` is a sealed trait with four cases for the types every RabbitMQ broker provides and one case for types added by plugins:

```scala
sealed trait ExchangeType extends Product with Serializable {
  def name: String
}

object ExchangeType {
  case object Direct                extends ExchangeType
  case object Fanout                extends ExchangeType
  case object Topic                 extends ExchangeType
  case object Headers               extends ExchangeType
  case class Custom(`type`: String) extends ExchangeType

  implicit def represent(`type`: ExchangeType): String
}
```

The `name` of each case is the string the broker expects. To list them:

```scala
List(ExchangeType.Direct, ExchangeType.Fanout, ExchangeType.Topic, ExchangeType.Headers).map(_.name)
// res4: List[String] = List("direct", "fanout", "topic", "headers")
```

The cases behave as follows:

| Case                   | Routes a message to                                                          |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ExchangeType.Direct`  | Queues bound with a routing key equal to the message's routing key.          |
| `ExchangeType.Fanout`  | Every bound queue; the routing key is ignored.                               |
| `ExchangeType.Topic`   | Queues whose binding pattern matches the routing key (`*` and `#` wildcards). |
| `ExchangeType.Headers` | Queues whose binding arguments match the message headers.                    |
| `ExchangeType.Custom`  | Whatever the plugin that provides the exchange type decides.                 |

`ExchangeType.Custom` carries the type name as given. To refer to an exchange type from a RabbitMQ plugin, such as the delayed-message plugin:

```scala
ExchangeType.Custom("x-delayed-message").name
// res5: String = "x-delayed-message"
```

The implicit conversion `ExchangeType.represent` turns an `ExchangeType` into its name where a `String` is expected, which is how [`Channel#exchangeDeclare`](./channel.md#channelexchangedeclare) passes it to the RabbitMQ client. You rarely need it yourself.

See [Route Messages with Exchanges](../how-to-route-with-exchanges.md) for a worked example of the first three types.
