## Configure Credentials and Region

In this guide, we will configure the region, the credentials and the client timeouts that every ZIO AWS client uses. By the end, you will know how to use the defaults, how to set the values in code and how to load them from a configuration source.

We'll take an incremental approach: first we use the defaults, then we set the values in code, and finally we load them from configuration.

### The Problem

Every AWS call needs a region, credentials and often a timeout. The AWS Java SDK can find these values on its own, but it looks in several places in a fixed order, such as environment variables, system properties and profile files. A program that runs on a laptop, in a container and in a test may need a different value in each place.

If the values are hard-coded in each service client, a change means editing every place that builds a client. If they are read from the environment without a shared place, each client can end up with a different setting.

ZIO AWS solves this with one common configuration layer, `AwsConfig`, that every service module depends on. The settings live in one `CommonAwsConfig` value, which you can build in code or load from configuration.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module, one service module and one HTTP client module to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core"  % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-ec2"   % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

The examples in this guide use these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.aws.core.config.{AwsConfig, CommonAwsConfig, CommonClientConfig}
import zio.aws.core.config.descriptors.commonAwsConfig
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.netty.NettyHttpClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.DefaultCredentialsProvider
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
```

### Using the Defaults

`AwsConfig.default` depends only on an `HttpClient`. It does not set the region, the credentials or any timeout, so the AWS SDK decides these on its own. This is the smallest setup, and it works when the environment already has the values:

```scala
val defaultLayers: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Ec2] =
  NettyHttpClient.default >>> AwsConfig.default >>> Ec2.live
```

The layer chain is read from left to right. `NettyHttpClient.default` provides the `HttpClient`, `AwsConfig.default` provides the `AwsConfig`, and `Ec2.live` provides the `Ec2` service.

### Setting the Values in Code

To set the values explicitly, build a `CommonAwsConfig` and pass it to `AwsConfig.configured()`. This layer depends on an `HttpClient` and on a `CommonAwsConfig`, so we provide both:

```scala
val explicitConfig: CommonAwsConfig = CommonAwsConfig(
  region = Some(Region.EU_WEST_1),
  credentialsProvider = DefaultCredentialsProvider.builder().build(),
  endpointOverride = None,
  commonClientConfig = Some(
    CommonClientConfig(
      extraHeaders = Map.empty,
      apiCallTimeout = Some(Duration.fromSeconds(30)),
      apiCallAttemptTimeout = Some(Duration.fromSeconds(10)),
      defaultProfileName = None
    )
  )
)

val configuredLayers: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Ec2] =
  (NettyHttpClient.default ++ ZLayer.succeed(explicitConfig)) >>> AwsConfig.configured() >>> Ec2.live
```

The code above:

- `region` sets the region for every client. `Some(Region.EU_WEST_1)` is the same as the `region` key in configuration.
- `credentialsProvider` chooses where the credentials come from. `DefaultCredentialsProvider` uses the same chain as the AWS SDK, so the same environment works. Pass `StaticCredentialsProvider` only for local tests, and never commit literal keys.
- `endpointOverride` sends requests to another URL, for example a local emulator. `None` keeps the regular AWS endpoint.
- `commonClientConfig` holds the timeouts and extra headers. `apiCallTimeout` limits the whole call, including retries, and `apiCallAttemptTimeout` limits one HTTP attempt.

:::note
When `commonClientConfig` is `Some`, `AwsConfig.configured()` also turns off the SDK's own retries. The recommended way to add retries is an aspect, as described in [Add Aspects](./guide-add-aspects.md). When `commonClientConfig` is `None`, the SDK keeps its default retry behaviour.
:::

### Loading the Values from Configuration

To keep the values out of the code, read them with ZIO Config. The `commonAwsConfig` descriptor in `zio.aws.core.config.descriptors` describes all the keys, so the same layer works with any ZIO Config provider:

```scala
val configFromSource: ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, CommonAwsConfig] =
  ZLayer.fromZIO(ZIO.config(commonAwsConfig))

val configuredFromSource: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Ec2] =
  (NettyHttpClient.default ++ configFromSource.mapError(e => new RuntimeException(e.toString))) >>> AwsConfig.configured() >>> Ec2.live
```

The keys are `region`, `credentials` (with a `type` of `default`, `anonymous`, `instance-profile` or `static`), `endpointOverride` and `client` (with `extraHeaders`, `apiCallTimeout`, `apiCallAttemptTimeout` and `defaultProfileName`). The [Configuration](./configuration.md) page lists every key and its format.

:::warning
Do not put literal access keys in a configuration file that is committed to source control. Use the `default` credentials type and let the AWS SDK read the keys from its own profile or the environment.
:::

### Going Further

- The [Configuration](./configuration.md) reference lists every `CommonAwsConfig` key.
- The [Use a Local Endpoint](./guide-use-a-local-endpoint.md) guide points the clients at LocalStack or MinIO.
- The HTTP client has its own settings. See [HTTP Clients](./http.md), and [Choose an HTTP Client](./guide-choose-http-client.md) for guidance on which one to use.

---

## Handle AWS Errors

In this guide, we will handle the failures of an AWS call with pattern matching on `AwsError`, read the AWS error code behind a failed request and recover from a missing field. By the end, you will know how to decide which failures to retry, which to report and which to ignore.

We'll take an incremental approach: first we catch every error, then we match the two error cases, and finally we read the error code of a service failure.

### The Problem

The AWS Java SDK reports failures by throwing exceptions, and it reports missing response fields by returning `null`. A program that calls the SDK directly has to catch both, and it must know which exception types a given service can throw.

ZIO AWS turns both into values of one type, `AwsError`, in the error channel of every effect. The compiler then requires you to handle the failure, and a missing field can no longer slip through as `null`.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module and a service module, such as EC2:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core"  % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-ec2"   % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.aws.core.{AwsError, FieldIsNone, GenericAwsError}
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.ec2.model._
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.ec2.model.Ec2Exception
```

### Catching Every Error

Each AWS call has the error type `AwsError`. The simplest way to recover is to provide a fallback for every failure. Here a failed `DescribeRegions` call returns an empty list of regions:

```scala
val regions: ZIO[Ec2, Nothing, Iterable[Region.ReadOnly]] =
  Ec2
    .describeRegions(DescribeRegionsRequest())
    .flatMap(_.getRegions)
    .catchAll(_ => ZIO.succeed(Iterable.empty))
```

The `catchAll` handler receives the `AwsError` and returns a fallback effect. The result has the error type `Nothing`, so the caller no longer has to handle failures.

:::warning
Catching every error hides the difference between a network problem and a rejected request. Use it only when a fallback is always acceptable.
:::

### Matching the Two Error Cases

`AwsError` is a sealed trait with two cases, so a pattern match with both cases is exhaustive:

- `GenericAwsError(reason)` wraps the exception that the AWS SDK threw. The `reason` is a `Throwable`.
- `FieldIsNone(field)` is produced when a field that the response must contain is absent. The `field` is the name of the field.

To handle each case differently:

```scala
val described: ZIO[Ec2, Nothing, Unit] =
  Ec2
    .describeRegions(DescribeRegionsRequest())
    .flatMap(_.getRegions)
    .flatMap(regions => ZIO.foreachDiscard(regions)(_.getRegionName))
    .catchAll {
      case GenericAwsError(reason) =>
        Console.printLine(s"The AWS call failed: ${reason.getMessage}").ignore
      case FieldIsNone(field) =>
        Console.printLine(s"The response has no $field field").ignore
    }
```

The code above handles the two failures with different messages. The `GenericAwsError` branch can use the exception message, and the `FieldIsNone` branch can name the field that was missing.

### Reading the AWS Error Code

Failures from the service itself carry the AWS error code, such as `UnauthorizedOperation` or `Throttling`. The `reason` of a `GenericAwsError` is the SDK exception, which is specific to the service. For EC2 it is `Ec2Exception`, and that exception gives access to the error code:

```scala
val errorCode: AwsError => Option[String] = {
  case GenericAwsError(ec2: Ec2Exception) =>
    Option(ec2.awsErrorDetails()).map(_.errorCode())
  case _ =>
    None
}
```

The code above returns the AWS error code when the failure comes from EC2, and `None` for any other failure. Each service module has its own exception class, named after the service.

### Converting to a Throwable

Code that still uses exceptions can convert an `AwsError` with `toThrowable`. Both cases have a `Throwable` form. The effect below fails with a `Throwable` instead of an `AwsError`:

```scala
val asThrowable: ZIO[Ec2, Throwable, Iterable[Region.ReadOnly]] =
  Ec2
    .describeRegions(DescribeRegionsRequest())
    .flatMap(_.getRegions)
    .mapError(_.toThrowable)
```

`toThrowable` returns the wrapped exception for a `GenericAwsError`, and a `NoSuchElementException` for a `FieldIsNone`.

### Retrying Failures

Retries are not part of the error model. ZIO AWS recommends adding retries with an aspect on the service layer, so that every call gets the same policy. See [Add Aspects](./guide-add-aspects.md) for an example. The [AWS Errors](./aws-error.md) reference describes every case of `AwsError`.

### Going Further

- The [AWS Errors](./aws-error.md) reference lists the full definition of `AwsError`.
- The [Paginate and Stream Results](./guide-paginate-and-stream.md) guide shows how errors appear inside a stream.

---

## Paginate and Stream Results

In this guide, we will read all the results of a paginated AWS operation without writing a loop that tracks the next-page token. By the end, you will know how to consume a stream of results, how to limit it and how to fetch one page when you need that instead.

We'll take an incremental approach: first we read the whole stream, then we count and limit it, and finally we fetch a single page.

### The Problem

Many AWS operations return only part of their results per call. The response carries a next-page token, and the caller must send that token back to get the next part. A complete listing needs a loop that keeps the token, stops when it is absent and handles failures on every page.

Writing that loop by hand is repetitive, and it is easy to get wrong. A missed token stops the listing early, and an error on the third page can leave the code without a clear way to recover.

ZIO AWS generates a stream for each paginated operation. The stream fetches the next page when it needs one, so your code sees one item at a time.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module and the EC2 service module, plus an HTTP client:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core"  % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-ec2"   % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.aws.core.AwsError
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.ec2.model._
```

### Reading the Whole Stream

`Ec2.describeInstances` is a paginated operation, so the wrapper returns a `ZStream` of `Reservation.ReadOnly` items. Each item is one reservation from one page:

```scala
val reservations: ZStream[Ec2, AwsError, Reservation.ReadOnly] =
  Ec2.describeInstances(DescribeInstancesRequest())
```

The stream type is `ZStream[Ec2, AwsError, Reservation.ReadOnly]`. Nothing runs yet. The AWS call happens when a consumer pulls the first item, and the next page is requested only after the previous items have been consumed.

To count every instance across all reservations:

```scala
val instanceCount: ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, Long] =
  Ec2
    .describeInstances(DescribeInstancesRequest())
    .mapZIO(_.getInstances)
    .flatMap(ZStream.fromIterable(_))
    .runCount
```

The code above:

- `mapZIO(_.getInstances)` reads the instances of each reservation. The getter is a ZIO effect, because the field is optional in the AWS model.
- `flatMap(ZStream.fromIterable(_))` turns each list of instances into individual stream items.
- `runCount` consumes the stream and returns the number of instances.

### Limiting the Stream

A stream can contain many pages, and the operation keeps paging until the listing is complete. Use the standard stream operators to stop early. This example reads at most ten reservations:

```scala
val firstTenReservations: ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, Chunk[Reservation.ReadOnly]] =
  Ec2
    .describeInstances(DescribeInstancesRequest())
    .take(10)
    .runCollect
```

`take(10)` stops the stream once it has ten items, so the operation stops requesting further pages. This matters for listings that run to thousands of items.

:::warning
`runCollect` loads every item it receives into memory. For a very large listing, process the items with `foreach` or `runCount` instead.
:::

### Fetching a Single Page

Sometimes you need the page itself, for example to forward it through an HTTP API that has its own paging. For those cases the library also generates a non-streaming wrapper with a `Paginated` suffix. It makes one call and returns the raw response:

```scala
val onePage: ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, DescribeInstancesResponse.ReadOnly] =
  Ec2.describeInstancesPaginated(DescribeInstancesRequest())
```

The response contains the `reservations` for that page and a `nextToken` field. Pass the token in the next request yourself to fetch the following page.

### Going Further

- The [Wrappers](./wrappers.md) reference describes every kind of operation wrapper.
- Errors raised while a stream is running are the same `AwsError` values as in a single call. See [Handle AWS Errors](./guide-handle-errors.md).

---

## Stream S3 Objects

In this guide, we will upload and download Amazon S3 objects as ZIO streams, so that a file of any size passes through the program without being loaded into memory. By the end, you will know how to upload from memory and from a file, how to download to a file, and how to list the objects of a bucket.

We'll take an incremental approach: first we upload, then we download, and finally we list a bucket.

### The Problem

An S3 object can be larger than the memory of the program that reads it. The AWS Java SDK streams object bodies through reactive-streams publishers and response transformers, which do not fit naturally into a ZIO program, and the bytes then have to be connected to a file or another stream by hand.

ZIO AWS generates S3 operations that take and return `ZStream[Any, AwsError, Byte]`. An upload consumes a stream, and a download returns one, so the bytes flow between S3 and any ZIO stream source or sink.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module, an HTTP client and the S3 module:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core"  % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-s3"    % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets
import java.nio.file.{Files, Path}
import zio._
import zio.stream.{ZSink, ZStream}
import zio.aws.core.AwsError
import zio.aws.s3.S3
import zio.aws.s3.model.{GetObjectRequest, ListObjectsV2Request, PutObjectRequest, S3Object}
import zio.aws.s3.model.primitives.{BucketName, ContentLength, ObjectKey}
```

### Uploading from Memory

`S3.putObject` takes the request and the body as a second argument. The body is a stream of bytes, and S3 needs to know its length before the upload starts, so we set `contentLength` in the request:

```scala
def uploadText(bucket: String, key: String, text: String): ZIO[S3, AwsError, Unit] = {
  val bytes = Chunk.fromArray(text.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
  S3.putObject(
    PutObjectRequest(
      bucket = BucketName(bucket),
      key = ObjectKey(key),
      contentLength = ContentLength(bytes.length.toLong)
    ),
    ZStream.fromChunk(bytes)
  ).unit
}
```

The code above:

- `BucketName`, `ObjectKey` and `ContentLength` are the S3 newtypes for these fields; the request case class does not accept plain strings or numbers.
- Optional request fields such as `contentLength` take the value directly; ZIO AWS wraps it in `Optional` for you.
- `ZStream.fromChunk(bytes)` is the body. It must produce exactly `contentLength` bytes.
- `S3.putObject` returns a `PutObjectResponse.ReadOnly`, which holds the object's ETag; `ZIO#unit` discards it here.

### Uploading a File

A file upload is the same call with a file stream as the body. `ZStream.fromPath` reads the file in chunks, and its failures are `Throwable` values, so we turn them into `AwsError` with `AwsError.fromThrowable`:

```scala
def uploadFile(bucket: String, key: String, path: Path): ZIO[S3, AwsError, Unit] =
  for {
    size <- ZIO.attempt(Files.size(path)).mapError(AwsError.fromThrowable)
    _ <- S3.putObject(
           PutObjectRequest(
             bucket = BucketName(bucket),
             key = ObjectKey(key),
             contentLength = ContentLength(size)
           ),
           ZStream.fromPath(path).mapError(AwsError.fromThrowable)
         )
  } yield ()
```

The file is never loaded into memory as a whole: the HTTP client pulls chunks from the stream as it sends them.

### Downloading to a File

`S3.getObject` returns a `StreamingOutputResult`. It pairs the response, which holds the object's metadata, with an `output` stream of the object's bytes:

```scala
def downloadFile(bucket: String, key: String, path: Path): ZIO[S3, AwsError, Long] =
  for {
    result <- S3.getObject(GetObjectRequest(bucket = BucketName(bucket), key = ObjectKey(key)))
    _ <- Console.printLine(s"Content type: ${result.response.contentType.getOrElse("unknown")}").orDie
    written <- result.output
                 .mapError(_.toThrowable)
                 .run(ZSink.fromPath(path))
                 .mapError(AwsError.fromThrowable)
  } yield written
```

The code above:

- `result.response` is a `GetObjectResponse.ReadOnly`, available before any byte of the body is read. Its `contentType` field is an `Optional`.
- `result.output` is a `ZStream[Any, AwsError, Byte]` that reads the HTTP response body as it arrives. Run it once.
- `ZSink.fromPath(path)` writes the bytes to a file and returns the number of bytes written. The sink fails with `Throwable`, so we map the stream's `AwsError` to a `Throwable` with `AwsError#toThrowable` before running it, and map the result back.

### Reading Part of an Object

`StreamingOutputResult` has two helpers that change one half of the result and keep the other. `mapOutput` changes the byte stream, and `mapResponse` changes the response. To read only the first kilobyte of an object:

```scala
def firstKilobyte(bucket: String, key: String): ZIO[S3, AwsError, Chunk[Byte]] =
  S3.getObject(GetObjectRequest(bucket = BucketName(bucket), key = ObjectKey(key)))
    .map(_.mapOutput(_.take(1024)))
    .flatMap(_.output.runCollect)
```

`take(1024)` stops reading after 1024 bytes. To ask S3 to send only a byte range instead, set the `range` field of `GetObjectRequest` to an HTTP range such as `bytes=0-1023`.

### Listing the Objects in a Bucket

`S3.listObjectsV2` is a paginated operation, so it returns a stream of `S3Object.ReadOnly` items and fetches the next page when the stream needs it:

```scala
def objectKeys(bucket: String): ZStream[S3, AwsError, String] =
  S3.listObjectsV2(ListObjectsV2Request(bucket = BucketName(bucket)))
    .mapZIO(_.getKey)
    .map(key => ObjectKey.unwrap(key))
```

Combined with the download function, this copies every object of a bucket to a local directory, one object at a time:

```scala
def downloadAll(bucket: String, directory: Path): ZIO[S3, AwsError, Unit] =
  objectKeys(bucket)
    .filterNot(_.endsWith("/"))
    .mapZIO { key =>
      val target = directory.resolve(key)
      ZIO.attempt(Files.createDirectories(target.getParent)).mapError(AwsError.fromThrowable) *>
        downloadFile(bucket, key, target)
    }
    .runDrain
```

### Going Further

- The [Wrappers](wrappers.md) reference describes the streaming operation signatures and `StreamingOutputResult`.
- The [Use a Local Endpoint](guide-use-a-local-endpoint.md) guide runs the same code against LocalStack or MinIO.
- The [Paginate and Stream Results](guide-paginate-and-stream.md) guide covers paginated operations in more depth.

## Test Code That Uses AWS

In this guide, we will put the AWS calls behind a small service of our own, implement that service once with ZIO AWS and once as a stub for tests. By the end, your business logic will run in tests without network access or credentials.

We'll take an incremental approach: first we define the service, then we write the live implementation, and finally we write a stub and use it in a test.

### The Problem

A function that calls AWS directly can only be tested against AWS. The test needs credentials, a network connection and a real account, and it becomes slow and flaky. Even a test that only checks the logic around the call has to set all of that up.

ZIO AWS does not generate mock objects for the service modules. Instead, you separate the part of your code that talks to AWS from the part that uses the result. The business logic depends on a small service of your own, and only the live implementation depends on the AWS client.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module, the service module and an HTTP client:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core"  % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-ec2"   % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.aws.core.AwsError
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.ec2.model._
```

### Defining the Service

We define a trait for the one question our code needs answered. The trait has no AWS types in its public methods, so code that uses it never needs to know about the AWS client:

```scala
trait RegionCatalog {
  def regionNames: ZIO[Any, AwsError, Iterable[String]]
}

object RegionCatalog {
  def regionNames: ZIO[RegionCatalog, AwsError, Iterable[String]] =
    ZIO.serviceWithZIO[RegionCatalog](_.regionNames)
}
```

The companion object provides an accessor, so a program can write `RegionCatalog.regionNames` and declare `RegionCatalog` in its environment.

### Implementing the Live Service

The live implementation calls EC2 through the `Ec2` service. It takes the `Ec2` service from the layer, and then it provides that service to the AWS calls:

```scala
val live: ZLayer[Ec2, Nothing, RegionCatalog] =
  ZLayer.fromZIO(
    ZIO.service[Ec2].map { ec2 =>
      new RegionCatalog {
        override def regionNames: ZIO[Any, AwsError, Iterable[String]] =
          Ec2
            .describeRegions(DescribeRegionsRequest())
            .flatMap(_.getRegions)
            .flatMap(regions => ZIO.foreach(regions)(_.getRegionName))
            .provideEnvironment(ZEnvironment(ec2))
      }
    }
  )
```

The code above:

- `ZIO.service[Ec2]` reads the EC2 service from the environment, which the caller provides.
- `provideEnvironment(ZEnvironment(ec2))` gives the AWS calls the `Ec2` service they need. The returned effect requires nothing, so callers do not have to provide `Ec2` again.
- `getRegionName` returns the region name as a plain `String`, so the public method has no AWS types.

### Writing the Stub

The stub implements the same trait without calling AWS. Its effect requires nothing, so a test can provide it directly:

```scala
val stub: ULayer[RegionCatalog] =
  ZLayer.succeed(
    new RegionCatalog {
      override def regionNames: ZIO[Any, AwsError, Iterable[String]] =
        ZIO.succeed(List("eu-west-1", "us-east-1"))
    }
  )
```

The stub returns a fixed list. You can make it return any value or fail with an `AwsError`, which lets a test check how the code reacts to failures.

### Using the Stub in a Test

Business logic depends only on `RegionCatalog`. The function below counts the regions and reports the count:

```scala
val regionReport: ZIO[RegionCatalog, AwsError, String] =
  RegionCatalog.regionNames.map(names => s"${names.size} regions available")
```

A test provides the stub in place of the live layer, and no network call happens:

```scala
val reportWithStub: ZIO[Any, AwsError, String] =
  regionReport.provideLayer(stub)
```

In a test suite built with ZIO Test, the same `provideLayer(stub)` call goes inside the test body, and the assertion checks the result.

:::tip
Keep the service trait small. Every operation you add to it needs a stub, so one method per question the business logic asks is a good size.
:::

### Going Further

- The [Configure Credentials and Region](./guide-configure-credentials-and-region.md) guide shows how the live layer receives its configuration.
- The [Handle AWS Errors](./guide-handle-errors.md) guide shows how a stub can fail with an `AwsError` to test error handling.

## Use a Local Endpoint such as LocalStack or MinIO

In this guide, we will send ZIO AWS requests to a local AWS-compatible server, such as [LocalStack](https://www.localstack.cloud/) or [MinIO](https://min.io/), instead of AWS. By the end, you will have a configuration for local development and tests that you can set in code or load from a configuration source.

We'll take an incremental approach: first we set the endpoint in code, then we fix S3 addressing, and finally we load the same settings from configuration.

### The Problem

Integration tests and local development should not need an AWS account. Local servers such as LocalStack emulate the AWS APIs on a port of your machine, and MinIO does the same for S3. A client only reaches them when three settings change together: the endpoint URL, credentials the local server accepts, and a region.

S3 needs a fourth change. The AWS SDK puts the bucket name in the host name (`my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com`), which a server on `localhost` cannot answer, so the client must put the bucket in the path instead.

ZIO AWS keeps the endpoint, credentials and region in one `CommonAwsConfig` value, so every service client in the program uses the local server once that value changes.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module, an HTTP client and the service modules you call. The examples use S3:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core"  % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-s3"    % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import java.net.URI
import zio._
import zio.aws.core.config.{AwsConfig, CommonAwsConfig}
import zio.aws.core.config.descriptors.commonAwsConfig
import zio.aws.netty.NettyHttpClient
import zio.aws.s3.S3
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.{AwsBasicCredentials, StaticCredentialsProvider}
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
```

### Setting the Endpoint in Code

`CommonAwsConfig` has an `endpointOverride` field. We set it to the local server's URL, together with fixed credentials and a region. LocalStack listens on port 4566 and accepts any credentials:

```scala
val localConfig: CommonAwsConfig =
  CommonAwsConfig(
    region = Some(Region.US_EAST_1),
    credentialsProvider = StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("test", "test")),
    endpointOverride = Some(URI.create("http://localhost:4566")),
    commonClientConfig = None
  )

val localAwsConfig: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, AwsConfig] =
  (NettyHttpClient.default ++ ZLayer.succeed(localConfig)) >>> AwsConfig.configured()
```

The code above:

- `region` must be set, because the AWS SDK signs every request for a region, even a local one.
- `StaticCredentialsProvider` returns the same keys on every request. Use it only for a local server; for AWS, keep the `DefaultCredentialsProvider` chain.
- `endpointOverride` replaces the AWS endpoint of every client that uses this `AwsConfig`.
- `commonClientConfig = None` keeps the AWS SDK's default timeouts and retries.

Any service layer built on `localAwsConfig` now talks to the local server, for example `localAwsConfig >>> S3.live`.

### Using Path-Style Addressing for S3

For S3, we also turn on path-style addressing, so that requests go to `http://localhost:4566/my-bucket/key`. The setting belongs to the S3 client builder, so we pass it to `S3.customized`, which applies a function to the builder after `AwsConfig` has configured it:

```scala
val localS3: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, S3] =
  localAwsConfig >>> S3.customized(_.forcePathStyle(true))
```

Other services do not need this step.

### Loading the Settings from Configuration

To switch between AWS and the local server without changing code, load `CommonAwsConfig` with the `commonAwsConfig` descriptor. It reads `region`, `endpointOverride` and a `credentials` section whose `type` is `static`, with `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`. To see the result, we load it from an in-memory `ConfigProvider`; in a real application the same keys come from environment variables or a HOCON file:

```scala
val localProvider: ConfigProvider =
  ConfigProvider.fromMap(
    Map(
      "region"                      -> "us-east-1",
      "endpointOverride"            -> "http://localhost:4566",
      "credentials.type"            -> "static",
      "credentials.accessKeyId"     -> "test",
      "credentials.secretAccessKey" -> "test"
    )
  )
// localProvider: ConfigProvider = zio.ConfigProvider$$anon$9@4edc5245

val loaded: CommonAwsConfig =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(localProvider.load(commonAwsConfig)).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
// loaded: CommonAwsConfig = CommonAwsConfig(
//   region = Some(value = us-east-1),
//   credentialsProvider = e(credentials=AwsCredentials(accessKeyId=test, providerName=e)),
//   endpointOverride = Some(value = http://localhost:4566),
//   commonClientConfig = None
// )

loaded.endpointOverride
// res0: Option[URI] = Some(value = http://localhost:4566)
loaded.region
// res1: Option[Region] = Some(value = us-east-1)
```

In an application, the provider is installed once, and the layer reads it with `ZIO.config`:

```scala
val awsConfigFromSource: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, AwsConfig] =
  (NettyHttpClient.default ++ ZLayer.fromZIO(ZIO.config(commonAwsConfig))) >>> AwsConfig.configured()
```

### Writing the Endpoint with Its Scheme

The `endpointOverride` value must start with `http://` or `https://`. A value without a scheme, such as `localhost:4566`, is not a valid endpoint for the AWS SDK, so the descriptor rejects it when the configuration is loaded instead of failing on the first request:

```scala
Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  Runtime.default.unsafe
    .run(
      ConfigProvider
        .fromMap(Map("endpointOverride" -> "localhost:4566"))
        .load(commonAwsConfig)
        .either
    )
    .getOrThrowFiberFailure()
    .left
    .map(_.getMessage)
}
// res2: Either[String, CommonAwsConfig] = Left(
//   value = "(Invalid data at endpointOverride: Invalid endpoint URI 'localhost:4566': scheme must be 'http' or 'https' (e.g., 'http://localhost:9000'))"
// )
```

### Going Further

- The [Configure Credentials and Region](guide-configure-credentials-and-region.md) guide covers the other `CommonAwsConfig` settings.
- The [Configuration](configuration.md) reference lists every configuration key.
- The [Stream S3 Objects](guide-stream-s3-objects.md) guide uploads and downloads objects, which works the same against a local server.

## HTTP Clients

ZIO AWS sends every request through an `HttpClient` layer, which the `AwsConfig` layer depends on. Each HTTP client is its own module, and each module provides one or more factory functions that build an `HttpClient` layer. The [Choose an HTTP Client](./guide-choose-http-client.md) guide explains how to pick one.

### HttpClient

`HttpClient` is a trait in `zio.aws.core.httpclient`. When a service builds its AWS SDK client, `AwsConfig` asks the `HttpClient` for an SDK HTTP client that fits the service:

```scala
trait HttpClient {
  def clientFor(serviceCaps: ServiceHttpCapabilities): Task[SdkAsyncHttpClient]
}

case class ServiceHttpCapabilities(supportsHttp2: Boolean)
```

`supportsHttp2` is `true` for the services generated with HTTP/2 support, `kinesis` and `transcribestreaming`, and `false` for the rest. The `Protocol` type, with the cases `Protocol.Http11`, `Protocol.Http2` and `Protocol.Dual`, chooses how a client answers:

| Protocol          | HTTP/2 services | Other services                             |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `Protocol.Http11` | HTTP/1.1 client | HTTP/1.1 client                            |
| `Protocol.Http2`  | HTTP/2 client   | fails with `UnsupportedOperationException` |
| `Protocol.Dual`   | HTTP/2 client   | HTTP/1.1 client                            |

Only the Netty module takes a `Protocol`. The http4s, Akka HTTP and AWS CRT modules return the same client for every service.

The following modules are available:

- `zio-aws-netty` uses Netty, which is the HTTP client the AWS SDK uses by default
- `zio-aws-http4s` uses the Blaze client from http4s
- `zio-aws-akka-http` uses Akka HTTP, through the [aws-spi-akka-http library](https://github.com/matsluni/aws-spi-akka-http)
- `zio-aws-crt-http` uses the AWS Common Runtime (CRT) client

### Netty

The object `zio.aws.netty.NettyHttpClient` provides these factories:

```scala
val default: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, HttpClient]
val dual: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, HttpClient]
def customized(protocol: Protocol, customization: NettyNioAsyncHttpClient.Builder => NettyNioAsyncHttpClient.Builder = identity): ZLayer[Any, Throwable, HttpClient]
def configured(tlsKeyManagersProvider: Option[TlsKeyManagersProvider] = None, tlsTrustManagersProvider: Option[TlsTrustManagersProvider] = None): ZLayer[NettyClientConfig, Throwable, HttpClient]
```

`default` uses HTTP/1.1. `dual` uses HTTP/2 for the services that support it and HTTP/1.1 for the rest. `customized` takes the `Protocol` (`Protocol.Http11`, `Protocol.Http2` or `Protocol.Dual`) and a function that changes the Netty builder. `configured` reads the settings from a `NettyClientConfig` layer, which you can load with `ZIO.config(nettyClientConfig)` from `zio.aws.netty.descriptors`. Only the TLS key and trust manager providers are passed as parameters, because they cannot be described in configuration.

### Akka HTTP

The object `zio.aws.akkahttp.AkkaHttpClient` provides the `client` factory:

```scala
def client(
    connectionPoolSettings: Option[ConnectionPoolSettings] = None,
    executionContext: Option[ExecutionContext] = None
): ZLayer[ActorSystem, Throwable, HttpClient]
```

The layer needs an `ActorSystem` in its environment. The client uses the [standard akka-http settings](https://doc.akka.io/docs/akka-http/current/configuration.html) from the application's Lightbend config, and it is not described with ZIO Config descriptors.

### http4s

The object `zio.aws.http4s.Http4sClient` provides these factories:

```scala
val default: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, HttpClient]
def customized(f: BlazeClientBuilder[Task] => BlazeClientBuilder[Task]): ZLayer[Any, Throwable, HttpClient]
def configured(
    sslContext: Option[SSLContext] = tryDefaultSslContext,
    maxConnectionsPerRequestKey: Option[RequestKey => Int] = None,
    asynchronousChannelGroup: Option[AsynchronousChannelGroup] = None,
    additionalSocketOptions: Seq[OptionValue[_]] = Seq.empty
): ZLayer[BlazeClientConfig, Throwable, HttpClient]
```

`default` uses the default Blaze settings. `customized` passes the `BlazeClientBuilder` to your function. `configured` reads the timeouts and other settings from a `BlazeClientConfig` layer, and the function parameters cover the settings that cannot be described in configuration:

### Custom HTTP Clients

You rarely need this; it is an advanced API for using an `SdkAsyncHttpClient` that has no ZIO AWS module, such as one built by other code in your application. `HttpClient.fromScopedPerProtocol` builds an `HttpClient` layer from two scoped effects, one that creates the HTTP/1.1 client and one that creates the HTTP/2 client, and a `Protocol` that chooses between them:

```scala
object HttpClient {
  def fromScopedPerProtocol[R, E, A <: SdkAsyncHttpClient](
      http11Client: ZIO[R & Scope, E, A],
      http2Client: ZIO[R & Scope, E, A]
  )(protocol: Protocol): ZLayer[R, E, HttpClient]
}
```

The effects only run for the protocols the `Protocol` value uses, and the clients are closed when the layer's scope ends. `HttpClient.fromScopedPerProtocolScoped` returns the same `HttpClient` as a scoped `ZIO` instead of a layer. The Netty module uses this function itself:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.aws.core.httpclient.{HttpClient, Protocol}
import software.amazon.awssdk.http.async.SdkAsyncHttpClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.http.nio.netty.NettyNioAsyncHttpClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.http.{Protocol => SdkProtocol}

def nettyFor(protocol: SdkProtocol): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, SdkAsyncHttpClient] =
  ZIO.fromAutoCloseable(
    ZIO.attempt(NettyNioAsyncHttpClient.builder().protocol(protocol).build())
  )

val myHttpClient: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, HttpClient] =
  HttpClient.fromScopedPerProtocol[Any, Throwable, SdkAsyncHttpClient](
    nettyFor(SdkProtocol.HTTP1_1),
    nettyFor(SdkProtocol.HTTP2)
  )(Protocol.Dual)
```

---

## Introduction to ZIO AWS

[ZIO AWS](https://zio.dev/zio-aws) is an AWS wrapper for [ZIO](https://zio.dev) for _all_ AWS services, built on the AWS Java SDK v2.

[![Production Ready](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Production%20Ready-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-aws/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-aws-core_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-aws-core_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-aws-core_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-aws-core_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-aws-core_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-aws-core_2.13) [![ZIO AWS](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-aws?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-aws)

### Introduction

ZIO AWS gives a ZIO application direct access to every AWS service. Use it on its own when a program only needs to call a few operations, or as a building block for higher-level libraries around one service.

Key features of ZIO AWS:

- A common configuration layer, `AwsConfig`, shared by every service client
- A ZIO service module per AWS service, with a wrapper for every operation
- HTTP client implementations (Netty, http4s, Akka HTTP and AWS CRT), provided as ZIO layers
- `ZStream` wrappers around paginated, byte-streaming and event-streaming operations
- Scala case classes, enums and newtypes in place of the Java builders and `null` values
- [Aspects](aspects.md) that add logging, metrics or retries to every call of a service

### Installation

ZIO AWS is published for Scala 2.13 and Scala 3, on the JVM. Every module of one release has the same version. A program needs the core module, one HTTP client module and one module for each AWS service it calls. This example adds EC2:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Core: AwsConfig, AwsError, aspects and streaming support. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core" % "7.59.5.2",

  // HTTP client that sends the requests, built on Netty. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2",

  // The EC2 service module; add one module per AWS service you call. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-ec2" % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

### Modules

Besides the core module, ZIO AWS has two kinds of modules: HTTP clients and AWS service modules.

#### HTTP Clients

Pick one HTTP client module. Netty is the default choice; the others fit an application that already runs on their stack:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Netty client, the one the AWS SDK uses by default. Supports HTTP/2. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2",

  // http4s Blaze client, for applications already on http4s. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-http4s" % "7.59.5.2",

  // Akka HTTP client; needs an ActorSystem layer. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-akka-http" % "7.59.5.2",

  // AWS Common Runtime (CRT) client. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-crt-http" % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

[Choose an HTTP Client](guide-choose-http-client.md) helps you pick one and links to the reference of each.

#### AWS Service Modules

There is one generated module per AWS service, named `zio-aws-<service>`, such as `zio-aws-s3`, `zio-aws-dynamodb` or `zio-aws-sqs`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Amazon S3. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-s3" % "7.59.5.2",

  // Amazon DynamoDB. JVM.
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-dynamodb" % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

The [Artifacts](artifacts.md) page lists every service module.

### Example

The following program prints the ID of every EC2 instance in the account. `describeInstances` is a paginated operation, so ZIO AWS returns it as a stream that fetches the next page when it is needed:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import zio.aws.core.config.AwsConfig
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.ec2.model.DescribeInstancesRequest
import zio.aws.netty.NettyHttpClient

object ListInstances extends ZIOAppDefault {
  val program =
    Ec2
      .describeInstances(DescribeInstancesRequest())
      .mapZIO(_.getInstances)
      .flatMap(ZStream.fromIterable(_))
      .mapZIO(_.getInstanceId)
      .foreach(id => Console.printLine(id).orDie)

  def run =
    program.provide(NettyHttpClient.default, AwsConfig.default, Ec2.live)
}
```

The [Getting Started](getting-started.md) page explains each part of a program like this one.

### Design

The library has a core module and one generated module for _each_ AWS service. A code generator reads the service models of the AWS Java SDK and produces a thin ZIO wrapper around each service's async client. Because the wrapper delegates every call to the Java SDK, the generator does not have to know how each AWS protocol works, and a new AWS SDK release becomes a new ZIO AWS release automatically.

Three layers build a service client. The HTTP client layer provides an `HttpClient`, `AwsConfig` applies the region, credentials and timeouts, and the service layer, such as `Ec2.live`, builds the client:

```
NettyHttpClient.default   provides HttpClient
        |
        v
AwsConfig.default         provides AwsConfig, needs HttpClient
        |
        v
Ec2.live                  provides Ec2, needs AwsConfig
```

The [Wrappers](wrappers.md) reference describes what the generated modules contain.

### Where to Start

If you are new to ZIO AWS, start with [Getting Started](getting-started.md), then build a complete program in the [tutorial](tutorial-first-program.md). The how-to guides cover single tasks, such as [configuring credentials and region](guide-configure-credentials-and-region.md), [using a local endpoint](guide-use-a-local-endpoint.md), [streaming S3 objects](guide-stream-s3-objects.md) and [adding retries](guide-add-retries.md). Related libraries, articles and talks are listed under [Resources](resources.md).

## Migration Guide

This page lists the changes that need code changes when upgrading ZIO AWS, newest first. The [Changelog](changelog.md) lists every important change.

### From 6.x to 7.x

The operator that attaches an [aspect](aspects.md) to a service layer is renamed from `@@` to `@@@`. ZIO 2.0.18 added its own `@@` operator on layers for `ZLayerAspect`, which conflicted with the ZIO AWS operator. Replace each use:

```scala
// 6.x
val ec2 = Ec2.live @@ callLogging

// 7.x
val ec2 = Ec2.live @@@ callLogging
```

The import stays `zio.aws.core.aspects._`.

### From 5.x to 6.x

ZIO AWS 6.x uses ZIO 2's built-in `Config` type and the config providers of ZIO Config 4.x. The descriptors in `zio.aws.core.config.descriptors` and in the HTTP client modules, such as `commonAwsConfig` and `nettyClientConfig`, are now `zio.Config` values instead of zio-config `ConfigDescriptor` values. Load them with `ZIO.config`, which reads from the `ConfigProvider` installed in the program:

```scala
val commonConfig: ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, CommonAwsConfig] =
  ZLayer.fromZIO(ZIO.config(commonAwsConfig))
```

To read from HOCON, environment variables or other sources, install the matching ZIO Config provider, for example with `Runtime.setConfigProvider`. The [Configure Credentials and Region](guide-configure-credentials-and-region.md) guide shows a complete layer.

### From 3.x and 4.x to 5.x

There are some major changes compared to the ZIO 1 versions (3.x.x.x and 4.x.x.x). This section describes what changed and how to modify existing code.

#### New package names
Previously the zio-aws packages had the root package `io.github.vigoo.zioaws`. By moving to the ZIO organisation this changed to be simply `zio.aws`. 

So imports for something using the EC2 and ElasticBeanstalk APIs would change from:

```scala
import io.github.vigoo.zioaws.core._
import io.github.vigoo.zioaws.ec2.Ec2
import io.github.vigoo.zioaws.ec2.model._
import io.github.vigoo.zioaws.elasticbeanstalk.ElasticBeanstalk
import io.github.vigoo.zioaws.elasticbeanstalk.model._
```

to 

```scala
import zio.aws.core._
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.ec2.model._
import zio.aws.ec2.model.primitives._
import zio.aws.elasticbeanstalk.ElasticBeanstalk
import zio.aws.elasticbeanstalk.model._
import zio.aws.elasticbeanstalk.model.primitives._
```

Some other changes to the imports may be necessary because of switching to the new service pattern of ZIO, described below.

#### New getter names

In previous version of zio-aws the generated models provided to ways to access fields:

- a ZIO effect that failed if the value is `None` with the name of the field (for example `.instanceId`)
- a simple value accessor returning an `Option` value with the `Value` suffix (for example `.instanceIdValue`)

This has been changed to match the convention used in `zio-k8s` to the following:

- the ZIO effect for requiring that a field has value now has the `get` prefix (for example `.getInstanceId`)
- the value with the field name is the simple accessor returning the optional value: (for example `.instanceId`)

So for example the following code that prints information about EC2 instances:

```scala
for {
    id <- instance.instanceId
    typ <- instance.instanceType
    launchTime <- instance.launchTime
    _ <- console.putStrLn(s"  instance $id:").ignore
    _ <- console.putStrLn(s"    type: $typ").ignore
    _ <- console.putStrLn(s"    launched at: $launchTime").ignore
} yield ()
```

would have to be changed to:

```scala
for {
    id <- instance.getInstanceId
    typ <- instance.getInstanceType
    launchTime <- instance.getLaunchTime
    _ <- Console.printLine(s"  instance $id:").ignore
    _ <- Console.printLine(s"    type: $typ").ignore
    _ <- Console.printLine(s"    launched at: $launchTime").ignore
} yield ()
```

#### New service pattern
Previous versions were following the _ZIO module pattern 1.0_, so all the generated AWS services consisted of a type alias using `Has`, a trait called `Service` and a package object with the service's name. With ZIO 2 we no longer have `Has` and the recommended way to structure services was changed to the simple new service pattern, where each service is just a `trait` and one or more implementation classes, constructed by layers.

In practice this means that:
- instead of the package object with lower-case name, the accessor functions are now in the service companion object (`ElasticBeanstalk.describeApplications` instead of `elasticbeanstalk.describeApplications`)
- same for the layers, for example `Ec2.live` instead of `ec2.live`
- the service trait has the name of the service (for example `Ec2`) instead of `Service` 

The new service pattern is also applied to the core services like `AwsConfig` and the http implementations.

#### Optional parameters
A very large part of the fields of AWS models are optional. These previously had the type `Option`, and although for extracting data from them the library already had the generated getters, constructing these data types still required wrapping most of the parameters in `Some(...)`. To reduce this boilerplate zio-aws now uses the `Optional` type instead of `Option`, which was first used in [zio-k8s](https://coralogix.github.io/zio-k8s/docs/overview/overview_resources#model). Now the two libraries share the same type which was moved to [zio-prelude](https://zio.github.io/zio-prelude/).

The following example:

```scala
kinesis.describeStreamConsumer(
  DescribeStreamConsumerRequest(
    consumerName = Some(consumerName),
    streamARN = Some(streamDescription.streamDescriptionValue.streamARNValue)
  )
)
```

becomes

```scala
Kinesis.describeStreamConsumer(
  DescribeStreamConsumerRequest(
    consumerName = consumerName,
    streamARN = streamDescription.streamDescription.streamARN
  )
)
```

#### Newtypes
Previously zio-aws generated simple Scala type aliases for primitive types in the AWS SDKs. For example the `TableName` type in `zio-aws-dynamodb` was just a type alias for `String`:

```scala
package io.github.vigoo.zioaws.dynamodb.model

package object primitives {
  type TableName = String
}
```

The new version uses [zio-prelude's newtype wrappers](https://zio.github.io/zio-prelude/docs/newtypes/) to provide better type safety:

```scala
package zio.aws.dynamodb.model

package object primitives {
  object TableName extends Subtype[String]
  type TableName = TableName.Type
}
```

In practice this means that we have to explicitly wrap these primitive values, for example instead of:

```scala
elasticbeanstalk.describeApplications(
  DescribeApplicationsRequest(applicationNames = Some(List("my-service")))
)
```

now we have to write

```scala
ElasticBeanstalk.describeApplications(
  DescribeApplicationsRequest(applicationNames = List(ApplicationName("my-service")))
)
```

and if we need to convert them to the underlying primitive type we need to call `unwrap`:

```scala
ResourceId.unwrap(id)
```

#### Aspects
zio-aws introduced `AwsCallAspect` soon after Adam Fraser's [talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gcqWdNwNEPg&t=2s) but it was a custom implementation, defined as:

```scala
trait AwsCallAspect[-R] { self =>
  def apply[R1 <: R, A](
    f: ZIO[R1, AwsError, Described[A]]
  ): ZIO[R1, AwsError, Described[A]]

  // ...
}
```

These aspects can be applied to whole zio-aws service layers to add logging, metrics, retries etc for every AWS Java SDK call.

The ZIO 2.0.0 version is now using ZIO's built-in aspect support as a base:

```scala
type AwsCallAspect[-R] =
  ZIOAspect[Nothing, R, AwsError, AwsError, Nothing, Described[_]]
```

##### New built-in aspects
With ZIO 2 we have logging and metrics support built-in, so zio-aws now provides ready to use aspects for logging and monitoring AWS calls:

```scala
val callLogging: AwsCallAspect[Any]
def callDuration(prefix: String, boundaries: MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries): AwsCallAspect[Any]
```

##### Changes in defining aspects
The following example aspect uses `rezilience` to add circuit breaking for an AWS service:

```scala
def circuitBreaking(cb: CircuitBreaker[AwsError]): AwsCallAspect[Any] =
  new AwsCallAspect[Any] {
    override final def apply[R1 <: Any, A](
      f: ZIO[R1, AwsError, Described[A]]
    ): ZIO[R1, AwsError, Described[A]] =
      cb(f).mapError(policyError =>
        AwsError.fromThrowable(policyError.toException)
      )
  }
```

because of the changed base type for `AwsCallAspect` with the new version the same aspect is defined like this:

```scala
def circuitBreaking(cb: CircuitBreaker[AwsError]): AwsCallAspect[Any] =
  new AwsCallAspect[Any] {
    override final def apply[R, E >: AwsError <: AwsError, A <: Described[_]](
      f: ZIO[R, E, A]
    )(implicit trace: Trace): ZIO[R, E, A] =
      cb(f).mapError(policyError =>
        AwsError.fromThrowable(policyError.toException)
      )
  }
```

The main differences:

- requiring the implicit `Trace` 
- the constraints on the error and result types are now expressed as type bounds because the ZIO aspect is more generic

#### New config library

The 3.x series of zio-aws was using `zio-config 1.x`, and the 4.x series was using `zio-config 2.x`, the ZIO 1 version of the config library's new API. The 5.x series uses `zio-config 3.x`, the same API for ZIO 2.

Coming from zio-aws 3.x requires upgrading to the new config API. For more information about the changes in zio-config, [see its release notes](https://github.com/zio/zio-config/releases/tag/v2.0.0-RC1). Version 6.x changed the configuration again; see [From 5.x to 6.x](#from-5x-to-6x).

## Tutorial: Build an EC2 Inventory Program

Welcome to ZIO AWS! In this tutorial we build one small but complete program: an inventory that lists every EC2 instance in every region of an AWS account. This tutorial is for developers who know basic Scala and ZIO effects and layers, and who have run the program on the [Getting Started](getting-started.md) page. You don't need any prior experience with EC2.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will understand:

- How a generated ZIO AWS service turns AWS responses into ZIO effects and streams
- How to turn the read-only AWS wrappers into your own data types
- How to build a service client for a different region with `Ec2.scoped`
- How to keep a program running when one AWS call fails

We'll learn these concepts through:

1. Setting up the project
2. Listing the regions
3. Turning instances into our own data
4. Building one client per region
5. Surviving a failing region
6. Putting it together

We recommend reading from top to bottom, because each section builds on the previous one.

### Background

EC2 is regional: each region has its own instances, and an EC2 client talks to one region. To list every instance in the account, the program first asks one region for the list of regions, then asks each region for its instances.

ZIO AWS gives us three tools for this. Each AWS operation is a ZIO effect, so we can sequence calls and run them in parallel. Operations that return many pages are streams, so we never deal with next-page tokens. And every service has constructors that let us change the client's settings, such as its region, while it is built.

### 1. Setting Up the Project

The program uses the core module, the Netty HTTP client and the EC2 module:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-core"  % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-netty" % "7.59.5.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-aws-ec2"   % "7.59.5.2"
)
```

Every later section uses these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import zio.aws.core.AwsError
import zio.aws.core.config.AwsConfig
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.ec2.model.{DescribeInstancesRequest, DescribeRegionsRequest}
import zio.aws.netty.NettyHttpClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.{Region => AwsRegion}
```

The `zio.aws.ec2.model` package holds the request and response types. The AWS SDK's own `Region` type is renamed to `AwsRegion`, because EC2's model also has a type named `Region`.

### 2. Listing the Regions

Let's start with one call. `Ec2.describeRegions` returns the regions that are enabled for the account:

```scala
val regionNames: ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, List[String]] =
  for {
    response <- Ec2.describeRegions(DescribeRegionsRequest())
    regions  <- response.getRegions
    names    <- ZIO.foreach(regions.toList)(_.getRegionName)
  } yield names
```

The code above:

- `Ec2.describeRegions(...)` performs the call. Its type is `ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, DescribeRegionsResponse.ReadOnly]`, so it needs the `Ec2` service and can fail with an `AwsError`.
- `response.getRegions` reads the `regions` field. The field is optional in the AWS model, so the getter is an effect that fails with `AwsError` when the field is absent.
- `ZIO.foreach(...)(_.getRegionName)` reads the name of each region the same way. In EC2's model the region name is a plain `String`; services that define their own value types use newtypes instead, as the [Wrappers](wrappers.md) reference describes.

Notice that nothing has run yet. `regionNames` is a description of the calls; it runs when we provide an `Ec2` service and execute it.

### 3. Turning Instances into Our Own Data

The program should not pass AWS wrapper types around, so let's define our own record for one instance:

```scala
case class InstanceInfo(
  region: String,
  id: String,
  instanceType: String,
  state: String
)
```

`Ec2.describeInstances` is a paginated operation, so it returns a stream of reservations instead of a single response. Each reservation holds a list of instances. We flatten the reservations into instances and convert each one:

```scala
def listInstances(region: String): ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, Chunk[InstanceInfo]] =
  Ec2
    .describeInstances(DescribeInstancesRequest())
    .mapZIO(_.getInstances)
    .flatMap(instances => ZStream.fromIterable(instances))
    .mapZIO { instance =>
      instance.getInstanceId.map { id =>
        InstanceInfo(
          region = region,
          id = id,
          instanceType = instance.instanceType.map(_.toString).getOrElse("unknown"),
          state = instance.state.flatMap(_.name).map(_.toString).getOrElse("unknown")
        )
      }
    }
    .runCollect
```

The code above:

- `Ec2.describeInstances(...)` is a `ZStream[Ec2, AwsError, Reservation.ReadOnly]`. The stream requests the next page only after the items of the previous page are consumed.
- `ZStream#mapZIO` with `_.getInstances` reads the instance list of each reservation, and `ZStream#flatMap` with `ZStream.fromIterable` turns the lists into one stream of instances.
- `instance.getInstanceId` fails with `AwsError` if the ID is missing, which never happens for a real instance, so we use the failing getter.
- `instance.instanceType` and `instance.state` are the non-failing accessors. They return `Optional` values, which we turn into text with a default. The `get`-prefixed getters fail; the plain ones return `Optional`.
- `ZStream#runCollect` runs the stream and collects the instances into a `Chunk`.

### 4. Building One Client per Region

`Ec2.live` builds a client for the region in the configuration. To ask another region, we build another client. Every service has a `scoped` constructor, such as `Ec2.scoped`, that takes a function to change the AWS SDK builder, and returns the client as a scoped effect:

```scala
def instancesIn(region: String): ZIO[AwsConfig, AwsError, Chunk[InstanceInfo]] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    Ec2
      .scoped(builder => builder.region(AwsRegion.of(region)))
      .mapError(AwsError.fromThrowable)
      .flatMap(ec2 => listInstances(region).provideEnvironment(ZEnvironment(ec2)))
  }
```

The code above:

- `Ec2.scoped(builder => builder.region(...))` builds an EC2 client whose region is `region`. The function runs after `AwsConfig` has applied the common settings, so its region wins.
- Building a client can fail with a `Throwable`, so `ZIO#mapError` with `AwsError.fromThrowable` turns that failure into an `AwsError`. Now every failure of `instancesIn` has the same type.
- `ZIO#provideEnvironment` with `ZEnvironment(ec2)` gives `listInstances` the client it needs.
- `ZIO.scoped` closes the client when the region is done.

The result only needs `AwsConfig`, which every client in the program shares.

### 5. Surviving a Failing Region

A region can fail even when the others work, for example when an organization policy denies EC2 calls there. We don't want one region to stop the whole inventory, so let's turn each region's result into an `Either` and query the regions in parallel:

```scala
val inventory: ZIO[Ec2 & AwsConfig, AwsError, Chunk[InstanceInfo]] =
  for {
    regions <- regionNames
    results <- ZIO.foreachPar(regions)(region => instancesIn(region).either.map(region -> _))
    _ <- ZIO.foreachDiscard(results) {
           case (region, Left(error)) =>
             Console.printLineError(s"Skipping $region: ${error.toThrowable.getMessage}").orDie
           case _ => ZIO.unit
         }
  } yield Chunk.fromIterable(results).collect { case (_, Right(instances)) => instances }.flatten
```

The code above:

- `ZIO.foreachPar` queries all regions at the same time.
- `ZIO#either` on `instancesIn(region)` turns a failure into a `Left` value, so the effect for that region always succeeds and the others keep running.
- The `ZIO.foreachDiscard` call reports each failed region on standard error. `AwsError#toThrowable` returns the AWS SDK exception, whose message names the problem.
- The `yield` keeps the instances of the regions that succeeded.

Try changing `instancesIn(region).either` to `instancesIn(region)` and the first failing region would fail the whole program.

### 6. Putting It Together

The complete program prints one line per instance. It combines every step: the regions come from a client built by `Ec2.live`, each region gets its own client, and failing regions are skipped. Unlike the sections above, it is a single self-contained file that you can copy into `src/main/scala`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import zio.aws.core.AwsError
import zio.aws.core.config.AwsConfig
import zio.aws.ec2.Ec2
import zio.aws.ec2.model.{DescribeInstancesRequest, DescribeRegionsRequest}
import zio.aws.netty.NettyHttpClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.{Region => AwsRegion}

object Ec2Inventory extends ZIOAppDefault {
  case class InstanceInfo(region: String, id: String, instanceType: String, state: String)

  val regionNames: ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, List[String]] =
    for {
      response <- Ec2.describeRegions(DescribeRegionsRequest())
      regions  <- response.getRegions
      names    <- ZIO.foreach(regions.toList)(_.getRegionName)
    } yield names

  def listInstances(region: String): ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, Chunk[InstanceInfo]] =
    Ec2
      .describeInstances(DescribeInstancesRequest())
      .mapZIO(_.getInstances)
      .flatMap(instances => ZStream.fromIterable(instances))
      .mapZIO { instance =>
        instance.getInstanceId.map { id =>
          InstanceInfo(
            region,
            id,
            instance.instanceType.map(_.toString).getOrElse("unknown"),
            instance.state.flatMap(_.name).map(_.toString).getOrElse("unknown")
          )
        }
      }
      .runCollect

  def instancesIn(region: String): ZIO[AwsConfig, AwsError, Chunk[InstanceInfo]] =
    ZIO.scoped {
      Ec2
        .scoped(builder => builder.region(AwsRegion.of(region)))
        .mapError(AwsError.fromThrowable)
        .flatMap(ec2 => listInstances(region).provideEnvironment(ZEnvironment(ec2)))
    }

  val inventory: ZIO[Ec2 & AwsConfig, AwsError, Chunk[InstanceInfo]] =
    for {
      regions <- regionNames
      results <- ZIO.foreachPar(regions)(region => instancesIn(region).either.map(region -> _))
      _ <- ZIO.foreachDiscard(results) {
             case (region, Left(error)) =>
               Console.printLineError(s"Skipping $region: ${error.toThrowable.getMessage}").orDie
             case _ => ZIO.unit
           }
    } yield Chunk.fromIterable(results).collect { case (_, Right(instances)) => instances }.flatten

  def run =
    inventory
      .flatMap(instances =>
        ZIO.foreachDiscard(instances) { i =>
          Console.printLine(s"${i.region}  ${i.id}  ${i.instanceType}  ${i.state}").orDie
        }
      )
      .provide(NettyHttpClient.default, AwsConfig.default, Ec2.live)
}
```

When you run it with credentials and a default region set (for example `AWS_REGION=eu-west-1`), it prints a line such as `eu-west-1  i-0abc123def4567890  t3.micro  running` for each instance, and a `Skipping ...` line on standard error for each region it could not read.

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned:

- How a generated service exposes each operation as a ZIO effect, and each paginated operation as a stream
- How to read the read-only wrappers with failing `get` getters and `Optional` accessors, and turn them into your own case class
- How to build a client for another region with `Ec2.scoped` and give it to an effect with `provideEnvironment`
- How to keep a program running when one call fails, with `either` and `ZIO.foreachPar`

You now have the foundation for working with any AWS service that ZIO AWS supports. The next step is to apply it to the tasks of a real application.

### Where to Go Next

- **Ready to configure it for production?** Read [Configure Credentials and Region](guide-configure-credentials-and-region.md) and [Add Retries](guide-add-retries.md).
- **Want to observe the calls?** Read [Add Aspects for Logging and Metrics](guide-add-aspects.md).
- **Want the full API?** Read the [Wrappers](wrappers.md) and [AWS Errors](aws-error.md) reference pages.
