## Wrappers

Every AWS service module, such as `zio-aws-ec2`, is generated from the AWS Java SDK's service model. All of them have the same shape, so this page describes the pattern with examples from a few services.

### Service Modules

Each module has a package `zio.aws.<service>` with a service trait and its companion object, a `model` package with the request, response and data types, and a `model.primitives` package with newtypes. For EC2 the service is `zio.aws.ec2.Ec2`:

```scala
trait Ec2 extends AspectSupport[Ec2] {
  val api: Ec2AsyncClient

  def describeRegions(request: DescribeRegionsRequest): ZIO[Any, AwsError, DescribeRegionsResponse.ReadOnly]
  // ... one method per operation
}
```

The `api` field is the AWS Java SDK's async client that the service wraps. Use it for SDK features that are not operations, such as waiters; the [Customize Clients and Call the AWS SDK Directly](guide-call-the-sdk-client-directly.md) guide shows how. `AspectSupport` lets [aspects](aspects.md) be attached to the service.

#### Layers

The companion object builds the service. All three constructors depend on [`AwsConfig`](configuration.md):

```scala
object Ec2 {
  val live: ZLayer[AwsConfig, Throwable, Ec2]
  def customized(customization: Ec2AsyncClientBuilder => Ec2AsyncClientBuilder): ZLayer[AwsConfig, Throwable, Ec2]
  def scoped(customization: Ec2AsyncClientBuilder => Ec2AsyncClientBuilder): ZIO[AwsConfig & Scope, Throwable, Ec2]
}
```

`live` builds the client with the settings of `AwsConfig`. `customized(f)` builds the same client, but first applies `f` to the SDK client builder, after `AwsConfig` has configured it, so `f` can change any setting, including service-specific ones. `scoped(f)` does the same as `customized(f)` but returns a scoped `ZIO` instead of a layer, so you can build several clients and manage their lifetimes yourself. The client is closed when its layer or scope ends.

While it builds a client, the service also:

- Runs the SDK's future completions on the ZIO executor, so the code after an AWS call continues on a ZIO thread.
- Asks the `HttpClient` for an HTTP/2 client for `kinesis` and `transcribestreaming`, the services generated with HTTP/2 support, and for an HTTP/1.1 client for every other service. See [Choose an HTTP Client](guide-choose-http-client.md).
- Sets the region to `aws-global` for the global services `cloudfront`, `globalaccelerator`, `iam`, `networkmanager`, `organizations`, `route53`, `shield` and `waf`, before applying `f`.

#### Accessors

The companion object also has one accessor per operation. An accessor calls the operation on the service from the environment, so it has the service in its `R` type:

```scala
object Ec2 {
  def describeRegions(request: DescribeRegionsRequest): ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, DescribeRegionsResponse.ReadOnly]
}
```

Use the accessors in code that has the service in its environment, and the trait's methods when you hold a service value, such as one built with `scoped`.

### Operations

The generator picks the wrapper shape from the operation's input and output. The signatures below are the accessors.

#### Request and Response

A simple request-response operation returns a `ZIO` with the read-only response wrapper:

```scala
def deleteVolume(request: DeleteVolumeRequest): ZIO[Ec2, AwsError, DeleteVolumeResponse.ReadOnly]
```

An operation without input has no parameter, and an operation without output returns `Unit`.

#### Byte Streams

For operations whose input or output is a byte stream, the generator uses `ZStream[Any, AwsError, Byte]`:

```scala
def getObject(request: GetObjectRequest): ZIO[S3, AwsError, StreamingOutputResult[Any, GetObjectResponse.ReadOnly, Byte]]
def putObject(request: PutObjectRequest, body: ZStream[Any, AwsError, Byte]): ZIO[S3, AwsError, PutObjectResponse.ReadOnly]
```

An input stream is sent with the length from the request's `contentLength` field, when the request has one. A streamed output comes in a `StreamingOutputResult`, described [below](#streamingoutputresult). The [Stream S3 Objects](guide-stream-s3-objects.md) guide uses both.

#### Event Streams

For operations with event streams, the input or output is a `ZStream` of model types:

```scala
def startStreamTranscription(
    request: StartStreamTranscriptionRequest,
    input: ZStream[Any, AwsError, AudioStream]
): ZStream[TranscribeStreaming, AwsError, TranscriptEvent.ReadOnly]
```

The AWS call starts when the stream is pulled.

#### Paginated Operations

For operations that return their results in pages, the generator creates a streaming wrapper that requests the next page when the stream needs more items, and a `Paginated` variant that makes one call. The streaming wrapper has one of two shapes. Most paginated operations return a `ZStream` of the items:

```scala
def scan(request: ScanRequest): ZStream[DynamoDb, AwsError, Map[AttributeName, AttributeValue.ReadOnly]]
def scanPaginated(request: ScanRequest): ZIO[DynamoDb, AwsError, ScanResponse.ReadOnly]
```

For operations whose request and response both have a `NextToken` field, ZIO AWS pages through the results itself, following the next-page token. Other paginated operations use the AWS Java SDK's paginator. When the response of an operation that ZIO AWS pages itself has fields besides the items and the token, the first page is fetched right away, and the result is a `StreamingOutputResult` whose `response` is the first page's response and whose `output` is the stream of items from all pages:

```scala
def listSomething(request: ListSomethingRequest): ZIO[Svc, AwsError, StreamingOutputResult[Any, ListSomethingResponse.ReadOnly, Item.ReadOnly]]
```

For operations that ZIO AWS pages itself, each page request is a separate AWS call that runs through the service's aspects; for operations that use the Java SDK paginator, the aspect runs once for the whole stream. Use the `Paginated` variant to forward pages through your own API, passing the next-page token yourself. The [Paginate and Stream Results](guide-paginate-and-stream.md) guide shows both.

### StreamingOutputResult

`StreamingOutputResult` pairs a response with a stream, for streamed downloads and for paginated operations whose response has extra fields:

```scala
case class StreamingOutputResult[R, Response, Item](
    response: Response,
    output: ZStream[R, AwsError, Item]
) {
  def mapResponse[Response2](f: Response => Response2): StreamingOutputResult[R, Response2, Item]
  def mapOutput[I](f: ZStream[R, AwsError, Item] => ZStream[R, AwsError, I]): StreamingOutputResult[R, Response, I]
  def provideEnvironment(r: ZEnvironment[R]): StreamingOutputResult[Any, Response, Item]
}
```

`mapResponse` and `mapOutput` change one half and keep the other, and `provideEnvironment` provides the stream's environment. A downloaded byte stream reads the HTTP response body as it arrives, so run it once.

### Model Wrappers

For each model type, the generator creates:

- A case class with default parameter values, used as input, instead of the SDK's builder
- A `ReadOnly` trait, used for output, that wraps the SDK's immutable object
- [ZIO Prelude newtypes](https://zio.dev/zio-prelude/newtypes/) in `model.primitives` for primitive values, such as S3's `BucketName` or `ObjectKey`
- Scala collections instead of Java collections
- A sealed trait with one case object per value instead of each Java enum
- ZIO Prelude's `Optional` type for optional fields, which accepts a plain value or `Optional.Absent` in a constructor

#### Input Case Classes

This example from `zio-aws-elasticsearch` shows a generated case class. Every optional field defaults to `Optional.Absent`, and `buildAwsValue()` builds the SDK object:

```scala
case class DescribePackagesFilter(
    name: Optional[DescribePackagesFilterName] = Optional.Absent,
    value: Optional[Iterable[primitives.DescribePackagesFilterValue]] = Optional.Absent
) {
  def buildAwsValue(): software.amazon.awssdk.services.elasticsearch.model.DescribePackagesFilter
  def asReadOnly: DescribePackagesFilter.ReadOnly
}
```

Newtypes are created with their `apply`, such as `ObjectKey("reports/2026.csv")`, and read back with the companion's `unwrap`, such as `ObjectKey.unwrap(key)`. Fields without a dedicated AWS type, such as EC2's region names and instance IDs, are plain Scala types.

#### Read-Only Wrappers

Responses and the values inside them are read-only wrappers around the SDK objects. This example is from `zio-aws-transcribe`:

```scala
object CreateMedicalVocabularyResponse {
  trait ReadOnly {
    def asEditable: CreateMedicalVocabularyResponse
    def vocabularyName: Optional[VocabularyName]
    def languageCode: Optional[LanguageCode]
    def getVocabularyName: ZIO[Any, AwsError, VocabularyName]
    def getLanguageCode: ZIO[Any, AwsError, LanguageCode]
    // ... one pair per field
  }

  def wrap(impl: software.amazon.awssdk.services.transcribe.model.CreateMedicalVocabularyResponse): ReadOnly
}
```

Each field has two accessors. The plain one, such as `vocabularyName`, returns the `Optional` value. The `get`-prefixed one, such as `getVocabularyName`, is an effect that fails with [`FieldIsNone`](aws-error.md) when the field is absent, which makes it easy to chain AWS calls in a for-comprehension. `asEditable` copies the values into the case class, so you can change them and send them in a new request, and `wrap` turns an SDK object into the wrapper.

### Testing

The library does not generate mock objects for the services. To test code that calls AWS, put the calls behind a small service of your own and provide a stub in tests. The [Test Code That Uses AWS](guide-test-code-with-stubs.md) guide shows the pattern.

---

## BsonBuilder

`BsonBuilder` is a small object of helpers that build `BsonValue` instances from Scala values. It is useful for writing MongoDB filters and updates by hand and for building the expected documents in tests. Except for `BsonBuilder.date`, which uses the `Instant` encoder, each helper wraps one constructor of the MongoDB Java driver, so no encoding or codec is involved.

To bring the helpers into scope:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
```

### Definition

The object has one helper per common BSON type:

```scala
object BsonBuilder {
  def doc(kv: (String, BsonValue)*): BsonDocument
  def element(k: String, v: BsonValue): BsonElement
  def array(elements: BsonValue*): BsonArray
  def str(s: String): BsonString
  def int(i: Int): BsonInt32
  def long(l: Long): BsonInt64
  def bool(b: Boolean): BsonBoolean
  def double(d: Double): BsonDouble
  def date(instant: Instant): BsonValue
  val bNull: BsonNull
}
```

### Building Documents and Arrays

To build a nested document, pass pairs of a key and a `BsonValue` to `BsonBuilder.doc`, and use `BsonBuilder.array` for lists:

```scala
val order = doc(
  "id"    -> long(42L),
  "items" -> array(str("apple"), str("pear")),
  "paid"  -> bool(true),
  "note"  -> bNull
)
// order: org.bson.BsonDocument = {"id": 42, "items": ["apple", "pear"], "paid": true, "note": null}
```

`BsonBuilder.element` builds one `BsonElement`, a key with its value, which some driver APIs take instead of a pair.

### Numbers

`BsonBuilder.int` writes `INT32`, `BsonBuilder.long` writes `INT64`, and `BsonBuilder.double` writes `DOUBLE`. Decoders accept several numeric BSON types, as the [type mappings](./types.md) list. An `Int` decoder reads all three values below, because each one is a whole number that fits:

```scala
doc("a" -> int(1), "b" -> long(1L), "c" -> double(1.0)).as[Map[String, Int]]
// res0: Either[String, Map[String, Int]] = Right(
//   value = Map("a" -> 1, "b" -> 1, "c" -> 1)
// )
```

### Dates

`BsonBuilder.date` converts an `Instant` with the same encoder as `Instant#toBsonValue`, so it writes a `DATE_TIME` with millisecond precision:

```scala
import java.time.Instant

date(Instant.ofEpochMilli(1700000000000L))
// res1: org.bson.BsonValue = BsonDateTime{value=1700000000000}
```

### Related Pages

- [BsonEncoder](./bson-encoder.md) converts any Scala value to a `BsonValue`.
- [BsonDecoder](./bson-decoder.md) reads a `BsonValue` back with `as`.
- [Type Mappings](./types.md) lists the BSON type of each Scala type.

---

## BsonCodecConfiguration and Annotations

### Overview

`DeriveBsonCodec.derive` builds a codec for a case class or sealed trait from its shape. Two things control the result: a `BsonCodecConfiguration` value that sets defaults for the whole derivation, and annotations that override those defaults for one field, one subtype, or one sealed trait.

Derivation is available from the `zio.bson.magnolia` package, which is the `zio-bson-magnolia` module. It supports Scala 2.13 and Scala 3.

### Definition

`BsonCodecConfiguration` is a case class with five fields. Each one has a default:

```scala
case class BsonCodecConfiguration(
  sumTypeHandling: BsonCodecConfiguration.SumTypeHandling = SumTypeHandling.WrapperWithClassNameField,
  skipNullsInCaseClass: Boolean = true,
  classNameMapping: String => String = identity,
  fieldNameMapping: String => String = identity,
  allowExtraFields: Boolean = true
)
```

The companion object also provides an implicit default value, so derivation works without any configuration.

| Field                  | Default                     | Effect                                                                                          |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sumTypeHandling`      | `WrapperWithClassNameField` | How a sealed trait is written. See [Sum Types](#sum-types).                                     |
| `skipNullsInCaseClass` | `true`                      | When `true`, a `None` field is left out of the document. When `false`, it is written as `null`. |
| `classNameMapping`     | `identity`                  | Converts a subtype's class name before it is used as a key or discriminator value.              |
| `fieldNameMapping`     | `identity`                  | Converts a field's name before it is used as a BSON key.                                        |
| `allowExtraFields`     | `true`                      | When `false`, a field that is not in the case class makes decoding fail.                        |

Annotations on a field, subtype, or sealed trait always win over the configuration. For example, `bsonField` replaces whatever `fieldNameMapping` would produce.

### Providing a Configuration

Derivation reads the configuration as an implicit value in the scope where `DeriveBsonCodec.derive` is written. The examples on this page use a small function that takes the configuration and derives the codec from it. Any implicit `BsonCodecConfiguration` in scope takes precedence over the default one, so the same configuration can also be an `implicit val` in the companion object. Writing it as a function keeps each example self-contained:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration.{SumTypeHandling, toSnakeCase, toUpperSnakeCase}

final case class Address(streetName: String, postalCode: Option[String])

def addressCodec(config: BsonCodecConfiguration): BsonCodec[Address] = {
  implicit val configuration: BsonCodecConfiguration = config
  DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

val snakeAddress: BsonCodec[Address] =
  addressCodec(BsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = toSnakeCase))
```

```scala
println(snakeAddress.encoder.toBsonValue(Address("Main Street", None)))
// {"street_name": "Main Street"}
```

The field `streetName` is written as `street_name`. The `None` field is omitted because `skipNullsInCaseClass` is still `true`.

When you have only one configuration for a type, you can also declare it as an `implicit val` in the scope where the codec is derived, and call `DeriveBsonCodec.derive` there. In Scala 3, the same value is declared with `given` instead of `implicit val`.

### Field Names

`fieldNameMapping` changes every field name in a derived codec. The following example writes `None` fields as `null` and uses upper snake case for keys:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration.{SumTypeHandling, toSnakeCase, toUpperSnakeCase}

final case class Address(streetName: String, postalCode: Option[String])

def addressCodec(config: BsonCodecConfiguration): BsonCodec[Address] = {
  implicit val configuration: BsonCodecConfiguration = config
  DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

val nullAddress: BsonCodec[Address] =
  addressCodec(
    BsonCodecConfiguration(
      fieldNameMapping = toUpperSnakeCase,
      skipNullsInCaseClass = false
    )
  )
```

```scala
println(nullAddress.encoder.toBsonValue(Address("Main Street", None)))
// {"STREET_NAME": "Main Street", "POSTAL_CODE": null}
```

The mapping functions are listed in [Name Mappers](#name-mappers).

### Class Names and Sum Types

A sealed trait needs a way to tell its subtypes apart in BSON. `classNameMapping` changes the name that is written for each subtype. The next example uses the default wrapper style, where each subtype name is a key that holds the subtype's fields:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration.{SumTypeHandling, toSnakeCase, toUpperSnakeCase}

sealed trait Shape

object Shape {
  final case class Circle(radius: Double) extends Shape
  final case class Square(side: Double)   extends Shape

  implicit val config: BsonCodecConfiguration =
    BsonCodecConfiguration(classNameMapping = toSnakeCase)

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Shape] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Shape].toBsonValue(Shape.Square(2.0)))
// {"square": {"side": 2.0}}
```

The output key is `square`. The name comes from the class name, so `Square` becomes `square` under `toSnakeCase`.

### Sum Types

`sumTypeHandling` picks one of two encodings for sealed traits:

- `SumTypeHandling.WrapperWithClassNameField` (the default) writes a document with one key, the subtype name, whose value holds the subtype's fields. For example, `{ Circle: { radius: 1.0 } }`.
- `SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField(name)` writes the subtype fields in the same document as a string field called `name`. For example, `{ radius: 1.0, kind: "Circle" }` when `name` is `"kind"`.

The next example uses a discriminator field called `kind`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration.{SumTypeHandling, toSnakeCase, toUpperSnakeCase}

sealed trait Pet

object Pet {
  final case class Dog(name: String) extends Pet
  final case class Cat(lives: Int)   extends Pet

  implicit val config: BsonCodecConfiguration =
    BsonCodecConfiguration(sumTypeHandling = SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField("kind"))

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Pet] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Pet].toBsonValue(Pet.Dog("rex")))
// {"name": "rex", "kind": "Dog"}
println(BsonDecoder[Pet].fromBsonValue(doc("kind" -> str("Cat"), "lives" -> int(9))))
// Right(Cat(9))
```

When the discriminator is given as an annotation with `bsonDiscriminator`, that annotation wins over the configuration for that sealed trait. See [Annotations](#annotations).

The decoder requires the discriminator to be present. If it is missing, decoding fails with `Missing disambiguator kind.`

### Extra Fields

With the default `allowExtraFields = true`, a document may contain fields the case class does not know, and they are skipped. Setting it to `false` makes decoding fail on any unknown field:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

def pointCodec(config: BsonCodecConfiguration): BsonCodec[Point] = {
  implicit val configuration: BsonCodecConfiguration = config
  DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

val strictPoint: BsonCodec[Point] =
  pointCodec(BsonCodecConfiguration(allowExtraFields = false))
```

```scala
println(strictPoint.decoder.fromBsonValue(doc("x" -> int(1), "y" -> int(2), "z" -> int(3))))
// Left(zio.bson.BsonDecoder$Error: Path: .z, error: Invalid extra field.. Don't use `decodeUnsafe` and `fromBsonValueUnsafe` methods.)
```

The error names the extra field, with the path to it. The `bsonNoExtraFields` annotation applies the same rule to one case class regardless of the configuration.

### Annotations

Annotations are classes in the `zio.bson` package. Import them with `import zio.bson._`, which is in the examples above.

| Annotation                | Target           | Effect                                                                                       |
| ------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `bsonField(name)`         | case class field | Uses `name` as the BSON key for this field, overriding `fieldNameMapping`.                   |
| `bsonDiscriminator(name)` | sealed trait     | Uses `name` as the discriminator field for this sealed trait, overriding `sumTypeHandling`. |
| `bsonHint(name)`          | subtype          | Uses `name` as the subtype's key or discriminator value, overriding `classNameMapping`.      |
| `bsonExclude`             | case class field | Leaves the field out when writing. See [Excluded Fields](#excluded-fields).                  |
| `bsonNoExtraFields`       | case class       | Rejects unknown fields when decoding this case class, even if `allowExtraFields` is `true`.  |

A field annotation and a subtype annotation work the same way as the configuration, but only for that one element. The next example renames a field and a subtype. It uses the default configuration, so the companion object's implicit codec is enough:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

sealed trait Fruit

object Fruit {
  final case class Banana(curvature: Double) extends Fruit

  @bsonHint("custom_type_name")
  final case class Apple(@bsonField("is_poisoned") poison: Boolean) extends Fruit

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Fruit] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Fruit].toBsonValue(Fruit.Apple(poison = true)))
// {"custom_type_name": {"is_poisoned": true}}
```

The output key is `custom_type_name`, and the field is `is_poisoned`. Neither depends on the configuration.

#### Excluded Fields

`bsonExclude` leaves a field out of the output when writing. The field's default value is used when reading, because the document does not contain it. A field marked `bsonExclude` without a default value cannot be decoded, because there is nothing to fall back to.

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Session(user: String, @bsonExclude attempts: Int = 0)

object Session {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Session] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Session].toBsonValue(Session("ada", 3)))
// {"user": "ada"}
println(BsonDecoder[Session].fromBsonValue(doc("user" -> str("ada"))))
// Right(Session(ada,0))
```

The decoder does not check the annotation. If a document does contain the excluded field, the decoder reads it. Only the writing side skips the field.

### Name Mappers

`BsonCodecConfiguration` provides five functions that convert a camel-case name. They can be used for `fieldNameMapping` or `classNameMapping`.

| Function               | Example input | Example output |
| ---------------------- | ------------- | -------------- |
| `toSnakeCase`          | `someField`   | `some_field`   |
| `toKebabCase`          | `someField`   | `some-field`   |
| `toScreamingSnakeCase` | `someField`   | `SOME_FIELD`   |
| `toUpperSnakeCase`     | `someField`   | `SOME_FIELD`   |
| `toUpperKebabCase`     | `someField`   | `SOME-FIELD`   |

`toUpperSnakeCase` is another name for `toScreamingSnakeCase`. Acronyms are split as well: `ABcDEFgHi` becomes `a_bc_de_fg_hi` under `toSnakeCase`.

### Scala 2 and Scala 3

The annotations and configuration are the same in both versions. The configuration is declared as an `implicit val` in Scala 2 and as a `given` in Scala 3. The derivation entry points also differ, as described in [Derivation](./bson-derivation.md).

### Related Pages

- [Derivation](./bson-derivation.md) describes the derivation entry points for Scala 2 and Scala 3.
- [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md) describes the value that derivation returns.
- [Use zio-bson with the MongoDB Driver](./how-to-use-with-mongodb-driver.md) shows derivation in an application.
- [Type Mappings](./types.md) lists the BSON type for each field type.

## BsonCodec

### Overview

`BsonCodec[A]` holds one `BsonEncoder[A]` and one `BsonDecoder[A]` together. Most user code needs only the codec: you define one in the companion object of a type, and the library finds it wherever an encoder or decoder for that type is needed.

Two things make a codec useful: it is what `DeriveBsonCodec.derive` produces for case classes and sealed traits, and it is what you write by hand when a type needs a custom format.

### Definition

`BsonCodec` is a case class with two fields and two transform methods:

```scala
final case class BsonCodec[A](encoder: BsonEncoder[A], decoder: BsonDecoder[A]) {
  def transform[B](to: A => B)(from: B => A): BsonCodec[B]
  def transformOrFail[B](to: A => Either[String, B])(from: B => A): BsonCodec[B]
}
```

`transform` builds a codec for a new type `B`. It takes two functions: `to` converts an `A` read from BSON into a `B`, and `from` converts a `B` into an `A` before writing. The `to` function runs after decoding and cannot fail. `transformOrFail` is the same, except that `to` returns `Either[String, B]`, so it can reject a value.

### Building a Codec from an Encoder and a Decoder

The companion object has an `apply` that takes an encoder and a decoder:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
```

```scala
val stringCodec: BsonCodec[String] = BsonCodec(BsonEncoder[String], BsonDecoder[String])
```

```scala
println(stringCodec.encoder.toBsonValue("hello"))
// BsonString{value='hello'}
```

You do not need this for the built-in types, because `BsonCodec` already has them in its companion object. Use the two-argument `apply` when you have an encoder and a decoder from separate sources.

### Summoning a Codec

`BsonCodec.apply` with a single implicit argument returns the codec in scope for a type. This is handy for checking which codec the compiler will use:

```scala
println(BsonCodec[Int].encoder.toBsonValue(5))
// BsonInt32{value=5}
```

### Transforming a Codec

`transform` reuses an existing codec for a new type. This example stores a `Username` as a plain string:

```scala
final case class Username(value: String)

val usernameCodec: BsonCodec[Username] =
  BsonCodec[String].transform(Username(_))(_.value)
```

The two functions run in opposite directions: the first builds a `Username` after reading, and the second unwraps it before writing.

```scala
println(usernameCodec.encoder.toBsonValue(Username("ada")))
// BsonString{value='ada'}
println(usernameCodec.decoder.fromBsonValue(str("ada")))
// Right(Username(ada))
```

### Transforming a Codec with Validation

`transformOrFail` is the variant to use when reading can fail. Here a `Port` must be between 1 and 65535:

```scala
final case class Port(number: Int)

val portCodec: BsonCodec[Port] =
  BsonCodec[Int].transformOrFail { n =>
    if (n >= 1 && n <= 65535) Right(Port(n))
    else Left(s"Port must be between 1 and 65535, but got $n.")
  }(_.number)
```

```scala
println(portCodec.decoder.fromBsonValue(int(8080)))
// Right(Port(8080))
println(portCodec.decoder.fromBsonValue(int(70000)).left.map(_.render))
// Left(: Port must be between 1 and 65535, but got 70000.)
```

The failure is returned as a `BsonDecoder.Error`, so the message is paired with the path at which the decoder ran.

### Codecs in Companion Objects

For a type you own, put its codec in the companion object as an `implicit val` (or `implicit lazy val`). The compiler then finds it without an import:

```scala
final case class Tag(name: String)

object Tag {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Tag] = BsonCodec[String].transform(Tag(_))(_.name)
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Tag].toBsonValue(Tag("scala")))
// BsonString{value='scala'}
```

For case classes and sealed traits, the codec usually comes from `DeriveBsonCodec.derive` instead. See [Use zio-bson with the MongoDB Driver](./how-to-use-with-mongodb-driver.md) for an example, and [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md) for the derivation options.

### Predefined Instances

The `BsonCodec` companion object has codecs for the same types as the encoder and decoder companions: primitives, the `java.time` types, `UUID`, `ObjectId`, `Currency`, `Option`, `Array`, `Iterable`, `Map`, `NonEmptyChunk`, and any `BsonValue` subtype. The exact list is in [BsonEncoder](./bson-encoder.md) and [Type Mappings](./types.md).

### Related Pages

- [BsonEncoder](./bson-encoder.md)
- [BsonDecoder](./bson-decoder.md)
- [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md)
- [Field Codecs](./bson-field-codecs.md) for map keys

## BsonDecoder

### Overview

`BsonDecoder[A]` is the typeclass that reads BSON and produces a Scala value of type `A`. Every decoding call either returns the value or a `BsonDecoder.Error` that says where in the document the problem is.

As with encoders, you usually get a decoder from a `BsonCodec`. This page covers the public methods, the error type, and the operations that build new decoders from existing ones.

### Definition

The trait has these members that users call:

```scala
trait BsonDecoder[A] {
  def decode(reader: BsonReader): Either[BsonDecoder.Error, A]
  def fromBsonValue(value: BsonValue): Either[BsonDecoder.Error, A]
  def map[B](f: A => B): BsonDecoder[B]
  def mapOrFail[B](f: A => Either[String, B]): BsonDecoder[B]
}
```

`decode` reads from a `BsonReader`, the streaming API used by the MongoDB driver. `fromBsonValue` reads from an in-memory `BsonValue`. Both return `Left` with a `BsonDecoder.Error` when the input does not match.

The members with `Unsafe` in their names, such as `decodeUnsafe` and `fromBsonValueUnsafe`, throw instead of returning `Left`. They exist for the derived decoders and for code that needs to avoid allocation. Use the safe methods in application code.

### Decoding a BsonValue

The syntax method `as` from the `zio.bson` package calls `fromBsonValue` and converts the error to a `String`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
```

To read an `Int` from a `BsonValue`:

```scala
println(int(42).as[Int])
// Right(42)
```

A `BsonDecoder` also accepts other numeric BSON types for the same Scala type. For example, a `DOUBLE` with no fractional part decodes to an `Int`:

```scala
println(double(7.0).as[Int])
// Right(7)
println(double(7.5).as[Int])
// Left(: Could not convert DOUBLE(7.5) to a Int without losing precision.)
```

The second line fails because `7.5` cannot be stored in an `Int` without losing precision. The full list of accepted BSON types for each Scala type is in [Type Mappings](./types.md).

### Decoding from a BsonReader

To decode directly from the driver's stream, call `decode` with a `BsonReader`. The example below reads the value of the `count` field from a `BsonDocumentReader`, which is a reader over an in-memory document. The reader must be positioned on the value, so the code first moves past the start of the document and the field name:

```scala
import org.bson.BsonDocumentReader

val reader = new BsonDocumentReader(doc("count" -> int(3)))
reader.readStartDocument()
reader.readName()
```

```scala
println(BsonDecoder[Int].decode(reader))
// Right(3)
```

For real code, the derived codec for a case class already calls `decode` for you when the MongoDB driver is configured. See [Use zio-bson with the MongoDB Driver](./how-to-use-with-mongodb-driver.md).

### Transforming Decoders

`map` changes the result type of a decoder. The function you pass runs after the original decoder and cannot fail:

```scala
final case class Celsius(degrees: Double)

val celsiusDecoder: BsonDecoder[Celsius] = BsonDecoder[Double].map(Celsius(_))
```

```scala
println(double(21.5).as(celsiusDecoder))
// Right(Celsius(21.5))
```

`mapOrFail` works the same way, but the function returns `Either[String, B]`. Use it when a value must pass a check, such as a range:

```scala
final case class Percent(value: Int)

val percentDecoder: BsonDecoder[Percent] =
  BsonDecoder[Int].mapOrFail { n =>
    if (n >= 0 && n <= 100) Right(Percent(n))
    else Left(s"Expected a percentage between 0 and 100, but got $n.")
  }
```

```scala
println(int(150).as(percentDecoder))
// Left(: Expected a percentage between 0 and 100, but got 150.)
```

When `mapOrFail` returns `Left`, the message becomes a `BsonDecoder.Error` at the current path, so the caller sees the field name as well.

For a full encoder and decoder pair, use `BsonCodec.transformOrFail`, described in [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md).

### Missing Fields

A decoder can say what happens when a field is absent from a document. The default is an error. `Option` overrides this and returns `None`. The derived case-class decoder calls this method for each field that is missing from the input. You can override `decodeMissingUnsafe` only when you write a decoder by hand.

### Errors

Every failure is a `BsonDecoder.Error`, a case class with two fields:

- `trace`: a list of `BsonTrace` steps that points from the root of the value to the failing part.
- `message`: a human-readable reason.

The `render` method combines both into one string. See [Errors and BsonTrace](./bson-errors.md) for the full format.

### Predefined Instances

The `BsonDecoder` companion object has a decoder for every type listed in [BsonEncoder](./bson-encoder.md), with the same set of accepted BSON types per type. Each one is documented in [Type Mappings](./types.md).

### Decoder Context and Helpers

You rarely need these directly; they matter when writing a decoder with `decodeUnsafe` and `fromBsonValueUnsafe` instead of wrapping an existing one with `BsonDecoder#map` or `BsonDecoder#mapOrFail`.

`BsonDecoder.BsonDecoderContext` carries the state that a decoder passes down to nested decoders. Its only field, `ignoreExtraField`, names one field that the enclosing derived decoder must not report as unexpected. Derived decoders use it to skip the discriminator field when `bsonNoExtraFields` is active. `BsonDecoder.BsonDecoderContext.default` is the empty context that `BsonDecoder#decode` and `BsonDecoder#fromBsonValue` start with:

```scala
object BsonDecoder {
  case class BsonDecoderContext(ignoreExtraField: Option[String] = None)
}
```

The `DecoderUtils` object in the `zio.bson` package has three helpers for failing with the right trace:

```scala
object DecoderUtils {
  def unsafeCall[R](trace: List[BsonTrace])(call: => R): R
  def throwInvalidType(trace: List[BsonTrace], expected: BsonType, actual: BsonType): Nothing
  def assumeType[T](trace: List[BsonTrace])(tpe: BsonType, value: BsonValue)(f: BsonValue => T): T
}
```

`DecoderUtils.unsafeCall` runs a reader call and turns a driver `BsonInvalidOperationException` or `IllegalStateException` into a `BsonDecoder.Error` with the given trace. `DecoderUtils.throwInvalidType` throws the `Expected BSON type X, but got Y.` error. `DecoderUtils.assumeType` checks the BSON type of a value before running a conversion.

### Related Pages

- [BsonEncoder](./bson-encoder.md) writes values.
- [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md) bundles an encoder and a decoder.
- [Errors and BsonTrace](./bson-errors.md) explains the error format.

## Derivation

The `zio-bson-magnolia` module derives encoders, decoders and codecs for case classes and sealed traits. It exposes three objects in the `zio.bson.magnolia` package: `DeriveBsonCodec`, `DeriveBsonEncoder` and `DeriveBsonDecoder`. Most programs only use `DeriveBsonCodec`. This page lists the entry points of each Scala version, because they differ.

### DeriveBsonCodec

`DeriveBsonCodec.derive` builds a `BsonCodec` from an encoder and a decoder derived for the same type. It is the entry point used throughout this documentation:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

object Point {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Point] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

The signature differs by Scala version. In Scala 2 it is a macro that reads the implicit `BsonCodecConfiguration` at the call site. In Scala 3 it requires a `Mirror.Of` instance and the configuration as a `using` parameter:

  

**Scala 2**

```scala
object DeriveBsonCodec {
  def derive[T]: BsonCodec[T] = macro genBoth[T]
}
```

  
  

**Scala 3**

```scala
object DeriveBsonCodec {
  inline def derive[T: Mirror.Of](using BsonCodecConfiguration): BsonCodec[T] = ???
}
```

  

### DeriveBsonEncoder and DeriveBsonDecoder

To derive only one direction, use `DeriveBsonEncoder` or `DeriveBsonDecoder`. The method name differs: Scala 2 uses `DeriveBsonEncoder.derive` and `DeriveBsonDecoder.derive`, and Scala 3 uses `DeriveBsonEncoder.derived` and `DeriveBsonDecoder.derived`.

  

**Scala 2**

```scala
case class Tag(name: String)

object Tag {
  implicit val encoder: BsonEncoder[Tag] = DeriveBsonEncoder.derive
  implicit val decoder: BsonDecoder[Tag] = DeriveBsonDecoder.derive
}
```

  
  

**Scala 3**

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

case class Tag(name: String)

object Tag {
  given BsonEncoder[Tag] = DeriveBsonEncoder.derived
  given BsonDecoder[Tag] = DeriveBsonDecoder.derived
}
```

  

The Scala 3 snippet is not compiled with the page, because the documentation is built with Scala 2.13.

### Extension Points

Both versions are built on [Magnolia](https://github.com/softwaremill/magnolia). Code that needs a custom derivation, for instance to change how a case class is written, can reuse the pieces.

In Scala 2, `DeriveBsonEncoder` and `DeriveBsonDecoder` are traits as well as objects. They declare `join` for case classes and `split` for sealed traits, each taking the implicit `BsonCodecConfiguration`, and the objects supply the `DeriveBsonEncoder.derive` and `DeriveBsonDecoder.derive` macros. In Scala 3, `DeriveBsonEncoder.Derive` and `DeriveBsonDecoder.Derive` are classes that take a `BsonCodecConfiguration` and extend Magnolia's `AutoDerivation`. The `DeriveBsonEncoder.Codec` and `DeriveBsonDecoder.Codec` objects have `join` and `split` methods that take the configuration as an explicit argument.

These are advanced APIs. To change the output of derived codecs, prefer the [annotations and configuration](./bson-codec-configuration.md).

### Related Pages

- [Configuration and Annotations](./bson-codec-configuration.md) lists every setting that derivation reads.
- [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md) describes the value that `DeriveBsonCodec.derive` returns.
- [Write a Codec by Hand](./how-to-write-a-codec-by-hand.md) shows the alternative to derivation.

## BsonEncoder

### Overview

`BsonEncoder[A]` is the typeclass that turns a Scala value of type `A` into BSON. ZIO Bson uses it everywhere a value is written, whether into a `BsonWriter` for the MongoDB driver or into an in-memory `BsonValue`.

You rarely write an encoder by hand. Most of the time you get one from a `BsonCodec` (see [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md)), either a built-in one or one derived with `DeriveBsonCodec.derive`. This page describes the methods every encoder has and the operations that build new encoders from existing ones.

### Definition

The trait has four members that matter to users:

```scala
trait BsonEncoder[A] {
  def encode(writer: BsonWriter, value: A, ctx: BsonEncoder.EncoderContext): Unit
  def toBsonValue(value: A): BsonValue
  def isAbsent(value: A): Boolean
  def contramap[B](f: B => A): BsonEncoder[B]
}
```

`encode` writes the value to a `BsonWriter`. `toBsonValue` builds a `BsonValue` directly. `isAbsent` tells the caller that a value can be left out of a document, and it returns `false` by default. `contramap` builds an encoder for a new type `B` by converting each `B` to an `A` first.

`EncoderContext` is a small case class with one flag, `inlineNextObject`. The derived encoders use it to avoid writing an extra document wrapper for a sum-type discriminator. `BsonEncoder.EncoderContext.default` has the flag off. It is the context to pass when calling `BsonEncoder#encode` directly, as the MongoDB driver integration does.

### Encoding a Value to a BsonValue

The syntax method `toBsonValue` from the `zio.bson` package calls the encoder for you. The encoder is found through implicit search:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
```

To convert a primitive value:

```scala
println(42.toBsonValue)
// BsonInt32{value=42}
println("zio".toBsonValue)
// BsonString{value='zio'}
```

To get the encoder itself, call `BsonEncoder.apply` with the type. This is useful when you want the encoder without the syntax:

```scala
val intEncoder: BsonEncoder[Int] = BsonEncoder[Int]
```

```scala
println(intEncoder.toBsonValue(7))
// BsonInt32{value=7}
```

### Building an Encoder with contramap

`contramap` lets you reuse an existing encoder for a type that wraps or converts to it. The function you pass runs before the original encoder, so the result is an encoder for the new type. For example, to encode a `Celsius` value as a plain `Double`:

```scala
final case class Celsius(degrees: Double)

val celsiusEncoder: BsonEncoder[Celsius] = BsonEncoder[Double].contramap(_.degrees)
```

Use it the same way as any other encoder:

```scala
println(celsiusEncoder.toBsonValue(Celsius(21.5)))
// BsonDouble{value=21.5}
```

For a full encoder and decoder pair, use `BsonCodec.transform`, described in [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md).

### Absent Values

An encoder reports absence through `isAbsent`. The derived case-class encoder checks it on each field. When `skipNullsInCaseClass` is `true` (the default), a field whose encoder says the value is absent is left out of the document entirely. Only `Option` says so today: `None` is absent, and `Some(x)` is not.

```scala
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Profile(name: String, nickname: Option[String])

object Profile {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Profile] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Profile].toBsonValue(Profile("ada", None)))
// {"name": "ada"}
```

With the default configuration, the `None` field is omitted from the document. See [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md) for how to change this.

### Predefined Instances

The `BsonEncoder` companion object has encoders for these types:

- `Boolean`, `String`, `Char`, `Symbol`, `UUID`, `org.bson.types.ObjectId`
- `Byte`, `Short`, `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `Double`
- `scala.math.BigDecimal`, `java.math.BigDecimal`, `scala.math.BigInt`, `java.math.BigInteger`
- `java.time` types: `Instant`, `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `LocalTime`, `OffsetDateTime`, `OffsetTime`, `ZonedDateTime`, `Duration`, `Period`, `Year`, `YearMonth`, `MonthDay`, `DayOfWeek`, `Month`, `ZoneId`, `ZoneOffset`
- `java.util.Currency`
- `Option[A]` when `A` has an encoder
- `Array[Byte]` and any `Iterable[Byte]` subtype, as `BINARY`
- `Array[A]`, `Iterable` subtypes, and `NonEmptyChunk[A]` for other `A`, as `ARRAY`
- `Map[K, V]` and other `Map` subtypes, when keys have a [BsonFieldEncoder](./bson-field-codecs.md)
- Any `T <: BsonValue`, passed through unchanged

The exact BSON type each one produces is listed in [Type Mappings](./types.md).

### Field Encoders

Map keys are strings in BSON, so an encoder for `Map[K, V]` also needs a `BsonFieldEncoder[K]`. See [Field Codecs](./bson-field-codecs.md).

### Related Pages

- [BsonDecoder](./bson-decoder.md) reads values back.
- [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md) bundles an encoder and a decoder.
- [Type Mappings](./types.md) lists the BSON type of each built-in encoder.

## Errors and BsonTrace

### Overview

When decoding fails, ZIO Bson reports the reason and the location of the failing value. The location is a path such as `.address.postalCode` or `.tags[2]`, built from `BsonTrace` steps. This page describes the error type, the path format, and the messages you can expect.

### BsonDecoder.Error

Every decoding failure is a `BsonDecoder.Error`, a case class with two fields:

```scala
case class Error(trace: List[BsonTrace], message: String) extends RuntimeException with NoStackTrace
```

`trace` lists the steps from the root to the failing value, with the most recent step first. `message` describes the problem. The `render` method joins both into one string in the form `<path>: <message>`. The exception message itself is different: it reads `Path: <path>, error: <message>` and ends with a hint not to use the `Unsafe` methods. The error has no stack trace.

`BsonDecoder#fromBsonValue` and `BsonDecoder#decode` return `Either[BsonDecoder.Error, A]`, so we can inspect the trace. The `as` syntax from the `zio.bson` package returns `Either[String, A]`, where the `String` is `render` applied to the error. The next example shows the rendered form, with a field name in the path:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Banana(curvature: Double)

object Banana {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Banana] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(doc("curvature" -> Array[Byte](1, 2, 3).toBsonValue).as[Banana])
// Left(.curvature: Expected BSON type Double, but got BINARY.)
```

The message says that the `Double` decoder received a `BINARY` value at the path `.curvature`.

Using `fromBsonValue` gives the structured error instead:

```scala
val document = doc("curvature" -> bool(true))
// document: org.bson.BsonDocument = {"curvature": true}
println(BsonDecoder[Banana].fromBsonValue(document).left.map(_.trace))
// Left(List(Field(curvature)))
```

### BsonTrace

`BsonTrace` is a sealed trait with two cases:

- `BsonTrace.Field(name)` stands for a field of a document. It renders as `.name`.
- `BsonTrace.Array(idx)` stands for an element of an array, counting from zero. It renders as `[idx]`.

`BsonTrace.render` turns a list of steps into the path string:

```scala
val steps: List[BsonTrace] = List(BsonTrace.Array(2), BsonTrace.Field("tags"))
```

```scala
println(BsonTrace.render(steps))
// .tags[2]
```

The list is stored with the most recent step first, which is why `render` reverses it before printing. Here `Field("tags")` is the outer step and `Array(2)` is the element inside it, so the path reads `.tags[2]`.

An array element error shows the index in the path:

```scala
println(array(int(1), bool(true)).as[List[Int]])
// Left([1]: Expected BSON type Int, but got BOOLEAN.)
```

### Common Messages

The table lists the messages most often seen, with the decoder that produces them.

| Message                                                    | Produced by                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `Expected BSON type <Type>, but got <BSON type>.`          | Any decoder that receives the wrong BSON type |
| `missing`                                                  | A required field that is absent               |
| `Invalid extra field.`                                     | A case class with unknown fields and extra fields disallowed |
| `Missing disambiguator <name>.`                            | A sealed trait with a missing discriminator   |
| `Invalid disambiguator <name>.`                            | A sealed trait with an unknown subtype name   |
| `Could not convert <BSON type>(<value>) to a <Type> without losing precision.` | A numeric value that does not fit the target type |
| `Expected one character, but got a string of length <n>.`  | `Char` decoder                                |
| `Invalid UUID: <reason>`                                   | `UUID` decoder                                |

The `missing` message comes from a field that is not present and has no default value. The example below derives a codec for a case class and omits the `y` field:

```scala
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

object Point {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Point] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(doc("x" -> int(1)).as[Point])
// Left(.y: missing)
```

The path `.y` names the missing field. Derivation is described in [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md).

### Reading an Error in Code

Use the `trace` and `message` fields when you need to act on the failing location, such as logging the path with the reason:

```scala
val result = BsonDecoder[Int].fromBsonValue(bool(false))
// result: Either[BsonDecoder.Error, Int] = Left(
//   value = Error(
//     trace = List(),
//     message = "Expected BSON type Int, but got BOOLEAN."
//   )
// )

result match {
  case Left(err) => println(s"path=${BsonTrace.render(err.trace)} message=${err.message}")
  case Right(v)  => println(v)
}
// path= message=Expected BSON type Int, but got BOOLEAN.
```

### Related Pages

- [BsonDecoder](./bson-decoder.md) describes the methods that return these errors.
- [Type Mappings](./types.md) lists the BSON types each decoder accepts.

## Field Codecs

### Overview

A BSON document has string keys only. When a Scala `Map` has keys of another type, such as `Int`, ZIO Bson needs a way to turn each key into a string and back. Two typeclasses do this: `BsonFieldEncoder[A]` turns a key into a string, and `BsonFieldDecoder[A]` turns a string into a key.

You need these only for `Map` keys. Ordinary fields use `BsonEncoder` and `BsonDecoder`.

### Definition

```scala
trait BsonFieldEncoder[-A] {
  def unsafeEncodeField(in: A): String
  def contramap[B](f: B => A): BsonFieldEncoder[B]
}

trait BsonFieldDecoder[+A] {
  def unsafeDecodeField(trace: List[BsonTrace], in: String): A
  def map[B](f: A => B): BsonFieldDecoder[B]
  def mapOrFail[B](f: A => Either[String, B]): BsonFieldDecoder[B]
}
```

The `unsafe` methods throw on failure, which is how the `Map` codecs use them. `contramap` and `map` build new instances from existing ones in the same way as `BsonEncoder` and `BsonDecoder`.

### Predefined Instances

ZIO Bson provides field codecs for three key types:

- `String`: the key is used as is.
- `Int`: the key is written with `toString` and read with `toInt`.
- `Long`: the key is written with `toString` and read with `toLong`.

A `Map[K, V]` encoder and decoder require both a field codec for `K` and a value codec for `V`. The keys in the output are the string forms of the keys:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Map[Int, String]].toBsonValue(Map(1 -> "one", 2 -> "two")))
// {"1": "one", "2": "two"}
```

Reading the document back gives the original keys:

```scala
println(BsonDecoder[Map[Int, String]].fromBsonValue(doc("1" -> str("one"), "2" -> str("two"))))
// Right(Map(1 -> one, 2 -> two))
```

A key that is not a number fails with the field's path:

```scala
println(BsonDecoder[Map[Int, String]].fromBsonValue(doc("one" -> str("x"))))
// Left(zio.bson.BsonDecoder$Error: Path: .one, error: Invalid Int: 'one': java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "one". Don't use `decodeUnsafe` and `fromBsonValueUnsafe` methods.)
```

### Custom Key Types

For another key type, build a field encoder and decoder from the `String` instances with `contramap` and `mapOrFail`. The next example uses a `Status` key that is stored by its lowercase name:

```scala
sealed trait Status
object Status {
  case object Active   extends Status
  case object Inactive extends Status
}

implicit val statusFieldEncoder: BsonFieldEncoder[Status] =
  BsonFieldEncoder[String].contramap {
    case Status.Active   => "active"
    case Status.Inactive => "inactive"
  }

implicit val statusFieldDecoder: BsonFieldDecoder[Status] =
  BsonFieldDecoder[String].mapOrFail {
    case "active"   => Right(Status.Active)
    case "inactive" => Right(Status.Inactive)
    case other      => Left(s"Unknown status: $other")
  }
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Map[Status, Int]].toBsonValue(Map(Status.Active -> 3)))
// {"active": 3}
```

The `Map` codec then works for `Map[Status, Int]` with no extra code.

### Related Pages

- [BsonEncoder](./bson-encoder.md) describes the encoder for the values of the map.
- [BsonDecoder](./bson-decoder.md) describes the decoder for the values of the map.
- [Type Mappings](./types.md) lists the BSON type of a `Map`.

## Getting Started with ZIO BSON

This page walks through the first program: declare a codec for a case class, convert values to and from `BsonValue`, and plug the codec into the MongoDB driver. To add the dependencies, see [Installation](./index.md#installation).

All the following code snippets assume that these imports have been declared:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
```

### Declaring Codecs

To get a codec for a case class or a sealed trait, derive it with `DeriveBsonCodec.derive`:

```scala
import zio.bson.magnolia._

case class Banana(curvature: Double)

object Banana {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Banana] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

### Converting to BsonValue

To use values in `Filter` or `Update` expressions, convert them to `BsonValue` with `toBsonValue`:

```scala
"str".toBsonValue

Banana(0.2).toBsonValue

import org.bson._

def method[T: BsonEncoder](value: T): BsonDocument = doc("key" -> value.toBsonValue)
```

### Creating a CodecProvider

To get a `CodecProvider` for a `BsonCodec`, use `zioBsonCodecProvider`:

```scala
val codecProvider = zioBsonCodecProvider[Banana]
```

### Parsing a BsonValue

In general, a `CodecProvider` parses a case class without an intermediate `BsonValue`. A `BsonValue` can still be parsed with `as`:

```scala
import org.bson._

val bsonVal: BsonValue = doc("curvature" -> double(0.2))
// bsonVal: BsonValue = {"curvature": 0.2}

bsonVal.as[Banana]
// res2: Either[String, Banana] = Right(value = Banana(curvature = 0.2))
```

### Errors

Bad BSON produces an error with the path and contextual information. To see one, decode a `BINARY` value where a `Double` is expected:

```scala
doc("curvature" -> Array[Byte](1, 2, 3).toBsonValue).as[Banana]
// res3: Either[String, Banana] = Left(
//   value = ".curvature: Expected BSON type Double, but got BINARY."
// )
```

### Configuration

To configure derivation, use annotations. A sealed trait is encoded as a document with one key per subtype by default, and the annotations rename the discriminator, the subtype and the field:

```scala
sealed trait Fruit

object Fruit {
  case class Pear(curvature: Double) extends Fruit
  case class Apple(poison: Boolean)  extends Fruit

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Fruit] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

@bsonDiscriminator("$type")
sealed trait FruitConfigured

object FruitConfigured {
  case class Pear(curvature: Double) extends FruitConfigured

  @bsonHint("custom_type_name")
  case class Apple(@bsonField("is_poisoned") poison: Boolean) extends FruitConfigured

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[FruitConfigured] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

Next, decode a document written in the default shape and one written in the configured shape:

```scala
doc("Pear" -> doc("curvature" -> double(0.5))).as[Fruit]
// res4: Either[String, Fruit] = Right(value = Pear(curvature = 0.5))

doc("$type" -> str("custom_type_name"), "is_poisoned" -> bool(true)).as[FruitConfigured]
// res5: Either[String, FruitConfigured] = Right(value = Apple(poison = true))
```

### Next Steps

See [Type Mappings](./types.md) for the supported Scala and Java types, [Configuration and Annotations](./bson-codec-configuration.md) for every setting, and the [tutorial](./tutorial-store-and-load.md) for a complete program.

## Customize Field Names and Discriminators

### Problem

Your BSON documents have a naming scheme that differs from Scala's, such as `snake_case` keys for a camel-case case class. Or you need to read a sealed trait that another system writes with a `kind` field, or with a type name you do not control. This guide shows how to change those names without changing the case classes.

### Rename One Field

To change the BSON key of a single field, put `bsonField` on the field. The annotation overrides every other naming rule for that field:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Order(orderId: String, @bsonField("total_cents") total: Long)

object Order {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Order] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Order].toBsonValue(Order("A-1", 1250L)))
// {"orderId": "A-1", "total_cents": 1250}
```

The key `orderId` keeps its name, because only `total` has an annotation.

### Rename All Fields

To change every field name in a type at once, set `fieldNameMapping` in a configuration. The next example writes `orderId` as `order_id` and reads it back:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration.toSnakeCase

final case class Order(orderId: String, customerName: String)

def orderCodec(config: BsonCodecConfiguration): BsonCodec[Order] = {
  implicit val configuration: BsonCodecConfiguration = config
  DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

val snakeOrder: BsonCodec[Order] =
  orderCodec(BsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = toSnakeCase))
```

```scala
println(snakeOrder.encoder.toBsonValue(Order("A-1", "Ada")))
// {"order_id": "A-1", "customer_name": "Ada"}
println(snakeOrder.decoder.fromBsonValue(doc("order_id" -> str("A-2"), "customer_name" -> str("Grace"))))
// Right(Order(A-2,Grace))
```

The mapping runs on each field name, so an annotation on a single field still wins over it. Other mapping functions are listed in [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md#name-mappers).

### Choose the Discriminator Field for a Sealed Trait

A sealed trait is written as a wrapper by default: the subtype name is the only key. To write the subtype name as a field in the same document, set `sumTypeHandling` to `DiscriminatorField`. The next example uses the field name `kind`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration.SumTypeHandling

sealed trait Payment

object Payment {
  final case class Card(last4: String)    extends Payment
  final case class Transfer(iban: String) extends Payment

  implicit val config: BsonCodecConfiguration =
    BsonCodecConfiguration(sumTypeHandling = SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField("kind"))

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Payment] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Payment].toBsonValue(Payment.Card("4242")))
// {"last4": "4242", "kind": "Card"}
println(BsonDecoder[Payment].fromBsonValue(doc("kind" -> str("Transfer"), "iban" -> str("DE00"))))
// Right(Transfer(DE00))
```

### Rename a Subtype

The discriminator value is the subtype's class name, unless you change it. `bsonHint` sets a different name for one subtype. The next example writes the `Transfer` subtype as `bank_transfer`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._
import zio.bson.magnolia.BsonCodecConfiguration.SumTypeHandling

@bsonDiscriminator("type")
sealed trait Event

object Event {
  final case class Login(user: String) extends Event

  @bsonHint("bank_transfer")
  final case class Transfer(amount: Long) extends Event

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Event] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Event].toBsonValue(Event.Transfer(500L)))
// {"amount": 500, "type": "bank_transfer"}
println(BsonDecoder[Event].fromBsonValue(doc("type" -> str("Login"), "user" -> str("ada"))))
// Right(Login(ada))
```

The `@bsonDiscriminator` annotation on the trait sets the field name to `type`. It overrides `sumTypeHandling` for this trait only.

### Related Pages

- [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md) lists every option and annotation.
- [Use zio-bson with the MongoDB Driver](./how-to-use-with-mongodb-driver.md) shows how a derived codec is used with a database.

## Handle Optional Fields and Default Values

### Problem

Documents in a collection are rarely uniform: older documents lack newer fields, and some fields are only set sometimes. This guide shows how to read and write such documents with `Option` fields, default values and the `skipNullsInCaseClass` setting.

### Use Option for Fields That May Be Missing

A field of type `Option[A]` decodes to `None` when the key is missing or the value is `NULL`. When encoding, `None` is left out of the document, because `skipNullsInCaseClass` is `true` by default:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class User(name: String, nickname: Option[String])

object User {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[User] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

To see what `User` writes and reads, encode a user without a nickname, then decode documents with the key missing and with `NULL`:

```scala
println(User("Ada", None).toBsonValue)
// {"name": "Ada"}
println(doc("name" -> str("Ada")).as[User])
// Right(User(Ada,None))
println(doc("name" -> str("Ada"), "nickname" -> bNull).as[User])
// Right(User(Ada,None))
```

### Use a Default Value for Documents Written Before a Field Existed

When a case class field has a default value and the key is missing, the decoder uses the default instead of failing. This lets us add a field without migrating old documents:

```scala
final case class Settings(theme: String, pageSize: Int = 20)

object Settings {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Settings] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

To decode a document written before `pageSize` existed:

```scala
doc("theme" -> str("dark")).as[Settings]
// res3: Either[String, Settings] = Right(
//   value = Settings(theme = "dark", pageSize = 20)
// )
```

A field without a default and without an `Option` type is required. Its absence is an error with the path of the field:

```scala
doc("pageSize" -> int(50)).as[Settings]
// res4: Either[String, Settings] = Left(value = ".theme: missing")
```

### Write Explicit Nulls

Some consumers expect every key to be present. To write `None` as `NULL` instead of leaving the key out, set `skipNullsInCaseClass` to `false` in the [configuration](./bson-codec-configuration.md):

```scala
final case class Profile(name: String, bio: Option[String])

object Profile {
  implicit val config: BsonCodecConfiguration =
    BsonCodecConfiguration(skipNullsInCaseClass = false)

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Profile] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

With the setting turned off, `None` is written as `NULL`:

```scala
println(Profile("Ada", None).toBsonValue)
// {"name": "Ada", "bio": null}
```

### Related Pages

- [Configuration and Annotations](./bson-codec-configuration.md) lists every setting of the derivation.
- [Type Mappings](./types.md) describes how `Option` maps to BSON.

## Store Dates, Times and Decimal Numbers

### Problem

MongoDB has a date type with millisecond precision and a decimal type with a fixed number of digits. Java's time classes and Scala's big numbers carry more information than that. This guide shows what each type becomes in BSON, so we can choose the right Scala type for a field.

### Know What Each Date Type Stores

`Instant`, `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime` and `LocalTime` are written as a BSON `DATE_TIME`, which counts milliseconds, and the value is interpreted in UTC. Any precision below a millisecond is lost when encoding:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import java.time.Instant

val precise = Instant.parse("2026-01-01T10:00:00.123456789Z")
// precise: Instant = 2026-01-01T10:00:00.123456789Z

val stored = precise.toBsonValue
// stored: org.bson.BsonValue = BsonDateTime{value=1767261600123}

stored.as[Instant]
// res0: Either[String, Instant] = Right(value = 2026-01-01T10:00:00.123Z)
```

If the sub-millisecond part matters, store the value as an ISO string instead, by wrapping a `String` codec as shown in [Write a Codec by Hand](./how-to-write-a-codec-by-hand.md).

### Keep the Zone with OffsetDateTime and ZonedDateTime

A `DATE_TIME` has no zone. When we need the offset or the zone id back, we use `OffsetDateTime` or `ZonedDateTime`. They are written as a document with the date and the offset or zone, as listed in [Type Mappings](./types.md):

```scala
import java.time.{OffsetDateTime, ZoneOffset}

val local = OffsetDateTime.of(2026, 1, 1, 10, 0, 0, 0, ZoneOffset.ofHours(3))
// local: OffsetDateTime = 2026-01-01T10:00+03:00

val bson = local.toBsonValue
// bson: org.bson.BsonValue = {"date_time": {"$date": "2026-01-01T07:00:00Z"}, "offset": "+03:00"}

println(bson)
// {"date_time": {"$date": "2026-01-01T07:00:00Z"}, "offset": "+03:00"}
bson.as[OffsetDateTime]
// res2: Either[String, OffsetDateTime] = Right(value = 2026-01-01T10:00+03:00)
```

### Choose Between Decimal and String for Big Numbers

`BigDecimal` and `java.math.BigDecimal` are written as `DECIMAL128`, which keeps up to 34 significant digits and supports range queries and arithmetic in the database. `BigInt` and `java.math.BigInteger` are written as `STRING`, so any size fits, but the database cannot compare them as numbers:

```scala
println(BigDecimal("12.50").toBsonValue)
// BsonDecimal128{value=12.50}
println(BigInt("123456789012345678901234567890").toBsonValue)
// BsonString{value='123456789012345678901234567890'}
```

Use `BigDecimal` for money and measurements that the database must filter or sort, and `BigInt` for large identifiers that are only stored and loaded.

### Related Pages

- [Type Mappings](./types.md) lists the BSON type and the decoder fallbacks of every supported type.
- [BsonBuilder](./bson-builder.md) has `BsonBuilder.date` for building a date value by hand.

## Use zio-bson with the MongoDB Driver

### Problem

The MongoDB Java driver, which the Scala driver also uses, converts Scala and Java objects to and from BSON through a `CodecRegistry`. A registry is a list of `CodecProvider`s. Each provider says whether it can convert a given class. You want the driver to use your zio-bson codecs for your own types, so that `insertOne` and `find` work on case classes without any extra mapping.

### Create a CodecProvider

`zioBsonCodecProvider` returns a `CodecProvider` for one type. It uses the codec in scope for that type, which is usually the one from `DeriveBsonCodec.derive`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Order(orderId: String, totalCents: Long)

object Order {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Order] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

val orderProvider = zioBsonCodecProvider[Order]
```

The provider is a plain value, so it can be listed with other providers when you build a registry.

### Build a Registry

A registry combines providers. The `bson` library's `CodecRegistries` builds one from a list, and `Bson.DEFAULT_CODEC_REGISTRY` already knows the standard types, such as `String` and `BsonDocument`. Put the zio-bson provider first, so it is checked before the defaults:

```scala
import org.bson.codecs.configuration.CodecRegistries
import org.bson.conversions.Bson

val registry = CodecRegistries.fromRegistries(
  CodecRegistries.fromProviders(orderProvider),
  Bson.DEFAULT_CODEC_REGISTRY
)
```

The MongoDB driver takes this kind of registry in its client settings. With the synchronous driver, the setup looks like this:

```scala
val settings = MongoClientSettings.builder()
  .applyConnectionString(new ConnectionString("mongodb://localhost:27017"))
  .codecRegistry(registry)
  .build()

val client     = MongoClients.create(settings)
val collection = client.getDatabase("shop").getCollection("orders", classOf[Order])

collection.insertOne(Order("A-1", 1250L))
```

The driver calls the codec for `Order`, which is the zio-bson codec. That snippet needs a running MongoDB server and the driver library, which this documentation build does not include, so it is shown as plain text. The rest of this guide runs without a server, using the same registry the driver uses.

### Encode and Decode Through the Registry

To check the registry, look up the codec for `Order` and write a value with it. The `BsonDocumentWriter` writes into an in-memory `BsonDocument`, which is the same kind of object the driver sends to the server:

```scala
import org.bson.{BsonDocument, BsonDocumentWriter}
import org.bson.codecs.EncoderContext

val orderCodec = registry.get(classOf[Order])
```

```scala
val stored = new BsonDocument()
// stored: BsonDocument = {"orderId": "A-1", "totalCents": 1250}
orderCodec.encode(new BsonDocumentWriter(stored), Order("A-1", 1250L), EncoderContext.builder().build())
println(stored)
// {"orderId": "A-1", "totalCents": 1250}
```

The reverse direction reads the document back into an `Order`:

```scala
import org.bson.BsonDocumentReader
import org.bson.codecs.DecoderContext

val loaded = orderCodec.decode(new BsonDocumentReader(stored), DecoderContext.builder().build())
// loaded: Order = Order(orderId = "A-1", totalCents = 1250L)
println(loaded)
// Order(A-1,1250)
```

### Check the Type You Asked For

The provider matches the class it was built for, and classes that extend it. Any other class returns `null` from the registry, so the driver falls back to its own codecs for those types. This is why the zio-bson provider goes first in the list. A type that has no provider and no default codec fails at lookup, so give every type you store a provider.

### Related Pages

- [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md) describes the codec that the provider wraps.
- [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md) controls how the derived codec writes fields.
- [Tutorial: Store and Load a Case Class with MongoDB](./tutorial-store-and-load.md) puts these steps in order.

## Write a Codec by Hand

### Problem

Derivation works for case classes whose BSON form matches their Scala shape. Some types need a different form: a value stored as one string, a number that must be checked, or a class you do not own, such as one from a library. This guide shows three ways to write a codec for those cases, from the simplest to the most work.

### Wrap an Existing Codec

If the BSON form of your type is the same as a type you already have a codec for, reuse that codec with `transform`. Use `transformOrFail` when reading can fail. This example stores an email address as a string and rejects values without an `@`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._

final case class Email(value: String)

object Email {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Email] =
    BsonCodec[String].transformOrFail[Email] { s =>
      if (s.contains("@")) Right(Email(s))
      else Left(s"Expected an email address, but got '$s'.")
    }(_.value)
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Email].toBsonValue(Email("ada@example.com")))
// BsonString{value='ada@example.com'}
println(doc("contact" -> str("not-an-email")).as[Map[String, Email]])
// Left(.contact: Expected an email address, but got 'not-an-email'.)
```

The `Left` message becomes the error for the field, so the path `.contact` appears when the value sits in a document.

### Store a Type as a Different BSON Form

Some types have a natural string form that differs from the default. This example stores `Money` as a single string such as `"12.50 USD"`. The encode side builds the string, and the decode side parses it. `scala.util.Try` turns a bad number into a `Left`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import scala.util.Try

final case class Money(amount: BigDecimal, currency: String)

object Money {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Money] =
    BsonCodec[String].transformOrFail[Money] { s =>
      s.split(" ").toList match {
        case amount :: currency :: Nil =>
          Try(Money(BigDecimal(amount), currency)).toEither.left.map(_.getMessage)
        case _                         =>
          Left(s"Expected '<amount> <currency>', but got '$s'.")
      }
    }(m => s"${m.amount} ${m.currency}")
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Money].toBsonValue(Money(BigDecimal("12.50"), "USD")))
// BsonString{value='12.50 USD'}
println(BsonDecoder[Money].fromBsonValue(str("3 EUR")))
// Right(Money(3,EUR))
println(BsonDecoder[Money].fromBsonValue(str("twelve EUR")).left.map(_.render))
// Left(: Character t is neither a decimal digit number, decimal point, nor "e" notation exponential mark.)
```

### Implement an Encoder and Decoder Directly

When there is no existing codec to reuse, implement `BsonEncoder` and `BsonDecoder` yourself. An encoder needs two methods: `encode`, which writes to a `BsonWriter`, and `toBsonValue`, which builds a `BsonValue`. The example below stores a `Celsius` temperature as a `DOUBLE`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import org.bson.{BsonDouble, BsonValue, BsonWriter}

final case class Celsius(degrees: Double)

object Celsius {
  implicit val encoder: BsonEncoder[Celsius] = new BsonEncoder[Celsius] {
    def encode(writer: BsonWriter, value: Celsius, ctx: BsonEncoder.EncoderContext): Unit =
      writer.writeDouble(value.degrees)

    def toBsonValue(value: Celsius): BsonValue =
      new BsonDouble(value.degrees)
  }

  implicit val decoder: BsonDecoder[Celsius] =
    BsonDecoder[Double].mapOrFail { d =>
      if (d >= -273.15) Right(Celsius(d))
      else Left(s"Temperature $d is below absolute zero.")
    }
}
```

```scala
println(BsonEncoder[Celsius].toBsonValue(Celsius(21.5)))
// BsonDouble{value=21.5}
println(BsonDecoder[Celsius].fromBsonValue(double(-300.0)).left.map(_.render))
// Left(: Temperature -300.0 is below absolute zero.)
```

The decoder is built from `BsonDecoder[Double]` with `mapOrFail`, rather than written from scratch. This keeps the BSON type checks of the built-in decoder, so an `Int` or `Long` value is also accepted.

### Use the Codec

A hand-written codec is found the same way as a derived one. Put it in the companion object as an `implicit val`, and any code that needs `BsonEncoder[Celsius]` or `BsonDecoder[Celsius]` finds it.

To check that the codec works with the MongoDB driver, see [Use zio-bson with the MongoDB Driver](./how-to-use-with-mongodb-driver.md).

### Related Pages

- [BsonCodec](./bson-codec.md) describes `transform` and `transformOrFail` in full.
- [BsonEncoder](./bson-encoder.md) and [BsonDecoder](./bson-decoder.md) describe the methods used above.
- [Errors and BsonTrace](./bson-errors.md) explains the messages returned by `mapOrFail` and `transformOrFail`.

## Introduction to ZIO BSON

[ZIO BSON](https://github.com/zio/zio-bson) is a BSON library for Scala that plugs into the MongoDB Java driver.

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-bson/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-bson_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-bson_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-bson_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-bson_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-bson_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-bson_2.13) [![ZIO Bson](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-bson?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-bson)

### Introduction

The goal of this project is to create the best all-round BSON library for Scala:

- **Native BSON support** to avoid intermediate JSON conversions and support BSON types.
- **Future-proof**, prepared for Scala 3 and next-generation Java.
- **Simple**, with a small codebase and concise documentation that covers everything.
- **Helpful errors** that are readable by humans and machines.
- **ZIO types** such as `Chunk` and `NonEmptyChunk` have codecs out of the box.

### Installation

To use ZIO BSON, add the following to the `build.sbt` file. The core module is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3, and the derivation module for Scala 2.13 and 3:

```sbt
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Encoders, decoders, codecs and syntax (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-bson"          % "1.0.12",

  // Automatic derivation of codecs for case classes and sealed traits (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-bson-magnolia" % "1.0.12"
)
```

If we only write codecs by hand, `zio-bson` is enough.

### Modules

The `zio-schema-bson` module of the [zio-schema](https://github.com/zio/zio-schema/) project derives BSON codecs from a `Schema`. It is published by that project, not by this one, and it depends on `zio-bson`, so the types stay the same.

### Example

To get a codec for a case class, derive it with `DeriveBsonCodec.derive`, then convert values to and from `BsonValue`:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

case class Banana(curvature: Double)

object Banana {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Banana] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

val bson = Banana(0.2).toBsonValue

bson.as[Banana]
```

### Where to Go Next

- [Getting Started](./getting-started.md) walks through codecs, `BsonValue` conversion, the MongoDB driver and errors.
- [Reference](./bson-encoder.md) pages describe the public types, the [type mappings](./types.md) and the [errors](./bson-errors.md).
- [Tutorial: Store and Load a Case Class with MongoDB](./tutorial-store-and-load.md) builds a complete program.
- [How-to guides](./how-to-use-with-mongodb-driver.md) answer one task each, such as renaming fields or writing a codec by hand.

Release notes are on the [releases page](https://github.com/zio/zio-bson/releases).

### Related Projects

- [MongoDB Java driver](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/java/sync/current/) provides `BsonValue`, `BsonReader`, `BsonWriter` and the `CodecProvider` that ZIO BSON plugs into.
- [zio-schema](https://github.com/zio/zio-schema/) provides the `zio-schema-bson` module, which derives BSON codecs from a `Schema`.
- [Magnolia](https://github.com/softwaremill/magnolia) is the derivation library that `zio-bson-magnolia` is built on.

### Community

Questions about ZIO BSON are welcome on the [ZIO Discord](https://discord.gg/2ccFBr4) in the ecosystem channels.
