## Tutorial: Model a Domain with Sealed Traits

In this tutorial, we will model a small payment domain with a sealed trait, derive a codec for it, and look at the BSON that each case produces. Then we will read documents back, including a bad one, and change the encoding with a discriminator field.

By the end of this tutorial, you will know how a sealed trait becomes a BSON document, how to read it back, and how to control the shape of the result. You do not need a MongoDB server. If you have not derived a codec before, start with [Store and Load a Case Class](./tutorial-store-and-load.md).

### Step 1: Define the Domain

A payment is either a card payment or a bank transfer. We model it as a sealed trait with one case class per kind, and we derive the codec in the companion object of the trait:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

sealed trait Payment

object Payment {
  final case class Card(last4: String, cents: Long) extends Payment
  final case class Transfer(iban: String)           extends Payment

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Payment] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

### Step 2: Encode Each Case

To see what the database would store, we convert two payments with `toBsonValue`:

```scala
val card: Payment     = Payment.Card("4242", 1999L)
// card: Payment = Card(last4 = "4242", cents = 1999L)
val transfer: Payment = Payment.Transfer("DE89370400440532013000")
// transfer: Payment = Transfer(iban = "DE89370400440532013000")

println(card.toBsonValue)
// {"Card": {"last4": "4242", "cents": 1999}}
println(transfer.toBsonValue)
// {"Transfer": {"iban": "DE89370400440532013000"}}
```

By default, each document has a single key, the name of the case class, and the value holds its fields. This is the `WrapperWithClassNameField` encoding.

### Step 3: Decode a Document

To read a document back, we use `as` with the type of the trait. The decoder picks the case class from the key:

```scala
doc("Transfer" -> doc("iban" -> str("NL91ABNA0417164300"))).as[Payment]
// res2: Either[String, Payment] = Right(
//   value = Transfer(iban = "NL91ABNA0417164300")
// )
```

Next, we try a document whose key names no case class of the trait:

```scala
doc("Cash" -> doc("amount" -> int(5))).as[Payment]
// res3: Either[String, Payment] = Left(
//   value = ".Cash: Invalid disambiguator Cash."
// )
```

The error says which key is not a known case, so a typo in stored data is easy to find.

### Step 4: Use a Discriminator Field

Many applications keep the case name inside the document as a field instead. To do that, we annotate the sealed trait with `bsonDiscriminator`:

```scala
@bsonDiscriminator("type")
sealed trait Refund

object Refund {
  final case class Full(orderId: String)                  extends Refund
  final case class Partial(orderId: String, cents: Long)  extends Refund

  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Refund] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

The case class fields and the `type` field now share one document:

```scala
val refund: Refund = Refund.Partial("o-1", 250L)
// refund: Refund = Partial(orderId = "o-1", cents = 250L)

println(refund.toBsonValue)
// {"orderId": "o-1", "cents": 250, "type": "Partial"}

println(refund.toBsonValue.as[Refund])
// Right(Partial(o-1,250))
```

### What We Learned

A sealed trait is encoded with one document per value, either keyed by the case name or tagged with a discriminator field. Decoding mirrors encoding, and a document that matches no case produces an error. To rename cases and fields, or to change the encoding for the whole codebase, see [Customize Field Names and Discriminators](./how-to-customize-field-names-and-discriminators.md) and [Configuration and Annotations](./bson-codec-configuration.md).

---

## Tutorial: Store and Load a Case Class with MongoDB

### What You Will Build

In this tutorial, we will define a case class, derive a BSON codec for it, and see the exact document that MongoDB would store. Then we will load that document back into a Scala value. At the end, we will connect the codec to the MongoDB driver.

By the end of this tutorial, you will know how to derive a codec for your own types, how the fields of a case class become BSON keys, and how to check that a stored document reads back correctly. You do not need a MongoDB server to follow the steps. The driver step is shown as text, because it needs a running server.

### Step 1: Add the Dependencies

Add the two zio-bson modules to your `build.sbt` file. `zio-bson` holds the encoders, decoders and codecs. `zio-bson-magnolia` derives codecs for case classes automatically:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-bson" % "1.0.12"
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-bson-magnolia" % "1.0.12"
```

The MongoDB driver is a separate library. You add it when you connect to a server, in Step 6.

### Step 2: Define a Case Class and Its Codec

We will store books. Each book has a title, a page count, and an optional subtitle. We need imports for the zio-bson types, the BSON document builders, and the derivation module:

```scala
import zio.bson._
import zio.bson.BsonBuilder._
import zio.bson.magnolia._

final case class Book(title: String, pages: Int, subtitle: Option[String])
```

To derive the codec, we put a `DeriveBsonCodec.derive` call in the companion object of `Book`. The compiler finds this codec wherever a `BsonEncoder[Book]` or `BsonDecoder[Book]` is needed:

```scala
object Book {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Book] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}
```

`DeriveBsonCodec.derive` reads the fields of `Book` and builds the encoder and decoder from them. We did not write any mapping code, and we will see the result in the next step.

### Step 3: Encode a Book to a BSON Document

When the driver stores a value, it first converts the value to BSON. We can do the same conversion ourselves with `toBsonValue`. We will create a book without a subtitle:

```scala
val dune = Book("Dune", 412, None)
// dune: Book = Book(title = "Dune", pages = 412, subtitle = None)

println(dune.toBsonValue)
// {"title": "Dune", "pages": 412}
```

The output has two keys, `title` and `pages`. The `subtitle` field is missing, because it is `None` and the default configuration leaves out empty optional fields. The key names match the field names of `Book`.

Now we create a book with a subtitle, and see that the key appears:

```scala
val hobbit = Book("The Hobbit", 310, Some("There and Back Again"))
// hobbit: Book = Book(
//   title = "The Hobbit",
//   pages = 310,
//   subtitle = Some(value = "There and Back Again")
// )

println(hobbit.toBsonValue)
// {"title": "The Hobbit", "pages": 310, "subtitle": "There and Back Again"}
```

### Step 4: Load a Document Back into a Book

Loading is the reverse of storing. The `as` method reads a `BsonValue` with the decoder for `Book`, and returns either the value or an error message:

```scala
println(hobbit.toBsonValue.as[Book])
// Right(Book(The Hobbit,310,Some(There and Back Again)))
```

The result is `Right` with a `Book` that equals the original. Now we read a document that is missing the `pages` field, which is required:

```scala
println(doc("title" -> str("Emma")).as[Book])
// Left(.pages: missing)
```

The error names the missing field with a leading dot, `.pages`, so we can see what to fix in the stored document.

### Step 5: Check the Round Trip

A good habit is to check that a value survives a round trip: encode it, decode it, and compare the result with the original. We will check both books from Step 3:

```scala
val roundTrip = List(dune, hobbit).map(b => b.toBsonValue.as[Book])
// roundTrip: List[Either[String, Book]] = List(
//   Right(value = Book(title = "Dune", pages = 412, subtitle = None)),
//   Right(
//     value = Book(
//       title = "The Hobbit",
//       pages = 310,
//       subtitle = Some(value = "There and Back Again")
//     )
//   )
// )

println(roundTrip)
// List(Right(Book(Dune,412,None)), Right(Book(The Hobbit,310,Some(There and Back Again))))
println(roundTrip == List(Right(dune), Right(hobbit)))
// true
```

The second line prints `true`, so both books came back unchanged.

### Step 6: Connect the Codec to MongoDB

The MongoDB driver stores values through a `CodecRegistry`. A registry holds a `CodecProvider` for each type. The provider returned by `zioBsonCodecProvider` wraps the `Book` codec:

```scala
import org.bson.codecs.configuration.CodecRegistries
import org.bson.conversions.Bson

val registry = CodecRegistries.fromRegistries(
  CodecRegistries.fromProviders(zioBsonCodecProvider[Book]),
  Bson.DEFAULT_CODEC_REGISTRY
)
```

With the registry in the driver's client settings, `insertOne` and `find` work on `Book` values. The driver writes the same document that we printed in Step 3. The driver code needs a running MongoDB server and the synchronous driver library, so it is shown as text:

```scala
val settings = MongoClientSettings.builder()
  .applyConnectionString(new ConnectionString("mongodb://localhost:27017"))
  .codecRegistry(registry)
  .build()

val collection = MongoClients.create(settings)
  .getDatabase("library")
  .getCollection("books", classOf[Book])

collection.insertOne(dune)
println(collection.find().first())
```

The [MongoDB driver how-to](./how-to-use-with-mongodb-driver.md) explains the registry in more detail and shows the same encode and decode steps that run without a server.

### Putting It Together

The complete example below holds the model, the codec, and the checks from Steps 2 to 5 in one place:

```scala
final case class Shelf(name: String, books: List[Book])

object Shelf {
  implicit val codec: BsonCodec[Shelf] = DeriveBsonCodec.derive
}

val shelf = Shelf("Science Fiction", List(dune, hobbit))
// shelf: Shelf = Shelf(
//   name = "Science Fiction",
//   books = List(
//     Book(title = "Dune", pages = 412, subtitle = None),
//     Book(
//       title = "The Hobbit",
//       pages = 310,
//       subtitle = Some(value = "There and Back Again")
//     )
//   )
// )

val stored = shelf.toBsonValue
// stored: org.bson.BsonValue = {"name": "Science Fiction", "books": [{"title": "Dune", "pages": 412}, {"title": "The Hobbit", "pages": 310, "subtitle": "There and Back Again"}]}
println(stored)
// {"name": "Science Fiction", "books": [{"title": "Dune", "pages": 412}, {"title": "The Hobbit", "pages": 310, "subtitle": "There and Back Again"}]}
println(stored.as[Shelf] == Right(shelf))
// true
```

We derived a codec for `Shelf`, which holds a list of `Book` values. The codec for `Book` is used for each element, so no extra code is needed.

### Next Steps

- [Customize Field Names and Discriminators](./how-to-customize-field-names-and-discriminators.md) changes the keys in the stored document.
- [Write a Codec by Hand](./how-to-write-a-codec-by-hand.md) covers types that derivation cannot handle.
- [BsonCodecConfiguration](./bson-codec-configuration.md) lists every setting that controls derivation.

## Type Mappings

### Scala / Java to BSON Type Mappings

ZIO Bson provides `BsonEncoder` and `BsonDecoder` typeclass instances for a wide range of Scala and Java types.
The encoder determines the primary BSON type a value is written as.
The decoder accepts the primary type and, where it makes sense, additional fallback BSON types.

| Scala / Java Type | Encoder → BSON | Decoder fallbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `Boolean` | `BOOLEAN` | — |
| `Byte` | `INT32` | `INT64` (range check), `DOUBLE` (lossless), `DECIMAL128` (lossless), `STRING` |
| `Short` | `INT32` | `INT64` (range check), `DOUBLE` (lossless), `DECIMAL128` (lossless), `STRING` |
| `Int` | `INT32` | `INT64` (range check), `DOUBLE` (lossless), `DECIMAL128` (lossless), `STRING` |
| `Long` | `INT64` | `INT32`, `DOUBLE` (lossless), `DECIMAL128` (lossless), `STRING` |
| `Float` | `DOUBLE` | `INT32`, `INT64`, `DECIMAL128` (lossless), `STRING` |
| `Double` | `DOUBLE` | `INT32`, `INT64`, `DECIMAL128` (lossless), `STRING` |
| `java.math.BigDecimal` | `DECIMAL128` | `INT32`, `INT64`, `DOUBLE`, `STRING` |
| `BigDecimal` | `DECIMAL128` | `INT32`, `INT64`, `DOUBLE`, `STRING` |
| `java.math.BigInteger` | `STRING` | `INT32`, `INT64`, `DOUBLE` (lossless), `DECIMAL128` (lossless) |
| `BigInt` | `STRING` | `INT32`, `INT64`, `DOUBLE` (lossless), `DECIMAL128` (lossless) |
| `String` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `Char` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `scala.Symbol` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `UUID` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `java.util.Currency` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `DayOfWeek` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `Month` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `MonthDay` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `Year` | `INT32` | `INT64` (range check), `DOUBLE` (lossless), `DECIMAL128` (lossless), `STRING` |
| `YearMonth` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `ZoneId` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `ZoneOffset` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `Duration` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `Period` | `STRING` | `SYMBOL` |
| `Instant` | `DATE_TIME` | — |
| `LocalDate` | `DATE_TIME` | — |
| `LocalDateTime` | `DATE_TIME` | — |
| `LocalTime` | `DATE_TIME` | — |
| `OffsetDateTime` | `DOCUMENT` | — |
| `OffsetTime` | `DOCUMENT` | — |
| `ZonedDateTime` | `DOCUMENT` | — |
| `org.bson.types.ObjectId` | `OBJECT_ID` | — |
| `Option[A]` | same as `A` / `NULL` | — |
| `Array[Byte]` | `BINARY` | — |
| `Iterable[Byte]` subtype | `BINARY` | — |
| `NonEmptyChunk[Byte]` | `BINARY` | — |
| `Array[A]` (non-byte) | `ARRAY` | — |
| `Iterable[A]` subtype (non-byte) | `ARRAY` | — |
| `NonEmptyChunk[A]` (non-byte) | `ARRAY` | — |
| `Map[K, V]` | `DOCUMENT` | — |
| `T <: BsonValue` | any (pass-through) | — |

### Special Cases

- **`Byte` and `Short`** are decoded via the `Int` decoder followed by a range check. All BSON numeric types and `STRING` are accepted, but the decoded value must fit within the type's range, otherwise a decoder error is returned.
- **`BigInt` and `java.math.BigInteger`** encode to `STRING` but decode from all numeric BSON types. Conversion from `DOUBLE` and `DECIMAL128` requires the value to be a lossless integer (no fractional part).
- **`String`** decoder also accepts `SYMBOL` for backward compatibility with legacy BSON documents. Every type that decodes through the `String` decoder (`Char`, `Symbol`, `UUID`, `Currency`, `DayOfWeek`, `Month`, `MonthDay`, `YearMonth`, `ZoneId`, `ZoneOffset`, `Duration`, `Period`) accepts `SYMBOL` as well. `DayOfWeek` and `Month` decode case-insensitively.
- **`Instant`, `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime` and `LocalTime`** are stored as `DATE_TIME`, which has millisecond precision. Sub-millisecond precision is lost when encoding, and the date and time are interpreted in UTC.
- **`Char`** decoder requires the string to be exactly one UTF-16 code unit. A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as an emoji, is stored as two code units and is rejected.
- **`OffsetDateTime`** and **`OffsetTime`** encode as a `DOCUMENT` with two fields: `date_time` (`DATE_TIME`) and `offset` (`STRING`). The decoder rejects any other field in the document.
- **`ZonedDateTime`** encodes as a `DOCUMENT` with two fields: `date_time` (`DATE_TIME`) and `zone_id` (`STRING`). The decoder rejects any other field in the document.
- **`Option[A]`** encodes `None` as `NULL` and `Some(a)` using the encoder for `A`. The decoder returns `None` for `NULL` and `Some(a)` for any value accepted by the decoder for `A`. When a field is missing from a document, the decoder also returns `None`.
- **`Map[K, V]`** needs a field codec for `K`. Only `String`, `Int` and `Long` keys have one built in. Other key types need a custom `BsonFieldEncoder` and `BsonFieldDecoder`, as described in [Field Codecs](./bson-field-codecs.md). A `None` value in a map is written as `NULL`, not skipped.

### BSON Types Without Scala Mappings

The following BSON types have no dedicated Scala or Java codec in this library. They are accessible only via the `T <: BsonValue` pass-through encoder/decoder using the underlying MongoDB Java driver:

| BSON Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| `SYMBOL` | Deprecated BSON type; accepted by the `String` decoder for backward compatibility, but no encoder exists |
| `UNDEFINED` | Deprecated BSON type |
| `REGULAR_EXPRESSION` | — |
| `DB_POINTER` | Deprecated BSON type |
| `JAVASCRIPT` | — |
| `JAVASCRIPT_WITH_SCOPE` | — |
| `TIMESTAMP` | MongoDB internal replication timestamp |
| `MIN_KEY` | — |
| `MAX_KEY` | — |
| `END_OF_DOCUMENT` | Internal sentinel used by the reader loop; never a value |

## Cache Statistics

ZIO Cache automatically tracks statistics for the whole cache: the number of cache hits and misses and the current size of the cache. You can use them to assess how well the cache works. You can access these statistics by using the `cacheStats` operator on `Cache`.

The `CacheStats` type is a case class with three fields:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, CacheStats}

def report(cache: Cache[String, Nothing, Int]): UIO[Unit] =
  cache.cacheStats.flatMap { stats: CacheStats =>
    ZIO.debug(s"hits=${stats.hits} misses=${stats.misses} size=${stats.size}")
  }
```

- `hits` is the number of lookups answered without running the lookup function. A lookup that waits for a value another fiber is still computing counts as a hit. For `Cache`, a lookup that finds an expired value counts as a miss.
- `misses` is the number of lookups that started a new computation.
- `size` is the number of values in the cache. Under concurrent access it is approximate.

The cache statistics represent a snapshot as of a point in time. Note that the cache statistics are designed for aggregate analysis and may not be fully consistent with each other when read during concurrent updates.

More cache statistics will be added over time. To track the statistics of one entry, see [Entry Statistics](./entry-statistics.md).

---

## Cache

A cache is defined in terms of a lookup function, a capacity, and a time to live.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

val cache: UIO[Cache[String, Nothing, Int]] =
  Cache.make(
    capacity = 100,
    timeToLive = 10.minutes,
    lookup = Lookup(key => ZIO.succeed(key.length))
  )
```

The most fundamental operator on a cache is `get`, which either returns the value in the cache if it exists or else computes a new value with the lookup function, puts it in the cache, and returns it.

### Concurrent Access

The cache is guaranteed to be safe for concurrent access. In addition, getting a value from the cache is efficient under concurrency.

If two concurrent processes attempt to get the same value and it does not exist in the cache, the value will be computed once and provided to both concurrent processes as soon as it is available. The concurrent processes will semantically block for the value to become available but no underlying operating system threads will block as a result of this operation.

In the event that the computation of the lookup function fails or is interrupted that will automatically be propagated to any concurrent processes waiting for the same value.

Failures will be cached and made available to subsequent calls to `get` to avoid repeatedly computing the same failed value. In the event of interruption the key will be removed from the cache so subsequent calls to `get` will attempt to compute the value again.

### Capacity

A cache is constructed with a specified capacity. When the cache is at capacity the least recently accessed values will be removed first.

Note that the size of the cache may slightly exceed the specified capacity between operations.

### Time To Live (TTL)

A cache also allows specifying a time to live. The cache guarantees that no value will be returned from the cache if its age is greater than the specified time to live.

The expiry time is set when the lookup completes: the time to live is added to that moment. A value whose expiry time has passed is treated as absent, so the next `get` computes it again.

The `Cache.make` constructor applies the same time to live to every value. To choose the time to live from the result of the lookup function, use `Cache.makeWith`. Its time to live function receives the `Exit` of the lookup, so a failure can expire sooner than a success:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, Int] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("Empty user id") else ZIO.succeed(userId.length)

val profiles: UIO[Cache[String, String, Int]] =
  Cache.makeWith(capacity = 100, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))(exit =>
    if (exit.isSuccess) 10.minutes else 5.seconds
  )
```

### Custom Keys

By default, the key of a cache entry is the input of the lookup function. The `Cache.makeWithKey` constructor accepts a `keyBy` function that converts each input into the key stored in the cache. Use it when the input is large and only a part of it identifies the value:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

final case class Request(id: String, payload: Array[Byte])

def process(request: Request): IO[Nothing, Int] =
  ZIO.succeed(request.payload.length)

val requests: UIO[Cache[Request, Nothing, Int]] =
  Cache.makeWithKey(capacity = 100, lookup = Lookup(process))(
    timeToLive = _ => 1.minute,
    keyBy = (request: Request) => request.id
  )
```

The `keyBy` function only changes the key that the cache stores. The lookup function still receives the full input, so two inputs with the same key share the cached value.

### Operators

In addition to `get`, `Cache` provides a variety of other operators.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.Cache

def operators(cache: Cache[String, Nothing, Int]): UIO[Unit] =
  for {
    stats   <- cache.cacheStats
    entry   <- cache.entryStats("key")
    present <- cache.contains("key")
    count   <- cache.size
    _       <- ZIO.debug(s"$stats $entry $present $count")
    _       <- cache.refresh("key")
    _       <- cache.invalidate("key")
    _       <- cache.invalidateAll
  } yield ()
```

The `refresh` operator is similar to `get`. The difference is `refresh` triggers a re-computation of the value without invalidating it. This allows any request to the associated key to be served while the value is being re-computed / retrieved by the lookup function. Note: `refresh` always triggers the lookup function, disregarding the last `Error`. 

The `size` operator returns the current size of the cache. Under concurrent access the size should be regarded as only approximate since by the time we observe a given size the cache may have a different size based on concurrent insertions or removals.

Similarly, the `contains` operator returns whether a value associated with the specified key exists in the cache. An expired value does not count, so `contains` returns `false` for it even before it is removed. Again, under concurrent access `contains` is guaranteed to return whether the cache contains a value associated with the specified key as of a given point in time but that value may be concurrently added or removed immediately after that.

There are also the `cacheStats` and `entryStats` operators which allow obtaining a snapshot of statistics either for the cache itself or for a specified entry. See the sections on cache statistics and entry statistics for further discussion of this functionality.

The `invalidate` and `invalidateAll` operators can be used to evict a value associated with a specified key and evict all values, respectively.

---

## Entry Statistics

ZIO Cache also tracks statistics for each entry, such as when the entry was loaded into the cache. You can access the statistics for a specified entry using the `entryStats` operator on `Cache`, passing the key of the entry.

The `EntryStats` type is a case class with one field, `loaded`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, EntryStats}

def loadedAt(cache: Cache[String, Nothing, Int], key: String): UIO[Option[java.time.Instant]] =
  cache.entryStats(key).map(_.map((stats: EntryStats) => stats.loaded))
```

`loaded` is the instant when the lookup for the entry completed. `entryStats` returns `None` when the cache holds no value for that key, including while the first lookup for the key is still running. An expired value that has not been removed yet still returns its statistics.

More entry statistics will be added over time.

---

## Getting Started with ZIO Cache

This page shows how to define a cache and read a value from it. To add ZIO Cache to your build, see [Installation](./index.md#installation).

### Defining a Cache

A cache is defined in terms of a lookup function that describes how to compute the value associated with a key if a value is not already in the cache.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.Lookup

val lookup: Lookup[String, Any, Nothing, Int] =
  Lookup(key => ZIO.succeed(key.length))
```

The lookup function takes a key of type `Key` and returns a `ZIO` effect that requires an environment of type `Environment` and can fail with an error of type `Error` or succeed with a value of type `Value`. Because the lookup function returns a `ZIO` effect it can describe both synchronous and asynchronous workflows.

We construct a cache using a lookup function as well as a maximum size and a time to live.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

val cache: UIO[Cache[String, Nothing, Int]] =
  Cache.make(
    capacity = 100,
    timeToLive = Duration.Infinity,
    lookup = Lookup(key => ZIO.succeed(key.length))
  )
```

Once we have created a cache the most idiomatic way to work with it is the `get` operator. The `get` operator will return the current value in the cache if it exists or else compute a new value, put it in the cache, and return it.

If multiple concurrent processes get the value at the same time the value will only be computed once, with all of the other processes receiving the computed value as soon as it is available. All of this will be done using ZIO's fiber based concurrency model without ever blocking any underlying operating system threads.

### Example: Concurrent Lookups

In this example, we are calling `timeConsumingEffect` three times in parallel with the same key. The ZIO Cache runs this effect only once. So the concurrent lookups will suspend until the value being computed is available:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

object ZIOCacheExample extends ZIOAppDefault {
  def timeConsumingEffect(key: String) =
    ZIO.sleep(5.seconds).as(key.hashCode)

  def run =
    for {
      cache <- Cache.make(
        capacity = 100,
        timeToLive = Duration.Infinity,
        lookup = Lookup(timeConsumingEffect)
      )
      result <- cache
        .get("key1")
        .zipPar(cache.get("key1"))
        .zipPar(cache.get("key1"))
      _ <- ZIO.debug(
        s"Result of parallel execution of three effects with the same key: $result"
      )

      hits <- cache.cacheStats.map(_.hits)
      misses <- cache.cacheStats.map(_.misses)
      _ <- ZIO.debug(s"Number of cache hits: $hits")
      _ <- ZIO.debug(s"Number of cache misses: $misses")
    } yield ()

}
```

The output of this program should be as follows:

```
Result of parallel execution of three effects with the same key: ((3288498,3288498),3288498)
Number of cache hits: 2
Number of cache misses: 1
```

### Where to Go Next

To build the same cache step by step, follow the [tutorial](./tutorial-first-cache.md).

## How to Decide Whether to Cache Failures

ZIO Cache stores a failed lookup just like a successful one. The next `Cache#get` for the same key returns the stored error until the entry expires, so the lookup does not run again. This avoids repeated calls to a broken service, but it also means a transient error can be returned for as long as the entry lives.

To decide what fits your service, first pick the lifetime for failures. Use `Cache.makeWith` and return a short time to live when the exit is a failure:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.succeed(s"profile of $userId")

val profiles: UIO[Cache[String, String, String]] =
  Cache.makeWith(capacity = 1000, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))(exit =>
    if (exit.isSuccess) 10.minutes else 5.seconds
  )
```

A short lifetime keeps a broken dependency from being hit on every request, and it lets the cache recover after a few seconds. If you do not want failures reused at all, return `Duration.Zero` for failures. The entry then expires as soon as it is stored, and the next `Cache#get` runs the lookup again.

Two details apply to every choice:

- Callers that are already waiting for a lookup in progress receive its failure, even when the failure is not stored for later calls.
- If the lookup is interrupted, the entry is removed and nothing is stored. The next `Cache#get` runs the lookup again.

:::caution
Keeping failures for a long time turns a short outage into a long one. Prefer a short lifetime for failures unless the lookup's errors are permanent, such as a missing record that cannot appear later.
:::

For the per-entry time to live function in more detail, see [How to Set a Time to Live per Entry](./how-to-per-entry-ttl.md).

---

## How to Cache Resources That Must Be Closed

A plain `Cache` is fine for values that need no cleanup. When each value is a resource, such as a database connection, it must be closed when the cache no longer needs it. `ScopedCache` closes each resource after it is evicted, invalidated, or expired, and after the last caller finishes using it.

This guide keeps one connection per database URL. A failed query removes the connection from the cache, so the next call opens a new one. The lookup acquires the connection and registers its release with `ZIO.acquireRelease`, and `runQuery` uses the cache inside a scope:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{ScopedCache, ScopedLookup}

final case class Connection(url: String) {
  def query(sql: String): IO[Throwable, String] = ZIO.succeed(s"result of $sql on $url")
}

val openConnection: ScopedLookup[String, Scope, Nothing, Connection] =
  ScopedLookup { (url: String) =>
    ZIO.acquireRelease(ZIO.succeed(Connection(url)))(connection =>
      ZIO.debug(s"closing ${connection.url}")
    )
  }

def runQuery(cache: ScopedCache[String, Nothing, Connection], url: String, sql: String): IO[Throwable, String] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    cache.get(url).flatMap(connection => connection.query(sql))
  }.tapError(_ => cache.invalidate(url))
```

`ZIO.acquireRelease` pairs the opening of the connection with its closing. The cache calls the release action only when no caller still uses the connection.

The `ZIO.scoped` block holds the connection only while the query runs. If the query fails, `tapError` invalidates the URL. The connection is then closed once its last caller has finished, and the next `runQuery` call opens a new connection.

The cache itself is built with `ScopedCache.make`, which needs a `Scope`, so the cache lives as long as the enclosing scope. Use `ZIO.scoped` at the top of the program to provide that scope.

:::caution
Do not return the connection from `ZIO.scoped`. The connection is released when the scope closes, so using it afterward uses a closed resource.
:::

For how the cache counts the callers of a resource and when it releases one, see the [Scoped Cache](./scoped-cache.md) reference page.

---

## How to Choose Capacity and Time to Live

Capacity and time to live are the two settings that decide how much a cache keeps and how long it keeps it. This guide shows how to choose both for a service that caches user profiles.

### Choose the Capacity

The capacity is the maximum number of values the cache holds. When the cache is full, it evicts the least recently accessed value to make room for a new one. A good capacity covers the keys that are requested again within a short period. Each value costs memory, so the capacity also caps how much memory the cache can use.

Start from the number of distinct keys you expect in the busiest period, and multiply it by the approximate size of one value to estimate memory use. If the estimate fits your memory budget, use that number as the capacity:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  ZIO.succeed(s"profile of $userId")

val profiles: UIO[Cache[String, String, String]] =
  Cache.make(
    capacity = 10000,
    timeToLive = 5.minutes,
    lookup = Lookup(loadProfile)
  )
```

The size of the cache can briefly exceed the capacity between operations, so treat the capacity as a target rather than an exact limit.

### Choose the Time to Live

The time to live is how long a value may be returned after it was loaded. Choose the longest time that still keeps the data acceptable for your users. A profile that changes rarely can live for minutes. A price that changes every second needs a short time to live, or no cache at all.

Use `Duration.Infinity` only when the value never changes while the process runs. Values then stay until they are evicted by capacity or invalidated by hand.

### Check the Results with Statistics

After you deploy, read the statistics to see whether the settings fit your traffic. A low hit rate means values are evicted or expire before they are reused. A high miss count with a small size suggests the time to live is too short. Use `Cache#cacheStats` for the totals, as described in [How to Monitor the Hit Rate](./how-to-monitor-hit-rate.md).

:::tip
Change one setting at a time and measure again. Changing the capacity and the time to live together makes it hard to tell which change helped.
:::

For the meaning of each parameter, see the [Cache](./cache.md) reference page.

---

## How to Invalidate a Cached Value After an Update

A cache serves the stored value until it expires. When our application updates the data behind a key, readers would see the old value for up to the time to live. This guide removes the stale value right after the update, so the next `Cache#get` runs the lookup again.

We use a small in-memory store as the source of truth, and a cache in front of it:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

final class Users(store: Ref[Map[String, String]], cache: Cache[String, Nothing, String]) {
  def name(id: String): UIO[String] = cache.get(id)

  def rename(id: String, newName: String): UIO[Unit] =
    store.update(_.updated(id, newName)) *> cache.invalidate(id)
}

object Users {
  val make: UIO[Users] =
    for {
      store <- Ref.make(Map("u-1" -> "Alice"))
      cache <- Cache.make(
                 capacity = 100,
                 timeToLive = 10.minutes,
                 lookup = Lookup((id: String) => store.get.map(_.getOrElse(id, "unknown")))
               )
    } yield new Users(store, cache)
}
```

`rename` writes to the store first and invalidates the key second. If we invalidated first, a concurrent `Cache#get` could reload the old value between the two steps and keep it until the time to live expires.

```scala
val program: UIO[Unit] =
  for {
    users  <- Users.make
    before <- users.name("u-1")
    _      <- users.rename("u-1", "Alicia")
    after  <- users.name("u-1")
    _      <- ZIO.debug(s"$before -> $after")
  } yield ()
```

The program prints `Alice -> Alicia`. To drop every entry at once, for example after a bulk import, use `Cache#invalidateAll`.

:::note
Use `Cache#refresh` instead of `Cache#invalidate` when readers must never wait for the lookup. See [How to Refresh Values in the Background](./how-to-refresh-in-background.md).
:::

---

## How to Monitor the Hit Rate

The hit rate is the share of lookups that the cache answered without running the lookup function. A low hit rate means the cache does little work for your service. This guide computes the hit rate from `Cache#cacheStats`, logs it on a schedule, and then checks a single entry.

The hit rate is the number of hits divided by the number of hits and misses together. The helper below returns zero when no lookups have happened yet. The `monitor` function logs the rate every minute in a background fiber, which is forked into the current scope and stops when that scope closes:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, CacheStats}

def hitRate(stats: CacheStats): Double = {
  val lookups = stats.hits + stats.misses
  if (lookups == 0L) 0.0 else stats.hits.toDouble / lookups.toDouble
}

def logHitRate[Key, Error, Value](cache: Cache[Key, Error, Value]): UIO[Unit] =
  cache.cacheStats.flatMap { stats =>
    ZIO.debug(f"hit rate: ${hitRate(stats) * 100}%.1f%% (size ${stats.size})")
  }

def monitor[Key, Error, Value](cache: Cache[Key, Error, Value]): URIO[Scope, Unit] =
  logHitRate(cache).repeat(Schedule.spaced(1.minute)).forkScoped.unit
```

The counters only grow, so the rate above covers the whole life of the cache. To see the rate for a recent period, read the statistics at the start and at the end of the period and subtract the counts.

To check one entry, call `Cache#entryStats` with its key. It returns the time the entry was loaded, or `None` when the cache holds no value for the key. The next example shows that call:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.Cache

def loadedAt[Key, Error, Value](cache: Cache[Key, Error, Value], key: Key): UIO[Option[java.time.Instant]] =
  cache.entryStats(key).map(_.map(_.loaded))
```

A very old `loaded` time for a key that is requested often can mean the time to live is longer than your data allows.

:::tip
Use the rate together with the size. A low rate with a size at the capacity suggests the capacity is too small. A low rate with a small size suggests the time to live is too short, or the keys rarely repeat.
:::

For the fields of each statistics type, see [Cache Statistics](./cache-statistics.md) and [Entry Statistics](./entry-statistics.md).

---

## How to Set a Time to Live per Entry

`Cache.make` gives every value the same time to live. When successful and failed lookups need different lifetimes, use `Cache.makeWith` instead. Its time to live function receives the `Exit` of each lookup and returns the time to live for that entry.

Suppose a profile lookup succeeds rarely enough to keep for ten minutes, but a failure should be retried after five seconds. We pass a function to `Cache.makeWith` that checks the `Exit`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.succeed(s"profile of $userId")

val profiles: UIO[Cache[String, String, String]] =
  Cache.makeWith(capacity = 1000, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))(exit =>
    if (exit.isSuccess) 10.minutes else 5.seconds
  )
```

The function runs once for each lookup, when the lookup completes. The expiry time of the entry is that moment plus the returned duration. A failed entry expires after five seconds, so the next `Cache#get` for that key runs the lookup again.

:::note
The time to live is fixed when the lookup completes. The function cannot change the lifetime of an entry after it is stored.
:::

To give each entry a time to live based on its key or value rather than its `Exit`, compute the duration from the key in your own code and store values with a separate cache per lifetime.

---

## How to Refresh Values in the Background

Sometimes a value must stay current, but a caller should never wait for the lookup to finish. `Cache#refresh` runs the lookup and replaces the stored value when the new one is ready. While that happens, `Cache#get` keeps returning the current value. This guide runs `Cache#refresh` on a fixed schedule in a background fiber.

We start by refreshing one key every thirty seconds. The fiber is forked into a `Scope`, so it stops when the scope closes:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  ZIO.succeed(s"profile of $userId at ${java.time.Instant.now}")

val refreshed: ZIO[Scope, String, Unit] =
  for {
    cache <- Cache.make(capacity = 100, timeToLive = 5.minutes, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))
    _     <- cache.get("alice")
    _     <- cache.refresh("alice").repeat(Schedule.spaced(30.seconds)).forkScoped
    _     <- cache.get("alice")
  } yield ()
```

Each `Cache#refresh` call runs the lookup again, even when the stored value has not expired. The old value stays in the cache, so the `Cache#get` calls in the meantime return it without waiting.

:::note
If the lookup fails during a refresh, the failure replaces the stored value and is cached like any other failure. The loop above stops at its first failure, because `Cache#refresh` returns the error. To keep the loop running, handle the error inside it, for example with `ZIO#ignore` or `ZIO#catchAll` plus a log message.
:::

Use `Cache#refresh` for values where a stale read is acceptable for a short time. For values that must never be stale, use `Cache#invalidate` followed by `Cache#get` instead.

---

## How to Test Cache Expiry Without Waiting

A cache entry expires after its time to live, and waiting that long in a test is slow and flaky. A cache reads the time from the ZIO `Clock` service, so `TestClock` can move time forward instantly. This guide checks that an entry is computed again after it expires.

The test counts how many times the lookup runs. We use a one-minute time to live and move the `TestClock` past it:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}
import zio.test._

object CacheExpirySpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec =
    test("an expired entry is computed again") {
      for {
        calls <- Ref.make(0)
        cache <- Cache.make(
                   capacity = 10,
                   timeToLive = 1.minute,
                   lookup = Lookup((key: String) => calls.updateAndGet(_ + 1).as(key.length))
                 )
        _     <- cache.get("key")
        _     <- cache.get("key")
        _     <- TestClock.adjust(2.minutes)
        _     <- cache.get("key")
        count <- calls.get
      } yield assertTrue(count == 2)
    }
}
```

The first two `Cache#get` calls run the lookup once, because the second finds the stored value. After `TestClock.adjust(2.minutes)` the entry has expired, so the third call runs the lookup again and the count is `2`.

`Cache#contains` follows the same clock. After the adjustment, `Cache#contains` returns `false` for the expired key even before another `Cache#get` replaces it.

:::note
Create the cache inside the test, as above, so it reads the `TestClock` that the test provides.
:::

---

## How to Cache by a Part of a Large Input

Sometimes the input of the lookup function is large, but only a small part of it identifies the value. Storing the whole input as the cache key wastes memory and makes two requests with the same identifier look different. `Cache.makeWithKey` converts each input into the key that the cache stores. This guide caches the result of processing a request by the request's `id`.

We start with a request type that carries a large payload, and a lookup function that processes it:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

final case class Request(id: String, payload: Array[Byte])

def process(request: Request): UIO[Int] =
  ZIO.succeed(request.payload.length)
```

Then we create the cache with `Cache.makeWithKey`. Its `keyBy` function maps a `Request` to the `String` that the cache stores:

```scala
val requests: UIO[Cache[Request, Nothing, Int]] =
  Cache.makeWithKey(capacity = 100, lookup = Lookup(process))(
    timeToLive = _ => 1.minute,
    keyBy = (request: Request) => request.id
  )
```

The cache is still used with the full `Request`. Two requests with the same `id` share one cached value, even when their payloads differ:

```scala
val program: UIO[Unit] =
  for {
    cache <- requests
    first <- cache.get(Request("r-1", Array[Byte](1, 2, 3)))
    other <- cache.get(Request("r-1", Array[Byte](9)))
    _     <- ZIO.debug(s"first=$first other=$other")
  } yield ()
```

Both results are `3`, because the second call finds the value stored under the key `"r-1"`. The lookup function runs only for the first call and still receives the full `Request`.

:::note
Choose a key that identifies the value completely. If two inputs with the same key should produce different values, they will share one entry and the second caller gets the first caller's value.
:::

`ScopedCache` has no `makeWithKey`. To cache resources by part of an input, wrap the input in a small key type and look up by that key instead.

## Introduction to ZIO Cache

ZIO Cache is a library that makes it easy to optimize the performance of our application by caching values.

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-cache/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-cache_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-cache_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-cache_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-cache_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-cache_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-cache_2.13) [![ZIO Cache](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-cache?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-cache)

### Introduction

Sometimes we may call or receive requests to do overlapping work. Assume we are writing a service that is going to handle all incoming requests. We don't want to handle duplicate requests. Using ZIO Cache we can make our application more **performant** by preventing duplicated work.

Some key features of ZIO Cache:

- **Compositionality** — If we want our applications to be **compositional**, different parts of our application may do overlapping work. ZIO Cache lets us keep that compositionality while using caching.
- **Unification of Synchronous and Asynchronous Caches** — Compositional definition of cache in terms of _lookup function_ unifies synchronous and asynchronous caches. So the lookup function can compute value either synchronously or asynchronously.

- **Deep ZIO Integration** — ZIO Cache is a ZIO native solution. So without losing the power of ZIO it includes support for _concurrent lookups_, _failure_, and _interruption_.
- **Capacity and Time to Live** — A cache holds at most a fixed number of values. When it is full, it removes the least recently accessed value. Each value also expires after a time to live, and that time can depend on whether the lookup succeeded or failed.

- **Cache/Entry Statistics** — ZIO Cache tracks hits, misses, and size for the whole cache, and the time each entry was loaded. So we can look at how our cache is doing and decide whether its capacity and time to live need to change.

### Installation

ZIO Cache is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3. Add the artifact that matches your platform to your `build.sbt`.

On the JVM:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Cache, ScopedCache, Lookup and statistics (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-cache" % "0.4.1"
)
```

On Scala.js or Scala Native, use `%%%` instead:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Cache, ScopedCache, Lookup and statistics (Scala.js and Scala Native)
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-cache" % "0.4.1"
)
```

### Learn More

Start with [Getting Started](./getting-started.md), then build your first cache step by step in the [tutorial](./tutorial-first-cache.md). To make specific decisions, read the how-to guides, starting with [How to Choose Capacity and Time to Live](./how-to-choose-capacity-and-ttl.md). The reference pages describe [Cache](./cache.md), [ScopedCache](./scoped-cache.md), [Lookup](./lookup.md), and the statistics types. Talks and articles are listed under [Resources](./resources.md).

## Lookup

A `Lookup` is a lookup function that, given a key of type `Key`, knows how to compute a value of type `Value`, requiring an environment of type `Environment` and potentially failing with an error of type `Error`.

`Lookup` is a case class that wraps a function from a key to a `ZIO` effect. Its type parameters are `Key`, `Environment`, `Error`, and `Value`. Because `Lookup` also extends the function type `Key => ZIO[Environment, Error, Value]`, calling `Lookup#apply` with a key runs the wrapped function on it.

You can think of a key as essentially an effectual function to compute a value. And in fact you can construct a `Lookup` from any effectual function using the `Lookup.apply` method on the `Lookup` companion object:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.Lookup

def timeConsumingEffect(key: String): UIO[Int] =
  ZIO.sleep(5.seconds).as(key.hashCode)

val lookup: Lookup[String, Any, Nothing, Int] = Lookup(timeConsumingEffect)
```

Since the lookup function can return a `ZIO` effect it can either return its result synchronously or asynchronously. It can also use an environment and potentially fail with an error.

In short, if you can describe it with a ZIO effect you can use it as the lookup function for a cache.

We will see how ZIO’s support for asynchrony and concurrency let us implement a cache in terms of a single lookup function and how we get many other things such as typed errors and compositional caching policies for free. See how easy it can be to add caching to your ZIO application!

## Scoped Cache

A `ScopedCache` is a [cache](./cache.md) whose values are resources, such as database connections, file handles, or temporary directories. Each value must be released when the cache no longer needs it. A `ScopedCache` keeps a resource open while the cache holds it or while any caller still uses it, and releases the resource after it is evicted, invalidated, or expired and no caller uses it anymore.

If the cached values need no cleanup, use a plain [Cache](./cache.md) instead.

### Defining a Scoped Lookup

A `ScopedLookup` describes how to compute a value of type `Value` for a key of type `Key`. Unlike a [Lookup](./lookup.md), the lookup function requires a `Scope`. Any resource it acquires with `ZIO.acquireRelease` stays open for as long as the cached value lives:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.ScopedLookup

final case class Connection(url: String)

val openConnection: ScopedLookup[String, Scope, Nothing, Connection] =
  ScopedLookup { (url: String) =>
    ZIO.acquireRelease(ZIO.succeed(Connection(url)))(connection =>
      ZIO.debug(s"Closing connection to ${connection.url}")
    )
  }
```

The `ScopedLookup` constructor takes a function from a key to a `ZIO` effect that requires `Scope`. Calling `ScopedLookup#apply` with a key returns that effect for the key.

### Creating a Scoped Cache

`ScopedCache.make` constructs a cache from a capacity, a time to live, and a `ScopedLookup`. The effect requires a `Scope`, which ties the lifetime of the cache to the enclosing scope. Closing that scope invalidates all values in the cache and releases the resources they hold:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{ScopedCache, ScopedLookup}

final case class Connection(url: String)

val openConnection: ScopedLookup[String, Scope, Nothing, Connection] =
  ScopedLookup { (url: String) =>
    ZIO.acquireRelease(ZIO.succeed(Connection(url)))(connection =>
      ZIO.debug(s"Closing connection to ${connection.url}")
    )
  }

val connections: ZIO[Scope, Nothing, ScopedCache[String, Throwable, Connection]] =
  ScopedCache.make(
    capacity = 10,
    timeToLive = 1.minute,
    lookup = openConnection
  )
```

To decide the time to live from the result of the lookup, use `ScopedCache.makeWith`. Its time to live function receives the `Exit` of the lookup, so a failed lookup can expire sooner than a successful one:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{ScopedCache, ScopedLookup}

final case class Connection(url: String)

val openConnection: ScopedLookup[String, Scope, Nothing, Connection] =
  ScopedLookup { (url: String) =>
    ZIO.acquireRelease(ZIO.succeed(Connection(url)))(connection =>
      ZIO.debug(s"Closing connection to ${connection.url}")
    )
  }

val connections: URIO[Scope, ScopedCache[String, Throwable, Connection]] =
  ScopedCache.makeWith(capacity = 10, scopedLookup = openConnection)(exit =>
    if (exit.isSuccess) 1.minute else 5.seconds
  )
```

### Using Scoped Values

The `ScopedCache#get` operator returns the cached value as a `ZIO[Scope, Error, Value]`. The `Scope` in its type tells the caller how long it uses the value. The cache counts each caller that holds the value, so the value stays alive until every caller's scope closes. A caller must not use the value after its scope closes.

To use a value for one operation, run `ScopedCache#get` inside `ZIO.scoped`, which opens a scope and closes it when the operation finishes:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{ScopedCache, ScopedLookup}

final case class Connection(url: String)

def query(cache: ScopedCache[String, Throwable, Connection], url: String): Task[Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    cache.get(url).flatMap { connection =>
      ZIO.debug(s"Running a query on ${connection.url}")
    }
  }
```

### Lifetime of Scoped Values

A resource is released only after two things are true. First, the value has left the cache, because it was evicted, invalidated, expired, or the cache itself was closed. Second, every caller that obtained the value through `get` has closed its scope.

Expired values are removed in two ways. A `ScopedCache#get` call on an expired key removes the old value before it computes a new one. A background fiber also checks the cache about every second and removes all expired values. Both paths release the resources of values that no caller uses.

If the lookup fails, the failure is cached, as with a plain [Cache](./cache.md). The failed lookup releases any resource it acquired before it failed.

### Operators

In addition to `ScopedCache#get`, `ScopedCache` provides these operators:

- `ScopedCache#refresh` computes a new value with the lookup function and replaces the cached one. Concurrent calls to `ScopedCache#get` keep using the old value until the new one is ready, and the old resource is released once no caller uses it.
- `invalidate` removes the value for a key from the cache. The resource is released after its last caller closes its scope.
- `invalidateAll` removes all values from the cache.
- `ScopedCache#contains` returns whether the cache holds a value for a key. As with `Cache#contains`, an expired value does not count, even before the background fiber removes it (see [Lifetime of Scoped Values](#lifetime-of-scoped-values)).
- `size` returns the approximate number of values in the cache. It counts expired values that the background fiber has not removed yet.
- `cacheStats` returns a snapshot of the cache statistics. See [Cache Statistics](./cache-statistics.md).
- `entryStats` returns the statistics of one entry. See [Entry Statistics](./entry-statistics.md).

The following example loads a connection, uses it, and then invalidates it, which releases the connection because no caller uses it anymore:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{ScopedCache, ScopedLookup}

final case class Connection(url: String)

object ScopedCacheExample extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val openConnection: ScopedLookup[String, Scope, Nothing, Connection] =
    ScopedLookup { (url: String) =>
      ZIO.acquireRelease(ZIO.debug(s"Opening connection to $url").as(Connection(url)))(connection =>
        ZIO.debug(s"Closing connection to ${connection.url}")
      )
    }

  def run =
    ZIO.scoped {
      for {
        cache <- ScopedCache.make(capacity = 10, timeToLive = 1.minute, lookup = openConnection)
        _ <- ZIO.scoped {
               cache.get("db-1").flatMap(connection => ZIO.debug(s"Using ${connection.url}"))
             }
        _ <- cache.invalidate("db-1")
      } yield ()
    }
}
```

## Tutorial: Your First Cache

Welcome to the ZIO Cache tutorial! This tutorial is for newcomers to ZIO who want to avoid repeating slow work. You need to know basic Scala syntax. You don't need any prior experience with caching or with ZIO Cache to follow along.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will understand:

- What a lookup function is, and how it describes the work a cache avoids repeating
- How to create a cache with `Cache.make`, including its capacity and time to live
- How `Cache#get` returns a stored value instead of computing it again
- How concurrent calls for the same key share one computation

We'll learn these concepts through:

1. A Slow Lookup
2. Creating a Cache
3. Getting a Value
4. Reading the Statistics
5. Concurrent Lookups Share One Computation
6. Invalidating a Value

We recommend reading from top to bottom, because each section builds on the previous one.

### 1. A Slow Lookup

Imagine a service that loads a user profile from a remote system. The call takes a long time, and the same user may be requested many times. The function below stands in for that remote call. It sleeps for 100 milliseconds to simulate the delay:

```scala
import zio._

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.sleep(100.millis).as(s"profile of $userId")
```

The function takes a `String` key and returns a `ZIO` effect:

- `IO[String, String]` means the effect can fail with a `String` error or succeed with a `String` value.
- `ZIO.sleep(100.millis)` simulates the slow remote call.
- `.as(...)` replaces the sleep's result with the profile text.

A function like this is what a cache needs. A cache does not know how to load a value by itself. It asks a lookup function for the value it does not have yet.

### 2. Creating a Cache

ZIO Cache wraps a lookup function in a `Lookup`. We pass the `Lookup`, a capacity, and a time to live to `Cache.make`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.sleep(100.millis).as(s"profile of $userId")

val cache: UIO[Cache[String, String, String]] =
  Cache.make(
    capacity = 10,
    timeToLive = 1.minute,
    lookup = Lookup(loadProfile)
  )
```

- `Lookup(loadProfile)` turns our function into a lookup function.
- `capacity = 10` lets the cache hold at most ten entries. When it is full, it evicts the least recently accessed one.
- `timeToLive = 1.minute` means a stored value expires once it is more than one minute old.
- `Cache.make` returns a `UIO` effect. Creating a cache cannot fail, so its error type is `Nothing`.

:::note
The cache's type is `Cache[String, String, String]`: the key type, the error type, and the value type. The environment type of the lookup is gone because `loadProfile` needs no environment.
:::

### 3. Getting a Value

`Cache#get` is the main operation. It returns the stored value when there is one. Otherwise it runs the lookup, stores the result, and returns it. We call `Cache#get` twice with the same key to see the difference:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.sleep(100.millis).as(s"profile of $userId")

val firstAndSecond: IO[String, (String, String)] =
  for {
    cache  <- Cache.make(capacity = 10, timeToLive = 1.minute, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))
    first  <- cache.get("alice") // runs loadProfile and stores the result
    second <- cache.get("alice") // returns the stored result without running loadProfile
  } yield (first, second)
```

The first call to `Cache#get` is slow because the lookup runs. The second call returns right away. Both calls return the same `"profile of alice"` value.

:::tip
Keep the cache in a `val` or a service and share it. A cache built inside every request starts empty each time, so it never gets a hit.
:::

### 4. Reading the Statistics

The cache counts hits and misses for us. A hit means a `Cache#get` call found a stored value. A miss means a `Cache#get` call ran the lookup. `Cache#cacheStats` reports these counts together with the current size:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.sleep(100.millis).as(s"profile of $userId")

val statistics: IO[String, (Long, Long, Int)] =
  for {
    cache <- Cache.make(capacity = 10, timeToLive = 1.minute, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))
    _     <- cache.get("alice")
    _     <- cache.get("alice")
    stats <- cache.cacheStats
  } yield (stats.hits, stats.misses, stats.size)
```

After the two calls above, the cache has one miss (the first call), one hit (the second call), and one stored value. The `statistics` value is `(1, 1, 1)`.

### 5. Concurrent Lookups Share One Computation

Several fibers may ask for the same key at the same time. ZIO Cache runs the lookup only once and gives the result to all of them. We start three concurrent calls for `"bob"`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.sleep(100.millis).as(s"profile of $userId")

val concurrent: IO[String, (List[String], Long, Long)] =
  for {
    cache   <- Cache.make(capacity = 10, timeToLive = 1.minute, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))
    results <- ZIO.foreachPar(List("bob", "bob", "bob"))(cache.get)
    stats   <- cache.cacheStats
  } yield (results, stats.hits, stats.misses)
```

All three calls return `"profile of bob"`. Only one of them is a miss, because the lookup ran once. The other two are hits, because they wait for the value that is already being computed. The result is `(List("profile of bob", "profile of bob", "profile of bob"), 2, 1)`.

### 6. Invalidating a Value

Sometimes we know a stored value is out of date. `Cache#invalidate` removes the value for one key, and `Cache#contains` tells us whether a value is stored for a key:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
  if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
  else ZIO.sleep(100.millis).as(s"profile of $userId")

val invalidation: IO[String, Boolean] =
  for {
    cache <- Cache.make(capacity = 10, timeToLive = 1.minute, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))
    _     <- cache.get("alice")
    _     <- cache.invalidate("alice")
    has   <- cache.contains("alice")
  } yield has
```

The `invalidation` value is `false`. The next `Cache#get` call for `"alice"` runs the lookup again.

### Putting It Together

This program combines the steps above into one runnable `ZIOAppDefault`. It creates one cache, calls `Cache#get` for a single key, reads the statistics, runs concurrent lookups, invalidates a key, and shows what a failed lookup returns:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cache.{Cache, Lookup}

object FirstCacheTutorial extends ZIOAppDefault {

  def loadProfile(userId: String): IO[String, String] =
    if (userId.isEmpty) ZIO.fail("user id must not be empty")
    else ZIO.sleep(100.millis).as(s"profile of $userId")

  def run =
    for {
      cache   <- Cache.make(capacity = 10, timeToLive = 1.minute, lookup = Lookup(loadProfile))
      first   <- cache.get("alice")
      _       <- ZIO.debug(s"first get: $first")
      second  <- cache.get("alice")
      _       <- ZIO.debug(s"second get: $second")
      stats   <- cache.cacheStats
      _       <- ZIO.debug(s"after alice: hits=${stats.hits} misses=${stats.misses} size=${stats.size}")
      results <- ZIO.foreachPar(List("bob", "bob", "bob"))(cache.get)
      _       <- ZIO.debug(s"concurrent results: $results")
      stats2  <- cache.cacheStats
      _       <- ZIO.debug(s"after bob: hits=${stats2.hits} misses=${stats2.misses} size=${stats2.size}")
      _       <- cache.invalidate("alice")
      has     <- cache.contains("alice")
      _       <- ZIO.debug(s"contains alice after invalidate: $has")
      failed  <- cache.get("").either
      _       <- ZIO.debug(s"empty id: $failed")
    } yield ()
}
```

Running this program prints the following lines:

```text
first get: profile of alice
second get: profile of alice
after alice: hits=1 misses=1 size=1
concurrent results: List(profile of bob, profile of bob, profile of bob)
after bob: hits=3 misses=2 size=2
contains alice after invalidate: false
empty id: Left(user id must not be empty)
```

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned:

- What a lookup function is, and how `Lookup` wraps it for a cache
- How to create a cache with `Cache.make`, choosing its capacity and time to live
- How `Cache#get` returns a stored value, and runs the lookup only when no value is stored
- How hits and misses appear in `Cache#cacheStats`
- How concurrent calls for the same key share one computation
- How `Cache#invalidate` and `Cache#contains` remove and check stored values

You now have a solid foundation for caching with ZIO Cache. The next step is to make the choices a real service needs, such as the right capacity and time to live.

### Where to Go Next

- **Ready to use this in practice?** Read [How to Choose Capacity and Time to Live](./how-to-choose-capacity-and-ttl.md) for guidance on sizing a cache.
- **Need a different expiry for each value?** Read [How to Set a Time to Live per Entry](./how-to-per-entry-ttl.md).
- **Want to dive deeper into the API?** Read the reference pages for [Cache](./cache.md), [Lookup](./lookup.md), and [Cache Statistics](./cache-statistics.md).
- **Caching resources that must be closed?** Read [Scoped Cache](./scoped-cache.md).

## Args

`Args[A]` describes the positional arguments of a command: the values a user types without a name, such as the repository URL in `git clone https://github.com/zio/zio-cli.git`. An `Args[A]` is a description, not a parsed value. It says which arguments the command accepts and how to build an `A` from them, and a [`Command`](commands.md) uses it to parse the user's input.

Arguments come after the command's [options](options.md). ZIO CLI stops reading options at the first token that is not an option, and a `--` token makes every later token an argument, even one that starts with `-`. [Options Come Before Arguments](parsing.md#options-come-before-arguments) describes the order in detail.

### Constructors

The `Args` companion object has one constructor per value type, plus constructors for enumerations, paths and commands without arguments.

#### Value Arguments

Each value type has a named and an unnamed constructor. The named form takes the name shown in the help, and the unnamed form uses the value type's placeholder as its name. `Args.localDate` is the only constructor without an unnamed form.

To declare a named integer argument and an unnamed one:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val count: Args[BigInt]    = Args.integer("count") // shown as <count>
val anyNumber: Args[BigInt] = Args.integer         // shown as <integer>
```

The value types and their constructors are `Args.text`, `Args.integer`, `Args.decimal`, `Args.bool`, `Args.duration`, `Args.instant`, `Args.localDate`, `Args.localDateTime`, `Args.localTime`, `Args.monthDay`, `Args.offsetDateTime`, `Args.offsetTime`, `Args.period`, `Args.year`, `Args.yearMonth`, `Args.zonedDateTime`, `Args.zoneId` and `Args.zoneOffset`. [Value Types](value-types.md) lists the Scala type, the placeholder and the accepted input of each one.

A value that cannot be converted fails with the value type's message, such as `ten is not a integer.`. A missing argument fails with `Missing argument <count>.`.

#### Enumeration Arguments

`Args.enumeration` accepts one of a fixed set of words. Each case is a pair of the word the user types and the value it stands for. `Args.enumeration(name)(cases*)` names the argument, and `Args.enumeration(cases*)` uses `choice` as the name.

To accept one of three log levels:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val level: Args[Int] = Args.enumeration("level")(("debug", 0), ("info", 1), ("warn", 2))
```

The word must match exactly, including its case. Any other word fails with `Expected one of the following cases: debug, info, warn`.

#### Path Arguments

`Args.file`, `Args.directory` and `Args.path` produce a `java.nio.file.Path`. `Args.file` and `Args.directory` take an `Exists` value that says whether the path must exist, and each has three forms: `(name, exists)`, `(exists)` without a name, and the unnamed value with `Exists.Either`. `Args.path(name)` and `Args.path` accept a file or a directory, existing or not.

To require an existing file and accept any directory:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val source = Args.file("source", exists = Exists.Yes)
val target = Args.directory("target")
```

An existing path must also be of the right kind: `Args.file` rejects an existing directory, and `Args.directory` rejects an existing file. These constructors are not available on Scala.js. [Paths](value-types.md#paths) and [Platform Support](value-types.md#platform-support) give the full rules.

#### No Arguments

`Args.none` is an `Args[Unit]` that consumes no input. A command built without arguments uses it, and it disappears from the command's value.

To declare a command that takes no arguments:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val status: Command[Boolean] = Command("status", Options.boolean("short"), Args.none)
```

#### Arguments From a PrimType

`Args.Single(pseudoName, primType, description)` wraps any `PrimType` directly. You rarely need it; it is for a value type that no constructor offers, such as a path that must exist but may be a file or a directory. [Custom Parameters From a PrimType](value-types.md#custom-parameters-from-a-primtype) shows an example.

### Methods

The `Args` trait has the following public methods:

```scala
sealed trait Args[+A] {
  def ++[B](that: Args[B])(implicit zippable: Zippable[A, B]): Args[zippable.Out]

  def * : Args[List[A]]
  def +[A1 >: A]: Args[::[A1]]
  def repeat: Args[List[A]]
  def repeat1[A1 >: A]: Args[::[A1]]
  def atLeast(min: Int): Args[List[A]]
  def atMost(max: Int): Args[List[A]]
  def between(min: Int, max: Int): Args[List[A]]

  def map[B](f: A => B): Args[B]
  def mapOrFail[B](f: A => Either[HelpDoc, B]): Args[B]
  def mapTry[B](f: A => B): Args[B]

  def ??(that: String): Args[A]

  def helpDoc: HelpDoc
  def synopsis: UsageSynopsis
  def minSize: Int
  def maxSize: Int
  def uid: Option[String]
  def validate(args: List[String], conf: CliConfig): IO[ValidationError, (List[String], A)]
}
```

`Args` has no `optional` or `withDefault`. To make an argument optional, accept at most one value with `Args#atMost` and take the first one with `Args#map`, as in `Args.text("name").atMost(1).map(_.headOption)`.

#### Combining Arguments With ++

A command takes a single `Args` value, so we combine several arguments into one with `Args#++`. The arguments are read in the order they are combined. The result is a flat tuple: `a ++ b ++ c` is an `Args[(A, B, C)]`, not a nested pair, and `Unit` values such as `Args.none` disappear from it.

To combine the two arguments of `git clone`:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val cloneArgs: Args[(String, String)] = Args.text("repository") ++ Args.text("directory")
```

The usage line of a command with these arguments shows them in order, as `<repository> <directory>`.

#### Repeating Arguments

These methods turn an argument into a list of arguments of the same type:

- `Args#*` (and its alias `Args#repeat`) accepts zero or more values.
- `Args#+` (and its alias `Args#repeat1`) accepts one or more values and returns a non-empty list, `::[A]`.
- `Args#atLeast(min)` accepts `min` or more values.
- `Args#atMost(max)` accepts up to `max` values.
- `Args#between(min, max)` accepts from `min` to `max` values.

To accept one or more file names, and between two and five numbers:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val files: Args[::[String]]       = Args.text("file").+
val numbers: Args[List[BigInt]]   = Args.integer("n").between(2, 5)
```

The help names the repetition rule, and the usage line shows the argument followed by `...`:

```scala
println(numbers.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// <n> 2 - 5
//   An integer.
// 
//   This argument must be repeated at least 2 times and may be repeated up to 5 times.
// 
//
```

`Args#*`, `Args#+` and `Args#atLeast` are greedy: they take every remaining token. An argument combined after them never receives a value, so a required one fails with `Missing argument <name>.`. If a remaining token is not a valid value, the command fails with that value's error; the token is not left for a later argument. `Args#atMost` and `Args#between` stop at their maximum, so another argument can follow them once that many values are given. With fewer values, a remaining token that is not valid for the repeated argument fails the command instead of going to the next argument.

:::caution
Tokens left over after the last argument is filled are ignored, without an error. With `Args.text("name")`, the input `alice bob` gives `"alice"`, and `bob` is dropped; see [Leftover Words](parsing.md#leftover-words).
:::

#### Transforming Values

`Args#map` converts the parsed value with a function that cannot fail. To turn a text argument into an upper-case name:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val shout: Args[String] = Args.text("name").map(_.toUpperCase)
```

`Args#mapOrFail` converts the value with a function that may reject it. The function returns `Right` with the new value, or `Left` with a `HelpDoc` that is shown to the user. To accept only positive counts:

```scala
val positive: Args[Int] =
  Args.integer("count").mapOrFail { (n: BigInt) =>
    if (n > 0) Right(n.toInt) else Left(HelpDoc.p("The count must be positive."))
  }
```

`Args#mapTry` converts the value with a function that may throw. An exception becomes a validation error whose text is the exception's message. To parse a URI:

```scala
val uri: Args[java.net.URI] = Args.text("uri").mapTry(java.net.URI.create)
```

With the input `not a uri`, the user sees `Illegal character in path at index 3: not a uri`. [How to validate and convert a parameter's value](how-to-validate-input.md) compares these methods with their `Options` counterparts.

#### Adding Help With ??

`Args#??` appends a paragraph to the help of an argument. To describe the repository argument:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val repository = Args.text("repository") ?? "The repository to clone."
```

The help shows the description after the sentence for the value type:

```scala
println(repository.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// <repository>
//   A user-defined piece of text.
// 
//   The repository to clone.
// 
//
```

On arguments combined with `Args#++`, `Args#??` appends the same paragraph to every argument, so call it on each argument before combining them.

#### Inspecting an Args

`Args#helpDoc` returns the help as a [`HelpDoc`](helpdoc.md), and `Args#synopsis` returns the usage line. `Args#minSize` and `Args#maxSize` give the number of tokens the arguments accept, and `Args#uid` returns their names, such as `<repository>, <directory>`. `Args#validate` parses a list of tokens and returns the leftover tokens with the value; tests use it to check an `Args` without building a command.

### How Args Are Represented

`Args` is a sealed trait. Its cases are `Args.Empty` (the result of `Args.none`), `Args.Single` (one argument), `Args.Both` (the result of `Args#++`), `Args.Variadic` (the result of `Args#*`, `Args#+`, `Args#atLeast`, `Args#atMost` and `Args#between`) and `Args.Map` (the result of `Args#map` and the methods built on it). They are public, but you build arguments with the constructors and methods above instead of constructing the cases yourself.

---

## Authorization with OAuth2

`Options.oauth2` lets a command-line application act on behalf of a user of a web service such as GitHub. It adds OAuth2 authorization to a command: the first run asks the user to approve the application in a browser, and every run gives the command an access token for the service's API. The types live in the `zio.cli.oauth2` package.

ZIO CLI obtains the token with the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant, defined in [RFC 8628](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628). The program prints a web address and a short code, the user opens the address in any browser and enters the code, and the program polls the service until the user approves. The token is saved in a file, so later runs do not ask again. ZIO CLI does not call the service's API for you: your command sends the token with its own requests.

OAuth2 support exists only on the JVM. [How to log users in with OAuth2](how-to-oauth2-login.md) walks through adding a login to an application and writing a provider for another service.

### Adding OAuth2 to a Command

`Options.oauth2` takes the provider of the service and the list of scopes to request, and returns an `Options[OAuth2Token]`:

```scala
object Options {
  def oauth2(provider: OAuth2Provider, scope: List[String]): Options[OAuth2Token]
}
```

The result combines with other options like any `Options` value, as described in [Options](options.md). We require GitHub authorization with the `read:user` scope in a `stars` command that also takes a flag:

```scala
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.oauth2._

val clientId = "Iv1.0123456789abcdef"

val github: Options[OAuth2Token] = Options.oauth2(OAuth2Provider.Github(clientId), List("read:user"))

val stars: Command[(OAuth2Token, Boolean)] = Command("stars", github ++ Options.boolean("verbose"))
```

`Options.oauth2` adds one option, `--oauth2-file <file>`, which sets the file that stores the token. It is optional. It also adds a section about the authorization to the help output. For an application named `gh-stars`, `--help` prints the following after the banner, on a machine where the home directory is `/home/user`:

```text
gh-stars 1.0.0 -- Lists your starred repositories

USAGE

  $ gh-stars [--oauth2-file <file>]

OPTIONS

  --oauth2-file <file>
    A file.

    File in which OAuth2 access token will be stored.

    This setting is optional. Default: '/home/user/oauth2_github_Iv1.0123456789abcdef_access_token.json'.

3RD PARTY AUTHORIZATION

  This application requires 3rd party authorization (using OAuth2 protocol)
  provided by Github. When the application is launched for the first time,
  instructions to perform the authorization will be displayed. Subsequent launches
  do not require any action unless the access has been revoked.

  Behavior of 3rd party authorization can be modified by options starting with '--oauth2-'.
```

### When Authorization Happens

The token is obtained while the command line is parsed, before your command's function runs. Parsing the OAuth2 option does the following:

1. It reads the token file. If the file holds a token that has not expired, the command gets that token.
2. If the stored token has expired, it is refreshed. The refresh uses the refresh token when the service issued one, and otherwise runs the authorization again.
3. If the file is missing or cannot be decoded, the authorization runs.
4. A new or refreshed token is written to the file.

The built-in options `--help` and the shell-completion options are handled before the command's own options, so they never start an authorization. `--wizard` starts it only when it runs the command line that the wizard built.

When the authorization fails, for example because the user denies access, the code expires or the service returns an error, the error message becomes a `ValidationError` of type `InvalidValue`.
