The `CliApp` prints the message and fails with `CliError.Parsing`, the same way as for invalid input. [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md) describes these types.

### The Device Authorization Flow

When the authorization runs, ZIO CLI talks to the service in three steps:

```text
CLI                                   Service                       User's browser
 |-- authorization request ------------>|                                 |
 |<-- device code, user code, URL ------|                                 |
 |   prints URL and user code, "Waiting..."                               |
 |                                      |<-- user opens URL, enters code -|
 |-- access token request (polling) --->|                                 |
 |<-- authorization_pending ... token --|                                 |
 |   saves the token to the file                                          |
```

The first request asks the service for a device code, a user code and a verification address. The program prints the address and the user code in a box, with the number of minutes until the code expires, followed by `Waiting...`.

The program then sends the access token request repeatedly. It waits the interval given by the service between requests, or 5 seconds when the service gives none. A `slow_down` answer makes every later wait longer by the interval in the answer, or by 5 seconds. Polling stops when the service returns a token, when it returns an error other than `authorization_pending` or `slow_down`, or when the lifetime of the device code has passed.

### Providers

An `OAuth2Provider` describes how to talk to one service. Three providers are included, each a case class in the `OAuth2Provider` companion object:

| Provider                                        | Parameters from the service's developer console | Scope separator | Sends refresh requests |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ---------------------- |
| `OAuth2Provider.Github(clientId)`               | The client ID of an OAuth app                   | `,`             | Yes                    |
| `OAuth2Provider.Google(clientId, clientSecret)` | The client ID and client secret                 | space           | Yes                    |
| `OAuth2Provider.Facebook(appId, clientToken)`   | The app ID and client token                     | `,`             | No                     |

The service must allow the device flow for the registered application. On GitHub, enable the device flow in the settings of the OAuth app. On Google, create an OAuth client of type "TVs and Limited Input devices". On Facebook, enable the device login option in the Facebook Login settings of the app.

We create one option per provider. Google requires at least one scope, so its example requests the `openid` and `email` scopes:

```scala
val githubLogin: Options[OAuth2Token] =
  Options.oauth2(OAuth2Provider.Github("github-client-id"), List("repo"))

val googleLogin: Options[OAuth2Token] =
  Options.oauth2(OAuth2Provider.Google("google-client-id", "google-client-secret"), List("openid", "email"))

val facebookLogin: Options[OAuth2Token] =
  Options.oauth2(OAuth2Provider.Facebook("facebook-app-id", "facebook-client-token"), List("public_profile"))
```

A provider for any other service that supports the device flow is a class that extends `OAuth2Provider`, as described in [Custom Providers](#custom-providers).

### Token Storage

The token is stored as JSON in a file in the user's home directory. The file name is `oauth2_<provider>_<client>_access_token.json`, where `<provider>` is the lower-case name of the provider, such as `github`, and `<client>` is its client identifier: the client ID for GitHub and Google, the app ID for Facebook. The `--oauth2-file <path>` option sets another file.

The file holds the access token, its type, its expiry time, the refresh token and the granted scopes, in plain text. Anyone who can read the file can use the token, so protect it like a password. Deleting the file makes the next run ask for authorization again.

### Using the Token

The command receives an `OAuth2Token`, which gives access to the current access token:

```scala
trait OAuth2Token {
  def accessToken: Task[AccessToken]
  def refreshTokenNow: Task[Unit]
}
```

`OAuth2Token#accessToken` returns the current token. If the token has expired, it is refreshed first, with the refresh token when there is one and otherwise by running the authorization again. `OAuth2Token#refreshTokenNow` refreshes the token immediately. Call it when the service rejects a token before its expiry time, for example because the user revoked it, which ZIO CLI cannot detect.

`AccessToken` is a case class with these fields:

```scala
final case class AccessToken(
  accessToken: String,
  tokenType: TokenType,
  expiresAt: Option[OffsetDateTime],
  refreshToken: Option[String],
  scope: List[String]
)
```

- `AccessToken#accessToken` is the token string to send to the API. Treat it as a secret and do not print it.
- `AccessToken#tokenType` says how the token must be sent.
- `AccessToken#expiresAt` is the expiry time, or `None` when the service gave no lifetime. A token without an expiry time is never refreshed automatically.
- `AccessToken#refreshToken` is the refresh token, when the service issued one.
- `AccessToken#scope` is the list of scopes the service reported as granted.

`TokenType` has three cases: `TokenType.Bearer`, `TokenType.Mac` and `TokenType.Other(tokenType)`, which keeps any other value as the service sent it.

:::caution
`TokenType.Bearer` and `TokenType.Mac` match only the lower-case strings `bearer` and `mac`. A service that sends `Bearer`, as Google does, produces `TokenType.Other("Bearer")`. Compare the type case-insensitively.
:::

We print the type of the GitHub token without printing the token itself:

```scala
import zio._

val tokenType = Command("token-type", Options.oauth2(OAuth2Provider.Github("github-client-id"), List("read:user")))

val tokenTypeApp = CliApp.make(
  name = "token-type",
  version = "1.0.0",
  summary = HelpDoc.Span.text("Shows the type of the GitHub token"),
  command = tokenType
) { (token: OAuth2Token) =>
  for {
    current <- token.accessToken
    isBearer = current.tokenType match {
                 case TokenType.Bearer       => true
                 case TokenType.Other(other) => other.equalsIgnoreCase("bearer")
                 case TokenType.Mac          => false
               }
    _ <- Console.printLine(s"Bearer token: $isBearer")
  } yield ()
}
```

### Custom Providers

To support another service, extend the `OAuth2Provider` trait. The service must support the device authorization flow, and the provider builds the HTTP requests of that flow with the JDK's `java.net.http.HttpRequest`:

```scala
trait OAuth2Provider {
  def name: String
  def clientIdentifier: String
  def authorizationRequest(scope: List[String]): HttpRequest
  def accessTokenRequest(authorization: AuthorizationResponse): HttpRequest
  def refreshTokenRequest(refreshToken: String): Option[HttpRequest]
  def decodeAuthorizationResponse(body: String): Either[String, AuthorizationResponse]
  def decodeAccessTokenResponse(body: String): Either[String, AccessTokenResponse]
}
```

| Member                                       | What it does                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OAuth2Provider#name`                        | The name shown in the help output. Its lower-case form is part of the default token file name.                  |
| `OAuth2Provider#clientIdentifier`            | The public client ID. It is part of the default token file name.                                                |
| `OAuth2Provider#authorizationRequest`        | Builds the request for a device code, with the requested scopes.                                                |
| `OAuth2Provider#accessTokenRequest`          | Builds the polling request for the token, from the device code in the `AuthorizationResponse`.                  |
| `OAuth2Provider#refreshTokenRequest`         | Builds the request that exchanges a refresh token for a new token, or returns `None` when the service has none. |
| `OAuth2Provider#decodeAuthorizationResponse` | Decodes the answer to the device-code request. The default reads the standard JSON of RFC 8628.                 |
| `OAuth2Provider#decodeAccessTokenResponse`   | Decodes each answer to the token request. The default reads the standard JSON of RFC 6749.                      |

The first five members are abstract. Override the two decoders only when the service does not answer with the standard JSON fields. The device-code request must answer with HTTP status 200, and so must a refresh request. Answers to the polling request are decoded whatever their status.

`AuthorizationResponse` is the decoded answer to the device-code request:

```scala
final case class AuthorizationResponse(
  deviceCode: String,
  userCode: String,
  verificationUri: String,
  verificationUriComplete: Option[String],
  expiresIn: Duration,
  interval: Duration
)
```

`deviceCode` is the value to send back in `OAuth2Provider#accessTokenRequest`. `userCode` and `verificationUri` are shown to the user. `expiresIn` is how long the codes are valid, and `interval` is the wait between polling requests, 5 seconds when the JSON has no `interval` field.

`AccessTokenResponse` is the decoded answer to a token request, and has two cases. `AccessTokenResponse.AccessToken(accessToken, tokenType, expiresIn, refreshToken, scope)` is a granted token, with its lifetime as a `Duration`. `AccessTokenResponse.Error(error, errorDescription, errorUri, interval)` is an error answer. Its `error` is an `AccessTokenResponse.Error.Kind`: `AuthorizationPending` and `SlowDown` keep the polling going, and every other kind ends it. The other kinds are `InvalidRequest`, `InvalidClient`, `InvalidGrant`, `UnauthorizedClient`, `UnsupportedGrantType`, `InvalidScope`, `AccessDenied`, `ExpiredToken` and `Other(code)`.

[How to log users in with OAuth2](how-to-oauth2-login.md) shows a complete custom provider.

### Platform Support

`Options.oauth2` is defined only in the JVM build of ZIO CLI. On Scala.js and Scala Native, code that calls it does not compile.

---

## Bash Completion

Every `CliApp` supports Tab completion in bash without extra code. The application gets three built-in options that generate a completion script and answer completion requests from the shell. The design follows the Haskell library [optparse-applicative](https://github.com/pcapriotti/optparse-applicative#bash-zsh-and-fish-completions).

Only bash is supported. The `zsh` value of `--shell-type` exists, but no zsh script generator is implemented. [How to add Tab completion in bash](how-to-add-shell-completion.md) walks through installing the script for an application.

### Built-in Options

The three options are recognized by the parser of every `CliApp`, next to `--help` and `--wizard`, which [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) describes. They are not listed in the help output:

| Option                      | Value                  | Purpose                                                              |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--shell-completion-script` | Path to the executable | Asks for the completion script. The path is written into the script. |
| `--shell-type`              | `bash`, `sh` or `zsh`  | Selects the shell. `sh` is another name for `bash`.                  |
| `--shell-completion-index`  | Integer                | Asks for the completions of the word at this position.               |

The options work in two combinations. `--shell-completion-script <path> --shell-type bash` prints the completion script. `--shell-type bash --shell-completion-index <n>` prints the completions for one Tab press, one per line. Any other combination is not a built-in request, so the input is parsed as a normal command line.

:::caution
`--shell-completion-script <path> --shell-type zsh` is not implemented. The program stops with a `scala.NotImplementedError` instead of printing a script. Use `--shell-type bash`.
:::

### The Completion Script

For an application whose top-level command is named `greet`, the following command line prints the script:

```bash
greet --shell-completion-script /usr/local/bin/greet --shell-type bash
```

The output is:

```bash
#/usr/bin/env bash
_greet()
{
  local CMDLINE
  local IFS=$'\n'
  CMDLINE=(--shell-type bash --shell-completion-index $COMP_CWORD)
  
  INDEX=0
  for arg in ${COMP_WORDS[@]}; do
    export COMP_WORD_$INDEX=${arg}
    (( INDEX++ ))
  done

  COMPREPLY=( $(/usr/local/bin/greet "${CMDLINE[@]}") )

  # Unset the environment variables.
  unset $(compgen -v | grep "^COMP_WORD_")
}

complete -F _greet greet
```

The script defines a function named after the first top-level command name and registers it with `complete -F` for every top-level command name. The `name` of the `CliApp` is used only when the command has no name of its own. The name of the executable file plays no part in the registration: bash calls the function only when the first word on the line is a command name. The path passed to `--shell-completion-script` is the program that the function runs, so pass the path where users run the installed executable. A path that contains spaces breaks the generated script, because the script does not quote it.

The first line of the script is a comment, not a shebang. Load the script with `source` or install it in a bash completion directory instead of running it.

### How a Completion Request Works

Each time the user presses Tab after a registered command name, the function in the script runs the executable again. It passes the words typed so far in the environment variables `COMP_WORD_0`, `COMP_WORD_1` and so on, and the position of the cursor word with `--shell-completion-index`.

When the user types `greet foo bar baz`, moves the cursor over `foo` and presses Tab, the function runs the executable with these variables and arguments:

```bash
COMP_WORD_0=greet          \
COMP_WORD_1=foo            \
COMP_WORD_2=bar            \
COMP_WORD_3=baz            \
/usr/local/bin/greet       \
--shell-type bash          \
--shell-completion-index 1
```

The application reads the `COMP_WORD_` variables, matches the words before the cursor against its `Command`, and prints every possible next word that starts with the word under the cursor. Bash reads these lines and shows them as candidates.

The `COMP_WORD_` names come from the `COMP_WORDS` array of bash's [programmable completion](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Programmable-Completion.html). An array cannot be passed as an environment variable, so each word gets its own variable.

### What Gets Completed

Completion follows the same grammar that the parser uses. The first word is not checked, so a completion request works under any program name. The other words complete as follows:

| Position                    | Candidates                                                          |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Subcommand name             | The names of the subcommands that can follow                        |
| Option name                 | The names and aliases of options not given yet                      |
| Value of an enumeration     | The case names given to `Options.enumeration` or `Args.enumeration` |
| Value of a boolean argument | `true` and `false`                                                  |
| Value of a `ZoneId`         | Time-zone IDs that start with the typed text                        |
| Path to a file              | File and directory names, on the JVM only                           |
| Path to a directory         | Directory names, on the JVM only                                    |
| Any other value             | Nothing                                                             |

A finished word ends with a space, so the cursor moves on to the next word. A directory name ends with `/` and no space, so Tab can be pressed again to go deeper. The built-in options themselves are not offered.

Path completion runs bash's `compgen` command in a child process. Scala.js and Scala Native builds do not run it, so path values get no candidates there. A GraalVM native image is built from the JVM artifact and uses the JVM implementation.

### Testing Completions

`Completion.complete` in the `zio.cli.completion` package computes completions without a shell. It takes the words of the line, the index of the word to complete, the command and the configuration:

```scala
object Completion {
  def complete(
    words: List[String],
    index: Int,
    command: Command[Any],
    cliConfig: CliConfig,
    compgen: Compgen = Compgen.live
  ): UIO[List[String]]
}
```

We define a command with a flag, an enumeration and an integer, and a helper that runs `Completion.complete`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.completion.Completion

val files: Command[(Boolean, String, Option[BigInt])] =
  Command(
    "files",
    Options.boolean("verbose").alias("v") ++
      Options.enumeration("format")("json" -> "json", "text" -> "text") ++
      Options.integer("depth").optional
  )

def complete(words: List[String], index: Int): List[String] =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(Completion.complete(words, index, files, CliConfig.default)).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

After the command name, every option is a candidate. After `--format`, the cases of the enumeration are. After `--depth`, an integer, nothing is:

```scala
complete(List("files", ""), 1)
// res1: List[String] = List("--depth ", "--format ", "--verbose ", "-v ")
complete(List("files", "--f"), 1)
// res2: List[String] = List("--format ")
complete(List("files", "--format", ""), 2)
// res3: List[String] = List("json ", "text ")
complete(List("files", "--depth", ""), 2)
// res4: List[String] = List()
complete(List("files", "-v", ""), 2)
// res5: List[String] = List("--depth ", "--format ")
```

`Compgen` is the service that lists file and directory names. On the JVM, `Compgen.live` runs `compgen` in the current directory, and `Compgen.test(workingDirectory)` runs it in the given directory, which keeps a test independent of where it runs. On Scala.js and Scala Native, `Compgen` returns no names.

### Platform Support

Completion of commands, options and values works on every platform. Only path completion needs the JVM:

| Feature                                  | JVM | Scala.js | Scala Native |
| ---------------------------------------- | --- | -------- | ------------ |
| Completion script and requests           | Yes | Yes      | Yes          |
| Commands, options, enumerations, ZoneIds | Yes | Yes      | Yes          |
| File and directory paths                 | Yes | No       | No           |

The sbt plugin declares `zioCliGenerateBashCompletion` and `zioCliGenerateZshCompletion` tasks, which only print `TODO: Not Implemented!`. See [sbt plugin](sbt-plugin.md). Generate the script with the built-in options instead.

---

## Built-in Commands

Every command built with zio-cli accepts a few options that you do not declare yourself. They show the help, start the interactive wizard, and support shell completion. `CliApp#run` handles them before your `execute` function would run, so `execute` never sees them.

The built-in options are:

| Option                             | Value                  | What it does                                                                           | Result of `CliApp#run`                       |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `--help`, `-h`                     | none                   | Prints the help of the command.                                                        | `None`                                       |
| `--wizard`                         | none                   | Starts [wizard mode](wizard.md), which asks for each value and then runs the command.  | The result of the command, or `None` on quit |
| `-w`                               | none                   | Starts wizard mode, but only when the rest of the input is invalid.                    | Same as `--wizard`                           |
| `--shell-completion-script <path>` | path of the executable | Prints a Bash completion script that calls `<path>`. Needs `--shell-type`.             | `None`                                       |
| `--shell-completion-index <n>`     | integer                | Prints the completions for word `n` of the line being completed. Needs `--shell-type`. | `None`                                       |
| `--shell-type <type>`              | `sh`, `bash` or `zsh`  | Selects the shell for the two completion options. `sh` is the same as `bash`.          | none on its own                              |

There is no built-in `--version` option, and the help does not list the built-in options.

When `Command#parse` sees a built-in option, it returns `CommandDirective.BuiltIn` holding one of these cases:

```scala
sealed trait BuiltInOption
object BuiltInOption {
  final case class ShowHelp(synopsis: UsageSynopsis, helpDoc: HelpDoc) extends BuiltInOption
  final case class ShowCompletionScript(pathToExecutable: java.nio.file.Path, shellType: ShellType) extends BuiltInOption
  final case class ShowCompletions(index: Int, shellType: ShellType) extends BuiltInOption
  final case class ShowWizard(command: Command[_]) extends BuiltInOption
}
```

`ShellType` is a sealed trait with two cases, `ShellType.Bash` and `ShellType.ZShell`. `ShellType.option` is the `Options[ShellType]` behind `--shell-type`: it maps `sh` and `bash` to `ShellType.Bash`, and `zsh` to `ShellType.ZShell`.

### How Built-in Options Are Matched

zio-cli looks for built-in options after the name of the top-level command and after the name of each subcommand. The following rules decide which one runs:

- The built-in options must be the only words after the command name. `greet --help` shows the help, while `greet --help Ada` is parsed as a normal command, so for a command with a text argument the argument becomes `--help`.
- When several built-in options are given, `--help` wins over `--wizard`, `--wizard` wins over `--shell-completion-script`, and `--shell-completion-script` wins over `--shell-completion-index`.
- When the input does not parse but contains `--help`, `-h`, `--wizard` or `-w` anywhere, zio-cli shows the help or starts the wizard instead of printing the error. [`CliConfig#finalCheckBuiltIn`](cli-config.md#final-built-in-check) turns this fallback off.

### Help

`--help` and `-h` print a banner, a header line with the app's name, version and summary, the usage line, and the help of the command. The examples on this page use a small Git-like app:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text

val git: Command[Any] =
  Command("git")
    .withHelp("A tiny version control tool.")
    .subcommands(
      Command("add", Args.file("path")).withHelp("Stages a file."),
      Command("clone", Options.boolean("quiet").alias("q"), Args.text("repository")).withHelp("Copies a repository.")
    )

val gitApp: CliApp[Any, java.io.IOException, Unit] =
  CliApp.make("git", "0.1.0", text("A tiny version control tool"), git)(value => Console.printLine(s"Got $value"))

// Prints the help of the app, the same as running it with no subcommand.
val rootHelp = gitApp.run(List("--help"))

// Prints the help of the add subcommand.
val addHelp = gitApp.run(List("add", "-h"))
```

For `rootHelp`, the parent's help lists the subcommands:

```text
          _ __
   ____ _(_) /_
  / __ `/ / __/
 / /_/ / / /_
 \__, /_/\__/
/____/

git 0.1.0 -- A tiny version control tool

USAGE

  $ git <command>

DESCRIPTION

  A tiny version control tool.

COMMANDS

  - add <path>                          Stages a file.
  - clone [(-q, --quiet)] <repository>  Copies a repository.
```

For `addHelp`, the usage line starts with the parent's name, and the help shows the subcommand's own sections:

```text
          _ __
   ____ _(_) /_
  / __ `/ / __/
 / /_/ / / /_
 \__, /_/\__/
/____/

git 0.1.0 -- A tiny version control tool

USAGE

  $ git add <path>

DESCRIPTION

  Stages a file.

ARGUMENTS

  <path>
    A file.
```

:::caution
`--help` and `-h` after any subcommand except the first one show the help of the first subcommand, as described in [Subcommands](commands.md#subcommands). Point users to `git --help`, which lists every subcommand with its usage.
:::

### Wizard

`--wizard` starts an interactive session that asks for the subcommand and for each option and argument, prints the equivalent command line, and runs it. `-w` starts the same session through the fallback described above. [Wizard Mode](wizard.md) describes the session in detail.

### Shell Completion

Two built-in options support Bash completion. Both need `--shell-type`:

- `--shell-completion-script <path> --shell-type bash` prints a Bash script that registers completion for the command's names. `<path>` is the executable that the script calls on each Tab press.
- `--shell-completion-index <n> --shell-type bash` prints the possible completions of word `n`, one per line. It reads the words typed so far from the environment variables `COMP_WORD_0`, `COMP_WORD_1`, and so on. The generated script calls the program this way.

For `gitApp`, `--shell-completion-script /usr/local/bin/git --shell-type bash` prints:

```text
#/usr/bin/env bash
_git()
{
  local CMDLINE
  local IFS=$'\n'
  CMDLINE=(--shell-type bash --shell-completion-index $COMP_CWORD)
  
  INDEX=0
  for arg in ${COMP_WORDS[@]}; do
    export COMP_WORD_$INDEX=${arg}
    (( INDEX++ ))
  done

  COMPREPLY=( $(/usr/local/bin/git "${CMDLINE[@]}") )

  # Unset the environment variables.
  unset $(compgen -v | grep "^COMP_WORD_")
}

complete -F _git git
```

:::caution
`--shell-type zsh` with `--shell-completion-script` is not implemented and stops with a `NotImplementedError`; see [Bash Completion](bash-and-zsh-completion.md). With `--shell-completion-index`, the shell type is ignored, so `zsh` behaves like `bash`.
:::

[Bash Completion](bash-and-zsh-completion.md) explains how zio-cli computes completions, and [How to add Tab completion in bash](how-to-add-shell-completion.md) shows how to install the script.

---

## CliApp and Running a CLI

A `CliApp[R, E, A]` is a complete command-line application. It holds the program's name, version and summary, the [`Command`](commands.md) that describes what the user may type, and the function that runs once the input is parsed. It needs an environment `R`, can fail with an error of type `E`, and produces a value of type `A`.

We build a `CliApp` with `CliApp.make`, run it with `CliApp#run`, and, for a stand-alone program, wrap it in `ZIOCliDefault`:

```scala
sealed trait CliApp[-R, +E, +A] {
  def run(args: List[String]): ZIO[R, CliError[E], Option[A]]
  def config(newConfig: CliConfig): CliApp[R, E, A]
  def map[B](f: A => B): CliApp[R, E, B]
  def flatMap[R1 <: R, E1 >: E, B](f: A => ZIO[R1, E1, B]): CliApp[R1, E1, B]
  def footer(newFooter: HelpDoc): CliApp[R, E, A]
  def summary(s: HelpDoc.Span): CliApp[R, E, A]
}
```

### Building a CliApp With CliApp.make

`CliApp.make` takes the description of the app in its first parameter list and the function that runs the command in its second:

```scala
object CliApp {
  def make[R, E, Model, A](
    name: String,
    version: String,
    summary: HelpDoc.Span,
    command: Command[Model],
    footer: HelpDoc = HelpDoc.Empty,
    config: CliConfig = CliConfig.default,
    figFont: FigFont = FigFont.Default
  )(execute: Model => ZIO[R, E, A]): CliApp[R, E, A]
}
```

The following app greets the name given with `--name`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text

val nameOpt: Options[String] = Options.text("name").withDefault("world") ?? "Who to greet."
val greet: Command[String]   = Command("greet", nameOpt).withHelp("Prints a greeting.")

val greetApp: CliApp[Any, java.io.IOException, Unit] = CliApp.make(
  name = "greet",
  version = "1.0.0",
  summary = text("Prints a greeting"),
  command = greet,
  footer = HelpDoc.p("Example footer text.")
)(name => Console.printLine(s"Hello, $name!"))
```

Each parameter of `CliApp.make` has the following meaning:

| Parameter | Type                    | Default             | What it does                                                                                                            |
| --------- | ----------------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`    | `String`                | none                | The program name. It is drawn as the banner and starts the header line of the help; the wizard header also contains it. |
| `version` | `String`                | none                | The version string, shown after the name in the header line.                                                            |
| `summary` | `HelpDoc.Span`          | none                | A one-line description, shown after `--` in the header line.                                                            |
| `command` | `Command[Model]`        | none                | The grammar of valid input. The value it parses is the `Model` passed to `execute`. See [Commands](commands.md).        |
| `footer`  | `HelpDoc`               | `HelpDoc.Empty`     | Text printed at the end of the help.                                                                                    |
| `config`  | `CliConfig`             | `CliConfig.default` | Parsing and help settings, such as case sensitivity and auto-correction. See [CLI Configuration](cli-config.md).        |
| `figFont` | `FigFont`               | `FigFont.Default`   | The font used to draw the name as a banner. See [Figlet banners](figlet.md).                                            |
| `execute` | `Model => ZIO[R, E, A]` | none                | The second parameter list. It runs with the parsed value of the command.                                                |

### The Help Screen

`--help` prints the banner, a header line with the name, version and summary, the `USAGE` section, the help of the command and the footer. For `greetApp`, the help is:

```text
                         __
   ____ _________  ___  / /_
  / __ `/ ___/ _ \/ _ \/ __/
 / /_/ / /  /  __/  __/ /_
 \__, /_/   \___/\___/\__/
/____/

greet 1.0.0 -- Prints a greeting

USAGE

  $ greet [--name <text>]

DESCRIPTION

  Prints a greeting.

OPTIONS

  --name <text>
    A user-defined piece of text.

    Who to greet.

    This setting is optional. Default: 'world'.

  Example footer text.
```

The built-in options themselves, such as `--help`, are not listed. See [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) for all of them.

### Running a CliApp With CliApp#run

`CliApp#run` takes the command-line words as a `List[String]`, without the program name, and returns `ZIO[R, CliError[E], Option[A]]`:

```scala
object GreetMain extends ZIOAppDefault {
  def run =
    greetApp.run(List("--name", "Ada"))
}
```

Before parsing, `CliApp#run` puts the name of the top-level command in front of the words, so the user never types it. For a command with subcommands, it adds the parent's name, and the user starts with the subcommand name. For a top-level command built with `Command#|`, it adds nothing, and the user types the name of one alternative first.

The result depends on the input:

| Input                                                     | What `CliApp#run` does                                | Result                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| A valid command                                           | Runs `execute` with the parsed value.                 | `Some(a)`, or `CliError.Execution(e)` on failure |
| `--help` or `-h`                                          | Prints the help.                                      | `None`                                           |
| A parent command with no subcommand                       | Prints the parent's help.                             | `None`                                           |
| `--shell-completion-script` or `--shell-completion-index` | Prints the completion script or the completions.      | `None`                                           |
| `--wizard`                                                | Asks for the values, then runs the command they form. | The result of that run, or `None` on `quit`      |
| Invalid input                                             | Prints the error message to standard output.          | Fails with `CliError.Parsing`                    |

Words left over after a complete command are ignored, so `greet --name Ada extra` still greets `Ada`. The error type `CliError[E]` has four cases, `Parsing`, `Execution`, `IO` and `BuiltIn`, described in [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md#clierror).

### Running a Stand-alone Program With ZIOCliDefault

`ZIOCli` is a `ZIOApp` whose `ZIOApp#run` reads the program arguments and passes them to `cliApp.run`. `ZIOCliDefault` combines it with `ZIOAppDefault` and is the usual way to write a command-line program:

```scala
trait ZIOCli extends ZIOApp {
  def cliApp: CliApp[Environment with ZIOAppArgs with Scope, Any, Any]
}

trait ZIOCliDefault extends ZIOCli with ZIOAppDefault
```

With `ZIOAppDefault`, `Environment` is `Any`, so `cliApp` may require at most `ZIOAppArgs` and `Scope`. Provide other services inside `execute`. The program becomes an object that names its `CliApp`:

```scala
object Greet extends ZIOCliDefault {
  val cliApp = greetApp
}
```

The program exits with code `0` when `cliApp.run` succeeds and with code `1` otherwise; [Exit Codes](validation-and-errors.md#exit-codes) lists each outcome. To choose other exit codes, see [How to choose the exit code for each error](how-to-exit-codes.md).

Use `ZIOCli` directly when your program extends another `ZIOApp` subtype.

### Changing a CliApp

These methods return a new `CliApp` and leave the original unchanged. Each one changes a single aspect of the app.

#### CliApp#map

`CliApp#map` transforms the value that `execute` returns. Built-in actions that return `None`, such as `--help`, are not affected:

```scala
val greetingApp: CliApp[Any, Nothing, String] = CliApp.make(
  name = "greet",
  version = "1.0.0",
  summary = text("Builds a greeting"),
  command = greet
)(name => ZIO.succeed(s"Hello, $name!"))

val lengthApp: CliApp[Any, Nothing, Int] = greetingApp.map(_.length)
```

#### CliApp#flatMap

`CliApp#flatMap` runs another effect after `execute`, with the value that `execute` returns. The environment and error types widen to include those of the new effect:

```scala
val loggedApp: CliApp[Any, java.io.IOException, Unit] =
  greetApp.flatMap(_ => Console.printLine("Greeting sent."))
```

#### CliApp#footer

`CliApp#footer` appends a `HelpDoc` to the footer. Calling it more than once keeps all the text, in call order:

```scala
val withFooter = greetApp.footer(HelpDoc.p("Report problems to the issue tracker."))
```

#### CliApp#summary

`CliApp#summary` appends a `HelpDoc.Span` to the summary in the header line. No space is added, so include one in the span:

```scala
val withSummary = greetApp.summary(text(" (beta)"))
```

#### CliApp#config

`CliApp#config` replaces the whole `CliConfig` of the app:

```scala
val caseSensitiveApp = greetApp.config(CliConfig.default.copy(caseSensitive = true))
```

### The Usage Line

The `USAGE` section of the help has one line per shape of input the command accepts. Each line starts with `$ `. The line comes from a `UsageSynopsis` value, which every `Command`, `Options` and `Args` has. The synopsis is built as follows:

- A command starts with its name, followed by the synopsis of its options and then of its arguments.
- An option is written as its names and, unless it is a flag, its value type, such as `--name <text>`. An enumeration option shows its choices, such as `--mode fast | slow`.
- An option with several names lists them in parentheses, such as `(-q, --quiet)`.
- Options with a default value, options made with `Options#optional`, and flags are wrapped in square brackets, such as `[--verbose]`.
- Two options combined with `Options#|` are joined by `|` with no spaces, such as `[-a]|[-b]`.
- A repeated argument, made with `Args#*` or `Args#+`, ends with `...`.
- A command with two or more subcommands shows `<command>` in their place. A command with exactly one subcommand shows that subcommand's name, options and arguments.
- Empty parts are removed, so a command with no options and no arguments shows only its name.

To print the usage line of a few commands, we render each synopsis with the default configuration:

```scala
def usage(command: Command[_]): String =
  command.synopsis.enumerate(CliConfig.default).map(_.text).mkString("\n")

val tail       = Command("tail", Options.integer("lines").alias("n").withDefault(BigInt(10)), Args.file("file").+)
val repo       = Command("repo").subcommands(Command("clone", Args.text("repository")), Command("add", Args.text("path")))
val singleRepo = Command("repo").subcommands(Command("clone", Args.text("repository")))
```

The three commands render as follows:

```scala
println(usage(tail))
// tail [(-n, --lines <integer>)] <file>...
println(usage(repo))
// repo <command>
println(usage(singleRepo))
// repo clone <repository>
```

`CliConfig#showAllNames` and `CliConfig#showTypes` change how names and types appear in the `USAGE` lines (see [Help Appearance](cli-config.md#help-appearance)). They do not affect the `OPTIONS` and `COMMANDS` sections, which always show every name and type.

`UsageSynopsis` has these public members:

```scala
sealed trait UsageSynopsis {
  def enumerate(config: CliConfig): List[HelpDoc.Span]
  def helpDoc: HelpDoc
  def +(that: UsageSynopsis): UsageSynopsis
  def optional: UsageSynopsis
}
```

`UsageSynopsis#enumerate` returns the lines for a given configuration. `UsageSynopsis#helpDoc` returns the same lines as a `HelpDoc`, always rendered with `CliConfig.default`. `UsageSynopsis#+` places two synopses one after the other, and `UsageSynopsis#optional` wraps a synopsis in square brackets. The cases that make up a synopsis (`UsageSynopsis.Named`, `Optional`, `Repeated`, `Sequence`, `Alternation`, `Mixed` and `None`) are public, but the constructors of `Command`, `Options` and `Args` create them for you.

---

## CLI Configuration

A `CliConfig` controls how a `CliApp` parses the command line and how its help looks. It covers case sensitivity, "Did you mean" suggestions, the fallback check for `--help` and `--wizard`, and the names and types shown in the usage line.

`CliConfig` is a case class with five fields:

```scala
final case class CliConfig(
  caseSensitive: Boolean,
  autoCorrectLimit: Int,
  finalCheckBuiltIn: Boolean = true,
  showAllNames: Boolean = true,
  showTypes: Boolean = true
)
```

| Field               | Type      | Value in `CliConfig.default` | What it controls                                                                                      |
| ------------------- | --------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `caseSensitive`     | `Boolean` | `false`                      | Whether upper and lower case letters are different in command names.                                  |
| `autoCorrectLimit`  | `Int`     | `2`                          | The largest number of typing mistakes for which a "Did you mean" hint is shown.                       |
| `finalCheckBuiltIn` | `Boolean` | `true`                       | Whether invalid input that contains `--help` or `--wizard` still shows the help or starts the wizard. |
| `showAllNames`      | `Boolean` | `true`                       | Whether the usage line shows every name of an option or only the long one.                            |
| `showTypes`         | `Boolean` | `true`                       | Whether the usage line shows the value type of each option.                                           |

### Setting the Configuration

`CliApp.make` uses `CliConfig.default` unless you pass the `config` parameter. `CliApp#config` replaces the configuration of an existing app. Both forms are shown here:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text

val strict: CliConfig = CliConfig(caseSensitive = true, autoCorrectLimit = 1)

val greet: Command[String] = Command("greet", Args.text("name"))

val app: CliApp[Any, java.io.IOException, Unit] = CliApp.make(
  name = "greet",
  version = "1.0.0",
  summary = text("Prints a greeting"),
  command = greet,
  config = strict
)(name => Console.printLine(s"Hello, $name!"))

val relaxedApp = app.config(CliConfig.default)
```

### Default Configuration

`CliConfig.default` is case-insensitive, suggests corrections for up to two mistakes, runs the fallback check for `--help` and `--wizard`, and shows all names and types:

```scala
CliConfig.default
// res1: CliConfig = CliConfig(
//   caseSensitive = false,
//   autoCorrectLimit = 2,
//   finalCheckBuiltIn = true,
//   showAllNames = true,
//   showTypes = true
// )
```

### Case Sensitivity

`caseSensitive` decides whether `GIT CLONE` means the same as `git clone`. With `caseSensitive = false`, upper and lower case letters are equal in these places:

- Command and subcommand names.
- The distance used for "Did you mean" hints.
- Matching words during shell completion.
- The words of a boolean argument, such as `YES` or `Off` for `Args.bool`.

Enumeration values are always case-sensitive.

:::caution
Option names are matched case-sensitively in practice, even with `caseSensitive = false`. For an option declared as `Options.text("name")`, the input `--NAME Ada` is rejected with `Expected to find --name option.` Type option names in the case they are declared.
:::

### Auto-Correction

`autoCorrectLimit` is the largest number of typing mistakes (inserted, deleted or replaced characters) for which zio-cli adds a "Did you mean" hint to a parse error. With the default limit of `2`, a required option `--limit` typed as `--limt` gives:

```text
The flag "--limt" is not recognized. Did you mean --limit?
```

The hint never changes the input: the parse still fails. An option name that is at most `autoCorrectLimit + 1` characters long never gets a hint, and `autoCorrectLimit = 0` turns hints off. [Auto-Correct Suggestions](validation-and-errors.md#auto-correct-suggestions) lists every condition, including when a misspelt option produces no hint at all.

### Final Built-in Check

`finalCheckBuiltIn` controls what happens when the input does not parse but contains `--help`, `-h`, `--wizard` or `-w` somewhere. With `true`, zio-cli shows the help, or starts the wizard, of the command that failed to parse, instead of printing the error. With `false`, it prints the error.

For a command with a required `--limit` option, the input `--limt 3 --help` shows the help with the default configuration and the error `The flag "--limt" is not recognized. Did you mean --limit?` with `finalCheckBuiltIn = false`. `-w` starts the wizard only through this check, so it works only when the rest of the input is invalid. See [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) for how the built-in options are matched.

### Help Appearance

`showAllNames` and `showTypes` change how options appear in the `USAGE` line of the help. They do not change the `OPTIONS` and `COMMANDS` sections. To compare the four combinations, we render the usage line of a command whose option has a short alias:

```scala
val command: Command[String] = Command("command", Options.text("option").alias("o"))

def usageWith(config: CliConfig): String =
  command.synopsis.enumerate(config).map(_.text).mkString("\n")
```

The four lines below use the default configuration, then `showAllNames = false`, then `showTypes = false`, then both set to `false`:

```scala
println(usageWith(CliConfig.default))
// command (-o, --option <text>)
println(usageWith(CliConfig.default.copy(showAllNames = false)))
// command --option <text>
println(usageWith(CliConfig.default.copy(showTypes = false)))
// command (-o, --option)
println(usageWith(CliConfig.default.copy(showAllNames = false, showTypes = false)))
// command --option
```

With `showAllNames = false`, an option with several names shows only its first long name (`--option`). An option with only short names shows all of them.

### Other Members

`CliConfig` also has a few helpers that zio-cli uses while parsing:

```scala
final case class CliConfig(/* ... */) {
  def normalizeCase(text: String): String
  def isLongOption(value: String): Boolean
  def isShortOption(value: String): Boolean
  def isOption(value: String): Boolean
}

object CliConfig {
  val default: CliConfig
  val cliConfig: URIO[CliConfig, CliConfig]
}
```

`CliConfig#normalizeCase` lowercases text when `caseSensitive` is `false` and returns it unchanged otherwise. `CliConfig#isLongOption`, `CliConfig#isShortOption` and `CliConfig#isOption` match only very short words: `--` or two dashes and one character, `-` or one dash and one character. `--name` is not a long option for `CliConfig#isLongOption`, so do not use these helpers to classify user input. `CliConfig.cliConfig` reads a `CliConfig` from the ZIO environment, for code that receives the configuration as a service.

---

## Commands

A `Command[A]` describes one command of a command-line application: its name, its [options](options.md), its [arguments](args.md), and, optionally, its subcommands. When the user's input matches the command, the parser produces a value of type `A`. You pass a `Command` to `CliApp.make`, and the value it produces is handed to your program (see [CliApp and Running a CLI](cli-app.md)).

Git is a familiar example. In `git clone https://github.com/zio/zio-cli`, `git` is the top-level command, `clone` is a subcommand, and the URL is an argument of `clone`.

### Creating a Command

`Command.apply` builds a command from a name and, optionally, `Options` and `Args`. It has four overloads:

```scala
object Command {
  def apply(name: String): Command[Unit]
  def apply[OptionsType](name: String, options: Options[OptionsType]): Command[OptionsType]
  def apply[ArgsType](name: String, args: Args[ArgsType]): Command[ArgsType]
  def apply[OptionsType, ArgsType](name: String, options: Options[OptionsType], args: Args[ArgsType]): Command[(OptionsType, ArgsType)]
}
```

The result types above are simplified. Each overload takes an implicit `Reducable` that removes `Unit` from the value: a command without options produces only the arguments' value, a command without arguments produces only the options' value, and a command with both produces the tuple `(options, args)`. `Options.none` and `Args.none` stand for "no options" and "no arguments", so `Command("git", Options.none, Args.none)` is the same as `Command("git")`.

The value type of each command follows from its options and arguments:

```scala
import zio.cli._
import java.nio.file.Path

val statusCmd: Command[Unit]             = Command("status")
val commitCmd: Command[Boolean]          = Command("commit", Options.boolean("quiet"))
val addCmd: Command[Path]                = Command("add", Args.file("path"))
val cloneCmd: Command[(Boolean, String)] = Command("clone", Options.boolean("quiet"), Args.text("repository"))
```

The name is the word the user types. `CliApp` adds the name of the top-level command for you, so users of an app built from `Command("git")` type only what follows `git`.

### Transforming the Value

A command's raw value is often a tuple or `Unit`. These methods turn it into a type that fits your program:

```scala
trait Command[+A] {
  def map[B](f: A => B): Command[B]
  def as[B](b: => B): Command[B]
}
```

#### Command#map

`Command#map` applies a function to the parsed value:

```scala
case class Clone(quiet: Boolean, repository: String)

val cloneCommand: Command[Clone] = cloneCmd.map { case (quiet, repository) => Clone(quiet, repository) }
```

#### Command#as

`Command#as` replaces the value with a constant, which suits commands that carry no data:

```scala
case object Status

val statusCommand: Command[Status.type] = statusCmd.as(Status)
```

To give every subcommand of an app one shared type, see [How to turn subcommands into one domain type](how-to-map-subcommands.md).

### Adding a Description

`Command#withHelp` sets the command's description:

```scala
trait Command[+A] {
  def withHelp(help: String): Command[A]
  def withHelp(help: HelpDoc): Command[A]
}
```

A `String` is wrapped in a paragraph (`HelpDoc.p`). The description replaces any earlier one. It appears under `DESCRIPTION` in the command's help, and next to the command in its parent's `COMMANDS` list. On a command built with `Command#|`, `Command#withHelp` sets the same description on every alternative. On a command built with `Command#subcommands`, it sets the description of the parent.

The help of a command with a description, an option and an argument looks like this:

```scala
val documentedClone: Command[(Boolean, String)] =
  Command("clone", Options.boolean("quiet").alias("q"), Args.text("repository"))
    .withHelp("Copies a repository.")
```

`Command#helpDoc` returns this help, which we render as plain text:

```scala
println(documentedClone.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// 
// DESCRIPTION
// 
//   Copies a repository.
// 
// ARGUMENTS
// 
//   <repository>
//     A user-defined piece of text.
// 
// OPTIONS
// 
//   (-q, --quiet)
//     A true or false value.
// 
//     This setting is optional. Default: 'false'.
// 
//
```

See [Help Documentation](helpdoc.md) for building richer `HelpDoc` values.

### Choosing Between Commands

These methods combine two commands so that the user can type either one:

```scala
trait Command[+A] {
  def |[A1 >: A](that: Command[A1]): Command[A1]
  def orElse[A1 >: A](that: Command[A1]): Command[A1]
  def orElseEither[B](that: Command[B]): Command[Either[A, B]]
}
```

The parser tries the left command first. When the first word is not the left command's name, it tries the right one. If neither name matches, the input is rejected.

#### Command#| and Command#orElse

`Command#orElse` is the same as `Command#|`. The value type is the common supertype of both commands:

```scala
val addOrStatus: Command[Any] = addCmd | statusCmd
```

#### Command#orElseEither

`Command#orElseEither` keeps track of which command matched by wrapping the value in an `Either`:

```scala
val addOrClone: Command[Either[Path, (Boolean, String)]] = addCmd.orElseEither(cloneCmd)
```

When a top-level command is built with `Command#|`, `CliApp` does not add any name before the input: the user types `add` or `status` first. Most apps instead put the alternatives under a parent command with `Command#subcommands`.

### Subcommands

`Command#subcommands` adds child commands to a parent:

```scala
trait Command[+A] {
  def subcommands[B](that: Command[B])(implicit ev: Reducable[A, B]): Command[ev.Out]
  def subcommands[B](c1: Command[B], c2: Command[B], cs: Command[B]*)(implicit ev: Reducable[A, B]): Command[ev.Out]
}
```

The second overload joins its arguments with `Command#|`, so the user picks exactly one child. The value combines the parent's value and the child's value with the same `Reducable` rule as `Command.apply`. When the parent has no options or arguments (a `Command[Unit]`), the value is the child's value. Otherwise it is the tuple `(parentValue, childValue)`.

A parent without options gives the child's value directly:

```scala
val git: Command[Any] =
  Command("git")
    .withHelp("A tiny version control tool.")
    .subcommands(Command("add", Args.file("path")).withHelp("Stages a file."), documentedClone)
```

A parent with options gives a tuple, and the parent's options go before the subcommand name, as in `git --verbose add file.txt`:

```scala
val verboseGit: Command[(Boolean, Any)] =
  Command("git", Options.boolean("verbose")).subcommands(addCmd, cloneCmd)
```

A child can have subcommands of its own, which gives nested commands such as `git remote add`. The parent's help lists every subcommand with its usage and description:

```scala
println(git.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// 
// DESCRIPTION
// 
//   A tiny version control tool.
// 
// COMMANDS
// 
//   - add <path>                          Stages a file.
//   - clone [(-q, --quiet)] <repository>  Copies a repository.
//
```

Parsing a command with subcommands follows these rules:

- When the input names no subcommand, the result is the parent's help, as if the user had typed `--help`.
- When the first word after the parent is not a subcommand, the input is rejected with `Invalid subcommand for git. Use one of 'add', 'clone'`.
- When the input continues after a complete subcommand, the extra words are ignored.

`--help` after a subcommand other than the first shows the first subcommand's help; see [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md#help).

### Inspecting a Command

These members describe a command without running it. `CliApp` uses them to print help and to parse input, and tests use them to check a command:

```scala
trait Command[+A] {
  def helpDoc: HelpDoc
  def synopsis: UsageSynopsis
  def names: Set[String]
  def getSubcommands: Map[String, Command[_]]
  def parse(args: List[String], conf: CliConfig): IO[ValidationError, CommandDirective[A]]
}
```

`Command#helpDoc` holds the sections that `--help` prints below the usage line: `DESCRIPTION`, `ARGUMENTS`, `OPTIONS` and, for a parent, `COMMANDS`. `Command#synopsis` is the usage line, described in [The Usage Line](cli-app.md#the-usage-line). `Command#names` returns the name of the command (for a command built with `Command#|`, the names of both alternatives). `Command#getSubcommands` maps each subcommand name to its command.

#### Command#parse

`Command#parse` parses a list of words. Unlike `CliApp#run`, the list must start with the command's own name. The result is a `CommandDirective`:

```scala
sealed trait CommandDirective[+A] {
  def map[B](f: A => B): CommandDirective[B]
  def mapBuiltIn(f: BuiltInOption => BuiltInOption): CommandDirective[A]
}
object CommandDirective {
  final case class BuiltIn(option: BuiltInOption)                   extends CommandDirective[Nothing]
  final case class UserDefined[A](leftover: List[String], value: A) extends CommandDirective[A]

  def builtIn(option: BuiltInOption): CommandDirective[Nothing]
  def userDefined[A](leftover: List[String], value: A): CommandDirective[A]
}
```

`UserDefined` carries the parsed value and any words the parser does not use. `BuiltIn` means the input asks for a [built-in command](built-in-commands.md) such as `--help`. A failure is a [`ValidationError`](validation-and-errors.md). `CommandDirective#map` changes the value of a `UserDefined` and leaves a `BuiltIn` unchanged, `CommandDirective#mapBuiltIn` changes the option of a `BuiltIn` and leaves a `UserDefined` unchanged, and `CommandDirective.builtIn` and `CommandDirective.userDefined` build the two cases with the wider type `CommandDirective`.

To run the parser outside a ZIO program, we use a small helper:

```scala
import zio._

def parse[A](command: Command[A], args: String*): CommandDirective[A] =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(command.parse(args.toList, CliConfig.default)).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

With the helper, we can parse a `clone` command line and an `add` command line:

```scala
parse(git, "git", "clone", "-q", "https://github.com/zio/zio-cli")
// res3: CommandDirective[Any] = UserDefined(
//   leftover = List(),
//   value = (true, "https://github.com/zio/zio-cli")
// )
parse(verboseGit, "git", "--verbose", "add", "build.sbt")
// res4: CommandDirective[(Boolean, Any)] = UserDefined(
//   leftover = List(),
//   value = (true, build.sbt)
// )
```

See [Testing CLI Applications](testing.md) for assertions built on `Command#parse`.

#### The -- Separator

A `--` word ends the options. Every word after it goes to the arguments, even a word that looks like an option:

```scala
val echo: Command[(Boolean, List[String])] = Command("echo", Options.boolean("n"), Args.text("word").*)
```

Parsing the words after the separator shows that `-n` stays an argument:

```scala
parse(echo, "echo", "--", "-n", "hello")
// res5: CommandDirective[(Boolean, List[String])] = UserDefined(
//   leftover = List(),
//   value = (false, List("-n", "hello"))
// )
```

### How Commands Are Represented

`Command` is a sealed trait. Its cases are `Command.Single` (a name, a description, options and arguments), `Command.Map` (the result of `Command#map`), `Command.OrElse` (the result of `Command#|`) and `Command.Subcommands` (the result of `Command#subcommands`). They are public, but you build commands with `Command.apply` and the methods above instead of constructing the cases yourself.

---

## Tutorial: Build a Git-Like CLI

Welcome! This tutorial builds a small command-line program that works like a few parts of `git`. You run it from a terminal, the way you run `git add` or `git remote add`. The program only prints what it would do. It does not change any files.

A **command-line interface (CLI)** is a program that reads its input from the words you type after its name. **ZIO CLI** is a Scala library that reads those words for you, checks them, and hands your code clean values. You describe the shape of the input, and **ZIO CLI** does the parsing.

The tutorial is for Scala developers who know sbt and have not used **ZIO CLI** before. If you have not done so yet, read [Getting Started](getting-started.md) first: it shows the smallest possible app.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will know how to:

- Describe options, arguments, commands and nested subcommands, and turn their parsed values into your own types
- Run the program and pass it a command line, knowing which words **ZIO CLI** adds for you
- Read an option that takes a value, such as `commit -m <message>`
- Add help text and read the help that **ZIO CLI** generates
- Generate a bash completion script for the program
- Test the command-line parsing with the **ZIO CLI** testkit

The tutorial uses four building blocks:

- An **option** is a named input, such as `-m`. A flag option is either present or absent; other options carry a value.
- An **argument** is a value given by its position, such as the directory `./src`.
- A **command** is a named action, such as `add`. It holds options and arguments.
- A **subcommand** is a command that sits under another command, such as `remote` under `git`.

You need an sbt project with the `zio-cli` dependency, as shown in [Installation](index.md#installation). Each step below adds one idea to the same program. We recommend reading from top to bottom, because each step builds on the previous one. The complete program is at the end of the page.

### Step 1: Define One Option and One Argument

An option and an argument are the two kinds of input your program reads. Each one has a Scala type that describes the value it produces. Let's define one of each:

```scala
import zio.cli._

import java.nio.file.{Path => JPath}

val modified: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("m")

val directory: Args[JPath] = Args.directory("directory")
```

The two values work like this:

- `Options.boolean("m")` reads the `-m` flag. It produces a `Boolean`: `true` when `-m` is present and `false` when it is not.
- `Args.directory("directory")` reads one positional value that names a directory. It produces a `java.nio.file.Path`. By default the directory does not have to exist.

The name you pass in (`"m"`, `"directory"`) is what appears on the command line and in help text. It is not the Scala variable name.

### Step 2: Build a Command

A command gives a name to a set of options and arguments. `Command("add", modified, directory)` means: the word `add`, then optionally `-m`, then one directory:

```scala
import zio.cli._

import java.nio.file.{Path => JPath}

val modified: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("m")
val directory: Args[JPath]     = Args.directory("directory")

val add: Command[(Boolean, JPath)] =
  Command("add", modified, directory).withHelp("Stage the files in a directory")
```

The type of the result is `Command[(Boolean, JPath)]`. **ZIO CLI** puts the option values and the argument values in a tuple, in the order you listed them. `Command#withHelp` attaches the description that appears in the help output.

### Step 3: Add Subcommands

A program usually has more than one action. The usual pattern is a root command, here `git`, with subcommands under it. Each subcommand is one action.

Two ideas are new in this step. `Command#map` changes a command's result type: the tuple from Step 2 becomes a value of a type we define, so the program can use a single `match` to decide what to do. `Command#subcommands` attaches child commands to a parent: `Command("git").subcommands(add, remote)` accepts `git add ...` and `git remote ...`:

```scala
import zio.cli._

import java.nio.file.{Path => JPath}

sealed trait Subcommand extends Product with Serializable
object Subcommand {
  case class Add(modified: Boolean, directory: JPath) extends Subcommand
  case object Remote                                  extends Subcommand
}

val modified: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("m")
val directory: Args[JPath]     = Args.directory("directory")

val add: Command[Subcommand] =
  Command("add", modified, directory)
    .withHelp("Stage the files in a directory")
    .map { case (modified, directory) => Subcommand.Add(modified, directory) }

val remote: Command[Subcommand] =
  Command("remote").withHelp("Manage the set of remotes").as(Subcommand.Remote)

val git: Command[Subcommand] =
  Command("git").subcommands(add, remote)
```

`Subcommand` is a `sealed trait`. The compiler then knows every possible case, so a `match` on it can be checked for completeness. `Command#as` replaces the result of `remote`, which has no options or arguments, with the fixed value `Subcommand.Remote`.

### Step 4: Add a Nested Subcommand

A subcommand can have its own subcommands. `git remote add <name> <url>` has three levels: the program `git`, the subcommand `remote`, and the sub-subcommand `add`.

In this step, `remote` stops being a plain command and becomes a parent with the children `add` and `remove`. The two children need their own result type, so we put them in a nested `Remote` group inside `Subcommand`:

```scala
import zio.cli._

import java.nio.file.{Path => JPath}

sealed trait Subcommand extends Product with Serializable
object Subcommand {
  case class Add(modified: Boolean, directory: JPath) extends Subcommand

  sealed trait Remote extends Subcommand
  object Remote {
    case class Add(name: String, url: String) extends Remote
    case class Remove(name: String)           extends Remote
  }
}

val modified: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("m")
val directory: Args[JPath]     = Args.directory("directory")

val add: Command[Subcommand] =
  Command("add", modified, directory)
    .withHelp("Stage the files in a directory")
    .map { case (modified, directory) => Subcommand.Add(modified, directory) }

val remoteAdd: Command[Subcommand.Remote] =
  Command("add", Args.text("name") ++ Args.text("url"))
    .withHelp("Add a remote with a name and a URL")
    .map { case (name, url) => Subcommand.Remote.Add(name, url) }

val remoteRemove: Command[Subcommand.Remote] =
  Command("remove", Args.text("name"))
    .withHelp("Remove the remote with this name")
    .map(name => Subcommand.Remote.Remove(name))

val remote: Command[Subcommand] =
  Command("remote")
    .withHelp("Manage the set of remotes")
    .subcommands(remoteAdd, remoteRemove)

val git: Command[Subcommand] =
  Command("git").subcommands(add, remote)
```

Two new constructors appear here. `Args.text` reads one text value, and `Args.text("name") ++ Args.text("url")` reads two text values in order and produces them as a tuple. The parts fit together like this:

```text
git
├── add [-m] <directory>
└── remote
    ├── add <name> <url>
    └── remove <name>
```

### Step 5: Run the App

The program needs one more piece: a function that runs for each parsed command. `CliApp.make` takes a name, a version, a one-line summary and the root command, plus that function:

```scala
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text

val cliApp = CliApp.make(
  name = "git",
  version = "0.9.2",
  summary = text("a client for the git dvcs protocol"),
  command = git
) {
  case Subcommand.Add(modified, directory) =>
    printLine(s"Executing `git add $directory` with modified flag set to $modified")
  case Subcommand.Remote.Add(name, url) =>
    printLine(s"Executing `git remote add $name $url`")
  case Subcommand.Remote.Remove(name) =>
    printLine(s"Executing `git remote remove $name`")
}
```

Create `src/main/scala/GitTutorial.scala`. Put the imports from Step 4 and from this step at the top of the file. Put the definitions from Step 4 and this `cliApp` inside an `object GitTutorial extends ZIOCliDefault`, with `Subcommand` and its cases inside the object too. `ZIOCliDefault` turns the object into a runnable program that hands the words from the command line to `cliApp`. Step 6 shows the finished file.

The text after `run` is what your program receives. Notice that it does not start with `git`. When you start an installed program as `git add ./src`, the operating system passes only `add ./src` to it, so `CliApp` adds the root command name `git` in front before it parses the words. You type only what comes after the program name:

```shell
sbt "run add -m ./src"
```

The program prints:

```text
Executing `git add ./src` with modified flag set to true
```

Without `-m`, the flag is `false`:

```shell
sbt "run add ./src"
```

The program prints:

```text
Executing `git add ./src` with modified flag set to false
```

The nested subcommands work the same way:

```shell
sbt "run remote add origin https://example.com/repo.git"
```

The program prints:

```text
Executing `git remote add origin https://example.com/repo.git`
```

If you type `git` yourself, as in `sbt "run git add ./src"`, the program sees `git git add ./src` and stops with an "Invalid subcommand for git" error.

Try one more line, with the flag after the directory:

```shell
sbt "run add ./src -m"
```

The program prints:

```text
Executing `git add ./src` with modified flag set to false
```

The flag is `false`, and there is no error. **ZIO CLI** reads a command's options before its arguments, and stops reading options at the first word that is not one. Once `./src` has been read as the argument, `-m` is a leftover word, and `CliApp` ignores leftover words. Always put options before arguments. [How ZIO CLI reads a command line](parsing.md) explains these rules in detail.

### Step 6: Read an Option That Takes a Value

The `-m` flag of `add` is either present or absent. Many options carry a value instead, like the message of `git commit -m "Fix the typo"`. Let's add a `commit` subcommand with a `--message` option, short name `-m`.

`Options.text("message")` reads the word after `--message` as a `String`. `Options#alias` gives the option a second name, `-m`. An option without a default is required: `commit` fails when the message is missing. Here is the whole program so far, as it goes into `GitTutorial.scala`, with the new `Commit` case, the `message` option, the `commit` command and its case in `cliApp`:

```scala
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text
import zio.cli._

import java.nio.file.{Path => JPath}

object GitTutorial extends ZIOCliDefault {

  sealed trait Subcommand extends Product with Serializable
  object Subcommand {
    case class Add(modified: Boolean, directory: JPath) extends Subcommand
    case class Commit(message: String)                  extends Subcommand

    sealed trait Remote extends Subcommand
    object Remote {
      case class Add(name: String, url: String) extends Remote
      case class Remove(name: String)           extends Remote
    }
  }

  val modified: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("m")
  val directory: Args[JPath]     = Args.directory("directory")
  val message: Options[String]   = Options.text("message").alias("m")

  val add: Command[Subcommand] =
    Command("add", modified, directory)
      .withHelp("Stage the files in a directory")
      .map { case (modified, directory) => Subcommand.Add(modified, directory) }

  val commit: Command[Subcommand] =
    Command("commit", message)
      .withHelp("Record the staged files with a message")
      .map(message => Subcommand.Commit(message))

  val remoteAdd: Command[Subcommand.Remote] =
    Command("add", Args.text("name") ++ Args.text("url"))
      .withHelp("Add a remote with a name and a URL")
      .map { case (name, url) => Subcommand.Remote.Add(name, url) }

  val remoteRemove: Command[Subcommand.Remote] =
    Command("remove", Args.text("name"))
      .withHelp("Remove the remote with this name")
      .map(name => Subcommand.Remote.Remove(name))

  val remote: Command[Subcommand] =
    Command("remote")
      .withHelp("Manage the set of remotes")
      .subcommands(remoteAdd, remoteRemove)

  val git: Command[Subcommand] =
    Command("git").subcommands(add, commit, remote)

  val cliApp = CliApp.make(
    name = "git",
    version = "0.9.2",
    summary = text("a client for the git dvcs protocol"),
    command = git
  ) {
    case Subcommand.Add(modified, directory) =>
      printLine(s"Executing `git add $directory` with modified flag set to $modified")
    case Subcommand.Commit(message) =>
      printLine(s"Executing `git commit` with message: $message")
    case Subcommand.Remote.Add(name, url) =>
      printLine(s"Executing `git remote add $name $url`")
    case Subcommand.Remote.Remove(name) =>
      printLine(s"Executing `git remote remove $name`")
  }
}
```

The changes from Step 5 are:

- `Subcommand.Commit(message: String)` is the new case for the parsed `commit` line.
- `Options.text("message").alias("m")` defines the option. Its type is `Options[String]`, because it carries a text value.
- `Command("commit", message)` takes only options, so its value is the message itself, and `Command#map` wraps it in `Subcommand.Commit`.
- `Command("git").subcommands(add, commit, remote)` adds `commit` to the root command.
- `cliApp` has a new case that prints the message.

Run `commit` with a message. The quotes keep the message together as one word:

```shell
sbt 'run commit -m "Fix the typo"'
```

The program prints:

```text
Executing `git commit` with message: Fix the typo
```

The long name works too, and so does the `--message=<text>` form. Without a message, parsing fails and the program prints the error:

```shell
sbt "run commit"
```

The program prints the error and exits with a failure code:

```text
Expected to find --message option.
```

### Step 7: Add Help Text

**ZIO CLI** generates help from the commands, options and arguments you define. `Command#withHelp` already gives each command a description. Options and arguments get one with the `??` operator, which adds a sentence to the help of an option or argument. In `GitTutorial`, we give each option and argument a description, and we pull the two remote arguments into vals so both remote commands share them:

```scala
val modified: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("m") ?? "Stage only the files that were modified."
val directory: Args[JPath]     = Args.directory("directory") ?? "The directory to stage."
val message: Options[String]   = Options.text("message").alias("m") ?? "The commit message."
val remoteName: Args[String]   = Args.text("name") ?? "The name of the remote."
val remoteUrl: Args[String]    = Args.text("url") ?? "The URL of the remote."
```

The remote commands then use the new vals: `Command("add", remoteName ++ remoteUrl)` and `Command("remove", remoteName)`. The complete program at the end of the page has every change.

Every app understands the built-in `--help` flag. Ask for the help of the whole program:

```shell
sbt "run --help"
```

The output starts with the app name drawn as a banner, then the name, version and summary, a usage line, and one line per subcommand with its description:

```text
          _ __ 
   ____ _(_) /_
  / __ `/ / __/
 / /_/ / / /_  
 \__, /_/\__/  
/____/         

git 0.9.2 -- a client for the git dvcs protocol

USAGE

  $ git <command>

COMMANDS

  - add [-m] <directory>           Stage the files in a directory
  - commit (-m, --message <text>)  Record the staged files with a message
  - remote                         Manage the set of remotes
  - remote add <name> <url>        Add a remote with a name and a URL
  - remote remove <name>           Remove the remote with this name
```

Notice the notation in the usage lines: `[-m]` is optional, `(-m, --message <text>)` lists two names of one required option that takes a text value, and `<directory>` is an argument. Running the program with no words at all prints the same help.

`--help` after a subcommand name shows the help of that subcommand:

```shell
sbt "run add --help"
```

The `??` texts appear under the arguments and options, below a sentence that **ZIO CLI** writes for each type:

```text
          _ __ 
   ____ _(_) /_
  / __ `/ / __/
 / /_/ / / /_  
 \__, /_/\__/  
/____/         

git 0.9.2 -- a client for the git dvcs protocol

USAGE

  $ git add [-m] <directory>

DESCRIPTION

  Stage the files in a directory

ARGUMENTS

  <directory>
    A directory.

    The directory to stage.

OPTIONS

  -m
    A true or false value.

    Stage only the files that were modified.

    This setting is optional. Default: 'false'.
```

:::caution
`--help` after any subcommand other than the first one in `subcommands(add, commit, remote)` shows the help of the first one, `add`. Running `sbt "run commit --help"` prints the help above. Use `sbt "run --help"` to see the usage line and description of every subcommand. See [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md#help) for the rule.
:::

[Help Documentation](helpdoc.md) covers `HelpDoc`, the type behind help text, and [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) lists every built-in flag.

### Step 8: Generate a Shell Completion Script

Shell completion lets a user press Tab to complete subcommand and option names. Every **ZIO CLI** app can print a bash script that sets this up. The built-in `--shell-completion-script` flag takes the path of the installed program, and `--shell-type bash` picks the shell:

```shell
sbt "run --shell-completion-script /usr/local/bin/git --shell-type bash"
```

The program prints the script:

```text
#/usr/bin/env bash
_git()
{
  local CMDLINE
  local IFS=$'\n'
  CMDLINE=(--shell-type bash --shell-completion-index $COMP_CWORD)
  
  INDEX=0
  for arg in ${COMP_WORDS[@]}; do
    export COMP_WORD_$INDEX=${arg}
    (( INDEX++ ))
  done

  COMPREPLY=( $(/usr/local/bin/git "${CMDLINE[@]}") )

  # Unset the environment variables.
  unset $(compgen -v | grep "^COMP_WORD_")
}

complete -F _git git
```

The script defines a bash function, `_git`, and its last line registers that function for the word `git`, the name of the root command. On each Tab press, the function calls the program at the path given to `--shell-completion-script`, with the built-in `--shell-completion-index` flag, and the program prints the possible completions.

Because our root command is called `git`, loading this script would replace the completion of the real `git` in that shell, so in this tutorial we only generate it and read it. To install completion for a program of your own, follow [How to add Tab completion in bash](how-to-add-shell-completion.md).

### Step 9: Test the Parsing

The testkit module, `zio-cli-testkit`, checks a command without a terminal. Add it to your build as a test dependency, as listed in [Modules](index.md#modules), together with ZIO Test. sbt 1.5 and later run ZIO Test specs without extra setup; on older sbt versions, add `testFrameworks += new TestFramework("zio.test.sbt.ZTestFramework")` to `build.sbt`.

`CliAssertion.assertCommand` parses each command line in a ZIO Test generator and checks that it produces the expected value. Each `CliRepr` pairs a command line with that value. Like `Command#parse`, it expects the full line, so each line starts with the root command name `git`, which `CliApp` adds when the program runs. `CliAssertion.assertCommandSuccess` takes an assertion on the result instead, which lets us check that a line fails. The spec goes into `src/test/scala/GitTutorialSpec.scala`:

```scala
import zio.cli.testkit.CliAssertion._
import zio.cli.testkit.CliRepr
import zio.test._

import java.nio.file.Paths

import GitTutorial._

object GitTutorialSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec = suite("git")(
    test("parses each subcommand") {
      assertCommand(
        git,
        Gen.fromIterable(
          List(
            CliRepr(List("git", "add", "-m", "src"), Subcommand.Add(true, Paths.get("src"))),
            CliRepr(List("git", "commit", "-m", "Fix the typo"), Subcommand.Commit("Fix the typo")),
            CliRepr(List("git", "remote", "remove", "origin"), Subcommand.Remote.Remove("origin"))
          )
        )
      )
    },
    test("commit without a message fails") {
      assertCommandSuccess(git, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("git", "commit"), Assertion.isLeft)))
    }
  )
}
```

The spec works like this:

- `import zio.cli.testkit.CliAssertion._` brings in the assertions and the `CliConfig` they use.
- `import GitTutorial._` gives access to `git` and `Subcommand`.
- `assertCommand(git, ...)` parses every line in the generator and compares the result with the expected `Subcommand` value.
- `assertCommandSuccess(git, ...)` runs `Assertion.isLeft` on the parse result, so the test passes only when `git commit` without a message is an error.

Run the spec with `sbt test`. Both tests pass. [Testing](testing.md) lists every testkit assertion, and [How to test a CLI app](how-to-test-a-cli.md) also tests help output and errors from the app's own code.

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned how to:

- Describe options, arguments, commands and nested subcommands, and map their values into a `sealed trait`
- Run the program, typing only the words after the program name, with options before arguments
- Read an option that takes a value with `Options.text` and give it a short name with `Options#alias`
- Describe options and arguments with `??` and read the help that `--help` prints
- Generate a bash completion script with `--shell-completion-script`
- Test the parsing with `CliAssertion.assertCommand` and `CliAssertion.assertCommandSuccess` from the testkit
