Some small changes to try on this program:

1. Give `-m` of `add` a long name with `Options.boolean("modified").alias("m")`, so `--modified` works too.
2. Add a `remote list` subcommand that prints a line such as "Executing `git remote list`": a `Command("list")` under `remote`, a new case in the `Subcommand.Remote` group and a new case in `cliApp`.
3. Add a `--depth` option to a new `clone` subcommand with `Options.integer("depth").optional`, and compare the help output.

### Complete Program

This is the whole program in one file, `src/main/scala/GitTutorial.scala`. It is the program from Step 6 with the help texts from Step 7:

```scala

      case class Remove(name: String)           extends Remote
    }
  }

  val modified: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("m") ?? "Stage only the files that were modified."
  val directory: Args[JPath]     = Args.directory("directory") ?? "The directory to stage."
  val message: Options[String]   = Options.text("message").alias("m") ?? "The commit message."
  val remoteName: Args[String]   = Args.text("name") ?? "The name of the remote."
  val remoteUrl: Args[String]    = Args.text("url") ?? "The URL of the remote."

  val add: Command[Subcommand] =
    Command("add", modified, directory)
      .withHelp("Stage the files in a directory")

  val commit: Command[Subcommand] =

      .map(name => Subcommand.Remote.Remove(name))
```

## Figlet banners

A `CliApp` prints its name as a banner of ASCII art at the top of the help output and of wizard mode. The art comes from a FIGlet font. FIGlet is a text format for fonts made of ASCII characters: a font file, called an FLF file after its file extension, holds one drawing for each character.

`FigFont` in the `zio.cli.figlet` package is a parsed font. ZIO CLI includes one font, `FigFont.Default`, so a banner works without any setup. On the JVM you can also load another font from a file, a classpath resource, a URL or any `scala.io.Source`.

### Setting the Banner Font

`CliApp.make` has a `figFont` parameter, which defaults to `FigFont.Default`. We pass the font explicitly:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.figlet.FigFont

val greetCommand: Command[String] = Command("hello", Options.text("name"))

val greetApp = CliApp.make(
  name = "hello",
  version = "1.0.0",
  summary = HelpDoc.Span.text("Greets someone."),
  command = greetCommand,
  figFont = FigFont.Default
)(name => Console.printLine(s"Hello, $name!"))
```

`FigFont.Default` is the "Slant" font. Its source text is part of the library and is parsed the first time `FigFont.Default` is used. [CliApp](cli-app.md) describes the other parameters of `CliApp.make`.

### Rendering Text

`FigFont#render` draws a string and returns the lines joined with `\n`. `FigFont#renderLines` returns the same lines as a `Chunk[String]`:

```scala
final case class FigFont(header: FigHeader, rightToLeft: Boolean, layout: Layouts, chars: Map[Char, FigChar]) {
  def render(text: String): String
  def renderLines(text: String): Chunk[String]
}
```

We draw the banner that the help output of `greetApp` shows:

```scala
println(FigFont.Default.render("hello"))
//     __         ____    
//    / /_  ___  / / /___ 
//   / __ \/ _ \/ / / __ \
//  / / / /  __/ / / /_/ /
// /_/ /_/\___/_/_/\____/ 
//
```

A `\n` in the text starts a new row of characters below the first one. A character that the font does not define is drawn with the font's glyph for character code 0, or left out when the font has none.

### Loading a Font

`FigFont.fromLines` parses a font from the lines of an FLF file. It is available on every platform and returns an error message when the lines are not a valid font. The message starts with the line number where parsing failed, followed by the column when the error is inside a line:

```scala
object FigFont {
  def fromLines(lines: Iterable[String]): Either[String, FigFont]
}
```

The loaders below read the lines from a source and then call `FigFont.fromLines`. They exist only on the JVM. Each one returns a `ZIO` that reads nothing until it runs, and fails with an `Either`: `Left` holds the `IOException` when the source could not be read, and `Right` holds the parse message when the text is not a valid font:

```scala
object FigFont {
  def fromFile(name: String): ZIO[Any, Either[IOException, String], FigFont]
  def fromResource(name: String, loader: ClassLoader): ZIO[Any, Either[IOException, String], FigFont]
  def fromURL(url: String): ZIO[Any, Either[IOException, String], FigFont]
  def fromSource[R, A, E >: IOException](source: => ZIO[R, E, Source]): ZIO[R, Either[E, String], FigFont]
}
```

| Loader                 | Reads                                    | Encoding                        |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `FigFont.fromFile`     | A file path                              | ISO-8859-1                      |
| `FigFont.fromResource` | A classpath resource of the class loader | The platform's default encoding |
| `FigFont.fromURL`      | A URL, over the network                  | ISO-8859-1                      |
| `FigFont.fromSource`   | A `Source` produced by a `ZIO`           | The encoding of the `Source`    |

We load a font from a file and from a classpath resource:

```scala
import java.io.IOException

val fontFromFile: ZIO[Any, Either[IOException, String], FigFont] =
  FigFont.fromFile("fonts/small.flf")

val fontFromResource: ZIO[Any, Either[IOException, String], FigFont] =
  FigFont.fromResource("fonts/small.flf", getClass.getClassLoader)
```

:::caution
When `FigFont.fromResource` cannot find the resource, the effect dies with a `NullPointerException` instead of failing with `Left`. Check that the resource exists, for example with `ClassLoader#getResource`, before loading it.
:::

`FigFont.fromURL` downloads the font when the effect runs:

```scala
val fontFromUrl: ZIO[Any, Either[IOException, String], FigFont] =
  FigFont.fromURL("https://example.com/fonts/small.flf")
```

`FigFont.fromSource` takes a `ZIO` that opens a `scala.io.Source`, reads its lines and closes it. The other loaders are built on it. We load a font whose text is already in memory, such as text read from a database:

```scala
import scala.io.Source

def fontFromText(text: String): ZIO[Any, Either[IOException, String], FigFont] =
  FigFont.fromSource(ZIO.attemptBlockingIO(Source.fromString(text)))
```

Because a loader returns a `ZIO`, the application is built after the font is loaded. `ZIO#orElseSucceed` falls back to the default font when loading fails:

```scala
def helloApp(font: FigFont) =
  CliApp.make(
    name = "hello",
    version = "1.0.0",
    summary = HelpDoc.Span.text("Greets someone."),
    command = greetCommand,
    figFont = font
  )(name => Console.printLine(s"Hello, $name!"))

val runHello: ZIO[Any, Any, Any] =
  FigFont.fromFile("fonts/small.flf").orElseSucceed(FigFont.Default).flatMap(font => helloApp(font).run(List("--help")))
```

### Font Model

The fields of `FigFont` and the types they use are public, so a program can inspect a parsed font. You rarely need them: they matter only if you write your own renderer.

| Type        | Holds                                                                                           |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `FigHeader` | The values of the font's header line, such as the hard-blank character and the character height |
| `Layouts`   | The horizontal and vertical `Layout` of the font                                                |
| `Layout`    | `Layout.FullWidth`, `Layout.Fitting` or `Layout.Smushing` with its `SmushingRule`               |
| `FigChar`   | The drawing of one character, as `FigCharLine` rows with a width and height                     |

### Platform Support

The parser and the renderer work on the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native. Only the loaders that read from a source are JVM-only:

| Method                 | JVM | Scala.js | Scala Native |
| ---------------------- | --- | -------- | ------------ |
| `FigFont.Default`      | Yes | Yes      | Yes          |
| `FigFont#render`       | Yes | Yes      | Yes          |
| `FigFont.fromLines`    | Yes | Yes      | Yes          |
| `FigFont.fromFile`     | Yes | No       | No           |
| `FigFont.fromResource` | Yes | No       | No           |
| `FigFont.fromURL`      | Yes | No       | No           |
| `FigFont.fromSource`   | Yes | No       | No           |

On Scala.js and Scala Native, a call to a JVM-only loader does not compile. To use another font there, read the file with the platform's own API and pass its lines to `FigFont.fromLines`.

The objects `FigFontParser` and `FigFontRenderer` are private to the library, and the `Parser` and `ParseResult` classes in the same package are its parser combinators. They are not meant for application code.

---

## Getting Started(Zio-cli)

This page builds a small command-line program with **ZIO CLI** from an empty project. It assumes you know Scala and sbt, but have not used ZIO CLI before. At the end you will have one command, one option and one argument, and you will see the help text that **ZIO CLI** generates from them.

The steps are:

1. Add the library to your build.
2. Write an app that describes one command.
3. Run the app and read its help output.

### 1. Add the Dependency

Add `zio-cli` to `build.sbt` as shown in [Installation](index.md#installation). This page uses the JVM and `sbt run`.

### 2. Write the App

Create a file such as `src/main/scala/Greet.scala`. The app is an `object` that extends `ZIOCliDefault`. That trait makes the object a runnable program, and it asks you to define one value, `cliApp`.

Building a CLI app takes three pieces:

- An **option**, a named parameter such as `--loud`. See [Options](options.md).
- An **argument**, a position-based parameter such as the name in `greet Ada`. See [Args](args.md).
- A **command**, the named instruction that owns the option and the argument. See [Commands](commands.md).

The complete app defines all three pieces and ties them to the code that prints the greeting:

```scala
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text

object Greet extends ZIOCliDefault {

  // An option: "--loud" or "-l". It is a boolean, so it is true only when the flag is present.
  val loud: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("loud").alias("l")

  // An argument: a text value found by its position, after the options.
  val who: Args[String] = Args.text("name")

  // The command "greet" takes the option and the argument, and carries a help text.
  val greet: Command[(Boolean, String)] =
    Command("greet", loud, who).withHelp("Prints a greeting for the given name")

  // CliApp.make ties the command to the code that runs after the user input is parsed.
  // The function receives the parsed values as a tuple: (loud, who).
  val cliApp = CliApp.make(
    name = "greet",
    version = "0.1.0",
    summary = text("Prints a greeting"),
    command = greet
  ) { case (isLoud, name) =>
    val message = s"Hello, $name!"
    printLine(if (isLoud) message.toUpperCase else message)
  }
}
```

Some details in this code:

- `Options.boolean("loud")` creates the option. `Options#alias` adds a short name, so `-l` works too.
- `Args.text("name")` creates the argument. The `"name"` string is only a label for the help text. It is not a flag.
- `Command("greet", loud, who)` combines the option and the argument. The result has the type `Command[(Boolean, String)]`, which is the type of the value the app receives.
- `CliApp.make` takes a display name, a version, a one-line summary and the command. Its last parameter list is the function that runs the app logic. The function receives the parsed values, so you do not parse text yourself.

### 3. Run the App

From the project root, run:

```shell
sbt "run --loud Ada"
```

The program parses `--loud` as true and `Ada` as the name, then prints `HELLO, ADA!` in upper case. Notice that you do not type `greet` at the start. `CliApp` adds the command name before it parses your input, so you only type the options and arguments. Options come before arguments: ZIO CLI stops reading options at the first argument, as [How ZIO CLI reads a command line](parsing.md) explains.

Now ask for help:

```shell
sbt "run --help"
```

The help text comes from the code you wrote, so you do not write it by hand. Below a banner that spells the app name in large letters, it prints:

```text
greet 0.1.0 -- Prints a greeting

USAGE

  $ greet [(-l, --loud)] <name>

DESCRIPTION

  Prints a greeting for the given name

ARGUMENTS

  <name>
    A user-defined piece of text.

OPTIONS

  (-l, --loud)
    A true or false value.

    This setting is optional. Default: 'false'.
```

The usage line shows the option in parentheses inside brackets, because it is optional, and the argument in angle brackets. If you change `Command#withHelp`, the `summary`, or the alias, rerun `--help` to see the change. The built-in `--help` flag is covered in [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md).

### Where to Go Next

Each of these pages takes one part further:

- [Commands](commands.md) explains how to build several commands and nest subcommands.
- [Options](options.md) lists the option types, such as text, integer and enumeration.
- [Args](args.md) explains position-based arguments, including repeated arguments.
- [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) covers `--help`, `--wizard` and shell completion, which every app gets for free.
- [Wizard Mode](wizard.md) shows how a user can build a command interactively, without knowing the options in advance.
- [How ZIO CLI reads a command line](parsing.md) explains the order in which the input is read.
- [Tutorial: Build a Git-Like CLI](examples.md) builds a larger program with subcommands, step by step.

## Help Documentation

`HelpDoc` is the text that a ZIO CLI application prints for `--help` and for errors. It lives in `zio.cli` and is a tree of headers, paragraphs, description lists and enumerations, joined into sequences with `HelpDoc#+`. The words inside each element are stored as `HelpDoc.Span` values, which also record how a piece of text is styled: plain, code, error, weak, strong or a link.

You attach a `HelpDoc` to a [`Command`](commands.md) with `Command#withHelp`, and to a [`CliApp`](cli-app.md) as its footer. [`Options`](options.md) and [`Args`](args.md) take a plain `String` with `Options#??` and `Args#??`, which is added as a paragraph. Parse errors also carry a `HelpDoc`, as described in [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md).

### Creating Help Documents

The constructors on the `HelpDoc` companion object build the elements of a document. Every constructor that takes a `String` also has an overload that takes a `Span`, so a header or paragraph can contain styled text.

#### Headers and Paragraphs

`HelpDoc.h1`, `HelpDoc.h2` and `HelpDoc.h3` create headers of level 1, 2 and 3. `HelpDoc.p` creates a paragraph, and `HelpDoc.empty` is a document with no content:

```scala
object HelpDoc {
  val empty: HelpDoc
  def h1(t: String): HelpDoc
  def h1(span: Span): HelpDoc
  def h2(t: String): HelpDoc
  def h2(span: Span): HelpDoc
  def h3(t: String): HelpDoc
  def h3(span: Span): HelpDoc
  def p(t: String): HelpDoc
  def p(span: Span): HelpDoc
}
```

We build a header and a paragraph from strings, and a second paragraph from spans:

```scala
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span

val title: HelpDoc   = HelpDoc.h1("Usage")
val intro: HelpDoc   = HelpDoc.p("Copies files from one place to another.")
val styled: HelpDoc  = HelpDoc.p(Span.text("Run ") + Span.code("copy --help") + Span.text(" for details."))
val nothing: HelpDoc = HelpDoc.empty
```

#### Description Lists

`HelpDoc.descriptionList` takes any number of `(Span, HelpDoc)` pairs. Each pair is a term and its description, the same layout the help output uses for options and arguments:

```scala
object HelpDoc {
  def descriptionList(definitions: (Span, HelpDoc)*): HelpDoc
}
```

We describe two flags:

```scala
val flags: HelpDoc = HelpDoc.descriptionList(
  Span.text("--verbose") -> HelpDoc.p("Prints more."),
  Span.text("--quiet")   -> HelpDoc.p("Prints less.")
)
```

#### Enumerations

`HelpDoc.enumeration` takes any number of documents and renders them as a bulleted list. An enumeration passed inside another enumeration is flattened, so its items become items of the outer list:

```scala
object HelpDoc {
  def enumeration(elements: HelpDoc*): HelpDoc
}
```

We list two steps:

```scala
val steps: HelpDoc = HelpDoc.enumeration(HelpDoc.p("first item"), HelpDoc.p("second item"))
```

#### Blocks

`HelpDoc.blocks` joins documents one after another, the same as chaining them with `HelpDoc#+`. One overload takes at least one document, the other takes a collection and returns `HelpDoc.empty` when the collection is empty:

```scala
object HelpDoc {
  def blocks(helpDoc: HelpDoc, helpDocs0: HelpDoc*): HelpDoc
  def blocks(bs: Iterable[HelpDoc]): HelpDoc
}
```

We stack the header, the paragraph and the flags into one document:

```scala
val page: HelpDoc = HelpDoc.blocks(title, intro, HelpDoc.h2("Options"), flags)
```

### Spans

A `Span` holds a piece of inline text together with its style. Help output and errors use the style to colour the text in a terminal or to pick a tag in HTML.

#### Creating Spans

The constructors on `HelpDoc.Span` cover every style:

```scala
object Span {
  def text(t: String): Span
  def code(t: String): Span
  def error(t: String): Span
  def error(span: Span): Span
  def weak(t: String): Span
  def weak(span: Span): Span
  def strong(t: String): Span
  def strong(span: Span): Span
  def uri(uri: java.net.URI): Span
  def space: Span
  def empty: Span
  def spans(span: Span, spans0: Span*): Span
  def spans(spans: Iterable[Span]): Span
}
```

| Constructor   | Result                                                  |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Span.text`   | Plain text.                                             |
| `Span.code`   | A command or code fragment.                             |
| `Span.error`  | Text marked as an error, from a string or another span. |
| `Span.weak`   | De-emphasised text, from a string or another span.      |
| `Span.strong` | Emphasised text, from a string or another span.         |
| `Span.uri`    | A link.                                                 |
| `Span.space`  | A single space, the same as `Span.text(" ")`.           |
| `Span.empty`  | An empty text span, the same as `Span.text("")`.        |
| `Span.spans`  | The given spans joined in order.                        |

We combine several styles in one span:

```scala
val hint: Span = Span.spans(
  Span.error("Unknown flag."),
  Span.space,
  Span.text("See "),
  Span.uri(java.net.URI.create("https://zio.dev/zio-cli/"))
)
```

#### Span Operations

A `Span` has three methods that read it and one that extends it:

```scala
sealed trait Span {
  def +(that: Span): Span
  def text: String
  def size: Int
  def isEmpty: Boolean
}
```

`Span#+` appends another span. `Span#text` returns the characters without any style, `Span#size` returns their number, and `Span#isEmpty` is `true` when the size is zero:

```scala
hint.text
// res1: String = "Unknown flag. See https://zio.dev/zio-cli/"
hint.size
// res2: Int = 42
Span.empty.isEmpty
// res3: Boolean = true
```

The cases of the sealed trait are `Span.Text`, `Span.Code`, `Span.Error`, `Span.Weak`, `Span.Strong`, `Span.URI` and `Span.Sequence`. They are public, so you can pattern match on a span, for example to write your own renderer.

### Combining Help Documents

Two operators join documents. `HelpDoc#+` places one document after another, and `HelpDoc#|` picks a fallback:

```scala
sealed trait HelpDoc {
  def +(that: HelpDoc): HelpDoc
  def |(that: HelpDoc): HelpDoc
}
```

`HelpDoc#+` returns a sequence of both documents. If either side is empty, it returns the other side unchanged, so adding `HelpDoc.empty` does nothing. `HelpDoc#|` returns the left document, or the right one when the left document is empty:

```scala
(HelpDoc.empty + intro) == intro
// res4: Boolean = true
(HelpDoc.empty | intro) == intro
// res5: Boolean = true
(title | intro) == title
// res6: Boolean = true
```

"Empty" follows `HelpDoc#isEmpty`, described in the next section. A paragraph or header built from an empty string is not empty, so `HelpDoc.p("") | intro` keeps the empty paragraph.

### Inspecting and Transforming

`HelpDoc` has methods that ask what kind of document it is, read its text and change description lists:

```scala
sealed trait HelpDoc {
  def isEmpty: Boolean
  def isHeader: Boolean
  def isParagraph: Boolean
  def isDescriptionList: Boolean
  def isEnumeration: Boolean
  def isSequence: Boolean
  def getSpan: Span
  def mapDescriptionList(f: (Span, HelpDoc) => (Span, HelpDoc)): HelpDoc
}
```

- `HelpDoc#isEmpty` is `true` for `HelpDoc.empty`, for a sequence or enumeration whose parts are all empty, and for a description list whose descriptions are all empty. A description list like that is dropped by `HelpDoc#+`, even when it has terms.
- `HelpDoc#isHeader`, `HelpDoc#isParagraph`, `HelpDoc#isDescriptionList` and `HelpDoc#isEnumeration` are `true` when the document is that element, or is a sequence that starts with it.
- `HelpDoc#isSequence` is `true` only for a sequence built with `HelpDoc#+`.
- `HelpDoc#getSpan` returns the span of a header or paragraph, and `Span.empty` for anything else.
- `HelpDoc#mapDescriptionList` changes every entry of a description list and leaves any other document unchanged.

We check the page built earlier and add a note to every flag:

```scala
page.isHeader
// res7: Boolean = true
page.isSequence
// res8: Boolean = true
title.getSpan.text
// res9: String = "Usage"

val annotated = flags.mapDescriptionList { case (term, description) =>
  term -> (description + HelpDoc.p("Can be given once."))
}
// annotated: HelpDoc = DescriptionList(
//   definitions = List(
//     (
//       Text(value = "--verbose"),
//       Sequence(
//         left = Paragraph(value = Text(value = "Prints more.")),
//         right = Paragraph(value = Text(value = "Can be given once."))
//       )
//     ),
//     (
//       Text(value = "--quiet"),
//       Sequence(
//         left = Paragraph(value = Text(value = "Prints less.")),
//         right = Paragraph(value = Text(value = "Can be given once."))
//       )
//     )
//   )
// )
println(annotated.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --verbose
//   Prints more.
// 
//   Can be given once.
// 
// --quiet
//   Prints less.
// 
//   Can be given once.
// 
//
```

The cases of the sealed trait are `HelpDoc.Empty`, `HelpDoc.Header(value, level)`, `HelpDoc.Paragraph(value)`, `HelpDoc.DescriptionList(definitions)`, `HelpDoc.Enumeration(elements)` and `HelpDoc.Sequence(left, right)`. They are public, so you can pattern match on a document. `HelpDoc.Enumeration#flatten` lifts the items of nested enumerations into the outer one, which `HelpDoc.enumeration` already does for you.

### Rendering

A `HelpDoc` renders to terminal text with `HelpDoc#toPlaintext` and to an HTML page with `HelpDoc#toHTML`:

```scala
sealed trait HelpDoc {
  def toPlaintext(columnWidth: Int = 100, color: Boolean = true): String
  def toHTML: String
}
```

#### Plain Text

`HelpDoc#toPlaintext` writes headers in upper case on their own line and indents the content under them by two spaces. All three header levels look the same in plain text. Words wrap at `columnWidth` characters. With `color = true`, the default, the text contains ANSI escape codes for the styles and ends with a reset code. With `color = false` there are no escape codes. The help screen of a `CliApp` uses a column width of 300, and parse errors use 80.

We render the page built earlier without colour:

```scala
println(page.toPlaintext(color = false))
// 
// USAGE
// 
//   Copies files from one place to another.
// 
// OPTIONS
// 
//   --verbose
//     Prints more.
// 
//   --quiet
//     Prints less.
// 
//
```

An enumeration puts a dash before each item:

```scala
println(steps.toPlaintext(color = false))
// - first item
// - second item
//
```

A narrow `columnWidth` wraps a long paragraph at the last space that fits:

```scala
println(HelpDoc.p("This paragraph is long enough to wrap at a narrow column width.").toPlaintext(columnWidth = 30, color = false))
// This paragraph is long enough
// to wrap at a narrow column
// width.
//
```

With `color = true`, each style maps to a terminal attribute:

| Element or span       | Terminal style       |
| --------------------- | -------------------- |
| Header                | Bold, upper case     |
| Description-list term | Bold                 |
| `Span.strong`         | Bold                 |
| `Span.weak`           | Bold                 |
| `Span.error`          | Red                  |
| `Span.uri`            | Underlined           |
| `Span.code`           | No style             |
| `Span.text`           | Style of the context |

#### HTML

`HelpDoc#toHTML` returns a complete HTML page, with a `<style>` element in the head and the document in the body. Headers become `<h1>` to `<h3>`, paragraphs `<p>`, enumerations `<ul>` with `<li>` items, and the parts of a sequence are separated by `<br/>`. Inside text, `Span.code` becomes `<pre><code>`, `Span.strong` becomes `<b>`, `Span.error` becomes `<span class='error'>`, `Span.uri` becomes an `<a>` link and `Span.weak` has no tag. The characters `<` and `>` in text are escaped.

We print the body of the page built earlier:

```scala
val html = page.toHTML
// html: String = """<html><head><style>
//         h1 {
//             color: rgb(36, 41, 46);
//             font-weight: 600;
//             line-height: 1.25;
//             margin-bottom: 16px;
//             font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, Segoe UI Symbol;
//         }
// 
//         h2 {
//             font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, Segoe UI Symbol;
//             font-size: 24px;
//             letter-spacing: 0px;
//             word-spacing: 2px;
//             color: rgb(36, 41, 46);
//             font-weight: 600;
//         }
// 
//         h3 {
//             font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, Segoe UI Symbol;
//             font-size: 21px;
//             letter-spacing: 0px;
//             word-spacing: 2px;
//             color: rgb(36, 41, 46);
//             font-weight: 700;
//         }
// 
//         p {
//             font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, Segoe UI Symbol;
//             color: #24292e;
//         }
// 
//         .error {
//             font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, Segoe UI Symbol;
//             color: #24292e;
//         }
// 
//         a {
//             border: 0;
//             color: rgb(189, 39, 26);
//             text-decoration: none;
//             font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, Segoe UI Symbol;
//             font-size: inherit;
// ...
println(html.substring(html.indexOf("<body>")))
// <body><h1>Usage</h1><br/><p>Copies files from one place to another.</p><br/><h2>Options</h2><br/>--quiet<p>Prints less.</p>--verbose<p>Prints more.</p></body></html>
```

:::caution
`HelpDoc#toHTML` writes the entries of a description list in reverse order, with no list markup around them: in the output above, `--quiet` comes before `--verbose`. `HelpDoc#toPlaintext` keeps the original order.
:::

### Attaching Help to Commands and Parameters

Help text reaches the help screen through the command, its options and arguments, and the application.

#### Options and Args

`Options#??` and `Args#??` add a sentence to the description of an option or argument. Each call adds one paragraph after the existing description. On options or arguments combined with `++`, the text is added to every option or argument in the combination, so call `??` on each one before combining them:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val verbose: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("verbose") ?? "Prints more."
val source: Args[String]      = Args.text("source") ?? "The file to copy."
```

#### Commands

`Command#withHelp` replaces the help of a command. The `String` overload wraps the text in a paragraph, and the `HelpDoc` overload takes any document:

```scala
sealed trait Command[+A] {
  def withHelp(help: String): Command[A]
  def withHelp(help: HelpDoc): Command[A]
}
```

On a command with subcommands, the help goes to the parent command only. On two commands joined with `Command#|`, the help replaces the help of both alternatives. We give the copy command a paragraph and an enumeration:

```scala
val copy: Command[(Boolean, String)] =
  Command("copy", verbose, source).withHelp(
    HelpDoc.p("Copies a file.") + HelpDoc.enumeration(HelpDoc.p("Keeps timestamps."), HelpDoc.p("Never overwrites."))
  )
```

#### Applications

A `CliApp` takes a `HelpDoc.Span` summary, shown on the first line of the help screen, and a `HelpDoc` footer, shown after the options and arguments. Both are parameters of `CliApp.make`, and `CliApp#summary` and `CliApp#footer` append to them on an existing application. We add a footer to an application built from the copy command:

```scala
val copyApp = CliApp.make(
  name = "copy",
  version = "1.0.0",
  summary = HelpDoc.Span.text("Copies files"),
  command = copy,
  footer = HelpDoc.p("Report problems at https://github.com/zio/zio-cli/issues.")
) { case (verbose, source) => zio.Console.printLine(s"Copying $source") }
```

[CliApp](cli-app.md) lists the other parameters of `CliApp.make`, and [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) shows the help screen that `--help` prints.

---

## How to add Tab completion in bash

We want users of our CLI to press Tab in bash and see the subcommands, options and values they can type next. Every `CliApp` already answers completion requests, so the work is to generate a bash completion script once and install it where bash loads it.

Only bash is supported. Zsh has no script generator yet. [Bash Completion](bash-and-zsh-completion.md) describes the built-in options and what gets completed.

You need:

- A CLI built with `CliApp.make`.
- An executable of the CLI installed on the user's `PATH`.
- Bash, and for permanent installation the `bash-completion` package that most Linux distributions and Homebrew provide.

### Steps

The steps below use an application whose command is named `greet`.

#### 1. Name the Command After the Executable

The completion script registers itself for the name of the top-level command, not for the file name of the executable. Give the top-level command the name users type to start the program:

```scala
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text

object GreetApp extends ZIOCliDefault {
  val greet: Command[String] = Command("greet", Options.text("name"))

  val cliApp = CliApp.make(
    name = "greet",
    version = "1.0.0",
    summary = text("Greets a user"),
    command = greet
  ) { name =>
    printLine(s"Hello, $name!")
  }
}
```

If the executable must have another name, such as a short alias, add one `complete` line for that name to the script that step 3 generates. For an alias `g`, the line is `complete -F _greet g`.

#### 2. Build and Install the Executable

Build the executable and install it under the name `greet` on the `PATH`. [How to package a CLI as a native binary](how-to-package-native-binary.md) covers GraalVM native images. The `installer.sh` launcher template in the ZIO CLI repository builds a native image and links it at `$XDG_DATA_HOME/<app>/bin/<app>` (`~/.local/share/<app>/bin/<app>` when `XDG_DATA_HOME` is not set and the user is not root) only when `native-image` is available. Without `native-image` it runs the downloaded JAR and creates no such file, so use it only with a native image, and add that directory to the `PATH`.

The completion script stores the path of the executable and runs it on every Tab press, so install the executable at its final location before generating the script.

#### 3. Generate the Completion Script

Run the executable with `--shell-completion-script` and the path to the executable, and with `--shell-type bash`. Both options are required:

```bash
greet --shell-completion-script "$(command -v greet)" --shell-type bash > greet-completion.bash
```

The file contains a bash function named `_greet` and the line `complete -F _greet greet`. [Bash Completion](bash-and-zsh-completion.md) shows the full script.

#### 4. Load the Script

To try completion in the current shell session only, load the file with `source`:

```bash
source greet-completion.bash
```

To enable completion in every new session for one user, copy the file to the user's completion directory of `bash-completion`, named after the command:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions
cp greet-completion.bash ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/greet
```

To enable it for all users, install the file in the system directory instead, such as `/etc/bash_completion.d/`. When you ship the CLI as a package, generate the script during the build and let the package install it there.

#### 5. Test It

Open a new bash session, type `greet ` with a trailing space, and press Tab. Bash shows `--name`, the only option of the command. [Bash Completion](bash-and-zsh-completion.md#how-a-completion-request-works) explains what the program does on each Tab press.

### Troubleshooting

When Tab shows nothing or shows file names instead of options, check these causes:

- The first word does not match the name of the top-level command. Add a `complete -F _greet <name>` line for the name you type, as described in step 1.
- The executable is no longer at the path stored in the script. Generate the script again with the new path.
- The path to the executable contains spaces. The generated script does not quote the path, so install the executable in a directory without spaces.
- A path option or argument shows no candidates in a Scala.js or Scala Native build. Path completion works only in JVM builds.
- The script request uses `--shell-type zsh`. Zsh scripts are not implemented, and the program stops with an error.

## How to choose the exit code for each error

Scripts and CI jobs read a program's exit code to decide what happened. A program built with `ZIOCliDefault` uses only two codes, `0` and `1`. This guide shows how to give each kind of failure its own exit code, such as `2` for invalid input and `3` for a missing file.

### What ZIOCliDefault Does

`ZIOCliDefault` passes the program arguments to `CliApp#run`. The program exits with `0` when `CliApp#run` succeeds, including after `--help`, and with `1` for every `CliError`. [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md#exit-codes) lists each case.

Because every failure ends with code `1`, a caller cannot tell a typing mistake from a failed command. To change that, we run the `CliApp` ourselves from a `ZIOAppDefault` and map each error to an exit code.

### Define the Errors of Your Command

Start with an error type for the failures your command can report. Here, a `show` command fails when the file does not exist or cannot be read:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text
import java.nio.file.{Files, Path}

sealed trait ShowError
object ShowError {
  case class NotFound(path: Path)   extends ShowError
  case class Unreadable(path: Path) extends ShowError
}

val show: Command[Path] = Command("show", Args.file("file"))

val showApp: CliApp[Any, ShowError, Unit] =
  CliApp.make(
    name = "show",
    version = "1.0.0",
    summary = text("Prints the size of a file"),
    command = show
  ) { path =>
    for {
      _    <- ZIO.fail(ShowError.NotFound(path)).unless(Files.exists(path))
      size <- ZIO.attempt(Files.size(path)).orElseFail(ShowError.Unreadable(path))
      _    <- Console.printLine(s"$path: $size bytes").orDie
    } yield ()
  }
```

### Map Each Error to an Exit Code

Next, write a function from `CliError[ShowError]` to `ExitCode`. Matching on `CliError.Execution` gives access to your own error. zio-cli prints nothing for your errors, so print a message for them here:

```scala
def exitCodeFor(error: CliError[ShowError]): UIO[ExitCode] =
  error match {
    case CliError.Parsing(_) =>
      ZIO.succeed(ExitCode(2))
    case CliError.Execution(ShowError.NotFound(path)) =>
      Console.printLineError(s"No such file: $path").orDie.as(ExitCode(3))
    case CliError.Execution(ShowError.Unreadable(path)) =>
      Console.printLineError(s"Cannot read: $path").orDie.as(ExitCode(4))
    case CliError.IO(_) | CliError.BuiltIn(_) =>
      ZIO.succeed(ExitCode(70))
  }
```

`CliError.Parsing` needs no message, because `CliApp#run` has already printed the validation error.

### Run the App From ZIOAppDefault

Finally, extend `ZIOAppDefault` instead of `ZIOCliDefault`. Read the arguments with `ZIOApp#getArgs`, run the app, and on failure call `ZIOApp#exit` with the chosen code:

```scala
object ShowMain extends ZIOAppDefault {
  def run =
    for {
      args <- getArgs
      _    <- showApp.run(args.toList).catchAll(error => exitCodeFor(error).flatMap(exit(_)))
    } yield ()
}
```

`ZIOApp#exit` stops the program at once with the given code. Returning an `ExitCode` value from `ZIOAppDefault#run` is not enough: the program exits with `0` whenever `ZIOAppDefault#run` succeeds, whatever value it returns.

With this program, the exit codes are:

| Command line       | Exit code | Reason                               |
| ------------------ | --------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `show build.sbt`   | `0`       | The file exists and its size prints. |
| `show --help`      | `0`       | Help is a successful run.            |
| `show`             | `2`       | The `<file>` argument is missing.    |
| `show missing.txt` | `3`       | `ShowError.NotFound`                 |

### Test the Mapping

`exitCodeFor` is an ordinary function, so tests can call it with each `CliError` case without starting the program:

```scala
Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  Runtime.default.unsafe.run(exitCodeFor(CliError.Parsing(ValidationError(ValidationErrorType.InvalidArgument, HelpDoc.empty)))).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
}
// res1: ExitCode = ExitCode(code = 2)
```

### Related Pages

- [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md) describes every `CliError` case and the messages users see.
- [CliApp and Running a CLI](cli-app.md) describes `CliApp#run` and `ZIOCliDefault`.

## How to turn subcommands into one domain type

An app with subcommands produces a different raw value for each one: `Unit` for a subcommand without parameters, a `Path` for one with a file argument, a tuple for one with an option and an argument. Combined with `Command#subcommands`, these values lose their types and become `Any`. This guide shows how to give every subcommand one shared domain type, so that the function you pass to `CliApp.make` is a single, exhaustive `match`.

We build a small Git-like app with three subcommands: `add <path>`, `clone [--quiet] <repository>` and `status`.

### Define the Domain Type

Start with a sealed trait that has one case per subcommand. Each case holds the values that subcommand needs:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text
import java.nio.file.Path

sealed trait GitCommand
object GitCommand {
  case class Add(path: Path)                           extends GitCommand
  case class Clone(quiet: Boolean, repository: String) extends GitCommand
  case object Status                                   extends GitCommand
}
```

### Map Each Subcommand to a Case

Next, map the raw value of each subcommand to its case. Use `Command#map` when the case holds values, and `Command#as` when the subcommand carries no data. Give each command the type `Command[GitCommand]`:

```scala
val add: Command[GitCommand] =
  Command("add", Args.file("path")).withHelp("Stages a file.").map(GitCommand.Add(_))

val cloneRepo: Command[GitCommand] =
  Command("clone", Options.boolean("quiet").alias("q"), Args.text("repository"))
    .withHelp("Copies a repository.")
    .map { case (quiet, repository) => GitCommand.Clone(quiet, repository) }

val status: Command[GitCommand] =
  Command("status").withHelp("Shows the working tree status.").as(GitCommand.Status)
```

The explicit type makes the three commands share one value type. Without it, each command has the type of its own case, such as `Command[GitCommand.Add]`.

### Combine the Subcommands

Then attach the subcommands to a parent. A parent without options or arguments produces exactly the child's value, so the whole command is a `Command[GitCommand]`:

```scala
val git: Command[GitCommand] =
  Command("git").withHelp("A tiny version control tool.").subcommands(add, cloneRepo, status)
```

To check the mapping without running the app, we parse a few command lines. `Command#parse` expects the parent's name as the first word:

```scala
def parse(args: String*): CommandDirective[GitCommand] =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(git.parse(args.toList, CliConfig.default)).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

Each command line now produces a `GitCommand` case:

```scala
parse("git", "add", "build.sbt")
// res1: CommandDirective[GitCommand] = UserDefined(
//   leftover = List(),
//   value = Add(path = build.sbt)
// )
parse("git", "clone", "-q", "https://github.com/zio/zio-cli")
// res2: CommandDirective[GitCommand] = UserDefined(
//   leftover = List(),
//   value = Clone(quiet = true, repository = "https://github.com/zio/zio-cli")
// )
parse("git", "status")
// res3: CommandDirective[GitCommand] = UserDefined(
//   leftover = List(),
//   value = Status
// )
```

### Handle Every Case in One Place

Finally, pass the command to `CliApp.make`. The function that runs the command matches on `GitCommand`, and the compiler warns if a case is missing:

```scala
val gitApp: CliApp[Any, java.io.IOException, Unit] =
  CliApp.make(
    name = "git",
    version = "0.1.0",
    summary = text("A tiny version control tool"),
    command = git
  ) {
    case GitCommand.Add(path)                 => Console.printLine(s"Staging $path")
    case GitCommand.Clone(quiet, repository) => Console.printLine(s"Cloning $repository (quiet: $quiet)")
    case GitCommand.Status                    => Console.printLine("Nothing to commit")
  }

object GitMain extends ZIOCliDefault {
  val cliApp = gitApp
}
```

### Parent Options

When the parent has options of its own, such as a global `--verbose` flag, the value becomes a tuple of the parent's value and the subcommand's value. Map the tuple to a type that holds both:

```scala
case class Invocation(verbose: Boolean, command: GitCommand)

val verboseGit: Command[Invocation] =
  Command("git", Options.boolean("verbose"))
    .subcommands(add, cloneRepo, status)
    .map { case (verbose, command) => Invocation(verbose, command) }
```

The parent's options go before the subcommand name on the command line:

```scala
Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  Runtime.default.unsafe.run(verboseGit.parse(List("git", "--verbose", "status"), CliConfig.default)).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
}
// res5: CommandDirective[Invocation] = UserDefined(
//   leftover = List(),
//   value = Invocation(verbose = true, command = Status)
// )
```

### Commands Combined With orElseEither

`Command#orElseEither` keeps the type of each alternative but nests the values in `Either`. With three commands, the value is an `Either[Either[A, B], C]`. Map the nested `Either` to the domain type once, right after combining:

```scala
val nested: Command[Either[Either[Path, (Boolean, String)], Unit]] =
  Command("add", Args.file("path"))
    .orElseEither(Command("clone", Options.boolean("quiet"), Args.text("repository")))
    .orElseEither(Command("status"))

val flattened: Command[GitCommand] =
  nested.map {
    case Left(Left(path))                 => GitCommand.Add(path)
    case Left(Right((quiet, repository))) => GitCommand.Clone(quiet, repository)
    case Right(())                        => GitCommand.Status
  }
```

Mapping each subcommand before combining, as in the sections above, avoids the nested `Either` altogether.

### Related Pages

- [Commands](commands.md) describes `Command#map`, `Command#as`, `Command#subcommands` and `Command#orElseEither`.
- [CliApp and Running a CLI](cli-app.md) describes `CliApp.make` and `ZIOCliDefault`.

## How to log users in with OAuth2

We want a command-line tool that calls a web API on behalf of its user, for example to read the user's GitHub profile. The user logs in once in a browser, and the tool keeps the access token for later runs. ZIO CLI does this with `Options.oauth2` and the OAuth 2.0 device authorization flow, described in [Authorization with OAuth2](auth.md).

You need:

- A JVM build of the application. `Options.oauth2` does not exist on Scala.js or Scala Native.
- An application registered with the service, with the device flow enabled. For GitHub, create an OAuth app, enable the device flow in the app's settings, and copy its client ID.
- The scopes your API calls need. Reading the user's profile on GitHub needs `read:user`.

### Steps

The first four steps build a `whoami` command that prints the GitHub profile of the user. The last step replaces the GitHub provider with one for another service.

#### 1. Require a Token in the Command

Add an option created with `Options.oauth2`, giving the provider and the scopes. The command then produces an `OAuth2Token`:

```scala
import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.{HttpClient, HttpRequest, HttpResponse}

import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.oauth2._

val githubClientId = "Iv1.0123456789abcdef"

val login: Options[OAuth2Token] =
  Options.oauth2(OAuth2Provider.Github(githubClientId), List("read:user"))

val whoami: Command[OAuth2Token] = Command("whoami", login)
```

Parsing this command obtains the token before your code runs. On the first run it prints a web address and a code and waits until the user approves the application in a browser.

#### 2. Send the Token with Each API Request

Read the current token with `OAuth2Token#accessToken` and put it in the `Authorization` header. `OAuth2Token#accessToken` refreshes an expired token before returning it:

```scala
val http: HttpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient()

def fetchProfile(token: OAuth2Token): Task[HttpResponse[String]] =
  for {
    current  <- token.accessToken
    request   = HttpRequest
                  .newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.github.com/user"))
                  .header("Authorization", s"Bearer ${current.accessToken}")
                  .header("Accept", "application/vnd.github+json")
                  .build()
    response <- ZIO.fromCompletableFuture(http.sendAsync(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()))
  } yield response
```

Never print `AccessToken#accessToken` or write it to a log. It gives full access to the scopes the user granted.

#### 3. Refresh a Rejected Token Once

A service can reject a token before its expiry time, for example after the user revoked it. ZIO CLI cannot detect that, so when the API answers `401 Unauthorized`, call `OAuth2Token#refreshTokenNow` and try once more:

```scala
def fetchProfileWithRetry(token: OAuth2Token): Task[HttpResponse[String]] =
  fetchProfile(token).flatMap { response =>
    if (response.statusCode() == 401) token.refreshTokenNow *> fetchProfile(token)
    else ZIO.succeed(response)
  }
```

`OAuth2Token#refreshTokenNow` uses the refresh token when the service issued one. GitHub OAuth apps issue refresh tokens only when expiring user tokens are enabled for the app. Without a refresh token, it runs the browser authorization again.

#### 4. Run the Command in a CliApp

Build the application with `CliApp.make` and print the API's answer:

```scala
object WhoAmI extends ZIOCliDefault {
  val cliApp = CliApp.make(
    name = "whoami",
    version = "1.0.0",
    summary = HelpDoc.Span.text("Prints your GitHub profile"),
    command = whoami
  ) { token =>
    fetchProfileWithRetry(token).flatMap(response => Console.printLine(response.body()))
  }
}
```

The first run prints the address and code and waits. Later runs read the token from `~/oauth2_github_<client id>_access_token.json` and print the profile at once. To keep the token somewhere else, pass `--oauth2-file <path>`. To log the user out, delete the file.

When the user denies access or the code expires, the run ends with the service's error message, printed like an input error.

#### 5. Write a Provider for Another Service

Any service that supports the device authorization flow of RFC 8628 can be used. Its documentation lists two addresses: the device authorization endpoint and the token endpoint. A provider extends `OAuth2Provider` and builds the three requests of the flow. The provider below sends form-encoded `POST` requests, which is what RFC 8628 specifies. Replace the `example.com` addresses with the endpoints of your service:

```scala
import java.net.URLEncoder

class DeviceFlowProvider(
  val name: String,
  clientId: String,
  deviceAuthorizationEndpoint: URI,
  tokenEndpoint: URI
) extends OAuth2Provider {
  val clientIdentifier: String = clientId

  private def post(uri: URI, fields: (String, String)*): HttpRequest = {
    val body = fields.map { case (key, value) => s"$key=${URLEncoder.encode(value, "UTF-8")}" }.mkString("&")
    HttpRequest
      .newBuilder(uri)
      .header("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
      .header("Accept", "application/json")
      .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body))
      .build()
  }

  def authorizationRequest(scope: List[String]): HttpRequest =
    post(deviceAuthorizationEndpoint, "client_id" -> clientId, "scope" -> scope.mkString(" "))

  def accessTokenRequest(authorization: AuthorizationResponse): HttpRequest =
    post(
      tokenEndpoint,
      "client_id"   -> clientId,
      "device_code" -> authorization.deviceCode,
      "grant_type"  -> "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"
    )

  def refreshTokenRequest(refreshToken: String): Option[HttpRequest] =
    Some(post(tokenEndpoint, "client_id" -> clientId, "grant_type" -> "refresh_token", "refresh_token" -> refreshToken))
}

val example = new DeviceFlowProvider(
  name = "Example",
  clientId = "example-client-id",
  deviceAuthorizationEndpoint = URI.create("https://auth.example.com/oauth/device"),
  tokenEndpoint = URI.create("https://auth.example.com/oauth/token")
)

val exampleLogin: Options[OAuth2Token] = Options.oauth2(example, List("profile"))
```

Return `None` from `OAuth2Provider#refreshTokenRequest` when the service has no refresh tokens. The token is then renewed by running the authorization again. The provider's `name` appears in the help output and, in lower case, in the default token file name, so keep it short and stable.

The default decoders read the standard JSON answers. If the service names a field differently, override the matching decoder. This service answers the device-code request with `verification_url` instead of `verification_uri`, so we decode that answer ourselves with zio-json, which ZIO CLI already depends on:

```scala
import zio.json._

case class LegacyDeviceCode(
  device_code: String,
  user_code: String,
  verification_url: String,
  expires_in: Long,
  interval: Long
)

object LegacyDeviceCode {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[LegacyDeviceCode] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[LegacyDeviceCode]
}

class LegacyProvider(clientId: String, deviceEndpoint: URI, tokenEndpoint: URI)
    extends DeviceFlowProvider("Legacy", clientId, deviceEndpoint, tokenEndpoint) {
  override def decodeAuthorizationResponse(body: String): Either[String, AuthorizationResponse] =
    body.fromJson[LegacyDeviceCode].map { answer =>
      AuthorizationResponse(
        deviceCode = answer.device_code,
        userCode = answer.user_code,
        verificationUri = answer.verification_url,
        verificationUriComplete = None,
        expiresIn = Duration.fromSeconds(answer.expires_in),
        interval = Duration.fromSeconds(answer.interval)
      )
    }
}
```

Use the new provider with `Options.oauth2` exactly like a built-in one. [Authorization with OAuth2](auth.md) lists every member of `OAuth2Provider`, the fields of `AuthorizationResponse`, and the cases of `AccessTokenResponse` that the token decoder returns.

## How to make an option optional or give it a default

An option built with a constructor such as `Options.text` is required: a command without it fails with `Expected to find --user option.`. This guide makes options optional, so the user can leave them out, and chooses what the program receives when they do.

You need the `zio-cli` library on your classpath (see [Installation](index.md#installation)) and a command whose options you want to relax; [Options](options.md) describes how options are built.

### Choose What a Missing Option Means

Pick the method by the value your program needs when the user leaves the option out:

| The program needs                    | Use                               | Value type  |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | ----------- |
| To know whether the option was given | `Options#optional`                | `Option[A]` |
| A fixed value                        | `Options#withDefault`             | `A`         |
| `true` or `false` from a flag        | `Options.boolean`, nothing to add | `Boolean`   |

### Steps

We build the options of a `serve` command step by step: a flag, an option with a default, an optional option, and a pair of alternatives.

#### 1. Use a Flag for a Yes-or-No Choice

A boolean option already has a default, the opposite of the value it gives when present. To declare a `--quiet` flag that is `false` unless given:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val quiet: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("quiet")
```

To invert a flag, pass `ifPresent = false`, as described in [Boolean Options](options.md#boolean-options).

#### 2. Give an Option a Default

`Options#withDefault` uses its value when the option is missing. To default the number of retries to 3, convert the `BigInt` of `Options.integer` first and annotate the type:

```scala
val retries: Options[Int] = Options.integer("retries").map(_.toInt).withDefault(3)
```

The type annotation matters: without it, `Options.integer("retries").withDefault(3)` compiles as an `Options[Any]`, as [Defaults](options.md#defaults) explains.

#### 3. Make an Option Optional

`Options#optional` gives `Some(value)` when the option is given and `None` when it is missing. To accept an optional user name:

```scala
val user: Options[Option[String]] = Options.text("user").optional
```

#### 4. Put a Default on Alternatives

For two alternative options combined with `Options#orElseEither` or `Options#|`, put the default on the whole alternative, not on each option. To accept `--port` or `--socket`, with port 8080 when neither is given:

```scala
val endpoint: Options[Either[BigInt, String]] =
  (Options.integer("port") orElseEither Options.text("socket")).withDefault(Left(BigInt(8080)))
```

An option with a default inside an alternative always reports a collision; see [Choosing Between Options](options.md#choosing-between-options).

#### 5. Combine the Options in a Command

`Options#++` combines the options, and the command receives a flat tuple with one value per option, in the order they are combined. To build the command:

```scala
val serve: Command[(Boolean, Int, Option[String], Either[BigInt, String])] =
  Command("serve", quiet ++ retries ++ user ++ endpoint)
```

#### 6. Check the Help

The help of a single option with `Options#withDefault` ends with `This setting is optional. Default: '<value>'.`, and the help of an option with `Options#optional` ends with `This setting is optional.`. Alternatives with a default get no such sentence. To print the help of the command:

```scala
println(serve.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// 
// OPTIONS
// 
//   --quiet
//     A true or false value.
// 
//     This setting is optional. Default: 'false'.
// 
//   --retries <integer>
//     An integer.
// 
//     This setting is optional. Default: '3'.
// 
//   --user <text>
//     A user-defined piece of text.
// 
//     This setting is optional.
// 
//   --port <integer>
//     An integer.
// 
//   --socket <text>
//     A user-defined piece of text.
// 
//
```

The usage line shows every optional option, including the alternatives with a default, in square brackets:

```scala
println(serve.synopsis.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// serve [--quiet] [--retries <integer>] [--user <text>] [--port <integer>|--socket <text>]
//
```

### What the Default Does Not Cover

A default is used only when the option is missing; an invalid value such as `--retries many` still fails with `many is not a integer.`, and the default itself is not validated (see [Defaults](options.md#defaults)).

Positional arguments have no counterpart of `Options#withDefault` or `Options#optional`. To make an argument optional, accept at most one value with `Args#atMost(1)`, as described in [Args](args.md#methods).

### Complete Example

The complete program runs the `serve` command and prints the values it receives:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._

object ServeApp extends ZIOCliDefault {
  val quiet: Options[Boolean]       = Options.boolean("quiet")
  val retries: Options[Int]         = Options.integer("retries").map(_.toInt).withDefault(3)
  val user: Options[Option[String]] = Options.text("user").optional
  val endpoint: Options[Either[BigInt, String]] =
    (Options.integer("port") orElseEither Options.text("socket")).withDefault(Left(BigInt(8080)))

  val serve = Command("serve", quiet ++ retries ++ user ++ endpoint)

  val cliApp = CliApp.make("serve", "1.0.0", HelpDoc.Span.text("Starts the server."), serve) {
    case (quiet, retries, user, endpoint) =>
      Console.printLine(s"quiet=$quiet retries=$retries user=$user endpoint=$endpoint")
  }
}
```

Run without options, the program prints `quiet=false retries=3 user=None endpoint=Left(8080)`.

### See Also

- [Options](options.md#defaults): the reference for `Options#optional` and `Options#withDefault`.
- [How to validate and convert a parameter's value](how-to-validate-input.md): reject values that parse but are not acceptable.

## How to package a CLI as a native binary

This guide turns a **ZIO CLI** app into a standalone native executable with GraalVM `native-image`, driven from sbt by the [sbt-native-image](https://github.com/scalameta/sbt-native-image) plugin. The executable starts without a JVM, which makes a command-line tool start almost instantly.

### Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

- An sbt project with an app object that extends `ZIOCliDefault`, such as the `Greet` app from [Getting Started](getting-started.md).
- Either sbt 1.x or sbt 2.x. sbt-native-image is published for both.

You do not need to install GraalVM. By default, sbt-native-image downloads a GraalVM distribution with [Coursier](https://get-coursier.io/) the first time it builds an image. `native-image` still needs a C toolchain on the machine. On Linux, install `gcc` and the zlib development headers, for example `zlib1g-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu. On macOS, install the Xcode command line tools. On Windows, install the Visual Studio C++ build tools.

### Step 1: Add the Plugin

Add sbt-native-image to `project/plugins.sbt`:

```scala
addSbtPlugin("org.scalameta" % "sbt-native-image" % "0.6.0")
```

### Step 2: Enable the Plugin and Set the Main Class

Enable `NativeImagePlugin` on the project that contains the app, and set `Compile / mainClass` to the fully qualified name of the app object. The binary is named after the project, so we also set `name`:

```scala
lazy val root = project
  .in(file("."))
  .enablePlugins(NativeImagePlugin)
  .settings(
    name                := "greet",
    Compile / mainClass := Some("Greet"),
    nativeImageOptions += "--no-fallback"
  )
```

`nativeImageOptions` holds extra arguments for `native-image`, and it is empty by default. The `--no-fallback` option makes the build fail when GraalVM cannot compile the app ahead of time, instead of producing an image that still needs a JVM to run. When the project has exactly one main class, sbt finds it without `Compile / mainClass`; with several, the build stops with `no mainClass is specified` until you set it.

### Step 3: Build the Executable

Run the `nativeImage` task:

```bash
sbt nativeImage
```

The task compiles the project, runs `native-image` (which takes a minute or more), and logs the absolute path of the binary. The binary is written to `native-image/<project name>` under the project's target directory: `target/native-image/greet` for the project above on sbt 1.x. The first build also downloads GraalVM, which takes longer.

### Step 4: Run the Executable

Run the binary like any other program. To print the app's help screen:

```bash
./target/native-image/greet --help
```

From sbt, `nativeImageRun` runs the binary that the last `nativeImage` built, passing the arguments that follow it:

```bash
sbt nativeImage "nativeImageRun --help"
```

To copy the binary to a fixed location, for example in a CI job that uploads it, use `nativeImageCopy` with the destination path:

```bash
sbt "nativeImageCopy greet-linux-x86_64"
```

### Use a Locally Installed GraalVM

To use a GraalVM that is already installed instead of downloading one, set the environment variable `NATIVE_IMAGE_INSTALLED=true` (or `GRAALVM_INSTALLED=true`) before starting sbt:

```bash
NATIVE_IMAGE_INSTALLED=true GRAALVM_HOME=/path/to/graalvm sbt nativeImage
```

sbt-native-image then runs `bin/native-image` from the first of `GRAAL_HOME`, `GRAALVM_HOME` and `JAVA_HOME` that is set. To keep the download but change the GraalVM release it fetches, set `nativeImageJvm` and `nativeImageVersion`; in sbt-native-image 0.6.0 they default to `"graalvm-java25"` and `"25.0.1"`.

### Apps That Use Reflection

`native-image` must know at build time about every class that is loaded by reflection. If the binary fails at runtime with a missing class or method while the same app works on the JVM, run the app once under the GraalVM tracing agent with `nativeImageRunAgent`, then pass the generated configuration to `nativeImageOptions` and rebuild. The [sbt-native-image README](https://github.com/scalameta/sbt-native-image#nativeimagerunagent) shows the exact settings.

### The ZIO CLI sbt Plugin

The ZIO CLI repository also contains an sbt plugin, `sbt-zio-cli`, whose `zioCliBuildNative` task wraps the same `nativeImage` task. It is not published, so the steps above are the shorter path. See [ZIO CLI sbt Plugin](sbt-plugin.md) for what it adds.

### See Also

- [ZIO CLI sbt Plugin](sbt-plugin.md) describes the `sbt-zio-cli` settings and tasks.
- [How to add Tab completion in bash](how-to-add-shell-completion.md) generates a bash completion script for the installed executable.
- The [sbt-native-image README](https://github.com/scalameta/sbt-native-image) lists every setting and task of the plugin.

## How to test a CLI app

This guide writes a [ZIO Test](https://zio.dev/reference/test/) spec for a **ZIO CLI** app with the `zio-cli-testkit` module. By the end, the spec checks that:

1. The usage line and the help document describe the command correctly.
2. Valid arguments, both hand-picked and randomly generated, produce the right value, and invalid arguments are rejected.
3. `--help` is recognized and prints the option names.
4. The app returns the right result, and parse errors and errors from the app's own code are reported as different `CliError` cases.

A **spec** is a ZIO Test object that holds tests, a **suite** groups tests under a name, and each **test** runs one check. Every assertion used here is described in the [testkit reference](testing.md).

### Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

- The `zio-cli-testkit` dependency in the `Test` configuration of your build. The dependency line is in [Modules](index.md#modules). sbt 1.5 and later run ZIO Test specs without extra setup; on older sbt versions, add `testFrameworks += new TestFramework("zio.test.sbt.ZTestFramework")` to `build.sbt`.
- A test source file, for example `src/test/scala/GreetCliSpec.scala`.
- A `Command` and a `CliApp` to test. This guide uses a small greeting app.

### Step 1: Define the Command and the App

We start with the code under test. The command `GreetCli.greet` has two required options, `--name` (text) and `--times` (integer). The app `GreetCli.app` returns a greeting, and a second app, `GreetCli.failingApp`, always fails so we can test the execution error path:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.testkit._
import zio.cli.testkit.CliAssertion._
import zio.test._

object GreetCli {

  val greet: Command[(String, BigInt)] =
    Command("greet", Options.text("name") ++ Options.integer("times"))

  val app: CliApp[Any, Nothing, String] =
    CliApp.make("greet", "1.0.0", HelpDoc.Span.text("Greets a person."), greet) { case (name, times) =>
      ZIO.succeed(s"Hello, $name x$times")
    }

  val failingApp: CliApp[Any, String, String] =
    CliApp.make[Any, String, (String, BigInt), String](
      "greet",
      "1.0.0",
      HelpDoc.Span.text("Greets a person."),
      greet
    ) { case (_, _) =>
      ZIO.fail("boom")
    }
}
```

Two details matter in every later step. First, the `import zio.cli.testkit.CliAssertion._` line brings the implicit `CliConfig` into scope, which the parsing assertions need; see [Imports and the Implicit CliConfig](testing.md#imports-and-the-implicit-cliconfig). Second, an argument list passed to a `Command` starts with the command name, while an argument list passed to a `CliApp` does not, because `CliApp#run` adds the name itself. That is why the command tests below start with `"greet"` and the app tests do not.

### Step 2: Check the Usage Line and the Help Document

`CliAssertion.assertSynopsis` compares the rendered usage line, and `CliAssertion.assertHelpDoc` compares the help document of the command. The expected usage line uses the placeholders that ZIO CLI prints for each value type, here `<text>` and `<integer>`:

```scala
val documentationTests =
  suite("documentation")(
    test("the usage line lists both options") {
      assertSynopsis(GreetCli.greet, "greet --name <text> --times <integer>")
    },
    test("the app uses the greet command's help document") {
      assertHelpDoc(GreetCli.app, GreetCli.greet.helpDoc)
    }
  )
```

These assertions return a `TestResult` directly, so no effect is involved. See [Synopsis and Help Assertions](testing.md#synopsis-and-help-assertions) for the other forms.

### Step 3: Test Parsing with Fixed Inputs

Next, we check how the command parses hand-picked argument lists. `CliAssertion.assertCommand` takes `CliRepr` pairs of arguments and the expected value. `CliAssertion.assertCommandSuccess` takes pairs of arguments and an `Assertion` on the whole `Either[ValidationError, A]`, which makes it the method for inputs that must be rejected:

```scala
val validInputs: Gen[Any, CliRepr[List[String], (String, BigInt)]] =
  Gen.fromIterable(
    List(
      CliRepr(List("greet", "--name", "Ada", "--times", "2"), ("Ada", BigInt(2))),
      CliRepr(List("greet", "--times", "1", "--name", "Lin"), ("Lin", BigInt(1)))
    )
  )

val invalidInputs: Gen[Any, CliRepr[List[String], Assertion[Either[ValidationError, (String, BigInt)]]]] =
  Gen.fromIterable(
    List(
      // --times is required and missing
      CliRepr(List("greet", "--name", "Ada"), Assertion.isLeft),
      // --times is not an integer
      CliRepr(List("greet", "--name", "Ada", "--times", "two"), Assertion.isLeft)
    )
  )

val parsingTests =
  suite("parsing")(
    test("valid arguments produce the parsed values") {
      assertCommand(GreetCli.greet, validInputs)
    },
    test("invalid arguments produce a validation error") {
      assertCommandSuccess(GreetCli.greet, invalidInputs)
    }
  )
```

Both methods return a ZIO effect, and returning that effect from `test` is enough. The check runs every input from the generator and fails if any of them does not match. See [Parsing Assertions](testing.md#parsing-assertions).

### Step 4: Test Parsing with Generated Inputs

Fixed inputs cover the cases we think of. A random generator covers many more: here every sample is a random alphanumeric name and a random count, and the expected value is built from the same random parts:

```scala
val randomInputs: Gen[Any, CliRepr[List[String], (String, BigInt)]] =
  (Gen.alphaNumericStringBounded(1, 10) <*> Gen.int(1, 100)).map { case (name, times) =>
    CliRepr(List("greet", "--name", name, "--times", times.toString), (name, BigInt(times)))
  }

val propertyTests =
  suite("property-based parsing")(
    test("any alphanumeric name and positive count parse") {
      assertCommand(GreetCli.greet, randomInputs)
    }
  )
```

ZIO Test draws 200 samples by default; change the count with `TestAspect.samples`. When ZIO Test finds a failing sample, it shrinks it to a smaller failing input before reporting it.

### Step 5: Test Help Output

There are two ways to check `--help`. `CliAssertion.assertCommandAll` checks that the command recognizes the built-in option, and `CliAssertion.outputContains` checks the text the app prints.

`--help` does not produce a value of the command's type, so `CliAssertion.assertCommand` cannot check it: it fails the test with a `java.lang.Exception` that has no message. `CliAssertion.assertCommandAll` passes the result as a [`TestReturn`](testing.md#testreturn), where every built-in option appears as `TestReturn.Help()`:

```scala
val helpInput: CliRepr[List[String], Assertion[Either[ValidationError, TestReturn[(String, BigInt)]]]] =
  CliRepr(List("greet", "--help"), Assertion.isRight(Assertion.equalTo(TestReturn.Help())))

val helpTests =
  suite("help")(
    test("--help returns the built-in help directive") {
      assertCommandAll(GreetCli.greet, Gen.const(helpInput))
    },
    test("--help prints the option names") {
      outputContains(GreetCli.app, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--help"), Seq("--name", "--times"))))
    }
  )
```

For `--help`, the app prints this help screen as a single console entry:

```text
                         __
   ____ _________  ___  / /_
  / __ `/ ___/ _ \/ _ \/ __/
 / /_/ / /  /  __/  __/ /_
 \__, /_/   \___/\___/\__/
/____/

greet 1.0.0 -- Greets a person.

USAGE

  $ greet --name <text> --times <integer>

OPTIONS

  --name <text>
    A user-defined piece of text.

  --times <integer>
    An integer.
```

`CliAssertion.outputContains` passes when each expected string is a substring of one captured console entry, so `--name` and `--times` both match. The captured output is not cleared between samples, so keep one input per `CliAssertion.outputContains` call when the inputs print different text. See [Console Output Assertion](testing.md#console-output-assertion).

### Step 6: Test Results and Failures

`CliAssertion.assertCliAppValues` checks that the app succeeds with an expected value. `CliAssertion.assertCliApp` passes the full `Either[CliError[E], A]` from `CliApp#run` to an `Assertion`, which lets us tell the two kinds of failure apart:

- `CliError.Parsing` means the arguments did not parse. The app prints only the error message, for example `Expected to find --times option.`, and stops before it runs its own code.
- `CliError.Execution` means the app's own code failed. It holds the error the app returned.

The following tests cover a successful run and both failure kinds:

```scala
val parseFailure: Gen[Any, CliRepr[List[String], Assertion[Either[CliError[Nothing], String]]]] =
  Gen.const(
    CliRepr(
      List("--name", "Ada"),
      Assertion.assertion[Either[CliError[Nothing], String]]("is a parsing error") {
        case Left(CliError.Parsing(_)) => true
        case _                         => false
      }
    )
  )

val executionFailure: Gen[Any, CliRepr[List[String], Assertion[Either[CliError[String], String]]]] =
  Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--name", "Ada", "--times", "2"), Assertion.isLeft(Assertion.equalTo(CliError.Execution("boom")))))

val appTests =
  suite("app")(
    test("valid arguments return the greeting") {
      assertCliAppValues(GreetCli.app, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--name", "Ada", "--times", "2"), "Hello, Ada x2")))
    },
    test("missing --times is a parsing error") {
      assertCliApp(GreetCli.app, parseFailure)
    },
    test("an error from the app is an execution error") {
      assertCliApp(GreetCli.failingApp, executionFailure)
    }
  )
```

Do not use `CliAssertion.assertCliAppZIO` for parse errors: it reports only `CliError.Execution` to the comparison and fails the whole check on any other error. Do not pass `--help` to the app assertions either; `CliApp#run` returns `None` for it, and they fail with a message-less `java.lang.Exception`. See [App Assertions](testing.md#app-assertions).

### Step 7: Assemble and Run the Spec

Finally, we put the suites in one spec object named after the app:

```scala
object GreetCliSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec =
    suite("GreetCli")(documentationTests, parsingTests, propertyTests, helpTests, appTests)
}
```

Run it with your build's test task, for example `sbt test`, or `sbt "testOnly GreetCliSpec"` for this spec alone.

### Troubleshooting

When a test fails for a reason unrelated to your app, check these common causes:

- `could not find implicit value for parameter cliConfig`: the file does not import `zio.cli.testkit.CliAssertion._`, or it imports both `CliAssertion._` and `GenerationAssertion._` with wildcards.
- `java.lang.Exception: null`: a built-in option such as `--help` reached `CliAssertion.assertCommand`, `CliAssertion.assertCommandSuccess` or one of the app assertions. Use `CliAssertion.assertCommandAll` or `CliAssertion.outputContains`.
- A valid input fails as a parsing error: a command test is missing the command name as its first argument, or an app test includes it.

### See Also

- [Testing CLI Applications](testing.md) lists every testkit method with its exact behaviour.
- [Commands](commands.md) and [Options](options.md) describe the values under test.
- [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) describes `--help`, shell completion and the wizard.
- [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md) describes `ValidationError` and `CliError`.
