## How to validate and convert a parameter's value

Every option and argument already checks that its input has the right type: `Options.integer` rejects `ten`. This guide adds the checks that the type cannot express, such as "a port between 1 and 65535" or "one of these three words", and converts the input into your own types. Each step shows the error message the user sees.

You need the `zio-cli` library on your classpath (see [Installation](index.md#installation)) and options and arguments to check; [Options](options.md) and [Args](args.md) describe how to build them.

### Choose a Method

Pick the method by the kind of check:

| Check                                              | Method                                    | Error text comes from            |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| The value is one word from a fixed list            | `Options.enumeration`, `Args.enumeration` | ZIO CLI                          |
| The value matches some cases of a partial function | `Options#collect`                         | the message you pass             |
| Any rule, on an option                             | `Options#mapOrFail`                       | the `ValidationError` you return |
| Any rule, on an argument                           | `Args#mapOrFail`                          | the `HelpDoc` you return         |
| A conversion that may throw, on an argument        | `Args#mapTry`                             | the exception's message          |
| A path that must exist, or must be new             | an `Exists` value, or a `PrimType.Path`   | ZIO CLI                          |

`Options#mapOrFail` and `Args#mapOrFail` look alike but differ in their error type: the `Options` version returns a `ValidationError`, and the `Args` version returns a `HelpDoc`. `Options` has no counterpart of `Args#mapTry`.

### Steps

We first define a helper that parses a command line and returns the error text, so each step can show what the user sees. `CliApp` prints the same text when parsing fails:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._

def errorFor[A](command: Command[A], input: String*): String =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe
      .run(command.parse(input.toList, CliConfig.default).flip.map(_.error.toPlaintext(color = false).trim))
      .getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

The input starts with the command name, because `Command#parse` expects it.

#### 1. Accept Only Fixed Words

`Options.enumeration` maps each accepted word to a value. To accept three log levels:

```scala
val level: Options[Int] = Options.enumeration("level")(("debug", 0), ("info", 1), ("warn", 2))
val log                 = Command("log", level)
```

A word outside the list fails, and so does a word in the wrong case:

```scala
println(errorFor(log, "log", "--level", "error"))
// Expected one of the following cases: debug, info, warn
println(errorFor(log, "log", "--level", "DEBUG"))
// Expected one of the following cases: debug, info, warn
```

#### 2. Keep Some Values With Options#collect

`Options#collect` takes the message to show and a partial function. Values that the partial function does not match are rejected. To accept two colors and map them to codes:

```scala
val color: Options[Int] =
  Options.text("color").collect("color must be red or blue") {
    case "red"  => 1
    case "blue" => 2
  }
val paint = Command("paint", color)
```

With an unmatched color, the user sees the message:

```scala
println(errorFor(paint, "paint", "--color", "green"))
// color must be red or blue
```

#### 3. Check an Option With Options#mapOrFail

`Options#mapOrFail` runs a function that returns `Right` with the converted value, or `Left` with a `ValidationError`. Use `ValidationErrorType.InvalidValue` for a value that does not meet the rule, and `HelpDoc.p` for the message. To accept only valid port numbers:

```scala
val port: Options[Int] =
  Options.integer("port").mapOrFail { (value: BigInt) =>
    if (value >= 1 && value <= 65535) Right(value.toInt)
    else Left(ValidationError(ValidationErrorType.InvalidValue, HelpDoc.p("Port must be between 1 and 65535.")))
  }
val serve = Command("serve", port)
```

The user sees the type error before our rule runs, and our message when the type is right but the rule fails:

```scala
println(errorFor(serve, "serve", "--port", "http"))
// http is not a integer.
println(errorFor(serve, "serve", "--port", "70000"))
// Port must be between 1 and 65535.
```

#### 4. Check an Argument With Args#mapOrFail

`Args#mapOrFail` works the same way for positional arguments, but the `Left` holds only a `HelpDoc`. To accept a positive count:

```scala
val count: Args[Int] =
  Args.integer("count").mapOrFail { (n: BigInt) =>
    if (n > 0) Right(n.toInt) else Left(HelpDoc.p("The count must be positive."))
  }
val repeat = Command("repeat", count)
```

A count of zero fails with our message:

```scala
println(errorFor(repeat, "repeat", "0"))
// The count must be positive.
```

#### 5. Convert With Code That Throws

`Args#mapTry` runs a conversion that may throw, and turns the exception's message into the error. To parse an argument as a URI:

```scala
val uri: Args[java.net.URI] = Args.text("uri").mapTry(java.net.URI.create)
val open                    = Command("open", uri)
```

The message of the exception that `java.net.URI.create` throws becomes the error:

```scala
println(errorFor(open, "open", "not a uri"))
// Illegal character in path at index 3: not a uri
```

`Options` has no counterpart of `Args#mapTry`. For an option, wrap the conversion in `scala.util.Try` inside `Options#mapOrFail`:

```scala
val endpoint: Options[java.net.URI] =
  Options.text("endpoint").mapOrFail { (text: String) =>
    scala.util.Try(java.net.URI.create(text)).toEither.left.map { e =>
      ValidationError(ValidationErrorType.InvalidValue, HelpDoc.p(e.getMessage))
    }
  }
```

#### 6. Check That a Path Exists

The `exists` parameter of the path constructors checks the file system. `Exists.Yes` rejects a missing path, and `Exists.No` rejects an existing one. To require an existing input file:

```scala
val input = Command("cat", Args.file("input", exists = Exists.Yes))
```

A missing file fails before your program runs:

```scala
println(errorFor(input, "cat", "/no/such/file"))
// Path '/no/such/file' must exist.
```

No constructor accepts "an existing file or directory". For that rule, wrap a `PrimType.Path` in `Options.Single` or `Args.Single`:

```scala
val source: Options[java.nio.file.Path] =
  Options.Single("source", Vector.empty, PrimType.Path(PathType.Either, Exists.Yes))
val copy = Command("copy", source)
```

The help describes the rule, and a missing path fails the same way:

```scala
println(source.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --source <path>
//   An existing file or directory.
// 
// 
println(errorFor(copy, "copy", "--source", "/no/such/dir"))
// Path '/no/such/dir' must exist.
```

### Complete Example

The complete program combines a checked option and a converted argument:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._

object FetchApp extends ZIOCliDefault {
  val port: Options[Int] =
    Options.integer("port").mapOrFail { (value: BigInt) =>
      if (value >= 1 && value <= 65535) Right(value.toInt)
      else Left(ValidationError(ValidationErrorType.InvalidValue, HelpDoc.p("Port must be between 1 and 65535.")))
    }

  val uri: Args[java.net.URI] = Args.text("uri").mapTry(java.net.URI.create)

  val fetch = Command("fetch", port, uri)

  val cliApp = CliApp.make("fetch", "1.0.0", HelpDoc.Span.text("Fetches a URI."), fetch) { case (port, uri) =>
    Console.printLine(s"Fetching $uri through port $port")
  }
}
```

### See Also

- [Value Types](value-types.md): the input each value type accepts, and the messages for type errors.
- [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md): the `ValidationError` type and how `CliApp` reports errors.

## Introduction to ZIO CLI

Rapidly build powerful command-line applications powered by ZIO

[![Experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Experimental-yellowgreen.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-cli/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-cli_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-cli_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-cli_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-cli_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-cli_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-cli_2.13) [![ZIO CLI](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-cli?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-cli)

### Introduction

**ZIO CLI** turns a typed description of a command line into a working program. We describe the commands, options and arguments a program accepts, and ZIO CLI parses the user's input into Scala values, reports errors, and generates the help text from the same description.

Key features of ZIO CLI:

- **Typed options and arguments**: Text, numbers, booleans, dates, paths, enumerations and key-value pairs are parsed into Scala types.
- **Commands and subcommands**: Programs such as `git remote add` are built from small commands that compose.
- **Generated help**: The `--help` output, usage line and error messages come from the command description, so they never drift from the code.
- **Built-in features**: Every app gets `--help`, an interactive `--wizard` mode and bash completion without extra code.
- **Testing support**: The `zio-cli-testkit` module checks parsing and app behaviour inside ZIO Test.
- **Cross-platform**: The library runs on the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native.

### Installation

ZIO CLI is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3. To use it on the JVM, add the following to your `build.sbt` file:

```scala
// Commands, options, arguments, generated help, wizard mode and shell completion (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-cli" % "0.8.3"
```

For Scala.js or Scala Native projects, use `%%%` instead:

```scala
// Commands, options, arguments, generated help, wizard mode and shell completion (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %%% "zio-cli" % "0.8.3"
```

The [Getting Started](getting-started.md) page walks through a first program.

### Modules

Besides the core library, ZIO CLI has a module for tests and an sbt plugin.

#### Testing

The testkit adds assertions and generators that check how commands parse their input and how apps behave. To use it on the JVM, add it as a test dependency:

```scala
// Assertions and generators for testing commands and apps with ZIO Test (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-cli-testkit" % "0.8.3" % Test
```

For Scala.js or Scala Native projects, use `%%%` instead:

```scala
// Assertions and generators for testing commands and apps with ZIO Test (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %%% "zio-cli-testkit" % "0.8.3" % Test
```

The [Testing](testing.md) reference lists the assertions, and [How to test a CLI app](how-to-test-a-cli.md) shows them in use.

#### sbt Plugin

The ZIO CLI sbt plugin is not published to Maven Central; the [sbt Plugin](sbt-plugin.md) page explains how to build it from source and what it provides.

### Example

The following program implements a small part of `git clone`, with one boolean option, one argument and help text for both:

```scala
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text

object GitClone extends ZIOCliDefault {

  val local: Options[Boolean] =
    Options.boolean("local").alias("l") ?? "Clone from a repository on this machine."

  val repository: Args[String] =
    Args.text("repository") ?? "The repository to clone."

  val cloneCommand: Command[(Boolean, String)] =
    Command("clone", local, repository).withHelp("Creates a copy of an existing repository.")

  val cliApp = CliApp.make(
    name = "Sample Git",
    version = "1.1.0",
    summary = text("Sample implementation of git clone"),
    command = cloneCommand
  ) { case (isLocal, repo) =>
    printLine(s"Cloning $repo (local: $isLocal)")
  }
}
```

Running the program with `-l https://github.com/zio/zio-cli.git` prints `Cloning https://github.com/zio/zio-cli.git (local: true)`. Running it with `--help` prints a banner with the app name, followed by help text generated from the description:

```text
Sample Git 1.1.0 -- Sample implementation of git clone

USAGE

  $ clone [(-l, --local)] <repository>

DESCRIPTION

  Creates a copy of an existing repository.

ARGUMENTS

  <repository>
    A user-defined piece of text.

    The repository to clone.

OPTIONS

  (-l, --local)
    A true or false value.

    Clone from a repository on this machine.

    This setting is optional. Default: 'false'.
```

---

## Options

`Options[A]` describes the named parameters of a command, such as `--quiet` or `--message "Fix typo"`. An `Options[A]` is a description, not a parsed value. It says which options the command accepts and how to build an `A` from them, and a [`Command`](commands.md) uses it to parse the user's input.

An option is written as `--name` when its name is longer than one character, and as `-n` when it is one character long. The same rule applies to aliases. ZIO CLI accepts these forms on the command line:

- A value after the name, as in `--name Ada`, or joined with `=`, as in `--name=Ada`.
- Clustered one-character flags, as in `-abc` for `-a -b -c`.
- Options in any order among themselves, but before the command's positional [arguments](args.md). Reading of options stops at the first token that is not an option, and a `--` token makes every later token an argument.

A misspelled option name close to a real one, such as `--firstnme`, fails with `The flag "--firstnme" is not recognized. Did you mean --firstname?`. [How to Write Options](parsing.md#how-to-write-options) describes these rules in detail.

### Constructors

The `Options` companion object has one constructor per value type, plus constructors for flags, key-value pairs and commands without options. Every constructor takes the option's name; there are no unnamed options.

#### Value Options

A value option reads the token after its name and converts it to its value type. The constructors are `Options.text`, `Options.integer`, `Options.decimal`, `Options.duration`, `Options.instant`, `Options.localDate`, `Options.localDateTime`, `Options.localTime`, `Options.monthDay`, `Options.offsetDateTime`, `Options.offsetTime`, `Options.period`, `Options.year`, `Options.yearMonth`, `Options.zonedDateTime`, `Options.zoneId` and `Options.zoneOffset`. [Value Types](value-types.md) lists the Scala type, the placeholder and the accepted input of each one.

To declare a required integer option:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val count: Options[BigInt] = Options.integer("count")
```

A value option is required. Without it, parsing fails with `Expected to find --count option.`, and a value that cannot be converted fails with `ten is not a integer.`. [Defaults](#defaults) shows how to make an option optional.

#### Boolean Options

`Options.boolean(name, ifPresent = true)` creates a flag. The flag alone gives `ifPresent`, and a missing flag gives the opposite value, so every boolean option already has a default.

To declare a flag that is `true` when present, and one that is `false` when present:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val quiet: Options[Boolean]    = Options.boolean("quiet")
val progress: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("progress", ifPresent = false)
```

The user can also give the value explicitly, as `--quiet true`, `--quiet false` or `--quiet=false`.

:::caution
A flag reads the next token as its value only when it is exactly `true` or `false`. Other boolean words such as `no`, `0` or `FALSE` are not read: `--quiet=no` and `--quiet no` give `true`, and `no` is left over as a positional argument. The words listed in [Boolean](value-types.md#boolean) work for `Args.bool`, not for flags. [Boolean Flags](parsing.md#boolean-flags) shows examples.
:::

#### Boolean Options With a Negation

`Options.boolean(name, ifPresent, negationName, negationNames*)` adds a second flag that gives the opposite value. With `ifPresent` set to `true`, `--color` gives `true`, `--no-color` gives `false`, and the value is `false` when neither flag is given. Extra `negationNames` are aliases of the negation flag. Giving both flags fails with `Options collision detected. You can only specify either --color or --no-color.`.

To declare a color flag with its negation:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val color: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("color", true, "no-color")
```

`Options.boolean(name, alias, ifPresent, negationName, negationNames*)` also gives the main flag an alias. To declare `-v`/`--verbose` with the negation `-q`/`--quiet`:

```scala
val verbose: Options[Boolean] = Options.boolean("verbose", "v", true, "quiet", "q")
```

:::caution
Do not call `Options#alias` on a boolean option with a negation. The alias is added to both flags, so using it always fails with `Options collision detected`. Pass the alias to `Options.boolean` instead, as in the example above.
:::

#### Enumeration Options

`Options.enumeration(name)(cases*)` accepts one of a fixed set of words. Each case is a pair of the word the user types and the value it stands for. The word must match exactly, including its case.

To accept one of three commit modes:

```scala
import zio.cli._

sealed trait Mode
object Mode {
  case object All         extends Mode
  case object Interactive extends Mode
  case object Patch       extends Mode
}

val mode: Options[Mode] =
  Options.enumeration[Mode]("mode")(("all", Mode.All), ("interactive", Mode.Interactive), ("patch", Mode.Patch))
```

The help lists the accepted words:

```scala
println(mode.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --mode all | interactive | patch
//   One of the following cases: all, interactive, patch.
// 
//
```

#### Path Options

`Options.file(name, exists)` and `Options.directory(name, exists)` produce a `java.nio.file.Path`. The `exists` parameter defaults to `Exists.Either`. An existing path must also be of the right kind, so `Options.file` rejects an existing directory.

To require an existing configuration file:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val config = Options.file("config", exists = Exists.Yes)
```

`Options.directory` is not available on Scala.js, and `Options.file` there rejects every value. There is no `Options.path`; an option that accepts a file or a directory is built from a `PrimType`. [Paths](value-types.md#paths), [Custom Parameters From a PrimType](value-types.md#custom-parameters-from-a-primtype) and [Platform Support](value-types.md#platform-support) give the details.

#### Key-Value Options

`Options.keyValueMap(name)` collects `key=value` pairs into a `Map[String, String]`. The user repeats the option for each pair, as in `-d a=1 -d b=2`, or lists several pairs after one option, as in `-d a=1 b=2`. Reading stops at the first token without `=` or with an empty value, and the rest is left for the next options or arguments. `Options.keyValueMap(option)` takes an `Options.Single[String]` instead of a name.

To collect definitions under `--define` and `-d`:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val defines: Options[Map[String, String]] = Options.keyValueMap("define").alias("d")
```

:::caution
A key-value option does not accept the `--define=a=1` form, and with the default case-insensitive [`CliConfig`](cli-config.md) it does not recognize a name or alias that contains capital letters, such as `-D`. Use lower-case names.
:::

#### No Options

`Options.none` is an `Options[Unit]` that consumes no input. A command built without options uses it, and it disappears from the command's value.

To declare a command that takes no options:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val status = Command("status", Options.none, Args.none)
```

#### Other Constructors

`Options.oauth2(provider, scope)` adds OAuth2 authorization and is available only on the JVM; see [Authorization with OAuth2](auth.md). `Options.Single(name, aliases, primType, description, pseudoName)` wraps any `PrimType` directly, as shown in [Custom Parameters From a PrimType](value-types.md#custom-parameters-from-a-primtype).

### Methods

The `Options` trait has the following public methods. `Options#as` and `Options#fold` have overloads for two to six values, and only the smallest is shown:

```scala
sealed trait Options[+A] {
  def ++[A1 >: A, B](that: Options[B])(implicit zippable: Zippable[A, B]): Options[zippable.Out]
  def |[A1 >: A](that: Options[A1]): Options[A1]
  def orElse[A1 >: A](that: Options[A1]): Options[A1]
  def orElseEither[B](that: Options[B]): Options[Either[A, B]]

  def optional: Options[Option[A]]
  def withDefault[A1 >: A](value: A1): Options[A1]

  def map[B](f: A => B): Options[B]
  def mapOrFail[B](f: A => Either[ValidationError, B]): Options[B]
  def collect[B](message: String)(f: PartialFunction[A, B]): Options[B]
  def as[B, C, Z](f: (B, C) => Z)(implicit ev: A <:< (B, C)): Options[Z]
  def fold[B, C, Z](f1: B => Z, f2: C => Z)(implicit ev: A <:< Either[B, C]): Options[Z]

  def ??(that: String): Options[A]
  def alias(name: String, names: String*): Options[A]
  def withPseudoName(name: String): Options[A]

  def helpDoc: HelpDoc
  def synopsis: UsageSynopsis
  def isBool: Boolean
  def flatten: List[Options[_] with Input]
  def validate(args: Map[String, List[String]], conf: CliConfig): IO[ValidationError, A]
  def uid: Option[String]
}
```

#### Combining Options With ++

`Options#++` requires both options. The result is a flat tuple: `a ++ b ++ c` is an `Options[(A, B, C)]`, not a nested pair, and `Unit` values such as `Options.none` disappear from it.

To combine a flag and a text option:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val commitOptions: Options[(Boolean, String)] = Options.boolean("all") ++ Options.text("message")
```

The usage line of a command with these options is `[--all] --message <text>`. A flag is in square brackets because it has a default.

#### Choosing Between Options

`Options#|` (and its alias `Options#orElse`) accepts exactly one of two options of a common type. `Options#orElseEither` does the same for options of different types and wraps the result in an `Either`, with `Left` for the first option. If both options are given, parsing fails with `Options collision detected. You can only specify either --name or --id.`. If neither is given, parsing fails with both missing-option messages, unless the whole alternative has a default.

To accept a user by name or by ID, with a default when neither is given:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val user: Options[Either[String, BigInt]] =
  Options.text("name") orElseEither Options.integer("id")

val userOrMe: Options[Either[String, BigInt]] = user.withDefault(Left("me"))
```

The usage line shows the alternatives separated by `|`, as `--name <text>|--id <integer>`.

:::caution
Do not combine options that already have a default with `Options#|`, `Options#orElse` or `Options#orElseEither`. Such an option always succeeds, so the alternative always reports a collision, even when the user gives no option at all. This includes every `Options.boolean` and every option built with `Options#optional` or `Options#withDefault`. Put the default on the whole alternative instead, and use an enumeration for mutually exclusive modes, as in [Enumeration Options](#enumeration-options).
:::

When the choice is between flags, separate flags with a check also work. To reject `--all` together with `--patch`:

```scala
val mode: Options[String] =
  (Options.boolean("all") ++ Options.boolean("patch")).mapOrFail {
    case (true, true) =>
      Left(ValidationError(ValidationErrorType.InvalidValue, HelpDoc.p("Use either --all or --patch.")))
    case (true, false) => Right("all")
    case (false, true) => Right("patch")
    case (false, false) => Right("default")
  }
```

### Defaults

An option without a default is required. These methods make it optional.

#### Options#optional

`Options#optional` wraps the value in `Some`, and gives `None` when the option is missing. To make a port optional:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val port: Options[Option[BigInt]] = Options.integer("port").optional
```

The help adds `This setting is optional.`, and the usage line shows the option in square brackets, as `[--port <integer>]`.

#### Options#withDefault

`Options#withDefault(value)` uses `value` when the option is missing. To default the output directory to `target`:

```scala
val output = Options.directory("output").withDefault(java.nio.file.Paths.get("target"))
```

The help shows the default:

```scala
println(output.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --output <directory>
//   A directory.
// 
//   This setting is optional. Default: 'target'.
// 
//
```

The default is used only when the option is missing. A value the user gives that is not valid is still an error. The default itself is not validated, so a default path is not checked against `Exists`. The default must have the option's type or a supertype of it: `Options.integer("retries").withDefault(3)` compiles as an `Options[Any]` unless the expected type is `Options[BigInt]`. [How to make an option optional or give it a default](how-to-optional-option-with-default.md) walks through the choices.

### Transforming Values

These methods convert the parsed value. Each one keeps the option's name, help and position on the command line.

#### Options#map

`Options#map` converts the value with a function that cannot fail. To convert an integer option to an `Int`:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val retries: Options[Int] = Options.integer("retries").map(_.toInt)
```

#### Options#mapOrFail

`Options#mapOrFail` converts the value with a function that may reject it. The function returns `Right` with the new value, or `Left` with a `ValidationError` whose text is shown to the user. To accept only valid port numbers:

```scala
val port: Options[Int] =
  Options.integer("port").mapOrFail { (value: BigInt) =>
    if (value >= 1 && value <= 65535) Right(value.toInt)
    else Left(ValidationError(ValidationErrorType.InvalidValue, HelpDoc.p("Port must be between 1 and 65535.")))
  }
```

#### Options#collect

`Options#collect` keeps the values that a partial function matches, and rejects the others with the given message. To accept two colors:

```scala
val colorCode: Options[Int] =
  Options.text("color").collect("color must be red or blue") {
    case "red"  => 1
    case "blue" => 2
  }
```

#### Options#as

`Options#as` turns a tuple into a value of a case class, or into the result of any function of two to six arguments. It is a shorthand for `Options#map` that spreads the tuple into the function's arguments. To build a `Bounds` from two options:

```scala
case class Bounds(from: BigInt, to: BigInt)

val bounds: Options[Bounds] = (Options.integer("from") ++ Options.integer("to")).as(Bounds.apply _)
```

#### Options#fold

`Options#fold` handles each side of an `Either`, such as the result of `Options#orElseEither`. It takes one function per side, and versions for two to six sides exist. With three or more sides, the nested `Either` is the one that chained `Options#orElseEither` calls produce, nested to the left. To turn a name or an ID into a description:

```scala
val nameOrId: Options[String] =
  (Options.text("name") orElseEither Options.integer("id"))
    .fold((name: String) => s"name $name", (id: BigInt) => s"id $id")
```

### Names and Help

These methods change how an option is named and described. On a combined option, such as `a ++ b` or `a | b`, they apply to every option inside it, so call them on each option before combining.

#### Options#alias

`Options#alias(name, names*)` adds one or more alternative names. A one-character alias is written with `-`, and a longer one with `--`. To let `-o` and `--out` stand for `--output`:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val output = Options.text("output").alias("o", "out")
```

The help lists every name:

```scala
println(output.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// (-o, --output, --out <text>)
//   A user-defined piece of text.
// 
//
```

#### Options#??

`Options#??` appends a paragraph to the help of an option. On an option with a default, the description comes before the sentence about the default. To describe the `--quiet` flag:

```scala
val quiet = Options.boolean("quiet") ?? "Suppress feedback messages."
```

```scala
println(quiet.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --quiet
//   A true or false value.
// 
//   Suppress feedback messages.
// 
//   This setting is optional. Default: 'false'.
// 
//
```

#### Options#withPseudoName

`Options#withPseudoName` replaces the placeholder that the help shows after the option name, such as `<text>`. It changes only the help, not what the option accepts. To show `<NAME>` instead of `<text>`:

```scala
val lastname = Options.text("lastname").withDefault("xyz").withPseudoName("NAME")
```

```scala
println(lastname.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --lastname <NAME>
//   A user-defined piece of text.
// 
//   This setting is optional. Default: 'xyz'.
// 
//
```

### Inspecting and Validating Options

`Options#helpDoc` returns the help as a [`HelpDoc`](helpdoc.md), and `Options#synopsis` returns the usage line. `Options#isBool` tells whether the option is a flag, and `Options#uid` returns its names, such as `--name, --id`.

`Options.validate(options, args, conf)` parses a list of tokens without a command, which is useful in tests. It returns a tuple of an optional parse error that is kept for the arguments to report, the tokens left for the arguments, and the value. To parse two tokens with the default configuration:

```scala
import zio.cli._

val parsed = Options.validate(Options.text("name"), List("--name", "Ada"), CliConfig.default)
```

`parsed` is a ZIO effect that succeeds with `(None, List(), "Ada")`.

### How Options Are Represented

`Options` is a sealed trait. Its cases are `Options.Empty` (the result of `Options.none`), `Options.Single` (one named option), `Options.WithDefault` (the result of `Options#optional` and `Options#withDefault`), `Options.Both` (the result of `Options#++`), `Options.OrElse` (the result of `Options#|`), `Options.Map` (the result of `Options#map` and the methods built on it), `Options.KeyValueMap` and `Options.OAuth2Options`. They are public, but you build options with the constructors and methods above instead of constructing the cases yourself.

---

## How ZIO CLI reads a command line

A user types a line such as `tail -n 5 app.log`, and your program receives clean values. This page explains what happens in between: in which order **ZIO CLI** reads the words, which spellings it accepts, and what it does with words it does not expect. It builds on [Getting Started](getting-started.md). Knowing these rules helps you design commands that read the way users type them, and explains results that look surprising at first, such as an option that is silently ignored.

### The Parse Pipeline

The shell splits the line into words before your program starts. **ZIO CLI** then reads those words from left to right, in a fixed order:

```text
 user types               -n 5 app.log
                               │
 CliApp#run               adds the command name in front
                               │
                               ▼
                          tail -n 5 app.log
                               │
 Command#parse            1. built-in flags? (--help, -h, --wizard, completion)
                               │ no
                          2. command name       tail
                          3. options            -n 5      (stops at the first word that is not an option)
                          4. arguments          app.log
                          5. subcommand         (when the command has subcommands: steps 2-4 again
                               │                 for the subcommand, on the words that are left)
                               │ parse failed?
                          6. --help, -h, --wizard or -w anywhere on the line? show help or the wizard
                               │
                               ▼
 result                   built-in action  or  value + leftover words
                               │
 CliApp#run               prints help / script, or runs your code with the value (leftover is ignored)
```

Each step is covered in its own section below. The reference pages hold the details of each building block: [Commands](commands.md), [Options](options.md), [Args](args.md), [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) and [CliConfig](cli-config.md).

### Trying It Yourself

`Command#parse` runs steps 1 to 6 without starting an app, so we can call it directly to see what **ZIO CLI** makes of a line. It takes the words and a `CliConfig`, and returns a ZIO effect. We wrap it in a small helper that runs the effect and prints the outcome on one line:

```scala
import zio.{Runtime, Unsafe}
import zio.cli._

def show[A](command: Command[A], line: String, config: CliConfig = CliConfig.default): Unit = {
  val words  = line.split(" ").toList
  val result = Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(command.parse(words, config).either).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
  val outcome = result match {
    case Right(CommandDirective.UserDefined(leftover, value)) =>
      s"value = $value, leftover = $leftover"
    case Right(CommandDirective.BuiltIn(BuiltInOption.ShowHelp(synopsis, _))) =>
      s"built-in: help for ${synopsis.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false).trim}"
    case Right(CommandDirective.BuiltIn(BuiltInOption.ShowWizard(_))) =>
      "built-in: wizard"
    case Right(CommandDirective.BuiltIn(other)) =>
      s"built-in: $other"
    case Left(error) =>
      s"error: ${error.error.toPlaintext(color = false).trim}"
  }
  println(s"$line  =>  $outcome")
}
```

A successful parse gives a `CommandDirective.UserDefined` with the parsed value and the leftover words that nothing consumed. A built-in flag gives a `CommandDirective.BuiltIn`, and a failure gives a `ValidationError` whose `error` field holds the message the user sees. See [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md) for the error types.

Most examples use a small `tail` command. It has an integer option `--lines` (short name `-n`, default 10), a flag `--follow` (short name `-f`) and one text argument:

```scala
val tail: Command[((BigInt, Boolean), String)] =
  Command(
    "tail",
    Options.integer("lines").alias("n").withDefault(BigInt(10)) ++ Options.boolean("follow").alias("f"),
    Args.text("file")
  )
```

The value is a tuple: first the values of the options, then the value of the argument.

### The Command Name Comes First

The first word must be the name of the command. `Command#parse` expects that word, so the lines in our examples start with `tail`:

```scala
show(tail, "tail -n 5 app.log")
// tail -n 5 app.log  =>  value = ((5,false),app.log), leftover = List()
show(tail, "head -n 5 app.log")
// head -n 5 app.log  =>  error: Missing command name: tail
```

A user of your program does not type the command name. When the program is started as `tail -n 5 app.log`, the operating system passes only `-n 5 app.log`, and `CliApp#run` adds the name in front before it calls `Command#parse`. For a command with subcommands, it adds the name of the parent command, so the user starts with the subcommand name. The one exception is a top-level command built with `|`, such as `Command("start", ...) | Command("stop", ...)`: `CliApp#run` adds nothing, and the user types `start` or `stop` as the first word. See [CliApp](cli-app.md) for how `CliApp#run` is called.

Command and subcommand names are matched without regard to case by default, so `TAIL` and `Tail` also select the `tail` command. The [Case Sensitivity](#case-sensitivity) section covers the details.

### Options Come Before Arguments

After the command name, **ZIO CLI** reads options. It takes the next word and compares it with the names of the command's options. If it matches, it reads the option (and its value, if the option takes one) and moves on to the next word. As soon as a word does not match any option, option reading stops, and that word and everything after it are positional arguments.

Options can be given in any order among themselves:

```scala
show(tail, "tail -n 5 -f app.log")
// tail -n 5 -f app.log  =>  value = ((5,true),app.log), leftover = List()
show(tail, "tail -f -n 5 app.log")
// tail -f -n 5 app.log  =>  value = ((5,true),app.log), leftover = List()
```

Options written after an argument are not read as options. They become leftover words, so an option that has a default silently keeps it, and users who write `tail app.log -n 5` get no error, only the default value. Put the options first in your own help text and examples, so users copy that order:

```scala
show(tail, "tail app.log -n 5")
// tail app.log -n 5  =>  value = ((10,false),app.log), leftover = List(-n, 5)
```

The output shows `lines` still at 10, and `-n 5` in the leftover list. If the option has no default, the same mistake is an error, because the option is never found. The `greet` command below has a required `--greeting` option:

```scala
val greet: Command[(String, String)] =
  Command("greet", Options.text("greeting"), Args.text("name"))
```

When `--greeting` comes after the name, parsing fails:

```scala
show(greet, "greet --greeting Hello Ada")
// greet --greeting Hello Ada  =>  value = (Hello,Ada), leftover = List()
show(greet, "greet Ada --greeting Hello")
// greet Ada --greeting Hello  =>  error: Expected to find --greeting option.
```

Two more consequences of the same rule are worth knowing. A word that looks like an option but matches none, such as `--nope`, also ends option reading, so it becomes a positional argument. And each option is read at most once: a second `--lines` is not a known option any more, so it ends option reading too:

```scala
show(tail, "tail --nope app.log")
// tail --nope app.log  =>  value = ((10,false),--nope), leftover = List(app.log)
show(tail, "tail --lines 5 --lines 6 app.log")
// tail --lines 5 --lines 6 app.log  =>  value = ((5,false),--lines), leftover = List(6, app.log)
```

### Ending Options With `--`

The word `--` ends option reading on purpose. Every word after it is a positional argument, even when it starts with `-`. This is how a user passes a value such as `-n` as an argument. The `echo` command below has a flag `-n` and takes any number of words:

```scala
val echo: Command[(Boolean, List[String])] =
  Command("echo", Options.boolean("n"), Args.text("word").*)
```

Without `--`, a leading `-n` is the flag. After `--`, it is one of the words:

```scala
show(echo, "echo -n hello")
// echo -n hello  =>  value = (true,List(hello)), leftover = List()
show(echo, "echo -- -n hello")
// echo -- -n hello  =>  value = (false,List(-n, hello)), leftover = List()
show(echo, "echo -n -- -n")
// echo -n -- -n  =>  value = (true,List(-n)), leftover = List()
```

:::caution
In a command with subcommands, the parent command reads the first `--` and removes it, so the subcommand never sees it. If the subcommand has options, a word such as `-f` after that `--` is read as one of the subcommand's options again. To pass such a word to a subcommand's argument, write `--` twice: `git add -- -- -f`.
:::

### How to Write Options

This section covers the spellings **ZIO CLI** accepts for an option on the command line. The [Options](options.md) reference page explains how to define each kind of option.

#### Long and Short Names

A name with more than one letter is written with two dashes (`--lines`), and a one-letter name with one dash (`-n`). `Options#alias` adds more names to the same option. Every name of an option is equivalent:

```scala
show(tail, "tail --lines 5 app.log")
// tail --lines 5 app.log  =>  value = ((5,false),app.log), leftover = List()
show(tail, "tail -n 5 app.log")
// tail -n 5 app.log  =>  value = ((5,false),app.log), leftover = List()
```

#### Values After `=`

A long name can carry its value after an equals sign. This form only works with two dashes. A short name always takes its value as the next word, and a value glued to it (`-n5`) is not recognised:

```scala
show(tail, "tail --lines=5 app.log")
// tail --lines=5 app.log  =>  value = ((5,false),app.log), leftover = List()
show(tail, "tail -n5 app.log")
// tail -n5 app.log  =>  value = ((10,false),-n5), leftover = List(app.log)
```

Notice that `-n5` does not match `-n`, so option reading stops and `-n5` becomes the file name.

#### Clustered Short Flags

Several one-letter flags can be joined into one word: `-la` means `-l -a`. Clustering works for flags only, meaning boolean options that take no value. The `ls` command below has two flags:

```scala
val ls: Command[(Boolean, Boolean)] =
  Command("ls", Options.boolean("long").alias("l") ++ Options.boolean("all").alias("a"))
```

Both orders of the cluster set both flags. A cluster that contains an option with a value, such as `-fn 5` for `tail`, is not split, and the whole word is taken as an argument:

```scala
show(ls, "ls -la")
// ls -la  =>  value = (true,true), leftover = List()
show(ls, "ls -al")
// ls -al  =>  value = (true,true), leftover = List()
show(tail, "tail -fn 5 app.log")
// tail -fn 5 app.log  =>  value = ((10,false),-fn), leftover = List(5, app.log)
```

#### Boolean Flags

A boolean option is a flag: writing its name is enough, and it takes no value. `Options.boolean` produces `true` when the flag is present and `false` when it is absent, unless you choose other values. The flag can also be followed by an explicit `true` or `false`, either as the next word or after `=`:

```scala
show(tail, "tail -f app.log")
// tail -f app.log  =>  value = ((10,true),app.log), leftover = List()
show(tail, "tail --follow false app.log")
// tail --follow false app.log  =>  value = ((10,false),app.log), leftover = List()
show(tail, "tail --follow=false app.log")
// tail --follow=false app.log  =>  value = ((10,false),app.log), leftover = List()
```

Only the exact words `true` and `false` are read as the flag's value. Any other word after a flag, such as `yes` or `0`, is not consumed by the flag, so it becomes the next positional argument:

```scala
show(tail, "tail --follow yes app.log")
// tail --follow yes app.log  =>  value = ((10,true),yes), leftover = List(app.log)
```

Here `yes` became the file name, and `app.log` is leftover.

### Alternatives With `|`

The `|` operator offers a choice, both between options and between commands.

Between two options, `a | b` accepts exactly one of them. The `load` command reads its input either from a file or from a URL:

```scala
val load: Command[String] =
  Command("load", Options.text("file") | Options.text("url"))
```

Either option alone works. Giving both is an error, and so is giving neither:

```scala
show(load, "load --file data.csv")
// load --file data.csv  =>  value = data.csv, leftover = List()
show(load, "load --url https://example.com/data.csv")
// load --url https://example.com/data.csv  =>  value = https://example.com/data.csv, leftover = List()
show(load, "load --file data.csv --url https://example.com/data.csv")
// load --file data.csv --url https://example.com/data.csv  =>  error: Options collision detected. You can only specify either --file or --url.
show(load, "load")
// load  =>  error: Expected to find --file option.
// 
// Expected to find --url option.
```

:::caution
Do not put an option that already has a default inside `|`. That includes every `Options.boolean` and every option built with `Options#optional` or `Options#withDefault`. The side with the default always counts as given, so the alternative reports "Options collision detected" for every input, even an empty line. For mutually exclusive modes, use `Options.enumeration`. To make the whole choice optional, add the default to the alternative: `(a | b).withDefault(x)`.
:::

Between two commands, `a | b` tries the first command, and tries the second one only when the first word is not the first command's name:

```scala
val service: Command[String] =
  Command("start", Args.text("service")) | Command("stop", Args.text("service"))
```

The first word picks the command:

```scala
show(service, "start web")
// start web  =>  value = web, leftover = List()
show(service, "stop web")
// stop web  =>  value = web, leftover = List()
show(service, "restart web")
// restart web  =>  error: Missing command name: stop
```

### Subcommands

A command with subcommands, such as `git` with `add` and `clone`, repeats the pipeline. The parent command reads its name and its own options. The first word that is not one of its options must be the name of a subcommand, and that subcommand then reads its own options and arguments from the rest of the line:

```scala
val git =
  Command("git", Options.boolean("verbose")).subcommands(
    Command("add", Options.boolean("force").alias("f"), Args.text("path")),
    Command("clone", Options.integer("depth").optional, Args.text("url"))
  )
```

The parent's options go before the subcommand name, and the subcommand's options go after it, before the subcommand's arguments:

```scala
show(git, "git --verbose add notes.txt")
// git --verbose add notes.txt  =>  value = (true,(false,notes.txt)), leftover = List()
show(git, "git clone --depth 1 https://example.com/repo.git")
// git clone --depth 1 https://example.com/repo.git  =>  value = (false,(Some(1),https://example.com/repo.git)), leftover = List()
```

An option in the wrong place follows the same rules as before. The parent's `--verbose` written after `add` is not an option of `add`, so it becomes the path. The subcommand's `--depth` written after the URL is leftover:

```scala
show(git, "git add --verbose notes.txt")
// git add --verbose notes.txt  =>  value = (false,(false,--verbose)), leftover = List(notes.txt)
show(git, "git clone https://example.com/repo.git --depth 1")
// git clone https://example.com/repo.git --depth 1  =>  value = (false,(None,https://example.com/repo.git)), leftover = List(--depth, 1)
```

A word that is not a known subcommand is an error that lists the valid names, and a line with no subcommand at all shows the help of the parent command:

```scala
show(git, "git push")
// git push  =>  error: Invalid subcommand for git. Use one of 'add', 'clone'
show(git, "git")
// git  =>  built-in: help for git [--verbose] <command>
```

See [Commands](commands.md) for building subcommands and for the type of the value they produce.

### Auto-Correct: "Did You Mean"

When a word looks like a misspelt option name, **ZIO CLI** can suggest the right one. A word is a candidate when its edit distance to the option's main name (such as `--greeting`) is at most `CliConfig#autoCorrectLimit`, which is 2 by default. The option's name must also be longer than the limit plus one character, so with the default limit, names of three letters or fewer never get a suggestion.

The suggestion is only shown when the whole line fails to parse. With `greet`, the misspelt `--greting` leaves the required `--greeting` missing, so the parse fails and the error carries the suggestion:

```scala
show(greet, "greet --greting Hello Ada")
// greet --greting Hello Ada  =>  error: The flag "--greting" is not recognized. Did you mean --greeting?
```

When the line can still be parsed without the option, there is no error and so no suggestion. The misspelt word ends option reading like any other unknown word, and becomes an argument or a leftover word. The `greetWithDefault` command gives `--greeting` a default:

```scala
val greetWithDefault: Command[(String, String)] =
  Command("greet", Options.text("greeting").withDefault("Hello"), Args.text("name"))
```

The same typo now runs the command with `--greting` as the name:

```scala
show(greetWithDefault, "greet --greting Hi Ada")
// greet --greting Hi Ada  =>  value = (Hello,--greting), leftover = List(Hi, Ada)
```

**ZIO CLI** only suggests. It never replaces the word with the corrected name. Set `CliConfig#autoCorrectLimit` in [CliConfig](cli-config.md) to change the threshold, and see [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md) for the `CorrectedFlag` error type.

### Case Sensitivity

`CliConfig.default` is case-insensitive (`caseSensitive = false`). This applies to command and subcommand names, so `TAIL` selects `tail`. With `CliConfig(caseSensitive = true, autoCorrectLimit = 2)`, the name must match exactly:

```scala
show(tail, "TAIL -n 5 app.log")
// TAIL -n 5 app.log  =>  value = ((5,false),app.log), leftover = List()
show(tail, "TAIL -n 5 app.log", CliConfig(caseSensitive = true, autoCorrectLimit = 2))
// TAIL -n 5 app.log  =>  error: Missing command name: tail
```

:::caution
The case-insensitive setting does not carry over to option names. An option name in a different case, such as `--LINES`, is not found, even with `CliConfig.default`: an option with a default silently keeps it, and a required option is reported as missing. Users must type option names in the case you declared them in. The values of `Options.enumeration` and `Args.enumeration` are also always compared with their exact case.
:::

To see the effect on a required option:

```scala
show(greet, "greet --GREETING Hello Ada")
// greet --GREETING Hello Ada  =>  error: Expected to find --greeting option.
```

### Built-In Flags

Every command understands a few flags that you do not declare: `--help` (or `-h`), `--wizard`, and the shell completion flags `--shell-completion-script` and `--shell-completion-index`, both used together with `--shell-type`. [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) describes what each one does.

A built-in flag is recognised in two situations. The first is when the words after the command name are only built-in flags:

```scala
show(greet, "greet --help")
// greet --help  =>  built-in: help for greet --greeting <text> <name>
show(greet, "greet --shell-completion-script /usr/local/bin/greet --shell-type bash")
// greet --shell-completion-script /usr/local/bin/greet --shell-type bash  =>  built-in: ShowCompletionScript(/usr/local/bin/greet,Bash)
```

When the line holds anything else, **ZIO CLI** parses it as a normal command line, and a successful parse runs the command. The built-in flag is then just another word. The `echo` command takes any words, so `--help` after `hello` is one of them:

```scala
show(echo, "echo hello --help")
// echo hello --help  =>  value = (false,List(hello, --help)), leftover = List()
```

The second situation is a fallback. When the line fails to parse and contains `--help`, `-h`, `--wizard` or `-w` anywhere, **ZIO CLI** shows the help or starts the [wizard](wizard.md) instead of reporting the error. This fallback is controlled by `CliConfig#finalCheckBuiltIn`, which is `true` by default. The `greet` line below fails because `--greeting` is missing, so the user gets help:

```scala
show(greet, "greet Ada --help")
// greet Ada --help  =>  built-in: help for greet --greeting <text> <name>
```

The short form `-w` only works through this fallback. Both completion flags need `--shell-type` next to them. Without it, the line is parsed as a normal command line:

```scala
show(greet, "greet --shell-completion-script /usr/local/bin/greet")
// greet --shell-completion-script /usr/local/bin/greet  =>  error: Expected to find --greeting option.
```

When several built-in flags are given, one wins, in this order: help, then the wizard, then the completion script, then completions:

```scala
show(greet, "greet --wizard --help")
// greet --wizard --help  =>  built-in: help for greet --greeting <text> <name>
```

For a subcommand, `--help` after the subcommand name shows the help of that subcommand, with the parent's name in its usage line:

```scala
show(git, "git add --help")
// git add --help  =>  built-in: help for git add [(-f, --force)] <path>
```

:::caution
`--help` after the name of any subcommand other than the first one in the `subcommands` list shows the help of the first subcommand. In the `git` example, `git clone --help` shows the help of `git add`. The help of the parent command (`git --help`) lists every subcommand with its usage line and description.
:::

### Leftover Words

A successful parse can leave words that nothing consumed: options after the arguments, an extra argument, or a word after a boolean flag. `Command#parse` returns them as `leftover`:

```scala
show(greet, "greet --greeting Hello Ada Bob")
// greet --greeting Hello Ada Bob  =>  value = (Hello,Ada), leftover = List(Bob)
```

`CliApp#run` ignores the leftover words. It runs your code with the parsed value and reports no error, so the line above greets Ada and drops `Bob` without a word. If your program must reject extra input, give the command an argument that collects the rest of the line, such as `Args.text("rest").*`, and check it in your own code.

### Where to Go Next

- [Tutorial: Build a Git-Like CLI](examples.md) uses these rules in a complete program with subcommands, options with values, help and tests.
- [Options](options.md) and [Args](args.md) list every option and argument type and the values each one accepts.
- [Commands](commands.md) covers `|`, subcommands and mapping the parsed value.
- [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) and [CliConfig](cli-config.md) describe the built-in flags and the settings used on this page.
- [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md) lists the error types a failed parse produces.

## ZIO CLI sbt Plugin

The `sbt-zio-cli` plugin is an sbt plugin in the **ZIO CLI** repository. It enables the [sbt-native-image](https://github.com/scalameta/sbt-native-image) plugin, sets a few native-image defaults, and adds one working task, `zioCliBuildNative`, which builds a native executable of your app. Its other tasks are placeholders that print `TODO: Not Implemented!`.

For most builds, the published sbt-native-image plugin alone does the same job with fewer steps; see [How to package a CLI as a native binary](how-to-package-native-binary.md).

### Availability

The plugin is not published to Maven Central or any other repository. To use it, publish it to your local Ivy repository from a clone of the ZIO CLI repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zio/zio-cli.git
cd zio-cli
sbt sbtZioCli/publishLocal
```

The published module is `"zio.cli.sbt" % "sbt-zio-cli"`. It is compiled with Scala 2.12, so it is a plugin for sbt 1.x builds. The plugin has no fixed version: sbt derives it from the latest git tag and commit, for example `0.8.2+28-5b6890e2-SNAPSHOT`. Use the version that `publishLocal` prints in its log, or print it on its own with `sbt "show sbtZioCli/version"`.

### Enabling the Plugin

The plugin is an `AutoPlugin` named `ZIOCLIPlugin`. It is not triggered automatically, and enabling it also enables sbt-native-image's `NativeImagePlugin`. Add the locally published version to `project/plugins.sbt`, replacing the version with the one that `publishLocal` printed:

```scala
addSbtPlugin("zio.cli.sbt" % "sbt-zio-cli" % "0.8.2+28-5b6890e2-SNAPSHOT")
```

`ZIOCLIPlugin` is defined in the root package and has no `autoImport` object, so sbt does not import its setting and task keys into `build.sbt`. Import them from the plugin object, then enable the plugin on the project that contains the app:

```scala
import ZIOCLIPlugin._

lazy val root = project
  .in(file("."))
  .enablePlugins(ZIOCLIPlugin)
  .settings(
    Compile / mainClass := Some("com.example.GreetApp")
  )
```

Without `import ZIOCLIPlugin._`, sbt reports the `zioCli*` keys as not found. The plugin object itself needs no import, because it is in the root package.

### Settings and Tasks

All keys are defined in the `ZIOCLIPluginKeys` trait, which `ZIOCLIPlugin` extends:

```scala
trait ZIOCLIPluginKeys {
  lazy val zioCliMainClass: SettingKey[Option[String]]
  lazy val zioCliNativeImageOptions: SettingKey[Seq[String]]
  lazy val zioCliNativeImageReady: SettingKey[() => Unit]

  lazy val zioCliBuildNative: TaskKey[Unit]
  lazy val zioCliGenerateBashCompletion: TaskKey[Unit]
  lazy val zioCliGenerateZshCompletion: TaskKey[Unit]
  lazy val zioCliInstallCli: TaskKey[Unit]
}
```

The settings configure the native-image build that `zioCliBuildNative` runs.

#### Settings

The plugin sets these defaults on every project that enables it:

| Setting                    | Type             | Default                                                                                                              | Effect                                                     |
| -------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `zioCliMainClass`          | `Option[String]` | `None`                                                                                                               | None in 0.8.2; see the caution below                       |
| `zioCliNativeImageOptions` | `Seq[String]`    | `--allow-incomplete-classpath`, `--report-unsupported-elements-at-runtime`, `--initialize-at-build-time`, `--no-fallback` | Copied into sbt-native-image's `nativeImageOptions`        |
| `zioCliNativeImageReady`   | `() => Unit`     | Prints `ZIO CLI App Native Image Ready!`                                                                             | Copied into sbt-native-image's `nativeImageReady` callback |

Because the plugin assigns `nativeImageOptions := zioCliNativeImageOptions.value`, the plugin's list replaces sbt-native-image's own default, which is empty. To add one option, append to the plugin's setting, for example `zioCliNativeImageOptions += "--verbose"`. A `nativeImageOptions` setting written later in your `build.sbt` overrides `zioCliNativeImageOptions` completely.

:::caution
In 0.8.2, `zioCliMainClass` does not choose the main class: `zioCliBuildNative` ignores it. sbt-native-image builds the class in `Compile / mainClass`, so set that setting instead, as in the example above. When the project has exactly one main class, sbt finds it on its own and neither setting is needed; with several main classes and no `Compile / mainClass`, the build stops with `no mainClass is specified`.
:::

#### Tasks

The plugin adds four tasks:

| Task                           | Behaviour                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `zioCliBuildNative`            | Runs sbt-native-image's `nativeImage` task and returns nothing                                    |
| `zioCliGenerateBashCompletion` | Prints `TODO: Not Implemented!` and does nothing else                                             |
| `zioCliGenerateZshCompletion`  | Prints `TODO: Not Implemented!` and does nothing else                                             |
| `zioCliInstallCli`             | Prints `TODO: Not Implemented!` and does nothing else                                             |

`zioCliBuildNative` produces the same executable as `nativeImage`: it compiles the project, runs GraalVM `native-image` with the options above, writes the binary to `native-image/<project name>` under the project's target directory, logs its absolute path, and then calls the `zioCliNativeImageReady` callback. Run it from the sbt shell:

```bash
sbt zioCliBuildNative
```

For shell completion, use the built-in `--shell-completion-script` option of the app instead; see [How to add Tab completion in bash](how-to-add-shell-completion.md).

### sbt-native-image Keys

Only the two settings above are forwarded to sbt-native-image. Every other sbt-native-image setting and task, such as `nativeImageVersion`, `nativeImageInstalled`, `nativeImageRun`, `nativeImageCopy` and `nativeImageRunAgent`, is available unchanged on a project that enables `ZIOCLIPlugin`. Those keys, how GraalVM is downloaded, and where the binary is written are described in [How to package a CLI as a native binary](how-to-package-native-binary.md). The plugin itself depends on sbt-native-image 0.5.0, so the defaults described there apply only when you also add sbt-native-image 0.6.0 to `project/plugins.sbt`.

### See Also

- [How to package a CLI as a native binary](how-to-package-native-binary.md) builds a native executable with sbt-native-image directly.
- [How to add Tab completion in bash](how-to-add-shell-completion.md) generates a bash completion script from the app's built-in options.
