## Testing CLI Applications

The `zio-cli-testkit` module provides [ZIO Test](https://zio.dev/reference/test/) assertions and generators for **ZIO CLI** [commands](commands.md) and [apps](cli-app.md). It checks the usage synopsis and help document of a command, how a command parses an argument list, what a `CliApp` returns, and what it prints. For a step-by-step walkthrough that builds a complete test spec, see [How to test a CLI app](how-to-test-a-cli.md).

### Overview

The testkit is published as a separate artifact for the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native, for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3. Every API on this page is available on all three platforms. [Modules](index.md#modules) gives the dependency line; add it to the `Test` configuration. The testkit brings in `zio-test` and `zio-test-sbt` (and, on the JVM and Scala.js, `zio-test-magnolia`).

All public types live in the `zio.cli.testkit` package:

| Type                  | Kind   | Purpose                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CliAssertion`        | object | Assertions on a `Command` or a `CliApp`                                 |
| `GenerationAssertion` | object | Assertions on a function that builds a `Command` or a `CliApp`          |
| `CliRepr`             | class  | Pairs an argument list with the expected result                         |
| `TestReturn`          | trait  | Parse result that also represents built-in options such as `--help`     |
| `Tree`                | class  | Builds generators of nested values, such as expressions                 |

Most assertions take a `Gen` of `CliRepr` values and run a ZIO Test `check` over it, so every generated input is checked. A `Gen` can be a fixed list (`Gen.const`, `Gen.fromIterable`) or a random generator for property-based testing.

### Imports and the Implicit CliConfig

Several assertion methods take an implicit [`CliConfig`](cli-config.md). `CliAssertion` and `GenerationAssertion` each define one, named `cliConfig` and equal to `CliConfig.default`. A wildcard import of the object brings it into scope:

```scala
import zio.cli.testkit._
import zio.cli.testkit.CliAssertion._
```

Without the import, the compiler reports a missing implicit value for `cliConfig`. Do not import both `CliAssertion._` and `GenerationAssertion._` with wildcards in the same scope: both objects define `cliConfig`, the two names clash, and the compiler again reports that it cannot find the implicit. Import one object with a wildcard and call the other with its prefix, for example `GenerationAssertion.commandCreation`.

Each method uses the implicit differently:

| Method                                                                                             | Uses the implicit `CliConfig` for                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `CliAssertion.assertSynopsis` with a `String` or `List[String]`                                    | Rendering the command's synopsis                                                     |
| `CliAssertion.assertSynopsis` with a `UsageSynopsis`                                               | Nothing: both sides are rendered with `CliConfig.default`                            |
| `CliAssertion.assertCommand`, `CliAssertion.assertCommandSuccess`, `CliAssertion.assertCommandAll` | Parsing the argument list                                                            |
| `CliAssertion.assertCliApp`, `CliAssertion.assertCliAppValues`                                     | Nothing: the app parses with its own config, set by `CliApp.make` or `CliApp#config` |
| `GenerationAssertion.commandCreation`                                                              | Parsing, through `CliAssertion.assertCommand`                                        |

To check a command against a different `CliConfig`, pass it explicitly as the second argument list instead of declaring a second implicit, which would be ambiguous with the imported one. To test an app with a different config, build the app with that config.

### Argument Lists for Commands and Apps

A `Command` is parsed directly, so its argument list starts with the command name. `CliApp#run` prepends the command name itself, so an app's argument list does not:

| Input under test  | Argument list                       | Example                          |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `Command[A]`      | First element is the command name   | `List("greet", "--name", "Ada")` |
| `CliApp[R, E, A]` | No command name                     | `List("--name", "Ada")`          |

The one exception is an app whose top-level command is built with `Command#orElse` (or `|`). `CliApp#run` prepends nothing for it, so the argument list starts with the name of the chosen command. See [Commands](commands.md) for how commands are combined.

### Example Definitions

The examples on this page share one command and one app. The command has two required options, and the app returns a greeting:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.testkit._
import zio.cli.testkit.CliAssertion._
import zio.test._

val greet: Command[(String, BigInt)] =
  Command("greet", Options.text("name") ++ Options.integer("times"))

val app: CliApp[Any, Nothing, String] =
  CliApp.make("greet", "1.0.0", HelpDoc.Span.text("Greets a person."), greet) { case (name, times) =>
    ZIO.succeed(s"Hello, $name x$times")
  }
```

### CliAssertion

`CliAssertion` holds the assertions on a single `Command` or `CliApp`. They fall into five groups: access methods, synopsis and help assertions, parsing assertions, app assertions, and the console output assertion.

#### Access Methods

Access methods read one part of a `CliApp` and run an `Assertion` you write on it. They return a `TestResult` directly, with no effect and no generator:

```scala
object CliAssertion {
  def accessCommand[R, E, A](cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A], assert: Assertion[Command[_]]): TestResult
  def accessHelpDoc[R, E, A](cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A], assert: Assertion[HelpDoc]): TestResult
  def accessSynopsis[R, E, A](cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A], assert: Assertion[UsageSynopsis]): TestResult
}
```

`CliAssertion.accessCommand` passes the app's `Command`, `CliAssertion.accessHelpDoc` passes that command's `HelpDoc`, and `CliAssertion.accessSynopsis` passes its unrendered `UsageSynopsis`. Use them when no other assertion covers your check. To render a `UsageSynopsis` inside the assertion, call `UsageSynopsis#enumerate` with a `CliConfig`.

Each access method takes the app and an assertion on the extracted part:

```scala
val isNamedGreet: TestResult =
  accessCommand(app, Assertion.assertion[Command[_]]("is named greet")(_.names.contains("greet")))

val hasGreetHelp: TestResult =
  accessHelpDoc(app, Assertion.equalTo(greet.helpDoc))

val hasOneUsageLine: TestResult =
  accessSynopsis(app, Assertion.assertion[UsageSynopsis]("has one usage line")(_.enumerate(CliConfig.default).size == 1))
```

#### Synopsis and Help Assertions

These assertions compare the usage synopsis or the help document of a command, or of the command inside an app:

```scala
object CliAssertion {
  def assertSynopsis[A](command: Command[A], synopsis: String)(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): TestResult
  def assertSynopsis[A](command: Command[A], synopsis: List[String])(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): TestResult
  def assertSynopsis[A](command: Command[A], synopsis: UsageSynopsis): TestResult
  def assertSynopsis[R, E, A](cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A], synopsis: String)(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): TestResult
  def assertSynopsis[R, E, A](cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A], synopsis: List[String])(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): TestResult
  def assertSynopsis[R, E, A](cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A], synopsis: UsageSynopsis): TestResult

  def assertHelpDoc[A](command: Command[A], helpDoc: HelpDoc): TestResult
  def assertHelpDoc[R, E, A](cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A], helpDoc: HelpDoc): TestResult
}
```

`CliAssertion.assertSynopsis` renders the synopsis and compares it with the expected text. The `String` form expects exactly one usage line. The `List[String]` form expects every line in order; a command built with `Command#orElse` has the single line `<command>`, and an `Options#orElse` whose alternatives are several words has one line per alternative. The `UsageSynopsis` form renders both sides with `CliConfig.default`. For an app, the synopsis is the one of the app's command, rendered with the implicit config, not the app's own config.

`CliAssertion.assertHelpDoc` compares the HTML rendering (`HelpDoc#toHTML`) of the command's help document with the expected one. For an app, it checks the command's help document only. The help screen that `CliApp#run` prints for `--help` also contains the app name, version, summary, a usage section and the footer; use `CliAssertion.outputContains` to check those.

Each form takes the expected value directly:

```scala
val synopsisFromText: TestResult =
  assertSynopsis(greet, "greet --name <text> --times <integer>")

val synopsisFromLines: TestResult =
  assertSynopsis(app, List("greet --name <text> --times <integer>"))

val synopsisFromValue: TestResult =
  assertSynopsis(greet, greet.synopsis)

val helpDocCheck: TestResult =
  assertHelpDoc(app, greet.helpDoc)
```

To render the synopsis with a non-default config, pass the config as the second argument list. With `showTypes = false` the value placeholders disappear:

```scala
val synopsisWithoutTypes: TestResult =
  assertSynopsis(greet, "greet --name --times")(CliConfig.default.copy(showTypes = false))
```

#### Parsing Assertions

Parsing assertions run `Command#parse` on every argument list that the generator produces. They return a `ZIO` effect that a ZIO Test `test` can return directly:

```scala
object CliAssertion {
  def assertCommand[A, R](
    command: Command[A],
    pairs: Gen[R, CliRepr[List[String], A]]
  )(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): ZIO[R, Throwable, TestResult]

  def assertCommandSuccess[A, R](
    command: Command[A],
    pairs: Gen[R, CliRepr[List[String], Assertion[Either[ValidationError, A]]]]
  )(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): ZIO[R, Throwable, TestResult]

  def assertCommandAll[A, R](
    command: Command[A],
    pairs: Gen[R, CliRepr[List[String], Assertion[Either[ValidationError, TestReturn[A]]]]]
  )(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): ZIO[R, Throwable, TestResult]
}
```

The three methods differ in what the expected result is:

- `CliAssertion.assertCommand` expects the parsed value to equal the value in the `CliRepr`. A `ValidationError` fails the assertion.
- `CliAssertion.assertCommandSuccess` runs your `Assertion` on the whole `Either[ValidationError, A]`. Despite its name, it is the method to use when an input must be rejected.
- `CliAssertion.assertCommandAll` runs your `Assertion` on `Either[ValidationError, TestReturn[A]]`. Use it for built-in options such as `--help`, which do not produce a value of type `A`. See [TestReturn](#testreturn).

Each method takes the command and a generator of inputs:

```scala
val parsesNameAndTimes: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  assertCommand(greet, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("greet", "--name", "Ada", "--times", "2"), ("Ada", BigInt(2)))))

val rejectsMissingTimes: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  assertCommandSuccess(greet, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("greet", "--name", "Ada"), Assertion.isLeft)))

val helpIsBuiltIn: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  assertCommandAll(
    greet,
    Gen.const(CliRepr(List("greet", "--help"), Assertion.isRight(Assertion.isSubtype[TestReturn.Help](Assertion.anything))))
  )
```

:::caution
`CliAssertion.assertCommand` and `CliAssertion.assertCommandSuccess` cannot handle built-in options. An input such as `--help` or `--wizard` makes the whole check fail with a `java.lang.Exception` that has no message, instead of an assertion failure. Use `CliAssertion.assertCommandAll` for those inputs. The app assertions below behave the same way for any input that makes `CliApp#run` return `None`.
:::

#### App Assertions

App assertions run `CliApp#run` on every argument list that the generator produces:

```scala
object CliAssertion {
  def assertCliApp[R, E, A, RGen](
    cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A],
    pairs: Gen[RGen, CliRepr[List[String], Assertion[Either[CliError[E], A]]]]
  )(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): ZIO[RGen with R, Throwable, TestResult]

  def assertCliAppValues[R, E, A, RGen](
    cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A],
    pairs: Gen[RGen, CliRepr[List[String], A]]
  )(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): ZIO[RGen with R, Throwable, TestResult]

  def assertCliAppZIO[R, E, A, RGen](
    cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A],
    pairs: Gen[RGen, CliRepr[List[String], ZIO[R, E, A]]]
  ): ZIO[RGen with R, Throwable, TestResult]
}
```

The three methods differ in how they treat errors:

- `CliAssertion.assertCliApp` runs your `Assertion` on the whole `Either[CliError[E], A]`. Every [`CliError`](validation-and-errors.md) case reaches the assertion: `CliError.Parsing` for an argument list that does not parse, `CliError.Execution` for an error from the app's own code, and `CliError.IO` or `CliError.BuiltIn` from built-in options.
- `CliAssertion.assertCliAppValues` expects the app to succeed with the value in the `CliRepr`.
- `CliAssertion.assertCliAppZIO` runs the effect in the `CliRepr` as the expected result and compares it with the app's result using `==`. A failure `e` of the effect is compared as `CliError.Execution(e)`. Any other `CliError` from the app, such as a parse error, fails the whole check with that error instead of an assertion result.

`CliAssertion.assertCliApp` and `CliAssertion.assertCliAppValues` accept an implicit `CliConfig` but do not use it; the app parses with its own config. Each method takes the app and a generator of inputs without the command name:

```scala
val returnsGreeting: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  assertCliAppValues(app, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--name", "Ada", "--times", "2"), "Hello, Ada x2")))

val reportsParseError: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  assertCliApp(app, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--name", "Ada"), Assertion.isLeft(Assertion.isSubtype[CliError.Parsing](Assertion.anything)))))

val matchesEffect: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  assertCliAppZIO(app, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--name", "Ada", "--times", "2"), ZIO.succeed("Hello, Ada x2"))))
```

#### Console Output Assertion

`CliAssertion.outputContains` runs the app and checks the console output that ZIO Test captures with `TestConsole`:

```scala
object CliAssertion {
  def outputContains[R, E, A, RGen](
    cliApp: CliApp[R, E, A],
    pairs: Gen[RGen, CliRepr[List[String], Seq[String]]]
  ): ZIO[RGen with R, Throwable, TestResult]
}
```

`TestConsole.output` holds one entry per `print` or `printLine` call. The check passes when every expected string is a substring of at least one entry. `CliApp#run` prints the whole help screen with a single `printLine`, so for `--help` all of the help text is one entry. The app must not fail: if `CliApp#run` fails, for example with a parse error, the whole check fails with that `CliError`, so the error message printed on a parse error cannot be checked this way.

To check that the help screen lists both options:

```scala
val helpListsOptions: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  outputContains(app, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--help"), Seq("--name", "--times"))))
```

:::caution
`CliAssertion.outputContains` does not clear the captured output before each run. Output from earlier samples of the same generator, and anything printed earlier in the same test, still counts. A later sample can therefore pass on text that only an earlier sample printed. Keep one sample per `CliAssertion.outputContains` call when the samples print different text.
:::

### GenerationAssertion

`GenerationAssertion` tests a function that builds a `Command` or a `CliApp` from a seed value, such as a name. Each method takes a two-level generator: the outer generator produces `(seed, inputs)` pairs, and `inputs` is the generator of `CliRepr` values that the command or app built from `seed` must satisfy:

```scala
object GenerationAssertion {
  def commandCreation[A, B, R1, R2](
    f: A => Command[B],
    response: Gen[R1, (A, Gen[R2, CliRepr[List[String], B]])]
  )(implicit cliConfig: CliConfig): ZIO[R1 with R2, Throwable, TestResult]

  def commandCreationZIO[A, B, R, E <: Throwable, RGen1, RGen2](
    f: A => ZIO[R, E, Command[B]],
    response: Gen[RGen1, (A, Gen[RGen2, CliRepr[List[String], B]])]
  ): ZIO[R with RGen1 with RGen2, Throwable, TestResult]

  def cliAppCreation[R, E, A, B, RGen](
    f: A => CliApp[R, E, B],
    response: Gen[RGen, (A, Gen[RGen, CliRepr[List[String], B]])]
  ): ZIO[R with RGen, Throwable, TestResult]

  def cliAppCreationZIO[R, E, A, B, RGen, RC, EC <: Throwable](
    f: A => ZIO[RC, EC, CliApp[R, E, B]],
    response: Gen[RGen, (A, Gen[RGen, CliRepr[List[String], B]])]
  ): ZIO[R with RC with RGen, Throwable, TestResult]
}
```

`GenerationAssertion.commandCreation` and `GenerationAssertion.commandCreationZIO` check each built command with `CliAssertion.assertCommand`, so their argument lists start with the command name. `GenerationAssertion.cliAppCreation` and `GenerationAssertion.cliAppCreationZIO` check each built app with `CliAssertion.assertCliAppValues`, so their argument lists do not. The `ZIO` variants build the command or app in an effect whose error type must be a `Throwable`. In the two app methods the outer and inner generators share one environment type `RGen`.

The following factories build a command and an app from a greeting word, and the generators pair each word with the input it must accept:

```scala
def greetingCommand(word: String): Command[String] =
  Command(word, Options.text("name")).map(name => s"$word, $name")

def greetingApp(word: String): CliApp[Any, Nothing, String] =
  CliApp.make(word, "1.0.0", HelpDoc.Span.text("Greets a person."), greetingCommand(word))(ZIO.succeed(_))

val words: Gen[Any, String] = Gen.fromIterable(List("hello", "bye"))

val commandSeeds: Gen[Any, (String, Gen[Any, CliRepr[List[String], String]])] =
  words.map(word => (word, Gen.const(CliRepr(List(word, "--name", "Ada"), s"$word, Ada"))))

val appSeeds: Gen[Any, (String, Gen[Any, CliRepr[List[String], String]])] =
  words.map(word => (word, Gen.const(CliRepr(List("--name", "Ada"), s"$word, Ada"))))
```

Each method takes the factory and the matching generator:

```scala
val commandsCheck: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  GenerationAssertion.commandCreation(greetingCommand, commandSeeds)

val commandsInEffectCheck: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  GenerationAssertion.commandCreationZIO((word: String) => ZIO.succeed(greetingCommand(word)), commandSeeds)

val appsCheck: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  GenerationAssertion.cliAppCreation(greetingApp, appSeeds)

val appsInEffectCheck: ZIO[Any, Throwable, TestResult] =
  GenerationAssertion.cliAppCreationZIO((word: String) => ZIO.succeed(greetingApp(word)), appSeeds)
```

:::note
Each `GenerationAssertion` method runs a `check` over the inner generator inside a `check` over the outer one, so the sample counts multiply. With random generators and the default of 200 samples, one call runs up to 40,000 parses. Use finite generators or lower the count with `TestAspect.samples`.
:::

### TestReturn

`TestReturn` is the parse result that `CliAssertion.assertCommandAll` passes to your assertion. Unlike `CommandDirective`, it is a plain value that is easy to compare:

```scala
sealed trait TestReturn[+A]

object TestReturn {
  def convert[A](res: CommandDirective[A]): TestReturn[A]

  sealed trait BuiltIn extends TestReturn[Nothing]
  case class Help()   extends BuiltIn
  case class Wizard() extends BuiltIn
  case class SH()     extends BuiltIn
  case class SHH()    extends BuiltIn
  case class Value[A](a: A) extends TestReturn[A]
}
```

`TestReturn.convert` turns a user-defined result into `Value(a)` and every built-in directive into `Help()`. This includes `--wizard` and the shell-completion options: `TestReturn.convert` never returns `Wizard`, `SH` or `SHH`, so match on `Help()` or on `TestReturn.BuiltIn` for any built-in option.

Converting a user-defined directive gives a `Value`:

```scala
TestReturn.convert(CommandDirective.userDefined(Nil, 5))
// res2: TestReturn[Int] = Value(a = 5)
```

### CliRepr

`CliRepr` pairs an input with its expected result:

```scala
final case class CliRepr[+A, +R](value: A, repr: R) {
  def map[B](f: A => B): CliRepr[B, R]
  def map2[B](f: R => B): CliRepr[A, B]
}
```

`value` is the input, usually the argument list. `repr` is the expected result: a value, a `ZIO` effect, or an `Assertion`, depending on the method. `CliRepr#map` changes `value`, and `CliRepr#map2` changes `repr`. Use `CliRepr#map2` to turn plain expected values into assertions or effects:

```scala
val input = CliRepr(List("--times", "2"), 2)
// input: CliRepr[List[String], Int] = CliRepr(
//   value = List("--times", "2"),
//   repr = 2
// )

input.map(_.size)
// res3: CliRepr[Int, Int] = CliRepr(value = 2, repr = 2)

input.map2(times => times * 10)
// res4: CliRepr[List[String], Int] = CliRepr(
//   value = List("--times", "2"),
//   repr = 20
// )
```

### Tree

`Tree` builds a generator of nested values, such as arithmetic expressions. Atoms are the leaves, operators combine two sub-trees, and mappers combine one sub-tree with a value drawn from a second generator:

```scala
final case class Tree[A](
  atoms: List[Gen[Any, A]],
  mappers: List[Tree.Mapper[A, Any]],
  operators: List[((A, A) => A)],
  depth: Int
) {
  def gen: Gen[Any, A]
  lazy val anyAtom: Gen[Any, A]
  def anyTree(depth: Int): Gen[Any, A]
}

object Tree {
  final case class Compare[A, Repr](a: A, repr: Repr)
  final case class Mapper[A, B](f: (A, B) => A, anyB: Gen[Any, B])
}
```

The members behave as follows:

- `Tree#anyAtom` picks one of the atom generators.
- `Tree#anyTree` builds values of exactly the nesting depth you pass; depth 0 is an atom.
- `Tree#gen` picks a depth between 0 and 2 and calls `Tree#anyTree`. It does not read the `depth` field.
- `Tree.Mapper` is invariant in its second type parameter, and the `mappers` field holds `Mapper[A, Any]`, so write every mapper as `Tree.Mapper[A, Any]`.
- `Tree.Compare` is a helper type that the testkit itself does not use.

With no mappers and no operators, every depth above 0 produces no values at all. A tree of sums, products and increments over the atoms 1, 2 and 3:

```scala
val arithmetic: Tree[Int] = Tree[Int](
  atoms = List(Gen.const(1), Gen.const(2), Gen.const(3)),
  mappers = List(Tree.Mapper[Int, Any]((a: Int, _: Any) => a + 1, Gen.const[Any](()))),
  operators = List((a: Int, b: Int) => a + b, (a: Int, b: Int) => a * b),
  depth = 2
)

val anyExpression: Gen[Any, Int] = arithmetic.gen

val nestedOnce: Gen[Any, Int] = arithmetic.anyTree(1)
```

### See Also

- [How to test a CLI app](how-to-test-a-cli.md) builds a complete test spec step by step.
- [Commands](commands.md) and [Options](options.md) describe the values under test.
- [HelpDoc](helpdoc.md) describes the help document that `CliAssertion.assertHelpDoc` compares.
- [CLI config](cli-config.md) describes `CliConfig`.
- [Validation and Errors](validation-and-errors.md) describes `ValidationError` and `CliError`.

## Validation and Errors

This page describes the errors a `CliApp` can produce, what the user sees for each one, and how the "Did you mean" hints work.

Two types describe failures:

- `ValidationError` describes why the command-line input does not match the command. The parser produces it.
- `CliError[E]` is the error type of `CliApp#run`. It wraps a `ValidationError`, a failure of a built-in option, or an error from your own code.

### ValidationError

`ValidationError` pairs a short code for the kind of failure with the message for the user:

```scala
final case class ValidationError(validationErrorType: ValidationErrorType, error: HelpDoc) extends Throwable {
  def isOptionMissing: Boolean
}
```

`ValidationError` extends `Throwable`, but zio-cli never throws it. `Command#parse` returns it in the error channel of a ZIO effect. `ValidationError#isOptionMissing` is `true` when `validationErrorType` is `MissingValue`.

#### Error Types Users See

These `ValidationErrorType` values reach the user. The messages come from a `count` command with a required `--limit` integer option and a `<start>` integer argument, and from a `git` command with the subcommands `add` and `clone`:

| Value             | Raised when                                                                                                | Example message                                              |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `MissingValue`    | A required option is absent, or an option is given without its value.                                      | `Expected to find --limit option.`, `Expected some value.`   |
| `InvalidValue`    | An option's value cannot be converted to its type, or a custom check on the option fails.                  | `x is not a integer.`                                        |
| `InvalidArgument` | An argument is missing, cannot be converted to its type, or fails a check from `Args#mapOrFail`.           | `abc is not a integer.`, `Missing argument <start>.`         |
| `CorrectedFlag`   | An option name is misspelt and the parse fails. See [Auto-Correct Suggestions](#auto-correct-suggestions). | `The flag "--limt" is not recognized. Did you mean --limit?` |
| `CommandMismatch` | The first word after a parent command is not one of its subcommands.                                       | `Invalid subcommand for git. Use one of 'add', 'clone'`      |

When several required options are missing, the message lists each of them, one per line.

#### Internal Error Types

The parser uses the remaining values to steer its own work and does not show them to users. `MissingFlag` means "the next word is not this option", `UnclusteredFlag` drives the splitting of `-abc` into `-a -b -c`, `KeyValuesDetected` drives key-value options, and `NoBuiltInMatch` means the input holds no built-in option. `MissingSubCommand` exists but is never produced.

#### Unknown Options and Extra Words

zio-cli does not reject words it does not recognise. Words left over after a complete command are ignored: for a command without arguments, `status --unknown` runs `status`. For a command with a text argument, an unknown `--option` can become the argument's value. Declare every option your users may type, and validate argument values in `execute` or with `Args#mapOrFail` when a stray option would cause harm.

### CliError

`CliApp#run` returns `ZIO[R, CliError[E], Option[A]]`. `CliError` is a sealed trait with four cases:

```scala
sealed trait CliError[+E] extends Exception
object CliError {
  case class Parsing(e: ValidationError) extends CliError[Nothing]
  case class Execution[+E](e: E)         extends CliError[E]
  case class IO(e: IOException)          extends CliError[Nothing]
  case class BuiltIn(e: Exception)       extends CliError[Nothing]
}
```

| Case           | Raised when                                                         | What the user sees                                                    |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Parsing(e)`   | The input does not match the command.                               | The text of `e.error`, printed to standard output before the failure. |
| `Execution(e)` | Your `execute` function fails with `e`.                             | Nothing from zio-cli, which passes your error on unchanged.           |
| `IO(e)`        | Writing the help or the completion script to standard output fails. | Nothing from zio-cli.                                                 |
| `BuiltIn(e)`   | Computing shell completions for `--shell-completion-index` fails.   | Nothing from zio-cli.                                                 |

Quitting the [wizard](wizard.md) is not an error: `CliApp#run` succeeds with `None`. To report each case in your own words, match on it:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.cli._

def report(error: CliError[String]): UIO[Unit] =
  error match {
    case CliError.Parsing(e)     => Console.printLineError(s"Input rejected: ${e.validationErrorType}").orDie
    case CliError.Execution(msg) => Console.printLineError(s"Command failed: $msg").orDie
    case CliError.IO(e)          => Console.printLineError(s"Could not write output: ${e.getMessage}").orDie
    case CliError.BuiltIn(e)     => Console.printLineError(s"Completion failed: ${e.getMessage}").orDie
  }
```

`CliError` extends `Exception`, and its `getMessage` is always `"zio-cli app failed"`. Use the case itself, or `getCause`, to find the reason. `getCause` returns the wrapped exception or `ValidationError`, the error of an `Execution` when it is a `Throwable`, and `null` otherwise.

### Exit Codes

`CliApp#run` does not choose an exit code. A program that extends `ZIOCliDefault` exits as follows:

| Outcome                                                   | Exit code | Output                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CliApp#run` succeeds, including after `--help`           | `0`       | Whatever the command or the built-in option prints.      |
| `CliError.Parsing`                                        | `1`       | The validation message, already printed by `CliApp#run`. |
| `CliError.Execution`, `CliError.IO` or `CliError.BuiltIn` | `1`       | ZIO logs the failure at the `ERROR` level.               |

To use different exit codes for different errors, see [How to choose the exit code for each error](how-to-exit-codes.md).

### Auto-Correct Suggestions

When a user misspells an option name, zio-cli can add a hint to the error. With the default configuration, a required option `--limit` typed as `--limt` gives:

```text
The flag "--limt" is not recognized. Did you mean --limit?
```

The hint appears only when all of these are true:

- The distance between the typed word and the option's main name, counted as Levenshtein edits (inserted, deleted or replaced characters), is at most [`CliConfig#autoCorrectLimit`](cli-config.md#auto-correction). The default is `2`. Aliases are not compared.
- The option's main name, without its dashes, is longer than `autoCorrectLimit + 1` characters. With the default, names of four or more characters qualify.
- No other option of the command has exactly the typed word as its name.
- The command as a whole fails to parse, typically because the misspelt option is required.

The hint never rewrites the input. The parse fails with a `CorrectedFlag` error, and the user types the command again. With `caseSensitive = false`, the distance ignores case.

:::caution
A misspelt option gets a hint only when the parse fails. When the option has a default value and the rest of the input still parses, the misspelt word is ignored and the command runs with the default. For example, `--verbos` for a flag `--verbose` runs the command with the flag off, and for a command with a text argument the word `--verbos` can become the argument's value.
:::

### See Also

- [CLI Configuration](cli-config.md) for `CliConfig#autoCorrectLimit` and the other parser settings.
- [Commands](commands.md) for how commands and subcommands are built.
- [Options](options.md) and [Args](args.md) for the values that produce `InvalidValue` and `InvalidArgument` errors.

---

## Value Types

Every basic [`Args`](args.md) and [`Options`](options.md) constructor reads one string from the command line and converts it to a Scala value. The conversion is described by a `PrimType`, a sealed trait whose cases are listed on this page. For each type, this page gives the constructors, the placeholder shown in the help, the input the user types, and any platform limits. `PrimType#validate(value)` parses a string and returns an `IO[String, A]` that fails with the messages on this page, which tests can use to check a type without a command.

### Summary

The table lists every value type, the constructors that use it, and the placeholder that the help and the usage line show for it:

| Value type        | `Args` constructor                                                         | `Options` constructor               | Scala type                 | Placeholder        |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
| Text              | `Args.text`, `Args.text(name)`                                             | `Options.text(name)`                | `String`                   | `text`             |
| Integer           | `Args.integer`, `Args.integer(name)`                                       | `Options.integer(name)`             | `BigInt`                   | `integer`          |
| Decimal           | `Args.decimal`, `Args.decimal(name)`                                       | `Options.decimal(name)`             | `BigDecimal`               | `decimal`          |
| Boolean           | `Args.bool`, `Args.bool(name)`                                             | `Options.boolean(name, ...)`        | `Boolean`                  | `boolean`          |
| Enumeration       | `Args.enumeration(cases*)`, `Args.enumeration(name)(cases*)`               | `Options.enumeration(name)(cases*)` | the case values            | `choice`           |
| Duration          | `Args.duration`, `Args.duration(name)`                                     | `Options.duration(name)`            | `java.time.Duration`       | `duration`         |
| Instant           | `Args.instant`, `Args.instant(name)`                                       | `Options.instant(name)`             | `java.time.Instant`        | `instant`          |
| Local date        | `Args.localDate(name)` only                                                | `Options.localDate(name)`           | `java.time.LocalDate`      | `date`             |
| Local date-time   | `Args.localDateTime`, `Args.localDateTime(name)`                           | `Options.localDateTime(name)`       | `java.time.LocalDateTime`  | `date-time`        |
| Local time        | `Args.localTime`, `Args.localTime(name)`                                   | `Options.localTime(name)`           | `java.time.LocalTime`      | `local-time`       |
| Month-day         | `Args.monthDay`, `Args.monthDay(name)`                                     | `Options.monthDay(name)`            | `java.time.MonthDay`       | `month-day`        |
| Offset date-time  | `Args.offsetDateTime`, `Args.offsetDateTime(name)`                         | `Options.offsetDateTime(name)`      | `java.time.OffsetDateTime` | `offset-date-time` |
| Offset time       | `Args.offsetTime`, `Args.offsetTime(name)`                                 | `Options.offsetTime(name)`          | `java.time.OffsetTime`     | `offset-time`      |
| Period            | `Args.period`, `Args.period(name)`                                         | `Options.period(name)`              | `java.time.Period`         | `period`           |
| Year              | `Args.year`, `Args.year(name)`                                             | `Options.year(name)`                | `java.time.Year`           | `year`             |
| Year-month        | `Args.yearMonth`, `Args.yearMonth(name)`                                   | `Options.yearMonth(name)`           | `java.time.YearMonth`      | `year-month`       |
| Zoned date-time   | `Args.zonedDateTime`, `Args.zonedDateTime(name)`                           | `Options.zonedDateTime(name)`       | `java.time.ZonedDateTime`  | `zoned-date-time`  |
| Zone ID           | `Args.zoneId`, `Args.zoneId(name)`                                         | `Options.zoneId(name)`              | `java.time.ZoneId`         | `zone-id`          |
| Zone offset       | `Args.zoneOffset`, `Args.zoneOffset(name)`                                 | `Options.zoneOffset(name)`          | `java.time.ZoneOffset`     | `zone-offset`      |
| File              | `Args.file`, `Args.file(exists)`, `Args.file(name, exists)`                | `Options.file(name, exists)`        | `java.nio.file.Path`       | `file`             |
| Directory         | `Args.directory`, `Args.directory(exists)`, `Args.directory(name, exists)` | `Options.directory(name, exists)`   | `java.nio.file.Path`       | `directory`        |
| File or directory | `Args.path`, `Args.path(name)`                                             | none                                | `java.nio.file.Path`       | `path`             |

An unnamed argument, such as `Args.integer`, uses the placeholder as its name: it appears as `<integer>` in the help. A named argument or an option uses its own name, and an option shows the placeholder after its name, as in `--count <integer>`. `Options#withPseudoName` replaces the placeholder of an option. `Args.localDate` has only the named form.

Options always need a name, so there is no unnamed `Options` constructor. There is also no `Options.path`; see [Custom Parameters From a PrimType](#custom-parameters-from-a-primtype) for an option that accepts a file or a directory.

To see the placeholder and the help sentence of a value type, we print the help of an option:

```scala
import zio.cli._

println(Options.localDate("since").helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --since <date>
//   A date in ISO_LOCAL_DATE format, such as 2007-12-03
// 
//
```

### Text and Numbers

`PrimType.Text` accepts any string, including an empty one. `PrimType.Integer` reads the input with `BigInt(...)` and `PrimType.Decimal` with `BigDecimal(...)`, so both accept numbers of any size. An integer may have a sign, such as `-42`, and a decimal may use an exponent, such as `1e3`.

A value that cannot be converted fails with `<input> is not a <placeholder>.`, for example `ten is not a integer.`. The same message format is used by every type in this section and in [Dates and Times](#dates-and-times).

### Boolean

`PrimType.Bool` accepts `true`, `1`, `y`, `yes` and `on` for `true`, and `false`, `0`, `n`, `no` and `off` for `false`. The words are compared case-insensitively unless the app uses a case-sensitive [`CliConfig`](cli-config.md#case-sensitivity).

For a positional `Args.bool`, the user types one of these words. For an `Options.boolean` flag, the flag alone gives its value, and an explicit value is read only when it is exactly `true` or `false`; see [Boolean Options](options.md#boolean-options).

### Enumeration

`PrimType.Enumeration` takes pairs of the word the user types and the value it stands for. The word must match exactly, including its case, even when the app is otherwise case-insensitive. The help lists the words, and the usage line shows them as `debug | info`. Any other word fails with `Expected one of the following cases: debug, info`.

To define an enumeration option and print its help:

```scala
val level = Options.enumeration("level")(("debug", 0), ("info", 1), ("warn", 2))
```

```scala
println(level.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --level debug | info | warn
//   One of the following cases: debug, info, warn.
// 
//
```

### Dates and Times

The `java.time` types are parsed with the matching `parse` or `of` method of `java.time`, so they accept the ISO-8601 forms below. `Year` reads a plain integer, and `YearMonth` reads a year, a dash and a two-digit month. The help sentence of each type is the one ZIO CLI prints under the option or argument.

| Placeholder        | Example input that parses                 | Help sentence printed by ZIO CLI                                                                         |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `duration`         | `PT1H30M`, `P1DT2H3M`                     | A time-based amount of time in the ISO-8601 format, such as 'P1DT2H3M'.                                  |
| `instant`          | `2007-12-03T10:15:30.00Z`                 | An instant in time in UTC format, such as 2007-12-03T10:15:30.00Z.                                       |
| `date`             | `2007-12-03`                              | A date in ISO_LOCAL_DATE format, such as 2007-12-03                                                      |
| `date-time`        | `2007-12-03T10:15:30`                     | A date-time without a time-zone in the ISO-8601 format, such as 2007-12-03T10:15:30.                     |
| `local-time`       | `10:15`, `10:15:30`                       | A time without a time-zone in the ISO-8601 format, such as 10:15:30.                                     |
| `month-day`        | `--12-03`                                 | A month-day in the ISO-8601 format such as 12-03.                                                        |
| `offset-date-time` | `2007-12-03T10:15:30+01:00`               | A date-time with an offset from UTC/Greenwich in the ISO-8601 format, such as 2007-12-03T10:15:30+01:00. |
| `offset-time`      | `10:15:30+01:00`                          | A time with an offset from UTC/Greenwich in the ISO-8601 format, such as 10:15:30+01:00.                 |
| `period`           | `P1Y2M3D`                                 | A date-based amount of time in the ISO-8601 format, such as 'P1Y2M3D'.                                   |
| `year`             | `2007`                                    | A year in the ISO-8601 format, such as 2007.                                                             |
| `year-month`       | `2007-12`                                 | A year-month in the ISO-8601 format, such as 2007-12.                                                    |
| `zoned-date-time`  | `2007-12-03T10:15:30+01:00[Europe/Paris]` | A date-time with a time-zone in the ISO-8601 format, such as 2007-12-03T10:15:30+01:00 Europe/Paris.     |
| `zone-id`          | `Europe/Paris`                            | A time-zone ID, such as Europe/Paris.                                                                    |
| `zone-offset`      | `+02:00`, `Z`                             | A time-zone offset from Greenwich/UTC, such as +02:00.                                                   |

:::caution
The help sentences for `month-day` and `zoned-date-time` show examples that do not parse. A month-day needs the leading dashes (`--12-03`, not `12-03`), and a zoned date-time needs the zone in square brackets (`2007-12-03T10:15:30+01:00[Europe/Paris]`). Add a correct example with `Args#??` or `Options#??` so your users see it.
:::

To add a correct example to the help of a month-day option:

```scala
val birthday = Options.monthDay("birthday") ?? "For example --12-03 for 3 December."
// birthday: Options[java.time.MonthDay] = Single(
//   name = "birthday",
//   aliases = Vector(),
//   primType = MonthDay,
//   description = Paragraph(
//     value = Text(value = "For example --12-03 for 3 December.")
//   ),
//   pseudoName = None
// )

println(birthday.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// --birthday <month-day>
//   A month-day in the ISO-8601 format such as 12-03.
// 
//   For example --12-03 for 3 December.
// 
//
```

### Paths

Path parameters return a `java.nio.file.Path`. Two small types configure them:

`PathType` says which kind of path is expected: `PathType.File`, `PathType.Directory`, or `PathType.Either` when both are acceptable. `Exists` says whether the path must exist: `Exists.Yes`, `Exists.No`, or `Exists.Either` when it does not matter.

`PrimType.Path(pathType, shouldExist)` combines the two. `Args.file(name, exists = Exists.Yes)`, for example, wraps `PrimType.Path(PathType.File, Exists.Yes)`. A third parameter, `fileSystem`, is a `zio.cli.files.FileSystem` and defaults to `FileSystem.live`. `FileSystem` has four methods, `parsePath(path: String): IO[String, Path]`, `exists(path: Path): UIO[Boolean]`, `isDirectory(path: Path): UIO[Boolean]` and `isRegularFile(path: Path): UIO[Boolean]`, so a test can pass its own implementation.

The `exists` parameter of `Args.file`, `Args.directory`, `Options.file` and `Options.directory` defaults to `Exists.Either`. The help sentence follows the combination, as in `A file.`, `An existing file.` or `A directory that must not exist.`. Validation checks the path in two steps:

1. The existence rule: `Exists.Yes` rejects a missing path with `Path '<input>' must exist.`, and `Exists.No` rejects an existing path with `Path '<input>' must not exist.`.
2. The kind rule: if the path exists and `Exists.No` is not used, a file parameter rejects a directory with `Expected path '<input>' to be a regular file.`, and a directory parameter rejects a file with `Expected path '<input>' to be a directory.`.

A path that does not exist is accepted by `Exists.Either` without a kind check. `Args.path` uses `PathType.Either` and `Exists.Either`, so it accepts any path.

To accept only existing files and only new directories:

```scala
val input  = Args.file("input", exists = Exists.Yes)
val output = Options.directory("output", exists = Exists.No)
```

### Custom Parameters From a PrimType

You rarely need this; it is an advanced API for a value type that no constructor offers, such as an option that accepts an existing file or directory. `Args.Single(pseudoName, primType, description)` and `Options.Single(name, aliases, primType, description, pseudoName)` are public case classes, so we can wrap any `PrimType` directly:

```scala
val source: Options[java.nio.file.Path] =
  Options.Single("source", Vector("s"), PrimType.Path(PathType.Either, Exists.Yes))

val target: Args[java.nio.file.Path] =
  Args.Single(Some("target"), PrimType.Path(PathType.Either, Exists.Yes))
```

The help of `source` shows its alias, its placeholder and the sentence for the combination:

```scala
println(source.helpDoc.toPlaintext(color = false))
// (-s, --source <path>)
//   An existing file or directory.
// 
//
```

`PrimType` is sealed, so we cannot add a new case. To convert text into a type of our own, we use `Options#mapOrFail` or `Args#mapOrFail` instead; see [How to validate and convert a parameter's value](how-to-validate-input.md).

### Platform Support

Some value types depend on the file system, so their constructors differ between platforms:

| Constructor         | JVM | Scala Native | Scala.js                                           |
| ------------------- | --- | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `Args.file`         | yes | yes          | no                                                 |
| `Args.directory`    | yes | yes          | no                                                 |
| `Args.path`         | yes | yes          | no                                                 |
| `Options.file`      | yes | yes          | compiles as `Options[String]`, rejects every value |
| `Options.directory` | yes | yes          | no                                                 |
| `Options.oauth2`    | yes | no           | no                                                 |

All other value types are available on every platform. On Scala.js there is no file system, so `Options.file` fails for every value the user passes with `FileSystem is not available in ScalaJS`. Only a default set with `Options#withDefault` can be used there. `Options.oauth2` is described in [Authorization with OAuth2](auth.md).

---

## Wizard Mode

Wizard mode is an interactive way to build a command. Instead of typing the full command line, the user answers questions in the terminal. The app asks which subcommand to run, then asks for each option and argument. When every answer is in, the app prints the equivalent command line and runs it.

Wizard mode helps users who do not know the options and arguments of an app, or who want a guided way to try a command. Scripts and experienced users type the full command instead.

### Starting Wizard Mode

Wizard mode is a [built-in option](built-in-commands.md), so every app has it. The user adds `--wizard` after the program name. For the app in [Getting Started](getting-started.md), that is:

```bash
sbt "run --wizard"
```

`--wizard` starts the wizard when it is the only word after the program name, or when the rest of the input is invalid. The short form `-w` works only in the second case, through the [final built-in check](cli-config.md#final-built-in-check).

`CliApp#run` returns the result of the command that the wizard runs, wrapped in `Some`, or `None` when the user quits.

### How a Session Runs

A session has three steps:

1. **Choose a subcommand.** For a command with two or more subcommands, the wizard prints a numbered list of them, each with its description, and the user types a name or a number. A chosen subcommand that has subcommands of its own leads to another list.
2. **Answer each option and argument.** For each option and argument of the chosen command, the wizard prints a short description and waits for input. An argument value that is not valid, such as `abc` for an integer, is rejected, and the question is asked again.
3. **Review and run.** The wizard prints the collected values as one command line, prints `Executing command...`, and runs the command with those values.

Before every question, the app prints a header: the banner, a line with `WIZARD of`, the name and the version, and a short explanation. Every question ends with a prompt made of the command's name followed by ` :> `.

The examples on this page use this app, with two subcommands that each take one argument:

```scala
import zio.cli._
import zio.cli.HelpDoc.Span.text
import zio.Console.printLine

val repo: Command[String] = Command("repo").subcommands(
  Command("clone", Args.text("repository")).withHelp("Copies a repository."),
  Command("add", Args.text("path")).withHelp("Stages a path.")
)

val cliApp = CliApp.make(
  name = "repo",
  version = "0.1.0",
  summary = text("Manages repositories"),
  command = repo
)(value => printLine(s"Selected: $value"))

// Starts wizard mode. It reads from the terminal, so the docs build does not run it.
val session = cliApp.run(List("--wizard"))
```

The first screen asks for the subcommand:

```text
   ________  ____  ____
  / ___/ _ \/ __ \/ __ \
 / /  /  __/ /_/ / /_/ /
/_/   \___/ .___/\____/
         /_/

WIZARD of repo0.1.0 -- Manages repositories

Wizard mode assist you in constructing commands for repo0.1.0

WIZARD

  Please, enter the command you would like to execute.

  Write help for more information about this parameter, restart to start again Wizard mode and quit
  to exit.

OPTIONS

  [1]    clone  Copies a repository.

  [2]    add    Stages a path.

repo :>
```

After the user types `1`, the wizard asks for the argument of `clone`:

```text
WIZARD

  Please, specify the following argument.

  Argument <repository>:

  Write help for more information about this parameter, restart to start again Wizard mode and quit
  to exit.

repo :>
```

After the user types `zio/zio-cli`, the wizard prints the command line and runs it:

```text
You may bypass the wizard and execute your command directly with the following options and
arguments:

  clone zio/zio-cli

Executing command...

Selected: zio/zio-cli
```

### Special Input Words

At any question, three words have a special meaning. The wizard compares the input to these words exactly: the match is case-sensitive and does not trim spaces, so `Help`, `QUIT` and ` quit` are ordinary input.

- `help` shows the full help of the current value. The question is asked again, and earlier answers are kept.
- `restart` throws away all answers and starts again from the first question.
- `quit` leaves wizard mode without running the command.

Empty input, which means pressing enter with nothing typed, is never accepted. The wizard prints `No text found.` and asks the same question again.

### Choosing by Number

When the wizard lists subcommands, the user can type either the name or the number shown next to it. A number outside the list, such as `0`, and text that is neither a name nor a number are rejected, and the question is asked again. The list follows the order in which the subcommands are declared for up to four subcommands. With five or more, the order of the list is not guaranteed, so users should check the number they type against the name next to it.

### Which Values the Wizard Asks For

The wizard asks for every option and every argument of the chosen command, in declaration order: first the options, then the arguments. Each kind of value accepts different input:

- For an option with a value, the user types the value, such as `Ada` for `--name`. The wizard accepts any non-empty text here and checks it only when the command runs, so `abc` for an integer option makes the final run fail with `abc is not a integer.`
- For a boolean flag, typing `true`, `1`, `y`, `yes` or `on` adds the flag to the command line. Any other text leaves it out.
- For an option with a default, the user must still type a value, because empty input is rejected.
- For a repeated argument, such as `Args.text("file").*`, the user types all values on one line, separated by spaces.

### The Final Command

The printed line holds the subcommand names, options and arguments in the order the wizard asked for them. It does not include the program's own name, because `CliApp#run` adds that name itself. For the app in [Getting Started](getting-started.md), the answers `yes` for `--loud` and `Ada` for the name print `--loud Ada`. To skip the wizard next time, the user passes the same values after the program name, as in `sbt "run --loud Ada"`.

:::caution
The wizard builds an invalid command line in two cases, and the run fails with `Invalid subcommand for <parent>`. The first is a parent with exactly one subcommand: the wizard does not ask for the subcommand and also leaves its name out of the line. The second is a session started after a subcommand name, as in `repo clone --wizard`: the line again lacks `clone`. Give the parent at least two subcommands, and start the wizard right after the program name.
:::

### Related Pages

- [Built-in Commands](built-in-commands.md) lists `--wizard` with `--help` and the shell completion options.
- [Commands](commands.md) explains how subcommands are built.
- [Args](args.md) and [Options](options.md) describe the values that the wizard asks for.

## Automatic Derivation of Config

By bringing in `zio-config-magnolia` we  avoid all the boilerplate required to define the config. With a single import, `Config` is automatically derived.

#### Example

##### Config
```scala
sealed trait X

object X {
  case object A extends X
  case object B extends X
  case object C extends X
  case class  DetailsWrapped(detail: Detail) extends X
  
  case class Detail(firstName: String, lastName: String, region: Region)
  case class Region(suburb: String, city: String)
}

case class MyConfig(x: X)
```

##### AutoDerivation

```scala
// Setting up imports

import zio._
import zio.config._, 
import zio.config.typesafe._
import zio.config.magnolia._

  import X._
```

```scala
// Defining different possibility of HOCON source

val aHoconSource =
  ConfigProvider
    .fromHoconString("x = A")
```

```scala
val bHoconSource =
  ConfigProvider
    .fromHoconString("x = B")
```

```scala
val cHoconSource =
  ConfigProvider
    .fromHoconString("x = C")
```

```scala
val dHoconSource =
  ConfigProvider
    .fromHoconString(
      s"""
         | x {
         |   DetailsWrapped {
         |    detail  {
         |      firstName : ff
         |      lastName  : ll
         |      region {
         |        city   : syd
         |        suburb : strath
         |     }
         |   }
         |  }
         |}
         |""".stripMargin
    )
```

```scala
// Let's try automatic derivation

aHoconSource.load(deriveConfig[MyConfig])
// res0: Right(MyConfig(A))

bHoconSource.load(deriveConfig[MyConfig])
// res0: Right(MyConfig(B))

cHoconSource.load(deriveConfig[MyConfig])
// res0: Right(MyConfig(C))

dHoconSource.load(deriveConfig[MyConfig])
// res0: Right(MyConfig(DetailsWrapped(Detail("ff", "ll", Region("strath", "syd")))))
```

**NOTE**

The fieldNames and class-names remain the same as that of case-classes and sealed-traits.

If you want custom names for your fields, use `name` annotation.

```
import zio.config.derivation.name

@name("detailsWrapped")
case class  DetailsWrapped(detail: Detail) extends X
```

```scala
import zio.config._

deriveConfig[MyConfig].mapKey(toKebabCase)
```

With the above change`firstName` and `lastName` in the above HOCON example can be `first-name` and `last-name` 
respectively.

There are various ways in which you can customise the derivation of sealed traits. 
This is a bit involving, and more documentations will be provided soon.

#### Documentation while automatic derivation

With `describe` annotation you can still document your config while automatically generating the config

```scala
import zio.config.magnolia.describe

@describe("This config is about aws")
case class Aws(region: String, dburl: DbUrl)
case class DbUrl(value: String)
```

This will be equivalent to the manual configuration of:

```scala
string("region").zip(string("dburl").to[DbUrl]).to[Aws] ?? "This config is about aws"
```

You could provide `describe` annotation at field level

Example:

```scala
case class Aws(@describe("AWS region") region: String, dburl: DbUrl)
```

This will be equivalent to the manual configuration of:

```scala
(string("region") ?? "AWS region" zip string("dburl").to[DbUrl]).to[Aws] ?? "This config is about aws"
```

#### Custom Config

Every field in a case class should have an instance of `DeriveConfig` (and not `Config`) in order for the automatic derivation to work.
This doesn't mean the entire design of zio-config is typeclass based. For the same reason, the typeclass
`DeriveConfig` exists only in zio-config-magnolia.

As an example, given below is a case class where automatic derivation won't work, and result in a compile time error:
Assume that, `AwsRegion` is a type that comes from AWS SDK.

```
import java.time.ZonedDateTime

case class Execution(time: AwsRegion, id: Int)
```

In this case, `deriveConfig[Execution]` will give us the following descriptive compile error.

```
magnolia: could not find Descriptor.Typeclass for type <outside.library.package>.AwsRegion
  in parameter 'time' of product type <your.packagename>.Execution
```

This is because zio-config-magnolia failed to derive an instance of Descriptor for AwsRegion.

In order to provide implicit instances, following choices are there

```
import zio.config.magnolia._

implicit val awsRegionConfig: DeriveConfig[Aws.Region] =
  DeriveConfig[String].map(string => AwsRegion.from(string))

```

Now `deriveConfig[Execution]` compiles.

Custom descriptors are also needed in case you use value classes to describe your configuration. You can use them
together with automatic derivation and those implicit custom descriptors will be taken automatically into account

```scala
import zio.config.magnolia._

final case class AwsRegion(value: String) extends AnyVal {
  override def toString: String = value
}

object AwsRegion {
  implicit val descriptor: DeriveConfig[AwsRegion] = 
    DeriveConfig[String].map(AwsRegion(_))
}
```

#### Where to place these implicits ?

If the types are owned by us, then the best place to keep implicit instance is the companion object of that type.

```scala
final case class MyAwsRegion(value: AwsRegion)

object MyAwsRegion {
  implicit val awsRegionDescriptor: DeriveConfig[MyAwsRegion] =
    DeriveConfig[String]
      .map(
        string => MyAwsRegion(AwsRegion.from(string))
      ) ?? "value of type AWS.Region"
}
```

However, sometimes, the types are owned by an external library.

In these situations, better off place the implicit closer to where we call the automatic derivation.
Please find the example in `magnolia` package in examples module.

#### Change Keys (CamelCase, kebab-case etc)

Please find the examples in ChangeKeys.scala in magnolia module to find how to manipulate keys in an automatic derivation such as being able to specify keys as camelCase, kebabCase or snakeCase in the source config.

### Scala3 Autoderivation
Works just like scala-2.12 and scala-2.13.
If possible, we will make this behaviour consistent in scala-2.12 and scala-2.13 in future versions of zio-config.

##### Example:

The name of the sealed trait itself is skipped completely by default.
However, if you put a `name` annotation on top of the sealed-trait itself,
then it becomes part of the config. 

The name of the case-class should be available in config-source, 
and by default it should the same name as that of the case-class.

```scala
sealed trait A
case class B(x: String) extends A
case class C(y: String) extends A

case class Config(a: A) 
```

With the above config, `deriveConfig[A]` can read following source.

```scala
{
  "a" : {
   "B" : {
      "x" : "abc"
     }
   }
  }
}

// or a.B.x="abc", if your source is just property file
```

However, if you give `name` annotation for A, the name of the sealed trait
should be part of the config too. This is rarely used.

```scala
@name("aaaaa")
sealed trait A
case class B(x: String) extends A
case class C(y: String) extends A

case class Config(a: A) 
```

With the above config, `deriveConfig[A]` can read following source.

```scala
{
  "a" : {
    "aaaaa" : 
      "B" : {
        "x" : "abc"
     }
   }
  }
}
```
Similar to scala-2.x, you can give name annotations to any case-class as well (similar to scala 2.x)

##### Example:

```scala
sealed trait A

@name("b")
case class B(x: String) extends A
case class C(y: String) extends A

case class Config(a: A) 
```

In this case, the config should be

```scala
{
  "a" : {
   "b" : {
      "x" : "abc"
     }
   }
  }
}
```

#### Config derivation via `derives` keyword

Scala 3 has introduced `derives` keyword to derive typeclasses without the need of explicitely declaring the implicit / given.
This syntax can be enabled for `zio.Config` by importing `zio.config.magnolia.*` and then using the `derives` keyword on the type that needs to be derived:

```scala 3
import zio.config.magnolia.*
import zio.{Config, ZIO}

sealed trait A
case class B(x: String) extends A
case class C(y: String) extends A

case class MyConfig(a: A) derives Config

// And then simply summon the `Config[MyConfig]` instance as you would normally:
val cfg = ZIO.config[MyConfig]
```

#### No guaranteed behavior for scala-3 enum yet
With the current release, there is no guaranteed support of scala-3 enum. 
Use `sealed trait` and `case class` pattern.

#### No support for recursive config in auto-derivation, but we can make it work

There is no support for auto-deriving recursive config with scala-3.
Please refer to examples in magnolia package (not in the main examples module)

#### Custom Keys

With zio-config-3.x, the only way to change keys is as follows:

```scala
// mapKey is just a function in `Config` that pre-existed

val config = deriveConfig[Config].mapKey(_.toUpperCase)
```

### Inbuilt support for pure-config

Many users make use of the label `type` in HOCON files to annotate the type of the coproduct. 
Just put `@nameWithLabel()` in sealed trait name. By default the `label` name is `type`, but you can provide
any custom name `@nameWithLabel("foo")`

```scala
import zio.config._, typesafe._, magnolia._

@nameWithLabel("type")
sealed trait X
case class A(name: String) extends X
case class B(age: Int) extends X

case class AppConfig(x: X)

val str =
  s"""
   x : {
     type = A
     name = jon
   }
  """

read(deriveConfig[AppConfig] from ConfigProvider.fromHoconString(str))
```

---

## Automatic Validations

By bringing in `zio-config-refined` module, you get validations for your config parameters almost for free. 
`zio-config` elegantly integrates with `Refined` library for you to achieve this with same ergonomics.

If you are not familiar with `refined` library, refer https://github.com/fthomas/refined.

There are various ways that zio-config can interact with refined library. 
Take a look at `zio.config.refined` package.

```scala
 import zio.Config
 import zio.ConfigProvider
 import zio.config._, refined._

```

A few examples are given below.

### Basic Example

```scala
 import eu.timepit.refined.types.string.NonEmptyString

 case class Jdbc(username: NonEmptyString, password: NonEmptyString)

 val jdbc: Config[Jdbc] =
   (refineType[NonEmptyString]("username") zip
     refineType[NonEmptyString]("password")).to[Jdbc]

 ConfigProvider.fromMap(Map("username" -> "", "password" -> "")).load(jdbc)
```

### Direct Interaction with Refined Predicates

If you need to directly interact with `Predicate`s (ex: `NonEmpty`), then
`refine[A, P]` method is useful.

```scala
 import eu.timepit.refined._, api._, string._, collection._
 
 type NonEmptyString = String Refined NonEmpty
 
 val refinedConfig: Config[NonEmptyString] = 
   refineType[NonEmptyString]("USERNAME")
  
 // Another way of doing it is
 val urlConfig: Config[Refined[String, Url]] =
   refine[String, Url]("URL")
   
 // refineType takes a fully formed type (String Refined NonEmpty) where as refine allows you to play with the predicate directly (NonEmpty)  
```

### Derive from existing Config

Of various methods available in `zio.config.refined` package, 
the most interesting one is being able to get a refined type out of an already derived Config.
This shows the composable nature of zio-config. 

Take a look at the below example

```scala
 import eu.timepit.refined._, api._, numeric._, collection._
 import zio.config.magnolia.deriveConfig

 case class MyConfig(url: String, port: Int)

 val configs: Config[List[MyConfig]] =
   Config.listOf("databases", deriveConfig[MyConfig])

 // A list of database configs, such that size should be greater than 2.
 val databaseList: Config[Refined[List[MyConfig], Size[Greater[W.`2`.T]]]] =
   refine[Size[Greater[W.`2`.T]]](configs)
```

### Auto-Derivation and Refined

You can also use auto derivations with refined.

```scala
import zio.ConfigProvider
import eu.timepit.refined.W
import eu.timepit.refined.api.Refined
import eu.timepit.refined.collection.{ NonEmpty, Size }
import zio.config.magnolia.deriveConfig

object RefinedReadConfig extends App {
  case class RefinedProd(
    ldap: Refined[String, NonEmpty],
    port: Refined[Int, GreaterEqual[W.`1024`.T]],
    dbUrl: Option[Refined[String, NonEmpty]]
  )

  val configMap =
    Map(
      "LDAP"     -> "ldap",
      "PORT"     -> "1999",
      "DBURL"   -> "ddd"
    )

  val result =
    ConfigProvider.fromMap(configMap).load(deriveConfig[RefinedProd].mapKey(_.toUpperCase))

  // RefinedProd(ldap,1999,Some(ddd))
}
```

## AWS Parameter Store

AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store keeps configuration values under hierarchical names such as `/myapp/prod/db/url`. zio-config can read every parameter under one base path and expose them as a `ConfigProvider`, so the same `Config` descriptions you use for files and strings work with Parameter Store too.

### Choosing a Module

zio-config offers two modules for Parameter Store. They expose the same entry point, `ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore`, and differ only in the AWS client library underneath:

| Module               | AWS client library             |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `zio-config-aws`     | AWS SDK for Java v1            |
| `zio-config-zio-aws` | `zio-aws`, a ZIO-native client |

Both modules define classes in the same package, `zio.config.aws.parameterstore`, so add only one of them to a project. The examples below use `zio-config-aws`. To use the ZIO-native client instead, replace the module name in the dependency and follow the ZIO-native example further down.

To add the SDK-based module to an sbt build:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-config-aws" % "4.1.2"
```

### Reading a Base Path

`ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore` loads all parameters under the base path in one call, including parameters in nested paths. The base path prefix is removed from each name, and the remaining path segments become config keys separated by `/`. A parameter named `/myapp/prod/db/url` is therefore read as the key `db/url`. Pass the base path without a trailing slash, because the prefix removal expects exactly one `/` after the base path.

To read the `url` and `port` values under `/myapp/prod/db`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.config._
import zio.config.aws.parameterstore._

final case class Database(url: String, port: Int)

val databaseConfig: Config[Database] =
  (Config.string("url") zip Config.int("port")).nested("db").map(pair => Database(pair._1, pair._2))
```

Next, build the provider from the base path and load the config from it:

```scala
val loadDatabase: ZIO[Any, Config.Error, Database] =
  for {
    provider <- ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore("/myapp/prod")
    database <- provider.load(databaseConfig)
  } yield database
```

The provider reads the parameters once, when `ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore` runs. Later changes in Parameter Store are not seen until you build a new provider.

### Credentials and Region

When you call `ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore` with only a base path, zio-config creates the client with `AWSSimpleSystemsManagementClientBuilder.defaultClient()`. That client follows the AWS default credential chain for credentials and region, so environment variables, a shared profile, and an instance role all work without code changes.

To control the client yourself, pass a `Task` that builds an `AWSSimpleSystemsManagement` client as the second argument:

```scala
import com.amazonaws.services.simplesystemsmanagement.AWSSimpleSystemsManagementClientBuilder

val withCustomClient: ZIO[Any, Config.Error, ConfigProvider] =
  ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore(
    "/myapp/prod",
    ZIO.attempt(AWSSimpleSystemsManagementClientBuilder.standard().withRegion("us-east-1").build())
  )
```

With the `zio-config-zio-aws` module, the caller provides an `Ssm` service instead. The following sketch builds the `Ssm` layer from the ZIO-native client and loads the same `databaseConfig`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.aws.core.config.AwsConfig
import zio.aws.netty.NettyHttpClient
import zio.aws.ssm.Ssm
import zio.config._
import zio.config.aws.parameterstore._

val loadWithZioAws: ZIO[Any, Config.Error, Database] =
  ZIO
    .serviceWithZIO[Ssm] { ssm =>
      ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore("/myapp/prod", ssm).flatMap(_.load(databaseConfig))
    }
    .provide(NettyHttpClient.default, AwsConfig.default, Ssm.live)
```

### Required Permissions

The identity that runs the application needs `ssm:GetParametersByPath` on the base path, because the provider reads parameters recursively. The provider also requests decrypted values, so the identity needs `kms:Decrypt` on the KMS key that encrypts any `SecureString` parameters under that path.

### Errors

If an AWS call fails, `ConfigProvider.fromParameterStore` returns a `Config.Error` whose message contains the text of the original exception. Handle it like any other `Config.Error`, for example with `catchAll` or by logging it at startup.

## Dive Into ZIO Config

__Note that this documentation is for 1.x series. For newer versions, please refer to [docs](https://github.com/zio/zio-config/tree/master/docs) section in GitHub.__

### Describe the config by hand

We must fetch the configuration from the environment to a case class (product) in scala. Let it be `MyConfig`

```scala
import zio.IO

import zio.config._
import zio.ConfigProvider
import zio.Config, Config._

```

```scala
case class MyConfig(ldap: String, port: Int, dburl: String)
```
To perform any action using zio-config, we need a configuration description.
Let's define a simple one.

```scala
val myConfig: Config[MyConfig] =
  (string("LDAP") zip int("PORT") zip string("DB_URL")).to[MyConfig]

 // Config[MyConfig]
```

To get a tuple,

```scala
val myConfigTupled: Config[(String, Int, String)] =
  (string("LDAP") zip int("PORT") zip string("DB_URL"))
```

### Fully automated Config Description

If you don't like describing your configuration manually, and rely on the names of the parameter in the case class (or sealed trait),
there is a separate module called `zio-config-magnolia`.

Note:  `zio-config-shapeless` is an alternative to `zio-config-magnolia` to support scala 2.11 projects.
It will be deprecated once we find users have moved on from scala 2.11.

```scala
import zio.config._
import zio.config.magnolia._

val myConfigAutomatic = deriveConfig[MyConfig]
```

`myConfig` and `myConfigAutomatic` are same description, and is of the same type.

Refer to API docs for more explanations on [descriptor](https://javadoc.io/static/dev.zio/zio-config-magnolia_2.13/1.0.0-RC31-1/zio/config/magnolia/index.html#descriptor[A](implicitconfig:zio.config.magnolia.package.Descriptor[A]):zio.Config[A])
More examples on automatic derivation is in examples module of [zio-config](https://github.com/zio/zio-config)

### Read config from various sources

There are more information on various sources in [here](read-from-various-sources.md).

Below given is a simple example.

```scala
val map =
  Map(
    "LDAP" -> "xyz",
    "PORT" -> "8888",
    "DB_URL" -> "postgres"
  )

val source = ConfigProvider.fromMap(map)

source.load(myConfig)

```

#### Documentations using Config

```scala
generateDocs(myConfig)
//Creates documentation (automatic)

val betterConfig =
  (string("LDAP") ?? "Related to auth" zip int("PORT") ?? "Database port" zip
    string("DB_URL") ?? "url of database"
   ).to[MyConfig]

generateDocs(betterConfig).toTable.toGithubFlavouredMarkdown
// Custom documentation along with auto generated docs
```

#### Accumulating all errors

For any misconfiguration, the ReadError collects all of them with proper semantics: `AndErrors` and `OrErrors`.
Instead of directly printing misconfigurations, the `ReadError.prettyPrint` shows the path, detail of collected misconfigurations.

1. All misconfigurations of `AndErrors` are put in parallel lines.
```text
╥
╠══╗ 
║  ║ FormatError
║ MissingValue
``` 
2. `OrErrors` are in the same line which indicates a sequential misconfiguration

```text
╥
╠MissingValue
║
╠FormatError
```

Here is a complete example:

```text
   ReadError:
   ╥
   ╠══╦══╗
   ║  ║  ║
   ║  ║  ╠─MissingValue
   ║  ║  ║ path: var2
   ║  ║  ║ Details: value of type string
   ║  ║  ║ 
   ║  ║  ╠─MissingValue path: envvar3
   ║  ║  ║ path: var3
   ║  ║  ║ Details: value of type string
   ║  ║  ║ 
   ║  ║  ▼
   ║  ║
   ║  ╠─FormatError
   ║  ║ cause: Provided value is wrong, expecting the type int
   ║  ║ path: var1
   ║  ▼
   ▼
```

#### Example of mapping keys

Now on, the only way to change keys is as follows:

```scala
  // mapKey is just a function in `Config` that pre-existed

  val config = deriveConfig[Config].mapKey(_.toUpperCase)
```

### Inbuilt support for pure-config

Many users make use of the label `type` in HOCON files to annotate the type of the coproduct.
Now on, zio-config has inbuilt support for reading such a file/string using `descriptorForPureConfig`.

```scala
import zio.config._, typesafe._, magnolia._

@nameWithLabel("type")
sealed trait X
case class A(name: String) extends X
case class B(age: Int) extends X

case class AppConfig(x: X)

val str =
  s"""
   x : {
     type = A
     name = jon
   }
  """

ConfigProvider.fromHoconString(str).load(deriveConfig[AppConfig])

```

### The `to` method for easy manual configurations

```scala
import zio.config._
import zio.Config

final case class AppConfig(port: Int, url: String)

val config = Config.int("PORT").zip(Config.string("URL")).to[AppConfig]

```

### A few handy methods

#### CollectAll

```scala
import zio.config._

  final case class Variables(variable1: Int, variable2: Option[Int])

  val listOfConfig: List[Config[Variables]] =
    List("GROUP1", "GROUP2", "GROUP3", "GROUP4")
      .map(group => (Config.int(s"${group}_VARIABLE1") zip Config.int(s"${group}_VARIABLE2").optional).to[Variables])

  val configOfList: Config[List[Variables]] =
    Config.collectAll(listOfConfig.head, listOfConfig.tail: _*)

```

#### orElseEither && Constant

```scala
import zio.config._ 

sealed trait Greeting

case object Hello extends Greeting
case object Bye extends Greeting

val configSource = 
  ConfigProvider.fromMap(Map("greeting" -> "Hello"))

val config: Config[Greeting] = 
  Config.constant("Hello").orElseEither(Config.constant("Bye")).map(_.merge)

```
