## SFTP Settings

`SecureFtpSettings` describes a connection to an SFTP server, which is file transfer over SSH. This page documents its fields and constructors, and the credential types it accepts: passwords, SSH keys held in memory, and SSH key files.

### Definition

`SecureFtpSettings` is a case class with seven fields, none of which has a default value in the case class itself:

```scala
final case class SecureFtpSettings(
  host: String,
  port: Int,
  credentials: FtpCredentials,
  strictHostKeyChecking: Boolean,
  knownHosts: Option[String],
  proxy: Option[java.net.Proxy],
  sshConfig: net.schmizz.sshj.Config
)
```

The settings value is passed to the `secure` layer or to `SecureFtp.connect`, both documented in [Connecting](connecting.md).

### Construction

The companion has two constructors that fill in the security and SSH fields:

```scala
object SecureFtpSettings {
  def apply(host: String, port: Int, credentials: FtpCredentials): SecureFtpSettings
  def apply(host: String, port: Int, credentials: FtpCredentials, proxy: Option[java.net.Proxy]): SecureFtpSettings
}
```

Both set `strictHostKeyChecking = false`, `knownHosts = None` and `sshConfig = new net.schmizz.sshj.DefaultConfig()`. The four-argument form also sets the proxy:

```scala
import zio.ftp._
import java.net.{ InetSocketAddress, Proxy }

val direct = SecureFtpSettings("sftp.example.com", 22, PasswordCredentials("foo", "bar"))

val viaProxy = SecureFtpSettings(
  "sftp.example.com",
  22,
  PasswordCredentials("foo", "bar"),
  Some(new Proxy(Proxy.Type.SOCKS, new InetSocketAddress("proxy.internal", 1080)))
)
```

:::warning
With `strictHostKeyChecking = false`, the client accepts any host key, so it cannot detect a server that impersonates the real one. Turn strict checking on for any server reached over a network you don't control.
:::

### Fields

The fields cover where to connect, how to log in, and how to trust the server.

#### Server and Proxy

The `host` field is the server's host name or IP address, and `port` is its SSH port, usually 22. The `proxy` field routes the SSH connection through a `java.net.Proxy`, such as a SOCKS proxy, when it is `Some`.

#### Host Key Verification

The `strictHostKeyChecking` and `knownHosts` fields decide which server keys the client trusts.

When `strictHostKeyChecking` is false, the client accepts any host key and ignores `knownHosts`. When it is true, the client loads the OpenSSH `known_hosts` file at the path in `knownHosts` and accepts only keys listed there for that host. If `knownHosts` is `None`, no key is trusted and every connection fails with a `ConnectionError`.

To trust the keys in your own `known_hosts` file:

```scala
import zio.ftp._

val strict = SecureFtpSettings("sftp.example.com", 22, PasswordCredentials("foo", "bar")).copy(
  strictHostKeyChecking = true,
  knownHosts = Some(sys.props("user.home") + "/.ssh/known_hosts")
)
```

#### SSH Configuration

The `sshConfig` field is the sshj `Config` used to create the SSH client. It controls the algorithms the client offers (ciphers, key exchange, MACs and signatures) and the keepalive provider. The default, `DefaultConfig`, is sshj's recommended set. Replace it only to work with servers that need algorithms sshj disables by default, or to restrict the client to a smaller set. For example, to offer only AES ciphers:

```scala
import zio.ftp._
import net.schmizz.sshj.DefaultConfig
import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters._

val config = new DefaultConfig()
config.setCipherFactories(config.getCipherFactories.asScala.filter(_.getName.startsWith("aes")).asJava)

val custom = SecureFtpSettings("sftp.example.com", 22, PasswordCredentials("foo", "bar")).copy(sshConfig = config)
```

The SFTP implementation has no timeout or TCP keepalive settings of its own; the connection uses sshj's defaults.

### Credentials

The `credentials` field takes any `FtpCredentials`, a sealed trait with two cases:

```scala
sealed trait FtpCredentials

final case class PasswordCredentials(username: String, password: String) extends FtpCredentials
final case class KeyCredentials(username: String, identity: SftpIdentity) extends FtpCredentials
```

`PasswordCredentials` logs in with SSH password authentication. `KeyCredentials` logs in with public key authentication, using the private key described by its `SftpIdentity`. [Connect over SFTP with a Key](../guides/connect-over-sftp-with-a-key.md) walks through key setup end to end.

### SftpIdentity

`SftpIdentity` is a sealed trait with two cases, one for a key held in a string and one for a key in a file. Both carry an optional passphrase that decrypts an encrypted private key:

```scala
sealed trait SftpIdentity {
  type KeyType
  val privateKey: KeyType
  val passphrase: Option[String]
}
```

`RawKeySftpIdentity` holds the private key as text, for example loaded from a secret store or an environment variable. Its optional `publicKey` is the matching public key text, which is only needed for key formats that don't embed it:

```scala
final case class RawKeySftpIdentity(
  privateKey: String,
  passphrase: Option[String] = None,
  publicKey: Option[String] = None
) extends SftpIdentity

object RawKeySftpIdentity {
  def apply(privateKey: String): RawKeySftpIdentity
  def apply(privateKey: String, passphrase: String): RawKeySftpIdentity
}
```

`KeyFileSftpIdentity` points at a private key file on the local disk:

```scala
final case class KeyFileSftpIdentity(privateKey: java.nio.file.Path, passphrase: Option[String] = None)
  extends SftpIdentity

object KeyFileSftpIdentity {
  def apply(privateKey: java.nio.file.Path): KeyFileSftpIdentity
}
```

Both accept the private key formats sshj reads, including OpenSSH, PEM (PKCS#1 and PKCS#8) and PuTTY keys. To log in with an encrypted key file:

```scala
import zio.ftp._
import java.nio.file.Paths

val keyFile = KeyFileSftpIdentity(Paths.get("/home/app/.ssh/id_ed25519"), Some("key passphrase"))

val settings = SecureFtpSettings("sftp.example.com", 22, KeyCredentials("app", keyFile))
```

To log in with a key held in an environment variable:

```scala
import zio.ftp._

val rawKey = RawKeySftpIdentity(sys.env("SFTP_PRIVATE_KEY"))

val settings = SecureFtpSettings("sftp.example.com", 22, KeyCredentials("app", rawKey))
```

### Related Pages

For FTP and FTPS, see [FTP and FTPS settings](unsecure-ftp-settings.md). For the differences between the protocols, see [FTP, FTPS and SFTP](../protocols.md).

---

## TestFtp

`TestFtp` is a test double for ZIO FTP that works on a local directory instead of a server. It implements every `FtpAccessors` operation with local file system calls, so code written against the `FtpAccessors` interface can be tested without starting an FTP or SFTP server.

### Definition

`TestFtp.create` builds the service, and the `stub` function in the `zio.ftp` package object wraps it in a layer. Both take the directory that plays the role of the server's root, as a ZIO NIO `Path`:

```scala
object TestFtp {
  def create(root: zio.nio.file.Path): FtpAccessors[Unit]
}

package object ftp {
  type StubFtp = FtpAccessors[Unit]
  def stub(path: zio.nio.file.Path): Layer[Any, StubFtp]
}
```

The `StubFtp` object offers the same accessor functions as `Ftp` and `SFtp`, documented in the [Ftp API](ftp-accessors.md). The underlying client type is `Unit`, so `StubFtp.execute` passes `()` to the function.

:::note
Open pull request [#464](https://github.com/zio/zio-ftp/pull/464) proposes removing the ZIO NIO dependency. If it is merged, `TestFtp.create` and `stub` would take a `java.nio.file.Path` instead of a `zio.nio.file.Path`. Until then, convert a Java path with `zio.nio.file.Path.fromJava`.
:::

### How Paths Map to the Root

Every path you pass is joined to the root directory: `/reports/a.csv` with root `/tmp/ftp-root` becomes `/tmp/ftp-root/reports/a.csv`. The leading `/` is optional. The stub does not normalize `..` segments, so a path containing them can leave the root. Paths in returned `FtpResource` values are relative to the root and start with `/`, so they look like server paths.

### Example

The following setup creates a temporary root directory with one file and a subdirectory, and defines a helper that runs an effect against the stub layer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.ftp._
import zio.stream._
import java.nio.file.Files

val root = Files.createTempDirectory("stub-ftp")
Files.createDirectories(root.resolve("dir1"))
Files.write(root.resolve("notes.txt"), "Hello from the stub".getBytes)
Files.write(root.resolve("dir1/users.csv"), "id,name\n1,Ada\n".getBytes)

def runStub[A](effect: ZIO[StubFtp, Throwable, A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe
      .run(effect.provide(stub(zio.nio.file.Path.fromJava(root))))
      .getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

Listing the root returns both entries, with paths relative to the root:

```scala
runStub(StubFtp.ls("/").map(_.path).runCollect.map(_.sorted))
// res3: Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq("/dir1", "/notes.txt")
```

`StubFtp.lsDescendant` returns only the files, from every level:

```scala
runStub(StubFtp.lsDescendant("/").map(_.path).runCollect.map(_.sorted))
// res4: Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq("/dir1/users.csv", "/notes.txt")
```

Uploads write real files under the root, so a later read sees them:

```scala
runStub(
  StubFtp.upload("/dir1/new.txt", ZStream.fromIterable("uploaded".getBytes)) *>
    StubFtp.readFile("/dir1/new.txt").via(ZPipeline.utf8Decode).runCollect.map(_.mkString)
)
// res5: String = "uploaded"
```

Reading a missing file fails with the same `InvalidPathError` as on FTP:

```scala
runStub(StubFtp.readFile("/missing.txt").runCollect.either)
// res6: Either[java.io.IOException, Chunk[Byte]] = Left(
//   value = InvalidPathError(message = "File does not exist /missing.txt")
// )
```

### Behavior

The stub follows FTP's behavior where it can, and the local file system's otherwise:

- `FtpAccessors#stat` returns `None` for a missing path and fills `isDirectory`, `size`, `lastModified` and `permissions` from the file system. On Windows, `permissions` is empty.
- `FtpAccessors#ls` and `FtpAccessors#lsDescendant` return an empty stream for a missing directory. `FtpAccessors#lsDescendant` emits regular files only.
- `FtpAccessors#readFile` reads the whole file into memory before streaming it, ignores `chunkSize`, and skips `fileOffset` bytes. A missing file fails with `InvalidPathError`.
- `FtpAccessors#upload` replaces an existing file and fails if the parent directory doesn't exist.
- `FtpAccessors#mkdir` creates missing parent directories, like SFTP and unlike FTP.
- `FtpAccessors#rm` and `FtpAccessors#rmdir` both delete the path, and fail on a non-empty directory.
- `FtpAccessors#rename` moves the file or directory and fails if the target exists.
- Errors other than a missing file for `FtpAccessors#readFile` are plain `IOException` values; see [Errors](errors.md).

### Testing Code Written for Ftp or SFtp

The accessor functions are tied to their environment type: code that calls `Ftp.ls` requires `Ftp`, and a `StubFtp` layer can't satisfy it, because `Ftp` and `StubFtp` are different types. To test such code with the stub, write it against `FtpAccessors[_]` instead of the `Ftp` or `SFtp` objects, and pass in the service. [Test Without a Server](../guides/test-without-a-server.md) shows this pattern with ZIO Test.

---

## FTP and FTPS Settings

`UnsecureFtpSettings` describes a connection to an FTP or FTPS server. Despite the name, it covers both: a value with `sslParams` set connects over TLS. This page documents every field, the two constructors, and the supporting types `SslParams`, `ProtectionLevel`, `KeepaliveSettings` and `PasswordCredentials`.

### Definition

`UnsecureFtpSettings` is a case class with twelve fields. The first seven have no default value, and the last five do:

```scala
final case class UnsecureFtpSettings(
  host: String,
  port: Int,
  credentials: PasswordCredentials,
  binary: Boolean,
  passiveMode: Boolean,
  remoteVerificationEnabled: Boolean,
  proxy: Option[java.net.Proxy],
  sslParams: Option[SslParams] = None,
  dataTimeout: Option[Duration] = Some(1.minute),
  defaultTimeout: Option[Duration] = Some(1.minute),
  keepalive: Option[KeepaliveSettings] = Some(KeepaliveSettings.default),
  controlEncoding: Option[String] = None
)
```

The settings value is passed to the `unsecure` layer or to `UnsecureFtp.connect`, both documented in [Connecting](connecting.md).

### Construction

Use the companion's constructors rather than the case class constructor. They fill in the fields without defaults:

```scala
object UnsecureFtpSettings {
  def apply(host: String, port: Int, creds: PasswordCredentials): UnsecureFtpSettings
  def secure(host: String, port: Int, creds: PasswordCredentials): UnsecureFtpSettings
}
```

`UnsecureFtpSettings.apply` creates plain FTP settings with binary transfers, passive mode and remote verification turned on, no proxy, and the case class defaults for the rest:

```scala
import zio.ftp._

UnsecureFtpSettings("127.0.0.1", 21, PasswordCredentials("one", "1234"))
// res0: UnsecureFtpSettings = UnsecureFtpSettings(
//   host = "127.0.0.1",
//   port = 21,
//   credentials = PasswordCredentials(username = "one", password = "1234"),
//   binary = true,
//   passiveMode = true,
//   remoteVerificationEnabled = true,
//   proxy = None,
//   sslParams = None,
//   dataTimeout = Some(value = PT1M),
//   defaultTimeout = Some(value = PT1M),
//   keepalive = Some(
//     value = KeepaliveSettings(
//       idle = Some(value = 60),
//       interval = Some(value = 10),
//       count = Some(value = 5)
//     )
//   ),
//   controlEncoding = None
// )
```

`UnsecureFtpSettings.secure` creates the same settings with `sslParams = Some(SslParams.default)`, which selects explicit FTPS:

```scala
UnsecureFtpSettings.secure("127.0.0.1", 21, PasswordCredentials("one", "1234")).sslParams
// res1: Option[SslParams] = Some(
//   value = SslParams(isImplicit = false, pbzs = 0L, prot = Clear)
// )
```

To change any other field, use `UnsecureFtpSettings#copy` on the result.

### Fields

The fields fall into four groups: where to connect, how to transfer, how to secure the connection, and how to keep it healthy.

#### Server and Credentials

The `host` field is the server's host name or IP address, and `port` is its control port, usually 21 for FTP and explicit FTPS and 990 for implicit FTPS. The `credentials` field is a `PasswordCredentials(username, password)` value; FTP has no key-based login. For anonymous FTP, servers conventionally accept the user name `anonymous` with an email address as the password.

The `proxy` field routes every socket through a `java.net.Proxy`, such as a SOCKS proxy, when it is `Some`:

```scala
import zio.ftp._
import java.net.{ InetSocketAddress, Proxy }

val viaSocks = UnsecureFtpSettings("ftp.example.com", 21, PasswordCredentials("one", "1234"))
  .copy(proxy = Some(new Proxy(Proxy.Type.SOCKS, new InetSocketAddress("proxy.internal", 1080))))
```

#### Transfer Mode

The `binary` field selects the transfer type. When it is true, the client sends `TYPE I` after login and files are transferred byte for byte. When it is false, the client keeps the server's default, which is ASCII mode on most servers and may rewrite line endings. Keep it true unless you know you need ASCII conversion.

The `passiveMode` field selects passive mode, where the client opens the data connection to a port the server announces. When it is false, the client uses active mode, where the server connects back to the client. Passive mode works through client-side firewalls and NAT, which is why both constructors turn it on.

The `remoteVerificationEnabled` field asks the client to check that each data connection comes from the same host as the control connection. Commons Net enables this check by default, and ZIO FTP only calls its setter when the field is true, so setting the field to false does not currently turn the check off.

The `controlEncoding` field sets the character encoding of the control connection, which carries commands and file names. When it is `None`, the client asks the server whether it supports UTF-8 and uses it if so. Set it, for example to `Some("ISO-8859-1")`, for servers with non-ASCII file names in another encoding.

#### TLS

The `sslParams` field turns on FTPS when it is `Some`. Its value is an `SslParams`:

```scala
final case class SslParams(isImplicit: Boolean, pbzs: Long, prot: ProtectionLevel)

object SslParams {
  val default: SslParams = SslParams(isImplicit = false, 0L, ProtectionLevel.Clear)
}
```

The three parameters map to the FTPS connection setup:

- `isImplicit` selects implicit FTPS when true, where the connection is TLS from the first byte, and explicit FTPS when false, where the client connects in plain text and upgrades with `AUTH TLS`.
- `pbzs` is the protection buffer size sent with the `PBSZ` command after login. With TLS it is always 0.
- `prot` is the data channel protection level sent with the `PROT` command.

`ProtectionLevel` has one case per `PROT` value:

| Case                           | `PROT` value | Meaning                                      |
| ------------------------------ | ------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `ProtectionLevel.Clear`        | `C`          | data connections are not encrypted           |
| `ProtectionLevel.Private`      | `P`          | data connections are encrypted with TLS      |
| `ProtectionLevel.Safe`         | `S`          | integrity protection only, not used with TLS |
| `ProtectionLevel.Confidential` | `E`          | confidentiality only, not used with TLS      |

FTPS servers normally accept only `C` and `P`. Since `SslParams.default` uses `Clear`, file contents are not encrypted unless you choose `Private`:

```scala
import zio.ftp._

val encrypted = UnsecureFtpSettings
  .secure("ftp.example.com", 21, PasswordCredentials("one", "1234"))
  .copy(sslParams = Some(SslParams(isImplicit = false, pbzs = 0L, prot = ProtectionLevel.Private)))
```

[Use FTPS](../guides/use-ftps.md) walks through explicit and implicit mode.

#### Timeouts and Keepalive

Two timeouts and a keepalive option protect long-running connections. Each one is turned off by setting it to `None`:

- `dataTimeout` is how long a read on a data connection can block before it fails. It defaults to one minute.
- `defaultTimeout` is the read timeout of the control connection, which bounds how long the client waits for a command reply. It doesn't limit the initial TCP connection attempt. It defaults to one minute.
- `keepalive` turns on TCP keepalive on every socket the client opens when it is `Some`. It defaults to `Some(KeepaliveSettings.default)`.

`KeepaliveSettings` holds the three TCP keepalive parameters, each in the units of `jdk.net.ExtendedSocketOptions`:

```scala
final case class KeepaliveSettings(idle: Option[Int], interval: Option[Int], count: Option[Int])

object KeepaliveSettings {
  val default: KeepaliveSettings = KeepaliveSettings(Some(60), Some(10), Some(5))
}
```

`idle` is the number of seconds a connection must be idle before the first probe, `interval` is the number of seconds between probes, and `count` is the number of unanswered probes after which the connection is dropped. A `None` parameter keeps the operating system's default. If the platform does not support one of the options, ZIO FTP logs a warning with `ZIO.logWarning` and continues without it. To set both timeouts and all three keepalive parameters at once:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.ftp._

val tunedSettings = UnsecureFtpSettings("127.0.0.1", 21, PasswordCredentials("foo", "bar")).copy(
  dataTimeout = Some(30.seconds),
  defaultTimeout = Some(10.seconds),
  keepalive = Some(KeepaliveSettings(idle = Some(30), interval = Some(5), count = Some(3)))
)
```

[Keep a Connection Alive](../guides/keep-a-connection-alive.md) explains when each setting matters.

### Related Pages

For SFTP, see [SFTP settings](secure-ftp-settings.md). For what happens with these fields when the connection opens, see the lifecycle section of [Connecting](connecting.md#connection-lifecycle).

---

## Tutorial: Back Up a Folder to a File Server

Welcome! In this tutorial we build a small backup tool: it copies a local folder, with its subfolders, to a file server, skips files that are already there, and checks that the copy matches. This tutorial is for Scala developers who know the basics of `ZIO` effects. You don't need any prior experience with ZIO FTP or with FTP servers.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will understand:

- How a ZIO FTP connection is provided as a layer and used as a service.
- How uploads, listings and downloads work as ZIO effects and streams.
- How to create remote directories and check whether a file exists.
- How to write file-transfer code once and run it against a test double or a real server.

We'll learn these concepts through:

1. Preparing a folder to back up
2. Connecting to a server
3. Uploading one file
4. Uploading a whole folder
5. Skipping unchanged files
6. Verifying the backup
7. Backing up to a real server

We recommend reading from top to bottom: each section builds on the previous one.

### Background

A file server stores files under paths like `/backup/photos/cat.jpg`, and a client sends it commands: list this directory, store these bytes, send me that file. ZIO FTP gives every command the shape of a ZIO value. Commands that return one thing, like "create a directory", are `ZIO` effects; commands that return many things or many bytes, like "list a directory" or "read a file", are `ZStream`s. Nothing happens until the effect runs, and the connection itself is a resource that opens before the first command and closes after the last.

So that every step runs right here on the page, we use ZIO FTP's test double, `StubFtp`, which behaves like a server but stores its files in a local directory. In the last section, we point the same code at a real FTP server.

### 1. Prepare a Folder to Back Up

First, we need something to back up. Let's create a temporary folder with a text file and two "photos", and a second, empty temporary folder that plays the role of the server's disk:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.ftp._
import zio.stream._
import java.io.IOException
import java.nio.file.{ Files, Path }
import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters._

val source = Files.createTempDirectory("my-documents")
Files.createDirectories(source.resolve("photos"))
Files.write(source.resolve("notes.txt"), "Buy milk".getBytes)
Files.write(source.resolve("photos/cat.jpg"), Array.fill[Byte](1200)(1))
Files.write(source.resolve("photos/dog.jpg"), Array.fill[Byte](800)(2))

val serverDisk = Files.createTempDirectory("server-disk")
```

The code above does the following:

- The imports bring in ZIO, ZIO FTP, ZIO Streams and the Java file API.
- `source` is the folder to back up. It holds `notes.txt` and a `photos` subfolder with two files of 1200 and 800 bytes.
- `serverDisk` is where the stub server keeps the files we upload. It starts empty.

### 2. Connect to a Server

A ZIO FTP connection is a service in the ZIO environment, and a layer creates it. For the stub, the layer is `stub(root)`; for a real FTP server, it is `unsecure(settings)`. Our backup code receives the service as a plain parameter of type `FtpAccessors[Any]`, which every connection type satisfies, so the same code works with any of them. Let's write a helper that builds the stub layer, hands its service to a function, and runs the result:

```scala
def runOnStub[A](f: FtpAccessors[Any] => ZIO[Any, IOException, A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe
      .run(ZIO.serviceWithZIO[StubFtp](f).provide(stub(zio.nio.file.Path.fromJava(serverDisk))))
      .getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

The helper has three parts:

- `ZIO.serviceWithZIO[StubFtp](f)` takes the connection out of the environment and passes it to `f`.
- `ZIO#provide` with `stub(...)` builds the stub layer around the `serverDisk` folder. A real program provides `unsecure` or `secure` here instead.
- `Runtime.default.unsafe.run` runs the effect so the page can show the result. A real program extends `ZIOAppDefault` instead, as we do in section 7.

Now let's ask the server what is in its root directory. `FtpAccessors#ls` returns a stream of entries, and `ZStream#runCollect` gathers them:

```scala
runOnStub(ftp => ftp.ls("/").map(_.path).runCollect)
// res4: Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq()
```

The listing is empty: the server has no files yet.

### 3. Upload One File

To upload a file, we need a directory to put it in and a stream of its bytes. `FtpAccessors#mkdir` creates the directory, `ZStream.fromPath` reads the local file as a stream, and `FtpAccessors#upload` sends that stream to the server:

```scala
def uploadFile(ftp: FtpAccessors[Any], local: Path, remote: String): ZIO[Any, IOException, Unit] =
  ftp.upload(remote, ZStream.fromPath(local))
```

Let's create `/backup` and upload `notes.txt` into it, then list the directory to check:

```scala
runOnStub { ftp =>
  ftp.mkdir("/backup") *>
    uploadFile(ftp, source.resolve("notes.txt"), "/backup/notes.txt") *>
    ftp.ls("/backup").map(f => s"${f.path} (${f.size} bytes)").runCollect
}
// res5: Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq("/backup/notes.txt (8 bytes)")
```

The file is on the server with its 8 bytes. Notice that the upload never loads the file into memory: `ZStream.fromPath` reads it in chunks while `FtpAccessors#upload` writes them, so the same code works for a file of any size.

### 4. Upload a Whole Folder

A folder backup repeats the single upload for every file, but subfolders add a twist: the remote directory must exist before we upload into it. On FTP servers, `FtpAccessors#mkdir` creates only one level at a time, so we create each level that is missing. `FtpAccessors#stat` tells us whether a path exists by returning `Some(resource)` or `None`:

```scala
def ensureDirectory(ftp: FtpAccessors[Any], dir: String): ZIO[Any, IOException, Unit] = {
  val levels = dir.split('/').filter(_.nonEmpty).scanLeft("")(_ + "/" + _).drop(1)
  ZIO.foreachDiscard(levels.toList) { level =>
    ftp.stat(level).flatMap(existing => ftp.mkdir(level).when(existing.isEmpty))
  }
}
```

The function first turns `/backup/photos` into `/backup` and `/backup/photos`, one entry per level. For each level, `FtpAccessors#stat` checks whether it exists, and `FtpAccessors#mkdir` runs only when it doesn't.

Next, we need the list of local files and a rule that maps each local path to a remote one:

```scala
def localFiles(dir: Path): ZIO[Any, IOException, List[Path]] =
  ZIO.acquireReleaseWith(ZIO.attemptBlockingIO(Files.walk(dir)))(s => ZIO.succeed(s.close())) { s =>
    ZIO.attemptBlockingIO(s.iterator().asScala.filter(Files.isRegularFile(_)).toList.sorted)
  }

def remotePath(local: Path): String =
  "/backup/" + source.relativize(local).asScala.mkString("/")
```

These two helpers do the local side of the work. `localFiles` walks the folder tree on the blocking thread pool and keeps only regular files, sorted so the output is stable. `remotePath` turns `<source>/photos/cat.jpg` into `/backup/photos/cat.jpg`.

Now the backup itself: for each local file, make sure its remote directory exists, then upload it:

```scala
def backupAll(ftp: FtpAccessors[Any]): ZIO[Any, IOException, Int] =
  localFiles(source).flatMap { files =>
    ZIO.foreach(files) { local =>
      val remote = remotePath(local)
      ensureDirectory(ftp, remote.substring(0, remote.lastIndexOf('/'))) *> uploadFile(ftp, local, remote)
    }.map(_.size)
  }
```

Let's run it and list everything under `/backup`. `FtpAccessors#lsDescendant` walks the remote tree and returns every file in it:

```scala
runOnStub { ftp =>
  backupAll(ftp) *> ftp.lsDescendant("/backup").map(f => s"${f.path} (${f.size} bytes)").runCollect.map(_.sorted)
}
// res6: Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq(
//   "/backup/notes.txt (8 bytes)",
//   "/backup/photos/cat.jpg (1200 bytes)",
//   "/backup/photos/dog.jpg (800 bytes)"
// )
```

All three files are on the server, in the same folder structure as on the local disk.

### 5. Skip Unchanged Files

Running the backup again uploads every file again, which is wasteful when most of them haven't changed. Let's upload a file only when the server doesn't have it, or has a copy with a different size. `FtpAccessors#stat` gives us the remote size:

```scala
def needsUpload(ftp: FtpAccessors[Any], local: Path, remote: String): ZIO[Any, IOException, Boolean] =
  for {
    localSize <- ZIO.attemptBlockingIO(Files.size(local))
    existing  <- ftp.stat(remote)
  } yield existing.forall(_.size != localSize)

def backupChanged(ftp: FtpAccessors[Any]): ZIO[Any, IOException, Int] =
  localFiles(source).flatMap { files =>
    ZIO.filter(files)(local => needsUpload(ftp, local, remotePath(local))).flatMap { changed =>
      ZIO.foreach(changed) { local =>
        val remote = remotePath(local)
        ensureDirectory(ftp, remote.substring(0, remote.lastIndexOf('/'))) *> uploadFile(ftp, local, remote)
      }.as(changed.size)
    }
  }
```

The new code changes the backup in two places. `needsUpload` returns true when `FtpAccessors#stat` finds nothing (`Option#forall` on `None` is true) or finds a file whose size differs. `backupChanged` keeps only the files that need uploading, uploads them like `backupAll`, and returns how many it uploaded.

Everything is already on the server, so a run now uploads nothing:

```scala
runOnStub(backupChanged)
// res7: Int = 0
```

Let's change one local file, so its size no longer matches the copy on the server:

```scala
Files.write(source.resolve("notes.txt"), "Buy milk and bread".getBytes)
```

Now we run the backup again. Only the changed file is uploaded:

```scala
runOnStub(backupChanged)
// res9: Int = 1
```

Comparing sizes is a simple rule that misses edits that keep the size the same. A real tool would also compare `lastModified` or a checksum; we keep the size rule so the tutorial stays focused.

### 6. Verify the Backup

A backup is only useful if it can be read back. `FtpAccessors#readFile` streams a remote file's bytes, so we can compare them with the local file:

```scala
def verify(ftp: FtpAccessors[Any]): ZIO[Any, IOException, List[String]] =
  localFiles(source).flatMap { files =>
    ZIO.foreach(files) { local =>
      for {
        remoteBytes <- ftp.readFile(remotePath(local)).runCollect
        localBytes  <- ZIO.attemptBlockingIO(Files.readAllBytes(local))
      } yield s"${remotePath(local)}: ${if (remoteBytes.toArray.sameElements(localBytes)) "OK" else "DIFFERENT"}"
    }
  }
```

The verification reads each remote file in full with `ZStream#runCollect` and compares it byte for byte with the local file. Let's run it:

```scala
runOnStub(verify)
// res10: List[String] = List(
//   "/backup/notes.txt: OK",
//   "/backup/photos/cat.jpg: OK",
//   "/backup/photos/dog.jpg: OK"
// )
```

Every file matches, including the `notes.txt` we changed in the previous section.

### 7. Back Up to a Real Server

Our functions only use `FtpAccessors[Any]`, so they run unchanged against a real server. The only new piece is the layer: instead of `stub`, we provide `unsecure` with the server's settings, and instead of `runOnStub`, we run the program as a `ZIOAppDefault`:

```scala
object BackupApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val settings =
    UnsecureFtpSettings("127.0.0.1", 2121, PasswordCredentials("username", "userpass"))

  private val program: ZIO[Ftp, IOException, Unit] =
    ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Ftp] { ftp =>
      for {
        uploaded <- backupChanged(ftp)
        _        <- Console.printLine(s"Uploaded $uploaded file(s)")
        report   <- verify(ftp)
        _        <- ZIO.foreachDiscard(report)(Console.printLine(_))
      } yield ()
    }

  override def run = program.provide(unsecure(settings))
}
```

The program differs from the stub runs in three places:

- `settings` describes the server; the values match the local server from [Getting Started](../getting-started.md).
- `ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Ftp]` takes the FTP connection from the environment, just as `runOnStub` did with `StubFtp`.
- `ZIO#provide` with `unsecure(settings)` connects before the program starts and disconnects when it ends.

Try it: start the Pure-FTPd container from Getting Started, run `BackupApp`, then run it a second time and notice that it uploads nothing.

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned:

- How a connection is provided as a layer (`stub`, `unsecure`) and used as an `FtpAccessors` service.
- How `FtpAccessors#upload`, `FtpAccessors#ls`, `FtpAccessors#lsDescendant` and `FtpAccessors#readFile` turn file transfers into effects and streams that can move a file in chunks.
- How `FtpAccessors#stat` and `FtpAccessors#mkdir` let you check for paths and create directory trees one level at a time.
- How code written against `FtpAccessors[Any]` runs on a test double and on a real server without changes.

You now have a working mental model of ZIO FTP. The next step is to apply it to your own servers and protocols.

### Where to Go Next

To keep going:

- **Connecting to SFTP?** Follow [Connect over SFTP with a Key](../guides/connect-over-sftp-with-a-key.md), then provide `secure` instead of `unsecure` and take `SFtp` from the environment instead of `Ftp`.
- **Testing your own code?** [Test Without a Server](../guides/test-without-a-server.md) uses the same stub with ZIO Test.
- **Want every operation in detail?** Read the [Ftp API](../reference/ftp-accessors.md) reference.
- **Wondering how FTP, FTPS and SFTP differ?** Read [FTP, FTPS and SFTP](../protocols.md).

## How Strict Is the Decoder

ZIO JSON decoders check everything they need to build your value, and little else. Some input that is not valid JSON under [RFC 8259](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259) therefore decodes without an error. This page explains which input that is, why the decoders work this way, and how to get stricter checks when you need them.

All examples on this page use these imports and types:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.Json

final case class Reading(value: Int)

object Reading {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Reading] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Reading]
}

final case class Name(name: String)

object Name {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Name] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Name]
}
```

### Why the Decoder Is Lenient

A `JsonDecoder` reads characters and builds your value directly, without building a syntax tree first (see [How ZIO JSON Works](how-it-works.md#decoding-reads-straight-into-your-types)). Each decoder reads only the part of the input that belongs to its value. An `Int` decoder reads digits, a case class decoder reads the fields it knows, and nothing is checked twice.

That design makes decoding fast and keeps memory use low, but it means no step looks at the whole document. Three things follow from it:

- The top-level decoder stops after the first complete value and never looks at the rest of the input.
- Values of fields the decoder does not know are skipped with a quick scan that does not validate them.
- Some built-in decoders accept common non-standard forms, such as numbers in quotes, so that JSON written by other tools still decodes.

None of these leniencies lets a wrongly typed value into your program. They decide only which *extra* text is tolerated around and between the values you asked for. That extra text can still change the meaning of a top-level number, as the next section shows: `1e3` decodes as the `Int` `1`. When you need the input itself to be valid JSON, for example because you store it or pass it on, add one of the checks in [Getting Stricter Checks](#getting-stricter-checks).

### Input After the First Value Is Ignored

`JsonDecoder#decodeJson`, and the `fromJson` extension method that calls it, read one complete JSON value from the start of the input and then stop. They do not check that the rest of the input is empty.

For a top-level number, the value ends at the first character that cannot continue it. The `Int` decoder reads digits only, so it stops at the `e` of `1e3` or the `.` of `1.5` and ignores the rest. The same holds for other scalar values and for whole objects:

```scala
"1e3".fromJson[Int]
// res1: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 1)

"1.5".fromJson[Int]
// res2: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 1)

"12x".fromJson[Int]
// res3: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 12)

"truex".fromJson[Boolean]
// res4: Either[String, Boolean] = Right(value = true)

"""{"value":1} {"value":2}""".fromJson[Reading]
// res5: Either[String, Reading] = Right(value = Reading(value = 1))
```

Inside an object or an array the same text fails, because after a value the decoder expects a `,` or a closing bracket:

```scala
"""{"value":1e3}""".fromJson[Reading]
// res6: Either[String, Reading] = Left(
//   value = "(expected ',' or '}' got 'e')"
// )

"[1.5]".fromJson[List[Int]]
// res7: Either[String, List[Int]] = Left(
//   value = "(expected ',' or ']' got '.')"
// )
```

So the trailing-input leniency matters mostly when a whole message is a single number, string or boolean, or when a second document follows the first one by mistake. The [JsonDecoder reference](../reference/json-decoder.md#trailing-input-is-ignored) states the rule as part of the API.

### Unknown Fields Are Skipped Without Validation

A derived case class decoder ignores fields it does not know, unless you forbid them (see [Reject Unknown Fields](#reject-unknown-fields)). To ignore a field, it skips over the field's value. Skipping is a fast scan that only looks for where the value ends. It does not check that the value is well-formed JSON, so a malformed value in an unknown field is accepted:

```scala
"""{"name":"Ada","x":tzzz}""".fromJson[Name]
// res8: Either[String, Name] = Right(value = Name(name = "Ada"))

"""{"name":"Ada","x":1-2e+}""".fromJson[Name]
// res9: Either[String, Name] = Right(value = Name(name = "Ada"))
```

The scan builds nothing and does not recurse, so an unknown field costs little time and memory even when it is large or deeply nested. That is what keeps decoding fast on payloads with many fields you do not need, and it is also why unknown fields are a cheap path for an attacker to send padding. [Security](security.md#redundant-data) discusses that side.

### Leniencies of the Built-in Decoders

Some decoders for standard types accept more than their encoders write. This keeps them compatible with JSON written by other libraries and languages. The full list is in [Built-in Instances](../reference/built-in-instances.md#leniencies); the number-related ones are the most visible.

Every number decoder accepts a number inside a string, and the integer decoders accept leading zeros:

```scala
"\"42\"".fromJson[Int]
// res10: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 42)

"""{"value":"42"}""".fromJson[Reading]
// res11: Either[String, Reading] = Right(value = Reading(value = 42))

"007".fromJson[Int]
// res12: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 7)
```

`Float` and `Double` accept the quoted strings `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"+Infinity"` and `"-Infinity"`, which are also what their encoders write for those values:

```scala
"\"NaN\"".fromJson[Double]
// res13: Either[String, Double] = Right(value = NaN)

"\"+Infinity\"".fromJson[Double]
// res14: Either[String, Double] = Right(value = Infinity)

"\"-Infinity\"".fromJson[Float]
// res15: Either[String, Float] = Right(value = -InfinityF)
```

`Map` keys go through a separate key decoder (see [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](../reference/json-field-codecs.md)). The `Int` and `Long` key decoders parse the key with `String#toInt` and `String#toLong`, so a key such as `"+5"` is accepted, although the value decoder rejects `+5`:

```scala
"""{"+5":1}""".fromJson[Map[Int, Int]]
// res16: Either[String, Map[Int, Int]] = Right(value = Map(5 -> 1))

"+5".fromJson[Int]
// res17: Either[String, Int] = Left(value = "(expected an Int)")
```

### What the Decoder Checks

Leniency is about tolerated extra text, not about types. Everything that decides what your value contains is checked, and the error names the path to the problem (see [Errors](../reference/errors.md)).

A value of the wrong type fails, and so does a required field that is missing:

```scala
"""{"value":"high"}""".fromJson[Reading]
// res18: Either[String, Reading] = Left(value = ".value(expected an Int)")

"{}".fromJson[Reading]
// res19: Either[String, Reading] = Left(value = ".value(missing)")
```

A derived decoder rejects a field that appears twice, instead of silently keeping one of the values:

```scala
"""{"value":1,"value":2}""".fromJson[Reading]
// res20: Either[String, Reading] = Left(value = "(duplicate)")
```

Strings must be well-formed, so a bad escape or a raw control character fails. Bare `NaN` and a leading `+` on a number are rejected too:

```scala
"\"a\\xb\"".fromJson[String]
// res21: Either[String, String] = Left(value = "(invalid '\\x' in string)")

"NaN".fromJson[Double]
// res22: Either[String, Double] = Left(value = "(expected a Double)")

"+1".fromJson[Int]
// res23: Either[String, Int] = Left(value = "(expected an Int)")
```

Unknown fields are rejected as soon as you ask for it with `@jsonNoExtraFields` or `allowExtraFields = false`, which the next section shows.

### Getting Stricter Checks

Which check you add depends on what you need to be strict about. Parsing to `Json` first validates the syntax of the whole document, forbidding extra fields rejects unknown fields, `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail` validates values, and a short helper rejects trailing input.

#### Parse to `Json` First

Decoding to the [`Json` AST](../reference/json-ast.md) parses every value fully, including the values of fields your type does not know. Converting the tree with `Json#as` then gives you your type:

```scala
"""{"name":"Ada","x":tzzz}""".fromJson[Json]
// res24: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = ".x(expected a Boolean)")

"""{"name":"Ada","x":tzzz}""".fromJson[Json].flatMap(_.as[Name])
// res25: Either[String, Name] = Left(value = ".x(expected a Boolean)")
```

Numbers are read in full too, so `1e3` becomes the number one thousand, not `1` followed by ignored text. Converting it to an `Int` then succeeds, while a number with a fraction is rejected:

```scala
"1e3".fromJson[Json]
// res26: Either[String, Json] = Right(value = Num(value = 1E+3))

"1e3".fromJson[Json].flatMap(_.as[Int])
// res27: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 1000)

"1.5".fromJson[Json].flatMap(_.as[Int])
// res28: Either[String, Int] = Left(value = "(expected a Int)")
```

Parsing to `Json` does not reject trailing input. The `Json` decoder also reads one value and stops, so text after it is still ignored:

```scala
"12x".fromJson[Json]
// res29: Either[String, Json] = Right(value = Num(value = 12))

"""{"name":"Ada"} trailing""".fromJson[Json]
// res30: Either[String, Json] = Right(
//   value = Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("name", Str(value = "Ada"))))
// )
```

The cost is a full tree in memory before your value is built, which makes decoding slower and uses more memory than decoding directly. The leniencies of the built-in decoders stay too: `Json#as[Int]` still accepts a quoted number. Use this approach where a complete syntax check matters more than speed, for example at a system boundary that stores the raw document.

#### Reject Unknown Fields

`@jsonNoExtraFields` on a case class, or `allowExtraFields = false` in a [`JsonCodecConfiguration`](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#allowextrafields), makes the derived decoder fail at the first field it does not know. The unknown value is then never skipped, so its contents no longer matter:

```scala
@jsonNoExtraFields
final case class StrictName(name: String)

object StrictName {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[StrictName] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[StrictName]
}
```

The same payload as before now fails:

```scala
"""{"name":"Ada","x":tzzz}""".fromJson[StrictName]
// res31: Either[String, StrictName] = Left(value = "(invalid extra field)")
```

This makes your API reject typos in field names and fields from a newer client version, so turn it on only where that is what you want. It also does not combine with a discriminator field, because the discriminator counts as an extra field of the case; [JSON Shapes and Round Trips](wire-format.md#a-discriminator-with-strict-field-checks) shows the failure. The [optional and default fields guide](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md#4-reject-unexpected-fields-with-jsonnoextrafields) covers the annotation in more detail.

#### Validate Values With `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail`

The decoders check types, not the rules of your domain. `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail` adds such a rule, and a value that breaks it fails with your message and the usual path:

```scala
final case class Percent(value: Int)

object Percent {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Percent] =
    JsonDecoder[Int].mapOrFail { n =>
      if (n >= 0 && n <= 100) Right(Percent(n))
      else Left(s"$n is not between 0 and 100")
    }
}
```

A number outside the range now fails:

```scala
"42".fromJson[Percent]
// res32: Either[String, Percent] = Right(value = Percent(value = 42))

"150".fromJson[Percent]
// res33: Either[String, Percent] = Left(
//   value = "(150 is not between 0 and 100)"
// )
```

[Validate on Decode](../how-to/validate-on-decode.md) shows more patterns, including rules that span several fields.

#### Check the Trailing Input Yourself

No public option makes `fromJson` reject trailing input. You can check it yourself by decoding from a reader and looking at what is left after the value. The helper below uses `WithRetractReader` and `JsonDecoder#unsafeDecode`:

```scala
import zio.json.internal.WithRetractReader
import scala.util.control.NonFatal

def fromJsonStrict[A](input: String)(implicit decoder: JsonDecoder[A]): Either[String, A] = {
  val in = new WithRetractReader(new java.io.StringReader(input))
  try {
    val value = decoder.unsafeDecode(Nil, in)
    val next  = Iterator.continually(in.read()).dropWhile(c => c == ' ' || c == '\t' || c == '\n' || c == '\r').next()
    if (next == -1) Right(value)
    else Left(s"(unexpected '${next.toChar}' after the value)")
  } catch {
    case NonFatal(_) | (_: StackOverflowError) => decoder.decodeJson(input)
  }
}
```

The helper works like this:

- `decoder.unsafeDecode(Nil, in)` decodes one value and leaves the reader just after it, exactly as `fromJson` does.
- `Iterator.continually(in.read())` reads the characters that follow, skipping the whitespace that JSON allows after a value. `in.read()` returns `-1` at the end of the input.
- Any other character means trailing input, which becomes a `Left`.
- If decoding itself fails, the `catch` runs the ordinary `JsonDecoder#decodeJson`, which reports the error in the usual format.

The earlier examples now fail, while input with only trailing whitespace still decodes:

```scala
fromJsonStrict[Int]("1e3")
// res34: Either[String, Int] = Left(
//   value = "(unexpected 'e' after the value)"
// )

fromJsonStrict[Boolean]("truex")
// res35: Either[String, Boolean] = Left(
//   value = "(unexpected 'x' after the value)"
// )

fromJsonStrict[Reading]("""{"value":1} {"value":2}""")
// res36: Either[String, Reading] = Left(
//   value = "(unexpected '{' after the value)"
// )

fromJsonStrict[Reading]("""{"value":1}  """)
// res37: Either[String, Reading] = Right(value = Reading(value = 1))

fromJsonStrict[Reading]("""{"value":"high"}""")
// res38: Either[String, Reading] = Left(value = ".value(expected an Int)")
```

:::caution
`WithRetractReader` and `JsonDecoder#unsafeDecode` belong to the low-level API. Everything in the `zio.json.internal` package can change in any release, as [Low-Level Codecs](../how-to/low-level-codecs.md) explains. Keep the helper in one place and cover it with a test.
:::

For a stricter check of the whole document, combine the approaches: call `fromJsonStrict[Json]` to validate the syntax and reject trailing input, then convert with `Json#as`.

### Upstream Status

The [JSONTestSuite](https://github.com/nst/JSONTestSuite) collects inputs that a strict parser must accept or reject. ZIO JSON accepts several of the inputs it marks as invalid, mostly for the reasons on this page: trailing input after a value, leading zeros, and number forms such as `2.e3`. GitHub issue [#55](https://github.com/zio/zio-json/issues/55) tracks these results upstream. Until it changes, treat the behaviour on this page as the current contract, and add the checks above where your application needs them.

### See Also

- [JsonDecoder](../reference/json-decoder.md) for the decoding API and its contract
- [Built-in Instances](../reference/built-in-instances.md#leniencies) for the leniencies of each standard type
- [Security](security.md) for how the decoder behaves under hostile input
- [JSON Shapes and Round Trips](wire-format.md) for what the encoder writes and which values survive a round trip

## How ZIO JSON Works

This page explains the ideas behind ZIO JSON. You do not need any of it to use the library. It helps when you wonder why the API looks the way it does, or why a decode failed the way it did.

### Decoding Reads Straight Into Your Types

Most JSON libraries parse the whole text into a tree of JSON nodes first, then convert the tree into your types. ZIO JSON skips the tree for normal decoding. A decoder reads characters from the input and builds your values as it goes.

The input is wrapped in a small reader. The reader hands out one character at a time and can step back by one character (`retract`). Stepping back matters for numbers: a number has no end marker, so the decoder only learns it has finished when it reads the next character. It then pushes that character back for the next step to see.

Several readers exist for different inputs:

- `FastStringReader` for a `String` or other `CharSequence`.
- `Utf8ChunkReader` for UTF-8 bytes in a `Chunk[Byte]`, read without first copying them into a `String`.
- `WithRetractReader` for any `java.io.Reader`, which is how streaming input is handled.

They live in `zio.json.internal`, and you normally reach them through `fromJson` and the decoding methods on `JsonDecoder`. `FastStringReader` and `Utf8ChunkReader` are private to the library. `RetractReader` is the public type that `unsafeDecode` receives, and `WithRetractReader` is public, so a hand-written decoder can be called directly on any `java.io.Reader`, for example in a test. See [Writing a Decoder by Hand](../reference/json-decoder.md#writing-a-decoder-by-hand).

The `Json` tree type does exist, and you can decode to it. See the [JSON AST reference](../reference/json-ast.md). It is a choice you make, not a step the library forces on you.

### No Reflection at Runtime

A `JsonEncoder` or `JsonDecoder` for a case class or sealed trait is plain code. That code is written for you at compile time, when you call `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` (or write `derives` on Scala 3). What the generated code does is controlled by [annotations](../reference/annotations.md) and by [`JsonCodecConfiguration`](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md), both read at compile time.

- On Scala 2, `DeriveJsonEncoder.gen`, `DeriveJsonDecoder.gen` and `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` are macros. The encoder and decoder derivation is built on the Magnolia library, which reads the shape of your type during compilation. The codec derivation is a macro that builds on the other two.
- On Scala 3, derivation uses native Scala 3 macros together with the compiler-provided `Mirror` of your type.

Neither route uses Shapeless. After compilation, the derived instance does not inspect classes, field names, or annotations by reflection. It reads the fields it was generated to read.

This has two visible effects:

1. A type that has no codec and cannot be derived is a compile error. Duplicate field names, aliases or case names are the exception: they compile, and are reported with an `AssertionError` when the codec is first initialised.
2. Derivation is done once when your code is compiled, not on every call.

### Nested Types and Subtypes

A derived codec needs a codec for every type it contains. When one is missing, derivation can often fill the gap itself:

- The subtypes of a sealed trait that have no codec of their own are derived together with the trait, on Scala 2 and Scala 3. You derive the codec of the trait, and its case classes and case objects come with it.
- On Scala 3, a case class field whose type has no codec is derived too, if it can be. On Scala 2, every field type needs a codec in implicit scope, and a missing one fails to compile with `magnolia: could not find zio.json.DeriveJsonEncoder.Typeclass[...]`.

A type derived this way is derived again at each place it is used, inside the outer codec, with the configuration in scope at the outer derivation call. Two outer codecs with different configurations can therefore write the same nested type differently. An instance that already exists in implicit scope is never re-derived: it is used as it is, with the configuration it was built with. Give a nested type its own codec when it must look the same everywhere, or when you also encode or decode it on its own. [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#passing-a-custom-configuration) shows both cases.

### Failing Early

A decoder reports a problem by throwing a small exception that has no stack trace. Building a stack trace is slow, and a flood of bad requests would make a server pay that cost again and again. The exception carries a short list of path steps instead, such as `.address.city`, followed by a message.

`fromJson` and `decodeJson` catch that exception at the top and turn it into a `Left` with the rendered path. That is why every error looks like `.address.city(...)` and why `fromJson` returns a `Left` instead of throwing. The JVM streaming methods are the exception: they fail the effect with a `java.lang.Exception` whose message is the same rendered path. [Errors](../reference/errors.md) describes the format.

Decoding stops at the first problem. It does not collect a list of errors, and it does not read the rest of the payload. This is the *early exit* strategy: a malformed or hostile payload is rejected as soon as it is known to be bad.

### Performance and Security Goals

Reading directly into your types allocates less and does less work than building a tree first. Early exit keeps a bad payload from costing more than the part that was read. The two ideas support each other.

Measurements and attack scenarios are covered in their own pages:

- [Performance](./performance.md) has the benchmarks.
- [Security](./security.md) walks through denial-of-service attacks and how the library resists them.

### Helpful Errors and Simple Patterns

The error path follows the `jq` query style, so you can paste a path into a JSON tool to find the spot. The design relies on the well-known typeclass pattern, where `JsonEncoder[A]` and `JsonDecoder[A]` are values you pass implicitly. To define your own, see [Build an Encoder or Decoder from an Existing One](../how-to/manual-instances.md).

## Performance(Explanation)

ZIO JSON decodes JSON text straight into your data types and encodes them straight to text, without building an intermediate syntax tree. This page describes the benchmark suite that measures it, how to read the published numbers, and what you can do in your own code to encode and decode faster.

### The Benchmark Suite

The benchmarks are [JMH](https://github.com/openjdk/jmh) benchmarks in [`zio-json/jvm/src/jmh`](https://github.com/zio/zio-json/tree/series/2.x/zio-json/jvm/src/jmh/scala/zio/json). The main ones compare ZIO JSON with [Circe](https://circe.github.io/circe/) and [jsoniter-scala](https://github.com/plokhotnyuk/jsoniter-scala) on four standard datasets:

| Benchmark class           | Dataset                  | What it stresses                              |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `GoogleMapsAPIBenchmarks` | Google Maps API response | Arrays and number parsing                     |
| `TwitterAPIBenchmarks`    | Twitter API response     | Nested case classes with many fields          |
| `GeoJSONBenchmarks`       | GeoJSON document         | Nested sealed traits that use a discriminator |
| `SyntheticBenchmarks`     | Generated recursive data | Nested recursive types                        |

Each class has `decode…` and `encode…` methods per library. `GoogleMapsAPIBenchmarks` also has `…Attack…` methods that decode the malicious payloads described on the [Security](security.md) page. Other classes measure single features: collections, decoding from bytes (`ChunkDecoderBenchmarks`), nesting depth, `UUID` parsing, `orElse` decoders and the number parser.

The suite runs on the JVM with `NeoJmhPlugin`, a rewrite of [sbt-jmh](https://github.com/sbt/sbt-jmh) defined in the build (`project/NeoJmhPlugin.scala`) that adds a `Jmh` configuration to the `zioJsonJVM` project. To run it on your own hardware, with the GC profiler that reports memory use:

```bash
sbt "zioJsonJVM/Jmh/run -prof gc"
```

To run only some benchmarks, add a regular expression that matches their names, for example `sbt "zioJsonJVM/Jmh/run -prof gc GoogleMaps.*"`.

There are two main factors to consider when comparing the performance of JSON libraries: memory usage and operations per second. The benchmarks run one thread at a time, but in a real server situation there are multiple threads, each consuming resources. JMH reports throughput as `ops/sec` (higher is better). The GC profiler reports the allocation rate as `MB/sec` (lower is better). A better metric for memory usage might be `MB` per decode or encode, since it can be misleading to have the same `MB/sec` but be processing more JSON: the library that allocates the least memory is likely to have the highest throughput.

### Historical Results

The tables below were published with the first version of ZIO JSON in July 2020. They compare ZIO JSON with Circe and Play JSON, measured on the hardware and library versions of that time.

:::note
These numbers cannot be reproduced with the current suite. The Play JSON benchmarks were removed in January 2025 ([#1220](https://github.com/zio/zio-json/pull/1220)), when jsoniter-scala encoding benchmarks were added, and all three libraries have changed a lot since 2020. Run the suite yourself to get numbers for your hardware and versions.
:::

<!-- zioJsonJVM/Jmh/run -prof gc GoogleMaps.*Success1 -->
<!-- zioJsonJVM/Jmh/run -prof gc GoogleMaps.*encode* -->

On the Google Maps API dataset:

```
       Decoding                    | Encoding
       ops/sec       MB/sec        | ops/sec      MB/sec
zio    15761 ± 283   1633 ± 29     | 14289 ±  84  2214 ± 12
circe   8832 ± 269   1816 ± 55     | 11980 ± 142  2030 ± 24
play    5756 ±  47   2260 ± 19     |  6669 ± 160  2677 ± 64
```

On the Twitter API dataset:

```
       ops/sec       MB/sec        | ops/sec      MB/sec
```

On the synthetic dataset:

```
       Decoding                    | Encoding
       ops/sec       MB/sec        | ops/sec       MB/sec
zio    59099 ± 1307  2108 ± 46     | 32048 ±  240  2573 ± 19
```
