
In these 2020 results, ZIO JSON has the highest ops/sec in every table: from about 1.1x to 3x the ops/sec of Circe, and from about 1.5x to 24x the ops/sec of Play JSON. On MB/sec it allocates the least memory when decoding, but it trails Circe in all four encoding columns, where Circe allocates less memory per second.

### Encoding Faster

Most encoders never need tuning, but a few details of how encoding works matter when you write encoders by hand or encode large volumes.

#### Reusable Buffers Behind `toJson`

`toJson` and `toJsonPretty` call `JsonEncoder#encodeJson`. It writes into a character buffer taken from a per-thread pool and returns the buffer's contents as a `String`, so repeated encoding on the same thread reuses the buffer instead of allocating a new one each time. The pool is held through a weak reference, so the garbage collector can reclaim it when memory is short.

Inside a hand-written encoder, write to the `Write` that `JsonEncoder#unsafeEncode` receives, or delegate to another encoder's `JsonEncoder#unsafeEncode`. Calling `toJson` inside `JsonEncoder#unsafeEncode` encodes into a second buffer and creates an intermediate `String` that is then copied into the first. [Writing an Encoder by Hand](../reference/json-encoder.md#writing-an-encoder-by-hand) shows the pattern.

#### Compact Versus Pretty Output

`toJsonPretty` writes a newline and indentation before every field and array element, and a space on each side of the `:`. The output is much larger than the compact form: for a list of small objects, it is roughly twice as many characters, and the encoder spends correspondingly longer writing them. Use `toJson` for data that machines read, and keep `toJsonPretty` for logs and files that people read.

#### Converting to the AST Directly

`JsonEncoder#toJsonAST` converts a value to the `Json` AST. The default implementation encodes the value to text and then parses that text back into a `Json`. The built-in encoders, the derived encoders and encoders built with `JsonEncoder#contramap` override it to build the `Json` directly. A hand-written encoder that implements only `JsonEncoder#unsafeEncode` uses the slow default, and so does every derived encoder that contains it as a field, whenever `JsonEncoder#toJsonAST` runs. Either build the encoder from an existing one with `JsonEncoder#contramap`, or override `JsonEncoder#toJsonAST` as shown in [Overriding `toJsonAST`](../reference/json-encoder.md#overriding-tojsonast).

#### Writing Straight to a `java.io.Writer`

`toJson` always builds the whole document as a `String`. When the output goes to a `java.io.Writer`, such as a file or a servlet response, `zio.json.internal.WriteWriter` adapts the writer to the `Write` interface, so `JsonEncoder#unsafeEncode` can write into it directly. The JVM streaming encoders use it internally:

```scala
import java.io.StringWriter

import zio.json._
import zio.json.internal.WriteWriter

final case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

object Point {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Point] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Point]
}

val writer = new StringWriter()

JsonEncoder[Point].unsafeEncode(Point(1, 2), None, new WriteWriter(writer))
```

The `StringWriter` now holds the encoded JSON:

```scala
writer.toString
// res2: String = "{\"x\":1,\"y\":2}"
```

`WriteWriter` passes a `String` to the underlying writer in one call, but every other character in a separate call, so wrap an unbuffered writer in a `java.io.BufferedWriter`. Everything in `zio.json.internal` is a low-level API without a compatibility guarantee. For ZIO streams, prefer the streaming encoders described in [Streaming API](../reference/streaming.md).

### Decoding Faster

The decoder reads input once, from left to right, and builds your data types as it goes. These choices keep that path short.

#### Decoding From Bytes

An HTTP body or a file usually arrives as bytes. Converting the bytes to a `String` first (`new String(bytes, UTF_8)`) copies the whole payload. `JsonDecoder#decodeJson` has overloads for `Chunk[Byte]` and `Array[Byte]` that decode UTF-8 while parsing, without that copy, and `fromJson` works on both types:

```scala
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8

import zio.Chunk

val bytes: Chunk[Byte] = Chunk.fromArray("""{"x":1,"y":2}""".getBytes(UTF_8))
// bytes: Chunk[Byte] = IndexedSeq(
//   123,
//   34,
//   120,
//   34,
//   58,
//   49,
//   44,
//   34,
//   121,
//   34,
//   58,
//   50,
//   125
// )

bytes.fromJson[Point]
// res3: Either[String, Point] = Right(value = Point(x = 1, y = 2))
```

`ChunkDecoderBenchmarks` measures this path against decoding a `String` and against copying the bytes into a `String` first. See [`decodeJson`](../reference/json-decoder.md#decodejson) for the full list of overloads.

#### Decoding Into Your Own Types

Decoding straight into a case class is the fastest path. The derived decoder matches field names without building a map, and skips fields it does not know without building values for them. Decoding into `Json` builds a tree of every value in the document, and decoding into `Map[String, V]` builds a hash map of every key, so use them only when the shape of the data is not known in advance.

When you do decode into `Json` first and convert it with `Json#as` or `JsonDecoder#fromJsonAST`, the conversion is direct only for decoders that override `unsafeFromJsonAST`: the primitive types, `Option`, `Chunk`, `java.time` types and derived case classes and sealed traits. Other decoders, such as those for `List`, `Vector`, `Set` and `Map`, and hand-written decoders, encode the `Json` back to text and parse that text. [Decoding from the AST](../reference/json-decoder.md#decoding-from-the-ast) explains how to override it.

#### Large Payloads

`Chunk[Byte]`, `Array[Byte]` and `String` inputs all hold the whole payload in memory. On the JVM, the streaming decoders (`JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStreamInput` for bytes and `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStream` for characters) read the input incrementally instead, and the pipelines decode a stream of many values. See [Streaming API](../reference/streaming.md).

### Even More Performance

If ZIO JSON isn't fast enough for you, try [jsoniter-scala](https://github.com/plokhotnyuk/jsoniter-scala). ZIO JSON is fully integrated into ZIO, including streams and pipelines, while jsoniter-scala is library agnostic.

JSON is an inefficient transport format, and everybody would benefit from a port of this library to msgpack or protobuf. For legacy services, a port supporting XML is also possible.

---

## Scala 2 and Scala 3 Differences

ZIO JSON has the same API on Scala 2 and Scala 3, and most code compiles on both without changes. The JSON it produces is not always the same, though. This page explains where the differences come from, lists each of them with the output of the same code on Scala 2.13.18 and Scala 3.9.0, and ends with a checklist for moving a project from Scala 2 to Scala 3.

### Why the Two Versions Differ

Codecs for your case classes and sealed traits are written at compile time by macros (code that runs inside the compiler and generates code). Scala 2 and Scala 3 have different macro systems, so ZIO JSON has two separate implementations of derivation:

- On Scala 2, `DeriveJsonEncoder.gen` and `DeriveJsonDecoder.gen` are built on [Magnolia](https://github.com/softwaremill/magnolia), a library that describes the shape of a type to the code that builds the instance. `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` is a small macro that calls the other two.
- On Scala 3, derivation uses native Scala 3 macros together with the `Mirror` that the compiler provides for case classes, sealed traits and enums. Magnolia is not used.

Both implementations read the same annotations and the same `JsonCodecConfiguration` options. Where they disagree, it is because each one decides a few details on its own: what counts as an enumeration value, what to do when a field type has no instance, or what an empty case class looks like inside another one. The defaults of `JsonCodecConfiguration` also live in two separate source files, one per version, and one default differs.

The rest of the library, the parser, the built-in instances for standard types and the `Json` tree, is shared code. Apart from a few instances for types that only exist on one version, it behaves the same on both. [How ZIO JSON works](how-it-works.md) describes derivation in general.

### The Differences at a Glance

The Scala 2 column is for Scala 2.13 (most rows also apply to 2.12):

| Behaviour                                                                | Scala 2                                                   | Scala 3                                                                                            |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Field type without a codec                                               | Compile error                                             | Derived with the outer configuration                                                               |
| Default of `enumValuesAsStrings`                                         | `false`: case objects are written as `{"Red":{}}`         | `true`: case objects are written as `"Red"`                                                        |
| Case class with no fields in a family of case objects                    | Counts as an enum value, written as `"Stop"`              | Does not count, the whole family is written as objects                                             |
| Case object with a hand-written codec, family as strings                 | String form is turned off, the hand-written codec is used | String form is used; the encoder ignores the hand-written codec, and the decoder passes `{}` to it |
| Empty case class field with `ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false)` | Field is left out of the JSON                             | Field is written as `{}`                                                                           |
| Recursive type with a plain `implicit val` or `implicit def`             | Fails at runtime, needs `lazy val`                        | Works, with `derives` or a plain `given`                                                           |
| Generic sealed trait with a case class extending `T[Nothing]`            | Works                                                     | Compiler crash, give the case class the type parameter                                             |
| Compile error for a missing instance                                     | `magnolia: could not find ... Typeclass[...]`             | `Cannot find or derive JsonEncoder for ...`                                                        |
| Sum type read from a `Json.Obj` with several keys                        | `expected single field object`                            | `expected object with a single field`                                                              |
| How a configuration is passed                                            | `implicit val`                                            | `given`, also picked up by `derives`                                                               |
| `derives JsonCodec`, Scala 3 `enum`, opaque types                        | Not available                                             | Available                                                                                          |
| String-literal union types, `IArray`, `T <: String` map keys             | Not available                                             | Built-in instances                                                                                 |
| `@jsonDerive` from `zio-json-macros`                                     | Available                                                 | Not published                                                                                      |

These behaviours are the same on both versions: the subtypes of a sealed trait are derived together with the trait, a nested sealed trait is flattened to its leaf cases, default values of fields are used when a field is missing (Scala 3 does not need the `-Yretain-trees` option for this), and every alias in `@jsonAliases` is accepted.

The sections below show each difference with code. Scala 2 code is compiled and run when this page is built. Scala 3 code is shown from example files, followed by the output of running them on Scala 3.9.0.

### Field Types Without a Codec

A derived codec needs an instance for the type of every field. On Scala 2, Magnolia looks the instance up in implicit scope and stops with a compile error when there is none. Here `Address` has no codec:

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Address(street: String)
final case class Person(name: String, address: Address)

object Person {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
}
// error: magnolia: could not find zio.json.DeriveJsonEncoder.Typeclass[repl.MdocSession.MdocApp0.Address]
//     in parameter 'address' of product type repl.MdocSession.MdocApp0.Person
// 
//   implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
//                                                              ^
```

On Scala 3, derivation looks for an instance first, and when it finds none, it derives one for the field type on the spot, with the configuration in scope at the outer type:

```scala
final case class Address(street: String)
final case class Person(name: String, address: Address) derives JsonCodec
```

Running it on Scala 3 prints:

```text
nested: {"name":"Ada","address":{"street":"Main St"}}
```

Scala 3 accepts every such codec that Scala 2 accepts, but not the other way round. When the nested type must look the same everywhere, or is also encoded on its own, give it its own codec on both versions. [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#passing-a-custom-configuration) shows how a nested type picks up the outer configuration.

### Case Objects as Strings

The `enumValuesAsStrings` option decides whether a family of case objects is written as plain strings. Its default is `false` on Scala 2 and `true` on Scala 3, so the same family is written in two ways. On Scala 2:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.Json

sealed trait Color
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color

object Color {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Color] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Color]
}
```

On Scala 2, a case object is written as an object with one key:

```scala
println((Red: Color).toJson)
// {"Red":{}}
```

The same family on Scala 3:

```scala
sealed trait Color derives JsonCodec
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color
```

Scala 3 writes the plain string:

```text
case objects: "Red"
```

This is the difference most likely to break a running system after a migration: a Scala 3 service sends `"Red"` to a Scala 2 client that expects `{"Red":{}}`, and each side rejects the other's JSON. Set the option explicitly in a shared configuration to get the same JSON on both versions. [Sealed traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md#5-write-case-objects-as-strings) covers the string form in full.

### What Counts as an Enumeration Value

Even with `enumValuesAsStrings = true` on both sides, the two versions disagree on which families qualify. Scala 2 accepts a case class with an empty parameter list as an enumeration value, like a case object. Scala 3 accepts only case objects and parameterless `enum` cases. A family with `Stop()` is written as strings on Scala 2:

```scala
object strings {
  implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

  sealed trait Signal
  case object Go          extends Signal
  final case class Stop() extends Signal

  object Signal {
    implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Signal] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Signal]
  }
}
```

Both cases become strings on Scala 2:

```scala
println((strings.Go: strings.Signal).toJson)
// "Go"
println((strings.Stop(): strings.Signal).toJson)
// "Stop"
```

On Scala 3, the empty case class makes the whole family use objects, the case object included:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

sealed trait Signal derives JsonCodec
case object Go          extends Signal
final case class Stop() extends Signal
```

Running it on Scala 3 prints:

```text
Go: {"Go":{}}
Stop(): {"Stop":{}}
```

The two versions also disagree when one case object has a codec of its own. Scala 2 then turns the string form off for the whole family and wraps the hand-written JSON in the usual object. Scala 3 keeps the string form: the encoder ignores the hand-written codec, and the decoder passes `{}` to it, so a hand-written decoder that expects anything else fails. On Scala 2:

```scala
object handwritten {
  implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

  sealed trait Light
  case object Amber extends Light
  case object Blue  extends Light

  implicit val amberCodec: JsonCodec[Amber.type] = JsonCodec.string.transform(_ => Amber, _ => "AMBER")

  object Light {
    implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Light] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Light]
  }
}
```

The hand-written JSON of `Amber` appears inside the wrapper, and `Blue` is an object too:

```scala
println((handwritten.Amber: handwritten.Light).toJson)
// {"Amber":"AMBER"}
println((handwritten.Blue: handwritten.Light).toJson)
// {"Blue":{}}
```

The same code on Scala 3:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

sealed trait Light
case object Amber extends Light
case object Blue  extends Light

given JsonCodec[Amber.type] = JsonCodec.string.transform(_ => Amber, _ => "AMBER")

object Light {
  given JsonCodec[Light] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}
```

Running it on Scala 3 prints the encoded cases, then the result of decoding `"Amber"`. The decoder passes `{}` to the string codec of `Amber`, which rejects it:

```text
Amber: "Amber"
Blue: "Blue"
Amber decoded: Left((expected string))
```

To get the same JSON on both versions, use only case objects in a family that should be written as strings, and change a string with `@jsonHint` rather than with a hand-written codec.

### Empty Case Classes as Fields

With `ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false)`, the encoder leaves out fields whose value is empty, such as an empty `List`. On Scala 2, the encoder of a case class with no fields also reports its value as empty, so a field of that type disappears too. With the default `decoding = true`, the decoder then rejects the JSON that the encoder wrote:

```scala
object emptyfield {
  implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
    JsonCodecConfiguration(explicitEmptyCollections = ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false))

  final case class Marker()

  object Marker {
    implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Marker] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Marker]
  }

  final case class Holder(name: String, marker: Marker)

  object Holder {
    implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Holder] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Holder]
  }
}
```

The `marker` field is missing from the JSON, so decoding it fails:

```scala
println(emptyfield.Holder("a", emptyfield.Marker()).toJson)
// {"name":"a"}
emptyfield.Holder("a", emptyfield.Marker()).toJson.fromJson[emptyfield.Holder]
// res12: Either[String, emptyfield.Holder] = Left(value = ".marker(missing)")
```

On Scala 3 the field is written as `{}`, and the round trip works:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(explicitEmptyCollections = ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false))

final case class Marker() derives JsonCodec
final case class Holder(name: String, marker: Marker) derives JsonCodec
```

Running it on Scala 3 prints:

```text
empty field: {"name":"a","marker":{}}
empty field round trip: Right(Holder(a,Marker()))
```

[JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#explicitemptycollections) describes the option.

### Recursive Types

A recursive type, such as a node whose children are nodes, refers to its own codec while that codec is being built. On Scala 2 the derived instance reads the instance of each field when it is created. With `implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Node] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Node]`, that instance is still `null` at that moment, and the first use fails with a `NullPointerException` inside an `ExceptionInInitializerError`. Declare the codec as an `implicit lazy val`:

```scala
final case class Node(name: String, children: List[Node])

object Node {
  implicit lazy val codec: JsonCodec[Node] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Node]
}
```

Encoding a tree with one child:

```scala
println(Node("root", List(Node("leaf", Nil))).toJson)
// {"name":"root","children":[{"name":"leaf","children":[]}]}
```

A generic recursive type with an `implicit def` fails with a `StackOverflowError` instead, and needs a local `implicit lazy val`, as shown in [Derive codecs for generic types](../how-to/generic-types.md#4-derive-a-recursive-generic-type).

The Scala 3 derivation reads field instances lazily, so `derives` works for recursive types without any extra code:

```scala
final case class Node(name: String, children: List[Node]) derives JsonCodec
```

Running it on Scala 3 prints:

```text
recursive: {"name":"root","children":[{"name":"leaf","children":[]}]}
```

A `lazy val` is also correct on Scala 3, so keep it in code that cross-builds.

### Generic Sealed Traits

A generic sealed trait such as `sealed trait Result[+A]` often has cases that do not use the type parameter, for example `final case class Failed(reason: String) extends Result[Nothing]`. Scala 2 derives such a family. On Scala 3.9.0 the same family makes the compiler crash with `java.lang.AssertionError: assertion failed: TypeRef(..., class Failed)`, because the derivation applies the type arguments of `Result` to `Failed`, which has none. Case objects are not affected. The workaround is to give the case class the type parameter: `final case class Failed[A](reason: String) extends Result[A]`. [Derive codecs for generic types](../how-to/generic-types.md#3-derive-a-generic-sealed-trait) shows both versions.

### Error Messages

When derivation cannot find or build an instance, the compile errors differ. Scala 2 reports the Magnolia type class, the field and the outer type, as in the first example on this page. Outside mdoc, with the types in an object `Err`, the message reads:

```text
magnolia: could not find zio.json.DeriveJsonEncoder.Typeclass[Err.Address]
    in parameter 'address' of product type Err.Person
```

Scala 3 reports only the field type, followed by an inline stack trace that points at the `derives` clause or the `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` call. For a case class with a `java.io.File` field:

```text
Cannot find or derive JsonDecoder for java.io.File
```

Runtime messages are almost all shared, because the decoders for standard types are shared code. One message from derived sum types differs: reading a sealed trait from a `Json.Obj` that has more than one key. On Scala 2:

```scala
sealed trait Fruit
final case class Banana(curvature: Double) extends Fruit
final case class Apple(poison: Boolean)    extends Fruit

object Fruit {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Fruit] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Fruit]
}
```

Decoding an object that has both keys fails on Scala 2 with:

```scala
Json.Obj("Banana" -> Json.Obj(), "Apple" -> Json.Obj()).as[Fruit]
// res16: Either[String, Fruit] = Left(
//   value = "(expected single field object)"
// )
```

On Scala 3 the same call returns `Left((expected object with a single field))`. Tests that compare error strings must allow for both. [Errors](../reference/errors.md) lists the messages.

### Features of Only One Version

Some features exist on one version only, because the language feature they build on exists on one version only.

Scala 3 adds:

- The `derives JsonCodec`, `derives JsonEncoder` and `derives JsonDecoder` clauses, and the `given` form of the configuration that they pick up. See [Derive codecs on Scala 3](../how-to/scala-3-derivation.md).
- Derivation for Scala 3 `enum` types. A parameterless enum is written as strings, an enum with parameters as objects.
- An encoder and a decoder for unions of string literals, such as `"EUR" | "USD"`, which also work as `Map` keys. See [JsonEncoder](../reference/json-encoder.md#scala-2-vs-scala-3).
- Key decoding for any subtype of `String` that has a `JsonDecoder`, such as an opaque type declared `<: String`. See [Use your own type as a Map key](../how-to/custom-map-keys.md#scala-3-string-subtypes-need-no-key-decoder).
- An instance for `IArray`. Both Scala 2.13 and Scala 3 have one for `immutable.ArraySeq`; Scala 2.12 has neither.

Opaque types are Scala 3 only, but ZIO JSON has no automatic support for them. Each one needs a hand-written codec, usually `JsonCodec.string.transform(...)` on the underlying type.

Scala 2 has `@jsonDerive` from the `zio-json-macros` module, which generates the companion codec for you. Scala 3 has no macro annotations, so the module is not published for Scala 3. A `derives` clause replaces it. See [@jsonDerive Macro Annotation](../reference/zio-json-macros.md#scala-3-alternative).

### Migrating From Scala 2 to Scala 3

Most of a migration is mechanical: the code compiles, and derived codecs keep working. The risk is JSON that changes without a compile error. Work through these steps:

1. Write [golden tests](../how-to/golden-testing.md) for every type that crosses a process boundary (HTTP payloads, messages, stored documents) while the project is still on Scala 2. They record the current JSON, so any change on Scala 3 fails a test instead of reaching production.
2. Decide on `enumValuesAsStrings`. To keep the Scala 2 JSON, put `JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = false)` in scope for every derivation. To switch to strings, change both sides of every integration at the same time.
3. Search for case classes with an empty parameter list, `final case class Stop()`, in sealed families written as strings. Replace them with case objects, or accept that Scala 3 writes the family as objects.
4. Search for hand-written codecs of case objects that belong to a derived family. When the family is written as strings, the Scala 3 encoder ignores them and the decoder passes `{}` to them. Use `@jsonHint` to change the string instead.
5. If you use `ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false)`, check fields whose type is a case class with no fields: Scala 3 starts writing them as `{}`.
6. Replace `@jsonDerive` with a `derives` clause, or with an explicit companion codec if the code must still compile on Scala 2.
7. Move each `implicit val` configuration next to the types it should affect. A `given` at the top level of a file applies to every `derives` clause in the whole package.
8. For generic sealed traits, give every case class the type parameter of the trait, so that the Scala 3 compiler does not crash.
9. Update tests that compare error strings, and drop `-Yretain-trees` from `scalacOptions` if it was only there for default values.

Scala 3 derives the instances of nested field types for you, so you can drop codecs that existed only to satisfy Scala 2. Keep a codec when the nested type is also encoded on its own, or when it must use a different configuration than the outer type.

### See Also

- [Derive codecs on Scala 3](../how-to/scala-3-derivation.md) shows `derives`, enums, union types and opaque types step by step.
- [Derive codecs for generic types](../how-to/generic-types.md) covers type parameters and recursive types on both versions.
- [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#scala-2-and-scala-3-differences) has a short version of the configuration-related differences.
- [Golden testing](../how-to/golden-testing.md) explains how to pin the JSON before you migrate.

---

## Security

A [Denial of Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denial-of-service_attack) (DoS) attack is a cyber-attack in which the perpetrator seeks to make a machine or network resource unavailable to its intended users by temporarily or indefinitely disrupting services. Any public-facing server that decodes JSON from its clients is a potential target.

Attacks that are in the form of a valid payload are designed to be stealthy and produce the same end result as a legitimate payload, but consume more resources along the way. This page goes through specific attacks, how ZIO JSON behaves under each one, and what you can do about it. The last section, [Mitigations](#mitigations), sums up the defences.

:::note
The benchmark tables on this page come from the first version of ZIO JSON, published in July 2020. They compare ZIO JSON with Circe and Play JSON on the hardware and library versions of that time. The Play JSON benchmarks have since been removed from the suite, so the tables cannot be reproduced as they are. The `…Attack…` benchmarks in `GoogleMapsAPIBenchmarks` still exist for ZIO JSON, Circe and jsoniter-scala; see [Performance](performance.md#the-benchmark-suite) for how to run them.
:::

### Resource Attack: Larger Payload

An obvious way to slow down a server is to give it more data to read. JSON is particularly susceptible to this kind of attack because it has a built-in mechanism to expand the size of the message without altering the contents: pad with whitespace. ZIO JSON skips whitespace without any limit. In our test, 20 million spaces followed by `1` decode as the `Int` `1`.

Many web frameworks fully consume the payload into a `String` before handing it to the JSON library, so a JSON message consisting of 1 GB of whitespace takes 1 GB of heap on that server, plus a copy if the body was read as bytes first.

The best way to mitigate message size attacks is to cap the request size (the `Content-Length`) at a reasonable value for the use case, in the HTTP server or proxy. Two further mitigations come from ZIO JSON itself:

- Decode the body from bytes. `JsonDecoder#decodeJson` and `fromJson` accept a `Chunk[Byte]` or an `Array[Byte]` and decode the UTF-8 while parsing, so the payload is not copied into a `String` first. See [`decodeJson`](../reference/json-decoder.md#decodejson).
- On the JVM, decode from a stream with `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStreamInput`, which reads the input incrementally instead of loading the whole message into memory. See [Streaming API](../reference/streaming.md).

<!-- zioJsonJVM/Jmh/run -prof gc GoogleMaps.*Attack0 -->

For all the remaining attacks, we cap the malicious message size to 100 KB (the original message is 25 KB) and compare the attacks against this baseline. The benchmark results for the original (unedited) payload are given in parentheses. The ops/sec drop for all libraries, along with the memory usage:

```
       ops/sec        MB/sec
zio    10104 (14823)  1047 (1537)
circe   7456 ( 8832)  1533 (1816)
play    3589 ( 5756)  1344 (2260)
```

### Redundant Data

Most JSON libraries (but not ZIO JSON) first create a representation of the JSON message in an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) that represents all the objects, arrays and values in a generic way. Their decoders typically read what they need from the AST.

<!-- zioJsonJVM/Jmh/run -prof gc GoogleMaps.*Attack1 -->

An intermediate AST enables attack vectors that insert redundant data. For example, in our Google Maps dataset we can add a new field called `redundant` at the top level, containing a 60K `String`. With this payload, Circe is heavily impacted, with a 70% reduction in capacity and an increase in memory usage. Play is also impacted, although not as severely. ZIO JSON's ops/sec are reduced, but its memory usage stays in line, so throughput is unlikely to be affected by this kind of attack:

```
       ops/sec       MB/sec
zio    5999 (10104)   622 (1047)
circe  2224 ( 7456)  1655 (1533)
play   2350 ( 3589)  1854 (1344)
```

ZIO JSON is not as badly affected because a derived decoder skips the values of fields it does not know. Skipping does not build anything, and it is not recursive, so even an unknown field nested 100,000 levels deep is skipped without trouble. Skipping also does not validate the skipped value fully, so some malformed values inside unknown fields are accepted. We define a small type to show it:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.Json

final case class Name(name: String)

object Name {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Name] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Name]
}
```

The value `tzzz` is not valid JSON, but it sits in an unknown field, so decoding succeeds:

```scala
"""{"name":"Ada","x":tzzz}""".fromJson[Name]
// res1: Either[String, Name] = Right(value = Name(name = "Ada"))
```

We can completely mitigate this kind of attack with the `@jsonNoExtraFields` annotation, or with `allowExtraFields = false` in a [`JsonCodecConfiguration`](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#allowextrafields). The decoder then rejects the payload at the first unknown field, at a rate of 5.5 million ops/sec in the 2020 benchmarks:

```scala
@jsonNoExtraFields
final case class StrictName(name: String)

object StrictName {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[StrictName] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[StrictName]
}

"""{"name":"Ada","x":1}""".fromJson[StrictName]
// res2: Either[String, StrictName] = Left(value = "(invalid extra field)")
```

Other kinds of redundant values attacks are also possible, such as an array of 60K full of high-precision decimal numbers that require slow parsing (also known as ["near halfway numbers"](https://www.exploringbinary.com/17-digits-gets-you-there-once-youve-found-your-way/)), attacking the CPU. However, the memory attack afforded by a redundant `String` is already quite effective.

### `hashCode` Collisions

Following on from the redundant data attack, we can place redundant data in the location of object fields.

JSON libraries that use an intermediate AST often store JSON objects as a `HashMap` keyed by string (Circe uses a [`java.util.LinkedHashMap`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/14/docs/api/java.base/java/util/LinkedHashMap.html)). If we insert redundant fields that have hash code collisions with legitimate fields, we can successfully attack both memory and CPU. We need to know the hashing algorithm that is being used, which often comes down to some version of the default Java `String.hashCode`, [which is very easy to exploit](https://github.com/plokhotnyuk/jsoniter-scala/blob/master/jsoniter-scala-benchmark/shared/src/main/scala/com/github/plokhotnyuk/jsoniter_scala/benchmark/HashCodeCollider.scala).

In this malicious payload, we add redundant fields that have hash code collisions, up to 4 collisions per field; we could add more with a brute-force search.

<!-- zioJsonJVM/Jmh/run -prof gc GoogleMaps.*Attack2 -->

ZIO JSON completely mitigates this attack if the `@jsonNoExtraFields` annotation is used. Even if Circe and Play rejected payloads of this nature, it would be too late, because the attack happens at the AST layer, not in the decoders. For the sake of comparison, here are the results with the ZIO JSON mitigation turned off:

```
       ops/sec       MB/sec
zio    3742 (10104)   695 (1047)
circe  1992 ( 7456)  1162 (1533)
play   1312 ( 3589)  1636 (1344)
```

ops/sec is down for all decoders relative to the baseline, but since ZIO JSON and Circe memory usage is also reduced, the throughput on a server might not be impacted as badly as it sounds. This attack hurts Play very badly: memory usage is up compared to the baseline, with throughput reduced to about 37% of the baseline (23% of the original).

There is a variant of this attack that can be devastating for libraries that rely on `HashMap`. In this attack, [developed by plokhotnyuk to DoS ujson](https://github.com/plokhotnyuk/jsoniter-scala/pull/325), an object is filled with many fields whose `String#hashCode` is zero. This exploits two facts:

- Before JDK 13, Java `String` did not cache a `String#hashCode` of zero, so it recomputed the hash every time it was requested.
- Many `HashMap` implementations re-request the hashes of all objects as the number of entries grows during construction.

#### Decoding Into a `Map`

Derived case class decoders match field names without hashing, and the `Json` AST keeps an object's fields in a `Chunk`, so neither builds a hash map from the payload's keys. Decoding into `Map[String, V]` (or `HashMap`, `mutable.Map` and the other map types) does build a hash map from attacker-chosen keys, so it is open to the same collision attack.

In our test, a 540 KB object with 16,384 keys that all share one `String.hashCode` took about 3 seconds to decode as a `Map[String, Int]`. The same object decoded as `Json` in about 5 ms, and an object of the same size with ordinary keys decoded as a `Map[String, Int]` in about 15 ms.

When the keys of an object come from untrusted input, decode it into a case class if the keys are known in advance. Otherwise decode it into `Json` or with `JsonDecoder.keyValueChunk`, which keeps the key-value pairs in a `Chunk` without hashing (duplicate keys stay as separate entries):

```scala
"""{"a":1,"b":2,"a":3}""".fromJson(JsonDecoder.keyValueChunk[String, Int])
// res3: Either[String, zio.Chunk[(String, Int)]] = Right(
//   value = IndexedSeq(("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("a", 3))
// )
```

### Death by a Thousand Zeros

Another kind of attack is to provide data that makes the decoder for a specific value do more work than it needs to. Numbers are always a great example of this.

The most brutal attack of this nature is to trick a deserialization library into constructing a gigantic number as a `BigDecimal` and then to convert it to a `BigInteger`. The JVM will happily attempt to reserve gigabytes of heap for the conversion. This expression, which is not run here, does exactly that:

```scala
new java.math.BigDecimal("1e214748364").toBigInteger
```

Fortunately, this kind of attack is prevented by all the mainstream libraries. But it is possible to perform a much weaker form of the attack on Circe, which (to its credit) goes to great effort to pre-validate numbers.

The Google Maps schema has fields of type `Int`, and Circe supports the conversion of floating point numbers to integers if the fractional part is zero, so we can pad an integer with as many zeros as possible:

```
       ops/sec       MB/sec
circe  4529 ( 7456)  2037 (1533)
```

This attack is very effective in schemas with lots of numbers, causing a 39% drop in ops/sec with a 33% increase in memory usage.

ZIO JSON is resistant to a wide range of number-based attacks because it uses a from-scratch number parser that exits early. `Int` and `Long` fail as soon as the value overflows. A `BigInt` or `BigInteger` fails when it needs more than 256 bits, and a `BigDecimal` (or a `Json.Num`) fails when its mantissa, the digits without the exponent, needs more than 256 bits. The limit is the constant `Lexer.NumberMaxBits`:

```scala
("1" + "0" * 100).fromJson[BigInt]
// res4: Either[String, BigInt] = Left(value = "(expected a 256-bit BigInt)")

("1." + "1" * 100).fromJson[BigDecimal]
// res5: Either[String, BigDecimal] = Left(
//   value = "(expected a BigDecimal with 256-bit mantissa)"
// )
```

The exponent of a `BigDecimal` is not capped by that limit, only by the range of `Int`. A number such as `1e2000000000` is accepted as a `BigDecimal` or a `Json.Num`, because it is stored as a small mantissa and a scale:

```scala
"1e2000000000".fromJson[BigDecimal]
// res6: Either[String, BigDecimal] = Right(value = 1E+2000000000)
```

ZIO JSON's own conversions from such a value are safe. Converting the `Json.Num` to a `BigInt` with `Json#as` fails at once:

```scala
"1e2000000000".fromJson[Json].flatMap(_.as[BigInt])
// res7: Either[String, BigInt] = Left(value = "(expected a 256-bit BigInt)")
```

Your own code is not protected in the same way. Calling `toBigInt` or `toBigInteger` (or anything that expands the number to all its digits) on a decoded `BigDecimal` from untrusted input reproduces the attack above. Check the size first, for example with `scale` and `precision`, or decode into a bounded type such as `Long` or `Double` when the domain allows it.

### Deeply Nested Input

The decoders are recursive: decoding an array inside an array calls the array decoder again, one level of the JVM call stack per level of nesting. ZIO JSON has no explicit limit on nesting depth. Instead, `JsonDecoder#decodeJson`, `fromJson` and `JsonDecoder#fromJsonAST` catch the `StackOverflowError` that very deep input causes and return the error `Unexpected structure`:

```scala
("[" * 1000000).fromJson[Json]
// res8: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = "Unexpected structure")
```

How deep a document can be before this happens depends on the stack size of the thread that decodes it. In our test on a JVM with default settings, 1,000 nested arrays decoded into `Json` and 10,000 failed with `Unexpected structure`.

Deep nesting only matters where the target type allows it. A case class decoder only descends as deep as the type itself is nested, and unknown fields are skipped without recursion. `Json`, recursive types such as trees, and nested collections follow the input as deep as it goes.

:::warning
The JVM streaming decoders `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStream` and `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStreamInput` do not catch `StackOverflowError`. ZIO treats that error as fatal, so it is not a normal failure of the effect. In our test, decoding 100,000 opening brackets into `Json` with `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStream` stopped a `ZIOAppDefault` application with a "Catastrophic error encountered" report. Do not decode untrusted input into recursive types such as `Json` with these methods.
:::

### Huge Strings

There is no limit on the length of a JSON string or on the number of elements in an array or object. In our test, a single string of 20 million characters decoded successfully. The only bound is the size of the input, which is why a request size limit in the HTTP server matters more than any check in your decoders: a `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail` that rejects long values runs only after the value has been read into memory.

### Mitigations

ZIO JSON avoids many of these attacks by design, but the following choices are yours:

| Risk                                     | Mitigation                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Large payloads, whitespace, huge strings | Cap the request size in the HTTP server or proxy.                                                                            |
| Copying the body into a `String`         | Decode from `Chunk[Byte]` or `Array[Byte]`, or, on the JVM, from a stream with `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStreamInput`.          |
| Redundant data in unknown fields         | Use `@jsonNoExtraFields` or `allowExtraFields = false`.                                                                      |
| Hash collisions in object keys           | Decode into case classes, `Json` or `JsonDecoder.keyValueChunk` instead of `Map[String, V]` when keys come from the client.  |
| Huge `BigDecimal` exponents              | Do not expand untrusted `BigDecimal` values to `BigInt`; check `scale` and `precision`, or use bounded number types.         |
| Deep nesting                             | Prefer non-recursive target types; avoid the JVM streaming decoders for untrusted input into recursive types such as `Json`. |

---

## JSON Shapes and Round Trips

The *wire format* of a type is the exact JSON its codec writes and reads. Other programs depend on it, so it pays to know what a derived codec produces before you publish an API, and to know when a value changes on the way through. A *round trip* is an encode followed by a decode. For most types the round trip gives back the value you started with, but a few combinations of types and settings do not.

This page first shows how the cases of a sealed trait or enum are written under each strategy, on Scala 2 and on Scala 3, and then lists the round-trip pitfalls.

### How Sum Type Cases Are Written

A case class is always written as a JSON object of its fields. A sealed trait or a Scala 3 `enum` (a *sum type*) also needs a *hint* that tells the decoder which case it is reading. ZIO JSON has three ways to write the hint:

- The wrapper object, the default, puts the case inside an object with a single key named after the case: `{"Circle":{"r":1.0}}`.
- A discriminator field, set with `@jsonDiscriminator("type")` or `SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField("type")`, adds the hint as a field of the case's own object: `{"type":"Circle","r":1.0}`.
- `enumValuesAsStrings = true` writes a case as a plain JSON string, `"Red"`, but only in a family where no case has fields.

The [sealed traits guide](../how-to/sealed-traits.md) shows how to set each one, and [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#sumtypehandling) documents the options.

#### The Shapes at a Glance

Every cell below comes from running the codecs on both Scala versions. Where the versions differ, the cell says so:

| Kind of case                                                   | Wrapper object                 | Discriminator field `type`          | `enumValuesAsStrings = true`             |
|----------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Case class with fields, `Circle(1.0)`                          | `{"Circle":{"r":1.0}}`         | `{"type":"Circle","r":1.0}`         | `{"Circle":{"r":1.0}}`                   |
| Case object next to cases with fields, `Unknown`               | `{"Unknown":{}}`               | `{"type":"Unknown"}`                | `{"Unknown":{}}`                         |
| Case object in a family of case objects only, `Red`            | `{"Red":{}}`                   | `{"type":"Red"}`                    | `"Red"`                                  |
| Empty case class in a family without fields, `Off()`           | `{"Off":{}}`                   | `{"type":"Off"}`                    | Scala 2: `"Off"`, Scala 3: `{"Off":{}}`  |
| Case object next to an empty case class, `On`                  | `{"On":{}}`                    | `{"type":"On"}`                     | Scala 2: `"On"`, Scala 3: `{"On":{}}`    |
| Scala 3 enum case with fields, `Banana(0.5)`                   | `{"Banana":{"curvature":0.5}}` | `{"type":"Banana","curvature":0.5}` | `{"Banana":{"curvature":0.5}}`           |
| Scala 3 parameterless case next to cases with fields, `Apple`  | `{"Apple":{}}`                 | `{"type":"Apple"}`                  | `{"Apple":{}}`                           |
| Scala 3 parameterless case in an enum of such cases, `Small`   | `{"Small":{}}`                 | `{"type":"Small"}`                  | `"Small"`                                |

Four rules explain the table:

- The discriminator always wins. With a discriminator, every case is an object, whatever `enumValuesAsStrings` says.
- The string form applies to a whole family or not at all. One case with fields keeps every case of the family in the object form, the case objects included.
- An empty case class counts as a fieldless case on Scala 2 only. On Scala 3, a family with a `final case class Off()` is not an enumeration, so `enumValuesAsStrings` has no effect on it.
- The defaults differ. `enumValuesAsStrings` is `false` by default on Scala 2 and `true` on Scala 3. Without any configuration, Scala 2 uses the wrapper column and Scala 3 uses the last column.

The last two rules are the reason the same model can produce different JSON on the two versions. If you cross-build a library, or move it from Scala 2 to Scala 3, set `enumValuesAsStrings` explicitly and use case objects rather than empty case classes. [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#scala-2-and-scala-3-differences) lists the remaining differences between the versions.

#### The Same Cases on Scala 2

The wrapper column is the Scala 2 default. We define one family with a field, one of case objects only, and one that mixes a case object with an empty case class:

```scala
import zio.json._

sealed trait Shape
final case class Circle(r: Double) extends Shape
case object Unknown                extends Shape

object Shape {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Shape] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Shape]
}

sealed trait Color
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color

object Color {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Color] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Color]
}

sealed trait Signal
case object On         extends Signal
final case class Off() extends Signal

object Signal {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Signal] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Signal]
}
```

Every case is a wrapper object, including the case objects:

```scala
println((Circle(1.0): Shape).toJson)
// {"Circle":{"r":1.0}}
println((Unknown: Shape).toJson)
// {"Unknown":{}}
println((Red: Color).toJson)
// {"Red":{}}
println((Off(): Signal).toJson)
// {"Off":{}}
```

With `enumValuesAsStrings = true`, the families without fields become strings. On Scala 2 that includes the family with the empty case class:

```scala
import zio.json._

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

sealed trait Color
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color

object Color {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Color] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Color]
}

sealed trait Signal
case object On         extends Signal
final case class Off() extends Signal

object Signal {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Signal] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Signal]
}
```

The case objects and the empty case class are now plain strings:

```scala
println((Red: Color).toJson)
// "Red"
println((On: Signal).toJson)
// "On"
println((Off(): Signal).toJson)
// "Off"
```

A discriminator turns every case into an object again, even with `enumValuesAsStrings = true` in scope:

```scala
import zio.json._

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

@jsonDiscriminator("type")
sealed trait Shape
final case class Circle(r: Double) extends Shape
case object Unknown                extends Shape

object Shape {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Shape] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Shape]
}

@jsonDiscriminator("type")
sealed trait Color
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color

object Color {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Color] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Color]
}
```

The hint is now a field of each case's object:

```scala
println((Circle(1.0): Shape).toJson)
// {"type":"Circle","r":1.0}
println((Unknown: Shape).toJson)
// {"type":"Unknown"}
println((Red: Color).toJson)
// {"type":"Red"}
```

#### The Same Cases on Scala 3

On Scala 3, `derives JsonCodec` uses the default configuration, where `enumValuesAsStrings` is on. The example file defines the same families, plus two enums:

```scala
object Defaults {
  sealed trait Shape derives JsonCodec
  final case class Circle(r: Double) extends Shape
  case object Unknown                extends Shape

  sealed trait Color derives JsonCodec
  case object Red   extends Color
  case object Green extends Color

  sealed trait Signal derives JsonCodec
  case object On         extends Signal
  final case class Off() extends Signal

  enum Fruit derives JsonCodec {
    case Banana(curvature: Double)
    case Apple
  }

  enum Size derives JsonCodec {
    case Small, Large
  }
}
```

Running the file prints the following for these families. Only `Red` and `Small` are strings, because `Shape`, `Fruit` and `Signal` each have a case with fields or an empty case class:

```text
Defaults, case class: {"Circle":{"r":1.0}}, decodes back to Right(Circle(1.0))
Defaults, case object next to a case class: {"Unknown":{}}, decodes back to Right(Unknown)
Defaults, case object in an all-object family: "Red", decodes back to Right(Red)
Defaults, case object next to an empty case class: {"On":{}}, decodes back to Right(On)
Defaults, empty case class: {"Off":{}}, decodes back to Right(Off())
Defaults, enum case with fields: {"Banana":{"curvature":0.5}}, decodes back to Right(Banana(0.5))
Defaults, parameterless case in a mixed enum: {"Apple":{}}, decodes back to Right(Apple)
Defaults, parameterless case in an all-parameterless enum: "Small", decodes back to Right(Small)
```

To get the Scala 2 default on Scala 3, put a `given` configuration with `enumValuesAsStrings = false` in scope where the codecs are derived:

```scala
object StringsOff {
  given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = false)

  sealed trait Color derives JsonCodec
  case object Red   extends Color
  case object Green extends Color

  enum Size derives JsonCodec {
    case Small, Large
  }
}
```

`StringsOff.Red` is then written as `{"Red":{}}` and `StringsOff.Size.Small` as `{"Small":{}}`.

A discriminator works on enums as it does on sealed traits:

```scala
object Discriminated {
  @jsonDiscriminator("type")
  sealed trait Signal derives JsonCodec
  case object On         extends Signal
  final case class Off() extends Signal

  @jsonDiscriminator("type")
  enum Fruit derives JsonCodec {
    case Banana(curvature: Double)
    case Apple
  }

  @jsonDiscriminator("type")
  enum Size derives JsonCodec {
    case Small, Large
  }
}
```

Every case becomes an object with a `type` field: `{"type":"On"}`, `{"type":"Off"}`, `{"type":"Banana","curvature":0.5}`, `{"type":"Apple"}` and `{"type":"Small"}`.

### Round-Trip Pitfalls

Each codec in the table above reads back what it writes. The pitfalls below are the cases where it does not: the value that comes back differs from the one that went in, or the decoder rejects the JSON its own encoder wrote. They behave the same on Scala 2 and Scala 3.

#### An `Option` Field With a `Some` Default

An encoder leaves a `None` field out of the JSON. A decoder fills a missing field with its default value, and only falls back to `None` when there is no default. So when the default is not `None`, a `None` comes back as the default:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.Json

final case class Timeout(seconds: Option[Int] = Some(30))

object Timeout {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Timeout] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Timeout]
}
```

`Timeout(None)` is written as `{}` and read back as `Timeout(Some(30))`:

```scala
println(Timeout(None).toJson)
// {}

Timeout(None).toJson.fromJson[Timeout]
// res18: Either[String, Timeout] = Right(
//   value = Timeout(seconds = Some(value = 30))
// )
```

`@jsonExplicitNull` does not help, because the decoder treats `null` like a missing field and uses the default too. If `None` must mean something other than the default, make `None` the default, or use a type of your own that can say "not set". The [optional and default fields guide](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md#6-keep-round-trips-in-mind) shows the rules behind this.

#### A Nested `Option[Option[A]]`

An `Option[Option[A]]` field looks like a way to tell "absent" apart from "explicitly `null`". The encoder treats both `None` and `Some(None)` as "nothing", so it writes the same JSON for them, and the decoder reads that JSON as `None`:

```scala
final case class Update(nickname: Option[Option[String]])

object Update {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Update] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Update]
}
```

`Some(None)` does not survive the trip:

```scala
println(Update(Some(None)).toJson)
// {}

Update(Some(None)).toJson.fromJson[Update]
// res20: Either[String, Update] = Right(value = Update(nickname = None))
```

To tell the three states apart, decode the object to the [`Json` AST](../reference/json-ast.md) and look at its keys yourself.

#### Omitting Empty Collections Without Filling Them In

`ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false)` makes the encoder leave out a field whose collection is empty. The `decoding` flag is separate and defaults to `true`, which means a missing collection field is an error. With only the encoding side turned off, the codec rejects its own output:

```scala
@jsonExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false)
final case class Basket(items: List[String])

object Basket {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Basket] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Basket]
}
```

The empty list is left out, and the missing field then fails to decode:

```scala
println(Basket(Nil).toJson)
// {}

Basket(Nil).toJson.fromJson[Basket]
// res22: Either[String, Basket] = Left(value = ".items(missing)")
```

Turn off both directions together, so that a missing field decodes as an empty collection:

```scala
@jsonExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false, decoding = false)
final case class Cart(items: List[String])

object Cart {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Cart] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Cart]
}
```

Now the round trip works:

```scala
Cart(Nil).toJson.fromJson[Cart]
// res23: Either[String, Cart] = Right(value = Cart(items = List()))
```

The same applies to `JsonCodecConfiguration(explicitEmptyCollections = ...)`, described in [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#explicitemptycollections).

#### A Discriminator With Strict Field Checks

With a discriminator, the decoder passes the whole object, discriminator field included, to the decoder of the case. When that case decoder rejects unknown fields, because of `allowExtraFields = false` or `@jsonNoExtraFields` on the case class, it rejects the discriminator too. Nothing warns at compile time:

```scala
object Strict {
  implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
    JsonCodecConfiguration(
      sumTypeHandling = JsonCodecConfiguration.SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField("type"),
      allowExtraFields = false
    )

  sealed trait Shape
  final case class Square(side: Double) extends Shape
  case object Point                     extends Shape

  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Shape] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Shape]
}
```

Neither case decodes the JSON that the encoder writes for it:

```scala
println((Strict.Square(2.0): Strict.Shape).toJson)
// {"type":"Square","side":2.0}

(Strict.Square(2.0): Strict.Shape).toJson.fromJson[Strict.Shape]
// res25: Either[String, Strict.Shape] = Left(
//   value = "(Square)(invalid extra field)"
// )

(Strict.Point: Strict.Shape).toJson.fromJson[Strict.Shape]
// res26: Either[String, Strict.Shape] = Left(
//   value = "(Point)(expected '}' got '\"')"
// )
```

Keep `allowExtraFields = true` for a family with a discriminator, or use the wrapper object when you need unknown fields rejected. The [sealed traits guide](../how-to/sealed-traits.md#3-use-a-discriminator-field-with-jsondiscriminator) has the same warning.

#### Comparing Numbers in the `Json` AST

`Json.Num` holds a `java.math.BigDecimal` and compares with `BigDecimal#equals`, which also compares the scale (see [Equality](../reference/json-ast.md#equality)). `1` and `1.0` decode to the same `Double`, but as `Json` values they are different. This bites in tests that compare an encoder's output with expected JSON as trees:

```scala
final case class Weight(kg: Double)

object Weight {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Weight] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Weight]
}
```

The `Double` encoder writes `1.0`, so the tree differs from one parsed from `{"kg":1}`, although both decode to the same `Weight`:

```scala
Weight(1.0).toJsonAST == """{"kg":1}""".fromJson[Json]
// res27: Boolean = false

"""{"kg":1}""".fromJson[Weight] == Right(Weight(1.0))
// res28: Boolean = true
```

Compare decoded values, or write the expected JSON with the scale the encoder produces. A `BigDecimal` keeps the scale it was given, so `BigDecimal("1.50")` is written as `1.50`, not `1.5`.

#### Non-Finite Doubles Become Strings

JSON has no literal for `NaN` or infinity. The `Double` and `Float` encoders write them as the strings `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"` and `"-Infinity"`, and the decoders accept those strings back:

```scala
println(Weight(Double.NaN).toJson)
// {"kg":"NaN"}

Weight(Double.NaN).toJson.fromJson[Weight]
// res30: Either[String, Weight] = Right(value = Weight(kg = NaN))
```

The round trip works within ZIO JSON, but another program that reads the JSON finds a string where it expects a number. `NaN` also never equals itself, so a round-trip test that compares with `==` fails for it even though the value came back. `JsonEncoder#toJsonAST` throws on these values instead of producing a string; [Non-Finite Numbers](../reference/json-encoder.md#non-finite-numbers) has the details.

### Pin the Format With Golden Tests

A change to a type or a setting can change the wire format without breaking any compile or any round-trip test: renaming a case renames its hint, adding a case with fields switches a whole family out of the string form, and moving to Scala 3 flips the `enumValuesAsStrings` default. A round-trip test still passes in all these cases, because the codec reads its own new output. Only the clients that depend on the old JSON break.

A *golden test* catches this. On its first run it writes the encoder's output for a set of generated sample values to a file for you to review and accept. From then on it fails whenever the output differs from the accepted file. The `zio-json-golden` module provides `goldenTest` for ZIO Test, and the [golden testing guide](../how-to/golden-testing.md) shows how to set it up. Add one for every type whose JSON leaves your program, and review a changed golden file as you would review a change to a public API.

### See Also

- [Work With Sealed Traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md) to choose and configure the hint
- [Optional, Default and Null Fields](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md) for the rules on missing and `null` fields
- [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md) for every derivation option and its defaults
- [How Strict Is the Decoder](decoder-strictness.md) for what the decoder accepts beyond what the encoder writes

## Getting Started(Zio-json)

On this page you will install ZIO JSON, turn Scala values into JSON, read JSON back into Scala values, and handle bad input. Every step builds on the one before it, so run the steps in order.

By the end you will have a small user-profile model: a `Profile` that holds a `Person` with an `Address`, an optional nickname, a list of tags, and a list of contacts of different kinds. You will encode it, decode it, and read the errors it reports for bad input.

### 1. Install

Add the library to your `build.sbt`:

```sbt
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

:::note[Scala.js and Scala Native]
ZIO JSON is published for the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native, for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3. In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use `%%%` instead of `%%`.

On those two platforms the `java.time` types come from the `scala-java-time` library. If you use `java.time.ZoneId` or `java.time.ZonedDateTime` there, also add the time-zone database in the same version as the `scala-java-time` in your dependency tree (`sbt dependencyTree` shows it), for example:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "io.github.cquiroz" %%% "scala-java-time-tzdb" % "2.10.0"
```

The add-on modules (YAML, golden testing, `@jsonDerive` macros and the integrations) are listed in the [Modules](index.md#modules) section of the Introduction page, with their platforms.
:::

The code on this page uses Scala 2.13 syntax. Where Scala 3 is shorter, a Scala 3 tip follows the example.

Every snippet below assumes this import:

```scala
import zio.json._
```

The import brings in the type classes `JsonEncoder` and `JsonDecoder`, the derivation helpers, and the extension methods `toJson` and `fromJson`.

### 2. Encode Your First Value

A *codec* is a pair of one encoder (Scala to JSON) and one decoder (JSON to Scala). The easiest way to get one for a case class is to let the compiler derive it. Put the codec on the companion object so Scala finds it without any import:

```scala
final case class Address(street: String, city: String)

object Address {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Address] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Address]
}
```

Now call `toJson` on a value:

```scala
val home = Address("1 Main St", "Springfield")
// home: Address = Address(street = "1 Main St", city = "Springfield")

println(home.toJson)
// {"street":"1 Main St","city":"Springfield"}
```

Use `toJsonPretty` when you want indented output for people to read:

```scala
println(home.toJsonPretty)
// {
//   "street" : "1 Main St",
//   "city" : "Springfield"
// }
```

:::tip[Scala 3]
On Scala 3 you can skip the companion and write `derives JsonCodec` on the class instead:

```scala
final case class Address(street: String, city: String) derives JsonCodec
```
:::

### 3. Decode Your First Value

`fromJson` goes the other way. It does not throw. It returns an `Either[String, A]`: a `Right` with the value, or a `Left` with an error message:

```scala
"""{"street":"1 Main St","city":"Springfield"}""".fromJson[Address]
// res4: Either[String, Address] = Right(
//   value = Address(street = "1 Main St", city = "Springfield")
// )
```

The same codec supplies the decoder, because a `JsonCodec` holds both halves.

### 4. Nest One Case Class in Another

A `Person` holds the `Address` from step 2. A case class field can be any type that has a codec, and `Address` got its codec in step 2:

```scala
final case class Person(name: String, age: Int, address: Address)

object Person {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
}
```

The nested value becomes a nested JSON object:

```scala
val alice = Person("Alice", 30, home)
// alice: Person = Person(
//   name = "Alice",
//   age = 30,
//   address = Address(street = "1 Main St", city = "Springfield")
// )

println(alice.toJsonPretty)
// {
//   "name" : "Alice",
//   "age" : 30,
//   "address" : {
//     "street" : "1 Main St",
//     "city" : "Springfield"
//   }
// }
```

Decoding the same text gives the original value back:

```scala
alice.toJson.fromJson[Person]
// res6: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(
//     name = "Alice",
//     age = 30,
//     address = Address(street = "1 Main St", city = "Springfield")
//   )
// )
```

### 5. Model Alternatives with a Sealed Trait

A person can be reached by email or by phone. A `sealed trait` models "one of several shapes". Derive the codec on the trait itself, and its subtypes are derived along with it:

```scala
sealed trait Contact

object Contact {
  final case class Email(address: String) extends Contact
  final case class Phone(number: String)  extends Contact

  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Contact] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Contact]
}
```

By default the JSON names the subtype in a single wrapper key. This key is the *tag* that tells the decoder which subtype to build:

```scala
val contacts: List[Contact] = List(Contact.Email("alice@example.com"), Contact.Phone("555-0100"))
// contacts: List[Contact] = List(
//   Email(address = "alice@example.com"),
//   Phone(number = "555-0100")
// )

println(contacts.toJson)
// [{"Email":{"address":"alice@example.com"}},{"Phone":{"number":"555-0100"}}]

"""[{"Phone":{"number":"555-0100"}}]""".fromJson[List[Contact]]
// res8: Either[String, List[Contact]] = Right(
//   value = List(Phone(number = "555-0100"))
// )
```

:::tip[Scala 3]
On Scala 3 the same alternatives can be an `enum` with `derives JsonCodec`:

```scala
enum Contact derives JsonCodec {
  case Email(address: String)
  case Phone(number: String)
}
```

An enum case is written the same way, so `Contact.Phone("555-0100")` encodes as `{"Phone":{"number":"555-0100"}}`.
:::

### 6. Put It Together with Optional and List Fields

Now combine everything into a `Profile`. It holds the `Person` from step 4, the `Contact` list from step 5, a nickname that may be missing, and a list of tags. `Option` and `List` already have codecs, so the derived codec needs nothing extra:

```scala
final case class Profile(
  person: Person,
  nickname: Option[String],
  tags: List[String],
  contacts: List[Contact]
)

object Profile {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Profile] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Profile]
}
```

A `None` is left out of the JSON, and a `List` becomes a JSON array:

```scala
val profile = Profile(alice, None, List("admin", "dev"), contacts)
// profile: Profile = Profile(
//   person = Person(
//     name = "Alice",
//     age = 30,
//     address = Address(street = "1 Main St", city = "Springfield")
//   ),
//   nickname = None,
//   tags = List("admin", "dev"),
//   contacts = List(
//     Email(address = "alice@example.com"),
//     Phone(number = "555-0100")
//   )
// )

println(profile.toJsonPretty)
// {
//   "person" : {
//     "name" : "Alice",
//     "age" : 30,
//     "address" : {
//       "street" : "1 Main St",
//       "city" : "Springfield"
//     }
//   },
//   "tags" : [
//     "admin",
//     "dev"
//   ],
//   "contacts" : [
//     {
//       "Email" : {
//         "address" : "alice@example.com"
//       }
//     },
//     {
//       "Phone" : {
//         "number" : "555-0100"
//       }
//     }
//   ]
// }
```

A missing `nickname` field decodes as `None`, so the encoded text decodes back to the same value:

```scala
profile.toJson.fromJson[Profile]
// res11: Either[String, Profile] = Right(
//   value = Profile(
//     person = Person(
//       name = "Alice",
//       age = 30,
//       address = Address(street = "1 Main St", city = "Springfield")
//     ),
//     nickname = None,
//     tags = List("admin", "dev"),
//     contacts = List(
//       Email(address = "alice@example.com"),
//       Phone(number = "555-0100")
//     )
//   )
// )
```

### 7. Handle a Decode Error

Bad input never throws. It comes back as a `Left` holding a message. The message is a path in `jq` style, followed by a note in parentheses that says what went wrong.

A value of the wrong type:

```scala
"""{"street":"1 Main St","city":42}""".fromJson[Address]
// res12: Either[String, Address] = Left(value = ".city(expected string)")
```

A missing field:

```scala
"""{"street":"1 Main St"}""".fromJson[Address]
// res13: Either[String, Address] = Left(value = ".city(missing)")
```

Text that is not JSON at all:

```scala
"""{"street": womp}""".fromJson[Address]
// res14: Either[String, Address] = Left(value = ".street(expected string)")
```

In the full `Profile`, a failure deep inside the model keeps the whole path, so you can see exactly where the problem sits:

```scala
"""{"person":{"name":"Alice","age":30,"address":{"street":"1 Main St","city":false}},"tags":[],"contacts":[]}""".fromJson[Profile]
// res15: Either[String, Profile] = Left(
//   value = ".person.address.city(expected string)"
// )
```

Because the result is an ordinary `Either`, you handle it with `fold`, `map`, or a `match`, as with any other `Either`:

```scala
"""{"street":"1 Main St"}""".fromJson[Address] match {
  case Right(address) => s"Got ${address.city}"
  case Left(error)    => s"Could not decode: $error"
}
// res16: String = "Could not decode: .city(missing)"
```

### 8. Where Next

You can now encode, decode, nest, model alternatives, and read errors. To practise on a larger example, continue with the next tutorial, [Model a Real API Payload](tutorial/model-an-api-payload.md). Or pick the guide that matches your next task:

- [Control the JSON a type encodes to](how-to/encoding.md) when the default JSON shape is not the one you need.
- [Decode JSON whose shape differs from your case class](how-to/decoding.md) when the JSON keys or nesting do not match your fields.
- [Rename fields](how-to/field-names.md) when the JSON names differ from your Scala names.
- [Change how sealed traits look in JSON](how-to/sealed-traits.md), for example with a discriminator field instead of the wrapper key.
- [Optional, default and null fields](how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md) for missing, `null` and empty fields.
- [Process large JSON as a stream](how-to/streaming.md) on the JVM.

For every option and method, see the [Reference](reference/index.md). For why ZIO JSON works the way it does, see [How ZIO JSON Works](explanation/how-it-works.md).
