## Use Your Own Type as a Map Key

Goal: write and read a `Map` whose keys are your own types, such as `java.time.LocalDate`, a wrapper around an `Int`, or a sealed-trait enumeration.

A JSON object key is always a string, so ZIO JSON writes a `Map[K, V]` as an object only when it knows how to turn a `K` into a `String` and back. Out of the box it knows this for `String`, `Int`, `Long` and `java.util.UUID` keys. For any other key type you write two small instances, a `JsonFieldEncoder[K]` and a `JsonFieldDecoder[K]`, usually in two lines each. In this guide we build a sales report with three maps, keyed by day, by store and by sales channel, and then check that it survives a round trip.

Steps 2 to 4 are alternatives, one per kind of key. Follow the one that matches your key type, then continue with steps 5 and 6.

### What You Need

Only the core module:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

All code on this page uses these imports:

```scala
import zio.json._

import java.time.LocalDate
import scala.util.Try
```

The guide assumes you know how to derive a codec for a case class (see the [Getting Started](../getting-started.md) tutorial). The [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](../reference/json-field-codecs.md) reference page describes both type classes in full.

### 1. Recognize the Missing Key Instance

The first sign of a missing key instance is a compile error. Encoding or decoding a `Map[LocalDate, Int]` does not compile, because `LocalDate` has no key instances:

```scala
Map(LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 1) -> 12).toJson

"""{"2024-03-01":12}""".fromJson[Map[LocalDate, Int]]
// error: could not find implicit value for parameter encoder: zio.json.JsonEncoder[scala.collection.immutable.Map[java.time.LocalDate,Int]]
// Map(LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 1) -> 12).toJson
// ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
// error: could not find implicit value for parameter decoder: zio.json.JsonDecoder[Map[java.time.LocalDate,Int]]
// """{"2024-03-01":12}""".fromJson[Map[LocalDate, Int]]
// ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

The error names the encoder or decoder for the whole map, `JsonEncoder[Map[LocalDate,Int]]`, and not the `JsonFieldEncoder[LocalDate]` that is actually missing. The values are not the problem: `Int` has a `JsonEncoder`. When the map is a field of a case class, the Scala 2 derivation macro reports the field instead, for example `magnolia: could not find zio.json.DeriveJsonEncoder.Typeclass[Map[java.time.LocalDate,Int]] in parameter 'byDay'`. In both cases the fix is the same: provide a `JsonFieldEncoder` and a `JsonFieldDecoder` for the key type.

### 2. Write a Key Codec for `LocalDate`

A key encoder turns a key into the string written as the object key, and a key decoder turns that string back into a key or fails. Both are easiest to build from the `String` instances. `JsonFieldEncoder#contramap` takes a function from your key to `String`, and `JsonFieldDecoder#mapOrFail` takes a function from `String` to `Either[String, K]`, where a `Left` is the error message:

```scala
implicit val localDateKeyEncoder: JsonFieldEncoder[LocalDate] =
  JsonFieldEncoder[String].contramap(_.toString)

implicit val localDateKeyDecoder: JsonFieldDecoder[LocalDate] =
  JsonFieldDecoder[String].mapOrFail { s =>
    Try(LocalDate.parse(s)).toOption.toRight(s"expected a date like 2024-03-01, got '$s'")
  }
```

`LocalDate#toString` and `LocalDate.parse` both use the ISO format, the same text the built-in `JsonEncoder[LocalDate]` writes for values, so keys and values look alike. With the two instances in scope, the map encodes and decodes, and an invalid date fails with our message at the key's path:

```scala
println(Map(LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 1) -> 12, LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 2) -> 9).toJson)
// {"2024-03-01":12,"2024-03-02":9}

"""{"2024-03-01":12,"2024-03-02":9}""".fromJson[Map[LocalDate, Int]]
// res3: Either[String, Map[LocalDate, Int]] = Right(
//   value = Map(2024-03-01 -> 12, 2024-03-02 -> 9)
// )

"""{"2024-02-30":12}""".fromJson[Map[LocalDate, Int]]
// res4: Either[String, Map[LocalDate, Int]] = Left(
//   value = ".2024-02-30(expected a date like 2024-03-01, got '2024-02-30')"
// )
```

`LocalDate` belongs to the JDK, so its key instances cannot go in its companion object. Keep them in an object of your own and import them where you need them, as [Encode a Type You Do Not Own](third-party-types.md) describes.

### 3. Write a Key Codec for a Wrapper Type

Wrapper types (sometimes called newtypes) give an `Int` or a `String` a name of its own, so the compiler keeps a store id apart from a quantity. A wrapper reuses the key instances of the type it wraps: `JsonFieldEncoder#contramap` unwraps, and `JsonFieldDecoder#map` wraps. Since we own `StoreId`, the instances go in its companion object, where the compiler finds them without an import:

```scala
final case class StoreId(value: Int)

object StoreId {
  implicit val keyEncoder: JsonFieldEncoder[StoreId] = JsonFieldEncoder[Int].contramap(_.value)
  implicit val keyDecoder: JsonFieldDecoder[StoreId] = JsonFieldDecoder[Int].map(StoreId(_))
}
```

`JsonFieldDecoder#map` cannot fail, but the `Int` key decoder underneath still checks that the key is a number:

```scala
println(Map(StoreId(7) -> 40, StoreId(12) -> 25).toJson)
// {"7":40,"12":25}

"""{"7":40,"12":25}""".fromJson[Map[StoreId, Int]]
// res6: Either[String, Map[StoreId, Int]] = Right(
//   value = Map(StoreId(value = 7) -> 40, StoreId(value = 12) -> 25)
// )

"""{"seven":40}""".fromJson[Map[StoreId, Int]]
// res7: Either[String, Map[StoreId, Int]] = Left(
//   value = ".seven(Invalid Int: seven)"
// )
```

The same two lines work when `StoreId` is a value class (`final case class StoreId(value: Int) extends AnyVal`). To also validate the wrapped value, for example to reject negative ids, use `JsonFieldDecoder#mapOrFail` instead of `JsonFieldDecoder#map`.

### 4. Write a Key Codec for a Sealed-Trait Enumeration

For a sealed trait of case objects, the key encoder writes each case's name and the key decoder looks the name up. An unknown name must fail, and a good error message lists the names that are accepted:

```scala
sealed trait Channel

object Channel {
  case object Web   extends Channel
  case object Store extends Channel
  case object Phone extends Channel

  val values: List[Channel] = List(Web, Store, Phone)

  def name(channel: Channel): String = channel.toString.toLowerCase

  implicit val keyEncoder: JsonFieldEncoder[Channel] =
    JsonFieldEncoder[String].contramap(name)

  implicit val keyDecoder: JsonFieldDecoder[Channel] =
    JsonFieldDecoder[String].mapOrFail { s =>
      values.find(name(_) == s).toRight(s"unknown channel '$s', expected one of: ${values.map(name).mkString(", ")}")
    }
}
```

Known names decode to the case objects, and the first unknown name stops decoding with our message:

```scala
println(Map[Channel, Int](Channel.Web -> 30, Channel.Store -> 35).toJson)
// {"web":30,"store":35}

"""{"web":30,"store":35}""".fromJson[Map[Channel, Int]]
// res9: Either[String, Map[Channel, Int]] = Right(
//   value = Map(Web -> 30, Store -> 35)
// )

"""{"web":30,"fax":1}""".fromJson[Map[Channel, Int]]
// res10: Either[String, Map[Channel, Int]] = Left(
//   value = ".fax(unknown channel 'fax', expected one of: web, store, phone)"
// )
```

Matching is exact, so `"Web"` is an unknown key here. If you use Enumeratum, its interop module builds these instances for you (see [Enumeratum Interop](../interop/enumeratum.md)).

### 5. Use the Keys in a Derived Codec

Derivation picks up the key instances for every `Map` field, so the report needs nothing beyond the instances from the previous steps:

```scala
final case class SalesReport(
  byDay: Map[LocalDate, Int],
  byStore: Map[StoreId, Int],
  byChannel: Map[Channel, Int]
)

object SalesReport {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[SalesReport] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[SalesReport]
}

val report = SalesReport(
  byDay = Map(LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 1) -> 12, LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 2) -> 9),
  byStore = Map(StoreId(7) -> 15, StoreId(12) -> 6),
  byChannel = Map(Channel.Web -> 13, Channel.Store -> 8)
)
```

The report encodes to nested objects, and a bad key deep inside it is reported with the full path, `.byChannel.fax`:

```scala
println(report.toJsonPretty)
// {
//   "byDay" : {
//     "2024-03-01" : 12,
//     "2024-03-02" : 9
//   },
//   "byStore" : {
//     "7" : 15,
//     "12" : 6
//   },
//   "byChannel" : {
//     "web" : 13,
//     "store" : 8
//   }
// }

"""{"byDay":{},"byStore":{},"byChannel":{"fax":1}}""".fromJson[SalesReport]
// res12: Either[String, SalesReport] = Left(
//   value = ".byChannel.fax(unknown channel 'fax', expected one of: web, store, phone)"
// )
```

### 6. Check the Round Trip

A key encoder and key decoder must agree: every string the encoder writes must decode back to the same key. The quickest check is to encode a value and decode the result:

```scala
report.toJson.fromJson[SalesReport] == Right(report)
// res13: Boolean = true
```

Run the same check in your tests, with keys that cover every case of an enumeration and the edge cases of your format, such as the first and last day of a year. A property-based test that generates keys catches a mismatch that a handful of examples miss.

### Pitfalls

A map round-trips only when its keys and values do, and three cases break that silently, without a compile error or a decoding error. The [Behaviour Notes](../reference/json-field-codecs.md#behaviour-notes) on the reference page list them with the other rules for map keys.

#### Duplicate Keys: The Last One Wins

JSON allows the same key twice in an object. Decoding into a `Map` keeps the last value and reports no error:

```scala
"""{"byDay":{"2024-03-01":12,"2024-03-01":20},"byStore":{},"byChannel":{}}""".fromJson[SalesReport]
// res14: Either[String, SalesReport] = Right(
//   value = SalesReport(
//     byDay = Map(2024-03-01 -> 20),
//     byStore = Map(),
//     byChannel = Map()
//   )
// )
```

If duplicates must be rejected or kept, decode the object with `JsonDecoder.keyValueChunk` or into a `Json.Obj`, and check the entries yourself.

#### Keys That Collide After Decoding

Two different strings can decode to the same key. The `Int` key decoder that `StoreId` reuses reads `"7"`, `"07"` and `"+7"` as the same number, so these entries collapse into one, and the last one wins again:

```scala
"""{"7":15,"07":4}""".fromJson[Map[StoreId, Int]]
// res15: Either[String, Map[StoreId, Int]] = Right(
//   value = Map(StoreId(value = 7) -> 4)
// )
```

A strict format avoids this: `LocalDate.parse` accepts only one spelling of each date. For a numeric key, use `JsonFieldDecoder#mapOrFail` and reject a key whose text differs from the encoded form of the number it decodes to.

#### `None` Values Are Dropped on Encode

The map encoder skips every entry whose value encodes to nothing, which for an `Option` value means `None`. The key disappears from the JSON, so the decoded map has fewer entries than the original:

```scala
val withGap = Map(LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 1) -> Some(12), LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 2) -> None)
// withGap: Map[LocalDate, Option[Int]] = Map(
//   2024-03-01 -> Some(value = 12),
//   2024-03-02 -> None
// )

println(withGap.toJson)
// {"2024-03-01":12}

withGap.toJson.fromJson[Map[LocalDate, Option[Int]]]
// res17: Either[String, Map[LocalDate, Option[Int]]] = Right(
//   value = Map(2024-03-01 -> Some(value = 12))
// )
```

Use `Map#getOrElse` or `Map#get` when reading such a map, so a missing key and a `None` value mean the same thing, or store a non-optional placeholder instead of `None`.

### Scala 3: String Subtypes Need No Key Decoder

On Scala 3, a key type that is a subtype of `String` and has a `JsonDecoder` needs no key instances at all. The encoder side is covered because `JsonFieldEncoder` is contravariant, so the `String` key encoder also serves every subtype of `String`. The decoder side is covered by a low-priority Scala 3 instance that decodes the key with the type's `JsonDecoder`.

A union of string literals has a built-in `JsonDecoder` on Scala 3, so it works as a key type as it is:

```scala
type Channel = "web" | "store" | "phone"

final case class ChannelSales(byChannel: Map[Channel, Int]) derives JsonCodec
```

An opaque type declared with an upper bound of `String` is a subtype of `String` too, so a `JsonDecoder` for it is enough. Its validation runs on keys as well as on values:

```scala
object Skus {
  opaque type Sku <: String = String

  def apply(code: String): Either[String, Sku] =
    if (code.matches("[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{3}")) Right(code) else Left(s"not a SKU: $code")

  given JsonDecoder[Sku] = JsonDecoder.string.mapOrFail(apply)
}
import Skus.Sku

final case class Stock(bySku: Map[Sku, Int]) derives JsonCodec
```

Running the example prints:

```text
union encode: {"byChannel":{"web":13,"store":8}}
union decode: Right(ChannelSales(Map(web -> 13, store -> 8)))
union bad key: Left(.byChannel.fax(expected one of: web, store, phone))
opaque encode: {"bySku":{"ABC-123":4}}
opaque decode: Right(Stock(Map(ABC-123 -> 4)))
opaque bad key: Left(.bySku.abc(not a SKU: abc))
```

This instance is Scala 3 only. On Scala 2, every key type other than `String`, `Int`, `Long` and `UUID` needs the instances shown in the steps above, and a Scala 3 `enum` or an opaque type without the `<: String` bound needs them too.

This instance does not escape the key again before decoding it, so a key that contains `"` or `\` is not read correctly. For example, the key `a"b` is cut to `a`. If your keys can contain these characters, write a `JsonFieldDecoder` with `mapOrFail` as in the steps above. See [Scala 3: Keys That Are Subtypes of `String`](../reference/json-field-codecs.md#scala-3-keys-that-are-subtypes-of-string).

### See Also

- [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](../reference/json-field-codecs.md) for the full API, the built-in key types and the map types that use key instances.
- [Built-in Instances](../reference/built-in-instances.md#maps) for the map types and how they are written.
- [Encode a Type You Do Not Own](third-party-types.md) for where to put instances of a type from another library.
- [Errors](../reference/errors.md) for how error paths such as `.byChannel.fax` are built.
- [Enumeratum Interop](../interop/enumeratum.md) and [Refined Interop](../interop/refined.md) for key instances those modules provide.

## Decode JSON Whose Shape Differs from Your Case Class

Goal: decode JSON into a case class whose field names, or layout, do not match the JSON you receive.

The running example is a stock quote from a third-party API. Its keys are not valid Scala identifiers:

```json
{
  "01. symbol": "IBM",
  "02. open": "182.4300",
  "03. high": "182.8000"
}
```

The case class we want to fill uses plain names:

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Quote(symbol: String, open: String, high: String)

object Quote {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Quote] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Quote]
}
```

A derived decoder looks for the keys `symbol`, `open` and `high`, so it fails on the first one it cannot find:

```scala
"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","02. open":"182.4300","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res1: Either[String, Quote] = Left(value = ".symbol(missing)")
```

Each step below is a separate option, and each one makes this input decode to `Quote(IBM,182.4300,182.8000)`. Pick the one that fits your situation:

| Option                              | Pick it when                                                                                   | Error messages                                                     |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1. Rename fields with `@jsonField`  | You can edit the case class, and only the key names differ                                     | Derived, with the field path                                       |
| 2. Decode an intermediate class     | The domain class must stay free of JSON details, and the JSON is a flat object with fixed keys | Derived, with the field path                                       |
| 3. Decode to `Json` and match on it | The layout differs, not only the names, or you compute values from several fields              | The messages you write                                             |
| 4. Decode to `Json` with cursors    | As option 3, but the paths are reusable values and reach into nested objects in one line       | The cursor's, which name a missing key but not a wrongly typed one |

Options 1 and 2 decode in one pass, straight from the text. Options 3 and 4 first build the whole document as a [`Json`](../reference/json-ast.md) tree and then read from it, which costs more time and memory. When only one field differs, because it arrives in two shapes, see [Accept a Field That Arrives in Two Shapes](#accept-a-field-that-arrives-in-two-shapes) instead.

### 1. Rename Fields with `@jsonField`

`@jsonField` on a field gives the key the derived decoder looks for. This works only when you can change the case class:

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Quote(
  @jsonField("01. symbol") symbol: String,
  @jsonField("02. open") open: String,
  @jsonField("03. high") high: String
)

object Quote {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Quote] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Quote]
}
```

The input now decodes, and a wrong value is reported at its JSON key:

```scala
"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","02. open":"182.4300","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res3: Either[String, Quote] = Right(
//   value = Quote(symbol = "IBM", open = "182.4300", high = "182.8000")
// )

"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","02. open":182.43,"03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res4: Either[String, Quote] = Left(value = ".02. open(expected string)")
```

The annotation also renames the key on encoding. When many keys follow one pattern, such as `snake_case`, use `@jsonMemberNames` instead (see [Field Names](field-names.md)).

### 2. Decode an Intermediate Case Class

A private case class can mirror the JSON exactly, and `JsonDecoder#map` converts it into the domain class. Keys that are not valid Scala identifiers go in backticks:

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Quote(symbol: String, open: String, high: String)

object Quote {
  private final case class JsonQuote(
    `01. symbol`: String,
    `02. open`: String,
    `03. high`: String
  )

  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Quote] =
    DeriveJsonDecoder
      .gen[JsonQuote]
      .map { case JsonQuote(s, o, h) => Quote(s, o, h) }
}
```

`Quote` itself has no JSON annotations, and the errors are those of the derived `JsonQuote` decoder:

```scala
"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","02. open":"182.4300","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res6: Either[String, Quote] = Right(
//   value = Quote(symbol = "IBM", open = "182.4300", high = "182.8000")
// )

"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res7: Either[String, Quote] = Left(value = ".02. open(missing)")
```

Use `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail` instead of `JsonDecoder#map` when the conversion can fail, for example to validate a value (see [Validate Data While Decoding](validate-on-decode.md)).

### 3. Decode to `Json` and Match on It

`JsonDecoder[Json]` reads any valid JSON into a `Json` tree, and `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail` turns that tree into a `Quote` or an error message. `Json#asString` returns the text of a `Json.Str` and `None` for any other case, so a field that holds a number or an object is rejected. Do not use `toString` here: it renders the node as JSON, so a string would keep its quotes:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.Json

final case class Quote(symbol: String, open: String, high: String)

object Quote {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Quote] = JsonDecoder[Json]
    .mapOrFail {
      case Json.Obj(fields) =>
        def findField(name: String): Either[String, String] =
          fields
            .find(_._1 == name)
            .flatMap(_._2.asString)
            .toRight(left = s"Field '$name' is missing or not a string")

        for {
          symbol <- findField("01. symbol")
          open   <- findField("02. open")
          high   <- findField("03. high")
        } yield Quote(symbol, open, high)
      case _ =>
        Left("Not a JSON record")
    }
}
```

The input decodes, and a failure carries the message you wrote, at the position of the whole object:

```scala
"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","02. open":"182.4300","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res9: Either[String, Quote] = Right(
//   value = Quote(symbol = "IBM", open = "182.4300", high = "182.8000")
// )

"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res10: Either[String, Quote] = Left(
//   value = "(Field '02. open' is missing or not a string)"
// )
```

### 4. Decode to `Json` with Cursors

A [cursor](../reference/json-ast.md#cursors) is a path into a `Json` tree, built once and applied with `Json#get`. `JsonCursor.field` selects a key, `>>>` continues the path, and `JsonCursor.isString` rejects a value that is not a string, as `Json#asString` does in option 3:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.{Json, JsonCursor}

final case class Quote(symbol: String, open: String, high: String)

object Quote {
  private val symbolC = JsonCursor.field("01. symbol") >>> JsonCursor.isString
  private val openC   = JsonCursor.field("02. open") >>> JsonCursor.isString
  private val highC   = JsonCursor.field("03. high") >>> JsonCursor.isString

  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Quote] = JsonDecoder[Json]
    .mapOrFail { c =>
      for {
        symbol <- c.get(symbolC)
        open   <- c.get(openC)
        high   <- c.get(highC)
      } yield Quote(symbol.value, open.value, high.value)
    }
}
```

The input decodes. A missing key is named in the error, but a value of the wrong type is not:

```scala
"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","02. open":"182.4300","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res12: Either[String, Quote] = Right(
//   value = Quote(symbol = "IBM", open = "182.4300", high = "182.8000")
// )

"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res13: Either[String, Quote] = Left(value = "(No such field: '02. open')")

"""{"01. symbol":"IBM","02. open":182.43,"03. high":"182.8000"}""".fromJson[Quote]
// res14: Either[String, Quote] = Left(value = "(expected string)")
```

For values deeper in the document, extend the path, adding a `JsonCursor#isObject` step before each further `JsonCursor#field`, for example `JsonCursor.field("data").isObject.field("symbol").isString`. [Cursor Errors](../reference/json-ast.md#cursor-errors) lists the messages a cursor produces.

### Accept a Field That Arrives in Two Shapes

Sometimes only one field is irregular. Here some producers send `categories` as a JSON array, and others as one comma-separated string. Keep the derived decoder and give that field a decoder that tries both shapes with `JsonDecoder#orElse` (`<>`):

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Animal(name: String, categories: List[String])

object Animal {
  private val commaSeparated: JsonDecoder[List[String]] =
    JsonDecoder[String].map(_.split(',').map(_.trim).toList)

  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Animal] = {
    implicit val categories: JsonDecoder[List[String]] =
      JsonDecoder.list[String] <> commaSeparated
    DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Animal]
  }
}
```

The local implicit is visible only to `DeriveJsonDecoder.gen` in that block, so other `List[String]` fields in your program keep the standard decoder. Both shapes now decode:

```scala
"""{"name": "Dog", "categories": "Warm-blooded, Mammal"}""".fromJson[Animal]
// res16: Either[String, Animal] = Right(
//   value = Animal(name = "Dog", categories = List("Warm-blooded", "Mammal"))
// )

"""{"name": "Snake", "categories": ["Cold-blooded", "Reptile"]}""".fromJson[Animal]
// res17: Either[String, Animal] = Right(
//   value = Animal(name = "Snake", categories = List("Cold-blooded", "Reptile"))
// )
```

A missing `categories` key decodes to an empty list instead of failing: the derived decoder no longer sees a plain collection decoder, so it asks the combined one for a value, and `JsonDecoder#orElse` passes the request on to the list decoder (see [Missing Fields](../reference/json-decoder.md#missing-fields)):

```scala
"""{"name": "Cat"}""".fromJson[Animal]
// res18: Either[String, Animal] = Right(
//   value = Animal(name = "Cat", categories = List())
// )
```

`JsonDecoder#orElse` buffers the input while the first decoder runs, so prefer `JsonDecoder.peekChar` when the first character tells the shapes apart (see [`peekChar`](../reference/json-decoder.md#peekchar)).

### See Also

- [Field Names](field-names.md) for renaming many keys at once, aliases and naming conventions
- [Validate Data While Decoding](validate-on-decode.md) for rejecting decoded values with `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail`
- [JSON AST](../reference/json-ast.md) for the `Json` type and cursors
- [JsonDecoder](../reference/json-decoder.md) for decoding from bytes, `JsonDecoder#map`, `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail`, `JsonDecoder#orElse` and missing fields
- [Annotations](../reference/annotations.md) for `@jsonField` and the other field annotations
- [Getting Started](../getting-started.md) for deriving a first decoder

## Read and Edit JSON of Unknown Shape

Goal: read a few values from a JSON document you have no case class for, such as a webhook payload, and forward a changed copy of it without losing the fields you do not model.

Use this guide when decoding into case classes would force you to model every level of nesting, or would drop the fields your case classes do not declare when you encode the document again. The `Json` AST keeps the whole document, and a `JsonCursor` points at one node inside it.

Step 1 parses the document, and step 2 defines the cursors the other steps use. Steps 3 to 8 are separate options that each start from the parsed document, so use the ones you need. Step 9 chains several edits into one function.

### What You Need

The AST and cursors are part of the core `zio-json` module:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

All code on this page uses these imports:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.{ Json, JsonCursor }
```

The [JSON AST](../reference/json-ast.md) reference page lists every method, case and error message in detail.

### 1. Parse the Payload into `Json`

The example payload is an `order.paid` event from a payment provider. The order is nested two levels down, and `metadata` holds information we do not want to forward:

```scala
val payload: String =
  """{
    |  "id": "evt_1001",
    |  "type": "order.paid",
    |  "data": {
    |    "order": {
    |      "id": 42,
    |      "customer": { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" },
    |      "items": [
    |        { "sku": "BOOK-1", "qty": 2, "price": 12.50 },
    |        { "sku": "PEN-7", "qty": 1, "price": 3.00 }
    |      ],
    |      "total": 28.00
    |    }
    |  },
    |  "metadata": { "source": "web", "debug": true }
    |}""".stripMargin
```

Decode it with `Json` as the target type. This accepts any valid JSON and returns `Either[String, Json]`, with a `Left` only when the text is not valid JSON:

```scala
val parsed: Either[String, Json] = payload.fromJson[Json]
```

To keep the next steps short, they work on the value taken out of the `Either`. In real code, stay inside the `Either`, as step 9 does:

```scala
val event: Json = parsed.fold(error => sys.error(error), identity)
```

### 2. Build Cursors for the Values You Need

A cursor is a path into a document. `JsonCursor#field` goes into a field of an object, `JsonCursor#element` goes into an element of an array, and the type steps (`JsonCursor#isObject`, `JsonCursor#isArray`, `JsonCursor#isString`, `JsonCursor#isNumber`, `JsonCursor#isBool` and `JsonCursor#isNull`) check the type of the current node. The `JsonCursor` companion has the same methods to start a path. Put `JsonCursor#isObject` before each deeper field step, and `JsonCursor#isArray` before an element step. Define the paths once and reuse them:

```scala
val order    = JsonCursor.field("data").isObject.field("order").isObject
val customer = order.field("customer").isObject
val email    = customer.field("email").isString
val items    = order.field("items").isArray
val total    = order.field("total").isNumber
```

Without the `JsonCursor#isObject` step, the path does not compile, because `JsonCursor#field` needs a cursor that ends on a `Json.Obj`:

```scala
JsonCursor.field("data").field("order")
// error: Cannot prove that zio.json.ast.Json <:< zio.json.ast.Json.Obj.
```

`Json#get` follows a cursor and returns the node it ends on. A cursor that ends with a type step returns that case of `Json`, so with `JsonCursor#isString` you get a `Json.Str`, and `Json.Str#value` gives the `String`. For a number, `Json.Num#value` is a `java.math.BigDecimal`. To read the event type, the customer's email and the order total from `event` (the payload parsed in step 1):

```scala
event.get(JsonCursor.field("type").isString).map(_.value)
// res2: Either[String, String] = Right(value = "order.paid")

event.get(email).map(_.value)
// res3: Either[String, String] = Right(value = "ada@example.com")

event.get(total).map(_.value)
// res4: Either[String, java.math.BigDecimal] = Right(value = 28.00)
```

To read an element of an array, add `JsonCursor#element` with a zero-based index after a `JsonCursor#isArray` step:

```scala
event.get(items.element(0).isObject.field("sku").isString).map(_.value)
// res5: Either[String, String] = Right(value = "BOOK-1")
```

The [Cursors](../reference/json-ast.md#cursors) reference section covers the cursor type and its other ways to build a path.

### 3. Handle Missing Fields and Wrong Types

`Json#get` returns a `Left` when the document does not match the cursor. Here `event` is the parsed payload from step 1, and `order` and `items` are the cursors to `data.order` and `data.order.items` from step 2. A field that does not exist gives `No such field`:

```scala
event.get(order.field("coupon"))
// res6: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = "No such field: 'coupon'")
```

A type step that does not match gives `expected <type>`. The order `id` is a number, not a string:

```scala
event.get(order.field("id").isString)
// res7: Either[String, Json.Str] = Left(value = "expected string")
```

An index past the end of an array has its own message:

```scala
event.get(items.element(5))
// res8: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = "The array does not have index 5")
```

The messages name only the last step that failed, not the whole path. When you read several values, add the path to the error yourself, for example with `left.map(error => s"data.order.id: $error")`. The full list of messages is in [Cursor Errors](../reference/json-ast.md#cursor-errors).

### 4. Decode Part of the Document into a Case Class

When one part of the document has a stable shape, decode just that part. Define case classes with a `JsonDecoder` for the parts you need:

```scala
final case class Customer(name: String, email: String)

object Customer {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Customer] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Customer]
}

final case class LineItem(sku: String, qty: Int, price: BigDecimal)

object LineItem {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[LineItem] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[LineItem]
}
```

Get the sub-tree with a cursor, then call `Json#as`, which uses the `JsonDecoder` of the target type. With `customer` and `items` (the cursors from step 2) and `event` (the payload from step 1), the customer object and the items array decode into domain types, while the rest of the payload stays untyped:

```scala
event.get(customer).flatMap(_.as[Customer])
// res9: Either[String, Customer] = Right(
//   value = Customer(name = "Ada", email = "ada@example.com")
// )

event.get(items).flatMap(_.as[List[LineItem]])
// res10: Either[String, List[LineItem]] = Right(
//   value = List(
//     LineItem(sku = "BOOK-1", qty = 2, price = 12.50),
//     LineItem(sku = "PEN-7", qty = 1, price = 3.00)
//   )
// )
```

If the sub-tree does not match, `Json#as` returns the usual decoder error, with a path that starts at the sub-tree, not at the root of the document. Decoding the order object as a `Customer` fails on the first missing field:

```scala
event.get(order).flatMap(_.as[Customer])
// res11: Either[String, Customer] = Left(value = ".name(missing)")
```

### 5. Replace a Value

`Json#transformAt` replaces the node at a cursor with the result of a function. The function receives the node with the type the cursor ends on, so with `email` (the cursor to `data.order.customer.email` from step 2) it receives a `Json.Str`. To mask the customer's email in `event`, the payload from step 1:

```scala
val masked: Either[String, Json] = event.transformAt(email)(_ => Json.Str("***"))
```

The email in the new document is masked:

```scala
masked.flatMap(_.get(email)).map(_.value)
// res12: Either[String, String] = Right(value = "***")
```

:::note
`Json` values are immutable: `Json#transformAt` and the other editing methods return a new document and leave `event` unchanged. They return an `Either` because the cursor may not match, with the same messages as `Json#get`.
:::

### 6. Delete a Field

`Json#delete` removes the node at a cursor. To drop the `debug` flag from `metadata` in `event`, the payload from step 1:

```scala
println(
  event
    .delete(JsonCursor.field("metadata").isObject.field("debug"))
    .flatMap(_.get(JsonCursor.field("metadata")))
)
// Right({"source":"web"})
```

:::warning
`Json#delete` does not check a type step that comes after the last field or element step. A cursor ending in `field("debug").isString` still deletes `debug`, although it is a boolean. Type steps earlier in the path are checked. If the type matters, check it with `Json#get` before deleting.
:::

### 7. Move a Field to a New Key

`Json#relocate(from, to)` copies the node at `from` over the node at `to`, then deletes the node at `from`. The target must already exist. In this example, the downstream service expects `customer` at the top level of `event` (the payload from step 1), not inside `data.order`, and relocating `customer` (the cursor from step 2) to a key that is not in the document fails with `No such field`:

```scala
event.relocate(customer, JsonCursor.field("customer"))
// res14: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = "No such field: 'customer'")
```

To move a node to a new key, add a placeholder first, then relocate over it. `JsonCursor.isObject` points at the root object, so `Json#transformAt` with it can add a field through `Json.Obj#add`:

```scala
val moved: Either[String, Json] =
  event
    .transformAt(JsonCursor.isObject)(_.add("customer", Json.Null))
    .flatMap(_.relocate(customer, JsonCursor.field("customer")))
```

The customer object is now at the top level, and `data.order` no longer contains it:

```scala
println(moved.flatMap(_.get(JsonCursor.field("customer"))))
// Right({"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com"})

moved.flatMap(_.get(order)).map(_.keys)
// res16: Either[String, zio.Chunk[String]] = Right(
//   value = IndexedSeq("id", "items", "total")
// )
```

### 8. Fill In Missing Defaults with `Json#merge`

`Json#merge` combines two documents: objects are merged key by key, recursively, and for two scalar values the right-hand side wins. To add only the values the event lacks, write the defaults as a `Json` document:

```scala
val defaults: Json = Json.Obj(
  "metadata" -> Json.Obj("source" -> Json.Str("unknown"), "retries" -> Json.Num(0)),
  "currency" -> Json.Str("EUR")
)
```

Then merge `event` (the payload from step 1) into the defaults, with the event on the right. The event's `source` wins over the default, while `retries` and `currency` come from the defaults:

```scala
println(defaults.merge(event).get(JsonCursor.field("metadata")))
// Right({"source":"web","retries":0,"debug":true})

defaults.merge(event).get(JsonCursor.field("currency").isString).map(_.value)
// res18: Either[String, String] = Right(value = "EUR")
```

The keys of the left-hand document come first in the result. Put the defaults on the right (`event.merge(defaults)`) only when the defaults should overwrite the event. [Combining Documents](../reference/json-ast.md#combining-documents) describes how arrays and other pairs of values merge.

### 9. Chain the Edits in One Function

Every editing method returns an `Either`, so a for-comprehension chains them and stops at the first error. This `clean` function parses a raw payload and applies the edits of steps 5 to 8, using the cursors `email` and `customer` from step 2 and `defaults` from step 8:

```scala
def clean(raw: String): Either[String, Json] =
  for {
    json      <- raw.fromJson[Json]
    masked    <- json.transformAt(email)(_ => Json.Str("***"))
    noDebug   <- masked.delete(JsonCursor.field("metadata").isObject.field("debug"))
    withSlot  <- noDebug.transformAt(JsonCursor.isObject)(_.add("customer", Json.Null))
    relocated <- withSlot.relocate(customer, JsonCursor.field("customer"))
  } yield defaults.merge(relocated)
```

`toJsonPretty` renders a `Json` value with indentation, and `toJson` renders it on one line. To print the cleaned payload:

```scala
clean(payload).foreach(json => println(json.toJsonPretty))
// {
//   "metadata" : {
//     "source" : "web",
//     "retries" : 0
//   },
//   "currency" : "EUR",
//   "id" : "evt_1001",
//   "type" : "order.paid",
//   "data" : {
//     "order" : {
//       "id" : 42,
//       "items" : [
//         {
//           "sku" : "BOOK-1",
//           "qty" : 2,
//           "price" : 12.50
//         },
//         {
//           "sku" : "PEN-7",
//           "qty" : 1,
//           "price" : 3.00
//         }
//       ],
//       "total" : 28.00
//     }
//   },
//   "customer" : {
//     "name" : "Ada",
//     "email" : "***"
//   }
// }
```

A payload that does not match fails with the error of the first step that did not match. This one has no `customer`:

```scala
clean("""{"data": {"order": {"id": 7}}, "metadata": {}}""")
// res20: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = "No such field: 'customer'")
```

### See Also

- [JSON AST](../reference/json-ast.md) for the other ways to read and change a document: the `as*` methods, the `Json.Obj` field methods, `transformDown` and `transformUp`, `foldDown` and `foldUp`, `intersect`, and composing cursors with `>>>`.
- [Embedding Raw JSON in Case Classes](../reference/json-ast.md#embedding-raw-json-in-case-classes) to keep a free-form part of a typed model in a field of type `Json` or `Json.Obj`.
- [Load a YAML Configuration File](load-yaml-config.md) to read YAML into the same `Json` type.

## Control the JSON a Type Encodes To

Goal: make one of your types encode to the exact JSON shape you need, such as the shape another service expects.

A derived encoder writes a case class as an object with one key per field, and a sealed trait as an object with one key that names the subtype (see the [Getting Started](../getting-started.md) tutorial). When the JSON you need differs from that, pick the step that matches the difference:

| The JSON you need                                         | Step                                                                       |
|-----------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Other field names, a field left out, `null` for `None`    | [1](#1-rename-drop-or-null-out-fields-with-annotations)                    |
| A wrapper type written as the value it wraps              | [2](#2-write-a-wrapper-type-as-its-bare-value)                             |
| Extra computed fields, or an array instead of an object   | [3](#3-write-a-different-shape-through-an-intermediate-type)               |
| A sealed trait tagged by a field such as `"type"`         | [4](#4-tag-a-sealed-trait-with-a-type-field)                               |
| One naming rule for every type in the program             | [5](#5-apply-one-format-to-every-type)                                     |

Each step below is a separate option; use the ones you need. The steps derive only a `JsonEncoder`, because this page is about writing JSON. Derive a `JsonCodec` instead when you also read the same JSON back.

### What You Need

Only the core module:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

Every example on this page uses one import:

```scala
import zio.json._
```

### 1. Rename, Drop or Null Out Fields with Annotations

When the shape is right but the details are not, keep the derived encoder and annotate the case class fields. `@jsonField` renames a field, `@jsonExclude` leaves it out, and `@jsonExplicitNull` writes `null` for a `None` instead of omitting the field:

```scala
final case class Account(
  @jsonField("user_name") userName: String,
  @jsonExclude password: String,
  @jsonExplicitNull nickname: Option[String]
)

object Account {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Account] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Account]
}
```

The password is gone, the name uses the new key, and the empty nickname is written as `null`:

```scala
println(Account("ada", "secret", None).toJson)
// {"user_name":"ada","nickname":null}
```

[Field Names](./field-names.md) covers renaming every field with one rule, and [Optional, Default and Null Fields](./optional-and-default-fields.md) covers `null`, empty collections and excluded fields, including what they mean for decoding. The [Annotations reference](../reference/annotations.md) lists every annotation.

### 2. Write a Wrapper Type as Its Bare Value

A case class that wraps one value, such as an `OrderId` around a `String`, derives to an object like `{"value":"A-17"}`. To write just the string, build the encoder from the `String` encoder with `JsonEncoder#contramap`, which takes a function from your type to a type that already has an encoder:

```scala
final case class OrderId(value: String)

object OrderId {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[OrderId] = JsonEncoder[String].contramap(_.value)
}
```

The id is now a plain JSON string:

```scala
println(OrderId("A-17").toJson)
// "A-17"
```

[Build an Encoder or Decoder from an Existing One](./manual-instances.md) adds the matching decoder and bundles both into a codec.

### 3. Write a Different Shape Through an Intermediate Type

When the JSON has a different structure from your type, for example a computed `total` that your `Order` does not store, define a case class with exactly the JSON's structure, derive its encoder, and build your type's encoder from it with `JsonEncoder#contramap`. An order line is an ordinary derived object:

```scala
final case class OrderLine(sku: String, price: BigDecimal)

object OrderLine {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[OrderLine] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[OrderLine]
}
```

`OrderJson` describes the JSON, and the `Order` encoder converts each order into it:

```scala
final case class OrderJson(id: OrderId, lines: List[OrderLine], total: BigDecimal)

object OrderJson {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[OrderJson] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[OrderJson]
}

final case class Order(id: OrderId, lines: List[OrderLine])

object Order {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Order] =
    JsonEncoder[OrderJson].contramap(o => OrderJson(o.id, o.lines, o.lines.map(_.price).sum))
}
```

The `Order` is written with the computed total, and its `id` uses the bare-string encoder from step 2:

```scala
val order = Order(OrderId("A-17"), List(OrderLine("pen", BigDecimal("1.50")), OrderLine("ink", BigDecimal("4.25"))))
// order: Order = Order(
//   id = OrderId(value = "A-17"),
//   lines = List(
//     OrderLine(sku = "pen", price = 1.50),
//     OrderLine(sku = "ink", price = 4.25)
//   )
// )

println(order.toJson)
// {"id":"A-17","lines":[{"sku":"pen","price":1.50},{"sku":"ink","price":4.25}],"total":5.75}
```

The intermediate type can also be a tuple. Tuples are written as JSON arrays, so going through a tuple writes a case class as an array:

```scala
final case class Point(x: Double, y: Double)

object Point {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Point] = JsonEncoder[(Double, Double)].contramap(p => (p.x, p.y))
}
```

The point is written as a two-element array:

```scala
println(Point(1.0, 2.5).toJson)
// [1.0,2.5]
```

### 4. Tag a Sealed Trait with a Type Field

Many APIs put the subtype name in a field of the object, such as `{"type":"card",...}`, instead of the default wrapper object. Put `@jsonDiscriminator` on the sealed trait to name that field, and `@jsonHint` on a subtype to change the name written for it:

```scala
@jsonDiscriminator("type")
sealed trait Payment

object Payment {
  @jsonHint("card") final case class Card(last4: String)            extends Payment
  @jsonHint("bank_transfer") final case class BankTransfer(iban: String) extends Payment

  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Payment] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Payment]
}
```

Each payment carries its tag in the `type` field:

```scala
val payments: List[Payment] = List(Payment.Card("4242"), Payment.BankTransfer("DE89"))
// payments: List[Payment] = List(
//   Card(last4 = "4242"),
//   BankTransfer(iban = "DE89")
// )

println(payments.toJson)
// [{"type":"card","last4":"4242"},{"type":"bank_transfer","iban":"DE89"}]
```

The encoder is for `Payment`, so encode values typed as `Payment`. On both Scala 2 and Scala 3, `Payment.Card("4242").toJson` does not compile, because the compiler then looks for a `JsonEncoder[Payment.Card]`. Write `(Payment.Card("4242"): Payment).toJson` instead, or derive an encoder for the subtype as well if you want it written without the tag.

[Sealed Traits](./sealed-traits.md) covers the other choices for a sealed family: renaming all hints with one rule, writing case objects as plain strings, and the cost of a discriminator field.

### 5. Apply One Format to Every Type

To use the same rule for every derived encoder instead of annotating each class, put an implicit `JsonCodecConfiguration` in scope where the encoders are derived. Here `fieldNameMapping` writes every field name in snake_case:

```scala
import zio.json._

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)

final case class Shipment(trackingCode: String, weightGrams: Int)

object Shipment {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Shipment] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Shipment]
}
```

The field names follow the configuration without any annotation on `Shipment`:

```scala
println(Shipment("X1", 250).toJson)
// {"tracking_code":"X1","weight_grams":250}
```

Annotations such as `@jsonField` and `@jsonMemberNames` take priority over the configuration. [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md) lists every option, including `sumTypeHandling` for a program-wide discriminator field.

### See Also

- [Build an Encoder or Decoder from an Existing One](./manual-instances.md) builds both directions from existing instances.
- [Encode a Type You Do Not Own](./third-party-types.md) applies `JsonEncoder#contramap` to a class from another library.
- [Write a Fast Encoder or Decoder by Hand](./low-level-codecs.md) for a shape that no existing encoder can produce.
- [Golden Testing](./golden-testing.md) catches unintended changes to the JSON your types encode to.
- [JsonEncoder reference](../reference/json-encoder.md) covers every encoder method, including `toJsonPretty` and `toJsonAST`.

## Field Names

Goal: make the JSON field names differ from the Scala field names of a case class.

By default, the JSON field names are the case class field names. This page shows three ways to change that:

- `@jsonField` renames one field.
- `@jsonMemberNames` renames every field with one rule.
- `@jsonAliases` accepts extra names when decoding.

Each step below is a separate option. Use the ones you need.

### What you need

Only `zio-json` and one import:

```scala
import zio.json._
```

### 1. Rename one field with `@jsonField`

Put `@jsonField` on a field and give it the JSON name:

```scala
case class Banana(@jsonField("bendiness") curvature: Double)

object Banana {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Banana] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Banana]
}
```

The field is written and read as `bendiness`:

```scala
println(Banana(0.5).toJson)
// {"bendiness":0.5}
"""{"bendiness":0.5}""".fromJson[Banana]
// res2: Either[String, Banana] = Right(value = Banana(curvature = 0.5))
```

### 2. Rename all fields with `@jsonMemberNames`

Put `@jsonMemberNames` on a case class. It takes a `JsonMemberFormat`, and the format is applied to every field name, for both encoding and decoding.

These formats are available:

| Format           | What it does                             |
|------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `SnakeCase`      | `passionFruit` becomes `passion_fruit`   |
| `KebabCase`      | `passionFruit` becomes `passion-fruit`   |
| `PascalCase`     | `passionFruit` becomes `PassionFruit`    |
| `CamelCase`      | `passion_fruit` becomes `passionFruit`   |
| `IdentityFormat` | Leaves the name as it is                 |
| `CustomCase(f)`  | Applies your own `String => String`      |

A `JsonMemberFormat` is itself a `String => String`, so you can call it to see what it does:

```scala
List[(String, JsonMemberFormat)](
  "SnakeCase"      -> SnakeCase,
  "KebabCase"      -> KebabCase,
  "PascalCase"     -> PascalCase,
  "CamelCase"      -> CamelCase,
  "IdentityFormat" -> IdentityFormat,
  "CustomCase"     -> CustomCase(_.toUpperCase)
).map { case (name, format) => name -> format("passionFruit") }
// res3: List[(String, String)] = List(
//   ("SnakeCase", "passion_fruit"),
//   ("KebabCase", "passion-fruit"),
//   ("PascalCase", "PassionFruit"),
//   ("CamelCase", "passionFruit"),
//   ("IdentityFormat", "passionFruit"),
//   ("CustomCase", "PASSIONFRUIT")
// )
```

Here is a basket where most fields are `snake_case` in JSON:

```scala
@jsonMemberNames(SnakeCase)
case class FruitBasket(
  passionFruit: Boolean,
  grannySmith: Boolean,
  dragonFruit: Boolean,
  @jsonField("blood-orange") bloodOrange: Boolean
)

object FruitBasket {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[FruitBasket] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[FruitBasket]
}
```

Three fields follow the format. `bloodOrange` has its own `@jsonField`, which takes priority over `@jsonMemberNames`:

```scala
println(FruitBasket(true, true, true, false).toJson)
// {"passion_fruit":true,"granny_smith":true,"dragon_fruit":true,"blood-orange":false}
```

The same names are expected when decoding:

```scala
"""{"passion_fruit":true,"granny_smith":true,"dragon_fruit":true,"blood-orange":false}""".fromJson[FruitBasket]
// res5: Either[String, FruitBasket] = Right(
//   value = FruitBasket(
//     passionFruit = true,
//     grannySmith = true,
//     dragonFruit = true,
//     bloodOrange = false
//   )
// )
```

### 3. Use a custom rule

`CustomCase` wraps any `String => String`. Define the function as a normal value, then pass it to the format:

```scala
object Rules {
  val shout: String => String = _.toUpperCase
}

@jsonMemberNames(CustomCase(Rules.shout))
case class Lemon(sourness: Int)

object Lemon {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Lemon] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Lemon]
}
```

The field name is written in upper case:

```scala
println(Lemon(7).toJson)
// {"SOURNESS":7}
```

### 4. Set the format for the whole program

Instead of annotating each class, set `fieldNameMapping` in an implicit `JsonCodecConfiguration`. It applies to every codec derived while the configuration is in scope. The `@jsonMemberNames` annotation on a class takes priority over it. To write every field in snake_case without annotating each class:

```scala
implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)

case class Cherry(sweetnessLevel: Int)

implicit val cherryCodec: JsonCodec[Cherry] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Cherry]
```

### 5. Read old names with `@jsonAliases`

After a field has been renamed, you may still receive JSON that uses the old name. `@jsonAliases` lists extra names that the decoder accepts for that field. It was added in zio-json 0.5.0. To accept two old names for `seedCount`:

```scala
case class Strawberry(@jsonAliases("seeds", "pips") seedCount: Int)

object Strawberry {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Strawberry] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Strawberry]
}
```

The old names and the new name decode to equal values:

```scala
"""{"seeds":32}""".fromJson[Strawberry]
// res8: Either[String, Strawberry] = Right(value = Strawberry(seedCount = 32))
"""{"pips":32}""".fromJson[Strawberry]
// res9: Either[String, Strawberry] = Right(value = Strawberry(seedCount = 32))
"""{"seedCount":32}""".fromJson[Strawberry]
// res10: Either[String, Strawberry] = Right(
//   value = Strawberry(seedCount = 32)
// )
```

Keep these points in mind:

- The annotation has no effect on encoding. The encoder always writes the main name.
- An alias is matched exactly as you wrote it. A `@jsonMemberNames` format is not applied to aliases.
- A field name and its aliases must not collide with another field or alias of the same class. If they do, the code still compiles, but on Scala 2 and Scala 3 the decoder throws an `AssertionError` at runtime when the codec is first initialised.

### See also

- [Annotations](../reference/annotations.md) lists every derivation annotation in one table.
- [Sealed traits](sealed-traits.md) shows how to rename the type hints of a sealed family.
- [Getting Started](../getting-started.md) covers the basics of derived codecs.

## Generate Case Classes from Sample JSON

Goal: get a first draft of case classes and codecs for a JSON document you only have a sample of, such as a response copied from an API's documentation.

`zio.json.codegen.Generator.printCaseClasses` reads the sample and prints Scala source code, which you copy into your project and review. It is a developer utility that you run once in a REPL or a small program, not a build step. Run the steps in order.

### What You Need

`Generator` is part of the core `zio-json` module, so there is nothing else to add:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

The model in step 3 uses the usual import for codecs:

```scala
import zio.json._
```

The generated code uses `DeriveJsonCodec`, described in [JsonCodec](../reference/json-codec.md).

### 1. Run the Generator on the Sample

`Generator.printCaseClasses(input: String): Unit` parses its argument and prints the generated code to standard output. It returns nothing, so call it where you can read the output: a REPL, a worksheet, or a small `main` method. With [Scala CLI](https://scala-cli.virtuslab.org/), start a REPL that has `zio-json` on the classpath:

```bash
scala-cli repl --dep dev.zio::zio-json:1.1.3
```

Then paste the sample into a call to `Generator.printCaseClasses`. The same code works as the body of a `main` method in a scratch file. For an order from a shop's API:

```scala
import zio.json.codegen.Generator

Generator.printCaseClasses(
  """{
    |  "id": 42,
    |  "orderNumber": 9876543210,
    |  "placedAt": "2024-05-01T10:15:30",
    |  "deliveryDate": "2024-05-03",
    |  "trackingId": "3f1c2a9e-8b7d-4c6e-9a1b-2d3e4f5a6b7c",
    |  "total": 28.5,
    |  "paid": true,
    |  "customer": { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" },
    |  "line_items": [
    |    { "sku": "BOOK-1", "qty": 2, "price": 12.5, "note": null },
    |    { "sku": "PEN-7", "qty": 1, "price": 3, "note": "gift", "giftWrap": true }
    |  ],
    |  "tags": ["new", "priority"]
    |}""".stripMargin
)
```

If the argument is not valid JSON, `Generator.printCaseClasses` prints `Invalid JSON: ` followed by the input, instead of failing.

### 2. Review the Printed Classes and Types

The call in step 1 prints the following code. It is the real output of that call, with the colour codes removed (see the note after it):

```scala title="Printed output"
final case class RootObject(
  id: Int,
  orderNumber: Long,
  placedAt: java.time.LocalDateTime,
  deliveryDate: java.time.LocalDate,
  trackingId: java.util.UUID,
  total: Double,
  paid: Boolean,
  customer: Customer,
  line_items: List[LineItems],
  tags: List[String]
)

object RootObject {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[RootObject] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}

final case class Customer(
  name: String,
  email: String
)

object Customer {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Customer] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}

final case class LineItems(
  sku: String,
  qty: Int,
  price: Double,
  note: Option[String],
  giftWrap: Option[Boolean]
)

object LineItems {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[LineItems] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}
```

:::note
`Generator.printCaseClasses` wraps the code in ANSI colour codes, so it shows in cyan in a terminal. If you redirect the output to a file, the file starts with the escape sequence `ESC[36m` and ends with `ESC[0m`. Remove them before compiling the file.
:::

The generator prints one case class for each JSON object, with a companion object that derives a `JsonCodec`. It does not print a package or an `import zio.json._` line. The root object is always called `RootObject`. A nested object is named after its key in PascalCase: `customer` becomes `Customer`, and the key is split at `_`, `-` and `.`, so the elements of `line_items` become `LineItems`. If the root of the sample is an array of objects, the generated class for its elements is called `RootObject`.

Check each field's type against this table, which shows how the generator picks a type from the value in the sample:

| JSON value in the sample                              | Scala type                |
|-------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| `true` or `false`                                     | `Boolean`                 |
| An integer in the `Int` range                         | `Int`                     |
| An integer in the `Long` range                        | `Long`                    |
| Any other number up to `Double.MaxValue`              | `Double`                  |
| A number larger than `Double.MaxValue`                | `BigDecimal`              |
| A string in ISO date-time format                      | `java.time.LocalDateTime` |
| A string in ISO date format (`2024-05-03`)            | `java.time.LocalDate`     |
| A string in UUID format                               | `java.util.UUID`          |
| Any other string                                      | `String`                  |
| An object                                             | A new case class          |
| An array                                              | `List[A]`                 |

For an array, the generator combines the types of all elements into one element type. Numbers widen: `Int` and `Long` give `Long`, an integer and a `Double` give `Double`, and anything with a `BigDecimal` gives `BigDecimal`. That is why `price` is a `Double`: the sample has `12.5` and `3`. For an array of objects, the fields of all the objects are combined. A field that is `null` in one element and has a value in another becomes an `Option`, like `note`, and a field that is missing from some elements becomes an `Option` too, like `giftWrap`.

### 3. Adapt the Output for Your Project

The printed code shown in step 2 compiles once `import zio.json._` is added, and it decodes the sample. Before you commit it, fix the names and types. For the order, give the classes domain names, use `BigDecimal` for money, which should not be a `Double`, and rename `line_items` to `lineItems` with `@jsonField` (see [Field Names](field-names.md)), so the Scala name follows Scala conventions while the JSON key stays the same:

```scala
final case class Order(
  id: Int,
  orderNumber: Long,
  placedAt: java.time.LocalDateTime,
  deliveryDate: java.time.LocalDate,
  trackingId: java.util.UUID,
  total: BigDecimal,
  paid: Boolean,
  customer: Customer,
  @jsonField("line_items") lineItems: List[LineItem],
  tags: List[String]
)

object Order {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Order] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}

final case class Customer(name: String, email: String)

object Customer {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Customer] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}

final case class LineItem(
  sku: String,
  qty: Int,
  price: BigDecimal,
  note: Option[String],
  giftWrap: Option[Boolean]
)

object LineItem {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[LineItem] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}
```

### 4. Check That the Sample Decodes

Decode the sample from step 1 into `Order`, the adapted model from step 3:

```scala
"""{
  |  "id": 42,
  |  "orderNumber": 9876543210,
  |  "placedAt": "2024-05-01T10:15:30",
  |  "deliveryDate": "2024-05-03",
  |  "trackingId": "3f1c2a9e-8b7d-4c6e-9a1b-2d3e4f5a6b7c",
  |  "total": 28.5,
  |  "paid": true,
  |  "customer": { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" },
  |  "line_items": [
  |    { "sku": "BOOK-1", "qty": 2, "price": 12.5, "note": null },
  |    { "sku": "PEN-7", "qty": 1, "price": 3, "note": "gift", "giftWrap": true }
  |  ],
  |  "tags": ["new", "priority"]
  |}""".stripMargin.fromJson[Order]
// res2: Either[String, Order] = Right(
//   value = Order(
//     id = 42,
//     orderNumber = 9876543210L,
//     placedAt = 2024-05-01T10:15:30,
//     deliveryDate = 2024-05-03,
//     trackingId = 3f1c2a9e-8b7d-4c6e-9a1b-2d3e4f5a6b7c,
//     total = 28.5,
//     paid = true,
//     customer = Customer(name = "Ada", email = "ada@example.com"),
//     lineItems = List(
//       LineItem(
//         sku = "BOOK-1",
//         qty = 2,
//         price = 12.5,
//         note = None,
//         giftWrap = None
//       ),
//       LineItem(
//         sku = "PEN-7",
//         qty = 1,
//         price = 3,
//         note = Some(value = "gift"),
//         giftWrap = Some(value = true)
//       )
//     ),
//     tags = List("new", "priority")
//   )
// )
```

Check the types against the API's documentation as well. A single sample cannot show that a field the sample always fills can be `null`, or that an ID that fits in an `Int` today can grow beyond it.

### Limitations

The generator has no options, and several inputs make it fail or print code that does not compile. Fix the sample before you run it, or fix the output by hand:

- An empty array anywhere in the sample throws `java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: empty.reduceLeft`, because there is no element to take a type from. Put one representative element in each array.
- An array whose elements have types that cannot be combined, such as `[1, "x"]`, throws an exception with the message `Cannot combine:` followed by the two types (`LEFT: JInt`, `RIGHT: JString`). The same happens when a field holds a number in one object of an array and a string in another.
- A field that is `null` in the sample and never has a value gets the type `null`, which is not a valid Scala type. Replace it with an `Option` of the right type.
- Field names are copied unchanged. A key such as `first-name` or `type` produces a field that does not compile. Rename the field and keep the JSON key with `@jsonField("first-name")`, or quote it with backticks.
- Two nested objects with the same key in different places produce two case classes with the same name, even when their fields differ. Rename one of them.
- An integer outside the `Long` range becomes a `Double`, which loses precision. Use `BigInt` or `BigDecimal` instead.
- A date-time with an offset, such as `2024-05-01T10:15:30Z`, becomes a `java.time.LocalDateTime`, but the `LocalDateTime` decoder rejects the offset. Change the type to `java.time.OffsetDateTime` or `java.time.Instant`.
- The generated code uses Scala 2 syntax (`implicit val`), which also compiles on Scala 3. The generator's tests run only on Scala 2.12 and 2.13.

For example, a sample whose keys are not valid Scala identifiers:

```scala
import zio.json.codegen.Generator

Generator.printCaseClasses("""{"first-name": "Ada", "type": "user"}""")
```

The call prints this code, which does not compile (colour codes removed):

```scala title="Printed output"
final case class RootObject(
  first-name: String,
  type: String
)

object RootObject {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[RootObject] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}
```

Rename `first-name` with `@jsonField`, and quote `type` with backticks. Both fields keep their JSON keys:

```scala
final case class Account(@jsonField("first-name") firstName: String, `type`: String)

object Account {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Account] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}

"""{"first-name": "Ada", "type": "user"}""".fromJson[Account]
// res4: Either[String, Account] = Right(
//   value = Account(firstName = "Ada", type = "user")
// )
```

### See Also

- [JsonCodec](../reference/json-codec.md) for the derived codecs the generator writes into each companion object.
- [Field Names](field-names.md) to rename fields or apply a naming convention such as snake_case to a whole class.
- [Optional, Default and Null Fields](optional-and-default-fields.md) for how `Option` fields and default values decode, which helps when you adjust the generated types.
- [Read and Edit JSON of Unknown Shape](edit-json-with-cursors.md) to read a few values from a document with cursors, without a model at all.

## Derive Codecs for Generic Types

Goal: derive one codec that works for every element type of a generic case class or sealed trait, such as `Box[A]`, `Page[A]` or `Result[A]`.

By the end of this guide you will have codecs for a generic wrapper, a generic page of results, a generic sealed trait and a generic tree, on Scala 2 and on Scala 3. We start with one type parameter and then add separate encoders and decoders, sealed families and recursion.

### The Problem

A codec for a non-generic type is a single value: `implicit val codec: JsonCodec[User]`. A generic type has no single codec, because the JSON for `Box[Int]` depends on how an `Int` is written, and the JSON for `Box[User]` depends on how a `User` is written. Writing a separate `implicit val` for `Box[Int]`, `Box[String]` and every other element type you use does not scale, and it breaks as soon as a new element type appears.

The fix is a codec that is a function of the element codecs: an `implicit def` (Scala 2) or a `given` with type parameters (Scala 3) that asks for the instances of `A` and derives the instance of `Box[A]` from them.

### What You Need

Only the core module:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

The Scala 2 examples on this page use this import:

```scala
import zio.json._
```

The guide assumes you know how to derive a codec for a plain case class (see the [Getting Started](../getting-started.md) tutorial). Higher-kinded types, such as a case class with a parameter `F[_]`, are not covered here.

### 1. Derive a Codec for a Generic Case Class

Put an `implicit def` in the companion object. Its context bounds ask for a `JsonEncoder[A]` and a `JsonDecoder[A]`, and its body derives the codec of `Box[A]` with them:

```scala
final case class Box[A](value: A)

object Box {
  implicit def codec[A: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder]: JsonCodec[Box[A]] =
    DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Box[A]]
}
```

Any element type that has an encoder and a decoder now works, including another `Box`:

```scala
println(Box(42).toJson)
// {"value":42}
println(Box(List("a", "b")).toJson)
// {"value":["a","b"]}
"""{"value":{"value":true}}""".fromJson[Box[Box[Boolean]]]
// res3: Either[String, Box[Box[Boolean]]] = Right(
//   value = Box(value = Box(value = true))
// )
```

Ask for `JsonEncoder[A]` and `JsonDecoder[A]` rather than `JsonCodec[A]`. A `JsonCodec[A]` also provides both, but the separate bounds also accept element types that have two separate instances and no codec, such as `Sku` here:

```scala
final case class Sku(code: String)

object Sku {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Sku] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Sku]
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Sku] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Sku]
}
```

`Box[Sku]` finds both instances of `Sku` through the bounds:

```scala
println(Box(Sku("A-1")).toJson)
// {"value":{"code":"A-1"}}
```

With more than one type parameter, add bounds for each of them:

```scala
final case class Pair[A, B](first: A, second: B)

object Pair {
  implicit def codec[A: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder, B: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder]: JsonCodec[Pair[A, B]] =
    DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Pair[A, B]]
}
```

Encoding a `Pair[String, Int]` uses both bounds:

```scala
println(Pair("id", 7).toJson)
// {"first":"id","second":7}
```

A variance annotation such as `Box[+A]` is fine here, because the type parameter of the `implicit def` is a new, invariant one. The `@jsonDerive` annotation from `zio-json-macros` cannot do this: it copies the variance annotation into the generated method, and `@jsonDerive final case class Box[+A](value: A)` does not compile. [@jsonDerive Macro Annotation](../reference/zio-json-macros.md#generic-classes) shows the error.

### 2. Derive Only an Encoder or a Decoder

A codec needs an encoder and a decoder for `A`. When some element types can only be written, for example events you send but never read, derive the two sides separately. Each side asks only for what it needs:

```scala
final case class Page[A](items: List[A], total: Int)

object Page {
  implicit def encoder[A: JsonEncoder]: JsonEncoder[Page[A]] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Page[A]]
  implicit def decoder[A: JsonDecoder]: JsonDecoder[Page[A]] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Page[A]]
}
```

`AuditEvent` has an encoder and no decoder:

```scala
final case class AuditEvent(action: String)

object AuditEvent {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[AuditEvent] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[AuditEvent]
}
```

A `Page[AuditEvent]` can still be encoded, and a `Page[Int]` can be decoded:

```scala
println(Page(List(AuditEvent("login")), 1).toJson)
// {"items":[{"action":"login"}],"total":1}
"""{"items":[1,2],"total":2}""".fromJson[Page[Int]]
// res7: Either[String, Page[Int]] = Right(
//   value = Page(items = List(1, 2), total = 2)
// )
```

The `Box` codec from the previous section cannot do this, because it needs both instances of `AuditEvent` even to encode:

```scala
Box(AuditEvent("login")).toJson
// error: could not find implicit value for parameter encoder: zio.json.JsonEncoder[repl.MdocSession.MdocApp0.Box[repl.MdocSession.MdocApp0.AuditEvent]]
```

### 3. Derive a Generic Sealed Trait

A generic sealed trait works the same way: the `implicit def` goes in the companion of the trait, and the cases are derived along with it. Cases that do not use the type parameter can extend `Result[Nothing]`, which the variance annotation `+A` allows:

```scala
sealed trait Result[+A]
final case class Ok[A](value: A)        extends Result[A]
final case class Failed(reason: String) extends Result[Nothing]
case object Pending                     extends Result[Nothing]

object Result {
  implicit def codec[A: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder]: JsonCodec[Result[A]] =
    DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Result[A]]
}
```

Each case is written with its name as the key, as for any sealed trait:

```scala
println((Ok(1): Result[Int]).toJson)
// {"Ok":{"value":1}}
println((Failed("timeout"): Result[Int]).toJson)
// {"Failed":{"reason":"timeout"}}
println((Pending: Result[Int]).toJson)
// {"Pending":{}}
"""{"Ok":{"value":"done"}}""".fromJson[Result[String]]
// res12: Either[String, Result[String]] = Right(value = Ok(value = "done"))
```

`Pending` is written as `{"Pending":{}}` because `enumValuesAsStrings` is off by default on Scala 2. [Sealed traits](sealed-traits.md) shows how to change the keys and how to use a discriminator field.

:::warning[Scala 3: a case class that extends `Result[Nothing]` crashes the compiler]
On Scala 3.9.0, deriving `Result` fails with a compiler crash (`java.lang.AssertionError: assertion failed: TypeRef(..., class Failed)`) when the family has a case class that does not take the type parameter, such as `Failed` above. Case objects are fine. Give such a case class the type parameter of the trait, `final case class Failed[A](reason: String) extends Result[A]`, as the Scala 3 example below does.
:::

### 4. Derive a Recursive Generic Type

A tree whose children are trees of the same type refers to its own codec. On Scala 2, the plain `implicit def` from the first section compiles, but it calls itself without end when the codec is built:

```scala
final case class BrokenTree[A](value: A, children: List[BrokenTree[A]])

object BrokenTree {
  implicit def codec[A: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder]: JsonCodec[BrokenTree[A]] =
    DeriveJsonCodec.gen[BrokenTree[A]]
}
```

Encoding any `BrokenTree`, even one without children, throws a `java.lang.StackOverflowError`. The derived codec looks up the codec for `List[BrokenTree[A]]`, which calls `BrokenTree.codec[A]` again, which derives a new codec, and so on.

Inside the method, derive the codec once and store it in a local `implicit lazy val`. The derivation then finds that value for the children instead of calling the method again:

```scala
final case class Tree[A](value: A, children: List[Tree[A]])

object Tree {
  implicit def codec[A: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder]: JsonCodec[Tree[A]] = {
    implicit lazy val self: JsonCodec[Tree[A]] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Tree[A]]
    self
  }
}
```

The tree now encodes and decodes at any depth:

```scala
println(Tree(1, List(Tree(2, Nil))).toJson)
// {"value":1,"children":[{"value":2,"children":[]}]}
"""{"value":1,"children":[{"value":2,"children":[]}]}""".fromJson[Tree[Int]]
// res15: Either[String, Tree[Int]] = Right(
//   value = Tree(value = 1, children = List(Tree(value = 2, children = List())))
// )
```

A recursive type without type parameters has the same problem on Scala 2 in another form: `implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Node] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Node]` fails at runtime with a `NullPointerException` inside an `ExceptionInInitializerError`. Declare it as an `implicit lazy val`, or wrap the derived instance in `JsonEncoder.suspend` and `JsonDecoder.suspend` as shown in [JsonEncoder](../reference/json-encoder.md#recursive-encoders). Scala 3 needs none of this, as the next section shows.

### 5. Derive Generic Types on Scala 3

On Scala 3, a `derives` clause on a generic case class does all of the above in one line:

```scala
final case class Box[A](value: A) derives JsonCodec
```

The given that `derives JsonCodec` generates asks for a `JsonCodec[A]`. When an element type has only a separate encoder and decoder, write the given yourself, with the same bounds as the Scala 2 `implicit def`:

```scala
final case class Page[A](items: List[A], total: Int)

object Page {
  given [A: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder]: JsonCodec[Page[A]] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen
}
```

Separate encoder and decoder givens take one bound each:

```scala
final case class Delta[A](before: A, after: A)

object Delta {
  given [A: JsonEncoder]: JsonEncoder[Delta[A]] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen
  given [A: JsonDecoder]: JsonDecoder[Delta[A]] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen
}
```

A generic sealed trait derives with `derives JsonCodec` on the trait. Every case class takes the type parameter, which avoids the compiler crash described in the warning above. A case object can still extend `Result[Nothing]`:

```scala
sealed trait Result[+A] derives JsonCodec
final case class Ok[A](value: A)           extends Result[A]
final case class Failed[A](reason: String) extends Result[A]
case object Pending                        extends Result[Nothing]
```

A recursive generic type needs no `lazy val` on Scala 3:

```scala
final case class Tree[A](value: A, children: List[Tree[A]]) derives JsonCodec
```

Running the example file on Scala 3.9.0 prints:

```text
Box: {"value":"x"}
Page: {"items":[1,2],"total":2}
Page decoded: Right(Page(List(a),1))
Delta: {"before":1,"after":2}
Ok: {"Ok":{"value":1}}
Failed: {"Failed":{"reason":"timeout"}}
Pending: {"Pending":{}}
Result decoded: Right(Failed(timeout))
Tree: {"value":1,"children":[{"value":2,"children":[]}]}
Tree decoded: Right(Tree(1,List(Tree(2,List()))))
```

Deriving a generic sealed trait on Scala 3 also prints an unchecked warning (E092) for the generated code. For the example above it reads `the type test for ...GenericTypesExample.Ok[A] cannot be checked at runtime because its type arguments can't be determined from ...GenericTypesExample.Result[A]`, with the full package names in place of the dots. The warning is harmless, but it fails a build that turns warnings into errors (`-Werror`). [Derive Codecs on Scala 3](scala-3-derivation.md#6-derive-codecs-for-generic-case-classes) shows the compile error you get when an element type has no `JsonCodec`.

### See Also

- [Derive Codecs on Scala 3](scala-3-derivation.md) covers `derives`, enums, union types and opaque types.
- [Sealed traits](sealed-traits.md) covers type hints and discriminator fields for any sealed family.
- [@jsonDerive Macro Annotation](../reference/zio-json-macros.md#generic-classes) shows what `@jsonDerive` generates for a generic class on Scala 2.
- [Scala 2 and Scala 3 differences](../explanation/scala-2-vs-scala-3.md) lists the recursion and generic sealed trait differences together with the others.
