## Sealed Traits

Goal: change how a sealed trait and its subtypes look in JSON.

By default, a value of a sealed family is written as an object with one key, the short class name, whose value is the encoded subtype:

```json
{"Banana":{"curvature":0.5}}
```

This page shows how to change the key (the type hint), how to use a discriminator field instead, and how case objects can become plain strings. Each step is a separate option. Use the ones you need.

### What you need

Every example on this page uses one import:

```scala
import zio.json._
```

### 1. Change a type hint with `@jsonHint`

Put `@jsonHint` on a subtype to choose its key:

```scala
sealed trait Fruit

@jsonHint("banaani") case class Banana(curvature: Double) extends Fruit
@jsonHint("omena") case class Apple(poison: Boolean)      extends Fruit

object Fruit {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Fruit] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Fruit]
}
```

The keys are now `banaani` and `omena`:

```scala
println((Banana(0.5): Fruit).toJson)
// {"banaani":{"curvature":0.5}}
println((Apple(false): Fruit).toJson)
// {"omena":{"poison":false}}
```

### 2. Transform all hints with `@jsonHintNames`

`@jsonHintNames` goes on the sealed trait and applies a `JsonMemberFormat` to every hint in the family. It accepts the same formats as `@jsonMemberNames`, which are listed in [Field names](field-names.md). A `@jsonHint` on a subtype wins over the format. To write every hint of a family in snake_case:

```scala
@jsonHintNames(SnakeCase)
sealed trait FruitKind

case class GoodFruit(good: Boolean) extends FruitKind
case class BadFruit(bad: Boolean)   extends FruitKind

object FruitKind {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[FruitKind] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[FruitKind]
}
```

Each hint is the class name in snake_case:

```scala
println((GoodFruit(true): FruitKind).toJson)
// {"good_fruit":{"good":true}}
println((BadFruit(true): FruitKind).toJson)
// {"bad_fruit":{"bad":true}}
```

The codec of `FruitKind` expects the hint. You cannot decode a bare `{"good":true}` with it, and you cannot encode a `GoodFruit` on its own with it either.

#### Decode a single subtype

To read one subtype without a hint, give that subtype its own codec in its companion. A case class does not need a discriminator to be decoded on its own:

```scala
import zio.json._

@jsonHintNames(SnakeCase)
sealed trait Nut

case class Almond(salted: Boolean) extends Nut
case class Cashew(roasted: Boolean) extends Nut

object Almond {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Almond] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Almond]
}

object Nut {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Nut] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Nut]
}
```

The codec of `Almond` reads the bare object:

```scala
"""{"salted":true}""".fromJson[Almond]
// res6: Either[String, Almond] = Right(value = Almond(salted = true))
```

To accept a subtype only when it arrives inside the sealed family, transform the codec of the family instead of deriving a new one. Keep this decoder out of implicit scope, or the codec of `Nut` would pick it up and call itself:

```scala
val cashewDecoder: JsonDecoder[Cashew] =
  Nut.codec.decoder.mapOrFail {
    case cashew: Cashew => Right(cashew)
    case other          => Left(s"Expected Cashew, got $other")
  }
```

The decoder accepts a cashew and rejects any other member of the family:

```scala
"""{"cashew":{"roasted":true}}""".fromJson[Cashew](cashewDecoder)
// res7: Either[String, Cashew] = Right(value = Cashew(roasted = true))
"""{"almond":{"salted":true}}""".fromJson[Cashew](cashewDecoder)
// res8: Either[String, Cashew] = Left(
//   value = "(Expected Cashew, got Almond(true))"
// )
```

### 3. Use a discriminator field with `@jsonDiscriminator`

Some schemas put the type name inside the object:

```json
{"type":"banaani","curvature":0.5}
```

Use `@jsonDiscriminator` on the sealed trait to get this shape. The value of the field is still the hint, so `@jsonHint` and `@jsonHintNames` work as before. The family from section 1, with a discriminator named `type`:

```scala
@jsonDiscriminator("type")
sealed trait Tropical

@jsonHint("banaani") case class TropicalBanana(curvature: Double) extends Tropical
@jsonHint("omena") case class TropicalApple(poison: Boolean)      extends Tropical

object Tropical {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Tropical] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Tropical]
}
```

The encoder writes the hint into the `type` field, and the decoder reads it from there:

```scala
println((TropicalBanana(0.5): Tropical).toJson)
// {"type":"banaani","curvature":0.5}
"""{"type":"omena","poison":false}""".fromJson[Tropical]
// res10: Either[String, Tropical] = Right(
//   value = TropicalApple(poison = false)
// )
```

The encoder always writes the discriminator as the first field. The decoder accepts it anywhere in the object, so input from a producer that writes it last decodes too:

```scala
"""{"poison":false,"type":"omena"}""".fromJson[Tropical]
// res11: Either[String, Tropical] = Right(
//   value = TropicalApple(poison = false)
// )
```

:::warning[Use it only when you must]
A discriminator is slower, uses more memory, and is more exposed to denial-of-service input than the default wrapper object. Use it only to match a schema that you do not control. Do not combine it with `@jsonNoExtraFields` or with `JsonCodecConfiguration(allowExtraFields = false)`, because the discriminator counts as an extra field of the subtype: decoding then fails with an `(invalid extra field)` error.
:::

### 4. Set it for the whole program

The configuration form of the same options is `JsonCodecConfiguration`. Use `SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField` for `sumTypeHandling`, and `sumTypeMapping` for the hint format:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.JsonCodecConfiguration.SumTypeHandling

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(
    sumTypeHandling = SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField("type"),
    sumTypeMapping = SnakeCase
  )

sealed trait Berry
case class BlueBerry(sweet: Boolean) extends Berry

object Berry {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Berry] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Berry]
}
```

The hint goes into the `type` field, in snake_case:

```scala
println((BlueBerry(true): Berry).toJson)
// {"type":"blue_berry","sweet":true}
```

An annotation on the sealed trait takes priority over the configuration. The default is `SumTypeHandling.WrapperWithClassNameField`, the single-key object.

### 5. Write case objects as strings

A sealed family made only of case objects can be written as a plain JSON string:

```json
"Red"
```

Whether this happens depends on the [`enumValuesAsStrings`](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#enumvaluesasstrings) setting of `JsonCodecConfiguration`:

| Scala version | Default of `enumValuesAsStrings` |
|---------------|----------------------------------|
| Scala 2       | `false`                          |
| Scala 3       | `true`                           |

The setting has no effect when a discriminator is used. Hints still apply, so `@jsonHint("crimson")` on a case object changes its string.

On Scala 3, a sealed family of case objects and an `enum` with only parameterless cases are both written as strings without any setup.

On Scala 2 the default is the single-key object, `{"Red":{}}`. Turn the setting on with an implicit configuration:

```scala
import zio.json._

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

sealed trait Color
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color

object Color {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Color] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Color]
}
```

The case objects are now written and read as strings:

```scala
println((Red: Color).toJson)
// "Red"
""""Green"""".fromJson[Color]
// res16: Either[String, Color] = Right(value = Green)
```

The two Scala versions disagree on what counts as an enumeration value. On Scala 2, a case class with an empty parameter list counts, like a case object. With the setting on, this family is written as strings:

```scala
sealed trait Signal
case object On         extends Signal
final case class Off() extends Signal

object Signal {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Signal] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Signal]
}
```

Both cases become strings on Scala 2:

```scala
println((On: Signal).toJson)
// "On"
println((Off(): Signal).toJson)
// "Off"
```

On Scala 3, only case objects and parameterless `enum` cases count. A family that contains a case class with no fields is not an enumeration, so every case, the case objects included, uses the object form. The same family on Scala 3:

```scala
sealed trait Signal derives JsonCodec
case object On         extends Signal
final case class Off() extends Signal
```

Running the example file on Scala 3, `(On: Signal).toJson` gives `{"On":{}}` and `(Off(): Signal).toJson` gives `{"Off":{}}`. A family made only of case objects is written as strings on Scala 3, as the `Color` family in the same file shows:

```scala
sealed trait Color derives JsonCodec
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color
```

`(Red: Color).toJson` gives `"Red"`. If the JSON must be the same on both versions, use case objects rather than empty case classes. The other Scala 2 and Scala 3 differences are listed in [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md#scala-2-and-scala-3-differences).

### 6. Nest sealed traits

A sealed trait can extend another one. The codec of the outer trait sees only the leaf cases, the case classes and case objects at the bottom of the hierarchy. An intermediate sealed trait gets no hint of its own, so the JSON is the same as for a flat family. This holds on Scala 2 and on Scala 3:

```scala
import zio.json._

sealed trait Animal
sealed trait Pet extends Animal

final case class Dog(name: String) extends Pet
final case class Cat(name: String) extends Pet
final case class Wolf(pack: Int)   extends Animal

object Animal {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Animal] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Animal]
}
```

A `Dog` is written with its own name as the hint, and a hint that names the intermediate trait is not accepted:

```scala
println((Dog("Rex"): Animal).toJson)
// {"Dog":{"name":"Rex"}}
"""{"Cat":{"name":"Tom"}}""".fromJson[Animal]
// res23: Either[String, Animal] = Right(value = Cat(name = "Tom"))
"""{"Pet":{"Dog":{"name":"Rex"}}}""".fromJson[Animal]
// res24: Either[String, Animal] = Left(value = "(invalid disambiguator)")
```

Because the leaf names share one namespace, two leaves in different branches must not have the same hint.

### 7. Keep hint names unique

Every case of a family must end up with a distinct hint after `@jsonHint` and `@jsonHintNames` are applied. A clash is not a compile error. The code compiles, and the derived decoder, and with it a derived `JsonCodec`, throws an `AssertionError` at runtime when it is first initialised, on Scala 2 and Scala 3 alike. The message names the family by its fully qualified name. For a family `com.example.Dup` where two cases both carry `@jsonHint("x")`, it reads:

```text
java.lang.AssertionError: Case names in ADT com.example.Dup must be distinct, name(s) x are duplicated
```

An encoder derived on its own with `DeriveJsonEncoder.gen` does not check, and writes the same hint for both cases. A test that decodes one value of each family is enough to catch the clash early.

### See also

- [Annotations](../reference/annotations.md) lists every derivation annotation in one table.
- [Field names](field-names.md) covers `@jsonMemberNames`, whose formats `@jsonHintNames` reuses.
- [Optional, default and null fields](optional-and-default-fields.md) covers `@jsonNoExtraFields`.

## Process Large JSON as a Stream

Goal: read and write JSON files that are too large to load into memory, one value at a time, with [ZIO Streams](https://zio.dev/reference/stream/).

The steps follow one data set through a round trip: a large JSON array export is read element by element, written out as [JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org/) (one value per line), read back while skipping damaged lines, and written as a JSON array again. Each step also works on its own. The [Streaming API](../reference/streaming.md) reference lists every method used here, with its exact output and error behaviour.

### What You Need

The streaming API is part of the core module, but it exists on the JVM only:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

The guide assumes you know how to derive a codec for a case class (see [Getting Started](../getting-started.md)) and how to run a `ZStream`. All steps use these imports, an `Event` type with a codec, and a small helper that runs an effect so this page can show results:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.json._

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets
import java.nio.file.{ Files, Path }

final case class Event(id: Int, kind: String)

object Event {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Event] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Event]
}

def runSync[A](effect: ZIO[Any, Throwable, A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(effect).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }

def readText(path: Path): String =
  new String(Files.readAllBytes(path), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
```

In a real program the export already exists. For this page we write a small one to a temporary directory, and name the files the later steps write:

```scala
val dir: Path = Files.createTempDirectory("events")

val exportFile: Path  = dir.resolve("events.json")
val linesFile: Path   = dir.resolve("events.jsonl")
val damagedFile: Path = dir.resolve("damaged.jsonl")
val arrayFile: Path   = dir.resolve("good-events.json")

Files.write(
  exportFile,
  """[
    |  {"id": 1, "kind": "created"},
    |  {"id": 2, "kind": "updated"},
    |  {"id": 3, "kind": "deleted"}
    |]""".stripMargin.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
)
```

### 1. Read a Large JSON Array One Element at a Time

`ZStream.fromPath` reads the file as bytes, `ZPipeline.decodeCharsWith` turns the bytes into characters, and `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonPipeline` decodes the elements of the array one by one. Its default delimiter, `JsonStreamDelimiter.Array`, expects one JSON array:

```scala
val exported: ZStream[Any, Throwable, Event] =
  ZStream
    .fromPath(exportFile)
    .via(ZPipeline.decodeCharsWith(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
    .via(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonPipeline())
```

The stream holds only the elements it is working on, so it can filter, count or transform an array of any size. To count the `deleted` events:

```scala
runSync(exported.filter(_.kind == "deleted").runCount)
// res1: Long = 1L
```

If the file holds one large object rather than an array, decode it with `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStreamInput(ZStream.fromPath(exportFile))` instead. It reads the bytes incrementally and returns the single value.

### 2. Write a Stream of Values as JSON Lines

`writeJsonLinesAs`, from the `zio.json` package, encodes every value of a stream on its own line and writes the result to a file as UTF-8. It creates the file or replaces its contents:

```scala
runSync(writeJsonLinesAs(linesFile, exported))

println(readText(linesFile))
// {"id":1,"kind":"created"}
// {"id":2,"kind":"updated"}
// {"id":3,"kind":"deleted"}
//
```

:::warning[Live consumers]
The stream encoders collect output in a 4096-character buffer, so a value written to a socket or a server-sent events response can wait until about 4 KB of later output arrives. When each value must reach the consumer as soon as it is produced, encode the values one at a time, for example `stream.map(_.toJson + "\n")` for a `stream` of values. See [Output Format and Buffering](../reference/streaming.md#output-format-and-buffering).
:::

### 3. Read JSON Lines Back

`readJsonLinesAs` reads a JSON Lines file into a stream of values:

```scala
runSync(readJsonLinesAs[Event](linesFile).runCollect)
// res4: Chunk[Event] = IndexedSeq(
//   Event(id = 1, kind = "created"),
//   Event(id = 2, kind = "updated"),
//   Event(id = 3, kind = "deleted")
// )
```

`readJsonLinesAs` stops the stream at the first line that does not decode, and values decoded just before that line can be lost with it (see [Errors in a Decoding Pipeline](../reference/streaming.md#errors-in-a-decoding-pipeline)). For files that may contain bad lines, use the next step instead.

### 4. Skip Bad Lines Instead of Failing

Log files and exports from other systems sometimes contain a damaged line. Here the line for event 2 has lost its `kind` field, the line for event 4 is cut short, and one line is blank:

```scala
Files.write(
  damagedFile,
  """{"id":1,"kind":"created"}
    |{"id":2}
    |
    |{"id":3,"kind":"deleted"}
    |{"id":4,"kind":
    |{"id":5,"kind":"restored"}
    |""".stripMargin.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
)
```

To keep going past a bad line, split the text into lines yourself with `ZPipeline.utf8Decode` and `ZPipeline.splitLines`, drop blank lines, and decode each line on its own with `fromJson`. Every line then gives an `Either`, and a bad line does not affect the others:

```scala
val decodedLines: ZStream[Any, Throwable, Either[String, Event]] =
  ZStream
    .fromPath(damagedFile)
    .via(ZPipeline.utf8Decode >>> ZPipeline.splitLines)
    .filter(_.trim.nonEmpty)
    .map(_.fromJson[Event])
```

Running the stream shows one result per non-blank line:

```scala
runSync(decodedLines.runCollect)
// res6: Chunk[Either[String, Event]] = IndexedSeq(
//   Right(value = Event(id = 1, kind = "created")),
//   Left(value = ".kind(missing)"),
//   Right(value = Event(id = 3, kind = "deleted")),
//   Left(value = "Unexpected end of input"),
//   Right(value = Event(id = 5, kind = "restored"))
// )
```

To log the errors and keep only the good values, tap the `Left` results and then collect the `Right` results:

```scala
val goodEvents: ZStream[Any, Throwable, Event] =
  decodedLines
    .tap {
      case Left(error) => Console.printLine(s"skipping bad line: $error")
      case Right(_)    => ZIO.unit
    }
    .collect { case Right(event) => event }
```

The stream prints a message for each bad line and keeps the three good events:

```scala
runSync(goodEvents.runCollect)
// skipping bad line: .kind(missing)
// skipping bad line: Unexpected end of input
// res7: Chunk[Event] = IndexedSeq(
//   Event(id = 1, kind = "created"),
//   Event(id = 3, kind = "deleted"),
//   Event(id = 5, kind = "restored")
// )
```

This approach uses only `fromJson`, so it also works on Scala.js and Scala Native with a stream source other than a file.

### 5. Write a Stream of Values as a JSON Array File

Some consumers expect one JSON document rather than JSON Lines. `JsonEncoder#encodeJsonArrayPipeline` writes the stream as a single array, `ZPipeline.encodeCharsWith` turns the characters into UTF-8 bytes, and `ZSink.fromPath` writes them to a file. Here the input is `goodEvents` from step 4, so the damaged file is read again and its bad lines are logged again; the sink returns the number of bytes written:

```scala
runSync(
  goodEvents
    .via(JsonEncoder[Event].encodeJsonArrayPipeline)
    .via(ZPipeline.encodeCharsWith(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
    .run(ZSink.fromPath(arrayFile))
)
// skipping bad line: .kind(missing)
// skipping bad line: Unexpected end of input
// res8: Long = 80L

println(readText(arrayFile))
// [{"id":1,"kind":"created"},{"id":3,"kind":"deleted"},{"id":5,"kind":"restored"}]
```

The output is compact; the stream encoders have no pretty-printed form. The file can be read back with step 1.

### See Also

- [Streaming API](../reference/streaming.md) for every streaming method, the delimiters, the file helpers and the exact error behaviour.
- [JsonEncoder](../reference/json-encoder.md#streaming) and [JsonDecoder](../reference/json-decoder.md#streaming) for the type classes that carry the streaming methods.
- [Errors](../reference/errors.md) for the error messages a failed stream carries.

## Encode a Type You Do Not Own

Goal: use a class from another library as a field in your case class, even though that library gives it no JSON support and you cannot edit its source.

ZIO JSON already covers common library types such as `java.util.UUID`, `java.time.Instant`, and `BigDecimal` (see [Built-in Instances](../reference/built-in-instances.md)). For anything else you supply the instances yourself. The example below uses a `Money` class that stands in for a type from a library. The `vendor` object plays the role of that library:

```scala
import zio.json._

object vendor {
  final class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String) {
    override def toString: String = s"Money($cents, $currency)"
  }

  object Money {
    def apply(cents: Long, currency: String): Money = new Money(cents, currency)
  }
}

import vendor.Money
```

`Money` is not a case class, so derivation cannot see inside it. You must say how it looks in JSON. Here it will be one string, such as `"1250 USD"`.

### 1. Write the conversion functions

Two small functions turn a `Money` into text and back. The parser returns an `Either`, so it can say why the text is bad:

```scala
def formatMoney(m: Money): String = s"${m.cents} ${m.currency}"

def parseMoney(s: String): Either[String, Money] =
  s.split(" ") match {
    case Array(amount, currency) =>
      amount.toLongOption.map(Money(_, currency)).toRight(s"invalid amount: $amount")
    case _ =>
      Left("expected '<cents> <currency>'")
  }
```

### 2. Build the encoder with contramap

`JsonEncoder#contramap` adapts an existing encoder to a new type. You give it a function from your type to a type that already has an encoder. Here that is `Money` to `String`:

```scala
val moneyEncoder: JsonEncoder[Money] = JsonEncoder[String].contramap(formatMoney)
```

### 3. Build the decoder with mapOrFail

`JsonDecoder#mapOrFail` adapts an existing decoder. The function may fail with a message, which becomes a decode error:

```scala
val moneyDecoder: JsonDecoder[Money] = JsonDecoder[String].mapOrFail(parseMoney)
```

Test each half on its own:

```scala
println(moneyEncoder.encodeJson(Money(1250, "USD"), None))
// "1250 USD"

moneyDecoder.decodeJson("\"1250 USD\"")
// res2: Either[String, Money] = Right(value = Money(1250, USD))

moneyDecoder.decodeJson("\"12x USD\"")
// res3: Either[String, Money] = Left(value = "(invalid amount: 12x)")
```

### 4. Put the instances where the compiler finds them

The compiler looks for an implicit `JsonEncoder[Money]` in two places: the scope around the call, and the companions of the types involved. The companion of `Money` belongs to the other library, so you cannot add anything there. You have two options.

The first is the companion of a type you own. Put the instances next to the case class that uses `Money`, and define them before the derived codec:

```scala
final case class Invoice(id: String, total: Money)

object Invoice {
  implicit val encodeMoney: JsonEncoder[Money] = moneyEncoder
  implicit val decodeMoney: JsonDecoder[Money] = moneyDecoder

  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Invoice] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Invoice]
}
```

The derived `Invoice` codec now writes `total` as one string, and a bad amount fails the decode:

```scala
val invoice = Invoice("A-1", Money(1250, "USD"))
// invoice: Invoice = Invoice(id = "A-1", total = Money(1250, USD))

println(invoice.toJson)
// {"id":"A-1","total":"1250 USD"}

"""{"id":"A-1","total":"1250 USD"}""".fromJson[Invoice]
// res5: Either[String, Invoice] = Right(
//   value = Invoice(id = "A-1", total = Money(1250, USD))
// )

"""{"id":"A-1","total":"abc USD"}""".fromJson[Invoice]
// res6: Either[String, Invoice] = Left(value = ".total(invalid amount: abc)")
```

The error path `.total` comes from the field that held the bad value, and the text in parentheses is your `Left` message.

The second option is a shared object that other files import. Use it when many of your types hold a `Money` and you do not want to repeat the instances.

### 5. Bundle both halves into a codec

A `JsonCodec[A]` is one value holding an encoder and a decoder. Make one with `JsonCodec(encoder, decoder)`, or start from a codec that exists and call `JsonCodec#transformOrFail`. Its two functions are the parse step, which may fail, and the format step, which cannot. Here the codec goes in a `MoneyCodecs` object that other files can import:

```scala
object MoneyCodecs {
  implicit val moneyCodec: JsonCodec[Money] =
    JsonCodec[String].transformOrFail(parseMoney, formatMoney)
}
```

`JsonCodec(moneyEncoder, moneyDecoder)` gives an equivalent result. Importing the codec makes both the encoder and the decoder available, because a codec in scope also serves as an encoder and a decoder:

```scala
final case class Receipt(number: Int, paid: Money)

object Receipt {
  import MoneyCodecs._

  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Receipt] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Receipt]
}
```

The `Receipt` codec writes `paid` with the imported codec:

```scala
println(Receipt(7, Money(300, "EUR")).toJson)
// {"number":7,"paid":"300 EUR"}
```

### 6. Choose a codec or separate instances

| Choice                | Gives you                    | Use it when                                  |
|-----------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `JsonEncoder` only    | Writing JSON                 | The type is only sent out, never read        |
| `JsonDecoder` only    | Reading JSON                 | The type is only received, never written     |
| `JsonCodec`           | Both, kept together          | The type is used in both directions          |

A codec keeps the two halves side by side, so a change to the format is made in one place. Separate instances let you supply only the direction you need. Pick one style per type, so that only one instance of each type is in scope.

### 7. Use the type as a map key

A `Map[Money, Int]` needs different instances. JSON object keys are always strings, so a key is written by a `JsonFieldEncoder` and read by a `JsonFieldDecoder`, not by `JsonEncoder` and `JsonDecoder`. They are built the same way, from the `String` instances, with `JsonFieldEncoder#contramap` and `JsonFieldDecoder#mapOrFail`:

```scala
object MoneyKeys {
  implicit val moneyKeyEncoder: JsonFieldEncoder[Money] =
    JsonFieldEncoder[String].contramap(formatMoney)

  implicit val moneyKeyDecoder: JsonFieldDecoder[Money] =
    JsonFieldDecoder[String].mapOrFail(parseMoney)
}
```

With the key instances imported, maps keyed by `Money` encode and decode, and a bad key fails with your message:

```scala
import MoneyKeys._

println(Map(Money(500, "USD") -> 3).toJson)
// {"500 USD":3}

"""{"500 USD":3}""".fromJson[Map[Money, Int]]
// res9: Either[String, Map[Money, Int]] = Right(
//   value = Map(Money(500, USD) -> 3)
// )

"""{"5x USD":3}""".fromJson[Map[Money, Int]]
// res10: Either[String, Map[Money, Int]] = Left(
//   value = ".5x USD(invalid amount: 5x)"
// )
```

See [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](../reference/json-field-codecs.md) for the built-in key types, and [Use Your Own Type as a Map Key](custom-map-keys.md) for more key types.

### See also

- [Build an encoder or decoder from an existing one](./manual-instances.md) shows more ways to build instances, such as `JsonDecoder#map` and tuple encodings.
- [JsonEncoder reference](../reference/json-encoder.md) and [JsonDecoder reference](../reference/json-decoder.md) describe `JsonEncoder#contramap`, `JsonDecoder#map` and `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail` in full.
- [JsonCodec reference](../reference/json-codec.md) lists the combinators on `JsonCodec`.

## Validate Data While Decoding

Goal: make decoding fail when a value is well-formed JSON but is not acceptable to your program, for example an age of zero or less, or an email with no `@`.

The tool is `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail`. It runs a function on a decoded value. The function returns `Right` to accept or `Left` with a message to reject. The failure is part of decoding, so the bad value never reaches your code. Every example below uses this import:

```scala
import zio.json._
```

### 1. Validate one value type

Wrap the raw type in a small case class, then build its decoder from an existing decoder with `mapOrFail`:

```scala
final case class Email(value: String)

object Email {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Email] =
    JsonDecoder[String].mapOrFail { s =>
      if (s.contains("@")) Right(Email(s))
      else Left("email must contain @")
    }

  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Email] =
    JsonEncoder[String].contramap(_.value)
}
```

`JsonEncoder#contramap` is the encoder side. It turns an `Email` back into a `String` so the JSON stays a plain string.

The same pattern validates `Map` keys: build a `JsonFieldDecoder` with `JsonFieldDecoder[String].mapOrFail`. See [Use Your Own Type as a Map Key](custom-map-keys.md).

### 2. Validate both directions with transformOrFail

When you want encoder and decoder together, use a `JsonCodec` and `transformOrFail`. Its first function can fail. Its second function cannot:

```scala
final case class Age(value: Int)

object Age {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Age] =
    JsonCodec[Int].transformOrFail(
      n => if (n > 0) Right(Age(n)) else Left("age must be positive"),
      _.value
    )
}
```

### 3. Use the types in a case class

Fields of these types are checked as the case class is decoded:

```scala
final case class Signup(name: String, age: Age, email: Email)

object Signup {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Signup] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Signup]
}
```

Valid input decodes as normal:

```scala
"""{"name":"Ada","age":36,"email":"ada@example.com"}""".fromJson[Signup]
// res1: Either[String, Signup] = Right(
//   value = Signup(
//     name = "Ada",
//     age = Age(value = 36),
//     email = Email(value = "ada@example.com")
//   )
// )
```

### 4. Read the error

A rejected value produces a `Left`. The string starts with the path to the field, written as `.fieldName`, then your message in parentheses:

```scala
"""{"name":"Ada","age":-1,"email":"ada@example.com"}""".fromJson[Signup]
// res2: Either[String, Signup] = Left(value = ".age(age must be positive)")

"""{"name":"Ada","age":36,"email":"ada.example.com"}""".fromJson[Signup]
// res3: Either[String, Signup] = Left(value = ".email(email must contain @)")
```

When the value is not nested in a field, such as decoding an `Age` alone, the path is empty and only the parenthesised message remains:

```scala
"0".fromJson[Age]
// res4: Either[String, Age] = Left(value = "(age must be positive)")
```

### 5. Know that the first failure wins

Decoding stops at the first bad value. It does not collect a list of errors. Fields are read in the order they appear in the JSON text, so when two fields are bad, only the first one in the text is reported:

```scala
"""{"name":"Ada","age":-1,"email":"nope"}""".fromJson[Signup]
// res5: Either[String, Signup] = Left(value = ".age(age must be positive)")

"""{"name":"Ada","email":"nope","age":-1}""".fromJson[Signup]
// res6: Either[String, Signup] = Left(value = ".email(email must contain @)")
```

If you need every error at once, decode to the [`Json` AST](../reference/json-ast.md) or to plain types and run your own validation after decoding.

### 6. Check a rule across fields

`mapOrFail` also works on a whole object. Use it for a rule that involves more than one field:

```scala
final case class Window(from: Int, to: Int)

object Window {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Window] =
    DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Window].mapOrFail { r =>
      if (r.from <= r.to) Right(r) else Left("from must not be after to")
    }
}
```

An object whose fields are each valid but break the rule fails as a whole:

```scala
"""{"from":5,"to":1}""".fromJson[Window]
// res7: Either[String, Window] = Left(value = "(from must not be after to)")
```

Because the check runs after the object is built, the error has no path below the object: here it is empty, and inside another case class it would be the path of the field that holds the `Window`.

### 7. Use refined types

The `zio-json-interop-refined` module gives you encoders and decoders for [refined](https://github.com/fthomas/refined) types, so a predicate such as `NonEmpty` or `Positive` replaces the hand-written check. Add it to your build:

```sbt
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-refined" % "1.1.3"
```

With the module on the classpath, import its instances and use a refined type as a field type:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.interop.refined._

import eu.timepit.refined.api.Refined
import eu.timepit.refined.collection.NonEmpty

final case class Account(owner: String Refined NonEmpty)

object Account {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Account] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Account]
}
```

A failed predicate shows up as a `Left` such as `.owner(Predicate isEmpty() did not fail.)`. See [Refined interop](../interop/refined.md) for the details.

### 8. Reject unknown fields

Validation can also mean refusing JSON that has extra keys. Put `@jsonNoExtraFields` on the case class, and any field not in the class makes decoding fail:

```scala
@jsonNoExtraFields
final case class Login(user: String)

object Login {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Login] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Login]
}
```

An unknown `admin` key is now an error:

```scala
"""{"user":"ada","admin":true}""".fromJson[Login]
// res9: Either[String, Login] = Left(value = "(invalid extra field)")
```

Without the annotation, extra fields are skipped. See [Optional, default and null fields](./optional-and-default-fields.md) for how missing fields are handled, and the [Annotations reference](../reference/annotations.md) for every annotation.

## Introduction to ZIO JSON

[ZIO JSON](https://github.com/zio/zio-json) is a fast and secure JSON library with tight ZIO integration.

[![Production Ready](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Production%20Ready-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-json/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-json_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-json_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-json_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-json_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-json_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-json_2.13) [![ZIO JSON](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-json?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-json)

### Introduction

The goal of this project is to create the best all-round JSON library for Scala:

- **Performance** to handle more requests per second than the incumbents, i.e. reduced operational costs.
- **Security** to mitigate against adversarial JSON payloads that threaten the capacity of the server.
- **Fast Compilation** no shapeless, no type astronautics.
- **Future-Proof**, prepared for Scala 3 and next-generation Java.
- **Simple** small codebase, concise documentation that covers everything.
- **Helpful errors** are readable by humans and machines.
- **ZIO Integration** so nothing more is required.

### Installation

Add the core module to your `build.sbt`. It is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Codecs, derivation, the Json AST and, on the JVM, streaming (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
)
```

In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use `%%%`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Codecs, derivation and the Json AST
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
)
```

[Getting Started](getting-started.md) continues from here with a first program.

### Modules

The optional modules below have the same version number as `zio-json` and depend on it, so adding one also brings in the core module. Add only the lines you need.

#### Formats

Read and write YAML with your JSON codecs. This module is JVM only:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Read and write YAML with your JSON codecs, through SnakeYAML (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-yaml" % "1.1.3"
)
```

See [YAML](reference/yaml.md).

#### Derivation

Generate codec instances with the `@jsonDerive` annotation. This module is published for Scala 2.12 and 2.13 only, and needs macro annotations turned on: the `-Ymacro-annotations` compiler option on Scala 2.13, or the macro paradise plugin on Scala 2.12 (the [@jsonDerive page](reference/zio-json-macros.md#installation) has both settings). Use `%%%` on Scala.js and Scala Native:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // The @jsonDerive annotation, which writes codec instances for you (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native; Scala 2 only)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-macros" % "1.1.3"
)
```

See [@jsonDerive Macro Annotation](reference/zio-json-macros.md).

#### Integrations

Codecs for types from other libraries:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // http4s 0.23 entity encoders and decoders built from ZIO JSON codecs (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-http4s"     % "1.1.3",

  // Codecs and map-key codecs for refined types (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-refined"    % "1.1.3",

  // Codecs for Scalaz 7 IList (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native; Scala 2 only)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-scalaz7x"   % "1.1.3",

  // Codecs and map-key codecs for enumeratum enums (JVM, Scala.js, Scala Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-enumeratum" % "1.1.3"
)
```

The http4s module is JVM only. The others are also built for Scala.js and Scala Native:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Codecs and map-key codecs for refined types
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-json-interop-refined"    % "1.1.3",

  // Codecs for Scalaz 7 IList (Scala 2 only)
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-json-interop-scalaz7x"   % "1.1.3",

  // Codecs and map-key codecs for enumeratum enums
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-json-interop-enumeratum" % "1.1.3"
)
```

See [HTTP4s Interop](interop/http4s.md), [Refined Interop](interop/refined.md), [Scalaz 7.x Interop](interop/scalaz-7x.md) and [Enumeratum Interop](interop/enumeratum.md).

#### Testing

Golden (snapshot) tests that catch unintended changes to encoded JSON. This module is JVM only and belongs in the `Test` configuration:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Golden tests for JSON codecs, built on ZIO Test (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-golden" % "1.1.3" % Test
)
```

See [Golden Testing API](reference/golden-testing.md) and [Catch Unintended Changes to Your JSON with Golden Tests](how-to/golden-testing.md).

### Documentation

The documentation is split by what you want to do:

- **[Getting Started](getting-started.md)** installs ZIO JSON and walks through encoding and decoding your first types.
- **[Concepts](explanation/index.md)** explain the design and the trade-offs: how derivation and decoding work, Scala 2 and Scala 3 differences, decoder strictness, JSON shapes, performance and security.
- **[Reference](reference/index.md)** pages list every type, method, annotation and option.
- **[Integrations](interop/index.md)** connect ZIO JSON to http4s, refined, Scalaz 7 and enumeratum.
- **Tutorials** teach a larger example step by step: [Model a Real API Payload](tutorial/model-an-api-payload.md).
- **[How-to Guides](how-to/index.md)** solve one task each, such as renaming fields, encoding sealed traits or streaming large JSON documents.
