## Enumeratum Interop

The `zio-json-interop-enumeratum` module connects ZIO JSON to [enumeratum](https://github.com/lloydmeta/enumeratum). It gives enumeratum enums `JsonEncoder` and `JsonDecoder` instances, plus `JsonFieldEncoder` and `JsonFieldDecoder` instances so enum members can be keys of a `Map`. A string enum (`Enum[A]`) is written as the member's name, and a value enum (`IntEnum[A]`, `StringEnum[A]` and the others) is written as the member's value.

### Installation

Add the module to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-enumeratum" % "1.1.3"
```

The module is published for the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native, for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3. In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use `%%%` instead of `%%`. On Scala 3, value enums need an extra compiler option, see [Scala 3](#scala-3).

### Imports

Unlike the other interop modules, which live under `zio.json.interop`, the enumeratum integration lives in enumeratum's own packages. The string-enum traits and builders are in `enumeratum`, and the value-enum ones are in `enumeratum.values`:

```scala
import enumeratum._        // ZioJsonEnum, ZioJsonKeyEnum, ZioJson
import enumeratum.values._ // IntZioJsonEnum, LongZioJsonEnum, ..., ZioJson
```

Both packages contain an object named `ZioJson`. When you import both packages in the same file, refer to the builders as `enumeratum.ZioJson` and `enumeratum.values.ZioJson`, as the examples below do.

### String Enums

The quickest way to give a string enum its codecs is to mix traits into its companion object. `ZioJsonEnum` adds an implicit `JsonEncoder` and `JsonDecoder`, and `ZioJsonKeyEnum` adds an implicit `JsonFieldEncoder` and `JsonFieldDecoder` for map keys:

```scala
import enumeratum._
import zio.json._

sealed trait ShirtSize extends EnumEntry

case object ShirtSize extends Enum[ShirtSize] with ZioJsonEnum[ShirtSize] with ZioJsonKeyEnum[ShirtSize] {
  case object Small  extends ShirtSize
  case object Medium extends ShirtSize
  case object Large  extends ShirtSize

  val values = findValues
}
```

A member is encoded as its `entryName`, which by default is the name of the case object. The instances are for the enum type `ShirtSize`, and `JsonEncoder` is invariant, so a value whose static type is `ShirtSize.Small.type` has no encoder. Widen it to `ShirtSize` first:

```scala
(ShirtSize.Small: ShirtSize).toJson
// res1: String = "\"Small\""

ShirtSize.values.toJson
// res2: String = "[\"Small\",\"Medium\",\"Large\"]"
```

Decoding accepts the exact name only. A name that is not a member fails, and so does a name in the wrong case:

```scala
""""Large"""".fromJson[ShirtSize]
// res3: Either[String, ShirtSize] = Right(value = Large)

""""XLarge"""".fromJson[ShirtSize]
// res4: Either[String, ShirtSize] = Left(
//   value = "('XLarge' is not a member of enum ShirtSize)"
// )

""""large"""".fromJson[ShirtSize]
// res5: Either[String, ShirtSize] = Left(
//   value = "('large' is not a member of enum ShirtSize)"
// )
```

Because the companion also mixes in `ZioJsonKeyEnum`, the enum works as a `Map` key. Keys are matched by exact name too:

```scala
Map[ShirtSize, Int](ShirtSize.Small -> 3, ShirtSize.Large -> 1).toJson
// res6: String = "{\"Small\":3,\"Large\":1}"

"""{"Medium":2}""".fromJson[Map[ShirtSize, Int]]
// res7: Either[String, Map[ShirtSize, Int]] = Right(value = Map(Medium -> 2))
```

### Choosing the Case of Names

The traits always write the exact `entryName` and accept only the exact name. When an API sends names in lower case or upper case, or in any case, build the instances yourself with the builders in `enumeratum.ZioJson`. Each one takes the enum's companion object, which is `this` when you call the builder inside the companion:

| Builder                  | Result                | Behaviour                                                                    |
| ------------------------ | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `encoder`                | `JsonEncoder[A]`      | Writes `entryName` (what `ZioJsonEnum` uses).                                |
| `encoderLowercase`       | `JsonEncoder[A]`      | Writes `entryName` in lower case.                                            |
| `encoderUppercase`       | `JsonEncoder[A]`      | Writes `entryName` in upper case.                                            |
| `decoder`                | `JsonDecoder[A]`      | Accepts the exact `entryName` (what `ZioJsonEnum` uses).                     |
| `decoderLowercaseOnly`   | `JsonDecoder[A]`      | Accepts only the lower-case `entryName`.                                     |
| `decoderUppercaseOnly`   | `JsonDecoder[A]`      | Accepts only the upper-case `entryName`.                                     |
| `decoderCaseInsensitive` | `JsonDecoder[A]`      | Accepts `entryName` in any case.                                             |
| `keyEncoder`             | `JsonFieldEncoder[A]` | Writes `entryName` as an object key (what `ZioJsonKeyEnum` uses).            |
| `keyDecoder`             | `JsonFieldDecoder[A]` | Accepts the exact `entryName` as an object key (what `ZioJsonKeyEnum` uses). |

Every decoder fails with the message `'<input>' is not a member of enum <EnumName>`. Use the builders instead of mixing in `ZioJsonEnum`, otherwise the companion object has two implicit encoders for the same type. This enum writes lower-case names and accepts any case:

```scala
sealed trait Color extends EnumEntry

case object Color extends Enum[Color] {
  case object Red       extends Color
  case object DarkGreen extends Color

  val values = findValues

  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Color] = enumeratum.ZioJson.encoderLowercase(this)
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Color] = enumeratum.ZioJson.decoderCaseInsensitive(this)
}
```

The encoder lower-cases the name, and the decoder accepts every spelling:

```scala
(Color.DarkGreen: Color).toJson
// res8: String = "\"darkgreen\""

""""DARKGREEN"""".fromJson[Color]
// res9: Either[String, Color] = Right(value = DarkGreen)

""""darkGreen"""".fromJson[Color]
// res10: Either[String, Color] = Right(value = DarkGreen)
```

### Value Enums

A value enum is an enumeratum enum whose members carry a value, such as an `Int` or a `String`, and it is encoded as that value. Mix the trait that matches the value type into the companion object:

| Value type | Enum type    | Trait               |
| ---------- | ------------ | ------------------- |
| `Int`      | `IntEnum`    | `IntZioJsonEnum`    |
| `Long`     | `LongEnum`   | `LongZioJsonEnum`   |
| `Short`    | `ShortEnum`  | `ShortZioJsonEnum`  |
| `String`   | `StringEnum` | `StringZioJsonEnum` |
| `Char`     | `CharEnum`   | `CharZioJsonEnum`   |
| `Byte`     | `ByteEnum`   | `ByteZioJsonEnum`   |

Each trait provides an implicit `JsonEncoder`, `JsonDecoder`, `JsonFieldEncoder` and `JsonFieldDecoder`, so value enums work as map keys without a second trait. All six extend the common trait `ZioJsonValueEnum`. Here is an `IntEnum`:

```scala
import enumeratum.values._

sealed abstract class LibraryItem(val value: Int, val name: String) extends IntEnumEntry

case object LibraryItem extends IntEnum[LibraryItem] with IntZioJsonEnum[LibraryItem] {
  case object Book     extends LibraryItem(value = 1, name = "book")
  case object Movie    extends LibraryItem(value = 2, name = "movie")
  case object Magazine extends LibraryItem(value = 3, name = "magazine")
  case object CD       extends LibraryItem(value = 4, name = "cd")

  val values = findValues
}
```

A member is written as its value, and decoding looks the value up. As with string enums, widen a member to the enum type before encoding it:

```scala
(LibraryItem.Book: LibraryItem).toJson
// res11: String = "1"

"3".fromJson[LibraryItem]
// res12: Either[String, LibraryItem] = Right(value = Magazine)

"999".fromJson[LibraryItem]
// res13: Either[String, LibraryItem] = Left(
//   value = "('999' is not a member of enum LibraryItem)"
// )
```

As a map key, the value is written as the key's text:

```scala
Map[LibraryItem, String](LibraryItem.CD -> "shelf 4").toJson
// res14: String = "{\"4\":\"shelf 4\"}"

"""{"2":"shelf 9"}""".fromJson[Map[LibraryItem, String]]
// res15: Either[String, Map[LibraryItem, String]] = Right(
//   value = Map(Movie -> "shelf 9")
// )
```

### Value Enum Builders

To create the instances without a trait, for example to give only some of them to an enum, use the builders in `enumeratum.values.ZioJson`:

| Builder      | Result                        | Requires                      |
| ------------ | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `encoder`    | `JsonEncoder[EntryType]`      | `JsonEncoder[ValueType]`      |
| `decoder`    | `JsonDecoder[EntryType]`      | `JsonDecoder[ValueType]`      |
| `keyEncoder` | `JsonFieldEncoder[EntryType]` | `JsonFieldEncoder[ValueType]` |
| `keyDecoder` | `JsonFieldDecoder[EntryType]` | `JsonFieldDecoder[ValueType]` |

ZIO JSON has built-in key codecs for `String`, `Int`, `Long` and `UUID` (see [Map Keys](../reference/json-field-codecs.md)), so `keyEncoder` and `keyDecoder` for a `Short`, `Char` or `Byte` enum need a key codec for that value type in scope. The `ShortZioJsonEnum`, `CharZioJsonEnum` and `ByteZioJsonEnum` traits bring their own. This `ShortEnum` gets only an encoder and a decoder:

```scala
sealed abstract class Priority(val value: Short) extends ShortEnumEntry

case object Priority extends ShortEnum[Priority] {
  case object Low  extends Priority(1)
  case object High extends Priority(9)

  val values = findValues

  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Priority] = enumeratum.values.ZioJson.encoder(this)
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Priority] = enumeratum.values.ZioJson.decoder(this)
}
```

The builders behave like the trait instances:

```scala
(Priority.High: Priority).toJson
// res16: String = "9"

"9".fromJson[Priority]
// res17: Either[String, Priority] = Right(value = High)

"5".fromJson[Priority]
// res18: Either[String, Priority] = Left(
//   value = "('5' is not a member of enum Priority)"
// )
```

### Scala 3

On Scala 3, enumeratum's `findValues` macro for value enums reads the arguments passed to each member's constructor, which needs the `-Yretain-trees` compiler option. Without it, the compiler stops at `findValues` with `Option -Yretain-trees must be set in scalacOptions`. Add the option to your build:

```scala
scalacOptions += "-Yretain-trees"
```

On Scala 3.9.0, string enums (`Enum[A]`) compile without the option. The module's own build sets it for Scala 3, so setting it in your build as well is the safe choice whenever you use enumeratum on Scala 3.

---

## HTTP4s Interop

The `zio-json-interop-http4s` module turns ZIO JSON codecs into [http4s](https://http4s.org/v0.23) entity codecs. An http4s `EntityDecoder[F, A]` reads a request or response body into an `A`, and an `EntityEncoder[F, A]` writes an `A` as a body. With this module, any type that has a `JsonDecoder` or `JsonEncoder` can be read from or written to an HTTP body as JSON.

The module targets http4s 0.23 and cats-effect 3 (the build uses http4s 0.23.38 and cats-effect 3.7.0). It is published for the JVM only, for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3.

### Installation

Add the module to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-http4s" % "1.1.3"
```

The module depends on `http4s-dsl`, `cats-effect` and `zio`, so those come in transitively. There is no Scala.js or Scala Native artifact, so always use `%%`.

### What the Module Provides

The module has two styles. You either create the instances you need with `jsonOf` and `jsonEncoderOf`, or you import implicit instances that cover every type with a ZIO JSON codec:

| Member                              | Result                         | Requires                          | Purpose                                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `jsonOf[F, A]`                      | `EntityDecoder[F, A]`          | `Concurrent[F]`, `JsonDecoder[A]` | Reads the body as UTF-8 text and decodes it with the `JsonDecoder`. |
| `jsonEncoderOf[F, A]`               | `EntityEncoder[F, A]`          | `JsonEncoder[A]`                  | Writes `A` with `toJson` and sets `Content-Type: application/json`. |
| `ZIOEntityDecoder.zioEntityDecoder` | implicit `EntityDecoder[F, A]` | `Concurrent[F]`, `JsonDecoder[A]` | `jsonOf[F, A]` for every `A` with a `JsonDecoder`.                  |
| `ZIOEntityEncoder.zioEntityEncoder` | implicit `EntityEncoder[F, A]` | `JsonEncoder[A]`                  | `jsonEncoderOf[F, A]` for every `A` with a `JsonEncoder`.           |
| `ZIOEntityCodec`                    | object                         |                                   | Both implicits above in one import.                                 |

`jsonOf` and `jsonEncoderOf` live in the `ZIOJsonInstances` trait. The package object `zio.json.interop.http4s` extends that trait, which is why `import zio.json.interop.http4s._` makes them available.

### Explicit Instances

The explicit style gives you full control over which types get JSON entity codecs. We define the payload types with ZIO JSON codecs, then declare one `EntityDecoder` for the request type and one `EntityEncoder` for the response type:

```scala
import cats.effect.IO
import org.http4s._
import org.http4s.dsl.io._
import org.http4s.headers.`Content-Type`
import org.http4s.implicits._
import zio.json._
import zio.json.interop.http4s._

final case class Greeting(name: String)

object Greeting {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Greeting] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Greeting]

  implicit val entityDecoder: EntityDecoder[IO, Greeting] = jsonOf[IO, Greeting]
}

final case class Reply(message: String)

object Reply {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Reply] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Reply]

  implicit val entityEncoder: EntityEncoder[IO, Reply] = jsonEncoderOf[IO, Reply]
}
```

The instances sit in the companion objects, so http4s finds them wherever `Greeting` and `Reply` are used. A route can now decode the body with `Request#as` and pass a `Reply` straight to `Ok`:

```scala
val routes: HttpRoutes[IO] = HttpRoutes.of[IO] { case req @ POST -> Root / "greet" =>
  for {
    greeting <- req.as[Greeting]
    response <- Ok(Reply(s"Hello, ${greeting.name}!"))
  } yield response
}
```

### Running the Routes in Memory

http4s routes are plain functions from a request to an effect, so we can call them without starting a server. This helper builds a `POST` request with a JSON body:

```scala
import cats.effect.unsafe.implicits.global

def jsonRequest(body: String): Request[IO] =
  Request[IO](Method.POST, uri"/greet")
    .withEntity(body)
    .withContentType(`Content-Type`(MediaType.application.json))
```

Sending a valid body runs the route and gives back the response:

```scala
val response = routes.orNotFound.run(jsonRequest("""{"name":"Ada"}""")).unsafeRunSync()
```

The response has the status `200 OK`, the JSON content type and a JSON body:

```scala
println(response.status)
// 200 OK
println(response.headers.get[`Content-Type`])
// Some(Content-Type(MediaType(application/json),None))
println(response.bodyText.compile.string.unsafeRunSync())
// {"message":"Hello, Ada!"}
```

### Decoding Errors

`jsonOf` turns every decoding problem into an http4s `MalformedMessageBodyFailure`. An empty body fails with the message `Invalid JSON: empty body`, and a ZIO JSON decoding error is passed on as the failure's message. `Request#attemptAs` shows the failure as a value:

```scala
jsonRequest("").attemptAs[Greeting].value.unsafeRunSync()
// res3: Either[DecodeFailure, Greeting] = Left(
//   value = MalformedMessageBodyFailure(
//     details = "Invalid JSON: empty body",
//     cause = None
//   )
// )

jsonRequest("""{"nom":"Ada"}""").attemptAs[Greeting].value.unsafeRunSync()
// res4: Either[DecodeFailure, Greeting] = Left(
//   value = MalformedMessageBodyFailure(details = ".name(missing)", cause = None)
// )

jsonRequest("""{"name":"Ada"""").attemptAs[Greeting].value.unsafeRunSync()
// res5: Either[DecodeFailure, Greeting] = Left(
//   value = MalformedMessageBodyFailure(
//     details = "Unexpected end of input",
//     cause = None
//   )
// )
```

Inside a route, `Request#as` raises the same failure in `IO`. `MalformedMessageBodyFailure` is an http4s `MessageFailure`, and the http4s server backends turn an unhandled `MessageFailure` into an error response. For this failure the response is `400 Bad Request`:

```scala
jsonRequest("""{"nom":"Ada"}""")
  .attemptAs[Greeting]
  .value
  .unsafeRunSync()
  .left
  .map(_.toHttpResponse[IO](HttpVersion.`HTTP/1.1`).status)
// res6: Either[Status, Greeting] = Left(value = Status(code = 400))
```

The decoder declares `application/json` as its media type. `Request#as` and `Request#attemptAs` decode non-strictly, so they also read a body sent with another `Content-Type`, such as `text/plain`. A strict decode, `jsonOf[IO, A].decode(request, strict = true)`, rejects such a request with a `MediaTypeMismatch` failure.

### Automatic Instances

When most of your payload types have ZIO JSON codecs, declaring an entity codec for each one gets repetitive. Importing `ZIOEntityCodec._` provides an `EntityEncoder` for every type with a `JsonEncoder` and an `EntityDecoder` for every type with a `JsonDecoder`. Use `ZIOEntityEncoder._` or `ZIOEntityDecoder._` to import only one direction.

The payload types now need only their ZIO JSON codecs:

```scala
import cats.effect.IO
import cats.effect.unsafe.implicits.global
import org.http4s._
import org.http4s.dsl.io._
import org.http4s.headers.`Content-Type`
import org.http4s.implicits._
import zio.json._
import zio.json.interop.http4s.ZIOEntityCodec._

final case class Order(item: String, quantity: Int)

object Order {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Order] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Order]
}

final case class Receipt(item: String, quantity: Int, total: BigDecimal)

object Receipt {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Receipt] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Receipt]
}

val orderRoutes: HttpRoutes[IO] = HttpRoutes.of[IO] { case req @ POST -> Root / "orders" =>
  req.as[Order].flatMap { order =>
    Ok(Receipt(order.item, order.quantity, BigDecimal("2.50") * order.quantity))
  }
}
```

The imported encoder also works for building requests, so `Request#withEntity` accepts an `Order` and writes it as JSON:

```scala
val orderRequest = Request[IO](Method.POST, uri"/orders").withEntity(Order("tea", 4))
```

The request carries the JSON content type, and the route decodes the `Order` and encodes the `Receipt` with the imported instances:

```scala
println(orderRequest.headers.get[`Content-Type`])
// Some(Content-Type(MediaType(application/json),None))
println(orderRoutes.orNotFound.run(orderRequest).unsafeRunSync().bodyText.compile.string.unsafeRunSync())
// {"item":"tea","quantity":4,"total":10.00}
```

:::warning
The imported instances apply to every type with a ZIO JSON codec, including `String`, numbers and collections. They take precedence over http4s's built-in instances, so with `ZIOEntityCodec._` in scope, `Ok("hello")` sends the JSON string `"hello"` (with the quotes) as `application/json`, not the plain text `hello`. The same applies to `Request#withEntity` with a `String` argument: the text is encoded as a JSON string instead of being sent as is. Keep the import in the files that serve JSON, or use the explicit style when a route also handles plain text.
:::

### Example Project

The repository contains an older example project in `examples/interop-http4s`. It is written for http4s 0.21 and cats-effect 2 and does not build against this module; the code on this page is the up-to-date reference.

---

## Integrations(Zio-json)

An interop module connects ZIO JSON to another library. It provides `JsonEncoder`, `JsonDecoder` and related instances for that library's types, or adapts ZIO JSON codecs to that library's own abstractions. Each module is a separate artifact, so you only add the ones you use.

### Modules

Each interop module has a short page with installation steps and examples:

| Module                      | What it gives you                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [http4s](http4s.md)         | `EntityEncoder` and `EntityDecoder` instances for http4s 0.23 built from ZIO JSON codecs, so routes can read and write JSON bodies. |
| [refined](refined.md)       | Encoders, decoders and map-key codecs for refined types (`A Refined P`); decoding checks the predicate.                             |
| [Scalaz 7.x](scalaz-7x.md)  | An encoder and a decoder for Scalaz's `IList`.                                                                                      |
| [enumeratum](enumeratum.md) | Traits and builders that give enumeratum enums (string enums and value enums) their codecs and map-key codecs.                      |

### Platforms and Scala Versions

The modules are not all published for the same platforms. The table below follows the project build (`build.sbt` and `project/BuildHelper.scala`):

| Artifact                      | JVM | Scala.js | Scala Native | Scala 2.12 | Scala 2.13 | Scala 3 |
| ----------------------------- | --- | -------- | ------------ | ---------- | ---------- | ------- |
| `zio-json-interop-http4s`     | Yes | No       | No           | Yes        | Yes        | Yes     |
| `zio-json-interop-refined`    | Yes | Yes      | Yes          | Yes        | Yes        | Yes     |
| `zio-json-interop-scalaz7x`   | Yes | Yes      | Yes          | Yes        | Yes        | No      |
| `zio-json-interop-enumeratum` | Yes | Yes      | Yes          | Yes        | Yes        | Yes     |

The http4s module is a JVM-only project. The other three are cross-built, so in a Scala.js or Scala Native project you add them with `%%%` instead of `%%`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %%% "zio-json-interop-refined" % "1.1.3"
```

The Scalaz module has no Scala 3 artifact. The enumeratum module works on Scala 3, but enumeratum's own `findValues` macro needs the `-Yretain-trees` compiler option there for value enums, see [enumeratum on Scala 3](enumeratum.md#scala-3).

The other add-on modules (YAML, golden testing and `@jsonDerive` macros) are listed with their platforms in the [Modules](../index.md#modules) section of the Introduction page.

---

## Refined Interop

The `zio-json-interop-refined` module provides ZIO JSON instances for [refined](https://github.com/fthomas/refined) types. A refined type `A Refined P` is a value of type `A` that is known to satisfy the predicate `P`, for example `String Refined NonEmpty`. Encoding writes the underlying `A`. Decoding reads an `A` and then checks the predicate, so a payload that breaks it fails to decode.

### Installation

Add the module to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-refined" % "1.1.3"
```

The module is published for the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native, for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3. In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use `%%%` instead of `%%`.

### Instances

One import, `zio.json.interop.refined._`, brings four implicit instances into scope:

| Instance             | Type                            | Requires                                             |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `encodeRefined`      | `JsonEncoder[A Refined P]`      | `JsonEncoder[A]`                                     |
| `decodeRefined`      | `JsonDecoder[A Refined P]`      | `JsonDecoder[A]` and refined's `Validate[A, P]`      |
| `encodeFieldRefined` | `JsonFieldEncoder[A Refined P]` | `JsonFieldEncoder[A]`                                |
| `decodeFieldRefined` | `JsonFieldDecoder[A Refined P]` | `JsonFieldDecoder[A]` and refined's `Validate[A, P]` |

The decoders use refined's `refineV`, so the error message is the one refined produces for the failed predicate. The field instances let a refined type be the key of a `Map`; see [Map Keys](../reference/json-field-codecs.md) for how keys are encoded.

### Encoding and Decoding a Case Class

With the import in place, a case class whose fields are refined types derives a full codec like any other case class:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.interop.refined._

import eu.timepit.refined.api.Refined
import eu.timepit.refined.auto._
import eu.timepit.refined.collection.NonEmpty
import eu.timepit.refined.numeric.Positive

final case class Person(name: String Refined NonEmpty, age: Int Refined Positive)

object Person {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
}
```

Encoding writes the plain values. The `eu.timepit.refined.auto._` import lets us write the literals `"Aurora"` and `32` where refined types are expected, checking them at compile time:

```scala
Person("Aurora", 32).toJson
// res1: String = "{\"name\":\"Aurora\",\"age\":32}"
```

:::note
On Scala 3, refined's `auto` conversion of literals is not available, so `Person("Aurora", 32)` does not compile there. Build the refined values with `refineV` instead, for example `refineV[NonEmpty]("Aurora")`, which returns an `Either`. The ZIO JSON instances from this module work the same on both versions.
:::

Decoding valid input succeeds:

```scala
"""{ "name": "Aurora", "age": 32 }""".fromJson[Person]
// res2: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = Aurora, age = 32)
// )
```

When a value breaks its predicate, decoding fails with refined's message and the path of the field:

```scala
"""{ "name": "", "age": 32 }""".fromJson[Person]
// res3: Either[String, Person] = Left(
//   value = ".name(Predicate isEmpty() did not fail.)"
// )

"""{ "name": "Aurora", "age": 0 }""".fromJson[Person]
// res4: Either[String, Person] = Left(
//   value = ".age(Predicate failed: (0 > 0).)"
// )
```

### Refined Types as Map Keys

`encodeFieldRefined` and `decodeFieldRefined` make a refined type usable as a `Map` key, as long as the underlying type has a key codec (`String`, `Int`, `Long` and `UUID` have built-in ones). Here the keys are stock-keeping unit codes that must match a pattern:

```scala
import eu.timepit.refined.string.MatchesRegex

type Sku = String Refined MatchesRegex["[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{4}"]

val stock: Map[Sku, Int] = Map(("ABC-1234": Sku) -> 5)
```

The key is written as its plain string:

```scala
stock.toJson
// res5: String = "{\"ABC-1234\":5}"
```

Decoding checks every key, and a key that does not match fails with the key in the error path:

```scala
"""{ "ABC-1234": 5 }""".fromJson[Map[Sku, Int]]
// res6: Either[String, Map[Sku, Int]] = Right(value = Map(ABC-1234 -> 5))

"""{ "abc": 5 }""".fromJson[Map[Sku, Int]]
// res7: Either[String, Map[Sku, Int]] = Left(
//   value = ".abc(Predicate failed: \"abc\".matches(\"[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{4}\").)"
// )
```

### See Also

- [Validate on Decode](../how-to/validate-on-decode.md) shows other ways to reject values while decoding, such as `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail`.
- [Manual Instances](../how-to/manual-instances.md) explains how to write a decoder for a refined type yourself.

---

## Scalaz 7.x Interop

The `zio-json-interop-scalaz7x` module provides a `JsonEncoder` and a `JsonDecoder` for [Scalaz 7](https://github.com/scalaz/scalaz)'s immutable list, `IList`. An `IList` is written as a JSON array, exactly like a Scala `List`.

### Installation

Add the module to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-interop-scalaz7x" % "1.1.3"
```

The module is published for Scala 2.12 and 2.13 only, on the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native. There is no Scala 3 artifact. In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use `%%%` instead of `%%`.

### Instances

The import `zio.json.interop.scalaz7x._` brings two implicit instances into scope:

| Instance           | Type                    | Requires         |
| ------------------ | ----------------------- | ---------------- |
| `ilistEncoder`     | `JsonEncoder[IList[A]]` | `JsonEncoder[A]` |
| `ilistJsonDecoder` | `JsonDecoder[IList[A]]` | `JsonDecoder[A]` |

Both convert through `List`: the encoder writes `IList#toList`, and the decoder reads a `List` and builds the `IList` with `IList.fromList`.

### Encoding

Encoding an `IList` produces a JSON array:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.interop.scalaz7x._

import scalaz._

IList(1, 2, 3).toJson
// res1: String = "[1,2,3]"
```

### Decoding

Decoding reads a JSON array into an `IList`. An element of the wrong type fails with its index in the error path:

```scala
"[1, 2, 3]".fromJson[IList[Int]]
// res2: Either[String, IList[Int]] = Right(
//   value = ICons(
//     head = 1,
//     tail = ICons(head = 2, tail = ICons(head = 3, tail = []))
//   )
// )

"""[1, "two"]""".fromJson[IList[Int]]
// res3: Either[String, IList[Int]] = Left(value = "[1](expected an Int)")
```

### In a Case Class

With the import in scope, case classes with `IList` fields derive their codecs like any other case class:

```scala
final case class Basket(items: IList[String])

object Basket {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Basket] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Basket]
}

Basket(IList("apple", "pear")).toJson
// res4: String = "{\"items\":[\"apple\",\"pear\"]}"

"""{"items":["plum"]}""".fromJson[Basket]
// res5: Either[String, Basket] = Right(
//   value = Basket(items = ICons(head = "plum", tail = []))
// )
```

---

## Annotations

ZIO JSON reads annotations on case classes, fields and sealed traits when it derives a codec with `DeriveJsonCodec.gen`, `DeriveJsonEncoder.gen` or `DeriveJsonDecoder.gen`. All of them live in the `zio.json` package, so `import zio.json._` brings them in. The table lists each annotation, what it can be placed on, and its arguments.

| Annotation                      | Applies to                                | Argument                                             | What it does                                                                        | How-to                                                                                                                 |
|---------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `@jsonField`                    | Field                                     | `name: String`                                       | Sets the JSON name of one field. Wins over `@jsonMemberNames`.                      | [Field names](../how-to/field-names.md#1-rename-one-field-with-jsonfield)                                              |
| `@jsonAliases`                  | Field                                     | `alias: String, aliases: String*`                    | Adds names the decoder also accepts for the field. No effect on encoding.           | [Field names](../how-to/field-names.md#5-read-old-names-with-jsonaliases)                                              |
| `@jsonMemberNames`              | Case class                                | `format: JsonMemberFormat`                           | Applies a name format to every field, for encoding and decoding.                    | [Field names](../how-to/field-names.md#2-rename-all-fields-with-jsonmembernames)                                       |
| `@jsonHint`                     | Subtype of a sealed family                | `name: String`                                       | Sets the type hint of the subtype. The default is the short class name.             | [Sealed traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md#1-change-a-type-hint-with-jsonhint)                                         |
| `@jsonHintNames`                | Sealed trait or class                     | `format: JsonMemberFormat`                           | Applies a name format to every type hint of the family.                             | [Sealed traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md#2-transform-all-hints-with-jsonhintnames)                                   |
| `@jsonDiscriminator`            | Sealed trait or class                     | `name: String`                                       | Writes the type hint as a field inside the object instead of a wrapper key.         | [Sealed traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md#3-use-a-discriminator-field-with-jsondiscriminator)                         |
| `@jsonNoExtraFields`            | Case class                                | None                                                 | Makes decoding fail when the JSON has a field the class does not have.              | [Optional fields](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md#4-reject-unexpected-fields-with-jsonnoextrafields)          |
| `@jsonExplicitNull`             | Case class or field                       | None                                                 | Writes `None` as `null` instead of leaving the field out.                           | [Optional fields](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md#2-write-nulls-with-jsonexplicitnull)                        |
| `@jsonExplicitEmptyCollections` | Case class or field                       | `encoding: Boolean = true, decoding: Boolean = true` | Sets whether empty collections are written and required. On a field, encoding only. | [Optional fields](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md#3-omit-empty-collections-with-jsonexplicitemptycollections) |
| `@jsonExclude`                  | Field                                     | None                                                 | Leaves the field out of the encoded JSON. The decoder still reads it.               | [Optional fields](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md#5-keep-a-field-out-of-the-json-with-jsonexclude)            |
| `@jsonDerive`                   | Case class or sealed trait (Scala 2 only) | `config: JsonDeriveConfig = JsonDeriveConfig.Codec`  | Generates the codec in the companion object at compile time.                        | [zio-json-macros](./zio-json-macros.md)                                                                                |

Most of these annotations have a program-wide form in `JsonCodecConfiguration`. The how-to page of each annotation names it.

### Member Formats

`@jsonMemberNames` and `@jsonHintNames` take a `JsonMemberFormat`. The built-in formats are `SnakeCase`, `KebabCase`, `PascalCase`, `CamelCase`, `IdentityFormat` and `CustomCase(f: String => String)`.

`ziojson_03.SnakeCase` and `ziojson_03.KebabCase` are the legacy formats of zio-json 0.3.0. They also put a separator before a digit, so `abc123Def` becomes `abc_123_def`. Use them only to keep JSON that was written by that version readable.

### jsonDerive

`@jsonDerive` is different from the other annotations: it does not change how a codec behaves, it writes the codec for you. It is a Scala 2 macro annotation from the separate `zio-json-macros` module, and it needs `-Ymacro-annotations` on Scala 2.13 or the macro paradise plugin on Scala 2.12. Placed on a case class or a sealed trait, it adds an `implicit val codecFor<Type>` (or `encode<Type>` / `decode<Type>`, depending on its `JsonDeriveConfig` argument) to the companion object. The other annotations on the class still apply to the generated codec. On Scala 3, use a `derives` clause instead.

See [@jsonDerive Macro Annotation](./zio-json-macros.md) for installation, the generated member names, generic classes and the limitations.

### See Also

- [Field names](../how-to/field-names.md) covers `@jsonField`, `@jsonAliases` and `@jsonMemberNames`.
- [Sealed traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md) covers `@jsonHint`, `@jsonHintNames` and `@jsonDiscriminator`.
- [Optional, default and null fields](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md) covers `@jsonNoExtraFields`, `@jsonExplicitNull`, `@jsonExplicitEmptyCollections` and `@jsonExclude`.
- [@jsonDerive Macro Annotation](./zio-json-macros.md) covers `@jsonDerive`.
- [JsonCodecConfiguration](./json-codec-configuration.md) sets the program-wide defaults that these annotations override per type.

---

## Built-in Instances

ZIO JSON ships a `JsonEncoder`, a `JsonDecoder` and usually a `JsonCodec` for the standard Scala and Java types. The instances live in the companion objects of the three type classes, so they are found without any import beyond `import zio.json._`. Derived encoders and decoders for your own case classes and sealed traits use these instances for their fields.

Every table below has the same columns. **JSON shape** is what the encoder writes and the decoder expects. **Encoder**, **Decoder** and **Codec** say whether an implicit `JsonEncoder`, `JsonDecoder` or `JsonCodec` exists for the type. A type with an encoder and a decoder but no codec still works with `toJson` and `fromJson`; only `JsonCodec[T]` itself does not resolve, and you can build it with `JsonCodec(JsonEncoder[T], JsonDecoder[T])`. **Notes** list the leniencies of the decoder and any Scala version or platform limits. Unless a note says otherwise, an instance exists on Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3, on the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native.

A few of the shapes, written by the built-in encoders:

```scala
import zio.json._
import java.time.Instant

(Left(1): Either[Int, String]).toJson
// res1: String = "{\"Left\":1}"

(1, "a", true).toJson
// res2: String = "[1,\"a\",true]"

Map("a" -> Some(1), "b" -> None).toJson
// res3: String = "{\"a\":1}"

Instant.parse("2024-01-02T03:04:05Z").toJson
// res4: String = "\"2024-01-02T03:04:05Z\""
```

### Text, Booleans and Unit

These types map to JSON strings, booleans and an empty object:

| Scala type | JSON shape              | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                           |
|------------|-------------------------|---------|---------|-------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `String`   | string                  | yes     | yes     | yes   | The encoder escapes `"`, `\` and control characters                             |
| `Char`     | string of one character | yes     | yes     | yes   | Decoding a longer or empty string fails with `expected single character string` |
| `Symbol`   | string                  | yes     | yes     | yes   | Written and read as the symbol's name                                           |
| `Boolean`  | `true` / `false`        | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                 |
| `Unit`     | `{}`                    | yes     | yes     | no    | The decoder accepts and skips any JSON value; see [Leniencies](#leniencies)     |

### Numbers

All number types encode as JSON numbers and accept the same number text when decoding, plus the leniencies listed in [Leniencies](#leniencies):

| Scala type                           | JSON shape | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|--------------------------------------|------------|---------|---------|-------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Byte`, `Short`, `Int`, `Long`       | number     | yes     | yes     | yes   | Out-of-range values fail. Quoted numbers and leading zeros are accepted; a leading `+` is not                                                                                                            |
| `Float`, `Double`                    | number     | yes     | yes     | yes   | `NaN` and the infinities are written as the strings `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"` ([Non-Finite Numbers](json-encoder.md#non-finite-numbers)). Values too large for the type decode as an infinity |
| `BigInt`, `java.math.BigInteger`     | number     | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder rejects values larger than 256 bits with `expected a 256-bit BigInt` (`expected a 256-bit BigInteger` for `BigInteger`). The encoder has no limit                                            |
| `BigDecimal`, `java.math.BigDecimal` | number     | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder limits the unscaled value (mantissa) to 256 bits; the exponent may be any `Int`. The encoder keeps the scale, so `1.50` stays `1.50`                                                         |

### Option and Either

`Option` and `Either` wrap another type, so they need an instance for each type they hold:

| Scala type     | JSON shape                     | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                                                                                    |
|----------------|--------------------------------|---------|---------|-------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Option[A]`    | the value, or `null`           | yes     | yes     | yes   | `None` is `null`. In a derived case class, a `None` field is left out by default and a missing field decodes as `None`. `Some(None)` encodes like `None` |
| `Either[A, B]` | `{"Left": a}` / `{"Right": b}` | yes     | yes     | yes   | See [Either Wire Format](#either-wire-format)                                                                                                            |

### Either Wire Format

The `Either` encoder wraps the value in an object with a single key, `"Left"` or `"Right"`. The decoder accepts more key names, for compatibility with other libraries:

| Side    | Keys accepted by the decoder |
|---------|------------------------------|
| `Left`  | `"Left"`, `"left"`, `"a"`    |
| `Right` | `"Right"`, `"right"`, `"b"`  |

Other keys in the object are skipped. An object with neither side fails with `missing fields`, one with both sides fails with `ambiguous either, zip present`, and one that names the same side twice fails with `duplicate`:

```scala
"""{"right":"x"}""".fromJson[Either[Int, String]]
// res5: Either[String, Either[Int, String]] = Right(
//   value = Right(value = "x")
// )

"""{"Left":1,"Right":"x"}""".fromJson[Either[Int, String]]
// res6: Either[String, Either[Int, String]] = Left(
//   value = "(ambiguous either, zip present)"
// )
```

For an untagged `Either`, use `JsonEncoder#orElseEither` and `JsonDecoder#orElseEither`; see [JsonEncoder](json-encoder.md#either-orelseeither-and-eitherwith).

### Tuples

Tuples of 1 to 22 elements are JSON arrays with one element per tuple member, each encoded with its own instance:

| Scala type            | JSON shape                | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                                                                                 |
|-----------------------|---------------------------|---------|---------|-------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Tuple1` to `Tuple22` | array of exactly N values | yes     | yes     | yes   | `(1, "a")` is `[1,"a"]`. Pretty output separates the elements with `", "` instead of putting each on its own line. An array of the wrong length fails |

### Sequences and Sets

Every sequence and set encodes as a JSON array of its elements. They differ in whether a `JsonCodec` exists and in what they need besides the element's instances:

| Scala type                               | JSON shape      | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                                                      |
|------------------------------------------|-----------------|---------|---------|-------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `List`, `Vector`, `Seq`                  | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                                            |
| `Chunk`                                  | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   | `zio.Chunk`                                                                                                                |
| `NonEmptyChunk`                          | non-empty array | yes     | yes     | yes   | `zio.NonEmptyChunk`. An empty array fails with `Chunk was empty`                                                           |
| `Array`                                  | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   | Needs a `ClassTag` for the element type, on the encoder too                                                                |
| `IndexedSeq`, `immutable.LinearSeq`      | array           | yes     | yes     | no    | No `JsonCodec`; build one with `JsonCodec(JsonEncoder[T], JsonDecoder[T])`                                                 |
| `Set`, `immutable.HashSet`               | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   | Duplicate elements in the input collapse silently                                                                          |
| `immutable.SortedSet`                    | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   | Needs an `Ordering` for the element type in both directions                                                                |
| `immutable.ListSet`, `immutable.TreeSet` | array           | yes     | yes     | no    | No `JsonCodec`. The `TreeSet` decoder needs an `Ordering`                                                                  |
| `immutable.ArraySeq`                     | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   | Scala 2.13 and 3 only. Needs a `ClassTag`                                                                                  |
| `IArray`                                 | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   | Scala 3 only. Needs a `ClassTag`                                                                                           |
| `Iterable[A]`                            | array           | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder builds a `List`                                                                                                |
| Any other `T[A] <: Iterable[A]`          | array           | yes     | no      | no    | A generic, low-priority encoder covers any `Iterable` subtype, for example `immutable.Queue`. There is no matching decoder |

When a derived decoder meets a missing field whose type is one of these collections, the result depends on the [explicitEmptyCollections](json-codec-configuration.md#explicitemptycollections) setting: by default the field is required.

### Maps

A JSON object's keys are strings, so every map type needs a `JsonFieldEncoder[K]` to write keys and a `JsonFieldDecoder[K]` to read them, in addition to the value's instances. The built-in key types are `String`, `Int`, `Long` and `UUID`; on Scala 3, any subtype of `String` that has a `JsonDecoder`, such as a string-literal union, can also be a decoded key. Any other key type needs instances of your own; [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](json-field-codecs.md) shows how.

| Scala type                                                        | JSON shape | Encoder  | Decoder  | Codec | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|------------|----------|----------|-------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Map[K, V]`, `immutable.HashMap[K, V]`, `immutable.ListMap[K, V]` | object     | yes      | yes      | yes   | Keys need a `JsonFieldEncoder` / `JsonFieldDecoder`. Entries whose value is `None` are left out when encoding. On duplicate keys, the last value wins                                                                       |
| `collection.SortedMap[K, V]`                                      | object     | yes      | yes      | yes   | As `Map`. The decoder and the codec also need an `Ordering[K]`                                                                                                                                                              |
| `mutable.Map[K, V]`                                               | object     | yes      | yes      | no    | As `Map`, but no `JsonCodec`                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `Chunk[(K, V)]`, other sequences of pairs                         | object     | explicit | explicit | no    | Only through `JsonEncoder.keyValueChunk`, `JsonEncoder.keyValueIterable` and `JsonDecoder.keyValueChunk`, which are not implicit and keep duplicate keys. Implicitly, a sequence of pairs is an array of two-element arrays |

### java.time

All 16 `java.time` types are written as ISO-8601 strings. The examples in the table are the exact text the encoder writes:

| Scala type       | JSON shape                                  | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                            |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------|---------|-------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Instant`        | `"2024-01-02T03:04:05.123Z"`                | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder needs a `Z` or an offset, which it converts to UTC                                   |
| `LocalDate`      | `"2024-01-02"`                              | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                  |
| `LocalTime`      | `"03:04:00"`                                | yes     | yes     | yes   | Seconds are always written, unlike `toString`; the decoder accepts `"03:04"`                     |
| `LocalDateTime`  | `"2024-01-02T03:04:05"`                     | yes     | yes     | yes   | Seconds are always written                                                                       |
| `OffsetTime`     | `"03:04:05+02:00"`                          | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                  |
| `OffsetDateTime` | `"2024-01-02T03:04:05+02:00"`               | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                  |
| `ZonedDateTime`  | `"2024-01-02T03:04:05+01:00[Europe/Paris]"` | yes     | yes     | yes   | Scala.js and Scala Native need the time-zone database (see below)                                |
| `ZoneId`         | `"Europe/Paris"`                            | yes     | yes     | yes   | Region ids and offsets such as `"+01:00"`. Scala.js and Scala Native need the time-zone database |
| `ZoneOffset`     | `"+02:00"`, `"Z"`                           | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                  |
| `Duration`       | `"PT1H30M"`                                 | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                  |
| `Period`         | `"P1Y2M3D"`                                 | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder also accepts weeks, such as `"P1W"`                                                  |
| `Year`           | `"2024"`                                    | yes     | yes     | yes   | A string, not a number. Years after 9999 carry a `+` sign                                        |
| `YearMonth`      | `"2024-01"`                                 | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                  |
| `MonthDay`       | `"--12-25"`                                 | yes     | yes     | yes   |                                                                                                  |
| `DayOfWeek`      | `"MONDAY"`                                  | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder ignores case: `"monday"` works. Abbreviations do not                                 |
| `Month`          | `"JANUARY"`                                 | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder ignores case                                                                         |

On Scala.js and Scala Native, `ZoneId` and `ZonedDateTime` with region ids need the time-zone database, `scala-java-time-tzdb`, as an extra dependency. Use the same version as the `scala-java-time` in your dependency tree, as described in the [installation notes](../index.md). For example, when that version is 2.10.0:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "io.github.cquiroz" %%% "scala-java-time-tzdb" % "2.10.0"
```

### UUID and Currency

Two more JDK types from `java.util` are written as strings:

| Scala type           | JSON shape                               | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                                                                                |
|----------------------|------------------------------------------|---------|---------|-------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `java.util.UUID`     | `"123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000"` | yes     | yes     | yes   | The decoder also accepts non-canonical forms with shorter groups, as `UUID.fromString` does: `"1-2-3-4-5"` is `00000001-0002-0003-0004-000000000005` |
| `java.util.Currency` | `"EUR"`                                  | yes     | yes     | yes   | The ISO 4217 code, read with `Currency.getInstance`, so it is case-sensitive                                                                         |

### JSON AST

The [`Json`](json-ast.md) type and each of its cases have instances, so a field of type `Json` holds any JSON value as it is:

| Scala type                                                               | JSON shape                                     | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                                                      |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|---------|---------|-------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Json`                                                                   | any JSON value                                 | yes     | yes     | yes   | Instances live in the `Json` companion                                                                                     |
| `Json.Obj`, `Json.Arr`, `Json.Str`, `Json.Num`, `Json.Bool`, `Json.Null` | object, array, string, number, boolean, `null` | yes     | yes     | yes   | Each case's companion has its own instances, which reject the other shapes. `Json.Num` decodes with the `BigDecimal` rules |

### Scala 3 Only

Besides `IArray` (see [Sequences and Sets](#sequences-and-sets)), Scala 3 adds instances for unions of string literal types:

| Scala type                                 | JSON shape | Encoder | Decoder | Codec | Notes                                                                                                |
|--------------------------------------------|------------|---------|---------|-------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| String-literal union, such as `"a" \| "b"` | string     | yes     | yes     | no    | Scala 3 only. Decoding any other string fails with `expected one of: a, b`. Works as a `Map` key too |

[JsonEncoder](json-encoder.md#scala-2-vs-scala-3) shows a union used as a field and as a `Map` key.

### Leniencies

Several decoders accept more than the JSON that the matching encoder writes. This keeps them compatible with JSON produced by other tools, but it also means that some unusual input decodes without an error:

- Every number type accepts a number inside a string: `"42"` decodes as `42`.
- Integer types accept leading zeros: `007` decodes as `7`. A leading `+` is rejected.
- `Float` and `Double` accept the quoted strings `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"+Infinity"` and `"-Infinity"`. Bare `NaN` and `Infinity`, which are not JSON, are rejected.
- `Unit` accepts any JSON value and skips it without checking that it is well-formed.
- `DayOfWeek` and `Month` ignore case, and `UUID` accepts non-canonical forms (see [java.time](#javatime) and [UUID and Currency](#uuid-and-currency)).
- Sets drop duplicate elements, and maps keep the last value for a duplicate key, without an error.

The first four, decoded at the top level:

```scala
"\"42\"".fromJson[Int]
// res7: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 42)

"007".fromJson[Int]
// res8: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 7)

"\"NaN\"".fromJson[Double]
// res9: Either[String, Double] = Right(value = NaN)

"""[1, {"x": 2}]""".fromJson[Unit]
// res10: Either[String, Unit] = Right(value = ())
```

The decoders also have leniencies that are not tied to one type, such as ignoring input after the first complete value at the top level and skipping unknown fields without validating them. [Decoder Strictness](../explanation/decoder-strictness.md) explains them and how to get stricter checks.

### See Also

- [JsonEncoder](json-encoder.md), [JsonDecoder](json-decoder.md) and [JsonCodec](json-codec.md), the three type classes
- [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](json-field-codecs.md) for map keys
- [Third-Party Types](../how-to/third-party-types.md) for types that have no built-in instance
- [JSON AST](json-ast.md) for the `Json` type
- [Decoder Strictness](../explanation/decoder-strictness.md) for how strict decoding is overall

## Derivation(Reference)

*Derivation* is how ZIO JSON writes a `JsonEncoder`, `JsonDecoder` or `JsonCodec` for your own case classes and sealed traits at compile time, so you don't write them by hand. This section is the reference for everything that controls it. The pages in it are:

- [JsonCodecConfiguration](../json-codec-configuration.md): the options that apply to every type derived where the configuration is in scope.
- [Annotations](../annotations.md): the annotations that change one type or one field.
- [@jsonDerive Macro Annotation](../zio-json-macros.md): a Scala 2 macro annotation that writes the derived codec into the companion object for you.

### Starting Derivation

On Scala 2 and Scala 3, call `gen` on one of the three derivation objects, usually in the companion object so the compiler finds the instance without an import:

| Call                     | Produces         |
|--------------------------|------------------|
| `DeriveJsonEncoder.gen`  | `JsonEncoder[A]` |
| `DeriveJsonDecoder.gen`  | `JsonDecoder[A]` |
| `DeriveJsonCodec.gen`    | `JsonCodec[A]`   |

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
}

println(Person("Ada", 36).toJson)
// {"name":"Ada","age":36}
```

On Scala 3 you can write a `derives` clause instead. It calls `JsonCodec.derived` (or `JsonEncoder.derived`, `JsonDecoder.derived`):

```scala
final case class Person(name: String, age: Int) derives JsonCodec
```

Derivation needs an instance for the parts of the type. For a sealed trait, the subtypes that have no instance of their own are derived together with the trait on both Scala versions. For a field whose type has no instance, Scala 3 derives one, while Scala 2 stops with a compile error, so give that type its own codec first. [Scala 2 and Scala 3 Differences](../../explanation/scala-2-vs-scala-3.md) lists every behaviour that differs between the two.

### Changing What Derivation Produces

There are three tools, and each works at a different scope:

| Tool                                                  | Scope                                                   | Example                                               |
|-------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| [Annotations](../annotations.md)                      | One type or one field                                   | `@jsonField("user_id")`, `@jsonDiscriminator("type")` |
| [JsonCodecConfiguration](../json-codec-configuration.md) | Every type derived where the implicit or `given` is in scope | `JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)` |
| [`@jsonDerive`](../zio-json-macros.md)                | Writes the derivation call for you (Scala 2 only)      | `@jsonDerive case class Person(...)`                  |

A configuration in scope sets the default for every derived type, and an annotation on a type or field takes priority over it. Here the configuration turns every field name into `snake_case`, and `@jsonField` still decides the name of one field:

```scala
import zio.json._

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)
// config: JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(
//   sumTypeHandling = WrapperWithClassNameField,
//   fieldNameMapping = <function1>,
//   allowExtraFields = true,
//   sumTypeMapping = <function1>,
//   explicitNulls = false,
//   explicitEmptyCollections = ExplicitEmptyCollections(
//     encoding = true,
//     decoding = true
//   ),
//   enumValuesAsStrings = false
// )

final case class Account(accountId: Int, @jsonField("name") displayName: String)

object Account {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Account] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Account]
}

println(Account(1, "Ada").toJson)
// {"account_id":1,"name":"Ada"}
```

On Scala 3 the configuration is a `given`:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)

final case class Account(accountId: Int, displayName: String) derives JsonCodec
```

When no configuration is in scope, derivation uses `JsonCodecConfiguration.default`, so `derives` and `gen` never need one.

### See Also

- [Rename Fields](../../how-to/field-names.md), [Sealed Traits](../../how-to/sealed-traits.md) and [Optional, Default and Null Fields](../../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md) for the common changes, step by step
- [Derive Codecs on Scala 3](../../how-to/scala-3-derivation.md) and [Derive Codecs for Generic Types](../../how-to/generic-types.md) for the cases derivation needs help with
- [JSON Shapes and Round Trips](../../explanation/wire-format.md) for how each kind of type is written under each setting
