## JSON AST

The JSON AST is a tree of values that represents any JSON document, using the `zio.json.ast.Json` type. Most code decodes JSON straight into domain types, but the AST is useful when the shape of the document is not known in advance, when you need to edit a document, when you want to combine several documents, or when a case class has a field that holds arbitrary JSON. For navigating the AST with cursors, see [Cursors](#cursors).

`Json` is a sealed class with one case class per kind of JSON value:

```scala
sealed abstract class Json

object Json {
  final case class Obj(fields: Chunk[(String, Json)]) extends Json
  final case class Arr(elements: Chunk[Json])         extends Json
  final case class Str(value: String)                 extends Json
  final case class Num(value: java.math.BigDecimal)   extends Json
  final case class Bool(value: Boolean)               extends Json
  case object Null                                    extends Json
  type Null = Null.type
}
```

:::warning
`Json.Num` holds a `java.math.BigDecimal` of any size. Converting it yourself with the standard library (for example `num.value.toBigInteger`) can be a denial-of-service vector: `new java.math.BigDecimal("1e214748364").toBigInteger` tries to allocate gigabytes of heap. Decode numbers with `Json#as[Int]`, `Json#as[BigInt]` and so on, whose decoders check the size first. See [Security](../explanation/security.md#death-by-a-thousand-zeros).
:::

### The Json Type

`Json` has six cases: `Json.Obj`, `Json.Arr`, `Json.Str`, `Json.Num`, `Json.Bool`, and `Json.Null`. Objects keep their fields in insertion order as a `Chunk` of key-value pairs. This section shows how to build values and how they compare.

#### Creating Values

The cases can be constructed directly:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.{ Json, JsonCursor, JsonType }

val user: Json = Json.Obj(
  "name"   -> Json.Str("Alice"),
  "age"    -> Json.Num(30),
  "admin"  -> Json.Bool(false),
  "tags"   -> Json.Arr(Json.Str("ops"), Json.Str("dev")),
  "avatar" -> Json.Null
)
// user: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     ("name", Str(value = "Alice")),
//     ("age", Num(value = 30)),
//     ("admin", Bool(value = false)),
//     ("tags", Arr(elements = IndexedSeq(Str(value = "ops"), Str(value = "dev")))),
//     ("avatar", null)
//   )
// )
```

`Json.Num` wraps a `java.math.BigDecimal`, and `Json.Num.apply` has overloads for `Byte`, `Short`, `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `Double`, `BigInt`, `BigDecimal` and `java.math.BigInteger`, so numbers keep their precision.

The companions have a few more constructors and constants:

```scala
object Json {
  def apply(fields: (String, Json)*): Json // an object, typed as Json

  object Obj {
    val empty: Obj
    def apply(fields: (String, Json)*): Obj
    def apply(chunk: Chunk[(String, Json)]): Obj
    def apply(key: String, value: Json): Obj
  }

  object Arr {
    val empty: Arr
    def apply(elements: Json*): Arr
    def apply(chunk: Chunk[Json]): Arr
  }

  object Bool {
    val True: Bool
    val False: Bool
  }
}
```

`Json.apply` builds an object but returns it as `Json`, which helps when a `val` should have the general type. `Json#widen` does the same for any case, turning a `Json.Obj` into a `Json` without a type ascription:

```scala
val settings = Json("theme" -> Json.Str("dark"))
// settings: Json = Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("theme", Str(value = "dark"))))

val single = Json.Obj("retries", Json.Num(3))
// single: Json.Obj = Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("retries", Num(value = 3))))

println(single.widen)
// {"retries":3}
```

#### Equality

`Json` overrides `Json#equals` and `Json#hashCode`. Two objects are equal when they have the same keys with equal values, in any order. Arrays compare element by element, in order:

```scala
Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Num(1), "b" -> Json.Num(2)) == Json.Obj("b" -> Json.Num(2), "a" -> Json.Num(1))
// res2: Boolean = true

Json.Arr(Json.Num(1), Json.Num(2)) == Json.Arr(Json.Num(2), Json.Num(1))
// res3: Boolean = false
```

Numbers compare with `java.math.BigDecimal#equals`, which also compares the scale. So `1` and `1.0` are different values, whether you build them or parse them:

```scala
Json.Num(1) == Json.Num(1.0)
// res4: Boolean = false

"1".fromJson[Json] == "1.0".fromJson[Json]
// res5: Boolean = false
```

Keep this in mind when you compare documents in tests, and when you use `Json#intersect`, which relies on the same equality.

### Converting Between Types and the AST

`JsonEncoder#toJsonAST` takes a value and returns `Either[String, Json]`, and the `value.toJsonAST` extension calls it with the implicit encoder. `JsonDecoder#fromJsonAST` goes from a `Json` value to a domain type. The `Json#as` method is the shortcut for decoding:

```scala
final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
}
```

To encode a value into the AST, call `toJsonAST` on the value:

```scala
Person("Bob", 41).toJsonAST
// res6: Either[String, Json] = Right(
//   value = Obj(
//     fields = IndexedSeq(("name", Str(value = "Bob")), ("age", Num(value = 41)))
//   )
// )
```

To decode an AST into a domain type, call `as` on the `Json` value:

```scala
user.as[Person]
// res7: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "Alice", age = 30)
// )
```

Decoding with `as` fails when the fields do not match, which lets you check the shape of a document:

```scala
Json.Obj("name" -> Json.Str("Carol")).as[Person]
// res8: Either[String, Person] = Left(value = ".age(missing)")
```

### Embedding Raw JSON in Case Classes

A field of type `Json` holds any JSON value, which is the main reason the AST exists: part of a business object can stay free-form while the rest is typed. `Json` and each of its cases have their own implicit `JsonEncoder`, `JsonDecoder` and `JsonCodec` (`Json.codec`, `Json.Obj.codec`, `Json.Arr.codec`, `Json.Str.codec`, `Json.Num.codec`, `Json.Bool.codec` and `Json.Null.codec`), so derivation finds them for fields of those types.

A field typed as one case, such as `Json.Obj`, accepts only that kind of value:

```scala
final case class Event(kind: String, payload: Json.Obj)

object Event {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Event] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Event]
}
```

The payload keeps whatever object was sent:

```scala
"""{"kind":"click","payload":{"x":1,"y":2}}""".fromJson[Event]
// res9: Either[String, Event] = Right(
//   value = Event(
//     kind = "click",
//     payload = Obj(
//       fields = IndexedSeq(("x", Num(value = 1)), ("y", Num(value = 2)))
//     )
//   )
// )
```

When the payload is not an object, decoding from text fails with the usual parser message:

```scala
"""{"kind":"click","payload":1}""".fromJson[Event]
// res10: Either[String, Event] = Left(
//   value = ".payload(expected '{' got '1')"
// )
```

Decoding from a `Json` value (with `Json#as` or `JsonDecoder#fromJsonAST`) reports the mismatch with the message of the case decoder:

```scala
Json.Obj("kind" -> Json.Str("click"), "payload" -> Json.Num(1)).as[Event]
// res11: Either[String, Event] = Left(value = ".payload(Not an object)")
```

The case decoders use these messages when the value has a different type:

| Decoder          | Message              |
|------------------|----------------------|
| `Json.Obj`       | `Not an object`      |
| `Json.Arr`       | `Not an array`       |
| `Json.Str`       | `Not a string value` |
| `Json.Num`       | `Not a number`       |
| `Json.Bool`      | `Not a bool value`   |
| `Json.Null.type` | `Not null`           |

The `Json` decoder itself accepts every value.

### Reading Values

The simplest way to read a value is to test which case it is. `Json` has six `as*` methods (`asString`, `asNumber`, `asArray`, `asObject`, `asBoolean`, `asNull`). Each returns `Some` only when the value is that case: `asString` gives a `String`, `asNumber` a `Json.Num`, `asArray` a `Chunk[Json]`, `asObject` a `Json.Obj`, `asBoolean` a `Boolean`, and `asNull` a `Unit`:

```scala
user.asObject.map(_.keys)
// res12: Option[zio.Chunk[String]] = Some(
//   value = IndexedSeq("name", "age", "admin", "tags", "avatar")
// )

user.asString
// res13: Option[String] = None
```

The `Obj#get` method reads one field by name, and `Obj#contains` checks whether a field exists:

```scala
println(user.asObject.map(_.get("name")))
// Some(Some("Alice"))
```

Checking for a field that is not present returns `false` inside an `Option`:

```scala
user.asObject.map(_.contains("nickname"))
// res15: Option[Boolean] = Some(value = false)
```

The `Json#get` method takes a [cursor](#cursors) and returns the node at that location as `Either[String, A]`, where `A` is the node type the cursor refines to. A cursor that ends in a type filter such as `isNumber` returns that case directly:

```scala
println(user.get(JsonCursor.field("age").isNumber).map(_.value))
// Right(30)
```

`Json#arrayOrObject(or, jsonArray, jsonObject)` handles the two container cases with one function each and returns `or` for every other case:

```scala
user.arrayOrObject("scalar", elements => s"array of ${elements.size}", obj => s"object with ${obj.keys.size} keys")
// res17: String = "object with 5 keys"
```

### Working with Objects

`Json.Obj` has its own methods for reading and editing fields. They return a `Json.Obj`, so they chain:

```scala
final case class Obj(fields: Chunk[(String, Json)]) extends Json {
  def contains(key: String): Boolean
  def get(key: String): Option[Json]
  def isEmpty: Boolean
  def nonEmpty: Boolean
  lazy val keys: Chunk[String]
  lazy val values: Chunk[Json]
  def toMap: Map[String, Json]
  def add(key: String, value: Json): Json.Obj
  def +:(entry: (String, Json)): Json.Obj
  def remove(key: String): Json.Obj
  def mapValues(f: Json => Json): Json.Obj
  def filter(pred: ((String, Json)) => Boolean): Json.Obj
  def filterKeys(pred: String => Boolean): Json.Obj
  def merge(that: Json.Obj): Json.Obj
}
```

`Json.Arr` has `isEmpty`, `nonEmpty` and a typed `merge(that: Json.Arr): Json.Arr`.

To inspect an object's fields:

```scala
val server = Json.Obj(
  "host"  -> Json.Str("localhost"),
  "tls"   -> Json.Obj("enabled" -> Json.Bool(false)),
  "debug" -> Json.Bool(true)
)
// server: Json.Obj = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     ("host", Str(value = "localhost")),
//     ("tls", Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("enabled", Bool(value = false))))),
//     ("debug", Bool(value = true))
//   )
// )

server.keys
// res18: zio.Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq("host", "tls", "debug")
server.values
// res19: zio.Chunk[Json] = IndexedSeq(
//   Str(value = "localhost"),
//   Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("enabled", Bool(value = false)))),
//   Bool(value = true)
// )
server.toMap.get("host")
// res20: Option[Json] = Some(value = Str(value = "localhost"))
server.isEmpty
// res21: Boolean = false
Json.Obj.empty.nonEmpty
// res22: Boolean = false
```

To remove, filter and rewrite fields:

```scala
println(server.remove("debug"))
// {"host":"localhost","tls":{"enabled":false}}
println(server.filterKeys(_ != "tls"))
// {"host":"localhost","debug":true}
println(server.filter { case (_, value) => value.asBoolean.isDefined })
// {"debug":true}
println(server.mapValues(_ => Json.Null))
// {"host":null,"tls":null,"debug":null}
```

`Obj#add` and its operator form `+:` add a field. A new key goes at the end of the object, even with `+:`:

```scala
println(server.add("port", Json.Num(8443)))
// {"host":"localhost","tls":{"enabled":false},"debug":true,"port":8443}
println(("id" -> Json.Num(1)) +: server)
// {"host":"localhost","tls":{"enabled":false},"debug":true,"id":1}
```

:::warning
`Obj#add` is implemented as `merge(Json.Obj(key -> value))`. When the key already exists and the old and the new value are both objects or both arrays, they are merged as `Json#merge` does (objects deep-merged, arrays element by element) instead of the new value replacing the old one.
:::

Adding a `tls` object to `server` merges it into the existing `tls` object. To replace the object, remove the key first:

```scala
println(server.add("tls", Json.Obj("port" -> Json.Num(8443))))
// {"host":"localhost","tls":{"enabled":false,"port":8443},"debug":true}
println(server.remove("tls").add("tls", Json.Obj("port" -> Json.Num(8443))))
// {"host":"localhost","debug":true,"tls":{"port":8443}}
```

For other combinations of values, `Obj#add` replaces the existing value in place:

```scala
println(server.add("debug", Json.Bool(false)))
// {"host":"localhost","tls":{"enabled":false},"debug":false}
```

### Cursors

A cursor, `JsonCursor[-From, +To <: Json]`, is a path into a `Json` document: a sequence of steps that go down into a field, down into an array element, or check the type of the current node. `From` is the type of node the path starts from and `To` is the type of node it ends on. Cursors are usually more convenient than pattern matching on `Json` directly, and the editing methods `Json#transformAt`, `Json#delete` and `Json#relocate` take them too. The trait has four cases, one per kind of step:

```scala
sealed trait JsonCursor[-From, +To <: Json]

object JsonCursor {
  case object Identity                                                      extends JsonCursor[Json, Json]
  final case class DownField(parent: JsonCursor[_, Json.Obj], name: String) extends JsonCursor[Json.Obj, Json]
  final case class DownElement(parent: JsonCursor[_, Json.Arr], index: Int) extends JsonCursor[Json.Arr, Json]
  final case class FilterType[A <: Json](parent: JsonCursor[_, _ <: Json], jsonType: JsonType[A])
      extends JsonCursor[Json, A]
}
```

For a step-by-step guide to reading and editing a document with cursors, see [Read and Edit JSON of Unknown Shape](../how-to/edit-json-with-cursors.md).

#### Building Cursors

The `JsonCursor` companion starts a path:

```scala
object JsonCursor {
  val identity: JsonCursor[Json, Json]
  def field(name: String): JsonCursor[Json.Obj, Json]
  def element(index: Int): JsonCursor[Json.Arr, Json]
  def filter[A <: Json](jsonType: JsonType[A]): JsonCursor[Json, A]
  val isObject: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Obj]
  val isArray: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Arr]
  val isString: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Str]
  val isNumber: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Num]
  val isBool: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Bool]
  val isNull: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Null]
}
```

`JsonCursor.identity` points at the root. `JsonCursor.field` and `JsonCursor.element` check that the root is an object or an array, and then step into it. The `is*` values and `JsonCursor.filter` only check the type of the root.

The cursor instance has the same steps, to extend a path:

```scala
sealed trait JsonCursor[-From, +To <: Json] {
  def field(field: String)(implicit ev: To <:< Json.Obj): JsonCursor.DownField
  def element(index: Int)(implicit ev: To <:< Json.Arr): JsonCursor.DownElement
  def isObject: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Obj]
  def isArray: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Arr]
  def isString: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Str]
  def isNumber: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Num]
  def isBool: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Bool]
  def isNull: JsonCursor[Json, Json.Null]
  def filterType[B <: Json](jsonType: JsonType[B]): JsonCursor[Json, B]
  def >>>[Next <: Json](that: JsonCursor[To, Next]): JsonCursor[From, Next]
  def andThen[Next <: Json](that: JsonCursor[To, Next]): JsonCursor[From, Next]
}
```

`JsonCursor#field` compiles only when the cursor already ends on a `Json.Obj`, and `JsonCursor#element` only when it ends on a `Json.Arr`. A field step ends on a plain `Json`, so add a `JsonCursor#isObject` or `JsonCursor#isArray` step before going deeper:

```scala
val profile: Json = Json.Obj(
  "user" -> Json.Obj(
    "name"  -> Json.Str("Ada"),
    "langs" -> Json.Arr(Json.Str("scala"), Json.Str("ocaml"))
  ),
  "visits" -> Json.Num(12)
)
// profile: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     (
//       "user",
//       Obj(
//         fields = IndexedSeq(
//           ("name", Str(value = "Ada")),
//           (
//             "langs",
//             Arr(
//               elements = IndexedSeq(Str(value = "scala"), Str(value = "ocaml"))
//             )
//           )
//         )
//       )
//     ),
//     ("visits", Num(value = 12))
//   )
// )

println(profile.get(JsonCursor.field("user").isObject.field("name").isString))
// Right("Ada")
println(profile.get(JsonCursor.field("user").isObject.field("langs").isArray.element(1)))
// Right("ocaml")
```

`JsonCursor#>>>` and its alias `JsonCursor#andThen` append a second cursor to the first, so you can build reusable path pieces. `JsonCursor.identity` is the neutral element: appending it changes nothing, and reading it returns the whole document:

```scala
val userCursor = JsonCursor.field("user") >>> JsonCursor.isObject
// userCursor: JsonCursor[Json.Obj, Json.Obj] = FilterType(
//   parent = DownField(
//     parent = FilterType(parent = Identity, jsonType = Obj),
//     name = "user"
//   ),
//   jsonType = Obj
// )

println(profile.get(userCursor.andThen(JsonCursor.field("name"))))
// Right("Ada")

profile.get(JsonCursor.identity) == Right(profile)
// res35: Boolean = true
```

#### Filtering by Type

`JsonType[A]` names one case of `Json`. It has six values, `JsonType.Obj`, `JsonType.Arr`, `JsonType.Str`, `JsonType.Num`, `JsonType.Bool` and `JsonType.Null`, and one method, `get(json: Json): Either[String, A]`, which returns the value as that case or an `expected ...` error. The `is*` steps are shortcuts for `JsonCursor#filterType` and `JsonCursor.filter` with one of these values:

```scala
println(profile.get(JsonCursor.field("visits").filterType(JsonType.Num)))
// Right(12)
println(profile.get(JsonCursor.filter(JsonType.Obj)).map(_.keys))
// Right(Chunk(user,visits))

JsonType.Str.get(Json.Num(1))
// res38: Either[String, Json.Str] = Left(value = "expected string")
```

#### Cursor Errors

The methods that take a cursor (`Json#get`, `Json#transformAt`, `Json#delete` and `Json#relocate`) return a `Left` with one of these messages when the cursor does not match the document:

| Message                              | Cause                                                              |
|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `No such field: 'name'`              | A `field` step names a key that the object does not have           |
| `The array does not have index n`    | An `element` step goes past the end of the array                   |
| `expected object`, `expected array`  | A type check failed; `field` and `element` start with such a check |
| `expected string`, `expected number` | A type check failed                                                |
| `expected boolean`, `expected null`  | A type check failed                                                |

For example, reading a missing field, an element past the end, and a value of the wrong type:

```scala
profile.get(JsonCursor.field("email"))
// res39: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = "No such field: 'email'")

profile.get(JsonCursor.field("user").isObject.field("langs").isArray.element(5))
// res40: Either[String, Json] = Left(
//   value = "The array does not have index 5"
// )

profile.get(JsonCursor.field("visits").isString)
// res41: Either[String, Json.Str] = Left(value = "expected string")
```

### Transforming Values

The `mapXxx` methods change one kind of node without touching the rest. Each applies only to the value it is called on, never to nested values, and returns the value unchanged when it is a different case:

| Method             | Changes     | Function type                                  |
|--------------------|-------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `mapBoolean`       | `Json.Bool` | `Boolean => Boolean`                           |
| `mapNumber`        | `Json.Num`  | `java.math.BigDecimal => java.math.BigDecimal` |
| `mapString`        | `Json.Str`  | `String => String`                             |
| `mapArray`         | `Json.Arr`  | `Chunk[Json] => Chunk[Json]`                   |
| `mapArrayValues`   | `Json.Arr`  | `Json => Json`, applied to each element        |
| `mapObject`        | `Json.Obj`  | `Json.Obj => Json.Obj`                         |
| `mapObjectKeys`    | `Json.Obj`  | `String => String`, applied to each key        |
| `mapObjectValues`  | `Json.Obj`  | `Json => Json`, applied to each value          |
| `mapObjectEntries` | `Json.Obj`  | `((String, Json)) => (String, Json)`           |

For example, `mapObjectKeys` renames the top-level keys of an object; nested objects are not changed (use `transformDownSome` for that):

```scala
println(user.mapObjectKeys(_.toUpperCase))
// {"NAME":"Alice","AGE":30,"ADMIN":false,"TAGS":["ops","dev"],"AVATAR":null}
```

`mapObjectValues` and `mapArrayValues` apply a function to each direct child:

```scala
println(user.mapObjectValues {
  case Json.Num(value) => Json.Num(value.add(java.math.BigDecimal.ONE))
  case other           => other
})
// {"name":"Alice","age":31,"admin":false,"tags":["ops","dev"],"avatar":null}
```

The `Json#transformDown` method walks the whole tree from the top and applies a function to every node. The `Json#transformUp` method works from the bottom, so the function sees each node after its children were transformed. Use the `transformDownSome` and `transformUpSome` variants when the function only applies to some nodes. The following replaces every string with its upper-case form and leaves other values unchanged:

```scala
println(user.transformDownSome { case Json.Str(value) => Json.Str(value.toUpperCase) })
// {"name":"ALICE","age":30,"admin":false,"tags":["OPS","DEV"],"avatar":null}
```

To change a single node located by a cursor, use `Json#transformAt`. It returns an `Either` because the cursor may not match the document:

```scala
println(user.transformAt(JsonCursor.field("age").isNumber)(age => Json.Num(age.value.add(java.math.BigDecimal.TEN))))
// Right({"name":"Alice","age":40,"admin":false,"tags":["ops","dev"],"avatar":null})
```

### Deleting and Relocating Values

The `Json#delete` method removes the node at a cursor:

```scala
println(user.delete(JsonCursor.field("avatar")))
// Right({"name":"Alice","age":30,"admin":false,"tags":["ops","dev"]})
```

Deleting `JsonCursor.identity` deletes the whole document and returns `Right(Json.Null)`.

:::warning
`Json#delete` does not check a type filter that comes after the last `field` or `element` step. `Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Num(1)).delete(JsonCursor.field("a").isString)` returns `Right({})`: the number is removed although the cursor asks for a string. Type filters earlier in the path are checked. If the type matters, check it with `Json#get` before deleting.
:::

The `Json#relocate` method copies the node at the `from` cursor over the existing node at the `to` cursor, then deletes the `from` node. Relocating `tags` to `avatar` replaces the `null` value there, and removes `tags` from its original location:

```scala
println(user.relocate(JsonCursor.field("tags"), JsonCursor.field("avatar")))
// Right({"name":"Alice","age":30,"admin":false,"avatar":["ops","dev"]})
```

The `to` location must already exist. Relocating to a key that is not in the object fails:

```scala
user.relocate(JsonCursor.field("tags"), JsonCursor.field("roles"))
// res48: Either[String, Json] = Left(value = "No such field: 'roles'")
```

To move a value to a new key, read it with `Json.Obj#get`, add it with `Json.Obj#add`, and remove the old key:

```scala
println(user.asObject.map(obj => obj.get("tags").fold(obj)(tags => obj.remove("tags").add("roles", tags))))
// Some({"name":"Alice","age":30,"admin":false,"avatar":null,"roles":["ops","dev"]})
```

### Combining Documents

The `Json#merge` method combines two values:

- When both values are objects, the result contains the fields of both. A key that appears on both sides is merged recursively, so nested objects are merged, and for scalar values the right-hand side wins.
- When both values are arrays, elements at the same index are merged with each other, and the extra elements of the longer array are kept.
- For any other combination, the right-hand side replaces the left.

Merging a set of overrides into defaults keeps the keys that are not overridden:

```scala
val defaults: Json = Json.Obj("admin" -> Json.Bool(false), "locale" -> Json.Str("en"))
// defaults: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     ("admin", Bool(value = false)),
//     ("locale", Str(value = "en"))
//   )
// )
val overrides: Json = Json.Obj("locale" -> Json.Str("de"))
// overrides: Json = Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("locale", Str(value = "de"))))

println(defaults.merge(overrides))
// {"admin":false,"locale":"de"}
```

Merging two arrays works index by index:

```scala
println(Json.Arr(Json.Num(1), Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Num(1))).merge(Json.Arr(Json.Num(2), Json.Obj("b" -> Json.Num(2)), Json.Num(3))))
// [2,{"a":1,"b":2},3]
```

`Json.Obj#merge` and `Json.Arr#merge` are typed versions that return a `Json.Obj` and a `Json.Arr`.

The `Json#intersect` method keeps only the key-value pairs (for objects) or elements (for arrays) that are equal on both sides. It returns `Left("Non compatible types")` unless both values are objects or both are arrays. A key whose value differs between the two sides is dropped:

```scala
val left: Json  = Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Num(1), "b" -> Json.Num(2), "c" -> Json.Num(3))
// left: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     ("a", Num(value = 1)),
//     ("b", Num(value = 2)),
//     ("c", Num(value = 3))
//   )
// )
val right: Json = Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Num(9), "b" -> Json.Num(2))
// right: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(("a", Num(value = 9)), ("b", Num(value = 2)))
// )

println(left.intersect(right))
// Right({"b":2})
println(left.intersect(Json.Arr()))
// Left(Non compatible types)
```

### Folding Over a Document

The `Json#foldDown` and `Json#foldUp` methods reduce the whole tree into one value, with `foldDownSome` and `foldUpSome` as the variants for partial functions. `foldDown` visits each node before its children (pre-order), and `foldUp` visits the children first (post-order). Both visit object fields in their insertion order. For example, to count the string values in a document:

```scala
user.foldDown(0) {
  case (count, Json.Str(_)) => count + 1
  case (count, _)           => count
}
// res54: Int = 3
```

The visiting order shows when the function collects the nodes it sees:

```scala
val small = Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Arr(Json.Num(1)))
// small: Json.Obj = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(("a", Arr(elements = IndexedSeq(Num(value = 1)))))
// )

small.foldDown(List.empty[String])((seen, json) => seen :+ json.toString)
// res55: List[String] = List("{\"a\":[1]}", "[1]", "1")

small.foldUp(List.empty[String])((seen, json) => seen :+ json.toString)
// res56: List[String] = List("1", "[1]", "{\"a\":[1]}")
```

### Rendering and Parsing

The `toJson` extension on `Json` renders the AST as a compact string, and `toJsonPretty` renders it with indentation. `Json#toString` also renders compact JSON, so string interpolation and logging show JSON text. The `fromJson[Json]` method parses a string into an AST:

```scala
println(user.toJsonPretty)
// {
//   "name" : "Alice",
//   "age" : 30,
//   "admin" : false,
//   "tags" : [
//     "ops",
//     "dev"
//   ],
//   "avatar" : null
// }

println(s"user = $user")
// user = {"name":"Alice","age":30,"admin":false,"tags":["ops","dev"],"avatar":null}
```

Parsing a string into the AST uses the same `fromJson` method as domain types, with `Json` as the type:

```scala
"""{"id": 7, "ok": true}""".fromJson[Json]
// res59: Either[String, Json] = Right(
//   value = Obj(
//     fields = IndexedSeq(("id", Num(value = 7)), ("ok", Bool(value = true)))
//   )
// )
```

For encoding and decoding in streams, see [Streaming API](streaming.md). For YAML, the AST is the intermediate form, as described in [YAML](./yaml.md).

---

## JsonCodecConfiguration

`JsonCodecConfiguration` is a case class that sets the defaults for derived codecs. `DeriveJsonCodec.gen`, `DeriveJsonEncoder.gen` and `DeriveJsonDecoder.gen` read it when they derive an instance. Annotations on a single type, such as `@jsonDiscriminator` or `@jsonMemberNames`, override the configuration for that type.

### Options

All options have defaults, so you only name the ones you want to change.

| Option                     | Type                       | Scala 2 default              | Scala 3 default              | What it controls                                   |
|----------------------------|----------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| `sumTypeHandling`          | `SumTypeHandling`          | `WrapperWithClassNameField`  | `WrapperWithClassNameField`  | How a sealed trait case is tagged                  |
| `fieldNameMapping`         | `JsonMemberFormat`         | `IdentityFormat`             | `IdentityFormat`             | How case class field names become JSON keys        |
| `allowExtraFields`         | `Boolean`                  | `true`                       | `true`                       | Whether unknown keys are accepted on decode        |
| `sumTypeMapping`           | `JsonMemberFormat`         | `IdentityFormat`             | `IdentityFormat`             | How case names become JSON tags                    |
| `explicitNulls`            | `Boolean`                  | `false`                      | `false`                      | Whether `None` is written as `null`                |
| `explicitEmptyCollections` | `ExplicitEmptyCollections` | `ExplicitEmptyCollections()` | `ExplicitEmptyCollections()` | Whether empty collections are written and required |
| `enumValuesAsStrings`      | `Boolean`                  | `false`                      | `true`                       | Whether case objects are plain JSON strings        |

The only difference in defaults between the two Scala versions is `enumValuesAsStrings`. A few behaviours also differ; see [Scala 2 and Scala 3 differences](#scala-2-and-scala-3-differences).

### Passing a Custom Configuration

The derivation macros take the configuration as an implicit parameter. The library provides `JsonCodecConfiguration.default` in the companion object. To use your own, put an implicit value in scope before the `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` call. A value in scope wins over the companion default. Here the companion of `User` holds a configuration that writes field names in snake case:

```scala
import zio.json._

case class User(firstName: String, lastName: String)

object User {
  implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
    JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)

  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[User] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[User]
}
```

Encoding and decoding both use the snake-case names:

```scala
User("Ada", "Lovelace").toJson
// res1: String = "{\"first_name\":\"Ada\",\"last_name\":\"Lovelace\"}"

"""{"first_name":"Ada","last_name":"Lovelace"}""".fromJson[User]
// res2: Either[String, User] = Right(
//   value = User(firstName = "Ada", lastName = "Lovelace")
// )
```

You can also start from the default and change one option with `copy`:

```scala
import zio.json._

val strict: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration.default.copy(allowExtraFields = false)
```

:::warning
`JsonCodecConfiguration#copy` is hand-written, and each of its parameters defaults to the library default, not to the current value. Call it only on `JsonCodecConfiguration.default`. On any other configuration, every option you do not name is reset: `JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase).copy(allowExtraFields = false)` loses the `SnakeCase` mapping. To set several options, name them all in one `JsonCodecConfiguration(...)` call.
:::

In Scala 3, supply it as a `given`. The macros take it as a `using` parameter, and so do `JsonCodec.derived`, `JsonEncoder.derived` and `JsonDecoder.derived`, which a `derives` clause calls. The following Scala 3 code writes `{"first_name":"Ada","last_name":"Lovelace"}` for `User("Ada", "Lovelace")`:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)

final case class User(firstName: String, lastName: String) derives JsonCodec
```

A `derives` clause does not need a given of your own. Without one, `JsonCodecConfiguration.default` from the companion object is used, so this Scala 3 class encodes as `{"accountId":7,"ownerName":"Ada"}`:

```scala
final case class Account(accountId: Long, ownerName: String) derives JsonCodec
```

The configuration is read at derivation time. Changing it afterwards has no effect on codecs that already exist.

The subtypes of a sealed trait that have no codec of their own are derived together with the trait, using the configuration in scope at the outer `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` call. Field types are different on the two Scala versions:

- On Scala 2, every field type needs a codec in implicit scope. A case class field whose type has none fails to compile with `magnolia: could not find zio.json.DeriveJsonEncoder.Typeclass[...]`.
- On Scala 3, a field type that has no codec and can be derived is derived with the outer configuration.

On Scala 3, the following writes `{"full_name":"Ada","home_address":{"street_name":"Main St"}}` for `Customer("Ada", Address("Main St"))`, although `Address` has no codec:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)

final case class Address(streetName: String)
final case class Customer(fullName: String, homeAddress: Address) derives JsonCodec
```

### sumTypeHandling

Type: `SumTypeHandling`, a sealed trait in `JsonCodecConfiguration.SumTypeHandling` with two values:

- `WrapperWithClassNameField` (the default) wraps the case in an object with one key, the case name.
- `DiscriminatorField(name)` writes the case name into a field called `name` inside the case object itself.

`SumTypeHandling#discriminatorField` returns the field name as an `Option[String]`: `Some(name)` for `DiscriminatorField(name)` and `None` for `WrapperWithClassNameField`.

`@jsonDiscriminator("name")` on a sealed trait does the same for that trait only. The scaladoc warns that a discriminator is slower, uses more memory, and is open to denial of service attacks that the wrapper form is not. Use it only to match an external schema.

The following configuration writes the case name into a `type` field:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.JsonCodecConfiguration.SumTypeHandling.DiscriminatorField

sealed trait Shape
case class Circle(radius: Double) extends Shape
case class Square(side: Double)   extends Shape

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(sumTypeHandling = DiscriminatorField("type"))

implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Shape] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Shape]
```

The `type` field comes first in the output, and the decoder reads it to pick the case:

```scala
(Circle(1.0): Shape).toJson
// res8: String = "{\"type\":\"Circle\",\"radius\":1.0}"

"""{"type":"Square","side":2.0}""".fromJson[Shape]
// res9: Either[String, Shape] = Right(value = Square(side = 2.0))
```

With the default, the same value encodes as `{"Circle":{"radius":1.0}}`. See [sealed traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md) for the how-to side.

:::warning
Do not combine a discriminator with `allowExtraFields = false`. The discriminator form passes the whole object, discriminator field included, to the decoder of the case class, and that decoder then rejects the discriminator as an unknown field. Every case of the family fails to decode with `(invalid extra field)`, and nothing warns at compile time. The same happens with `@jsonDiscriminator` on the trait and `@jsonNoExtraFields` on a case.
:::

### fieldNameMapping

Type: `JsonMemberFormat`. It rewrites every case class field name. `@jsonMemberNames` overrides it per type, and `@jsonField` overrides it per field. The available formats are `IdentityFormat`, `SnakeCase`, `KebabCase`, `CamelCase`, `PascalCase`, and `CustomCase(f: String => String)`. The `ziojson_03` object holds the `SnakeCase` and `KebabCase` variants from zio-json 0.3.0, which put a separator before digits. The example under [Passing a custom configuration](#passing-a-custom-configuration) uses `SnakeCase`. See [field names](../how-to/field-names.md) for the how-to side.

### allowExtraFields

Type: `Boolean`. When `false`, decoding fails if the JSON has a key that the case class does not declare. `@jsonNoExtraFields` sets it per type. It breaks decoding of sum types that use a discriminator; see [sumTypeHandling](#sumtypehandling).

The configuration below makes a plain case class strict:

```scala
import zio.json._

case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(allowExtraFields = false)

implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Point] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Point]
```

The extra `z` key makes decoding fail:

```scala
"""{"x":1,"y":2,"z":3}""".fromJson[Point]
// res11: Either[String, Point] = Left(value = "(invalid extra field)")
```

### sumTypeMapping

Type: `JsonMemberFormat`. It rewrites the case names of a sealed trait, for both the wrapper key and the discriminator value. `@jsonHintNames` overrides it per trait, and `@jsonHint` overrides it per case.

With `KebabCase`, a case named `RoundCircle` is tagged `round-circle`:

```scala
import zio.json._

sealed trait Shape
case class RoundCircle(radius: Double) extends Shape

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(sumTypeMapping = KebabCase)

implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Shape] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Shape]
```

The wrapper key uses the rewritten name:

```scala
(RoundCircle(1.0): Shape).toJson
// res13: String = "{\"round-circle\":{\"radius\":1.0}}"
```

### explicitNulls

Type: `Boolean`. When `true`, an `Option` field that is `None` is written as `null`. By default the key is left out. `@jsonExplicitNull` sets it per type or per field. This option only affects encoding.

The configuration below writes `None` as `null`:

```scala
import zio.json._

case class Profile(name: String, nickname: Option[String])

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(explicitNulls = true)

implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Profile] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Profile]
```

The `nickname` key is now present with a `null` value:

```scala
Profile("Ada", None).toJson
// res15: String = "{\"name\":\"Ada\",\"nickname\":null}"
```

### explicitEmptyCollections

Type: `ExplicitEmptyCollections`, a case class `ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding: Boolean = true, decoding: Boolean = true)`.

- `encoding = false` leaves out fields whose collection is empty.
- `decoding = false` lets a missing collection field decode as an empty collection.

With the defaults, empty collections are written, and a missing collection field is an error. `@jsonExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding, decoding)` sets it per type. On a single field it changes encoding only; the `decoding` flag of a field annotation is ignored.

The configuration below turns off both directions:

```scala
import zio.json._

case class Basket(items: List[String])

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(explicitEmptyCollections = ExplicitEmptyCollections(encoding = false, decoding = false))

implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Basket] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Basket]
```

The empty list is left out, and a missing `items` key decodes as an empty list:

```scala
Basket(Nil).toJson
// res17: String = "{}"

"{}".fromJson[Basket]
// res18: Either[String, Basket] = Right(value = Basket(items = List()))
```

### enumValuesAsStrings

Type: `Boolean`. It applies to a sealed trait whose cases all have no fields. On Scala 3 that means case objects and parameterless enum cases. On Scala 2 it also includes case classes with an empty parameter list, and it is skipped if any case has its own hand-written codec. When `true`, each case is a plain JSON string. When `false`, each case is a wrapper object with an empty body, as for any other sum type. It has no effect when a discriminator is set, since the discriminator form always uses objects.

This is the one option with a different default per Scala version, so set it explicitly if your JSON must be the same on both. The how-to side is in [Write case objects as strings](../how-to/sealed-traits.md#5-write-case-objects-as-strings).

With all cases as case objects, the cases become strings:

```scala
import zio.json._

sealed trait Color
case object Red   extends Color
case object Green extends Color

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Color] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Color]
```

Each case is written and read as a JSON string:

```scala
(Red: Color).toJson
// res20: String = "\"Red\""

""""Green"""".fromJson[Color]
// res21: Either[String, Color] = Right(value = Green)
```

With `enumValuesAsStrings = false`, `Red` encodes as `{"Red":{}}`.

A case class with an empty parameter list counts as an enum value on Scala 2 only. On Scala 2, this family is written as strings:

```scala
import zio.json._

sealed trait Signal
case class Stop() extends Signal
case object Go    extends Signal

implicit val config: JsonCodecConfiguration =
  JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Signal] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Signal]
```

Both cases encode as JSON strings:

```scala
(Stop(): Signal).toJson
// res23: String = "\"Stop\""

(Go: Signal).toJson
// res24: String = "\"Go\""
```

The same family on Scala 3 uses the wrapper form for every case, because `Stop()` is not an enum value there. It writes `{"Stop":{}}` and `{"Go":{}}`:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(enumValuesAsStrings = true)

sealed trait Signal derives JsonCodec
case class Stop() extends Signal
case object Go    extends Signal
```

To get the same JSON on both versions, use case objects (or, on Scala 3, parameterless enum cases) for the values.

### Scala 2 and Scala 3 Differences

The options and their meaning are the same on both versions. These behaviours differ:

| Behaviour                                   | Scala 2                                     | Scala 3                                                                                            |
|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Default of `enumValuesAsStrings`            | `false`                                     | `true`                                                                                             |
| Case class with no fields, as an enum value | Counts, so it can be written as a string    | Does not count, so the family uses objects                                                         |
| Case object with a hand-written codec       | String form is skipped for the whole family | String form is used; the encoder ignores the hand-written codec, and the decoder passes `{}` to it |
| Field type without a codec                  | Compile error                               | Derived with the outer configuration                                                               |
| Configuration parameter                     | `implicit` value                            | `given` value, also used by `derives`                                                              |

---

## JsonCodec

`JsonCodec[A]` is a case class that holds a `JsonEncoder[A]` and a `JsonDecoder[A]` for the same type.
Use it when one value should describe both directions: you define the type's JSON shape once and get both halves.
Its instances should round-trip: encoding a value and decoding the result gives the value back.
Unlike `JsonEncoder` and `JsonDecoder`, `JsonCodec` is a `final case class`, not a trait.

| Member                                             | What it does                                             | Details                                         |
|----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| `JsonCodec(encoder, decoder)`                      | Builds a codec from two instances                        | [Construction](#construction)                   |
| `encoder`, `decoder`                               | The two halves                                           | [Construction](#construction)                   |
| `encodeJson(a, indent)`                            | Encodes with the encoder                                 | [Encoding and Decoding](#encoding-and-decoding) |
| `decodeJson(str)`                                  | Decodes with the decoder                                 | [Encoding and Decoding](#encoding-and-decoding) |
| `transform`, `transformOrFail`                     | Maps both directions, the decode side optionally failing | [Transforming a Codec](#transforming-a-codec)   |
| `orElse` (`<>`), `orElseEither` (`<+>`)            | Falls back to another codec when decoding                | [orElse](#orelse-and-orelseeither)              |
| `zip` (`<*>`), `zipLeft` (`<*`), `zipRight` (`*>`) | Pairs two codecs as a JSON array                         | [zip](#zip-zipleft-and-zipright)                |

### Construction

`JsonCodec` is a case class with one field for each half:

```scala
final case class JsonCodec[A](encoder: JsonEncoder[A], decoder: JsonDecoder[A])
```

The companion object offers three ways to get a codec:

- `JsonCodec(encoder, decoder)` builds one from two existing instances.
- `JsonCodec[A]` summons the implicit instance.
- `DeriveJsonCodec.gen[A]` derives both halves together (Scala 2 and Scala 3). Scala 3 also has `JsonCodec.derived`, used by `derives JsonCodec`.

The companion also declares `implicit def fromEncoderDecoder[A](encoder: JsonEncoder[A], decoder: JsonDecoder[A]): JsonCodec[A]`, which is the same as `JsonCodec(encoder, decoder)`.
Its two parameters are ordinary, not implicit, so implicit search never uses it to assemble a codec from an encoder and a decoder in scope. Call it, or `JsonCodec(encoder, decoder)`, explicitly.

The companion has codec instances for the primitive types, `Option`, `Either`, tuples of 1 to 22 elements, the common collections (`List`, `Vector`, `Seq`, `Set`, `Chunk`, `NonEmptyChunk`, `Array`, `Map` and others), `java.time` types, `UUID` and `Currency`.
A few types have an encoder and a decoder but no codec: `Unit`, `IndexedSeq`, `LinearSeq`, `ListSet`, `TreeSet` and `mutable.Map`. Build those with `JsonCodec(JsonEncoder[T], JsonDecoder[T])`.
[Built-in Instances](built-in-instances.md) lists every type with its JSON shape and says which of the three instances it has.

The examples on this page use a `Person` type with a derived codec:

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
}
```

A `JsonCodec[A]` in implicit scope also supplies a `JsonEncoder[A]` and a `JsonDecoder[A]`.
Both companions define `fromCodec` for this, so `toJson` and `fromJson` work with only the codec defined:

```scala
Person("Ada", 36).toJson
// res1: String = "{\"name\":\"Ada\",\"age\":36}"

"""{"name":"Ada","age":36}""".fromJson[Person]
// res2: Either[String, Person] = Right(value = Person(name = "Ada", age = 36))
```

### Encoding and Decoding

The codec's own `encodeJson` and `decodeJson` delegate to its encoder and decoder:

```scala
final def encodeJson(a: A, indent: Option[Int]): CharSequence
final def decodeJson(str: CharSequence): Either[String, A]
```

See [JsonEncoder](json-encoder.md#encodejson) and [JsonDecoder](json-decoder.md#decodejson) for the behavior of `indent` and for the `Left(String)` errors.

:::note[No default for indent]
`JsonEncoder#encodeJson` defaults `indent` to `None`. `JsonCodec#encodeJson` has no default, so you must pass it.
The codec has only the `CharSequence` overload of `decodeJson`. To decode bytes, use `codec.decoder.decodeJson(bytes)` or `fromJson`.
:::

Calling both methods on the `Person` codec, with `None` for compact output:

```scala
Person.codec.encodeJson(Person("Ada", 36), None)
// res3: CharSequence = "{\"name\":\"Ada\",\"age\":36}"

Person.codec.decodeJson("""{"name":"Ada","age":36}""")
// res4: Either[String, Person] = Right(value = Person(name = "Ada", age = 36))
```

### Transforming a Codec

`transform` and `transformOrFail` turn a codec for `A` into a codec for `B`:

```scala
final def transform[B](f: A => B, g: B => A): JsonCodec[B]
final def transformOrFail[B](f: A => Either[String, B], g: B => A): JsonCodec[B]
```

`transform` maps the decoded value with `f` and contramaps the encoder with `g`.
`transformOrFail` is the same, but `f` may fail with an error message, as in `JsonDecoder#mapOrFail`.
`g` cannot fail: the type `B` must always be encodable.
Internally they are `JsonCodec(encoder.contramap(g), decoder.map(f))` and `JsonCodec(encoder.contramap(g), decoder.mapOrFail(f))`.

To decode only strings that contain `@` into an `Email`, and to write an `Email` back as its string:

```scala
final case class Email(value: String)

val emailCodec: JsonCodec[Email] =
  JsonCodec[String].transformOrFail[Email](
    s => if (s.contains("@")) Right(Email(s)) else Left("not an email address"),
    _.value
  )
```

The encoder writes the plain string, and the decoder rejects a string without `@`:

```scala
emailCodec.encodeJson(Email("ada@example.com"), None)
// res5: CharSequence = "\"ada@example.com\""

emailCodec.decodeJson("\"ada\"")
// res6: Either[String, Email] = Left(value = "(not an email address)")
```

### Combining Codecs

Two codecs combine either as alternatives, where decoding falls back from one to the other, or as the elements of a JSON array.

#### `orElse` and `orElseEither`

Both methods take the fallback codec by name:

```scala
final def orElse(that: => JsonCodec[A]): JsonCodec[A]
final def orElseEither[B](that: => JsonCodec[B]): JsonCodec[Either[A, B]]
```

`<>` is an alias for `orElse`, and `<+>` is an alias for `orElseEither`.
The decoder tries this codec first and falls back to `that` if it fails.
For `orElseEither`, the encoder writes a `Left` with this codec's encoder and a `Right` with the other, with no tag in the JSON.
`orElse` is `orElseEither` followed by `transform`. It decodes with either codec, but its transform encodes every value as a `Right`, so it always writes with `that`, not with this codec.
The fallback rewinds the input, so it has the same memory caveat as [`JsonDecoder#orElse`](json-decoder.md#orelse-and-orelseeither).

To accept either a number or a string:

```scala
val intOrString: JsonCodec[Either[Int, String]] = JsonCodec[Int] <+> JsonCodec[String]
```

The `Left` is written with the `Int` codec and carries no tag, and a string falls through to the second decoder:

```scala
intOrString.encodeJson(Left(1), None)
// res7: CharSequence = "1"

intOrString.decodeJson("\"one\"")
// res8: Either[String, Either[Int, String]] = Right(
//   value = Right(value = "one")
// )
```

To see which codec `orElse` writes with, we pair the plain `Int` codec with a fallback whose encoder doubles the number:

```scala
val doubling: JsonCodec[Int] = JsonCodec(JsonEncoder[Int].contramap[Int](_ * 2), JsonDecoder[Int])

val primaryFirst: JsonCodec[Int] = JsonCodec[Int] <> doubling
```

Decoding succeeds with the first codec, but encoding uses the fallback's encoder:

```scala
primaryFirst.decodeJson("5")
// res9: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 5)

primaryFirst.encodeJson(5, None)
// res10: CharSequence = "10"
```

#### `zip`, `zipLeft` and `zipRight`

The three methods pair this codec with another one:

```scala
final def zip[B](that: => JsonCodec[B]): JsonCodec[(A, B)]
final def zipLeft(that: => JsonCodec[Unit]): JsonCodec[A]
final def zipRight[B](that: => JsonCodec[B])(implicit ev: Unit <:< A): JsonCodec[B]
```

`<*>` is `zip`, `<*` is `zipLeft`, and `*>` is `zipRight`.
`zip` pairs two codecs as a two-element JSON array.
`zipLeft` and `zipRight` drop the `Unit` side, which still takes up a slot in the array.
`zipRight` is only available when `Unit` is a subtype of `A` (usually `A` is `Unit`), because it encodes `()` for the dropped side.
There is no implicit `JsonCodec[Unit]`, so you build one from `JsonEncoder.unit` and `JsonDecoder.unit`.

A codec for a pair, and one that keeps only the count of a `[unit, count]` array:

```scala
val pair: JsonCodec[(String, Int)] = JsonCodec[String] <*> JsonCodec[Int]

val unitCodec: JsonCodec[Unit] = JsonCodec(JsonEncoder.unit, JsonDecoder.unit)

val countOnly: JsonCodec[Int] = unitCodec *> JsonCodec[Int]
```

`pair` writes a two-element array, and `countOnly` writes `{}` in the `Unit` slot and skips that slot when decoding:

```scala
pair.encodeJson(("apples", 3), None)
// res11: CharSequence = "[\"apples\",3]"

countOnly.encodeJson(3, None)
// res12: CharSequence = "[{},3]"

countOnly.decodeJson("""[{},3]""")
// res13: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 3)
```

### Scala 2 vs Scala 3

In Scala 2, derive with `DeriveJsonCodec.gen`, as above. It works on Scala 3 too.
In Scala 3, `derives JsonCodec` calls `JsonCodec.derived`.
It takes a `JsonCodecConfiguration` as a `using` parameter. The default configuration is found automatically, so a `derives` clause is all that is needed:

```scala
final case class Person(name: String, age: Int) derives JsonCodec
```

Define a given of your own only to change the defaults. A given in the enclosing scope is used by every `derives` clause that can see it:

```scala
given JsonCodecConfiguration = JsonCodecConfiguration(fieldNameMapping = SnakeCase)

final case class Account(accountId: Int, displayName: String) derives JsonCodec
```

Running the example file on Scala 3 prints:

```text
default configuration: {"name":"Ada","age":36}
decoded: Right(Person(Ada,36))
snake_case given: {"account_id":1,"display_name":"Ada"}
```

Scala 2.13 and Scala 3 also have a codec for `immutable.ArraySeq`, and Scala 3 has one for `IArray`. A union of string literal types has an encoder and a decoder on Scala 3, but no `JsonCodec`. See [JsonEncoder](json-encoder.md#scala-2-vs-scala-3).

- [Build an Encoder or Decoder from an Existing One](../how-to/manual-instances.md) for `contramap`, `map`, `mapOrFail`, `transform` and `transformOrFail`
- [JsonCodecConfiguration](json-codec-configuration.md) and [Annotations](annotations.md) for the derivation options
- [Built-in Instances](built-in-instances.md) for every type that has a codec out of the box
