## Streaming API

The streaming API connects ZIO JSON codecs to [ZIO Streams](https://zio.dev/reference/stream/). It encodes values into a `ZStream` of characters and decodes a `ZStream` of characters or bytes back into values, so a program can read or write a large JSON document, or a long sequence of documents, without holding all of the text in memory. It supports three shapes of input and output: a single JSON value, a JSON array read or written one element at a time, and [JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org/) (one value per line).

The API is a set of methods on `JsonEncoder` and `JsonDecoder`, one small type, `JsonStreamDelimiter`, and a few file helpers in the `zio.json` package object:

```scala
trait JsonEncoder[A] {
  def encodeJsonStream(a: A): ZStream[Any, Throwable, Char]
  lazy val encodeJsonLinesPipeline: ZPipeline[Any, Throwable, A, Char]
  lazy val encodeJsonArrayPipeline: ZPipeline[Any, Throwable, A, Char]
}

trait JsonDecoder[A] {
  def decodeJsonStream[R](stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, Char]): ZIO[R, Throwable, A]
  def decodeJsonStreamInput[R](
    stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, Byte],
    charset: Charset = StandardCharsets.UTF_8
  ): ZIO[R, Throwable, A]
  def decodeJsonPipeline(
    delimiter: JsonStreamDelimiter = JsonStreamDelimiter.Array
  ): ZPipeline[Any, Throwable, Char, A]
}

sealed trait JsonStreamDelimiter
object JsonStreamDelimiter {
  case object Newline extends JsonStreamDelimiter
  case object Array   extends JsonStreamDelimiter
}
```

:::note[JVM only]
Every method on this page exists only on the JVM. The `JsonEncoder` and `JsonDecoder` methods come from the `JsonEncoderPlatformSpecific` and `JsonDecoderPlatformSpecific` traits, and the file helpers from `JsonPackagePlatformSpecific`. On Scala.js and Scala Native these traits are empty. `JsonStreamDelimiter` is defined on every platform, but only the JVM `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonPipeline` uses it.
:::

### Usage

The examples on this page share one type and a helper that runs an effect and returns its result:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.json._

final case class Event(id: Int, kind: String)

object Event {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Event] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Event]
}

def runSync[A](effect: ZIO[Any, Throwable, A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(effect).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }

val events: ZStream[Any, Nothing, Event] =
  ZStream(Event(1, "created"), Event(2, "updated"), Event(3, "deleted"))
```

A round trip through JSON Lines encodes a stream of events with one pipeline and decodes the text with another:

```scala
val jsonLines: String =
  runSync(events.via(JsonEncoder[Event].encodeJsonLinesPipeline).runCollect.map(_.mkString))
// jsonLines: String = """{"id":1,"kind":"created"}
// {"id":2,"kind":"updated"}
// {"id":3,"kind":"deleted"}
// """

runSync(
  ZStream
    .fromIterable(jsonLines)
    .via(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonPipeline(JsonStreamDelimiter.Newline))
    .runCollect
)
// res1: Chunk[Event] = IndexedSeq(
//   Event(id = 1, kind = "created"),
//   Event(id = 2, kind = "updated"),
//   Event(id = 3, kind = "deleted")
// )
```

### Installation

The streaming API is part of the core `zio-json` artifact, which depends on `zio-streams`. No extra module is needed:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json" % "1.1.3"
```

### Encoding

The encoding side has one method that turns a single value into a character stream and two pipelines that turn a stream of values into a character stream. A `ZPipeline[Any, Throwable, A, Char]` is applied with `ZStream#via`.

#### Encoding a Single Value

`JsonEncoder#encodeJsonStream` returns the JSON text of one value as a `ZStream[Any, Throwable, Char]`:

```scala
trait JsonEncoder[A] {
  def encodeJsonStream(a: A): ZStream[Any, Throwable, Char]
}
```

To collect the characters of one event into a `String`:

```scala
runSync(JsonEncoder[Event].encodeJsonStream(Event(1, "created")).runCollect.map(_.mkString))
// res2: String = "{\"id\":1,\"kind\":\"created\"}"
```

#### Encoding JSON Lines

`JsonEncoder#encodeJsonLinesPipeline` writes each value followed by a newline character (`\n`), including the last one. An empty input stream produces no characters:

```scala
trait JsonEncoder[A] {
  lazy val encodeJsonLinesPipeline: ZPipeline[Any, Throwable, A, Char]
}
```

The `jsonLines` value from the [Usage](#usage) example holds three lines, each ending with `\n`:

```scala
jsonLines.count(_ == '\n')
// res3: Int = 3
```

#### Encoding a JSON Array

`JsonEncoder#encodeJsonArrayPipeline` writes the whole stream as one JSON array: an opening `[`, the values separated by commas, and a closing `]`. An empty input stream produces `[]`:

```scala
trait JsonEncoder[A] {
  lazy val encodeJsonArrayPipeline: ZPipeline[Any, Throwable, A, Char]
}
```

To encode the three events, and then an empty stream, as arrays:

```scala
runSync(events.via(JsonEncoder[Event].encodeJsonArrayPipeline).runCollect.map(_.mkString))
// res4: String = "[{\"id\":1,\"kind\":\"created\"},{\"id\":2,\"kind\":\"updated\"},{\"id\":3,\"kind\":\"deleted\"}]"

runSync(ZStream.empty.via(JsonEncoder[Event].encodeJsonArrayPipeline).runCollect.map(_.mkString))
// res5: String = "[]"
```

#### Output Format and Buffering

The three encoders share one implementation, so they format and emit output the same way:

- The output is always compact, written without indentation. There is no pretty-printed streaming form.
- The characters go through a `java.io.BufferedWriter` with a buffer of `ZStream.DefaultChunkSize` (4096) characters. Characters reach the output stream only when the buffer fills, in whole 4096-character blocks, or when the input stream ends and the rest is flushed. The pipelines can also emit empty chunks in between.
- Writing happens inside `ZIO.attemptBlocking`, on ZIO's blocking thread pool.

The buffering affects slow or never-ending sources, such as server-sent events or a log tail: a value can wait in the buffer until about 4 KB of later output arrives. An event such as `{"id":1,"kind":"created"}` takes 26 characters with its newline, so about 150 events fill one block. To send each value as soon as it is produced, encode the values one at a time instead, for example with `events.map(_.toJson + "\n")`.

### Decoding

The decoding side has two methods that read one value and one pipeline that reads many values.

#### Decoding a Single Value

`JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStream` decodes one value from a stream of characters. `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStreamInput` decodes one value from a stream of bytes, using the given `Charset` (UTF-8 by default):

```scala
trait JsonDecoder[A] {
  def decodeJsonStream[R](stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, Char]): ZIO[R, Throwable, A]
  def decodeJsonStreamInput[R](
    stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, Byte],
    charset: Charset = StandardCharsets.UTF_8
  ): ZIO[R, Throwable, A]
}
```

Both turn the stream into a `java.io.Reader` (through an `InputStream` for bytes) and decode from it on ZIO's blocking thread pool, so the input is read incrementally. To decode one event from characters and another from UTF-8 bytes:

```scala
runSync(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonStream(ZStream.fromIterable("""{"id":4,"kind":"archived"}""")))
// res6: Event = Event(id = 4, kind = "archived")

runSync(
  JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonStreamInput(
    ZStream.fromChunk(Chunk.fromArray("""{"id":5,"kind":"restored"}""".getBytes("UTF-8")))
  )
)
// res7: Event = Event(id = 5, kind = "restored")
```

Both methods stop after the first value. They do not read or check the rest of the stream, so text after the value, even a second value or invalid JSON, is not an error:

```scala
runSync(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonStream(ZStream.fromIterable("""{"id":6,"kind":"first"} not json""")))
// res8: Event = Event(id = 6, kind = "first")
```

#### Decoding Many Values

`JsonDecoder#decodeJsonPipeline` returns a pipeline from characters to values. It decodes one value at a time and passes the values downstream as they are decoded, so a long input never has to fit in memory:

```scala
trait JsonDecoder[A] {
  def decodeJsonPipeline(
    delimiter: JsonStreamDelimiter = JsonStreamDelimiter.Array
  ): ZPipeline[Any, Throwable, Char, A]
}
```

The `delimiter` argument selects how the values are laid out in the input. The decoding runs in a background fiber on ZIO's blocking thread pool, and the pipeline passes the decoded values on in batches: up to `ZStream.DefaultChunkSize` (4096) values for each chunk of input, and all remaining values when the input ends.

The pipeline takes characters. For a byte source, such as a file, put a character decoder in front of it, for example `ZPipeline.utf8Decode` followed by a step that splits the strings into characters, or `ZPipeline.decodeCharsWith(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`.

#### `JsonStreamDelimiter`

`JsonStreamDelimiter` has two cases, which choose the input layout for `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonPipeline`:

| Case                           | Input layout                                | Default |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `JsonStreamDelimiter.Array`    | One JSON array; each element is one value   | Yes     |
| `JsonStreamDelimiter.Newline`  | JSON Lines; one value per line              | No      |

With `JsonStreamDelimiter.Array`, the input must start with `[` (leading whitespace is allowed). An empty array gives an empty stream. Between elements the pipeline expects a `,` or the closing `]`:

```scala
runSync(
  ZStream
    .fromIterable("""[{"id":1,"kind":"created"}, {"id":2,"kind":"updated"}]""")
    .via(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonPipeline())
    .runCollect
)
// res9: Chunk[Event] = IndexedSeq(
//   Event(id = 1, kind = "created"),
//   Event(id = 2, kind = "updated")
// )
```

With `JsonStreamDelimiter.Newline`, the pipeline consumes one `\n` or `\r\n` after each value. The decoder skips whitespace before a value, so blank lines are accepted, and so are several values on one line separated by spaces:

```scala
runSync(
  ZStream
    .fromIterable("{\"id\":1,\"kind\":\"created\"}\r\n\r\n{\"id\":2,\"kind\":\"updated\"} {\"id\":3,\"kind\":\"deleted\"}")
    .via(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonPipeline(JsonStreamDelimiter.Newline))
    .runCollect
)
// res10: Chunk[Event] = IndexedSeq(
//   Event(id = 1, kind = "created"),
//   Event(id = 2, kind = "updated"),
//   Event(id = 3, kind = "deleted")
// )
```

A trailing newline after the last value is optional. An empty input gives an empty stream with either delimiter.

### File Helpers

The `zio.json` package object (through `JsonPackagePlatformSpecific`) has helpers that read and write files of JSON Lines. They combine the pipelines above with `ZStream.fromPath`, `ZSink.fromPath` and UTF-8 conversion:

```scala
package object json {
  def readJsonLinesAs[A: JsonDecoder](file: File): ZStream[Any, Throwable, A]
  def readJsonLinesAs[A: JsonDecoder](path: Path): ZStream[Any, Throwable, A]
  def readJsonLinesAs[A: JsonDecoder](path: String): ZStream[Any, Throwable, A]
  def readJsonLinesAs[A: JsonDecoder](url: URL): ZStream[Any, Throwable, A]

  def readJsonAs(file: File): ZStream[Any, Throwable, ast.Json]
  def readJsonAs(path: Path): ZStream[Any, Throwable, ast.Json]
  def readJsonAs(path: String): ZStream[Any, Throwable, ast.Json]
  def readJsonAs(url: URL): ZStream[Any, Throwable, ast.Json]

  def writeJsonLinesAs[R, A: JsonEncoder](file: File, stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, A]): RIO[R, Unit]
  def writeJsonLinesAs[R, A: JsonEncoder](path: Path, stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, A]): RIO[R, Unit]
  def writeJsonLinesAs[R, A: JsonEncoder](path: String, stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, A]): RIO[R, Unit]

  def writeJsonLines[R](file: File, stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, ast.Json]): RIO[R, Unit]
  def writeJsonLines[R](path: Path, stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, ast.Json]): RIO[R, Unit]
  def writeJsonLines[R](path: String, stream: ZStream[R, Throwable, ast.Json]): RIO[R, Unit]
}
```

The helpers behave as follows:

- `readJsonLinesAs` reads the file (or URL) as UTF-8 and decodes it with `decodeJsonPipeline(JsonStreamDelimiter.Newline)`. A `String` argument is a file path, converted with `Paths.get`.
- `readJsonAs` is `readJsonLinesAs[ast.Json]`. Despite its name, it reads JSON Lines, not one JSON document, so a file that holds a single document gives a stream of one `Json` value.
- `writeJsonLinesAs` encodes the stream with `JsonEncoder#encodeJsonLinesPipeline`, converts the characters to UTF-8 and writes them with `ZSink.fromPath`, which creates the file or replaces its contents.
- `writeJsonLines` is `writeJsonLinesAs` for a stream of `ast.Json` values.

There is no helper for a file that holds one JSON array. Combine `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonPipeline` or `JsonEncoder#encodeJsonArrayPipeline` with `ZStream.fromPath` and `ZSink.fromPath` yourself, as [Process Large JSON as a Stream](../how-to/streaming.md) shows.

The example below writes to a temporary file:

```scala
val file: java.nio.file.Path = java.nio.file.Files.createTempFile("events", ".jsonl")
```

Writing the three events to it and reading them back gives the same events:

```scala
runSync(writeJsonLinesAs(file, events) *> readJsonLinesAs[Event](file).runCollect)
// res11: Chunk[Event] = IndexedSeq(
//   Event(id = 1, kind = "created"),
//   Event(id = 2, kind = "updated"),
//   Event(id = 3, kind = "deleted")
// )
```

### Errors

Every streaming method reports failures in the `Throwable` error channel. A decoding failure is a `java.lang.Exception` whose message is the rendered error path, in the same format as the `Left` from `fromJson` (see [Errors](errors.md)). Reading a file that does not exist fails with the I/O exception from the file system.

#### Errors When Decoding a Single Value

`JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStream` and `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonStreamInput` fail the effect when the value does not decode. When the input ends in the middle of the value, the message is `unexpected end of input`, in lower case:

```scala
runSync(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonStream(ZStream.fromIterable("""{"id":7}""")).either)
// res12: Either[Throwable, Event] = Left(
//   value = java.lang.Exception: .kind(missing)
// )

runSync(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonStream(ZStream.fromIterable("""{"id":7,"ki""")).either)
// res13: Either[Throwable, Event] = Left(
//   value = java.lang.Exception: unexpected end of input
// )
```

#### Errors in a Decoding Pipeline

In the current implementation, `JsonDecoder#decodeJsonPipeline` behaves as follows when the input is not valid:

- The first value that fails to decode fails the whole stream. The values after it are not decoded, and a failed stream cannot resume, so `ZStream#catchAll` can only replace the rest of the stream.
- Values decoded before the failing one are not guaranteed to be emitted. The pipeline passes values downstream in batches, and when a batch contains the failure, the values in that batch are dropped.
- When the input ends in the middle of the last value, the stream ends without an error, and the incomplete value is left out. With `JsonStreamDelimiter.Array`, a missing closing `]` is not reported either.
- With `JsonStreamDelimiter.Array`, input that does not start with `[` fails with a message such as `(expected '[' got '{')`.

A missing field in the second of three lines fails the stream:

```scala
val withBadLine: String =
  """{"id":1,"kind":"created"}
    |{"id":2}
    |{"id":3,"kind":"deleted"}
    |""".stripMargin
// withBadLine: String = """{"id":1,"kind":"created"}
// {"id":2}
// {"id":3,"kind":"deleted"}
// """

runSync(
  ZStream
    .fromIterable(withBadLine)
    .via(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonPipeline(JsonStreamDelimiter.Newline))
    .runCollect
    .either
)
// res14: Either[Throwable, Chunk[Event]] = Left(
//   value = java.lang.Exception: .kind(missing)
// )
```

A last line cut short ends the stream after the complete values:

```scala
runSync(
  ZStream
    .fromIterable("{\"id\":1,\"kind\":\"created\"}\n{\"id\":2,\"ki")
    .via(JsonDecoder[Event].decodeJsonPipeline(JsonStreamDelimiter.Newline))
    .runCollect
)
// res15: Chunk[Event] = IndexedSeq(Event(id = 1, kind = "created"))
```

To keep going past bad lines in JSON Lines input, split the text with `ZPipeline.splitLines` and decode each line with `fromJson`, as [Process Large JSON as a Stream](../how-to/streaming.md#4-skip-bad-lines-instead-of-failing) shows. That technique uses only `fromJson`, so it also works on Scala.js and Scala Native.

### See Also

- [Process Large JSON as a Stream](../how-to/streaming.md) for task-oriented examples with files.
- [JsonEncoder](json-encoder.md#streaming) and [JsonDecoder](json-decoder.md#streaming) for the type classes that carry these methods.
- [Errors](errors.md) for the error message format.
- [Performance](../explanation/performance.md) for when to decode from a stream instead of from a `String` or bytes.

---

## Type Classes

ZIO JSON is built on a few *type classes*: a trait with one type parameter, such as `JsonEncoder[A]`, plus values (instances) of that trait for each type you use. The compiler finds the instance for a type through implicit search, so `toJson` and `fromJson` work for any type that has one.

| Type class                  | What an instance does                              | Page                                                         |
|-----------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `JsonEncoder[A]`            | Writes an `A` as JSON                              | [JsonEncoder](../json-encoder.md)                            |
| `JsonDecoder[A]`            | Reads JSON into an `A`, or fails with an error     | [JsonDecoder](../json-decoder.md)                            |
| `JsonCodec[A]`              | An encoder and a decoder for `A` in one value      | [JsonCodec](../json-codec.md)                                |
| `JsonFieldEncoder[A]`       | Writes an `A` as a JSON object key                 | [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](../json-field-codecs.md) |
| `JsonFieldDecoder[A]`       | Reads a JSON object key into an `A`                | [JsonFieldEncoder and JsonFieldDecoder](../json-field-codecs.md) |

Two more pages belong to this group: [Built-in Instances](../built-in-instances.md) lists every type that has instances out of the box, and [Errors](../errors.md) describes what a failed decode returns.

### How They Relate

A `JsonCodec[A]` holds a `JsonEncoder[A]` and a `JsonDecoder[A]`. When a codec is in implicit scope, the compiler also finds the encoder and the decoder through it, so one codec is enough for both directions. Each type class has an `apply` method that returns the instance in scope:

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

object Point {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Point] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Point]
}

val encoder: JsonEncoder[Point] = JsonEncoder[Point]
// encoder: JsonEncoder[Point] = zio.json.DeriveJsonEncoder$$anon$10@a9cee31
val decoder: JsonDecoder[Point] = JsonDecoder[Point]
// decoder: JsonDecoder[Point] = zio.json.DeriveJsonDecoder$$anon$1@3d100eea

println(encoder.encodeJson(Point(1, 2), None))
// {"x":1,"y":2}

decoder.decodeJson("""{"x":1,"y":2}""")
// res2: Either[String, Point] = Right(value = Point(x = 1, y = 2))
```

`JsonFieldEncoder` and `JsonFieldDecoder` are separate, because a JSON object key is always a string. The `Map` encoders and decoders use them for the keys and a `JsonEncoder` or `JsonDecoder` for the values:

```scala
println(Map(1 -> Point(1, 2)).toJson)
// {"1":{"x":1,"y":2}}
```

### Where Instances Come From

The compiler looks for an instance in four places, and the reference page of each type class describes them in detail:

- **Built in.** The companion objects hold instances for the standard types: primitives, collections, `Option`, `Either`, `java.time` and more. See [Built-in Instances](../built-in-instances.md).
- **Derived.** `DeriveJsonEncoder.gen`, `DeriveJsonDecoder.gen` and `DeriveJsonCodec.gen`, or `derives` on Scala 3, write instances for case classes and sealed traits. See [Derivation](../derivation/index.md).
- **Built from another instance.** `contramap` on an encoder, `map` and `mapOrFail` on a decoder, and `transform` on a codec adapt an existing instance to a new type.
- **Written by hand.** For full control or speed, implement `unsafeEncode` or `unsafeDecode` directly. See "Writing an Encoder by Hand" on [JsonEncoder](../json-encoder.md#writing-an-encoder-by-hand) and "Writing a Decoder by Hand" on [JsonDecoder](../json-decoder.md#writing-a-decoder-by-hand).

Put an instance for your own type in that type's companion object. The compiler searches there without an import.

---

## YAML

The `zio-json-yaml` module converts between YAML and any type that has a `JsonEncoder` or `JsonDecoder`. It goes through the [JSON AST](./json-ast.md): values are encoded to a `Json` value and then rendered as YAML, and YAML is parsed into a `Json` value before decoding. Because of this, the same codec that you use for JSON also works for YAML, and there is no separate YAML codec to write.

The module is available for the JVM only, since it depends on [SnakeYAML](https://bitbucket.org/snakeyaml/snakeyaml).

### Installation

Add the module to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-yaml" % "1.1.3"
```

### Encoding to YAML

Importing `zio.json.yaml._` adds the `toYaml` extension method to any value that has a `JsonEncoder` in scope. We define a case class with a derived codec first:

```scala
import zio.json._
import zio.json.ast.Json
import zio.json.yaml._

case class Person(name: String, age: Int, email: Option[String])

object Person {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[Person] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Person]
}
```

On a value with an encoder, calling `toYaml` returns an `Either[String, String]`. The `email` field is `None`, so it is absent from the output:

```scala
println(Person("Alice", 30, None).toYaml().getOrElse(""))
// name: Alice
// age: 30
//
```

`toYaml` also works on a `Json` value directly, which is useful when you already have an AST:

```scala
println(Json.Obj("name" -> Json.Str("Alice"), "tags" -> Json.Arr(Json.Str("admin"), Json.Str("ops"))).toYaml().getOrElse(""))
// name: Alice
// tags:
//   - admin
//   - ops
//
```

On a `Json` value, `toYaml` returns `Either[YAMLException, String]`, where `YAMLException` is `org.yaml.snakeyaml.error.YAMLException`. The version for encodable values first converts the value to `Json`, and turns a `YAMLException` into its message.

### Decoding from YAML

The `String#fromYaml` extension method parses YAML and decodes the result with a `JsonDecoder`:

```scala
val yaml: String =
  """name: Bob
    |age: 41
    |email: bob@example.com""".stripMargin
// yaml: String = """name: Bob
// age: 41
// email: bob@example.com"""

yaml.fromYaml[Person]
// res3: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(
//     name = "Bob",
//     age = 41,
//     email = Some(value = "bob@example.com")
//   )
// )
```

If the input is not valid YAML, or the resulting structure does not match the decoder, `String#fromYaml` returns a `Left` with an error message:

```scala
"name: [unclosed".fromYaml[Person]
// res4: Either[String, Person] = Left(
//   value = """while parsing a flow sequence
//  in 'reader', line 1, column 7:
//     name: [unclosed
//           ^
// expected ',' or ']', but got <stream end>
//  in 'reader', line 1, column 16:
//     name: [unclosed
//                    ^
// """
// )
```

YAML scalars that SnakeYAML resolves to a boolean, integer or floating-point number become `Json.Bool` and `Json.Num`, `null` and `~` become `Json.Null`, and every other scalar, such as a date, becomes a `Json.Str` with its text. Mapping keys must be scalars.

### Decoding Limits

`String#fromYaml` parses with `new Yaml()`, so it uses SnakeYAML's default `LoaderOptions`. There is no parameter to pass different options. The defaults set these limits:

| Limit              | Default                      | What happens when it is exceeded                                            |
|--------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Documents          | One                          | `Left` with `expected a single document in the stream`                      |
| Nesting depth      | 50 levels                    | `Left(Nesting Depth exceeded max 50)`                                       |
| Collection aliases | 50 aliases                   | `Left(Number of aliases for non-scalar nodes exceeds the specified max=50)` |
| Input size         | 3 MB (3,145,728 code points) | `Left(The incoming YAML document exceeds the limit: 3145728 code points.)`  |

The alias limit counts only aliases (`*name`) that point at a mapping or a sequence; aliases of scalars are not limited. Duplicate keys are accepted, and the last value wins:

```scala
"a: 1\na: 2".fromYaml[Json]
// res5: Either[String, Json] = Right(
//   value = Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("a", Num(value = 2))))
// )
```

A stream with more than one document (separated by `---`) fails, so split such input yourself before decoding each part:

```scala
"a: 1\n---\na: 2\n".fromYaml[Json].isLeft
// res6: Boolean = true
```

An empty input, or one that holds only comments, has no document at all. `fromYaml` then returns a `Left` whose message comes from a `NullPointerException` (`Cannot invoke "org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.Node.getClass()" because "node" is null` on current JDKs) rather than a clear "empty document" error. Check for blank input yourself if you need a better message, as [Load a YAML Configuration File](../how-to/load-yaml-config.md) does.

### Options

`YamlOptions` controls how YAML is rendered. `YamlOptions.default` is used when no options are given, and you can change individual settings with `copy`:

```scala
val nested: Json = Json.Obj(
  "server" -> Json.Obj("host" -> Json.Str("localhost"), "port" -> Json.Num(8080)),
  "debug"  -> Json.Null
)
// nested: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     (
//       "server",
//       Obj(
//         fields = IndexedSeq(
//           ("host", Str(value = "localhost")),
//           ("port", Num(value = 8080))
//         )
//       )
//     ),
//     ("debug", null)
//   )
// )

println(nested.toYaml(YamlOptions.default.copy(dropNulls = false, indentation = 4)).getOrElse(""))
// server:
//     host: localhost
//     port: 8080
// debug: null
//
```

The settings are:

- `dropNulls` (default `true`): removes object fields whose value is `Json.Null`. A `null` element of an array is still written. Option fields that are `None` are controlled by the codec, not by this setting.
- `indentation` (default `2`): spaces per nesting level.
- `sequenceIndentation` (default `2`): spaces placed before the `-` indicator of sequence entries (SnakeYAML's indicator indent).
- `indentWithIndicator` (default `true`): adds the `-` indicator indent to the general indentation, so sequence item content is indented past the `-` instead of sharing its column. If you set it to `false`, also set `sequenceIndentation = 0`: with the default indicator indent, SnakeYAML writes sequences of mappings that `String#fromYaml` cannot read back.
- `maxScalarWidth` (default `Some(80)`): long string scalars are split across lines. Set it to `None` to keep each scalar on one line.
- `lineBreak`: the line separator. The default follows the platform.
- `flowStyle`, `scalarStyle` and `keyStyle`: functions that choose the SnakeYAML presentation style for each value or key. `flowStyle` receives each object and array, `scalarStyle` each scalar value, and `keyStyle` each key.
- `nonPrintableStyle`: how strings that contain non-printable characters are written. The default escapes them, and `NonPrintableStyle.BINARY` writes them as base64 `!!binary` values.
- `newDumperOptions`: a function that creates the SnakeYAML `DumperOptions` used for rendering.

The `sequenceIndentation` setting moves the `-` indicator. With `0`, the indicator sits in the same column as the parent key:

```scala
val list: Json = Json.Obj("items" -> Json.Arr(Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Num(1), "b" -> Json.Num(2)), Json.Str("x")))
// list: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     (
//       "items",
//       Arr(
//         elements = IndexedSeq(
//           Obj(fields = IndexedSeq(("a", Num(value = 1)), ("b", Num(value = 2)))),
//           Str(value = "x")
//         )
//       )
//     )
//   )
// )

println(list.toYaml(YamlOptions.default.copy(sequenceIndentation = 0)).getOrElse(""))
// items:
// - a: 1
//   b: 2
// - x
//
```

The style functions take SnakeYAML types from `org.yaml.snakeyaml.DumperOptions`. To write every object and array in flow style, on one line:

```scala
import org.yaml.snakeyaml.DumperOptions.{ FlowStyle, ScalarStyle }

println(list.toYaml(YamlOptions.default.copy(flowStyle = _ => FlowStyle.FLOW)).getOrElse(""))
// {items: [{a: 1, b: 2}, x]}
//
```

When `scalarStyle` returns `PLAIN` for a string that contains a line break, the string is written as a literal block scalar (`|`) instead. Other styles are kept as chosen:

```scala
val text: Json = Json.Obj("text" -> Json.Str("line1\nline2"))
// text: Json = Obj(
//   fields = IndexedSeq(
//     (
//       "text",
//       Str(
//         value = """line1
// line2"""
//       )
//     )
//   )
// )

println(text.toYaml().getOrElse(""))
// text: |-
//   line1
//   line2
// 

println(text.toYaml(YamlOptions.default.copy(scalarStyle = _ => ScalarStyle.DOUBLE_QUOTED)).getOrElse(""))
// text: "line1\nline2"
//
```

If you need an option that is not exposed by `YamlOptions`, use `newDumperOptions` to supply your own SnakeYAML `DumperOptions`. The settings that `YamlOptions` exposes (indentation, sequence indentation, width, line break, indentWithIndicator) are always overwritten from `YamlOptions`, so set those through `YamlOptions` instead. Other settings take effect, for example an explicit `---` document start:

```scala
import org.yaml.snakeyaml.DumperOptions

val withStart = YamlOptions.default.copy(newDumperOptions = () => {
  val options = new DumperOptions()
  options.setExplicitStart(true)
  options
})
// withStart: YamlOptions = YamlOptions(
//   newDumperOptions = <function0>,
//   dropNulls = true,
//   indentation = 2,
//   sequenceIndentation = 2,
//   maxScalarWidth = Some(value = 80),
//   lineBreak = Line break: UNIX,
//   flowStyle = zio.json.yaml.YamlOptions$$$Lambda$19931/0x00007373271488d8@7770d94,
//   scalarStyle = zio.json.yaml.YamlOptions$$$Lambda$19932/0x0000737327148ca0@bd029cc,
//   keyStyle = zio.json.yaml.YamlOptions$$$Lambda$19933/0x0000737327149068@547e18d6,
//   nonPrintableStyle = ESCAPE,
//   indentWithIndicator = true
// )

println(nested.toYaml(withStart).getOrElse(""))
// ---
// server:
//   host: localhost
//   port: 8080
//
```

### Number Rendering

`Json.Num` values are written as YAML integers when they have no fractional part after `stripTrailingZeros`, and as floats otherwise. A number that was a decimal in JSON can therefore come back as an integer:

```scala
println(Json.Obj("a" -> Json.Num(1.0), "b" -> Json.Num(BigDecimal("2.50")), "c" -> Json.Num(BigDecimal("1E+3"))).toYaml().getOrElse(""))
// a: 1
// b: 2.5
// c: 1000
//
```

:::warning
An integral number outside the `Long` range is not written correctly: only its low 64 bits are kept, so `Json.Num(BigInt("123456789012345678901234567890"))` is written as `-4362896299872285998`. Encode such numbers as strings if they must go through YAML.
:::

### Working with the YAML Node Tree

The `toYamlAST` method returns the SnakeYAML `Node` tree instead of a string. Use it when you need to change the document before it is emitted. On a value with an encoder it returns `Either[String, Node]`, because the encoding to `Json` can fail:

```scala
val node = Person("Carol", 25, None).toYamlAST()
// node: Either[String, org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.Node] = Right(
//   value = <org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.MappingNode (tag=tag:yaml.org,2002:map, values={ key=<org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.ScalarNode (tag=tag:yaml.org,2002:str, value=name)>; value=<NodeTuple keyNode=<org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.ScalarNode (tag=tag:yaml.org,2002:str, value=name)>; valueNode=<org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.ScalarNode (tag=tag:yaml.org,2002:str, value=Carol)>> }{ key=<org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.ScalarNode (tag=tag:yaml.org,2002:str, value=age)>; value=<NodeTuple keyNode=<org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.ScalarNode (tag=tag:yaml.org,2002:str, value=age)>; valueNode=<org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.ScalarNode (tag=tag:yaml.org,2002:int, value=25)>> })>
// )
node.map(_.getNodeId)
// res14: Either[String, org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.NodeId] = Right(
//   value = mapping
// )
```

On a `Json` value, `toYamlAST` returns the `Node` directly:

```scala
nested.toYamlAST().getNodeId
// res15: org.yaml.snakeyaml.nodes.NodeId = mapping
```

To go from a YAML string to a `Json` value without decoding into a domain type, use `String#fromYaml` with `Json` as the type:

```scala
"""items:
  |  - 1
  |  - true
  |  - null""".stripMargin.fromYaml[Json]
// res16: Either[String, Json] = Right(
//   value = Obj(
//     fields = IndexedSeq(
//       (
//         "items",
//         Arr(elements = IndexedSeq(Num(value = 1), Bool(value = true), null))
//       )
//     )
//   )
// )
```

---

## @jsonDerive Macro Annotation

`@jsonDerive` is a macro annotation from the `zio-json-macros` module. Placed on a case class or a sealed trait, it adds an implicit codec (or only an encoder, or only a decoder) to the companion object at compile time, so you do not write the `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` line yourself. It is available on Scala 2.12 and 2.13 only; on Scala 3, a `derives` clause does the same job.

The module's public API is one annotation class and one configuration type:

```scala
class jsonDerive(val config: JsonDeriveConfig = JsonDeriveConfig.Codec) extends scala.annotation.StaticAnnotation

sealed abstract class JsonDeriveConfig

object JsonDeriveConfig {
  case object Codec   extends JsonDeriveConfig
  case object Encoder extends JsonDeriveConfig
  case object Decoder extends JsonDeriveConfig
}
```

### Installation

The module is published for Scala 2.12 and 2.13, on the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native. There is no Scala 3 artifact. Add it next to `zio-json`, and turn on macro annotations in the compiler.

On Scala 2.13, macro annotations are a compiler option:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-macros" % "1.1.3"
scalacOptions += "-Ymacro-annotations"
```

On Scala 2.12, they need the macro paradise compiler plugin instead:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-macros" % "1.1.3"
addCompilerPlugin("org.scalamacros" % "paradise" % "2.1.1" cross CrossVersion.full)
```

For Scala.js or Scala Native, use `%%%` instead of `%%`.

### Usage

With no argument, `@jsonDerive` generates a `JsonCodec`, so the class can be encoded and decoded right away:

```scala
import zio.json._

@jsonDerive final case class Watermelon(pips: Int)

Watermelon(3).toJson
// res1: String = "{\"pips\":3}"

"""{"pips":5}""".fromJson[Watermelon]
// res2: Either[String, Watermelon] = Right(value = Watermelon(pips = 5))
```

The generated code calls the usual derivation macros, so every [annotation](./annotations.md) on the class and an implicit [`JsonCodecConfiguration`](./json-codec-configuration.md) in scope apply as they would to a hand-written `DeriveJsonCodec.gen` call.

### What `@jsonDerive` Generates

The macro adds one `implicit` member to the companion object of the annotated type. If the type has no companion, the macro creates one; if it has one, the member is added next to the existing definitions. The member name is a prefix followed by the type name:

| `config`                   | Generated member                                                         |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `JsonDeriveConfig.Codec`   | `implicit val codecFor<Type>: JsonCodec[<Type>] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen`   |
| `JsonDeriveConfig.Encoder` | `implicit val encode<Type>: JsonEncoder[<Type>] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen` |
| `JsonDeriveConfig.Decoder` | `implicit val decode<Type>: JsonDecoder[<Type>] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen` |

So `@jsonDerive final case class Watermelon(pips: Int)` is the same as writing:

```scala
import zio.json._

final case class Watermelon(pips: Int)

object Watermelon {
  implicit val codecForWatermelon: JsonCodec[Watermelon] =
    DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Watermelon]
}
```

The names matter when you refer to the instance explicitly, and when you define a member with the same name in the companion, which then fails to compile as a duplicate definition. The generated codec is an ordinary member:

```scala
Watermelon.codecForWatermelon.encodeJson(Watermelon(1), None)
// res4: CharSequence = "{\"pips\":1}"
```

### Choosing What to Generate

The `config` argument chooses what to generate: `JsonDeriveConfig.Codec` (the default), `JsonDeriveConfig.Encoder` for an encoder only, or `JsonDeriveConfig.Decoder` for a decoder only. It can be passed by position or by name. Write it with its full package, as below. The macro type-checks the argument on its own, before the surrounding code, so it does not see an `import zio.json._` that sits in the same class body or block; the expansion then fails with `not found: value JsonDeriveConfig`. An import at the top of the file works too.

A type with only an encoder can be written but not read:

```scala
@jsonDerive(zio.json.JsonDeriveConfig.Encoder) final case class Melon(pips: Int)

@jsonDerive(config = zio.json.JsonDeriveConfig.Decoder) final case class Gourd(pips: Int)

Melon(2).toJson
// res5: String = "{\"pips\":2}"

"""{"pips":1}""".fromJson[Gourd]
// res6: Either[String, Gourd] = Right(value = Gourd(pips = 1))
```

These two classes get the members `Melon.encodeMelon` and `Gourd.decodeGourd`.

The macro decides what to generate from the static type of the argument, at compile time. If the type is not one of the three `JsonDeriveConfig` objects, for example a `val` typed as `JsonDeriveConfig`, the compiler prints a warning and the macro generates a full codec:

```text
warning: Couldn't determine type of configuration zio.json.JsonDeriveConfig; will produce both encoder and decoder
```

Pass one of the three objects directly so that the choice is the one you intended.

### Sealed Traits

On a sealed trait or sealed abstract class, the generated codec covers the whole family. Subtypes without a codec of their own are derived along with it, and the sum-type annotations such as `@jsonDiscriminator` and `@jsonHint` work as usual. The subtypes come first here, for the reason given below:

```scala
final case class Apple(radius: Int) extends Fruit

@jsonHint("pear")
case object Pear extends Fruit

@jsonDerive
@jsonDiscriminator("kind")
sealed trait Fruit

(Apple(3): Fruit).toJson
// res7: String = "{\"kind\":\"Apple\",\"radius\":3}"

"""{"kind":"pear"}""".fromJson[Fruit]
// res8: Either[String, Fruit] = Right(value = Pear)
```

The generated companion sits right after the trait. At the top level of a file, or in an object at the top level, the subtypes can follow the trait as usual. Inside a class body, a method, or an object nested in a class, the derivation then runs before the compiler has registered the subtypes, and compilation fails with `magnolia: could not find any direct subtypes of trait Fruit`. In those places, define the subtypes before the trait, as in the example above.

### Generic Classes

For a class with type parameters, the macro generates an `implicit def` instead of an `implicit val`. It takes, for every type parameter `A`, an implicit `JsonEncoder[A]` (encoder or codec) and an implicit `JsonDecoder[A]` (decoder or codec). The codec for `Pair[A, B]` is roughly:

```scala
object Pair {
  implicit def codecForPair[A, B](implicit
    decode0: JsonDecoder[A],
    decode1: JsonDecoder[B],
    encode0: JsonEncoder[A],
    encode1: JsonEncoder[B]
  ): JsonCodec[Pair[A, B]] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Pair[A, B]]
}
```

Any element types that have an encoder and a decoder then work:

```scala
@jsonDerive final case class Pair[A, B](first: A, second: B)

Pair(1, "one").toJson
// res9: String = "{\"first\":1,\"second\":\"one\"}"

"""{"first":2,"second":"two"}""".fromJson[Pair[Int, String]]
// res10: Either[String, Pair[Int, String]] = Right(
//   value = Pair(first = 2, second = "two")
// )
```

The macro copies the type parameters, variance annotations included, into the generated method. A method cannot declare a covariant or contravariant type parameter, so `@jsonDerive final case class Box[+A](value: A)` does not compile. The error is reported on the annotation:

```text
error: covariant type A occurs in invariant position in type [+A](implicit decode0: zio.json.JsonDecoder[A], encode0: zio.json.JsonEncoder[A]): zio.json.JsonCodec[Box[A]] of method codecForBox
```

For such a class, write the instance by hand in the companion object:

```scala
final case class Crate[+A](value: A)

object Crate {
  implicit def codec[A: JsonEncoder: JsonDecoder]: JsonCodec[Crate[A]] =
    DeriveJsonCodec.gen[Crate[A]]
}

Crate(List(1, 2)).toJson
// res11: String = "{\"value\":[1,2]}"
```

### Limitations

Compilation stops with an error in these cases. The macro reports the first two itself, after checking its target and its own name; the compiler reports the third:

| Situation                                                          | Compile error                                                             |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| The annotated class is neither a case class nor sealed             | `Invalid annotation target: must be a case class or a sealed trait/class` |
| The annotation is written with its package, `@zio.json.jsonDerive` | `Unsupported macroname supplied to @zio.json.jsonDerive`                  |
| A type parameter has a variance annotation                         | `covariant type A occurs in invariant position ...`                       |

Import the annotation (`import zio.json._` or `import zio.json.jsonDerive`) and write it as `@jsonDerive`.

### Scala 3 Alternative

`zio-json-macros` is not published for Scala 3, because Scala 3 has no macro annotations. On Scala 3, add a `derives` clause to the type instead. `derives JsonCodec`, `derives JsonEncoder` and `derives JsonDecoder` match the three `JsonDeriveConfig` values, and they also work for classes with variant type parameters:

```scala
final case class Watermelon(pips: Int) derives JsonCodec
final case class Melon(pips: Int) derives JsonEncoder
final case class Gourd(pips: Int) derives JsonDecoder
final case class Box[+A](a: A) derives JsonCodec
```

Run on Scala 3, `Box(List(1, 2)).toJson` writes `{"a":[1,2]}` and `"""{"a":"x"}""".fromJson[Box[String]]` returns `Right(Box(x))`. For code that cross-builds for Scala 2 and Scala 3, a hand-written `implicit val codec: JsonCodec[T] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[T]` in the companion works on both versions. See [Derive codecs on Scala 3](../how-to/scala-3-derivation.md) for `derives`, enums and the other Scala 3 features.

---

## Tutorial: Model a Real API Payload

Welcome to the second ZIO JSON tutorial! It continues where [Getting Started](../getting-started.md) ends. You already know how to derive a codec, encode a value with `toJson` and decode one with `fromJson`. Here we use those skills on a payload that looks like the ones real services send, and we make the model match the JSON exactly, instead of making the JSON match the model.

Our example is an online shop that sends us webhook events about orders. A *webhook* is an HTTP request that another service sends to our server when something happens, with a JSON body describing the event. We do not control the format of that body, so our codecs must follow it.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will know how to:

- Rename every field of a case class to `snake_case` with one annotation
- Model a family of events that share a `type` field
- Use `BigDecimal` for money, `Instant` for timestamps, and defaults and `Option` for fields that may be missing
- Use your own type as a `Map` key
- Turn a decode error into a response instead of an exception
- Pin the JSON format with a golden test, so a later change cannot break it unnoticed

We work through these steps:

1. Give Product IDs Their Own Type
2. Model the Events
3. Decode the Sample Payload
4. Handle a Decode Error
5. Encode a Response
6. Pin the Format With a Golden Test

We recommend reading from top to bottom, because each step uses the code of the steps before it.

### The Payload

The shop sends three kinds of events. This is an `order_placed` event, the one we decode first:

```json
{
  "type": "order_placed",
  "order_id": "ord-1001",
  "customer_email": "ada@example.com",
  "items": { "sku-42": 2, "sku-7": 1 },
  "total": 59.90,
  "placed_at": "2026-03-14T09:26:53Z",
  "source": "web"
}
```

Notice four things about it. The field names use `snake_case`, while Scala uses `camelCase`. The `type` field says which kind of event this is. The `items` object maps product IDs to quantities. And the shop sends a `source` field that we do not need. The other two events, `order_shipped` and `order_cancelled`, follow the same pattern.

### 1. Give Product IDs Their Own Type

A product ID is a string, but not every string is a product ID. Let's give it a type of its own, so the compiler keeps it apart from order IDs and email addresses. The shop's product IDs always start with `sku-`, so we check that while decoding.

The `items` object uses product IDs as keys. A JSON key is always a string, and ZIO JSON reads and writes keys with two small type classes, `JsonFieldEncoder` and `JsonFieldDecoder`. We define both in the companion object of `ProductId`:

```scala
import zio.json._
import java.time.Instant

final case class ProductId(value: String)

object ProductId {
  private def parse(s: String): Either[String, ProductId] =
    if (s.startsWith("sku-")) Right(ProductId(s)) else Left(s"not a product id: $s")

  implicit val keyEncoder: JsonFieldEncoder[ProductId] =
    JsonFieldEncoder.string.contramap(_.value)

  implicit val keyDecoder: JsonFieldDecoder[ProductId] =
    JsonFieldDecoder.string.mapOrFail(parse)
}
```

The code above works like this:

- `import java.time.Instant` brings in the timestamp type we use in the next step.
- `ProductId.parse` accepts a string only when it starts with `sku-`, and returns a `Left` with a message otherwise.
- `JsonFieldEncoder.string.contramap(_.value)` reuses the encoder for `String` keys: it unwraps the `ProductId` first, then writes the string.
- `JsonFieldDecoder.string.mapOrFail(parse)` reads the key as a string, then runs `ProductId.parse`, so a key that is not a product ID fails decoding.

Let's try a map with these keys in both directions:

```scala
println(Map(ProductId("sku-42") -> 2, ProductId("sku-7") -> 1).toJson)
// {"sku-42":2,"sku-7":1}

"""{"sku-42":2,"oops":1}""".fromJson[Map[ProductId, Int]]
// res2: Either[String, Map[ProductId, Int]] = Left(
//   value = ".oops(not a product id: oops)"
// )
```

Notice that the error path names the bad key, `oops`, and is followed by our message. The [custom map keys guide](../how-to/custom-map-keys.md) shows more kinds of key types.

### 2. Model the Events

Now we model the three events as a sealed trait, so a single codec can read any of them. Three annotations make the JSON match the shop's format:

- `@jsonDiscriminator("type")` on the trait stores the kind of event in a `type` field inside the object, instead of the default wrapper object `{"OrderPlaced":{...}}` that you saw in Getting Started.
- `@jsonHintNames(SnakeCase)` on the trait turns each case name into `snake_case`, so `OrderPlaced` is written as `order_placed`.
- `@jsonMemberNames(SnakeCase)` on each case class turns every field name into `snake_case`, so `orderId` is written as `order_id`.

With those annotations in place, the whole model fits in one block:

```scala
@jsonDiscriminator("type")
@jsonHintNames(SnakeCase)
sealed trait OrderEvent {
  def orderId: String
}

object OrderEvent {
  @jsonMemberNames(SnakeCase)
  final case class OrderPlaced(
    orderId: String,
    customerEmail: String,
    items: Map[ProductId, Int],
    total: BigDecimal,
    currency: String = "EUR",
    placedAt: Instant,
    note: Option[String] = None
  ) extends OrderEvent

  @jsonMemberNames(SnakeCase)
  final case class OrderShipped(
    orderId: String,
    carrier: String,
    trackingNumber: Option[String],
    shippedAt: Instant
  ) extends OrderEvent

  @jsonMemberNames(SnakeCase)
  final case class OrderCancelled(orderId: String, reason: String) extends OrderEvent

  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[OrderEvent] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[OrderEvent]
}
```

Here is what each part of the model does:

- `def orderId: String` on the trait lets us read the order ID of any event without matching on its kind. Each case class implements it with its `orderId` field.
- `items: Map[ProductId, Int]` uses the key codecs from step 1.
- `total: BigDecimal` holds money. A `Double` stores numbers in binary and cannot hold `59.90` exactly, while a `BigDecimal` keeps the decimal digits as they were sent, including the trailing zero.
- `placedAt: Instant` and `shippedAt: Instant` read timestamps written in the ISO-8601 format, such as `2026-03-14T09:26:53Z`. ZIO JSON has a built-in codec for `Instant` and the other `java.time` types.
- `currency: String = "EUR"` has a default value, which the decoder uses when the field is missing.
- `note: Option[String] = None` and `trackingNumber: Option[String]` may be missing. A missing field decodes as `None`, and the encoder leaves a `None` out.
- The single `DeriveJsonCodec.gen[OrderEvent]` derives the codec of the trait together with the codecs of its three cases.

Let's encode an event to see the result:

```scala
val placed: OrderEvent = OrderEvent.OrderPlaced(
  orderId = "ord-1001",
  customerEmail = "ada@example.com",
  items = Map(ProductId("sku-42") -> 2),
  total = BigDecimal("59.90"),
  placedAt = Instant.parse("2026-03-14T09:26:53Z")
)
// placed: OrderEvent = OrderPlaced(
//   orderId = "ord-1001",
//   customerEmail = "ada@example.com",
//   items = Map(ProductId(value = "sku-42") -> 2),
//   total = 59.90,
//   currency = "EUR",
//   placedAt = 2026-03-14T09:26:53Z,
//   note = None
// )

println(placed.toJsonPretty)
// {
//   "type" : "order_placed",
//   "order_id" : "ord-1001",
//   "customer_email" : "ada@example.com",
//   "items" : {
//     "sku-42" : 2
//   },
//   "total" : 59.90,
//   "currency" : "EUR",
//   "placed_at" : "2026-03-14T09:26:53Z"
// }
```

Notice that `type` comes first, every field name is in `snake_case`, the total keeps its trailing zero, and `note` is missing because it is `None`. We typed `placed` as `OrderEvent` on purpose: the codec belongs to the trait, so we encode and decode through the trait.

### 3. Decode the Sample Payload

Now let's decode the payload from the start of this tutorial:

```scala
val payload =
  """{
    |  "type": "order_placed",
    |  "order_id": "ord-1001",
    |  "customer_email": "ada@example.com",
    |  "items": { "sku-42": 2, "sku-7": 1 },
    |  "total": 59.90,
    |  "placed_at": "2026-03-14T09:26:53Z",
    |  "source": "web"
    |}""".stripMargin
// payload: String = """{
//   "type": "order_placed",
//   "order_id": "ord-1001",
//   "customer_email": "ada@example.com",
//   "items": { "sku-42": 2, "sku-7": 1 },
//   "total": 59.90,
//   "placed_at": "2026-03-14T09:26:53Z",
//   "source": "web"
// }"""

payload.fromJson[OrderEvent]
// res4: Either[String, OrderEvent] = Right(
//   value = OrderPlaced(
//     orderId = "ord-1001",
//     customerEmail = "ada@example.com",
//     items = Map(
//       ProductId(value = "sku-42") -> 2,
//       ProductId(value = "sku-7") -> 1
//     ),
//     total = 59.90,
//     currency = "EUR",
//     placedAt = 2026-03-14T09:26:53Z,
//     note = None
//   )
// )
```

The decoder uses the `type` field to pick `OrderPlaced`. It fills in `currency` with the default `"EUR"` and `note` with `None`, because the payload has neither field. It also skips the `source` field, which our model does not have. Skipping unknown fields is the default, and it lets the shop add new fields without breaking our server. [How Strict Is the Decoder](../explanation/decoder-strictness.md) explains what else the decoder tolerates.

The other events decode with the same codec. This `order_shipped` event has no tracking number yet:

```scala
"""{"type":"order_shipped","order_id":"ord-1001","carrier":"DHL","shipped_at":"2026-03-15T08:00:00Z"}""".fromJson[OrderEvent]
// res5: Either[String, OrderEvent] = Right(
//   value = OrderShipped(
//     orderId = "ord-1001",
//     carrier = "DHL",
//     trackingNumber = None,
//     shippedAt = 2026-03-15T08:00:00Z
//   )
// )
```

### 4. Handle a Decode Error

Real webhooks sometimes carry data our model does not accept. As in Getting Started, a bad payload gives a `Left` with a message, never an exception. Let's look at four typical mistakes.

A kind of event that our model does not know:

```scala
"""{"type":"order_refunded","order_id":"ord-1001"}""".fromJson[OrderEvent]
// res6: Either[String, OrderEvent] = Left(value = "(invalid disambiguator)")
```

A timestamp that is not in the ISO-8601 format:

```scala
"""{"type":"order_placed","order_id":"ord-1001","customer_email":"ada@example.com","items":{},"total":10,"placed_at":"yesterday"}""".fromJson[OrderEvent]
// res7: Either[String, OrderEvent] = Left(
//   value = "(order_placed).placed_at(expected an Instant)"
// )
```

A product ID that our key decoder rejects:

```scala
"""{"type":"order_placed","order_id":"ord-1001","customer_email":"ada@example.com","items":{"42":1},"total":10,"placed_at":"2026-03-14T09:26:53Z"}""".fromJson[OrderEvent]
// res8: Either[String, OrderEvent] = Left(
//   value = "(order_placed).items.42(not a product id: 42)"
// )
```

A required field that is missing:

```scala
"""{"type":"order_placed","order_id":"ord-1001","items":{},"total":10,"placed_at":"2026-03-14T09:26:53Z"}""".fromJson[OrderEvent]
// res9: Either[String, OrderEvent] = Left(
//   value = "(order_placed).customer_email(missing)"
// )
```

Each message starts with the kind of event in parentheses, such as `(order_placed)`, then gives the path to the bad field, then says what went wrong. Notice that the path uses the JSON names, `placed_at` and `customer_email`, so you can match it against the payload directly. An unknown `type` value gives `(invalid disambiguator)`, which does not repeat the value, so log the payload as well when you report it.

### 5. Encode a Response

Our server answers each webhook with a small JSON body that says whether we accepted the event. The shop expects `snake_case` here too:

```scala
@jsonMemberNames(SnakeCase)
final case class WebhookAck(accepted: Boolean, orderId: Option[String], error: Option[String] = None)

object WebhookAck {
  implicit val codec: JsonCodec[WebhookAck] = DeriveJsonCodec.gen[WebhookAck]
}

def respond(body: String): WebhookAck =
  body.fromJson[OrderEvent] match {
    case Right(event) => WebhookAck(accepted = true, orderId = Some(event.orderId))
    case Left(error)  => WebhookAck(accepted = false, orderId = None, error = Some(error))
  }
```

The code above works like this:

- `WebhookAck` is a plain case class. It only needs to be encoded, but a `JsonCodec` is just as easy to derive and lets tests decode it too.
- `respond` decodes the request body and matches on the result. A `Right` gives an event, and `event.orderId` works for every kind of event thanks to the `def` on the trait.
- A `Left` becomes a rejected acknowledgement that carries the decode error.

Let's respond to the good payload and to a bad one:

```scala
println(respond(payload).toJson)
// {"accepted":true,"order_id":"ord-1001"}

println(respond("""{"type":"order_refunded","order_id":"ord-1001"}""").toJson)
// {"accepted":false,"error":"(invalid disambiguator)"}
```

Notice that `order_id` is in `snake_case`, and that the `None` fields are left out of each response.

### 6. Pin the Format With a Golden Test

Our codecs now match the shop's format. The danger is a later change that alters the JSON by accident: renaming a case class renames its `type` value, and removing an annotation changes every field name. The code still compiles, and decoding our own output still works, so ordinary tests stay green while the shop's requests start to fail.

A *golden test* guards against this. It encodes a set of sample values, stores the JSON in a file the first time it runs, and fails whenever the output differs from the stored file later. The `zio-json-golden` module provides it for [ZIO Test](https://zio.dev/reference/test/).

Add the module to `build.sbt`. It brings ZIO Test with it, so the only other line tells sbt to run ZIO Test specs:

```sbt
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-json-golden" % "1.1.3" % Test

testFrameworks += new TestFramework("zio.test.sbt.ZTestFramework")
```

Then write the test in `src/test/scala`. We list one sample of each event, so the stored file is small and easy to review:

```scala
import zio.test._
import zio.json.golden._

object OrderEventGoldenSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  val samples: List[OrderEvent] = List(
    OrderEvent.OrderPlaced(
      orderId = "ord-1001",
      customerEmail = "ada@example.com",
      items = Map(ProductId("sku-42") -> 2, ProductId("sku-7") -> 1),
      total = BigDecimal("59.90"),
      placedAt = Instant.parse("2026-03-14T09:26:53Z")
    ),
    OrderEvent.OrderShipped("ord-1001", "DHL", Some("JD0123"), Instant.parse("2026-03-15T08:00:00Z")),
    OrderEvent.OrderCancelled("ord-1002", "customer request")
  )

  implicit val config: GoldenConfiguration =
    GoldenConfiguration.default.copy(sampleSize = samples.size)

  def spec = suite("OrderEventGoldenSpec")(
    goldenTest(Gen.fromIterable(samples))
  )
}
```

The test works like this:

- `samples` holds fixed values. A golden test needs the same samples on every run, so we avoid random or clock-based values.
- `Gen.fromIterable(samples)` turns the list into a ZIO Test generator, which is what `goldenTest` expects.
- `GoldenConfiguration.default.copy(sampleSize = samples.size)` takes exactly our three samples instead of the default 20.
- `goldenTest` encodes the samples with the `OrderEvent` codec and compares them with the file `src/test/resources/golden/OrderEvent.json`.

The first run has no stored file yet. It writes `OrderEvent_new.json` and fails with a message asking you to accept it. Review the file, remove the `_new` suffix, and run the test again. Our file looks like this, and the test now passes:

```json
{
  "samples" : [
    {
      "type" : "order_placed",
      "order_id" : "ord-1001",
      "customer_email" : "ada@example.com",
      "items" : {
        "sku-42" : 2,
        "sku-7" : 1
      },
      "total" : 59.90,
      "currency" : "EUR",
      "placed_at" : "2026-03-14T09:26:53Z"
    },
    {
      "type" : "order_shipped",
      "order_id" : "ord-1001",
      "carrier" : "DHL",
      "tracking_number" : "JD0123",
      "shipped_at" : "2026-03-15T08:00:00Z"
    },
    {
      "type" : "order_cancelled",
      "order_id" : "ord-1002",
      "reason" : "customer request"
    }
  ]
}
```

Try changing `@jsonHintNames(SnakeCase)` to `@jsonHintNames(KebabCase)` and running the test again. It fails, shows that `"order_placed"` became `"order-placed"`, and writes the new output to `OrderEvent_changed.json` so you can compare. That is exactly the kind of change the shop would notice first if the test did not. Commit the golden file together with the code.

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned how to:

- Rename all fields of a case class with `@jsonMemberNames(SnakeCase)`, and all case names with `@jsonHintNames(SnakeCase)`
- Model a family of events with a `type` field using `@jsonDiscriminator`
- Use `BigDecimal` for money and `Instant` for timestamps, and handle missing fields with defaults and `Option`
- Write key codecs so your own type can be a `Map` key, with validation
- Turn a decode error into a response, and read the path in the error message
- Pin the JSON format with a golden test

You can now model a third-party JSON format end to end and keep it stable as your code changes.

### Where to Go Next

- **Need other names or rules?** [Field Names](../how-to/field-names.md) covers single renames and old names with `@jsonAliases`, and [Work With Sealed Traits](../how-to/sealed-traits.md) covers other hint formats.
- **Fields that can be `null` or empty?** [Optional, Default and Null Fields](../how-to/optional-and-default-fields.md) explains every rule for missing, `null` and empty values.
- **Rules beyond types?** [Validate on Decode](../how-to/validate-on-decode.md) shows how to check values and fields while decoding.
- **More about golden tests?** [Golden Testing API](../reference/golden-testing.md) covers the configuration and the file lifecycle.
- **Want to see every shape a sum type can take?** [JSON Shapes and Round Trips](../explanation/wire-format.md) has the full table and the values that do not survive a round trip.
- **Looking for an API?** [JsonCodecConfiguration](../reference/json-codec-configuration.md) lists every derivation option, and [Built-in Instances](../reference/built-in-instances.md) lists every type that has a codec out of the box.
