## Admin Client

`AdminClient` manages a Kafka cluster from ZIO: it creates and deletes topics, reads and changes configuration, inspects and resets consumer groups, lists offsets, describes the cluster, and manages access control lists (ACLs). It wraps the Java [`Admin`](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#adminapi) client, turns every Kafka future into a ZIO effect, and replaces Java collections and nullable values with Scala collections, `Option` and small case classes. Unlike the Java client, a write operation (for example creating a topic) completes only after its effect is visible, wherever that is possible; see [Write Operations Wait Until They Are Visible](#write-operations-wait-until-they-are-visible). The main types are `AdminClient`, `AdminClientSettings`, the model case classes nested in the `AdminClient` companion object (`NewTopic`, `ConfigResource`, `OffsetSpec`, and so on), and the ACL types in the `zio.kafka.admin.acl` and `zio.kafka.admin.resource` packages.

The shape of the two entry points is:

```scala
trait AdminClient {
  def createTopic(newTopic: AdminClient.NewTopic, validateOnly: Boolean = false): Task[Unit]
  def listTopics(listTopicsOptions: Option[AdminClient.ListTopicsOptions] = None): Task[Map[String, AdminClient.TopicListing]]
  // ... about 40 more operations
}

final case class AdminClientSettings(closeTimeout: Duration, properties: Map[String, AnyRef])
```

### Write Operations Wait Until They Are Visible

The Java admin client completes a write operation as soon as the broker accepts it, but the change is not yet visible to the next read: a topic that was just created may be missing from `listTopics` for a while (see [KAFKA-18818](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-18818)). Zio-kafka hides this. Its write operations only complete once the change is visible, using one of two strategies:

- **Polling:** after the broker accepts the request, zio-kafka waits 50 ms and then repeatedly reads the state back, with exponential backoff starting at 50 ms, until the change shows up. If it does not show up within 5 seconds, the operation still succeeds: zio-kafka assumes that the write succeeded and was undone by another write.
- **Fixed sleep:** where polling is impractical, the operation sleeps for its `visibilitySleep` parameter (default 1 second) after the broker accepts the request. Pass `Duration.Zero` when you don't care when the operation takes effect.

The table lists which operations wait and how:

| Operation                                                             | How it waits                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `createTopic`, `createTopics`                                         | Polls `listTopics` until every new topic is listed                                                                              |
| `deleteTopic`, `deleteTopics`                                         | Polls `listTopics` until no deleted topic is listed                                                                             |
| `createPartitions`                                                    | Polls `describeTopics` until each topic has at least the requested partition count                                              |
| `deleteConsumerGroups`                                                | Polls `listConsumerGroups` until no deleted group is listed                                                                     |
| `alterConsumerGroupOffsets`                                           | Polls `listConsumerGroupOffsets` until every partition shows the new offset                                                     |
| `incrementalAlterConfigs`, `incrementalAlterConfigsAsync`             | Polls `describeConfigs` for `Set`/`Delete` ops; sleeps `visibilitySleep` when the request contains an `Append` or `Subtract` op |
| `createAcls`, `createAclsAsync`                                       | Polls `describeAcls` until every new binding is listed                                                                          |
| `deleteAcls`, `deleteAclsAsync`                                       | Polls `describeAcls` with each filter until it matches nothing                                                                  |
| `deleteRecords`                                                       | Sleeps `visibilitySleep`                                                                                                        |
| `removeMembersFromConsumerGroup`, `removeAllMembersFromConsumerGroup` | Sleeps `visibilitySleep`                                                                                                        |

A request made with `validateOnly = true` changes nothing, so `createTopic`, `createTopics`, `createPartitions` and `incrementalAlterConfigs` skip the waiting when `validateOnly` is set and return as soon as the broker has validated the request. `incrementalAlterConfigsAsync` does not skip it: with `validateOnly = true` its inner effects still wait as described above, which for a `Set` op usually means polling until the 5-second limit, because the validated change never shows up. The waiting uses the ZIO `Clock`; in a ZIO Test spec that uses `TestClock`, add `@@ TestAspect.withLiveClock` (see [Writing Tests](writing-tests.md)).

### Creating an Admin Client

An `AdminClient` holds a network connection that must be closed when you are done with it. `AdminClient.make` and `AdminClient.live` close it automatically when their scope ends. With `AdminClient.fromScopedJavaClient`, the scoped effect you pass must close the Java client, for example by creating it with `ZIO.acquireRelease`. With `AdminClient.fromJavaClient` you close the Java client yourself. All constructors are in the `AdminClient` companion object:

```scala
object AdminClient {
  def make(settings: AdminClientSettings): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, AdminClient]
  val live: ZLayer[AdminClientSettings, Throwable, AdminClient]
  def fromJavaClient(javaClient: org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin): URIO[Any, AdminClient]
  def fromScopedJavaClient[R, E](scopedJavaClient: ZIO[R & Scope, E, Admin]): ZIO[R & Scope, E, AdminClient]
  def javaClientFromSettings(settings: AdminClientSettings): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Admin]
}
```

`AdminClient.make` is the usual entry point. It runs zio-kafka's SSL endpoint check (see [Security](security.md)), creates the Java client, and closes it, waiting at most `AdminClientSettings#closeTimeout`, when the scope closes. To create a topic and then list all topic names inside one scope:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.{ AdminClient, AdminClientSettings }
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient.NewTopic

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val topicNames: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Set[String]] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      admin <- AdminClient.make(AdminClientSettings(bootstrapServers))
      _ <- admin.createTopic(
             NewTopic(
               name = "orders",
               numPartitions = 6,
               replicationFactor = 3,
               configs = Map("cleanup.policy" -> "compact")
             )
           )
      topics <- admin.listTopics()
    } yield topics.keySet
  }
```

Alternatively, you can provide an `AdminClient` as a ZIO layer. `AdminClient.live` builds the client from an `AdminClientSettings` in the environment, so the rest of the application can depend on `AdminClient` as a service:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.{ AdminClient, AdminClientSettings }

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val adminLayer: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, AdminClient] =
  ZLayer.succeed(AdminClientSettings(bootstrapServers)) >>> AdminClient.live

val clusterId: ZIO[AdminClient, Throwable, String] =
  ZIO.serviceWithZIO[AdminClient](_.describeClusterId())
```

The other constructors work with a Java `Admin` client:

- `AdminClient.fromJavaClient(javaClient)` wraps a Java client that you created. You must close the Java client yourself.
- `AdminClient.fromScopedJavaClient(effect)` wraps the Java client that a scoped effect creates. It does not close the client itself: create the client with `ZIO.acquireRelease` in that effect so that it is closed when the scope ends.
- `AdminClient.javaClientFromSettings(settings)` creates a Java client from settings and closes it when the scope ends. `AdminClient.make` uses it. Use it when you also need the Java client, for example for an operation that zio-kafka does not wrap.

`AdminClient.fromJavaClient` and `AdminClient.fromScopedJavaClient` do not run the [SSL endpoint check](security.md#ssl-endpoint-check); `AdminClient.javaClientFromSettings` (and so `AdminClient.make`) does.

### AdminClientSettings

`AdminClientSettings` holds the Java client properties and the close timeout. Construct it from the bootstrap servers, which also sets a close timeout of 30 seconds, and refine it with the `with*` methods, which keeps your code source compatible with future releases. The close timeout has no `with` method; change it with `copy`. For every member, see the [`AdminClientSettings` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/admin/AdminClientSettings.html).

Any [Java admin client configuration](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#adminclientconfigs) can be set as a property, and `AdminClientSettings#withCredentials` adds the TLS properties of a `KafkaCredentialStore` (see [Security](security.md)). To set a client id and a shorter request timeout, and to close faster:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.AdminClientConfig
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClientSettings

val settings: AdminClientSettings =
  AdminClientSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withProperty(AdminClientConfig.CLIENT_ID_CONFIG, "ops-tool")
    .withProperties(AdminClientConfig.REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS_CONFIG -> "15000")
    .copy(closeTimeout = 10.seconds)
```

### How the Types Work Together

Every operation takes zio-kafka model values and returns zio-kafka model values; the Java types stay inside the wrapper. Most operations also accept an optional options value (`Option[...Options] = None`) that carries a request `timeout` and operation-specific flags:

```
AdminClientSettings ──> AdminClient.make / AdminClient.live ──> AdminClient
                                                                   │
  NewTopic, NewPartitions ─────────────> topics ───────────────────┤──> TopicListing, TopicDescription
  ConfigResource + AlterConfigOp ──────> configs ──────────────────┤──> KafkaConfig (entries: ConfigEntry)
  groupId, ListConsumerGroupOffsetsSpec > consumer groups ─────────┤──> ConsumerGroupListing, ConsumerGroupDescription,
                                                                   │    OffsetAndMetadata
  TopicPartition + OffsetSpec ─────────> offsets ──────────────────┤──> ListOffsetsResultInfo
  DescribeClusterOptions ──────────────> cluster ──────────────────┤──> Node, cluster id, AclOperation
  AclBinding, AclBindingFilter ────────> ACLs ─────────────────────┘──> AclBinding
```

A typical admin task follows the same steps:

1. Build `AdminClientSettings` and create the client with `AdminClient.make` or `AdminClient.live`.
2. Describe the target with model values: a `NewTopic`, a `ConfigResource`, a `TopicPartition` with an `OffsetSpec`, an `AclBinding`.
3. Call the operation. Write operations return once the change is visible; read operations return Scala maps keyed by topic name, `TopicPartition`, `ConfigResource` or group id.
4. Close the scope, which closes the client.

:::note[Name clashes]
The `AdminClient` companion defines its own `TopicPartition`, `OffsetAndMetadata`, `Node`, `Metric` and `IsolationLevel`, which clash with the Java classes of the same name. Import the model types you need by name, for example `import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient.{ NewTopic, TopicPartition }`, rather than with a wildcard.
:::

### Operations by Task

The operations group naturally by the part of the cluster they manage. Every operation returns a `Task` (`ZIO[Any, Throwable, *]`), and a Kafka error, such as a `TopicExistsException` or a `GroupNotEmptyException`, becomes the failure of that task. The sections below show one task per group; for every operation, its parameters and its options type, see the [`AdminClient` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/admin/AdminClient.html), and for the model case classes, the [`AdminClient` companion API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/admin/AdminClient$.html).

#### Topics

`createTopic`, `createTopics`, `deleteTopic`, `deleteTopics`, `listTopics`, `describeTopics`, `createPartitions` and `deleteRecords` create, inspect and remove topics and their data. A `NewTopic` describes a topic to create and `NewPartitions` raises a topic's partition count; `listTopics` leaves out internal topics unless `ListTopicsOptions#listInternal` is set, and `TopicDescription#authorizedOperations` is `None` unless the request set `includeAuthorizedOperations = true`. `deleteRecords` takes the Java `RecordsToDelete` class, for example `RecordsToDelete.beforeOffset(offset)`.

To add partitions to an existing topic and then read back its partition leaders:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient.NewPartitions

def growTopic(admin: AdminClient, topic: String, partitions: Int): Task[Map[Int, Option[Int]]] =
  for {
    _            <- admin.createPartitions(Map(topic -> NewPartitions(totalCount = partitions)))
    descriptions <- admin.describeTopics(List(topic))
  } yield descriptions(topic).partitions.map(p => p.partition -> p.leader.map(_.id)).toMap
```

#### Configuration

`describeConfigs` and `incrementalAlterConfigs`, and their `*Async` variants, read and change the configuration of topics, brokers and other resources. A `ConfigResource` names the resource; for a broker, its name is the broker id as a string, for example `"0"`. Each change is an `AlterConfigOp`: `AlterConfigOpType.Set` sets a value, `Delete` reverts it to the default, and `Append` and `Subtract` add to or remove from a list-valued config. The `AlterConfigsOptions` parameter of `incrementalAlterConfigs` is required, but `AlterConfigsOptions()` is enough in most cases. The result, a `KafkaConfig`, maps each config name to a Java `ConfigEntry`.

To set a topic's retention and read the new value back:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ConfigEntry
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient.{ AlterConfigOp, AlterConfigOpType, AlterConfigsOptions, ConfigResource, ConfigResourceType }

def setRetention(admin: AdminClient, topic: String, retention: Duration): Task[Option[String]] = {
  val resource = ConfigResource(ConfigResourceType.Topic, topic)
  val setOp    = AlterConfigOp(new ConfigEntry("retention.ms", retention.toMillis.toString), AlterConfigOpType.Set)
  for {
    _       <- admin.incrementalAlterConfigs(Map(resource -> List(setOp)), AlterConfigsOptions())
    configs <- admin.describeConfigs(List(resource))
  } yield configs.get(resource).flatMap(_.entries.get("retention.ms")).map(_.value())
}
```

Because `incrementalAlterConfigs` polls until the `Set` is visible, the `describeConfigs` call that follows already sees the new value.

#### Consumer Groups

`listConsumerGroups`, `listGroups`, `describeConsumerGroups`, `listConsumerGroupOffsets`, `alterConsumerGroupOffsets`, `deleteConsumerGroups` and the `remove*MembersFromConsumerGroup` operations list, inspect, reset and delete consumer groups. `listConsumerGroups` returns consumer groups only, while `listGroups` returns groups of every type. A group must be empty before `deleteConsumerGroups` can delete it, and must have no active members before `alterConsumerGroupOffsets` can change its offsets; `removeMembersFromConsumerGroup` removes static members by their group instance id. As always in Kafka, a committed `OffsetAndMetadata` holds the offset of the *next* record the group will read.

To compute the lag of every partition a consumer group has committed offsets for, combine the group's committed offsets with the partitions' end offsets:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient.{ OffsetSpec, TopicPartition }

def consumerLag(admin: AdminClient, groupId: String): Task[Map[TopicPartition, Long]] =
  for {
    committed  <- admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets(groupId)
    endOffsets <- admin.listOffsets(committed.map { case (tp, _) => tp -> OffsetSpec.LatestSpec })
  } yield committed.flatMap { case (tp, committedOffset) =>
    endOffsets.get(tp).map(end => tp -> (end.offset - committedOffset.offset))
  }
```

To rewind a group to the start of its partitions, for example to reprocess a topic after a bug fix, stop all members of the group first and then alter its offsets:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient.{ GroupState, OffsetAndMetadata, OffsetSpec }

def rewindGroup(admin: AdminClient, groupId: String): Task[Unit] =
  for {
    description <- admin.describeConsumerGroups(groupId).map(_(groupId))
    _ <- ZIO.fail(new IllegalStateException(s"Group $groupId still has members"))
           .unless(description.state == GroupState.Empty)
    committed <- admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets(groupId)
    earliest  <- admin.listOffsets(committed.map { case (tp, _) => tp -> OffsetSpec.EarliestSpec })
    _ <- admin.alterConsumerGroupOffsets(
           groupId,
           earliest.map { case (tp, info) => tp -> OffsetAndMetadata(info.offset) }
         )
  } yield ()
```

#### Offsets

`listOffsets` and `listOffsetsAsync` look up offsets in the partitions themselves, independently of any consumer group. Each partition, given as the zio-kafka admin `TopicPartition` case class rather than the Java one, comes with an `OffsetSpec`: `OffsetSpec.EarliestSpec` (the first offset still in the log), `OffsetSpec.LatestSpec` (the offset the next produced record will get), or `OffsetSpec.TimestampSpec(timestamp)` (the first offset whose timestamp is at or after `timestamp`, in epoch milliseconds). The isolation level in `ListOffsetsOptions` defaults to `IsolationLevel.ReadUncommitted`; with `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted`, `LatestSpec` returns the last stable offset, which excludes records of open transactions, so use it for topics written by a [transactional producer](transactions.md).

#### Cluster

The `describeCluster*` operations (`describeClusterNodes`, `describeClusterController`, `describeClusterId` and `describeClusterAuthorizedOperations`), `describeLogDirs` and `metrics` describe the brokers, their log directories and the client itself. `describeClusterAuthorizedOperations` returns an empty set unless `DescribeClusterOptions#includeAuthorizedOperations` is set. A `Node` describes a broker, with `Option` fields where Kafka uses empty or negative placeholders. `metrics` returns the Java admin client's own metrics; see [Metrics](metrics.md) for the consumer and producer metrics zio-kafka publishes.

#### Access Control Lists

`describeAcls`, `createAcls` and `deleteAcls` (the last two also have `*Async` variants) need a broker with an authorizer configured; `deleteAcls` returns the bindings it deleted. They use the types from the `zio.kafka.admin.acl` and `zio.kafka.admin.resource` packages. An ACL is an `AclBinding(pattern, entry)` that binds a resource pattern to an access control entry:

```
AclBinding ──> ResourcePattern(resourceType, name, patternType)
           └─> AccessControlEntry(principal, host, operation, permissionType)

AclBindingFilter ──> ResourcePatternFilter(resourceType, name, patternType)
                 └─> AccessControlEntryFilter(principal, host, operation, permissionType)
```

A `PatternType.Literal` pattern matches the exact name (or `*` for all), and `PatternType.Prefixed` matches every name that starts with it. The `principal` is a Kafka principal such as `"User:alice"` (or `"User:*"`), and `host` is a client host, or `"*"` for any host. `AclBindingFilter(ResourcePatternFilter.Any, AccessControlEntryFilter.Any)` selects every ACL.

To let a principal read every topic whose name starts with a prefix, and then list the ACLs on that prefix:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient
import zio.kafka.admin.acl._
import zio.kafka.admin.resource.{ PatternType, ResourcePattern, ResourcePatternFilter, ResourceType }

def allowReadOnPrefix(admin: AdminClient, principal: String, prefix: String): Task[Set[AclBinding]] = {
  val binding = AclBinding(
    ResourcePattern(ResourceType.Topic, name = prefix, patternType = PatternType.Prefixed),
    AccessControlEntry(
      principal = principal,
      host = "*",
      operation = AclOperation.Read,
      permissionType = AclPermissionType.Allow
    )
  )
  val filter = AclBindingFilter(
    ResourcePatternFilter(ResourceType.Topic, prefix, PatternType.Prefixed),
    AccessControlEntryFilter.Any
  )
  admin.createAcls(Set(binding)) *> admin.describeAcls(filter)
}
```

### The Async Variants

Several operations come in two flavours: `describeConfigs` and `describeConfigsAsync`, `incrementalAlterConfigs` and `incrementalAlterConfigsAsync`, `listOffsets` and `listOffsetsAsync`, `describeLogDirs` and `describeLogDirsAsync`, `createAcls` and `createAclsAsync`, `deleteAcls` and `deleteAclsAsync`. The plain variant waits for the whole request and fails if any part of it fails. The `*Async` variant returns a nested effect, `Task[Map[K, Task[V]]]`:

- The outer effect sends the request and completes as soon as the Java client returns its per-item futures, without waiting for the broker's answer.
- Each inner effect waits for the result of one item (one config resource, partition, broker, ACL binding or filter). For `incrementalAlterConfigsAsync`, `createAclsAsync` and `deleteAclsAsync`, the inner effect also does the visibility wait described above.

This gives you a result, or a failure, per item: one missing topic does not fail the lookup of the others. The request is sent when the outer effect runs, so not running an inner effect does not cancel anything. To describe the configuration of several topics and keep a separate outcome for each:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClient.{ ConfigResource, ConfigResourceType, KafkaConfig }

def describeEach(admin: AdminClient, topics: List[String]): Task[Map[ConfigResource, Either[Throwable, KafkaConfig]]] =
  admin
    .describeConfigsAsync(topics.map(ConfigResource(ConfigResourceType.Topic, _)))
    .flatMap { perResource =>
      ZIO.foreachPar(perResource) { case (resource, config) => config.either.map(resource -> _) }
    }
```

### Using the Java Admin Client Directly

Zio-kafka wraps most, but not all, operations of the Java `Admin` interface. For an operation it does not wrap, create the Java client with `AdminClient.javaClientFromSettings` and convert its `KafkaFuture` results with the public helpers `AdminClient.fromKafkaFuture` and `AdminClient.fromKafkaFutureVoid`. To describe the cluster's feature flags, which zio-kafka does not wrap:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.FeatureMetadata
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.{ AdminClient, AdminClientSettings }

val features: ZIO[Any, Throwable, FeatureMetadata] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      javaAdmin <- AdminClient.javaClientFromSettings(AdminClientSettings(List("localhost:9092")))
      metadata  <- AdminClient.fromKafkaFuture(ZIO.attempt(javaAdmin.describeFeatures().featureMetadata()))
    } yield metadata
  }
```

Operations called this way get none of zio-kafka's visibility waiting.

### See Also

- [Security](security.md) for TLS and SASL settings and the SSL endpoint check that `AdminClient.make` runs.
- [Writing Tests](writing-tests.md) for the testkit helpers that create admin clients against an embedded broker.
- [Transactions](transactions.md) for when `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted` matters.

## Avoiding Chunk-Breakers

### A warning about `mapZIO` and other chunk-breakers

ZIO streams are not just a simple sequence of elements. The elements are grouped into chunks, which makes many
operations faster. Zio-kafka helps with this by guaranteeing that all records (for a given partition), fetched together
from the broker, are in the same chunk.

Be careful when using `mapZIO`, `tap` and some other stream operators that break the chunking structure of the stream
(or more precisely, the resulting stream has chunks with a single element). The throughput may be significantly lower
than with the original chunking structure intact.

Chunk-breaking operators can be found by looking at their scaladocs. Since zio-streams 2.1.17, the scaladocs of chunk-breaking operators such as `mapZIO`, `tap`, `buffer`, `mapZIOPar` and `flattenZIO` contain the words `This combinator destroys the chunking structure`.

You can regain full throughput by processing all elements in a chunk together in one go. However, there is a catch: the
order of processing changes. For example, given a stream with elements `a` and `b` in the same chunk, for
`stream.mapZIO(f).mapZIO(g)` the evaluation order is `f(a), g(a), f(b), g(b)`. For the alternatives listed below the
evaluation order changes to `f(a), f(b), g(a), g(b)`. Now imagine that `g(a)` fails, with `mapZIO`, `f(b)` is not
executed, but with the alternatives it _is_ executed. It is up to you to decide if this is a problem.

#### Use `mapZIOChunked`

_Available since zio-streams 2.1.17._

The simplest alternative is the stream operator `mapZIOChunked`; it has the same signature as `mapZIO`:

```scala
def f(a: A): ZIO[R, E, B]

stream               // ZStream[R, E, A]
  .mapZIOChunked(f)  // ZStream[R, E, B]
```

#### Use `chunksWith`

If you have a single processing step that needs to work on a chunk, you can use `chunksWith`:

```scala
def f(a: A): ZIO[R, E, B]

stream             // ZStream[R, E, A]
  .chunksWith { chunkStream =>
    chunkStream.mapZIO(chunk => ZIO.foreach(chunk)(f))
  }                // ZStream[R, E, B]
```

#### Expose chunking structure with `chunks`

Use `chunks` when you have multiple processing steps that can all work on a chunk at a time. Since `chunks` exposes the
chunking structure explicitly, the program can no longer accidentally break the chunking structure (unless
`flattenChunks` is also used):

```scala
def f(a: A): ZIO[R, E, B]
def g(b: B): ZIO[R, E, C]

stream                                         // ZStream[R, E, A]
  .chunks                                      // ZStream[R, E, Chunk[A]]
  .mapZIO { chunk => ZIO.foreach(chunk)(f) }   // ZStream[R, E, Chunk[B]]
  .mapZIO { chunk => ZIO.foreach(chunk)(g) }   // ZStream[R, E, Chunk[C]]
  .flattenChunks                               // ZStream[R, E, C]
```

#### Side effects per chunk with `tapChunks`

_Available since zio-streams 2.1.17._

Unlike `tap`, the `tapChunks` stream operator preserves the chunking structure and allows side effects per chunk:

```scala
stream                                                     // ZStream[R, E, A]
  .tapChunks(c => ZIO.logInfo(s"Chunk of size ${c.size}")) // ZStream[R, E, A]
```

#### Avoid `rechunk`

ZStream also provides the `rechunk` operator. This operator rebuilds the chunking structure by grouping elements into
chunks of fixed size. If there are not enough elements available for a chunk, the operator waits for these elements to
arrive. Only when the stream ends a smaller chunk is emitted.

In low-volume kafka applications, waiting for enough elements to arrive can take a long time! In high-volume kafka
applications, this operator causes data from multiple polls to be processed together. This results in increased
processing latency and memory usage.

Therefore, we recommend that you avoid `rechunk` in kafka applications.

---

## Tuning the Consumer

Zio-kafka's consumer can be tuned for:

* throughput
* latency
* memory usage
* long-running processes / slow consumers

All tuning is done via `ConsumerSettings` (see [consumer](consumer.md)):

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")
val groupId          = "my-group"
val properties       = Map[String, AnyRef]("fetch.min.bytes" -> "1")

val settings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
  .withGroupId(groupId)
  .withProperties(properties)
```

Read on for more details.

### Names

Two very similarly named settings are relevant. Don't mix them up:

* `pollTimeout` — how long a poll may take
* `max.poll.interval.ms` — the maximum time between polls

### Throughput and latency

The kafka client can be tuned for either high throughput or low latency, unfortunately not both.
The most important settings for tuning throughput and latency are:

* zio-kafka's `pollTimeout` — This is the maximum time to block while polling the Kafka consumer. Zio-kafka's default
  is `50ms` which is good for low latency applications. Set this higher, e.g. `500ms` for better throughput.
* kafka's [configuration `max.poll.records`](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#consumerconfigs_max.poll.records) — The maximum number of records a poll will return. Kafka defaults
  this to `500`. You can set this higher for more throughput, or lower for lower latency.
* zio-kafka's fetch-strategy `partitionPreFetchBufferLimit` — when the number of records in a partition queue is
  at or below this value, zio-kafka will start to pre-fetch and buffer more records from Kafka. The default value for
  this parameter is `1024`; 2 * the default `max.poll.records` of 500, rounded to the nearest power of 2.

Zio-kafka provides 2 methods that set these settings for 2 common use cases: `ConsumerSettings.tuneForHighThroughput`
and `ConsumerSettings.tuneForLowLatency`.
Note that their implementation may vary over time. You can use them as follows:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val highThroughputSettings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers).tuneForHighThroughput
val lowLatencySettings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers).tuneForLowLatency
```

The scaladoc of `ConsumerSettings#tuneForHighThroughput` and `ConsumerSettings#tuneForLowLatency` lists the exact values they set. Both methods replace the configured `FetchStrategy` with a `QueueSizeBasedFetchStrategy`, and so does `ConsumerSettings#withPartitionPreFetchBufferLimit`. Call them before `ConsumerSettings#withFetchStrategy`, otherwise a custom fetch strategy is silently discarded.

### Small and large records

Kafka’s performance is not very sensitive to record size. However, when records become very small (< 100 bytes) it
might be beneficial to increase `max.poll.records` and `partitionPreFetchBufferLimit`. Similarly, when records are
very large (> 100Kb), `max.poll.records` can be decreased. Also, pre-fetching can be limited by decreasing
`partitionPreFetchBufferLimit` or even disabled by using `ConsumerSettings#withoutPartitionPreFetching`.

### High number of partitions

When a lot of partitions need to be consumed, we need to take into account that heap is needed to store the records in
the partition queues. A very rough estimate for the maximum amount of heap needed is given by: `average record size` *
`number of partitions` * max(`partitionPreFetchBufferLimit`, `max.poll.records`).

The total can be tuned by changing the `partitionPreFetchBufferLimit`, `max.poll.records` settings.

Another option is to use a different `FetchStrategy`, for example the built-in
`zio.kafka.consumer.fetch.ManyPartitionsQueueSizeBasedFetchStrategy` (since zio-kafka 2.8.1), which also caps the total
queue size over all partitions:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings
import zio.kafka.consumer.fetch.ManyPartitionsQueueSizeBasedFetchStrategy

val settings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
  .withFetchStrategy(
    ManyPartitionsQueueSizeBasedFetchStrategy(maxPartitionQueueSize = 1024, maxTotalQueueSize = 20480)
  )
```

You can also write a custom `FetchStrategy`, see [Writing a Custom Fetch Strategy](#writing-a-custom-fetch-strategy).

### Writing a Custom Fetch Strategy

A fetch strategy decides, before every poll, which partitions may receive records. It implements a single method:

```scala
package zio.kafka.consumer.fetch

trait FetchStrategy {
  def selectPartitionsToFetch(streams: Chunk[PartitionStream]): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Set[TopicPartition]]
}

abstract class PartitionStream {
  def tp: TopicPartition
  def queueSize: UIO[Int]
}
```

The consumer passes one `PartitionStream` for every partition stream that has not ended. `PartitionStream#tp` is the Kafka `TopicPartition` of the stream, and `PartitionStream#queueSize` is the number of records that are buffered for it and not yet pulled by your program. The consumer resumes the partitions in the returned set and pauses all other assigned partitions for the next poll.

A paused partition receives no records, even when its stream is waiting for them, so make sure every partition is selected again eventually. The built-in strategies select a partition whenever its queue size is at or below a limit, which always includes partitions with an empty queue. The method runs before every poll, so keep it fast.

The following strategy gives one topic a larger buffer than the others, so that its partitions keep more records ready:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings
import zio.kafka.consumer.fetch.{ FetchStrategy, PartitionStream }

final case class PriorityTopicFetchStrategy(
  priorityTopic: String,
  priorityLimit: Int = 4096,
  defaultLimit: Int = 256
) extends FetchStrategy {
  override def selectPartitionsToFetch(streams: Chunk[PartitionStream]): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Set[TopicPartition]] =
    ZIO
      .filter(streams) { stream =>
        val limit = if (stream.tp.topic() == priorityTopic) priorityLimit else defaultLimit
        stream.queueSize.map(_ <= limit)
      }
      .map(_.map(_.tp).toSet)
}

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withFetchStrategy(PriorityTopicFetchStrategy(priorityTopic = "payments"))
```

`PartitionStream` is part of the public API since zio-kafka 4.1.0; in earlier versions, a custom fetch strategy had to depend on an internal type.

### Long-running processes / slow consumers

To detect stalled consumers, Kafka revokes a partition when a consumer does not poll within the max poll interval (see
[configuration `max.poll.interval.ms`](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#consumerconfigs_max.poll.interval.ms)). The default max poll interval is 5 minutes. After a partition is revoked,
it will be assigned to another consumer.

In zio-kafka a stream needs to pull data within the max stream pull interval (`ConsumerSettings#withMaxStreamPullInterval`,
since zio-kafka 2.9.0), which defaults to `max.poll.interval.ms` (in versions 2.6.0 up to 2.8.x it is always the max poll
interval). If this doesn't happen, the stream is interrupted with a failure and the whole consumer shuts down.

To prevent the above failure states, either decrease `max.poll.records` (so that time between polling gets shorter),
and/or increase `max.poll.interval.ms` (so that the time between polls may be longer).

To see if your application must be configured with a lower `max.poll.records` and/or a higher `max.poll.interval.ms`
value we need to consider the maximum duration between polls. If processing is sequential, we can obtain this maximum by
multiplying `max.poll.records` with the maximum duration to process a single record. To also accommodate things like
long garbage collections and buffering, configuration `max.poll.interval.ms` should be substantially higher than the
maximum processing time.

`max.poll.records`, `max.poll.interval.ms` and the max stream pull interval can be set with:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val settings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
  .withMaxPollRecords(1)
  .withMaxPollInterval(15.minutes)
  .withMaxStreamPullInterval(15.minutes)
```

On older zio-kafka versions `ConsumerSettings#withMaxPollInterval` is not available. Use the following instead:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val settings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
  .withProperty("max.poll.interval.ms", 15.minutes.toMillis.toString)
```

#### Long-running processes and `rebalance-safe-commits`

When `rebalance-safe-commits` is enabled, additional settings are needed for long-running processes. See
[preventing duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md) for more details.

#### Long-running processes and silent authorization failures

When topics are quiet or experience long idle periods, configuring a low threshold for silent authorization failure
detection (`emptyPollCountToMetaRefresh`) can trigger excessive offset-fetch requests.
See [detecting authorization failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md) for how to tune this setting for low-volume
topics.

### Using metrics to tune the consumer

Zio-kafka exposes [metrics](metrics.md) that can be used to further tune the consumer. To interpret these metrics you need to know how zio-kafka works internally.

![](consumer-internals.svg)

The runloop is at the heart of every zio-kafka consumer.
It creates a zstream for each partition, eventually this is the zstream your applications consumes from.
When the zstream starts, and every time the records queue is empty, it sends a request for data to the runloop.
The request makes the runloop poll. Partitions whose queue size is at or below the `FetchStrategy`'s limit are resumed, so the next poll may receive records for them.
Any received records are put in the records queue.
When the queue reaches a certain size (as determined by the configured `FetchStrategy`), the partition is paused.
Meanwhile, the zstream reads from the queue and emits the records to your application.

An optimally configured consumer has the following properties:

- the zstreams never have to wait for new records (to get high throughput),
- most of the time, the record queues are empty (to get low latency and low heap usage).

The following strategy can help you get to this state:

1. First make sure that `pollTimeout` and `max.poll.records` make sense for the latency and throughput requirements
   of your application.
2. Configure `partitionPreFetchBufferLimit` to `0` (`ConsumerSettings#withPartitionPreFetchBufferLimit(0)`).
3. Observe metric `ziokafka_consumer_queue_polls` which gives the number of polls during which records are idling in
   the queue.
4. Increase `partitionPreFetchBufferLimit` in steps until most measurements of the `ziokafka_consumer_queue_polls`
   histogram are in the lowest bucket (`le="1.0"`; zio-metrics ignores the `0` bucket boundary, so this bucket counts both 0 and 1 idle polls).

During this process, it is useful to observe metric `ziokafka_consumer_queue_size` (number of records in the queues) to
see if the queues are indeed increasing in size.

When many (hundreds of) partitions need to be consumed, the metric `ziokafka_consumer_all_queue_size` should also be
observed as increasing `partitionPreFetchBufferLimit` can lead to high heap usage. (See 'High number of partitions'
above.)

---

## Consumer

`Consumer` is the **zio-kafka service for reading records from Kafka**. It wraps a single Apache Kafka `KafkaConsumer` and exposes its records as ZIO streams of `CommittableRecord`s, so that each record carries an `Offset` you can commit once you have processed it. One `Consumer` can serve several streams at once, each with its own subscription and deserializers.

The `Consumer` service:

- Polls for you — a background loop owns the Kafka consumer, fetches records ahead of demand, and pauses partitions whose streams are not pulling.
- Streams per partition — records of one partition arrive in order, and you choose between one merged stream or one stream per partition.
- Never auto-commits — offsets are committed explicitly after processing (by your code or by `Consumer#consumeWith`), which gives at-least-once delivery.
- Is scoped — the Kafka consumer is closed when the `Scope` that created it closes.

The shape of the service, with representative members:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def plainStream[R, K, V](subscription: Subscription, keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K], valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V], bufferSize: Int = 4): ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]]
  def partitionedStream[R, K, V](subscription: Subscription, keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K], valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V]): Stream[Throwable, (TopicPartition, ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]])]
  def consumeWith[R: EnvironmentTag, R1: EnvironmentTag, K, V](subscription: Subscription, keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K], valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V], commitRetryPolicy: Schedule[Any, Any, Any] = Schedule.exponential(1.second) && Schedule.recurs(3))(f: ConsumerRecord[K, V] => URIO[R1, Unit]): ZIO[R & R1, Throwable, Unit]
  def stopConsumption: UIO[Unit]
  def assignment: Task[Set[TopicPartition]]
  def committed(partitions: Set[TopicPartition], timeout: Duration = Duration.Infinity): Task[Map[TopicPartition, Option[OffsetAndMetadata]]]
  val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings
  // ... more streams and metadata queries, see below
}

object Consumer {
  def make(settings: ConsumerSettings): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Consumer]
  def live: RLayer[ConsumerSettings, Consumer]
  // ...
}
```

The how-to guides walk through common tasks step by step: [creating a consumer](creating-a-consumer.md), [consuming Kafka topics using ZIO Streams](consuming-kafka-topics-using-zio-streams.md) and [sharing a consumer between streams](sharing-consumer.md). This page is the reference for the whole API.

### Usage

To consume a topic, we create a consumer from `ConsumerSettings`, stream its records, and commit their offsets in batches:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("my-group")
    .withClientId("my-client")

val program: Task[Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      consumer <- Consumer.make(settings)
      _ <- consumer
             .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
             .tap(record => ZIO.logInfo(s"${record.key}: ${record.value}"))
             .map(_.offset)
             .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
             .mapZIO(_.commit)
             .runDrain
    } yield ()
  }
```

`Consumer.collectOffsets` merges the offsets that arrive while a commit is running into one `OffsetBatch`, so committing does not slow down the stream. See [Offsets and Committing](offsets-and-committing.md) for the details.

### Creating a Consumer

A `Consumer` needs a `Scope`, because it owns a connection to the Kafka cluster that must be closed. There are three ways to create one.

#### Consumer.make

`Consumer.make` creates a consumer from settings. It validates the settings first and fails with an `IllegalArgumentException` when they are invalid (see [Settings Validation](#settings-validation)):

```scala
object Consumer {
  def make(settings: ConsumerSettings): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Consumer]
}
```

When the scope closes, zio-kafka stops consuming and closes the Kafka consumer, giving it at most `closeTimeout` (30 seconds by default) to close. The [creating a consumer](creating-a-consumer.md) guide shows how to use it with `ZIO.scoped` and `ZLayer.scoped`.

#### Consumer.live

`Consumer.live` is a layer that reads `ConsumerSettings` from the environment and produces a `Consumer`. It is the natural choice when the settings come from another layer, for example from configuration:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._

val settingsLayer: ULayer[ConsumerSettings] =
  ZLayer.succeed(ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("my-group"))

val consumerLayer: TaskLayer[Consumer] =
  settingsLayer >>> Consumer.live
```

#### Consumer.fromJavaConsumerWithPermit

`Consumer.fromJavaConsumerWithPermit` wraps a `KafkaConsumer` that you create yourself. You rarely need this; it is an advanced API for when your application also needs direct access to the Java consumer. Prefer `Consumer.make` otherwise. Its signature:

```scala
object Consumer {
  def fromJavaConsumerWithPermit(
    javaConsumer: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.Consumer[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]],
    settings: ConsumerSettings,
    access: Semaphore
  ): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Consumer]
}
```

The Java consumer and zio-kafka share the semaphore `access`. While you hold its permit, zio-kafka cannot poll, so hold it as briefly as possible. Unlike `Consumer.make`, this method does not validate `settings`. You are responsible for all of the following:

- Create the `KafkaConsumer` and close it after the zio-kafka consumer.
- Disable auto commit (`enable.auto.commit=false`).
- Create `access` as a semaphore with exactly one permit.
- Acquire a permit from `access` before every use of the Java consumer, and release it afterwards.
- Never call `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `assign`, `poll`, `commit*`, `seek`, `pause`, `resume` or `enforceRebalance` on the Java consumer.
- Keep the configuration of the Java consumer in sync with `settings`, for example by building `settings` with `ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers).withProperties(config)`.

Breaking any of these rules is likely to cause errors that are hard to track down. To create the Java consumer in a scope and hand it to zio-kafka:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.{ ConsumerConfig, KafkaConsumer }
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.ByteArrayDeserializer
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._

import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters._

val config: Map[String, AnyRef] = Map(
  ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG  -> "localhost:9092",
  ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG           -> "my-group",
  ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG -> "false"
)

val consumerWithJavaAccess: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, (Consumer, Task[Set[String]])] =
  for {
    javaConsumer <- ZIO.fromAutoCloseable(
                      ZIO.attempt(
                        new KafkaConsumer[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]](
                          config.asJava,
                          new ByteArrayDeserializer(),
                          new ByteArrayDeserializer()
                        )
                      )
                    )
    access   <- Semaphore.make(1)
    settings  = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withProperties(config)
    consumer <- Consumer.fromJavaConsumerWithPermit(javaConsumer, settings, access)
    // Every direct use of the Java consumer holds the permit:
    listTopicNames = access.withPermit(ZIO.attemptBlocking(javaConsumer.listTopics().keySet().asScala.toSet))
  } yield (consumer, listTopicNames)
```

Because finalizers run in reverse order, the scope closes the zio-kafka consumer before the Java consumer.

### Consumer Settings

`ConsumerSettings` is an immutable case class holding the Kafka client properties plus zio-kafka's own settings. Build it with `ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)` followed by `with*` methods; the Scaladoc recommends this style to stay source compatible with future releases:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.consumer.Consumer.{ AutoOffsetStrategy, OffsetRetrieval }

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withClientId("orders-service-1")
    .withOffsetRetrieval(OffsetRetrieval.Auto(AutoOffsetStrategy.Earliest))
    .withRebalanceSafeCommits(true)
    .withMaxPollInterval(10.minutes)
    .withProperty("fetch.min.bytes", "1024")
```

Any Kafka consumer property can be set with `ConsumerSettings#withProperty` or `ConsumerSettings#withProperties`; the common ones, such as `group.id`, `client.id`, `max.poll.records` and `isolation.level`, also have their own `with*` method. A group id is needed for `Topics` and `Pattern` subscriptions and for committing to Kafka; a `Manual` subscription works without it. The other settings control zio-kafka itself, for example the poll and commit timeouts, the offset retrieval strategy (by default `OffsetRetrieval.Auto(AutoOffsetStrategy.Latest)`, so a partition without a committed offset starts at its end), rebalance-safe commits, pre-fetching, metrics and diagnostics. For every setting and its default, see the [`ConsumerSettings` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/consumer/ConsumerSettings.html).

Related pages explain when to change these settings: [consumer tuning](consumer-tuning.md) for poll, pre-fetch and slow-consumer settings, [partition assignment and offset retrieval](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md) for `OffsetRetrieval`, [preventing duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md) for rebalance-safe commits, [detecting authorization failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md) for the authorization settings, and [metrics](metrics.md) for the metrics settings.

:::note
When rebalance-safe commits are enabled and you do not set `partition.assignment.strategy` yourself, zio-kafka configures Kafka's `RangeAssignor`, which revokes all partitions during a rebalance.
:::

#### Settings Validation

`Consumer.make` checks the settings before it connects. It fails with an `IllegalArgumentException` listing every problem when:

- `enable.auto.commit` is set to `true` (zio-kafka pre-fetches records, so auto commit could commit records you have not processed; zio-kafka always disables it).
- `commitTimeout` is not larger than twice `pollTimeout`.
- The settings contain the deprecated `OffsetRetrieval.Manual` directly instead of `OffsetRetrieval.External`. `ConsumerSettings#withOffsetRetrieval` converts `Manual` to `External` for you.

### Consuming Records

Every way to consume takes a `Subscription` and a key and a value `Deserializer`. A subscription names topics (`Subscription.topics("a", "b")`), a topic pattern (`Subscription.pattern("orders-.*".r)`), or a fixed set of partitions (`Subscription.manual("a" -> 0)`); [partition assignment and offset retrieval](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md) covers them in detail. Deserializers are described in [serialization and deserialization](serialization-and-deserialization.md).

All streams emit records of one partition in order, and the records fetched for a partition in one poll land in the same chunk. Use chunk-preserving operators to keep processing fast, as explained in [avoiding chunk breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md).

#### Plain Stream

`Consumer#plainStream` emits the records of all assigned partitions in a single stream. The order within a partition is preserved; how partitions interleave is not deterministic. Internally it merges the partition streams, buffering up to `bufferSize` chunks:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def plainStream[R, K, V](
    subscription: Subscription,
    keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K],
    valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V],
    bufferSize: Int = 4
  ): ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]]
}
```

The [Usage](#usage) section shows a complete plain stream.

#### Partitioned Streams

`Consumer#partitionedStream` emits one inner stream per assigned partition, paired with its `TopicPartition`. Processing each partition stream in its own fiber gives parallelism across partitions while keeping each partition sequential. `Consumer#partitionedAssignmentStream` emits the same partition streams, but grouped in one `Chunk` per rebalance, so you can react to the set of newly assigned partitions as a whole:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def partitionedStream[R, K, V](
    subscription: Subscription,
    keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K],
    valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V]
  ): Stream[Throwable, (TopicPartition, ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]])]

  def partitionedAssignmentStream[R, K, V](
    subscription: Subscription,
    keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K],
    valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V]
  ): Stream[Throwable, Chunk[(TopicPartition, ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]])]]
}
```

With a `Topics` or `Pattern` subscription the outer stream emits again on every rebalance: new partition streams start, and the streams of revoked partitions complete. With a `Manual` subscription there are no rebalances. To process every partition in parallel and commit from a single place:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def processPartitions(consumer: Consumer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .partitionedStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .flatMapPar(Int.MaxValue) { case (topicPartition, partitionStream) =>
      partitionStream
        .tap(record => ZIO.logInfo(s"$topicPartition: ${record.value}"))
        .map(_.offset)
    }
    .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
    .mapZIO(_.commit)
    .runDrain
```

Use `Int.MaxValue` (or at least the number of partitions you can be assigned) as the parallelism of `flatMapPar`. A partition stream that is never pulled stops making progress, and after `maxStreamPullInterval` zio-kafka fails it and shuts down the consumer. The [consuming Kafka topics using ZIO Streams](consuming-kafka-topics-using-zio-streams.md) guide explains these patterns further.

#### consumeWith

`Consumer#consumeWith` is the simplest way to process a topic. It runs your effect for each record and commits offsets for you:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def consumeWith[R: EnvironmentTag, R1: EnvironmentTag, K, V](
    subscription: Subscription,
    keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K],
    valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V],
    commitRetryPolicy: Schedule[Any, Any, Any] = Schedule.exponential(1.second) && Schedule.recurs(3)
  )(f: ConsumerRecord[K, V] => URIO[R1, Unit]): ZIO[R & R1, Throwable, Unit]
}

object Consumer {
  def consumeWith[R: EnvironmentTag, R1: EnvironmentTag, K, V](
    settings: ConsumerSettings,
    subscription: Subscription,
    keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K],
    valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V],
    commitRetryPolicy: Schedule[Any, Any, Any] = Schedule.exponential(1.second) && Schedule.recurs(3)
  )(f: ConsumerRecord[K, V] => URIO[R1, Unit]): RIO[R & R1, Unit]
}
```

`R` is the environment of the deserializers and `R1` the environment of your effect. The effect receives Kafka's `ConsumerRecord`, not a `CommittableRecord`. Records of one partition are processed one after another, while different partitions are processed in parallel. Offsets are committed after the effect completes, batched while a commit is in progress; commits that fail with a `RetriableCommitFailedException` or `Consumer.CommitTimeout` are retried according to `commitRetryPolicy` (by default up to 3 retries with exponential backoff starting at 1 second). The returned effect only completes when it is interrupted, or fails when the consumer fails.

The effect's error type is `Nothing`, so it must handle its own failures, by retrying or by ignoring the error and skipping the record. The companion variant creates and closes its own consumer from `settings`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("my-group")

val program: Task[Unit] =
  Consumer.consumeWith(settings, Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string) { record =>
    ZIO.logInfo(s"${record.key()}: ${record.value()}")
  }
```

Delivery is at least once: a record whose effect has run may not have its offset committed yet when the stream stops. See [committing with consumeWith](offsets-and-committing.md#committing-with-consumewith).

#### Streams With Control

Each stream method has a `*WithControl` variant that returns a `StreamControl` instead of a bare stream. A `StreamControl` lets you stop fetching records for one subscription and let the stream finish its in-flight records, which makes a graceful shutdown possible. The `*WithControl` methods and `Consumer.runWithGracefulShutdown` are experimental: they may change or disappear in any zio-kafka release. Their signatures:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def plainStreamWithControl[R, K, V](subscription: Subscription, keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K], valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V], bufferSize: Int = 4): ZIO[Scope with R, Throwable, StreamControl[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]]]
  def partitionedStreamWithControl[R, K, V](subscription: Subscription, keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K], valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V]): ZIO[Scope with R, Throwable, StreamControl[R, Throwable, (TopicPartition, ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]])]]
  def partitionedAssignmentStreamWithControl[R, K, V](subscription: Subscription, keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K], valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V]): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, StreamControl[R, Throwable, Chunk[(TopicPartition, ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]])]]]
}

trait StreamControl[-R, +E, +A] {
  def stream: ZStream[R, E, A]
  def end: UIO[Unit]
}

object Consumer {
  def runWithGracefulShutdown[R1, R2, E, A](control: StreamControl[R1, E, A], shutdownTimeout: Duration)(
    withStream: ZStream[R1, E, A] => ZIO[R2 & Scope, E, Any]
  ): ZIO[R1 & R2, E, Any]
}
```

The `Scope` controls the subscription: zio-kafka unsubscribes when the scope ends. `StreamControl#end` stops fetching records for the subscription's partitions and ends the stream, but does not unsubscribe until the scope ends. Run `StreamControl#stream` at most once; running it twice divides the chunks over both runs. `StreamControl#map` transforms the stream while keeping `StreamControl#end`.

`Consumer.runWithGracefulShutdown` runs `withStream` on the controlled stream. When the surrounding fiber is interrupted, for example at application shutdown, it calls `StreamControl#end` and waits up to `shutdownTimeout` for `withStream` to finish processing and committing:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def runGracefully(consumer: Consumer): Task[Any] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      control <- consumer.plainStreamWithControl(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
      result <- Consumer.runWithGracefulShutdown(control, shutdownTimeout = 30.seconds) { stream =>
                  stream
                    .tap(record => ZIO.logInfo(record.value))
                    .map(_.offset)
                    .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
                    .mapZIO(_.commit)
                    .runDrain
                }
    } yield result
  }
```

If `withStream` does not finish within `shutdownTimeout`, zio-kafka logs an error and gives up waiting; some in-flight records may not have been processed. The [controlled shutdown](consuming-kafka-topics-using-zio-streams.md#controlled-shutdown-experimental) section of the streams guide shows how to call `StreamControl#end` yourself.

#### Multiple Subscriptions on One Consumer

You can run several streams on one `Consumer`, each with its own subscription and deserializers. Zio-kafka subscribes the Kafka consumer to the union of all active subscriptions, and each stream receives only the partitions that match its own subscription. When a stream completes, its subscription is removed from the union.

All subscriptions on one consumer must be of the same kind: all `Topics`, all `Pattern`, or all `Manual`. Two `Pattern` subscriptions are combined into one regular expression. Starting a stream whose subscription is of a different kind fails that stream with `InvalidSubscriptionUnion`, which lists the subscriptions that could not be combined. When subscriptions overlap, for example `Subscription.topics("a", "b")` and `Subscription.topics("b", "c")`, the records of topic `b` are divided over both streams in a non-deterministic way.

Settings such as `max.poll.records` and the offset retrieval strategy apply to all subscriptions together. The [sharing a consumer](sharing-consumer.md) guide has a full example.

#### Stopping Consumption

`Consumer#stopConsumption` stops fetching for every subscription, drains the buffered records, and ends all streams of this consumer. Commits are still processed while the streams finish, so a stream can stop the consumer and then commit the offsets of the records it has processed:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def stopConsumption: UIO[Unit]
}
```

To end a single subscription and leave the others running, use the `StreamControl` of that subscription instead.

### Querying Metadata and Offsets

The `Consumer` forwards a set of read-only queries to the Kafka consumer, converting Java collections to Scala ones: `Consumer#assignment`, `Consumer#subscription`, `Consumer#committed`, `Consumer#beginningOffsets`, `Consumer#endOffsets`, `Consumer#offsetsForTimes`, `Consumer#position`, `Consumer#listTopics`, `Consumer#partitionsFor` and `Consumer#metrics` (the Kafka client's own metrics; for zio-kafka's metrics, see [metrics](metrics.md)). Every query that takes a `timeout` defaults to `Duration.Infinity`. The queries share the Kafka consumer with the polling loop, so each one waits until the current poll completes. `Consumer#committed` returns `None` for a partition the group has not committed, and `Consumer#offsetsForTimes` leaves out partitions that have no record at or after the given timestamp. For the signatures, see the [`Consumer` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/consumer/Consumer.html).

Except for `Consumer#position`, the queries do not need the partitions to be assigned to this consumer, so they also work for monitoring. To compute the lag of a consumer group for the partitions it has committed:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._

def lag(consumer: Consumer, topic: String): Task[Map[TopicPartition, Long]] =
  for {
    partitions <- consumer.partitionsFor(topic, timeout = 10.seconds)
    tps         = partitions.map(p => new TopicPartition(p.topic(), p.partition())).toSet
    ends       <- consumer.endOffsets(tps, timeout = 10.seconds)
    committed  <- consumer.committed(tps, timeout = 10.seconds)
  } yield ends.flatMap { case (tp, end) =>
    committed.get(tp).flatten.map(c => tp -> (end - c.offset()))
  }
```

Partitions without a committed offset are left out: where a consumer starts on them depends on its offset retrieval setting (by default the end of the partition, see [Consumer Settings](#consumer-settings)).

### Committing Offsets

Records are committed through their `Offset`, not through the `Consumer`. The `Consumer` companion provides the sinks that combine offsets into an `OffsetBatch`, and the service accepts commits made elsewhere:

```scala
object Consumer {
  val collectOffsets: ZSink[Any, Nothing, Offset, Nothing, OffsetBatch]
  val collectOffsetBatches: ZSink[Any, Nothing, OffsetBatch, Nothing, OffsetBatch]
  case object CommitTimeout extends RuntimeException
}

trait Consumer {
  def registerExternalCommits(offsetBatch: OffsetBatch): Task[Unit]
}
```

`Consumer.collectOffsets` folds `Offset`s into a batch, and `Consumer.collectOffsetBatches` merges batches (`Consumer.offsetBatches` is an alias of `Consumer.collectOffsets`). `Consumer.CommitTimeout` is the error of a commit that does not complete within `commitTimeout`. `Consumer#registerExternalCommits` tells the consumer about offsets you stored outside Kafka, so that rebalance-safe commits can wait for them; a `TransactionalProducer` calls it for you. [Offsets and Committing](offsets-and-committing.md) covers all of these, and [transactions](transactions.md) covers committing inside a transaction.

### Rebalance Listener

A `RebalanceListener` runs your effects when the consumer group changes the partitions assigned to this consumer. It is a ZIO wrapper around Kafka's `ConsumerRebalanceListener`:

```scala
final case class RebalanceListener(
  onAssigned: Set[TopicPartition] => Task[Unit],
  onRevoked: Set[TopicPartition] => Task[Unit],
  onLost: Set[TopicPartition] => Task[Unit]
) {
  def ++(that: RebalanceListener): RebalanceListener
  def runOnExecutor(executor: Executor): RebalanceListener
}

object RebalanceListener {
  def apply(onAssigned: Set[TopicPartition] => Task[Unit], onRevoked: Set[TopicPartition] => Task[Unit]): RebalanceListener
  val noop: RebalanceListener
}
```

Kafka calls `onAssigned` with the partitions newly given to this consumer, `onRevoked` with partitions taken away in an orderly rebalance, and `onLost` with partitions the consumer lost without a chance to commit, for example after its session timed out. The two-argument `RebalanceListener.apply` uses `onRevoked` for lost partitions too. `RebalanceListener#++` combines two listeners so that both run, one after the other, and `RebalanceListener#runOnExecutor` runs the callbacks on the given `Executor`. Register a listener with `ConsumerSettings#withRebalanceListener`:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._

val listener: RebalanceListener =
  RebalanceListener(
    onAssigned = (assigned: Set[TopicPartition]) => ZIO.logInfo(s"Assigned: ${assigned.mkString(", ")}"),
    onRevoked = (revoked: Set[TopicPartition]) => ZIO.logInfo(s"Revoked: ${revoked.mkString(", ")}"),
    onLost = (lost: Set[TopicPartition]) => ZIO.logWarning(s"Lost: ${lost.mkString(", ")}")
  )

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("my-group")
    .withRebalanceListener(listener)
```

Zio-kafka runs your listener after its own rebalance handling. By the time your `onRevoked` runs, zio-kafka has told the streams of the revoked partitions to end and, with rebalance-safe commits enabled, has waited (up to `maxRebalanceDuration`) for their offsets to be committed.

:::warning
The callbacks run inside the Kafka consumer's poll, while zio-kafka holds exclusive access to the Kafka consumer. Polling for all partitions waits until the callback completes, so keep callbacks short. Do not call `Consumer` methods or commit offsets from a callback: they need that same access and cannot complete until the callback returns. A failing callback makes the poll fail, so handle errors inside the callback.
:::

### CommittableRecord

A `CommittableRecord[K, V]` is what the consumer streams emit: a deserialized Kafka `ConsumerRecord` together with what is needed to commit it. Its commit handle and consumer group metadata are private:

```scala
final case class CommittableRecord[K, V](
  record: ConsumerRecord[K, V],
  nextOffset: OffsetAndMetadata,
  // private: commit handle and consumer group metadata
) {
  def key: K
  def value: V
  def partition: Int
  def timestamp: Long
  def offset: Offset
  def deserializeWith[R, K1, V1](keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K1], valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V1])(implicit
    ev1: K <:< Array[Byte],
    ev2: V <:< Array[Byte]
  ): RIO[R, CommittableRecord[K1, V1]]
}
```

Besides `key`, `value`, `partition` and `timestamp`, use `record`, the underlying Kafka `ConsumerRecord`, for everything else, such as `record.topic()` and `record.leaderEpoch()`. `offset.offset` is the consumed offset, and `offset.commit` commits it. `nextOffset` is the offset a consumer should resume from after this record: usually the record's offset + 1, but for the last record of a partition in a poll it is the next offset Kafka reports, which is larger when transaction control records follow the record. For every member, see the [`CommittableRecord` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/consumer/CommittableRecord.html).

The headers of a record are only available through `record.headers()`; see [record headers](record-headers.md). How `offset` and `nextOffset` relate to committing is explained in [Offsets and Committing](offsets-and-committing.md).

`CommittableRecord#deserializeWith` lets you defer deserialization, for example to handle a deserialization failure per record. When both deserializers of a stream are `Serde.byteArray`, zio-kafka skips deserialization entirely, so you can deserialize inside the stream instead:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def consumeRaw(consumer: Consumer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.byteArray, Serde.byteArray)
    .mapChunksZIO(_.mapZIO(_.deserializeWith(Serde.string, Serde.string)))
    .tap(record => ZIO.logInfo(s"partition ${record.partition}, offset ${record.offset.offset}: ${record.value}"))
    .map(_.offset)
    .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
    .mapZIO(_.commit)
    .runDrain
```

## Consuming Kafka Topics Using ZIO Streams

You can stream data from Kafka using the `plainStream` method:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

val consumer: Consumer = ??? // see "Creating a zio-kafka Consumer"

consumer
  .plainStream(Subscription.topics("topic150"), Serde.string, Serde.string) // (1)
  .tap(cr => printLine(s"key: ${cr.record.key}, value: ${cr.record.value}")) // (2)
  .map(_.offset) // (3)
  .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis)) // (4)
  .mapZIO(_.commit) // (5)
  .runDrain
```

(1) There are several types of subscriptions: a set of topics, a topic name pattern, or fully specified set of
topic-partitions (see [subscriptions](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md)).

(2) The `plainStream` method returns a stream of `CommittableRecord` objects. In this line, we access the key
and value from the `CommittableRecord` and print them to the console.

:::caution
Some stream operators (like `tap` and `mapZIO`) break the chunking structure of the stream which heavily reduces
throughput. See [avoiding chunk-breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md) for more information and alternatives.
:::

(3) Here we get the offset of the record, so we now have a stream of offsets.

(4) The offsets are aggregated into an `OffsetBatch`. Per partition, the offset batch keeps the highest next offset (the offset to resume consuming from). ZStream operator `aggregateAsyncWithin` runs upstream in a separate fiber, allowing consuming and committing to run in parallel.

The offset batches are emitted every 100 milliseconds. The delay should be longer than the typical commit-duration in
your system. For example, lets assume the delay is set to 2ms and a commit operation takes 10ms. Then, when some records
are consumed, 2ms later `aggregateAsyncWithin` emits an offset batch and starts collecting offsets for the next batch.
In addition, the commit operation starts. Again 2ms later `aggregateAsyncWithin` tries to emit the next batch. However,
this will block because the commit is still ongoing. Since `aggregateAsyncWithin` is now blocked, it stops accepting
offsets from upstream, halting the consumer until the commit completes.

For applications that only see a few records per second or less, you can remove line (4) and commit the offset for each
record separately. In this approach the commit executes on the same fiber as the rest of the stream. This lowers
throughput. Explicitly committing every record is therefore almost never the best approach.

To get the lowest commit latency you can commit continuously; a new commit is started as soon as the previous completes.
This is done by replacing line (4) with `.aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)`. Be aware that registering commits is
an intensive operation for the kafka brokers. With dozens of consumers continuously committing, the high load may slow
down everything.

(5) All offsets in the `OffsetBatch` are committed. As soon as the commit is done, the next offset batch is pulled
from upstream.

See [offsets and committing](offsets-and-committing.md) for the other ways to commit offsets.

### Consuming with more parallelism

To process partitions (assigned to the consumer) in parallel, you may use the `partitionedStream` method, which creates
a nested stream of partitions:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import zio.stream._

val consumer: Consumer = ??? // see "Creating a zio-kafka Consumer"

consumer
  .partitionedStream(Subscription.topics("topic150"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
  .flatMapPar(Int.MaxValue) { case (topicPartition, partitionStream) => // (1)
    ZStream.fromZIO(
      printLine(s"Starting stream for topic '${topicPartition.topic}' partition ${topicPartition.partition}")
    ) *>
      partitionStream
        .tap(record => printLine(s"key: ${record.key}, value: ${record.value}")) // (2)
        .map(_.offset) // (3)
  }
  .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis)) // (4)
  .mapZIO(_.commit)  // (5)
  .runDrain
```

In this example, each partition is processed in parallel on separate fibers, while a single fiber is doing commits.

(1) When using partitionedStream with `flatMapPar(n)`, it is recommended to set n to `Int.MaxValue`. N must be equal to or greater than the number of partitions your consumer subscribes to, otherwise some partition streams are never pulled. Once such a stream has buffered records and has not been pulled for `maxStreamPullInterval` (by default `max.poll.interval.ms`), zio-kafka fails the stream and shuts down the consumer.

Each time a new partition is assigned to the consumer, a new partition stream is created and the body of the
`flatMapPar` is executed.

(2) As before, here we process the received `CommittableRecord`.

(3) Note how the offsets from all the sub-streams are merged into a single stream of `Offset`s. This ensures only a
single stream is doing commits.

(4) and (5) The offsets are aggregated into an `OffsetBatch` and committed as in the previous section.

### Controlled shutdown (experimental)

The examples above will keep processing records forever, or until the fiber is interrupted, typically at application
shutdown. When interrupted, some records may be 'in-flight', e.g. being processed by one of the stages of your consumer
stream user code. Those records will be processed partly and their offsets may not be committed. For fast shutdown in an
at-least-once processing scenario this is fine.

Zio-kafka also supports a _graceful shutdown_, where the fetching of records for the subscribed topics/partitions is
stopped, the streams are ended and all downstream stages are completed, allowing in-flight records to be fully
processed.

Use the `*StreamWithControl` variants of `plainStream`, `partitionedStream` and `partitionedAssignmentStream` for this
purpose. These methods return a `StreamControl` object allowing you to stop fetching records and terminate the execution
of the stream gracefully.

The `StreamControl` can be used with `Consumer.runWithGracefulShutdown`, which can gracefully terminate the stream upon
fiber interruption. This is useful for a controlled shutdown when your application is terminated:

```scala
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import zio._

val consumer: Consumer = ??? // see "Creating a zio-kafka Consumer"

ZIO.scoped {
  for {
    control <- consumer.partitionedStreamWithControl(
      Subscription.topics("topic150"),
      Serde.string,
      Serde.string
    )
    _ <- Consumer.runWithGracefulShutdown(control, shutdownTimeout = 30.seconds) { stream =>
        stream.flatMapPar(Int.MaxValue) { case (topicPartition, partitionStream) =>
          partitionStream
            .tap(record => printLine(s"key: ${record.key}, value: ${record.value}"))
            .map(_.offset)
        }
        .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
        .mapZIO(_.commit)
        .runDrain
      }
  } yield ()
}
```

For more control over when to end the stream, use the `StreamControl` construct like this:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

val consumer: Consumer = ??? // see "Creating a zio-kafka Consumer"

ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      control <- consumer.partitionedStreamWithControl(
          Subscription.topics("topic150"),
          Serde.string,
          Serde.string
        )
      fiber <- control.stream.flatMapPar(Int.MaxValue) { case (topicPartition, partitionStream) =>
            partitionStream
              .tap(record => printLine(s"key: ${record.key}, value: ${record.value}"))
              .map(_.offset)
          }
          .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
          .mapZIO(_.commit)
          .runDrain
          .forkScoped
      // At some point in your code, when some condition is met
      _ <- control.end // Stop fetching more records
      _ <- fiber.join // Wait for graceful completion of the stream
    } yield ()
}
```

This functionality is experimental: the API may change in incompatible ways in any zio-kafka version. If no issues are reported and the API has good usability, it will eventually be marked as stable.
