## Consuming, Producing and Committing Offsets

Consuming from Kafka and then producing a transformed message back to Kafka, is a regular pattern in systems that use
Kafka. This page shows an example of an application that does this. Next we discuss how throughput can be improved.

This page is also useful as a deep dive into producing to Kafka with data from other streaming sources.

### Example application

This is what the example application does:

1. consumes messages from topic `my-input-topic`,
2. transforms the received records,
3. produces the transformed records to topic `my-output-topic`,
4. commits the consumer offsets.

The application uses the zio-kafka streaming APIs. We need to explicitly commit offsets; applications that use the streaming API process records asynchronously with the consumer, and therefore, committing offsets automatically is not possible. See [offsets and committing](offsets-and-committing.md) for an overview of the ways to commit, and [Producer](producer.md) for the producer API.

The application consumes, transforms, produces and commits in a single stream:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord

val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("my-application")
val producerSettings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))

val app: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Unit] = for {
  consumer <- Consumer.make(consumerSettings)
  producer <- Producer.make(producerSettings)
  _ <-
    consumer
      // Create a stream of records, consuming all records from a topic
      .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-input-topic"), Serde.int, Serde.long)
      // Convert every record in a ProducerRecord, and the ConsumerRecord's offset
      .map { record =>
        val key: Int = record.record.key()
        val value: Long = record.record.value()
        val newValue: String = value.toString

        val producerRecord: ProducerRecord[Int, String] =
          new ProducerRecord("my-output-topic", key, newValue)
        (producerRecord, record.offset)
      }
      // For every chunk of producerRecords and offsets
      .mapChunksZIO { chunk =>
        val records = chunk.map(_._1)
        val offsetBatch = OffsetBatch(chunk.map(_._2))

        // produce the chunk of records, when acked by kafka, commit the consumed offsets,
        // returning an empty chunk (`mapChunksZIO` requires this function to return a ZIO[Chunk])
        producer.produceChunk(records, Serde.int, Serde.string) *>
          offsetBatch.commit.as(Chunk.empty)
      }
      .runDrain
} yield ()
```

#### Performance analysis

To analyze throughput performance of a zio-streams program, it is important to find out the characteristics of the
stream's chunks, and to make sure that the chunking structure stays intact. (See [avoiding
chunk-breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md) for more information.)

The program above uses a zio-kafka consumer as stream source. Kafka consumers poll the broker to get new records.
Zio-kafka guarantees that all records that were received in a poll for a given partition, are in the same stream chunk.
This is ideal; partitions can be processed in parallel, and we can process as many records as are available.

By default, the zio-kafka consumer does pre-fetching. The result is that as soon as the stream processed a chunk of
records, the next chunk of records is already available. This increases throughput compared to having to wait for the
next poll.

The next operation —`map`— keeps the chunking structure intact. Nothing to improve here.

The next operation —`mapChunksZIO`— also keeps the chunking structure intact. In this operator, we produce a chunk of
records. Once they are acknowledged by the Kafka broker, we commit the offsets of the consumed records.

#### Optimizing consumer throughput

Let's zoom in on the consumer part of the example program.

Method `plainStream` produces a single stream, and chunks from different partitions are processed serially. At the
cost of making the program more complex, we can increase throughput with per-partition parallel processing. See
[consuming with more parallelism](consuming-kafka-topics-using-zio-streams.md#consuming-with-more-parallelism) for more
details. On this page, we do not explore this optimization further.

Zio-kafka's prefetching automatically adapts and is usually as good as it can be. Only for very small/large records, or for large numbers of partitions, you may need to configure it better. Please see [consumer tuning](consumer-tuning.md) to find out how.

#### Optimizing producer throughput

ℹ️ Know your domain. In cases where messages need to be produced in a certain order, the techniques in this section are
not suitable.

Let's focus on the producer part of the program, that is, the `mapChunksZIO` operation in the example above. The
operator pulls a chunk of records from upstream, produces that chunk to Kafka, awaits the acknowledgements, and then the
process repeats. All these tasks are executed sequentially.

We can optimize througput by pulling and producing the next chunk of records concurrently with waiting for the
acknowledgements.

To implement this with zio-streams, we need to split the `mapChunksZIO` operation from the example above in separate
stream operations:

1. produce the records
2. await the acknowledgements and commits offsets

We then use the `buffer` operator between those operations. Buffer allows upstream to run ahead in a separate fiber.

The following diagram compares the two approaches. The rectangles represent stream operations.

![](producer-stream-seq-and-par.svg)

And now in code. The `mapChunksZIO` operator is replaced with the following operators. In this snippet, `stream` stands for the stream that the `map` step of the example application returns:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord

val producer: Producer = ???
// The output of the `map` step in the example application
val stream: ZStream[Any, Throwable, (ProducerRecord[Int, String], Offset)] = ???

stream
  // Expose the chunking structure of the stream
  .chunks         // ZStream[_, _, Chunk[(ProducerRecord, Offset)]]

  // For every exposed chunk
  .mapZIO { chunk =>
    val records = chunk.map(_._1)
    val offsetBatch = OffsetBatch(chunk.map(_._2))
    // Produce asynchronously
    producer.produceChunkAsync(records, Serde.int, Serde.string)
      .map(await => (await, offsetBatch))
  }               // ZStream[_, _, (Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]], OffsetBatch)]

  // Allow the producer to run ahead, producing up to 4 extra chunks
  .buffer(4)      // ZStream[_, _, (Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]], OffsetBatch)]

  // Await acknowledgements for a chunk, and commit
  .mapZIO { case (await, offsetBatch) =>
    // 'await' is a ZIO, run it, and then commit offsets
    await *> offsetBatch.commit
  }               // ZStream[_, _, Unit]
```

Method `Producer#produceChunkAsync` returns a `RIO[R, Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]]]`. The outer effect completes when the records have been enqueued in the producer's internal buffer. Completion gives us the inner task, which completes when the broker acknowledges the records.

In the code we use `buffer(4)` which allows the program to produce up to 4 extra chunk of records while awaiting
acknowledgements.

##### Aside, when commits are not needed

When commits are not needed, we can simplify the code a bit:

```scala
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord

val producer: Producer = ???
val stream: ZStream[Any, Throwable, ProducerRecord[Int, String]] = ???

stream
  // Expose the chunking structure of the stream
  .chunks         // ZStream[_, _, Chunk[ProducerRecord]]
  // Every chunk gets produced asynchronously
  .mapZIO { records =>
    producer.produceChunkAsync(records, Serde.int, Serde.string)
  }               // ZStream[_, _, Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]]]
  // Allow the producer to run ahead, producing up to 4 extra chunks
  .buffer(4)      // ZStream[_, _, Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]]]
  // Await acknowledgements per chunk
  .flattenZIO     // ZStream[_, _, Chunk[RecordMetadata]]
```

#### Optimizing committing consumer offsets

Commiting offsets can become the bottleneck in highly optimized zio-kafka programs. This is because high commit rates
can put a high strain on the broker. Next up, we split off committing to its own fiber as well by using
`aggregateAsyncWithin`. See [consuming with zio-streams](consuming-kafka-topics-using-zio-streams.md) to learn how this
works.

Replace the part after `ZStream#buffer` with the following operators. In this snippet, `buffered` stands for the stream that `buffer(4)` returns:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.RecordMetadata

// The output of `buffer(4)` in the previous section
val buffered: ZStream[Any, Throwable, (Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]], OffsetBatch)] = ???

buffered
  // Await acknowledgements for a chunk
  .mapZIO { case (await, offsetBatch) =>
    // 'await' is a ZIO, run it, and then return the offsets
    await.as(offsetBatch)
  }                   // ZStream[_, _, OffsetBatch]
  .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsetBatches, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
                      // ZStream[_, _, OffsetBatch]
  .mapZIO(_.commit)   // ZStream[_, _, Unit]
```

---

## Creating a zio-kafka Consumer

Create a consumer with `Consumer.make`, passing some `ConsumerSettings`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, ConsumerSettings }

val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("group")
val consumer: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Consumer] =
  Consumer.make(consumerSettings)
```

The consumer settings are not only used for passing properties to the underlying Kafka consumer. You can also configure
zio-kafka features such as `rebalanceSafeCommits` (see [preventing duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md)), external offset
retrieval (see [offset retrieval](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md)), the pre-fetch strategy (see
[consumer tuning](consumer-tuning.md)), and silent authorization failure detection
(see [detecting authorization failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md)).

For an overview of all consumer settings and operations, see the [Consumer](consumer.md) reference page.

Notice that the consumer requires a `Scope` in the environment. When this scope closes, the consumer closes its
connection with the Kafka cluster. A scope can be created with the `ZIO.scoped` method:

```scala
ZIO.scoped {
  // make the consumer
  // use the consumer
}
// end of scope, consumer has closed connection to Kafka cluster.
```

If the consumer is provided as a layer, you can use a scoped layer (see below).

:::caution
If no explicit `Scope` is provided, the consumer uses the application's scope, and it will only close the connection
with the Kafka cluster when the application exits.
:::

### Providing a consumer as a layer

If your application uses the [ZIO service pattern](https://zio.dev/reference/service-pattern/), the consumer can
be provided as a layer. Here's an example of how to construct a consumer layer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, ConsumerSettings }

val consumerLayer: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Consumer] =
  ZLayer.scoped { // (1)
    val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings =
      ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("group")
    Consumer.make(consumerSettings)
  }
```

(1) By using `ZLayer.scoped`, the consumer is closed when the layer is no longer needed.

### Consumer settings from a layer

If you wish to create the `ConsumerSettings` and the `Consumer` from a layer, you can use `Consumer.live`. It takes
the consumer settings as a layer and produces a consumer.

The `provide` section of the main program could look like this:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, ConsumerSettings }

val consumerSettingsLayer: ULayer[ConsumerSettings] =
  ZLayer.succeed(ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("group"))

// Any program that needs a Consumer
val program: ZIO[Consumer, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Consumer](_.listTopics()).unit

val app: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  program.provide(
    consumerSettingsLayer,
    Consumer.live
  )
```

In zio-kafka 2.x, `Consumer.live` also needed a diagnostics layer. Since zio-kafka 3.0, diagnostics are set with `ConsumerSettings.withDiagnostics` instead; see [migrating to zio-kafka 3](migrating-to-zio-kafka-3.md).

---

## Detecting Authorization Failures

When a Kafka consumer's `READ` access control list (ACL) is revoked at runtime, the Apache Kafka broker stops sending
records to the consumer for the affected topic. However, the underlying Java Kafka consumer client's `poll()` method
silently returns zero records instead of throwing an error. In a standard stream setup, this causes zio-kafka's consumer
stream (such as `plainStream`, `partitionedStream` or `consumeWith`) to run indefinitely in a silent, zombie-like state, without any
indication that authorization was lost.

To detect these silent authorization losses, zio-kafka provides an _opt-in_ metadata-refresh probe. By configuring
`ConsumerSettings.withEmptyPollCountToMetaRefresh(n)`, you instruct zio-kafka to count consecutive empty polls for each
topic that is being fetched (topics whose partitions are all paused because of back-pressure are not counted). (We define 'empty poll' as a `poll()` operation resulting in zero records for a topic.) Once a topic
reaches `n` consecutive polls that return no records, the consumer issues a `committed()` request to the broker for one
of the assigned partitions of that topic. Afterwards the counter for that topic is reset, so the probe repeats every `n`
consecutive empty polls. Unlike `poll()`, calling `committed()` forces a broker round-trip that immediately
throws a `TopicAuthorizationException` if access is denied, causing the consumer to fail.

Here is how you can configure the probe in your consumer settings:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val settings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
  .withGroupId("my-group")
  .withEmptyPollCountToMetaRefresh(3) // Triggers a probe after 3 consecutive empty polls
```

:::note
The probe uses the consumer group's committed offsets, so the consumer needs a group id (`ConsumerSettings#withGroupId`); without one, the Java consumer throws an `InvalidGroupIdException` as soon as the probe runs. The `committed()` call runs inside the consumer's poll loop and can block it for up to the Kafka setting `default.api.timeout.ms`.
:::

#### When to use this feature

You should use this feature if your Kafka cluster enforces dynamic topic-level ACLs that may be revoked at runtime, and
you want your consumer application to fail-fast, generate alerts, or restart to refresh credentials when authorization
is lost. Setting the threshold to a small value (such as `3` or `5`) ensures that your application detects the
permission loss within a few poll intervals.

For low-volume topics that are naturally quiet or experience long idle periods, setting a higher threshold for
`emptyPollCountToMetaRefresh` is prudent. If the threshold is set too low, the consumer will frequently hit the empty
poll threshold and execute `committed()` queries against the broker, creating unnecessary network traffic and offset-fetch
request load on the group coordinator of your Kafka cluster.

#### When to avoid this feature

This feature is disabled by default (`None`) and should remain disabled if you do not use dynamic topic-level ACLs, as
keeping it turned off avoids all bookkeeping and potential broker overhead.

---

## Diagnostics

Diagnostics is a callback API that lets your program observe key events inside a zio-kafka consumer or producer: polls, data requests, commits, rebalances, batches of produced records and shutdown. You plug a `Diagnostics` into `ConsumerSettings` or `ProducerSettings`, and zio-kafka calls it for every event. Use it to log rebalances, count failed records, or check in a test that the consumer did what you expect.

The API consists of a callback trait, two event hierarchies and a ready-made implementation for tests:

```scala
package zio.kafka.diagnostics

trait Diagnostics[-DiagnosticEvent] {
  def emit(event: => DiagnosticEvent): UIO[Unit]
}

object SlidingDiagnostics {
  def make[DiagnosticEvent](queueSize: Int = 16): ZIO[Scope, Nothing, QueuingDiagnostics[DiagnosticEvent]]
}
```

The consumer emits subtypes of `zio.kafka.consumer.diagnostics.DiagnosticEvent`, and the producer emits subtypes of `zio.kafka.producer.ProducerEvent`.

Diagnostics and [metrics](metrics.md) complement each other. Metrics are aggregated numbers (counters, gauges, histograms) meant for dashboards and alerting. Diagnostics hands you each individual event, with full details such as the exact topic-partitions of a rebalance or the indices of the records that failed to be produced.

### How They Work Together

You create a `Diagnostics` and put it in the settings. When the consumer or producer starts, zio-kafka wraps your callback so that it runs on its own fiber:

1. Create a `Diagnostics[DiagnosticEvent]` (consumer) or a `Diagnostics[ProducerEvent]` (producer), either by implementing the trait or with `SlidingDiagnostics.make`.
2. Pass it to `ConsumerSettings#withDiagnostics` or `ProducerSettings#withDiagnostics`.
3. While running, the consumer or producer places every event in an unbounded in-memory queue.
4. A separate fiber takes the events from that queue, in order, and calls your `Diagnostics#emit` for each of them, one at a time.
5. When the consumer or producer closes, it emits a final event (`DiagnosticEvent.ConsumerFinalized` or `ProducerEvent.ProducerFinalized`), waits until your `Diagnostics` has handled every queued event including the final one. The fiber ends after the final event.

The diagram shows the flow of events from the consumer or producer to your callback:

```
 Consumer / Producer                        separate fiber
 ───────────────────                        ──────────────
   Poll, Request,      ┌──────────────────┐
   Commit.*, ...  ───> │ unbounded queue  │ ───> your Diagnostics#emit(event)
   ...Finalized   ───> │ (in memory)      │      (one event at a time, in order)
                       └──────────────────┘
```

### The Diagnostics Trait

`Diagnostics[-DiagnosticEvent]` is a single-method trait. Its `emit` method receives one event and returns a `UIO[Unit]`, so it cannot fail:

```scala
trait Diagnostics[-DiagnosticEvent] {
  def emit(event: => DiagnosticEvent): UIO[Unit]
}

object Diagnostics {
  val NoOp: Diagnostics[Any]
}
```

The type parameter is contravariant: a `Diagnostics[Any]` is a `Diagnostics[DiagnosticEvent]` and a `Diagnostics[ProducerEvent]` at the same time, so one generic implementation can serve both a consumer and a producer. The event is passed by name, so when diagnostics are turned off, zio-kafka never builds the event objects at all.

The no-op implementation is available under three names: `Diagnostics.NoOp`, `Consumer.NoDiagnostics` and `Producer.NoDiagnostics`. It is the default in both `ConsumerSettings` and `ProducerSettings`. When the settings hold the no-op implementation, zio-kafka creates neither the queue nor the fiber.

Two type aliases name the consumer and producer variants:

```scala
object Consumer {
  type ConsumerDiagnostics = zio.kafka.diagnostics.Diagnostics[DiagnosticEvent]
  val NoDiagnostics: ConsumerDiagnostics
}

object Producer {
  type ProducerDiagnostics = zio.kafka.diagnostics.Diagnostics[ProducerEvent]
  val NoDiagnostics: ProducerDiagnostics
}
```

### Configuring Diagnostics

Diagnostics are part of the consumer and producer settings. The consumer takes a `Consumer.ConsumerDiagnostics` through `ConsumerSettings#withDiagnostics`, and the producer takes a `Producer.ProducerDiagnostics` through `ProducerSettings#withDiagnostics`. `TransactionalProducerSettings` has no diagnostics setting of its own. Set the diagnostics on the `ProducerSettings` you pass to `TransactionalProducerSettings.apply`, and the transactional producer uses them.

To log every consumer and producer event at debug level with one generic `Diagnostics[Any]`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.diagnostics.Diagnostics
import zio.kafka.producer._

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val logEverything: Diagnostics[Any] = new Diagnostics[Any] {
  override def emit(event: => Any): UIO[Unit] = ZIO.logDebug(s"zio-kafka event: $event")
}

val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
    .withGroupId("my-group")
    .withDiagnostics(logEverything)

val producerSettings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers)
    .withDiagnostics(logEverything)

val transactionalProducerSettings: TransactionalProducerSettings =
  TransactionalProducerSettings(producerSettings, "my-transactional-id")
```

:::warning[Keep Up With the Events]
The queue between zio-kafka and your `Diagnostics` is unbounded. Because `Diagnostics#emit` runs on a separate fiber, a slow implementation does not slow down consuming or producing, but events pile up in memory when it cannot keep up. A busy consumer emits a `Poll` event for every poll and a `Request` event for every data request, so a slow implementation eventually leads to out-of-memory errors. Keep `Diagnostics#emit` fast: filter out the events you don't need, and hand expensive work to another fiber or a bounded queue. `SlidingDiagnostics` (below) is bounded by design.
:::

A slow `Diagnostics#emit` also delays shutdown, because closing the consumer or producer waits until every queued event has been handled.

:::warning[Never Throw or Die in Emit]
When `Diagnostics#emit` throws an exception or dies with a defect, the fiber that delivers the events stops. From then on, every attempt of the consumer or producer to emit an event dies with that same defect, so the problem surfaces instead of events piling up in memory unnoticed. Consumer streams fail with the defect, and so do commits. New produce calls die, and a produce call that is already waiting for its acknowledgement may never complete. Events emitted between the defect and the moment zio-kafka notices it are lost. Keep the body of `Diagnostics#emit` inside a ZIO effect (for example `ZIO.suspend { ... }`) and recover from every failure and defect with `catchAllCause`.
:::

### Consumer Events

The consumer emits subtypes of the sealed trait `zio.kafka.consumer.diagnostics.DiagnosticEvent`. Each event carries the Kafka `TopicPartition`s it is about:

```scala
sealed trait DiagnosticEvent

object DiagnosticEvent {
  final case class Poll(
    tpRequested: Set[TopicPartition],
    tpWithData: Set[TopicPartition],
    tpWithoutData: Set[TopicPartition]
  ) extends DiagnosticEvent

  final case class Request(partition: TopicPartition) extends DiagnosticEvent

  sealed trait Commit extends DiagnosticEvent
  object Commit {
    final case class Started(offsets: Map[TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata])                   extends Commit
    final case class Success(offsets: Map[TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata])                   extends Commit
    final case class Failure(offsets: Map[TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata], cause: Throwable) extends Commit
  }

  final case class Rebalance(
    revoked: Set[TopicPartition],
    assigned: Set[TopicPartition],
    lost: Set[TopicPartition],
    ended: Set[TopicPartition]
  ) extends DiagnosticEvent

  case object SubscriptionFinalized extends DiagnosticEvent
  case object RunloopFinalized      extends DiagnosticEvent
  case object ConsumerFinalized     extends DiagnosticEvent
}
```

The events fall into four groups: fetching data, committing, rebalancing and shutdown.

#### Fetching Data

Partition streams ask the consumer for records, and the consumer polls the Kafka brokers to fulfill those requests. Two events describe this:

| Event                | Emitted when                                                                                                |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Request(partition)` | A partition stream requests more records, which happens each time the stream pulls and its buffer is empty. |
| `Poll(...)`          | After every poll of the underlying Kafka consumer.                                                          |

`Poll` describes the outcome of one poll. `tpRequested` holds the partitions whose streams had an outstanding request at the time of the poll. `tpWithData` holds the partitions for which the poll returned records, which can include partitions that did not request data (zio-kafka pre-fetches). `tpWithoutData` holds the requested partitions for which the poll returned nothing, that is `tpRequested -- tpWithData`.

#### Committing

Committing produces a `Started` event when a commit is requested, and a `Success` or a `Failure` event when it completes. `Started` is emitted just after the commit is queued, so occasionally it arrives after its own `Success` or `Failure`:

| Event                            | Emitted when                                                                   |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Commit.Started(offsets)`        | A commit is requested, for example by `Offset#commit` or `OffsetBatch#commit`. |
| `Commit.Success(offsets)`        | The Kafka broker confirmed a commit.                                           |
| `Commit.Failure(offsets, cause)` | A commit to the Kafka broker failed.                                           |

All offsets in these events are the committed *next* offsets, see [Offsets and Committing](offsets-and-committing.md). A `Started` event is emitted for every commit attempt, with the offsets of that attempt. Each retry of `Offset#commitOrRetry` or `OffsetBatch#commitOrRetry` (which `Consumer.consumeWith` uses) is a new attempt. The consumer combines commits that are waiting to be sent into a single Kafka commit, so one `Success` or `Failure` event can cover several `Started` events. Its `offsets` field holds the combined offsets.

Some commits produce no `Success` or `Failure` event:

- When the broker rejects a commit because a rebalance is in progress, there is no event for the rejection. The consumer silently retries the commit later, without a new `Started` event, and the outcome of that retry produces the `Success` or `Failure` event.
- When a commit takes longer than the commit timeout, the caller fails with `Consumer.CommitTimeout`, but there is no event for the timeout itself.
- Commits registered with `Consumer#registerExternalCommits` and offsets committed by a `TransactionalProducer` do not emit commit events at all.

#### Rebalancing

The `Rebalance` event is emitted after the consumer has handled a poll during which Kafka changed the partition assignment. Its fields hold the partitions that were revoked, newly assigned, and lost, plus the partitions whose streams were ended. A partition stream ends when its partition is revoked or lost, so `ended` lists the revoked and lost partitions that had a running stream.

Manual subscriptions (`Subscription.manual`) assign partitions directly, without the Kafka group protocol, so they never produce `Rebalance` events.

#### Shutdown

Three events mark the end of the consumer's resources. When a consumer shuts down, they arrive in this order:

1. `SubscriptionFinalized` is emitted when the scope of a subscription ends, for example when a stream created by `Consumer#plainStream` completes. It is emitted once for every subscription.
2. `RunloopFinalized` is emitted when the consumer's internal run loop shuts down. The run loop starts when it is first needed, usually with the first subscription, and stops when the consumer closes. A consumer whose run loop never started does not emit this event.
3. `ConsumerFinalized` is emitted when the consumer closes. It is always the last event.

### Producer Events

The producer emits subtypes of the sealed trait `zio.kafka.producer.ProducerEvent`. The producer always handles records in batches, and a single record is a batch of one, so every event is about a batch:

```scala
sealed trait ProducerEvent

object ProducerEvent {
  val NoPartition = -1
  val NoValue     = -1

  final case class ProducedRecord(topic: String, partition: Int, size: Int)

  final case class RecordsOffered(batchId: Long, records: Chunk[ProducedRecord]) extends ProducerEvent

  final case class RecordsSent(batchId: Long, records: Chunk[ProducedRecord], failed: Set[Int]) extends ProducerEvent

  case object ProducerFinalized extends ProducerEvent
}
```

The events do not contain the records themselves. Each record is summarized by a `ProducedRecord` that holds the topic, the partition from the `ProducerRecord`, and the size of the serialized value in bytes. For a record without a value (a tombstone), `size` is `ProducerEvent.NoValue` (`-1`). The partition is the one set on the `ProducerRecord`, not the partition the Kafka partitioner picks. For records that leave the partition choice to the partitioner, it is `ProducerEvent.NoPartition` (`-1`), so you can tell them apart from records sent to partition `0`.

The producer emits three kinds of events:

| Event                                   | Emitted when                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `RecordsOffered(batchId, records)`      | A batch of records is about to be offered to the producer's internal send queue. The offer can still wait for space, or never happen if the produce call is interrupted. |
| `RecordsSent(batchId, records, failed)` | Sending all records of the batch completed, successfully or not.                                                                                                         |
| `ProducerFinalized`                     | The producer closes. It is always the last event.                                                                                                                        |

The moment of `RecordsSent` depends on the `acks` producer configuration. With `acks=0` it is emitted as soon as all records are added to the socket buffer, with any other value it is emitted after the broker acknowledged the records. When the producer retries records after an authentication or authorization error (see `ProducerSettings#withAuthErrorRetrySchedule`), `RecordsSent` is emitted once, after the last attempt.

The `failed` field of `RecordsSent` holds the indices (into `records`) of the records that failed, together with the records that were not sent because an earlier record failed. When every record succeeded, `failed` is empty.

The `batchId` links the events of one batch. It starts at `0` and increases by one for every batch, separately for each producer. The `RecordsOffered` and `RecordsSent` events of the same batch have the same `batchId` and the same `records`. Batches are sent concurrently, so the `RecordsSent` events of different batches can arrive in any order, and interleaved with the `RecordsOffered` events of other batches. The `RecordsOffered` event of a batch always arrives before its own `RecordsSent` event, When several fibers produce concurrently, the order of the `RecordsOffered` events (and of the `batchId`s) can differ from the order in which the batches enter the send queue. An empty batch produces no events.

### Writing Your Own Diagnostics

To write your own diagnostics, implement `Diagnostics#emit` and pattern match on the events you are interested in. Return `ZIO.unit` for the others, so that the queue drains quickly.

#### Logging Consumer Rebalances

The `Rebalance` event shows exactly which partitions moved, which helps when you investigate duplicate processing or lag after a deployment. To log every rebalance of a consumer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.consumer.diagnostics.DiagnosticEvent
import zio.kafka.diagnostics.Diagnostics

val logRebalances: Consumer.ConsumerDiagnostics = new Diagnostics[DiagnosticEvent] {
  override def emit(event: => DiagnosticEvent): UIO[Unit] =
    event match {
      case DiagnosticEvent.Rebalance(revoked, assigned, lost, ended) =>
        ZIO.logInfo(
          s"Rebalance: assigned=${assigned.mkString(",")} revoked=${revoked.mkString(",")} " +
            s"lost=${lost.mkString(",")} ended=${ended.mkString(",")}"
        )
      case DiagnosticEvent.Commit.Failure(offsets, cause) =>
        ZIO.logWarningCause(s"Commit of $offsets failed", Cause.fail(cause))
      case _ =>
        ZIO.unit
    }
}

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("my-group")
    .withDiagnostics(logRebalances)
```

The example also logs failed commits, because they often accompany a rebalance.

#### Counting Failed Producer Records

The `failed` field of `RecordsSent` tells you how many records of a batch were not written. To keep a running count of failed records in a `Ref` that the rest of the program can read:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.diagnostics.Diagnostics
import zio.kafka.producer._

def countFailures(failedRecords: Ref[Long]): Producer.ProducerDiagnostics =
  new Diagnostics[ProducerEvent] {
    override def emit(event: => ProducerEvent): UIO[Unit] =
      event match {
        case ProducerEvent.RecordsSent(_, _, failed) if failed.nonEmpty =>
          failedRecords.update(_ + failed.size)
        case _ =>
          ZIO.unit
      }
  }

val producerWithFailureCount: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, (Producer, Ref[Long])] =
  for {
    failedRecords <- Ref.make(0L)
    settings = ProducerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withDiagnostics(countFailures(failedRecords))
    producer <- Producer.make(settings)
  } yield (producer, failedRecords)
```

To feed such a count into your monitoring system, increment a ZIO metric instead of a `Ref`.

### SlidingDiagnostics

`SlidingDiagnostics.make` creates a `Diagnostics` that stores the events in a sliding queue of `queueSize` elements (default `16`). When the queue is full, the oldest event is dropped to make room for the new one, so memory use stays bounded no matter how many events arrive. This makes it a good fit for tests, and for any other situation where a slow consumer of the events must not cause high memory use:

```scala
object SlidingDiagnostics {
  def make[DiagnosticEvent](queueSize: Int = 16): ZIO[Scope, Nothing, QueuingDiagnostics[DiagnosticEvent]]
}

final case class QueuingDiagnostics[DiagnosticEvent] private[diagnostics] (queue: Queue[DiagnosticEvent])
  extends Diagnostics[DiagnosticEvent]
```

The result is a `QueuingDiagnostics`, which exposes the underlying ZIO `Queue` as `queue`. Read the collected events from it, for example with `Queue#takeAll`. The queue is shut down when the `Scope` of `SlidingDiagnostics.make` closes, so read the events before that.

In a test, create the diagnostics in an outer scope, run the consumer in an inner scope, and inspect the events once the consumer has closed. To collect the rebalances a consumer went through:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.consumer.diagnostics.DiagnosticEvent
import zio.kafka.diagnostics.SlidingDiagnostics
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val rebalances: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Chunk[DiagnosticEvent.Rebalance]] =
  for {
    diagnostics <- SlidingDiagnostics.make[DiagnosticEvent](queueSize = 1000)
    settings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
                 .withGroupId("test-group")
                 .withDiagnostics(diagnostics)
    _ <- ZIO.scoped {
           Consumer.make(settings).flatMap { consumer =>
             consumer
               .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
               .take(10)
               .runDrain
           }
         }
    events <- diagnostics.queue.takeAll
  } yield events.collect { case rebalance: DiagnosticEvent.Rebalance => rebalance }
```

Because the consumer has closed when `Queue#takeAll` runs, `events` ends with `DiagnosticEvent.ConsumerFinalized`. Choose a `queueSize` that is large enough for the events you want to inspect: the consumer also emits `Poll` and `Request` events, and those push older events out of a small queue.

## Getting Started with ZIO Kafka

This page gets you from an empty sbt project to a running program that produces records to Kafka and consumes them again. We add the zio-kafka dependencies, start a single Kafka broker on our machine with Docker, and then walk through a small application that runs a producer and a consumer side by side.

### Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

- A JDK, version 17 or later (zio-kafka is tested on Java 17, 21 and 25).
- [sbt](https://www.scala-sbt.org), to build and run the example.
- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with Docker Compose, to run a local Kafka broker.

### Adding the Dependencies

Zio-kafka is published for Scala 2.13 and Scala 3. Add the library, and the test kit for your tests, to your `build.sbt` file:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka"         % "4.2.0"
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka-testkit" % "4.2.0" % Test
```

The `zio-kafka` artifact brings in ZIO, zio-streams and the Apache Kafka Java client, so you don't need to add them separately. The `zio-kafka-testkit` artifact provides an embedded Kafka broker and helpers for tests, see [Writing Tests](writing-tests.md).

Two situations need extra build settings: using the test kit on Scala 3, and trying out unreleased versions.

#### Using the Test Kit With Scala 3

The test kit depends on `embedded-kafka`, which pulls in the Scala 2.13 build of `scala-collection-compat`. On Scala 3 this clashes with the Scala 3 build of the same library, and sbt fails with "Modules were resolved with conflicting cross-version suffixes". If you use zio-kafka 3.x or later, Scala 3, `zio-kafka-testkit` and `embedded-kafka`, exclude the Scala 2.13 artifact in your `build.sbt` file:

```scala
excludeDependencies += "org.scala-lang.modules" % "scala-collection-compat_2.13"
```

#### Using Snapshot Versions

Snapshots of zio-kafka are published to Sonatype's Central snapshot repository at https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/. The repository's [metadata file for zio-kafka](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-kafka_3/maven-metadata.xml) lists the available versions. To let sbt resolve snapshot versions, add the repository as a resolver:

```scala
resolvers += "Sonatype Central Snapshots" at "https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/"
```

### Running a Local Kafka Broker

Before we can produce or consume anything, we need a running Kafka broker. Save the following file as `docker-compose.yml`. It starts a single Kafka node in KRaft mode (Kafka's built-in cluster coordination, so no ZooKeeper is needed) that acts as both broker and controller:

```yaml
services:
  broker:
    image: apache/kafka:4.4.0
    container_name: broker
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://broker:29092,CONTROLLER://broker:29093,PLAINTEXT_HOST://0.0.0.0:9092
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://broker:29092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT_HOST:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@broker:29093
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: PLAINTEXT
```

The `PLAINTEXT_HOST` listener is published on port 9092 of your machine, so programs running outside Docker connect to `localhost:9092`. The replication factors are set to 1 because there is only one broker.

Start the broker in the background:

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

When you are done, `docker compose down` stops and removes the container.

### Writing a Producer and a Consumer

The following application, one of the examples in the zio-kafka repository, produces a record with a random number every two seconds, and at the same time consumes those records, prints them and commits their offsets:

```scala title="zio-kafka-example/src/main/scala/zio/kafka/example/ReadmeExample.scala"
// format: off
// Manually formatted for the small width of readme
package zio.kafka.example

import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer.{ Producer, ProducerSettings }
import zio.kafka.serde._
import zio.stream.ZStream

object ReadmeExample extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val producerRun: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
    ZIO.scoped {
      for {
        producer <-
          Producer.make(
            ProducerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
          )
        _ <- ZStream
          .fromSchedule(Schedule.fixed(2.seconds))
          .mapZIO(_ => Random.nextIntBetween(0, Int.MaxValue))
          .mapZIO { random =>
            producer.produce[Any, Long, String](
              topic = "random-topic",
              key = (random % 4).toLong,
              value = random.toString,
              keySerializer = Serde.long,
              valueSerializer = Serde.string
            )
          }
          .runDrain
      } yield ()
    }

  private val consumerRun: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
    ZIO.scoped {
      for {
        consumer <-
          Consumer.make(
            ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
              .withGroupId("group")
          )
        _ <- consumer
          .plainStream(Subscription.topics("random-topic"), Serde.long, Serde.string)
          .tap(r => Console.printLine(r.value))
          .map(_.offset)
          .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
          .mapZIO(_.commit)
          .runDrain
      } yield ()
    }

  override def run: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
    ZIO.raceFirst(producerRun, List(consumerRun))
}
```

Run it with `sbt run`. After a few seconds, the consumer prints a new random number every two seconds. Stop the program with `Ctrl+C`.

### How the Example Works

The application has two independent parts, a producer and a consumer, that both connect to the broker at `localhost:9092`.

#### The Producer

`Producer.make` creates a `Producer` from a `ProducerSettings`. It needs a `Scope`: when the scope closes, the producer is closed and disconnects from Kafka. `ZIO.scoped` provides that scope and closes it when `producerRun` ends.

`ZStream.fromSchedule` emits an element every two seconds. For each element, we draw a random number and call `Producer#produce` to send a record to the `random-topic` topic. Kafka stores keys and values as bytes, so `Producer#produce` takes a serializer for the key and one for the value. Here the key is a `Long` (the random number modulo 4) and the value is a `String`, so we use the built-in `Serde.long` and `Serde.string`. `Producer#produce` completes when the broker has acknowledged the record. The broker creates the `random-topic` topic automatically the first time a record is sent to it, because Kafka brokers allow automatic topic creation by default.

#### The Consumer

`Consumer.make` creates a `Consumer` from a `ConsumerSettings`. Like the producer, it lives as long as its `Scope`. `ConsumerSettings#withGroupId` sets the consumer group: consumers in the same group share the partitions of a topic, and Kafka remembers per group which records were already processed.

`Consumer#plainStream` subscribes to the `random-topic` topic and returns a `ZStream` of `CommittableRecord`s, with keys and values deserialized by `Serde.long` and `Serde.string`. For each record we print the value, then keep only its offset (`CommittableRecord#offset`).

Committing an offset tells Kafka that the group has processed the record, so it is not delivered to this group again after a restart. Committing every record separately is slow, so `ZStream#aggregateAsyncWithin` with the `Consumer.collectOffsets` sink merges the offsets into an `OffsetBatch` every 100 milliseconds, and `OffsetBatch#commit` commits each batch in one call.

By default a new consumer group starts reading at the end of the topic. Records produced before the consumer joined are skipped, but because the producer keeps producing, new records soon arrive. See [Partition Assignment and Offset Retrieval](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md) to start from the beginning of the topic instead.

:::note
`ZStream#tap` is used here to keep the example short. It breaks the chunking structure of the stream and lowers throughput. See [Avoiding Chunk Breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md) for alternatives.
:::

#### Running Both

`ZIO.raceFirst` runs `producerRun` and `consumerRun` concurrently and completes as soon as one of them completes, interrupting the other. Both streams run until they are interrupted or fail, so the application runs until you stop it or one side fails.

- The [tutorial](tutorial.md), a longer guided tour of producing and consuming with ZIO workflows, zio-streams and JSON data.

- [Producer](producer.md), for all the ways to produce records.

- [Writing Tests](writing-tests.md), for testing your zio-kafka code with the embedded Kafka broker from the test kit.

## Introduction to ZIO Kafka

[ZIO Kafka](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka) is a Kafka client for ZIO. It provides a purely functional, streams-based interface to the Kafka
client and integrates effortlessly with ZIO and zio-streams. Often zio-kafka programs have a _higher_ throughput than
programs that use the Java Kafka client directly (see section [Performance](#performance) below).

[![Production Ready](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Production%20Ready-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-kafka_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-kafka_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13) [![ZIO Kafka](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-kafka?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka) [![Scala Steward badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/Scala_Steward-helping-blue.svg?style=flat&logo=data:image/png;base64,)](https://scala-steward.org)

### Introduction

Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform that acts as a distributed publish-subscribe messaging system. It enables us to build distributed streaming data pipelines and event-driven applications.

Kafka has a mature Java client for producing and consuming events, but it has a low-level API. Zio-kafka is a ZIO native client for Apache Kafka. It has a high-level streaming API on top of the Java client. So we can produce and consume events using the declarative concurrency model of zio-streams. In addition, zio-kafka supports an even higher level API where you only write the processing part and the rest is handled by zio-kafka.

### Features

- Exposes the Java Kafka consumer, producer and admin clients with a ZIO based interface.
- Consuming (see [Consumer](consumer.md)):
  - 2 APIs: streaming and ZIO workflow based
  - supports [custom deserialization](serialization-and-deserialization.md)
  - can process each partition in parallel for highest throughput
  - allows batched processing for highest throughput
  - configurable per partition pre-fetching (with back-pressure)
  - the only async Kafka consumer [without duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md) after a rebalance (as far as we know)
  - very [configurable](consumer-tuning.md)
  - automatic or manual [starting offset](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md)
  - supports [external commits](offsets-and-committing.md)
  - retries after authentication/authorization errors
  - detects [silent authorization failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md) when a READ ACL is revoked at runtime
  - exposes [metrics](metrics.md)
  - [diagnostics](diagnostics.md) API
- Producing (see [Producer](producer.md)):
  - 2 APIs: streaming and ZIO workflow based
  - supports [custom serialization](serialization-and-deserialization.md)
  - allows for batches for highest throughput
  - optionally await broker acknowledgements
  - supports [transactions](transactions.md)
  - optional retries after authentication/authorization errors
  - exposes [metrics](metrics.md)
  - [diagnostics](diagnostics.md) API
- [Admin API](admin-client.md):
  - exposes most of the admin client methods with a ZIO based interface
  - safer than the wrapped java client by waiting for the operation to be done
- Proper errors when broker expects SSL (no [OOM crashes](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-4090)), see [Security](security.md)
- [Test kit](writing-tests.md) with embedded kafka broker
- Well documented
- Community support via [Discord](https://discord.com/channels/629491597070827530/629497941719121960)
- Commercial support via [Ziverge](https://www.ziverge.com)

### Installation

To use zio-kafka, add the following lines to your `build.sbt` file:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka"         % "4.2.0"
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka-testkit" % "4.2.0" % Test
```

The [Getting Started](getting-started.md) page walks through running a local Kafka broker and writing a first producer and consumer. For a longer tour of the different ways you can use zio-kafka, read the [zio-kafka tutorial](tutorial.md).

### Performance

Often, _zio-kafka programs consume with a higher throughput_ than programs that use the java-kafka client directly.
Read on for the details.

Zio-kafka makes it easy to process partitions in parallel: `Consumer.consumeWith` does so by default, and with the streaming API you can use `Consumer#partitionedStream` with `ZStream#flatMapPar`. The default java-kafka client does not provide parallel processing. Of course, there is some overhead in buffering records and distributing them to the fibers that need them. On 2024-11-23, we estimated that zio-kafka consumes faster than the java-kafka client when processing takes more than ~1.2ms per 1000 records. The precise time depends on many factors. Please see [this article](https://day-to-day-stuff.blogspot.com/2024/12/zio-kafka-faster-than-java-kafka.html) for more details.

If you do not care for the convenient ZStream based API that zio-kafka brings, and latency is of absolute importance,
using the java based Kafka client directly is still the better choice.

* [Benchmarks and Flame graphs](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka/blob/master/zio-kafka-bench/README.md)
