## Metrics Observers

Metrics observers are the extension point that decides where the zio-kafka consumer and producer metrics go. While it runs, the consumer reports every poll, commit, rebalance and a periodic snapshot of its internal queues to a `ConsumerMetricsObserver`. The producer reports every completed produce call and the state of its send queue to a `ProducerMetricsObserver`. By default, both observers record the measurements as ZIO metrics, so any ZIO metrics backend can export them. When you implement your own observer, you can send the same measurements to another metrics library, add logging, change histogram boundaries, or turn metrics off.

The module consists of two observer traits, their default implementations, and two case classes that describe every metric with a `MetricInfo`:

```scala
// package zio.kafka.consumer.metrics
trait ConsumerMetricsObserver { /* 6 callbacks, see below */ }
final class ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver(consumerMetrics: ConsumerMetrics, metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel])
    extends ConsumerMetricsObserver
final case class ConsumerMetrics(pollCounter: MetricInfo.Counter = ???, /* 23 more descriptors */)

// package zio.kafka.producer.metrics
trait ProducerMetricsObserver { /* 4 callbacks, see below */ }
final class ZioMetricsProducerMetricsObserver(producerMetrics: ProducerMetrics, metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel])
    extends ProducerMetricsObserver
final case class ProducerMetrics(produceCallsCounter: MetricInfo.Counter = ???, /* 6 more descriptors */)

// package zio.kafka.metrics
sealed trait MetricInfo { def name: String; def description: String }
```

The metric names, their meaning and how to read them on a dashboard are on the [Metrics](metrics.md) page. This page covers the API behind them: when each callback runs, what it receives, and how to install your own observer.

:::warning[Unstable API]
The scaladoc of `ConsumerMetricsObserver`, `ProducerMetricsObserver`, `ConsumerMetrics`, `ProducerMetrics` and `MetricInfo` marks them as an UNSTABLE API: they may change in an incompatible way in any zio-kafka version, without notice. Expect to adapt a custom observer when you upgrade.
:::

### How They Work Together

When a consumer or producer starts, it picks one observer and calls it from its own code paths for the rest of its life:

1. You optionally pass an observer with `ConsumerSettings#withMetricsObserver` or `ProducerSettings#withMetricsObserver`.
2. When the consumer or producer is created, it uses that observer. When none is set, it creates a `ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver` or `ZioMetricsProducerMetricsObserver` with the default descriptors and the labels from `withMetricsLabels`.
3. The consumer calls the observer after every poll, commit, aggregated commit and rebalance, and on a schedule for the runloop snapshot. The producer calls it when a produce call completes, when the send fiber takes a batch from the send queue, after authorization failures, and every 10 seconds for the send queue size.
4. The default observers turn each `MetricInfo` of `ConsumerMetrics` or `ProducerMetrics` into a ZIO metric (`Metric.counter`, `Metric.gauge` or `Metric.histogram`), tagged with the labels, and update it on every callback.

The following diagram shows where the callbacks come from:

```
ConsumerSettings#metricsObserver
  Some(observer) -> observer
  None           -> new ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver(ConsumerMetrics(), metricLabels)
        │
        ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐     observePoll              after every poll
│  ConsumerMetricsObserver  │ ◄── observePollAuthError     each poll that fails with an auth error
└───────────────────────────┘     observeRebalance         after a poll during which a rebalance ran
                                  observeCommit            each successful Offset#commit
                                  observeAggregatedCommit  each successful commit to the broker
                                  observeRunloopMetrics    on runloopMetricsSchedule

ProducerSettings#metricsObserver
  Some(observer) -> observer
  None           -> new ZioMetricsProducerMetricsObserver(ProducerMetrics(), metricLabels)
        │
        ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐     observeProduce           each fully acknowledged produce call
│  ProducerMetricsObserver  │ ◄── observeSendAuthError     each send with auth errors
└───────────────────────────┘     observeSendQueueTake     each batch the send fiber takes
                                  observeSendQueueSize     every 10 seconds
```

Every callback returns `UIO[Unit]`. Most callbacks run inside the consumer's or producer's own processing (the poll loop, commit handling, or a produce call), so the scaladoc of both traits asks them to return quickly. `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observeRunloopMetrics` and `ProducerMetricsObserver#observeSendQueueSize` are the exception: they run on their own fibers, on a schedule.

### Installing an Observer

Each settings class has a `metricsObserver: Option[...]` field, `None` by default, and a method that sets it:

```scala
final case class ConsumerSettings(/* ... */) {
  def withMetricsLabels(metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel]): ConsumerSettings
  def withMetricsObserver(observer: ConsumerMetricsObserver): ConsumerSettings
  def withRunloopMetricsSchedule(runloopMetricsSchedule: Schedule[Any, Unit, Long]): ConsumerSettings
}

final case class ProducerSettings(/* ... */) {
  def withMetricsLabels(metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel]): ProducerSettings
  def withMetricsObserver(observer: ProducerMetricsObserver): ProducerSettings
}
```

`withMetricsLabels` only configures the default observer. As soon as an observer is set, the consumer and producer use it as is, and the labels from `withMetricsLabels` are ignored. When you install a `ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver` or `ZioMetricsProducerMetricsObserver` yourself, pass the labels to its constructor instead.

The two settings below record the consumer metrics with the same `group-id` label, the first through the settings and the second through the constructor of the default observer:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings
import zio.kafka.consumer.metrics.{ ConsumerMetrics, ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver }
import zio.metrics.MetricLabel

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")
val labels           = Set(MetricLabel("group-id", "orders-service"))

// The default observer, created by the consumer, gets the labels from the settings
val withLabels: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withMetricsLabels(labels)

// An explicit observer: labels set with withMetricsLabels would be ignored
val withObserver: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withMetricsObserver(new ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver(ConsumerMetrics(), labels))
```

When no observer is set, every consumer and producer creates its own default observer when it starts, in `Consumer.make`, `Producer.make` and the other constructors, including those of `TransactionalProducer`. An observer is just a value, so you can share one instance between several consumers; they then report into the same metrics. When an application runs several consumers or producers with the default observer, give each one distinct labels, or their measurements land in the same ZIO metrics.

### ConsumerMetricsObserver

`ConsumerMetricsObserver` has six callbacks, each called from a different place in the consumer:

```scala
trait ConsumerMetricsObserver {
  def observePoll(resumedCount: Int, pausedCount: Int, latency: Duration, pollSize: Int): UIO[Unit]
  def observeCommit(latency: Duration): UIO[Unit]
  def observeAggregatedCommit(latency: Duration, commitSize: Long): UIO[Unit]
  def observeRebalance(currentlyAssignedCount: Int, assignedCount: Int, revokedCount: Int, lostCount: Int): UIO[Unit]
  def observeRunloopMetrics(state: ConsumerMetricsObserver.ConsumerState): UIO[Unit]
  def observePollAuthError: UIO[Unit]
}
```

The sections below describe when the consumer calls each one. See the [Consumer](consumer.md) page for the runloop, partition streams and commits these callbacks report on.

#### Polling

The runloop calls `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observePoll` once after every successful call to the Java consumer's `poll`. Before polling, the runloop asks the fetch strategy which partitions to fetch: it resumes those and pauses the other assigned partitions, which applies backpressure to slow streams. The arguments are:

- `resumedCount` is the number of assigned partitions resumed for this poll.
- `pausedCount` is the number of assigned partitions paused for this poll.
- `latency` is the duration of the poll, including any retries after authentication or authorization errors.
- `pollSize` is the number of records the poll returned.

`ConsumerMetricsObserver#observePollAuthError` takes no arguments. The consumer calls it every time a poll fails with an `AuthorizationException` or `AuthenticationException`, while it decides whether to retry the poll according to `ConsumerSettings#authErrorRetrySchedule` (by default 5 retries, 500 ms apart). Only errors thrown by `poll` itself count; see [Detecting Authorization Failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md) for failures that `poll` does not report.

#### Committing

Committing produces two kinds of measurements: one per commit request and one per commit sent to the broker.

The consumer calls `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observeCommit` once for every commit request made through the zio-kafka API, such as `Offset#commit` or `OffsetBatch#commit`, when the request completes successfully. `latency` runs from the moment the request is queued until the broker acknowledges it. A commit that fails or exceeds `ConsumerSettings#commitTimeout` is not observed, and neither are offsets that a `TransactionalProducer` commits as part of a transaction.

In each runloop cycle, the consumer merges all queued commit requests into one aggregated commit and sends it to the broker with the Java consumer's `commitAsync`. When the broker acknowledges that commit, the consumer calls `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observeAggregatedCommit`, provided the aggregated commit contained at least one request:

- `latency` runs from the `commitAsync` call until the acknowledgement arrives.
- `commitSize` is the sum, over all partitions in the commit, of how far the committed offset moved since the previous commit of this consumer. A partition this consumer has not committed to before counts as 0, so the value is an approximation of the number of committed records.

#### Rebalancing

When the rebalance listener runs during a poll, the runloop updates its partition streams after that poll and then calls `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observeRebalance` once. When the listener runs more than once during the same poll, the consumer merges those events into one call. The arguments are:

- `currentlyAssignedCount` is the number of partitions assigned to the consumer after the rebalance.
- `assignedCount` is the number of newly assigned partitions.
- `revokedCount` is the number of revoked partitions.
- `lostCount` is the number of lost partitions.

#### Sampling Runloop State

The other callbacks report events, but `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observeRunloopMetrics` reports a snapshot. When the consumer starts, it forks a fiber that takes the snapshot immediately and then repeats it according to `ConsumerSettings#runloopMetricsSchedule`, `Schedule.fixed(500.millis)` by default. The snapshot is a `ConsumerState`:

```scala
object ConsumerMetricsObserver {
  final case class ConsumerState(
    pendingRequestCount: Int,
    assignedPartitionCount: Int,
    perPartitionQueueSizes: Chunk[Int],
    perPartitionOutstandingPolls: Chunk[Int],
    isSubscribed: Boolean,
    commandQueueSize: Int,
    commitQueueSize: Int,
    pendingCommitCount: Int
  ) {
    val totalQueueSize: Int = perPartitionQueueSizes.sum
  }
}
```

The pending requests, the partition streams and the subscription come from the runloop state as of its most recent cycle; the queue sizes and commit counts are read when the snapshot is taken. The field names mostly speak for themselves, but a few need a word of explanation: `pendingRequestCount` is the number of partition streams that ran out of records and requested more, `perPartitionOutstandingPolls` counts, per partition stream, the polls during which records idled in its queue, `commitQueueSize` is the number of commit requests waiting to be merged into the next aggregated commit, and `pendingCommitCount` is the number of commits sent to the broker and awaiting completion.

To sample the runloop less often, for example every 5 seconds, change the schedule in the consumer settings:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withRunloopMetricsSchedule(Schedule.fixed(5.seconds))
```

### ProducerMetricsObserver

`ProducerMetricsObserver` has four callbacks:

```scala
trait ProducerMetricsObserver {
  def observeProduce(latency: Duration, batchSize: Int): UIO[Unit]
  def observeSendQueueSize(size: Int): UIO[Unit]
  def observeSendQueueTake(latency: Duration): UIO[Unit]
  def observeSendAuthError(errorCount: Int): UIO[Unit]
}
```

To read them, it helps to know how the producer works (see [Producer](producer.md)): every produce call serializes its records and offers them as one batch to an internal send queue; a background fiber takes the batches from the queue and sends their records to Kafka. `Producer` and `TransactionalProducer` call the observer in the same places.

The producer calls `ProducerMetricsObserver#observeProduce` once per produce call, after the broker has acknowledged every record of the call, including records sent again after an authorization error. `latency` runs from the moment the producer starts to enqueue the serialized batch until the last acknowledgement. `batchSize` is 1 for `Producer#produce` and `Producer#produceAsync`, and the number of records for the chunk variants such as `Producer#produceChunk`, `Producer#produceChunkAsync` and `Producer#produceChunkAsyncWithFailures`. A produce call with at least one failed record is not observed.

`ProducerMetricsObserver#observeSendQueueSize` receives the number of batches (produce calls, not records) in the send queue. A background fiber samples it every 10 seconds; this interval is not configurable. The capacity of the queue is set with `ProducerSettings#withSendBufferSize`.

`ProducerMetricsObserver#observeSendQueueTake` runs each time the send fiber takes a batch from the queue. `latency` is the time the batch spent in the queue, including waiting for queue capacity.

`ProducerMetricsObserver#observeSendAuthError` runs when a send attempt gets authentication or authorization errors. For a single-record produce call (`Producer#produce`, `Producer#produceAsync`), it runs with `errorCount` 1 each time the record fails with such an error. For a chunk produce call (`Producer#produceChunk` and its variants, including `Producer#produceAll`), it runs when some records fail with such an error and no record fails with another error; `errorCount` is the number of records that failed with an authentication or authorization error. In both cases the producer calls it before it asks `ProducerSettings#authErrorRetrySchedule` whether to retry, so it also runs with the default schedule, `Schedule.stop`, which never retries.

### The Default Observers

`ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver` and `ZioMetricsProducerMetricsObserver` record every callback as ZIO metrics. Each has a primary constructor that takes the descriptors and the labels, and an auxiliary constructor that takes only the labels and uses the default descriptors:

```scala
final class ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver(consumerMetrics: ConsumerMetrics, metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel])
    extends ConsumerMetricsObserver {
  def this(metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel]) = this(ConsumerMetrics(), metricLabels)
}

final class ZioMetricsProducerMetricsObserver(producerMetrics: ProducerMetrics, metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel])
    extends ProducerMetricsObserver {
  def this(metricLabels: Set[MetricLabel]) = this(ProducerMetrics(), metricLabels)
}
```

The default observers convert every descriptor into a ZIO metric with the same name and description, tagged with `metricLabels`:

- A `MetricInfo.Counter` becomes a `Metric.counter` that counts in `Long`.
- A `MetricInfo.Gauge[Int]` becomes a `Metric.gauge`; the `Int` value is converted to `Double`.
- A `MetricInfo.Histogram[Duration]` becomes a `Metric.histogram` with the descriptor's boundaries, and records the duration in seconds.
- A `MetricInfo.Histogram[Int]` or `MetricInfo.Histogram[Long]` becomes a `Metric.histogram` with the descriptor's boundaries.

Each callback updates the descriptors named after it, for example `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observePoll` updates `pollCounter`, `pollLatencyHistogram` and the other poll descriptors, and `ProducerMetricsObserver#observeProduce` updates the `produce*` descriptors. Counters such as `partitionsAssignedCounter`, `produceRecordsCounter` (by `batchSize`) and `sendAuthErrorCounter` (by `errorCount`) grow by the matching count, and the gauges are set to the latest value. `ConsumerMetricsObserver#observeRunloopMetrics` adds one observation per partition stream to `queueSizeHistogram` and `queuePollsHistogram`, sets `subscriptionStateGauge` to 1 or 0, and does not record `assignedPartitionCount`.

### Metric Descriptors

`ConsumerMetrics` and `ProducerMetrics` are repositories of metric names, descriptions and histogram boundaries. Every field has a default, so `ConsumerMetrics()` describes the standard metrics, and `ConsumerMetrics#copy` changes only the fields you name. A custom observer for another metrics library can read the same descriptors to keep the standard names.

Each field is a `MetricInfo`, a sealed trait with one case class per metric kind:

```scala
sealed trait MetricInfo {
  def name: String
  def description: String
}

object MetricInfo {
  final case class Counter(name: String, description: String)  extends MetricInfo
  final case class Gauge[A](name: String, description: String) extends MetricInfo
  final case class Histogram[A](
    name: String,
    description: String,
    boundaries: zio.metrics.MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries
  ) extends MetricInfo
}
```

The type parameter of `Gauge` and `Histogram` is the type of the measured value (`Int`, `Long` or `Duration`); `MetricInfo` stores no value itself. The boundaries are ZIO's `Histogram.Boundaries`, usually built with `Histogram.Boundaries.fromChunk`, `Histogram.Boundaries.linear` or `Histogram.Boundaries.exponential`. Latency boundaries are in seconds, because the default observers record durations in seconds.

The companion objects define the default boundaries as methods, such as `ConsumerMetrics.defaultLatencyBoundaries`, so you can reuse them. Most follow an exponential series based on 𝑒. For every default and the histograms that use it, see the [`ConsumerMetrics`](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/consumer/metrics/ConsumerMetrics$.html) and [`ProducerMetrics`](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/producer/metrics/ProducerMetrics$.html) API docs.

:::note
`Histogram.Boundaries.fromChunk` drops every boundary that is not greater than 0 and appends `Double.MaxValue` as the last boundary (the `+Inf` bucket). The `0` that several default series start with therefore never reaches `Boundaries#values`, for the default observer and for a custom observer that reads the descriptor alike. The lowest bucket of those histograms is the first positive boundary, and it also counts the value 0.
:::

### Common Patterns

The examples below cover the usual reasons to touch this API. All of them only build settings and observers; nothing connects to Kafka until the settings are passed to `Consumer.make` or `Producer.make`.

#### Customizing Histogram Boundaries

When the default buckets are too coarse for your workload, copy the default descriptors, replace the boundaries you need, and pass the result to the default observer. Here, polls usually take a few milliseconds, so the poll latency histogram gets boundaries from 1 ms to 512 ms, doubling each step:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings
import zio.kafka.consumer.metrics.{ ConsumerMetrics, ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver }
import zio.kafka.metrics.MetricInfo
import zio.metrics.MetricKeyType.Histogram
import zio.metrics.MetricLabel

val defaults = ConsumerMetrics()

// 0.001, 0.002, 0.004, ..., 0.512 seconds
val fastPollBoundaries: Histogram.Boundaries = Histogram.Boundaries.exponential(0.001, 2.0, 10)

val pollLatency: MetricInfo.Histogram[Duration] =
  defaults.pollLatencyHistogram.copy(boundaries = fastPollBoundaries)

val consumerMetrics: ConsumerMetrics = defaults.copy(pollLatencyHistogram = pollLatency)

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withMetricsObserver(
      new ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver(consumerMetrics, Set(MetricLabel("group-id", "orders-service")))
    )
```

The same approach renames a metric: copy the `MetricInfo` with a different `name`. For the producer, copy `ProducerMetrics()` and pass it to `ZioMetricsProducerMetricsObserver`.

#### Adding Logging to the Default Observer

An observer can delegate to another observer and do extra work around it. This one keeps all the default ZIO metrics, and also logs slow polls and every rebalance:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings
import zio.kafka.consumer.metrics.{ ConsumerMetricsObserver, ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver }
import zio.kafka.consumer.metrics.ConsumerMetricsObserver.ConsumerState
import zio.metrics.MetricLabel

final class LoggingConsumerMetricsObserver(underlying: ConsumerMetricsObserver, slowPoll: Duration)
    extends ConsumerMetricsObserver {

  override def observePoll(resumedCount: Int, pausedCount: Int, latency: Duration, pollSize: Int): UIO[Unit] =
    underlying.observePoll(resumedCount, pausedCount, latency, pollSize) *>
      ZIO
        .logWarning(s"Slow poll: ${latency.toMillis} ms for $pollSize records")
        .when(latency > slowPoll)
        .unit

  override def observeRebalance(
    currentlyAssignedCount: Int,
    assignedCount: Int,
    revokedCount: Int,
    lostCount: Int
  ): UIO[Unit] =
    underlying.observeRebalance(currentlyAssignedCount, assignedCount, revokedCount, lostCount) *>
      ZIO.logInfo(
        s"Rebalance: $assignedCount assigned, $revokedCount revoked, $lostCount lost, $currentlyAssignedCount now assigned"
      )

  override def observeCommit(latency: Duration): UIO[Unit] =
    underlying.observeCommit(latency)

  override def observeAggregatedCommit(latency: Duration, commitSize: Long): UIO[Unit] =
    underlying.observeAggregatedCommit(latency, commitSize)

  override def observeRunloopMetrics(state: ConsumerState): UIO[Unit] =
    underlying.observeRunloopMetrics(state)

  override def observePollAuthError: UIO[Unit] =
    underlying.observePollAuthError
}

val labels = Set(MetricLabel("group-id", "orders-service"))

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withMetricsObserver(
      new LoggingConsumerMetricsObserver(new ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver(labels), slowPoll = 1.second)
    )
```

Because a custom observer replaces the default one, the labels go into the `ZioMetricsConsumerMetricsObserver` constructor, not into `withMetricsLabels`. `ZIO.logInfo` and `ZIO.logWarning` are cheap with ZIO's default logger; with a logging backend that writes synchronously, keep the extra work in the callback small.

#### Bridging to Another Metrics Backend

To send zio-kafka metrics to a library other than ZIO metrics, implement the trait and translate each callback into calls on that library. The example below uses a small in-memory registry as a stand-in for that library, and reads the metric names from `ProducerMetrics` so the exported names match the standard ones. It records counters and keeps the latest value of each histogram as a gauge, to stay short:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.metrics.MetricInfo
import zio.kafka.producer.{ Producer, ProducerSettings }
import zio.kafka.producer.metrics.{ ProducerMetrics, ProducerMetricsObserver }

// Stand-in for the API of another metrics library
final class Registry(counters: Ref[Map[String, Long]], gauges: Ref[Map[String, Double]]) {
  def increment(metric: MetricInfo, by: Long): UIO[Unit] =
    counters.update(m => m.updated(metric.name, m.getOrElse(metric.name, 0L) + by))

  def set(metric: MetricInfo, value: Double): UIO[Unit] =
    gauges.update(_.updated(metric.name, value))
}

object Registry {
  val make: UIO[Registry] =
    for {
      counters <- Ref.make(Map.empty[String, Long])
      gauges   <- Ref.make(Map.empty[String, Double])
    } yield new Registry(counters, gauges)
}

final class RegistryProducerMetricsObserver(registry: Registry, metrics: ProducerMetrics)
    extends ProducerMetricsObserver {

  override def observeProduce(latency: Duration, batchSize: Int): UIO[Unit] =
    registry.increment(metrics.produceCallsCounter, 1L) *>
      registry.increment(metrics.produceRecordsCounter, batchSize.toLong) *>
      registry.set(metrics.produceLatencyHistogram, latency.toNanos.toDouble / 1e9)

  override def observeSendQueueSize(size: Int): UIO[Unit] =
    registry.set(metrics.sendQueueSizeHistogram, size.toDouble)

  override def observeSendQueueTake(latency: Duration): UIO[Unit] =
    ZIO.unit

  override def observeSendAuthError(errorCount: Int): UIO[Unit] =
    registry.increment(metrics.sendAuthErrorCounter, errorCount.toLong)
}

val producer: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Producer] =
  for {
    registry <- Registry.make
    settings = ProducerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
                 .withMetricsObserver(new RegistryProducerMetricsObserver(registry, ProducerMetrics()))
    producer <- Producer.make(settings)
  } yield producer
```

Each callback only updates a `Ref`, which keeps it fast. With a real library, prefer its non-blocking update calls; if an update can block, hand the measurement to a queue that another fiber drains, so the producer never waits for the metrics backend.

#### Disabling Metrics

`ConsumerMetricsObserver.NoOp` and `ProducerMetricsObserver.NoOp` implement every callback as `ZIO.unit`. Installing them turns off zio-kafka's own metrics, which is useful in tests or when you do not export metrics at all:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings
import zio.kafka.consumer.metrics.ConsumerMetricsObserver
import zio.kafka.producer.ProducerSettings
import zio.kafka.producer.metrics.ProducerMetricsObserver

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
    .withGroupId("orders-service")
    .withMetricsObserver(ConsumerMetricsObserver.NoOp)

val producerSettings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers)
    .withMetricsObserver(ProducerMetricsObserver.NoOp)
```

`NoOp` only silences the zio-kafka metrics. The Java client metrics stay available through `Consumer#metrics` and `Producer#metrics`. With the consumer `NoOp`, the runloop still runs its sampling fiber on `ConsumerSettings#runloopMetricsSchedule`, but every snapshot is discarded.

### Related Pages

Metrics observers sit next to several other parts of zio-kafka:

- [Metrics](metrics.md) lists every metric name with its type and description, and explains how to read them.
- [Consumer](consumer.md) and [Producer](producer.md) describe `ConsumerSettings` and `ProducerSettings`, including their metrics settings, and the internals the callbacks report on.
- [Diagnostics](diagnostics.md) is the event-based counterpart: it hands you each individual event with full details on a separate fiber, while metrics observers receive numeric measurements inline, meant to become counters, gauges and histograms.
- [Consumer Tuning](consumer-tuning.md) shows how to use the consumer metrics to tune the consumer.

## Metrics

Zio-kafka exposes all the metrics of the wrapped Java based consumer and producer, plus some more metrics about the
zio-kafka consumer and producer themselves.

### Java client metrics

The metrics from the Java metrics can be obtained via the `Consumer#metrics` and `Producer#metrics` methods. Both
return a live view on the internal metrics of the consumer/producer. We currently do not expose these metrics elsewhere,
a PR to copy them to the zio-metrics API is welcome.

### Zio-kafka Metrics

The zio-kafka consumer and producer collect some additional metrics using the zio-metrics API. This allows any
zio-metrics backend to access and process the observed values.

By default, no tags are added. Tags can be configured via `ConsumerSettings.withMetricsLabels` / `ProducerSettings.withMetricsLabels`.

To send these metrics to another backend, change histogram boundaries, or turn metrics off, see [Metrics Observers](metrics-observers.md).

Like the zio-metrics we follow Prometheus conventions. This means that:

- durations are expressed in seconds,
- counters can only increase,
- metric names use snake_case and end with the unit name where possible.

Each histogram defines 10 bucket boundaries (zio-metrics ignores a boundary of `0` and adds a `+Inf` bucket). To reach a decent range while keeping sufficient accuracy at the low end, most
bucket boundaries use an exponential series based on 𝑒.

### Zio-kafka Consumer Metrics

To interpret the metrics you need to know how zio-kafka works internally.

![](consumer-internals.svg)

See the [tuning guide](consumer-tuning.md#using-metrics-to-tune-the-consumer) for more details on the internals.

#### Poll metrics

| Type      | Name                                                  | Description                                                                        |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| counter   | `ziokafka_consumer_polls`                             | The number of polls.                                                               |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_poll_latency_seconds`              | The duration of a single poll in seconds.                                          |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_poll_size`                         | The number of records fetched by a single poll.                                    |
| gauge     | `ziokafka_consumer_partitions_resumed_in_latest_poll` | The number of partitions resumed in the latest poll call.                          |
| gauge     | `ziokafka_consumer_partitions_paused_in_latest_poll`  | The number of partitions paused in the latest poll call (because of backpressure). |
| counter   | `ziokafka_consumer_poll_auth_errors`                  | The number of polls that ended with an authentication or authorization error.      |

:::note
Note that `ziokafka_consumer_poll_auth_errors` only tracks errors surfaced directly during `poll()` calls. Silent
runtime authorization failures (such as a revoked `READ` ACL) are silently swallowed by `poll()` and will not increment
this metric. To detect and surface these failures as exceptions, configure the empty-poll metadata-refresh probe (
see [Detecting Authorization Failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md)).
:::

#### Partition stream metrics

These metrics are sampled periodically, by default every 500ms (see `ConsumerSettings#withRunloopMetricsSchedule`).

| Type      | Name                                 | Description                                                            |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_pending_requests` | The number of partitions that ran out of records (the queue is empty). |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_queue_size`       | The number of records queued for a partition.                          |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_all_queue_size`   | The total number of records queued for all partitions.                 |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_queue_polls`      | The number of polls during which records are idling in a queue.        |

#### Commit metrics

These metrics measure the separate commit requests issued through zio-kafka's api. Metric
`ziokafka_consumer_pending_commits` is sampled periodically, like the partition stream metrics.

| Type      | Name                                       | Description                                         |
|-----------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_pending_commits`        | The number of commits that are awaiting completion. |
| counter   | `ziokafka_consumer_commits`                | The number of commits.                              |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_commit_latency_seconds` | The duration of a commit in seconds.                |

#### Aggregated commit metrics

In each runloop cycle zio-kafka combines all outstanding commit requests into 1 aggregated commit. These metrics are for the aggregated commits.

| Type      | Name                                                  | Description                                                                |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| counter   | `ziokafka_consumer_aggregated_commits`                | The number of aggregated commits.                                          |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_aggregated_commit_latency_seconds` | The duration of an aggregated commit in seconds.                           |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_aggregated_commit_size`            | An approximation of the number of records (offsets) per aggregated commit. |

#### Rebalance metrics

| Type    | Name                                              | Description                                                  |
|---------|---------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| counter | `ziokafka_consumer_rebalances`                    | The number of rebalances.                                    |
| gauge   | `ziokafka_consumer_partitions_currently_assigned` | The number of partitions currently assigned to the consumer. |
| counter | `ziokafka_consumer_partitions_assigned`           | The number of partitions assigned to the consumer.           |
| counter | `ziokafka_consumer_partitions_revoked`            | The number of partitions revoked to the consumer.            |
| counter | `ziokafka_consumer_partitions_lost`               | The number of partitions lost to the consumer.               |

#### Runloop metrics

These metrics are sampled periodically, by default every 500ms (see `ConsumerSettings#withRunloopMetricsSchedule`).

| Type      | Name                                   | Description                                        |
|-----------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| gauge     | `ziokafka_consumer_subscription_state` | Whether the consumer is subscribed (1) or not (0). |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_command_queue_size` | The number of commands queued in the consumer.     |
| histogram | `ziokafka_consumer_commit_queue_size`  | The number of commits queued in the consumer.      |

See [ConsumerMetrics.scala](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka/blob/master/zio-kafka/src/main/scala/zio/kafka/consumer/metrics/ConsumerMetrics.scala) for the exact details.

### Example

Here is an example dashboard that could be built with these metrics:

![metrics-dashboard.png](metrics-dashboard.png)

### Zio-kafka Producer Metrics

To understand the producer metrics it is useful to know how the producer works.

When you call the producer it first serializes the given batch of records (a single record is treated like a batch of
one). The batch is then offered to an internal send queue. Once the queue accepts the batch, the `produce*Async` methods
return immediately. The `produce` and `produceChunk` methods return later, when all acknowledgements are in. Once the fiber is ready
for it, it pulls a batch from the queue and sends the records to the Kafka broker one by one. Meanwhile, the broker
acknowledges records.

![](producer-internals.svg)

#### Producer metrics

| Type      | Name                                | Description                                                                             |
|-----------|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| counter   | `ziokafka_producer_calls`           | The number of produce calls that completed successfully.                                |
| histogram | `ziokafka_producer_latency_seconds` | The duration of a single produce, from after serialization to acknowledged, in seconds. |
| counter   | `ziokafka_producer_records`         | The number of records produced.                                                         |
| histogram | `ziokafka_producer_batch_size`      | The number of records per produce call.                                                 |

These metrics are only updated for produce calls in which every record was produced successfully.

#### Queue metrics

| Type      | Name                                           | Description                                                                                  |
|-----------|------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| histogram | `ziokafka_producer_send_queue_size`            | The number of batches (produce calls) in the zio-kafka send queue, sampled every 10 seconds. |
| histogram | `ziokafka_producer_send_queue_latency_seconds` | Time in send queue, including waiting for capacity, in seconds.                              |

The capacity of the send queue is set with `ProducerSettings#withSendBufferSize`.

#### Send metrics

| Type    | Name                            | Description                                                                           |
|---------|---------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| counter | `ziokafka_producer_auth_errors` | The number of record sends that resulted in an authentication or authorization error. |

See [ProducerMetrics.scala](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka/blob/master/zio-kafka/src/main/scala/zio/kafka/producer/metrics/ProducerMetrics.scala) for the exact details.

## Migrating to zio-kafka 3

Zio-kafka 3.0.0 brings a number of backwards incompatible changes:

1. Removal of all deprecated methods, _including accessor methods,_
2. Kafka 4.x
3. The transactional producer is now much easier to use,
4. Diagnostics set via consumer settings, 
5. `restartStreamOnRebalancing` mode is no longer supported.

This document helps you migrate from zio-kafka 2 to zio-kafka 3. To upgrade further, from zio-kafka 3 to zio-kafka 4, see [Migrating to zio-kafka 4](migrating-to-zio-kafka-4.md).

In the examples below, code marked as zio-kafka 2.x shows the old API; it is not meant to compile with zio-kafka 3.

### 1. Deprecations

Zio-kafka 3.0.0 removes everything that was deprecated in the zio-kafka 2.x series. In particular, this includes
accessor methods. To prepare for zio-kafka 3.0, _you should always first migrate to zio-kafka 2.12.0_ and solve all
deprecation issues, using this page as a guide.

#### Renamed methods

Some methods have just been renamed. Read the deprecation message and try the new method name. If it compiles, you're
done. Otherwise, read on.

#### Consumer, Producer and TransactionalProducer accessor methods

Accessor methods are little helper methods that look up a service from the environment, and then forward your call to
that service. Accessor methods have not been recommended for some time; they were deprecated in zio-kafka 2.11 and have
been removed in zio-kafka 3.0. The
[ZIO service pattern](https://zio.dev/reference/service-pattern/) provides a much cleaner approach for accessing
services.

All accessor methods provided by zio-kafka were deprecated in zio-kafka 2.11 and have been removed in zio-kafka 3.0. If
you use these accessor methods follow one of these approaches:

##### Use the ZIO Service pattern

This is the best option. For established codebases it may be a lot of work to get here. If you are already follow
this pattern, using it for zio-kafka services as well will be easy. See [ZIO service pattern](https://zio.dev/reference/service-pattern/) for more information.

Here is an example with a `Consumer`, but it works the same with `Producer` and `TransactionalProducer`. We get the
`Consumer` from the environment in the layer with the `ZIO.service` method, and then inject it into the service class.
The service now uses the consumer directly, with `consumer` instead of `Consumer`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, Subscription }
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

trait Service {
  def someMethod: ZIO[Any, Throwable, String]
}

object Service {

  def layer: ZLayer[Consumer, Throwable, Service] = ZLayer {
    for {
      consumer <- ZIO.service[Consumer]
    } yield ServiceLive(consumer)
  }

}

case class ServiceLive(consumer: Consumer) extends Service {

  override def someMethod: ZIO[Any, Throwable, String] =
    // use `consumer`, not `Consumer`:
    consumer
      .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
      .runHead
      .map(_.fold("")(_.value))
}
```

Constructing a `Consumer` layer is described in [creating a consumer](creating-a-consumer.md). Constructing a
`Producer` or `TransactionalProducer` layer works in a similar way.

##### YOLO, use `ZIO.service` everywhere

The other option is to replace all accessor methods of `Consumer`, `Producer` and `TransactionalProducer` as follows:

- `Consumer.method(...)` => `ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Consumer](_.method(...))`
- `Producer.method(...)` => `ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Producer](_.method(...))`
- `TransactionalProducer.method(...)` => `ZIO.serviceWithZIO[TransactionalProducer](_.method(...))`

The accessors that return a stream or a pipeline need a different replacement. For `Consumer.plainStream`, `Consumer.partitionedStream` and `Consumer.partitionedAssignmentStream`, use `ZStream.serviceWithStream[Consumer](_.plainStream(...))` (and likewise for the other two). For `Producer.produceAll`, get the producer with `ZIO.service[Producer]` and use the `Producer#produceAll` pipeline.

Or, alternatively, use `ZIO.service`.

For example: `Consumer.method(...)` is transformed to:
```scala
for {
  consumer <- ZIO.service[Consumer]
  _        <- consumer.method(...)
} yield () 
```

#### Zio-test-kit

Zio-kafka provides a `zio-kafka-testkit` library to help you test your code using zio-kafka. Several methods in the
`KafkaTestUtils` class have been replaced:

- The `produce*` and `scheduledProduce*` methods, which get a producer from the environment, were deprecated in
  zio-kafka 2.11 and have been removed in zio-kafka 3.0. Each of these methods now only exists as a variant with an
  explicit producer parameter.
- All methods that produce a layer (e.g. `consumer`, `producer`) have _not_ been deprecated, but they have been given a
  more convenient alternative: `makeConsumer`, `makeProducer`, etc. The exception is `minimalConsumer()`, which is
  deprecated since zio-kafka 3.0.0; use `Consumer.live` instead.
- The `withAdmin`, `withSaslAdmin`, `withSslAdmin` methods have been removed and are replaced by `makeAdminClient`,
  `makeSaslAdminClient` and `makeSslAdminClient`.

Here is a typical zio-kafka 2.x test suite:

```scala
// Old (zio-kafka 2.x)
override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment, Any] =
  suite("old example suite")(
    test("uses a producer") {
      for {
        _ <- KafkaTestUtils.produceOne("topic", "key", "message")
      } yield assertCompletes
    }
  )
    .provideSome[Kafka](KafkaTestUtils.producer)
    .provideShared(Kafka.embedded)
```

In zio-kafka 3.x, the same suite looks like this:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.testkit.{ Kafka, KafkaTestUtils }
import zio.test._

object NewExampleSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  // New (zio-kafka 3.x)
  // Added `Scope`:
  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope, Any] =
    suite("new example suite")(
      test("uses a producer") {
        for {
          // Make a producer explicitly (instead of via a layer):
          producer <- KafkaTestUtils.makeProducer
          // Notice explicit producer parameter:
          _ <- KafkaTestUtils.produceOne(producer, "topic", "key", "message")
        } yield assertCompletes
      }
    )
      // Producer layer removed.
      // Using `provideSomeShared[Scope]` instead of `provideShared`:
      .provideSomeShared[Scope](Kafka.embedded)
}
```

`KafkaTestUtils.makeProducer` and the other `make*` methods require a `Scope` in the environment. This scope is
normally provided by the test framework (notice how `Scope` was added to the type parameter of `Spec`). If needed, a
smaller scope can be given with the `ZIO.scoped` method. See also [writing tests](writing-tests.md) for details on how
to provide more layers.

Here is code that uses one of the removed `with*Admin` methods:

```scala
// Old (zio-kafka 2.x)
KafkaTestUtils.withAdmin { adminClient =>
  adminClient.method() // Use the admin client...
}
```

In zio-kafka 3.x, we make the admin client explicitly instead:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.testkit.{ Kafka, KafkaTestUtils }

// New (zio-kafka 3.x)
val useAdminClient: ZIO[Scope & Kafka, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    adminClient <- KafkaTestUtils.makeAdminClient
    _           <- adminClient.listTopics() // Use the admin client...
  } yield ()
```

### 2. Kafka 4.x

Starting with 3.0.0, zio-kafka is based on the kafka 4.0.0 client. This has a number of consequences:

* Java 11 support is dropped. Even though the kafka client library still supports java 11, zio-kafka's unit tests
  depend on an embedded kafka broker and the kafka brokers no longer support it.
* `ConsumerGroupState` (used in the admin client) was renamed to `GroupState`, unfortunately without a deprecation
  cycle.
* Due to [KAFKA-18818](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-18818), admin operations are eventually consistent.
  Zio-kafka 3.0 to 3.3 added a fixed 550ms delay after operations like `createTopic`, `deleteTopic` and `createAcls`
  in the admin client; 3.4 removed it, after earlier releases had already replaced it for some operations. Since zio-kafka 3.6.0, the admin client polls
  the broker until the change is visible (for at most 5 seconds), and operations whose effect it cannot check accept a
  `visibilitySleep` parameter (default 1 second).
* Two deprecated methods of kafka's admin client were removed. Their equivalent in zio-kafka were unfortunately not
  deprecated yet but had to be removed as well:
  * `AdminClient.alterConfigs` was removed, use `AdminClient.incrementalAlterConfigs` instead.
  * `AdminClient.alterConfigsAsync` was removed, use `AdminClient.incrementalAlterConfigsAsync` instead.

There may be more changes that affect you. See the [Kafka 4.0.0 release announcement](https://kafka.apache.org/blog#apache_kafka_400_release_announcement) for more details.

### 3. Changes in the transactional producer

The transactional producer is now much easier to use. The zio-kafka 2.x transactional API is so complicated that we
expect only a few very experienced users to make use of it. Therefore, only the new API is described in
[transactions](transactions.md).

### 4. Diagnostics set via consumer settings

Diagnostics, an optional callback for key events in the consumer life-cycle, is now set via
`ConsumerSettings.withDiagnostics`. In zio-kafka 2.x it was the second (optional) argument to `Consumer.make`, or an
additional input layer for `Consumer.live`.

#### Migrate a layers app without diagnostics

If your program uses ZIO layers, but you don't need diagnostics, it will look like this:

```scala
// zio-kafka 2.x
.provide(
  consumerSettingsLayer,
  ZLayer.succeed(Consumer.NoDiagnostics), // 1
  Consumer.live
)
```

For zio-kafka 3.x simply remove the line marked with `// 1` and you are done.

#### Migrate uses of `Consumer.make` with diagnostics

In zio-kafka 2.x, the diagnostics were the second argument of `Consumer.make`:

```scala
// zio-kafka 2.x
val diagnostics = ???
val settings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrap)
val consumer = Consumer.make(settings, diagnostics)
```

Rewrite your code so that the diagnostics are part of the settings:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, ConsumerSettings }

val bootstrap = List("localhost:9092")

// zio-kafka 3.x
val diagnostics: Consumer.ConsumerDiagnostics = ???
val settings                                  = ConsumerSettings(bootstrap).withDiagnostics(diagnostics)
val consumer: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Consumer] = Consumer.make(settings)
```

#### Migrate a layers app with diagnostics

In case your application provides diagnostics via a layer, providing the layers looks like this:

```scala
// zio-kafka 2.x
.provide(
  consumerSettingsLayer,
  diagnosticsLayer,
  Consumer.live
)
```

The cleanest solution is to merge the code that constructs `diagnosticsLayer` into the code that constructs
`consumerSettingsLayer`.

The other option is to apply a 'quick fix' that transforms the two layers into a single layer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, ConsumerSettings }

val consumerSettingsLayer: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, ConsumerSettings]        = ???
val diagnosticsLayer: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Consumer.ConsumerDiagnostics] = ???
val program: ZIO[Consumer, Throwable, Unit]                                = ???

// zio-kafka 3.x
program.provide(
  (consumerSettingsLayer ++ diagnosticsLayer) >>> ZLayer {
    for {
      settings    <- ZIO.service[ConsumerSettings]
      diagnostics <- ZIO.service[Consumer.ConsumerDiagnostics]
    } yield settings.withDiagnostics(diagnostics)
  },
  Consumer.live
)
```

### 5. `restartStreamOnRebalancing` mode

This mode is no longer available in zio-kafka 3. With `restartStreamOnRebalancing` all streams are ended during a
rebalance, even when the partition for that stream was not revoked. One of its purposes was to enable transactional
consuming. Since zio-kafka 3 however, transactional consuming no longer needs this mode.

If your goal is to [prevent duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md), please use `rebalanceSafeCommits` instead.

### Other changes?

If you find a change that is not documented here then please let us know via a
[new issue](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka/issues/new).

---

## Migrating to zio-kafka 4

Zio-kafka 4.0.0 changes how offsets are committed. Before 4.0, zio-kafka committed the offset of the last consumed record plus 1. Since KIP-1094, the Kafka client reports the actual _next offset_ of a partition, which skips the invisible control records that transactional producers write. Zio-kafka 4.0 attaches this next offset to every record and commits it. As a result, consumer lag can now go down to 0, where before a consumer of a transactional topic always showed some lag.

This change is the only one in 4.0.0. The Scala, ZIO and Kafka client versions are the same as in zio-kafka 3.8.2, and 4.0.0 removes no deprecated APIs. Most applications only need to update the dependency. You need to change code if it:

- Reads `OffsetBatch.offsets`, for example to store offsets outside Kafka.
- Implements the `Offset` trait, for example as a fake in tests.
- Constructs a `CommittableRecord` directly, for example in tests.
- Reads the offsets of `DiagnosticEvent.Commit.Started` in a diagnostics callback.
- Assumes that a committed offset always equals the last consumed offset plus 1.

If you are still on zio-kafka 2.x, first follow [migrating to zio-kafka 3](migrating-to-zio-kafka-3.md).

### Update the Dependency

To upgrade, change the version of zio-kafka (and of the testkit, if you use it) in `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka"         % "4.1.0"
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka-testkit" % "4.1.0" % Test
```

As with any major release, zio-kafka 4 is not binary compatible with zio-kafka 3. A library that was compiled against zio-kafka 3 and uses the APIs below needs a release built against zio-kafka 4.

### Replace `OffsetBatch.offsets` With `OffsetBatch#nextOffsets`

`OffsetBatch.offsets` is gone. Its replacement, `OffsetBatch#nextOffsets`, holds per partition the offset to commit, which is the next offset, not the consumed offset. This affects you if you combine offsets into a batch and then store them outside Kafka, as described in [preventing duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md).

In zio-kafka 3.x, the batch held consumed offsets, so code that stored offsets added 1:

```scala
// zio-kafka 3.x
def offsetsToStore(batch: OffsetBatch): Map[TopicPartition, Long] =
  batch.offsets.map { case (tp, offsetAndMetadata) => tp -> (offsetAndMetadata.offset() + 1) }
```

In zio-kafka 4, the values are already the next offsets, so we store them as they are:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio.kafka.consumer.OffsetBatch

def offsetsToStore(batch: OffsetBatch): Map[TopicPartition, Long] =
  batch.nextOffsets.map { case (tp, offsetAndMetadata) => tp -> offsetAndMetadata.offset() }
```

:::warning
Do not only rename `OffsetBatch.offsets` to `OffsetBatch#nextOffsets`. If you keep adding 1, the code still compiles, but after a restart or rebalance each partition skips one record.
:::

The values of `OffsetBatch#nextOffsets` are `OffsetAndMetadata`s, so they also carry the leader epoch and any metadata added with `Offset#withMetadata`. Values that are not inside an `OffsetBatch`, such as `record.offset.offset`, keep their meaning: they are still consumed offsets.

### Prefer `CommittableRecord#nextOffset` When Storing Single Offsets

This step is optional; the 3.x code keeps compiling and working. Code that stores the offset of a single record by adding 1 to the consumed offset ignores the control records that follow it, so the stored offset can lag behind. Each record now carries its exact next offset in `CommittableRecord#nextOffset`, and each `Offset` in `Offset#nextOffset`.

In zio-kafka 3.x, we compute the next offset ourselves:

```scala
// zio-kafka 3.x
def offsetToStore(record: CommittableRecord[String, String]): (TopicPartition, Long) =
  record.offset.topicPartition -> (record.offset.offset + 1)
```

In zio-kafka 4, we read it from the record:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio.kafka.consumer.CommittableRecord

def offsetToStore(record: CommittableRecord[String, String]): (TopicPartition, Long) =
  record.offset.topicPartition -> record.nextOffset.offset()
```

To also store the leader epoch, use `record.nextOffset.leaderEpoch()`. [Offsets and Committing](offsets-and-committing.md) explains the difference between the consumed offset and the next offset.

### Implement `Offset#nextOffset`

The `Offset` trait has a new abstract member, `def nextOffset: OffsetAndMetadata`, and lost its package-private `metadata` and `asJavaOffsetAndMetadata` members. A custom implementation of `Offset` must now provide `Offset#nextOffset`. To match zio-kafka's own implementation, take `Offset#leaderEpoch` from the next offset, let `Offset#commit` commit the next offset, and let `Offset#withMetadata` store the metadata in the next offset.

In zio-kafka 3.x, a fake offset for tests had no next offset:

```scala
// zio-kafka 3.x
final case class FakeOffset(topic: String, partition: Int, offset: Long) extends Offset {
  def leaderEpoch: Optional[Integer] = Optional.empty()
  // ... commit, batch, consumerGroupMetadata, withMetadata, metadata
}
```

In zio-kafka 4, it takes the next offset as an extra field:

```scala
import java.util.Optional

import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.{ ConsumerGroupMetadata, OffsetAndMetadata }
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Offset, OffsetBatch }

final case class FakeOffset(topic: String, partition: Int, offset: Long, nextOffset: OffsetAndMetadata)
    extends Offset {
  def leaderEpoch: Optional[Integer]                       = nextOffset.leaderEpoch()
  def commit: Task[Unit]                                   = ZIO.unit
  def batch: OffsetBatch                                   = OffsetBatch.empty // this fake is never committed in a batch
  def consumerGroupMetadata: Option[ConsumerGroupMetadata] = None
  def withMetadata(metadata: String): Offset =
    copy(nextOffset = new OffsetAndMetadata(nextOffset.offset(), nextOffset.leaderEpoch(), metadata))
}
```

### Pass the Next Offset When Constructing a `CommittableRecord`

`CommittableRecord` has a new second parameter, `nextOffset: OffsetAndMetadata`, both in its constructor and in `CommittableRecord.apply`. Code that builds records by hand, typically tests, must pass it, and a pattern such as `case CommittableRecord(record, _, _)` needs an extra `_`.

In zio-kafka 3.x, a test record needed only the Kafka record, a commit handle and the group metadata:

```scala
// zio-kafka 3.x
val record: CommittableRecord[String, String] =
  CommittableRecord(
    record = consumerRecord,
    commitHandle = _ => ZIO.unit,
    consumerGroupMetadata = None
  )
```

In zio-kafka 4, we also pass the next offset. For a record that is not followed by control records, it is the record's offset plus 1:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.{ ConsumerRecord, OffsetAndMetadata }
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.CommittableRecord

val consumerRecord = new ConsumerRecord[String, String]("my-topic", 0, 41L, "key", "value")

val record: CommittableRecord[String, String] =
  CommittableRecord(
    record = consumerRecord,
    nextOffset = new OffsetAndMetadata(consumerRecord.offset() + 1),
    commitHandle = (_: Map[TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata]) => ZIO.unit,
    consumerGroupMetadata = None
  )
```

### Expect Commits to Skip Control Records

This change needs no code changes. `Offset#commit`, `OffsetBatch#commit`, `Consumer#consumeWith` and transactions of a `TransactionalProducer` now commit the actual next offset. When control records follow the last consumed record of a partition, the committed offset is larger than that record's offset plus 1.

Review code, tests and dashboards that assume otherwise. For example, a test that checks `committed == lastConsumedOffset + 1` on a transactional topic can now fail, and a dashboard that showed a lag of 1 on such a topic now shows 0.

### Expect Next Offsets in `Commit.Started` Diagnostic Events

In zio-kafka 3.x, the `DiagnosticEvent.Commit.Started` event carried the consumed offsets, while `Commit.Success` and `Commit.Failure` carried the next offsets. In zio-kafka 4, `Commit.Started` also carries the next offsets, the same values that are committed. If a [diagnostics](diagnostics.md) callback compares or logs the offsets of `Commit.Started`, remove any `+ 1` it applies to them.

### Checklist

To migrate an application from zio-kafka 3.x to zio-kafka 4:

- [ ] Update `zio-kafka` and `zio-kafka-testkit` to the latest 4.x release (4.1.0 at the time of writing).
- [ ] Replace every use of `OffsetBatch.offsets` with `OffsetBatch#nextOffsets`, and remove any `+ 1` applied to its values.
- [ ] Optionally, replace `record.offset.offset + 1` with `record.nextOffset.offset()` where you store offsets.
- [ ] Add `Offset#nextOffset` to custom implementations of `Offset`.
- [ ] Pass the `nextOffset` parameter wherever you construct a `CommittableRecord`, and add a field to positional patterns on it.
- [ ] Remove any `+ 1` applied to the offsets of `DiagnosticEvent.Commit.Started` in diagnostics callbacks.
- [ ] Check tests and monitoring that compare committed offsets with consumed offsets.

### Upgrading From zio-kafka 4.0 to 4.1

Zio-kafka 4.1.0 fixes a number of small problems and adds a few APIs; most applications only need to update the dependency. Check the following points:

- **Producer diagnostics:** `ProducerEvent.ProducedRecord#partition` is now `ProducerEvent.NoPartition` (`-1`) for a record that leaves the partition choice to the Kafka partitioner. In 4.0 it was `0`, which could not be told apart from a record sent to partition `0`. Update [diagnostics](diagnostics.md) callbacks that group or filter by this field.
- **Custom fetch strategies:** `PartitionStream`, the type a `FetchStrategy` receives, moved from an internal package to `zio.kafka.consumer.fetch.PartitionStream`. Change the import of a custom `FetchStrategy`, see [Writing a Custom Fetch Strategy](consumer-tuning.md#writing-a-custom-fetch-strategy).
- **SSL endpoint check:** `TransactionalProducer.make` and `TransactionalProducer.live` now run the same SSL endpoint check as the other clients, so with a plain-text protocol they fail when no bootstrap server is reachable at startup. The `KafkaException` of a failed check now has the message `"Failed to connect to Kafka"` instead of `"Failed to create new KafkaAdminClient"`; update code or alerts that match on the old message. See [Security](security.md#ssl-endpoint-check).
- **Failing diagnostics:** when a `Diagnostics` implementation throws or dies, the consumer or producer now fails with that defect, instead of queueing events in memory without bound. See [Diagnostics](diagnostics.md).
- **Metrics:** `ziokafka_producer_send_queue_latency_seconds` now records the actual (positive) time a batch spends in the send queue; in 4.0 the values had the wrong sign. `ziokafka_producer_auth_errors` now also counts authentication and authorization errors of single-record produce calls. Review dashboards and alerts built on these metrics, see [Metrics](metrics.md).
- **Admin client:** `createTopic`, `createTopics`, `createPartitions` and `incrementalAlterConfigs` with `validateOnly = true` no longer wait for the change to become visible, so they return sooner. See [Admin Client](admin-client.md).

Zio-kafka 4.1.0 also adds the serdes `Serde.intOption`, `Serde.longOption`, `Serde.shortOption`, `Serde.floatOption` and `Serde.doubleOption`, which turn a `null` key or value into `None` (see [Handling Missing Data](serialization-and-deserialization.md#handling-missing-data)).

---

## Offsets and Committing

Kafka remembers how far a consumer group has read each partition by storing a *committed offset* per partition. When a consumer restarts, or when a partition moves to another consumer during a rebalance, consumption continues from that committed offset. Zio-kafka never commits on its own (Kafka's `enable.auto.commit` is not supported, and `Consumer.make` fails when you set it to `true`), so your program decides when an offset is committed. This page explains what an offset is in zio-kafka, how to commit offsets one by one or in batches, how to retry failed commits, and how commits relate to external storage and transactions.

The core types are `Offset`, the position of one consumed record, and `OffsetBatch`, the combined positions of many records, at most one per partition. You get an `Offset` from a `CommittableRecord`, the record type that the [consumer](consumer.md) streams emit:

```scala
final case class CommittableRecord[K, V](record: ConsumerRecord[K, V], nextOffset: OffsetAndMetadata, ...) {
  def offset: Offset
}

trait Offset {
  def offset: Long
  def nextOffset: OffsetAndMetadata
  def commit: Task[Unit]
  def batch: OffsetBatch
}

sealed trait OffsetBatch {
  def nextOffsets: Map[TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata]
  def commit: Task[Unit]
  def add(offset: Offset): OffsetBatch
  def merge(offsets: OffsetBatch): OffsetBatch
}
```

You rarely need to commit by hand when you use `Consumer.consumeWith`: it commits the offsets of processed records for you (see [Committing With consumeWith](#committing-with-consumewith)).

### How They Work Together

A consumer stream emits records, and each record carries the offset to commit once it has been processed. The typical flow is:

1. The consumer stream emits a `CommittableRecord` for every record it reads.
2. Your program processes the record and keeps its `Offset` (`CommittableRecord#offset`).
3. Offsets are collected into an `OffsetBatch`, which keeps only the highest next offset per partition. The `Consumer.collectOffsets` sink does this for a stream of offsets.
4. Your program calls `OffsetBatch#commit` (or `Offset#commit` for a single record). The commit goes through the consumer to the Kafka brokers.
5. After a restart or rebalance, a consumer of the same group starts from the committed offsets.

The diagram shows how the types relate:

```
 CommittableRecord ──offset──> Offset ──add──> OffsetBatch ──commit──> Kafka broker
        │                        │                  ▲                (committed offsets
        └─ nextOffset            ├─ commit          │                 per partition)
                                 └─ batch ──────────┘
                                                    merge
                                        OffsetBatch ─────> OffsetBatch
```

### Kafka Commits the Next Offset

In Kafka you never commit the offset of the record you processed. You commit the *next offset*: the offset from which a consumer should continue reading. If you processed the record at offset 42, you commit 43.

Most of the time the next offset is the record's offset plus one. It can be larger when a partition contains *control records*. A transactional producer writes such a control record (a transaction marker) when it commits or aborts a transaction. Control records occupy an offset but are never delivered to your program. In the diagram, the record at offset 44 is the last record that a poll returned for partition 0, and it is followed by a control record at offset 45:

```
  offset          40     41     42     43     44     45     46
               ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
  partition 0  │  r   │  r   │  r   │  r   │  r   │ ctrl │  r   │
               └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘

  record at 42:  Offset#offset = 42   Offset#nextOffset.offset() = 43
  record at 44:  Offset#offset = 44   Offset#nextOffset.offset() = 46  (last record of its poll; skips the control record)
```

Zio-kafka gives you both values, so you don't have to compute the next offset yourself. `Offset#offset` (a `Long`) is the offset of the consumed record. `Offset#nextOffset` (a Kafka `OffsetAndMetadata`) is the offset to commit; it also carries the leader epoch and, optionally, metadata. The same value is available directly on the record as `CommittableRecord#nextOffset`.

For most records `Offset#nextOffset` is `Offset#offset + 1`. For the last record of each partition in a poll, zio-kafka uses the position that the Kafka consumer reports, which already skips any control records that follow the record. As a result, committing the offsets of all processed records moves the committed offset past the control records, and the consumer lag of a transactionally written topic can reach 0.

:::note[Changed in zio-kafka 4.0.0]
`Offset#nextOffset` and `CommittableRecord#nextOffset` were added in zio-kafka 4.0.0, when commits started to skip control records. In the same release `OffsetBatch#offsets` was replaced by `OffsetBatch#nextOffsets`, whose values are already the next offsets to commit. See [Migrating to zio-kafka 4](migrating-to-zio-kafka-4.md).
:::

### Offset

`Offset` is the position of one consumed record. You get it from `CommittableRecord#offset`; there is no public constructor. Besides the record's position, an `Offset` knows how to commit itself through the consumer that read the record:

```scala
trait Offset {
  def topic: String
  def partition: Int
  lazy val topicPartition: TopicPartition
  def leaderEpoch: java.util.Optional[Integer]

  def offset: Long
  def nextOffset: OffsetAndMetadata

  def commit: Task[Unit]
  def commitOrRetry[R](policy: Schedule[R, Throwable, Any]): RIO[R, Unit]

  def batch: OffsetBatch
  def withMetadata(metadata: String): Offset
  def consumerGroupMetadata: Option[ConsumerGroupMetadata]
}
```

The members fall into four groups:

- **Position:** `Offset#topic`, `Offset#partition` and `Offset#topicPartition` identify the partition. `Offset#offset` is the consumed offset, `Offset#nextOffset` the offset to commit, and `Offset#leaderEpoch` the leader epoch stored with the next offset.
- **Committing:** `Offset#commit` commits `Offset#nextOffset` for this record's partition. `Offset#commitOrRetry` does the same and retries retriable failures (see [Retrying Commits](#retrying-commits)).
- **Batching:** `Offset#batch` turns the offset into an `OffsetBatch` with one entry.
- **Metadata:** `Offset#withMetadata` returns a copy whose next offset carries the given metadata string (see [Committing Metadata](#committing-metadata)). `Offset#consumerGroupMetadata` is the consumer group metadata that a `TransactionalProducer` needs to commit offsets as part of a transaction.

To commit after every record, call `Offset#commit` once the record is processed:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def process(key: String, value: String): Task[Unit] = ZIO.logInfo(s"$key -> $value")

def consumeAndCommitEach(consumer: Consumer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .mapZIO(record => process(record.key, record.value) *> record.offset.commit)
    .runDrain
```

Committing every record is simple but slow: each commit is a round trip to the broker, and a high commit rate puts a heavy load on the brokers. Unless your topic sees only a few records per second, commit in batches instead.

### OffsetBatch

`OffsetBatch` holds the next offsets of many records, at most one per partition. When an offset is added for a partition that already has one, the batch keeps the highest next offset. Committing a batch therefore commits the progress of every record that went into it, with a single commit request:

```scala
sealed trait OffsetBatch {
  def nextOffsets: Map[TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata]
  def commit: Task[Unit]
  def commitOrRetry[R](policy: Schedule[R, Throwable, Any]): RIO[R, Unit]
  def add(offset: Offset): OffsetBatch
  def merge(offsets: OffsetBatch): OffsetBatch
  def consumerGroupMetadata: Option[ConsumerGroupMetadata]
}

object OffsetBatch {
  val empty: OffsetBatch
  def apply(offset: Offset): OffsetBatch
  def apply(offsets: Iterable[Offset]): OffsetBatch
}

case object EmptyOffsetBatch extends OffsetBatch
```

#### Creating Offset Batches

There are three ways to start a batch. `OffsetBatch.empty` is the batch without offsets. It is the `EmptyOffsetBatch` object, whose `EmptyOffsetBatch.commit` does nothing. `OffsetBatch.apply(offset)` creates a batch from one offset (the same as `Offset#batch`), and `OffsetBatch.apply(offsets)` creates a batch from a collection of offsets.

To build one batch from the records of a chunk:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._

def batchOf(records: Chunk[CommittableRecord[String, String]]): OffsetBatch =
  OffsetBatch(records.map(_.offset))
```

#### Combining and Committing

Batches grow with `OffsetBatch#add`, which adds one `Offset`, and `OffsetBatch#merge`, which combines two batches. Both keep, per partition, the entry with the highest next offset, so the order in which offsets arrive doesn't matter. `OffsetBatch#nextOffsets` returns the result as a map from partition to the `OffsetAndMetadata` that is committed.

`OffsetBatch#commit` commits all next offsets in one request, and `OffsetBatch#commitOrRetry` adds retries. `OffsetBatch#consumerGroupMetadata` is used by the `TransactionalProducer`, see [Transactional Commits](#transactional-commits).

### Committing in Streams

In a stream, you rarely build batches by hand. The `Consumer` object provides sinks that fold a stream of offsets or batches into one `OffsetBatch`:

```scala
object Consumer {
  val collectOffsets: ZSink[Any, Nothing, Offset, Nothing, OffsetBatch]
  val collectOffsetBatches: ZSink[Any, Nothing, OffsetBatch, Nothing, OffsetBatch]
}
```

`Consumer.collectOffsets` adds each `Offset` to a batch with `OffsetBatch#add`, and `Consumer.collectOffsetBatches` merges each incoming `OffsetBatch` with `OffsetBatch#merge`. `Consumer.offsetBatches` is an alias of `Consumer.collectOffsets`; both names are supported.

Combine these sinks with `ZStream#aggregateAsync` or `ZStream#aggregateAsyncWithin`. Both run the upstream on a separate fiber: while a commit is in progress, the offsets of newly processed records are collected into the next batch, so consuming and committing run in parallel.

#### Batching a Plain Stream

With `ZStream#aggregateAsync`, a new commit starts as soon as the previous commit completes. To process records and commit their offsets in batches:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def process(key: String, value: String): Task[Unit] = ZIO.logInfo(s"$key -> $value")

def consumeAndCommitInBatches(consumer: Consumer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .mapChunksZIO(records => ZIO.foreach(records)(record => process(record.key, record.value).as(record.offset)))
    .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
    .mapZIO(_.commit)
    .runDrain
```

The example processes records with `ZStream#mapChunksZIO` to keep the stream's chunks intact (see [Avoiding Chunk Breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md)).

Committing continuously gives the lowest commit latency, but with many consumers the steady stream of commits can load the brokers. `ZStream#aggregateAsyncWithin` with a schedule limits the commit rate. To emit at most one batch every 100 milliseconds, replace the aggregation line with:

```scala
.aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
```

Choose an interval that is longer than a typical commit. The trade-offs are explained in [Consuming Kafka Topics Using ZIO Streams](consuming-kafka-topics-using-zio-streams.md).

#### Batching a Partitioned Stream

With `Consumer#partitionedStream`, each partition has its own stream, and you merge the partition streams before committing. When each partition stream emits one `OffsetBatch` per processed chunk, aggregate the batches with `Consumer.collectOffsetBatches`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def processChunk(records: Chunk[CommittableRecord[String, String]]): Task[Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo(s"Processing ${records.size} records")

def consumePartitions(consumer: Consumer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .partitionedStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .flatMapPar(Int.MaxValue) { case (_, partitionStream) =>
      partitionStream.mapChunksZIO { records =>
        processChunk(records).as(Chunk.single(OffsetBatch(records.map(_.offset))))
      }
    }
    .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsetBatches)
    .mapZIO(_.commit)
    .runDrain
```

Each partition stream processes its chunks sequentially, partitions are processed in parallel, and all their offsets are committed together.

### Retrying Commits

A commit can fail. Some failures are temporary: Kafka signals them with a `RetriableCommitFailedException`, and zio-kafka fails a commit with `Consumer.CommitTimeout` when it does not complete within the commit timeout. `Offset#commitOrRetry` and `OffsetBatch#commitOrRetry` retry exactly these two failures, for as long as the given schedule allows. Any other failure, and the last failure once the schedule is exhausted, fails the effect.

To retry a batch commit up to three times with exponential back-off:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def consumeWithRetriedCommits(consumer: Consumer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .map(_.offset)
    .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
    .mapZIO(_.commitOrRetry(Schedule.exponential(100.millis) && Schedule.recurs(3)))
    .runDrain
```

The commit timeout is set with `ConsumerSettings#withCommitTimeout` and defaults to 15 seconds (`ConsumerSettings.defaultCommitTimeout`). It must be larger than twice the poll timeout (`ConsumerSettings#withPollTimeout`); otherwise `Consumer.make` fails. A timed-out commit may still complete later.

### Committing With consumeWith

`Consumer.consumeWith` (and the `Consumer#consumeWith` instance method) runs your effect for each record and commits for you. Partitions are processed in parallel. After the effect for a record completes, the record's offset joins a batch: offsets are aggregated with `ZStream#aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)` while the previous commit is still running, and each batch is committed with `OffsetBatch#commitOrRetry`.

The retry schedule is the `commitRetryPolicy` parameter, with the default `Schedule.exponential(1.second) && Schedule.recurs(3)`. To use a different policy:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("my-group")

val program: Task[Unit] =
  Consumer.consumeWith(
    settings = settings,
    subscription = Subscription.topics("my-topic"),
    keyDeserializer = Serde.string,
    valueDeserializer = Serde.string,
    commitRetryPolicy = Schedule.spaced(500.millis) && Schedule.recurs(10)
  ) { record =>
    ZIO.logInfo(s"${record.key()} -> ${record.value()}")
  }
```

When a commit still fails after the retries, `Consumer.consumeWith` fails.

### Committing Metadata

Kafka stores an optional metadata string with each committed offset. Use it to record, for example, which service or version committed. `Offset#withMetadata` returns a copy of the offset whose next offset carries the metadata. When offsets are combined into a batch, the batch keeps the metadata of the offset it keeps for that partition, which is the one with the highest next offset.

`Consumer#committed` reads the committed offsets of a set of partitions back from the broker. A partition without a committed offset maps to `None`. To commit with metadata and read the metadata back:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def commitWithMetadata(consumer: Consumer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .map(_.offset.withMetadata("committed-by=my-service"))
    .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
    .mapZIO(_.commit)
    .runDrain

def committedMetadata(consumer: Consumer): Task[Option[String]] = {
  val partition0 = new TopicPartition("my-topic", 0)
  consumer
    .committed(Set(partition0))
    .map(_.get(partition0).flatten.map(_.metadata()))
}
```

The offset that `Consumer#committed` returns is a next offset, the offset from which consumption continues.

### Delivery Semantics
