When you commit an offset only after the record has been processed, as all examples on this page do, you get *at-least-once* processing: every record is processed, but some records may be processed more than once. Records whose processing finished but whose offset was not yet committed are consumed again after a crash, a restart or a rebalance. Committing *before* processing gives at-most-once processing instead: records whose processing was interrupted are lost.

Rebalances are a common source of duplicates, because a partition can move to another consumer while its last offsets are still being committed. Enable rebalance-safe commits with `ConsumerSettings#withRebalanceSafeCommits` to hold up a rebalance until the offsets of all consumed records are committed, for at most the duration set by `ConsumerSettings#withMaxRebalanceDuration`. See [Preventing Duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md) for the details and the timing constraints. For exactly-once processing from Kafka to Kafka, use [transactions](transactions.md).

### External Commits

Instead of committing to Kafka, you can store offsets in an external system, for example in the same database transaction that stores the processing results. Then the database is the source of truth for the consumer's progress, and two things need to be wired up:

1. When partitions are assigned, the consumer must start from the stored offsets. Configure this with `OffsetRetrieval.External`, see [Partition Assignment and Offset Retrieval](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md).
2. When rebalance-safe commits are enabled, the consumer must know about the external commits, otherwise it waits in vain for commits to Kafka. Report every external commit with `Consumer#registerExternalCommits`.

`Consumer#registerExternalCommits` takes an `OffsetBatch` and only records it as committed in the consumer; it does not commit anything to Kafka:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def registerExternalCommits(offsetBatch: OffsetBatch): Task[Unit]
}
```

Store the next offset (`CommittableRecord#nextOffset`) rather than the consumed offset. Then your `OffsetRetrieval.External` function returns the stored value as is. To store offsets in an external store and resume from them:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.consumer.Consumer.{ OffsetEpoch, OffsetRetrieval }
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

import scala.jdk.OptionConverters._

trait OffsetStore {
  def save(partition: TopicPartition, nextOffset: OffsetEpoch): Task[Unit]
  def load(partitions: Set[TopicPartition]): Task[Map[TopicPartition, OffsetEpoch]]
}

def settings(store: OffsetStore): ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("my-group")
    .withRebalanceSafeCommits(true)
    .withOffsetRetrieval(OffsetRetrieval.External(store.load))

def consumeWithExternalCommits(consumer: Consumer, store: OffsetStore): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .mapChunksZIO { records =>
      // Process the records here, then store the highest next offset per partition once per chunk.
      val batch = OffsetBatch(records.map(_.offset))
      ZIO.foreachDiscard(batch.nextOffsets) { case (tp, next) =>
        store.save(tp, OffsetEpoch(next.offset(), next.leaderEpoch().toScala.map(_.intValue)))
      } *> consumer.registerExternalCommits(batch).as(records)
    }
    .runDrain
```

The example stores and registers offsets once per chunk instead of once per record. In a real program, save the offsets in the same database transaction as the processing results.

### Transactional Commits

With a `TransactionalProducer`, consumed offsets are committed as part of a Kafka transaction, together with the records the transaction produces. You don't call `OffsetBatch#commit` yourself. Instead, you pass the offsets to the transaction: `Transaction#produce` and `Transaction#produceChunk` take an `offset: Option[Offset]`, and `Transaction#produceChunkBatch` takes an `OffsetBatch`. When the transaction commits, the producer sends the collected offsets to the broker, using the batch's consumer group metadata, and registers them with the consumer as external commits. A transactional producer therefore requires rebalance-safe commits on its consumer.

To copy records to another topic and commit their offsets in one transaction per chunk:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

def copyTransactionally(consumer: Consumer, producer: TransactionalProducer): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("input-topic"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .mapChunksZIO { records =>
      ZIO.scoped {
        producer.createTransaction.flatMap { transaction =>
          transaction.produceChunkBatch(
            records.map(record => new ProducerRecord("output-topic", record.key, record.value)),
            Serde.string,
            Serde.string,
            OffsetBatch(records.map(_.offset))
          )
        }
      }.as(Chunk.empty[Unit])
    }
    .runDrain
```

See [Transactions](transactions.md) for the setup of the consumer and the transactional producer.

---

## Partition Assignment and Offset Retrieval

### Consumer partition assignment

Zio-kafka offers several ways to control which Kafka topics and partitions are assigned to your application.

| Use case                                           | Method                                                  |
|----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| One or more topics, automatic partition assignment | `Subscription.topics("my_topic", "other_topic")`        |
| Topics matching a pattern                          | `Subscription.pattern("topic.*".r)`                     |
| Manual partition assignment                        | `Subscription.manual("my_topic" -> 1, "my_topic" -> 2)` |

The example `Subscription.manual("my_topic" -> 1, "my_topic" -> 2)` subscribes to partitions `1` and `2` of topic `my_topic`.

`Subscription.pattern` also accepts a `java.util.regex.Pattern`. The overload that takes a `String`, `Subscription.pattern("topic.*")`, returns a `Task[Subscription]` that fails when the pattern is not a valid regular expression.

### Consumer starting offsets / offset retrieval

By default `zio-kafka` starts streaming a partition from the last committed offset for the active consumer group, or
else the latest offset on the partition in case no offset has yet been committed.

You can also choose to store offsets externally, outside of Kafka. This is useful when consistency between external
data and the consumer offset is required. For example, you can store the offset in a transactional database together
with the data that is derived from the record of that offset. Although it is optional, Kafka recommends you store a
`leaderEpoch` together with the offset as it prevents consuming from a broker that is unaware it is no longer a leader.
For more details about why leaderEpoch is important
see https://www.confluent.io/blog/guide-to-consumer-offsets/#part-ii-in-depth-analysis-and-insights.

| Use case                                                          | `OffsetRetrieval` method                                            |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Offsets in Kafka, start at latest record if no offset committed   | `Auto()`                                                            |
| Offsets in Kafka, start at earliest record if no offset committed | `Auto(AutoOffsetStrategy.Earliest)`                                 |
| Offsets in Kafka, fail if no offset committed                     | `Auto(AutoOffsetStrategy.None)`                                     |
| External offset storage                                           | `External(getOffsets, defaultStrategy = AutoOffsetStrategy.Latest)` |

`OffsetRetrieval` and `AutoOffsetStrategy` are defined in the `Consumer` companion object; bring them into scope with `import zio.kafka.consumer.Consumer._`.

For external offset retrieval, the `getOffsets` function has type `Set[TopicPartition] => Task[Map[TopicPartition, OffsetEpoch]]`. It is called with the set of topic-partitions that are newly assigned to the consumer, either via Kafka's rebalancing or via a manual assignment. When the returned map has no entry for a topic-partition, consuming continues from the last committed offset. When the returned offset is out of range, or there is no committed offset to fall back to, `defaultStrategy` decides where consuming starts.

Offset retrieval is configured via `ConsumerSettings.withOffsetRetrieval()`. You can find more details in the scaladocs
of that method.

:::caution
To prevent off-by-one bugs you should clearly decide to store either the consumed offset, or the next-offset. Read more
about this on
the [preventing duplicates](preventing-duplicates.md#be-clear-about-what-offset-you-persist-to-prevent-off-by-one-bugs)
page.
:::

---

## Preventing Duplicates

In zio-kafka processing of records runs asynchronously with partition management. This brings substantial performance
advantages but causes some records to be consumed and processed _twice_ when a rebalance occurs. To prevent this,
since version 2.7.1 zio-kafka supports a new mode in which we prevent duplicates due to rebalances. You can enable it
as follows:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withGroupId("group")
    .withRebalanceSafeCommits(true)       // enable rebalance-safe-commits mode
    .withMaxRebalanceDuration(30.seconds) // defaults to 3 minutes
    .withCommitTimeout(15.seconds)        // defaults to 15 seconds
```

With rebalance-safe-commits mode enabled, rebalances are held up for up to max-rebalance-duration to wait for pending
commits to be completed. Once pending commits are completed, it is safe for another consumer in the group to take over
a partition.

For this to work correctly, your program must process a chunk (of up to `max.poll.records` records) within the
configured max-rebalance-duration. The clock starts the moment the chunk is pushed into the stream and ends when the
commits for these records complete. Zio-kafka uses `commit-timeout` as the worse case time to commit. Therefore, with
the default settings, your program has 2 minutes and 45 seconds until the offsets should be committed.

It is probably clear now that your program should commit the offsets of consumed records. The most straightforward way
is to commit to the kafka brokers. This is done by calling `Offset#commit` on the offset of consumed records (see
[offsets and committing](offsets-and-committing.md)). However, there are more options: external commits and transactional producing.

#### Commit to an external system

When you commit to an external system (e.g. by writing to a relational database) the zio-kafka consumer needs to know
about those commits before it can work in rebalance-safe-commits mode. Inform zio-kafka about external commits by
invoking method `Consumer#registerExternalCommits(offsetBatch: OffsetBatch)` (available since zio-kafka 2.10.0).

Here is what this could look like:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

trait Database {
  def store(offset: Offset): Task[Unit]
}

def consumeAndStore(consumer: Consumer, database: Database): Task[Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("topic2000"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .mapZIO { record =>
      database.store(record.offset) *> // <-- the external commit
        consumer.registerExternalCommits(OffsetBatch(record.offset))
    }
    .runDrain
```

See [starting offsets](partition-assignment-and-offset-retrieval.md#consumer-starting-offsets--offset-retrieval)
for letting a consumer start consuming a partition from the offset you persisted after a rebalance.

##### Be clear about what offset you persist to prevent off-by-one bugs!

In the example above `record.offset` represents the offset of the consumed record. However, in Kafka you always commit
the _next offset_. It represents the record's offset another consumer should continue from after a rebalance.
Normally the _next offset_ is the offset of the consumed record `+ 1`. The difference can be a bit larger when Kafka
placed some 'control records' on the partition. Since it is fine to consume control records multiple times (they are
invisible), adding `1` to get the next offset is fine. Since zio-kafka 4.0.0 it is also possible to get the exact
next-offset with `record.nextOffset` (also available as `record.offset.nextOffset`).

:::caution
You should decide on what offset you want to persist per partition, either the _consumed offset_, or the _next offset_.
:::

Unless there are good reasons to do otherwise, we recommend you persist the 'next offset'.

**Persisting the consumed offset**

- Per partition, persist the offset `record.offset.offset` (ideally persist `record.offset.leaderEpoch` as well).
- From your `OffsetRetrieval.External` implementation, return the persisted offset + 1 (ideally, also include the
  persisted leader-epoch).

**Persisting the next offset**

- Per partition, persist the offset `record.offset.offset + 1`, or better yet: `record.nextOffset.offset()` (ideally
  persist `record.nextOffset.leaderEpoch()` as well).
- From your `OffsetRetrieval.External` implementation, return the persisted offset (ideally, also include the persisted
  leader-epoch).

#### Commit with a transactional producer

Transactional producing is described in [transactions](transactions.md).

### Long-running processes / slow consumers

When rebalance-safe-commits mode is enabled, consumers have tighter dead-lines. Besides a suitable `max.poll.records`
and `max.poll.interval.ms` (see [consumer tuning](consumer-tuning.md#long-running-processes--slow-consumers)), a
consumer must also be able to process `max.poll.records` within `maxRebalanceDuration`, with some margin to complete
commits.

With the default values of `500` for `max.poll.records`, 3 minutes for `maxRebalanceDuration` (which is 3/5 of 5
minutes for `max.poll.interval.ms`), and 15 seconds for `commitTimeout`, a consumer must be able to process and commit
`500` records in 2 minutes, 45 seconds (_3 records per second_). **This is a hard threshold.** Change the settings such
that there is sufficient head-room for busy services, network delays, garbage collections or reduced CPU capacity due to
other processes.

When rebalance-safe-commits mode is enabled, zio-kafka configures the Range Assignor by default (since zio-kafka 3.2.0). In case the consumer can handle less than 10 times the minimum records per second, it is important to keep the Range Assignor: do not override `partition.assignment.strategy` with a cooperative assignor (see [PR 1576](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka/pull/1576) for an extensive explanation).

Settings described in this section can be changed as follows:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val settings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
  .withRebalanceSafeCommits(true)
  .withMaxPollRecords(1)
  .withMaxPollInterval(15.minutes)
  .withMaxRebalanceDuration(4.minutes)
  .withCommitTimeout(10.seconds)
```

### More information

There is more information in the scaladocs of `ConsumerSettings` and the description of
[pull request #1098](https://github.com/zio/zio-kafka/pull/1098) that introduced this feature.
You can also watch the presentation
[Making ZIO-Kafka Safer And Faster](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MJoRwEyyVxM). The relevant part starts at 10:24.

---

## Producer

`Producer` is the **zio-kafka client for writing records to Kafka**. It wraps the Java `KafkaProducer` in a ZIO-friendly API: every produce call is an effect, serialization uses zio-kafka's effectful [`Serializer`](serialization-and-deserialization.md), and the producer's lifetime is tied to a `Scope` so it is always closed. The fundamental operations are `Producer#produce`, `Producer#produceAsync` and their chunk-based variants `Producer#produceChunk` and `Producer#produceChunkAsync`.

`Producer`:

- Two-Layer Async — the async variants separate "accepted by the producer" from "acknowledged by the broker", so you can send many records and await all acknowledgements at once.
- Batch-Oriented — the producer handles records in chunks internally; a single record is a chunk of one.
- Backpressured — records wait in a bounded send queue, so a fast caller slows down instead of exhausting memory.
- Shareable — one `Producer` can serve many fibers.

The trait has the following shape (bodies and overloads omitted; see the sections below for every overload):

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produce[R, K, V](record: ProducerRecord[K, V], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, RecordMetadata]
  def produceAsync[R, K, V](record: ProducerRecord[K, V], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, Task[RecordMetadata]]
  def produceChunk[R, K, V](records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[K, V]], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, Chunk[RecordMetadata]]
  def produceChunkAsync[R, K, V](records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[K, V]], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]]]
  def produceChunkAsyncWithFailures(records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]]): UIO[UIO[Chunk[Either[Throwable, RecordMetadata]]]]
  final def produceAll[R, K, V](keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): ZPipeline[R, Throwable, ProducerRecord[K, V], RecordMetadata]

  def partitionsFor(topic: String): Task[Chunk[PartitionInfo]]
  def flush: Task[Unit]
  def metrics: Task[Map[MetricName, Metric]]
}
```

`ProducerRecord`, `RecordMetadata`, `PartitionInfo`, `MetricName` and `Metric` are the Kafka client's own classes (`org.apache.kafka.clients.producer` and `org.apache.kafka.common`).

### Usage

To produce a record, we build `ProducerSettings`, provide them to the `Producer.live` layer, and call `Producer#produce` with a serializer for the key and one for the value:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

object ProducerApp extends ZIOAppDefault {
  val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

  val program: ZIO[Producer, Throwable, Unit] =
    for {
      producer <- ZIO.service[Producer]
      metadata <- producer.produce("orders", "order-1", "created", Serde.string, Serde.string)
      _        <- ZIO.logInfo(s"Written to partition ${metadata.partition()} at offset ${metadata.offset()}")
    } yield ()

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers).withClientId("orders-producer")),
      Producer.live
    )
}
```

`Producer#produce` completes when the broker acknowledges the record. For higher throughput, see [Choosing a Produce Method](#choosing-a-produce-method).

### Creating a Producer

A producer holds network connections and a background fiber, so every constructor returns it inside a `Scope` (or a layer, which manages the scope for you). When the scope closes, the producer stops its background fibers. `Producer.make` and `Producer.live` also close the underlying Java producer; with `Producer.fromJavaProducer` you close it yourself.

#### Producer.make

`Producer.make` creates a scoped producer from `ProducerSettings`. It validates the SSL endpoint configuration, creates the Java `KafkaProducer` on the blocking thread pool, and closes it with `ProducerSettings#closeTimeout` when the scope ends:

```scala
object Producer {
  def make(settings: ProducerSettings): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Producer]
}
```

To use the producer inside a single scoped workflow:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val program: Task[Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      producer <- Producer.make(ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers))
      _        <- producer.produce("events", "key", "value", Serde.string, Serde.string)
    } yield ()
  }
```

#### Producer.live

`Producer.live` is a layer that reads `ProducerSettings` from the environment and calls `Producer.make`:

```scala
object Producer {
  val live: RLayer[ProducerSettings, Producer]
}
```

To build the layer and share one producer across the application:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val producerLayer: TaskLayer[Producer] =
  ZLayer.succeed(ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers)) >>> Producer.live
```

#### Producer.fromJavaProducer

`Producer.fromJavaProducer` wraps a Java producer that you create yourself, for example to configure it in a way `ProducerSettings` does not cover. The Java producer must use byte-array keys and values, because zio-kafka serializes records itself:

```scala
object Producer {
  def fromJavaProducer(
    javaProducer: org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Producer[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]],
    settings: ProducerSettings
  ): ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Producer]
}
```

You are responsible for creating and closing the Java producer. From `settings`, only the zio-kafka parts apply (send buffer size, auth error retry schedule, diagnostics and metrics); the Kafka properties and `ProducerSettings#closeTimeout` are not used. To create and close the Java producer in the same scope:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.ByteArraySerializer
import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters._

val config: Map[String, AnyRef] = Map("bootstrap.servers" -> "localhost:9092")

val producer: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Producer] =
  for {
    javaProducer <- ZIO.acquireRelease(
                      ZIO.attemptBlocking(
                        new KafkaProducer[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]](
                          config.asJava,
                          new ByteArraySerializer(),
                          new ByteArraySerializer()
                        )
                      )
                    )(p => ZIO.attemptBlocking(p.close()).orDie)
    producer     <- Producer.fromJavaProducer(javaProducer, ProducerSettings())
  } yield producer
```

Because the scope releases resources in reverse order, the zio-kafka producer stops before the Java producer closes.

### Producing Records

The produce methods differ in two ways: whether they take one record or a chunk, and whether they wait for the broker's acknowledgement or hand it back as a separate effect. This section starts with a guide to choosing, then covers each method.

#### Choosing a Produce Method

Waiting for an acknowledgement costs a network round trip. A method that waits for every record before sending the next one is easy to reason about but slow. The async variants let you send many records and wait for all their acknowledgements once, and the chunk variants put a whole batch into the send queue in one step. As a rule of thumb, use `Producer#produce` for low volumes or when each record must be confirmed before the next, `Producer#produceAsync` when records arrive one at a time and throughput matters, `Producer#produceChunk` or `Producer#produceChunkAsync` when you already have a batch (the async one gives the highest throughput, because sending one chunk overlaps with waiting for the acknowledgement of another), `Producer#produceChunkAsyncWithFailures` when you need to know which records of a chunk failed, and `Producer#produceAll` to produce every element of a `ZStream`.

For streaming applications that also commit consumer offsets, [Consuming, Producing and Committing Offsets](consuming-producing-and-committing-offsets.md) shows how to combine `Producer#produceChunkAsync` with `ZStream#buffer` to keep the producer busy while acknowledgements arrive.

#### Byte Arrays or Serializers

Every produce method except `Producer#produceChunkAsyncWithFailures` and `Producer#produceAll` comes in two forms. One takes `ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]` values that are already serialized. The other takes a `ProducerRecord[K, V]` plus a key `Serializer[R, K]` and a value `Serializer[R, V]`, and serializes the record before sending it; serialization runs as part of the effect and can use the environment `R`. The single-record methods also accept `topic`, `key` and `value` directly instead of a `ProducerRecord`:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produce(record: ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]): Task[RecordMetadata]
  def produce[R, K, V](record: ProducerRecord[K, V], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, RecordMetadata]
  def produce[R, K, V](topic: String, key: K, value: V, keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, RecordMetadata]
}
```

Use a full `ProducerRecord` when you need to set the partition, the timestamp or [record headers](record-headers.md). The serializers receive the record's headers and may read or add to them. See [Serialization and Deserialization](serialization-and-deserialization.md) for the predefined serdes such as `Serde.string` and `Serde.long`.

:::note
Because `ProducerRecord` is a Java class, give its type parameters explicitly when the compiler cannot infer them, for example `new ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]](topic, key, value)`. Build a new `ProducerRecord` for every send instead of reusing one: the Kafka client marks the headers of a sent byte-array record read-only, and a serializer may add headers to the record you pass in.
:::

#### Producing One Record and Waiting

`Producer#produce` puts one record in the send queue and completes with its `RecordMetadata` (topic, partition, offset and timestamp) after the broker acknowledges it. It has the three overloads shown in [Byte Arrays or Serializers](#byte-arrays-or-serializers). To produce a record with a header and an explicit partition:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.{ ProducerRecord, RecordMetadata }

def produceOrder(producer: Producer): Task[RecordMetadata] = {
  val record = new ProducerRecord[String, String]("orders", 0, "order-1", "created")
  record.headers().add("source", "web-shop".getBytes("UTF-8"))
  producer.produce(record, Serde.string, Serde.string)
}
```

#### Producing Without Waiting

`Producer#produceAsync` returns an effect with two layers. The outer effect completes when the record is in the producer's send queue; it waits while the queue is full. Its result, the inner `Task`, completes when the broker acknowledges the record:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produceAsync(record: ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]): Task[Task[RecordMetadata]]
  def produceAsync[R, K, V](record: ProducerRecord[K, V], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, Task[RecordMetadata]]
  def produceAsync[R, K, V](topic: String, key: K, value: V, keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, Task[RecordMetadata]]
}
```

Running only the outer effect for many records and then awaiting all inner tasks lets the Kafka client batch the records into fewer requests. To enqueue 100 records and then wait for all acknowledgements:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.RecordMetadata

def produceMany(producer: Producer): Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]] =
  for {
    acks     <- ZIO.foreach(Chunk.fromIterable(1 to 100)) { i =>
                  producer.produceAsync("events", i.toString, s"event $i", Serde.string, Serde.string)
                }
    metadata <- ZIO.collectAll(acks)
  } yield metadata
```

Every `Producer#produceAsync` call is one entry in the send queue, whose capacity is `ProducerSettings#sendBufferSize` (4096 by default). If you produce many records one by one, consider raising it, for example to `10240`, or switch to the chunk variants.

#### Producing a Chunk

`Producer#produceChunk` sends a `Chunk` of records as one batch and completes with their metadata, in the same order as the input, after the broker acknowledges all of them:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produceChunk(records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]]): Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]]
  def produceChunk[R, K, V](records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[K, V]], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, Chunk[RecordMetadata]]
}
```

To produce three records in one call:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.{ ProducerRecord, RecordMetadata }

def produceBatch(producer: Producer): Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]] = {
  val records = Chunk(
    new ProducerRecord("orders", "order-1", "created"),
    new ProducerRecord("orders", "order-2", "created"),
    new ProducerRecord("orders", "order-1", "paid")
  )
  producer.produceChunk(records, Serde.string, Serde.string)
}
```

If any record fails, the whole effect fails, even though other records of the chunk may already be written. See [Error Handling](#error-handling).

#### Producing a Chunk Without Waiting

`Producer#produceChunkAsync` is the two-layer form of `Producer#produceChunk`. The outer effect completes when the chunk is in the send queue, and the inner task completes when the broker acknowledges every record of the chunk:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produceChunkAsync(records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]]): Task[Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]]]
  def produceChunkAsync[R, K, V](records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[K, V]], keySerializer: Serializer[R, K], valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]): RIO[R, Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]]]
}
```

This variant gives the highest throughput: while one chunk waits for acknowledgements, the next chunk is already on its way. To enqueue two chunks before awaiting either:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.{ ProducerRecord, RecordMetadata }

def produceTwoBatches(
  producer: Producer,
  first: Chunk[ProducerRecord[String, String]],
  second: Chunk[ProducerRecord[String, String]]
): Task[Chunk[RecordMetadata]] =
  for {
    ackFirst  <- producer.produceChunkAsync(first, Serde.string, Serde.string)
    ackSecond <- producer.produceChunkAsync(second, Serde.string, Serde.string)
    metadata1 <- ackFirst
    metadata2 <- ackSecond
  } yield metadata1 ++ metadata2
```

#### Per-Record Results

`Producer#produceChunkAsyncWithFailures` reports a result for each record instead of failing the whole chunk. It never fails: the inner effect completes with one `Either[Throwable, RecordMetadata]` per input record, in input order:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produceChunkAsyncWithFailures(records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]]): UIO[UIO[Chunk[Either[Throwable, RecordMetadata]]]]
}

object Producer {
  case object PublishOmittedException
      extends RuntimeException("Publish omitted due to a publish error for a previous record in the chunk")
      with NoStackTrace
}
```

When a record fails while the chunk is still being handed to the Java producer, the producer does not attempt the remaining records of the chunk; their result is `Left(Producer.PublishOmittedException)`. Records handed over before the failure was reported are still sent and get their own result. This variant accepts only byte-array records, because a failing serializer cannot be reported per record. Serialize the records first, for example with `Serializer#serialize`. To log which records of a chunk failed:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord

def produceAndReport(producer: Producer, records: Chunk[ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]]): UIO[Unit] =
  for {
    await   <- producer.produceChunkAsyncWithFailures(records)
    results <- await
    _       <- ZIO.foreachDiscard(results.zipWithIndex) {
                 case (Right(_), _)                                  => ZIO.unit
                 case (Left(Producer.PublishOmittedException), index) => ZIO.logWarning(s"Record $index was not sent")
                 case (Left(error), index)                           => ZIO.logError(s"Record $index failed: $error")
               }
  } yield ()
```

#### Producing a Stream

`Producer#produceAll` is a `ZPipeline` that produces every record of a stream and emits its `RecordMetadata`. It calls `Producer#produceChunk` once per chunk of the stream and waits for the acknowledgements before pulling the next chunk, so the stream's chunk size is the batch size:

```scala
trait Producer {
  final def produceAll[R, K, V](
    keySerializer: Serializer[R, K],
    valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]
  ): ZPipeline[R, Throwable, ProducerRecord[K, V], RecordMetadata]
}
```

To produce a stream of 1000 records:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord

def produceStream(producer: Producer): Task[Unit] =
  ZStream
    .fromIterable(1 to 1000)
    .map(i => new ProducerRecord("events", i.toString, s"event $i"))
    .via(producer.produceAll(Serde.string, Serde.string))
    .runDrain
```

Operators such as `ZStream#mapZIO` and `ZStream#tap` turn a stream into chunks of one record, which makes `Producer#produceAll` send one record per request. See [Avoiding Chunk Breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md).

### Error Handling

A produce effect can fail at two moments. With the serializer overloads, serialization runs before anything is queued, so a serializer failure fails the outer effect and nothing of that call is sent. Send failures reported by Kafka fail the effect that waits for the acknowledgement: the inner task of the async variants, or the single effect of `Producer#produce` and `Producer#produceChunk`.

For chunks, `Producer#produceChunk`, `Producer#produceChunkAsync` and `Producer#produceAll` fail with the first error of the chunk. The other records of that chunk may or may not be written: records sent before the failure is noticed can succeed, and the remaining ones are not attempted. When you need to know which records were written, use `Producer#produceChunkAsyncWithFailures`.

The Java producer already retries transient errors according to Kafka's `retries` and `delivery.timeout.ms` properties. On top of that, zio-kafka can retry records that fail with an `AuthorizationException` or `AuthenticationException`, which some brokers report while access rights are still being set up. The retry is off by default (`Schedule.stop`); enable it with `ProducerSettings#withAuthErrorRetrySchedule`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val settings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers)
    .withAuthErrorRetrySchedule(Schedule.recurs(5) && Schedule.spaced(500.millis))
```

For a chunk, only the failed and omitted records are sent again, so a retry can change the order in which records are written. For detecting revoked read access on the consumer side, see [Detecting Authorization Failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md).

### Other Operations

Besides producing, `Producer` exposes three operations that pass through to the Java producer. Each runs on the blocking thread pool:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def partitionsFor(topic: String): Task[Chunk[PartitionInfo]]
  def flush: Task[Unit]
  def metrics: Task[Map[MetricName, Metric]]
}
```

`Producer#partitionsFor` returns the partition metadata of a topic, which is useful for choosing a partition yourself. `Producer#flush` blocks until every record in the Java producer's buffer has been sent. `Producer#metrics` returns the Java client's metrics; zio-kafka's own producer metrics are covered in [Metrics](metrics.md). To count the partitions of a topic:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._

def partitionCount(producer: Producer, topic: String): Task[Int] =
  producer.partitionsFor(topic).map(_.size)
```

### ProducerSettings

`ProducerSettings` is an immutable case class holding the Kafka client properties plus zio-kafka's own options. Build it with `ProducerSettings.apply(bootstrapServers)` and refine it with the `with*` methods; this stays source compatible when new fields are added. Any Kafka producer property can be set with `ProducerSettings#withProperty` or `ProducerSettings#withProperties`, and the common ones, such as `client.id`, `linger.ms`, `compression.type` and `enable.idempotence`, also have their own `with*` method. The zio-kafka options include the close timeout, the size of the send queue (`ProducerSettings#withSendBufferSize`, counted in chunks, one per produce call, not in records), the retry schedule for authorization errors (see [Error Handling](#error-handling)), diagnostics and metrics. For every setting and its default, see the [`ProducerSettings` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/producer/ProducerSettings.html).

`ProducerSettings#driverSettings` returns the properties passed to the Java producer. To see which Kafka properties the `with*` methods set:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._

val exampleSettings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
    .withClientId("orders-producer")
    .withLinger(20.millis)
    .withCompression(ProducerCompression.Zstd(3))
```

The resulting driver properties are:

```scala
exampleSettings.driverSettings
// res12: Map[String, AnyRef] = Map(
//   "compression.type" -> "zstd",
//   "bootstrap.servers" -> "localhost:9092",
//   "client.id" -> "orders-producer",
//   "compression.zstd.level" -> 3,
//   "linger.ms" -> "20"
// )
```

Higher `linger.ms` values give larger batches, which also improves compression, at the cost of latency. With idempotence enabled (Kafka's default), the broker discards duplicates caused by the client's own retries. For transactional producing, wrap the settings in `TransactionalProducerSettings`, see [Transactions](transactions.md).

#### Compression

`ProducerCompression` selects the codec for `ProducerSettings#withCompression`. Kafka compresses whole batches, so better batching (see `ProducerSettings#withLinger`) gives a better compression ratio. The codecs are `NoCompression`, `Gzip`, `Snappy`, `Lz4` and `Zstd`; `Gzip`, `Lz4` and `Zstd` accept a compression level as a constructor argument. For the valid levels and their defaults, see the [`ProducerCompression` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/producer/ProducerCompression$.html).

To compress with LZ4 at its default level:

```scala
import zio.kafka.producer._

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val settings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers).withCompression(ProducerCompression.Lz4())
```

#### Diagnostics and Metrics

`ProducerSettings#withDiagnostics` registers a callback for `ProducerEvent`s: `ProducerEvent.RecordsOffered` just before a batch is offered to the send queue, `ProducerEvent.RecordsSent` when the broker has handled it (with the indices of failed records), and `ProducerEvent.ProducerFinalized` when the producer closes. Events of the same batch share a `batchId`. The callback runs in a separate fiber, and unhandled events queue up in memory, so it must keep up. See [Diagnostics](diagnostics.md) for the full event model.

The producer records zio-kafka metrics such as produce latency, batch size and send queue size through ZIO metrics. When an application runs several producers, label their metrics with `ProducerSettings#withMetricsLabels`. To send metrics elsewhere, or to turn them off with `ProducerMetricsObserver.NoOp`, use `ProducerSettings#withMetricsObserver`; labels are then ignored. To label a producer's metrics:

```scala
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.metrics.MetricLabel

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")

val settings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers).withMetricsLabels(Set(MetricLabel("producer-id", "orders")))
```

See [Metrics](metrics.md) for the list of metrics.

These pages build on `Producer`:

- [Record Headers](record-headers.md) explains how to attach metadata to produced records.
- [Transactions](transactions.md) covers `TransactionalProducer`, which produces records and commits consumer offsets atomically.
- [Consumer](consumer.md) and [Offsets and Committing](offsets-and-committing.md) cover the reading side of consume-transform-produce applications.
- [Writing Tests](writing-tests.md) shows how to create a producer against an embedded Kafka broker with the testkit.

## Record Headers

A Kafka record carries an optional list of **headers** next to its key and value. Each header has a `String` key and an `Array[Byte]` value (which may be `null`). Headers keep the order in which they are added, and several headers can share a key. Applications use them for metadata that does not belong in the payload, such as a content type, a schema version, a trace id or the name of the producing service.

Zio-kafka has no header type of its own. It uses the Kafka client's `org.apache.kafka.common.header.Headers` and `Header` interfaces directly, and passes them along at every step:

- When producing, the headers of a `ProducerRecord` are written with the record.
- When consuming, `CommittableRecord#record` returns the Kafka `ConsumerRecord`, whose `headers()` method returns the headers.
- Every `Serializer` and `Deserializer` receives the record's headers as a parameter.

### Adding Headers When Producing

A `ProducerRecord` always has a mutable `Headers` collection, so the simplest way to add a header is `Headers#add` on `ProducerRecord#headers`. To produce a record with two headers:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.{ ProducerRecord, RecordMetadata }
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8

def produceOrder(producer: Producer): Task[RecordMetadata] = {
  val record = new ProducerRecord("orders", "order-1", "created")
  record.headers().add("source", "web-shop".getBytes(UTF_8))
  record.headers().add("trace-id", "4bf92f3577b34da6".getBytes(UTF_8))
  producer.produce(record, Serde.string, Serde.string)
}
```

You can also pass the headers to the `ProducerRecord` constructor, which accepts any `java.lang.Iterable[Header]` after the topic, partition, timestamp, key and value. Pass `null` for the partition and timestamp to let Kafka choose them. Kafka's own implementations are `RecordHeader` and `RecordHeaders` in the `org.apache.kafka.common.header.internals` package. That package is not part of Kafka's documented public API, but the classes are widely used (zio-kafka's own tests use them). To build the headers first and then the record:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.{ ProducerRecord, RecordMetadata }
import org.apache.kafka.common.header.internals.RecordHeaders
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8

def produceWithHeaders(producer: Producer): Task[RecordMetadata] = {
  val headers = new RecordHeaders()
    .add("source", "web-shop".getBytes(UTF_8))
    .add("schema-version", "2".getBytes(UTF_8))

  val record = new ProducerRecord[String, String]("orders", null, null, "order-1", "created", headers)
  producer.produce(record, Serde.string, Serde.string)
}
```

Headers work the same with every produce method of the [Producer](producer.md), including the chunk variants and `Producer#produceAll`, and with the [transactional producer](transactions.md): `Transaction#produce`, `Transaction#produceChunk` and `Transaction#produceChunkBatch` send records through the same code path.

:::warning
Create a new `ProducerRecord` for every send. When you produce a byte-array record, the Kafka client marks that record's headers read-only, so a later `Headers#add` on it throws an `IllegalStateException`. With the serializer overloads, zio-kafka sends a copy, but a serializer that adds headers changes the record you pass in (see [Header-Aware Serializers and Deserializers](#header-aware-serializers-and-deserializers)).
:::

### Reading Headers When Consuming

A `CommittableRecord` has no header accessor of its own; read them from the wrapped Kafka record with `record.record.headers()`. The `Headers` interface offers `Headers#lastHeader` for the most recent header with a key (or `null` when there is none), `Headers#headers` for all headers with a key, and iteration over all headers. Since both a missing header and a header value can be `null`, wrap them in `Option`. To read a header as a string and to list all headers of a record:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters._
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8

def headerValue[K, V](record: CommittableRecord[K, V], key: String): Option[String] =
  Option(record.record.headers().lastHeader(key))
    .flatMap(header => Option(header.value()))
    .map(bytes => new String(bytes, UTF_8))

def allHeaders[K, V](record: CommittableRecord[K, V]): List[(String, Option[String])] =
  record.record
    .headers()
    .asScala
    .map(header => header.key() -> Option(header.value()).map(new String(_, UTF_8)))
    .toList
```

In a consumer stream, read the headers in an operator that keeps the chunk structure, such as `ZStream#map`. To pair each record's `source` header with its offset for later committing:

```scala
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8

def sources(consumer: Consumer): ZStream[Any, Throwable, (String, Offset)] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("orders"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .map { record =>
      val source = Option(record.record.headers().lastHeader("source"))
        .flatMap(header => Option(header.value()))
        .map(new String(_, UTF_8))
        .getOrElse("unknown")
      (source, record.offset)
    }
```

`Consumer#consumeWith` hands your function a `ConsumerRecord` directly, so there you call `record.headers()`. See [Consumer](consumer.md) for the stream methods and [Offsets and Committing](offsets-and-committing.md) for committing the collected offsets.

### Header-Aware Serializers and Deserializers

Every `Serializer` and `Deserializer` receives the topic and the headers along with the value, so the encoding of a record can depend on its headers. The function-based constructors make this explicit:

```scala
object Serializer {
  def apply[R, A](ser: (String, Headers, A) => RIO[R, Array[Byte]]): Serializer[R, A]
}

object Deserializer {
  def apply[R, A](deser: (String, Headers, Array[Byte]) => RIO[R, A]): Deserializer[R, A]
}
```

A serializer may also add headers. When producing with a serializer, zio-kafka runs the key serializer and then the value serializer on the record's headers, and writes the record with the headers as they are afterwards. The serializer below encodes a `Greeting` as JSON and records that in a `content-type` header. The deserializer reads the header and accepts both the JSON format and an older `name:message` text format, which it assumes when the header is missing:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.json._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8

final case class Greeting(name: String, message: String)

object Greeting {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Greeting] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Greeting]
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Greeting] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Greeting]
}

val ContentTypeHeader = "content-type"

val greetingSerializer: Serializer[Any, Greeting] =
  Serializer { (_, headers, greeting) =>
    ZIO.attempt {
      headers.add(ContentTypeHeader, "application/json".getBytes(UTF_8))
      greeting.toJson.getBytes(UTF_8)
    }
  }

val greetingDeserializer: Deserializer[Any, Greeting] =
  Deserializer { (_, headers, data) =>
    val contentType = Option(headers.lastHeader(ContentTypeHeader))
      .flatMap(header => Option(header.value()))
      .map(new String(_, UTF_8))
    val text = new String(data, UTF_8)

    contentType match {
      case Some("application/json") =>
        ZIO.fromEither(text.fromJson[Greeting]).mapError(new RuntimeException(_))
      case Some("text/plain") | None =>
        text.split(":", 2) match {
          case Array(name, message) => ZIO.succeed(Greeting(name, message))
          case _                    => ZIO.fail(new RuntimeException(s"Invalid greeting: $text"))
        }
      case Some(other) =>
        ZIO.fail(new RuntimeException(s"Unsupported content type: $other"))
    }
  }

val greetingSerde: Serde[Any, Greeting] = Serde(greetingDeserializer)(greetingSerializer)
```

Because the serializer changes the headers of the `ProducerRecord` you pass in, producing the same record object twice adds the header twice; create a new record for every send. The predefined serdes such as `Serde.string` ignore headers. See [Serialization and Deserialization](serialization-and-deserialization.md) for more ways to build serdes.

### Headers in CommittableRecord#deserializeWith

`CommittableRecord#deserializeWith` turns a record of byte arrays into a typed record. It passes the record's headers to both deserializers, and the new record keeps the same headers. This is useful when you consume with `Serde.byteArray` and deserialize inside the stream, where you can handle failures per record. Reusing `greetingDeserializer` from the previous section:

```scala
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka.consumer._

def greetings(consumer: Consumer): ZStream[Any, Throwable, CommittableRecord[String, Greeting]] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics("greetings"), Serde.byteArray, Serde.byteArray)
    .mapChunksZIO(records => ZIO.foreach(records)(_.deserializeWith(Serde.string, greetingDeserializer)))
```

The deserializers you pass to `Consumer#plainStream` and the other stream methods go through `CommittableRecord#deserializeWith` as well, so they receive the headers in the same way.

## Security: TLS and Credentials

Zio-kafka clients connect to Kafka through the Java clients, so encryption (TLS) and authentication (mutual TLS or SASL) are configured with the usual Java client properties. Zio-kafka adds two things on top: `KafkaCredentialStore`, which turns PEM-encoded certificates into the TLS properties, and an SSL endpoint check that catches a client configured for plain text that connects to a TLS listener, a mistake that otherwise crashes the application with an `OutOfMemoryError`.

### Security Protocols

The Java property `security.protocol` (constant `CommonClientConfigs.SECURITY_PROTOCOL_CONFIG`) selects how a client talks to the brokers. It must match the broker listener the bootstrap servers point to:

| `security.protocol`   | Encryption | Authentication                                                            |
| --------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PLAINTEXT` (default) | None       | None                                                                      |
| `SSL`                 | TLS        | Optional: a client certificate (mutual TLS)                               |
| `SASL_PLAINTEXT`      | None       | SASL (`PLAIN`, `SCRAM-SHA-256`, `SCRAM-SHA-512`, `OAUTHBEARER`, `GSSAPI`) |
| `SASL_SSL`            | TLS        | SASL, as above                                                            |

Every zio-kafka settings type accepts arbitrary Java client properties, so any security setup the Java clients support also works in zio-kafka:

| Settings type                   | Generic properties                                                       | TLS credentials                          |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| `ConsumerSettings`              | `ConsumerSettings#withProperty`, `ConsumerSettings#withProperties`       | `ConsumerSettings#withCredentials`       |
| `ProducerSettings`              | `ProducerSettings#withProperty`, `ProducerSettings#withProperties`       | `ProducerSettings#withCredentials`       |
| `AdminClientSettings`           | `AdminClientSettings#withProperty`, `AdminClientSettings#withProperties` | `AdminClientSettings#withCredentials`    |
| `TransactionalProducerSettings` | Configure the wrapped `ProducerSettings`                                 | Configure the wrapped `ProducerSettings` |

`TransactionalProducerSettings` has no `with` methods of its own: configure security on a `ProducerSettings` and pass it to `TransactionalProducerSettings.apply(producerSettings, transactionalId)`. In all settings types, a property set later replaces a property with the same key set earlier.

### TLS from PEM Strings

`KafkaCredentialStore` holds a set of TLS properties. Its only constructor, `KafkaCredentialStore.fromPemStrings`, takes PEM-encoded strings, which is convenient when the certificates come from environment variables or a secret manager rather than from key store files:

```scala
sealed trait KafkaCredentialStore {
  def properties: Map[String, String]
}

object KafkaCredentialStore {
  def fromPemStrings(caCertificate: String, clientPrivateKey: String, clientCertificate: String): KafkaCredentialStore
}
```

`KafkaCredentialStore.fromPemStrings` sets the following properties. It replaces every newline in the PEM strings with a space, so the strings can be passed as single-line property values:

| Property                         | Value                                                    |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `security.protocol`              | `SSL`                                                    |
| `ssl.truststore.type`            | `PEM`                                                    |
| `ssl.truststore.certificates`    | `caCertificate`: the CA certificate(s) the client trusts |
| `ssl.keystore.type`              | `PEM`                                                    |
| `ssl.keystore.key`               | `clientPrivateKey`: the client's private key             |
| `ssl.keystore.certificate.chain` | `clientCertificate`: the client's certificate chain      |

The result is a mutual TLS setup: the client verifies the brokers with the CA certificate, and the brokers authenticate the client by its certificate. The Java client only accepts a private key in PKCS#8 format; if the key is encrypted, also set its password with `withProperty("ssl.key.password", ...)`.

`ConsumerSettings#withCredentials`, `ProducerSettings#withCredentials` and `AdminClientSettings#withCredentials` add `KafkaCredentialStore#properties` to the settings. To read the PEM strings from environment variables and use the same credentials for a consumer, a producer and an admin client:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.admin.AdminClientSettings
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings
import zio.kafka.producer.ProducerSettings
import zio.kafka.security.KafkaCredentialStore

val bootstrapServers = List("kafka-1.example.com:9093", "kafka-2.example.com:9093")

def requiredEnv(name: String): Task[String] =
  System.env(name).someOrFail(new IllegalStateException(s"Missing environment variable $name"))

val credentials: Task[KafkaCredentialStore] =
  for {
    ca   <- requiredEnv("KAFKA_CA_PEM")
    key  <- requiredEnv("KAFKA_CLIENT_KEY_PEM")
    cert <- requiredEnv("KAFKA_CLIENT_CERT_PEM")
  } yield KafkaCredentialStore.fromPemStrings(caCertificate = ca, clientPrivateKey = key, clientCertificate = cert)

val settings: Task[(ConsumerSettings, ProducerSettings, AdminClientSettings)] =
  credentials.map { creds =>
    (
      ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers).withGroupId("billing").withCredentials(creds),
      ProducerSettings(bootstrapServers).withCredentials(creds),
      AdminClientSettings(bootstrapServers).withCredentials(creds)
    )
  }
```

`KafkaCredentialStore.fromPemStrings` always includes a client key and certificate. For one-way TLS, where only the client verifies the brokers, set the properties yourself. To trust a private CA from a PEM string, without a client certificate:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.CommonClientConfigs
import org.apache.kafka.common.config.SslConfigs
import zio.kafka.producer.ProducerSettings

val caPem: String = "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n...\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----"

val settings: ProducerSettings =
  ProducerSettings(List("kafka.example.com:9093")).withProperties(
    CommonClientConfigs.SECURITY_PROTOCOL_CONFIG    -> "SSL",
    SslConfigs.SSL_TRUSTSTORE_TYPE_CONFIG           -> "PEM",
    SslConfigs.SSL_TRUSTSTORE_CERTIFICATES_CONFIG   -> caPem.replace('\n', ' ')
  )
```

When the brokers use certificates from a public CA that the JVM already trusts, `security.protocol` set to `SSL` is enough. Key store and trust store files (JKS or PKCS12) work too, through `ssl.truststore.location`, `ssl.truststore.password`, `ssl.keystore.location` and the related properties.

### SASL Authentication

SASL authenticates the client with a user name and password (or a token) instead of a certificate. Configure it with three properties: `security.protocol` set to `SASL_SSL` (or `SASL_PLAINTEXT` on an unencrypted listener), `sasl.mechanism` (constant `SaslConfigs.SASL_MECHANISM`), and `sasl.jaas.config` (constant `SaslConfigs.SASL_JAAS_CONFIG`) with the login module and credentials. To connect a consumer with SCRAM over TLS:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.CommonClientConfigs
import org.apache.kafka.common.config.SaslConfigs
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val username = "billing-service"
val password = "change-me" // load from a secret store in real code

val settings: ConsumerSettings =
  ConsumerSettings(List("kafka.example.com:9094"))
    .withGroupId("billing")
    .withProperties(
      CommonClientConfigs.SECURITY_PROTOCOL_CONFIG -> "SASL_SSL",
      SaslConfigs.SASL_MECHANISM                   -> "SCRAM-SHA-512",
      SaslConfigs.SASL_JAAS_CONFIG ->
        s"""org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule required username="$username" password="$password";"""
    )
```

The `PLAIN` mechanism works the same way, with `sasl.mechanism` set to `PLAIN` and the login module `org.apache.kafka.common.security.plain.PlainLoginModule`. Managed Kafka services usually document the exact `sasl.mechanism` and `sasl.jaas.config` values to use; copy them into the settings as shown. To combine SASL with a private CA, add the `ssl.truststore.*` properties from the previous section.

### SSL Endpoint Check

A long-standing Kafka client bug ([KAFKA-4090](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-4090)) makes a client that uses a plain-text protocol (`PLAINTEXT` or `SASL_PLAINTEXT`) against a TLS listener read the broker's TLS handshake bytes as the size of a response. It then tries to allocate a buffer of that size, and the application dies with an `OutOfMemoryError`. Zio-kafka protects against this with `zio.kafka.utils.SslHelper.validateEndpoint`, which probes the brokers before the Java client is created and turns the mismatch into an ordinary error.

#### When the Check Runs

The check runs while a client is created, before the Java client exists, in these constructors:

- `Consumer.make` and `Consumer.live`.
- `Producer.make` and `Producer.live`.
- `TransactionalProducer.make` and `TransactionalProducer.live`, using the properties of the wrapped `ProducerSettings`.
- `AdminClient.make`, `AdminClient.live` and `AdminClient.javaClientFromSettings`.

It is skipped when `security.protocol` contains `SSL`, ignoring case, that is for `SSL` and `SASL_SSL`: such a client speaks TLS and is not affected by the bug. It does not run in `Producer.fromJavaProducer`, `Consumer.fromJavaConsumerWithPermit`, `AdminClient.fromJavaClient` and `AdminClient.fromScopedJavaClient`, because these wrap a Java client that you create yourself. There is no setting to turn the check off.

#### What the Check Does

For a client with a plain-text protocol, the check goes through these steps:

1. It reads `bootstrap.servers`, and fails with `IllegalArgumentException("Empty bootstrapServers list")` when the property is missing. This step runs for every protocol, before the `SSL` skip described above. An empty value, such as the one `AdminClientSettings(Nil)` produces, passes this step and fails at the address lookup in step 2 instead.
2. It resolves every bootstrap server to all of its IP addresses and opens a plain socket to each address, in parallel, on a blocking thread.
3. On each socket it sends a Kafka `ApiVersions` request, reads the first 5 bytes of the answer, and closes the socket.
4. If the first byte is a TLS record type, the broker answered with TLS, and the check fails with `IllegalArgumentException("Received an unexpected SSL packet from the server. Please ensure the client is properly configured with SSL enabled")`.

Each probe times out after the client's `request.timeout.ms` (30 seconds when it is not set or not a positive number). The overall outcome is:

| Situation                                                   | Outcome                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| At least one address answers without TLS, none with TLS     | Succeeds; unreachable addresses are ignored                                                            |
| Any address answers with TLS                                | Fails with the "unexpected SSL packet" error                                                           |
| Any non-timeout error after a connection is open            | Fails with that error                                                                                  |
| No address can be reached (connection refused or timed out) | Fails with the first connection error, for example a `TimeoutException("Failed to contact <address>")` |

Every failure is wrapped in an `org.apache.kafka.common.KafkaException` with the message `"Failed to connect to Kafka"`, for every kind of client; the actual reason is the exception's cause. Because the check needs at least one reachable broker, `Consumer.make`, `Producer.make`, `TransactionalProducer.make` and `AdminClient.make` with a plain-text protocol fail when none of the bootstrap servers is reachable at startup.

To log the real reason when a client cannot be created:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.KafkaException
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer.{ Producer, ProducerSettings }

val producer: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Producer] =
  Producer
    .make(ProducerSettings(List("localhost:9092")))
    .tapSomeError { case e: KafkaException if e.getCause != null =>
      ZIO.logError(s"Cannot connect to Kafka: ${e.getCause.getMessage}")
    }
```

### Testing Secured Clients

The `zio-kafka-testkit` module starts embedded brokers with security enabled. `Kafka.saslEmbedded` starts a broker whose listener uses `SASL_PLAINTEXT` with the `PLAIN` mechanism and an ACL authorizer, with `admin` (password `admin-secret`) as super user; `KafkaTestUtils.makeSaslAdminClient` connects to it. `Kafka.sslEmbedded` starts a broker with a TLS listener, but clients cannot actually use it: it only serves to test the SSL endpoint check. See [Writing Tests](writing-tests.md) for details.

- [Admin Client](admin-client.md) for managing ACLs with `AdminClient#createAcls` and related operations.
- [Detecting Authorization Failures](detecting-authorization-failures.md) for how consumers and producers retry and report authorization errors.
- The Kafka documentation on [security](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#security) for broker-side setup and every client property.
