## Serialization and Deserialization

Kafka stores keys and values as plain byte arrays. Zio-kafka converts them to and from your own types with three types from the `zio.kafka.serde` package: a `Serializer` turns a value into bytes when producing, a `Deserializer` turns bytes into a value when consuming, and a `Serde` is both at once. All three are effectful: they return a ZIO effect, so a conversion can fail with a `Throwable`, use the ZIO environment, or call another service, such as a schema registry.

The core types have this shape:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.header.Headers
import zio.RIO

trait Serializer[-R, -A] {
  def serialize(topic: String, headers: Headers, value: A): RIO[R, Array[Byte]]
}

trait Deserializer[-R, +A] {
  def deserialize(topic: String, headers: Headers, data: Array[Byte]): RIO[R, A]
}

trait Serde[-R, A] extends Deserializer[R, A] with Serializer[R, A]
```

The type parameter `R` is the ZIO environment the conversion needs; it is `Any` for every built-in serde. `A` is the value type. Because `Serde` extends both traits, a `Serde` can be passed wherever a `Serializer` or a `Deserializer` is expected, which is why most code only ever names `Serde.string`, `Serde.long` and friends.

### How They Work Together

Serdes are not part of the `Consumer` or `Producer` themselves. You pass a key and a value deserializer (or serializer) to every call that reads (or writes) records, so one consumer or producer can handle topics with different formats.

A typical application uses them like this:

1. Pick a built-in serde such as `Serde.string`, or build one: from functions, from an existing Kafka serde, or by transforming another serde.
2. Pass a key and a value deserializer to a [consumer](consumer.md) stream method: `Consumer#plainStream`, `Consumer#partitionedStream`, `Consumer#partitionedAssignmentStream`, their `WithControl` variants, or `Consumer#consumeWith` (and `Consumer.consumeWith`). Zio-kafka reads every record from Kafka as raw bytes and runs your deserializers on each record inside the stream, with `CommittableRecord#deserializeWith`. A failed deserialization fails the stream.
3. Pass a key and a value serializer to a [producer](producer.md) method: `Producer#produce`, `Producer#produceAsync`, `Producer#produceChunk`, `Producer#produceChunkAsync`, or the `Producer#produceAll` pipeline. In a [transaction](transactions.md), `Transaction#produce`, `Transaction#produceChunk` and `Transaction#produceChunkBatch` take serializers in the same way. Serialization runs in the calling fiber before the record is handed to the producer. A failed serialization fails the call, and nothing is sent; for the chunk methods, all records are serialized first, so one failure means no record of the chunk is sent.

The diagram shows how the types relate and where they are used:

```
              Serializer[-R, -A]               Deserializer[-R, +A]
                      ^                                  ^
                      |             extends              |
                      +-------- Serde[-R, A] ------------+

 Producer#produce*(record, keySerializer, valueSerializer)
   key: K, value: V --Serializer#serialize(topic, headers, _)--> Array[Byte] --> Kafka

 Consumer#plainStream(subscription, keyDeserializer, valueDeserializer)
   Kafka --> Array[Byte] --Deserializer#deserialize(topic, headers, _)--> key: K, value: V
```

The producer methods that take a `ProducerRecord[Array[Byte], Array[Byte]]` have no serializer parameters; they send the bytes as they are. `Producer#produceChunkAsyncWithFailures` exists only in this byte-array form, because serializers could fail for each record independently.

`Serializer#serialize` and `Deserializer#deserialize` both receive the record's topic and its Kafka `Headers`. A serializer may read the headers or add to them, and a deserializer may use them to decide how to decode the bytes, for example from a content-type header. The built-in serdes ignore both the topic and the headers. [Record Headers](record-headers.md#header-aware-serializers-and-deserializers) shows a header-aware serde.

### Built-in Serdes

The `Serde` companion object provides ready-made serdes for common types: `Serde.string`, `Serde.int`, `Serde.long`, `Serde.short`, `Serde.float`, `Serde.double`, their option variants `Serde.intOption`, `Serde.longOption`, `Serde.shortOption`, `Serde.floatOption` and `Serde.doubleOption`, and `Serde.uuid`, `Serde.bytes`, `Serde.byteBuffer` and `Serde.byteArray`. All of them have environment `Any` and, except for `Serde.byteArray`, delegate to a serializer and a deserializer from Kafka's `org.apache.kafka.common.serialization` package. For their types, see the [`Serde` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/serde/Serde$.html).

Zio-kafka never calls `configure` on these Kafka classes, so they use Kafka's defaults; for example, `Serde.string` and `Serde.uuid` always use UTF-8. To use another configuration, wrap a Kafka serde yourself, as shown in [From Kafka Serdes](#from-kafka-serdes). `Serde.byteArray` returns its input unchanged and cannot fail. The other serdes catch exceptions from the Kafka code and turn them into failures, such as a `Serde.int` deserializer that receives anything other than 4 bytes.

The `Serializer` and `Deserializer` companion objects contain the same set of serdes (`Serializer.string`, `Deserializer.long`, and so on), also typed as `Serde`. They are distinct instances from the ones on `Serde`, though, and only `Serde.byteArray` enables the consumer's byte-array shortcut described in [Deserialization in the Consumer Stream](#deserialization-in-the-consumer-stream), so prefer the `Serde` versions.

Serdes need no broker, so we can call them directly. For the examples on this page, we use a small helper that runs an effect and returns its result:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.common.header.internals.RecordHeaders

def unsafeRun[A](effect: Task[A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit u =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(effect).getOrThrow()
  }
```

`Serde.int` writes an `Int` as 4 big-endian bytes and reads it back:

```scala
val intBytes = unsafeRun(Serde.int.serialize("numbers", new RecordHeaders, 258))
// intBytes: Array[Byte] = Array(0, 0, 1, 2)

unsafeRun(Serde.int.deserialize("numbers", new RecordHeaders, intBytes))
// res0: Int = 258
```

### Creating Serdes

When no built-in serde fits, you can create one from scratch: from plain functions, or by wrapping a serializer or deserializer written for the Kafka Java client. To derive a serde from an existing one instead, see [Custom Data Type Serdes](#custom-data-type-serdes).

#### From Functions

`Serializer.apply`, `Deserializer.apply` and `Serde.apply` build an instance from functions of the topic, the headers and the data. `Serde.apply` comes in two forms: one takes two functions, the other combines an existing `Deserializer` and `Serializer`:

```scala
object Serializer {
  def apply[R, A](ser: (String, Headers, A) => RIO[R, Array[Byte]]): Serializer[R, A]
}

object Deserializer {
  def apply[R, A](deser: (String, Headers, Array[Byte]) => RIO[R, A]): Deserializer[R, A]
}

object Serde {
  def apply[R, A](deser: (String, Headers, Array[Byte]) => RIO[R, A])(ser: (String, Headers, A) => RIO[R, Array[Byte]]): Serde[R, A]
  def apply[R, A](deser: Deserializer[R, A])(ser: Serializer[R, A]): Serde[R, A]
}
```

The functions signal a failure with a failed effect, so wrap code that can throw in `ZIO.attempt`. To build a serde for a `Point` that is stored as the text `x,y`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8

final case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

val pointDeserializer: Deserializer[Any, Point] =
  Deserializer { (_, _, data) =>
    new String(data, UTF_8).split(",") match {
      case Array(x, y) => ZIO.attempt(Point(x.trim.toInt, y.trim.toInt))
      case _           => ZIO.fail(new IllegalArgumentException("A point needs two coordinates"))
    }
  }

val pointSerializer: Serializer[Any, Point] =
  Serializer((_, _, point) => ZIO.succeed(s"${point.x},${point.y}".getBytes(UTF_8)))

val pointSerde: Serde[Any, Point] = Serde(pointDeserializer)(pointSerializer)
```

`Serializer` and `Deserializer` each have a single abstract method, so you can also implement them, or `Serde`, directly with `new Serde[Any, Point] { ... }`, overriding `Serde#serialize` and `Serde#deserialize`.

#### From Kafka Serdes

Many serialization formats already have an implementation for the Kafka Java client: a class implementing `org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.Serializer`, `Deserializer` or `Serde`. Third-party serdes, such as the Avro serdes that work with a schema registry, are usually distributed this way. Three constructors turn them into zio-kafka serdes:

```scala
object Serializer {
  def fromKafkaSerializer[A](serializer: KafkaSerializer[A], props: Map[String, AnyRef], isKey: Boolean): Task[Serializer[Any, A]]
}

object Deserializer {
  def fromKafkaDeserializer[A](deserializer: KafkaDeserializer[A], props: Map[String, AnyRef], isKey: Boolean): Task[Deserializer[Any, A]]
}

object Serde {
  def fromKafkaSerde[A](serde: KafkaSerde[A], props: Map[String, AnyRef], isKey: Boolean): Task[Serde[Any, A]]
}
```

Each constructor first calls the Kafka object's `configure(props, isKey)` method, which is why it returns a `Task`: if `configure` throws, the task fails. The `props` map is the configuration the Kafka class expects, the same keys you would give the Java client, for example the URL of a schema registry. `isKey` tells the Kafka class whether it handles keys or values; many classes read different configuration keys for each, so configure a separate instance for keys and for values. Every later call passes the topic, the headers and the data to the Kafka class and turns an exception into a failed effect. A `Serde` built with `Serde.fromKafkaSerde` takes the serializer and the deserializer from the Kafka serde once, when it is created.

Kafka's `StringSerializer` reads its character encoding from `value.serializer.encoding` when `isKey` is `false`. To serialize strings as UTF-16 instead of the default UTF-8:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.{ IntegerDeserializer, StringSerializer }

unsafeRun(
  Serializer
    .fromKafkaSerializer(new StringSerializer, Map("value.serializer.encoding" -> "UTF-16"), isKey = false)
    .flatMap(_.serialize("greetings", new RecordHeaders, "hi"))
)
// res2: Array[Byte] = Array(-2, -1, 0, 104, 0, 105)
```

A wrapped Kafka class keeps its Java types; Kafka's `IntegerDeserializer` produces a `java.lang.Integer`. To get a Scala `Int`, map the result:

```scala
unsafeRun(
  Deserializer
    .fromKafkaDeserializer(new IntegerDeserializer, Map.empty, isKey = true)
    .flatMap(_.map(_.intValue).deserialize("numbers", new RecordHeaders, Array[Byte](0, 0, 1, 2)))
)
// res3: Int = 258
```

Because the constructors return a `Task`, create the serdes once, before you start consuming or producing, and pass them on. To consume a topic whose keys are UTF-16 and whose values are ISO-8859-1 text, using Kafka's `Serdes.String()` factory, imported as `KafkaSerdes`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.{ Serdes => KafkaSerdes }

val consumerSettings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("group")

val program: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    keySerde   <- Serde.fromKafkaSerde(KafkaSerdes.String(), Map("key.deserializer.encoding" -> "UTF-16"), isKey = true)
    valueSerde <- Serde.fromKafkaSerde(KafkaSerdes.String(), Map("value.deserializer.encoding" -> "ISO-8859-1"), isKey = false)
    consumer   <- Consumer.make(consumerSettings)
    _ <- consumer
           .plainStream(Subscription.topics("legacy-events"), keySerde, valueSerde)
           .mapChunksZIO(records => ZIO.foreach(records)(record => ZIO.logInfo(record.value).as(record.offset)))
           .aggregateAsync(Consumer.collectOffsets)
           .mapZIO(_.commit)
           .runDrain
  } yield ()
```

Zio-kafka never calls `close` on a wrapped Kafka object. If it holds resources, such as a connection to a schema registry, keep a reference to it and close it yourself, for example with `ZIO.acquireRelease`. If its calls block on network I/O, run it on the blocking thread pool, see [Running on the Blocking Thread Pool](#running-on-the-blocking-thread-pool).

### Custom Data Type Serdes

Serializers and deserializers for custom data types can be created from scratch, as described in [Creating Serdes](#creating-serdes), or by converting existing ones. Converting is usually shorter: you only write the step between your type and a type that already has a serde.

#### Transforming Deserializers

A `Deserializer` produces values, so it is transformed in the same direction as the data, from `A` to `B`:

```scala
trait Deserializer[-R, +A] {
  def map[B](f: A => B): Deserializer[R, B]
  def mapZIO[R1 <: R, B](f: A => RIO[R1, B]): Deserializer[R1, B]
}
```

`Deserializer#map` applies a pure function. The function must not throw: an exception thrown inside it is a defect, not a failure, so it kills the consumer stream and `Deserializer#asTry` cannot catch it. For a conversion that can fail, use `Deserializer#mapZIO` and return a failed effect. To parse a count that is stored as text:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.serde._

val countDeserializer: Deserializer[Any, Int] =
  Serde.string.mapZIO(text => ZIO.attempt(text.trim.toInt))
```

#### Transforming Serializers

A `Serializer` consumes values, so it is transformed against the direction of the data: you supply a function from your new type `B` to the type `A` that the serializer already handles:

```scala
trait Serializer[-R, -A] {
  def contramap[B](f: B => A): Serializer[R, B]
  def contramapZIO[R1 <: R, B](f: B => RIO[R1, A]): Serializer[R1, B]
}
```

`Serializer#contramap` takes a pure function, and `Serializer#contramapZIO` an effectful one, for example one that looks up data before serializing. To write an `Instant` as its ISO-8601 text:

```scala
import java.time.Instant

new String(
  unsafeRun(
    Serde.string
      .contramap((instant: Instant) => instant.toString)
      .serialize("events", new RecordHeaders, Instant.EPOCH)
  ),
  "UTF-8"
)
// res6: String = "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"
```

#### Transforming Both Directions

Calling `Deserializer#map` or `Serializer#contramap` on a `Serde` returns only a `Deserializer` or a `Serializer`. To transform a `Serde` and keep both directions, give one function for each direction:

```scala
trait Serde[-R, A] extends Deserializer[R, A] with Serializer[R, A] {
  def inmap[B](f: A => B)(g: B => A): Serde[R, B]
  def inmapZIO[R1 <: R, B](f: A => RIO[R1, B])(g: B => RIO[R1, A]): Serde[R1, B]
}
```

`Serde#inmap` takes pure functions; the same rule as for `Deserializer#map` applies, so `f` must not throw. For example, to create a serde for an `Instant` from a serde for a `Long`:

```scala
import java.time.Instant
import zio.kafka.serde._

val instantSerde: Serde[Any, Instant] =
  Serde.long.inmap(java.time.Instant.ofEpochMilli)(_.toEpochMilli)
```

`Serde#inmapZIO` takes effectful functions, so decoding can fail cleanly. To accept only order ids with the right prefix:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.serde._

final case class OrderId(value: String)

val orderIdSerde: Serde[Any, OrderId] =
  Serde.string.inmapZIO { text =>
    if (text.startsWith("order-")) ZIO.succeed(OrderId(text))
    else ZIO.fail(new IllegalArgumentException(s"Not an order id: $text"))
  }(orderId => ZIO.succeed(orderId.value))
```

For a complete example of creating a custom serde with ZIO JSON, see the [Producing and Consuming JSON Data](tutorial.md#producing-and-consuming-json-data) section in the tutorial.

### Handling Missing Data

A Kafka key or value can be `null`: many records have no key, and a tombstone record, which marks a key as deleted in a compacted topic, has a `null` value. The plain built-in serdes handle `null` poorly. `Serde.string` and the other reference-type serdes return a `null` value, and the numeric serdes, such as `Serde.long`, silently turn Kafka's `null` into `0` (Scala unboxes a `null` number to zero), so a tombstone or a missing key looks like a real zero.

For numeric keys and values that can be `null`, use the option variants `Serde.intOption`, `Serde.longOption`, `Serde.shortOption`, `Serde.floatOption` and `Serde.doubleOption`. They deserialize `null` to `None` and serialize `None` to `null`:

```scala
unsafeRun(Serde.longOption.deserialize("users", new RecordHeaders, null))
// res9: Option[Long] = None

unsafeRun(Serde.longOption.serialize("users", new RecordHeaders, None))
// res10: Array[Byte] = null
```

For any other serde, use `Serializer#asOption`, `Deserializer#asOption` or `Serde#asOption`; `Serde.longOption` behaves the same as `Serde.long.asOption`:

```scala
trait Serializer[-R, -A] {
  def asOption[A1 <: A]: Serializer[R, Option[A1]]
}

trait Deserializer[-R, +A] {
  def asOption: Deserializer[R, Option[A]]
}

trait Serde[-R, A] extends Deserializer[R, A] with Serializer[R, A] {
  override def asOption: Serde[R, Option[A]]
}
```

For example, `Serde.string.asOption` results in a `None` if the key or value is `null`, and in a `Some(string)` otherwise; the underlying deserializer is not called for `null`. When serializing, `None` is written as `null`. An empty byte array is not `null`, so it still goes through the deserializer:

```scala
unsafeRun(Serde.string.asOption.serialize("users", new RecordHeaders, None))
// res11: Array[Byte] = null

unsafeRun(Serde.long.asOption.deserialize("users", new RecordHeaders, null))
// res12: Option[Long] = None

unsafeRun(Serde.string.asOption.deserialize("users", new RecordHeaders, Array.emptyByteArray))
// res13: Option[String] = Some(value = "")
```

### Handling Failures in a Serde

Ideally, a serde can not fail serializing and deserializing. This is for example the case with the provided `Serde.byteArray` and `Serde.string`. This is not the case for any serde that needs to handle invalid input (for example `Serde.long`), or a serde that needs to do a remote lookup.

By default, a consumer stream fails if it encounters a deserialization error in the serde. The resulting error does not always show that the serde is the cause.

There are three ways to improve this, described in the sections below: fall back to another deserializer with `Deserializer#orElse`, wrap the result of the deserializer in a `Try` with `Deserializer#asTry`, or consume with `Serde.byteArray` and do the deserialization in the consumer stream (or serialize before handing the data to zio-kafka), so that you can handle failures any way you want.

#### Falling Back to Another Deserializer

When a topic contains data in more than one format, `Deserializer#orElse` tries a second deserializer when the first one fails:

```scala
trait Deserializer[-R, +A] {
  def orElse[R1 <: R, A1 >: A](alternative: Deserializer[R1, A1]): Deserializer[R1, A1]
}
```

If both deserializers fail, the result fails with the error of the alternative. To read amounts that are stored either as 8-byte numbers or as text:

```scala
unsafeRun(
  Serde.long
    .orElse(Serde.string.mapZIO(text => ZIO.attempt(text.toLong)))
    .deserialize("amounts", new RecordHeaders, "42".getBytes("UTF-8"))
)
// res14: Long = 42L
```

#### Custom Serdes That Wrap Invalid Data

Any `Deserializer[R, A]` for a given type `A` can be converted into a `Deserializer[R, Try[A]]`, where deserialization failures are converted to a `Failure`, using the `Deserializer#asTry` method. `Serde#asTry` is also available; it is inherited from `Deserializer` and returns a `Deserializer`, so the result can only be used for consuming:

```scala
trait Deserializer[-R, +A] {
  def asTry: Deserializer[R, Try[A]]
}
```

The deserializer then always succeeds, and the failure becomes part of the value:

```scala
unsafeRun(Serde.int.asTry.deserialize("numbers", new RecordHeaders, Array[Byte](1, 2)))
// res15: util.Try[Int] = Failure(
//   exception = org.apache.kafka.common.errors.SerializationException: Size of data received by IntegerDeserializer is not 4
// )
```

`Deserializer#asTry` converts failures only. A defect, such as an exception thrown inside the function given to `Deserializer#map`, still fails the stream.

Below is an example of skipping records that fail to deserialize. The offset is passed downstream to be committed. The example uses `ZStream#mapZIO` for brevity; see [avoiding chunk-breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md) before using it in production:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import scala.util.{Try, Success, Failure}

val consumerSettings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("group")
def someEffect(value: String): Task[Unit] = ???

val keySerde = Serde.string
val valueDeserializer = Serde.string.asTry   // <-- using `asTry`

val program: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Unit] =
  Consumer.make(consumerSettings).flatMap { consumer =>
    consumer
      .plainStream(Subscription.topics("topic150"), keySerde, valueDeserializer)
      .mapZIO { record => // ⚠️ mapZIO is a chunk-breaker, see "Avoiding chunk-breakers"
        val tryValue: Try[String] = record.record.value()
        val offset: Offset = record.offset

        tryValue match {
          case Success(value) =>
            // Action for successful deserialization
            someEffect(value).as(offset)
          case Failure(exception) =>
            // Possibly log the exception or take alternative action
            ZIO.succeed(offset)
        }
      }
      .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
      .mapZIO(_.commit)
      .runDrain
  }
```

The `Serde` companion object also has an implicit conversion that does the same as `Deserializer#asTry` for code that passes deserializers implicitly:

```scala
object Serde {
  implicit def deserializerWithError[R, A](implicit deser: Deserializer[R, A]): Deserializer[R, Try[A]]
}
```

The zio-kafka consumer methods take their deserializers as explicit arguments, so you rarely need it. It is defined on `Serde`, not on `Deserializer`, so it is not found automatically; import it to use it:

```scala
import zio.kafka.serde._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde.deserializerWithError
import scala.util.Try

implicit val stringDeserializer: Deserializer[Any, String] = Serde.string

val tryDeserializer: Deserializer[Any, Try[String]] = implicitly[Deserializer[Any, Try[String]]]
```

#### Deserialization in the Consumer Stream

In this approach we provide zio-kafka with the `Serde.byteArray` serde (which is a pass-through serde) and do the deserialization in the consumer stream. The deserialization can be done with regular ZIO operators.

This approach provides more freedom at the cost of having to write more code. It also allows for optimizations such as operating on chunks of records (see [avoiding chunk-breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md)), and more contextual failure handling. When both the key and the value deserializer are `Serde.byteArray`, the consumer recognizes that exact instance and skips the deserialization step entirely. Other instances, such as `Deserializer.byteArray`, do not trigger this shortcut.

The following example deserializes each value in the stream and falls back to another effect when deserialization fails:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

final case class Message(text: String)

val consumerSettings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("group")
def deserialize(value: Array[Byte]): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Message] = ???
def someEffect(value: Array[Byte]): ZIO[Any, Throwable, Message] = ???
def processMessage(message: Message): Task[Unit] = ???

val program: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Unit] =
  Consumer.make(consumerSettings).flatMap { consumer =>
    consumer
      .plainStream(Subscription.topics("topic150"), Serde.byteArray, Serde.byteArray)
      .mapZIO { record => // ⚠️ mapZIO is a chunk-breaker, see "Avoiding chunk-breakers"
        val value: Array[Byte] = record.record.value()
        val offset: Offset = record.offset

        deserialize(value)
          // possible action to take if deserialization fails:
          .catchAll(_ => someEffect(value))
          .flatMap(processMessage)
          .as(offset)
      }
      .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
      .mapZIO(_.commit)
      .runDrain
  }
```

To apply ordinary deserializers to such a record later in the stream, call `CommittableRecord#deserializeWith(keyDeserializer, valueDeserializer)`. It runs both deserializers with the record's topic and headers and returns a typed `CommittableRecord` with the same offset; see [CommittableRecord](consumer.md#committablerecord).

### Running on the Blocking Thread Pool

The fibers that run serdes share ZIO's default thread pool, which is sized for non-blocking work. A serde that blocks a thread, for example one that calls a remote service synchronously, should run on ZIO's blocking thread pool instead. `Serializer#blocking`, `Deserializer#blocking` and `Serde#blocking` do that:

```scala
trait Serializer[-R, -A] {
  def blocking: Serializer[R, A]
}

trait Deserializer[-R, +A] {
  def blocking: Deserializer[R, A]
}

trait Serde[-R, A] extends Deserializer[R, A] with Serializer[R, A] {
  override def blocking: Serde[R, A]
}
```

The result runs every call of the original inside `ZIO.blocking`. To run a wrapped Kafka serde, whose calls may block on network I/O, on the blocking thread pool:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.{ Serde => KafkaSerde }

def blockingSerde[A](kafkaSerde: KafkaSerde[A], props: Map[String, AnyRef]): Task[Serde[Any, A]] =
  Serde.fromKafkaSerde(kafkaSerde, props, isKey = false).map(_.blocking)
```

### A Warning About `mapZIO`

Moved to [avoiding chunk-breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md).

---

## Sharing a Consumer between Multiple Streams

Often in a single application, you want to consume from multiple Kafka topics and process each topic in a distinct way. With `zio-kafka` you can use a single `Consumer` instance for multiple streams from different topics. It is not only easier to create a single `Consumer` layer instead of one for each topic, but it may be more resource efficient as well. The underlying Apache Kafka consumer, its thread pool and communication with the Kafka brokers will be shared, resulting in less resource consumption compared to when you create a Consumer instance for every topic.

For each of the topics/patterns you subscribe to, you can define a dedicated stream to process the records, a dedicated `Deserializer` for the keys, and a dedicated `Deserializer` for the values. Other settings like poll interval and offset strategy are common to all subscriptions. For example, the value of the `max.poll.records` setting is the maximum number of records returned in each poll for all the subscriptions combined. If you need different settings for each topic/pattern, you need to create a `Consumer` instance per topic/pattern.

The following example runs two streams, each for a different topic and with different key and value types, on a single consumer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.Console.printLine
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

// Create a single Consumer instance
val consumerSettings: ConsumerSettings = ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092")).withGroupId("group")
val consumer: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Consumer] = ZLayer.scoped(Consumer.make(consumerSettings))

// Define two streams, each for a different topic and key-value types
val stream1 = ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Consumer] { consumer =>
  consumer.plainStream(Subscription.topics("topic1"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
    .tap(cr => printLine(s"For topic1, got key: ${cr.record.key}, value: ${cr.record.value}"))
    .map(_.offset)
    .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
    .mapZIO(_.commit)
    .runDrain
}

val stream2 = ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Consumer] { consumer =>
  consumer.plainStream(Subscription.topics("topic2"), Serde.uuid, Serde.int)
    .tap(cr => printLine(s"For topic2, got key: ${cr.record.key}, value: ${cr.record.value}"))
    .map(_.offset)
    .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
    .mapZIO(_.commit)
    .runDrain
}

// Run both streams with the same consumer instance
(stream1 zipPar stream2).provideLayer(consumer)
```

Each Stream can have a different lifetime. Subscriptions are tied to their Stream's scope, so when a Stream completes (successfully, via failure or interruption), the corresponding subscription is removed. 

Consumer sharing is only possible when using the same type of `Subscription`: `Topics`, `Pattern` or `Manual`. Mixing different types will result in a failed stream. Note that every `Topics` subscription can also be written as a `Pattern` subscription, so if you want to mix `Topics` and `Pattern` subscriptions, you can just use `Pattern`. 

If your subscriptions overlap, e.g. `Subscription.topics("topic1", "topic2")` and `Subscription.topics("topic2", "topic3")`, the records of `topic2` are divided non-deterministically over both streams.

:::note
Upon starting or ending subscriptions, Kafka may also reassign (with the default eager assignor: revoke and reassign) all partitions of the _other_ subscriptions. Record fetching will resume from the last committed offset, so records may be processed twice when not all offsets are committed yet. This works the same as for regular rebalancing. To minimize this issue, commit frequently or enable [rebalance safe commits](preventing-duplicates.md).
:::

---

## Transactions

> This document describes Kafka transactions for zio-kafka version 3.0.0 and later.

### What are Kafka Transactions?

[Kafka transactions](https://www.confluent.io/blog/transactions-apache-kafka/) are different from what you may know from
relational databases. In Kafka a transaction means that your program consumes some records, then produces some other
records (to the same broker) and then by committing the _consumed_ records the transaction is committed, and the
produced records become available to other consumers.

I can imagine that went a bit fast, here is a more gentle introduction with more background:
[Kafka Transactions Explained (Twice!)](https://www.warpstream.com/blog/kafka-transactions-explained-twice).

### A warning about consuming transactional records

By default, produced records become immediately visible for consumers, even if they are produced in a not yet committed
Kafka transaction! To prevent reading transactional records before they are committed, you need to configure every
consumer with the `isolation.level` property set to `read_committed`. For example as follows:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.ConsumerSettings

val bootstrapServers = List("localhost:9092")
val groupId          = "my-group"

val settings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers)
  .withGroupId(groupId)
  .withReadCommitted(true) // Only read committed records
```

### Producing transactional records

In order to produce records transactionally, we need a `Consumer` and a `TransactionalProducer` that will work together
to safely commit transactions.

On this page we assume you're using [ZIO service pattern](https://zio.dev/reference/service-pattern/) and that the
`Consumer` and `TransactionalProducer` are created as a layer.

First we create the `Consumer` layer.
Note that rebalance-safe-commits must be enabled (see the background section below for more information). The consumer must also use a partition assignor that revokes all partitions during a rebalance, so the `CooperativeStickyAssignor` is not supported. When rebalance-safe-commits is enabled, zio-kafka uses the `RangeAssignor` unless you configure another assignor. `TransactionalProducer.make` fails with an `IllegalArgumentException` when rebalance-safe-commits is off or the `CooperativeStickyAssignor` is configured. It cannot detect other incremental rebalance protocols, such as a custom cooperative assignor or the `consumer` group protocol (`group.protocol=consumer`), so do not use those with a transactional producer either.
Since the default `maxRebalanceDuration` is quite high, you may also consider setting it to a lower duration, one in
which you are sure all records of a poll can be processed:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, ConsumerSettings }

val bootstrapBrokers = List("localhost:9092")

val consumerLayer: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Consumer] = ZLayer.scoped {
  val consumerSettings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapBrokers)
    .withGroupId("somegroupid")
    .withRebalanceSafeCommits(true) // required!
    .withMaxRebalanceDuration(30.seconds)
  Consumer.make(consumerSettings)
}
```

Now we can create the `TransactionalProducer` layer.
Note that the producer connects (and must connect) to the same brokers as the consumer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.Consumer
import zio.kafka.producer.{ ProducerSettings, TransactionalProducer, TransactionalProducerSettings }

import java.util.UUID

val bootstrapBrokers = List("localhost:9092")

val producerLayer: ZLayer[Consumer, Throwable, TransactionalProducer] =
  ZLayer.scoped {
    // See text below for a better transactionalId
    val transactionalId = UUID.randomUUID().toString
    val producerSettings = ProducerSettings(bootstrapBrokers)
    val transactionalProducerSettings = TransactionalProducerSettings(producerSettings, transactionalId)

    for {
      consumer <- ZIO.service[Consumer]
      tp       <- TransactionalProducer.make(transactionalProducerSettings, consumer)
    } yield tp
  }
```

Notice that the `producerLayer` requires a `Consumer`. The producer coordinates with the consumer to make sure
that transactions are accepted by the brokers. The consumer does this by holding up rebalances until all records
consumed before the rebalance are committed by the producer. (Again, see the background section below for more
information.)

The `transactionalId` uniquely identifies a producer and is (ideally) retained across restarts. It allows the Kafka
brokers to identify zombies, producers that are accidentally still running. Records produced by a zombie are rejected.
For a more complete description see [Kafka’s transactional.id – your first guess is probably wrong. It’s actually all about zombies](https://community.ibm.com/community/user/integration/blogs/kim-clark1/2024/06/19/kafka-transactionalid).

Ideally, the `transactionalId` is stable and is provided by the environment. For example, the first producer uses a
`transactionalId` that ends with `0`, the second producer uses a `transactionalId` that ends with `1` and so on.

With these in place we can look at the application logic of consuming and producing. In this example we use the
`plainStream` method to consume records with a `Long` value and an `Int` key:

```scala
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Consumer, Subscription }
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

val consumer: Consumer = ??? // the consumer from the layer above

val consumedRecordsStream = consumer
  .plainStream(Subscription.topics("my-input-topic"), Serde.int, Serde.long)
```

For each consumed records, we then create a `ProducerRecord` with a `String` value containing `Copy of <input value>`.
Note, that we also keep the offset of the consumed record so that we can commit it later:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.CommittableRecord
import zio.stream.ZStream

val consumedRecordsStream: ZStream[Any, Throwable, CommittableRecord[Int, Long]] = ??? // from the previous step

val producedRecordsStream = consumedRecordsStream
  .mapChunks { (records: Chunk[CommittableRecord[Int, Long]]) =>
    records.map { record =>
      val key: Int    = record.record.key()
      val value: Long = record.record.value()
      val newValue: String = "Copy of " + value.toString

      val producerRecord: ProducerRecord[Int, String] =
        new ProducerRecord("my-output-topic", key, newValue)
      (producerRecord, record.offset)
    }
  }
```

Typically, to optimize throughput, we want to produce records in batches. The underlying chunking structure of the
consumer stream is ideal for that because zio-kafka guarantees that each chunk in the stream contains records that
were fetched together from the broker. However, we need to be careful to retain the chunking structure. For example, we
should not use `ZStream#mapZIO` because it results in a stream where each chunk contains only a single item. Therefore, we use
`ZStream#mapChunksZIO` instead (see also [avoiding chunk-breakers](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md)).

These new records can now be produced. Let's build it up slowly:

```scala
producedRecordsStream
  .mapChunksZIO { (recordsAndOffsets: Chunk[(ProducerRecord[Int, String], Offset)]) =>
    ???
  }
```

Let's work on those question marks. We need to create a transaction.
Each zio-kafka transaction runs in a ZIO `Scope`; the transaction commits when the scope closes successfully, and is aborted when the scope closes with a failure or interruption (for example after `Transaction#abort`, as long as its failure is not caught inside the scope). We start with the scope:

```scala
ZIO.scoped {
  ??? // transaction stuff
}
```

We also want to try to complete the transaction, even when the program is shutting down.
Therefore, we add `ZIO#uninterruptible` and get:

```scala
ZIO
  .scoped {
    ??? // transaction stuff
  }
  .uninterruptible
```

Now we can fill in the 'transaction stuff': we create the transaction and use it to produce some records:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.{ Offset, OffsetBatch }
import zio.kafka.producer.TransactionalProducer
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

val transactionalProducer: TransactionalProducer                    = ??? // the producer from the layer above
val recordsAndOffsets: Chunk[(ProducerRecord[Int, String], Offset)] = ??? // the input of `mapChunksZIO`

val transactionStuff =
  for {
    tx <- transactionalProducer.createTransaction
    _  <- {
      val (records, offsets) = recordsAndOffsets.unzip
      tx.produceChunkBatch(
        records,
        Serde.int,
        Serde.string,
        OffsetBatch(offsets)
      )
    }
    // running inside `mapChunksZIO`, we need to return a Chunk.
    // Since we're not using the result, the empty chunk will do.
  } yield Chunk.empty
```

Notice how we pass the offsets of the consumed records. When the transaction commits, these offsets are committed with it.
`Transaction#produce` and `Transaction#produceChunk` work the same way, but take an `Option[Offset]` instead of an `OffsetBatch`.

Putting it all together we get:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

import java.util.UUID

object Transactional extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val topic = "transactional-test-topic"

  val bootstrapBrokers = List("localhost:9092")

  val consumerSettings = ZLayer.succeed {
    ConsumerSettings(bootstrapBrokers)
      .withGroupId("transactional-example-app")
      .withRebalanceSafeCommits(true) // required for transactional producing
      .withMaxRebalanceDuration(30.seconds)
  }

  val producerSettings = ZLayer.succeed {
    TransactionalProducerSettings(
      bootstrapServers = bootstrapBrokers,
      transactionalId = UUID.randomUUID().toString
    )
  }

  private val runConsumerStream: ZIO[Consumer & TransactionalProducer, Throwable, Unit] =
    for {
      consumer              <- ZIO.service[Consumer]
      transactionalProducer <- ZIO.service[TransactionalProducer]
      _                     <- ZIO.logInfo(s"Consuming messages from topic $topic...")
      _ <- consumer
        .plainStream(Subscription.topics(topic), Serde.int, Serde.long)
        .mapChunks { (records: Chunk[CommittableRecord[Int, Long]]) =>
          records.map { record =>
            val key: Int         = record.record.key()
            val value: Long      = record.record.value()
            val newValue: String = "Copy of " + value.toString

            val producerRecord: ProducerRecord[Int, String] =
              new ProducerRecord("my-output-topic", key, newValue)
            (producerRecord, record.offset)
          }
        }
        .mapChunksZIO { (recordsAndOffsets: Chunk[(ProducerRecord[Int, String], Offset)]) =>
          ZIO.scoped {
            for {
              _  <- ZIO.addFinalizer(ZIO.logInfo("Completing transaction"))
              tx <- transactionalProducer.createTransaction
              _ <- {
                val (records, offsets) = recordsAndOffsets.unzip
                tx.produceChunkBatch(
                  records,
                  Serde.int,
                  Serde.string,
                  OffsetBatch(offsets)
                )
              }
            } yield Chunk.empty
          }.uninterruptible
        }
        .runDrain
    } yield ()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, Any] =
    runConsumerStream
      .provide(
        consumerSettings,
        Consumer.live,
        producerSettings,
        TransactionalProducer.live
      )

}
```

### How a Transaction Ends

A transaction ends when its scope closes. When the scope closes successfully, zio-kafka commits the transaction, including the collected offsets. When the scope closes with a failure or an interruption, zio-kafka aborts the transaction. Committing and aborting are each retried up to 5 times; when they keep failing, the effect dies.

A `TransactionalProducer` runs one transaction at a time: `TransactionalProducer#createTransaction` waits until the scope of the previous transaction has closed. Do not keep a `Transaction` after its scope closes; producing with it then fails with `TransactionalProducer.TransactionLeaked`.

To abort a transaction on purpose, call `Transaction#abort`. It fails the effect with `TransactionalProducer.UserInitiatedAbort` (not a `Throwable`). The transaction is aborted only if this failure reaches the end of the scope: if you catch it inside the scope, the scope closes successfully and the transaction commits. So we catch it outside the scope when the abort is expected:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer.TransactionalProducer
import zio.kafka.producer.TransactionalProducer.UserInitiatedAbort
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde

val transactionalProducer: TransactionalProducer = ???

val abortedTransaction =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      tx <- transactionalProducer.createTransaction
      _  <- tx.produce(new ProducerRecord("my-output-topic", "key", "value"), Serde.string, Serde.string, None)
      _  <- tx.abort // the record above is never visible to read_committed consumers
    } yield ()
  }.catchSome { case UserInitiatedAbort => ZIO.unit }
```

### Technical background - How does it all work?

Kafka must ensure that each record is only processed once, even though a partition can be revoked, assigned to another
consumer, all while the original consumer knows nothing about this. In this situation the original consumer will happily
continue producing records even though another consumer is doing the same thing with the same records.

Kafka does this by validating the group epoch. The group epoch is a number that gets increased after every rebalance.
When the transactional producer commits a transaction with the offsets of consumed records, it also includes the group
epoch of when the records were consumed. If the broker detects a commit with a group epoch that is not equal to the
current epoch, it will reject the commit.

In addition, to prevent an old consumer from continuing to poll into the next epoch without participating in the
rebalance, consumers polling within the wrong group epoch are 'fenced'. The broker rejects the commits of a fenced
consumer.

#### How zio-kafka helps

With zio-kafka you can use ZIO scopes to define the transaction boundaries. Within the scope you can produce records one
by one, all in 1 batch or in multiple batches. Once the scope closes successfully, the records are committed together with all
collected offsets. If the scope fails, the transaction is aborted.

In addition, zio-kafka prevents failed commits. The `TransactionalProducer` informs the `Consumer` which offsets were
committed. When a rebalance starts, the consumer holds it up until all records consumed so far are committed. (This
feature is called rebalance-safe-commits.) Because of this, every transaction commits in the same group epoch as the
epoch in which the records were consumed, and the brokers can accept the transaction.

When a zio-kafka consumer misses a rebalance and continues polling, there is nothing that can be done. The broker rejects
its transactions; zio-kafka retries the commit 5 times and then the effect dies. In these cases the consumer (or perhaps
simpler, the whole program) should restart.

---

## Tutorial: How to Produce/Consume Data to/from Kafka Topics

### Introduction

Kafka is a distributed, fault-tolerant, message-oriented event-store platform. It is used as a message broker for distributed applications. Zio-kafka is a library that provides a way to consume and produce data from Kafka topics, and it also supports the ability to have streaming consumers and producers.

In this tutorial, we will learn how to use zio-streams and zio-kafka to produce and consume data from Kafka topics.

### Running Examples

To access the code examples, you can clone the [ZIO Quickstarts](http://github.com/zio/zio-quickstarts) project:

```bash
$ git clone https://github.com/zio/zio-quickstarts.git
$ cd zio-quickstarts/zio-quickstart-kafka
```

Start a Kafka broker with the `docker-compose.yml` that ships with the project (see [Setting Up The Kafka Cluster](#setting-up-the-kafka-cluster) for what it contains):

```bash
$ docker compose up -d
```

Then run the application using sbt:

```bash
$ sbt run
```

The project contains several applications (`SimpleKafkaApp`, `StreamingKafkaApp` and `JsonStreamingKafkaApp`), so `sbt run` asks which one to start.

### Adding Dependencies to The Project

In this tutorial, we will be using the following dependencies. So, let's add them to the `build.sbt` file:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka" % "4.2.0",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-json"  % "1.1.2"
)
```

Zio-kafka depends on zio and zio-streams, so these two libraries are added to the project as well.

1. **Zio-kafka** is a ZIO native client for Apache Kafka. It provides a high-level streaming API on top of the Java client. So we can produce and consume events using the declarative concurrency model of zio-streams.

2. **Zio-streams** introduces a high-level API for working with streams of values. It is designated to work in a highly concurrent environment. It has seamless integration with ZIO, so we have the ability to use all the features of the ZIO along with the streams, e.g. `Scope`, `Schedule`, `ZLayer`, `Queue`, `Hub` etc. To learn more about zio-stream, there is a comprehensive section on that [here](https://zio.dev/reference/stream/).

3. **Zio-json** is a library to serialize and deserialize data from/to JSON data type. We will be using this library to serialize and deserialize data when reading and writing JSON data from/to Kafka topics.

### Setting Up The Kafka Cluster

Before we start, we need to set up a Kafka cluster. To start a kafka cluster for testing purposes we can use the following `docker-compose.yml` file:

```yaml
services:
  broker:
    image: apache/kafka:4.4.0
    container_name: broker
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://broker:29092,CONTROLLER://broker:29093,PLAINTEXT_HOST://0.0.0.0:9092
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://broker:29092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT_HOST:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@broker:29093
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: PLAINTEXT
```

Now we can run the `docker compose up -d` command to start the Kafka cluster:

```bash
$ docker compose up -d
```

### Writing a Simple Producer and Consumer Using ZIO Workflows

To write producers and consumers, using the zio-kafka library, we have two choices:

1. Using ZIO workflows
2. Using zio-streams workflows

In this section, we will try the first option.

#### 1. Serializing and Deserializing Data

Before we can write a producer and consumer, let's talk about how data is stored in Kafka. Kafka is an event-store platform that stores records, records are key-value pairs as raw bytes. So a Kafka broker knows nothing about its records, it just appends the records to its internal log file.

To produce and consume data from Kafka, we need a way to serialize our data to a byte array and deserialize byte arrays to our data types. This is where the `Serde` data type comes in handy. A `Serde[R, A]` is a `Serializer` and `Deserializer` for values of type `A`, which can use the environment `R` to serialize and deserialize values.

Here is the simplified definition of the `Serde` data type:

```scala
trait Serde[-R, A] extends Deserializer[R, A] with Serializer[R, A] {
  def deserialize(topic: String, headers: Headers, data: Array[Byte]): RIO[R, A]
  def serialize(topic: String, headers: Headers, value: A)           : RIO[R, Array[Byte]]
}
```

The companion object of `Serde` trait contains a set of built-in serializers and deserializers for primitive types:

- `Serde.long`
- `Serde.int`
- `Serde.short`
- `Serde.float`
- `Serde.double`
- `Serde.bytes`
- `Serde.string`
- `Serde.byteArray`
- `Serde.byteBuffer`
- `Serde.uuid`

In this example, the type of the `key` is `Long` and the type of the `value` is `String`. So we can use the `Serde.long` for the `key` and the `Serde.string` for the `value`.

#### 2. Creating a Producer

Now we can create a `Producer`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka._
import zio.kafka.producer._

val producer: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Producer] =
  Producer.make(
    ProducerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
  )
```

The `ProducerSettings` as constructed in this code fragment is already sufficient for many applications. However, more configuration options are available on `ProducerSettings`.

Notice that the created producer requires a `Scope` in the environment. When this scope closes, the producer closes its
connection with the Kafka cluster. An explicit scope can be created with the `ZIO.scoped` method.

#### 3. Producing records

Zio-kafka has several producers that can be used to produce data on Kafka topics. In this example, we will be using the `Producer.produce` method:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produce[R, K, V](
    topic: String,
    key: K,
    value: V,
    keySerializer: Serializer[R, K],
    valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]
  ): RIO[R, RecordMetadata]
}
```

Notice how the type parameters of `produce` method ensure that the value's type, corresponds to the type produced by the value's `Serializer` (and the same for the key and the `Serializer` for the key).

Here is a helper function that shows how we could use the `produce` method:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.RecordMetadata
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

def produceRecord(producer: Producer, topic: String, key: Long, value: String): RIO[Any, RecordMetadata] =
  producer.produce[Any, Long, String](
    topic = topic,
    key = key,
    value = value,
    keySerializer = Serde.long,
    valueSerializer = Serde.string
  )
```

#### 4. Creating a Consumer

Zio-kafka provides several ways to consume data from Kafka topics. In this example, we will use the `Consumer.consumeWith` function.

The following helper function creates a ZIO workflow that if we run it, runs forever and consumes records from the given topic and prints them to the console, and then commits the offsets of the consumed records:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

def consumeAndPrintEvents(bootstrapServers: List[String], groupId: String, topic: String, topics: String*): RIO[Any, Unit] =
  Consumer.consumeWith(
    settings = ConsumerSettings(bootstrapServers).withGroupId(groupId),
    subscription = Subscription.topics(topic, topics: _*),
    keyDeserializer = Serde.long,
    valueDeserializer = Serde.string
  ) { record =>
    Console.printLine(s"Consumed key: ${record.key}, value: ${record.value}").orDie
  }
```

For performance reasons, records are always consumed in batches. `Consumer.consumeWith` commits the offsets of processed records in the background. Offsets of records that are processed while a commit is in progress are combined into the next commit. Commits that fail with a temporary error (a `RetriableCommitFailedException` or a commit timeout) are retried according to the `commitRetryPolicy` parameter (by default `Schedule.exponential(1.second) && Schedule.recurs(3)`). Any other commit failure, or a failure that remains after the retries, fails `consumeWith`.

For more options see [consumer tuning](consumer-tuning.md).

#### 5. The Complete Example

Now it's time to combine all the above steps to create a ZIO workflow that will produce and consume data from the Kafka cluster:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer.{Producer, ProducerSettings}
import zio.kafka.serde._

/** A simple app that produces and consumes messages from a kafka cluster
 * without using ZIO Streams.
 */
object SimpleKafkaApp extends ZIOAppDefault {
  private val BOOSTRAP_SERVERS = List("localhost:9092")
  private val KAFKA_TOPIC      = "hello"

  def run: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Unit] = {
    for {
      c <- Consumer
        .consumeWith(
          settings =
            ConsumerSettings(BOOSTRAP_SERVERS).withGroupId("simple-kafka-app"),
          subscription = Subscription.topics(KAFKA_TOPIC),
          keyDeserializer = Serde.long,
          valueDeserializer = Serde.string
        ) { record =>
          Console.printLine(s"Consumed ${record.key()}, ${record.value()}").orDie
        }
        .fork

      producer <- Producer.make(ProducerSettings(BOOSTRAP_SERVERS))
      p <- Clock.currentDateTime
        .flatMap { time =>
          producer.produce[Any, Long, String](
            topic = KAFKA_TOPIC,
            key = time.getHour.toLong,
            value = s"$time -- Hello, World!",
            keySerializer = Serde.long,
            valueSerializer = Serde.string
          )
        }
        .schedule(Schedule.spaced(1.second))
        .fork

      _ <- (c <*> p).join
    } yield ()
  }

}
```

### Zio-kafka With Zio-streams

As we said before, to write producers and consumers using the zio-kafka library, we have two choices:

1. Using ZIO workflows
2. Using zio-streams workflows

In this section we show zio-kafka's seamless integration with zio-streams.

#### 1. Streaming Producer API

With zio-kafka's `Producer.produceAll` we get a `ZPipeline`. It takes streams of `ProducerRecord[K, V]`, produces these records to a Kafka topic, and then returns a stream of `RecordMetadata`:

```scala
trait Producer {
  def produceAll[R, K, V](
    keySerializer: Serializer[R, K],
    valueSerializer: Serializer[R, V]
  ): ZPipeline[R, Throwable, ProducerRecord[K, V], RecordMetadata]
}
```

Here is an example that uses `Producer.produceAll`:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer._
import zio.kafka.serde._
import zio.stream._

val topic              = "my-topic"
val producer: Producer = ???

val produceRecords: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZStream
    .fromIterator(Iterator.from(0), maxChunkSize = 50)
             // ZStream[Any, Throwable, Int]
    .map(i => new ProducerRecord(topic, i, s"record $i"))
             // ZStream[Any, Throwable, ProducerRecord[Int, String]]
    .via(producer.produceAll(Serde.int, Serde.string))
             // ZStream[Any, Throwable, RecordMetadata]
    .runDrain
```

For performance reasons, method `produceAll` produces records in batches, every chunk of the input stream results in a batch. Once all acknowledges are received, the next batch is produced.

See [this page](consuming-producing-and-committing-offsets.md) for tips that can increase producing throughput.

#### 2. Creating a Consumer

When we use the streaming API we need to construct a Consumer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka._
import zio.kafka.consumer._

val consumer: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Consumer] =
  Consumer.make(
    ConsumerSettings(List("localhost:9092"))
      .withGroupId("streaming-kafka-app")
  )
```

Notice that the consumer requires a `Scope` in the environment. When this scope closes, the consumer closes its
connection with the Kafka cluster. An explicit scope can be created with the `ZIO.scoped` method.

For more options see [creating a consumer](creating-a-consumer.md) and [consumer tuning](consumer-tuning.md).

#### 3. Streaming Consumer API

The `Consumer.plainStream` method gives a `ZStream` that, when run, consumes records from a Kafka topic and gives a stream of `CommittableRecord[K, V]`:

```scala
trait Consumer {
  def plainStream[R, K, V](
    subscription: Subscription,
    keyDeserializer: Deserializer[R, K],
    valueDeserializer: Deserializer[R, V],
    bufferSize: Int = 4
  ): ZStream[R, Throwable, CommittableRecord[K, V]]
}
```

Parameter `subscription` indicates which topics and partitions should be consumed from. For example `Subscription.topics("events")` to consume from the `events` topic.

Parameters `keyDeserializer` and `valueDeserializer` are the `Serde` that will be used to deserialize the raw record bytes to whatever type you want them to be in.

Parameter `bufferSize` sets how many chunks of records the stream may buffer in memory (4 by default).

To indicate that a record has been consumed successfully, and make sure that no other consumer in the same group will consume this record again (even when the application crashes and restarts), we need to commit the offset of the record. This is how it works: first get the `Offset` of the `CommittableRecord` with the `offset` method, then call `commit` on the returned `Offset`.

Here is an example:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

val KAFKA_TOPIC = "my-topic"
val consumer: Consumer = ???

val c: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics(KAFKA_TOPIC), Serde.int, Serde.string)
    .tap(e => Console.printLine(e.value))
    .map(_.offset)      // Get the offset of the record
    .mapZIO(_.commit)   // Commit the offset
    .runDrain
```

While this works, it is not very performant. The problem with this approach is that we are committing offsets for each record separately. This causes a lot of overhead and slows down the consumption of records. To avoid this, we can aggregate offsets into batches and commit them all at once. This can be done by using the `ZStream#aggregateAsyncWithin` along with the `Consumer.collectOffsets` sink:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.kafka._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.serde._

val KAFKA_TOPIC = "my-topic"
val consumer: Consumer = ???

val c: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  consumer
    .plainStream(Subscription.topics(KAFKA_TOPIC), Serde.int, Serde.string)
    .tap(e => Console.printLine(e.value))
    .map(_.offset)                           // Get the offset of the record
                                             // Group offsets in an OffsetBatch
    .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
    .mapZIO(_.commit)                        // Commit the batch of offsets
    .runDrain
```

Notice that because we are using `aggregateAsyncWithin`, the commits run asynchronously with the upstream of `aggregateAsyncWithin`. Every 100 milliseconds the next `OffsetBatch` is committed.

:::caution
Keeping the chunking structure intact is important.

In the example so far we have used `tap` to print the records as they are consumed. Unfortunately, methods like `tap` and `mapZIO` destroy the chunking structure and lead to much lower throughput. Please read [a warning about mapZIO](avoiding-chunk-breakers.md) for more details and alternatives.
:::

For more details see [consuming Kafka topics using ZIO Streams](consuming-kafka-topics-using-zio-streams.md).

#### 4. The Complete Streaming Example

It's time to create a full working example of zio-kafka with zio-streams:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer.{Producer, ProducerSettings}
import zio.kafka.serde._
import zio.stream.ZStream

object StreamingKafkaApp extends ZIOAppDefault {
  private val BOOSTRAP_SERVERS = List("localhost:9092")
  private val KAFKA_TOPIC      = "streaming-hello"

  private val producerSettings = ProducerSettings(BOOSTRAP_SERVERS)
  private val consumerSettings =
    ConsumerSettings(BOOSTRAP_SERVERS).withGroupId("streaming-kafka-app")

  def run: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] = {
    val p: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
      ZIO.scoped {
        for {
          producer <- Producer.make(producerSettings)
          _ <- ZStream
            .repeatZIO(Clock.currentDateTime)
            .schedule(Schedule.spaced(1.second))
            .map { time =>
              new ProducerRecord(
                KAFKA_TOPIC,
                time.getMinute,
                s"$time -- Hello, World!"
              )
            }
            .via(producer.produceAll(Serde.int, Serde.string))
            .runDrain
        } yield ()
      }

    val c: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
      ZIO.scoped {
        for {
          consumer <- Consumer.make(consumerSettings)
          _ <- consumer
            .plainStream(
              Subscription.topics(KAFKA_TOPIC),
              Serde.int,
              Serde.string
            )
            // Do not use `tap` in throughput sensitive applications because it
            // destroys the chunking structure and leads to lower performance.
            // See the previous section for more info.
            .tap(r => Console.printLine("Consumed: " + r.value))
            .map(_.offset)
            .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
            .mapZIO(_.commit)
            .runDrain
        } yield ()
      }

    p <&> c
  }

}
```

### Producing and Consuming JSON Data

Until now, we learned how to work with simple types like `Int`, `String`, and how to use their `Serde` instances to serialize and deserialize the data.

In this section, we are going to learn how to serialize/deserialize user-defined data types (like case classes), and in particular how to use the JSON format. We also will learn how to use the `Serde` built-in instances to create more complex `Serde` instances.

#### 1. Writing Custom Serializer and Deserializer

In zio-kafka all the built-in serializers/deserializers are instances of the `Serde` trait. All `Serde`s offers several combinators with which we can create new `Serde`s. We take a closer look at 2 of them:

- Method `inmap` transforms the `Serde` with pure transformations from the source type to the target type and back.
- Method `inmapZIO` transforms the `Serde` with effectful transformations from the source type to the target type and back. As it accepts effectful transformations, we can encode any parsing failure with a `ZIO` workflow.

In this example, we use `inmap` to transform the built-in `Serde.long` to a `Serde[Any, Instant]`. The `inmap` method gets 2 pure functions, the first converts from `Long` to `Instant`, the second from `Instant` to `Long`:

```scala
import java.time.Instant
import zio.kafka.serde._

val instantSerde: Serde[Any, Instant] =
  Serde.long.inmap[Instant](Instant.ofEpochMilli)(_.toEpochMilli)
```

In the following example, we will use `inmapZIO` to transform the built-in `Serde.string` to a `Serde[Any, Event]` where `Event` is a case class that is serialized to/deserialized from a String containing JSON.

Let's say we have the `Event` case class with the following fields:

```scala
import java.time.OffsetDateTime
import java.util.UUID

case class Event(
  uuid: UUID,
  timestamp: OffsetDateTime,
  message: String
)
```

First, we need to define a JSON decoder and encoder for it:

```scala
import zio.json._

object Event {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Event] =
    DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Event]

  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Event] =
    DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Event]
}
```

Then we need to create a `Serde` for the `Event` type. To convert `Event` to JSON and back, we will use the zio-json library. To define a `Serde` for the `Event` type, we will use the `Serde.string.inmapZIO` combinator:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.serde._

object EventKafkaSerde {
  val event: Serde[Any, Event] =
    Serde.string.inmapZIO[Any, Event](s =>
      ZIO
        .fromEither(s.fromJson[Event])
        .mapError(e => new RuntimeException(e))
    )(r => ZIO.succeed(r.toJson))
}
```

As we can see, we use the `String#fromJson` to convert the string to an `Event` object, and we also encode any parsing failure with a `RuntimeException` in the `ZIO` workflow.

See [zio-kafka serialization and deserialization](serialization-and-deserialization.md) for more details.

#### 2. The Complete JSON Streaming Example

Here is a full working example of producing and consuming JSON data with zio-kafka, zio-streams and zio-json:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.json._
import zio.kafka.consumer._
import zio.kafka.producer.{Producer, ProducerSettings}
import zio.kafka.serde._
import zio.stream.ZStream

import java.time.OffsetDateTime
import java.util.UUID

/** This is the data we will be sending to Kafka in JSON format. */
case class Event(uuid: UUID, timestamp: OffsetDateTime, message: String)

/** A zio-json encoder/decoder for [[Event]]. */
object Event {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[Event] =
    DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[Event]

  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[Event] =
    DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[Event]
}

/** A zio-kafka serializer/deserializer for [[Event]]. */
object EventKafkaSerde {
  val event: Serde[Any, Event] =
    Serde.string.inmapZIO[Any, Event](s =>
      ZIO
        .fromEither(s.fromJson[Event])
        .mapError(e => new RuntimeException(e))
    )(r => ZIO.succeed(r.toJson))
}

object JsonStreamingKafkaApp extends ZIOAppDefault {
  private val BOOSTRAP_SERVERS = List("localhost:9092")
  private val KAFKA_TOPIC      = "json-streaming-hello"

  def run: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] = {
    val p: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
      ZIO.scoped {
        for {
          producer <- Producer.make(ProducerSettings(BOOSTRAP_SERVERS))
          _ <- ZStream
            .repeatZIO(Random.nextUUID <*> Clock.currentDateTime)
            .schedule(Schedule.spaced(1.second))
            .map { case (uuid, time) =>
              new ProducerRecord(
                KAFKA_TOPIC,
                time.getMinute,
                Event(uuid, time, "Hello, World!")
              )
            }
            .via(producer.produceAll(Serde.int, EventKafkaSerde.event))
            .runDrain
        } yield ()
      }

    val c: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
      ZIO.scoped {
        for {
          consumer <- Consumer.make(
            ConsumerSettings(BOOSTRAP_SERVERS).withGroupId("streaming-kafka-app")
          )
          _ <- consumer
            .plainStream(
              Subscription.topics(KAFKA_TOPIC),
              Serde.int,
              EventKafkaSerde.event
            )
            .tap { r =>
              val event: Event = r.value
              Console.printLine(
                s"Event ${event.uuid} was sent at ${event.timestamp} with message ${event.message}"
              )
            }
            .map(_.offset)
            .aggregateAsyncWithin(Consumer.collectOffsets, Schedule.fixed(100.millis))
            .mapZIO(_.commit)
            .runDrain
        } yield ()
      }

    p <&> c
  }

}
```

### Conclusion

In this tutorial we first learned how to create a producer and consumer for Kafka using the ZIO workflow with zio-kafka. Then we learned how to do the same with zio-streams. We also learned how to create a custom serializer and deserializer for the Kafka records and how to produce and consume JSON data using the zio-json library.

Runnable versions of these applications are in the [ZIO Quickstart](https://github.com/zio/zio-quickstarts) project on GitHub. Note that the quickstart may pin an older zio-kafka version than the one used on this page.

More information:

- [zio-kafka](https://zio.dev/zio-kafka/)
- [zio-streams](https://zio.dev/reference/stream/)
- [zio-json](https://zio.dev/zio-json/)
