## Writing Tests with the `zio-kafka-testkit` Library

Zio-kafka provides a `zio-kafka-testkit` library to help you test your code using zio-kafka.

To add it in your project, add the following dependency in your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-kafka-testkit" % "4.2.0" % Test
```

Let's study some examples of tests you can write with the `zio-kafka-testkit` and `zio-test` and let's see what this
library provides you.

### Testing a producer

This suite creates a producer and produces one record to an embedded Kafka broker:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde
import zio.kafka.testkit.Kafka
import zio.kafka.testkit.KafkaTestUtils
import zio.test.TestAspect.{timeout, withLiveClock}
import zio.test._

object ProducerSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope, Any] =
    (
      suite("Producer test suite")(
        test("minimal example") {
          for {
            producer <- KafkaTestUtils.makeProducer // (1)
            _ <- producer.produce(new ProducerRecord("topic", "boo", "baa"), Serde.string, Serde.string) // (2)
          } yield assertCompletes // (3)
        }
        // ... more tests ...
      )
        .provideSomeShared[Scope](Kafka.embedded) // (4) Provide an embedded Kafka instance, shared in the entire suite
      ) @@ withLiveClock @@ timeout(2.minutes) // (5)
}
```

The main entry points for zio-kafka test kit are the classes `KafkaTestUtils` and `Kafka`.

(1) A producer is created with lots of default settings. It knows how to connect to the Kafka broker by getting a
`Kafka` instance from the environment (see (4)).

(2) The producer is used to produce a record.

Take a look at the `produce*` methods in `KafkaTestUtils` when you need to produce a lot of records.

(3) The `assertCompletes` assertion from zio-test is used to check that the effect completes without errors.

(4) Provide a `Kafka` instance as a layer shared between all the tests. In this test we provide an **Embedded Kafka**,
meaning that a complete Kafka cluster is started and stopped inside the current JVM.

See further below for more options, such as connecting to an external Kafka cluster.

Note that any services that are _not_ provided at this line, must be given as type parameter to `provideSomeShared`. In
this case we are not providing a `Scope` (it is provided by the test framework).

(5) Zio-kafka requires a live clock.

#### Producer layer

In this example above, we decided to make a new `Producer` in each test. We could have decided to share one instance of
`Producer` between all the tests of this suite. For this purpose we can get a Producer layer using
`KafkaTestUtils.producer`. The result is:

```scala
suite("producer test suite")(
  // ... tests ...
).provideSomeShared[Scope](Kafka.embedded, KafkaTestUtils.producer)
```

#### More Kafka sharing options

Kafka is slow to start, so it is better to only start it once and share it between all tests of the suite.

However, if we insist on a separate embedded Kafka _per test_, we can provide the `Kafka.embedded` layer with
`provideSome` (instead of `provideSomeShared`), which looks like this:

```scala
suite("producer test suite")(
  // ... tests ...
).provideSome[Scope](Kafka.embedded)
```

We can also share one embedded `Kafka` instance between different test suites (i.e. between different test files) by
mixing in the `ZIOSpecWithKafka` trait, this looks like this:

```scala
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import zio._
import zio.kafka.producer.Producer
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde
import zio.kafka.testkit.{ Kafka, KafkaTestUtils, ZIOSpecWithKafka }
import zio.test.TestAspect.{ timeout, withLiveClock }
import zio.test._

object ProducerSpec extends ZIOSpecWithKafka { // (1)
  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope & Kafka, Any] =
    (
      suite("Producer test suite")(
        test("minimal example") {
          for {
            producer <- ZIO.service[Producer]
            _        <- producer.produce(new ProducerRecord("topic", "boo", "baa"), Serde.string, Serde.string)
          } yield assertCompletes
        }
        // ... more tests ...
      )
        .provideSome[Scope & Kafka](KafkaTestUtils.producer) // (2)
    ) @@ withLiveClock @@ timeout(2.minutes)
}
```

(1) Note the `ZIOSpecWithKafka` trait usage here instead of `ZIOSpecDefault`.

(2) When we need to provide additional layers with `provideSome` or `provideSomeShared`, both `Scope` and `Kafka` are
now provided by the test framework. Therefore, we need to include both in the type parameter.

More details about this `ZIOSpecWithKafka` trait [below](#ziospecwithkafka-trait).

### Considerations for sharing Kafka between tests

Zio tests by default all run concurrently. Tests may interfere with each other through the shared Kafka resource. The
best way to prevent interference is by making sure each test uses a different topic. If this is not feasible, we can use
the `TestAspect.sequential` aspect from zio-test to run the tests one by one:

```scala
import zio.test.TestAspect.sequential

suite("test suite")(
 // ... tests ...
) @@ sequential
```

### Testing a consumer

This suite produces records to a new topic and checks that a consumer reads them back:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.consumer.Subscription
import zio.kafka.serde.Serde
import zio.kafka.testkit.KafkaTestUtils
import zio.kafka.testkit._
import zio.test.Assertion.hasSameElements
import zio.test.TestAspect.{timeout, withLiveClock, withLiveRandom}
import zio.test._

object ConsumerSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope, Any] =
    (
      suite("Consumer test suite")(
        test("minimal example") {
          // Records (as key/value pairs) to produce and consume
          val kvs: List[(String, String)] = (1 to 5).toList.map(i => (s"key-$i", s"msg-$i"))
          for {
            topic <- Random.nextUUID.map("topic-" + _.toString) // (1)
            client <- Random.nextUUID.map("client-" + _.toString)
            group <- Random.nextUUID.map("group-" + _.toString)

            _ <- KafkaTestUtils.createCustomTopic(topic, partitionCount = 3) // (2)

            producer <- KafkaTestUtils.makeProducer
            _ <- KafkaTestUtils.produceMany(producer, topic, kvs) // (3)

            consumer <- KafkaTestUtils.makeConsumer(clientId = client, groupId = Some(group)) // (4)
            records <- consumer
              .plainStream(Subscription.topics(topic), Serde.string, Serde.string)
              .take(5)
              .runCollect // (5)
            consumed = records.map(r => (r.record.key, r.record.value)).toList
          } yield assert(consumed)(hasSameElements(kvs))
        }
      )
        .provideSomeShared[Scope](Kafka.embedded) // (6)
      ) @@ withLiveClock @@ withLiveRandom @@ timeout(2.minutes) // (7)
}
```

(1) Using random values for these parameters is important to avoid conflicts between tests as we share one Kafka
instance between all the tests of the suite.

(2) Here we create a topic with 3 partitions. Note that by default Kafka auto-creates topics. Therefore, creating
a topic explicitly is only needed when we want to control the number of partitions, or when your Kafka cluster does
not allow auto-created topics.

(3) A producer is constructed and 5 records are produced with `KafkaTestUtils.produceMany`.

(4) A consumer is constructed with `KafkaTestUtils.makeConsumer`.

(5) The consumer reads 5 records from the topic.

Be careful with the `take` method, due to pre-fetching, the consumer may have fetched more from the topic than expected.

(6) Similarly as in the producer test above, we provide the `Kafka.embedded` layer.

(7) Besides a live clock, this suite needs `withLiveRandom`. The default `TestRandom` of zio-test starts every test with the same fixed seed, so without `withLiveRandom` every test would generate the same "random" topic, client and group names. The `KafkaRandom` trait (see [below](#kafkarandom-trait)) avoids this problem as well.

### More consumer options

If we want to share a consumer between tests, we can use the `KafkaTestUtils.consumer` layer and provide it with the
`provideSomeShared` method (see the producer example above for more details).

### Utilities provided by the `zio-kafka-testkit` library

#### `Kafka` service

This trait represents a Kafka instance in your tests. It is used to provide the bootstrap servers to the constructor
methods in `KafkaTestUtils`:

```scala
trait Kafka {
  def bootstrapServers: List[String]

  def stop(): UIO[Unit]
}
```

The companion object provides a few layers to provide a Kafka instance in your tests:

```scala
object Kafka {
  /**
   * Creates an in-memory Kafka instance with a random port.
   */
  val embedded: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Kafka]

  /**
   * Like `embedded`, with extra or overridden broker properties.
   */
  def embeddedWith(customBrokerProps: Ports => Map[String, String]): ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Kafka]

  /**
   * Will connect to a Kafka instance running on localhost:9092 (with Docker, for example).
   */
  val local: ULayer[Kafka]

  /**
   * Creates an in-memory Kafka instance with a random port and SASL authentication configured.
   */
  val saslEmbedded: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Kafka.Sasl]

  /**
   * Creates an in-memory Kafka instance with a random port and SSL authentication configured.
   * Note: this broker does not actually work for clients; it only supports testing
   * zio-kafka's SSL check before connecting.
   */
  val sslEmbedded: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Kafka]

  final case class Sasl(value: Kafka)
}
```

The in-memory Kafka instances are created using [embedded-kafka](https://github.com/embeddedkafka/embedded-kafka). When the embedded broker cannot start, the layer fails with `EmbeddedKafkaStartException` (a `RuntimeException` from `zio.kafka.testkit`), whose `cause` holds the original error.

`Kafka.saslEmbedded` and `Kafka.sslEmbedded` also have `saslEmbeddedWith` and `sslEmbeddedWith` variants that accept custom broker properties. The `Ports` argument of these functions holds the `kafkaPort` and `controllerPort` of the embedded broker. `Kafka.saslEmbedded` provides a `Kafka.Sasl` (a wrapper around a `Kafka`) instead of a `Kafka`, so helpers that require a `Kafka`, such as `KafkaTestUtils.makeProducer`, cannot use it. Use the SASL helpers instead, such as `KafkaTestUtils.makeSaslAdminClient`, which logs in as user `admin` with password `admin-secret` by default.

#### `KafkaTestUtils` utilities

This object provides utilities to simplify writing your tests: settings, scoped values and layers for a `Producer`, a `Consumer`, a `TransactionalProducer`, a read-committed transactional consumer and an `AdminClient` (also over SASL and SSL), helpers that produce and consume records with `String` keys and values, and `KafkaTestUtils.createCustomTopic`. Each one is documented in the [`KafkaTestUtils` API docs](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-kafka-testkit_2.13/latest/zio/kafka/testkit/KafkaTestUtils$.html), and the tests in the `zio-kafka-test` module show them in use. The consumer settings are tuned for tests, for example with a 100 ms poll timeout and a 3 second session timeout. Tests that run in parallel need different transactional ids, because the transactional helpers without a transactional id parameter use the fixed id `test-transaction`.

The `make*` functions require a `Scope` and a `Kafka` (or `Kafka.Sasl`) in the environment. The consumer you pass to `KafkaTestUtils.makeTransactionalProducer` must have rebalance-safe-commits enabled, for example `KafkaTestUtils.makeConsumer(clientId, rebalanceSafeCommits = true)`.

#### `ZIOSpecWithKafka` trait

This trait can be used if you want to share one Kafka instance between different test suites.    
This allows you to speed up your tests by booting a Kafka instance only once for all your test suites using this trait.

Usage example:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.kafka.testkit.{ Kafka, KafkaTestUtils, ZIOSpecWithKafka }
import zio.test.TestAspect.{ timeout, withLiveClock }
import zio.test._

// In `src/test/scala/io/example/producer/ProducerSpec.scala`
object ProducerSpec extends ZIOSpecWithKafka { // Note `ZIOSpecWithKafka`
  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope & Kafka, Any] =
    suite("Producer test suite")(
      test("makes a producer") {
        KafkaTestUtils.makeProducer.as(assertCompletes)
      }
      // ... more tests ...
    ) @@ withLiveClock @@ timeout(2.minutes)
}

// In `src/test/scala/io/example/consumer/ConsumerSpec.scala`
object ConsumerSpec extends ZIOSpecWithKafka { // Note `ZIOSpecWithKafka`
  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope & Kafka, Any] =
    suite("Consumer test suite")(
      test("makes a consumer") {
        KafkaTestUtils.makeConsumer(clientId = "client").as(assertCompletes)
      }
      // ... more tests ...
    ) @@ withLiveClock @@ timeout(2.minutes)
}
```

This is a capability offered by ZIO2.    
See related zio-test documentation: https://zio.dev/reference/test/sharing-layers-between-multiple-files/

#### `KafkaRandom` trait

The `KafkaRandom` trait provides a few methods to generate random values.
To use it, you need to mix it in your test suite, like this:

```scala
import zio.kafka.testkit.Kafka
import zio.kafka.testkit.KafkaRandom
import zio.kafka.testkit.KafkaTestUtils
import zio.test.TestAspect.withLiveClock
import zio.test._
import zio._

object MyServiceSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault with KafkaRandom {
  // Required when mixing in the `KafkaRandom` trait
  // The best is to use a different prefix for each test suite
  override def kafkaPrefix: String = "my-service"

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope, Any] =
    suite("MyService")(
      test("minimal example") {
        for {
          topic    <- randomTopic  // Comes from `KafkaRandom`
          clientId <- randomClient // Comes from `KafkaRandom`
          groupId  <- randomGroup  // Comes from `KafkaRandom`
          _        <- KafkaTestUtils.createCustomTopic(topic)
          // ...
        } yield assertCompletes
      }
    ).provideSomeShared[Scope](Kafka.embedded) @@ withLiveClock
}
```

## How to Deploy to AWS Lambda

ZIO Lambda functions run on AWS Lambda through a custom runtime. You package the function as a GraalVM native image, which starts quickly and needs no JVM, and then deploy it either as a zip file or as a container image. This page covers both paths.

Lambda layers, which put the ZIO Lambda runtime in a separate package, are not covered here yet.

### Building the Native Image

To build the native binary of the example project, run this command from the root of the zio-lambda repository:

```shell
sbt "zio-lambda-example/GraalVMNativeImage/packageBin"
```

The build writes the binary to `lambda-example/target/graalvm-native-image/zio-lambda-example`. The example project sets `containerBuildImage` to `ghcr.io/graalvm/native-image-community:21.0.2`, so the build runs `native-image` inside Docker. To package your own handler, copy the GraalVM settings of the `zioLambdaExample` project in `build.sbt`, and set `GraalVMNativeImage / mainClass` to your `ZIOAppDefault` object.

### Deploying a Native Binary as a Zip File

Lambda reads its custom runtime from a `bootstrap` file at the root of the zip. The binary is your program, and `bootstrap` starts it.

To create the `bootstrap` file, write a script that runs your binary and place it next to the binary:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash

set -euo pipefail

./zio-lambda-example
```

Make both files executable, then zip them together:

```shell
chmod +x bootstrap zio-lambda-example
zip upload.zip bootstrap zio-lambda-example
```

To create the function, open the AWS Lambda console and choose **Author from scratch**. Under **Runtime**, choose **Amazon Linux 2023** (`provided.al2023`). Under **Code source**, upload `upload.zip`. Then open the **Test** tab, create an event with a JSON body that matches your handler's event type, and run it. The response shows the JSON that your handler returns.

### Deploying a Native Binary in a Container Image

Lambda also runs container images. The image contains the same native binary, and Lambda starts it as the container's command, so it needs no `bootstrap` file.

Create a `Dockerfile` in the root of the repository:

```Dockerfile
FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12
COPY lambda-example/target/graalvm-native-image/zio-lambda-example /app/zio-lambda-example
CMD ["/app/zio-lambda-example"]
```

Adjust the `COPY` path to match your project. Build the image and tag it for your Amazon ECR repository:

```shell
docker build -t native-image-binary .
```

Log in to Amazon ECR, then push the image. Replace the placeholders with your own registry and tag:

```shell
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <your_AWS_ECR_REPO>
docker tag native-image-binary <your-particular-ecr-image-repository>:<your-tag>
docker push <your-particular-ecr-image-repository>:<your-tag>
```

In the AWS Lambda console, choose **Author from scratch**, then choose **Container image** as the deployment type. Select the image you pushed. Because the binary runs inside a container, it adds some start-up overhead compared with the zip deployment.

---

## Event and Response Types

The `zio-lambda-event` and `zio-lambda-response` modules provide Scala case classes that match the JSON that AWS services send to Lambda and expect back from it. Use them as the event and response types of your handler, so you do not have to write those case classes yourself.

Most types come with their codec in their companion object, so `ZLambdaRunner.serve` finds it without an extra import. The exceptions are `DynamoDBEvent`, which has no codec, and five types whose codec sits in a differently named object, so you must import that object: `APIGatewayProxyRequestEvent` (`APIGatewayProxyRequest`), `APIGatewayV2CustomAuthorizerEvent` (`APIGatewayV2CustomAuthorizer`), `ConfigEvent` (`Config`), `CognitoUserPoolCreateAuthChallengeEvent` (`CognitoUserPoolCreateAuthChallenge`) and `CognitoUserPoolPreAuthenticationEvent` (`CognitoUserPoolPreAuthentication`). The tables below list the most common types. The reference pages describe every type and its fields:

- [API Gateway Events](./reference/events-api-gateway.md): API Gateway REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, custom authorizers and Application Load Balancer.
- [Messaging Events](./reference/events-messaging.md): SQS, SNS, Kafka, ActiveMQ, Kinesis, Firehose, Kinesis Analytics and DynamoDB.
- [Cognito Events](./reference/events-cognito.md): Cognito Sync and the user pool triggers.
- [Other Events](./reference/events-other.md): S3, S3 Batch, scheduled events, CloudWatch Logs, CloudFormation, CloudFront, CodeCommit, Config, Connect, IoT Button, Lex, Lambda destinations and Secrets Manager rotation.
- [Response Types](./reference/responses.md): all eight response types.

### Event Types

Event types live in the `zio.lambda.event` package. Each type decodes the JSON that the named AWS service sends:

| Type                                       | AWS source                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `APIGatewayProxyRequestEvent`              | API Gateway REST API with Lambda proxy integration      |
| `APIGatewayV2HttpEvent`                    | API Gateway HTTP API, payload format 2.0                |
| `APIGatewayV2WebSocketEvent`               | API Gateway WebSocket API                               |
| `ApplicationLoadBalancerRequestEvent`      | Application Load Balancer target group                  |
| `SQSEvent`                                 | Amazon SQS, a batch of messages                         |
| `KinesisEvent`                             | Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, a batch of records         |
| `KafkaEvent`                               | Amazon MSK or self-managed Apache Kafka                 |
| `ActiveMQEvent`                            | Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ                                  |
| `ScheduledEvent`                           | EventBridge scheduled rule                              |
| `CloudWatchLogsEvent`                      | CloudWatch Logs subscription filter                     |
| `CloudFormationCustomResourceEvent`        | CloudFormation custom resource                          |
| `ConnectEvent`                             | Amazon Connect contact flow                             |
| `CodeCommitEvent`                          | AWS CodeCommit repository trigger                       |
| `CloudFrontEvent`                          | CloudFront event for Lambda@Edge                        |

`APIGatewayProxyRequestEvent` is the exception to the companion rule: its codec is in the `APIGatewayProxyRequest` object in the same file, so import that object to use it with `ZLambdaRunner.serve`:

```scala
import zio.lambda.event.APIGatewayProxyRequest._
```

### Response Types

Response types live in the `zio.lambda.response` package. Each type encodes the JSON that the named AWS integration expects:

| Type                                                   | AWS integration                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `APIGatewayProxyResponse`                              | API Gateway REST API with Lambda proxy integration      |
| `APIGatewayV2HTTPResponse`                             | API Gateway HTTP API, payload format 2.0                |
| `APIGatewayV2WebSocketResponse`                        | API Gateway WebSocket API                               |
| `ApplicationLoadBalancerResponse`                      | Application Load Balancer target group                  |
| `KinesisAnalyticsInputPreprocessingResponse`           | Kinesis Analytics input preprocessing Lambda            |
| `KinesisAnalyticsOutputDeliveryResponse`               | Kinesis Analytics output delivery Lambda                |

To use a response type, return it from your function. The example below pairs an HTTP API event with an HTTP API response:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.lambda._
import zio.lambda.event._
import zio.lambda.response._

object HttpHandler extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val hello = (event: APIGatewayV2HttpEvent, _: Context) =>
    ZIO.succeed(APIGatewayV2HTTPResponse(body = s"You called ${event.rawPath}", statusCode = 200))

  override val run = ZLambdaRunner.serve(hello)
}
```

### Placeholder Types

Some types in the two modules are empty case classes with no fields. A placeholder event decodes any payload and discards its contents, so it carries no data. Placeholder events include `S3Event`, `SNSEvent`, `S3BatchEvent`, `LexEvent`, `LambdaDestinationEvent`, `SecretsManagerRotationEvent` and most of the Cognito user pool trigger events. The placeholder responses are `S3BatchResponse` and `SimpleIAMPolicyResponse`. The reference pages mark every placeholder.

`DynamoDBEvent` is different: it has no decoder at all, so it does not compile with `ZLambdaRunner.serve`. Do not rely on a placeholder to read data from an event. Define your own case class for the fields you need, as described in [How to Define Your Own Event Type](./how-to/decode-only-the-fields-you-need.md).

### Custom Types

If the AWS event you receive is not in the modules, or you need only some of its fields, write your own case class and codec, as shown in [How to Define Your Own Event Type](./how-to/decode-only-the-fields-you-need.md). zio-json ignores JSON fields that your case class does not declare, so you can decode a subset of a larger event.

---

## Getting Started(Zio-lambda)

A ZIO Lambda function is an ordinary function from an event and a `Context` to a ZIO effect. ZIO Lambda decodes the JSON event into your Scala type, runs the function, and encodes the result back to JSON for AWS.

### Writing a Handler

To write a handler, define an `object` that extends `ZIOAppDefault` and pass your function to `ZLambdaRunner.serve` in its `run` method. The function takes the decoded event and the `Context`, and returns a `ZIO`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.lambda._
import zio.json._

final case class GreetingEvent(name: String)

object GreetingEvent {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[GreetingEvent] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[GreetingEvent]
}

final case class GreetingResponse(message: String)

object GreetingResponse {
  implicit val encoder: JsonEncoder[GreetingResponse] = DeriveJsonEncoder.gen[GreetingResponse]
}

object GreetingHandler extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val greet = (event: GreetingEvent, context: Context) =>
    ZIO.succeed(GreetingResponse(s"Hello, ${event.name}! Request ${context.awsRequestId}"))

  override val run = ZLambdaRunner.serve(greet)
}
```

`ZLambdaRunner.serve` needs a `JsonDecoder` for the event type and a `JsonEncoder` for the response type. It looks them up as implicits, so put each codec in the companion object of its type, as the example does. The error type of your function must be a subtype of `Throwable`. The example's effect cannot fail, so its error type is `Nothing`, which satisfies that rule.

The runner loops forever. It asks the AWS Lambda Runtime API for the next invocation, decodes the payload, runs your function, and sends back the encoded result. A ZIO failure from your function is reported to Lambda as an invocation error, so the caller sees the failure instead of a silent timeout.

### Reading the Context

The `Context` describes the current invocation. It is a case class with these fields:

- `awsRequestId` is the ID of the current request, which is useful for logging.
- `remainingTimeInMillis` holds the deadline of the invocation as a Unix time in milliseconds, not a duration. See [Context](./reference/context.md).
- `logGroupName` and `logStreamName` name the CloudWatch Logs group and stream.
- `functionName`, `functionVersion` and `invokedFunctionArn` identify the function that runs.
- `memoryLimitInMB` is the memory size configured for the function.
- `clientContext` and `cognitoIdentity` are `Option` values that Lambda fills in only for invocations from the AWS Mobile SDK.

Your function receives the `Context` as its second argument. Use it to read these values, and do not construct one in production code, because the runtime creates it for each invocation.

### Working with Raw JSON

If you want to decode the JSON yourself, use `ZLambdaRunner.serveRaw` instead of `ZLambdaRunner.serve`. It passes the event as a `String` and expects a `String` in return, so no codecs are needed:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.lambda._

object RawHandler extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val echo = (json: String, _: Context) => ZIO.succeed(json)

  override val run = ZLambdaRunner.serveRaw(echo)
}
```

This form suits functions that only forward or log the payload. For typed events, prefer `ZLambdaRunner.serve`.

### Using Event Types from zio-lambda-event

The `zio-lambda-event` module provides types for common AWS event sources. Use them as the event type of your function, and the codecs are already in place. This function logs each message in an SQS batch and returns the number of messages, which the runner encodes as a JSON number:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.lambda._
import zio.lambda.event._

object QueueHandler extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val handle = (event: SQSEvent, _: Context) =>
    ZIO.foreachDiscard(event.records)(record => ZIO.logInfo(s"Message: ${record.body}")).as(event.records.size)

  override val run = ZLambdaRunner.serve(handle)
}
```

The [Event and Response Types](./event-and-response-types.md) page lists the types that the modules provide.

---

## How to Consume an SQS Batch

An SQS trigger sends your function a batch of messages in one `SQSEvent`. This guide shows how to process each message and how the outcome of the invocation affects the batch.

### Process Each Message

Use `SQSEvent` from the `zio-lambda-event` module as the event type. Its `records` field is the list of messages, and each `SQSRecord` has the message text in `body`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.lambda._
import zio.lambda.event._

object QueueConsumer extends ZIOAppDefault {

  def process(record: SQSRecord): Task[Unit] =
    ZIO.logInfo(s"Processing ${record.messageId}: ${record.body}")

  val handler = (event: SQSEvent, _: Context) =>
    ZIO.foreachDiscard(event.records)(process).as("done")

  override val run = ZLambdaRunner.serve(handler)
}
```

The function returns a `String`, which the runner encodes as a JSON string. The function must return a value that has a `JsonEncoder`, so the runner has something to send back.

### Fail the Invocation When a Message Fails

`ZIO.foreachDiscard` stops at the first failure. When the effect fails, the runner reports an invocation error to Lambda, and Lambda treats the whole batch as failed. SQS then makes the messages visible again after the visibility timeout, according to your queue settings. Make `process` safe to run twice, because messages that were already processed in the failed batch are delivered again.

### Read Message Attributes

`messageAttributes` is a `Map[String, SQSMessageAttribute]`. Each attribute has a `stringValue` and a `dataType` of `SQSMessageAttributeDataType.String`, `Number` or `Binary`:

```scala
import zio.lambda.event._

def priority(record: SQSRecord): Option[String] =
  record.messageAttributes.get("priority").map(_.stringValue)
```

For all fields of the event, see [Messaging Events](../reference/events-messaging.md).

---

## How to Define Your Own Event Type

Define your own event type when the AWS event you receive has no type in `zio-lambda-event`, when the provided type is an empty placeholder, or when you only need a few fields. This guide shows how.

### Write a Case Class and a Decoder

Declare only the fields you need, and put a `JsonDecoder` in the companion object so `ZLambdaRunner.serve` finds it. zio-json ignores JSON fields that your case class does not declare. For an Amazon DynamoDB Streams event, a type that reads the event name and the event source ARN of each record could look like this:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.json._
import zio.lambda._

final case class StreamRecord(eventName: String, eventSourceARN: String)

object StreamRecord {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[StreamRecord] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[StreamRecord]
}

final case class StreamEvent(@jsonField("Records") records: List[StreamRecord])

object StreamEvent {
  implicit val decoder: JsonDecoder[StreamEvent] = DeriveJsonDecoder.gen[StreamEvent]
}

object StreamHandler extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val handler = (event: StreamEvent, _: Context) =>
    ZIO.foreachDiscard(event.records)(r => ZIO.logInfo(s"${r.eventName} from ${r.eventSourceARN}")).as("ok")

  override val run = ZLambdaRunner.serve(handler)
}
```

`@jsonField("Records")` maps the capitalised JSON key `Records` to the Scala field `records`.

### Why Not the Provided Type

`DynamoDBEvent` in `zio-lambda-event` has no decoder, so `ZLambdaRunner.serve` does not compile with it. Other events, such as `S3Event` and `SNSEvent`, are empty placeholders. They decode, but they hold no data. See [Event and Response Types](../event-and-response-types.md) for the list.

### Make Fields Optional When They Can Be Missing

If a field is not always present in the JSON, declare it as an `Option`. A required field that is missing makes decoding fail, and the runner then reports an invocation error.

---

## Introduction to ZIO Lambda

ZIO Lambda is a ZIO-based AWS Custom Runtime compatible with GraalVM Native Image. It lets you write an AWS Lambda function as a ZIO program, with typed JSON events in and typed JSON responses out, and deploy it as a GraalVM native binary.

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-lambda/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-lambda_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-lambda_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-lambda_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-lambda_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-lambda_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-lambda_2.13) [![ZIO Lambda](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-lambda?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-lambda)

### Installation

ZIO Lambda is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3, and runs on the JVM, including as a GraalVM native image. Add the core module to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // The runtime: ZLambdaRunner, Context. JVM only. It brings zio-json with it
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-lambda" % "1.0.7"
)
```

### Modules

The event and response modules are optional. Add them when you want ready-made Scala types for AWS events and responses:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Scala types for the events that AWS services send to Lambda. JVM only
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-lambda-event" % "1.0.7",

  // Scala types for the responses that some AWS integrations expect. JVM only
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-lambda-response" % "1.0.7"
)
```

See [Event and Response Types](./event-and-response-types.md) for what the two modules contain.

### Where to Go Next

1. [Getting Started](./getting-started.md) shows how to write a handler with custom event and response types.
2. The Reference section describes [`ZLambdaRunner`](./reference/zlambda-runner.md), [`Context`](./reference/context.md) and every event and response type.
3. [Build an HTTP API](./tutorials/http-api-on-api-gateway.md) walks through an HTTP API on API Gateway step by step.
4. The how-to guides cover [testing a handler locally](./testing-locally.md) and [deploying it to AWS Lambda](./deployment.md).
