## Formatting Log Records

A `LogFormat` represents a DSL to describe the format of text log messages. Loggers accept a format through `ConsoleLoggerConfig` or `FileLoggerConfig`. Every member of the Scala DSL is listed in the [LogFormat Reference](reference-log-format.md).

To build a format from the DSL and pass it to a console logger layer:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogFormat._
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat }

val myLogFormat: LogFormat = timestamp.fixed(32) |-| level |-| label("message", quoted(line))
val myConsoleLogger        = consoleLogger(ConsoleLoggerConfig(myLogFormat, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default))
```

`LogFormat#filter` returns a new log format that produces the same result, if `LogFilter` is satisfied. The following format only outputs the `cause` label when the log event has a non-empty cause:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LogFormat }

val causeFormat: LogFormat = LogFormat.label("cause", LogFormat.cause).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)
```

### Log Format Configuration

The string representation of a `LogFormat` uses the following tokens:

| format                                   | description                                                                                                                                                                |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| %timestamp\{date-format\}%timestamp | Timestamp, where date format is a `java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter` pattern; without a pattern, ISO offset date-time,example: `%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ}` |
| %fiberId                                 | Fiber name, such as `zio-fiber-7`                                                                                                                                          |
| %fixed\{size\}\{format\}                 | Fixed size for format,example: `%fixed{7}{%level}`                                                                                                                    |
| %label\{name\}\{format\}                 | Labeled format, example: `%label{abcSpan}{%span{abc}}`. When `format` contains `%cause`, the label is written only for events with a cause                                 |
| %color\{LogColor\}\{format\}             | Colored format, log color values in upper case: `RED`, `BLUE`, `YELLOW`, `CYAN`, `GREEN`, `MAGENTA`, `WHITE`, `RESET`,example: `%color{CYAN}{%timestamp}`             |
| %level                                   | Log level                                                                                                                                                                  |
| %name                                    | Logger name (from the `logger_name` annotation or `Trace`)                                                                                                                 |
| %line                                    | Line number of the log call (from `Trace`)                                                                                                                                 |
| %message                                 | Log message                                                                                                                                                                |
| %cause                                   | Cause                                                                                                                                                                      |
| %kvs                                     | Key-values: every string annotation and every `LogAnnotation` in the logger context, except `logger_name`                                                                  |
| %kv\{key\}                               | Key-value: the string annotation `key`, or, when there is none, the `LogAnnotation` named `key` in the logger context                                                      |
| %spans                                   | All log spans                                                                                                                                                              |
| %span\{span\}                            | Log span with the given name                                                                                                                                               |
| %highlight\{format\}                     | Highlight given format with colors based on log Level                                                                                                                      |
| %%                                       | % character                                                                                                                                                                |
| %\{                                      | \{ character                                                                                                                                                               |
| %\}                                      | \} character                                                                                                                                                               |

Examples of format strings:

```
%timestamp %level [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %cause

%highlight{%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ} %fixed{7}{%level} [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %cause}

%label{timestamp}{%fixed{32}{%timestamp}} %label{level}{%level} %label{thread}{%fiberId} %label{message}{%message} %label{cause}{%cause}
```

The parsed form of a format string is a `LogFormat.Pattern`. See [LogFormat.Pattern](reference-log-format.md#logformatpattern) for parsing a string in code.

### Pattern Syntax Rules

When a format string does not parse, `LogFormat.config` fails with `Expected a LogFormat, but found <the string>`, without the position of the error. These rules cover the cases that most often fail or surprise:

- Plain text cannot contain a bare `%`, `{` or `}`. Write `%%`, `%{` and `%}` instead, as in `100%% done` or `%{id%}`. The name in `%label{name}` cannot contain these characters at all.
- Color names in `%color{...}` must be upper case. `%color{RED}{%level}` parses, `%color{red}{%level}` does not. Only `LogColor.config`, which reads a single color value, accepts any case.
- When the inner format of `%label{name}{...}` contains `%cause` directly, the whole label is written only for events that have a cause. This keeps `cause=` out of ordinary lines, but it also means that `%label{message}{%message %cause}` writes nothing for events without a cause. Give `%cause` a label of its own. When `%cause` is nested inside another element, as in `%label{cause}{%highlight{%cause}}`, the label is written on every line.
- `%kvs` leaves out the `logger_name` annotation; `%name` writes the logger name instead. To write it as a key-value, add `%kv{logger_name}`.
- The argument of `%timestamp{...}` must be a valid `DateTimeFormatter` pattern, and the size in `%fixed{...}` must be a number.

To check a pattern before it reaches a configuration file, parse it with `LogFormat.Pattern.parse`. The upper-case color name parses and the lower-case one does not:

```scala
LogFormat.Pattern.parse("%color{RED}{%level} 100%% done").isRight
// res0: Boolean = true
LogFormat.Pattern.parse("%color{red}{%level}").isRight
// res1: Boolean = false
```

### Creating a Custom LogFormat

Use `LogFormat.make` when the DSL cannot express the output you need. The function receives a `LogAppender` and all log inputs that ZIO core provides for each log event:

```scala
object LogFormat {
  def make(format: (LogAppender, Trace, FiberId, LogLevel, () => String, Cause[Any], FiberRefs, List[LogSpan], Map[String, String]) => Any): LogFormat
}
```

The format function arguments can be split into two sections:

* `LogAppender` - the output sink for the formatted log line
* All other arguments - the log inputs provided by ZIO core logging:
    * `Trace` - current trace (`zio.Trace`)
    * `FiberId` - fiber id (`zio.FiberId`)
    * `LogLevel` - log level (`zio.LogLevel`)
    * `() => String` - log message
    * `Cause[Any]` - cause (`zio.Cause`)
    * `FiberRefs` - fiber refs (`zio.FiberRefs`), collection of `zio.FiberRef` - ZIO's equivalent of Java's ThreadLocal
    * `List[LogSpan]` - log spans (`zio.LogSpan`)
    * `Map[String, String]` - ZIO core log annotations values, where key is annotation key/name, and value is annotation value

The function runs once for every log line, so anything it computes is computed per line.

The following predefined-style formats show how `LogFormat.make` combines the `LogAppender` functions described in the next section. Each block uses only the `LogAppender` argument and the annotations or cause that it needs:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogFormat

def annotation(name: String): LogFormat =
  LogFormat.make { (builder, _, _, _, _, _, _, _, annotations) =>
    annotations.get(name).foreach { value =>
      builder.appendKeyValue(name, value)
    }
  }

val cause: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.make { (builder, _, _, _, _, cause, _, _, _) =>
    if (!cause.isEmpty) {
      builder.appendCause(cause)
    }
  }

def text(value: => String): LogFormat =
  LogFormat.make { (builder, _, _, _, _, _, _, _, _) =>
    builder.appendText(value)
  }
```

This `text` function evaluates `value` again for every line. The library's own `LogFormat.text` evaluates its argument only once, when the format is built, so use a `LogFormat.make` function like this one for a value that changes between lines.

### LogFormat and LogAppender

The `LogAppender` provides these essential functions, which the predefined log formats use:

* `appendCause(cause: Cause[Any])` - appends a `zio.Cause` to the log, some logging backends may have special support for logging failures
* `appendNumeric[A](numeric: A)` - appends a numeric value to the log
* `appendText(text: String)` - appends unstructured text to the log
* `appendKeyValue(key: String, value: String)` - appends a key/value string pair to the log

How these functions render depends on the logging backend:

* [SLF4J v1](slf4j1.md) logging backend - key/value pairs from annotations and spans are put into the SLF4J [MDC context](https://logback.qos.ch/manual/mdc.html) while the line is logged, the cause is transformed to a `Throwable` and passed as the SLF4J throwable, and all other text and numeric parts, including `LogFormat.label` output written as `name=value`, are added to the SLF4J log message.
* [SLF4J v2](slf4j2.md) logging backend - the same as SLF4J v1, except that key/value pairs are added to the SLF4J 2 event as key-value pairs (`addKeyValue`), not to the MDC. Use a provider layout that prints key-value pairs, such as `%kvp` in Logback, to see them.
* Console and file logging backends - in general all values are added to the log line, `Cause.prettyPrint` renders the cause details.
* JSON loggers (`consoleJsonLogger`, `fileJsonLogger`) - each label and key/value pair becomes a JSON field, see [How to Log JSON](how-to-json-logs.md).

---

## Getting Started with ZIO Logging

This page shows how to add ZIO Logging to a project, which extra module to pick for your setup, and how to run a first program that writes its log lines through a ZIO Logging logger.

### Installation

Add the core module to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
// ZIO Logging core module (JVM)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

The core module is also published for Scala.js and Scala Native. In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, or in a cross-built project, use `%%%` instead of `%%`:

```scala
// ZIO Logging core module (JVM, Scala.js or Scala Native)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %%% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

The core module holds the [console loggers](console-logger.md), the [file loggers](file-logger.md), the [reconfigurable logger](reconfigurable-logger.md), [log formats](formatting-log-records.md), [log filters](log-filter.md) and [log metrics](metrics.md). Many applications need nothing else. See [Platforms](index.md#platforms) for what works on JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native.

### Choosing Extra Modules

The other modules connect ZIO Logging to Java logging libraries. All of them are JVM only. Pick a module by the direction the log lines travel:

- A **backend** sends the log lines of your ZIO code to a Java logging library, which then formats and writes them.
- A **bridge** does the opposite: it takes the log lines that Java libraries write and sends them to your ZIO Logging loggers.

| Module                      | Kind    | Use it when                                                                                                     | Page                                  |
| --------------------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `zio-logging-slf4j2`        | backend | your project already writes logs through SLF4J 2 (for example with Logback 1.3+ or Log4j 2), and ZIO logs should go there too | [SLF4J v2](slf4j2.md)                  |
| `zio-logging-slf4j`         | backend | the same, with an SLF4J 1.x setup                                                                               | [SLF4J v1](slf4j1.md)                  |
| `zio-logging-jpl`           | backend | your project writes logs through the Java Platform/System Logger (`System.Logger`)                              | [Java Platform/System Logger](jpl.md) |
| `zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge` | bridge  | a library you depend on logs through SLF4J 2, and its lines should reach your ZIO loggers                       | [SLF4J v2 bridge](slf4j2-bridge.md)   |
| `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge`  | bridge  | the same, for a library that logs through SLF4J 1.x                                                             | [SLF4J v1 bridge](slf4j1-bridge.md)   |
| `zio-logging-jul-bridge`    | bridge  | a library you depend on logs through `java.util.logging` (JUL), and its lines should reach your ZIO loggers     | [java.util.logging bridge](jul-bridge.md) |

Add the line for each module you need:

```scala
// Backends: send ZIO log lines to a Java logging library
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j2" % "2.5.5" // SLF4J v2
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j"  % "2.5.5" // SLF4J v1
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-jpl"    % "2.5.5" // Java Platform/System Logger

// Bridges: send Java library log lines to ZIO Logging
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge" % "2.5.5" // SLF4J v2
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j-bridge"  % "2.5.5" // SLF4J v1
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-jul-bridge"    % "2.5.5" // java.util.logging
```

:::caution
Do not combine a backend and a bridge for the same logging system in one application. For example, the SLF4J backend sends ZIO log lines to SLF4J, and the SLF4J bridge sends SLF4J log lines back to ZIO, so each line goes round in a loop. Also pick either the v1 or the v2 variant of a module, never both. [How They Work Together](reference-integrations.md#how-they-work-together) lists the combinations.
:::

### Your First Program

ZIO already logs through `ZIO.logInfo`, `ZIO.logError` and the other `ZIO.log*` methods. ZIO Logging does not change those calls. It provides loggers that decide how the log lines look and where they go.

Install the logger in the application's `bootstrap` layer. The logger then serves the whole application runtime, so the failure at the end of the program below is logged with it too:

```scala
import zio.logging.consoleLogger
import zio.{ ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }

object SimpleApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Start")
      _ <- ZIO.fail("FAILURE")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Done")
    } yield ExitCode.success

}
```

The `bootstrap` layer does two things:

1. `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` removes ZIO's built-in logger. Without this step, every line is printed twice: once by ZIO's default logger and once by the console logger.
2. `consoleLogger()` adds the ZIO Logging console logger. With no arguments, it reads its settings from the `logger` path of the application's configuration. When nothing is configured there, it uses the default format and logs at level `Info` and above. [Configuration](reference-configuration.md) lists every setting.

Running the program prints lines like these:

```
timestamp=2023-03-15T08:36:24.421098+01:00 level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-4 message="Start"
timestamp=2023-03-15T08:36:24.440181+01:00 level=ERROR thread=zio-fiber-0 message="" cause=Exception in thread "zio-fiber-4" java.lang.String: FAILURE
	at zio.logging.example.SimpleApp.run(SimpleApp.scala:29)
```

`"Done"` never appears, because `ZIO.fail` ends the program before it. The `ERROR` line comes from the ZIO runtime, which logs the failure through the same console logger.

### Next Steps

- Follow the [ZIO Logging Basics](tutorial.md) tutorial to learn log levels, annotations and JSON output step by step.
- Read [Console Logger](console-logger.md) to change the format, the level or the output stream.
- Browse the [Logger Layers reference](reference-logger-layers.md) for every logger ZIO Logging provides.
- Find task-focused recipes, such as [JSON logs](how-to-json-logs.md) or [correlation IDs](how-to-correlation-id.md), under How-to Guides.
- See the [examples](https://github.com/zio/zio-logging/tree/master/examples) folder for complete programs.

## How to Send Java Library Logs Through ZIO Logging

You want the logs from third-party Java libraries to appear in the same output as your ZIO logs, with the same format and the same level filter. Many libraries log through SLF4J, the common Java logging facade, or through `java.util.logging` (JUL), the logging package that ships with the JDK. Without a bridge, those libraries write to their own backend, so you end up with two formats, two level settings, and logs that a shipper may not collect. ZIO Logging provides `Slf4jBridge` for SLF4J v2 and `JULBridge` for `java.util.logging`. Each one forwards the library's log calls to the ZIO logger and applies a `LogFilter`.

The steps are:

1. Add the bridge modules to your build.
2. Install the SLF4J bridge with a filter from config.
3. Install the SLF4J bridge with a filter in code.
4. Install the JUL bridge, and install both bridges together.
5. Check for conflicting logging modules.

### Prerequisites

Add the bridge modules. The `slf4j2-bridge` module is for SLF4J v2 (`slf4j-api` 2.x) only. For libraries on `slf4j-api` 1.7.x, use the [SLF4J v1 bridge](./slf4j1-bridge.md) module, `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge`, instead; its `Slf4jBridge` object has the same layers, so the steps below apply to it unchanged. All bridge modules require Java 17 or later. Add both bridge modules to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge" % "2.5.5",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-jul-bridge"    % "2.5.5"
)
```

:::warning
Do not use `zio-logging-slf4j2` together with the SLF4J bridge. The `zio-logging-slf4j2` module sends ZIO logs to an SLF4J provider, and the bridge sends SLF4J logs to ZIO. Using both creates a loop. Choose the direction you need. For the other direction, see [SLF4J v2](./slf4j2.md).
:::

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import zio.{ ExitCode, LogLevel, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogFilter, consoleJsonLogger }
import zio.logging.jul.bridge.JULBridge
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge
```

### Install the SLF4J Bridge With a Filter From Config

We install `Slf4jBridge.init()` next to the console logger. The bridge reads its level from the `logger.filter` path by default, which is the same filter the console logger uses. The order of the layers matters: when the bridge's layer is built, it captures the ZIO runtime with the loggers installed at that moment, and library logs, including those from threads that run no ZIO fiber, go to those loggers. The `>>>` and `>+>` operators build their left side first, so the console logger must stand to the left of the bridge. The `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` call stops ZIO's default logger from writing the same lines a second time. The program looks like this:

```scala
object Slf4jFromConfigApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> Slf4jBridge.init()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    ZIO.logInfo("Service started").as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

`Slf4jBridge.init()` reads the filter from `logger.filter`, which is also available as the `Slf4jBridge.logFilterConfigPath` value. When the application keeps its logging settings under another key, pass the path as a `NonEmptyChunk[String]`. The following layer reads both the console logger's settings and the bridge's filter from under `app.logger`:

```scala
import zio.NonEmptyChunk

val appPathLogging =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
    consoleJsonLogger(NonEmptyChunk("app", "logger")) >+>
    Slf4jBridge.init(NonEmptyChunk("app", "logger", "filter"))
```

The matching HOCON nests the usual `filter` block one level deeper:

```hocon
app {
  logger {
    filter {
      rootLevel = INFO
      mappings {
        "com.example.thirdparty" = WARN
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The config keys are the same as in [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](./how-to-log-levels-from-config.md).

### Install the SLF4J Bridge With a Filter in Code

When the levels are fixed and do not need to change at runtime, pass the `LogFilter` directly. The following filter sets `INFO` as the root level and `WARN` for a noisy third-party package:

```scala
val thirdPartyFilter: LogFilter[Any] =
  LogFilter.logLevelByName[Any](LogLevel.Info, "com.example.thirdparty" -> LogLevel.Warning)
```

We pass this value to `Slf4jBridge.init`:

```scala
object Slf4jFromCodeApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> Slf4jBridge.init(thirdPartyFilter)

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    ZIO.logInfo("Service started").as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

The SLF4J library's own code still calls `org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger(...)`, and it does not change. Only the destination of its log calls changes.

### Install the JUL Bridge

The `JULBridge` layers follow the same pattern as `Slf4jBridge`. `JULBridge.init()` reads the filter from `logger.filter`, and `JULBridge.init(filter)` takes a `LogFilter` in code. The following program forwards a `java.util.logging` warning to the ZIO console:

```scala
object JulApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val legacyLogger = java.util.logging.Logger.getLogger("com.example.legacy")

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> JULBridge.init()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    ZIO.succeed(legacyLogger.warning("Connection pool is almost full")).as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

Installing the JUL bridge resets the global JUL configuration. It calls `LogManager#readConfiguration` with the single setting `.level= ALL`, which removes every JUL handler and level configured before, including those from `logging.properties` and the default console handler, and then adds the bridge's handler to the root logger. From then on, JUL itself filters nothing: every JUL logger creates a record for every level, and the bridge's `LogFilter` decides alone what is kept. Any JUL handler added after the bridge receives records of every level. See [What Installing the Bridge Changes in JUL](./jul-bridge.md#what-installing-the-bridge-changes-in-jul) for details.

### Install Both Bridges Together

The two bridge layers can be chained, so that SLF4J and JUL logs go through the same ZIO logger:

```scala
object BothBridgesApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
      consoleJsonLogger() >+>
      Slf4jBridge.init(thirdPartyFilter) >+>
      JULBridge.init(thirdPartyFilter)

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    ZIO.logInfo("Service started").as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

### Check for Conflicting Logging Modules

A bridge reverses the direction of a backend, and SLF4J allows only one provider, so some module combinations do not work together. Before you ship, check the runtime classpath for these cases:

- **The SLF4J backend and the SLF4J bridge together**: `zio-logging-slf4j2` with `zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge`, or `zio-logging-slf4j` with `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge`, send every line round in a loop.
- **Another SLF4J provider next to the bridge**, such as `logback-classic`, `slf4j-simple` or `log4j-slf4j2-impl`: if SLF4J picks the other provider, building the bridge layer fails at startup with a `ClassCastException` defect. Remove the other provider, or with SLF4J 2.0.9 and later, choose the bridge with `-Dslf4j.provider=zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.ZioSLF4JServiceProvider`.
- **The v1 bridge with `slf4j-api` 2.x**: SLF4J 2 ignores the v1 binding and discards library logs, although the bridge layer builds without an error. Use the v2 bridge.
- **The JPL backend and the JUL bridge together**: the JDK's `System.Logger` writes to JUL by default, so the [JPL backend](./jpl.md) and the JUL bridge send every line round in a loop.

### See also

- [SLF4J v2](./slf4j2.md) for sending ZIO logs to an SLF4J provider.
- [SLF4J v2 Bridge](./slf4j2-bridge.md) and [SLF4J v1 Bridge](./slf4j1-bridge.md) for the full reference of the SLF4J bridge layers.
- [JUL Bridge](./jul-bridge.md) for the full reference of the JUL bridge layers.
- [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](./how-to-log-levels-from-config.md) for the filter keys that the bridges read.
- [How to Log JSON](./how-to-json-logs.md) for the JSON format these examples use.

---

## How to Change Log Levels at Runtime

You want to turn on `DEBUG` output for a running service while you chase a problem, and turn it off again afterwards, without a restart. ZIO Logging does this with `ReconfigurableLogger`, a logger that forwards every log call to an inner logger that can be swapped while the program runs.

In this guide, we cover the two ways to swap it. In the first, the logger polls a configuration file on a schedule and rebuilds itself when the file changes. In the second, your own code pushes a new configuration, for example from an admin endpoint. We finish with the cases where today's behaviour can surprise you.

The steps are:

1. Load the logger configuration from a file that can change.
2. Install a logger that polls that configuration.
3. Keep polling after a bad edit.
4. Push a new level from your own code instead.
5. Know what is not reloaded or closed.

### The Problem

A logger built in the `bootstrap` layer from a config file reads the file once, at startup. Consider a service that runs with the root level at `INFO`. A customer reports an error that you cannot reproduce, and the lines that would explain it are at `DEBUG`. With a logger that reads its configuration once, you have to edit the file and restart the service, which drops the in-flight requests and may make the problem go away before you see it. Then you restart again to turn `DEBUG` off, because leaving it on fills the disk.

What you want is to edit the level, see `DEBUG` lines within seconds, and edit it back, while the service keeps running.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module, and `zio-config-typesafe` to read HOCON files. The examples read a file from disk, so they target the JVM:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging"         % "2.5.5",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-config-typesafe" % "4.1.2"
)
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, ReconfigurableLogger, makeConsoleLogger }
```

This guide assumes you know the `logger` configuration block from [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md).

### Load the Configuration From a File That Can Change

The reload works by running a load effect again and again, so that effect must read the source each time it runs. We use `TypesafeConfigProvider.fromHoconFilePathZIO`, which reads and parses the file inside the effect, and then load a `ConsoleLoggerConfig` from it with `ConsoleLoggerConfig.load`:

```scala
val loggerConfPath: String = "/etc/orders/logger.conf"

val loadLoggerConfig: ZIO[Any, Throwable, ConsoleLoggerConfig] =
  TypesafeConfigProvider
    .fromHoconFilePathZIO(loggerConfPath)
    .flatMap(provider => ConsoleLoggerConfig.load().withConfigProvider(provider))
```

The file holds the usual `logger` block:

```hocon
logger {
  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO
    mappings {
      "com.example.orders" = INFO
    }
  }
}
```

A config provider that is built once, outside the effect, would return the same values on every load. For example, `TypesafeConfigProvider.fromHoconFilePath` without the `ZIO` suffix parses the file when it is called, so wrapping its result in the load effect does not pick up later edits.

### Install a Logger That Polls the Configuration

`ReconfigurableLogger.make` takes three arguments: the load effect, a function that builds a logger from a loaded configuration, and the schedule for reloading. It loads the configuration and builds the first logger at once. Then it starts a background fiber that, on each step of the schedule, loads the configuration again and, if it differs from the current one, builds a new logger and swaps it in. We build console loggers with `makeConsoleLogger` and poll every 10 seconds, which is also the default schedule:

```scala
val reloadingLogger: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ReconfigurableLogger
    .make[Any, Throwable, String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig](
      loadLoggerConfig,
      (config, _) => makeConsoleLogger(config),
      Schedule.fixed(10.seconds)
    )
    .installUnscoped[Any]
```

The second argument of the build function is the logger that is being replaced: `None` on the first build, and `Some(previous)` on later ones. Ignore it unless your new logger needs something from the old one.

`ReconfigurableLogger.make` returns a scoped effect, and the `installUnscoped` syntax turns it into a layer that installs the logger and stops the reload fiber when the layer is released. See [Logger Layers](reference-logger-layers.md) for the other `install` variants and the other `make*` constructors. The application installs the layer in `bootstrap`, in place of the default logger:

```scala
object OrdersApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> reloadingLogger

  override def run: ZIO[Any, Any, Any] =
    (ZIO.logDebug("Polling the order queue") *> ZIO.logInfo("Orders processed"))
      .repeat(Schedule.spaced(2.seconds))
}
```

With `rootLevel = INFO`, only `Orders processed` lines appear. Change `rootLevel` to `DEBUG` and save the file; within one schedule step, about 10 seconds here, the `Polling the order queue` lines start to appear. Change it back to `INFO` and they stop. The first reload happens one schedule step after startup, not at startup.

The loaded configuration is compared with the current one through its `zio.prelude.Equal` instance, which is why `ReconfigurableLogger.make` needs a `C: Equal`. `ConsoleLoggerConfig` and `FileLoggerConfig` both provide one. When the two are equal, nothing is rebuilt, so polling an unchanged file costs one file read per step. One exception: the format part is compared with `==`, and a `format` key that contains `%timestamp{...}` with a pattern creates a new `DateTimeFormatter` on each load, which never equals the previous one. With such a key, the logger is rebuilt on every step. That is harmless for a console logger, but see the note on replaced loggers below.

### Keep Polling After a Bad Edit

The reload fiber stops at the first failed load. If someone saves the file with a HOCON syntax error or an unknown level name, the load fails, the background fiber ends, and nothing reports it. The logger keeps the last configuration it had, but no later edit is picked up until the service restarts.

A missing file is different: the Typesafe parser reads a missing file as an empty one by default, so the load succeeds with the default configuration (root level `INFO`, no mappings) and the logger switches to it.

To keep polling, make the load effect itself never fail: remember the last configuration that loaded, and return it when a load fails. The startup load still fails loudly, because a service that cannot read its logging configuration at startup should not start:

```scala
val resilientLogger: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZLayer.scoped[Any] {
    for {
      lastGood <- loadLoggerConfig.flatMap(config => Ref.make(config))
      safeLoad  = loadLoggerConfig.tap(config => lastGood.set(config)).orElse(lastGood.get)
      logger   <- ReconfigurableLogger.make[Any, Throwable, String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig](
                    safeLoad,
                    (config, _) => makeConsoleLogger(config),
                    Schedule.fixed(10.seconds)
                  )
      _        <- ZIO.withLoggerScoped(logger)
    } yield ()
  }
```

A failed load now returns the configuration that is already in use, so the comparison finds no change and the loop goes on to the next step. The same rule applies to the build function: if it fails, the loop stops too. `makeConsoleLogger` cannot fail, so this example is not affected.

### Push a New Level From Your Own Code

Polling suits a level kept in a file. When the change comes from an operator instead, through an admin endpoint, a command, or a message, push it directly. `ReconfigurableLogger.apply` creates the logger from a configuration and a first logger, with no polling. `ReconfigurableLogger#get` returns the current configuration and logger, and `ReconfigurableLogger#set` replaces both.

We create the logger in a layer that both installs it and returns it, so the rest of the program can reach it as a service:

```scala
type AdminLogger = ReconfigurableLogger[String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig]

val adminLogger: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, AdminLogger] =
  ZLayer.scoped[Any] {
    for {
      initial <- makeConsoleLogger(ConsoleLoggerConfig.default)
      logger   = ReconfigurableLogger[String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig](ConsoleLoggerConfig.default, initial)
      _       <- ZIO.withLoggerScoped(logger)
    } yield logger
  }
```

The `setLevel` function is what an admin endpoint calls. It reads the current configuration, changes the root level or the level of one logger name, builds a logger for the new configuration, and swaps it in:

```scala
def setLevel(logger: AdminLogger, loggerName: Option[String], level: LogLevel): UIO[Unit] =
  ZIO.suspendSucceed {
    val (current, _) = logger.get
    val filter       = loggerName match {
      case Some(name) => current.filter.withMapping(name, level)
      case None       => current.filter.withRootLevel(level)
    }
    val updated      = current.copy(filter = filter)
    makeConsoleLogger(updated).map(newLogger => logger.set(updated, newLogger))
  }
```

The program gets the logger from the environment and calls `setLevel`. In a real service, the call sits in the handler of your HTTP route or command; here it runs between two log calls, so the effect is visible:

```scala
object AdminApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers

  val program: ZIO[AdminLogger, Nothing, Unit] =
    for {
      logger <- ZIO.service[AdminLogger]
      _      <- ZIO.logDebug("Not written: the root level is INFO")
      _      <- setLevel(logger, None, LogLevel.Debug)
      _      <- ZIO.logDebug("Written: the root level is now DEBUG")
    } yield ()

  override def run: ZIO[Any, Any, Any] =
    program.provideLayer(adminLogger)
}
```

`ReconfigurableLogger#get` and `ReconfigurableLogger#set` are separate steps, so two calls to `setLevel` at the same moment can lose one of the changes. If several operators can call it at once, run the calls one at a time, for example behind a `Semaphore` with one permit.

The [Reconfigurable Logger](reconfigurable-logger.md) page shows a complete example with ZIO HTTP endpoints, built on a filter that can be changed in place.

### Know What Is Not Reloaded or Closed

A few parts of today's behaviour matter when you rely on runtime changes:

- When a new logger is swapped in, the old one is dropped without being closed. For console loggers this does not matter. For a file logger, the old logger's file stays open, so each rebuild with a different configuration leaves one more open file until the program ends.
- Only the logger built by the build function changes. The SLF4J and JUL bridges read their own filter once, when the bridge starts, and keep it. Lowering the level of the ZIO logger to `DEBUG` does not let through Java `DEBUG` lines that the bridge filter drops; see [How to Send Java Library Logs Through ZIO Logging](how-to-bridge-java-logs.md).
- Every log call first reads the current inner logger from an atomic reference, which adds a small cost per call. The [Reconfigurable Logger](reconfigurable-logger.md) page links benchmarks if this matters for your service.

### See also

- [Reconfigurable Logger](reconfigurable-logger.md) for the `ReconfigurableLogger` API and complete example applications.
- [Logger Layers](reference-logger-layers.md) for `makeConsoleLogger`, the file logger constructors, and the `install` syntax.
- [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md) for the `logger.filter` keys.
- [Log Filter](log-filter.md) for how logger names are matched against the mappings.

## How to Add a Correlation ID to Every Log Line

You want every log line written while one request is handled to carry the same ID, so that you can search the logs for that ID and see the whole story of the request, even when many requests run at the same time. ZIO Logging does this with a log annotation: a named value attached to an effect with `@@`, which every log call inside the effect, and every fiber it starts, picks up.

In this guide, we attach a request ID to a request handler, make sure the ID reaches the work the handler runs in parallel, and change the log format so the ID is printed. We finish with the JSON and SLF4J variants and a test.

The steps are:

1. Choose the annotation for the ID.
2. Read the ID from the request or generate one.
3. Apply the annotation around the handler.
4. Check that forked fibers carry the ID.
5. Print the ID in the log format.
6. Send the ID to JSON and SLF4J output.
7. Test that every line carries the ID.

### The Problem

Without an annotation, the only way to get the ID into each line is to pass it to every function and write it into every message. Each function that logs needs an extra parameter, and one forgotten call leaves a line that cannot be traced back to its request:

```scala
import zio._

def checkStockManually(item: String, requestId: String): UIO[Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo(s"[$requestId] Checking stock for $item")

def handleManually(path: String, requestId: String): UIO[Unit] =
  for {
    _ <- ZIO.logInfo(s"[$requestId] Handling $path")
    _ <- ZIO.foreachParDiscard(List("book", "pen"))(item => checkStockManually(item, requestId))
    _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Request done") // the ID is missing here
  } yield ()
```

The ID is also baked into the message text, so a log tool cannot filter on it as a field. In this guide, the ID lives in the fiber's log context instead, and the logger adds it to each line.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module to your build. Use `%%%` instead of `%%` for Scala.js or Scala Native:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

The examples use these imports and a small request handler. The handler is a plain function, `handle`, standing in for whatever HTTP library you use. It logs once at the start, checks two items in parallel, and logs once at the end:

```scala
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import java.util.UUID
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LogFilter, LogFormat, consoleJsonLogger, consoleLogger }

case class Request(path: String, headers: Map[String, String])
case class Response(status: Int)

def checkStock(item: String): UIO[Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo(s"Checking stock for $item")

def handle(req: Request): UIO[Response] =
  for {
    _ <- ZIO.logInfo(s"Handling ${req.path}")
    _ <- ZIO.foreachParDiscard(List("book", "pen"))(checkStock)
    _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Request done")
  } yield Response(200)
```

This guide assumes you know how to install a console logger. See [Console Logger](console-logger.md) if not.

### Choose the Annotation

A `LogAnnotation[A]` has a name, which becomes the key in the output, a `combine` function, and a `render` function that turns the value into a string. ZIO Logging ships `LogAnnotation.TraceId`, a `LogAnnotation[UUID]` named `trace_id`. Use it when your IDs are always UUIDs.

When IDs come from outside, for example from a load balancer or another service, they are often not UUIDs. Then define your own annotation over `String`:

```scala
val RequestId: LogAnnotation[String] =
  LogAnnotation[String](
    name = "request_id",
    combine = (_, newer) => newer,
    render = identity
  )
```

The `combine` function decides what happens when the same annotation is applied twice, once inside the other. Keeping the newer value means an inner `@@ RequestId(...)` replaces the outer one, which is what `LogAnnotation.TraceId` does too. For more on annotations, see [Log Annotations](reference-log-annotations.md).

### Read the ID From the Request or Generate One

If the caller sent an ID, reuse it, so that your lines match the caller's lines. If not, generate a fresh one with `Random.nextUUID`, which ZIO Test can make deterministic. The `requestIdOf` function reads an `X-Request-Id` header and falls back to a new UUID:

```scala
def requestIdOf(req: Request): UIO[String] =
  req.headers.get("X-Request-Id").filter(_.nonEmpty) match {
    case Some(id) => ZIO.succeed(id)
    case None     => Random.nextUUID.map(_.toString)
  }
```

Real HTTP header names are case-insensitive; your HTTP library's header lookup takes care of that, while this `Map` lookup does not.

With `LogAnnotation.TraceId`, the header value must parse as a UUID. The `traceIdOf` function treats a missing or malformed header the same way and generates a new ID:

```scala
def traceIdOf(req: Request): UIO[UUID] =
  ZIO.attempt(UUID.fromString(req.headers.getOrElse("X-Trace-Id", ""))).orElse(Random.nextUUID)
```

### Apply the Annotation Around the Handler

`RequestId(id)` returns a `ZIOAspect`. Applying it with `@@` sets the annotation for the whole wrapped effect, and removes it again when the effect ends, so the next request starts clean. We wrap the handler once, at the point where the request enters the application:

```scala
def handleWithId(req: Request): UIO[Response] =
  requestIdOf(req).flatMap(id => handle(req) @@ RequestId(id))
```

The typed variant looks the same with `LogAnnotation.TraceId`:

```scala
def handleWithTraceId(req: Request): UIO[Response] =
  traceIdOf(req).flatMap(traceId => handle(req) @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId))
```

Neither `handle` nor `checkStock` changes. They log as before, and the ID comes from the context they run in.

:::tip
ZIO core has its own string annotations, set with `ZIO.logAnnotate("request_id", id)`. They work for this purpose too. The two kinds are stored in different places, so the format must read the right one: `LogFormat.logAnnotation` reads only `LogAnnotation` values, `LogFormat.annotation(name)` reads only ZIO core annotations, and `LogFormat.anyAnnotation(name)`, `LogFormat.allAnnotations` and the `%kv{...}` and `%kvs` patterns read both.
:::

### Check That Forked Fibers Carry the ID

The handler checks its two items with `ZIO.foreachParDiscard`, which runs each check on a new fiber. Those lines still carry the ID. The annotations live in `logContext`, a `FiberRef[LogContext]`, and a fiber that is forked copies its parent's value. When a child fiber is joined, its context is merged back into the parent's with each annotation's `combine` function.

The copy happens when the fiber starts. A fiber that was started before the request, such as a background worker that reads jobs from a `Queue`, does not see the request's ID. Pass the ID along with the job and apply the annotation again in the worker:

```scala
case class AuditJob(requestId: String, message: String)

def auditWorker(jobs: Queue[AuditJob]): UIO[Nothing] =
  jobs.take.flatMap(job => ZIO.logInfo(job.message) @@ RequestId(job.requestId)).forever
```

### Print the ID in the Log Format

The annotation is now attached to every line, but the console logger does not print it yet. `LogFormat.default`, the format the console and file loggers use when none is given, writes the timestamp, level, fiber, message and cause, and no annotations. We build a format that also writes the request ID. `LogFormat.logAnnotation(RequestId)` writes `request_id=<value>`, and writes nothing on lines that have no ID:

```scala
val requestIdFormat: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.label("timestamp", LogFormat.timestamp(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME)) |-|
    LogFormat.label("level", LogFormat.level) |-|
    LogFormat.label("thread", LogFormat.fiberId) |-|
    LogFormat.label("message", LogFormat.quoted(LogFormat.line)) |-|
    LogFormat.logAnnotation(RequestId) +
    (LogFormat.space + LogFormat.label("cause", LogFormat.cause)).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)
```

The application installs a console logger with this format and handles two requests at the same time, one with an `X-Request-Id` header and one without:

```scala
object OrdersApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger(
      ConsoleLoggerConfig(requestIdFormat, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default)
    )

  override def run: ZIO[Any, Any, Any] =
    ZIO.foreachParDiscard(
      List(
        Request("/orders/1", Map("X-Request-Id" -> "req-7f3a")),
        Request("/orders/2", Map.empty)
      )
    )(handleWithId)
}
```

The lines of the two requests interleave, but each carries its own ID, including the lines written by the forked stock checks. The shape of the output looks like this, with the timestamps and fiber numbers shortened:

```text
timestamp=2026-11-17T09:15:02.104+01:00 level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-9 message="Handling /orders/1" request_id=req-7f3a
timestamp=2026-11-17T09:15:02.104+01:00 level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-10 message="Handling /orders/2" request_id=5b0e8c1a-...
timestamp=2026-11-17T09:15:02.109+01:00 level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-12 message="Checking stock for book" request_id=req-7f3a
timestamp=2026-11-17T09:15:02.109+01:00 level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-13 message="Checking stock for pen" request_id=req-7f3a
...
```

If your logger reads its format from configuration, add `%kv{request_id}` to the pattern instead. It prints the annotation with that name, whether it is a `LogAnnotation` or a ZIO core annotation. `%kvs` prints all annotations except the logger name:

```hocon
logger {
  format = "%timestamp %level [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %kv{request_id} %cause"
}
```

See [Formatting Log Records](formatting-log-records.md#log-format-configuration) for every pattern element, and [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md) for loading the `logger` block.

### Send the ID to JSON and SLF4J Output

In a JSON format, the same `LogFormat.logAnnotation(RequestId)` becomes a `request_id` field, so a log tool can filter on it directly. The following layer writes the request ID as its own JSON key:

```scala
val requestIdJsonFormat: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.label("timestamp", LogFormat.timestamp(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME)) +
    LogFormat.label("level", LogFormat.level) +
    LogFormat.label("message", LogFormat.line) +
    LogFormat.logAnnotation(RequestId) +
    LogFormat.label("cause", LogFormat.cause).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)

val jsonLoggerLayer: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger(
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(requestIdJsonFormat, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default)
  )
```

Each line then looks like `{"timestamp":"...","level":"INFO","message":"Handling /orders/1","request_id":"req-7f3a"}`. See [How to Log JSON](how-to-json-logs.md) for the other fields.

When ZIO Logging writes through SLF4J, you do not change the ZIO format. The default format of `SLF4J.slf4j` already passes every annotation except the logger name and the SLF4J marker to SLF4J:

```scala
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val slf4jLayer: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j
```

What SLF4J does with the annotations depends on the module. The `zio-logging-slf4j` module (SLF4J 1.x) puts them in the MDC for the duration of the call, so a Logback 1.2 pattern prints the ID with `%X{request_id}`, or all of them with `%mdc`. The `zio-logging-slf4j2` module adds them as SLF4J 2 key-value pairs, which a Logback 1.3+ pattern prints with `%kvp`. The Log4j 2 example in this repository prints them with `%X`. A Logback 1.3+ pattern that prints the key-value pairs looks like this:

```xml
<pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} [%kvp] %msg%n</pattern>
```

See [SLF4J v2](slf4j2.md), [SLF4J v1](slf4j1.md), and [How to Use ZIO Logging With Logback or Log4j 2](how-to-logback-log4j2.md).

### Test That Every Line Carries the ID

A test can check the context of every recorded line instead of parsing text. ZIO Test records each log call with `ZTestLogger`, and each entry's `context` holds the fiber's `logContext`. The following test handles one request and checks that every line, including those from forked fibers, has the request's ID:

```scala
import zio.logging.logContext
import zio.test._

val everyLineHasTheId = test("every line of a request carries its ID") {
  for {
    _       <- handleWithId(Request("/orders/1", Map("X-Request-Id" -> "req-1")))
    entries <- ZTestLogger.logOutput
  } yield assertTrue(
    entries.nonEmpty,
    entries.forall(_.context.get(logContext).flatMap(_.get(RequestId)).contains("req-1"))
  )
}
```

For more ways to check log output, see [How to Test Log Output](how-to-test-log-output.md).

### See also

- [Log Annotations](reference-log-annotations.md) for `LogAnnotation`, `LogContext`, `logContext` and `LogAnnotationZIOSyntax#logAnnotate`.
- [Logger Context and Annotations](logger-context-and-annotations.md) for an overview of annotations.
- [LogFormat Reference](reference-log-format.md) for `LogFormat.logAnnotation`, `LogFormat.anyAnnotation` and `LogFormat.allAnnotations`.
- [How to Write a Custom Log Format](how-to-custom-log-format.md) for building the rest of the line.

## How to Write a Custom Log Format

You want log lines in a layout your team has agreed on, for example the timestamp without the time zone, a padded level, the logger name in brackets, the message, and the user ID, with the error only when there is one. ZIO Logging builds such a layout from small `LogFormat` values joined with operators, and the same layout can be written as a pattern string in configuration.

In this guide, we build the layout from the `LogFormat` combinators, write the same layout as a pattern string, derive a JSON variant, add one value that the combinators cannot express with `LogFormat.make`, and check the result in a test.

The steps are:

1. Build the layout from combinators.
2. Add colors for the terminal.
3. Write the same layout as a pattern string.
4. Derive a JSON variant.
5. Compute a value per line with `LogFormat.make`, only when needed.
6. Test the format.

### The Problem

The default console format writes `timestamp=... level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-7 message="..."`. If your team reads logs with tools that expect another layout, or simply wants a shorter line, you might be tempted to put the layout into each message by hand:

```scala
import java.time.LocalDateTime
import zio._

def chargeCard(userId: String): UIO[Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo(s"${LocalDateTime.now()} INFO  [com.example.checkout] Charging card user_id=$userId")
```

Every call site now repeats the layout, the level is written twice, and nothing keeps the hundreds of calls consistent when the layout changes. The layout belongs in the logger, written once.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module to your build. Use `%%%` instead of `%%` for Scala.js or Scala Native:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import zio._
import zio.logging.{
  ConsoleLoggerConfig,
  LogColor,
  LogFilter,
  LogFormat,
  LoggerNameExtractor,
  consoleJsonLogger,
  consoleLogger
}
```

### Build the Layout From Combinators

Each part of the line is one `LogFormat` value from the `LogFormat` companion object. `LogFormat#|-|` joins two formats with a space, and `LogFormat#+` joins them with nothing in between. We build the line in two parts: the timestamp, which changes on every call, and the body, which we can test with fixed inputs later:

```scala
val timePart: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.timestamp(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS"))

val body: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.level.fixed(5) |-|
    LogFormat.bracketed(LogFormat.loggerName(LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace)) |-|
    LogFormat.line |-|
    LogFormat.anyAnnotation("user_id") +
    (LogFormat.space + LogFormat.cause).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)

val teamFormat: LogFormat = timePart |-| body
```

Each part does one thing:

- `LogFormat.timestamp` writes the current time with the given `DateTimeFormatter`. Without an argument, it uses ISO offset date-time.
- `LogFormat.level` writes the level label, such as `INFO` or `WARN`. `LogFormat#fixed` pads it with spaces, or cuts it, to exactly 5 characters, so the following columns line up.
- `LogFormat.loggerName` writes the logger name. `LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace` takes it from the `zio.logging.loggerName` aspect when one is set, and otherwise from the class that made the log call. `LogFormat.bracketed` wraps it in `[` and `]`.
- `LogFormat.line` writes the message.
- `LogFormat.anyAnnotation` writes `user_id=<value>` when the line has a `user_id` annotation, either a ZIO core annotation or a `LogAnnotation`, and nothing otherwise.
- `LogFormat.cause` writes the error. `LogFormat#filter` with `LogFilter.causeNonEmpty` drops the space and the cause on lines without an error.

`LogFormat#|-|` binds more loosely than `LogFormat#+`, so the last two lines read as `anyAnnotation("user_id") + (...)`. The output is the same either way, because joining formats is associative.

To use the format, pass it to a logger in a `ConsoleLoggerConfig`, together with a filter:

```scala
val teamLogger: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger(
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(teamFormat, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default)
  )
```

A line from this logger looks like `2026-11-17 09:15:02.104 INFO  [com.example.checkout] Charging card user_id=u-42`.

### Add Colors for the Terminal

For local development, colors make the level easier to spot. `LogFormat#highlight` colors a format by the level of the line, and `LogFormat#color` gives it one fixed `LogColor`. Both write ANSI escape codes, so keep them out of formats that go to files or log collectors. The following variant colors the timestamp blue and the level by severity:

```scala
val teamColoredFormat: LogFormat =
  timePart.color(LogColor.BLUE) |-|
    LogFormat.level.fixed(5).highlight |-|
    LogFormat.bracketed(LogFormat.loggerName(LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace)) |-|
    LogFormat.line |-|
    LogFormat.anyAnnotation("user_id") +
    (LogFormat.space + LogFormat.cause.highlight).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)
```

The default highlighter uses red for `ERROR`, yellow for `WARN`, cyan for `INFO`, green for `DEBUG`, and white for every other level, including `FATAL`. Pass your own `LogLevel => LogColor` function to `LogFormat#highlight` to change it.

### Write the Same Layout as a Pattern String

When the layout should change without a rebuild, write it as a pattern string under the `format` key of the logger configuration. Each element of the Scala format has a pattern counterpart:

```hocon
logger {
  format = "%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS} %fixed{5}{%level} [%name] %message %kv{user_id} %cause"
}
```

`%fixed{5}{%level}` is `LogFormat.level.fixed(5)`, `%name` is the logger name taken from the annotation or the trace, and `%kv{user_id}` is `LogFormat.anyAnnotation("user_id")`. A bare `%cause` writes nothing on lines without an error, but the space before it is still written, so those lines end with a trailing space. If you want a `cause=` key, write `%label{cause}{%cause}`, which is written only on lines with an error. For colors, the names in `%color{...}` are upper case: `%color{BLUE}{%timestamp}` parses and `%color{blue}{%timestamp}` does not.

`consoleLogger()`, with no arguments, reads this key from the application's `ConfigProvider` (see [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md)). A typo in the pattern fails the whole logger at startup with a configuration error, so check the string first with `LogFormat.Pattern.parse`:

```scala
LogFormat.Pattern.parse(
  "%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS} %fixed{5}{%level} [%name] %message %kv{user_id} %cause"
).isRight
// res1: Boolean = true
```

See [Formatting Log Records](formatting-log-records.md#log-format-configuration) for every pattern element and its syntax rules.

### Derive a JSON Variant

For machine-read output, the same parts go into a JSON logger. `LogFormat.label` gives each part a JSON key, and annotation formats such as `LogFormat.anyAnnotation` already write their own key. Leave out `LogFormat#fixed`, the brackets and the colors, which only make sense in text:

```scala
val teamJsonFormat: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.label("timestamp", LogFormat.timestamp(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME)) +
    LogFormat.label("level", LogFormat.level) +
    LogFormat.label("logger", LogFormat.loggerName(LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace)) +
    LogFormat.label("message", LogFormat.line) +
    LogFormat.anyAnnotation("user_id") +
    LogFormat.label("cause", LogFormat.cause).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)

val teamJsonLogger: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger(
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(teamJsonFormat, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default)
  )
```

Each line becomes one object, such as `{"timestamp":"...","level":"INFO","logger":"com.example.checkout","message":"Charging card","user_id":"u-42"}`. See [How to Log JSON](how-to-json-logs.md) for how values are written into the JSON.

### Compute a Value Per Line With LogFormat.make

The combinators cover the parts of a log event. When a part must be computed differently, for example the level in lower case because your log tool expects `info` and not `INFO`, write it with `LogFormat.make`. The function receives an appender and every input of the log event, and runs once per line:

```scala
val lowerCaseLevel: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.make { (builder, _, _, level, _, _, _, _, _) =>
    builder.appendText(level.label.toLowerCase)
  }
```

The nine arguments are the appender, the trace, the fiber ID, the level, the message, the cause, the fiber refs, the spans, and the ZIO core annotations. Write to the appender with its `appendText`, `appendNumeric`, `appendKeyValue` and `appendCause` methods; see [LogFormat Reference](reference-log-format.md#custom-formats-with-logformatmake) for each one.

Reach for `LogFormat.make` only when a value must be computed for each line. A value that never changes, such as the host name, is simpler as `LogFormat.text`. But note the opposite trap: the arguments of `LogFormat.text`, `LogFormat.label` and `LogFormat.timestamp(formatter)` look like by-name parameters, yet they are evaluated once, when the format is built, and not on each line. A format such as `LogFormat.text(java.time.Instant.now().toString)` writes the same instant on every line. Anything that changes between lines needs `LogFormat.make`, or one of the built-in formats such as `LogFormat.timestamp`, which reads the clock on each line.

### Test the Format

A format is a pure value, so you can check its output without running a program. `LogFormat#toLogger` turns it into a `ZLogger[String, String]` that returns the formatted line, and you call it with the inputs of one log event. We render the body of the team format for a `WARN` line with a logger name and a user ID passed as ZIO core annotations:

```scala
def render(format: LogFormat, level: LogLevel, message: String, annotations: Map[String, String]): String =
  format.toLogger(
    Trace.empty,
    FiberId.None,
    level,
    () => message,
    Cause.empty,
    FiberRefs.empty,
    Nil,
    annotations
  )
```

The output contains no timestamp, so it is the same on every run:

```scala
println(render(body, LogLevel.Warning, "Payment retried", Map("logger_name" -> "com.example.checkout", "user_id" -> "u-42")))
// WARN  [com.example.checkout] Payment retried user_id=u-42
println(render(lowerCaseLevel, LogLevel.Warning, "Payment retried", Map.empty))
// warn
```

In a ZIO Test spec, assert on the same `render` result with `assertTrue`. To check the lines a whole program writes, including annotations set with `LogAnnotation` values, use `ZTestLogger` and render each recorded entry; see [How to Test Log Output](how-to-test-log-output.md).

### See also

- [LogFormat Reference](reference-log-format.md) for every `LogFormat` value and operator.
- [Formatting Log Records](formatting-log-records.md) for the pattern syntax.
- [How to Log JSON](how-to-json-logs.md) for JSON output in detail.
- [How to Add a Correlation ID to Every Log Line](how-to-correlation-id.md) for printing a request ID with the format.

## How to Log to a File With Rotation

You want your application to write logs to a file on disk, with a new file for each day, so that each file stays small and old days are easy to archive or delete. A single file that grows forever is hard to move, search, and clean up. ZIO Logging writes to a file with `fileLogger`, and its only rolling policy, `TimeBasedRollingPolicy`, starts a new file each day.

The file logger is available on the JVM and Native platforms only. Scala.js has no file logger, so this guide applies to JVM and Native builds.

The steps are:

1. Choose the file settings.
2. Write the settings in a HOCON file.
3. Load the file in the `bootstrap` layer.
4. Understand the file names and when a new file starts.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module and the Typesafe config module to your build. The file logger is part of the JVM and Native artifact, and the examples below assume a JVM build. The Typesafe config module belongs to ZIO Config, which has its own version numbers:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging"         % "2.5.5",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-config-typesafe" % "4.1.2"
)
```

The examples use these imports:

```scala
import zio.{ Config, ConfigProvider, ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.{ FileLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat, fileLogger }
```

### Choose the File Settings

The `logger` configuration controls the file logger. Each key below maps to a field of `FileLoggerConfig`:

| Key                  | Default             | Meaning                                                                                  |
| -------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `path`               | none, required      | Destination as a `file:///` URI, for example `file:///var/log/orders.log`.               |
| `format`             | `LogFormat.default` | Text layout of each line. See [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md).     |
| `charset`            | `UTF-8`             | Character encoding of the file. An unknown name is a configuration error.                |
| `autoFlushBatchSize` | `1`                 | The writer flushes after this many lines. `1` flushes every line.                        |
| `bufferedIOSize`     | none                | Size of the character buffer in front of the file writer. When unset, no buffer is added. |
| `rollingPolicy.type` | none                | Rolling policy. The only supported value is `TimeBasedRollingPolicy`.                    |

The `filter` block sets the levels, as in [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](./how-to-log-levels-from-config.md). When `FileLoggerConfig#rollingPolicy` is `None`, the logger appends to the single file named by `path`, and nothing rotates.

### Write the Settings in a Config File

We write the settings in HOCON under the `logger` key. The `path` value must be a `file:///` URI, because `FileLoggerConfig` parses it with `Paths.get(URI.create(...))`. A plain path such as `/var/log/orders.log` is rejected as an invalid path. The settings file uses the URI form:

```hocon
logger {
  format = "%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ} %fixed{7}{%level} [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %cause"
  path = "file:///var/log/orders.log"
  charset = "UTF-8"
  autoFlushBatchSize = 1
  bufferedIOSize = 8192
  rollingPolicy {
    type = TimeBasedRollingPolicy
  }
  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO
  }
}
```

The directory `/var/log` must exist and be writable by the process. The logger does not create directories.

### Load the Config in the Bootstrap Layer

We load the HOCON text with `TypesafeConfigProvider.fromHoconString` and install the file logger in the `bootstrap` layer, the same way the `FileApp` example does. The `fileLogger()` layer reads the `logger` key by default. The application installs it as follows:

```scala
object OrdersFileLoggingApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val configString: String =
    """logger {
      |  format = "%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ} %fixed{7}{%level} [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %cause"
      |  path = "file:///var/log/orders.log"
      |  bufferedIOSize = 8192
      |  rollingPolicy {
      |    type = TimeBasedRollingPolicy
      |  }
      |  filter {
      |    rootLevel = INFO
      |  }
      |}
      |""".stripMargin

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Config.Error, Unit] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
      Runtime.setConfigProvider(TypesafeConfigProvider.fromHoconString(configString)) >>>
      fileLogger()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Order service started")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Order accepted")
    } yield ExitCode.success
}
```

The file logger can also be built in code. The following value sets the same destination and rolling policy as a `FileLoggerConfig`, and prints two of its fields so that you can see them:

```scala
import java.net.URI
import java.nio.file.Paths

val ordersFileConfig: FileLoggerConfig = FileLoggerConfig(
  destination = Paths.get(URI.create("file:///var/log/orders.log")),
  format = LogFormat.default,
  filter = LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default,
  bufferedIOSize = Some(8192),
  rollingPolicy = Some(FileLoggerConfig.FileRollingPolicy.TimeBasedRollingPolicy)
)
```

Printing the two fields shows the destination and the rolling policy:

```scala
println(ordersFileConfig.destination)
// /var/log/orders.log
println(ordersFileConfig.rollingPolicy)
// Some(TimeBasedRollingPolicy)
```

To install the file logger from this value, pass it to `fileLogger(config)` in a layer, as `fileLogger(ordersFileConfig)`.

### Understand the File Names and When a New File Starts

With `TimeBasedRollingPolicy`, the logger does not write to the file named in `path`. It inserts the date, in the form `yyyy-MM-dd`, before the last extension of the file name. The directory stays the same:

```text
file:///var/log/orders.log   ->  /var/log/orders-2026-11-10.log
file:///var/log/app.v2.log   ->  /var/log/app.v2-2026-11-10.log
file:///var/log/audit        ->  /var/log/audit-2026-11-10
```

The date comes from the local time zone of the JVM. The logger checks the date on every write. When the date has changed, it closes the current file, opens the file for the new date, and writes the line there. A new file therefore starts at the first log line after local midnight. A process that logs nothing does not create the new file until it logs again.

The library does not delete old files. Its source contains no code that removes files, so keeping a fixed number of days needs a separate job, such as `logrotate` or a scheduled cleanup.

:::warning
The file logger opens the file for the current date when its layer is built. If the directory is missing at that point, building the layer fails with a `java.io.FileNotFoundException` defect and the application does not start, so create the directory before the application starts.

After startup, the file logger ignores write errors. Each write is wrapped in a `try` block that drops any exception other than a `VirtualMachineError`. If the disk fills up, or the directory is removed before the next day's file is opened, log lines disappear without an error in the application. Monitor the file, or check its size and modification time, to detect this.
:::

### See also

- [File Logger](./file-logger.md) for the file logger configuration keys and the async variant `fileAsyncLogger`.
- [How to Log JSON](./how-to-json-logs.md) for writing the same file as JSON with `fileJsonLogger`.
- [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](./how-to-log-levels-from-config.md) for the `filter` block used by the file logger.
- [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md) for the `format` key.

## How to Log JSON

You want your application to write each log line as a JSON object, so that a log shipper or search tool can read each field by name without parsing free text. The default text layout puts the timestamp, level, message, and annotations into one string, so a tool has to guess where each value starts and ends. ZIO Logging solves this with `consoleJsonLogger` for the console and `fileJsonLogger` for a file. Both take the same `LogFormat` that the text loggers use, but they emit one JSON object per line.

In this guide, we define a format that picks the fields we want, install a JSON logger, and then read what each field looks like in the output.

The steps are:

1. Define the fields with a `LogFormat`.
2. Install the console JSON logger.
3. Write the same logs to a file.
4. Read the output.

### Prerequisites

Add the core module to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

The examples below use these imports:

```scala
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import java.util.UUID
import zio.{ Cause, ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LogFilter, LogFormat, consoleJsonLogger }
```

`LogFormat` is the building block for log layouts. A `LogFormat` value describes which parts of a log event to write, and `LogFormat#+` joins two formats together.

### Choose the Log Fields

We build a `LogFormat` where each field is wrapped in `LogFormat.label`. A label gives the field a JSON key. Text without a label is not lost, but all of it goes into one field named `text_content`, so a shipper cannot tell the parts apart. When the unlabelled text of a line is only spaces, such as the separators that `LogFormat#|-|` writes between labels, no `text_content` field is written. The following format labels every field:

```scala
val jsonFormat: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.label("timestamp", LogFormat.timestamp(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME)) +
    LogFormat.label("level", LogFormat.level) +
    LogFormat.label("fiber", LogFormat.fiberId) +
    LogFormat.label("message", LogFormat.line) +
    LogFormat.label("cause", LogFormat.cause).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty) +
    LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set.empty) +
    LogFormat.spans

val jsonConfig: ConsoleLoggerConfig = ConsoleLoggerConfig(jsonFormat, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default)
```

Each part of this format maps to a JSON key:

- `LogFormat.line` is the log message, which becomes the `message` key.
- `LogFormat.cause` is the error cause. The `filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)` call drops the `cause` key when there is no error, so successful log lines stay short.
- `LogFormat.allAnnotations` writes every log annotation as its own key. An annotation's key is its name, such as `user_id` for `LogAnnotation.UserId`.
- `LogFormat.spans` writes each active span as a key with its elapsed time, such as `"checkout":"12ms"`.

String values in the JSON are escaped, so a message that contains quotes or line breaks still produces one valid JSON object per line. A few kinds of value are written differently:

- A value that is itself a valid JSON object or array is embedded as JSON, not as a string. The `ConsoleJsonApp` example renders a `user` annotation as JSON, and the line contains `"user":{"first_name":"John","last_name":"Doe"}`.
- When a value starts and ends with a double quote, those two quotes are removed. This is why `LogFormat.quoted(LogFormat.line)` from a text format still writes a plain JSON string, but it also removes the quotes from a message such as `"done"`.
- A value made only of spaces is written as an empty string, `""`.
- ANSI color codes from `LogFormat#color` and `LogFormat#highlight` are removed, so a colored format writes plain values. `LogFormat#fixed` still pads or cuts the value, so leave it out of JSON formats.

:::caution
Keep a JSON value in a label of its own. When one label holds both plain text and a JSON value, the JSON logger can write a value that is not valid JSON.
:::

### Install the Console JSON Logger

`Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` stops ZIO from also writing its default text logger, so each event appears only once. We replace the default logger with the JSON logger in the `bootstrap` layer:

```scala
object JsonLogsApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger(jsonConfig)

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    (for {
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Order received")
      _ <- ZIO
             .fail(new RuntimeException("card declined"))
             .catchAll(e => ZIO.logErrorCause("Payment failed", Cause.fail(e)))
    } yield ExitCode.success) @@ LogAnnotation.UserId("user-42") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(UUID.randomUUID())
}
```

The `@@ LogAnnotation.UserId(...)` and `@@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(...)` calls attach annotations to every log line inside the effect, so each line carries the same `user_id` and `trace_id` values.

Each line that the program writes is one JSON object. The shape of the two lines looks like this, with long values shortened:

```text
{"timestamp":"2026-11-10T09:15:02.104+01:00","level":"INFO","fiber":"zio-fiber-7","message":"Order received","user_id":"user-42","trace_id":"3f2c9d1e-..."}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-10T09:15:02.109+01:00","level":"ERROR","fiber":"zio-fiber-7","message":"Payment failed","cause":"...java.lang.RuntimeException: card declined...","user_id":"user-42","trace_id":"3f2c9d1e-..."}
```

The `cause` key appears only on the second line, because the first line has no error.

### Write the Same Logs to a File

We use `fileJsonLogger` when the logs must go to a file. It takes a `FileLoggerConfig`, which holds the destination path, the format, and the filter. The file logger is available on the JVM and Native platforms only. Scala.js has no file logger. The following layer writes the same format to a file:

```scala
import java.net.URI
import java.nio.file.Paths
import zio.logging.{ FileLoggerConfig, fileJsonLogger }

val jsonFileLayer: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] = fileJsonLogger(
  FileLoggerConfig(Paths.get(URI.create("file:///tmp/orders.json.log")), jsonFormat, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default)
)
```

The destination is a `file:///` URI. `FileLoggerConfig` parses it with `Paths.get(URI.create(...))`, so a plain path such as `/tmp/orders.json.log` does not work in the `path` key. For rotation and file naming, see [How to Log to a File With Rotation](./how-to-file-logging-rotation.md).

### Read the Output

Each line is one JSON object, so a log shipper can split the stream on newlines and parse each line on its own. The keys come from the labels you chose in the format. If you rename a label, the key changes too. Downstream dashboards and alerts that read the old key stop matching, so pick the key names once and keep them stable.

Use `LogFormat.default` when you want the standard text layout from the console and file loggers for development. Use the JSON format for production, where machines read the output.

:::tip
To choose the fields with a config file instead of code, set the `logger/format` key to a format string, as the `ConsoleJsonApp` example does in `examples/core/jvm/src/main/scala/zio/logging/example/ConsoleJsonApp.scala`. The format string uses the same `%label{key}{%field}` syntax, such as `%label{message}{%message}`.
:::

### See also

- [Console Logger](./console-logger.md) for the full list of console logger configuration keys and the JSON console example.
- [File Logger](./file-logger.md) for the file logger configuration keys.
- [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md) for the `LogFormat` building blocks.
- [Logger Context and Annotations](./logger-context-and-annotations.md) for how annotations and spans are attached to log events.
- [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](./how-to-log-levels-from-config.md) for filtering which lines are written.
