## Log Filter

A `LogFilter` decides whether a log event is written. Every console and file logger has one, and the usual filter sets a minimum level per logger name: one root level for everything, and other levels for chosen packages or classes. This lets you keep your own code at `Debug` while a chatty library such as Netty only writes `Info` and above. This page explains how such a filter matches logger names. Every `LogFilter` member is listed in [LogFilter and LogGroup Reference](reference-log-filter.md).

The following filter sets `Debug` as the root level and overrides the level for specific logger names:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.LogFilter

val filter: LogFilter[Any] = LogFilter.logLevelByName[Any](
  LogLevel.Debug,
  "io.netty"              -> LogLevel.Info,
  "io.grpc.netty"         -> LogLevel.Info,
  "org.my.**.ServiceX"    -> LogLevel.Trace, // any number of segments between org.my and ServiceX
  "org.my.X*Layers"       -> LogLevel.Info   // one segment such as XLayers or XServiceLayers
)
```

This filter uses the `Debug` level for every logger except those whose name matches one of the mappings. A mapping covers the named package or class and everything below it, so `io.netty` also sets `Info` for `io.netty.channel.nio.NioEventLoop`. A level means "this level and above": for `io.netty`, an `Info` line is written and a `Debug` line is dropped.

The logger name comes from the `logger_name` annotation, which the `zio.logging.loggerName` aspect sets. When that annotation is missing, the name comes from the `zio.Trace` of the log call, which gives the enclosing class, such as `example.LivePingService`.

### How Logger Names Are Matched

The filter splits the logger name and each mapping at the dots into segments. A mapping matches when its segments match the first segments of the logger name, one by one; the logger name may have more segments after them. Each segment of a mapping takes one of these forms:

| Mapping segment                      | Matches                                         | Example                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A literal, such as `netty`           | Exactly that segment                            | `io.netty` matches `io.netty` and `io.netty.channel.Foo`, not `io.nettyx.Foo`     |
| `*`                                  | Exactly one segment, whatever its text          | `a.*.c` matches `a.b.c.Exec` and `a.b2.c.Exec`, not `a.c.Exec` or `a.b.b2.c.Exec` |
| `**`                                 | Any number of segments, including none          | `a.**.c` matches `a.c.Exec`, `a.b.c.Exec` and `a.b.b2.c.Exec`                     |
| `X*Y`, such as `*Impl` or `X*Layers` | One segment that contains `X` and ends with `Y` | `a.**.*y` matches `a.b.xy.Exec`, not `a.b.xyz.Exec`                               |

:::caution[Partial wildcards inside a segment]
For a segment with a `*` inside it, the filter looks for the pieces of text between the stars from left to right, each at its first occurrence, and the segment must end right after the last piece. This differs from a usual glob in three ways:

- A `*` at the end of a segment does not match a longer name. `org.my.Serv*` does not match `org.my.ServiceImpl`; it matches only segments that end in `Serv`, such as `Serv` or `MyServ`.
- A suffix is found at its first occurrence, not at the end. `*Impl` matches `ServiceImpl`, but not `ImplServiceImpl`.
- The text before the first `*` can appear anywhere in the segment. `X*Layers` also matches `MyXLayers`.

When you need a predictable match, use a whole-segment `*` or `**`, or write the full name.
:::

### Which Mapping Wins

A logger name often matches more than one mapping, for example a package and a class inside it. Before matching, the filter sorts the mappings from most specific to least specific. For each event, it uses the first mapping that matches the logger name, or the root level when none matches. The sort follows these rules:

- A mapping comes before every shorter mapping that is a prefix of it: `a.b.c` before `a.b` before `a`.
- At the first segment where two mappings differ, a literal segment comes before `*`, and `*` comes before `**`.
- When code maps the same name twice, the lower level comes first. A configuration file cannot map a name twice.

The order of the mappings in your code or configuration file does not matter. The following filter has a package mapping, a more specific sub-package mapping, and a wildcard mapping:

```scala
import zio.{ Cause, FiberId, FiberRefs, Trace }

val serviceLevels: LogFilter[Any] = LogFilter.logLevelByName[Any](
  LogLevel.Info,
  "org.my"         -> LogLevel.Warning,
  "org.my.service" -> LogLevel.Debug,
  "org.*.Repo"     -> LogLevel.Error
)

def accepts(loggerName: String, level: LogLevel): Boolean =
  serviceLevels(
    Trace.empty,
    FiberId.None,
    level,
    () => "",
    Cause.empty,
    FiberRefs.empty,
    Nil,
    Map(zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey -> loggerName)
  )
```

The class under `org.my.service` gets `Debug`. The logger `org.my.Repo` gets `Warning` from `org.my`, not `Error` from `org.*.Repo`: at the second segment, the literal `my` sorts before `*`, even though `org.*.Repo` is longer. A logger in another package, such as `org.other.Repo`, gets `Error`:

```scala
accepts("org.my.service.UserService", LogLevel.Debug)
// res0: Boolean = true
accepts("org.my.Repo", LogLevel.Warning)
// res1: Boolean = true
accepts("org.other.Repo", LogLevel.Warning)
// res2: Boolean = false
```

### Configuration

The configuration for the filter (`zio.logging.LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig`) has the following structure. In console and file logger configurations, it is set under the `filter` key, so with the default `logger` path the full keys are `logger.filter.rootLevel` and `logger.filter.mappings`:

```hocon
logger {
  filter {
    # LogLevel values: ALL, FATAL, ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG, TRACE, OFF

    # root LogLevel, default value: INFO
    rootLevel = DEBUG

    # LogLevel configurations for specific logger names or glob patterns, default value: empty
    mappings {
      "io.netty" = "INFO"
      "io.grpc.netty" = "INFO"
      "org.my.**.ServiceX" = "TRACE"
      "org.my.X*Layers" = "INFO"
    }
  }
}
```

Quote every key under `mappings`. HOCON reads an unquoted key with dots as a path, so `io.netty = INFO` becomes an object `io` that holds a key `netty`, not a mapping named `io.netty`. An unquoted key also cannot contain `*`. Level names are not case-sensitive.

The following config value is equivalent to the first two mappings of the configuration above:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.LogFilter

val nettyConfig: LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig =
  LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(LogLevel.Debug, Map("io.netty" -> LogLevel.Info, "io.grpc.netty" -> LogLevel.Info))

val configuredFilter: LogFilter[Any] = LogFilter.logLevelByName[Any](nettyConfig)
```

To read the filter from a configuration file at startup, see [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md).

### Apply a Filter to a Logger

The console and file logger layers apply the filter from their configuration for you. When you build a `ZLogger` yourself, for example from a `LogFormat` or for a custom backend, you apply the filter yourself. `LogFilter#filter` wraps a logger so that it runs only for accepted events, and the `ZLoggerOps#filter` syntax, written `logger.filter(logFilter)` after `import zio.logging._`, does the same with the arguments the other way round. Both return a `FilteredLogger`, whose output is `None` for a rejected event:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, Runtime, ZLayer, ZLogger }
import zio.logging._

val nettyQuiet: LogFilter[String] =
  LogFilter.logLevelByName[String](LogLevel.Debug, "io.netty" -> LogLevel.Info)

val lineLogger: ZLogger[String, String] = LogFormat.colored.toLogger

val filteredByFilter: ZLogger[String, Option[String]] = nettyQuiet.filter(lineLogger)
val filteredBySyntax: ZLogger[String, Option[String]] = lineLogger.filter(nettyQuiet)

val printing: ZLogger[String, Unit] = filteredBySyntax.map(_.foreach(line => println(line)))

val printingLayer: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> Runtime.addLogger(printing)
```

For the ready-made layers and constructors that install a logger, see [Logger Layers](reference-logger-layers.md).

---

## Logger Context and Annotations

A service handles many requests at once, so its log lines from different requests interleave. To follow one request through the log, each line needs to carry who and what it belongs to: a trace id, a user id, the part of the program that wrote it. Writing those values into every message by hand is tedious and easy to forget, and it buries them in free text that log tools cannot filter on.

Annotations solve this. You attach a value to an effect once, and every log line that the effect and the fibers it forks emit carries the value as a separate key and value, which a format writes next to the message or into a JSON field. This page explains the two kinds of annotations, how logger names fit in, and what happens when annotations nest. Every member it mentions is listed in [Log Annotations and LogContext Reference](reference-log-annotations.md).

### Typed Annotations

ZIO Logging's annotations are typed. A `LogAnnotation[A]` is a key with a name, a value type `A`, a `LogAnnotation#combine` rule for nested values, and a `LogAnnotation#render` rule that turns the value into text. The values for the current fiber live in a `LogContext`, which the fiber reference `zio.logging.logContext` holds. You define an annotation once and apply it to an effect with `@@`:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation

import java.util.UUID

val Tenant: LogAnnotation[String] =
  LogAnnotation[String](name = "tenant", combine = (_, inner) => inner, render = identity)

def handle(requestId: UUID): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo("Handling request") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(requestId) @@ Tenant("acme")
```

Compared with a plain string key, the typed form gives you three things. The compiler checks the value: `LogAnnotation.TraceId` accepts a `UUID`, so a user id cannot end up in the trace id field. The annotation decides what happens when an inner effect sets it again, through `LogAnnotation#combine`. And the name and rendering live in one `val` that the whole code base shares, so every module writes `trace_id` the same way.

ZIO Logging predefines three annotations: `LogAnnotation.TraceId` for a `UUID` named `trace_id`, `LogAnnotation.UserId` for a `String` named `user_id`, and `LogAnnotation.TraceSpans` for a `List[String]` named `trace_spans`.

### A Complete Example

The program below handles a checkout. It names its loggers, tags each request with a trace id and a user id, and adds a ZIO string annotation for the cart size. The format writes the level, the logger name, the quoted message, and the three annotations:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZIO, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{
  ConsoleLoggerConfig,
  LogAnnotation,
  LogFilter,
  LogFormat,
  LoggerNameExtractor,
  appendLoggerName,
  consoleLogger,
  loggerName
}

import java.util.UUID

object CheckoutApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val format: LogFormat =
    LogFormat.level |-|
      LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace.toLogFormat() |-|
      LogFormat.quoted(LogFormat.line) |-|
      LogFormat.logAnnotation(LogAnnotation.TraceId) |-|
      LogFormat.logAnnotation(LogAnnotation.UserId) |-|
      LogFormat.annotation("cart_size")

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
      consoleLogger(ConsoleLoggerConfig(format, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default))

  val chargeCard: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    ZIO.logInfo("Charging card") @@ appendLoggerName("payment")

  def checkout(userId: String, items: Int): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    ZIO.logAnnotate("cart_size", items.toString) {
      ZIO.logInfo("Checkout started") *> chargeCard
    } @@ LogAnnotation.UserId(userId) @@ loggerName("checkout")

  val run =
    checkout("user-42", 3) @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(UUID.fromString("7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7"))
}
```

Running it prints two lines:

```text
INFO checkout "Checkout started" trace_id=7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7 user_id=user-42 cart_size=3
INFO checkout.payment "Charging card" trace_id=7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7 user_id=user-42 cart_size=3
```

Neither `ZIO.logInfo` call mentions the trace id, the user id or the cart size. The aspects attach them to everything inside: the outermost `LogAnnotation.TraceId`, then `LogAnnotation.UserId` and the logger name, then the string annotation. `chargeCard` adds `payment` to the logger name it inherits. With `zio.logging.consoleJsonLogger` and the same format, each annotation becomes a JSON field instead; see [How to Log JSON](how-to-json-logs.md).

`LogFormat.default`, which the console and file loggers use when you configure no format, writes no annotations at all. You always choose which annotations reach the output, by name as above, or all at once with `LogFormat.allAnnotations` or the `%kvs` pattern. The full list of annotation formats is in [LogFormat Reference](reference-log-format.md#annotations).

### String Annotations and Typed Annotations

The `cart_size` value in the example is not a `LogAnnotation`. It comes from ZIO itself: `ZIO.logAnnotate(key, value)` and `ZIOAspect.annotated(key, value)` attach a string under a string key. These string annotations are stored apart from `logContext`, and ZIO passes them to every logger, including its own default logger.

Both kinds are useful, for different jobs. A string annotation suits a one-off key in one place of the code, or a value that every logger, including loggers outside ZIO Logging, should receive. A typed annotation suits a value used across the code base, a value with a real type, or a value that needs a merge rule when scopes nest.

Formats keep the two apart. `LogFormat.annotation(name)` and `LogFormat.annotations` read string annotations; `LogFormat.logAnnotation(annotation)` and `LogFormat.logAnnotations` read typed ones. `LogFormat.allAnnotations`, and in string patterns `%kv{name}` and `%kvs`, read both, so a format written as a pattern does not need to know which kind a key is.

:::caution
ZIO core also has a class named `zio.LogAnnotation`, the string pair. If a file has both `import zio._` and `import zio.logging._`, the name `LogAnnotation` is ambiguous. Import ZIO Logging's class by name with `import zio.logging.LogAnnotation`.
:::

### Logger Names

A logger name says which part of the program wrote a line. By default ZIO Logging derives it from the source location of the log call: a call inside `com.example.CheckoutService` has the logger name `com.example.CheckoutService`. That default works well for filtering, because per-name levels in the [log filter](log-filter.md) configuration, such as `"com.example" = "DEBUG"`, select by this name.

The aspects `zio.logging.loggerName` and `zio.logging.appendLoggerName` replace the default with a name you choose. `loggerName("checkout")` sets the name for everything inside; `appendLoggerName("payment")` adds a dot and `payment` to the name an outer aspect set, which is how `chargeCard` above logs as `checkout.payment`. A third form, `loggerName(fn)`, computes the new name from the current one. Use these aspects when the source location is not a good name: code generated by a library, a shared helper called from many services, or a name that must stay stable when you move code between packages.

The logger name is itself a string annotation with the key `logger_name`. So `LogFormat.annotations` and `LogFormat.allAnnotations` write it as `logger_name=checkout`, while the `%kvs` pattern leaves it out; write it with `%name` or `%kv{logger_name}` instead.

### Nesting and Combine

Effects nest, so an annotation is often applied to an effect that already has a value for it. The annotation's `LogAnnotation#combine` function decides the result, called as `combine(outer, inner)`. `LogAnnotation.TraceId` and `LogAnnotation.UserId` keep the inner value, so a nested call can switch to another id for its own scope. `LogAnnotation.TraceSpans` appends the inner list to the outer one and renders the result with `:` between the names, so nested spans build a path.

To record the path of nested operations with `LogAnnotation.TraceSpans`:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation

val loadUser: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo("Loading user") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceSpans(List("db"))

val handleRequest: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  (ZIO.logInfo("Request received") *> loadUser) @@ LogAnnotation.TraceSpans(List("http"))
```

With `LogFormat.logAnnotation(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans)` in the format, the first line carries `trace_spans=http` and the second `trace_spans=http:db`. When the inner effect ends, the outer value comes back: a line logged after `loadUser` inside `handleRequest` carries `trace_spans=http` again.

A custom annotation picks its own rule. To collect the feature flags that are active along the call path, union the sets:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation

val FeatureFlags: LogAnnotation[Set[String]] =
  LogAnnotation[Set[String]](
    name = "feature_flags",
    combine = _ ++ _,
    render = _.toList.sorted.mkString(",")
  )

val newCheckout: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo("Using the new checkout") @@ FeatureFlags(Set("new-checkout"))

val session: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  newCheckout @@ FeatureFlags(Set("dark-mode"))
```

With `LogFormat.logAnnotation(FeatureFlags)` in the format, the line logged when `session` runs carries `feature_flags=dark-mode,new-checkout`. Had `LogAnnotation#combine` returned the inner value, it would carry only `new-checkout`.

Annotations also follow fibers. A fiber forked inside an annotated effect, for example by `ZIO.foreachPar`, starts with the annotations of its parent, so parallel work keeps the trace id without any extra code.

### Next Steps

To put these pieces to work on a request handler, follow [How to Add a Correlation ID to Every Log Line](how-to-correlation-id.md). To read the context directly, combine contexts, or look up the exact behaviour of each aspect, see [Log Annotations and LogContext Reference](reference-log-annotations.md).

## Log Metrics

Log metrics count how many log lines an application writes, per log level. A sudden rise in `error` lines, or `warn` lines that never stop, is often the first sign that something is wrong, and a counter is cheap to scrape and to alert on, unlike the log text itself.

ZIO supports several loggers at the same time, so the counting is done by its own `ZLogger`, a `zio.logging.MetricLogger`. It writes nothing; for every `ZIO.log*` call it increments a counter. Because it is a separate logger, it works next to any other logger, such as the [console logger](console-logger.md) or the [file logger](file-logger.md).

### Installing the Log Metrics Logger

The `zio.logging.logMetrics` layer installs a `MetricLogger` with the default counter. Add it next to your output logger, usually in the `bootstrap` layer:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, logMetrics }
import zio.{ Runtime, ZIOAppArgs, ZLayer }

val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> (consoleLogger() ++ logMetrics)
```

### The `zio_log_total` Counter

`logMetrics` counts into a ZIO counter metric (`Metric.Counter[Long]`) named `zio_log_total`. Each increment carries the label `level`, whose value is the log level of the call in lower case:

| Log level          | `level` label value |
| ------------------ | ------------------- |
| `LogLevel.All`     | `all`               |
| `LogLevel.Fatal`   | `fatal`             |
| `LogLevel.Error`   | `error`             |
| `LogLevel.Warning` | `warn`              |
| `LogLevel.Info`    | `info`              |
| `LogLevel.Debug`   | `debug`             |
| `LogLevel.Trace`   | `trace`             |
| `LogLevel.None`    | `off`               |

The counter counts every log call, including the calls that the output logger drops. The level filter of a console or file logger belongs to that logger only, so a `ZIO.logDebug` call increments `zio_log_total{level="debug"}` even when the console logger is set to `INFO` and prints nothing. To count only some calls, add a filter to the metric logger itself, as shown in [Custom Counters](#custom-counters).

Every metric tag of the logging fiber also becomes a label of the count. `MetricLogger` reads the fiber's current metric tags, the ones set with `ZIOAspect.tagged` or `ZIO.tagged`, and adds the `level` label to them. Tagging a request handler with its service name therefore splits the counts per service:

```scala
import zio.{ UIO, ZIO, ZIOAspect }

def checkout(orderId: String): UIO[Unit] =
  (ZIO.logInfo(s"Order $orderId placed") *> ZIO.logWarning("Stock is low")) @@
    ZIOAspect.tagged("service" -> "checkout")
```

These two calls increment `zio_log_total` with the labels `level="info", service="checkout"` and `level="warn", service="checkout"`. Each distinct set of labels is a separate time series in a metrics backend, so tag with values that have a small, fixed set of possible values, such as a service or endpoint name, and never with ids such as an order id.

### Custom Metric and Label Names

To use a different metric name or a different name for the level label, for example to follow the naming rules of an existing dashboard, call `logMetricsWith(name, logLevelLabel)` instead of `logMetrics`:

```scala
import zio.logging.logMetricsWith

val customLayer = logMetricsWith("log_counter", "log_level")
```

This layer counts into the counter `log_counter`, with the level in the label `log_level`. Everything else works as for `logMetrics`.

### Custom Counters

`logMetrics` and `logMetricsWith` are built on `makeMetricLogger(counter, logLevelLabel)`, which returns the `MetricLogger` as an effect instead of a layer. Use it when you need something the layers do not offer, such as a counter that only counts some calls. The constructor and the logger are defined as follows:

```scala
// members of the zio.logging package
def makeMetricLogger(counter: Metric.Counter[Long], logLevelLabel: String): ZIO[Any, Nothing, MetricLogger]

final case class MetricLogger(counter: Metric.Counter[Long], logLevelLabel: String) extends ZLogger[String, Unit]
```

The following layer installs a second metric logger that counts only `ERROR` and `FATAL` calls, into a counter named `app_errors_total`. It can run next to `logMetrics`:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, ZLoggerZIOLayerOps, makeMetricLogger }
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.{ LogLevel, ZLayer }

val errorMetrics: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  makeMetricLogger(Metric.counter("app_errors_total"), "level")
    .filter(LogFilter.logLevel(LogLevel.Error))
    .install
```

The `filter` and `install` syntax comes from `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps`, which the example imports, and is described in [Logger Layers and Constructors Reference](reference-logger-layers.md).

### Reading the Counter in a Test

A counter can be read back with `Metric#value`, which returns its current state. To check the count in a test, create a `Metric` with the same name and the same labels, and read its `count`. ZIO keeps metrics in one global registry for the whole process, so other tests that log with the same counter add to it; give the test its own counter name with `logMetricsWith`, or compare the value before and after the code under test, as this spec does:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.logMetricsWith
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.test._

object CheckoutLogMetricsSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    test("counts one error line for the checkout service") {
      val checkoutErrors =
        Metric.counter("checkout_log_total").tagged("level", "error").tagged("service", "checkout")

      (for {
        before <- checkoutErrors.value
        _      <- (ZIO.logError("Payment declined") *> ZIO.logInfo("Order cancelled")) @@
                    ZIOAspect.tagged("service" -> "checkout")
        after  <- checkoutErrors.value
      } yield assertTrue(after.count - before.count == 1d))
        .provideLayer(logMetricsWith("checkout_log_total", "level"))
    }
}
```

The `info` call increments a different series, the one with `level="info"`, so it does not change the count that the test reads. The [Testing](testing.md) page shows how to check the log lines themselves.

### Exporting to Prometheus

ZIO metrics stay inside the application until a connector publishes them. To expose the counter to Prometheus, add the ZIO Metrics Connectors Prometheus module, which has its own version numbers:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors-prometheus" % "2.6.0"
```

The following application prints log lines with the console logger, counts them with `logMetrics`, and then prints the metrics in the Prometheus text format from the `PrometheusPublisher`. `MetricsConfig(200.millis)` sets how often the connector collects the metrics:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, logMetrics }
import zio.metrics.connectors.MetricsConfig
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus.{ PrometheusPublisher, prometheusLayer, publisherLayer }
import zio.{ ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer, _ }

object MetricsApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> (consoleLogger() ++ logMetrics)

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    (for {
      _            <- ZIO.logInfo("Start")
      _            <- ZIO.logWarning("Some warning")
      _            <- ZIO.logError("Some error")
      _            <- ZIO.logError("Another error")
      _            <- ZIO.sleep(1.second)
      metricValues <- ZIO.serviceWithZIO[PrometheusPublisher](_.get)
      _            <- Console.printLine(metricValues)
      _            <- ZIO.logInfo("Done")
    } yield ExitCode.success)
      .provideLayer((ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(200.millis)) ++ publisherLayer) >+> prometheusLayer)

}
```

The application is also in the example project, at `examples/core/jvm/src/main/scala/zio/logging/example/MetricsApp.scala`. In a real service, an HTTP endpoint returns the publisher's text for Prometheus to scrape instead of printing it.

The output below is illustrative. It was recorded with an earlier version of the connector, and the exact layout of the Prometheus text, such as the comment lines and the timestamps, depends on the connector version. What stays the same is one `zio_log_total` sample per `level` label value:

```text
timestamp=2023-03-15T08:44:39.93193+01:00  level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-6 message="Start"
timestamp=2023-03-15T08:44:39.951764+01:00 level=WARN thread=zio-fiber-6 message="Some warning"
timestamp=2023-03-15T08:44:39.95388+01:00  level=ERROR thread=zio-fiber-6 message="Some error"
timestamp=2023-03-15T08:44:39.954738+01:00 level=ERROR thread=zio-fiber-6 message="Another error"
```

## Reconfigurable Logger

`ReconfigurableLogger` is a `ZLogger` whose configuration and underlying logger can be replaced while the application runs. Every log call goes to the logger that is current at that moment, so a change takes effect on the next log line without a restart.

There are two ways to change it. With `ReconfigurableLogger.make`, the logger pulls its configuration: it reloads the configuration on a schedule and rebuilds the underlying logger when the configuration has changed. With `ReconfigurableLogger.apply`, your own code pushes a new configuration and logger with `ReconfigurableLogger#set`, for example from an admin endpoint. For a task-oriented walk-through of both, see [How to Change Log Levels at Runtime](how-to-change-levels-at-runtime.md).

### Reloading the Configuration on a Schedule

To create a console logger layer that reloads its configuration from a `ConfigProvider` every 5 seconds, wrap [console logger](console-logger.md) construction in `ReconfigurableLogger.make`:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, ReconfigurableLogger, makeConsoleLogger }
import zio._

val reconfigurableConfigProvider: ConfigProvider =
  ConfigProvider.fromMap(Map("logger/filter/rootLevel" -> "INFO"), "/")

val reconfigurableLoggerLayer = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> Runtime.setConfigProvider(reconfigurableConfigProvider) >>> ReconfigurableLogger
  .make[Any, Nothing, String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig](
    ConsoleLoggerConfig.load().orDie, // loading current configuration
    (config, _) => makeConsoleLogger(config), // make logger from loaded configuration
    Schedule.fixed(5.second) // default is 10 seconds
  )
  .installUnscoped[Any]
```

`ReconfigurableLogger.make` returns a `ZIO` that needs a `Scope`, because it starts a background fiber that reloads the configuration, and that fiber must stop when the logger is no longer used. The `installUnscoped` syntax turns this effect into a layer: the layer supplies the `Scope` itself, installs the logger for as long as the layer lives, and stops the reload fiber when the layer is released. The `install`, `installUnscoped` and `installScoped` helpers are described in [Logger Layers and Constructors Reference](reference-logger-layers.md).

### How `ReconfigurableLogger.make` Works

`ReconfigurableLogger.make` is defined as follows:

```scala
object ReconfigurableLogger {
  def make[R, E, M, O, C: Equal](
    loadConfig: => ZIO[R, E, C],
    makeLogger: (C, Option[ZLogger[M, O]]) => ZIO[R, E, ZLogger[M, O]],
    updateLogger: Schedule[R, Any, Any] = Schedule.fixed(10.seconds)
  ): ZIO[R with Scope, E, ReconfigurableLogger[M, O, C]]
}
```

The type parameters are the environment `R` and error `E` of loading and building, the message type `M` and output type `O` of the logger, and the configuration type `C`. The function works in these steps:

1. It runs `loadConfig` once and calls `makeLogger(config, None)` to build the first logger. If either fails, `ReconfigurableLogger.make` fails with that error.
2. It forks a fiber in the scope that runs `loadConfig` again on the `updateLogger` schedule. The first reload happens after the schedule's first interval, not at startup, so with the default schedule the first reload is 10 seconds after the logger is built.
3. On each reload, it compares the new configuration with the current one. Only when they differ does it call `makeLogger(newConfig, Some(currentLogger))` and switch to the new logger. When they are equal, nothing is rebuilt.

The comparison uses the ZIO Prelude `Equal` instance for `C`, which is why `C` needs one. ZIO Logging provides `ConsoleLoggerConfig.equal`, `FileLoggerConfig.equal`, `LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.equal` and `LogFilter.equal` (see [Configuration Keys Reference](reference-configuration.md#config-descriptors-and-equal-instances)). For a configuration type of your own, define an implicit `Equal`, for example `Equal.default` for a case class whose fields compare correctly with `==`.

The second argument of `makeLogger` is the logger that is about to be replaced: `None` when the first logger is built, and `Some(previousLogger)` on every rebuild. Use it when the new logger can reuse something from the old one, or ignore it with `(config, _) =>` as in the example above.

When the schedule ends, for example with `Schedule.recurs(3)`, the reloading stops and the last logger stays in place.

:::caution
Reloading stops at the first failure. If `loadConfig` or `makeLogger` fails during a reload, for example because the configuration source holds an invalid value for a moment, the reload fiber ends, the current logger stays in place, and later configuration changes are not picked up until the application restarts. Handle errors inside `loadConfig` and `makeLogger` if the reloading must survive them.

The replaced logger is not closed either. A logger that holds a resource, such as a file logger with its open file, keeps that resource after it has been replaced.
:::

### Pushing a New Configuration

`ReconfigurableLogger.apply` creates a reconfigurable logger with no reload fiber. It starts with the configuration and logger you pass, and your code replaces them by calling `ReconfigurableLogger#set`. Use it when the change comes from inside the application, such as an admin endpoint or a feature flag, rather than from a configuration source that can be polled. The trait has these members:

```scala
sealed trait ReconfigurableLogger[-Message, +Output, Config] extends ZLogger[Message, Output] {
  def get: (Config, ZLogger[Message, Output])
  def set[M <: Message, O >: Output](config: Config, logger: ZLogger[M, O]): Unit
}

object ReconfigurableLogger {
  def apply[Message, Output, Config](
    config: Config,
    logger: ZLogger[Message, Output]
  ): ReconfigurableLogger[Message, Output, Config]
}
```

`ReconfigurableLogger#get` returns the current configuration and logger, and `ReconfigurableLogger#set` replaces both at once. Both are plain methods, not effects, and they work on an atomic reference, so they are safe to call from any fiber. A `get` followed by a `set` is not one atomic step, though: two fibers that update the logger at the same time can overwrite each other's change. `ReconfigurableLogger#set` does not compare configurations, so it needs no `Equal` instance.

The following application installs a console logger that starts at the `INFO` level, exposes the `ReconfigurableLogger` as a service, and lowers the root level to `DEBUG` from inside the program:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, ReconfigurableLogger, makeConsoleLogger }

object LevelSwitchApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  type ConsoleReconfigurableLogger = ReconfigurableLogger[String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig]

  val reconfigurableConsole: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, ConsoleReconfigurableLogger] =
    ZLayer.scoped {
      for {
        initial <- makeConsoleLogger(ConsoleLoggerConfig.default)
        logger   = ReconfigurableLogger[String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig](ConsoleLoggerConfig.default, initial)
        _       <- ZIO.withLoggerScoped(logger)
      } yield logger
    }

  def setRootLevel(level: LogLevel): URIO[ConsoleReconfigurableLogger, Unit] =
    ZIO.serviceWithZIO[ConsoleReconfigurableLogger] { logger =>
      val (config, _) = logger.get
      val newConfig   = config.copy(filter = config.filter.withRootLevel(level))
      makeConsoleLogger(newConfig).map(newLogger => logger.set(newConfig, newLogger))
    }

  override def run: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    (for {
      _ <- ZIO.logDebug("Not written: the root level is INFO")
      _ <- setRootLevel(LogLevel.Debug)
      _ <- ZIO.logDebug("Written: the root level is now DEBUG")
    } yield ()).provideLayer(Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> reconfigurableConsole)
}
```

`ZIO.withLoggerScoped` adds the reconfigurable logger to the loggers of the layer's scope, and the layer also returns it as a service, so `setRootLevel` can reach it. The first `ZIO.logDebug` call is dropped by the `INFO` filter; after `ReconfigurableLogger#set`, the second one is written.

### Performance

Consider whether your application needs this feature, as it may affect performance (see [benchmarks](https://github.com/zio/zio-logging/blob/master/benchmarks/src/main/scala/zio/logging/FilterBenchmarks.scala)).

### Examples

You can find the source code [here](https://github.com/zio/zio-logging/tree/master/examples).

#### Console Logger With Re-configuration From Configuration File In Runtime

This example from `examples/core/jvm/src/main/scala/zio/logging/example/LoggerReconfigureApp.scala` reloads the logger configuration when the `logger.conf` file changes. It is an application, not library API.

The `logger.conf` configuration:

```hocon
logger {
  format = "%highlight{%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ} %fixed{7}{%level} [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %kv{trace_id} %kv{user_id} %cause}"
  filter {
    rootLevel = "INFO"
    mappings {
      "zio.logging.example" = "DEBUG"
    }
  }
}
```

Application:

```scala
import com.typesafe.config.ConfigFactory
import zio._
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, ReconfigurableLogger, makeConsoleLogger }

import java.util.UUID

object LoggerReconfigureApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  def configuredLogger(
    loadConfig: => ZIO[Any, Config.Error, ConsoleLoggerConfig]
  ): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit] =
    ReconfigurableLogger
      .make[Any, Config.Error, String, Any, ConsoleLoggerConfig](
        loadConfig,
        (config, _) => makeConsoleLogger(config),
        Schedule.fixed(500.millis)
      )
      .installUnscoped[Any]

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> configuredLogger(
      for {
        config       <- ZIO.succeed(ConfigFactory.load("logger.conf"))
        _            <- Console.printLine(config.getConfig("logger")).orDie
        loggerConfig <- ConsoleLoggerConfig.load().withConfigProvider(TypesafeConfigProvider.fromTypesafeConfig(config))
      } yield loggerConfig
    )

  def exec(): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    for {
      ok      <- Random.nextBoolean
      traceId <- ZIO.succeed(UUID.randomUUID())
      _       <- ZIO.logDebug("Start") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
      userIds <- ZIO.succeed(List.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID().toString))
      _       <- ZIO.foreachPar(userIds) { userId =>
        {
          ZIO.logDebug("Starting operation") *>
            ZIO.logInfo("OK operation").when(ok) *>
            ZIO.logError("Error operation").when(!ok) *>
            ZIO.logDebug("Stopping operation")
        } @@ LogAnnotation.UserId(userId)
      } @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
      _       <- ZIO.logDebug("Done") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
    } yield ()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- exec().repeat(Schedule.fixed(500.millis))
    } yield ExitCode.success

}
```

#### Console Logger With Configuration By Http APIs

This example from `examples/core/jvm/src/main/scala/zio/logging/example/ConfigurableLoggerApp.scala` changes the logger configuration through HTTP endpoints. It is example-project code, not library API. It depends on zio-http and on the classes `ConfigurableLogger`, `LoggerConfigurer` and `ApiHandlers`, which live in the example project under `examples/core/shared/src/main/scala/zio/logging/ConfigurableLogger.scala` and `examples/core/jvm/src/main/scala/zio/logging/api/http/`. It is not type-checked by mdoc.

Logger configurations APIs:
* get logger configurations
 ```bash
  curl -u "admin:admin" 'http://localhost:8080/example/logger'
 ```
* get `root` logger configuration
 ```bash
  curl -u "admin:admin" 'http://localhost:8080/example/logger/root'
 ```
* set `root` logger configuration
 ```bash
  curl -u "admin:admin" --location --request PUT 'http://localhost:8080/example/logger/root' --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '"WARN"'
 ```
* set `zio.logging.example` logger configuration
 ```bash
  curl -u "admin:admin" --location --request PUT 'http://localhost:8080/example/logger/zio.logging.example' --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '"WARN"'
 ```

The `logger.conf` configuration:

```hocon
logger {
  format = "%highlight{%timestamp{yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ} %fixed{7}{%level} [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %kv{trace_id} %kv{user_id} %cause}"
  filter {
    rootLevel = "INFO"
    mappings {
      "zio.logging.example" = "DEBUG"
    }
  }
}
```

Application:

```scala
package zio.logging.example

import com.typesafe.config.ConfigFactory
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.http._
import zio.logging.api.http.ApiHandlers
import zio.logging.{ ConfigurableLogger, ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LoggerConfigurer, makeSystemOutLogger }
import zio.{ ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppDefault, _ }

import java.util.UUID

object ConfigurableLoggerApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  def configurableLogger(): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit] =
    ConsoleLoggerConfig
      .load()
      .flatMap { config =>
        makeSystemOutLogger(config.format.toLogger).map { logger =>
          ConfigurableLogger.make(logger, config.filter)
        }
      }
      .install

  val configProvider: ConfigProvider = TypesafeConfigProvider.fromTypesafeConfig(ConfigFactory.load("logger.conf"))

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> Runtime.setConfigProvider(configProvider) >>> configurableLogger()

  def exec(): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    for {
      ok      <- Random.nextBoolean
      traceId <- ZIO.succeed(UUID.randomUUID())
      _       <- ZIO.logDebug("Start") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
      userIds <- ZIO.succeed(List.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID().toString))
      _       <- ZIO.foreachPar(userIds) { userId =>
        {
          ZIO.logDebug("Starting operation") *>
            ZIO.logInfo("OK operation").when(ok) *>
            ZIO.logError("Error operation").when(!ok) *>
            ZIO.logDebug("Stopping operation")
        } @@ LogAnnotation.UserId(userId)
      } @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
      _       <- ZIO.logDebug("Done") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
    } yield ()

  val httpApp: Routes[LoggerConfigurer with Any, Nothing] =
    ApiHandlers.routes("example" :: Nil) @@ Middleware.basicAuth("admin", "admin")

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    (for {
      _ <- Server.serve(httpApp).fork
      _ <- exec().repeat(Schedule.fixed(500.millis))
    } yield ExitCode.success).provide(LoggerConfigurer.layer ++ Server.default)

}
```

:::note
`ConfigurableLogger`, `LoggerConfigurer` and `ApiHandlers` live in the example project, not in the published `zio-logging` artifacts. If you want to use them in your app, copy them from the example project. For the same effect with the library alone, push a new configuration with `ReconfigurableLogger#set` as shown in [Pushing a New Configuration](#pushing-a-new-configuration).
:::

When the configuration for `logger/filter/mappings/zio.logging.example` changes from `DEBUG` to `WARN`, send the following request:

```bash
curl -u "admin:admin" --location --request PUT 'http://localhost:8080/example/logger/zio.logging.example' --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '"WARN"'
```

## Configuration Keys Reference

Each built-in logger reads its settings from a configuration source through ZIO Config. This page lists every key for the console logger, the file logger, and the level filter they share. The keys are relative to a root path, which is `logger` by default. Each feature has its own page with examples: [Console Logger](./console-logger.md), [File Logger](./file-logger.md), and [Log Filter](./log-filter.md).

### Default Config Path

The default root path lives in `zio.logging.loggerConfigPath`, as the single segment `logger`. The `ConsoleLoggerConfig.load`, `ConsoleLoggerConfig.make`, `FileLoggerConfig.load`, and `FileLoggerConfig.make` functions, and the logger layers such as `zio.logging.consoleLogger` and `zio.logging.fileLogger`, read from this path unless you pass another path. The source declares the value as follows:

```scala
val loggerConfigPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = NonEmptyChunk("logger")
```

A custom path is a `NonEmptyChunk[String]`. The first element is the top-level key, and the remaining elements are nested keys under it. For example, `NonEmptyChunk("app", "logging")` reads the keys from `app.logging`.

### Console Logger Keys

The console logger config is `zio.logging.ConsoleLoggerConfig`. It has a format and a level filter. The table lists its keys under the root path.

| Key                | Type                              | Default             | Meaning                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `format`           | Format string                     | `LogFormat.default` | The layout of each line. The string form is described in [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md).                                                    |
| `filter.rootLevel` | Log level name                    | `INFO`              | The minimum level for every logger name that has no mapping.                                                                                                       |
| `filter.mappings`  | Table of logger name to log level | Empty table         | Minimum levels for logger names. A key is a dot-separated logger name, which also covers the names under it, or a glob pattern; see [Log Filter](./log-filter.md). |

### File Logger Keys

The file logger config is `zio.logging.FileLoggerConfig`. It adds a destination path and the options for writing and rolling the file. The table lists its keys under the root path.

| Key                  | Type                                          | Default             | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `path`               | URI string, such as `file:///var/log/app.log` | None, required      | The file to write. The value is read with `URI.create`, so it must be a URI, not a plain path. An invalid value fails the config load.                                                                  |
| `format`             | Format string                                 | `LogFormat.default` | The layout of each line. See [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md).                                                                                                                     |
| `filter.rootLevel`   | Log level name                                | `INFO`              | The minimum level for every logger name that has no mapping.                                                                                                                                            |
| `filter.mappings`    | Table of logger name to log level             | Empty table         | Minimum levels for logger names, with the same rules as the console logger.                                                                                                                             |
| `charset`            | Charset name, such as `UTF-8`                 | `UTF-8`             | The character encoding of the file. The name is read with `Charset.forName`, and an unknown name fails the config load.                                                                                 |
| `autoFlushBatchSize` | Integer                                       | `1`                 | The number of lines written before the writer flushes its buffer. The value `1` flushes after every line. Use `1` or more; see [Flushing and Write Errors](./file-logger.md#flushing-and-write-errors). |
| `bufferedIOSize`     | Integer                                       | None, unbuffered    | When set, the writer wraps the file in a `java.io.BufferedWriter` with a buffer of this many characters.                                                                                                |
| `rollingPolicy.type` | Rolling policy name                           | None, no rolling    | When set, the file rolls over with the rolling policy. The only supported value is `TimeBasedRollingPolicy`.                                                                                            |

The `rollingPolicy.type` key is optional. When the key is absent, the file is not rolled.

### Log Level Filter Keys

The level filter config is `zio.logging.LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig`. The console and file loggers read it under the `filter` key, so the full keys are `filter.rootLevel` and `filter.mappings`. The class and its helper methods are described in [LogFilter and LogGroup Reference](./reference-log-filter.md#loglevelbynameconfig).

| Key         | Type                              | Default     | Meaning                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------- | --------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `rootLevel` | Log level name                    | `INFO`      | The minimum level for every event that matches no mapping.                                                                                  |
| `mappings`  | Table of logger name to log level | Empty table | Minimum levels for logger names. Dot-separated names select the mapping. The matching rules are described in [Log Filter](./log-filter.md). |

### Config Descriptors and Equal Instances

The layers and the `ConsoleLoggerConfig.load` and `FileLoggerConfig.load` functions are built on public values that you can also use directly. `ConsoleLoggerConfig.config`, `FileLoggerConfig.config` and the other descriptors below are ZIO `Config` descriptors for the keys in the tables above. A descriptor is not nested under any path; `ConsoleLoggerConfig.load` and `FileLoggerConfig.load` nest it under the root path for you. Use a descriptor when the logger settings are part of a larger config type of your own, or when you need the config value without building a logger. `ConsoleLoggerConfig.equal` and the other `Equal` values below are ZIO Prelude `Equal` instances, which [`ReconfigurableLogger.make`](./reconfigurable-logger.md) needs to decide whether a reloaded config has changed.

| Member                                      | Type                                         | Description                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ConsoleLoggerConfig.default`               | `ConsoleLoggerConfig`                        | `LogFormat.default` with `LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default`, which has root level `INFO` and no mappings.                               |
| `ConsoleLoggerConfig.config`                | `Config[ConsoleLoggerConfig]`                | Reads `format` (default `LogFormat.default`) and the `filter` keys.                                                                           |
| `ConsoleLoggerConfig.equal`                 | `Equal[ConsoleLoggerConfig]`                 | Two configs are equal when their formats are equal (`==`) and their filters are equal.                                                        |
| `FileLoggerConfig.config`                   | `Config[FileLoggerConfig]`                   | Reads every key in [File Logger Keys](#file-logger-keys), with the defaults listed there.                                                     |
| `FileLoggerConfig.equal`                    | `Equal[FileLoggerConfig]`                    | Two configs are equal when the destination, charset, `autoFlushBatchSize`, `bufferedIOSize`, rolling policy, format and filter are all equal. |
| `FileLoggerConfig.FileRollingPolicy.config` | `Config[FileLoggerConfig.FileRollingPolicy]` | Reads the `type` key. The only accepted value is `TimeBasedRollingPolicy`; any other value fails the config load.                             |
| `LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.config`     | `Config[LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig]`     | Reads `rootLevel` (default `INFO`) and `mappings` (default empty).                                                                            |
| `LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.equal`      | `Equal[LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig]`      | Structural equality of the root level and the mappings.                                                                                       |

`FileLoggerConfig` is defined on every platform, but `FileLoggerConfig.config` turns the `path` value into a file path with `java.nio.file.Paths`, which Scala.js does not provide. File configuration is therefore usable on the JVM and Scala Native only, the same platforms that have the file loggers.

To read the console logger settings as one field of an application config, nest the descriptor under the key you choose:

```scala
import zio.{ Config, ZIO }
import zio.logging.ConsoleLoggerConfig

case class AppConfig(port: Int, logging: ConsoleLoggerConfig)

val appConfig: Config[AppConfig] =
  (Config.int("port") ++ ConsoleLoggerConfig.config.nested("logging")).map { case (port, logging) =>
    AppConfig(port, logging)
  }

val loadAppConfig: ZIO[Any, Config.Error, AppConfig] = ZIO.config(appConfig)
```

With this descriptor, the logger keys are `logging.format`, `logging.filter.rootLevel` and `logging.filter.mappings`, next to the application's own `port` key.

### Log Level Names

Every level key accepts the names below. ZIO's `Config.logLevel` reader accepts them case-insensitively, so `info` and `INFO` both parse.

| Name    | Level       |
| ------- | ----------- |
| `ALL`   | Every event |
| `TRACE` | Trace       |
| `DEBUG` | Debug       |
| `INFO`  | Info        |
| `WARN`  | Warning     |
| `ERROR` | Error       |
| `FATAL` | Fatal       |
| `OFF`   | No events   |

The name `WARNING` is not accepted. Use `WARN`.

### Complete Example

The following HOCON configures the console logger with a custom level for one package. Only the keys in the tables above appear:

```hocon
logger {
  format = "%timestamp %level %name %message %cause"

  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO

    mappings {
      "zio.logging.example" = "DEBUG"
    }
  }
}
```

The file logger takes the same keys under a separate path, such as `logger-file`, when you pass that path to `FileLoggerConfig.make`:

```hocon
logger-file {
  path = "file:///var/log/app.log"
  charset = "UTF-8"
  autoFlushBatchSize = 100
  bufferedIOSize = 8192

  rollingPolicy {
    type = TimeBasedRollingPolicy
  }

  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO
  }
}
```

This example trades safety for throughput: with `autoFlushBatchSize = 100`, up to 99 lines can still be in the buffer when the application stops, and the logger does not flush them at shutdown.

---

## Backends and Bridges Reference

ZIO Logging connects to the Java logging world in two directions. A **backend** sends ZIO log records to a Java logging system: `SLF4J` writes to whatever SLF4J provider is on the classpath (Logback, Log4j 2, ...) and `JPL` writes to the JDK's `java.lang.System.Logger`. A **bridge** does the opposite: `Slf4jBridge` and `JULBridge` capture log calls that Java libraries make through SLF4J or `java.util.logging` (JUL) and send them to the ZIO loggers. This page lists every public entry point of the six integration modules, their defaults, their level mappings, and what each one keeps or drops. For walkthroughs, see the per-module pages: [SLF4J v2](slf4j2.md), [SLF4J v1](slf4j1.md), [SLF4J v2 bridge](slf4j2-bridge.md), [SLF4J v1 bridge](slf4j1-bridge.md), [java.util.logging bridge](jul-bridge.md) and [Java Platform/System Logger](jpl.md).

The entry points are four objects:

```scala
object SLF4J       // zio.logging.backend, modules zio-logging-slf4j and zio-logging-slf4j2
object JPL         // zio.logging.backend, module zio-logging-jpl
object Slf4jBridge // zio.logging.slf4j.bridge, modules zio-logging-slf4j-bridge and zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge
object JULBridge   // zio.logging.jul.bridge, module zio-logging-jul-bridge
```

### Choosing a Module

Pick the module by the direction the logs travel and, for SLF4J, by the version of `slf4j-api` that ends up on the classpath. Libraries compiled against SLF4J 1.7 still call SLF4J 2.x correctly, so the classpath version is what counts:

| You want to                                                                | Module                      | Entry point        | Page                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| Write ZIO logs through SLF4J 2.x (Logback 1.3+, `log4j-slf4j2-impl`)       | `zio-logging-slf4j2`        | `SLF4J.slf4j`      | [SLF4J v2](slf4j2.md)               |
| Write ZIO logs through SLF4J 1.7 (Logback 1.2)                             | `zio-logging-slf4j`         | `SLF4J.slf4j`      | [SLF4J v1](slf4j1.md)               |
| Write ZIO logs to `java.lang.System.Logger`                                | `zio-logging-jpl`           | `JPL.jpl`          | [JPL](jpl.md)                       |
| Send SLF4J logs from Java libraries to ZIO loggers, `slf4j-api` 2.x        | `zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge` | `Slf4jBridge.init` | [SLF4J v2 bridge](slf4j2-bridge.md) |
| Send SLF4J logs from Java libraries to ZIO loggers, `slf4j-api` 1.7        | `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge`  | `Slf4jBridge.init` | [SLF4J v1 bridge](slf4j1-bridge.md) |
| Send logs from Java libraries that call `java.util.logging` to ZIO loggers | `zio-logging-jul-bridge`    | `JULBridge.init`   | [JUL bridge](jul-bridge.md)         |

All six modules are JVM-only and are published for Java 17 and later. Every module depends on the `zio-logging` core module. The SLF4J modules also depend on `slf4j-api`: version 1.7.36 for `zio-logging-slf4j` and `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge`, and version 2.0.20 for `zio-logging-slf4j2` and `zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge`.

The v1 and v2 variants of a module declare classes with the same names in the same packages, so an application uses one or the other, never both.

### How They Work Together

A backend is a `ZLogger` that ZIO calls for every log record; a bridge is a Java logger implementation that turns each Java log call into a ZIO log record. The arrows show where each module sits:

```
Backends: ZIO log calls go out to a Java logging system

  ZIO.logInfo(...) ──▶ ZIO runtime ──┬──▶ SLF4J.slf4j ──▶ SLF4J provider (Logback, Log4j 2, ...)
                                     └──▶ JPL.jpl     ──▶ java.lang.System.Logger

Bridges: Java log calls come in to the ZIO loggers

  Java library ──▶ SLF4J API         ──▶ Slf4jBridge ──┐
  Java library ──▶ java.util.logging ──▶ JULBridge   ──┴──▶ ZIO runtime ──▶ ZIO loggers
                                                                           (console, file, JSON, ...)
```

The typical setups are:

1. A ZIO application that already runs on Logback or Log4j 2 installs `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j` and configures levels and appenders in `logback.xml` or `log4j2.xml`.
2. A ZIO application that writes with the ZIO console or file loggers installs a bridge after the logger layer, so that libraries such as database drivers or HTTP clients log into the same output: `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> Slf4jBridge.init()`.
3. A bridge captures the ZIO runtime when its layer is built, and with it the loggers installed at that point. That is why the logger layer comes first and the bridge layer second.

:::caution
Never combine a backend and a bridge for the same logging system. `SLF4J.slf4j` together with `Slf4jBridge` sends each record from ZIO to SLF4J and from SLF4J back to ZIO. The same loop appears with `JPL.jpl` and `JULBridge` when the `System.Logger` implementation is backed by `java.util.logging`, which is the JDK default.
:::

### SLF4J Backends

The `zio-logging-slf4j` and `zio-logging-slf4j2` modules provide the same `SLF4J` object in package `zio.logging.backend`. Both versions share every public member, and they differ only in how annotations reach the provider. Add one of these dependencies:

```scala
// SLF4J 2.x API (Logback 1.3 and later, log4j-slf4j2-impl)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j2" % "2.5.5"

// SLF4J 1.7 API (Logback 1.2)
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j" % "2.5.5"
```

#### SLF4J Entry Points

The `SLF4J` object has three overloads that return a layer, one that returns the bare logger, and helpers for the logger name, the marker and the cause. The members are declared as follows:

```scala
object SLF4J {
  val causeToThrowableDefault: Cause[Any] => Option[Throwable]
  val logMarkerNameAnnotationKey: String // "slf4j_log_marker_name"
  val logFormatDefault: LogFormat

  def logMarkerName(value: String): ZIOAspect[Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any]
  def getLoggerName(default: String = "zio-slf4j-logger"): Trace => String

  def slf4j(
    format: LogFormat,
    loggerName: Trace => String,
    causeToThrowable: Cause[Any] => Option[Throwable]
  ): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def slf4j(format: LogFormat): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def slf4j: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]

  def slf4jLogger(
    format: LogFormat,
    loggerName: Trace => String,
    causeToThrowable: Cause[Any] => Option[Throwable]
  ): ZLogger[String, Unit]
}
```

The table describes each member:

| Member                                              | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SLF4J.slf4j`                                       | Adds an SLF4J logger with `SLF4J.logFormatDefault`, `SLF4J.getLoggerName()` and `SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault`.                                                                                                                          |
| `SLF4J.slf4j(format)`                               | Same, with a custom `LogFormat`.                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `SLF4J.slf4j(format, loggerName, causeToThrowable)` | Same, with all three settings chosen by the caller. The layer calls `Runtime.addLogger` with the result of `SLF4J.slf4jLogger`.                                                                                                           |
| `SLF4J.slf4jLogger`                                 | Returns the `ZLogger` without installing it, for wrapping in a `LogFilter` or combining with other loggers. It calls `LoggerFactory.getLogger` once, so SLF4J initialises as soon as the logger exists rather than on the first log call. |
| `SLF4J.logFormatDefault`                            | `LogFormat.allAnnotations(excludeKeys = Set(logger_name, slf4j_log_marker_name)) + LogFormat.line + LogFormat.cause`.                                                                                                                     |
| `SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault`                     | Returns `None` for an empty cause and `Some(FiberFailure(cause))` otherwise.                                                                                                                                                              |
| `SLF4J.getLoggerName(default)`                      | Derives the SLF4J logger name from the `Trace` of the log call: `example.LivePingService.ping(PingService.scala:22)` becomes `example.LivePingService`. Returns `default` when the trace cannot be parsed.                                |
| `SLF4J.logMarkerName(value)`                        | An aspect that annotates an effect with `slf4j_log_marker_name = value`. The backend turns the annotation into an SLF4J `Marker` with `MarkerFactory.getMarker`.                                                                          |
| `SLF4J.logMarkerNameAnnotationKey`                  | The annotation key `"slf4j_log_marker_name"` that `SLF4J.logMarkerName` sets.                                                                                                                                                             |

Each `SLF4J.slf4j` layer adds one more logger to the runtime. Install it once, and remove ZIO's default logger with `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers`, or ZIO's own console logger prints the same records a second time in its own format.

To install the backend with a custom message format and a fixed fallback logger name:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.LogFormat
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val customSlf4j: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j(
    format = LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set(zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey, SLF4J.logMarkerNameAnnotationKey)) +
      LogFormat.text("[") + LogFormat.fiberId + LogFormat.text("] ") + LogFormat.line + LogFormat.cause,
    loggerName = SLF4J.getLoggerName("my-app"),
    causeToThrowable = SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault
  )
```

#### SLF4J Logger Names and Markers

For each record the backend picks the SLF4J logger name in this order:

1. The value of the `logger_name` annotation, which the `zio.logging.loggerName` and `zio.logging.appendLoggerName` aspects set.
2. The result of the `loggerName` function for the record's `Trace`; with `SLF4J.getLoggerName`, that is the class that makes the log call, or the fallback `"zio-slf4j-logger"`.

A record carries at most one marker: the one named by the `slf4j_log_marker_name` annotation. The backend passes the marker both to the level check (`isInfoEnabled(marker)` and so on) and to the log call, so provider features such as Logback's `MarkerFilter` work on it.

To set the logger name and a marker on one effect:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val audited =
  ZIO.logInfo("Card number changed") @@ zio.logging.loggerName("com.example.audit") @@ SLF4J.logMarkerName("CONFIDENTIAL")
```

#### SLF4J Level Mapping

The SLF4J provider decides which levels are written. Before formatting a record, the backend asks the SLF4J logger whether the mapped level is enabled, so the levels in `logback.xml` or `log4j2.xml` apply, and a ZIO `LogFilter` does not take part unless you wrap the logger yourself. The mapping is:

| ZIO `LogLevel`  | SLF4J level |
| --------------- | ----------- |
| `All`           | `TRACE`     |
| `Trace`         | `TRACE`     |
| `Debug`         | `DEBUG`     |
| `Info`          | `INFO`      |
| `Warning`       | `WARN`      |
| `Error`         | `ERROR`     |
| `Fatal`         | `ERROR`     |
| `None`          | not logged  |
| any other level | not logged  |

To apply a ZIO `LogFilter` in front of the provider's own level check, wrap the logger from `SLF4J.slf4jLogger` with `LogFilter#filter` and install it with `Runtime.addLogger`:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.LogFilter
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val filter: LogFilter[String] = LogFilter.logLevelByName(LogLevel.Info, "com.example.db" -> LogLevel.Warning)

val filteredSlf4j: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> Runtime.addLogger(
    filter.filter(SLF4J.slf4jLogger(SLF4J.logFormatDefault, SLF4J.getLoggerName(), SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault))
  )
```

#### SLF4J Annotations: MDC Versus Key-Value Pairs

The backend splits the output of the `LogFormat` into three parts. Every key-value pair that the format emits (from `LogFormat.allAnnotations`, `LogFormat.annotations`, `LogFormat.annotation`, `LogFormat.logAnnotation` or `LogFormat.spans`) goes to the provider as structured data. Everything else, such as `LogFormat.line`, `LogFormat.text`, `LogFormat.level` or `LogFormat.label`, is appended to the message string. `LogFormat.cause` becomes the `Throwable` of the log call, converted with `causeToThrowable`.

The two versions pass the structured data differently:

| Module               | Structured data       | How it reaches the provider                                                                                                                                                              | Logback pattern       |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `zio-logging-slf4j`  | MDC (`org.slf4j.MDC`) | For each record that has at least one key-value pair, the backend saves the thread's MDC, replaces it with the record's pairs, logs, and restores the saved MDC, all on the same thread. | `%mdc`, `%X{user_id}` |
| `zio-logging-slf4j2` | Key-value pairs       | The backend logs through the fluent API: `atLevel(...).setMessage(...).setCause(...).addMarker(...).addKeyValue(...)...log()`. The MDC is not touched.                                   | `%kvp`                |

:::note
In the v1 module the MDC is replaced, not merged: values that Java code put into the thread's MDC are hidden while a ZIO record with annotations is logged. When a record has no key-value pairs, the backend leaves the MDC untouched, so whatever the worker thread's MDC holds at that moment is printed with the record.
:::

#### SLF4J Backend: Kept and Dropped

With `SLF4J.logFormatDefault`, a record reaches the provider like this:

| Part of the ZIO record                       | What the provider receives                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Message                                      | The SLF4J message.                                                                          |
| Level                                        | The mapped SLF4J level; `None` and custom levels are dropped.                               |
| Fiber annotations and `LogAnnotation` values | MDC entries (v1) or key-value pairs (v2), except `logger_name` and `slf4j_log_marker_name`. |
| `logger_name` annotation                     | The SLF4J logger name.                                                                      |
| `slf4j_log_marker_name` annotation           | One SLF4J `Marker`.                                                                         |
| Cause                                        | The `Throwable`, by default a `FiberFailure` that wraps the whole cause.                    |
| Log spans, fiber id, call-site trace         | Not sent. Add `LogFormat.spans` or `LogFormat.fiberId` to the format to include them.       |

### SLF4J Bridges

The `zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge` and `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge` modules make ZIO Logging an SLF4J provider. Java code keeps calling `org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger(...)`, and the bridge turns each call into a ZIO log record. Both modules provide the same `Slf4jBridge` object in package `zio.logging.slf4j.bridge`. Add one of these dependencies:

```scala
// SLF4J 2.x API
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge" % "2.5.5"

// SLF4J 1.7 API
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j-bridge" % "2.5.5"
```

#### Slf4jBridge Entry Points

The bridge has layer constructors for application bootstrap and `Slf4jBridge.make` effects for code that sets up logging by hand. The members are declared as follows:

```scala
object Slf4jBridge {
  val logFilterConfigPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] // "logger", "filter"

  def initialize: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def init(filter: LogFilter[Any]): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def init(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = logFilterConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def initializeWithoutFiberRefPropagation: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def initWithoutFiberRefPropagation(filter: LogFilter[Any]): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]

  def make(filter: LogFilter[Any]): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def make(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = logFilterConfigPath): ZIO[Any, Config.Error, Unit]
}
```

The table describes each member:

| Member                                               | Returns                           | Fiber ref propagation      | Filter                                         |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `Slf4jBridge.initialize`                             | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | on                         | `LogFilter.acceptAll`                          |
| `Slf4jBridge.init(filter)`                           | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | on                         | the given filter                               |
| `Slf4jBridge.init(configPath)`, `Slf4jBridge.init()` | `ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]` | on                         | loaded from config, by default `logger.filter` |
| `Slf4jBridge.initializeWithoutFiberRefPropagation`   | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | off                        | `LogFilter.acceptAll`                          |
| `Slf4jBridge.initWithoutFiberRefPropagation(filter)` | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | off                        | the given filter                               |
| `Slf4jBridge.make(filter)`                           | `ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit]`         | off unless already enabled | the given filter                               |
| `Slf4jBridge.make(configPath)`, `Slf4jBridge.make()` | `ZIO[Any, Config.Error, Unit]`    | off unless already enabled | loaded from config                             |
| `Slf4jBridge.logFilterConfigPath`                    | `NonEmptyChunk[String]`           | —                          | the default config path, `logger.filter`       |

The config-based variants read a `LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig`, that is the `rootLevel` and `mappings` keys under the path; see [Configuration Keys Reference](reference-configuration.md#log-level-filter-keys). There is no config-based variant without fiber ref propagation; use `Slf4jBridge.initWithoutFiberRefPropagation` with a filter built in code instead.

Every variant captures the runtime of the fiber that builds the layer or runs `Slf4jBridge.make`, including the loggers installed at that moment, and attaches it to the SLF4J logger factory under a lock. Building the layer again replaces the runtime. Until the bridge is initialised, the factory reports every level as disabled, so SLF4J calls made before that point are dropped.

To install the bridge after a JSON console logger, with the filter read from the default config path:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZIOAppArgs, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.consoleJsonLogger
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge

val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> Slf4jBridge.init()
```

#### Fiber Ref Propagation

The `Slf4jBridge.initialize` and `Slf4jBridge.init` layers are `Runtime.enableCurrentFiber ++` the bridge layer. With the current-fiber runtime flag on, the bridge can see which ZIO fiber makes the SLF4J call, and copies that fiber's annotations, log spans and `LogAnnotation` context into the record. When a Java library runs inside `ZIO.logAnnotate("request_id", "r-1")(...)`, its records therefore carry `request_id = r-1`.

The `WithoutFiberRefPropagation` variants and the `Slf4jBridge.make` effects do not enable the flag. Records then carry only the fiber refs of the runtime captured at initialisation, plus what the bridge adds itself. Use them when you do not need the caller's annotations. To get propagation with `Slf4jBridge.make`, provide `Runtime.enableCurrentFiber` yourself.

#### SLF4J Bridge Level Mapping

The SLF4J level of each call maps to a ZIO level through the public value `ZioLoggerRuntime.logLevelMapping`:

| SLF4J level | ZIO `LogLevel` |
| ----------- | -------------- |
| `TRACE`     | `Trace`        |
| `DEBUG`     | `Debug`        |
| `INFO`      | `Info`         |
| `WARN`      | `Warning`      |
| `ERROR`     | `Error`        |

#### What the Bridge Filter Sees

The bridge runs its `LogFilter` inside SLF4J's `isTraceEnabled`, `isDebugEnabled` (and so on), before the message exists. The filter receives the mapped level and a single annotation, `logger_name`, set to the SLF4J logger name. Trace, cause, fiber refs, spans and message are empty. Filters by level and logger name, such as `LogFilter.logLevelByName`, work as expected; filters that test the message text, the cause or fiber annotations never match there.

Records that pass the bridge filter then go to every installed ZIO logger, and each logger applies its own filter to the full record.

#### SLF4J Bridge: Kept and Dropped

Each SLF4J call becomes one ZIO record. The table lists what survives:

| Part of the SLF4J call                               | v1 bridge                                                                       | v2 bridge                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Message pattern and arguments                        | Formatted with SLF4J's `MessageFormatter`.                                      | Same.                                                                        |
| Throwable                                            | `Cause.die(throwable)`.                                                         | Same.                                                                        |
| Logger name                                          | The `logger_name` annotation, plus a log span named after the logger.           | Same.                                                                        |
| Key-value pairs (`atInfo().addKeyValue(k, v).log()`) | Not part of the SLF4J 1.7 API.                                                  | Kept as ZIO log annotations. A `null` value throws a `NullPointerException`. |
| Markers                                              | Dropped.                                                                        | Dropped.                                                                     |
| MDC values set by Java code                          | Dropped: the bridge's MDC adapter stores them, but the bridge never reads them. | Dropped, for the same reason.                                                |
