| Caller fiber's annotations, spans and log context    | Kept when fiber ref propagation is on.                                          | Same.                                                                        |

### JUL Bridge

The `zio-logging-jul-bridge` module installs a `java.util.logging.Handler` on the JUL root logger and turns each `LogRecord` into a ZIO log record. The entry point is `JULBridge` in package `zio.logging.jul.bridge`. Add the dependency:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-jul-bridge" % "2.5.5"
```

#### JULBridge Entry Points

`JULBridge` has the same family of constructors as `Slf4jBridge`, with the same return types, the same fiber ref propagation rules and the same default config path `logger.filter`:

```scala
object JULBridge {
  val logFilterConfigPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] // "logger", "filter"

  def initialize: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def init(filter: LogFilter[Any]): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def init(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = logFilterConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def initializeWithoutFiberRefPropagation: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def initWithoutFiberRefPropagation(filter: LogFilter[Any]): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]

  def make(filter: LogFilter[Any]): ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def make(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = logFilterConfigPath): ZIO[Any, Config.Error, Unit]
}
```

The JUL filter has the same limits as described in [What the Bridge Filter Sees](#what-the-bridge-filter-sees): it receives the level, the `logger_name` annotation and a `Trace` built from the logger name, while the message, cause and fiber refs are empty. Each record gets a log span and a `logger_name` annotation named after the JUL logger.

To install the JUL bridge with a filter built in code:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, Runtime, ZIOAppArgs, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, consoleJsonLogger }
import zio.logging.jul.bridge.JULBridge

val julFilter: LogFilter[Any] = LogFilter.logLevelByName[Any](LogLevel.Info, "com.example.legacy" -> LogLevel.Warning)

val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> JULBridge.init(julFilter)
```

#### Global LogManager Side Effects

JUL keeps its configuration in one JVM-wide `LogManager`, and the bridge changes it. Each `JULBridge` layer or `JULBridge.make` call:

1. Calls `LogManager.getLogManager.readConfiguration` with the single line `.level= ALL`. This resets the whole JUL configuration: it removes every handler from every logger, including the default console handler, and drops levels set earlier from `logging.properties` or code.
2. Adds the bridge handler to the root logger.

From then on the bridge's `LogFilter` decides which JUL records are kept. Initialising the bridge again repeats the reset, so the old bridge handler is removed and a new one is added. Handlers or levels that other code adds to JUL after the bridge is initialised still apply.

#### JUL Level Mapping

JUL has more levels than ZIO, so several of them share a ZIO level:

| JUL `Level` | ZIO `LogLevel` |
| ----------- | -------------- |
| `SEVERE`    | `Fatal`        |
| `WARNING`   | `Warning`      |
| `INFO`      | `Info`         |
| `CONFIG`    | `Info`         |
| `FINE`      | `Debug`        |
| `FINER`     | `Debug`        |
| `FINEST`    | `Trace`        |
| `ALL`       | `All`          |
| `OFF`       | `None`         |

:::caution
Only these nine levels are mapped. A record with a custom `java.util.logging.Level` has no entry, and the bridge's `publish` throws `NoSuchElementException` back to the JUL caller.
:::

#### JUL Bridge: Kept and Dropped

The bridge copies the message, the level, the logger name and the thrown exception (as `Cause.die`). It uses `LogRecord#getMessage` as the message, so the bridge does not substitute JUL parameters such as `{0}` and does not apply resource bundles: `logger.log(Level.INFO, "Hi {0}", name)` is logged as `Hi {0}`. Fiber annotations of the calling fiber are kept when fiber ref propagation is on.

### JPL Backend

The `zio-logging-jpl` module writes ZIO log records to `java.lang.System.Logger`, the logging API built into the JDK (Java Platform Logging). The entry point is `JPL` in package `zio.logging.backend`. Add the dependency:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-jpl" % "2.5.5"
```

#### JPL Entry Points

`JPL` has two layer overloads, a default layer and a function that returns the bare logger:

```scala
object JPL {
  val logFormatDefault: LogFormat

  def jpl(format: LogFormat, loggerName: Trace => String): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def jpl(format: LogFormat): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  val jpl: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]

  def jplLogger(format: LogFormat, loggerName: Trace => String = getLoggerName()): ZLogger[String, Unit]
}
```

The table describes each member:

| Member                        | Description                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `JPL.jpl`                     | Adds a JPL logger with `JPL.logFormatDefault` and the trace-based logger name.                 |
| `JPL.jpl(format)`             | Same, with a custom `LogFormat`.                                                               |
| `JPL.jpl(format, loggerName)` | Same, with a custom logger-name function.                                                      |
| `JPL.jplLogger`               | Returns the `ZLogger` without installing it. The loggers come from `System.getLogger(name)`.   |
| `JPL.logFormatDefault`        | `LogFormat.allAnnotations(excludeKeys = Set(logger_name)) + LogFormat.line + LogFormat.cause`. |

The logger name is the `logger_name` annotation when present, and otherwise the class derived from the trace, with the fallback `"zio-jpl-logger"`. The trace-based function is `private[backend]`; to choose another fallback, pass your own `Trace => String`.

Unlike SLF4J, `System.Logger` has no structured data. Key-value pairs from the format are written into the message as `key=value ` text, so the default format produces `user=alice trace_id=... Starting user operation`. For the cause, the backend passes the first `Throwable` failure or defect of the cause, or a `FiberFailure` that wraps the cause when it contains none.

To install the JPL backend in place of the default logger:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.backend.JPL

val jplLogger: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> JPL.jpl
```

#### JPL Level Mapping

The backend checks `System.Logger#isLoggable` with the mapped level before formatting, so the `System.Logger` implementation decides which levels are written:

| ZIO `LogLevel` | `System.Logger.Level` |
| -------------- | --------------------- |
| `All`          | `ALL`                 |
| `Trace`        | `TRACE`               |
| `Debug`        | `DEBUG`               |
| `Info`         | `INFO`                |
| `Warning`      | `WARNING`             |
| `Error`        | `ERROR`               |
| `Fatal`        | `ERROR`               |
| `None`         | `OFF`                 |

:::note
`LogLevel.None` maps to `OFF` rather than being dropped. Whether a record at `OFF` is written depends on the `System.Logger` implementation; the default implementation, which is backed by `java.util.logging`, can still write it.
:::

### SPI Classes

SLF4J and JUL find their logger implementations by class name or through Java's `ServiceLoader`, so the bridge modules contain public classes that application code never calls. They are public only because the logging system loads them:

| Class                                                                     | Module             | Role                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `org.slf4j.impl.StaticLoggerBinder`                                       | v1 bridge          | SLF4J 1.7 looks up this class by name to find the logger factory.                            |
| `org.slf4j.impl.StaticMDCBinder`                                          | v1 bridge          | SLF4J 1.7 looks it up for the MDC adapter (a `BasicMDCAdapter` that the bridge never reads). |
| `org.slf4j.impl.StaticMarkerBinder`                                       | v1 bridge          | SLF4J 1.7 looks it up for the marker factory.                                                |
| `org.slf4j.helpers.ZioLoggerBase`                                         | v1 bridge          | Base logger; extends SLF4J's `MarkerIgnoringBase`, which is why v1 markers are ignored.      |
| `org.slf4j.impl.ZioLoggerFactory`, `ZioLogger`, `LoggerRuntime`           | v1 bridge          | The logger factory, the logger, and the interface between them and the ZIO runtime.          |
| `zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.ZioSLF4JServiceProvider`                        | v2 bridge          | The SLF4J 2 provider, registered in `META-INF/services/org.slf4j.spi.SLF4JServiceProvider`.  |
| `zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.ZioLoggerFactory`, `ZioLogger`, `LoggerRuntime` | v2 bridge          | The logger factory, the logger, and the interface to the ZIO runtime.                        |
| `zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.LoggerData`                                     | both SLF4J bridges | Holds a logger name and its `logger_name` annotation.                                        |
| `zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.ZioLoggerRuntime`                               | both SLF4J bridges | Turns SLF4J calls into ZIO records; its companion holds `ZioLoggerRuntime.logLevelMapping`.  |
| `zio.logging.jul.bridge.ZioLoggerRuntime`                                 | JUL bridge         | The JUL `Handler` that `JULBridge` adds to the root logger.                                  |

The v2 bridge jar also ships a `module-info` for the Java module system. It declares the module `org.slf4j.zio`, which requires `org.slf4j` and provides `org.slf4j.spi.SLF4JServiceProvider` with `ZioSLF4JServiceProvider`. The backend modules ship no `module-info`.

Because a bridge is an SLF4J provider, it conflicts with every other provider on the classpath, such as `logback-classic` or `log4j-slf4j2-impl`:

- With SLF4J 2.x, when several providers are present SLF4J picks one and prints a warning. If it picks another provider, building the `Slf4jBridge` layer fails with a `ClassCastException` defect. SLF4J 2.0.9 and later let you choose the provider with the system property `slf4j.provider=zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.ZioSLF4JServiceProvider`.
- With SLF4J 1.7, the first `org.slf4j.impl.StaticLoggerBinder` on the classpath wins, and the same `ClassCastException` appears when it is not the bridge's.
- SLF4J 2.x does not load SLF4J 1.7 bindings, so the v1 bridge has no effect when `slf4j-api` 2.x ends up on the classpath, for example through dependency eviction.

---

## Log Annotations and LogContext Reference

`LogAnnotation[A]` is a **typed key for structured log data**: a name, a value type `A`, a rule for combining two values, and a rule for rendering a value as text. `LogContext` is the immutable map from those keys to their values, and the fiber reference `zio.logging.logContext` holds the `LogContext` of the current fiber. Together they let you attach values such as a trace id or a user id to every log line emitted by an effect, without passing them to each `ZIO.log*` call. The fundamental operation is `LogAnnotation#apply`, which turns a value into a `ZIOAspect` that you apply with `@@`.

This page also covers the logger-name aspects `zio.logging.loggerName` and `zio.logging.appendLoggerName`. They set a plain string annotation, not a `LogAnnotation`, but they are the other half of "adding context to log lines".

The types and values have these shapes:

```scala
final case class LogAnnotation[A: Tag](name: String, combine: (A, A) => A, render: A => String) {
  type Id
  type Type = A
  def apply(value: A): ZIOAspect[Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any]
  def id: Id
  def tag: Tag[A]
}

final case class LogContext private (private val map: Map[LogAnnotation[_], Any])

package object logging {
  val logContext: FiberRef[LogContext]
}
```

`LogAnnotation`:
- Is typed: a `LogAnnotation[java.util.UUID]` only accepts a `UUID`, and `LogContext#get` gives the `UUID` back, not a string.
- Merges on nesting: when the same annotation is applied inside an effect that already has it, `combine(outer, inner)` decides the new value.
- Is compared by name and type: two annotations are equal when their `name` and their type `A` are equal, whatever their `LogAnnotation#combine` and `LogAnnotation#render` functions are.

:::caution[Two classes are called LogAnnotation]
ZIO core has its own `zio.LogAnnotation`, a plain `(key: String, value: String)` pair. With `import zio._` and `import zio.logging._` together, the name `LogAnnotation` is ambiguous and does not compile. Import ZIO Logging's class by name, as in `import zio.logging.LogAnnotation`, or import only the `zio` members you use.
:::

### Usage

To tag every log line of a request with a trace id and a user id, and to print both values next to the message:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZIO, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LogFilter, LogFormat, consoleLogger }

import java.util.UUID

object AnnotatedApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val format: LogFormat =
    LogFormat.level |-| LogFormat.line |-|
      LogFormat.logAnnotation(LogAnnotation.TraceId) |-|
      LogFormat.logAnnotation(LogAnnotation.UserId)

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
      consoleLogger(ConsoleLoggerConfig(format, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default))

  val handleRequest: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
    ZIO.logInfo("Request received") *> ZIO.logInfo("Request done")

  val run =
    handleRequest @@
      LogAnnotation.TraceId(UUID.fromString("7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7")) @@
      LogAnnotation.UserId("user-42")
}
```

Both lines carry both values:

```text
INFO Request received trace_id=7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7 user_id=user-42
INFO Request done trace_id=7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7 user_id=user-42
```

[Logger Context and Annotations](logger-context-and-annotations.md) explains when to use typed annotations, and [How to Add a Correlation ID to Every Log Line](how-to-correlation-id.md) builds a full request-scoped example.

### Creating Annotations

A custom annotation is an instance of the case class. Its declaration is:

```scala
final case class LogAnnotation[A: Tag](name: String, combine: (A, A) => A, render: A => String)
```

The three fields have these roles:

| Field     | Type             | Role                                                                                                                                        |
| --------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`    | `String`         | The key under which formats write the value, such as `trace_id`. It is also the key that `LogContext#get(name)` and `LogContext#asMap` use. |
| `combine` | `(A, A) => A`    | Called as `combine(current, added)` when a value is added for an annotation that already has one. The result replaces the current value.   |
| `render`  | `A => String`    | Turns the value into the text that formats write.                                                                                           |

The implicit `Tag[A]` records the value type. `LogAnnotation#tag` returns it, and `LogAnnotation#id` returns the pair of name and tag that `equals` and `hashCode` use.

The `LogAnnotation#combine` function is where the design choice lies. Return the added value to make an inner scope override the outer one. Concatenate or merge to accumulate. To define an annotation for feature flags that accumulates flags as scopes nest, and an annotation for a tenant id where the innermost value wins:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation

val FeatureFlags: LogAnnotation[Set[String]] =
  LogAnnotation[Set[String]](
    name = "feature_flags",
    combine = _ ++ _,
    render = _.toList.sorted.mkString(",")
  )

val TenantId: LogAnnotation[String] =
  LogAnnotation[String](
    name = "tenant_id",
    combine = (_, added) => added,
    render = identity
  )
```

Define each annotation once, as a `val`, and reuse it. Because equality ignores `LogAnnotation#combine` and `LogAnnotation#render`, a second `LogAnnotation[String]("tenant_id", ...)` with different functions is the same key as the first one, and which functions run depends on which instance the context stored first.

### Predefined Annotations

The `LogAnnotation` companion object defines three annotations:

| Annotation                 | Type             | `name`        | `combine(current, added)` | `render`                                        |
| -------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `LogAnnotation.TraceId`    | `java.util.UUID` | `trace_id`    | `added`                   | `UUID#toString`                                 |
| `LogAnnotation.UserId`     | `String`         | `user_id`     | `added`                   | the string itself                               |
| `LogAnnotation.TraceSpans` | `List[String]`   | `trace_spans` | `current ++ added`        | the elements joined with `:`, such as `http:db` |

`LogAnnotation.TraceId` and `LogAnnotation.UserId` keep the innermost value. `LogAnnotation.TraceSpans` builds a path of span names, outermost first, as the effect nests.

### Applying Annotations

An annotation does nothing until you give it a value and apply it to an effect. There are three ways to do that, and they all end in the same aspect.

#### As an Aspect

`LogAnnotation#apply` returns a `ZIOAspect`. Applying it with `@@` runs the effect with `logContext` locally set to the current context plus the new value, so every log call inside the effect, including calls in fibers it forks, sees the value. When the effect ends, `logContext` goes back to what it was:

```scala
final case class LogAnnotation[A: Tag](name: String, combine: (A, A) => A, render: A => String) {
  def apply(value: A): ZIOAspect[Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any]
}
```

`effect @@ a @@ b` reads as `(effect @@ a) @@ b`, so `b` is the outer aspect and `a` the inner one. For an annotation applied twice, the context first gets the outer value, then `combine(outer, inner)`. To nest `LogAnnotation.TraceSpans` by applying it at two levels:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation

val query: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo("Running query") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceSpans(List("db"))

val request: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  (ZIO.logInfo("Handling request") *> query) @@ LogAnnotation.TraceSpans(List("http"))
```

With a format that writes `LogFormat.logAnnotation(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans)`, the first line carries `trace_spans=http` and the second `trace_spans=http:db`.

Two annotation aspects composed with each other, as in `LogAnnotation.UserId("a") @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(id)` without an effect on the left, become one aspect holding both values. When both sides set the same annotation, the right-hand value replaces the left-hand one without calling `LogAnnotation#combine`.

#### With the logAnnotate Syntax

The implicit class `LogAnnotationZIOSyntax` adds `LogAnnotationZIOSyntax#logAnnotate` to every `ZIO`. It is the same as `effect @@ key(value)`, written as a method call:

```scala
implicit final class LogAnnotationZIOSyntax[R, E, A](self: ZIO[R, E, A]) {
  def logAnnotate[V: Tag](key: LogAnnotation[V], value: V): ZIO[R, E, A]
}
```

Bring the syntax into scope with `import zio.logging.LogAnnotationZIOSyntax` or `import zio.logging._`. To annotate a call with the user id in method style:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.{ LogAnnotation, LogAnnotationZIOSyntax }

val audited: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo("Password changed").logAnnotate(LogAnnotation.UserId, "user-42")
```

#### Typed Annotations Versus ZIO String Annotations

ZIO core has its own annotations: `ZIO.logAnnotate(key, value)` and `ZIOAspect.annotated(key, value)` attach a `String` value under a `String` key. They are stored in a different place from `logContext`, and the two kinds never mix:

| Aspect                     | ZIO core string annotations                         | ZIO Logging typed annotations                                   |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Created with               | `ZIO.logAnnotate(key, value)`, `ZIOAspect.annotated` | `LogAnnotation#apply` with `@@`, or `effect.logAnnotate(annotation, value)` |
| Value type                 | `String`                                            | Any `A`, rendered with `LogAnnotation#render`                   |
| Nested value for same key  | Inner value replaces the outer one                  | `LogAnnotation#combine(outer, inner)`                           |
| Stored in                  | ZIO's log annotations, passed to every `ZLogger`    | The `zio.logging.logContext` fiber reference                    |
| Read in code with          | `ZIO.logAnnotations`                                | `logContext.get`                                                |
| Written by formats         | `LogFormat.annotation(name)`, `LogFormat.annotations` | `LogFormat.logAnnotation(annotation)`, `LogFormat.logAnnotations` |
| Seen by other `ZLogger`s   | Yes, as the `annotations` argument                  | Only by loggers that read `logContext` from their `FiberRefs` argument, such as a logger built from a `LogFormat` that writes it |

Use a string annotation for a quick key that every `ZLogger`, including ZIO's default logger, should see. The default formats of the [SLF4J](slf4j2.md) and [JPL](jpl.md) backends write both kinds. Use a typed annotation when the value has a type worth keeping, needs a merge rule, or is defined once and shared across a code base.

### The logContext Fiber Reference

`zio.logging.logContext` is an ordinary `FiberRef[LogContext]`. It starts as `LogContext.empty`, a forked fiber starts with a copy of its parent's context, and a joined fiber's context is merged into its parent's with `LogContext#++`:

```scala
package object logging {
  val logContext: FiberRef[LogContext]
}
```

You rarely touch it directly; the aspects above are the idiomatic way to change it. Reading it is useful in tests and in custom loggers. To read the user id that the surrounding aspect set:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.{ LogAnnotation, logContext }

val currentUser: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Option[String]] =
  logContext.get.map(_.get(LogAnnotation.UserId))

val program: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Option[String]] =
  currentUser @@ LogAnnotation.UserId("user-42")
```

`FiberRef#update` and `FiberRef#set` change the context for the rest of the fiber, not only for one block, which is rarely what you want. `FiberRef#locallyWith` gives the scoped behaviour of the aspect. To add a value with `LogContext#annotate` for one block:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.{ LogAnnotation, logContext }

val withUser: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  logContext.locallyWith(_.annotate(LogAnnotation.UserId, "user-42"))(ZIO.logInfo("Inside"))
```

A custom `ZLogger` receives the fiber refs as its `context: FiberRefs` argument and reads the context with `context.get(logContext)`, which returns an `Option[LogContext]`.

### LogContext Operations

`LogContext` is an immutable map from annotations to values. Its constructor is private: start from `LogContext.empty` and add values with `LogContext#annotate`.

#### Creating and Adding Values

`LogContext.empty` is the context with no values. `LogContext#annotate` adds a value, combining it with the current value when the annotation already has one:

```scala
object LogContext {
  val empty: LogContext
}

final case class LogContext private (private val map: Map[LogAnnotation[_], Any]) {
  def annotate[A](annotation: LogAnnotation[A], newA: A): LogContext
}
```

To build a context with a user id and two trace spans:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogAnnotation, LogContext }

val context: LogContext =
  LogContext.empty
    .annotate(LogAnnotation.UserId, "user-1")
    .annotate(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans, List("http"))
    .annotate(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans, List("db"))
```

#### Reading Values

`LogContext#get` with an annotation returns the typed value. `LogContext#apply` returns the rendered value. `LogContext#get` with a name returns the rendered value of the annotation with that name. `LogContext#asMap` renders every entry:

```scala
final case class LogContext private (private val map: Map[LogAnnotation[_], Any]) {
  def get[A](annotation: LogAnnotation[A]): Option[A]
  def apply[A](logAnnotation: LogAnnotation[A]): Option[String]
  def get(name: String): Option[String]
  def asMap: Map[String, String]
}
```

Reading the context built above gives the typed list, the rendered list, the rendered user id, and the whole context as strings:

```scala
context.get(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans)
// res7: Option[List[String]] = Some(value = List("http", "db"))
context(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans)
// res8: Option[String] = Some(value = "http:db")
context.get("user_id")
// res9: Option[String] = Some(value = "user-1")
context.asMap
// res10: Map[String, String] = Map(
//   "user_id" -> "user-1",
//   "trace_spans" -> "http:db"
// )
```

:::caution[Two annotations with the same name]
Annotations with the same name but different types, such as a `LogAnnotation[String]("id", ...)` and a `LogAnnotation[Int]("id", ...)`, are different keys, so a context can hold both. `LogContext#get(name)` then returns one of them, and `LogContext#asMap` keeps only one entry for the name; which one is not specified. Give every annotation a distinct name.
:::

#### Merging Contexts

`LogContext#merge` and its alias `LogContext#++` combine two contexts. For an annotation present in both, the result is `combine(left, right)`; otherwise the value comes from whichever side has it:

```scala
final case class LogContext private (private val map: Map[LogAnnotation[_], Any]) {
  def ++(that: LogContext): LogContext
  def merge(that: LogContext): LogContext
}
```

To merge two contexts that both have trace spans:

```scala
val left: LogContext  = LogContext.empty.annotate(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans, List("a"))
val right: LogContext = LogContext.empty.annotate(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans, List("b"))

val merged: LogContext = left ++ right
```

The merged context holds both spans, left first, because `LogAnnotation.TraceSpans` concatenates:

```scala
merged(LogAnnotation.TraceSpans)
// res11: Option[String] = Some(value = "a:b")
```

### Logger Names

A logger name groups log lines by the part of the program that wrote them. Level filters with per-name mappings, such as `filter.mappings` in the [configuration](reference-configuration.md), select lines by it, and the `%name` pattern and `LogFormat.loggerName` write it. By default the name comes from the `Trace` of the log call: the enclosing class or object, such as `com.example.UserService`. These aspects override it:

```scala
package object logging {
  val loggerNameAnnotationKey: String // "logger_name"

  def loggerName(value: String): ZIOAspect[Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any]
  def loggerName(fn: Option[String] => String): ZIOAspect[Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any]
  def appendLoggerName(value: String): ZIOAspect[Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any]
}
```

The name is stored as a ZIO core string annotation under the key `zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`, whose value is `logger_name`, not in `logContext`:

| Aspect                                 | New name                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `zio.logging.loggerName(value)`        | `value`, replacing any name set by an outer aspect.                                            |
| `zio.logging.loggerName(fn)`           | `fn(current)`, where `current` is the current `logger_name` annotation, usually set by an outer aspect, or `None` when there is none. The trace-based default is not passed in. |
| `zio.logging.appendLoggerName(value)`  | `current.value` when an outer aspect set a name, otherwise `value`.                             |

To name a service once and let each method add its own suffix:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.{ appendLoggerName, loggerName }

val charge: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  ZIO.logInfo("Charging card") @@ appendLoggerName("charge")

val payments: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  charge @@ loggerName("payments")

val versioned: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  charge @@ loggerName((current: Option[String]) => current.fold("payments")(_ + ".v2"))
```

The line from `payments` has the logger name `payments.charge`. In `versioned`, no outer aspect set a name, so the function returns `payments`, and `charge` then appends to it, giving the same `payments.charge`.

Because the name is a string annotation, `LogFormat.annotations` and `LogFormat.allAnnotations` write it as `logger_name=...` next to your other annotations. The `%kvs` pattern leaves it out.

### Writing Annotations to the Output

`LogFormat.default` and `LogFormat.colored`, which the console and file loggers use unless configured otherwise, write no annotations. Add one of these members to your format:

| Member or pattern                      | Writes                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.logAnnotation(annotation)`  | One typed annotation from `logContext`, as `name=rendered value`.                                   |
| `LogFormat.logAnnotations`             | Every typed annotation in `logContext`.                                                             |
| `LogFormat.annotation(name)`           | One ZIO string annotation.                                                                          |
| `LogFormat.annotations`                | Every ZIO string annotation, including `logger_name`.                                               |
| `LogFormat.allAnnotations`             | Every string annotation, then every typed annotation.                                               |
| `%kv{name}` pattern                    | The string annotation `name`, or when there is none, the typed annotation with that name.           |
| `%kvs` pattern                         | Every string and typed annotation, except `logger_name`.                                            |

In a text format each entry is written as `name=value`, with a space between entries. In a JSON format each entry becomes a field. The full signatures, including the `excludeKeys` overloads, are in [LogFormat Reference](reference-log-format.md#annotations), and the pattern syntax is in [Formatting Log Records](formatting-log-records.md).

---

## LogFilter and LogGroup Reference

`LogFilter` decides whether a log event is written. `LogGroup` extracts one value from a log event, such as its level or logger name, and a filter tests that value with a predicate. `LoggerNameExtractor` is a small helper that finds the logger name in a log event. This page lists the members of all three types. For how filters are set up in a logger configuration, see [Log Filter](./log-filter.md).

### LogFilter Members

`LogFilter` is a sealed trait, so you create filters with the companion functions and combinators, not by extending the trait. A filter has two abstract parts: a group that extracts a value, and a predicate that tests the value. The trait is declared as follows:

```scala
sealed trait LogFilter[-Message] {
  type Value
  def group: LogGroup[Message, Value]
  def predicate(value: Value): Boolean
}
```

The instance methods combine filters or change their input type. In the table, `LogFilter#and` means the `and` method called on a filter value, as in `warnings.and(failures)`; it is not a member of the `LogFilter` companion object.

| Instance method       | Signature                                                                                                                                                                                             | Description                                                                                                     |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFilter#apply`     | `final def apply(trace: Trace, fiberId: FiberId, logLevel: LogLevel, message: () => Message, cause: Cause[Any], context: FiberRefs, spans: List[LogSpan], annotations: Map[String, String]): Boolean` | Runs the group on the event, then the predicate on the result. Returns `true` when the event passes.            |
| `LogFilter#and`       | `final def and[M <: Message](other: LogFilter[M]): LogFilter[M]`                                                                                                                                      | Accepts an event only when both filters accept it. The alphanumeric form of `&&`.                               |
| `LogFilter#&&`        | `final def &&[M <: Message](other: LogFilter[M]): LogFilter[M]`                                                                                                                                       | Same as `LogFilter#and`.                                                                                        |
| `LogFilter#or`        | `final def or[M <: Message](other: LogFilter[M]): LogFilter[M]`                                                                                                                                       | Accepts an event when either filter accepts it. The alphanumeric form of `\|\|`.                                |
| `LogFilter#\|\|`      | `final def \|\|[M <: Message](other: LogFilter[M]): LogFilter[M]`                                                                                                                                     | Same as `LogFilter#or`.                                                                                         |
| `LogFilter#not`       | `final def not: LogFilter[Message]`                                                                                                                                                                   | Negates the result. The alphanumeric form of `unary_!`.                                                         |
| `LogFilter#unary_!`   | `final def unary_! : LogFilter[Message]`                                                                                                                                                              | Same as `LogFilter#not`. Written as a prefix, as in `!LogFilter.causeNonEmpty`.                                 |
| `LogFilter#cached`    | `final def cached: LogFilter[Message]`                                                                                                                                                                | Remembers the predicate result for each group value. The cache has no size limit and never evicts entries.      |
| `LogFilter#contramap` | `final def contramap[M](f: M => Message): LogFilter[M]`                                                                                                                                               | Returns a filter for a different message type. The function `f` runs before the group.                          |
| `LogFilter#filter`    | `final def filter[M <: Message, O](logger: zio.ZLogger[M, O]): zio.ZLogger[M, Option[O]]`                                                                                                             | Wraps a logger so that it runs only for accepted events. The wrapped logger returns `None` for rejected events. |

Calling `LogFilter#cached` on an already cached filter creates a new, empty cache around the same inner filter. Use `LogFilter#cached` when the group is expensive to compute, or when many events share the same group value, such as the same logger name.

The next example combines three filters. It accepts events at WARN or above, unless the event has a cause:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.LogFilter

val quietWarnings: LogFilter[Any] = LogFilter.logLevel(LogLevel.Warning) && !LogFilter.causeNonEmpty
```

`LogFilter#contramap` adapts a filter written for one message type to a logger whose messages have another type. The next example reuses a filter on the message text for a logger of audit events, by reading the text out of each event:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LogGroup }

case class AuditEvent(action: String, user: String)

val messageText: LogGroup[String, String] =
  LogGroup[String, String]((_, _, _, message, _, _, _, _) => message())

val notHealthCheck: LogFilter[String] =
  LogFilter[String, String](messageText, (text: String) => !text.startsWith("GET /health"))

val auditFilter: LogFilter[AuditEvent] = notHealthCheck.contramap[AuditEvent](_.action)
```

To run a filter in front of a logger, call `LogFilter#filter` with the logger, or call `logger.filter(logFilter)` on the logger. Both return a `FilteredLogger`. The second form is the `ZLoggerOps#filter` syntax from the `zio.logging` package and needs `import zio.logging._`, as shown on [Log Filter](log-filter.md#apply-a-filter-to-a-logger). The layers that install loggers, and `FilteredLogger` itself, are described in [Logger Layers](reference-logger-layers.md).

### Companion Constructors

The companion object creates filters from groups and predicates, and provides two ready-made filters.

| Member                    | Signature                                                                         | Description                                                                                  |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFilter.apply`         | `def apply[M, V](group0: LogGroup[M, V], predicate0: V => Boolean): LogFilter[M]` | Creates a filter that accepts an event when `predicate0` returns `true` for the group value. |
| `LogFilter.apply`         | `def apply[M](group0: LogGroup[M, Boolean]): LogFilter[M]`                        | Creates a filter that accepts an event when the group value is `true`.                       |
| `LogFilter.acceptAll`     | `val acceptAll: LogFilter[Any]`                                                   | Accepts every event.                                                                         |
| `LogFilter.causeNonEmpty` | `val causeNonEmpty: LogFilter[Any]`                                               | Accepts an event only when its cause is not empty.                                           |

The next example builds a filter from a group and a predicate. It accepts only ERROR and FATAL events:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LogGroup }

val errorsOnly: LogFilter[Any] = LogFilter(LogGroup.logLevel, (level: LogLevel) => level >= LogLevel.Error)
```

### Level Filters

The level filter functions accept events by log level, or by log level for each logger name. The rules for the name mappings are shown in [Log Filter](./log-filter.md).

| Member                      | Signature                                                                                                                                    | Description                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `LogFilter.logLevel`        | `def logLevel(predicate: LogLevel => Boolean): LogFilter[Any]`                                                                               | Accepts events whose level passes `predicate`.                                                                                                                     |
| `LogFilter.logLevel`        | `def logLevel(rootLevel: LogLevel): LogFilter[Any]`                                                                                          | Accepts events at `rootLevel` or above.                                                                                                                            |
| `LogFilter.logLevelByGroup` | `def logLevelByGroup[M, A](rootLevel: LogLevel, group: LogGroup[M, A], matcher: (A, A) => Boolean, groupings: (A, LogLevel)*): LogFilter[M]` | Uses the level of the first grouping that `matcher` accepts. When none matches, uses `rootLevel`.                                                                  |
| `LogFilter.logLevelByGroup` | `def logLevelByGroup[M](rootLevel: LogLevel, group: LogGroup[M, String], mappings: (String, LogLevel)*): LogFilter[M]`                       | Matches the dot-separated name against the mappings, most specific mapping first, with the glob rules in [Log Filter](log-filter.md#how-logger-names-are-matched). |
| `LogFilter.logLevelByGroup` | `def logLevelByGroup[M](group: LogGroup[M, String], config: LogLevelByNameConfig): LogFilter[M]`                                             | Same as the previous overload, with the root level and mappings read from the config argument.                                                                     |
| `LogFilter.logLevelByName`  | `def logLevelByName[M](rootLevel: LogLevel, mappings: (String, LogLevel)*): LogFilter[M]`                                                    | Same as `LogFilter.logLevelByGroup` with `LogGroup.loggerName`.                                                                                                    |
| `LogFilter.logLevelByName`  | `def logLevelByName[M](config: LogLevelByNameConfig): LogFilter[M]`                                                                          | Same as `LogFilter.logLevelByName` with the root level and mappings read from the config argument.                                                                 |

The example below sets DEBUG as the root level, and sets INFO for the `io.netty` logger and everything under it:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.LogFilter

val nettyQuieter: LogFilter[Any] = LogFilter.logLevelByName[Any](LogLevel.Debug, "io.netty" -> LogLevel.Info)
```

The generic `LogFilter.logLevelByGroup` overload takes any group and your own `matcher`. Unlike the `String` overloads, it does not sort the groupings: it tries them in the order given and uses the first one for which `matcher(groupValue, grouping)` returns `true`. The next example matches logger names by plain string prefix instead of by dot-separated segments, so `com.acme.legacy` also covers `com.acme.legacyBilling`:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LogGroup }

val byPrefix: LogFilter[Any] =
  LogFilter.logLevelByGroup[Any, String](
    LogLevel.Info,
    LogGroup.loggerName,
    (loggerName: String, prefix: String) => loggerName.startsWith(prefix),
    "com.acme.legacy" -> LogLevel.Warning,
    "com.acme"        -> LogLevel.Debug
  )
```

Because the order matters here, the more specific prefix comes first.

### LogLevelByNameConfig

`LogLevelByNameConfig` holds the root level and the name mappings for a level filter. It is the value that `LogFilter.logLevelByName` accepts when you build the filter from configuration. The class is declared as follows:

```scala
final case class LogLevelByNameConfig(rootLevel: LogLevel, mappings: Map[String, LogLevel])
```

The class has helper methods that return a new config. The companion object provides the defaults and the parser.

| Member                               | Signature                                                                                   | Description                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig#withRootLevel` | `def withRootLevel(rootLevel: LogLevel): LogLevelByNameConfig`                              | Returns a copy with a new root level.                                                                                                                   |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig#withMapping`   | `def withMapping(name: String, level: LogLevel): LogLevelByNameConfig`                      | Returns a copy with one more mapping, or with the level of an existing mapping replaced.                                                                |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig#withMappings`  | `def withMappings(mappings: Map[String, LogLevel]): LogLevelByNameConfig`                   | Returns a copy with the given mappings, replacing all current mappings.                                                                                 |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig#toFilter`      | `def toFilter[M]: LogFilter[M]`                                                             | Builds the filter from this config. Same as `LogFilter.logLevelByName` with this config.                                                                |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig.apply`         | `def apply(rootLevel: LogLevel, mappings: (String, LogLevel)*): LogLevelByNameConfig`       | Companion constructor that takes the mappings as pairs.                                                                                                 |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig.default`       | `val default: LogLevelByNameConfig`                                                         | Root level INFO, with no mappings.                                                                                                                      |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig.config`        | `val config: Config[LogLevelByNameConfig]`                                                  | Reads `rootLevel` and `mappings`. The keys are described in [Configuration Keys Reference](./reference-configuration.md).                               |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig.load`          | `def load(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String]): ZIO[Any, Config.Error, LogLevelByNameConfig]` | Reads the config from the given path in the configuration source.                                                                                       |
| `LogLevelByNameConfig.equal`         | `implicit val equal: Equal[LogLevelByNameConfig]`                                           | Compares two configs by their root level and mappings. `ReconfigurableLogger` uses it through `ConsoleLoggerConfig.equal` and `FileLoggerConfig.equal`. |

### Filter Equality

`LogFilter.equal` is an implicit `zio.prelude.Equal[LogFilter[_]]`. `ReconfigurableLogger` uses `Equal` instances to decide whether a newly loaded configuration differs from the current one, and builds a new logger only when it does; see [Reconfigurable Logger](reconfigurable-logger.md). Two filters are equal when they have the same structure and equal parts. Filters made from functions are equal only when they hold the same function instance. Filters built from a `LogLevelByNameConfig`, through `LogFilter.logLevelByName(config)` or `LogFilter.logLevelByGroup(group, config)`, compare only their config, so two such filters with different groups and the same config are equal.

### LogGroup

`LogGroup` extracts one value from a log event. It is the first half of a filter: `LogFilter.apply` and `LogFilter.logLevelByGroup` take a group, and the filter tests the value it extracts. There is no API that turns a `LogGroup` into a `LogFormat`; to write a value into the log line, use `LogFormat.make`. The trait is declared as follows:

```scala
sealed trait LogGroup[-Message, Out] {
  def apply(
    trace: Trace,
    fiberId: FiberId,
    logLevel: LogLevel,
    message: () => Message,
    cause: Cause[Any],
    context: FiberRefs,
    spans: List[LogSpan],
    annotations: Map[String, String]
  ): Out
}
```

The companion object provides the ready-made groups and the constructor that accepts a function.

| Member                             | Signature                                                                                                                                  | Description                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogGroup.apply`                   | `def apply[M, O](fn: (Trace, FiberId, LogLevel, () => M, Cause[Any], FiberRefs, List[LogSpan], Map[String, String]) => O): LogGroup[M, O]` | Creates a group from a function over the event parts.                                                         |
| `LogGroup.cause`                   | `val cause: LogGroup[Any, Cause[Any]]`                                                                                                     | Extracts the cause of the event.                                                                              |
| `LogGroup.constant`                | `def constant[O](value: O): LogGroup[Any, O]`                                                                                              | Always returns `value`.                                                                                       |
| `LogGroup.fromLoggerNameExtractor` | `def fromLoggerNameExtractor(loggerNameExtractor: LoggerNameExtractor, loggerNameDefault: String = "zio-logger"): LogGroup[Any, String]`   | Extracts the logger name with `loggerNameExtractor`, or uses `loggerNameDefault` when none is found.          |
| `LogGroup.logLevel`                | `val logLevel: LogGroup[Any, LogLevel]`                                                                                                    | Extracts the level of the event.                                                                              |
| `LogGroup.loggerName`              | `val loggerName: LogGroup[Any, String]`                                                                                                    | Extracts the logger name from the logger name annotation, or from the `Trace` when the annotation is missing. |
| `LogGroup.loggerNameAndLevel`      | `val loggerNameAndLevel: LogGroup[Any, (String, LogLevel)]`                                                                                | Extracts the logger name and the level as a pair.                                                             |

`LogGroup.apply` builds a group from a function over the parts of the event. The next example reads a `tenant` string annotation, and a filter built from it lets every line of one tenant through while the root level is WARN for the rest:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LogGroup }

val tenant: LogGroup[Any, String] =
  LogGroup[Any, String]((_, _, _, _, _, _, _, annotations) => annotations.getOrElse("tenant", ""))

val tenantAndLevel: LogGroup[Any, (String, LogLevel)] = tenant ++ LogGroup.logLevel

val debugOneTenant: LogFilter[Any] =
  LogFilter[Any, (String, LogLevel)](
    tenantAndLevel,
    (value: (String, LogLevel)) => value._1 == "acme-beta" || value._2 >= LogLevel.Warning
  )
```

The instance methods change the output of a group or combine two groups. The `++` method is an alias for `LogGroup#zip`.

| Instance method      | Signature                                                                                                                       | Description                                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogGroup#++`        | `final def ++[M <: Message, O, Out2](other: LogGroup[M, O])(implicit zippable: Zippable.Out[Out, O, Out2]): LogGroup[M, Out2]`  | Same as `LogGroup#zip`.                                                             |
| `LogGroup#map`       | `final def map[O](f: Out => O): LogGroup[Message, O]`                                                                           | Applies `f` to the output of the group.                                             |
| `LogGroup#contramap` | `final def contramap[M](f: M => Message): LogGroup[M, Out]`                                                                     | Applies `f` to the message before the group runs.                                   |
| `LogGroup#zip`       | `final def zip[M <: Message, O, Out2](other: LogGroup[M, O])(implicit zippable: Zippable.Out[Out, O, Out2]): LogGroup[M, Out2]` | Returns both outputs as one value. The `Zippable` instance decides the tuple shape. |
| `LogGroup#zipWith`   | `final def zipWith[M <: Message, O, Out2](other: LogGroup[M, O])(f: (Out, O) => Out2): LogGroup[M, Out2]`                       | Combines both outputs with `f`.                                                     |

The next example builds a group that returns the logger name and the level as one string:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogGroup

val nameAndLevel: LogGroup[Any, String] =
  LogGroup.loggerName.zipWith(LogGroup.logLevel)((name, level) => s"$name/${level.label}")
```

### LoggerNameExtractor

`LoggerNameExtractor` finds the logger name from the parts of a log event. It returns `None` when it has no name, so you can chain extractors with `||` to try each one in turn. The trait is declared as follows:

```scala
sealed trait LoggerNameExtractor {
  def apply(trace: Trace, context: FiberRefs, annotations: Map[String, String]): Option[String]
}
```

The instance methods chain extractors and convert them into a format or a group.

| Instance method                   | Signature                                                                     | Description                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LoggerNameExtractor#\|\|`        | `final def \|\|(other: LoggerNameExtractor): LoggerNameExtractor`             | Uses this extractor's name, or the name of `other` when this one returns `None`.                    |
| `LoggerNameExtractor#or`          | `final def or(other: LoggerNameExtractor): LoggerNameExtractor`               | Same as `\|\|`, with an alphanumeric name.                                                          |
| `LoggerNameExtractor#toLogFormat` | `final def toLogFormat(default: String = "zio-logger"): LogFormat`            | Converts the extractor into a `LogFormat` that writes the name, using `default` when none is found. |
| `LoggerNameExtractor#toLogGroup`  | `final def toLogGroup(default: String = "zio-logger"): LogGroup[Any, String]` | Converts the extractor into a `LogGroup`, using `default` when none is found.                       |

The companion object provides the constructors and the extractors that the library uses:

| Member                                            | Signature                                                                                      | Description                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `LoggerNameExtractor.make`                        | `def make(fn: (Trace, FiberRefs, Map[String, String]) => Option[String]): LoggerNameExtractor` | Creates an extractor from a function.                                                                                                                                    |
| `LoggerNameExtractor.trace`                       | `val trace: LoggerNameExtractor`                                                               | Takes the name from the `Trace`, without the method name. For `example.LivePingService.ping(PingService.scala:22)` the name is `example.LivePingService`.                |
| `LoggerNameExtractor.annotation`                  | `def annotation(name: String): LoggerNameExtractor`                                            | Takes the name from the string annotation `name`.                                                                                                                        |
| `LoggerNameExtractor.annotationOrTrace`           | `def annotationOrTrace(name: String): LoggerNameExtractor`                                     | Takes the name from the annotation `name`, or from the `Trace` when the annotation is missing.                                                                           |
| `LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace` | `val loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace: LoggerNameExtractor`                                         | Same as `LoggerNameExtractor.annotationOrTrace` with the key `zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`. This is the default for `LogGroup.loggerName` and the `%name` token. |

The next example takes the name from a `component` annotation, and falls back to the trace:

```scala
import zio.logging.LoggerNameExtractor

val componentOrTrace: LoggerNameExtractor = LoggerNameExtractor.annotation("component") || LoggerNameExtractor.trace
```

`LoggerNameExtractor.make` builds an extractor from a function, for names that no predefined extractor gives. The next example puts every `component` annotation under one `app` namespace, so that a single mapping such as `app` -> INFO covers all components, and falls back to the trace:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LoggerNameExtractor }

val appComponent: LoggerNameExtractor =
  LoggerNameExtractor.make((_, _, annotations) => annotations.get("component").map(component => s"app.$component"))

val appFilter: LogFilter[Any] =
  LogFilter.logLevelByGroup[Any](
    LogLevel.Debug,
    (appComponent || LoggerNameExtractor.trace).toLogGroup(),
    "app" -> LogLevel.Info
  )
```

For a logger name in a format, see `LogFormat.loggerName` in [LogFormat Reference](./reference-log-format.md#logger-name).

---

## LogFormat Reference

`LogFormat` is a sealed trait that describes how one log line is laid out. You build a format from the values and functions in the `LogFormat` companion object, join formats with the instance methods, and pass the result to a logger through its configuration. Each part of a format either writes fixed text or reads one part of the log event, such as the level, the message, or an annotation.

The string form of the same DSL, such as `%timestamp{...}` and `%level`, is described in [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md). This page covers only the Scala API.

### Building Blocks

The companion object provides values and functions that write fixed text or wrap other formats. Each row lists one member of `LogFormat`.

| Member                   | Signature                                                  | Description                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.text`         | `def text(value: => String): LogFormat`                    | Writes the given string. `value` is evaluated once, when the format is built.                                               |
| `LogFormat.space`        | `val space: LogFormat`                                     | Writes one space character.                                                                                                 |
| `LogFormat.newLine`      | `val newLine: LogFormat`                                   | Writes the platform line separator.                                                                                         |
| `LogFormat.quote`        | `val quote: LogFormat`                                     | Writes one double quote character.                                                                                          |
| `LogFormat.quoted`       | `def quoted(inner: LogFormat): LogFormat`                  | Wraps `inner` in double quotes.                                                                                             |
| `LogFormat.bracketed`    | `def bracketed(inner: LogFormat): LogFormat`               | Wraps `inner` in square brackets.                                                                                           |
| `LogFormat.bracketStart` | `val bracketStart: LogFormat`                              | Writes `[`.                                                                                                                 |
| `LogFormat.bracketEnd`   | `val bracketEnd: LogFormat`                                | Writes `]`.                                                                                                                 |
| `LogFormat.label`        | `def label(label: => String, value: LogFormat): LogFormat` | Writes `label=value`, where `value` is the output of the inner format. `label` is evaluated once, when the format is built. |
| `LogFormat.empty`        | `val empty: LogFormat`                                     | Writes nothing.                                                                                                             |

`LogFormat.label` writes its name as a key, then the inner format as the value. In plain text output the result looks like `level=INFO`. The JSON output uses the same name as a JSON key.

:::note[By-name arguments are evaluated once]
`LogFormat.text`, `LogFormat.label` and `LogFormat.timestamp(formatter)` take by-name parameters, but each evaluates its argument once, when the format value is built, not for every line. `LogFormat.text(java.lang.System.currentTimeMillis().toString)` writes the same number on every line. For a value computed per line, write that part with [`LogFormat.make`](#custom-formats-with-logformatmake).
:::

### Composing Formats

The instance methods join formats together, add styling, or convert a format into a logger. Each method returns a new `LogFormat` and leaves the original unchanged.

| Method                   | Signature                                                        | Description                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `+`                      | `final def +(other: LogFormat): LogFormat`                       | Joins two formats with no separator.                                                                        |
| `LogFormat#concat`       | `final def concat(other: LogFormat): LogFormat`                  | Same as `+`, with an alphanumeric name.                                                                     |
| `\|-\|`                  | `final def \|-\|(other: LogFormat): LogFormat`                   | Joins two formats with one space between them.                                                              |
| `LogFormat#spaced`       | `final def spaced(other: LogFormat): LogFormat`                  | Same as `\|-\|`, with an alphanumeric name.                                                                 |
| `LogFormat#color`        | `final def color(color: LogColor): LogFormat`                    | Wraps the output in the ANSI code of `color`, followed by the reset code.                                   |
| `LogFormat#highlight`    | `final def highlight: LogFormat`                                 | Colors the output by log level: ERROR red, WARN yellow, INFO cyan, DEBUG green, and all other levels white. |
| `LogFormat#highlight`    | `final def highlight(fn: LogLevel => LogColor): LogFormat`       | Colors the output with the color that `fn` returns for the event's level.                                   |
| `LogFormat#fixed`        | `final def fixed(size: Int): LogFormat`                          | Cuts the output to `size` characters, or pads it with spaces up to `size`. The output becomes plain text.   |
| `LogFormat#filter`       | `final def filter[M >: String](filter: LogFilter[M]): LogFormat` | Writes the output only when `filter` accepts the event.                                                     |
| `LogFormat#toLogger`     | `final def toLogger: ZLogger[String, String]`                    | Converts the format into a text logger that returns the formatted line.                                     |
| `LogFormat#toJsonLogger` | `final def toJsonLogger: ZLogger[String, String]`                | Converts the format into a logger that returns one JSON object per event.                                   |

The `LogFormat#fixed` method destroys structure. Use it only for plain text output, because it turns every part of the format into characters.

The `LogFormat#color` method and the `LogFormat#highlight` methods add ANSI escape codes. Terminals display them as colors, but log files show the raw codes unless the output goes to a console.

The following example builds a format from the building blocks and a logger name extractor:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogFormat, LoggerNameExtractor }

val customLine: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.bracketed(LogFormat.level) |-| LoggerNameExtractor.trace.toLogFormat() |-| LogFormat.quoted(LogFormat.line)
```

The `LogFormat#fixed` method gives the level a column of seven characters, so lines line up when the level names differ in length:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogFormat

val levelColumn: LogFormat = LogFormat.level.fixed(7)
```

To color only the cause, and to show it only when the event has one, the example combines `LogFormat#color` and `LogFormat#filter`:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogColor, LogFilter, LogFormat }

val errorDetails: LogFormat =
  (LogFormat.space + LogFormat.label("cause", LogFormat.cause).color(LogColor.RED)).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)
```

### Timestamps

Two members write the current time at the moment the line is built. The time does not come from the event itself.

| Member                | Signature                                                   | Description                                                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.timestamp` | `val timestamp: LogFormat`                                  | Writes the time in ISO offset date-time format, from `DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME`.                                                                 |
| `LogFormat.timestamp` | `def timestamp(formatter: => DateTimeFormatter): LogFormat` | Writes the time with the given `java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter`. `formatter` is evaluated once, when the format is built; the time is read for every line. |

The following example writes the time with a custom pattern:

```scala
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import zio.logging.LogFormat

val clockOnly: LogFormat = LogFormat.timestamp(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss"))
```

### Levels

Two members write the log level of the event. The level label comes from `zio.LogLevel`, so the warning level prints as `WARN`.

| Member                  | Signature                    | Description                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.level`       | `val level: LogFormat`       | Writes the level label, such as `INFO`.                                                                                                 |
| `LogFormat.levelSyslog` | `val levelSyslog: LogFormat` | Writes the syslog severity number of the level, such as `6` for INFO. FATAL is `2`, ERROR is `3`, WARN is `4`, DEBUG and TRACE are `7`. |

### Logger Name

Two members write the name of the logger that sent the event. The name comes from an extractor. The extractor members are listed in [LogFilter and LogGroup Reference](./reference-log-filter.md#loggernameextractor).

| Member                     | Signature                                                                                                       | Description                                                                                            |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `LogFormat.loggerName`     | `def loggerName(loggerNameExtractor: LoggerNameExtractor, loggerNameDefault: String = "zio-logger"): LogFormat` | Writes the name from `loggerNameExtractor`, or `loggerNameDefault` when the extractor returns nothing. |
| `LogFormat.enclosingClass` | `val enclosingClass: LogFormat`                                                                                 | Writes the source file name from the `Trace` of the log call, or `not-available` when no trace exists. |

`LoggerNameExtractor#toLogFormat` calls `LogFormat.loggerName` for you, so you rarely call `LogFormat.loggerName` with an extractor directly.

### Message and Trace

These members write the message text and the source position of the log call.

| Member                | Signature                  | Description                                                                                    |
| --------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.line`      | `val line: LogFormat`      | Writes the log message.                                                                        |
| `LogFormat.traceLine` | `val traceLine: LogFormat` | Writes the line number of the log call, from the `Trace`. Writes nothing when no trace exists. |
| `LogFormat.fiberId`   | `val fiberId: LogFormat`   | Writes the thread name of the fiber that logged the event.                                     |
| `LogFormat.cause`     | `val cause: LogFormat`     | Writes the cause of the event when it is not empty. Writes nothing otherwise.                  |

Use `LogFormat.cause` with `LogFormat#filter` and `LogFilter.causeNonEmpty` when the cause should appear only on failures. The Composing Formats section shows an example.

### Spans

Log spans measure how long a named block of work has run. These members write the elapsed time of each span as a key and value, such as `db=12ms`.

| Member            | Signature                           | Description                                                                     |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.spans` | `val spans: LogFormat`              | Writes every active span in the event.                                          |
| `LogFormat.span`  | `def span(name: String): LogFormat` | Writes the span with the label `name`. Writes nothing when no such span exists. |

### Annotations

Annotations are key and value pairs that the program attaches to log events. The string annotations come from the event itself. The typed annotations are stored in the logger context, which is described in [Logger Context and Annotations](./logger-context-and-annotations.md).

| Member                     | Signature                                                 | Description                                                                                                          |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.annotation`     | `def annotation(name: String): LogFormat`                 | Writes the string annotation with key `name`, if the event has it.                                                   |
| `LogFormat.annotation`     | `def annotation[A](ann: LogAnnotation[A]): LogFormat`     | Same as `LogFormat.logAnnotation`.                                                                                   |
| `LogFormat.logAnnotation`  | `def logAnnotation[A](ann: LogAnnotation[A]): LogFormat`  | Writes the value of a typed `LogAnnotation` from the logger context, rendered with the annotation's `render` method. |
| `LogFormat.anyAnnotation`  | `def anyAnnotation(name: String): LogFormat`              | Writes the string annotation `name` from the event. When the event lacks it, looks for `name` in the logger context. |
| `LogFormat.annotations`    | `val annotations: LogFormat`                              | Writes every string annotation on the event.                                                                         |
| `LogFormat.annotations`    | `def annotations(excludeKeys: Set[String]): LogFormat`    | Writes every string annotation on the event, except the keys in `excludeKeys`.                                       |
| `LogFormat.logAnnotations` | `val logAnnotations: LogFormat`                           | Writes every typed annotation in the logger context.                                                                 |
| `LogFormat.logAnnotations` | `def logAnnotations(excludeKeys: Set[String]): LogFormat` | Writes every typed annotation in the logger context, except the keys in `excludeKeys`.                               |
| `LogFormat.allAnnotations` | `val allAnnotations: LogFormat`                           | Writes the string annotations on the event and the entries in the logger context.                                    |
| `LogFormat.allAnnotations` | `def allAnnotations(excludeKeys: Set[String]): LogFormat` | Same as `LogFormat.allAnnotations`, except the keys in `excludeKeys` are skipped.                                    |

The annotation members differ in where they look, so choose by how the program sets the value:

| The program sets the value with                                                  | Use                                     | Key in the output       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `ZIO.logAnnotate("key", "value")` or `ZIOAspect.annotated` (a string annotation) | `LogFormat.annotation("key")`           | `key`                   |
| A typed `LogAnnotation`, such as `effect @@ LogAnnotation.UserId("u-1")`         | `LogFormat.logAnnotation(annotation)`   | the annotation's `name` |
| Either of the two, and the format should not care which                          | `LogFormat.anyAnnotation("key")`        | `key`                   |
| Many keys that you do not want to list one by one                                | `LogFormat.allAnnotations(excludeKeys)` | each annotation's key   |

`LogFormat.anyAnnotation` is what the `%kv{key}` element of a format string uses, and `LogFormat.allAnnotations` without the logger name is what `%kvs` uses. See [Log Annotations](reference-log-annotations.md) for the two kinds of annotation.

`LogFormat.allAnnotations` writes the string annotations first, then the logger context, and does not remove duplicate keys. When a string annotation and a `LogAnnotation` share a name, the key is written twice, which a JSON parser may reject or resolve by keeping only one of the values. Give the two kinds of annotation different names, or exclude one of them with `excludeKeys`.

The logger name travels as the string annotation whose key is `zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`, which holds the value `logger_name`. To write every annotation except the logger name, pass that key to `LogFormat.allAnnotations`:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogFormat

val withoutLoggerName: LogFormat = LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set(zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey))
```

### Presets and Configuration

Two presets give ready-made formats. The `LogFormat.config` value reads a format from a configuration file.

| Member              | Signature                       | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.default` | `val default: LogFormat`        | Writes labelled parts separated by spaces: `timestamp=` with the time in a 32-character column, `level=`, `thread=` with the fiber name, `message=` with the quoted message, and `cause=` only when the cause is not empty. |
