| `LogFormat.colored` | `val colored: LogFormat`        | Writes the same labelled parts as `default`. The timestamp is blue and the thread is white; the level, the message and the cause are colored by log level, as `LogFormat#highlight` does.                                   |
| `LogFormat.config`  | `val config: Config[LogFormat]` | Reads a format from a string in the configuration file, using the string form described in [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md#log-format-configuration).                                                  |

A line written with `LogFormat.default` looks like this:

```text
timestamp=2026-11-17T10:15:30.123456+01:00 level=INFO thread=zio-fiber-7 message="Order received"
```

:::caution[The default timestamp column is 32 characters]
`LogFormat.default` and `LogFormat.colored` write the timestamp with `LogFormat#fixed(32)`. When the JDK clock has more than microsecond precision, the ISO timestamp is longer than 32 characters and the end of the time-zone offset is cut, as in `2026-11-17T10:15:30.915147744+03`. Shorter timestamps are padded with spaces.
:::

To keep the full offset, build the same layout with `LogFormat.timestamp` and no fixed width:

```scala
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LogFormat }
import zio.logging.LogFormat._

val fullTimestamp: LogFormat =
  label("timestamp", timestamp(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME)) |-|
    label("level", level) |-|
    label("thread", fiberId) |-|
    label("message", quoted(line)) +
    (space + label("cause", cause)).filter(LogFilter.causeNonEmpty)
```

The console and file logger configurations read their `format` key through `LogFormat.config`. See [Configuration Keys Reference](./reference-configuration.md) for the keys.

### LogFormat.Pattern

`LogFormat.Pattern` is the parsed form of a format string. Each element of the string form, such as `%level` or `%label{name}{...}`, becomes one case of the sealed trait `Pattern`, and `Pattern#toLogFormat` turns the tree into a `LogFormat`. The elements are listed in [Log Format Configuration](./formatting-log-records.md#log-format-configuration), and the rules for escaping and labels in [Pattern Syntax Rules](./formatting-log-records.md#pattern-syntax-rules).

You rarely need `Pattern` directly, because `LogFormat.config` parses the string and converts it in one step. Use it when you want to validate a format string yourself, for example to report the parser error at startup, since `LogFormat.config` replaces the parser error with a generic message.

| Member                     | Signature                                                                 | Description                                                                                                                               |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogFormat.Pattern.parse`  | `def parse(pattern: String): Either[Parser.ParserError[String], Pattern]` | Parses the string form into a `Pattern` tree. `Parser` is `zio.parser.Parser`.                                                            |
| `LogFormat.Pattern.config` | `val config: Config[Pattern]`                                             | Reads a string from the configuration and parses it, without converting it to a `LogFormat`.                                              |
| `Pattern#toLogFormat`      | `def toLogFormat: LogFormat`                                              | Converts the pattern into the `LogFormat` it describes.                                                                                   |
| `Pattern#isDefinedFilter`  | `def isDefinedFilter: Option[LogFilter[Any]]`                             | The filter that a `%label` around this pattern applies. It is `LogFilter.causeNonEmpty` for `%cause`, and `None` for most other elements. |

The following example parses a format string and keeps the parser error, so that a startup check can print where the string is wrong:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogFormat

val parsed: Either[String, LogFormat] =
  LogFormat.Pattern
    .parse("%timestamp %level [%fiberId] %name:%line %message %cause")
    .left
    .map(error => s"Invalid log format: $error")
    .map(_.toLogFormat)
```

### LogColor

`LogColor` is an ANSI color for `LogFormat#color` and for the function given to `LogFormat#highlight`. Its constructor is private, so the values below are the only colors.

| Member             | Signature                      | Description                                                                                 |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogColor.RED`     | `val RED: LogColor`            | Red.                                                                                        |
| `LogColor.BLUE`    | `val BLUE: LogColor`           | Blue.                                                                                       |
| `LogColor.YELLOW`  | `val YELLOW: LogColor`         | Yellow.                                                                                     |
| `LogColor.CYAN`    | `val CYAN: LogColor`           | Cyan.                                                                                       |
| `LogColor.GREEN`   | `val GREEN: LogColor`          | Green.                                                                                      |
| `LogColor.MAGENTA` | `val MAGENTA: LogColor`        | Magenta.                                                                                    |
| `LogColor.WHITE`   | `val WHITE: LogColor`          | White.                                                                                      |
| `LogColor.RESET`   | `val RESET: LogColor`          | The reset code, which ends the current color. Use it for levels that should not be colored. |
| `LogColor.config`  | `val config: Config[LogColor]` | Reads a color name from a string, in any case, such as `red` or `RED`.                      |

`LogColor.config` accepts any case, but the `%color{...}` element of a format string accepts only upper-case names.

The default highlighter of `LogFormat#highlight` writes FATAL in white. The following highlighter gives FATAL its own color and leaves TRACE uncolored:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.{ LogColor, LogFormat }

val levelColors: LogLevel => LogColor = {
  case LogLevel.Fatal   => LogColor.MAGENTA
  case LogLevel.Error   => LogColor.RED
  case LogLevel.Warning => LogColor.YELLOW
  case LogLevel.Info    => LogColor.CYAN
  case LogLevel.Debug   => LogColor.GREEN
  case _                => LogColor.RESET
}

val coloredLevel: LogFormat = LogFormat.level.fixed(5).highlight(levelColors)
```

### Custom Formats With LogFormat.make

`LogFormat.make` creates a format from a function. The function receives the parts of the log event and writes into a builder. Only use it when no combinator above fits your output.

:::warning[Internal builder type]
The first argument of the function is a `LogAppender`. The type is internal to the library, so you cannot name it in your own code, and its methods can change between releases. The builder is an advanced interface for writing a custom backend. Use the combinators on this page for ordinary formats.
:::

Choose `LogFormat.make` over the combinators in two cases: when a value must be computed for every line from something the members above do not read, such as the clock in another unit or the name of the current thread, and when a value must be rendered differently from the members above, such as the level in lower case. For text that never changes, `LogFormat.text` is simpler. For anything the members above already write, combine those members instead.

The signature of `LogFormat.make` is:

```scala
def make(
  format: (
    LogAppender,
    Trace,
    FiberId,
    LogLevel,
    () => String,
    Cause[Any],
    FiberRefs,
    List[LogSpan],
    Map[String, String]
  ) => Any
): LogFormat
```

The following format writes the time as epoch milliseconds, which some log stores expect. The function runs for every line, so each line gets the current time. `LogFormat.text(System.currentTimeMillis().toString)` would instead repeat one fixed time, taken when the format is built, on every line:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogFormat

val epochMillis: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.make { (builder, _, _, _, _, _, _, _, _) =>
    builder.appendNumeric(java.lang.System.currentTimeMillis())
  }

val epochLine: LogFormat =
  LogFormat.label("ts", epochMillis) |-| LogFormat.label("level", LogFormat.level) |-| LogFormat.label("message", LogFormat.line)
```

Because the value is written with `LogAppender#appendNumeric`, the JSON loggers write `ts` as a JSON number, not as a string. For the string-based way to write output, and for a walkthrough of the builder, see [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md#creating-a-custom-logformat) and [How to Write a Custom Log Format](how-to-custom-log-format.md).

### LogAppender Methods

A `LogAppender` writes text, numbers, causes, and key and value pairs to a backend. It is advanced, and it exists to write a custom backend, such as a logging library adapter. The methods below are the operations that the builder exposes to the function given to `LogFormat.make`. They are not part of the stable public API. For a worked custom format, see [Creating a Custom LogFormat](./formatting-log-records.md#creating-a-custom-logformat).

| Method                                | Signature                                                                        | Description                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogAppender#appendText`              | `def appendText(text: String): Unit`                                             | Writes unstructured text.                                           |
| `LogAppender#appendNumeric`           | `def appendNumeric[A](numeric: A): Unit`                                         | Writes a number.                                                    |
| `LogAppender#appendCause`             | `def appendCause(cause: Cause[Any]): Unit`                                       | Writes a cause. Backends that know causes can keep their structure. |
| `LogAppender#appendKeyValue`          | `def appendKeyValue(key: String, value: String): Unit`                           | Writes one key and value pair.                                      |
| `LogAppender#appendKeyValue`          | `def appendKeyValue(key: String, appendValue: LogAppender => Unit): Unit`        | Writes one key, then lets `appendValue` write the value.            |
| `LogAppender#appendKeyValues`         | `def appendKeyValues(keyValues: Iterable[(String, String)]): Unit`               | Writes many pairs, with a separator between each pair.              |
| `LogAppender#appendKeyValueSeparator` | `def appendKeyValueSeparator(): Unit`                                            | Writes the separator between two pairs.                             |
| `LogAppender#openLogEntry`            | `def openLogEntry(): Unit`                                                       | Marks the start of one log entry.                                   |
| `LogAppender#closeLogEntry`           | `def closeLogEntry(): Unit`                                                      | Marks the end of one log entry.                                     |
| `LogAppender#openKey`                 | `def openKey(): Unit`                                                            | Marks the start of a key.                                           |
| `LogAppender#closeKeyOpenValue`       | `def closeKeyOpenValue(): Unit`                                                  | Marks the end of a key and the start of its value.                  |
| `LogAppender#closeValue`              | `def closeValue(): Unit`                                                         | Marks the end of a value.                                           |
| `LogAppender#withAppendText`          | `final def withAppendText(f: (String => Unit) => (String => Unit)): LogAppender` | Returns a new appender whose text output passes through `f`.        |

---

## Logger Layers and Constructors Reference

The `zio.logging` package object is where ZIO Logging's ready-made loggers live. It gives you three kinds of members: **layers** such as `zio.logging.consoleLogger`, which you put in your application's `bootstrap`; **constructors** such as `zio.logging.makeConsoleLogger`, which are ZIO effects that build a `ZLogger` without installing it; and **syntax** such as `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#install`, which turns a constructor into a layer. Two small logger classes, `FilteredLogger` and `MetricLogger`, are what the config forms of the file constructors and `zio.logging.makeMetricLogger` return.

All members below are public as `zio.logging.<name>`. In the source, the `private[logging]` traits `LoggerLayers`, `FileLoggerLayers` and `LoggingPackageAllPlatforms` define them and the package object mixes those traits in, so you never refer to those trait names in your code. The shape of the package object is:

```scala
package object logging {
  // layers, ready to use in bootstrap
  def consoleLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def consoleLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]
  // ... and the JSON, standard-error, file and metric variants

  // constructors, for composing your own layer
  def makeConsoleLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
  // ... and the other make* constructors

  // syntax
  implicit final class ZLoggerZIOLayerOps[RIn, +E, ROut <: ZLogger[String, Any]: Tag](self: ZIO[RIn, E, ROut])
  implicit final class ZLoggerOps[-Message, +Output](self: ZLogger[Message, Output])
}
```

Prefer the layers. Reach for a `make*` constructor when you need something a layer cannot express: two loggers with different filters, a logger that writes to your own `PrintStream`, or a logger wrapped by [`ReconfigurableLogger`](reconfigurable-logger.md).

### Installation

The console, metric and syntax members are in the core module, published for JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %%% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

Use `%%` instead of `%%%` in a JVM-only build. The file members exist on the JVM and Scala Native only; see [Platform Support](#platform-support).

### How They Work Together

Every layer on this page is built from the same steps. A layer such as `zio.logging.consoleLogger(config)` is literally `makeConsoleLogger(config).install`, so knowing the steps lets you build any variant yourself:

1. Pick a format and a filter. A `ConsoleLoggerConfig` or `FileLoggerConfig` carries both, or you use a `LogFormat` and a `LogFilter` directly.
2. Build the logger with a `make*` constructor. The result is a ZIO effect that produces a `ZLogger[String, Any]`. Constructors that take a config apply the config's filter for you; the multi-argument constructors do not.
3. Optionally call `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#filter` to wrap the logger in a `FilteredLogger`.
4. Call `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#install` (or `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#installUnscoped`, `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#installScoped`) to get a `ZLayer[..., Unit]`. Building that layer adds the logger to ZIO's set of loggers with `ZIO.withLoggerScoped`, and removes it again when the layer's scope closes.
5. Put the layer after `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` in `bootstrap`. Installing a logger only adds it; ZIO's default console logger keeps running until you remove it.

The data flow through these steps is:

```text
 ConsoleLoggerConfig / FileLoggerConfig            LogFormat#toLogger / #toJsonLogger
   (format + filter)                                  (ZLogger[String, String])
          │                                                     │
          ▼                                                     ▼
  make*Logger(config)                          make*Logger(..., logger, ...)
  filter applied                               no filter
          │                                                     │
          └──────────────► ZIO[R, E, ZLogger[String, Any]] ◄────┘
                                    │
                                    │  .filter(LogFilter)   ──► FilteredLogger
                                    │
                                    │  .install / .installUnscoped / .installScoped
                                    ▼
                          ZLayer[R', E, Unit]   ◄── consoleLogger, fileLogger, logMetrics, ...
                                    │                 are prebuilt layers of this shape
                                    ▼
             bootstrap = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> layer
```

### Platform Support

The file members live in source shared by the JVM and Scala Native builds only. Everything else is in source shared by all three platforms.

| Member                                                                                                                | JVM | JS  | Native |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- | ------ |
| `consoleLogger`, `consoleJsonLogger`, `consoleErrLogger`, `consoleErrJsonLogger`                                      | yes | yes | yes    |
| `makeConsoleLogger`, `makeConsoleJsonLogger`, `makeConsoleErrLogger`, `makeConsoleErrJsonLogger`                      | yes | yes | yes    |
| `makeSystemOutLogger`, `makeSystemErrLogger`, `makePrintStreamLogger`                                                 | yes | yes | yes    |
| `logMetrics`, `logMetricsWith`, `makeMetricLogger`, `MetricLogger`                                                    | yes | yes | yes    |
| `fileLogger`, `fileJsonLogger`, `fileAsyncLogger`, `fileAsyncJsonLogger`                                              | yes | no  | yes    |
| `makeFileLogger`, `makeFileJsonLogger`, `makeFileAsyncLogger`, `makeFileAsyncJsonLogger`                              | yes | no  | yes    |
| `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps` syntax, `ZLoggerOps#filter`, `FilteredLogger`                                                   | yes | yes | yes    |
| `loggerConfigPath`                                                                                                    | yes | yes | yes    |

### Reading Configuration

Every console and file layer comes in two overloads. One takes a config value and cannot fail. The other takes a config path, reads the config with `ConsoleLoggerConfig.load` or `FileLoggerConfig.load`, and fails with `Config.Error` when the config is missing or invalid.

The default path is `zio.logging.loggerConfigPath`, which is `NonEmptyChunk("logger")`:

```scala
package object logging {
  val loggerConfigPath: NonEmptyChunk[String]
}
```

`ConsoleLoggerConfig.load` and `FileLoggerConfig.load` call `ZIO.config`, so the values come from the `ConfigProvider` of the running effect. By default that provider reads environment variables and system properties; set another one with `Runtime.setConfigProvider` before the logger layer. To read a console logger from the default `logger` path and a second one from `app.audit`:

```scala
import zio.{ Config, ConfigProvider, NonEmptyChunk, Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ consoleErrJsonLogger, consoleLogger }

val provider: ConfigProvider =
  ConfigProvider.fromMap(
    Map(
      "logger/filter/rootLevel"    -> "INFO",
      "app/audit/filter/rootLevel" -> "WARN"
    ),
    "/"
  )

val loggers: ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
    Runtime.setConfigProvider(provider) >>>
    consoleLogger() >>>
    consoleErrJsonLogger(NonEmptyChunk("app", "audit"))
```

Every key under the path is listed in [Configuration Keys Reference](reference-configuration.md).

### Logger Layers

A logger layer has the type `ZLayer[Any, E, Unit]`: it needs nothing, outputs no service, and installs one logger while it is alive. Use it as, or as part of, your application's `bootstrap`.

#### Console Layers

The console layers write one formatted line per log event to standard output or standard error. The `Json` variants format with `LogFormat#toJsonLogger`, the others with `LogFormat#toLogger`:

```scala
package object logging {
  def consoleLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def consoleLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def consoleJsonLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def consoleJsonLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def consoleErrLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def consoleErrLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def consoleErrJsonLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def consoleErrJsonLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]
}
```

| Layer                  | Writes to         | Line format | When to use                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------- | ----------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `consoleLogger`        | `System.out`      | Text        | Local development and any environment where people read the output directly.                                |
| `consoleJsonLogger`    | `System.out`      | JSON        | Containers whose log collector parses JSON from standard output. See [JSON logs](how-to-json-logs.md).      |
| `consoleErrLogger`     | `System.err`      | Text        | Command-line tools that keep standard output for their real output, such as data piped to another program. |
| `consoleErrJsonLogger` | `System.err`      | JSON        | The same, when the collector reads standard error and expects JSON.                                         |

To send text logs to standard output and only errors, as JSON, to standard error, combine two layers built from config values:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat, consoleErrJsonLogger, consoleLogger }

val errorsOnly: ConsoleLoggerConfig =
  ConsoleLoggerConfig(LogFormat.default, LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(LogLevel.Error))

val bootstrap: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
    consoleLogger(ConsoleLoggerConfig.default) >>>
    consoleErrJsonLogger(errorsOnly)
```

More examples are on [Console Logger](console-logger.md).

#### File Layers

The file layers write to the file at `FileLoggerConfig#destination`, opened in append mode. They exist on the JVM and Scala Native only:

```scala
package object logging {
  def fileLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def fileLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def fileJsonLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def fileJsonLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def fileAsyncLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def fileAsyncLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]

  def fileAsyncJsonLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def fileAsyncJsonLogger(configPath: NonEmptyChunk[String] = loggerConfigPath): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]
}
```

| Layer                 | Line format | Who writes the file                                    | When to use                                                                     |
| --------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fileLogger`          | Text        | The thread that logs, during the `ZIO.log*` call       | Low log volume, or when every line must be on disk before the call returns.     |
| `fileJsonLogger`      | JSON        | The same                                               | The same, for files read by a log shipper that expects JSON.                    |
| `fileAsyncLogger`     | Text        | A background fiber that takes lines from a queue       | High log volume, where the logging fiber should not wait for disk I/O.          |
| `fileAsyncJsonLogger` | JSON        | The same                                               | The same, for JSON files.                                                       |

To write JSON lines to a file through the background writer:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ FileLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat, fileAsyncJsonLogger }

import java.nio.file.Paths

val config: FileLoggerConfig =
  FileLoggerConfig(
    destination = Paths.get("/var/log/my-app/app.log"),
    format = LogFormat.default,
    filter = LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default
  )

val bootstrap: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> fileAsyncJsonLogger(config)
```

:::caution[How file loggers behave today]
- The file is opened when the layer is built. When its directory does not exist, building the layer dies with a `FileNotFoundException`; it is not reported as a `Config.Error`.
- No file logger flushes or closes its writer when its layer's scope closes. With `autoFlushBatchSize` above `1` or a `bufferedIOSize`, lines still in the buffer at shutdown can be lost.
- The async loggers use a bounded queue of 1000 entries. When the queue is full, the thread that logs waits until there is room. When the layer's scope closes, the background fiber is interrupted, and lines still in the queue are not written.
:::

Rolling and the other file options are on [File Logger](file-logger.md) and [Rolling Log Files](how-to-file-logging-rotation.md).

#### Metric Layers

The metric layers install a `MetricLogger`, which writes nothing and instead increments a counter for every log event, labelled with the event's level:

```scala
package object logging {
  val logMetrics: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
  def logMetricsWith(name: String, logLevelLabel: String): ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]
}
```

`zio.logging.logMetrics` counts into a counter named `zio_log_total` with the label name `level`. `zio.logging.logMetricsWith` uses your own counter name and label name, for example to match a naming convention in your metrics backend. Both count every event they receive, whatever the filters of your other loggers say. To keep the console logger and count log lines with custom names:

```scala
import zio.{ Config, Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, logMetricsWith }

val bootstrap: ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger() >>> logMetricsWith("app_log_lines_total", "severity")
```

See [Log Metrics](metrics.md) for exporting the counter.

### Logger Constructors

A constructor is a ZIO effect that builds a `ZLogger[String, Any]` without installing it. You rarely call one directly; it is the building block for the layers above. Use one when you need to change the logger before it is installed, such as adding a filter, writing to your own stream, or passing it to `ReconfigurableLogger.make`.

#### Console and Stream Constructors

These constructors write formatted lines with `PrintStream#println`. The `makeConsole*` constructors take a `ConsoleLoggerConfig` and apply its filter. The `makeSystem*` and `makePrintStreamLogger` constructors take a formatting logger, usually `LogFormat#toLogger` or `LogFormat#toJsonLogger`, and apply no filter:

```scala
package object logging {
  def makeConsoleLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
  def makeConsoleJsonLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
  def makeConsoleErrLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
  def makeConsoleErrJsonLogger(config: ConsoleLoggerConfig): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]

  def makeSystemOutLogger(logger: ZLogger[String, String]): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
  def makeSystemErrLogger(logger: ZLogger[String, String]): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
  def makePrintStreamLogger(logger: ZLogger[String, String], stream: PrintStream): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
}
```

`zio.logging.makeSystemOutLogger` and `zio.logging.makeSystemErrLogger` pass `System.out` and `System.err` to `zio.logging.makePrintStreamLogger`. The stream is read once, when the constructor is called, so a later `System.setOut` does not redirect a logger that already exists. Any exception from `PrintStream#println`, other than a `VirtualMachineError`, is ignored.

`zio.logging.makePrintStreamLogger` is the one to use when you want the lines somewhere you control. To capture formatted lines in memory, for example in a test:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.{ LogFormat, ZLoggerZIOLayerOps, makePrintStreamLogger }

import java.io.{ ByteArrayOutputStream, PrintStream }

val buffer: ByteArrayOutputStream = new ByteArrayOutputStream()

val captureLines: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
    makePrintStreamLogger(LogFormat.level.toLogger, new PrintStream(buffer, true)).install
```

After the program runs, `buffer.toString` holds one line per event, such as `INFO` and `WARN`.

#### File Constructors

The file constructors come in a config form, which applies the config's filter and returns a `FilteredLogger`, and a six-argument form, which applies no filter. The async forms need a `Scope`, because they fork the background writer fiber into it:

```scala
package object logging {
  def makeFileLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZIO[Any, Nothing, FilteredLogger[String, Any]]
  def makeFileJsonLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZIO[Any, Nothing, FilteredLogger[String, Any]]
  def makeFileAsyncLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZIO[Scope, Nothing, FilteredLogger[String, Any]]
  def makeFileAsyncJsonLogger(config: FileLoggerConfig): ZIO[Scope, Nothing, FilteredLogger[String, Any]]

  def makeFileLogger(
    destination: Path,
    logger: ZLogger[String, String],
    charset: Charset,
    autoFlushBatchSize: Int,
    bufferedIOSize: Option[Int],
    rollingPolicy: Option[FileLoggerConfig.FileRollingPolicy]
  ): ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]

  def makeFileAsyncLogger(
    destination: Path,
    logger: ZLogger[String, String],
    charset: Charset,
    autoFlushBatchSize: Int,
    bufferedIOSize: Option[Int],
    rollingPolicy: Option[FileLoggerConfig.FileRollingPolicy]
  ): ZIO[Scope, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]]
}
```

There is no six-argument form of `makeFileJsonLogger` or `makeFileAsyncJsonLogger`; pass `LogFormat#toJsonLogger` as `logger` to the six-argument `makeFileLogger` or `makeFileAsyncLogger` instead. The arguments mean the same as the `FileLoggerConfig` fields of the same names, listed in [Configuration Keys Reference](reference-configuration.md#file-logger-keys). The file is opened when the effect runs.

To build an unfiltered async file logger from a format, and install it so it lives as long as the layer:

```scala
import zio.ZLayer
import zio.logging.{ LogFormat, ZLoggerZIOLayerOps, makeFileAsyncLogger }

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets
import java.nio.file.Paths

val everything: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  makeFileAsyncLogger(
    destination = Paths.get("/var/log/my-app/debug.log"),
    logger = LogFormat.default.toLogger,
    charset = StandardCharsets.UTF_8,
    autoFlushBatchSize = 1,
    bufferedIOSize = None,
    rollingPolicy = None
  ).installUnscoped
```

#### Metric Constructor

`zio.logging.makeMetricLogger` builds a `MetricLogger` for any `Long` counter. `zio.logging.logMetrics` and `zio.logging.logMetricsWith` are this constructor followed by `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#install`:

```scala
package object logging {
  def makeMetricLogger(counter: Metric.Counter[Long], logLevelLabel: String): ZIO[Any, Nothing, MetricLogger]
}
```

Use it when you want to build the counter yourself, for example to add a fixed tag to it:

```scala
import zio.ZLayer
import zio.logging.{ ZLoggerZIOLayerOps, makeMetricLogger }
import zio.metrics.Metric

val counter: Metric.Counter[Long] = Metric.counter("log_events_total").tagged("service", "checkout")

val countLogs: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] = makeMetricLogger(counter, "level").install
```

### Installing and Filtering Loggers

The syntax that turns a constructor into a layer is the implicit class `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps`, defined in the `zio.logging` package object. It applies to any `ZIO[RIn, E, ROut]` whose result `ROut` is a `ZLogger[String, Any]`. When `ROut` is a type from `zio.logging`, such as `FilteredLogger`, Scala finds the syntax on its own; otherwise bring it into scope with `import zio.logging.ZLoggerZIOLayerOps` or `import zio.logging._`.

#### Choosing an Install Method

The three install methods differ only in what happens to the `Scope` that keeps the logger installed:

```scala
implicit final class ZLoggerZIOLayerOps[RIn, +E, ROut <: ZLogger[String, Any]: Tag](self: ZIO[RIn, E, ROut]) {
  def filter(filter: LogFilter[String]): ZIO[RIn, E, FilteredLogger[String, Any]]
  def install: ZLayer[RIn, E, Unit]
  def installUnscoped[RIn2](implicit ev: RIn2 with Scope =:= RIn): ZLayer[RIn2, E, Unit]
  def installScoped: ZLayer[Scope with RIn, E, Unit]
}
```

| Method                                | Use it when                                           | Effect                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#install`          | The constructor needs no `Scope` (`RIn` is `Any`)     | Builds a scoped layer. The logger is installed while the layer is alive and removed when the layer is released.                              |
| `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#installUnscoped`  | The constructor needs a `Scope`, such as `makeFileAsyncLogger` or `ReconfigurableLogger.make` | Same as `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#install`, and the layer's own scope satisfies the constructor's `Scope`, so the layer's input type drops it: `RIn2` is `RIn` without `Scope`. |
| `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#installScoped`    | You want the logger tied to a `Scope` that you provide | Builds a non-scoped layer that needs `Scope with RIn`. The logger stays installed until that outer scope closes, not when the layer is released. |

`ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#filter` wraps the produced logger in a `FilteredLogger`, which passes only the events the `LogFilter` accepts. Filtering before installing is how you give two loggers different levels. To keep every event at `INFO` and above on standard output, and also send `ERROR` and above to standard error in color:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, Runtime, ZIO, ZLayer, ZLogger }
import zio.logging.{
  ConsoleLoggerConfig,
  FilteredLogger,
  LogFilter,
  LogFormat,
  ZLoggerZIOLayerOps,
  makeConsoleLogger,
  makeSystemErrLogger
}

val stdout: ZIO[Any, Nothing, ZLogger[String, Any]] =
  makeConsoleLogger(ConsoleLoggerConfig.default)

val stderrErrors: ZIO[Any, Nothing, FilteredLogger[String, Any]] =
  makeSystemErrLogger(LogFormat.colored.toLogger).filter(LogFilter.logLevel(LogLevel.Error))

val bootstrap: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> stdout.install >>> stderrErrors.install
```

An error event goes to both loggers. An info event goes only to standard output, because the `FilteredLogger` around the second logger rejects it.

#### Filtering a Plain ZLogger

`ZLoggerOps#filter` does the same wrapping for a `ZLogger` value that is not inside a ZIO effect. `LogFilter#filter` is the same operation called from the filter's side:

```scala
implicit final class ZLoggerOps[-Message, +Output](self: ZLogger[Message, Output]) {
  def filter[M <: Message](filter: LogFilter[M]): ZLogger[M, Option[Output]]
}
```

The returned value is a `FilteredLogger`, typed as `ZLogger[M, Option[Output]]`. Its output is `None` for an event the filter rejects. This is useful for a logger you write yourself. To collect the messages of error events in memory, and install that logger with `ZIO.succeed` and `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#install`:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, ZIO, ZLayer, ZLogger }
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, LogFormat, ZLoggerOps, ZLoggerZIOLayerOps }

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue

val collected: ConcurrentLinkedQueue[String] = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue[String]()

val collector: ZLogger[String, Unit] =
  LogFormat.line.toLogger.map { line => collected.add(line); () }

val errorsOnly: ZLogger[String, Option[Unit]] =
  collector.filter(LogFilter.logLevel(LogLevel.Error))

val collectErrors: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit] = ZIO.succeed(errorsOnly).install
```

### FilteredLogger

`FilteredLogger` is a `ZLogger` that runs a `LogFilter` before delegating to another logger. It is what `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps#filter`, `ZLoggerOps#filter`, `LogFilter#filter` and the config forms of the file constructors return:

```scala
final case class FilteredLogger[Message, Output](logger: ZLogger[Message, Output], filter: LogFilter[Message])
    extends ZLogger[Message, Option[Output]] {
  def withFilter(newFilter: LogFilter[Message]): FilteredLogger[Message, Output]
}
```

For each event, it calls `FilteredLogger#filter` with the event's trace, fiber id, level, message, cause, fiber refs, spans and annotations. When the filter accepts the event, it calls `FilteredLogger#logger` and returns `Some` of its output; otherwise it returns `None` and the inner logger never sees the event. `FilteredLogger#withFilter` returns a copy with the same inner logger and a different filter. The filters themselves are described in [LogFilter and LogGroup Reference](reference-log-filter.md).

### MetricLogger

`MetricLogger` is a `ZLogger[String, Unit]` that increments a counter by one for every event it receives. It is what `zio.logging.makeMetricLogger`, `zio.logging.logMetrics` and `zio.logging.logMetricsWith` install:

```scala
final case class MetricLogger(counter: Metric.Counter[Long], logLevelLabel: String) extends ZLogger[String, Unit]
```

Each increment carries the label `logLevelLabel` with the event's level label in lower case, such as `info`, `warn` or `off`, plus every metric tag set on the logging fiber with `ZIOAspect.tagged`. It never reads the message, so it does not format anything and costs one counter update per event.

## SLF4J v1 bridge

Many third-party Java libraries log through [SLF4J](https://www.slf4j.org/). The `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge` module is an SLF4J v1 binding (for `slf4j-api` 1.7.x) that forwards those log calls to the ZIO loggers, so library logs get the same format, level filter and destination as your ZIO logs. SLF4J 1.7 finds the binding through the class `org.slf4j.impl.StaticLoggerBinder`, which this module provides. The module requires Java 17 or later. If your build resolves `slf4j-api` 2.x, use the [SLF4J v2 bridge](slf4j2-bridge.md) instead.

To use the bridge, add the module to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j-bridge" % "2.5.5"
```

:::warning
Use either `zio-logging-slf4j`, which sends ZIO logs to an SLF4J provider such as Logback, or `zio-logging-slf4j-bridge`, which sends SLF4J logs to ZIO Logging. Enabling both makes every line go round in a loop.
:::

### Installing the Bridge

Install the bridge by adding one of the `Slf4jBridge` layers to the `bootstrap` layer of your application:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge

object BridgeApp extends zio.ZIOAppDefault {
  override val bootstrap: zio.ZLayer[zio.ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] = Slf4jBridge.init()

  override def run: zio.ZIO[Any, Any, zio.ExitCode] = zio.ZIO.logInfo("Program output").as(zio.ExitCode.success)
}
```

`Slf4jBridge` has three groups of entry points. The `Slf4jBridge.init` and `Slf4jBridge.initialize` layers are the usual choice. The `WithoutFiberRefPropagation` layers skip the per-fiber context described in [Fiber-Ref Propagation](#fiber-ref-propagation). The `Slf4jBridge.make` effects install the bridge from inside a running program, using the runtime of the fiber that runs them:

| Entry point                                          | Type                              | Filter                                    | Fiber-ref propagation |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `Slf4jBridge.init(configPath)`                       | `ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]` | from config, default path `logger.filter` | yes                   |
| `Slf4jBridge.init(filter)`                           | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | the given `LogFilter[Any]`                | yes                   |
| `Slf4jBridge.initialize`                             | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | none, every level is accepted             | yes                   |
| `Slf4jBridge.initWithoutFiberRefPropagation(filter)` | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | the given `LogFilter[Any]`                | no                    |
| `Slf4jBridge.initializeWithoutFiberRefPropagation`   | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | none, every level is accepted             | no                    |
| `Slf4jBridge.make(configPath)`                       | `ZIO[Any, Config.Error, Unit]`    | from config, default path `logger.filter` | no                    |
| `Slf4jBridge.make(filter)`                           | `ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit]`         | the given `LogFilter[Any]`                | no                    |

The default config path is also available as the value `Slf4jBridge.logFilterConfigPath`. When the config has no `rootLevel`, the root level is `INFO`. For the full API of every backend and bridge, see [Backends and Bridges](reference-integrations.md).

When the bridge's layer is built, it captures the current ZIO runtime, including the loggers installed at that moment. Every line that a Java library logs later goes to the loggers in that captured runtime, in particular lines from threads that do not run a ZIO fiber. The logger layer must therefore be built before the bridge layer. The `>>>` and `>+>` operators build their left side first, so put the logger on the left and the bridge on the right:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.consoleJsonLogger
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge

val logger = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> Slf4jBridge.init()
```

Install the bridge early in `bootstrap`. Until the bridge is initialized, it reports every level as disabled and discards every call, so lines that libraries log before that point, for example while another layer starts up, are lost without a warning.

### Filtering Bridged Logs

Java libraries often guard expensive log statements with checks such as [`org.slf4j.Logger#isDebugEnabled`](https://www.slf4j.org/api/org/slf4j/Logger.html#isDebugEnabled()) before they build the message and its arguments. The bridge answers those checks with its `LogFilter`, so a level that the filter rejects costs the library almost nothing. Without a filter (`Slf4jBridge.initialize`), every check answers `true`, and libraries build every `TRACE` and `DEBUG` message only for the ZIO loggers to drop it later.

#### What the Filter Can See

The bridge's filter runs inside `org.slf4j.Logger#isDebugEnabled` and its siblings, before the message exists. It receives only the level and one annotation, `logger_name`, which holds the SLF4J logger name; it receives no trace, message, cause, spans or fiber annotations. A filter that looks at fiber annotations or message text therefore never matches in the bridge. After the bridge accepts a line, the line still passes through the filter of each ZIO logger, such as the console logger's filter, and those filters see the complete record.

The SLF4J logger name is stored in the log annotation with key `logger_name` (`zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`). The following extractor reads the logger name from that annotation, or from the ZIO `Trace` when the annotation is missing, and turns it into a log format:

```scala
import zio.logging.LoggerNameExtractor

val loggerName       = LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace
val loggerNameFormat = loggerName.toLogFormat()
```

`LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig` uses the same extractor, so a filter built from it, or from config, applies its levels by SLF4J logger name.

#### Filter by Logger Name From Config

`Slf4jBridge.init()` reads the same keys as the `filter` block of the console and file loggers: `rootLevel` and a `mappings` table from logger-name prefix to level. Mapping keys contain dots, so quote them. The following HOCON keeps `INFO` and above, but only `WARN` and above for HikariCP and the Kafka client:

```hocon
logger {
  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO
    mappings {
      "com.zaxxer.hikari" = WARN
      "org.apache.kafka" = WARN
    }
  }
}
```

The bridge loads this block with `ZIO.config`, from the `ConfigProvider` of the runtime. To read it from `application.conf`, install `TypesafeConfigProvider` from `zio-config-typesafe` first. Because `consoleJsonLogger()` reads its filter from the same `logger.filter` block, one block sets the levels for both ZIO and library logs:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZIOAppArgs, ZLayer }
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.consoleJsonLogger
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge

val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
    Runtime.setConfigProvider(TypesafeConfigProvider.fromResourcePath()) >>>
    consoleJsonLogger() >+>
    Slf4jBridge.init()
```

See [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md) for how names match the mapping keys, and [Configuration Reference](reference-configuration.md) for every key.

### What the Bridge Keeps and Drops

The bridge turns each SLF4J call into one ZIO log record, but SLF4J and ZIO model a log call differently, so not everything carries over:

| SLF4J input                                | In the ZIO log record                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Message pattern and arguments              | The message, with `{}` placeholders filled in by SLF4J's `MessageFormatter`                       |
| `Throwable`, including a trailing argument | The cause, as `Cause.die(throwable)`                                                              |
| Logger name                                | The `logger_name` annotation, and an extra log span named after the logger                        |
| Level                                      | `TRACE` to `Trace`, `DEBUG` to `Debug`, `INFO` to `Info`, `WARN` to `Warning`, `ERROR` to `Error` |
| Markers                                    | Dropped; the filter cannot see them either                                                        |
| MDC values put by Java code                | Ignored; the bridge stores them but never reads them                                              |

The extra log span means that a format with `LogFormat.spans` prints the SLF4J logger name as a span label on every bridged line. SLF4J 1.7 has no key-value pairs; to attach structured values to library lines, annotate the calling fiber and rely on [fiber-ref propagation](#fiber-ref-propagation).

### Fiber-Ref Propagation

A Java library that runs inside a ZIO effect, for example a JDBC driver called in `ZIO.attempt`, logs on the thread of the calling fiber. Fiber-ref propagation lets the bridge read that fiber's state, so the library's lines carry the fiber's log annotations, such as a `LogAnnotation.TraceId` or a `ZIOAspect.annotated` value, and its log spans, just like the fiber's own lines.

The `Slf4jBridge.init` and `Slf4jBridge.initialize` layers turn this on by adding `Runtime.enableCurrentFiber`, which makes ZIO record in a thread-local which fiber is running on each thread. ZIO documents this runtime flag as having a performance cost, because the thread-local is updated every time a fiber starts or resumes running on a thread. When you do not need fiber annotations on library lines, use `Slf4jBridge.initializeWithoutFiberRefPropagation` or `Slf4jBridge.initWithoutFiberRefPropagation(filter)`: the lines are still logged, but they carry only the logger name, its span, and what was set in the runtime that the bridge captured. The `Slf4jBridge.make` effects never enable the flag themselves. Lines logged from threads that run no fiber, such as a library's own thread pool, never carry fiber annotations, whatever variant you choose.

### Conflicts With Other SLF4J Bindings

The bridge only works when it is the one SLF4J binding in use, and two situations break that:

- **Another v1 binding on the classpath**, such as `logback-classic` 1.2, `slf4j-simple` 1.7 or `log4j-slf4j-impl`. Each binding ships its own `org.slf4j.impl.StaticLoggerBinder`; SLF4J prints a "multiple bindings" warning and the JVM loads only one of them. If it loads the other binding's class, building the bridge layer fails with a `ClassCastException` defect. Remove the other binding from the runtime classpath.
- **`slf4j-api` 2.x on the classpath**, for example because another dependency evicts 1.7.x. SLF4J 2 no longer looks for `StaticLoggerBinder`; it prints a warning that it ignores the binding and falls back to a no-operation logger. The bridge layer still builds, but library logs never reach it. Use the [SLF4J v2 bridge](slf4j2-bridge.md) in that case.

For the overall setup, including the `java.util.logging` bridge, see [How to Send Java Library Logs Through ZIO Logging](how-to-bridge-java-logs.md).

### Examples

The following example shows the bridge in a complete application.

#### SLF4J Bridge with JSON Console Logger

The following application logs through an SLF4J logger and a ZIO logger. The SLF4J logger name and the ZIO logger name appear in the JSON output, filtered by level:

```scala
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LogFilter, LogFormat, LoggerNameExtractor, consoleJsonLogger }
import zio.{ ExitCode, LogLevel, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }

import java.util.UUID

object Slf4jBridgeExampleApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val slf4jLogger = org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger("SLF4J-LOGGER")

  private val logFilterConfig = LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(
    LogLevel.Info,
    "zio.logging.slf4j" -> LogLevel.Debug,
    "SLF4J-LOGGER"      -> LogLevel.Warning
  )

  private val logFormat = LogFormat.label(
    "name",
    LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace.toLogFormat()
  ) + LogFormat.logAnnotation(LogAnnotation.UserId) + LogFormat.logAnnotation(
    LogAnnotation.TraceId
  ) + LogFormat.default

  private val loggerConfig = ConsoleLoggerConfig(logFormat, logFilterConfig)

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger(loggerConfig) >+> Slf4jBridge.init(loggerConfig.toFilter)

  private val uuids = List.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID())

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Start")
      _ <- ZIO.foreachPar(uuids) { u =>
        ZIO.succeed(slf4jLogger.info("Test {}!", "INFO")) *> ZIO.succeed(
          slf4jLogger.warn("Test {}!", "WARNING")
        ) @@ LogAnnotation.UserId(
          u.toString
        )
      } @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(UUID.randomUUID())
      _ <- ZIO.logDebug("Done")
    } yield ExitCode.success

}
```

The `SLF4J-LOGGER` mapping drops the SLF4J `INFO` lines. The final `DEBUG` line, `Done`, is not written either: the application's logger name, `zio.logging.example.Slf4jBridgeExampleApp`, does not match the `zio.logging.slf4j` mapping, so the root level `INFO` applies. Expected console output:

```
{"name":"zio.logging.example.Slf4jBridgeExampleApp","timestamp":"2024-02-16T08:10:45.373807+01:00","level":"INFO","thread":"zio-fiber-6","message":"Start"}
{"name":"SLF4J-LOGGER","user_id":"d13f90ad-6b0a-45fd-bf94-1db7a0d8c0b7","trace_id":"561300a9-e6f1-4f61-8dcc-dfef476dab20","timestamp":"2024-02-16T08:10:45.421448+01:00","level":"WARN","thread":"zio-fiber-10","message":"Test WARNING!"}
{"name":"SLF4J-LOGGER","user_id":"0f28521f-ac8f-4d8e-beeb-13c85c90c041","trace_id":"561300a9-e6f1-4f61-8dcc-dfef476dab20","timestamp":"2024-02-16T08:10:45.421461+01:00","level":"WARN","thread":"zio-fiber-9","message":"Test WARNING!"}
```

### Feature Changes

The following changes affect the logger name annotation of this bridge.

#### Version 2.1.9

SLF4J logger name is stored in log annotation with key `logger_name` (`zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`).
In previous versions, the logger name was stored in log annotation with key `slf4j_logger_name`.
`Slf4jBridge.initialize` takes no arguments, so no annotation key needs to be passed when setting it up.

The following log format gets the logger name from the log annotation with key `logger_name`, or from the ZIO `Trace` if that annotation is absent:

```scala
import zio.logging.LoggerNameExtractor

val loggerName       = LoggerNameExtractor.annotationOrTrace(zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey)
val loggerNameFormat = loggerName.toLogFormat()
```

This logger name extractor can also be used in a log filter, which applies log filtering by defined logger name and level:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.LogFilter
import zio.logging.LoggerNameExtractor

val loggerName = LoggerNameExtractor.annotationOrTrace(zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey)

val logFilter: LogFilter[String] = LogFilter.logLevelByGroup(
  LogLevel.Info,
  loggerName.toLogGroup(),
  "zio.logging.slf4j" -> LogLevel.Debug,
  "SLF4J-LOGGER"      -> LogLevel.Warning
)
```

#### Version 2.2.0

The deprecated log annotation with key `slf4j_logger_name` was removed.
The common log annotation with key `logger_name` (`zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`) is now the only supported annotation for the logger name.

---

## SLF4J v1

[SLF4J](https://www.slf4j.org/) (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is the common logging API of the Java ecosystem; frameworks such as Logback and Log4j 2 implement it as providers. The `zio-logging-slf4j` module is a backend for SLF4J v1: it sends every ZIO log line to the `slf4j-api` 1.7.x API, and the SLF4J provider on the classpath, for example Logback 1.2, writes it. The module requires Java 17 or later.

In order to use this logging backend, we need to add the following line to our build.sbt file:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j" % "2.5.5"
```

### Choosing SLF4J v1 or v2

ZIO Logging has two SLF4J backends, and both require Java 17 or later. They differ in the version of `slf4j-api` they are built against and in how they pass annotations to the provider. This v1 backend puts annotations into the [MDC](https://logback.qos.ch/manual/mdc.html) (Mapped Diagnostic Context, a per-thread map that the provider can print, for example with `%mdc` in Logback). The [v2 backend](slf4j2.md) passes them as [key-value pairs](https://www.slf4j.org/manual.html#fluent) of the SLF4J 2 API. Use v1 when your provider only supports `slf4j-api` 1.7.x, such as Logback 1.2; use v2 for Logback 1.3 or later and for Log4j 2 with `log4j-slf4j2-impl`. [How to Use ZIO Logging With Logback or Log4j 2](how-to-logback-log4j2.md) walks through both setups.

:::note[How the MDC is set]
For each line, this backend formats the annotations into a map, then, on the same thread and before the log call returns, it saves the thread's current MDC, replaces it with that map, calls the SLF4J logger, and restores the saved MDC. Fibers that log in parallel therefore never see each other's annotations. Two effects follow from this design. While a line with annotations is logged, the thread's existing MDC is replaced rather than merged, so MDC values that Java code put on that thread do not appear in the line. When a line has no annotations, the backend leaves the thread's MDC untouched, so any values that Java code left in the MDC of that worker thread appear in the line.
:::

### Installing the Backend

To replace the default ZIO loggers with the `SLF4J` logger, combine `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` with `SLF4J.slf4j` in a logger layer:

```scala
import zio.Runtime
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val logger = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j
```

With the default setup, each ZIO log line becomes one SLF4J call:

* The SLF4J logger name comes from the `logger_name` annotation when it is set, and otherwise from the `zio.Trace` of the log call; for example, the trace `zio.logging.example.Slf4jSimpleApp.run(Slf4jSimpleApp.scala:17)` gives the logger name `zio.logging.example.Slf4jSimpleApp`.
* All annotations, except the logger name and the marker name, are placed into the MDC.
* The cause, when there is one, is passed to SLF4J as a `Throwable`.

To set a custom logger name for a single effect, apply the `zio.logging.loggerName` aspect:

```scala
import zio.ZIO

ZIO.logInfo("Starting user operation") @@ zio.logging.loggerName("zio.logging.example.UserOperation")
```

To attach an SLF4J marker name to a single effect, apply the `SLF4J.logMarkerName` aspect:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

ZIO.logInfo("Confidential user operation") @@ SLF4J.logMarkerName("CONFIDENTIAL")
```

### Customizing the Backend

The no-argument `SLF4J.slf4j` layer is enough for most applications. The overloads below change what goes into each SLF4J call, and the last part of this section explains which levels are written. For the complete API, see [Backends and Bridges](reference-integrations.md).

#### Format, Logger Name and Cause

`SLF4J.slf4j(format)` replaces the default format, `SLF4J.logFormatDefault`, which is `LogFormat.allAnnotations` (without the logger name and marker name keys) followed by `LogFormat.line` and `LogFormat.cause`. The appender behind this backend routes each part of a format to a different place: text such as `LogFormat.line` builds the message, key-value parts such as `LogFormat.allAnnotations` and `LogFormat.spans` go into the MDC, and `LogFormat.cause` becomes the `Throwable`. See [Creating a Custom LogFormat](formatting-log-records.md#creating-a-custom-logformat) for how formats talk to an appender.

`SLF4J.slf4j(format, loggerName, causeToThrowable)` also takes two functions. The `loggerName` function turns the `Trace` into a logger name when no `logger_name` annotation is set; `SLF4J.getLoggerName(default)` builds the standard one, which falls back to `default` (`"zio-slf4j-logger"` when omitted) for traces it cannot parse. The `causeToThrowable` function turns a ZIO `Cause` into the `Throwable` that SLF4J receives; the default, `SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault`, wraps a non-empty cause in a `zio.FiberFailure`, so the provider prints the full ZIO cause.

The following layer adds every log span to the MDC, names lines whose trace cannot be parsed `billing-service`, and passes the original exception to SLF4J instead of a `FiberFailure`, so that Logback shows the exception's own class and stack trace:

```scala
import zio.{ Cause, Runtime }
import zio.logging.LogFormat
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val originalThrowable: Cause[Any] => Option[Throwable] =
  cause => cause.failureOption.collect { case t: Throwable => t }.orElse(cause.dieOption)

val billingLogger =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j(
    SLF4J.logFormatDefault + LogFormat.spans,
    SLF4J.getLoggerName("billing-service"),
    originalThrowable
  )
```

With this function, a cause that holds only an interruption, or a failure that is not a `Throwable`, reaches SLF4J without a `Throwable`.

#### Composing the Logger

`SLF4J.slf4j` returns a layer, so it cannot be combined with other logger operators. `SLF4J.slf4jLogger(format, loggerName, causeToThrowable)` returns the underlying `ZLogger[String, Unit]` instead. Use it when you want to wrap the SLF4J logger before installing it, for example to drop ZIO lines with a ZIO `LogFilter` before they are formatted and handed to SLF4J. The following logger keeps `INFO` and above, and only `WARN` and above for the `com.example.db` package:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, Runtime }
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, ZLoggerOps }
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val slf4jLogger =
  SLF4J.slf4jLogger(SLF4J.logFormatDefault, SLF4J.getLoggerName(), SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault)

val filteredLogger =
  slf4jLogger.filter(LogFilter.logLevelByName[String](LogLevel.Info, "com.example.db" -> LogLevel.Warning))

val filteredLayer = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> Runtime.addLogger(filteredLogger)
```

#### Which Levels Are Written

This backend applies no ZIO `LogFilter` of its own. For each line, it asks the SLF4J logger whether the level is enabled (`isInfoEnabled`, `isDebugEnabled` and so on, with the marker when one is set), so the provider's configuration, such as `logback.xml`, decides which levels are written. A ZIO `LogFilter` runs only if you add one, as in the previous example. ZIO levels map to SLF4J levels as follows:

| ZIO `LogLevel` | SLF4J level |
| -------------- | ----------- |
| `All`          | `TRACE`     |
| `Trace`        | `TRACE`     |
| `Debug`        | `DEBUG`     |
| `Info`         | `INFO`      |
| `Warning`      | `WARN`      |
| `Error`        | `ERROR`     |
| `Fatal`        | `ERROR`     |
| `None`         | not logged  |

### Examples

You can find the source code [here](https://github.com/zio/zio-logging/tree/master/examples)

#### SLF4J Logger Name and Annotations

The following application logs from two concurrent user operations. It sets a logger name and a log marker name with aspects, and it adds a `user` annotation and a trace ID:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J
import zio.{ ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZIOAspect, ZLayer, _ }

import java.util.UUID

object Slf4jSimpleApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j

  private val users = List.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID())

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Start")
      traceId <- ZIO.succeed(UUID.randomUUID())
      _       <- ZIO.foreachPar(users) { uId =>
        {
          ZIO.logInfo("Starting user operation") *>
            ZIO.logInfo("Confidential user operation") @@ SLF4J.logMarkerName("CONFIDENTIAL") *>
            ZIO.sleep(500.millis) *>
            ZIO.logInfo("Stopping user operation")
        } @@ ZIOAspect.annotated("user", uId.toString)
      } @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId) @@ zio.logging.loggerName("zio.logging.example.UserOperation")
      _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Done")
    } yield ExitCode.success

}
```

Logback configuration, which filters out logs with the `CONFIDENTIAL` marker:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<configuration>
    <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <layout class="ch.qos.logback.classic.PatternLayout">
            <Pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] [%mdc] %-5level %logger{36} %msg%n</Pattern>
        </layout>
    </appender>
    <turboFilter class="ch.qos.logback.classic.turbo.MarkerFilter">
        <Name>CONFIDENTIAL_FILTER</Name>
        <Marker>CONFIDENTIAL</Marker>
        <OnMatch>DENY</OnMatch>
    </turboFilter>
    <root level="debug">
        <appender-ref ref="STDOUT" />
    </root>
</configuration>
```

Expected Console Output:
```

12:16:22.024 [ZScheduler-Worker-12] [user=0e3bd69c-ee62-4096-82b2-593760d3fb19, trace_id=6e956bcf-d534-4c16-9402-fb6bca13c9ab] INFO  zio.logging.example.UserOperation Starting user operation
```

#### Custom Tracing Annotation

The following application has a custom aspect `currentTracingSpanAspect`, which takes the current span from a `Tracing` service and adds it to logs with a log annotation:

```scala
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J
import zio.{ ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZIOAspect, ZLayer, _ }

import java.util.UUID

trait Tracing {
  def getCurrentSpan(): UIO[String]
}

final class LiveTracing extends Tracing {
  override def getCurrentSpan(): UIO[String] = ZIO.succeed(UUID.randomUUID().toString)
}

object LiveTracing {
  val layer: ULayer[Tracing] = ZLayer.succeed(new LiveTracing)
}

object CustomTracingAnnotationApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private def currentTracingSpanAspect(key: String): ZIOAspect[Nothing, Tracing, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any] =
    new ZIOAspect[Nothing, Tracing, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any] {
      def apply[R <: Tracing, E, A](zio: ZIO[R, E, A])(implicit trace: Trace): ZIO[R, E, A] =
        ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Tracing] { tracing =>
          tracing.getCurrentSpan().flatMap { span =>
            ZIO.logAnnotate(key, span)(zio)
          }
        }
    }

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j

  private val users = List.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID())

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    (for {
      _ <- ZIO.foreachPar(users) { uId =>
        {
          ZIO.logInfo("Starting operation") *>
            ZIO.sleep(500.millis) *>
            ZIO.logInfo("Stopping operation")
        } @@ ZIOAspect.annotated("user", uId.toString)
      } @@ currentTracingSpanAspect("trace_id")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Done")
    } yield ExitCode.success).provide(LiveTracing.layer)

}
```

Expected Console Output:
```
15:53:20.145 [ZScheduler-Worker-9] [user=1abd8458-aefd-4780-88ec-cccd1310d4c8, trace_id=71436dd4-22d5-4e06-aaa7-f3ff7b108037] INFO  z.l.e.CustomTracingAnnotationApp Starting operation
15:53:20.145 [ZScheduler-Worker-13] [user=878689e0-da30-49f8-8923-ed915c00db9c, trace_id=71436dd4-22d5-4e06-aaa7-f3ff7b108037] INFO  z.l.e.CustomTracingAnnotationApp Starting operation
15:53:20.688 [ZScheduler-Worker-15] [user=1abd8458-aefd-4780-88ec-cccd1310d4c8, trace_id=71436dd4-22d5-4e06-aaa7-f3ff7b108037] INFO  z.l.e.CustomTracingAnnotationApp Stopping operation
```

### Feature Changes

The following changes affect the logger name annotation of this backend.

#### Version 2.2.0

The deprecated log annotation with key `slf4j_logger_name` was removed.
The common log annotation with key `logger_name` (`zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`) is now the only supported annotation for the logger name.
