## SLF4J v2 bridge

Many third-party Java libraries log through [SLF4J](https://www.slf4j.org/). The `zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge` module is an SLF4J provider for [SLF4J v2](https://www.slf4j.org/faq.html#changesInVersion200) (`slf4j-api` 2.x) that forwards those log calls to the ZIO loggers, so library logs get the same format, level filter and destination as your ZIO logs. The module requires Java 17 or later. It also ships a JPMS module descriptor, module `org.slf4j.zio`, which provides `org.slf4j.spi.SLF4JServiceProvider` with `zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.ZioSLF4JServiceProvider`.

To use the bridge, add the module to your build:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge" % "2.5.5"
```

:::warning
Use either `zio-logging-slf4j2`, which sends ZIO logs to an SLF4J provider such as Logback or Log4j 2, or `zio-logging-slf4j2-bridge`, which sends SLF4J logs to ZIO Logging. Enabling both makes every line go round in a loop.
:::

### Installing the Bridge

Install the bridge by adding one of the `Slf4jBridge` layers to the `bootstrap` layer of your application:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge

object BridgeApp extends zio.ZIOAppDefault {
  override val bootstrap: zio.ZLayer[zio.ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] = Slf4jBridge.init()

  override def run: zio.ZIO[Any, Any, zio.ExitCode] = zio.ZIO.logInfo("Program output").as(zio.ExitCode.success)
}
```

`Slf4jBridge` has three groups of entry points. The `Slf4jBridge.init` and `Slf4jBridge.initialize` layers are the usual choice. The `WithoutFiberRefPropagation` layers skip the per-fiber context described in [Fiber-Ref Propagation](#fiber-ref-propagation). The `Slf4jBridge.make` effects install the bridge from inside a running program, using the runtime of the fiber that runs them:

| Entry point                                          | Type                              | Filter                                    | Fiber-ref propagation |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `Slf4jBridge.init(configPath)`                       | `ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit]` | from config, default path `logger.filter` | yes                   |
| `Slf4jBridge.init(filter)`                           | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | the given `LogFilter[Any]`                | yes                   |
| `Slf4jBridge.initialize`                             | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | none, every level is accepted             | yes                   |
| `Slf4jBridge.initWithoutFiberRefPropagation(filter)` | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | the given `LogFilter[Any]`                | no                    |
| `Slf4jBridge.initializeWithoutFiberRefPropagation`   | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Unit]`      | none, every level is accepted             | no                    |
| `Slf4jBridge.make(configPath)`                       | `ZIO[Any, Config.Error, Unit]`    | from config, default path `logger.filter` | no                    |
| `Slf4jBridge.make(filter)`                           | `ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit]`         | the given `LogFilter[Any]`                | no                    |

The default config path is also available as the value `Slf4jBridge.logFilterConfigPath`. When the config has no `rootLevel`, the root level is `INFO`. For the full API of every backend and bridge, see [Backends and Bridges](reference-integrations.md).

When the bridge's layer is built, it captures the current ZIO runtime, including the loggers installed at that moment. Every line that a Java library logs later goes to the loggers in that captured runtime, in particular lines from threads that do not run a ZIO fiber. The logger layer must therefore be built before the bridge layer. The `>>>` and `>+>` operators build their left side first, so put the logger on the left and the bridge on the right:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZLayer }
import zio.logging.consoleJsonLogger
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge

val logger = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger() >+> Slf4jBridge.init()
```

Install the bridge early in `bootstrap`. Until the bridge is initialized, it reports every level as disabled and discards every call, so lines that libraries log before that point, for example while another layer starts up, are lost without a warning.

### Filtering Bridged Logs

Java libraries often guard expensive log statements with checks such as [`org.slf4j.Logger#isDebugEnabled`](https://www.slf4j.org/api/org/slf4j/Logger.html#isDebugEnabled()) before they build the message and its arguments. The bridge answers those checks with its `LogFilter`, so a level that the filter rejects costs the library almost nothing. Without a filter (`Slf4jBridge.initialize`), every check answers `true`, and libraries build every `TRACE` and `DEBUG` message only for the ZIO loggers to drop it later.

#### What the Filter Can See

The bridge's filter runs inside `org.slf4j.Logger#isDebugEnabled` and its siblings, before the message exists. It receives only the level and one annotation, `logger_name`, which holds the SLF4J logger name; it receives no trace, message, cause, spans or fiber annotations. A filter that looks at fiber annotations or message text therefore never matches in the bridge. After the bridge accepts a line, the line still passes through the filter of each ZIO logger, such as the console logger's filter, and those filters see the complete record.

The SLF4J logger name is stored in the log annotation with key `logger_name` (`zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey`). The following extractor reads the logger name from that annotation, or from the ZIO `Trace` when the annotation is missing, and turns it into a log format:

```scala
import zio.logging.LoggerNameExtractor

val loggerName       = LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace
val loggerNameFormat = loggerName.toLogFormat()
```

`LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig` uses the same extractor, so a filter built from it applies its levels by SLF4J logger name. The following filter keeps `INFO` and above by default, `DEBUG` for `zio.logging.slf4j`, and only `WARN` and above for the `SLF4J-LOGGER` logger:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.LogFilter

val logFilterConfig = LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(
  LogLevel.Info,
  "zio.logging.slf4j" -> LogLevel.Debug,
  "SLF4J-LOGGER"      -> LogLevel.Warning
)

val logFilter: LogFilter[String] = logFilterConfig.toFilter
```

#### Filter by Logger Name From Config

`Slf4jBridge.init()` reads the same keys as the `filter` block of the console and file loggers: `rootLevel` and a `mappings` table from logger-name prefix to level. Mapping keys contain dots, so quote them. The following HOCON keeps `INFO` and above, but only `WARN` and above for HikariCP and the Kafka client:

```hocon
logger {
  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO
    mappings {
      "com.zaxxer.hikari" = WARN
      "org.apache.kafka" = WARN
    }
  }
}
```

The bridge loads this block with `ZIO.config`, from the `ConfigProvider` of the runtime. To read it from `application.conf`, install `TypesafeConfigProvider` from `zio-config-typesafe` first. Because `consoleJsonLogger()` reads its filter from the same `logger.filter` block, one block sets the levels for both ZIO and library logs:

```scala
import zio.{ Runtime, ZIOAppArgs, ZLayer }
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.consoleJsonLogger
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge

val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
    Runtime.setConfigProvider(TypesafeConfigProvider.fromResourcePath()) >>>
    consoleJsonLogger() >+>
    Slf4jBridge.init()
```

See [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md) for how names match the mapping keys, and [Configuration Reference](reference-configuration.md) for every key.

### What the Bridge Keeps and Drops

The bridge turns each SLF4J call into one ZIO log record, but SLF4J and ZIO model a log call differently, so not everything carries over:

| SLF4J input                                         | In the ZIO log record                                                                             |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Message pattern and arguments                       | The message, with `{}` placeholders filled in by SLF4J's `MessageFormatter`                       |
| `Throwable`, including a trailing argument          | The cause, as `Cause.die(throwable)`                                                              |
| Logger name                                         | The `logger_name` annotation, and an extra log span named after the logger                        |
| Level                                               | `TRACE` to `Trace`, `DEBUG` to `Debug`, `INFO` to `Info`, `WARN` to `Warning`, `ERROR` to `Error` |
| Key-value pairs (`LoggingEventBuilder#addKeyValue`) | Log annotations, with each value converted with `toString`                                        |
| Markers                                             | Dropped; the filter cannot see them either                                                        |
| MDC values put by Java code                         | Ignored; the bridge stores them but never reads them                                              |

Key-value pairs from the SLF4J 2 fluent API, such as `logger.atInfo().addKeyValue("orderId", id).log("Order paid")`, become ordinary ZIO log annotations, so `LogFormat.allAnnotations` or a JSON logger prints them next to the fiber's own annotations. When a key-value pair and a fiber annotation share a key, the key-value pair wins, and the `logger_name` annotation always holds the SLF4J logger name. A `null` value is not supported: `addKeyValue("k", null)` throws a `NullPointerException` in the calling code.

The extra log span means that a format with `LogFormat.spans` prints the SLF4J logger name as a span label on every bridged line.

### Fiber-Ref Propagation

A Java library that runs inside a ZIO effect, for example a JDBC driver called in `ZIO.attempt`, logs on the thread of the calling fiber. Fiber-ref propagation lets the bridge read that fiber's state, so the library's lines carry the fiber's log annotations, such as a `LogAnnotation.TraceId` or a `ZIOAspect.annotated` value, and its log spans, just like the fiber's own lines.

The `Slf4jBridge.init` and `Slf4jBridge.initialize` layers turn this on by adding `Runtime.enableCurrentFiber`, which makes ZIO record in a thread-local which fiber is running on each thread. ZIO documents this runtime flag as having a performance cost, because the thread-local is updated every time a fiber starts or resumes running on a thread. When you do not need fiber annotations on library lines, use `Slf4jBridge.initializeWithoutFiberRefPropagation` or `Slf4jBridge.initWithoutFiberRefPropagation(filter)`: the lines are still logged, but they carry only the logger name, its span, and what was set in the runtime that the bridge captured. The `Slf4jBridge.make` effects never enable the flag themselves. Lines logged from threads that run no fiber, such as a library's own thread pool, never carry fiber annotations, whatever variant you choose.

### Conflicts With Other SLF4J Providers

SLF4J 2 uses exactly one provider. When another provider is also on the classpath, such as `logback-classic` 1.3 or later, `slf4j-simple` 2.x or `log4j-slf4j2-impl`, SLF4J prints a warning and picks one of them. If it picks the other provider, building the bridge layer fails with a `ClassCastException` defect, because the bridge expects its own logger factory. Remove the other provider from the runtime classpath; if you cannot, choose the bridge explicitly with the `slf4j.provider` system property (supported since SLF4J 2.0.9), for example `-Dslf4j.provider=zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.ZioSLF4JServiceProvider`.

For SLF4J v1 libraries on `slf4j-api` 1.7.x, use the [SLF4J v1 bridge](slf4j1-bridge.md) instead. For the overall setup, including the `java.util.logging` bridge, see [How to Send Java Library Logs Through ZIO Logging](how-to-bridge-java-logs.md).

### Examples

You can find the source code [here](https://github.com/zio/zio-logging/tree/master/examples)

#### SLF4J Bridge with JSON Console Logger

The following application logs through an SLF4J logger and a ZIO logger. The SLF4J logger name and the ZIO logger name appear in the JSON output, filtered by level:

```scala
import zio.logging.slf4j.bridge.Slf4jBridge
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LogFilter, LogFormat, LoggerNameExtractor, consoleJsonLogger }
import zio.{ ExitCode, LogLevel, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZLayer }

import java.util.UUID

object Slf4jBridgeExampleApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val slf4jLogger = org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger("SLF4J-LOGGER")

  private val logFilterConfig = LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(
    LogLevel.Info,
    "zio.logging.slf4j" -> LogLevel.Debug,
    "SLF4J-LOGGER"      -> LogLevel.Warning
  )

  private val logFormat = LogFormat.label(
    "name",
    LoggerNameExtractor.loggerNameAnnotationOrTrace.toLogFormat()
  ) + LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set(zio.logging.loggerNameAnnotationKey)) + LogFormat.default

  private val loggerConfig = ConsoleLoggerConfig(logFormat, logFilterConfig)

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger(loggerConfig) >+> Slf4jBridge.init(loggerConfig.toFilter)

  private val uuids = List.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID())

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Start")
      _ <- ZIO.foreachPar(uuids) { u =>
        ZIO.succeed(slf4jLogger.info("Test {}!", "INFO")) *> ZIO.succeed(
          slf4jLogger.atWarn().addArgument("WARNING").log("Test {}!")
        ) @@ LogAnnotation.UserId(
          u.toString
        )
      } @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(UUID.randomUUID())
      _ <- ZIO.logDebug("Done")
    } yield ExitCode.success

}
```

The `SLF4J-LOGGER` mapping drops the SLF4J `INFO` lines. The final `DEBUG` line, `Done`, is not written either: the application's logger name, `zio.logging.example.Slf4jBridgeExampleApp`, does not match the `zio.logging.slf4j` mapping, so the root level `INFO` applies. Expected console output:

```
{"name":"zio.logging.example.Slf4jBridgeExampleApp","timestamp":"2024-05-28T08:05:48.056029+02:00","level":"INFO","thread":"zio-fiber-735317063","message":"Start"}
{"name":"SLF4J-LOGGER","trace_id":"416f3886-717c-4359-9f6e-c260e49fd158","user_id":"580376aa-f851-43a2-8b17-9456ce005e93","timestamp":"2024-05-28T08:05:48.065133+02:00","level":"WARN","thread":"zio-fiber-1749629949","message":"Test WARNING!"}
{"name":"SLF4J-LOGGER","trace_id":"416f3886-717c-4359-9f6e-c260e49fd158","user_id":"76d49e0d-7c28-47fd-b5a1-d05afb487cfe","timestamp":"2024-05-28T08:05:48.065174+02:00","level":"WARN","thread":"zio-fiber-697454589","message":"Test WARNING!"}
```

## SLF4J v2

[SLF4J](https://www.slf4j.org/) (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is the common logging API of the Java ecosystem; frameworks such as Logback and Log4j 2 implement it as providers. The `zio-logging-slf4j2` module is a backend for SLF4J v2: it sends every ZIO log line to the `slf4j-api` 2.x API, and the SLF4J provider on the classpath, for example Logback 1.3 or later, or Log4j 2 with `log4j-slf4j2-impl`, writes it. The module requires Java 17 or later.

In order to use this logging backend, we need to add the following line to our build.sbt file:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging-slf4j2" % "2.5.5"
```

### Choosing SLF4J v1 or v2

ZIO Logging has two SLF4J backends, and both require Java 17 or later. They differ in the version of `slf4j-api` they are built against and in how they pass annotations to the provider. This v2 backend passes annotations as [key-value pairs](https://www.slf4j.org/manual.html#fluent) of the SLF4J 2 fluent API, which Logback prints with `%kvp`; it never touches the thread's MDC. The [v1 backend](slf4j1.md) puts annotations into the MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context, a per-thread map), which is the only option for providers that support only `slf4j-api` 1.7.x, such as Logback 1.2. Prefer v2 when your provider supports it. [How to Use ZIO Logging With Logback or Log4j 2](how-to-logback-log4j2.md) walks through both setups.

### Installing the Backend

To replace the default ZIO loggers with the `SLF4J` logger, combine `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` with `SLF4J.slf4j` in a logger layer:

```scala
import zio.Runtime
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val logger = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j
```

With the default setup, each ZIO log line becomes one SLF4J call:

* The SLF4J logger name comes from the `logger_name` annotation when it is set, and otherwise from the `zio.Trace` of the log call; for example, the trace `zio.logging.example.Slf4jSimpleApp.run(Slf4jSimpleApp.scala:17)` gives the logger name `zio.logging.example.Slf4jSimpleApp`.
* All annotations, except the logger name and the marker name, are passed as [key-value pairs](https://www.slf4j.org/manual.html#fluent).
* The cause, when there is one, is passed to SLF4J as a `Throwable`.

To set a custom logger name for a single effect, apply the `zio.logging.loggerName` aspect:

```scala
import zio.ZIO

ZIO.logInfo("Starting user operation") @@ zio.logging.loggerName("zio.logging.example.UserOperation")
```

To attach an SLF4J marker name to a single effect, apply the `SLF4J.logMarkerName` aspect:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

ZIO.logInfo("Confidential user operation") @@ SLF4J.logMarkerName("CONFIDENTIAL")
```

### Customizing the Backend

The no-argument `SLF4J.slf4j` layer is enough for most applications. The overloads below change what goes into each SLF4J call, and the last part of this section explains which levels are written. For the complete API, see [Backends and Bridges](reference-integrations.md).

#### Format, Logger Name and Cause

`SLF4J.slf4j(format)` replaces the default format, `SLF4J.logFormatDefault`, which is `LogFormat.allAnnotations` (without the logger name and marker name keys) followed by `LogFormat.line` and `LogFormat.cause`. The appender behind this backend routes each part of a format to a different place: text such as `LogFormat.line` builds the message, key-value parts such as `LogFormat.allAnnotations` and `LogFormat.spans` become SLF4J key-value pairs, and `LogFormat.cause` becomes the `Throwable`. See [Creating a Custom LogFormat](formatting-log-records.md#creating-a-custom-logformat) for how formats talk to an appender.

`SLF4J.slf4j(format, loggerName, causeToThrowable)` also takes two functions. The `loggerName` function turns the `Trace` into a logger name when no `logger_name` annotation is set; `SLF4J.getLoggerName(default)` builds the standard one, which falls back to `default` (`"zio-slf4j-logger"` when omitted) for traces it cannot parse. The `causeToThrowable` function turns a ZIO `Cause` into the `Throwable` that SLF4J receives; the default, `SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault`, wraps a non-empty cause in a `zio.FiberFailure`, so the provider prints the full ZIO cause.

The following layer adds every log span as a key-value pair, names lines whose trace cannot be parsed `billing-service`, and passes the original exception to SLF4J instead of a `FiberFailure`, so that Logback shows the exception's own class and stack trace:

```scala
import zio.{ Cause, Runtime }
import zio.logging.LogFormat
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val originalThrowable: Cause[Any] => Option[Throwable] =
  cause => cause.failureOption.collect { case t: Throwable => t }.orElse(cause.dieOption)

val billingLogger =
  Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j(
    SLF4J.logFormatDefault + LogFormat.spans,
    SLF4J.getLoggerName("billing-service"),
    originalThrowable
  )
```

With this function, a cause that holds only an interruption, or a failure that is not a `Throwable`, reaches SLF4J without a `Throwable`.

#### Composing the Logger

`SLF4J.slf4j` returns a layer, so it cannot be combined with other logger operators. `SLF4J.slf4jLogger(format, loggerName, causeToThrowable)` returns the underlying `ZLogger[String, Unit]` instead. Use it when you want to wrap the SLF4J logger before installing it, for example to drop ZIO lines with a ZIO `LogFilter` before they are formatted and handed to SLF4J. The following logger keeps `INFO` and above, and only `WARN` and above for the `com.example.db` package:

```scala
import zio.{ LogLevel, Runtime }
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, ZLoggerOps }
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J

val slf4jLogger =
  SLF4J.slf4jLogger(SLF4J.logFormatDefault, SLF4J.getLoggerName(), SLF4J.causeToThrowableDefault)

val filteredLogger =
  slf4jLogger.filter(LogFilter.logLevelByName[String](LogLevel.Info, "com.example.db" -> LogLevel.Warning))

val filteredLayer = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> Runtime.addLogger(filteredLogger)
```

#### Which Levels Are Written

This backend applies no ZIO `LogFilter` of its own. For each line, it asks the SLF4J logger whether the level is enabled (`isInfoEnabled`, `isDebugEnabled` and so on, with the marker when one is set), so the provider's configuration, such as `logback.xml` or `log4j2.xml`, decides which levels are written. A ZIO `LogFilter` runs only if you add one, as in the previous example. ZIO levels map to SLF4J levels as follows:

| ZIO `LogLevel` | SLF4J level |
| -------------- | ----------- |
| `All`          | `TRACE`     |
| `Trace`        | `TRACE`     |
| `Debug`        | `DEBUG`     |
| `Info`         | `INFO`      |
| `Warning`      | `WARN`      |
| `Error`        | `ERROR`     |
| `Fatal`        | `ERROR`     |
| `None`         | not logged  |

### Examples

You can find the source code [here](https://github.com/zio/zio-logging/tree/master/examples)

#### SLF4J Logger Name and Annotations

The following application logs from two concurrent user operations. It sets a logger name and a log marker name with aspects, and it adds a `user` annotation and a trace ID:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation
import zio.logging.backend.SLF4J
import zio.{ ExitCode, Runtime, Scope, ZIO, ZIOAppArgs, ZIOAppDefault, ZIOAspect, ZLayer, _ }

import java.util.UUID

object Slf4jSimpleApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] = Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> SLF4J.slf4j

  private val users = List.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID())

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Start")
      traceId <- ZIO.succeed(UUID.randomUUID())
      _       <- ZIO.foreachPar(users) { uId =>
        {
          ZIO.logInfo("Starting user operation") *>
            ZIO.logInfo("Confidential user operation") @@ SLF4J.logMarkerName("CONFIDENTIAL") *>
            ZIO.sleep(500.millis) *>
            ZIO.logInfo("Stopping user operation")
        } @@ ZIOAspect.annotated("user", uId.toString)
      } @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId) @@ zio.logging.loggerName("zio.logging.example.UserOperation")
      _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Done")
    } yield ExitCode.success

}
```

Logback configuration, which filters out logs with the `CONFIDENTIAL` marker:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<configuration>
    <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <layout class="ch.qos.logback.classic.PatternLayout">
            <Pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] [%kvp] %-5level %logger{36} %msg%n</Pattern>
        </layout>
    </appender>
    <turboFilter class="ch.qos.logback.classic.turbo.MarkerFilter">
        <Name>CONFIDENTIAL_FILTER</Name>
        <Marker>CONFIDENTIAL</Marker>
        <OnMatch>DENY</OnMatch>
    </turboFilter>
    <root level="debug">
        <appender-ref ref="STDOUT" />
    </root>
</configuration>
```

Expected Console Output:
```
12:13:17.495 [ZScheduler-Worker-8] [] INFO  zio.logging.example.Slf4jSimpleApp Start
12:13:17.601 [ZScheduler-Worker-11] [trace_id="7826dd28-7e37-4b54-b84d-05399bb6cbeb" user="7b6a1af5-bad2-4846-aa49-138d31b40a24"] INFO  zio.logging.example.UserOperation Starting user operation
12:13:17.601 [ZScheduler-Worker-10] [trace_id="7826dd28-7e37-4b54-b84d-05399bb6cbeb" user="4df9cdbc-e770-4bc9-b884-756e671a6435"] INFO  zio.logging.example.UserOperation Starting user operation
12:13:18.167 [ZScheduler-Worker-13] [trace_id="7826dd28-7e37-4b54-b84d-05399bb6cbeb" user="7b6a1af5-bad2-4846-aa49-138d31b40a24"] INFO  zio.logging.example.UserOperation Stopping user operation
12:13:18.167 [ZScheduler-Worker-15] [trace_id="7826dd28-7e37-4b54-b84d-05399bb6cbeb" user="4df9cdbc-e770-4bc9-b884-756e671a6435"] INFO  zio.logging.example.UserOperation Stopping user operation
12:13:18.173 [ZScheduler-Worker-13] [] INFO  zio.logging.example.Slf4jSimpleApp Done
```

## Testing

Log lines are often part of what a program promises: an audit line for every payment, a warning when a retry gives up, a user id on every line of a request. ZIO Test records every log call a test makes, so a test can check what was logged as data, without reading the console. This page describes the parts involved: the recorded entries, the two kinds of annotations, rendering an entry with a format, testing a filter, and capturing the real console output. For a task-oriented walk-through, see [How to Test Log Output](how-to-test-log-output.md).

### Adding ZIO Test

The test logger is part of ZIO Test. Add `zio-test` and its sbt runner to the test scope of your build, with the same version as your ZIO dependency (`%%%` in a Scala.js or Scala Native project):

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-test"     % "2.1.27" % Test,
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-test-sbt" % "2.1.27" % Test
)
```

### Reading the Recorded Log Entries

ZIO Test installs a test logger, `zio.test.ZTestLogger`, around every test. It records each log call of the test, and `ZTestLogger.logOutput` returns the records so far, in the order they were made. No extra layer is needed: `ZTestLogger.logOutput` works in any test of a `ZIOSpecDefault`.

The test logger only adds itself to the loggers; it does not replace them. ZIO's default logger, and any logger the test installs, such as a ZIO Logging console logger, still run. Provide `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` to the test if you want to keep ZIO's default logger from printing to the console. The `ZTestLogger.default` layer adds one more test logger; a test that uses the logger ZIO Test installs does not need it.

`ZTestLogger.logOutput` returns a `UIO[Chunk[ZTestLogger.LogEntry]]`. Each `LogEntry` holds the same arguments that every `ZLogger` receives:

| Field         | Type                  | Content                                                                                                         |
| ------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `trace`       | `Trace`               | The source location of the log call. ZIO Logging derives the default logger name from it.                       |
| `fiberId`     | `FiberId`             | The fiber that logged.                                                                                          |
| `logLevel`    | `LogLevel`            | The level of the call, such as `LogLevel.Info`.                                                                 |
| `message`     | `() => String`        | The message. It is a function, so call it: `entry.message()`.                                                   |
| `cause`       | `Cause[Any]`          | The cause passed to the log call, or `Cause.empty`.                                                             |
| `context`     | `FiberRefs`           | The fiber refs of the logging fiber, including ZIO Logging's `logContext` with the typed log annotations.       |
| `spans`       | `List[LogSpan]`       | The active log spans.                                                                                           |
| `annotations` | `Map[String, String]` | ZIO's string annotations, set with `ZIO.logAnnotate`, `ZIOAspect.annotated` or ZIO Logging's `loggerName`.       |

`LogEntry#call(logger)` passes the entry's fields to any `ZLogger[String, A]` and returns its result, which is how an entry is [rendered with a log format](#rendering-an-entry-with-a-log-format).

The following spec runs an operation for two users and checks the message, the level, the trace id and the user annotation of each entry. Each `ZIO.logInfo` call produces one entry, `ZIOAspect.annotated` adds a string annotation, and `LogAnnotation.TraceId` sets a typed trace id for the wrapped effect:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogAnnotation, logContext }
import zio.test.Assertion._
import zio.test._
import zio.{ Chunk, LogLevel, Runtime, ZIO, ZIOAspect, _ }

import java.util.UUID

object LoggingSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] = suite("LoggingSpec")(
    test("start stop log output") {
      val users = Chunk.fill(2)(UUID.randomUUID())
      for {
        traceId      <- ZIO.succeed(UUID.randomUUID())
        _            <- ZIO.foreach(users) { uId =>
                          {
                            ZIO.logInfo("Starting operation") *> ZIO.sleep(500.millis) *> ZIO.logInfo("Stopping operation")
                          } @@ ZIOAspect.annotated("user", uId.toString)
                        } @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
        _            <- ZIO.logInfo("Done")
        loggerOutput <- ZTestLogger.logOutput
      } yield assertTrue(loggerOutput.size == 5) && assertTrue(
        loggerOutput.forall(_.logLevel == LogLevel.Info)
      ) && assert(loggerOutput.map(_.message()))(
        equalTo(
          Chunk(
            "Starting operation",
            "Stopping operation",
            "Starting operation",
            "Stopping operation",
            "Done"
          )
        )
      ) && assert(loggerOutput.map(_.context.get(logContext).flatMap(_.asMap.get(LogAnnotation.TraceId.name))))(
        equalTo(
          Chunk.fill(4)(Some(traceId.toString)) :+ None
        )
      ) && assert(loggerOutput.map(_.annotations.get("user")))(
        equalTo(users.flatMap(u => Chunk.fill(2)(Some(u.toString))) :+ None)
      )
    }
  ).provideLayer(Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers) @@ TestAspect.withLiveClock
}
```

A version of this spec is in the [example project](https://github.com/zio/zio-logging/tree/master/examples/core/shared/src/test/scala/zio/logging/example). It also provides `ZTestLogger.default`, which works but is not needed.

### String Annotations and Typed Log Annotations

A log entry carries annotations in two places, and a test has to look in the right one. ZIO's own string annotations, set with `ZIO.logAnnotate` or `ZIOAspect.annotated`, are in `entry.annotations`, a `Map[String, String]`. ZIO Logging's `loggerName` aspect also sets one of these, under the key `logger_name`.

ZIO Logging's typed annotations, the `LogAnnotation` values such as `LogAnnotation.UserId` and `LogAnnotation.TraceId`, are not in that map. They are stored in the `logContext` fiber ref, which the entry keeps in `entry.context`. `entry.context.get(logContext)` returns an `Option[LogContext]`; `LogContext#get(annotation)` returns the typed value, and `LogContext#asMap` returns every typed annotation rendered as a string. The [Log Annotations and LogContext Reference](reference-log-annotations.md) describes both kinds.

The following test sets one annotation of each kind and reads each one from its place:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ LogAnnotation, logContext }
import zio.test._

object AnnotationsSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    test("reads a string annotation and a typed annotation") {
      for {
        _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Payment accepted") @@
                     ZIOAspect.annotated("request_id", "req-7") @@
                     LogAnnotation.UserId("alice")
        entries <- ZTestLogger.logOutput
        entry    = entries.head
      } yield assertTrue(
        entry.annotations.get("request_id") == Some("req-7"),
        entry.annotations.get("user_id") == None,
        entry.context.get(logContext).flatMap(_.get(LogAnnotation.UserId)) == Some("alice")
      )
    }
}
```

The typed `user_id` annotation does not appear in `entry.annotations`, even though a format such as `LogFormat.allAnnotations` prints both kinds side by side.

### Rendering an Entry With a Log Format

Checking the fields of an entry tells you what was logged, but not what the line looks like. To test the line your application writes, render the entry with the same `LogFormat`: `LogFormat#toLogger` turns the format into a `ZLogger[String, String]`, and `LogEntry#call` runs it on the entry. This tests the format without a console or a file. See [Formatting Log Records](formatting-log-records.md) for the formats themselves:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.LogFormat
import zio.test._

object CheckoutFormatSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  val checkoutFormat: LogFormat =
    LogFormat.level |-| LogFormat.line |-| LogFormat.annotation("user")

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    test("the checkout line shows the level, the message and the user") {
      for {
        _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Payment accepted") @@ ZIOAspect.annotated("user", "alice")
        entries <- ZTestLogger.logOutput
      } yield assertTrue(entries.map(_.call(checkoutFormat.toLogger)) == Chunk("INFO Payment accepted user=alice"))
    }
}
```

Formats that write the time or the fiber id, such as `LogFormat.default`, produce a different line on each run. Compare such lines with a pattern, or test a format without those parts.

### Testing a Log Filter

The test logger records every log call, whatever the level. ZIO Logging filters, such as the `filter` settings of a console logger, belong to the logger they are attached to, and the test logger has none. A debug line that your console logger drops is therefore still in `ZTestLogger.logOutput`.

To test which lines a `LogFilter` keeps, apply the filter to the recorded entries. `LogFilter#apply` takes the same eight arguments as a logger and returns `true` when the line passes. The following spec checks a filter that keeps only warnings and errors from the database code:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ LogFilter, loggerName }
import zio.test._

object DbLogFilterSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  val dbFilter: LogFilter[String] =
    LogFilter.logLevelByName(LogLevel.Info, "com.example.db" -> LogLevel.Warning)

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    test("the db logger keeps only warnings and errors") {
      for {
        _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Query took 3 ms") @@ loggerName("com.example.db")
        _       <- ZIO.logWarning("Query took 2 s") @@ loggerName("com.example.db")
        _       <- ZIO.logInfo("Order placed") @@ loggerName("com.example.orders")
        entries <- ZTestLogger.logOutput
        kept     = entries.filter { e =>
                     dbFilter(e.trace, e.fiberId, e.logLevel, e.message, e.cause, e.context, e.spans, e.annotations)
                   }
      } yield assertTrue(
        entries.size == 3,
        kept.map(_.message()) == Chunk("Query took 2 s", "Order placed")
      )
    }
}
```

The `loggerName` aspect fixes the logger name, so the test does not depend on the file and package the test lives in. Without it, the filter would use the name derived from each entry's `trace`. The filter rules are described in [Log Filter](log-filter.md).

### Capturing Console Output

Sometimes the test must see exactly what the console logger prints, filter and format together. The console layers write to `System.out` or `System.err`, which a test cannot read easily. `zio.logging.makePrintStreamLogger(logger, stream)` builds the same kind of logger but writes to the `java.io.PrintStream` you pass. `makeConsoleLogger(config)` is `makePrintStreamLogger(config.format.toLogger, System.out)` with the config's filter added, so the following layer behaves like `consoleLogger` but writes into a buffer:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, ZLoggerZIOLayerOps, makePrintStreamLogger }
import zio.test._

import java.io.{ ByteArrayOutputStream, PrintStream }

object ConsoleOutputSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  def capturingConsoleLogger(stream: PrintStream): ZLayer[Any, Config.Error, Unit] =
    ConsoleLoggerConfig
      .load()
      .flatMap(config => makePrintStreamLogger(config.format.toLogger, stream).filter(config.toFilter))
      .install

  val testConfig: ConfigProvider =
    ConfigProvider.fromMap(
      Map(
        "logger/format"           -> "%level %message",
        "logger/filter/rootLevel" -> "INFO"
      ),
      "/"
    )

  override def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    test("the console logger drops debug lines and prints the rest") {
      val buffer = new ByteArrayOutputStream()
      val stream = new PrintStream(buffer, true, "UTF-8")

      for {
        _     <- (ZIO.logDebug("Cache miss") *> ZIO.logInfo("Order placed"))
                   .provideLayer(Runtime.setConfigProvider(testConfig) >>> capturingConsoleLogger(stream))
        lines <- ZIO.succeed(buffer.toString("UTF-8").linesIterator.toList)
      } yield assertTrue(lines == List("INFO Order placed"))
    }
}
```

The `filter` and `install` syntax on the `ZIO` value comes from `ZLoggerZIOLayerOps`, which the test imports; see [Logger Layers and Constructors Reference](reference-logger-layers.md).

The test also shows how to drive a logger from configuration. `ConfigProvider.fromMap` holds the keys the test needs, with `/` as the path separator, and `Runtime.setConfigProvider` makes them the source that `ConsoleLoggerConfig.load` reads. The keys are listed in [Configuration Keys Reference](reference-configuration.md). For a test that changes a value while it runs, such as a test of a [reconfigurable logger](reconfigurable-logger.md), set the values with `TestSystem.putProperty` and read them with `ConfigProvider.fromProps("/")`. That provider reads the properties through ZIO's `System` service, which ZIO Test replaces with `TestSystem`, and it reads them again on every load, so each reload sees the latest values.

---

## Tutorial: Logging for a Small Service

Welcome to the second ZIO Logging tutorial! In this tutorial, we add logging to a small order service, one step at a time, the way you would in a real application. This tutorial continues from the first one, [ZIO Logging Basics](tutorial.md). You should already know how to install a console logger in the `bootstrap` layer, how log levels work, how to attach an annotation with `@@`, and how to switch to `consoleJsonLogger`. If any of that is new, start with the first tutorial.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will understand:

- How to give each part of a service its own logger name, and why a name lets you set a level for that part only
- How to attach a trace id and a user id to every log line of one request
- How to move the log format and the levels out of the code into a HOCON config file
- How to send the same JSON log lines to the console and to a file, and how to count log lines with a metric
- How to write a test that checks what the service logged

We learn these concepts through the following steps:

1. Name the Components
2. Annotate Each Request
3. Move the Format and Levels to a Config File
4. Write JSON to a File as Well
5. Count Log Lines
6. Test the Log Output

We recommend reading from top to bottom. Each step adds one thing to the same service, and the service code from step 1 stays the same until the end.

### Background

A service handles many requests at once, and its log lines arrive mixed together. To make sense of them later, each line has to answer three questions: which part of the service wrote it, which request it belongs to, and how serious it is. ZIO Logging answers the first question with a **logger name**, the second with **log annotations** that you attach once per request, and the third with the log level. Once a line carries all three, you can filter it, search for it, ship it to a log store as JSON, count it, and assert on it in a test. The six steps below add these pieces in that order.

### 1. Name the Components

Our service has two components: `Orders`, which processes an order, and `Payments`, which charges for it. When a log line has no explicit name, ZIO Logging takes the name from the code location of the log call, which is the class or package. That name changes when you move or rename code. The `zio.logging.loggerName` aspect sets a stable name for every log call inside the effect it wraps.

We define the order model and the two components:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.loggerName

case class Order(id: String, userId: String, amount: BigDecimal)

object Payments {
  def charge(order: Order): UIO[Unit] =
    (for {
      _ <- ZIO.logDebug(s"Charging ${order.amount} for order ${order.id}")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo(s"Payment accepted for order ${order.id}")
    } yield ()) @@ loggerName("shop.payments")
}

object Orders {
  def processOrder(order: Order): UIO[Unit] =
    (for {
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo(s"Processing order ${order.id}")
      _ <- ZIO.logWarning(s"Large order ${order.id}: ${order.amount}").when(order.amount > 500)
      _ <- Payments.charge(order)
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo(s"Order ${order.id} completed")
    } yield ()) @@ loggerName("shop.orders")
}
```

The code above does the following:

- `Order` is a plain case class with an order id, a user id, and an amount.
- `Payments.charge` writes a `Debug` line and an `Info` line. The `@@ loggerName("shop.payments")` at the end names every log call inside the `for` block.
- `Orders.processOrder` writes an `Info` line, a `Warning` line when the amount is over 500, calls `Payments.charge`, and writes a final `Info` line. Its log calls are named `shop.orders`.
- `Payments.charge` runs inside `Orders.processOrder`, but its own `loggerName` replaces `shop.orders` while it runs. After it returns, the name is `shop.orders` again.

The `loggerName` aspect stores the name as a log annotation with the key `logger_name`. Next, we install a console logger that prints the annotations and sets a lower level for one name only:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat }

object ShopApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val config: ConsoleLoggerConfig =
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(
      LogFormat.default |-| LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set.empty[String]),
      LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(LogLevel.Info, "shop.payments" -> LogLevel.Debug)
    )

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger(config)

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    Orders.processOrder(Order("o-1", "u-42", BigDecimal(750))).as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

The code above does the following:

- `LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set.empty[String])` adds every annotation to the end of the line, so we can see the `logger_name` annotation.
- `LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(LogLevel.Info, "shop.payments" -> LogLevel.Debug)` keeps `Info` as the root level, and lowers the level to `Debug` for `shop.payments` and every name below it.
- `run` processes one order of 750, which is large enough to trigger the warning.

When you run the program, you see five lines. The timestamp and the fiber change on every run, so this is example output:

```text
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Processing order o-1" logger_name=shop.orders
timestamp=<time> level=WARN thread=<fiber> message="Large order o-1: 750" logger_name=shop.orders
timestamp=<time> level=DEBUG thread=<fiber> message="Charging 750 for order o-1" logger_name=shop.payments
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Payment accepted for order o-1" logger_name=shop.payments
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Order o-1 completed" logger_name=shop.orders
```

Notice that the `DEBUG` line from `shop.payments` is printed, while the root level is still `Info`. Try adding a `ZIO.logDebug` call to `Orders.processOrder`: it stays hidden, because `shop.orders` uses the root level. A name is what lets you turn up the detail for one component while the rest of the service stays quiet.

### 2. Annotate Each Request

The lines from step 1 tell us which component wrote them, but not which request. When two orders run at the same time, their lines interleave. We fix this by attaching a trace id and a user id to every line of one request. A **trace id** is a unique id for one request, so all its lines can be found with one search.

ZIO Logging has two predefined typed annotations for this. `LogAnnotation.TraceId` holds a `java.util.UUID`, and `LogAnnotation.UserId` holds a `String`. They are typed because the value keeps its Scala type until a logger renders it as text. We wrap the call to `Orders.processOrder` in a request handler:

```scala
import zio.logging.LogAnnotation

def handleRequest(order: Order): UIO[Unit] =
  for {
    traceId <- Random.nextUUID
    _       <- Orders.processOrder(order) @@
                 LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId) @@
                 LogAnnotation.UserId(order.userId)
  } yield ()
```

The code above does the following:

- `Random.nextUUID` creates a new UUID for this request. In a real HTTP service, you would usually read the trace id from a request header instead.
- `LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)` and `LogAnnotation.UserId(order.userId)` are aspects. With `@@`, they apply to every log call that runs inside `Orders.processOrder`, including the calls in `Payments.charge`.
- `Orders` and `Payments` do not change. The handler adds the request context from the outside.

To see the result, we change `run` in the step 1 program to call `handleRequest` instead of `Orders.processOrder`. The rest of the program stays the same:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat }

object ShopApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val config: ConsoleLoggerConfig =
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(
      LogFormat.default |-| LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set.empty[String]),
      LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(LogLevel.Info, "shop.payments" -> LogLevel.Debug)
    )

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger(config)

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    handleRequest(Order("o-1", "u-42", BigDecimal(750))).as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

Each line now ends with the logger name, the trace id, and the user id. `LogFormat.allAnnotations` writes the `logger_name` annotation first, followed by the typed annotations, whose order is not fixed. The first two lines look like this example output:

```text
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Processing order o-1" logger_name=shop.orders trace_id=<uuid> user_id=u-42
timestamp=<time> level=WARN thread=<fiber> message="Large order o-1: 750" logger_name=shop.orders trace_id=<uuid> user_id=u-42
```

All five lines of the request carry the same `trace_id`. A second request gets a new UUID, so the lines of the two requests can be told apart.

### 3. Move the Format and Levels to a Config File

So far, the format and the levels are Scala values. To change them, we have to rebuild the service. A config file lets operations staff change the levels without touching the code. We use HOCON, the config format of the Typesafe Config library, and the `zio-config-typesafe` module, which turns a HOCON file into a ZIO `ConfigProvider`. A `ConfigProvider` is the source that ZIO reads configuration values from.

We add the module to `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-config-typesafe" % "4.1.2"
```

Then we create the file `src/main/resources/application.conf`. The logger layers read their settings from the `logger` key:

```hocon
logger {
  format = "%label{timestamp}{%timestamp} %label{level}{%level} %label{logger}{%name} %label{message}{%message} %label{cause}{%cause} %kvs"
  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO
    mappings {
      "shop.payments" = DEBUG
    }
  }
}
```

The file does the following:

- `format` is a format pattern. Each `%label{key}{...}` becomes one JSON field named `key`. `%timestamp` is the time, `%level` the level, `%name` the logger name, `%message` the message, and `%cause` the error, if any.
- `%label{cause}{%cause}` is left out of a line that has no error, so successful lines stay short.
- `%kvs` writes every annotation as its own field, except `logger_name`, which `%name` already covers.
- `filter` holds the same levels as the `LogLevelByNameConfig` value from step 1. The mapping key is quoted because it contains a dot, which HOCON would otherwise read as nesting.

Now we load the file in the `bootstrap` layer and use `consoleJsonLogger()` with empty parentheses, which reads its configuration from the `logger` key:

```scala
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.consoleJsonLogger

object ShopApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
      Runtime.setConfigProvider(TypesafeConfigProvider.fromResourcePath()) >>>
      consoleJsonLogger()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    handleRequest(Order("o-1", "u-42", BigDecimal(750))).as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

The code above does the following:

- `TypesafeConfigProvider.fromResourcePath()` loads `application.conf` from the classpath.
- `Runtime.setConfigProvider(...)` makes it the config provider for the layers that come after it with `>>>`.
- `consoleJsonLogger()` reads `logger.format` and `logger.filter` from that provider and installs a console logger that prints JSON. If the file has an invalid value, the layer fails with a `Config.Error` when the application starts.

The program prints one JSON object per line. With the trace id shortened to `<uuid>`, the first two lines look like this example output:

```text
{"timestamp":"2026-11-17T10:15:02.104123+01:00","level":"INFO","logger":"shop.orders","message":"Processing order o-1","trace_id":"<uuid>","user_id":"u-42"}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-17T10:15:02.109481+01:00","level":"WARN","logger":"shop.orders","message":"Large order o-1: 750","trace_id":"<uuid>","user_id":"u-42"}
```

Try changing `"shop.payments" = DEBUG` to `INFO` in the file and run the program again. The `Charging 750 for order o-1` line disappears, and you did not change a line of Scala.

### 4. Write JSON to a File as Well

A container platform usually collects the console output, but you may also want a log file on disk, for example for a log shipper that reads files. The `fileJsonLogger` layer writes the same JSON lines to a file. It reads its configuration from the same `logger` key, and needs one more setting: the `path` of the file.

We add one line to the `logger` block in `application.conf`:

```hocon
logger {
  path = "file:///tmp/shop.log"
  format = "%label{timestamp}{%timestamp} %label{level}{%level} %label{logger}{%name} %label{message}{%message} %label{cause}{%cause} %kvs"
  filter {
    rootLevel = INFO
    mappings {
      "shop.payments" = DEBUG
    }
  }
}
```

The `path` is a `file:///` URI, not a plain file path. The console logger ignores the `path` key, so both loggers can share the format and the filter. Next, we install both loggers with `++`, which combines two layers into one:

```scala
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.{ consoleJsonLogger, fileJsonLogger }

object ShopApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
      Runtime.setConfigProvider(TypesafeConfigProvider.fromResourcePath()) >>>
      (consoleJsonLogger() ++ fileJsonLogger())

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    handleRequest(Order("o-1", "u-42", BigDecimal(750))).as(ExitCode.success)
}
```

The only change is `(consoleJsonLogger() ++ fileJsonLogger())` in the bootstrap. Every log call now goes to both loggers. Run the program, then open `/tmp/shop.log`: it holds the same JSON lines that the console shows. The file logger appends to the file, so each run adds five more lines.

:::caution
The directory of the file must exist before the application starts. If it is missing, the `fileJsonLogger()` layer fails at startup with a `FileNotFoundException` defect. The file logger is available on the JVM and Scala Native, not on Scala.js.
:::

### 5. Count Log Lines

A sudden rise in warnings or errors is often the first sign of trouble. The `logMetrics` layer counts every log call in a ZIO counter metric named `zio_log_total`, with a `level` label that holds the level in lower case, such as `warn`. A metrics backend such as Prometheus can then chart the count and alert on it.

The `logMetrics` layer installs a third logger next to the two from step 4:

```text
                         ┌──> console JSON logger (logger.filter) ──> standard output
ZIO.logInfo(...),        │
ZIO.logWarning(...), ... ┼──> file JSON logger    (logger.filter) ──> /tmp/shop.log
                         │
                         └──> metric logger       (no filter)     ──> zio_log_total{level="..."}
```

We add `logMetrics` to the bootstrap and read the counter at the end of `run`:

```scala
import zio.config.typesafe.TypesafeConfigProvider
import zio.logging.{ consoleJsonLogger, fileJsonLogger, logMetrics }
import zio.metrics.Metric

object ShopApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>>
      Runtime.setConfigProvider(TypesafeConfigProvider.fromResourcePath()) >>>
      (consoleJsonLogger() ++ fileJsonLogger() ++ logMetrics)

  private val warnings = Metric.counter("zio_log_total").tagged("level", "warn")

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _     <- handleRequest(Order("o-1", "u-42", BigDecimal(750)))
      _     <- handleRequest(Order("o-2", "u-7", BigDecimal(20)))
      state <- warnings.value
      _     <- Console.printLine(s"Warnings logged: ${state.count.toLong}")
    } yield ExitCode.success
}
```

The code above does the following:

- `logMetrics` installs a logger that adds one to `zio_log_total` for each log call. It writes nothing to the console or the file.
- `Metric.counter("zio_log_total").tagged("level", "warn")` refers to the same counter with the label `level` set to `warn`. ZIO identifies a metric by its name and labels, so this value reads the count that `logMetrics` updates.
- `warnings.value` returns the current state of the counter, and `state.count` is the number of calls as a `Double`.
- The first order is large and logs a warning. The second order is small and does not.

After the JSON lines of the two requests, the program prints this line:

```text
Warnings logged: 1
```

The metric logger has no filter, so it counts every log call, including calls that the console and file filters drop. To publish the counter to Prometheus, see [Log Metrics](metrics.md).

### 6. Test the Log Output

The warning for a large order is part of the service's behaviour: an alert depends on it, and the trace id is how an operator finds the rest of the request. We write a test so that a change to `Orders.processOrder` cannot drop the warning or its trace id without anyone noticing.

ZIO Test records every log call of a test in a test logger, `ZTestLogger`, and `ZTestLogger.logOutput` returns the recorded entries. We add ZIO Test to `build.sbt`, at the same version as your ZIO dependency:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-test"     % "2.1.27" % Test,
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-test-sbt" % "2.1.27" % Test
)
```

Then we write the spec in `src/test/scala`:

```scala
import zio.logging.{ LogAnnotation, logContext }
import zio.test._

object OrdersSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    suite("Orders")(
      test("a large order logs a warning with the trace id") {
        val order = Order("o-1", "u-42", BigDecimal(750))
        for {
          traceId <- Random.nextUUID
          _       <- Orders.processOrder(order) @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)
          output  <- ZTestLogger.logOutput
          warnings = output.filter(_.logLevel == LogLevel.Warning)
          traceIds = warnings.map(_.context.get(logContext).flatMap(_.get(LogAnnotation.TraceId)))
        } yield assertTrue(
          warnings.map(_.message()) == Chunk("Large order o-1: 750"),
          traceIds == Chunk(Some(traceId))
        )
      }
    )
}
```

The code above does the following:

- `Orders.processOrder(order) @@ LogAnnotation.TraceId(traceId)` runs the service with a trace id that the test knows, in the same way that `handleRequest` does.
- `ZTestLogger.logOutput` returns a `Chunk` of `LogEntry` values, one per log call in this test. We don't install anything: ZIO Test adds a fresh `ZTestLogger` around every test.
- `output.filter(_.logLevel == LogLevel.Warning)` keeps only the warnings. `message()` is a function call, because the message is computed only when a logger asks for it.
- `context.get(logContext)` reads the typed annotations of the entry as a `LogContext`, and `get(LogAnnotation.TraceId)` returns the trace id as a `UUID`, not as text.
- `assertTrue` checks that there is exactly one warning, with the expected message and the trace id of this test.

Run the test with `sbt test`. It passes. Now try changing the limit in `Orders.processOrder` from `500` to `1000`: the test fails, because the order of 750 no longer logs a warning.

:::note
`ZTestLogger` records every log call, including `Debug` calls that the console filter would hide. The test checks what the service logs, not what a configured logger prints. [How to Test Log Output](how-to-test-log-output.md) shows how to check the printed line too.
:::

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned:

- How to give each component a stable logger name with `loggerName`, and set a lower level for one name only
- How to attach `LogAnnotation.TraceId` and `LogAnnotation.UserId` to every line of a request with `@@`
- How to read the format and the levels from `application.conf` with `TypesafeConfigProvider` and `consoleJsonLogger()`
- How to send the same JSON lines to a file with `fileJsonLogger()`, and count log calls with `logMetrics`
- How to check in a test that a warning was logged with the right trace id, using `ZTestLogger.logOutput`

You now have the logging setup of a small production service. The next step is to adapt each piece to your own project.

### Next Steps

- **Add a trace id from a request header:** Read [How to Add a Correlation ID to Every Log Line](how-to-correlation-id.md).
- **Write more log tests:** Read [How to Test Log Output](how-to-test-log-output.md) to assert on annotations, logger names and the formatted line.
- **Tune the levels:** Read [How to Set Log Levels Per Package From Config](how-to-log-levels-from-config.md), and [How to Change Log Levels at Runtime](how-to-change-levels-at-runtime.md) to change them without a restart.
- **Rotate the log file:** Read [How to Log to a File With Rotation](how-to-file-logging-rotation.md).
- **Shape the JSON fields:** Read [How to Log JSON](how-to-json-logs.md) and the [Log Format Reference](reference-log-format.md).
- **Look up the APIs:** Read the [Log Annotations](reference-log-annotations.md), [Logger Layers](reference-logger-layers.md), and [Configuration](reference-configuration.md) reference pages, and [Log Metrics](metrics.md) for publishing the counter.

## Tutorial: ZIO Logging Basics

Welcome to the ZIO Logging tutorial! This tutorial is for developers who are new to ZIO Logging. You should know the basics of ZIO, such as effects (values of type `ZIO` that describe work to run), `for` comprehensions, and `ZIOAppDefault`. You don't need any experience with logging libraries.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will understand:

- How to add ZIO Logging to a project and install a console logger
- How the log levels `Debug`, `Info`, `Warning`, and `Error` affect what gets printed
- How to attach log annotations (extra key-value data) to a group of log messages
- How to switch the output from plain text to JSON

We learn these concepts through the following steps:

1. Add the Dependency
2. Print Your First Log Message
3. Choose a Log Level
4. Attach Log Annotations
5. Print JSON Output
6. Filter by Logger Name

We recommend reading from top to bottom. Each step changes the same program a little, so the steps build on each other.

Some terms come up often in this tutorial. A **logger** is the part of your program that writes messages to a destination, such as the terminal. A **fiber** is a lightweight thread that ZIO uses to run your effects. Every log line records the fiber that wrote it. A **bootstrap** is a layer that ZIO builds and runs before your main program starts. We use the bootstrap to install the logger. A **layer** (`ZLayer`) is a recipe that builds a service your program needs.

### 1. Add the Dependency

We start by adding the ZIO Logging library to an sbt project. Add this line to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

The line tells sbt to download the `zio-logging` library. The library depends on ZIO, so the same line also brings ZIO into your project.

This tutorial runs on the JVM. The core module is also published for Scala.js and Scala Native; in such a project, write `%%%` instead of `%%`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %%% "zio-logging" % "2.5.5"
```

### 2. Print Your First Log Message

We write a small program that logs two messages. The program uses `ZIO.logInfo` to write a message at the `Info` level. The `bootstrap` value installs the console logger before the program starts:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.consoleLogger

object TutorialApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger()

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Application started")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Application finished")
    } yield ExitCode.success
}
```

The code above does the following:

- `import zio.logging.consoleLogger` brings the console logger constructor into scope.
- `Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers` removes ZIO's built-in logger, so the console logger is the only logger that prints.
- `>>> consoleLogger()` chains the removal into a layer that installs the console logger. The empty parentheses use the default configuration.
- `ZIO.logInfo("Application started")` writes one log message at the `Info` level.

When you run this program, each `ZIO.logInfo` call prints one line. The shape of each line looks like this. The timestamp and the fiber name change on every run, so this is an illustrative shape, not exact output:

```text
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Application started"
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Application finished"
```

Each line has four parts: a timestamp, the level, the fiber, and the message. This layout is the default format, `LogFormat.default`.

### 3. Choose a Log Level

A log level tells you how serious a message is. ZIO Logging has four levels that you use most often:

- `ZIO.logDebug` writes detailed messages for developers.
- `ZIO.logInfo` writes normal progress messages.
- `ZIO.logWarning` writes messages about a problem that the program can recover from.
- `ZIO.logError` writes messages about a failure.

The console logger prints only messages at or above its root level. The default root level is `Info`, so `ZIO.logDebug` messages are hidden by default. To see them, we build a `ConsoleLoggerConfig` with a root level of `Debug`. We use `LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default` and change its root level with `withRootLevel`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat }

object TutorialApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val config: ConsoleLoggerConfig =
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(
      LogFormat.default,
      LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default.withRootLevel(LogLevel.Debug)
    )

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger(config)

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- ZIO.logDebug("Loading settings")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Application started")
      _ <- ZIO.logWarning("Cache is almost full")
      _ <- ZIO.logError("Payment service is unreachable")
    } yield ExitCode.success
}
```

The new `config` value replaces the empty parentheses from step 2. The `consoleLogger(config)` call accepts a `ConsoleLoggerConfig` directly. The four log calls cover all four levels. Because the root level is `Debug`, all four messages are printed. The output has one line per call, with the level changed on each line:

```text
timestamp=<time> level=DEBUG thread=<fiber> message="Loading settings"
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Application started"
timestamp=<time> level=WARN thread=<fiber> message="Cache is almost full"
timestamp=<time> level=ERROR thread=<fiber> message="Payment service is unreachable"
```

:::note
Set the root level to `Info` again and the `DEBUG` line disappears. The other three lines stay. The level is a threshold, not a switch for one message at a time.
:::

### 4. Attach Log Annotations

A log annotation is extra data that you attach to log messages. An annotation is a key and a value, such as `user_id` and `user-42`. Annotations are useful when many messages belong to one request, because each message carries the same context. We attach annotations with the `@@` operator. `LogAnnotation.UserId` is a built-in annotation for user ids. `ZIOAspect.annotated` creates an annotation from any string key and value.

The program below handles one request. Both messages inside `handleRequest` get the two annotations. The last message in `run` does not:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ consoleLogger, ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LogFilter, LogFormat }

object TutorialApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val config: ConsoleLoggerConfig =
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(
      LogFormat.default |-| LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set.empty[String]),
      LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default.withRootLevel(LogLevel.Debug)
    )

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleLogger(config)

  private def handleRequest(userId: String): UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.logInfo("Request received") *> ZIO.logInfo("Request finished")) @@
      LogAnnotation.UserId(userId) @@
      ZIOAspect.annotated("request_id", "req-7")

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- handleRequest("user-42")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Application finished")
    } yield ExitCode.success
}
```

The code above does the following:

- `LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set.empty[String])` adds the annotations to each line. The default format does not print them, so we append this format with `|-|`. The empty set means no annotation key is hidden.
- `handleRequest` uses `*>` to run two log calls one after the other. The `@@` operator then applies the annotations to that whole group.
- `LogAnnotation.UserId(userId)` attaches the user id. `ZIOAspect.annotated("request_id", "req-7")` attaches a request id.
- The last log call in `run` is outside `handleRequest`, so it has no annotations.

The output shows the annotations after the message on the lines from `handleRequest`. The spacing and the exact order of fields are illustrative. The rest of each line follows the step 3 pattern:

```text
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Request received" user_id=user-42 request_id=req-7
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Request finished" user_id=user-42 request_id=req-7
timestamp=<time> level=INFO thread=<fiber> message="Application finished"
```

Annotations stop at the end of the effect they wrap. This is why the last line has none.

### 5. Print JSON Output

Many log systems read JSON, a text format for structured data. Instead of `consoleLogger`, we use `consoleJsonLogger`. It takes the same `ConsoleLoggerConfig` and prints each line as a JSON object. We change only the bootstrap line and keep the rest of the program from step 4:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.logging.{ consoleJsonLogger, ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogAnnotation, LogFilter, LogFormat }

object TutorialApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  private val config: ConsoleLoggerConfig =
    ConsoleLoggerConfig(
      LogFormat.default |-| LogFormat.allAnnotations(Set.empty[String]),
      LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig.default.withRootLevel(LogLevel.Debug)
    )

  override val bootstrap: ZLayer[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Any] =
    Runtime.removeDefaultLoggers >>> consoleJsonLogger(config)

  private def handleRequest(userId: String): UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.logInfo("Request received") *> ZIO.logInfo("Request finished")) @@
      LogAnnotation.UserId(userId) @@
      ZIOAspect.annotated("request_id", "req-7")

  override def run: ZIO[Scope, Any, ExitCode] =
    for {
      _ <- handleRequest("user-42")
      _ <- ZIO.logInfo("Application finished")
    } yield ExitCode.success
}
```

The only change is `consoleJsonLogger(config)` in the bootstrap. Each log line is now one JSON object. The fields come from the same format as the text output. The exact key layout is illustrative, so the sample below shows only the shape:

```text
{"timestamp":"<time>","level":"INFO","thread":"<fiber>","message":"Request received","user_id":"user-42","request_id":"req-7"}
```

:::tip
JSON output works well with log collectors because each line is one complete record. If you need a different layout, change the `LogFormat` value. You don't need to change the logger.
:::

### 6. Filter by Logger Name

Each log line has a logger name. ZIO Logging takes the name from the code location, or you can set it with the `loggerName` aspect. A filter can then set a different level for each name. A name matches its own name and any name below it, with dots as separators. For example, `"payments" -> LogLevel.Debug` prints debug messages from `payments` and `payments.checkout`, while the root level still applies to every other name.

The snippet below sets the root level to `Info` and sets `payments` to `Debug`:

```scala
import zio.LogLevel
import zio.logging.{ ConsoleLoggerConfig, LogFilter, LogFormat }

val filteredConfig: ConsoleLoggerConfig =
  ConsoleLoggerConfig(
    LogFormat.default,
    LogFilter.LogLevelByNameConfig(LogLevel.Info, "payments" -> LogLevel.Debug)
  )
```

To learn the full set of filter options, read the [Log Filter](./log-filter.md) page.

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned:

- How to add `zio-logging` to an sbt project and install a console logger in the bootstrap
- How the four log levels work, and how the root level hides messages below it
- How to attach annotations to a group of log messages with `@@`
- How to print JSON output with `consoleJsonLogger`
- How to set a different log level for one logger name

You now have a foundation for logging in a ZIO application. The next step is to change the output format and the destination to suit your project.

### Next Steps

- **Change the console output:** Read [Console Logger](./console-logger.md) for every option of the console logger.
- **Shape the log lines:** Read [Formatting Log Records](./formatting-log-records.md) to build your own format.
- **Control which messages print:** Read [Log Filter](./log-filter.md) for the full filter API.
- **Learn about annotations in depth:** Read [Logger Context and Annotations](./logger-context-and-annotations.md).
- **Send SLF4J logs through ZIO Logging:** Read [SLF4J 2](./slf4j2.md) if your project uses SLF4J.

## Getting Started(Zio-metrics-connectors)

ZIO Metrics Connectors reports the metrics that ZIO records, both your own and those of the ZIO runtime and the JVM, to Prometheus, StatsD, Datadog, New Relic, or Micrometer. The core library keeps the metric state, and a connector reads it and sends or serves it. See [How It Works](how-it-works.md) for details, and [How to Report ZIO Runtime and JVM Metrics](how-to/report-runtime-and-jvm-metrics.md) for the runtime and JVM metrics.

To get started, add the dependencies from [Installation](#installation), then follow the [tutorial](tutorial/instrument-and-scrape.md).

### Installation

Add the core library and the connector for your monitoring backend to your `build.sbt`. The [Introduction](index.md#installation)
lists the dependency line for each module.

### Next Steps

- To instrument an application and see its metrics in Prometheus, follow the [tutorial](tutorial/instrument-and-scrape.md).
- To pick a connector, see [How to Choose a Connector](how-to/choose-a-connector.md).
- To see how the connectors read the metrics, see [How It Works](how-it-works.md).

## How ZIO Metrics Connectors Work

A connector reads the metric state that ZIO keeps in its metrics registry. The state is kept in an internal data structure that is optimized to update as efficiently as possible, and the data that a backend needs is generated only when it is required. To define and apply metrics, see [Metric Reference](reference/metric-reference.md).

> Changing which platform the metrics are reported to has no impact on the application at all. Once instrumented
> properly, the decision where to report to happens 'at the end of the world', that is, in the ZIO application's main
> entry point, by providing one or more of the available reporting clients.

### Polling and Listening

The Prometheus, StatsD, Datadog, and New Relic connectors poll the registry on the interval of a `MetricsConfig`. The Prometheus connector republishes every metric on each poll. The StatsD, Datadog, and New Relic connectors skip metrics that did not change since the last poll, and Datadog sends them anyway when `sendUnchanged` is `true`. The Micrometer connector registers a listener, so every change reaches the Micrometer registry as it happens, and it does not need a `MetricsConfig`.

The Datadog connector also listens, for histograms only: it queues each recorded histogram value and sends it as a
distribution, while it polls for every other metric type.

### Push and Pull

Prometheus is a pull backend: your application serves the encoded text and the Prometheus server scrapes it. The
other connectors push to the backend. For a comparison of the connectors and how to pick one, see
[How to Choose a Connector](how-to/choose-a-connector.md).

### Where to Go Next

To add a connector to your build, see [Installation](index.md#installation). Then:

* [Metric Reference](reference/metric-reference.md) lists the metric types that ZIO Metrics supports.
* [Prometheus Client](reference/prometheus-client.md), [StatsD Client](reference/statsd-client.md),
  [Datadog Client](reference/datadog-client.md), [New Relic Client](reference/new-relic-client.md), and
  [Micrometer Connector](reference/micrometer-connector.md) describe each connector.
* [Configuration](reference/configuration.md) and [Metric Type Mapping](reference/metric-type-mapping.md) list every
  setting and how each metric type is encoded.
