## How to Add Labels to Metrics

Labels split one metric into several series, so that a dashboard can group or filter the values by a dimension such as
the service or the route. This guide shows how to attach a fixed label to a metric and how to vary a label per call.

### Attach a Fixed Label

`Metric#tagged` returns a copy of the metric with one more label. Every series of that metric carries the label, so
the label is set once where the metric is defined:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric

val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
  Metric.counter("http_requests", "Number of HTTP requests")
    .tagged("service", "orders")
    .fromConst(1L)
```

Call `Metric#tagged` again to add another label. Each call returns a new metric and leaves the original unchanged.

### Vary a Label per Call

To set a label that depends on the work being done, apply a tagged copy of the metric at the call site. The next
block records one request for each route it handles:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric

def handle(route: String): UIO[Unit] =
  ZIO.unit @@ requests.tagged("route", route)
```

When the application calls `handle("/orders")` twice and `handle("/health")` once, the Prometheus output contains one
series per distinct combination of labels:

```
# TYPE http_requests counter
# HELP http_requests Number of HTTP requests
http_requests{service="orders",route="/orders"} 2.0 1794253765088
http_requests{service="orders",route="/health"} 1.0 1794253765088
```

The order of labels inside the braces is not guaranteed, because the connector stores them in a set.

:::warning[Keep label values bounded]
Each distinct label value creates a new series. Label values taken from user input, such as customer IDs, email
addresses, or raw URL paths that contain IDs, can create an unbounded number of series. Use a route template such as
`/orders/:id` instead of the actual path.
:::

For the full list of labels that each connector forwards, see [Metric Type Mapping](../reference/metric-type-mapping.md).

---

## How to Choose a Connector

Your instrumented code does not change when you change the monitoring backend. You only decide which connector to provide
when the application starts. This guide explains how the connectors differ, so that you can pick the one your monitoring
setup needs.

The connectors differ in two ways. The first is direction: a pull connector waits for a backend to request the data,
while a push connector sends the data to the backend. The second is what your application must provide: some connectors
need an HTTP endpoint, others need a network address or an API key.

| Connector | Direction | How Data Leaves the App |
| ----------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Prometheus | Pull | Your HTTP route returns the publisher text |
| StatsD | Push | UDP datagrams, or a Unix domain socket |
| Datadog | Push | DogStatsD datagrams to a Datadog agent |
| New Relic | Push | HTTPS requests to the New Relic Metric API |
| Micrometer | In-process | Listener that updates a Micrometer registry |

Use the following steps to pick a connector:

1. If you run a Prometheus server, use the Prometheus connector. Prometheus scrapes the endpoint that you serve, so
   the application needs no address for the server.
2. If your hosts run a Datadog agent, use the Datadog connector. If you run a different StatsD server, use the StatsD
   connector instead.
3. If you send metrics to New Relic, use the New Relic connector. It needs an API key and reports over HTTPS.
4. If your application already uses a Micrometer registry, use the Micrometer connector. Micrometer then forwards the
   metrics to whichever backend that registry supports.

Each connector has its own page with the details: [Prometheus](../reference/prometheus-client.md),
[StatsD](../reference/statsd-client.md), [Datadog](../reference/datadog-client.md),
[New Relic](../reference/new-relic-client.md), and [Micrometer](../reference/micrometer-connector.md).

Avoid providing two connectors that send to the same backend, because each metric is then reported twice. Read the
[Datadog page](../reference/datadog-client.md) before you combine the Datadog and StatsD layers.

---

## How to Instrument an Application

This guide shows how to define one metric of each type and update them from a running program. For the definition of each metric type, see [Metric Reference](../reference/metric-reference.md). To see how the captured metrics are reported, see [StatsD](../reference/statsd-client.md) and [Prometheus](../reference/prometheus-client.md).

The following trait is used in the [zio metrics sample application](https://github.com/zio/zio-metrics-connectors/blob/series/2.x/sample-app/src/main/scala/sample/SamplePrometheusStatsDApp.scala) of the repository:

```scala
trait InstrumentedSample {

  // Create a gauge, it can be applied to effects yielding a Double
  val aspGauge1 = Metric.gauge("gauge1", "Description of gauge1")
    .tagged("tag1", "tag value")
    .tagged("tag2", "another tag value")

  val aspGauge2 = Metric.gauge("gauge2")

  // Create a histogram with 12 buckets: 0..100 in steps of 10, Infinite
  // It also can be applied to effects yielding a Double
  val aspHistogram =
    Metric.histogram("my_histogram", MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.linear(0.0d, 10.0d, 11))

  // Create a summary that can hold 100 samples, the max age of the samples is 1 day.
  // The summary should report the 10%, 50% and 90% quantile
  // It can be applied to effects yielding an Int
  val aspSummary =
    Metric.summary("my_summary", 1.day, 100, 0.03d, Chunk(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)).contramap[Int](_.toDouble)

  // Create a Set to observe the occurrences of unique Strings
  // It can be applied to effects yielding a String
  val aspSet = Metric.frequency("my_set")

  // Create a counter applicable to any effect
  val aspCountAll = Metric.counter("count_all").contramap[Any](_ => 1L)

  private lazy val gaugeSomething = for {
    _ <- Random.nextDoubleBetween(0.0d, 100.0d) @@ aspGauge1 @@ aspCountAll
    _ <- Random.nextDoubleBetween(-50d, 50d) @@ aspGauge2 @@ aspCountAll
  } yield ()

  // Record something into a histogram
  private lazy val observeNumbers = for {
    _ <- Random.nextDoubleBetween(0.0d, 120.0d) @@ aspHistogram @@ aspCountAll
    _ <- Random.nextIntBetween(100, 500) @@ aspSummary @@ aspCountAll
  } yield ()

  // Observe Strings in order to capture unique values
  private lazy val observeKey = for {
    _ <- Random.nextIntBetween(10, 20).map(v => s"my_key_$v") @@ aspSet @@ aspCountAll
  } yield ()

  def program: ZIO[Any, Nothing, Unit] = for {
    _ <- gaugeSomething.schedule(Schedule.spaced(200.millis)).forkDaemon
    _ <- observeNumbers.schedule(Schedule.spaced(150.millis)).forkDaemon
    _ <- observeKey.schedule(Schedule.spaced(300.millis)).forkDaemon
  } yield ()
}
```

---

## How to Migrate from the Deprecated StatsD and Datadog Layers

Version 2.4.0 deprecated `statsd.statsdLayer`, `datadog.datadogLayer`, and the `DatadogConfig` type. This guide shows
the replacement for each and how the settings move.

### Replace `statsd.statsdLayer`

`statsd.statsdLayer` needed a `StatsdConfig` and a `MetricsConfig`, and it produced no output. Replace it with
`statsd.statsdUDP`. It needs the same two configurations and works the same way, and it also provides a `StatsdClient`.
To send to a Unix domain socket instead, use `statsd.statsdUDS` with a `DatagramSocketConfig`.

### Replace `datadog.datadogLayer` and `DatadogConfig`

`datadog.datadogLayer` read a `DatadogConfig`, which held both the agent address and the Datadog settings. The
replacement splits them:

- The agent address, `host` and `port`, moves to a `StatsdConfig`, or to a `DatagramSocketConfig` with a `path`. A
  StatsD layer, `statsd.statsdUDP` or `statsd.statsdUDS`, uses it to provide the `StatsdClient`.
- The Datadog settings move to a `DatadogPublisherConfig`. It keeps the field names `histogramSendInterval`,
  `maxBatchedMetrics`, `maxQueueSize`, `containerId`, `entityId` and `sendUnchanged` with the same defaults, and it adds
  `constantTags` and `prefix`.
- The `datadog.live` layer replaces `datadog.datadogLayer`. It needs the `StatsdClient`, the
  `DatadogPublisherConfig` and a `MetricsConfig`.

The following application uses the new layers with the values that `DatadogConfig.default` had:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.{datadog, statsd, MetricsConfig}

object MigratedDatadogApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("dd_requests", "Requests handled").fromConst(1L)

  val program: UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.unit @@ requests *> ZIO.sleep(1.second)).forever

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(10.seconds)),
      ZLayer.succeed(statsd.StatsdConfig("localhost", 8125)),
      ZLayer.succeed(datadog.DatadogPublisherConfig()),
      statsd.statsdUDP,
      datadog.live,
    )
}
```

Read the [Datadog connector page](../reference/datadog-client.md) about the datagrams that this layer combination sends.
For every field, see the [configuration reference](../reference/configuration.md#datadog).

---

## How to Report ZIO Runtime and JVM Metrics

Besides the metrics that you define, ZIO can record metrics about its own runtime, such as fiber counts and execution
times, and about the JVM, such as memory and garbage collection. A connector reports them together with your own
metrics. This guide shows how to turn both on.

### Enable the Metrics

Provide `Runtime.enableRuntimeMetrics` to record the ZIO runtime metrics. Provide `DefaultJvmMetrics.liveV2` to record
the JVM metrics. Both layers go in the same `provide` call as the connector layers:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.connectors.{prometheus, MetricsConfig}
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus.PrometheusPublisher
import zio.metrics.jvm.DefaultJvmMetrics

object RuntimeMetricsApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val program: ZIO[PrometheusPublisher, Nothing, Unit] =
    for {
      _    <- ZIO.sleep(1.second)
      body <- ZIO.serviceWithZIO[PrometheusPublisher](_.get)
      _    <- ZIO.succeed(println(body))
    } yield ()

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(500.millis)),
      prometheus.publisherLayer,
      prometheus.prometheusLayer,
      Runtime.enableRuntimeMetrics,
      DefaultJvmMetrics.liveV2.unit,
    )
}
```

Add `.unit` to `DefaultJvmMetrics.liveV2`. The layer produces a value that the application does not use, and `.unit`
turns it into a layer that only starts the metrics.

The same two layers work with every connector, because they only record metrics. The connector decides where the
metrics go. The program prints the Prometheus text once, so that you can see the runtime and JVM metrics next to your own.

### Choose a JVM Metrics Layer

`DefaultJvmMetrics.live` is deprecated. It uses metric names from an older Prometheus client. `DefaultJvmMetrics.liveV2`
uses names that follow the OpenMetrics convention, so use it in new code. A dashboard that was built on the old names
must be updated when you switch.

---

## How to Send Metrics to Datadog

This guide shows how to run a Datadog agent in Docker, send the metrics of a ZIO application to it over a Unix domain
socket, and import a ready-made dashboard. You need a [Datadog](https://www.datadoghq.com/) account and its API key,
which this guide refers to as `$APIKEY`, and Docker on a Linux host. The Datadog agent accepts datagrams on a Unix
domain socket starting with version 6.0.0.

### Start the Datadog Agent

The application writes to a socket file, so the agent and the application must share a directory. Create the directory,
then start the agent with that directory mounted and `DD_DOGSTATSD_SOCKET` pointing at a socket inside it. Use the
`DD_SITE` of your account, such as `datadoghq.com` or `datadoghq.eu`:

```
mkdir -p /var/run/datadog

docker run --name dd-agent -e DD_API_KEY=$APIKEY -e DD_SITE=datadoghq.eu \
  -e DD_DOGSTATSD_SOCKET=/var/run/datadog/datadog.sock \
  -v /var/run/datadog:/var/run/datadog \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro \
  datadog/agent
```

The agent creates the socket file when it starts. Keep it running while you test.

### Send the Metrics over the Socket

Add the Datadog module to your build, as listed in the [Introduction](../index.md#modules). Then provide the
`statsd.statsdUDS` layer, which sends to the socket, together with `datadog.live`. The following application counts a
request every second and reports it to the socket that the agent created:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.{datadog, statsd, MetricsConfig}

object DatadogSocketApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("dd_requests", "Requests handled").fromConst(1L)

  val program: UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.unit @@ requests *> ZIO.sleep(1.second)).forever

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(10.seconds)),
      ZLayer.succeed(statsd.DatagramSocketConfig("/var/run/datadog/datadog.sock")),
      ZLayer.succeed(datadog.DatadogPublisherConfig()),
      statsd.statsdUDS,
      datadog.live,
    )
}
```

Read the [Datadog connector page](../reference/datadog-client.md) before you run this combination, because it explains
what each layer reports and a known duplication of datagrams.

If your agent listens on UDP instead of a socket, use `statsd.statsdUDP` with a `StatsdConfig`, as shown on the
connector page. To forward UDP datagrams from a host port to the socket, you can run `socat` next to the agent:

```
sudo socat -s -u udp-recv:8125 unix-sendto:/var/run/datadog/datadog.sock
```

Add `-v` to print the traffic that `socat` forwards, which shows whether datagrams are sent.

### Import the Example Dashboard

The repository has a dashboard that charts the metrics of the example application. To import it:

1. Log in to Datadog.
2. Select **Dashboards** and then **New Dashboard**.
3. In the upper right corner, open the dashboard settings and select **Import Dashboard JSON**.
4. Choose the file `examples/statsd/ZIOMetrics.json` from a checkout of the repository.
5. Confirm that you want to override the dashboard configuration, then save the dashboard.
6. Open **ZIO metrics** from the dashboard list.

![A simple Datadog Dashboard](../img/Datadog.png)

The dashboard shows data for the metric names that the example application records. Rename the metrics in your own
application to match the dashboard queries, or edit the queries.

---

## How to Serve Prometheus Metrics over HTTP

The Prometheus connector does not run an HTTP server. It stores the latest encoded metrics in a `PrometheusPublisher`, and
your application decides how to expose that text. This guide shows how to serve the text with zio-http, how to change the
path and port, and how to control how often the text is refreshed.

### Read the Text from the Publisher

`PrometheusPublisher#get` returns the current text as a `UIO[String]`, so any route can call it. The route must set the
content type to `text/plain; version=0.0.4` so that Prometheus reads the body as the text format. The following route serves
the metrics at `/internal/prometheus`:

```scala
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets

import zio._
import zio.http._
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus.PrometheusPublisher

val prometheusRoute: Route[PrometheusPublisher, Nothing] =
  Method.GET / "internal" / "prometheus" -> handler {
    ZIO.serviceWithZIO[PrometheusPublisher](_.get).map { body =>
      Response(
        status = Status.Ok,
        headers = Headers(Header.Custom(Header.ContentType.name, "text/plain; version=0.0.4")),
        body = Body.fromString(body, StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
      )
    }
  }
```

To change the path, change the segments after `Method.GET`. Keep the path in your Prometheus scrape configuration in sync
with the route.

### Choose the Port

The server port comes from `Server.Config`. The following layer makes the server listen on port 9090 instead of the
default 8080:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.http._

val serverConfig: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, Server.Config] =
  ZLayer.succeed(Server.Config.default.port(9090))
```

### Set the Refresh Interval

The connector refreshes the publisher text on the interval in `MetricsConfig`. A scrape returns the text from the most
recent refresh, not a new snapshot. A shorter interval gives fresher values and more work for the connector. A longer
interval does less work but returns older values. A reasonable starting point is the same interval as your Prometheus
scrape interval:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.connectors.MetricsConfig

val metricsConfig: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, MetricsConfig] =
  ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(15.seconds))
```

The first refresh runs about 10 milliseconds after the layer starts. Until then, the publisher text is empty, so a scrape
that arrives very early returns an empty body.

### Wire the Route into a Server

The application provides the server, the metrics layers, and the publisher. The routes need the `PrometheusPublisher`
in their environment, which `prometheus.publisherLayer` provides:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.http._
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus

object MetricsServer extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override def run =
    Server.serve(Routes(prometheusRoute))
      .provide(
        serverConfig,
        Server.live,
        metricsConfig,
        prometheus.publisherLayer,
        prometheus.prometheusLayer,
      )
}
```

### Test the Endpoint

To check the response headers as well as the body, request the endpoint with `curl -i`:

```
curl -i http://localhost:9090/internal/prometheus
```

The response status is 200, the `Content-Type` header is `text/plain; version=0.0.4`, and once the first refresh has run,
the body lists the metrics in the Prometheus text format, as shown in the [tutorial](../tutorial/instrument-and-scrape.md).

---

## How to Check Metrics Locally and in Tests

You can check which metrics an application records without running a monitoring backend. The Prometheus publisher keeps
the encoded text in memory, so a program or a test can read that text directly and check it. This guide shows how to read
the publisher in a local program and in a ZIO Test spec.

### Read the Publisher in a Local Program

The publisher refreshes on the `MetricsConfig` interval, so a program must wait longer than one interval before it reads
the text. The following program uses an interval of 100 milliseconds and waits 300 milliseconds before it reads:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.{prometheus, MetricsConfig}
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus.PrometheusPublisher

object LocalCheckApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("local_requests", "Requests seen by the local check").fromConst(1L)

  val program: ZIO[PrometheusPublisher, Throwable, Unit] =
    for {
      _    <- ZIO.unit @@ requests
      _    <- ZIO.sleep(300.millis)
      body <- ZIO.serviceWithZIO[PrometheusPublisher](_.get)
      _    <- Console.printLine(body)
    } yield ()

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(100.millis)),
      prometheus.publisherLayer,
      prometheus.prometheusLayer,
    )
}
```

The program prints the text that a scrape would return. For a single request, the output is:

```
# TYPE local_requests counter
# HELP local_requests Requests seen by the local check
local_requests 1.0 1794253765088
```

### Check Values in a ZIO Test

A ZIO Test spec can use the same publisher. The spec reads the text and asserts that the expected series is present:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.{prometheus, MetricsConfig}
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus.PrometheusPublisher
import zio.test._

object OrdersMetricsSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {

  val orders: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("test_orders_processed", "Orders processed in the test").fromConst(1L)

  def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment & Scope, Any] =
    suite("Orders metrics")(
      test("record the processed order in the Prometheus text") {
        for {
          _    <- ZIO.unit @@ orders
          _    <- ZIO.sleep(300.millis)
          body <- ZIO.serviceWithZIO[PrometheusPublisher](_.get)
        } yield assertTrue(body.contains("test_orders_processed 1.0"))
      },
    ).provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(100.millis)),
      prometheus.publisherLayer,
      prometheus.prometheusLayer,
    ) @@ TestAspect.withLiveClock
}
```

The spec ends with `TestAspect.withLiveClock`. The connector starts its refresh fiber when the layers are built, and that
fiber waits on the clock. ZIO Test replaces the clock with a test clock by default, and that clock does not advance on its
own, so the publisher would never refresh. The aspect must cover the layers, which is why it is applied to the whole spec.

:::tip[Use unique metric names]
ZIO Metrics keeps one registry for the whole JVM. If two tests record the same metric name, their values add up. Give
each test its own metric name, or check only the series that the test records.
:::

For a unit test that does not need the Prometheus text, the Micrometer connector can use an in-memory
`SimpleMeterRegistry`, which records values without any output format. See [Micrometer Connector](../reference/micrometer-connector.md).

---

## How to Visualize Prometheus Metrics in Grafana

This guide shows how to scrape an application that serves Prometheus metrics, and how to chart them in Grafana with the dashboard from the repository. It assumes that your application already serves the metrics at `http://localhost:8080/metrics`, as described in [How to Serve Prometheus Metrics over HTTP](serve-prometheus-metrics.md). You also need a checkout of the repository, which this guide refers to as `$DIR`.

### Run Prometheus

[Download Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/download/) and extract it to a directory that this guide refers to as `$PROMDIR`. The repository has a sample configuration, `examples/prometheus/promcfg.yml`, with a job named `zio` that polls `localhost:8080` every 10 seconds. Prometheus reads the default path, `/metrics`. Start Prometheus with it:

```
cd $PROMDIR
./prometheus --config.file $DIR/examples/prometheus/promcfg.yml
```

If your application serves the metrics on another host, port, or path, edit the `targets` of the `zio` job in the configuration file, and add a `metrics_path` for a path other than `/metrics`.

### Run Grafana

[Download Grafana](https://grafana.com/grafana/download) and start its server. Then open `http://localhost:3000`. The default user is `admin` with the password `admin`, and Grafana asks you to change the password at the first login.

Add Prometheus as a data source of Grafana. Use the address of the Prometheus server, which is `http://localhost:9090` by default.

### Import the Example Dashboard

The repository has a dashboard for the metrics of the example application. To import it:

1. In the Grafana menu, open **Dashboards** and select **Import**.
2. Paste the content of `examples/prometheus/ZIOMetricsDashboard.json` into the text field and select **Load**.
3. Import the dashboard and open it from the dashboard list.

![A simple Grafana Dashboard](../img/ZIOMetrics-Grafana.png)

The dashboard queries the metric names of the example application. Rename the metrics in your own application to match the queries, or edit the queries.

For the setup of Prometheus and Grafana beyond this example, see their own documentation.

## Introduction to ZIO Metrics Connectors

ZIO Metrics Connectors provides integration between ZIO metrics and industry-leading monitoring and observability systems such as
  * [Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/)
  * [Datadog](https://docs.datadoghq.com/)
  * [New Relic](https://newrelic.com)
  * [StatsD](https://github.com/statsd/statsd)
  * [Micrometer](https://micrometer.io)

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-metrics-connectors/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-metrics-connectors_3.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-metrics-connectors_3) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-metrics-connectors_3%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-metrics-connectors_3/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-metrics-connectors_3/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-metrics-connectors_3) [![ZIO Metrics Connectors](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-metrics-connectors?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-metrics-connectors)

### Installation

Add the core library to your `build.sbt`. All modules are published for Scala 2.12, Scala 2.13 and Scala 3, and run on the JVM only:

```sbt
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Core library: connector settings and the shared metrics client (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors" % "2.6.1"
)
```

Then add the connector for your monitoring backend, as described in [Modules](#modules).

### Modules

Each connector is a separate module. Add only the ones that you use:

```sbt
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Prometheus: encodes metrics as Prometheus text for you to serve over HTTP (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors-prometheus" % "2.6.1",

  // StatsD: sends datagrams over UDP or a Unix domain socket (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors-statsd" % "2.6.1",

  // Datadog: sends DogStatsD datagrams through a StatsD client, also adds `zio-metrics-connectors-statsd` (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors-datadog" % "2.6.1",

  // New Relic: sends metrics to the New Relic Metric API over HTTPS, also adds `zio-http` and `zio-json` (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors-newrelic" % "2.6.1",

  // Micrometer: forwards every metric update to a Micrometer `MeterRegistry` (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors-micrometer" % "2.6.1"
)
```

Each module depends on the core library, so you do not need to list it separately. Learn more about each module in its
reference page: [Prometheus](reference/prometheus-client.md), [StatsD](reference/statsd-client.md),
[Datadog](reference/datadog-client.md), [New Relic](reference/new-relic-client.md), and
[Micrometer](reference/micrometer-connector.md).

To pick a connector, see [How to Choose a Connector](how-to/choose-a-connector.md). To instrument an application and see
its metrics in Prometheus, follow the [tutorial](tutorial/instrument-and-scrape.md).

---

## Configuration Reference

This page lists every configuration type that the connectors use, with its fields, defaults, and the layers that need it.
Each connector page describes how to wire these configurations into an application.

### MetricsConfig

`MetricsConfig` sets how often the connector reads the ZIO Metrics registry. The Prometheus, StatsD, Datadog, and New Relic
connectors need it. The Micrometer connector does not, because it receives updates as they happen.

| Field      | Type       | Default  | Description                                                            |
| ---------- | ---------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `interval` | `Duration` | Required | How often the connector reads the registry and sends or publishes it. |

`MetricsConfig` has no default instance. Create one with the interval you need:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.connectors.MetricsConfig

val metricsConfig: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, MetricsConfig] =
  ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(5.seconds))
```

### Prometheus

The Prometheus connector has no configuration type. Its layers are `prometheus.publisherLayer`, which provides a `PrometheusPublisher`, and `prometheus.prometheusLayer`, which requires a `MetricsConfig` and a `PrometheusPublisher`.

`PrometheusPublisher` has two methods. `get` returns the current Prometheus text, and `set` replaces it. The application
reads `get` in an HTTP route. See [Serve Prometheus Metrics](../how-to/serve-prometheus-metrics.md).

### StatsD

`StatsdConfig` describes the StatsD agent that receives UDP datagrams:

| Field          | Type               | Default  | Description                                                                             |
| -------------- | ------------------ | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `host`         | `String`           | Required | Host name of the agent.                                                                 |
| `port`         | `Int`              | Required | UDP port of the agent.                                                                  |
| `prefix`       | `Option[String]`   | `None`   | Prepended to every metric name. Include any separator, such as `"orders."`.             |
| `constantTags` | `List[MetricLabel]` | `Nil`   | Added to every datagram.                                                                |
| `suffix`       | `Option[String]`   | `None`   | Appended to every datagram, after the tags.                                             |

`StatsdConfig.default` points at `localhost` on port 8125, and `StatsdConfig.defaultLayer` provides it as a layer.

`DatagramSocketConfig` describes a Unix domain socket instead of UDP. It has the same `prefix`, `constantTags`, and
`suffix` fields, and it adds one required field:

| Field  | Type     | Default  | Description                                |
| ------ | -------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `path` | `String` | Required | Path of the socket that the agent listens on. |

The layers are `statsd.statsdUDP`, which requires a `StatsdConfig` and a `MetricsConfig`, and `statsd.statsdUDS`, which
requires a `DatagramSocketConfig` and a `MetricsConfig`. The `statsd.statsdLayer` and `DatadogConfig` APIs are deprecated since
version 2.4.0, so new code should not use them.

The following values set a UDP agent with a prefix and one constant tag, and a socket path:

```scala
import zio.metrics.MetricLabel
import zio.metrics.connectors.statsd.{DatagramSocketConfig, StatsdConfig}

val udpConfig: StatsdConfig =
  StatsdConfig(
    host = "localhost",
    port = 8125,
    prefix = Some("orders."),
    constantTags = List(MetricLabel("env", "prod")),
  )

val socketConfig: DatagramSocketConfig =
  DatagramSocketConfig(path = "/var/run/datadog/datadog.sock")
```

### Datadog

`DatadogPublisherConfig` configures the Datadog connector. Every field has a default, so `DatadogPublisherConfig()` is a
valid configuration:

| Field                   | Type             | Default   | Description                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------- | --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `histogramSendInterval` | `Option[Duration]` | `None` | Sends distributions more often than the general interval.                                |
| `maxBatchedMetrics`     | `Int`            | `10`      | Maximum number of metrics per packet. Affects packet size.                               |
| `maxQueueSize`          | `Int`            | `100000`  | Maximum number of queued histogram values. Affects memory use.                           |
| `containerId`           | `Option[String]` | `None`    | Docker container ID, sent as a suffix on each datagram.                                  |
| `entityId`              | `Option[String]` | `None`    | Sent as the `dd.internal.entity_id` tag.                                                 |
| `sendUnchanged`         | `Boolean`        | `false`   | Sends metrics that did not change since the last poll.                                   |
| `constantTags`          | `List[MetricLabel]` | `Nil` | Added to every metric.                                                                   |
| `prefix`                | `Option[String]` | `None`    | Prepended to every metric name. Include any separator.                                   |

The `datadog.live` layer requires a `StatsdClient`, a `DatadogPublisherConfig`, and a `MetricsConfig`. Provide the
`StatsdClient` with `statsd.statsdUDP` or `statsd.statsdUDS`. The [Datadog page](./datadog-client.md) shows a
complete setup.

### New Relic

`NewRelicConfig` configures the New Relic connector. The constructor has no defaults. The `fromEnvLayer` and
`fromEnvEULayer` layers read these environment variables and apply the defaults listed in the table below:

| Environment Variable                 | Required | Default   | Description                                                             |
| ------------------------------------ | -------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NEW_RELIC_API_KEY`                  | Yes      | None      | Your New Relic API key. The application fails to start without it.      |
| `NEW_RELIC_URI`                      | No       | US endpoint | Custom Metric API endpoint. Ignored by `fromEnvEULayer`.              |
| `NEW_RELIC_MAX_METRICS_PER_REQUEST`  | No       | `500`     | Maximum number of metrics in one HTTPS request.                          |
| `NEW_RELIC_MAX_PUBLISHING_DELAY`     | No       | `PT5S`    | Longest time to wait before sending a partial batch, as an ISO-8601 duration. |

The `NewRelicConfig` fields are `apiKey`, `newRelicURI`, `maxMetricsPerRequest`, and `maxPublishingDelay`. The
`newRelicURI` field takes one of three values from `NewRelicUri`:

- `NewRelicUri.NA` sends to `https://metric-api.newrelic.com/metric/v1`, the US endpoint.
- `NewRelicUri.EU` sends to `https://metric-api.eu.newrelic.com/metric/v1`, the EU endpoint.
- `NewRelicUri.Custom(endpoint)` sends to any other endpoint.

The `newRelicLayer` requires a `NewRelicConfig` and a `MetricsConfig`. It creates its own HTTP client.

### Micrometer

`MicrometerConfig` configures the Micrometer connector:

| Field                              | Type  | Default | Description                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------- | ----- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `summaryPercentileDigitsOfPrecision` | `Int` | `3`   | Digits of precision for the percentiles that summaries publish.                   |

`MicrometerConfig.default` uses the default value. The `micrometer.micrometerLayer` requires a `MeterRegistry` and a
`MicrometerConfig` in its environment. It does not require a `MetricsConfig`.

### Layers by Connector

The following table lists the layers to provide for each connector, and the configuration each one needs in its
environment:

| Connector  | Layers You Provide                                  | Environment Required                                        |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Prometheus | `prometheus.publisherLayer`, `prometheus.prometheusLayer` | `MetricsConfig`                                       |
| StatsD     | `statsd.statsdUDP` or `statsd.statsdUDS`            | `StatsdConfig` or `DatagramSocketConfig`, `MetricsConfig`  |
| Datadog    | `datadog.live`, plus a StatsD client layer          | `StatsdClient`, `DatadogPublisherConfig`, `MetricsConfig`  |
| New Relic  | `newRelicLayer`                                     | `NewRelicConfig`, `MetricsConfig`                          |
| Micrometer | `micrometer.micrometerLayer`                        | `MeterRegistry`, `MicrometerConfig`                        |

---

## Datadog Client

In a normal Datadog setup we will find a Datadog agent with an open UDP port where applications send their
metrics to. The format of the metrics is defined by the [DogStatsD protocol](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/datagram_shell/?tab=metrics).

The Datadog connector creates the relevant DogStatsD datagrams and sends them through a `StatsdClient`, over UDP or a Unix domain socket.

> The instrumented code is exactly the same as for the Prometheus instrumentation. The only difference is that
> another client is provided when the App is configured.

### ZIO Metrics in DogStatsD

DogStatsD normally has its own definition how histograms and summaries are configured. In the default setup this
is defined in the config file of the statsd agent. Furthermore, a StatsD Histogram is more or less the
equivalent of a Prometheus summary.

However, whenever the desired quantiles need to change, the config must be adjusted and the agent restarted.

Therefore, the ZIO Metrics Datadog connector maps summaries and frequencies to sets of related gauges, and histograms to distributions. This allows us to achieve
the same visualization without the need to adjust any of the agents config files.

#### Counter

Counters are reported periodically within a configurable time interval, as in:

```
countAll:1|c
```

#### Gauge

Gauges are reported periodically within a configurable time interval, as in:

```
adjustGauge:32.2787317766752|g
```

#### Histogram

A histogram is reported as a datadog distribution. Each submitted value is queued and sent at the next flush, which runs every `histogramSendInterval`. Values for the same histogram that are queued together are sent in one datagram. The bucket configuration is 
ignored in this case, as Datadog expects raw values to be recorded. 

```
myHistogram:3|d
```

#### Summary

A summary is periodically reported as a set of related gauges, within a configurable time interval. Each quantile will 
be reported within its own gauge. The additional labels are `quantile` to address the quantile and `error` to display 
the configured error margin.

```
mySummary:123|g|#quantile:0.1,error:0.03
mySummary:254|g|#quantile:0.5,error:0.03
mySummary:441|g|#quantile:0.9,error:0.03
```

#### Frequencies

Frequencies are reported as sets of related gauges. An additional label is used to differentiate the distinct
values in the set. The label is named `bucket`.

```
mySet:6|g|#bucket:my_key_18
mySet:1|g|#bucket:my_key_19
mySet:2|g|#bucket:my_key_13
mySet:3|g|#bucket:my_key_14
mySet:1|g|#bucket:my_key_16
mySet:3|g|#bucket:my_key_10
mySet:2|g|#bucket:my_key_11
mySet:1|g|#bucket:my_key_12
```

### The ZIO Metrics Datadog Example

The Datadog connector sends its datagrams through a `StatsdClient`. We need a client that can send them to a specified
UDP destination or a unix domain socket, and we do not need to start a server in the application. The following
application counts a request every second. It provides the `datadog.live` layer together with the `statsd.statsdUDP`
layer that supplies its `StatsdClient`. Building these layers starts the reporting, so they are provided even though the
program does not use the client directly:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.{datadog, statsd, MetricsConfig}

object DatadogApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("dd_requests", "Requests handled").fromConst(1L)

  val program: UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.unit @@ requests *> ZIO.sleep(1.second)).forever

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(100.millis)),
      ZLayer.succeed(statsd.StatsdConfig("localhost", 8125)),
      ZLayer.succeed(datadog.DatadogPublisherConfig()),
      statsd.statsdUDP,
      datadog.live,
    )
}
```

:::warning[Each metric is sent twice with this layer combination]
The `datadog.live` layer needs a `StatsdClient`. The public layers that provide one, `statsd.statsdUDP` and `statsd.statsdUDS`, also start their own sender for every metric. With the combination above, counters, gauges, summaries, and frequencies are therefore sent once by each sender, and the Datadog agent receives two datagrams per update. With default settings the two datagrams are identical. Histograms are sent as `le` gauges by the StatsD sender and as `d` distributions by the Datadog sender.
:::

To send datagrams over a unix domain socket instead of UDP, use `statsd.statsdUDS` with a `statsd.DatagramSocketConfig`, as shown in [How to Send Metrics to Datadog](../how-to/send-metrics-to-datadog.md). This can be used with the Datadog agent starting with version 6.0.0 on the Linux platform.

### Configuration

The `datadog.live` layer reads a `DatadogPublisherConfig`, and it needs a `StatsdClient` to send the datagrams. That client comes from the `statsd.statsdUDP` or `statsd.statsdUDS` layer. The layer also reads `MetricsConfig`, which sets how often the metrics registry is polled.

Every field and default of `DatadogPublisherConfig` is listed in the [configuration reference](./configuration.md#datadog).

The older `DatadogConfig` is deprecated since version 2.4.0. It has no `prefix` or `constantTags` fields, so use `DatadogPublisherConfig` instead.

#### Prefix and Constant Tags

The `prefix` is prepended to every metric name, and the `constantTags` are added to every datagram before the tags of the metric itself. Any separator has to be part of the prefix. To report under `myapp.` with the environment and service as tags:

```scala
import zio.metrics.MetricLabel
import zio.metrics.connectors.datadog.DatadogPublisherConfig

val publisherConfig = DatadogPublisherConfig(
  prefix = Some("myapp."),
  constantTags = List(MetricLabel("env", "prod"), MetricLabel("service", "checkout")),
)
```

With this configuration, a counter named `countAll` is sent as:

```
myapp.countAll:1|c|#env:prod,service:checkout
```

Histograms are sent as distributions with the same prefix and tags, so the same settings apply to them. A histogram named `myHistogram` with the value 3 is sent as `myapp.myHistogram:3|d|#env:prod,service:checkout`.

#### Entity ID

When `entityId` is set, the client adds the internal `dd.internal.entity_id` tag after the constant tags. The tag lets Datadog track the client entity that sent the metric. To set an entity ID:

```scala
import zio.metrics.connectors.datadog.DatadogPublisherConfig

val publisherConfig = DatadogPublisherConfig(entityId = Some("pod-uid-123"))
```

With both `constantTags` and `entityId` set, the counter above is sent as `myapp.countAll:1|c|#env:prod,service:checkout,dd.internal.entity_id:pod-uid-123`.

The `containerId` is sent as a suffix after the tags. For example, a gauge named `m1` with the container ID `aaa` is sent as `m1:1|g|c:aaa`.

To run the connector against a local Datadog agent, see [How to Send Metrics to Datadog](../how-to/send-metrics-to-datadog.md).

---

## ZIO Metric Reference

### Measuring

All ZIO metrics are defined in the form of aspects that can be applied with `@@` to measure an effect. Applying an
aspect to an effect does not change the type of the effect. For example:

```scala
val metric = Metric.counter("effect_counter").fromConst(1L)
val effect: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Double] = ZIO.succeed(1.0)
val effectWithMeasurement: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Double] = effect @@ metric
```

#### Name, Description, and Labels

Every metric has a name and optionally a description. The name may be augmented by zero or more `Label`s (sometimes
called `tag`s). Labels are useful, because some reporting platforms support them and provide aggregation mechanisms
for them.

> For example, think of a counter that counts how often a particular service has been invoked. If the application is
> deployed across several hosts, we can model our counter with the name `my_service` and an additional label
> `(host, ${hostname})`. With this definition we can see the number of executions for each host, but we can also
> create a query in Grafana or Datadog to visualize the aggregated value over all hosts. Using more than one label
> allows us to create visualizations across any combination of the labels.

Name and description are always given as part of the metric constructor, labels can be added via one of the `tagged`
methods. Here is an example:

```scala
val hostname = "host-1"
val path     = "/orders"

val countRequests =
  Metric.counter("count_requests", "Description of the counter").fromConst(1L).tagged("hostname", hostname)
val effectWithTaggedMeasurement = effect @@ countRequests.tagged("path", path)
```

We recommend you follow the [Prometheus best practices](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/) guide for the metric name and labels.

#### Supported Type

Every `Metric` has the type parameter `In` which indicates what types of values can be measured by the metric. When
applying the metric as an aspect to an effect, the metric's `In` type must be compatible with the output type of the
effect (the `A` in `ZIO[R, E, A]`). For example, a `Metric.Counter[Any]` can be applied to any effect while a
`Metric.Counter[Double]` can only be applied to an effect that produces a `Double`.

In the underlying implementation, each metric type supports only one base type. _Counters_, _Gauges_, _Histograms_ and
_Summaries_ all support `Double` values, while a _Frequency_ supports `String` values. To support a different type, we
can use the `contramap` method. For example, a Gauge that supports `Long`s is written as:

```scala
val longGauge: Metric.Gauge[Long] =
  Metric.gauge("my_metric").contramap[Long](_.toDouble)
```

Method `fromConst` works like `contramap` but always returns the same value. For example a counter that always increases
with the same value is written as:

```scala
val occurrenceCounter: Metric.Counter[Any] =
  Metric.counter("my_metric").fromConst(1L)
```

#### Measuring Durations

To measure how long an effect takes, we can use methods `trackDuration` and `trackDurationWith`. See the histogram
section below for an example.

#### Measuring Failures

Normally, we only measure effects that succeed. To measure an effect that failed, we can use methods like `trackAll`,
`trackDefectWith`, `trackErrorWith` and `trackSuccessWith`. For example `trackError` lets you measure the error output
of an effect:

```scala
val countAllErrors =
  Metric.counter("all_errors").fromConst(1L).trackError

// counts the errors of `effect`
val errorMeasurement = effect @@ countAllErrors
```

### Metric Types

Each metric type measures a different kind of value. The following sections show how to create each type and how to apply it.

#### Counter

A counter is a metric of which the value can only increase over time. A counter can be created with one of these
methods:

```scala
val longCounter: Metric.Counter[Long] = Metric.counter(name = "my_metric")
val intCounter: Metric.Counter[Int] = Metric.counterInt(name = "my_metric")
val doubleCounter: Metric.Counter[Double] = Metric.counterDouble(name = "my_metric")
```

Besides using a counter as an aspect (with the `@@` operator), counter metrics can also measure values with their
`increment` and `incrementBy` methods. For example:

```scala
longCounter.incrementBy(10L)
```

##### Examples

Create a counter named `count_all` which is incremented by `1` every time it is invoked. Since the metric type is `Any`
the aspect can be applied to effect of any type.

```scala
val aspCountAll: Metric.Counter[Any] =
  Metric.counter("count_all").fromConst(1L)
```

The same aspect can be applied to more than one effect. In the following example we count the sum of executions of both
effects in the for comprehension:

```scala
val countAll = for {
  _ <- ZIO.unit @@ aspCountAll
  _ <- ZIO.unit @@ aspCountAll
} yield ()
```  

Create a counter named `count_bytes` that can be applied to effects having the output type `Double`.

```scala
val aspCountBytes = Metric.counterDouble("count_bytes")
```

Now we can apply it to effects producing `Double` (in a real application the value might be the number of bytes read
from a stream or something similar):

```scala
val countBytes = Random.nextDoubleBetween(0.0d, 100.0d) @@ aspCountBytes
```

#### Gauges

A gauge is a metric that can change over time. A gauge can be created as follows:

```scala
val doubleGauge: Metric.Gauge[Double] = Metric.gauge(name = "my_metric")
```

Besides using a gauge as an aspect (with the `@@` operator), gauge metrics can also measure values with their `set`,
`increment`, `incrementBy`, `decrement` and `decrementBy` methods. For example:

```scala
for {
  _ <- doubleGauge.set(10.0) // sets the gauge to 10.0
  _ <- doubleGauge.decrement // decreases the gauge with 1.0
} yield ()
```

##### Examples

Create a gauge that can be applied to effects that produce a Double:

```scala
val aspGauge = Metric.gauge("set_gauge")
```

Now we can apply the metric to effects that produce `Double`s. Note that we can instrument an effect with any number of
aspects if the type constraints are satisfied.

```scala
val measuredEffect = Random.nextDoubleBetween(0.0d, 100.0d) @@ aspGauge @@ aspCountAll
```

#### Histograms

A histogram is a metric that counts the measured values in buckets. Each bucket is defined by an upper boundary. The
count in a bucket with upper boundary `b` increases by `1` if an observed value `v` is less or equal to `b`. As a
consequence, all buckets that have a boundary `b1` with `b1 > b` will increase by `1` after observing `v`.

A histogram also keeps track of the overall count of observed values and the sum of all observed values.

The last bucket is always defined as `Double.MaxValue`, so that the count of observed values in the last bucket is
always equal to the overall count of observed values within the histogram.

The used histogram model is inspired by [Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/concepts/metric_types/#histogram).

Boundaries can be created as follows:

```scala
// given boundaries: 100.0, 200.0, 300.0, 400.0, MaxValue
MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.fromChunk(Chunk(100.0, 200.0, 300.0, 400.0))
// linear boundaries: 100.0, 200.0, 300.0, 400.0, 500.0, 600.0, 700.0, 800.0, 900.0, 1000.0, MaxValue
MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.linear(100.0, 100.0, 10)
// exponential boundaries: 100.0, 200.0, 400.0, 800.0, 1600.0, 3200.0, 6400.0, 12800.0, 25600.0, 51200.0, MaxValue
MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.exponential(100.0, 2.0, 10)
```

A histogram can be created with the `Metric.histogram(name, boundaries)` method. For example:

```scala
val latencyHistogram: Metric.Histogram[Double] =
  Metric.histogram("queue_size", MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.fromChunk(Chunk(100.0, 200.0, 300.0, 400.0)))
```

##### Examples

Create a histogram with 11 buckets: `0..90` in steps of `10` and `Double.MaxValue`. It can be applied to effects
yielding a `Double`.

```scala
val aspHistogram =
  Metric.histogram("my_histogram", MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.linear(0.0d, 10.0d, 10))
```

Now we can apply the histogram to effects producing `Double`:

```scala
val measuredEffect = Random.nextDoubleBetween(0.0d, 120.0d) @@ aspHistogram
```

Create a histogram that observes `Duration`s in seconds. Use `trackDuration` to track the duration of an effect.
Note that using seconds as unit is the recommended convention in many metric platforms such as Prometheus and
OpenTelemetry.

```scala
val latencyHistogram: Metric.Histogram[Duration] =
  Metric.histogram(
      "my_latency_seconds",
      "The latency in seconds.",
      MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.exponential(0.01, 2.0, 10)
    )
    .contramap[Duration](_.toNanos.toDouble / 1e9) // convert to seconds

val timedEffect: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] = ZIO.unit

val measuredLatency = timedEffect @@ latencyHistogram.trackDuration
```

#### Summaries

Similar to a histogram a summary also observes `Double` values. While a histogram directly modifies the bucket counters
and does not keep the individual samples, the summary keeps the observed samples in its internal state. To avoid the set
of samples grow uncontrolled, the summary need to be configured with a maximum age `t` and a maximum size `n`. To
calculate the statistics, maximal `n` samples will be used, all of which are not older than `t`.

Essentially the set of samples is a sliding window over the last observed samples matching the conditions above.

A summary is used to calculate a set of quantiles over the current set of samples. A quantile is defined by a `Double`
value `q` with `0 <= q <= 1` and resolves to a `Double` as well.

The value of a given quantile `q` is the maximum value `v` out of the current sample buffer with size `n` where at most
`q * n` values out of the sample buffer are less or equal to `v`.

Typical quantiles for observation are `0.5` (the median) and the `0.95`. Quantiles are very good for monitoring Service
Level Agreements.

The ZIO Metrics API also allows summaries to be configured with an error margin `e`. The error margin is applied to the
count of values, so that a quantile `q` for a set of size `s` resolves to value `v` if the number `n` of values less or
equal to `v` is `(1 - e) * q * s <= n <= (1 + e) * q * s`.

A summary can be created with the `summary` method:

```scala
val signature: Metric.Summary[Double] =
  Metric.summary(
    name = "my_summary",
    maxAge = 1.day,
    maxSize = 100,
    error = 0.03d,
    quantiles = Chunk(0.1, 0.5, 0.9),
  )
```

##### Examples

Create a summary that can hold 100 samples, the max age of the samples is `1 day` and the error margin is `3%`. The
summary should report the `10%`, `50%` and `90%` quantiles. It can be applied to effects producing an `Int`.

```scala
val aspSummary =
  Metric.summary("my_summary", 1.day, 100, 0.03d, Chunk(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)).contramap[Int](_.toDouble)
```

Now we can apply this aspect to an effect producing an `Int`:

```scala
val summary = Random.nextIntBetween(100, 500) @@ aspSummary
```

#### Frequencies

Frequencies are used to count the occurrences of distinct string values. For example an application that uses logical
names for its services, the number of invocations for each service can be tracked.

Essentially, a Frequency is a set of related counters sharing the same name and tags. The counters are set apart from
each other by an additional configurable tag. The values of the tag represent the observed distinct values.

The connectors report the distinct values in a label named `bucket`. See [Metric Type Mapping](metric-type-mapping.md).

A frequency can be created with the `frequency` method, which takes the name of the metric:

```scala
val frequency: Metric.Frequency[String] = Metric.frequency("my_frequency")
```

##### Examples

Create a Frequency to observe the occurrences of unique Strings. It can be applied to effects producing a String.

```scala
val aspSet = Metric.frequency("my_set")
```  

Now we can generate some keys within an effect and start counting the occurrences
for each value.

```scala
val set = Random.nextIntBetween(10, 20).map(v => s"my_key_$v") @@ aspSet
```

---

## Metric Type Mapping

Each ZIO metric type has a different shape, and each backend has its own shape for the same data. This page shows how
every connector encodes each type, so that you can build dashboards and queries against the output. For the definition of
each type and how to create it, see [Metric Reference](./metric-reference.md).

The table below gives the output of each connector for each metric type. The Prometheus column shows the metric family
name and the suffixes that the connector adds. The StatsD and Datadog columns show the datagram type code (`c`, `g`, or `d`).

| Metric Type | Prometheus                                              | StatsD and Datadog                                      | New Relic                                       | Micrometer                                       |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Counter     | `counter`, with the total count as the value            | `c`, with the change since the last poll                | `count`, with the change and `interval.ms`      | `Counter`                                        |
| Gauge       | `gauge`, with the current value                         | `g`, with the current value                             | `gauge`, with the current value                 | `Gauge`, backed by an atomic double              |
| Histogram   | `histogram`: `_bucket{le}`, `_sum`, `_count`, `_min`, `_max` | StatsD: one `g` per bucket with an `le` tag. Datadog: `d` distribution of raw values | `summary`, with count, sum, min, and max | `DistributionSummary`, with the bucket boundaries as service level objectives |
| Summary     | `summary`: `{quantile,error}`, `_sum`, `_count`, `_min`, `_max` | `g` per quantile, with `quantile` and `error` tags | `summary`, with count, sum, min, max, and `zio.error.margin` | `DistributionSummary`, with the quantiles as percentiles and an `error` tag |
| Frequency   | `counter`, one series per value with a `bucket` label   | `g` per value, with a `bucket` tag                      | `count` per value, with a `zio.frequency.name` attribute | `Counter` per value, with a `bucket` tag     |

### Prometheus

Prometheus output has a `# TYPE` and a `# HELP` line for each metric family. Metric names are changed so that they are
valid in Prometheus: hyphens, spaces, and dots become underscores. Counters do not get a `_total` suffix.

Histograms produce one `_bucket` series for each boundary, with an `le` label, and the `+Inf` bucket is last. Summaries
produce one series for each quantile, with `quantile` and `error` labels, and no buckets. Both types also produce `_sum`,
`_count`, `_min`, and `_max` series.

Frequencies produce a `counter` family. Each observed value becomes one series, with the value in the `bucket` label.

### StatsD and Datadog

StatsD and Datadog share the same datagram format. Each metric becomes one or more datagrams of the form
`name:value|type|#tags`. Constant tags come first in the tags section, followed by the metric's own labels.

Counters send the change since the last poll, so the backend must sum them. Gauges send the current value. Histograms
and summaries send one gauge per bucket or quantile, distinguished by the `le` or `quantile` tag. Frequencies send one
gauge per observed value, distinguished by the `bucket` tag.

The Datadog connector differs in one case. Histograms become `d` distributions, which carry raw values. Datadog then
computes the percentiles itself, so the bucket boundaries are not sent. See the [Datadog page](./datadog-client.md).

### New Relic

The New Relic connector sends JSON events to the Metric API. Counters become `count` events with an `interval.ms`
field, which is the time from the start of the application to the latest event. Gauges become `gauge` events.

Histograms and summaries become `summary` events with count, sum, min, and max. Quantiles are not sent. The error margin is
sent as the `zio.error.margin` attribute. Frequencies become `count` events, one for each observed value, with the value in the
`zio.frequency.name` attribute. Metric labels become event attributes, with their names sanitized.

### Micrometer

The Micrometer connector creates Micrometer meters directly, so the registry decides the final format. The connector sets
the following properties:

- Histograms use the boundaries as service level objectives. Boundaries of zero or less are dropped, because Micrometer
  does not accept them.
- A histogram's base unit comes from a `time_unit` label. The connector removes that label from the tags.
- Summaries publish their quantiles as percentiles. The number of digits comes from `MicrometerConfig`.
- Frequencies are counters, with one meter for each observed value.

---

## Micrometer Connector

The Micrometer connector forwards ZIO metrics to [Micrometer](https://micrometer.io/), a vendor-neutral metrics facade for
the JVM. Micrometer then sends the metrics to whichever monitoring system its registry supports, such as Prometheus,
Datadog, or Graphite, so you can change the backend by changing the registry and not your instrumented code.

### How It Works

The connector registers a listener with the ZIO Metrics core client. Every metric update is forwarded to the Micrometer
registry as it happens, so the registry always reflects the current state of the application and no polling interval
is involved.

### Layers and Configuration

The connector needs a Micrometer `MeterRegistry` and a `MicrometerConfig`. The `micrometer.micrometerLayer` layer requires both in its environment. `MicrometerConfig.default` sets `summaryPercentileDigitsOfPrecision` to 3, and `MicrometerConfig(summaryPercentileDigitsOfPrecision = 2)` changes it. Micrometer ships a `SimpleMeterRegistry` that keeps metrics in memory, which is useful for tests. `Runtime.enableRuntimeMetrics` and `DefaultJvmMetrics.liveV2` are optional layers that add the ZIO runtime and JVM metrics.

Add the connector and a registry for your backend to your `build.sbt`. This example uses the Prometheus registry from Micrometer, which lives in the `io.micrometer.prometheusmetrics` package in Micrometer 1.17.2:

```sbt
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio"      %% "zio-metrics-connectors-micrometer" % "2.6.1",
  "io.micrometer" % "micrometer-registry-prometheus"    % "1.17.2",
)
```

The following application records a counter and provides all the layers:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.micrometer
import zio.metrics.connectors.micrometer.MicrometerConfig
import zio.metrics.jvm.DefaultJvmMetrics

import io.micrometer.prometheusmetrics.{PrometheusConfig, PrometheusMeterRegistry}

object MicrometerApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("micrometer_requests", "Requests seen by Micrometer").fromConst(1L)

  val program: UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.unit @@ requests *> ZIO.sleep(1.second)).forever

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(new PrometheusMeterRegistry(PrometheusConfig.DEFAULT)),
      ZLayer.succeed(MicrometerConfig.default),
      micrometer.micrometerLayer,
      Runtime.enableRuntimeMetrics,
      DefaultJvmMetrics.liveV2.unit,
    )
}
```

The registry is a `PrometheusMeterRegistry`, so the application can serve its output with `PrometheusMeterRegistry#scrape`.
The [sample application](https://github.com/zio/zio-metrics-connectors/blob/series/2.x/sample-app/src/main/scala/sample/SampleMicrometerApp.scala)
serves that output on `/micrometer/prometheusMetrics`. For the general approach to serving metrics over HTTP, see
[Serving Prometheus Metrics](../how-to/serve-prometheus-metrics.md). For the Micrometer metric type mapping, see
[Metric Type Mapping](./metric-type-mapping.md).

---

## New Relic Client

The New Relic connector sends metrics to the [New Relic Metric API](https://docs.newrelic.com/docs/data-apis/ingest-apis/metric-api/report-metrics-metric-api/)
over HTTPS. The instrumented code is the same as for the other connectors. The only difference is the layer that you
provide when the application starts. For a comparison of the connectors, see [Choose a Connector](../how-to/choose-a-connector.md).

### How Metrics Are Sent

The connector reads the ZIO Metrics registry on the `MetricsConfig` interval. It converts each changed metric into a JSON
event, as described in [Metric Type Mapping](./metric-type-mapping.md#new-relic). The events wait in a queue
until one of two conditions is met. Either the queue holds `maxMetricsPerRequest` events, or `maxPublishingDelay` elapses
after the last request. Then the connector sends the batch in one HTTPS request with the `Api-Key` header set to
your API key.

The queue holds up to twice `maxMetricsPerRequest` events. When the queue is full, the connector waits for room
before it queues more events.

The connector creates its own [zio-http](https://zio.dev/zio-http/) client with the default settings and uses `zio-json`
to build the request body. Both come with the `zio-metrics-connectors-newrelic` module as transitive dependencies. The
application cannot supply its own client, so the client's default TLS and proxy settings apply.

### Configure the Connector from the Environment

The `NewRelicConfig.fromEnvLayer` layer reads its settings from environment variables. The API key is required, and the
other settings have defaults. The [configuration reference](./configuration.md#new-relic) lists them all.

Set the API key in the shell before you start the application:

```bash
export NEW_RELIC_API_KEY="your-api-key"
```

Then provide the layers in your application. The following application records a counter every second:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.MetricsConfig
import zio.metrics.connectors.newrelic.{newRelicLayer, NewRelicConfig}

object NewRelicApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("nr_requests", "Requests handled").fromConst(1L)

  val program: UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.unit @@ requests *> ZIO.sleep(1.second)).forever

  override def run =
    program.provide(
      ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(10.seconds)),
      NewRelicConfig.fromEnvLayer,
      newRelicLayer,
    )
}
```

The application fails to start if `NEW_RELIC_API_KEY` is not set, because `NewRelicConfig.fromEnvLayer` reads it as a required value.

### Use the EU Endpoint

New Relic accounts in the EU region use a different endpoint. The `NewRelicConfig.fromEnvEULayer` layer reads the same
variables but always sends to the EU endpoint, so it ignores `NEW_RELIC_URI`. Replace `NewRelicConfig.fromEnvLayer` with
`NewRelicConfig.fromEnvEULayer` in the `provide` call above to use it.

### Configure the Connector in Code

To set the values in code, construct a `NewRelicConfig` directly. The constructor takes the API key, the endpoint, the
batch size, and the maximum publishing delay:

```scala
import java.time.Duration

import zio.metrics.connectors.newrelic.{NewRelicConfig, NewRelicUri}

val config: NewRelicConfig =
  NewRelicConfig(
    apiKey = sys.env("NEW_RELIC_API_KEY"),
    newRelicURI = NewRelicUri.EU,
    maxMetricsPerRequest = 500,
    maxPublishingDelay = Duration.ofSeconds(5),
  )
```

Provide the config with `ZLayer.succeed(config)` in place of `NewRelicConfig.fromEnvLayer`. Use `NewRelicUri.Custom` with
your own endpoint URL when you need an endpoint that the connector does not list.

### Next Steps

The [configuration reference](./configuration.md) lists every New Relic setting and default. The
[metric type mapping](./metric-type-mapping.md#new-relic) shows the events that the connector sends for each
metric type.

---

## Prometheus Client

In a normal prometheus setup we will find prometheus agents which query configured endpoints at regular intervals. The
endpoints are HTTP endpoints serving the current metric state in an encoding defined by
[prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/exposition_formats/#text-based-format).

ZIO Metrics Connectors provides the Prometheus encoding for the captured metrics out of the box. To avoid enforcing a
particular HTTP implementation, an instrumented application needs to expose the encoded format as an endpoint with the
HTTP server of its choice.

### ZIO Metrics in Prometheus

Most of the ZIO metrics have a direct representation in the Prometheus encoding.

#### Counter

A counter is represented as a prometheus counter.

```scala
Metric.counter("count_all", "The counter description.")
```

```
# TYPE count_all counter
# HELP count_all The counter description.
count_all 460.0 1623586224730
```

#### Gauge

A gauge is represented as a prometheus gauge.

```scala
Metric.gauge("adjust_gauge", "The gauge description.")
```

```
# TYPE adjust_gauge gauge
# HELP adjust_gauge The gauge description.
adjust_gauge -1.2485836762095701 1623586224730
```

#### Histogram

A histogram is represented as a prometheus histogram.

```scala
Metric.histogram(
  "my_histogram",
  "My histogram description.",
  MetricKeyType.Histogram.Boundaries.linear(0.0, 10.0, 11)
)
```

```
# TYPE my_histogram histogram
# HELP my_histogram My histogram description.
my_histogram_bucket{le="0.0"} 0.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="10.0"} 8.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="20.0"} 18.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="30.0"} 30.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="40.0"} 44.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="50.0"} 51.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="60.0"} 59.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="70.0"} 65.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="80.0"} 76.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="90.0"} 88.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="100.0"} 95.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_bucket{le="+Inf"} 115.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_sum 6828.578655207023 1623586224730
my_histogram_count 115.0 1623586224730
my_histogram_min 0.2 1623586224730
my_histogram_max 118.4 1623586224730
```

#### Summary

A summary is represented as a prometheus summary.

```scala
Metric.summary(
  "my_summary",
  "The summary description.",
  maxAge = ???,
  maxSize = ???,
  error = ???,
  quantiles = Chunk(0.1, 0.5, 0.9),
)
```

```
# TYPE my_summary summary
# HELP my_summary The summary description. 
my_summary{quantile="0.1",error="0.03"} 147.0 1623589839194
my_summary{quantile="0.5",error="0.03"} 286.0 1623589839194
my_summary{quantile="0.9",error="0.03"} 470.0 1623589839194
my_summary_sum 42582.0 1623589839194
my_summary_count 139.0 1623589839194
my_summary_min 3.0 1623589839194
my_summary_max 512.0 1623589839194
```

#### Frequency

A frequency is represented by a set of prometheus counters, distinguished from each other with a label.

```scala
val aspSet = Metric.frequency("my_set", "My set description.")
ZIO.succeed("my_key_10") @@ aspSet
ZIO.succeed("my_key_11") @@ aspSet
// etc.
```

```
# TYPE my_set counter
# HELP my_set My set description.
my_set{bucket="my_key_17"} 7.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_18"} 9.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_19"} 12.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_13"} 6.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_14"} 4.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_15"} 6.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_16"} 5.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_10"} 10.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_11"} 1.0 1623589839194
my_set{bucket="my_key_12"} 10.0 1623589839194
```

### Serving the Encoded Metrics

The encoded state is stored in the `PrometheusPublisher`, and the application retrieves it with `PrometheusPublisher#get`. The resulting string can be used in an HTTP response that has a `Content-Type` header with value `text/plain; version=0.0.4`. For a complete route and server, see [How to Serve Prometheus Metrics over HTTP](../how-to/serve-prometheus-metrics.md). For a walkthrough from instrumentation to a scraped endpoint, follow the [tutorial](../tutorial/instrument-and-scrape.md). To chart the metrics, see [How to Visualize Prometheus Metrics in Grafana](../how-to/visualize-metrics-in-grafana.md).
