## StatsD Client

In a normal StatsD setup we will find a StatsD agent with an open UDP port where applications send their 
metrics to. The format of the metrics is defined in simple [datagrams](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/datagram_shell/?tab=metrics). 

The StatsD client creates the relevant StatsD datagrams and sends them via UDP.

> The instrumented code is exactly the same as for the Prometheus instrumentation. The only difference is that 
> another client is provided when the App is configured. 

### ZIO Metrics in StatsD

StatsD normally has its own definition how histograms and summaries are configured. In the default setup this 
is defined in the config file of the statsd agent. Furthermore, a StatsD Histogram is more or less the
equivalent of a Prometheus summary. 

However, whenever the desired quantiles need to change, the config must be adjusted and the agent restarted. 

Therefore, the client maps the more complex metrics to a set of related gauges. This allows us to achieve 
the same visualization without the need to adjust any of the agents config files. 

#### Counter 

On each poll, a datagram is sent with the change since the previous poll, as in:

```
countAll:1|c
```

#### Gauge 

Whenever a gauge changes, a datagram with the current absolute value of the gauge is reported.
```
adjustGauge:32.2787317766752|g
```

#### Histogram 

A histogram is reported in a datagram built from related gauges. The individual records share the same name
and the buckets are encoded in an extra label `le`. 

```
myHistogram:0|g|#le:0.0
myHistogram:3|g|#le:10.0
myHistogram:6|g|#le:20.0
myHistogram:10|g|#le:30.0
myHistogram:13|g|#le:40.0
myHistogram:16|g|#le:50.0
myHistogram:19|g|#le:60.0
myHistogram:22|g|#le:70.0
myHistogram:24|g|#le:80.0
myHistogram:27|g|#le:90.0
myHistogram:29|g|#le:100.0
myHistogram:37|g|#le:Inf
```

#### Summary 

A summary is also reported as a set of related gauges. Each quantile will be reported within its own gauge. 
The additional labels are `quantile` to address the quantile and `error` to display the configured error margin. 

```
mySummary:123|g|#quantile:0.1,error:0.03
mySummary:254|g|#quantile:0.5,error:0.03
mySummary:441|g|#quantile:0.9,error:0.03
```

#### Frequencies

Frequencies are reported as sets of related gauges. An additional label is used to differentiate the distinct 
values in the set. The label is named `bucket`.

```
mySet:6|g|#bucket:my_key_18
mySet:1|g|#bucket:my_key_19
mySet:2|g|#bucket:my_key_13
mySet:3|g|#bucket:my_key_14
mySet:1|g|#bucket:my_key_16
mySet:3|g|#bucket:my_key_10
mySet:2|g|#bucket:my_key_11
mySet:1|g|#bucket:my_key_12
```

### The ZIO Metrics StatsD example

For StatsD we do not need to start a server in the application. We provide a client that sends datagrams to a specified
UDP destination. The following application counts a request every second. It provides the `statsdUDP` layer. Building
this layer starts the reporting, so it is provided even though the program does not use the `StatsdClient` directly:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric
import zio.metrics.connectors.MetricsConfig
import zio.metrics.connectors.statsd.{statsdUDP, StatsdConfig}

object StatsdApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val requests: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("countAll", "Requests handled").fromConst(1L)

  val program: UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.unit @@ requests *> ZIO.sleep(1.second)).forever

  override def run =
    program.provideLayer(
      (ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(100.millis)) ++ ZLayer.succeed(StatsdConfig("localhost", 8125))) >>> statsdUDP
    )
}
```

The layer polls the ZIO Metrics registry on the `MetricsConfig` interval. On each poll it sends the metrics that changed since the previous poll to StatsD as datagrams.

### Configuration

The StatsD client takes a `StatsdConfig` when it sends datagrams over UDP, and a `DatagramSocketConfig` when it sends them to a unix domain socket. The `statsdUDP` and `statsdUDS` layers read these settings. They also read `MetricsConfig`, which sets how often the metrics registry is polled.

Every field and default of `StatsdConfig` and `DatagramSocketConfig` is listed in the [configuration reference](./configuration.md#statsd).

`StatsdConfig.default` points to `localhost` on port `8125`. `DatagramSocketConfig` has a `path` field instead of `host` and `port`, and it accepts the same `prefix`, `constantTags` and `suffix` fields. If a datagram cannot be sent, the client drops it without raising an error.

#### Prefix

The `prefix` is prepended to every metric name, including each bucket line of a histogram. Any separator has to be part of the prefix. To report all metrics under `myapp.`:

```scala
import zio.metrics.connectors.statsd.StatsdConfig

val config = StatsdConfig("localhost", 8125, prefix = Some("myapp."))
```

With this configuration, a counter named `countAll` that reaches 1 is sent as:

```
myapp.countAll:1|c
```

#### Constant Tags

The `constantTags` are added to every datagram, before the tags of the metric itself. Use them for values that are the same across the whole application, such as the environment:

```scala
import zio.metrics.MetricLabel
import zio.metrics.connectors.statsd.StatsdConfig

val config = StatsdConfig(
  host = "localhost",
  port = 8125,
  constantTags = List(MetricLabel("env", "prod"), MetricLabel("service", "checkout")),
)
```

With these tags, the same counter is sent as:

```
countAll:1|c|#env:prod,service:checkout
```

A metric with its own tags, such as `region:eu`, appends them after the constant tags: `countAll:1|c|#env:prod,service:checkout,region:eu`.

The `suffix` is appended to the end of every datagram, after the tags. The client adds it as written, so include any separator in the value yourself.

To send these datagrams to a Datadog agent, see [How to Send Metrics to Datadog](../how-to/send-metrics-to-datadog.md).

---

## Tutorial: Instrument an App and Scrape Metrics with Prometheus

In this tutorial, we instrument a small ZIO application with two metrics, a counter and a gauge. We serve the metrics
over HTTP at `/metrics`, check the output with `curl`, and point a Prometheus server at the endpoint. By the end, you
will have a working setup that you can adapt to your own application.

The tutorial uses sbt and assumes you know how to write a basic `ZIOAppDefault`.

### Add the Dependencies

We need the Prometheus connector to encode the metrics, and zio-http to serve them. Add both to your `build.sbt`:

```sbt
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-metrics-connectors-prometheus" % "2.6.1",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-http"                          % "3.4.0",
)
```

The connector brings in the core ZIO Metrics library, so no other dependency is needed for metrics.

### Define the Metrics

We define a counter that counts processed orders and a gauge that shows how many orders are waiting. A metric is a value
that you apply to an effect with `@@`. The effect keeps its type, so applying a metric does not change how the code runs. The `OrderService` object defines both metrics:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.Metric

object OrderService {

  val ordersProcessed: Metric.Counter[Any] =
    Metric.counter("orders_processed", "Number of processed orders").fromConst(1L)

  val queueDepth: Metric.Gauge[Double] =
    Metric.gauge("queue_depth", "Number of orders waiting to be processed")

  def processOrder(id: Int): UIO[Unit] =
    (ZIO.sleep(50.millis) *> ZIO.unit) @@ ordersProcessed

}
```

The counter uses `fromConst(1L)`, so each call to `OrderService.processOrder` adds 1 to the count. The `Metric.Counter[Any]` type
means that the counter can be applied to any effect. The gauge takes a `Double`, and we set its value directly in the
next steps.

### Serve the Metrics Endpoint

The connector stores the encoded metrics in a `PrometheusPublisher`. The HTTP route reads that text with
`PrometheusPublisher#get` and returns it with the content type that Prometheus expects:

```scala
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets

import zio._
import zio.http._
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus.PrometheusPublisher

val metricsRoute: Route[PrometheusPublisher, Nothing] =
  Method.GET / "metrics" -> handler {
    ZIO.serviceWithZIO[PrometheusPublisher](_.get).map { body =>
      Response(
        status = Status.Ok,
        headers = Headers(Header.Custom(Header.ContentType.name, "text/plain; version=0.0.4")),
        body = Body.fromString(body, StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
      )
    }
  }

val routes: Routes[PrometheusPublisher, Nothing] = Routes(metricsRoute)
```

The `text/plain; version=0.0.4` content type identifies the Prometheus text format that the encoder produces.

### Run the Workload

We run the workload in a background fiber. Each second it processes five orders, then sets the queue depth to 3:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.metrics.connectors.prometheus.PrometheusPublisher

val workload: UIO[Unit] =
  (for {
    _ <- ZIO.foreachDiscard(1 to 5)(OrderService.processOrder)
    _ <- OrderService.queueDepth.set(3.0)
    _ <- ZIO.sleep(1.second)
  } yield ()).forever
```

### Wire the Layers and Start the Server

The application provides the server, the metrics layers, and the publisher. The `MetricsConfig` sets how often the connector
copies the metrics into the publisher. Five seconds is enough for this tutorial:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.http._
import zio.metrics.connectors.{prometheus, MetricsConfig}

object TutorialApp extends ZIOAppDefault {

  override def run =
    (workload.forkDaemon *> Server.serve(routes))
      .provide(
        ZLayer.succeed(Server.Config.default.port(8080)),
        Server.live,
        ZLayer.succeed(MetricsConfig(5.seconds)),
        prometheus.publisherLayer,
        prometheus.prometheusLayer,
      )
}
```

The `publisherLayer` creates the `PrometheusPublisher`, and `prometheusLayer` starts the background task that refreshes
it. The `MetricsConfig` interval controls that refresh. For more on the interval, see
[Configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

### Check the Output

We start the application with `sbt run` and request the endpoint from another terminal:

```
curl http://localhost:8080/metrics
```

After a few seconds, the response looks similar to this. The timestamps and counts depend on when you request the page:

```
# TYPE queue_depth gauge
# HELP queue_depth Number of orders waiting to be processed
queue_depth 3.0 1794253675282
# TYPE orders_processed counter
# HELP orders_processed Number of processed orders
orders_processed 20.0 1794253675282
```

Each metric appears with a `# TYPE` line and a `# HELP` line, followed by its current value and a timestamp in
milliseconds. The counter name is unchanged, with no `_total` suffix added.

### Scrape the Endpoint with Prometheus

Prometheus pulls metrics from the endpoint on a schedule that you configure. This `prometheus.yml` entry scrapes the
application every 15 seconds:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: zio-orders
    scrape_interval: 15s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["localhost:8080"]
```

Start Prometheus with this file, and the two metrics appear in its expression browser under the names `orders_processed`
and `queue_depth`.

### Next Steps

You now have a complete pipeline from a ZIO effect to a Prometheus scrape. To go further:

- [Serving Prometheus Metrics](../how-to/serve-prometheus-metrics.md) explains the endpoint in more detail.
- [Adding Labels to Metrics](../how-to/add-labels.md) shows how to split one metric into several series.
- [Choosing a Connector](../how-to/choose-a-connector.md) compares Prometheus with the push-based connectors.
- [Metric Type Mapping](../reference/metric-type-mapping.md) lists how each metric type appears in every backend.

## Error Handling(Zio-parser)

Parsing and printing both report failures as values. This page explains the error types, how to name the parts of a grammar so errors say where they happened, and how to turn errors into readable messages.

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
import zio.parser.Parser.ParserError
```

### Error Types

`parseString` and `parseChars` return `Either[StringParserError[Err], Value]`. A `StringParserError` holds the original `input` and a `ParserError[Err]`. `parseChunk` returns the `ParserError[Err]` directly. A `ParserError` has these cases:

| Case                                  | Meaning                                                              |
|---------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Failure(nameStack, position, failure)` | A syntax failed with your own error value of type `Err`            |
| `UnknownFailure(nameStack, position)` | A failure without a custom value (only from `unsafe*` syntaxes)     |
| `UnexpectedEndOfInput(nameStack)`     | The input ended before the syntax was complete                       |
| `NotConsumedAll(nameStack, position)` | `Syntax.end` found input left over                                   |
| `AllBranchesFailed(left, right)`      | Every alternative of a `\|` failed. Each branch's error is kept      |

`nameStack` lists the names of the enclosing named syntaxes (see [Naming Syntaxes](#naming-syntaxes)). `position` is the index in the input.

```scala
val number: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.transform(_.toInt, _.toString)

val pair: Syntax[String, Char, Char, (Int, Int)] =
  number ~ Syntax.char(',') ~ number
```

A syntax stops as soon as it has parsed a value and does not look at the rest of the input. To require that everything is consumed, finish with `Syntax.end`:

```scala
val completePair: Syntax[String, Char, Char, (Int, Int)] = pair <~ Syntax.end
```

```scala
pair.parseString("1;2")
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], Tuple2[Int, Int]] = Left(
//   StringParserError(
//     input = "1;2",
//     error = Failure(nameStack = List(), position = 1, failure = "not ','")
//   )
// )
pair.parseString("1,")
// res1: Either[StringParserError[String], Tuple2[Int, Int]] = Left(
//   StringParserError(input = "1,", error = UnexpectedEndOfInput(List()))
// )
pair.parseString("1,2 and more")
// res2: Either[StringParserError[String], Tuple2[Int, Int]] = Right((1, 2))
completePair.parseString("1,2 and more")
// res3: Either[StringParserError[String], Tuple2[Int, Int]] = Left(
//   StringParserError(
//     input = "1,2 and more",
//     error = NotConsumedAll(nameStack = List(), position = 3)
//   )
// )
```

You can match on the error like any other value:

```scala
pair.parseString("1;2") match {
  case Left(StringParserError(_, ParserError.Failure(_, position, message))) =>
    s"$message at $position"
  case Left(other)  => other.toString
  case Right(value) => value.toString
}
// res4: String = "not ',' at 1"
```

### Pretty Printing Errors

`StringParserError#pretty` renders the error together with the relevant lines of the input and a caret under the failing position:

```scala
println(pair.parseString("1;2").left.map(_.pretty).merge)
// 1;2
//  ^
// error: Failure at position 1: not ','
//
```

Errors without a position, such as `UnexpectedEndOfInput` and `AllBranchesFailed`, are printed as a single line without the input. For a multi-line input only the lines around the error are shown.

### Custom Error Types

Most constructors default to a `String` error, and most also have a variant that takes your own failure value, for example `Syntax.char(c, failure)`, `Syntax.regex(regex, failure)` and `Syntax.filterChar(p, failure)`. Combine them with `mapError` to move to a richer error type:

```scala
enum ConfigError {
  case BadNumber(text: String)
  case Other(message: String)
}

val port: Syntax[ConfigError, Char, Char, Int] =
  Syntax
    .digit
    .repeat
    .string
    .mapError(ConfigError.Other(_))
    .transformEither[ConfigError, Int](
      s => s.toIntOption.toRight(ConfigError.BadNumber(s)),
      n => Right(n.toString)
    )
```

```scala
port.parseString("8080")
// res6: Either[StringParserError[ConfigError], Int] = Right(8080)
port.parseString("99999999999")
// res7: Either[StringParserError[ConfigError], Int] = Left(
//   StringParserError(
//     input = "99999999999",
//     error = Failure(
//       nameStack = List(),
//       position = 11,
//       failure = BadNumber("99999999999")
//     )
//   )
// )
```

`transformEither` and `filter` are the usual places to produce domain errors, while `transformOption` reports failures as `None`.

### Naming Syntaxes

Add a name to a syntax with `named` or its alias `??`. The name is pushed on the `nameStack` of any error raised inside, and `pretty` shows the chain:

```scala
val namedNumber = number ?? "number"
val namedPair   = (namedNumber ~ Syntax.char(',') ~ namedNumber) ?? "pair"
```

```scala
println(namedPair.parseString("1;2").left.map(_.pretty).merge)
// 1;2
//  ^
// error: Failure at position 1: not ',' in pair
//
```

### Errors from Alternatives

With `|`, the parser tries each branch in order. If one succeeds, the failures of the earlier branches are discarded. If all fail, you get `AllBranchesFailed`, which `pretty` prints as `All branches failed: ... and ...`:

```scala
val boolean: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Boolean] =
  Syntax.string("true", true) | Syntax.string("false", false)
```

```scala
boolean.parseString("maybe") match {
  case Left(StringParserError(_, ParserError.AllBranchesFailed(left, right))) =>
    (left.getClass.getSimpleName, right.getClass.getSimpleName)
  case other => other
}
// res9: Tuple2[String, String] | Either[StringParserError[String], Boolean] = (
//   "Failure",
//   "Failure"
// )
```

### Backtracking and Errors

By default a failing branch of `|` rewinds the input, so the next branch starts at the same position. `manualBacktracking` disables that rewind for a syntax and `backtrack` restores it at selected points. See [Building Syntaxes](syntax.md#backtracking).

### Printing Errors

The `Err` type is shared between the parser and the printer, and printing returns `Either[Err, ...]`. A printer fails when a `filter` condition does not hold, when a `transformTo` partial function does not cover a value, or when a `widen` finds no matching alternative:

```scala
Syntax.digit.filter[String, Char](_ != '0', "no zeros").printString('0')
// res10: Either[String, String] = Left("no zeros")
```

Next: the [worked example](example-json.md).

## Example: a GraphQL Parser

The `zio-parser-caliban` module is a real-world parser built with ZIO Parser. It parses GraphQL documents, the query language used by the [Caliban](https://github.com/ghostdogpr/caliban) library. Unlike the JSON example, it is a production grammar with many rules, and it shows how a large grammar is organized into small named parts.

This page shows how to call the parser and what it accepts. The full source is in [`zio-parser-caliban/src/main/scala/zio/parser/caliban/CalibanParser.scala`](https://github.com/zio/zio-parser/blob/master/zio-parser-caliban/src/main/scala/zio/parser/caliban/CalibanParser.scala).

### Using the Module

The module lives in this repository, next to the core library. It is not published as a separate artifact, so use it from a checkout of the repository or copy its source into your project. The examples on this page run against the same source during the documentation build.

```scala
import zio.parser.caliban.CalibanParser
```

### Parsing a Query

`CalibanParser.document` is a `Syntax` for a whole GraphQL document. Calling `parseString` on it gives an `Either`, just like any other syntax in this library. We parse a small query with a field and a nested selection:

```scala
CalibanParser.document.parseString("{ hero { name } }").map(_.definitions.length)
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], Int] = Right(1)
```

The result has one definition. A document with a syntax error returns a `Left` with the same `StringParserError` type you saw in the [error handling](errors.md) page:

```scala
CalibanParser.document.parseString("{ hero { name } ").left.map(_.pretty).merge
// res1: String | ParsedDocument = "All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: Failure at position 0: Not 'query' and Failure at position 0: Not 'mutation' and Failure at position 0: Not 'subscription' and Unexpected end of input and Failure at position 0: Not 'fragment' and All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: All branches failed: Failure at position 0: Not 'type' and Failure at position 0: Not 'interface' and Failure at position 0: Not 'input' and Failure at position 0: Not 'enum' and Failure at position 0: Not 'union' and Failure at position 0: Not 'scalar' and Failure at position 0: Not 'schema' and Failure at position 0: Not 'directive @' and Failure at position 0: Not 'extend '"
```

### Checking a Query

When you only need to know whether a query is valid, `CalibanParser.check` returns `None` for a valid query, and `Some` with the error text for an invalid one:

```scala
CalibanParser.check("{ hero { name } }")
// res2: Option[String] = None
```

:::note
`CalibanParser.parseQuery` wraps the same parser in a `ZIO`, and turns parse failures into a `ParsingError` that Caliban can report. It also catches unexpected exceptions. Use it inside a `ZIO` program.
:::

### What the Grammar Accepts

GraphQL allows commas as optional separators, and `#` comments anywhere between tokens. The module handles both by defining a shared whitespace syntax that skips spaces, line breaks, commas, the byte order mark, and comments. This is the same technique described in the [whitespace and comments](how-to-whitespace-and-comments.md) guide.

The grammar is split into many named `lazy val`s, one per GraphQL construct, such as `typeDefinition`, `objectTypeExtension` and `directiveDefinition`. The top-level `document` refers to them, and each one can be read on its own. Recursive constructs, such as selection sets inside fields, are `lazy val`s for the same reason explained in [recursive syntaxes](how-to-recursive-syntaxes.md).

### Where to Go Next

- Read the module's [tests](https://github.com/zio/zio-parser/tree/master/zio-parser-caliban/src/test/scala/zio/parser/caliban) for more query examples, including invalid ones.
- Compare with [Example: a JSON Syntax](example-json.md), which builds a small grammar from scratch.

---

## Example: a JSON Syntax

This example builds a complete JSON syntax. One definition parses JSON text into a small AST and prints the AST back to text. It is adapted from the example in the library's tests.

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
```

### The AST

```scala
sealed abstract class Json
object Json {
  final case class Obj(fields: Chunk[(String, Json)]) extends Json
  final case class Arr(elements: Chunk[Json])         extends Json
  final case class Bool(value: Boolean)               extends Json
  final case class Str(value: String)                 extends Json
  final case class Num(value: BigDecimal)             extends Json
  case object Null                                    extends Json
}
```

### Whitespace

JSON allows any amount of whitespace between tokens. The parser accepts all of it, and the printer writes a single space:

```scala
val whitespace: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Char]  = Syntax.charIn(' ', '\t', '\r', '\n')
val whitespaces: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] = whitespace.*.asPrinted((), Chunk(' '))
```

### Scalar Values

Every scalar syntax produces its own subtype of `Json`:

```scala
val nul: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Json.Null.type] =
  Syntax.string("null", Json.Null)

val bool: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Json.Bool] =
  Syntax.string("true", Json.Bool(true)) | Syntax.string("false", Json.Bool(false))

val quote: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] = Syntax.char('"')

val str: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Json.Str] =
  (quote ~> Syntax.charNotIn('"').*.string <~ quote)
    .transform(Json.Str.apply, (s: Json.Str) => s.value)

val digits: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Chunk[Char]] = Syntax.digit.repeat

val num: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Json.Num] =
  (Syntax.char('-').? ~ digits ~ (Syntax.char('.') ~> digits).?).string
    .transform(s => Json.Num(BigDecimal(s)), (n: Json.Num) => n.value.toString)
```

The string syntax does not handle escape sequences, to keep the example short.

### Arrays and Objects

Arrays and objects contain `Json` values, so these syntaxes are recursive. Define them as `lazy val`:

```scala
val listSep: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  Syntax.char(',').surroundedBy(whitespaces)

lazy val list: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Json.Arr] =
  (Syntax.char('[') ~> json.repeatWithSep0(listSep) <~ Syntax.char(']'))
    .transform(Json.Arr.apply, (arr: Json.Arr) => arr.elements)

val keyValueSep: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  Syntax.char(':').surroundedBy(whitespaces)

lazy val keyValue: Syntax[String, Char, Char, (String, Json)] =
  (str ~ keyValueSep ~ json).transform[(String, Json)](
    { case (key, value) => (key.value, value) },
    { case (key, value) => (Json.Str(key), value) }
  )

lazy val obj: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Json.Obj] =
  (Syntax.char('{') ~> keyValue.repeatWithSep0(listSep).surroundedBy(whitespaces) <~ Syntax.char('}'))
    .transform(Json.Obj.apply, (o: Json.Obj) => o.fields)
```

### Putting It Together

`widen[Json]` turns each alternative into a `Syntax[..., Json]`. The parser tries them in order, and the printer uses the type of the value to find the alternative to print with:

```scala
lazy val json: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Json] =
  (nul.widen[Json] | bool.widen[Json] | str.widen[Json] | num.widen[Json] |
    list.widen[Json] | obj.widen[Json]) ?? "json"
```

### Parsing

```scala
val input = """{ "name": "zio-parser", "stars": [1, 2, 3], "stable": false, "next": null }"""
// input: String = "{ \"name\": \"zio-parser\", \"stars\": [1, 2, 3], \"stable\": false, \"next\": null }"

val parsed = json.parseString(input)
// parsed: Either[StringParserError[String], Json] = Right(
//   Obj(
//     IndexedSeq(
//       ("name", Str("zio-parser")),
//       ("stars", Arr(IndexedSeq(Num(1), Num(2), Num(3)))),
//       ("stable", Bool(false)),
//       ("next", Null)
//     )
//   )
// )
```

### Printing

The same `json` value prints the AST back:

```scala
parsed.flatMap(json.printString(_))
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String] | String, String] = Right(
//   "{ \"name\" : \"zio-parser\" , \"stars\" : [1 , 2 , 3] , \"stable\" : false , \"next\" : null }"
// )
```

Whitespace in the input is normalized, because `whitespaces` always prints a single space. Parsing the printed output gives the same AST:

```scala
parsed.flatMap(json.printString(_)).flatMap(json.parseString(_)) == parsed
// res1: Boolean = true
```

You can also build a document by hand and print it:

```scala
json.printString(Json.Arr(Chunk(Json.Num(BigDecimal(1)), Json.Bool(true), Json.Null)))
// res2: Either[String, String] = Right("[1 , true , null]")
```

### Errors

Parse failures are reported like in any other syntax. Because `json` tries six alternatives, `AllBranchesFailed` carries one failure per branch. See [Error handling](errors.md) for how to read them.

---

## Getting Started with ZIO Parser

This page parses a first value, prints it back and reads an error. Add ZIO Parser to your project first, as described in [Installation](index.md#installation).

### Importing

On Scala 3, import everything from the `zio.parser` package:

```scala
import zio.parser.*
```

On Scala 2, write `import zio.parser._` instead. The rest of the documentation uses the Scala 3 syntax.

### Declaring a Syntax

A `Syntax` is the description of a grammar. `Syntax.digit` matches one digit:

```scala
val digitSyntax: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Char] = Syntax.digit
```

### Parsing a String

`parseString` runs the syntax on a string and returns an `Either`:

```scala
val result: Either[StringParserError[String], Char] = digitSyntax.parseString("1")
// result: Either[StringParserError[String], Char] = Right('1')
```

### Printing a Value

The same syntax prints a value back with `printString`:

```scala
digitSyntax.printString('7')
// res0: Either[String, String] = Right("7")
```

### Reading an Error

When the input does not match, `parseString` returns a `StringParserError`. Its `pretty` method shows the failing position:

```scala
println(digitSyntax.parseString("Hello").left.map(_.pretty).merge)
// Hello
// ^
// error: Failure at position 0: not a digit
//
```

### Next Steps

- [Tutorial: Parse and Print a Config Language](tutorial.md) builds a complete parser and printer step by step.
- [Building Syntaxes](syntax.md) lists the combinators.
- [Printing and Invertible Syntaxes](printing.md) explains why one syntax works in both directions.

---

## How to Get Readable Error Messages

A parse error is only useful if it says what was expected and where. This guide shows how to name the parts of a grammar so that errors describe the failing part, and how to show the position of an error in a multi-line input.

The goal is a parser for points written as `x,y`, where the separator between the coordinates is named. A point written with `;` instead of `,` then produces a message such as `Not ',' at 1 in comma -> point`.

### The Problem

By default, an error only says what the failing rule was, such as `Not ','`. In a larger grammar, the same rule appears in many places, so the message alone does not tell you which field was wrong. A line number and a column help, but a bare index into the input is hard to map back to a line of a multi-line file.

ZIO Parser records a name stack for each error. Naming a syntax adds its name to that stack, and the error reports the chain of names that led to the failure.

### Prerequisites

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
import zio.parser.Parser.ParserError
```

### Naming the Parts

We parse a number, and then give the number a name for each coordinate. We also name the separator and the whole point. The `??` operator attaches a name to a syntax:

```scala
val int: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.transform(_.toInt, _.toString)

val x: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] = int ?? "x coordinate"
val y: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] = int ?? "y coordinate"

val point: Syntax[String, Char, Char, (Int, Int)] =
  (x ~ (Syntax.char(',') ?? "comma") ~ y) ?? "point"
```

The code above:

- `int ?? "x coordinate"` is the same number syntax, with a name that appears in errors inside it
- `Syntax.char(',') ?? "comma"` names the separator
- `(...) ?? "point"` names the whole point, so errors inside it also mention `point`

Now we parse a point whose separator is a `;`:

```scala
point.parseString("3;4").left.map(_.pretty).merge
// res0: String | Tuple2[Int, Int] = """3;4
//  ^
// error: Failure at position 1: not ',' in comma -> point
// """
```

The message names the separator and the point, and the caret under the `;` shows the position.

### Reading the Position Directly

When your code needs the position rather than the text, match on the error. `StringParserError` holds the input and a `ParserError`, and the failure cases carry the position:

```scala
point.parseString("3;4") match {
  case Left(StringParserError(_, ParserError.Failure(names, position, message))) =>
    s"$message at $position in ${names.mkString(" -> ")}"
  case Left(other)  => other.toString
  case Right(value) => value.toString
}
// res1: String = "not ',' at 1 in comma -> point"
```

The name stack lists the innermost name first, and then the names around it. In this message, `comma` is inside `point`, so the stack is `comma -> point`.

### Errors in Multi-Line Input

For a file with one point per line, each line is a point followed by a newline. A repetition stops at the first line it cannot read, so `Syntax.end` is what reports the failure. Its position is where reading stopped. The `pretty` message then shows the lines around that position, not the whole file:

```scala
val points: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Chunk[(Int, Int)]] =
  (point <~ Syntax.char('\n')).repeat0 <~ Syntax.end
```

```scala
points.parseString("1,2\n3,4\n5;6\n7,8\n").left.map(_.pretty).merge
// res2: String | Chunk[Tuple2[Int, Int]] = """1,2
// 3,4
// 5;6
// ^
// error: Parser did not consume all input at position 8
// 7,8
// """
```

The output shows up to two lines before and after the position, marks `...` where lines were left out, and puts a caret under the position.

:::tip
Name each syntax that a user writes, such as a field, a value or a section. A single character, such as a separator, is often clear enough without a name, but a name makes the message more precise.
:::

---

## How to Tune Parser Performance

A parser can be fast enough for most inputs without any tuning. When it is not, a few choices in how you write the syntax make a large difference. This guide covers the choices that matter most, and how to check their effect with a measurement.

The goal is to replace a character-by-character token with one regex step, and to pick the parser implementation that fits your input.

### The Problem

A syntax such as `Syntax.digit.repeat` runs one parsing step per character. Each step has overhead, and a long token pays that overhead for every character. Parsing a large file of numbers can then spend most of its time on that overhead.

ZIO Parser compiles a `Regex` into one matcher, so a whole token is checked in a single step.

### Prerequisites

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
```

### Matching Tokens with a Regex

We write the same token two ways. The first repeats a character syntax. The second matches the whole token with `Regex.digits`:

```scala
val charByChar: Syntax[String, Char, Char, String] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string

val wholeToken: Syntax[String, Char, Char, String] =
  Syntax.regex(Regex.digits, "not digits").string
```

Both produce the same result for the same input:

```scala
charByChar.parseString("2024")
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Right("2024")
wholeToken.parseString("2024")
// res1: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Right("2024")
```

The difference shows up in speed, not in the output. The regex version is preferred for tokens such as numbers, identifiers and whitespace, and combinators are the right tool for the structure that joins them. The [Regex reference](regex.md) lists the available regexes.

:::caution
Do not claim a speed-up from this change without measuring it on your own input. The repository has a `benchmarks` module with JMH benchmarks for the parser, and you can add your own benchmark with your real data.
:::

### Choosing the Parser Implementation

Parsing defaults to `ParserImplementation.Recursive`, which is the faster option. `ParserImplementation.StackSafe` is slower, but it does not overflow the stack on deeply nested input. Keep the default unless your input can be nested deeply enough to overflow the stack. The [Syntax reference](syntax.md#choosing-the-parser-implementation) describes both options in detail.

### Limiting Backtracking

By default, a failing branch of `|` rewinds the input, so the next branch starts at the same position. Rewinding costs work, and you can avoid it in grammars where the first character already tells you which branch to take. The [Syntax reference](syntax.md#backtracking) describes `manualBacktracking` and `backtrack`.

Turning backtracking off changes which inputs parse. A branch that consumed input and then failed will no longer hand the input back to the next branch. Make this change only where the grammar guarantees the choice from the first character, and test the change with inputs that take each branch.

### Measuring a Change

A single timing run on a laptop is not a reliable measure. Use a benchmark that runs the parser many times on realistic input, warms up the JVM first, and reports the spread of results. The `benchmarks` module in the repository shows how JMH benchmarks are set up for this library.

---

## How to Parse Nested Data

Many formats nest: a list can contain lists, a directory can contain directories, an expression can contain expressions. This guide shows how to describe such data with one recursive syntax that both parses and prints.

The goal is a syntax for a tree of numbers, written as nested brackets. For example, `[1,[2,3],[]]` is a node with three children: the leaf `1`, a node with two leaves, and an empty node.

### The Problem

A parser that calls itself directly, without a pause, never finishes building: the definition of the syntax would refer to itself before its value exists. Languages handle this with functions and lazy values. Writing the parser and the printer as two separate recursive functions doubles the work, and the two can drift apart.

ZIO Parser lets you write the recursive definition once, as a `lazy val`, and both directions follow from it.

### Prerequisites

The examples use these imports and the data types below:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*

sealed trait Tree
object Tree {
  final case class Leaf(value: Int)         extends Tree
  final case class Node(children: Chunk[Tree]) extends Tree
}
```

### Parsing a Leaf

A leaf is a single number. We parse the digits and convert them to an `Int`. The conversion can fail, so we use `transformEither`, which reports a failure instead of throwing an exception:

```scala
val leaf: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Tree.Leaf] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.transformEither[String, Tree.Leaf](
    digits => digits.toIntOption.map(Tree.Leaf(_)).toRight("number out of range"),
    leaf => Right(leaf.value.toString)
  )
```

The leaf does not refer to the tree, so it does not need `lazy`.

### Parsing a Node

A node is a pair of brackets around a list of trees separated by commas. The list refers back to `tree`, so both syntaxes are `lazy val`s:

```scala
lazy val tree: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Tree] =
  (leaf.widen[Tree] | node.widen[Tree]) ?? "tree"

lazy val node: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Tree.Node] =
  (Syntax.char('[') ~> tree.repeatWithSep0(Syntax.char(',')) <~ Syntax.char(']'))
    .transform[Tree.Node](Tree.Node(_), _.children)
```

The code above:

- `tree` is a leaf or a node. `widen` lets each alternative produce its own subtype and be used as `Tree`
- `??` gives the whole tree a name, so error messages can say where a failure happened
- `node` matches the brackets, and in between a comma-separated list of `tree`
- `transform` converts the list to a `Tree.Node`, and back when printing

Because `tree` is a `lazy val`, the reference inside `node` is evaluated only when the parser runs, not when the definitions are created. Without `lazy`, Scala would try to build `tree` while building `node`, which needs `tree` first.

### Parsing and Printing Nested Input

We parse a nested list, then print a tree built by hand:

```scala
tree.parseString("[1,[2,3],[]]")
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], Tree] = Right(
//   Node(
//     IndexedSeq(Leaf(1), Node(IndexedSeq(Leaf(2), Leaf(3))), Node(IndexedSeq()))
//   )
// )
```

```scala
tree.printString(Tree.Node(Chunk(Tree.Leaf(1), Tree.Node(Chunk(Tree.Leaf(2))))))
// res1: Either[String, String] = Right("[1,[2]]")
```

The printer writes the brackets and commas back in the same places the parser expects them, because both directions come from the same definition.

:::caution
Deeply nested input can overflow the JVM stack with the default parser implementation. If your data can be nested that deeply, pass `ParserImplementation.StackSafe` to `parseString`, as explained in the [Syntax reference](syntax.md#choosing-the-parser-implementation).
:::

---

## How to Print to a ZStream

Printing with `printString` builds the whole result in memory. When the output is large, or when another part of your program wants to consume it as it is produced, you can print into a `ZStream` instead. This guide shows how to use `ZStreamTarget` to do that.

The goal is to print a stream of characters from a syntax and read the first few characters from the stream.

### The Problem

`print` and `printString` return a finished `Chunk` or `String`. For a value that produces megabytes of output, the whole output sits in memory before anything can use it. A streaming API lets the consumer start working on the first characters right away.

`Printer` writes each output element to a `Target`. A `Target` is the destination for the output. `ChunkTarget` collects the output, and `ZStreamTarget` pushes it into a queue that a `ZStream` reads from.

### Prerequisites

```scala
import zio.{Runtime, Unsafe}
import zio.parser.*
import zio.parser.target.ZStreamTarget
```

### Creating the Target

`ZStreamTarget` needs a `zio` runtime to run its queue operations. The companion object's `apply` is an effect that captures the runtime of the fiber that runs it, and returns the target. In an example like this one, we run that effect directly:

```scala
val target: ZStreamTarget[Any, Char] = Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  Runtime.default.unsafe.run(ZStreamTarget[Char]).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
}
```

The code above:

- `ZStreamTarget[Char]` creates a target for `Char` output, and returns it as a `UIO`
- `Runtime.default.unsafe.run` runs that effect, and `getOrThrowFiberFailure` returns the target or throws if creating it failed
- `Unsafe.unsafe` is required to run an effect outside of a `ZIO` program

In an application that already runs effects, use `ZStreamTarget[Char]` inside your `ZIO` code instead.

### Printing into the Target

We print a number with a syntax, writing its characters into the target:

```scala
val number: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.transform(_.toInt, _.toString)
```

```scala
number.print(42, target)
// res0: Either[String, Unit] = Right(())
```

The result is `Right(())` when printing succeeds. The characters are now in the target's queue, and nothing has read them yet.

### Reading the Stream

The target's `stream` field is a `ZStream` that reads the queue. We read two characters from it, and collect them into a `Chunk`:

```scala
val firstTwo = Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  Runtime.default.unsafe.run(target.stream.take(2).runCollect).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
}
// firstTwo: Chunk[Char] = IndexedSeq('4', '2')

firstTwo.mkString
// res1: String = "42"
```

We used `take(2)` on purpose. The stream never ends by itself, because nothing closes the queue when printing finishes. A consumer must take the number of elements it needs, or stop the stream with an interrupt.

:::caution
`ZStreamTarget` does not signal the end of the output. Reading the stream without `take` waits forever after the last character. Use `take`, `takeUntil` or a timeout to bound the read.
:::

:::tip
When a printer tries an alternative, the target captures its output first. Output from an alternative that fails is discarded and never reaches the stream.
:::

---

## How to Parse Whitespace and Comments

Real input is rarely tight. People put spaces around separators, break lines in odd places and leave comments. This guide shows how to accept all of that when parsing, while keeping control of what the printer writes.

The goal is a syntax for a list of numbers, such as `1, 2, 3`, that also accepts `#` comments and extra whitespace anywhere between the items.

### The Problem

A parser that only expects `1,2,3` rejects `1 , 2  # two`, even though a human reads both the same way. Writing the whitespace handling by hand in every place it may appear makes the grammar hard to read and easy to get wrong.

ZIO Parser solves this by describing "skippable text" once and reusing that description. The printer then decides separately how much whitespace to write.

### Prerequisites

The examples use the same imports as the [tutorial](tutorial.md):

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
```

### Matching a Comment

A comment starts with `#` and runs to the end of the line. We match the `#` and then every character that is not a newline. The matched text is not needed, so we discard it with `unit`, which takes the value the printer should use for the discarded result:

```scala
val comment: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  (Syntax.char('#') ~> Syntax.notChar('\n').repeat0).unit(Chunk.empty)
```

The code above:

- `Syntax.char('#')` matches the `#` and produces no value
- `~>` drops that result and keeps the result of `Syntax.notChar('\n').repeat0`
- `unit(Chunk.empty)` discards the text, and tells the printer to write nothing for it

### Skipping Whitespace and Comments

We combine a single space and a comment into one syntax, and repeat it to skip any amount of both:

```scala
val skip: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  (Syntax.whitespace.unit(' ') | comment).repeat0.unit(Chunk.empty)
```

The code above:

- `Syntax.whitespace.unit(' ')` matches one whitespace character, and would print a space
- `|` tries the whitespace first, and falls back to a comment
- `repeat0` allows zero or more of either
- `unit(Chunk.empty)` makes the whole skip print nothing

The last point matters when we print. Because `skip` prints nothing, the printer must get its spacing from somewhere else. We come back to this below.

### Parsing Items Between Skippable Text

Each number is surrounded by `skip`, and the items are separated by commas:

```scala
val number: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.transform(_.toInt, _.toString)

val numbers: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Chunk[Int]] =
  (skip ~> number <~ skip).repeatWithSep0(Syntax.char(','))
```

Now we parse input with spaces and comments in several places:

```scala
numbers.parseString("1 , 2  # two\n, 3")
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], Chunk[Int]] = Right(
//   IndexedSeq(1, 2, 3)
// )
```

The parser skipped the spaces around each number, skipped the comment `# two` and the newline after it, and read the three numbers.

### Printing with Explicit Spacing

Because `skip` prints nothing, printing the same syntax gives no spaces:

```scala
numbers.printString(Chunk(1, 2, 3))
// res1: Either[String, String] = Right("1,2,3")
```

To print a space after each comma, we build the separator from a comma followed by optional whitespace. The parser accepts any amount of whitespace there, and `asPrinted` makes the printer write exactly one space:

```scala
val spaces: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  Syntax.whitespace.repeat0.asPrinted((), Chunk(' '))

val comma: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  Syntax.char(',') ~> spaces

val spacedNumbers: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Chunk[Int]] =
  (skip ~> number <~ skip).repeatWithSep0(comma)
```

Printing now writes a space after each comma, and the parser still accepts the same input:

```scala
spacedNumbers.printString(Chunk(1, 2, 3))
// res2: Either[String, String] = Right("1, 2, 3")
spacedNumbers.parseString("1 , 2  # two\n, 3")
// res3: Either[StringParserError[String], Chunk[Int]] = Right(
//   IndexedSeq(1, 2, 3)
// )
```

:::tip
To skip whitespace with no comments, `Syntax.unsafeRegexDiscard(Regex.whitespace, Chunk(' '))` skips any amount of whitespace, including line breaks, in one regex step, and prints one space. Regexes match faster than repeated single-character syntaxes. See the [Regex reference](regex.md).
:::

:::caution
Whitespace and comments are both skipped when parsing, so you cannot tell them apart in the result. If the output needs the original comments, parse them into a value of their own instead of discarding them.
:::

## Introduction to ZIO Parser

Library for constructing parsers and pretty printers based on invertible syntax descriptions

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-parser/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-parser_3.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-parser_3) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-parser_3%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-parser_3/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-parser_3/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-parser_3) [![ZIO Parser](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-parser?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-parser)

### Introduction

ZIO Parser describes a grammar once, as a `Syntax`, and uses that description in both directions: it parses text into values and prints values back to text. Because one value drives both, a parser and its pretty printer cannot drift apart.

The library gives you small building blocks (characters, strings, regexes), operators to combine them, and error values that say where and why a parse failed.

### Installation

Add ZIO Parser to your `build.sbt`. It is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3.

On the JVM, use `%%`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // ZIO Parser: syntaxes, parsers, printers and regexes (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-parser" % "0.1.13"
)
```

On Scala.js and Scala Native, use `%%%`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // ZIO Parser: syntaxes, parsers, printers and regexes (Scala.js and Scala Native)
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-parser" % "0.1.13"
)
```
