## Printing and Invertible Syntaxes

What sets ZIO Parser apart from most parser libraries is that the description of a grammar is *invertible*. The same `Syntax` value that parses a string can also print a value back to a string, so the two directions cannot drift apart.

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
```

### Printing a Value

Every `Syntax` has three printing methods:

| Method                     | Result                    | Description                                      |
|----------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `printString(value)`       | `Either[Err, String]`     | Prints to a `String` (requires `Out` to be `Char`) |
| `print(value)`             | `Either[Err, Chunk[Out]]` | Prints to a `Chunk` of output elements           |
| `print(value, target)`     | `Either[Err, Unit]`       | Writes to a [`Target`](#printing-to-a-target)    |

```scala
val number: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.transform(_.toInt, _.toString)

val range: Syntax[String, Char, Char, (Int, Int)] =
  number ~ Syntax.char('-') ~ number
```

```scala
range.parseString("10-20")
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], Tuple2[Int, Int]] = Right((10, 20))
range.printString((10, 20))
// res1: Either[String, String] = Right("10-20")
range.print((1, 2))
// res2: Either[String, Chunk[Char]] = Right(IndexedSeq('1', '-', '2'))
```

### Round Trips

For a well-formed syntax, parsing the printed output gives back the original value:

```scala
range.printString((3, 9)).flatMap(range.parseString(_))
// res3: Either[String | StringParserError[String], Tuple2[Int, Int]] = Right(
//   (3, 9)
// )
```

### Writing Syntaxes That Print

A parser only has to turn text into a value. A printer has to do the opposite, so every step that loses information on the way in needs a hint on how to restore it on the way out.

#### Constant results

`as(value)` maps a `Unit` syntax to a constant. When printing, the printer is given that constant and writes the original text again:

```scala
sealed trait Op
case object Plus  extends Op
case object Minus extends Op

val op: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Op] =
  Syntax.char('+').as(Plus: Op) | Syntax.char('-').as(Minus: Op)
```

`Syntax.char('+').as(Plus)` parses `+` into `Plus`, and when asked to print `Plus` it prints `+`. The printer compares the value it is given with `Plus`, so the second alternative is tried for `Minus`:

```scala
op.parseString("-")
// res4: Either[StringParserError[String], Op] = Right(Minus)
op.printString(Minus)
// res5: Either[String, String] = Right("-")
op.printString(Plus)
// res6: Either[String, String] = Right("+")
```

#### Discarded results need a value to print

A syntax whose result is thrown away, such as whitespace, has no value for the printer. `asPrinted(result, value)` says what to print instead:

```scala
val spaces: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  Syntax.whitespace.repeat0.asPrinted((), Chunk(' '))

val assignment: Syntax[String, Char, Char, (String, Int)] =
  (Syntax.letter.repeat.string ~ Syntax.char('=').surroundedBy(spaces) ~ number)
```

```scala
assignment.parseString("x   =   5")
// res7: Either[StringParserError[String], Tuple2[String, Int]] = Right(
//   ("x", 5)
// )
assignment.printString(("x", 5))
// res8: Either[String, String] = Right("x = 5")
```

The parser accepts any amount of whitespace around `=`, and the printer produces exactly one space.

#### Subtypes need `widen` or `transformTo`

When a syntax produces a parent type but each alternative produces a subtype, the printer needs to find the alternative that fits a value. `widen[T]` does this with a runtime class check, and `transformTo` takes a partial function and an error for the values it does not cover:

```scala
sealed trait Shape
final case class Circle(r: Int)         extends Shape
final case class Square(side: Int)      extends Shape

val circle: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Circle] =
  (Syntax.string("circle ", ()) ~> number).transform(Circle.apply, _.r)

val square: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Square] =
  (Syntax.string("square ", ()) ~> number).transform(Square.apply, _.side)

val shape: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Shape] =
  circle.widen[Shape] | square.widen[Shape]
```

```scala
shape.parseString("square 4")
// res9: Either[StringParserError[String], Shape] = Right(Square(4))
shape.printString(Circle(2))
// res10: Either[String, String] = Right("circle 2")
shape.printString(Square(7))
// res11: Either[String, String] = Right("square 7")
```

#### Printing can fail

Printing returns an `Either`. A syntax can reject values it cannot print, for example when a `filter` condition is not met or a `transformTo` partial function is not defined:

```scala
val small: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  number.filter[String, Int](_ < 100, "too big")
```

```scala
small.printString(5)
// res12: Either[String, String] = Right("5")
small.printString(500)
// res13: Either[String, String] = Left("too big")
```

### Printers on Their Own

`Syntax` is a pair of a `Parser` and a `Printer`, available as `asParser` and `asPrinter`. A `Printer` can be used independently, for example for pretty printing a data structure that you never parse:

```scala
val printer: Printer[String, Char, Int] = number.asPrinter
```

```scala
printer.printString(42)
// res14: Either[String, String] = Right("42")
```

`Printer.printString(str)`, `Printer.char(c)` and `Printer.byValue` let you build printers by hand. Combine a `Parser` and a `Printer` into a syntax with `parser <=> printer`.

### Printing to a Target

`print(value, target)` writes the output elements to a `Target`. A `Target[Output]` is a small interface with `write`, and `capture`/`emit`/`drop` used by the printer internally for backtracking. ZIO Parser ships two implementations:

- `zio.parser.target.ChunkTarget`, which accumulates the output in a `Chunk` and is used by `print`.
- `zio.parser.target.ZStreamTarget`, which pushes the output into a `ZStream`.

Next: [Error handling](errors.md).

---

## Parser Reference

A `Parser[Err, In, Result]` reads input of type `In` and produces a `Result`, or fails with an `Err`. Parsers are one half of a `Syntax`, available as `Syntax#asParser`. You usually build a `Syntax` and use its parser through `parseString`, but a `Parser` can be used on its own when you never need the printer.

The type has three parameters. `Err` is the error type, which is `String` for most constructors. `In` is the input element type, which is `Char` for text. `Result` is the value the parser produces. `Parser` is covariant in `Err` and `Result` and contravariant in `In`, so a parser that needs fewer input types can be used where more are available.

For combinators that take a `Syntax` or `Printer` as an argument, see the [Syntax reference](syntax.md). Every method on `Parser` below has the same behavior as the `Syntax` method of the same name, applied to the parser half only.

### Running a Parser

| Method                                  | Result                                       | Description                                                     |
|-----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `parseString(input)`                    | `Either[StringParserError[Err], Result]`     | Parses a `String`. Requires `In` to be `Char`                   |
| `parseString(input, implementation)`    | `Either[StringParserError[Err], Result]`     | As above, with a `ParserImplementation`                         |
| `parseChars(input)`                     | `Either[StringParserError[Err], Result]`     | Parses a `Chunk[Char]`                                          |
| `parseChars(input, implementation)`     | `Either[StringParserError[Err], Result]`     | As above, with a `ParserImplementation`                         |
| `parseChunk(input)`                     | `Either[ParserError[Err], Result]`           | Parses any `Chunk[In]`. Returns the raw error, without the input |

`StringParserError` holds the input and the `ParserError`, and `pretty` formats it. See [Error Handling](errors.md) for the cases of `ParserError`.

### Transforming Results

| Method                           | Description                                                                              |
|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `map(f)`                         | Transforms the result                                                                    |
| `as(value)`                      | Replaces the result with a constant                                                      |
| `unit`                           | Discards the result                                                                      |
| `flatMap(f)`                     | Runs the parser returned by `f` on the rest of the input. Use it when the next step depends on this result |
| `transformEither(to)`            | Transforms the result. `to` returns an `Either`, and a `Left` fails the parser           |
| `transformOption(to)`            | Transforms the result. `to` returns an `Option`, and `None` fails the parser             |
| `filter(condition, failure)`     | Fails with `failure` when the result does not satisfy `condition`                        |
| `string`                         | Converts a `Chunk[Char]` result into a `String`                                           |
| `to[CaseClass]`                  | Maps a tuple result to a case class. Needs a `TupleConversion` for the case class       |
| `strip`                          | Removes all name information to make parsing faster. Failure messages become less detailed |
| `flatten`                        | Joins a `Chunk[String]` result into one `String`. Available only when the result is a `Chunk[String]` |
| `mapError(f)`                    | Transforms the error type                                                                |

### Sequencing and Alternatives

| Method                              | Result                                          | Description                                                        |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `~` / `zip`                         | `Parser[..., (A, B)]`                           | Runs this parser, then the other one, and pairs the results        |
| `<~` / `zipLeft`                    | `Parser[..., A]`                                | Runs both and keeps the left result                                |
| `~>` / `zipRight`                   | `Parser[..., B]`             | Runs both and keeps the right result                              |
| `\|` / `<>` / `orElse`              | `Parser[..., A]`                                | Tries this parser, then the other one, if this one fails          |
| `<+>` / `orElseEither`              | `Parser[..., Either[A, B]]`                     | As `orElse`, but keeps which branch matched                       |
| `??` / `named(name)`                | `Parser[..., A]`                                | Adds a name to errors raised inside this parser                   |

### Repetition and Optional Results

| Method                              | Result                       | Description                                              |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `repeat` / `+`                      | `Chunk[A]`                   | One or more times                                        |
| `repeat0` / `*`                     | `Chunk[A]`                   | Zero or more times                                       |
| `atLeast(n)`                        | `Chunk[A]`                   | At least `n` times                                       |
| `exactly(n)`                        | `Chunk[A]`                   | Exactly `n` times                                        |
| `repeatWithSep(sep)`                | `Chunk[A]`                   | One or more times with `sep` between them                |
| `repeatWithSep0(sep)`               | `Chunk[A]`                   | Zero or more times with `sep` between them               |
| `repeatUntil(stop)`                 | `Chunk[A]`                   | Repeats until `stop` succeeds                            |
| `optional` / `?`                    | `Option[A]`                  | Zero or one time                                         |
| `between(left, right)`              | `Parser[..., A]`             | Runs `left` and `right` around this parser and keeps the result |
| `surroundedBy(other)`               | `Parser[..., A]`             | Runs `other` before and after this parser                |
| `not(failure)`                      | `Parser[..., Unit]`          | Succeeds when this parser fails, and fails with `failure` when this parser succeeds |

### Backtracking

| Method                         | Description                                                                                  |
|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `backtrack`                    | Rewinds the input to where this parser started if it fails                                   |
| `autoBacktracking`             | Turns automatic backtracking on for this parser                                              |
| `manualBacktracking`           | Turns automatic backtracking off for this parser                                             |
| `setAutoBacktracking(enabled)` | Sets the backtracking mode for this parser                                                   |

The [Syntax reference](syntax.md#backtracking) explains when to use each of them.

### The Companion Object

These constructors are available on `Parser` directly. Most have a `Syntax` counterpart with the same name.

| Constructor                                 | Description                                                             |
|---------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `succeed(value)`                            | Succeeds with `value` without consuming input                           |
| `fail(failure)`                             | Fails with `failure`                                                    |
| `char(c)` / `char(c, failure)`              | Matches one character                                                   |
| `notChar(c)` / `notChar(c, failure)`        | Matches any character except `c`                                        |
| `charIn(chars*)` / `charNotIn(chars*)`      | Matches a character in or outside a set                                 |
| `anyChar`                                   | Matches any one character                                               |
| `any[T]`                                    | Matches any one element of type `T`                                     |
| `string(str, value)`                        | Matches `str` and produces `value`                                      |
| `anyString`                                 | Matches the rest of the input as a `String`                             |
| `ignoreRest`                                | Consumes the rest of the input without producing a value                |
| `digit`, `letter`, `alphaNumeric`, `whitespace` | Match one character of that class                                   |
| `regex(regex, failure)`                     | Matches a `Regex` and produces the matched `Chunk[Char]`                |
| `regexChar(regex, failure)`                 | Matches a `Regex` and produces its last character                       |
| `regexDiscard(regex, failure)`              | Matches a `Regex` and discards it                                       |
| `unit`                                      | Succeeds with `()`                                                      |
| `index`                                     | Produces the current position in the input                              |
| `end`                                       | Succeeds only at the end of the input                                   |

The `unsafe` variants, such as `unsafeRegex` and `unsafeRegexChar`, have no failure value, so a failure is reported as an `UnknownFailure`. Use them only with regexes that cannot fail.

### Error Cases

`Parser.ParserError` has five cases: `Failure`, `UnknownFailure`, `UnexpectedEndOfInput`, `NotConsumedAll` and `AllBranchesFailed`. Each case, what it means and how `pretty` shows it, is described in [Error Handling](errors.md#error-types).

---

## Printer Reference

A `Printer[Err, Out, Value]` takes a `Value` and writes it as a sequence of `Out` elements, or fails with an `Err`. Like `Parser`, it is one half of a `Syntax`, available as `Syntax#asPrinter`. Use a printer on its own when you only need to write values, and never parse them back.

The type has three parameters. `Err` is the error type, which is `String` for most constructors. `Out` is the output element type, which is `Char` for text. `Value` is the type of the value to print. The `Value` parameter is contravariant, so a printer for a supertype can print any subtype.

For combinators that take a `Syntax` as an argument, see the [Syntax reference](syntax.md). A printer method below has the same behavior as the `Syntax` method of the same name, applied to the printer half only.

### Printing a Value

| Method                    | Result                      | Description                                                       |
|---------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `printString(value)`      | `Either[Err, String]`       | Prints to a `String`. Requires `Out` to be `Char`                 |
| `print(value)`            | `Either[Err, Chunk[Out]]`   | Prints to a `Chunk` of output elements                            |
| `print(value, target)`    | `Either[Err, Unit]`         | Writes the output elements to a `Target`, see [Targets](#targets) |

### Transforming the Value

| Method                              | Description                                                                              |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `contramap(f)`                      | Converts a new value type to the value type of this printer with `f`                    |
| `contramapEither(f)`                | As `contramap`, but `f` returns an `Either`, and a `Left` fails printing                 |
| `contramapTo(from, failure)`        | As `contramap`, but `from` is a `PartialFunction`, and printing fails with `failure` where it is not defined |
| `transformOption(f)`                | As `contramapEither`, with `None` as the failure                                         |
| `filter(condition, failure)`        | Fails printing with `failure` when the value does not satisfy `condition`                |
| `asPrinted(matches, value)`         | Accepts `matches` as the value to print, and prints `value` instead                      |
| `widenWith(narrow, failure)`        | Prints a parent type, using `narrow` to find the subtype to print, and fails with `failure` otherwise |
| `mapError(f)`                       | Transforms the error type                                                                |
| `from[CaseClass]`                   | Prints a case class through a printer of its tuple. Needs a `TupleConversion` for the case class |

### Combining Printers

| Method                              | Description                                                                              |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `<~` / `zipLeft`                    | Prints this value, then the `Unit` printer on the right                                  |
| `~>` / `zipRight`                   | Prints the `Unit` printer on the left, then this value                                   |
| `\|` / `<>` / `orElse`              | Prints with this printer if it accepts the value, otherwise with the other one           |
| `<+>` / `orElseEither`              | As `orElse`, but takes an `Either` as input and prints the side that holds the value     |
| `repeat` / `+`                      | Prints a `Chunk` of values, one after another                                            |
| `repeat0` / `*`                     | As `repeat`, for a possibly empty `Chunk`                                                |
| `repeatWithSep(sep)`                | Prints a `Chunk`, with `sep` printed between the values                                  |
| `repeatWithSep0(sep)`               | As `repeatWithSep`, for a possibly empty `Chunk`                                         |
| `repeatUntil(stop)`                 | Prints a `Chunk` of values, followed by `stop`                                           |
| `optional` / `?`                    | Prints an `Option`: nothing for `None`, and the value for `Some`                         |
| `between(left, right)`              | Prints `left`, the value and `right`                                                     |
| `surroundedBy(other)`               | Prints `other` before and after the value                                                |

### The Companion Object

| Constructor                                       | Description                                                                              |
|---------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `unit`                                            | Prints nothing for `()`                                                                  |
| `fail(failure)`                                   | Always fails printing with `failure`                                                     |
| `any[T]`                                          | Prints the value unchanged, as an element of type `T`                                    |
| `byValue(f)`                                      | Chooses the printer to use from the value, using `f`                                      |
| `print(value)`                                    | Prints a constant output element                                                         |
| `printString(str)`                                | Prints the constant `str` as `Char` elements                                             |
| `apply(value)`                                    | Prints the constant `value`, for any output type other than `Char`                       |
| `char(c)`                                         | Prints the character `c`, and accepts only the value `()`                                |
| `notChar(c)` / `notChar(c, failure)`              | Prints a character that is not `c`                                                       |
| `exactly(value)` / `exactly(value, failure)`      | Prints `value` only when the value to print equals it                                    |
| `except(value)` / `except(value, failure)`        | Prints any value except `value`                                                          |
| `charIn(chars*)` / `charNotIn(chars*)`            | Prints a character in or outside a set                                                   |
| `anyChar`                                         | Prints any one character                                                                 |
| `anyString`                                       | Prints a `String` as its characters                                                      |
| `string(str, value)`                | Prints `str` when asked to print `value`, the mirror of `Syntax.string`                  |
| `digit`, `letter`, `alphaNumeric`, `whitespace`   | Print one character of that class, and fail for any other value                          |
| `regex(regex, failure)`                           | Prints a `Chunk[Char]` after checking that the regex matches it                          |
| `unsafeRegex(regex)`                              | As `regex`, without a failure value. Use only with regexes that cannot fail              |
| `regexChar(regex, failure)`                       | Prints a `Char` after checking that the regex matches it                                 |
| `unsafeRegexChar(regex)`                          | As `regexChar`, without a failure value                                                  |
| `regexDiscard(regex, value)`                      | Prints `value`, a `Chunk[Char]`, for a `Unit` value                                      |

### Targets

A `Target[Output]` receives output elements one at a time, so a printer can write them without building a `Chunk` first. The printer uses `capture`, `emit` and `drop` to handle alternatives: it captures the output of a branch, then either emits it to the target or drops it when the branch fails.

| Member                 | Description                                                              |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `write(value)`         | Writes one output element                                                |
| `capture()`            | Starts capturing output for a branch, and returns a `Capture` token      |
| `emit(capture)`        | Writes the output captured by `capture` to the target                    |
| `drop(capture)`        | Discards the output captured by `capture`                                |

The library ships two targets:

- `zio.parser.target.ChunkTarget` collects the output in memory. `result` returns the output as a `Chunk`. `print(value)` uses it internally.
- `zio.parser.target.ZStreamTarget` pushes the output into a queue, and its `stream` field reads the queue as a `ZStream`. See [How to Print to a ZStream](how-to-stream-printing.md).

---

## Regex

Character-level syntaxes such as `Syntax.digit` or `Syntax.string` are built on top of `Regex`, a small model of regular expressions that ZIO Parser compiles to an efficient matcher. You can use it directly when you need to match a whole token in a single step instead of composing it from many small syntaxes.

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
```

### Building a `Regex`

`Regex` is not `java.util.regex.Pattern`. It is a set of combinators:

| Combinator                              | Description                                                   |
|-----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Regex.char(c)`, `Regex.string(s)`      | Match a character or a literal string                         |
| `Regex.charIn(cs*)`, `Regex.charNotIn(cs*)` | Match a character in or not in a set                      |
| `Regex.filter(p)`                       | Match one character that satisfies a predicate                |
| `Regex.anyChar`, `Regex.anyDigit`, `Regex.anyLetter`, `Regex.anyAlphaNumeric`, `Regex.anyWhitespace` | Match one character of a class |
| `Regex.digits`, `Regex.letters`, `Regex.alphaNumerics`, `Regex.whitespace` | Repeated classes (`whitespace` matches zero or more) |
| `Regex.empty`                           | Matches the empty string                                      |
| `a ~ b`                                 | `a` followed by `b`                                           |
| `a \| b`                                | Either `a` or `b`                                             |
| `a & b`                                 | Input matched by both `a` and `b`                             |
| `a.atLeast(n)`, `a.atMost(n)`, `a.between(min, max)` | Repetition                                       |

```scala
val identifier: Regex =
  Regex.anyLetter ~ (Regex.anyLetter | Regex.anyDigit | Regex.char('_')).atLeast(0)

val hexByte: Regex =
  Regex.charIn("0123456789abcdefABCDEF".toList*).between(2, 2)
```

A regex can be compiled and tested on its own:

```scala
val compiled = identifier.compile
// compiled: Compiled = zio.parser.Regex$Parser$$anon$1@2ab7c4e5
compiled.matches("user_42")
// res0: Boolean = true
compiled.matches("42user")
// res1: Boolean = false
```

### Regex-based Syntaxes

The `Syntax.regex*` constructors turn a `Regex` into a syntax. They differ in what the syntax results in:

| Constructor                                      | Value          | Description                                                           |
|--------------------------------------------------|----------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Syntax.regex(regex, failure)`                   | `Chunk[Char]`  | The matched characters                                                |
| `Syntax.regexChar(regex, failure)`               | `Char`         | The last matched character. Use it for regexes that match one character |
| `Syntax.regexDiscard(regex, failure, printed)`   | `Unit`         | Discards the match. When printing, `printed` is written               |

The `unsafeRegex`, `unsafeRegexChar` and `unsafeRegexDiscard` variants have no failure value and must only be used with regexes that cannot fail.

```scala
val identifierSyntax: Syntax[String, Char, Char, String] =
  Syntax.regex(identifier, "not an identifier").string

val whitespace: Syntax[Nothing, Char, Char, Unit] =
  Syntax.unsafeRegexDiscard(Regex.whitespace, Chunk(' '))
```

```scala
identifierSyntax.parseString("count_1")
// res2: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Right("count_1")
identifierSyntax.parseString("1count")
// res3: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Left(
//   StringParserError(
//     input = "1count",
//     error = Failure(
//       nameStack = List(),
//       position = 0,
//       failure = "not an identifier"
//     )
//   )
// )
whitespace.parseString("   ")
// res4: Either[StringParserError[Nothing], Unit] = Right(())
whitespace.printString(())
// res5: Either[Nothing, String] = Right(" ")
```

`whitespace` accepts any amount of whitespace when parsing, and prints a single space.

When printing, the regex acts as a validator: a `Chunk[Char]` that the regex does not match makes the printer fail with the failure value.

```scala
Syntax.regex(identifier, "not an identifier").printString(Chunk.fromIterable("abc".toList))
// res6: Either[String, String] = Right("abc")
Syntax.regex(identifier, "not an identifier").printString(Chunk.fromIterable("1bc".toList))
// res7: Either[String, String] = Left("not an identifier")
```

### Why Use Regexes?

Each `Regex` is compiled once into a table-driven matcher that runs over the input in a tight loop. A syntax such as `Syntax.digit.repeat` is made of many parsing steps, while `Syntax.regex(Regex.digits, ...)` checks the whole token in one step. Prefer regexes for lexical tokens, like numbers, identifiers and whitespace, and combinators for structure.

The built-in `Syntax.digit`, `Syntax.letter`, `Syntax.alphaNumeric` and `Syntax.whitespace` are themselves defined with `Syntax.regexChar`.

Next: [Printing](printing.md).

## Building Syntaxes

A `Syntax[Err, In, Out, Value]` describes a grammar once and gives you both directions: a parser that turns input into a `Value`, and a printer that turns a `Value` back into output. This page covers the combinators you use to build syntaxes.

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
```

### The `Syntax` Type

`Syntax` has four type parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning                                                                        |
|-----------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Err`     | The custom error type, for example `String`                                    |
| `In`      | The element type of the input stream. For text this is `Char`                  |
| `Out`     | The element type of the printed stream. For text this is `Char`                |
| `Value`   | The type of the parsed value, which is also the type of the value to be printed |

Every syntax exposes its two halves as `asParser` and `asPrinter`, but you normally work with the syntax itself and call `parseString` or `printString` on it.

### Primitives

`Syntax` provides constructors for single characters, strings and common character classes:

| Constructor                                | Value    | Description                                       |
|--------------------------------------------|----------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `Syntax.char(c)`                           | `Unit`   | Matches the exact character `c`                   |
| `Syntax.charIn(cs)` / `Syntax.charNotIn(cs)` | `Char` | Matches a character in (or not in) the given set  |
| `Syntax.notChar(c)`                        | `Char`   | Matches any character except `c`                  |
| `Syntax.anyChar`                           | `Char`   | Matches any single character                      |
| `Syntax.digit`                             | `Char`   | Matches a digit                                   |
| `Syntax.letter`                            | `Char`   | Matches a letter                                  |
| `Syntax.alphaNumeric`                      | `Char`   | Matches a letter or a digit                       |
| `Syntax.whitespace`                        | `Char`   | Matches a whitespace character                    |
| `Syntax.filterChar(p, failure)`            | `Char`   | Matches a character that satisfies `p`            |
| `Syntax.string(s, value)`                  | `Result` | Matches the exact string `s` and results in `value` |
| `Syntax.succeed(v)` / `Syntax.fail(e)`     |          | Always succeed with `v` / always fail with `e`    |
| `Syntax.end`                               | `Unit`   | Succeeds only at the end of the input             |
| `Syntax.anyString`                         | `String` | Matches all the remaining input as a `String`     |
| `Syntax.index`                            | `Int`    | Produces the current position in the input. Prints nothing          |
| `Syntax.any[T]`                           | `T`      | Matches any single element of type `T`, for any input type         |

```scala
val comma: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit]       = Syntax.char(',')
val vowel: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Char]       = Syntax.charIn("aeiou")
val trueSyntax: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Boolean] = Syntax.string("true", true)
```

```scala
vowel.parseString("a")
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], Char] = Right('a')
vowel.parseString("x")
// res1: Either[StringParserError[String], Char] = Left(
//   StringParserError(
//     input = "x",
//     error = Failure(
//       nameStack = List(),
//       position = 0,
//       failure = "Not the expected character (a, e, i, o, u)"
//     )
//   )
// )
trueSyntax.parseString("true")
// res2: Either[StringParserError[String], Boolean] = Right(true)
```

### Sequencing

The `~` operator runs two syntaxes in order and combines their results into a tuple. Results of type `Unit` are dropped, so you do not end up with `Unit` entries in the tuple:

```scala
val pair: Syntax[String, Char, Char, (Char, Char)] =
  Syntax.digit ~ comma ~ Syntax.letter
```

```scala
pair.parseString("1,a")
// res3: Either[StringParserError[String], Tuple2[Char, Char]] = Right(
//   ('1', 'a')
// )
pair.printString(('1', 'a'))
// res4: Either[String, String] = Right("1,a")
```

If you only care about one side, use `~>` to keep the right result or `<~` to keep the left result. The discarded side must be a `Syntax[..., Unit]`, because the printer has no value to give it:

```scala
val parenthesizedDigit: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Char] =
  Syntax.char('(') ~> Syntax.digit <~ Syntax.char(')')
```

```scala
parenthesizedDigit.parseString("(7)")
// res5: Either[StringParserError[String], Char] = Right('7')
parenthesizedDigit.printString('7')
// res6: Either[String, String] = Right("(7)")
```

### Alternatives

`|` (or `orElse`, or its alias `<>`) tries the left syntax first and falls back to the right one if it fails. Both sides must have the same value type. When the types differ, `orElseEither` (alias `<+>`) returns an `Either`:

```scala
val boolean: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Boolean] =
  Syntax.string("true", true) | Syntax.string("false", false)

val digitOrLetter: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Either[Char, Char]] =
  Syntax.digit <+> Syntax.letter
```

```scala
boolean.parseString("false")
// res7: Either[StringParserError[String], Boolean] = Right(false)
digitOrLetter.parseString("x")
// res8: Either[StringParserError[String], Either[Char, Char]] = Right(
//   Right('x')
// )
```

When the alternatives are subtypes of a common type, `widen[T]` lifts each alternative to the parent type so they can be combined with `|`. The printer picks the first alternative that accepts the value. See the [worked example](example-json.md).

### Repetition

| Combinator                  | Result          | Description                                         |
|-----------------------------|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| `repeat` / `+`              | `Chunk[Value]`  | One or more times                                   |
| `repeat0` / `*`             | `Chunk[Value]`  | Zero or more times                                  |
| `atLeast(n)`                | `Chunk[Value]`  | At least `n` times                                  |
| `repeatWithSep(sep)`        | `Chunk[Value]`  | One or more times, separated by `sep`               |
| `repeatWithSep0(sep)`       | `Chunk[Value]`  | Zero or more times, separated by `sep`              |
| `repeatUntil(stop)`         | `Chunk[Value]`  | Repeats until `stop` succeeds                       |
| `optional` / `?`            | `Option[Value]` | Zero or one time                                    |

`string` turns a repeated character syntax into a `String`:

```scala
val number: Syntax[String, Char, Char, String] = Syntax.digit.repeat.string
val numbers: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Chunk[String]] = number.repeatWithSep(comma)
val maybeSign: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Option[Unit]] = Syntax.char('-').optional
```

```scala
number.parseString("2024")
// res9: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Right("2024")
numbers.parseString("1,22,333")
// res10: Either[StringParserError[String], Chunk[String]] = Right(
//   IndexedSeq("1", "22", "333")
// )
numbers.printString(Chunk("4", "5", "6"))
// res11: Either[String, String] = Right("4,5,6")
maybeSign.parseString("")
// res12: Either[StringParserError[String], Option[Unit]] = Right(None)
```

`Syntax.digit.repeat` has `Chunk[Char]` as its value type, and `.string` replaces it with the matched text. When printing, the whole string is written as is.

### Surrounding Syntaxes

`between(left, right)` and `surroundedBy(other)` wrap a syntax with `Unit` syntaxes and keep the inner result:

```scala
val quoted: Syntax[String, Char, Char, String] =
  Syntax.notChar('"').repeat0.string.surroundedBy(Syntax.char('"'))

val bracketed: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Chunk[String]] =
  number.repeatWithSep0(comma).between(Syntax.char('['), Syntax.char(']'))
```

```scala
quoted.parseString("\"hello\"")
// res13: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Right("hello")
bracketed.parseString("[1,2,3]")
// res14: Either[StringParserError[String], Chunk[String]] = Right(
//   IndexedSeq("1", "2", "3")
// )
bracketed.printString(Chunk("1", "2"))
// res15: Either[String, String] = Right("[1,2]")
```

### Mapping Values

Because a syntax works in both directions, a mapping needs a function for each direction:

| Combinator                       | Description                                                                                       |
|----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `transform(to, from)`            | Maps the parsed value with `to`, and the value to print with `from`                               |
| `transformEither(to, from)`      | Both functions can fail with an `Either`                                                          |
| `transformOption(to, from)`      | Both functions can fail with an `Option`, and the error becomes `Option[Err]`                     |
| `transformTo(to, from, failure)` | `from` is a `PartialFunction`. If it is not defined for a value, printing fails with `failure`    |
| `asPrinted(result, value)`       | Always parses to `result`, and prints `value` when asked to print `result`                        |
| `as(value)`                      | For `Unit` syntaxes: result in `value` when parsing                                               |
| `of[CaseClass]`                  | Converts a tuple result to a case class, and back when printing                  |
| `filter(p, failure)`             | Fails with `failure` when the value does not satisfy `p`                                          |
| `unit(printed)`                  | Discards the parsed value and results in `Unit`. When printing, `printed` is written              |
| `toList`                         | Converts a `Chunk[Item]` result to a `List[Item]`, and back when printing                         |
| `flatten`                        | Joins a `Chunk[String]` result into one `String`, and prints the whole string as one element      |
| `widenWith(narrow, failure)`     | Widens the value to a parent type. `narrow` is a `PartialFunction` that finds the subtype to print, and printing fails with `failure` where it is not defined |

```scala
val int: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  number.transformEither[String, Int](
    s => s.toIntOption.toRight("number out of range"),
    n => Right(n.toString)
  )

final case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)

val point: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Point] =
  (int ~ comma ~ int).of[Point].between(Syntax.char('('), Syntax.char(')'))
```

```scala
int.parseString("42")
// res16: Either[StringParserError[String], Int] = Right(42)
int.parseString("99999999999")
// res17: Either[StringParserError[String], Int] = Left(
//   StringParserError(
//     input = "99999999999",
//     error = Failure(
//       nameStack = List(),
//       position = 11,
//       failure = "number out of range"
//     )
//   )
// )
point.parseString("(3,4)")
// res18: Either[StringParserError[String], Point] = Right(Point(x = 3, y = 4))
point.printString(Point(5, 6))
// res19: Either[String, String] = Right("(5,6)")
```

The `of[CaseClass]` combinator works on both Scala 2 and Scala 3 for case classes. The conversion is a `TupleConversion`, which Scala 2 generates with a macro and Scala 3 derives from the case class's `Mirror`. The same conversion exists on the two halves: `to[CaseClass]` on a `Parser` and `from[CaseClass]` on a `Printer`.

### Recursive Syntaxes

A syntax can refer to itself as long as the reference sits behind a `lazy val` (or a `def`). The `~`, `~>`, `<~`, `|` operators take their right-hand side by name, so the recursion is resolved lazily. For a full example see the [worked example](example-json.md).

```scala
lazy val nested: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Int] =
  (Syntax.char('(') ~> nested <~ Syntax.char(')')).transform(_ + 1, _ - 1) |
    Syntax.succeed(0)
```

```scala
nested.parseString("((()))")
// res20: Either[StringParserError[String], Int] = Right(3)
```

### Choosing the Parser Implementation

`parseString` and `parseChars` take an optional `ParserImplementation`. The default, `ParserImplementation.Recursive`, is fast but uses the JVM stack for nested syntaxes. `ParserImplementation.StackSafe` is slower but does not overflow on deeply nested input:

```scala
nested.parseString("(((())))", ParserImplementation.StackSafe)
// res21: Either[StringParserError[String], Int] = Right(4)
```

### Debugging and Performance

`debug(msg)` prints `msg` and the parsed value each time the syntax succeeds while parsing. It does not change printing, so use it to follow a grammar while you build it and remove it afterwards:

```scala
Syntax.digit.repeat.string.debug("digits").parseString("42")
// digits: 42
// res22: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Right("42")
```

Syntaxes keep the names you add with `named` so errors can show where they happened. `strip` removes all name information from a syntax to make parsing faster, at the cost of less detailed failure messages. Apply it after the grammar works:

```scala
val fastNumber: Syntax[String, Char, Char, String] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.named("number").strip
```

### Backtracking

When a syntax fails after consuming input, the parser backtracks to where that syntax started, so that an alternative can try again from the same position. This automatic backtracking is on by default. `manualBacktracking` turns it off for a syntax, `autoBacktracking` turns it on again, and `backtrack` inserts an explicit backtracking point. Disabling it can make failures cheaper in grammars where you know which branch to take from the first character.

Next: [Regex](regex.md), [Printing](printing.md), [Error handling](errors.md).

---

## Tutorial: Parse and Print a Config Language

Welcome to ZIO Parser! This tutorial is for newcomers who know basic Scala and have never used a parser library. You don't need any prior experience with parsing to follow along.

We build a parser and printer for a tiny configuration language, one piece at a time. Each piece is a single `Syntax` value, and we combine them into a bigger one.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will understand:

- What a `Syntax` is, and why one value can both parse and print
- How to build small syntaxes from primitives and combine them with operators
- How to turn parsed text into your own case classes
- How to read the error that a failed parse returns

We learn these concepts through:

1. Parsing a Single Key
2. Parsing Values of Three Types
3. Parsing a Setting
4. Parsing a Whole File
5. Reading Errors

We recommend reading from top to bottom, because each section builds on the previous one.

### 1. Parsing a Single Key

A key in our language is one or more letters, such as `timeout`. In ZIO Parser, a `Syntax` describes one piece of text and the value it produces. The type has four parameters: the error type, the input element type, the output element type, and the value type.

For text, the input and output are both `Char`, so a key syntax has the type `Syntax[String, Char, Char, String]`. We start by importing the library:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.parser.*
```

To describe a key, we take a letter and repeat it. Then `string` turns the repeated characters into a `String`:

```scala
val key: Syntax[String, Char, Char, String] =
  Syntax.letter.repeat.string
```

The code above:

- `Syntax.letter` matches one letter and produces that `Char`
- `repeat` matches one or more of them and produces a `Chunk[Char]`
- `string` converts that chunk into a `String`

Now we run the syntax in both directions. `parseString` reads text into a value, and `printString` writes a value back into text:

```scala
key.parseString("timeout")
// res0: Either[StringParserError[String], String] = Right("timeout")
key.printString("timeout")
// res1: Either[String, String] = Right("timeout")
```

Both calls return an `Either`. `Right` holds the result, and `Left` holds the error. Notice that the same `key` value did both jobs, so we describe the grammar only once.

### 2. Parsing Values of Three Types

A setting value can be an integer, a boolean, or a quoted string. We model these with a small `sealed trait`, so that each kind of value has its own case class:

```scala
sealed trait Value
object Value {
  final case class IntValue(value: Int) extends Value
  final case class BoolValue(value: Boolean) extends Value
  final case class Text(value: String) extends Value
}
```

Each syntax below produces one of these subtypes. An integer is one or more digits. We parse the digits as a `String` and convert them to an `Int`. The conversion can fail, so we use `transformEither`, which returns an error instead of throwing:

```scala
val intValue: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Value.IntValue] =
  Syntax.digit.repeat.string.transformEither[String, Value.IntValue](
    digits => digits.toIntOption.map(Value.IntValue(_)).toRight("number out of range"),
    intValue => Right(intValue.value.toString)
  )
```

The code above:

- The first function turns the digits into a `Value.IntValue`, or into the error `"number out of range"`
- The second function is used when printing, and turns the `Int` back into digits

A boolean is either the text `true` or the text `false`. The `|` operator tries the left alternative first, and falls back to the right one if it fails:

```scala
val boolValue: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Value.BoolValue] =
  (Syntax.string("true", true) | Syntax.string("false", false))
    .transform[Value.BoolValue](Value.BoolValue(_), _.value)
```

A quoted string starts and ends with a double quote, and everything in between is kept. We drop the quotes with `~>` and `<~`, which keep only the value of the side that has one:

```scala
val text: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Value.Text] =
  (Syntax.char('"') ~> Syntax.notChar('"').repeat0.string <~ Syntax.char('"'))
    .transform[Value.Text](Value.Text(_), _.value)
```

The `Syntax.char('"')` parts produce no value, so the quotes disappear from the result. When printing, they come back, because the printer writes them again.

To combine the three alternatives, we widen each one to the common type `Value`. Then `|` can join them:

```scala
val value: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Value] =
  intValue.widen[Value] | boolValue.widen[Value] | text.widen[Value]
```

Now we try all three kinds of value in both directions:

```scala
value.parseString("8080")
// res2: Either[StringParserError[String], Value] = Right(IntValue(8080))
value.parseString("true")
// res3: Either[StringParserError[String], Value] = Right(BoolValue(true))
value.parseString("\"zio-parser\"")
// res4: Either[StringParserError[String], Value] = Right(Text("zio-parser"))
value.printString(Value.Text("zio-parser"))
// res5: Either[String, String] = Right("\"zio-parser\"")
```

:::tip
`widen` checks the type of a value at runtime when printing. It picks the first alternative whose case class matches the value, so the order of the alternatives matters only when two of them could match the same value.
:::

### 3. Parsing a Setting

A setting puts a key, an equals sign and a value together, such as `port = 8080`. Spaces around the equals sign are allowed when parsing, but we want the printer to write exactly one space on each side. The `asPrinted` method does this. It keeps the parsed result as `Unit` and tells the printer which text to write:

```scala
val spaces: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] =
  Syntax.whitespace.repeat0.asPrinted((), Chunk(' '))
```

Next, we combine the key, the equals sign and the value. A `final case class` holds the result of one setting:

```scala
final case class Setting(key: String, value: Value)

val setting: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Setting] =
  (key ~ (Syntax.char('=').surroundedBy(spaces) ~> value)).of[Setting]
```

The code above:

- `key ~ (...)` runs the key first, then the right side, and pairs their results
- `Syntax.char('=').surroundedBy(spaces) ~> value` matches the equals sign with spaces around it, and then the value
- `of[Setting]` turns the pair `(String, Value)` into a `Setting`, and back again when printing

Parsing and printing a setting show the whitespace being normalized:

```scala
setting.parseString("timeout   =   30")
// res6: Either[StringParserError[String], Setting] = Right(
//   Setting(key = "timeout", value = IntValue(30))
// )
setting.printString(Setting("timeout", Value.IntValue(30)))
// res7: Either[String, String] = Right("timeout = 30")
```

The input had three spaces on each side of the equals sign, and the printed output has one.

### 4. Parsing a Whole File

A file is a list of settings, one per line. We need a syntax for the newline character, and a rule that the file ends after the last setting. `repeatWithSep` repeats a syntax with a separator between the repetitions, and `Syntax.end` makes sure nothing is left over:

```scala
val newline: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Unit] = Syntax.char('\n')

val config: Syntax[String, Char, Char, Chunk[Setting]] =
  setting.repeatWithSep(newline) <~ Syntax.end
```

Now we parse a small file with three settings:

```scala
val source = "name = \"zio-parser\"\nport = 8080\ndebug = true"
// source: String = """name = "zio-parser"
// port = 8080
// debug = true"""

config.parseString(source)
// res8: Either[StringParserError[String], Chunk[Setting]] = Right(
//   IndexedSeq(
//     Setting(key = "name", value = Text("zio-parser")),
//     Setting(key = "port", value = IntValue(8080)),
//     Setting(key = "debug", value = BoolValue(true))
//   )
// )
```

Printing works the same way. We give the printer a `Chunk` of settings, and it writes them back one per line:

```scala
config.printString(
  Chunk(
    Setting("name", Value.Text("zio-parser")),
    Setting("port", Value.IntValue(8080))
  )
)
// res9: Either[String, String] = Right(
//   """name = "zio-parser"
// port = 8080"""
// )
```

Because `config` describes both directions, the printed text parses back to the same settings. You can check this yourself by parsing the output of `printString`.

### 5. Reading Errors

A parse that fails returns a `Left` with a `StringParserError`. The `pretty` method turns that error into a message that points at the place in the input where things went wrong.

Suppose a line has an extra word after the value, such as `port = 8080 extra`. The setting matches `port = 8080`, and then `Syntax.end` finds the text ` extra` that it did not expect:

```scala
config.parseString("port = 8080 extra").left.map(_.pretty).merge
// res10: String | Chunk[Setting] = """port = 8080 extra
//            ^
// error: Parser did not consume all input at position 11
// """
```

The message shows the input line and a caret under the first character the parser could not use. It is the position where the parser stopped, so you can read the message and go straight to the problem.

When every alternative of a `|` fails, the error lists the failure of each branch instead. For example, a value such as `port = 99999999999` fails the integer rule with `"number out of range"`, and the text and boolean rules fail too, so the message names all three.

:::note
A syntax returns as soon as it has matched its value. It does not look at the rest of the input, unless you finish it with `Syntax.end`, as `config` does.
:::

### What You've Learned

In this tutorial, you learned:

- What a `Syntax` is, and how its four type parameters describe the input, the output and the value
- How to build a syntax from primitives such as `Syntax.letter` and `Syntax.digit`, and combine them with `~`, `~>`, `<~` and `|`
- How to convert parsed text into your own types with `transform`, `transformEither` and `of`
- How `widen` lets alternatives of different subtypes share one syntax
- How to read an error with `pretty`

You now have a solid foundation for writing parsers and printers with ZIO Parser. The next step is to apply these ideas to common tasks.

### Where to Go Next

- **Ready to use this in practice?** The how-to guide [Whitespace and Comments](how-to-whitespace-and-comments.md) shows how to skip the text you do not need, and [Recursive Syntaxes](how-to-recursive-syntaxes.md) shows how to parse nested data.
- **Want to dive deeper into the API?** Read the [Syntax reference](syntax.md) for every combinator, and the [Regex reference](regex.md) for fast token matching.
- **Interested in a larger example?** [Example: a JSON Syntax](example-json.md) builds a complete parser and printer for JSON.

## Arithmetic

These abstractions describe types with a notion of addition and multiplication, and optionally subtraction and division. The shared base is `DistributiveProd`, which pairs a sum with a product that distributes over it. `Annihilation`, `Subtract`, `PartialDivide` and `Divide` each strengthen one of the two operations. The two operations are expressed through the `Sum` and `Prod` newtypes, which let one type carry both an additive and a multiplicative `Associative` instance.

The core declarations of the family are:

```scala
trait DistributiveProd[A] {
  def Sum: Associative[Sum[A]]
  def Prod: Associative[Prod[A]]
  def sum(l: => A, r: => A): A
  def prod(l: => A, r: => A): A
}
trait Subtract[A] extends DistributiveProd[A]      { def Sum: Inverse[Sum[A]];          def subtract(l: => A, r: => A): A }
trait PartialDivide[A] extends DistributiveProd[A] { def Prod: PartialInverse[Prod[A]]; def divideOption(l: => A, r: => A): Option[A] }
```

All of the types on this page are in `zio.prelude.experimental`. The [overview](index.md) shows how they relate to the other families.

### DistributiveProd

`DistributiveProd[A]` provides `sum` and `prod`, defined through the `Sum` and `Prod` instances, with the infix operators `+++` (alias `sum`) and `***` (alias `prod`). Its laws object, `DistributiveProdLaws`, checks that `prod` distributes over `sum` on both sides: `a1 *** (a2 +++ a3)` equals `(a1 *** a2) +++ (a1 *** a3)`, and `(a1 +++ a2) *** a3` equals `(a1 *** a3) +++ (a2 *** a3)`.

The built-in instances are provided for `Byte`, `Char`, `Short`, `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `Double` and `BigDecimal` and, as plain `DistributiveProd` instances, for `ParSeq[Unit, A]` and `zio.Cause[A]`. To add and multiply with the operators:

```scala
import zio.prelude.experimental._

10 +++ 5
// res0: Int = 15

10 *** 5
// res1: Int = 50
```

### Annihilation

`Annihilation[A]` extends `DistributiveProd[A]` and requires `Sum` to be an `Identity`. It defines `annihilation` as the identity of `Sum`, the zero of the type. `AnnihilationLaws` adds that zero absorbs the product on both sides: `annihilation *** a` and `a *** annihilation` both equal `annihilation`. The numeric instances above are all `Annihilation`.

To read the zero of `Int` through its instance:

```scala
Annihilation[Int].annihilation
// res2: Int = 0
```

### Subtract

`Subtract[A]` extends `DistributiveProd[A]` and requires `Sum` to be an `Inverse`, which is what makes subtraction possible. `subtract` is defined through `Sum.inverse`, and the infix forms are `---` and `subtract`. It has no laws object, because the inverse laws belong to the `Inverse` instance of `Sum`. The numeric types, from `Byte` to `BigDecimal`, have `Subtract` instances.

To subtract with the operator:

```scala
10 --- 4
// res3: Int = 6
```

### PartialDivide

`PartialDivide[A]` extends `DistributiveProd[A]` and requires `Prod` to be a `PartialInverse`. Division can fail, for example when the divisor is zero, so `divideOption` returns an `Option`, and the infix forms are `-/-` and `divideOption`. The instances are provided for `Float`, `Double` and `BigDecimal`, which return `None` when the divisor is zero.

To divide, and to divide by zero:

```scala
10.0 -/- 4.0
// res4: Option[Double] = Some(value = 2.5)

10.0 -/- 0.0
// res5: Option[Double] = None
```

### Divide

`Divide[A]` extends `PartialDivide[A]` and requires `Prod` to be an `Inverse`, so division always succeeds. It adds `divide`, with the infix forms `-:-` and `divide`, and `divideOption` is derived from the product's partial inverse. ZIO Prelude does not provide a built-in `Divide` instance for any type, so `Divide` is an extension point for our own types whose product is a total inverse.

### Writing an Instance

To support our own type, we provide `Sum` and `Prod` instances for it and extend the most specific abstraction it satisfies, overriding `sum` and `prod` only when we want something faster than combining through the newtypes. We then test the instance with `DistributiveProdLaws` or `AnnihilationLaws` from `zio-prelude-experimental-laws`, as shown on the [overview](index.md#laws).

---

## Composition

These abstractions describe arrow-like type constructors `=>:[-_, +_]`, such as functions, that can be composed and that gain extra structure on top of composition. `BothCompose` adds products (pairing outputs), `EitherCompose` adds sums (choosing between inputs), and `ApplicationCompose` adds currying and application. They build on [`AssociativeCompose`](../functional-abstractions/parameterized-types/associativecompose.md) from the core module, which provides `compose`.

The core declarations of `BothCompose` are:

```scala
trait BothCompose[=>:[-_, +_]] extends AssociativeCompose[=>:] {
  type :*:[+_, +_]
  def fromFirst[A]: (A :*: Any) =>: A
  def fromSecond[B]: (Any :*: B) =>: B
  def toBoth[A, B, C](a2b: A =>: B)(a2c: A =>: C): A =>: (B :*: C)
}
```

All of the types on this page are in `zio.prelude.experimental`. The [overview](index.md) shows how they relate to the other families.

### BothCompose

`BothCompose` adds a product type, the abstract type member `:*:`, together with its two projections, `fromFirst` and `fromSecond`, and `toBoth`, which builds an arrow into the product from two arrows with the same source. The `BothCompose#bothCompose` method checks the three laws that tie these together (the projections undo `toBoth`, and `toBoth` of the projections of an arrow gives the arrow back) for the arrows we supply, and returns a `Boolean`. It needs an `Equal` instance for the arrow type.

The only built-in instance is for `Function`, and it lives in the `BothCompose` companion. It is declared as an `ApplicationCompose[Function]` whose product is `Tuple2`. To pair the results of two functions on the same input:

```scala
import zio.prelude.experimental._

val increment: Int => Int = _ + 1
// increment: Int => Int = <function1>
val describe: Int => String = _.toString
// describe: Int => String = <function1>

val both = BothCompose.FunctionApplicationCompose.toBoth(increment)(describe)
// both: Function[Int, BothCompose.FunctionApplicationCompose.:*:[Int, String]] = zio.prelude.experimental.BothCompose$$anon$1$$Lambda$17571/0x00007f348ac79810@47f5da4b

println(both(1))
// (2,1)
```

The product type is an abstract member of the instance, so `both(1)` is typed with `:*:` rather than `Tuple2`, and we read the result as the pair `(2,1)` only at runtime. When a function over `Tuple2` is needed, we cast or provide our own instance with a concrete product.

### EitherCompose

`EitherCompose` is the dual of `BothCompose`. It adds a sum type, the abstract member `:+:`, with the injections `toLeft` and `toRight`, and `fromEither`, which builds an arrow out of the sum from two arrows with the same target. `EitherCompose#eitherCompose` checks the corresponding three laws and returns a `Boolean`, again requiring `Equal` for the arrow type.

The built-in `Function` instance, `EitherCompose.FunctionEitherCompose`, uses `Either` as the sum. To combine two functions that return the same type into one function over the sum:

```scala
val either = EitherCompose.FunctionEitherCompose.fromEither((i: Int) => i.toString)((s: String) => s)
// either: Function[EitherCompose.FunctionEitherCompose.:+:[Int, String], String] = zio.prelude.experimental.EitherCompose$$anon$1$$Lambda$17572/0x00007f348ac7a248@3fcaa39f
```

As with `BothCompose`, the sum is an abstract member, so values of the sum type are not statically known to be `Either`.

### ApplicationCompose

`ApplicationCompose` extends `BothCompose` with an exponential type, the abstract member `-->:`, which represents arrows as values. It adds `application` (apply an arrow value to its input), `curry` and `uncurry`. A `BothCompose` plus an `ApplicationCompose` together make a cartesian closed category, which is the structure behind functions of several arguments. `ApplicationCompose#applicationCompose` checks that `curry` and `uncurry` are inverses and that `application` recovers the original arrow, again for the arguments we supply.

The `Function` instance `BothCompose.FunctionApplicationCompose` is an `ApplicationCompose[Function]`, with `Tuple2` as the product and `Function` as the exponential. It is the same instance used for `BothCompose` above, so `BothCompose.FunctionApplicationCompose.curry` and `BothCompose.FunctionApplicationCompose.uncurry` convert between functions of a pair and curried functions.

### Syntax

The package object provides `&&&` and `toBoth` for `BothCompose`, `|||` and `fromEither` for `EitherCompose`, and `curry` and `uncurry` for `ApplicationCompose`. They take the matching `Aux` instance as an implicit parameter, which pins down the product, sum and exponential types. Because the built-in `Function` instances expose those types abstractly, as described above, the `Aux` evidence is not found for plain `Function1` values, and the operators are most useful with instances of our own whose members are concrete. For `Function` we call the instance methods directly.

### Classic Aliases

The `zio.prelude.experimental.classic` object defines type aliases that combine these abstractions with the `Category` type from `zio.prelude.classic`: `CartesianCategory`, `ClosedCartesianCategory` and `CoCartesianCategory`. They name the usual category-theory combinations: `Category` with `BothCompose`, with `ApplicationCompose` added, and with `EitherCompose`.

---

## Experimental Abstractions

The experimental module collects abstractions that are not part of the core ZIO Prelude API yet. They describe structure that the core abstractions do not cover: two operations that interact (addition with multiplication, join with meet), a complement operation, subtraction and division, and arrows that can pair or choose between values. Because they are experimental, their names and shapes can change between releases.

The abstractions fall into three families, each documented on its own page: [Lattices and Boolean Algebra](lattice-and-boolean-algebra.md) (`Absorption`, `DistributiveAbsorption`, `Complement`, `ExcludedMiddle`, `Noncontradiction`, `Involution`), [Arithmetic](arithmetic.md) (`DistributiveProd`, `Annihilation`, `Subtract`, `PartialDivide`, `Divide`) and [Composition](compose.md) (`BothCompose`, `EitherCompose`, `ApplicationCompose`).

The core declarations of one abstraction from each family are:

```scala
trait Absorption[A]       { def Or: Associative[OrF[A]];  def And: Associative[AndF[A]] }
trait DistributiveProd[A] { def Sum: Associative[Sum[A]]; def Prod: Associative[Prod[A]] }
trait BothCompose[=>:[-_, +_]] extends AssociativeCompose[=>:] { type :*:[+_, +_] }
```

### Installation

The abstractions live in `zio-prelude-experimental`, and their laws live in a separate module, `zio-prelude-experimental-laws`, that we add to the `Test` configuration. Both are available for the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-prelude-experimental"      % "1.0.0-RC49",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-prelude-experimental-laws" % "1.0.0-RC49" % Test
)
```

The infix syntax for every abstraction comes from the package object, so a single import brings it into scope:

```scala
import zio.prelude.experimental._
```

### How They Work Together

Every abstraction is a type class built from the core abstractions. Each operation is expressed as an `Associative`, `Identity` or `Inverse` instance over a newtype that names it (`Sum`, `Prod`, `OrF`, `AndF`), and the experimental type class adds the relationship between the operations. The hierarchy below shows which abstraction extends which:

```
DistributiveProd  (Sum, Prod: Associative)
 ├── Annihilation   (Sum: Identity, annihilation = Sum.identity)
 ├── Subtract       (Sum: Inverse)
 └── PartialDivide  (Prod: PartialInverse)
      └── Divide    (Prod: Inverse)

Absorption  (Or, And: Associative)
 ├── DistributiveAbsorption
 └── Complement  (complement)
      ├── ExcludedMiddle     (top, And: Identity)
      ├── Noncontradiction   (bottom, Or: Identity)
      └── Involution         (ExcludedMiddle with Noncontradiction)

AssociativeCompose  (core)
 ├── BothCompose
 │    └── ApplicationCompose
 └── EitherCompose
```

The typical workflow has four steps:

1. Pick the abstraction that matches the structure of the type, for example `DistributiveAbsorption` for sets or `Subtract` for numbers.
2. Import `zio.prelude.experimental._` for the operators, such as `vvv`, `^^^`, `+++`, `***` and `---`.
3. Use the built-in instance, or provide our own implicit instance for our type.
4. Check our own instance with the matching `*Laws` object from `zio-prelude-experimental-laws`, as described on the [Laws](../laws/index.md) page.

### Laws

The laws module contains a `Lawful` object for each abstraction that has laws as data: `AbsorptionLaws`, `DistributiveAbsorptionLaws`, `ExcludedMiddleLaws`, `NoncontradictionLaws`, `InvolutionLaws`, `DistributiveProdLaws` and `AnnihilationLaws`. They live in `zio.prelude.experimental.laws`, and each one includes the laws of the abstractions it extends. `Subtract`, `PartialDivide`, `Divide` and `Complement` have no laws object of their own, and the composition abstractions state their laws as methods on the traits themselves.

To check the laws for `Boolean`, we pass a generator to `checkAllLaws`:

```scala
import zio.prelude.experimental.laws._
import zio.test._
import zio.test.laws._

object BooleanLawsSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec =
    test("Boolean is an involution")(checkAllLaws(InvolutionLaws)(Gen.boolean))
}
```

---

## Lattices and Boolean Algebra

These abstractions describe types that have two combining operations, a join (`or`, written `vvv`) and a meet (`and`, written `^^^`), and optionally a complement. `Boolean` and `Set` are the standard examples. Together they build up from a lattice (`Absorption`) to a full Boolean algebra (`Involution`).

The core declarations of the family are:

```scala
trait Absorption[A] {
  def or(l: => A, r: => A): A
  def and(l: => A, r: => A): A
  def Or: Associative[OrF[A]]
  def And: Associative[AndF[A]]
}
trait Complement[A] extends Absorption[A] { def complement(a: => A): A }
```

All of the types on this page are in `zio.prelude.experimental`. The [overview](index.md) shows how they relate to the other families.

### Absorption

`Absorption[A]` is the base of the family. It provides `or` and `and`, defined through two `Associative` instances over the `OrF` and `AndF` newtypes, and the infix operators `vvv` (alias `or`) and `^^^` (alias `and`). The name refers to the absorption laws that its laws object checks: `a1 vvv (a1 ^^^ a2)` equals `a1`, and `a1 ^^^ (a1 vvv a2)` equals `a1`.

The built-in instances are for `Boolean` and `Set[A]`. To join and meet values:

```scala
import zio.prelude.experimental._

true vvv false
// res0: Boolean = true

true ^^^ false
// res1: Boolean = false

Set(1, 2) vvv Set(2, 3)
// res2: Set[Int] = Set(1, 2, 3)

Set(1, 2) ^^^ Set(2, 3)
// res3: Set[Int] = Set(2)
```

For `Set`, `vvv` is union and `^^^` is intersection. To implement `Absorption` for our own type, we provide the two associative operations as `Or` and `And` and let `or` and `and` default to combining through them.

### DistributiveAbsorption

`DistributiveAbsorption[A]` extends `Absorption[A]` without adding members. It marks an instance whose join and meet distribute over each other, and `DistributiveAbsorptionLaws` adds the two distributive laws on top of the absorption laws: `a1 vvv (a2 ^^^ a3)` equals `(a1 vvv a2) ^^^ (a1 vvv a3)`, and the same with join and meet exchanged. The `Boolean` and `Set` instances are both `DistributiveAbsorption`.

### Complement

`Complement[A]` extends `Absorption[A]` with a single operation, `complement`. The package object adds the syntax `!a` and `a.complement`, available for any type with a `Complement` instance. It has no laws of its own; the two abstractions below attach laws to it.

### ExcludedMiddle and Noncontradiction

`ExcludedMiddle[A]` and `Noncontradiction[A]` extend `Complement[A]` with the two bounds of the lattice. `ExcludedMiddle` adds `top`, which it defines as the identity of `And`, so its `And` must be an `Identity`. `Noncontradiction` adds `bottom`, the identity of `Or`, so its `Or` must be an `Identity`.

Their laws state how the complement interacts with the bounds. `ExcludedMiddleLaws` checks that `!a vvv a` equals `top`, and `NoncontradictionLaws` checks that `!a ^^^ a` equals `bottom`. Each object also includes the absorption laws.

### Involution

`Involution[A]` is `ExcludedMiddle[A] with Noncontradiction[A]` and declares no members of its own. It is the Boolean algebra: a bounded lattice whose complement satisfies both laws above. `InvolutionLaws` adds `!(!a)` equals `a` on top of the `ExcludedMiddle` and `Noncontradiction` laws. The `Boolean` instance is an `Involution`.

To read the bounds and the complement of `Boolean` through its instance (the instance is used explicitly because `Boolean` already has its own `!` operator):

```scala
Involution[Boolean].top
// res4: Boolean = true

Involution[Boolean].bottom
// res5: Boolean = false

Complement[Boolean].complement(true)
// res6: Boolean = false
```

### Writing an Instance

To support our own type, we implement the most specific abstraction it satisfies and test it with the matching laws object, which also checks every weaker abstraction. For a type that forms a Boolean algebra we implement `Involution`, and then run `checkAllLaws(InvolutionLaws)(gen)` as shown on the [overview](index.md#laws). The generic law-testing workflow is described on the [Laws](../laws/index.md) page.

---

## Design Principles

ZIO Prelude does not copy the type class hierarchy of Haskell, Scalaz or Cats. It starts from the algebraic properties that operators can have, and builds small abstractions around each one.

### Properties Instead of a Hierarchy

The classic hierarchy bundles several ideas into one name. A `Monoid` is an associative operation plus an identity element. A `Monad` is a mapping operation, a flattening operation and an identity, all at once.

ZIO Prelude names each property on its own, and a type that has several properties just mixes in several traits:

- [Associative](../functional-abstractions/concrete-types/associative.md) - the order of grouping does not matter.
- [Commutative](../functional-abstractions/concrete-types/commutative.md) - the order of the two operands does not matter.
- [Identity](../functional-abstractions/concrete-types/identity.md) - there is a value that changes nothing when combined.

The same properties exist for type constructors, for example [AssociativeBoth](../functional-abstractions/parameterized-types/associativeboth.md) and [IdentityBoth](../functional-abstractions/parameterized-types/identityboth.md). The [abstraction diagrams](../functional-abstractions/abstraction-diagrams.md) show how they fit together.

### Orthogonality

Each abstraction does one thing, and no two abstractions overlap. That keeps each one small enough to teach in a page, and it lets you ask for exactly the capability you need. A function that only combines values asks for `Associative`, not for a `Monoid` it does not use.

### Laws

Every abstraction comes with laws that its instances must obey, such as `combine(a, combine(b, c)) == combine(combine(a, b), c)` for `Associative`. The laws are written down in the [laws module](../laws/index.md) as properties you can run against your own instances with ZIO Test.

### Pragmatism

Some useful data types break a law in a corner case. ZIO Prelude still provides an instance when the type is useful and the deviation is small, and the documentation of the abstraction says which laws to expect.

### Scala First

Where Haskell has no subtyping, Scala does, and ZIO Prelude uses it. Combined abstractions are ordinary traits, so a type that is both `Covariant` and `IdentityBoth` is automatically what you need for the combinations built on both. See [Syntax and Instances](../syntax-and-instances.md) for how instances and syntax are found.

### Data Types for Domain Modeling

Besides abstractions, the library provides data types that make illegal states hard to express: [NonEmptyList](../functional-data-types/nonemptylist.md), [Validation](../functional-data-types/validation.md), and [newtypes](../newtypes/index.md) with no runtime overhead.

---

## Concepts(Zio-prelude)

These pages explain the ideas behind ZIO Prelude. They answer "why" rather than "how". For tasks use the how-to guides, and for exact APIs use the reference.

- [Design Principles](design-principles.md) - why the abstractions are small, lawful and orthogonal, and how that differs from the classic functor hierarchy.
- [Scala Versions and Platforms](scala-versions-and-platforms.md) - what is the same and what differs across Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3, and across JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native.

---

## Scala Versions and Platforms

### Platforms

All modules are published for the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native, except `zio-prelude-scala-parallel-collections`, which is published for the JVM and Scala Native only. Use `%%%` instead of `%%` on Scala.js and Scala Native.

### Scala Versions

ZIO Prelude is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3. The abstractions and data types behave the same in all of them. The differences are in the macro-based features and in a few APIs that rely on language features.

| Area | Scala 2 | Scala 3 |
|------|---------|---------|
| Newtypes | Defined in `Newtype` and `Subtype`. `wrap` and `derive` are `protected`, so only code inside the newtype object can call them. | The same API with `wrap` and `derive` public. See [Constructing Newtypes](../newtypes/constructing.md). |
| Smart newtype validation | Checked by macros from `zio-prelude-macros`. | Checked by inline macros, and you can add a custom [Validator](../newtypes/validator.md). |
| Deriving `Equal` | No `derived` method. Define the instance with `Equal.default` or `Equal.make`. | `Equal.derived` builds an instance for case classes and sealed traits from the standard `Mirror`. |
| `Debug` for arrays | Not applicable. | A `Debug[IArray[A]]` instance is provided. |

Scala 2.12 has parallel collections in its standard library, while Scala 2.13 and 3 need the separate `scala-parallel-collections` library. See [Scala Parallel Collections](../scala-parallel-collections/index.md) for how that module handles it.

```mermaid
  }

  }

    + bottom: A
  }

    + top: A
  }
  class Involution~A~{
    Boolean
  }
```
