## Talk to an Interactive Process

This guide shows how to talk to a program that reads a request, write a response, and then wait for the next request. Examples include a REPL like `node -i` or `python -i`, and an SSH session. To talk to such a program, we need to send input while it is still running and read its output as it arrives, instead of waiting for it to finish.

Three pieces make this work. A `Queue` holds the requests we want to send. `ProcessInput.fromQueue` feeds that queue into the process's standard input and flushes each chunk right away. `Command#run` starts the process without waiting for it to end, so we can read its standard output while we keep sending input. The example needs these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.process._

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets
```

### Sending Requests to a Node.js REPL

To talk to an interactive Node.js shell, we create the queue, start `node -i` with the queue as its input, and read each response line on a separate fiber:

```scala
val replSession: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    commandQueue <- Queue.unbounded[Chunk[Byte]]
    process      <- Command("node", "-i").stdin(ProcessInput.fromQueue(commandQueue)).run
    sep          <- System.lineSeparator
    fiber        <- process.stdout.linesStream.foreach { line =>
                      ZIO.debug(s"Response from REPL: $line")
                    }.fork
    _            <- commandQueue.offer(Chunk.fromArray(s"1+1${sep}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)))
    _            <- commandQueue.offer(Chunk.fromArray(s"2**8${sep}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)))
    _            <- commandQueue.offer(Chunk.fromArray(s"process.exit(0)${sep}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)))
    _            <- fiber.join
  } yield ()
```

The `ProcessStream#linesStream` fiber prints each line as the REPL writes it. Requests go in through the queue, so the REPL receives them one at a time, and the `process.exit(0)` request ends the session so that `fiber.join` can finish.

A helper for the repeated `Queue#offer` calls is useful in real code. This example keeps everything inline so the steps are easy to follow.

### Platform Support

The Node.js REPL example is tested on the JVM and Scala Native, and it is skipped on Scala.js. The test that feeds a shell script through a queue and expects each reply right away runs only on the JVM. Treat queue-based interaction as JVM-tested, and check it on your own process before relying on it in Scala.js.

Node.js must be installed for the REPL example to run. See [Platform Support](./platform-support.md) for the runtime requirements on each platform.

---

## Pipe One Command into Another

This guide shows how to connect the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next, in the same way that `ps -ef | grep java` works in a shell. ZIO Process builds the pipeline as a value, so nothing starts until you run it. There is no shell involved, so each command in the pipeline is a program with its own arguments. The examples on this page need these imports:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.process._

import java.io.File
```

### Building a Pipeline

`Command#|` joins two commands, and `Command#pipe` is the same operation with a name. To return the process IDs of all running Java processes, we pipe three commands together:

```scala
val javaProcessIds: ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[String]] =
  (Command("ps", "-ef") | Command("grep", "java") | Command("awk", "{print $2}")).lines
```

The pipeline behaves as one command. Its methods, such as `Command#lines`, `Command#string` and `Command#exitCode`, read from the rightmost command, and the output of each command feeds the next.

### Connecting Commands Manually

Under the hood, a pipe connects the stream of one command to the input of the next. You can make the same connection yourself with `ProcessInput.fromStream`, which is useful when the stream comes from somewhere other than a command:

```scala
val processes = Command("ps", "-ef").stream
val javaProcesses = Command("grep", "java").stdin(ProcessInput.fromStream(processes)).stream
val processIds = Command("awk", "{print $2}").stdin(ProcessInput.fromStream(javaProcesses)).lines
```

The operator form in the previous section does the same work and is easier to read.

### How Settings Apply to a Pipeline

A pipeline is a single `Command` value, so you can call the usual setting methods on it. Each setting reaches only the commands that need it:

| Setting                       | Applies to                                                  |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Command#env`                 | Every command in the pipeline                               |
| `Command#workingDirectory`    | Every command in the pipeline                               |
| `Command#stdin`               | The leftmost command, because the others read from the pipe |
| `Command#stdout`              | The rightmost command, which produces the result            |
| `Command#stderr`              | The rightmost command                                       |
| `Command#redirectErrorStream` | The rightmost command                                       |

For example, `Command#stdin` on a pipeline feeds the leftmost command, and the rightmost command's output is the result:

```scala
val javaLineCount: ZIO[Any, CommandError, String] =
  (Command("grep", "java") | Command("wc", "-l"))
    .stdin(ProcessInput.fromUTF8String("java\nrust\njava\n"))
    .string
```

Redirecting the output of a pipeline writes the rightmost command's output to the file:

```scala
val javaFile: ZIO[Any, CommandError, ExitCode] =
  (Command("ps", "-ef") | Command("grep", "java")).stdout(ProcessOutput.FileRedirect(new File("java-processes.txt"))).exitCode
```

For more on redirects, see [Redirect Output to a File](./how-to-redirect-output-to-a-file.md).

### Platform Support

Three of the piping tests are skipped on Scala Native: the basic pipe, pipe associativity, and `Command#stdin` on a piped command. The tests for how settings apply to a pipeline run on all three platforms. On Scala.js, `Command#redirectErrorStream` is ignored, as described on [Redirect Output to a File](./how-to-redirect-output-to-a-file.md).

---

## Platform Support

ZIO Process is one codebase built for three platforms: the JVM, Scala Native, and Scala.js. Most code runs the same way on all three, but some features, error cases, and runtime requirements differ. This page explains how to add the library for each platform and lists the differences to check before you rely on a feature.

### Supported Platforms

Each platform runs programs in its own way. The JVM uses the Java process API, Scala Native uses its own native runtime, and Scala.js runs on Node.js and uses its `child_process` module.

| Platform     | Runtime                           | Scala Versions   |
| ------------ | --------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| JVM          | JDK, 9 or later for some features | 2.12, 2.13 and 3 |
| Scala Native | Native binary                     | 2.12, 2.13 and 3 |
| Scala.js     | Node.js                           | 2.12, 2.13 and 3 |

The project builds and runs its JVM tests on JDK 17, 21 and 25. Programs that call `Process#killTree`, `Process#killTreeForcibly`, `Command#string` or `ProcessStream#string` need JDK 9 or later.

### Adding the Dependency

The [Installation](./index.md#installation) section of the introduction has the dependency blocks for the JVM and for Scala.js. Scala Native artifacts are not on Maven Central yet, because the build skips publishing the Native project, so there is no dependency line to add for Native. Scala Native support is in the code and in the tests, but a release that includes the Native artifact is needed before you can add it to a build. Check the release notes before you plan to use it.

### Behavior Differences

The table below lists the differences that matter most in practice. "Not tested" means the project's test suite does not check that feature on that platform, so verify it in your own program.

| Feature                         | JVM                    | Scala Native        | Scala.js                                |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `Process#killTree`              | Available              | Not available       | Not available                           |
| `Process#killTreeForcibly`      | Available              | Not available       | Not available                           |
| `Process#pid`                   | Available              | Available (parsed)  | Available                               |
| `Process#isAlive`               | Reports the real state | Not tested          | `true` even after exit                  |
| `Process#killForcibly`          | Sends SIGKILL on Unix  | Not tested          | Sends the same signal as `Process#kill` |
| `CommandError.ProgramNotFound`  | Raised                 | Not tested          | Raised                                  |
| `CommandError.PermissionDenied` | Raised                 | Not tested          | Raised                                  |
| `Command#env` with no map set   | Inherits the parent    | Inherits the parent | Empty, with no `PATH`                   |
| `Command#env` with a map        | Adds to the parent     | Adds to the parent  | Replaces the whole environment          |
| `Command#redirectErrorStream`   | Honored                | Honored             | Ignored                                 |
| `File` type                     | `java.io.File`         | `java.io.File`      | `String` path                           |
| `.sh` commands                  | Run as given           | Run through `bash`  | Run as given                            |
| Streaming standard input        | Tested                 | Not tested          | Not tested                              |

#### JVM

The JVM is the most complete platform. It is the only one with `Process#killTree`, the only one where streaming standard input is tested, and the one the examples in this documentation are compiled against. It uses the standard Java `ProcessBuilder`, so a program's arguments reach the program unchanged.

#### Scala Native

On Scala Native, a command whose name ends in `.sh` runs through `bash`, so a shell script runs without needing to be executable. The tests skip `CommandError.ProgramNotFound` and `CommandError.PermissionDenied` on this platform, so these errors may not be raised here. Check the exit code or the output as well.

Streaming standard input is not tested on Scala Native, so verify it in your own program before you rely on it. The same applies to `ProcessInput.fromFile`, whose test is skipped on Native.

#### Scala.js

On Scala.js, the library runs on Node.js. It cannot run in a browser, because it uses the Node.js `child_process` module. The `File` type is a `String` path, so a path that works on the JVM is written as a plain string.

Several features behave differently on Scala.js. `Process#isAlive` stays `true` after the program has exited, so do not use it to detect that a program has finished. `Process#killForcibly` sends the same signal as `Process#kill`, so a program that ignores the terminate signal keeps running after either call. A command that does not call `Command#env` also runs with an empty environment, with no `PATH`. `Command#redirectErrorStream` has no effect.

On Scala.js, a working directory is a plain path string:

```scala
Command("ls", "-l").workingDirectory("/")
```

On the JVM the same call takes `new File("/")`, as shown in [Set the Environment and Working Directory](./how-to-set-the-environment-and-working-directory.md).

---

## CommandError

Every failure in the error channel of a command is a `CommandError`. It is a sealed class that extends `Exception`, so it can also be logged or rethrown like any exception. [Errors and Exit Codes](../concepts/errors-and-exit-codes.md) explains when each failure happens.

### Cases

Match on a case to handle a specific failure.

| Case                                          | Raised when                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CommandError.NotStarted`                     | The base class of the three cases below. Match on those instead.                             |
| `CommandError.ProgramNotFound(cause)`         | The program does not exist. Not reliably raised on Scala Native.                             |
| `CommandError.PermissionDenied(cause)`        | The operating system refuses to run the program. Not reliable on Scala Native.               |
| `CommandError.WorkingDirectoryMissing(workingDirectory)` | The directory set with `Command#workingDirectory` does not exist. Raised on every platform. |
| `CommandError.NonZeroErrorCode(exitCode)`     | The program exits with a non-zero code and the code calls `successfulExitCode`.            |
| `CommandError.IOError(cause)`                 | Reading or writing a stream failed. `cause` is a `java.io.IOException`.                      |
| `CommandError.Error(cause)`                   | Any other failure. Treat it as a catch-all.                                                  |

`cause` is the underlying exception. On Scala.js, the `cause` of `ProgramNotFound` and `PermissionDenied` is a `JavaScriptException`, and `WorkingDirectoryMissing` holds the directory as a `String`.

### Matching a Case

To run a fallback when the first program is missing:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.process._

val output: ZIO[Any, CommandError, String] =
  Command("some-program-that-may-not-exist").string.catchSome {
    case CommandError.ProgramNotFound(_) => Command("fallback-program").string
  }
```

[Handle Command Errors](../how-to-handle-command-errors.md) shows more recipes.

---

## Command

`Command` describes a program, its arguments and how it runs. Creating or configuring a `Command` starts nothing. The type has two shapes, `Command.Standard` for a single program and `Command.Piped` for a pipeline, and most code never needs to tell them apart. For the ideas behind it, see [Commands and Processes](../concepts/commands-and-processes.md).

### Construction

To create a command, call `Command.apply`, which takes the program name and any number of arguments and returns a `Command.Standard`:

```scala
import zio.process._

val ls: Command = Command("ls", "-l", "/tmp")
```

A `Command.Standard` is a case class with the fields `command`, `env`, `workingDirectory`, `stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr` and `redirectErrorStream`. A `Command.Piped(left, right)` joins two commands. The defaults of `Command.apply` are an empty environment, no working directory, inherited standard input, captured standard output and standard error, and no merging of the error stream.

### Settings

Each setting method returns a new `Command`. On a pipeline, each setting reaches only the commands that need it, as described in [Pipe One Command into Another](../piping.md).

| Member                                   | Description                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Command#env(env: Map[String, String])`  | Sets the environment variables. A second call replaces the earlier map.        |
| `Command#workingDirectory(workingDirectory: File)` | Sets the directory the program starts in.                                      |
| `Command#redirectErrorStream(redirectErrorStream: Boolean)` | Merges standard error into standard output. Ignored on Scala.js.               |
| `Command#stdin(stdin: ProcessInput)` | Sets where standard input comes from.                                          |
| `Command#stdout(stdout: ProcessOutput)` | Sets where standard output goes.                                               |
| `Command#stderr(stderr: ProcessOutput)` | Sets where standard error goes.                                                |
| `Command#inheritIO`                      | Sends all three standard streams to the current program's terminal.            |
| `Command#>(redirectTo: File)` | Redirects standard output to a file, overwriting it.                           |
| `Command#>>(redirectTo: File)` | Redirects standard output to a file, appending to it.                          |
| `Command#<<(input: String)`              | Sends a UTF-8 string to standard input.                                        |
| `Command#\|(into: Command)`              | Pipes the output of this command into the input of the next command.           |
| `Command#pipe(into: Command)`            | A named alias for `Command#\|`.                                                |

`ProcessInput` and `ProcessOutput` are described in [ProcessInput, ProcessOutput and ProcessStream](./process-input-output.md). On Scala.js, `File` is a `String` path, and the environment behaves differently, as listed in [Platform Support](../platform-support.md).

### Running

These members start the program. Each one runs the command again every time the effect runs.

| Member                                | Returns                                 | Description                                                            |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Command#run`                         | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, Process]`       | Starts the program and returns its handle.                             |
| `Command#exitCode`                    | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, ExitCode]`      | Runs the program and returns its exit code, zero or not.               |
| `Command#successfulExitCode`          | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, ExitCode]`      | Fails with `CommandError.NonZeroErrorCode` unless the code is zero.    |
| `Command#lines`                       | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[String]]` | Collects standard output as lines, decoded as UTF-8.                   |
| `Command#lines(charset)`              | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[String]]` | Collects standard output as lines in the given encoding.               |
| `Command#linesStream`                  | `ZStream[Any, CommandError, String]`    | Emits standard output as lines, decoded as UTF-8.                      |
| `Command#string`                      | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, String]`        | Returns standard output as one UTF-8 string. Needs JDK 9 or later.     |
| `Command#string(charset)`             | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, String]`        | Returns standard output as one string in the given encoding.           |
| `Command#stream`                      | `ZStream[Any, CommandError, Byte]`      | Emits standard output as bytes.                                        |

The reading members read only standard output and never look at the exit code, as explained in [Errors and Exit Codes](../concepts/errors-and-exit-codes.md).

### Inspecting a Pipeline

`Command#flatten` returns the standard commands of a pipeline as a `NonEmptyChunk[Command.Standard]`, from left to right. For a single command, it returns a chunk with that one command:

```scala
import zio.process._

val pipeline: Command = Command("ps", "-ef") | Command("grep", "java") | Command("wc", "-l")

val programs: List[String] = pipeline.flatten.map(_.command.head).toList
```

---

## ProcessInput, ProcessOutput and ProcessStream

Three types describe the standard streams of a program. `ProcessInput` says where standard input comes from, `ProcessOutput` says where standard output and standard error go, and `ProcessStream` reads a captured output of a running `Process`. [Streams and Redirects](../concepts/streams-and-redirects.md) explains how they fit together.

### ProcessInput

Pass a `ProcessInput` to `Command#stdin`. The values `Inherit` and `Pipe` are objects, and the rest are constructors on `ProcessInput`.

| Member                                         | Description                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ProcessInput.Inherit`                         | Uses the current program's standard input. This is the default.                              |
| `ProcessInput.Pipe`                            | Creates a pipe for standard input but copies nothing into it. Most code uses a constructor.  |
| `ProcessInput.fromFile(file, chunkSize)`       | Streams a file. Scala Native takes no `chunkSize`.                                           |
| `ProcessInput.fromPath(path, chunkSize)`       | Streams a `java.nio.file.Path`, or a `String` path on Scala.js.                              |
| `ProcessInput.fromByteArray(bytes)`            | Sends an array of bytes.                                                                     |
| `ProcessInput.fromString(text, charset)`       | Sends a string in the given encoding.                                                        |
| `ProcessInput.fromUTF8String(text)`            | Sends a string in UTF-8.                                                                     |
| `ProcessInput.fromStream(stream, flushChunksEagerly)` | Sends a `ZStream` of bytes. `flushChunksEagerly` defaults to `false`.                 |
| `ProcessInput.fromQueue(queue)`                | Sends chunks of bytes from a `Queue`, flushing each one right away.                          |

The case classes `ProcessInput.FromStream` and `ProcessInput.JavaStream` are what the constructors build. You rarely create them directly: prefer the constructors above.

### ProcessOutput

Pass a `ProcessOutput` to `Command#stdout` or `Command#stderr`.

| Member                                  | Description                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ProcessOutput.Pipe`                    | Captures the output so that the output methods can read it. This is the default.    |
| `ProcessOutput.Inherit`                 | Sends the output to the current program's terminal.                                 |
| `ProcessOutput.FileRedirect(file)`      | Writes the output to a file, overwriting it.                                        |
| `ProcessOutput.FileAppendRedirect(file)`| Appends the output to a file.                                                       |

With a file redirect, the output is not captured, so the reading methods have nothing to read.

### ProcessStream

`ProcessStream` is the type of `Process#stdout` and `Process#stderr`. Each member reads the stream once, so a second read finds no output.

| Member                                 | Returns                                 | Description                                                   |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ProcessStream#lines`                  | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[String]]` | Reads all lines, decoded as UTF-8.                            |
| `ProcessStream#lines(charset)`         | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[String]]` | Reads all lines in the given encoding.                        |
| `ProcessStream#linesStream`            | `ZStream[Any, CommandError, String]`    | Emits lines as they arrive.                                   |
| `ProcessStream#string`                 | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, String]`        | Reads everything as one UTF-8 string. Needs JDK 9 or later.   |
| `ProcessStream#string(charset)`        | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, String]`        | Reads everything as one string in the given encoding.         |
| `ProcessStream#stream`                 | `ZStream[Any, CommandError, Byte]`      | Emits bytes as they arrive.                                   |

---

## Process

`Process` is the handle that `Command#run` returns once the program has started. It gives access to the program's output streams and controls the program. The idea behind it, and who owns a running program, is explained in [Commands and Processes](../concepts/commands-and-processes.md).

### Streams

The output streams are values on the handle. Both are [ProcessStream](./process-input-output.md#processstream) values.

| Member                 | Returns         | Description                                       |
| ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `Process#stdout`       | `ProcessStream` | Standard output of the program.                   |
| `Process#stderr`       | `ProcessStream` | Standard error of the program.                    |
| `Process#stdoutJava`   | `InputStream`   | Standard output as a Java `InputStream`.          |

### Waiting and Inspecting

| Member                        | Returns                            | Description                                                                         |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Process#exitCode`            | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, ExitCode]` | Waits for the program and returns its exit code, zero or not.                       |
| `Process#successfulExitCode`  | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, ExitCode]` | Waits for the program and fails with `CommandError.NonZeroErrorCode` unless zero.   |
| `Process#isAlive`             | `UIO[Boolean]`                     | Whether the program is still running. Always `true` on Scala.js.                    |
| `Process#pid`                 | `ZIO[Any, CommandError, Long]`     | The operating system's process ID. Needs JDK 9 or later on the JVM.                 |

Interrupting a fiber that waits in `Process#exitCode` or `Process#successfulExitCode` destroys the program.

### Stopping

Each of these waits until the program has exited. [Stop a Running Process](../how-to-stop-a-running-process.md) shows when to use which.

| Member                       | Description                                                                          |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Process#kill`               | Sends the terminate signal (SIGTERM on Unix).                                        |
| `Process#killForcibly`       | Forcefully stops the program (SIGKILL on Unix). On Scala.js, it sends the same signal as `Process#kill`. |
| `Process#killTree`           | Stops the program and its descendants. JVM only, JDK 9 or later.                     |
| `Process#killTreeForcibly`   | Forcefully stops the program and its descendants. JVM only, JDK 9 or later.          |

### Platform Access

`Process#execute` runs a function on the platform's own process object and returns the result as an effect. That object is `java.lang.Process` on the JVM and Scala Native, and a Node.js child process on Scala.js, so code that uses it is not portable:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.process._

val javaPid: ZIO[Any, CommandError, Long] =
  for {
    process <- Command("sleep", "1").run
    pid     <- process.execute(_.pid)
  } yield pid
```

`Process#getOutputStream` returns the program's standard input as a Java `OutputStream`. On Scala.js, it wraps the Node.js standard input stream. It is meant for programs that write to a process by hand.

---

## Tutorial: Build a Disk Usage Report Tool

Welcome! In this tutorial, we build a small command-line tool that reports the biggest files and folders under a directory. Along the way we run a command, pipe three commands together, turn the output into Scala values, handle a failure, and write the result to a file. By the end, you will have used the main parts of ZIO Process in one program.

The tool relies on the Unix programs `du`, `sort` and `head`, so it runs on Linux and macOS. We assume that you know basic ZIO, such as `for` comprehensions and `ZIOAppDefault`, and that ZIO Process is on your classpath as described in [Installation](./index.md#installation).

### Step 1: Run a Command

We start with the simplest possible use: run `du` for a directory and read its output as lines. `du -ak` prints the size in kilobytes of every file and folder, one per line, as the size, a tab, and the path:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.process._

import java.io.File

def allEntries(dir: File): ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[String]] =
  Command("du", "-ak", ".").workingDirectory(dir).lines
```

`Command("du", "-ak", ".")` only describes the program. `Command#workingDirectory` returns a new `Command` that starts in `dir`, and `Command#lines` runs it and collects standard output as a `Chunk[String]`. Nothing runs until the effect itself runs.

### Step 2: Pipe Commands Together

The output has one line for every file, which is far too much. In a shell, we write `du -ak . | sort -rn | head -n 5`. ZIO Process has the same idea with the `Command#|` operator, which connects the output of one command to the input of the next:

```scala
def biggestLines(dir: File, count: Int): ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[String]] =
  (Command("du", "-ak", ".").workingDirectory(dir) |
    Command("sort", "-rn") |
    Command("head", "-n", count.toString)).lines
```

The pipeline is also a `Command`, so `Command#lines` reads the output of its last command. The pipe works without a shell, so each command is a program with its own arguments. `Command#workingDirectory` on a pipeline applies to every command in it.

### Step 3: Turn Lines into Values

Lines of text are awkward to work with, so we parse each one into an `Entry` with a size and a path. A line that does not match the format is skipped:

```scala
final class Entry(val sizeKb: Long, val path: String)

def parse(line: String): Option[Entry] =
  line.split("\t", 2) match {
    case Array(size, path) => scala.util.Try(size.toLong).toOption.map(new Entry(_, path))
    case _                 => None
  }

def biggest(dir: File, count: Int): ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[Entry]] =
  biggestLines(dir, count).map(_.map(parse).collect { case Some(entry) => entry })
```

The result of `biggest` is an ordinary ZIO effect that returns typed values, so it composes with the rest of a program.

### Step 4: Handle a Failure

What happens when the directory does not exist? `Command#workingDirectory` makes the effect fail with `CommandError.WorkingDirectoryMissing` before any program starts. Every failure of ZIO Process is a `CommandError`, so we can match on the case that we want to handle and let the rest through:

```scala
def biggestOrEmpty(dir: File, count: Int): ZIO[Any, CommandError, Chunk[Entry]] =
  biggest(dir, count).catchSome { case CommandError.WorkingDirectoryMissing(_) => ZIO.succeed(Chunk.empty) }
```

Returning an empty chunk hides the problem, so a real tool prints a message instead. We keep the example short. [Handle Command Errors](./how-to-handle-command-errors.md) covers the other cases.

### Step 5: Write a Report to a File

To save the report, we send a string to the standard input of `cat` and redirect its output to a file. `Command#<<` feeds the string to standard input, and `Command#>` writes standard output to the file:

```scala
def report(entries: Chunk[Entry]): String =
  entries.map(entry => f"${entry.sizeKb}%10d KB  ${entry.path}").mkString("", "\n", "\n")

def save(entries: Chunk[Entry], file: File): ZIO[Any, CommandError, ExitCode] =
  ((Command("cat") << report(entries)) > file).exitCode
```

`Command#exitCode` runs the command and returns its exit code. Because the output goes to a file, there is nothing for the program to read.

### Putting It Together

We now have all the pieces. The complete tool takes a directory from the command line, defaulting to the current one, prints the report, and saves it to `report.txt`:

```scala
object DiskUsage extends ZIOAppDefault {
  override def run: ZIO[ZIOAppArgs, Any, Unit] =
    for {
      args    <- getArgs
      dir      = new File(args.headOption.getOrElse("."))
      entries <- biggest(dir, 10)
      _       <- Console.print(report(entries))
      _       <- save(entries, new File("report.txt"))
    } yield ()
}
```

That's it! We built a tool from three commands and a few lines of parsing.

### Next Steps

To go further, read how to [Run a Command and Read Its Output](./how-to-run-a-command-and-read-its-output.md) with streams for very large output, or how to [Stop a Running Process](./how-to-stop-a-running-process.md) that takes too long.

## How ZIO Profiling Works

A thread profiler sees only the ZIO runtime's evaluation loop. ZIO Profiling instead asks each fiber where in your program it is, and reports per named location. This page explains the pieces and their limits.

### Cost centers

A [`CostCenter`](../reference/cost-center.md) is a path of names, such as `handle;parse`. The path is stored in a `FiberRef`. Running an effect with `CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("parse")` extends the path for the duration of that effect. A fiber that is forked inherits the path of its parent. When it is joined, the parent keeps its own path.

Names come from two places: the [compiler plugin](../reference/tagging-plugin.md), which wraps every `def` and `val` of type `ZIO` or `ZStream`, and the calls you write yourself ([Tag effects by hand](../how-to/tag-effects-by-hand.md)). Code outside any tag runs in the root cost center.

### The sampling profiler

The sampling profiler is a ZIO `Supervisor`. It keeps the set of fibers that are currently running: a fiber joins the set when it starts or resumes and leaves it when it suspends or ends. A background fiber wakes up every `samplingPeriod` and adds one to the count of each running fiber's cost center.

Two consequences follow:

- Time spent waiting on an asynchronous result, such as a queue `take` or a sleep with `ZIO.sleep`, is not counted, because the fiber is suspended. Blocking code, such as `Thread.sleep` inside `ZIO.succeed`, is counted.
- Parallel fibers are all counted on each tick, so the total can exceed the wall-clock time.

### The causal profiler

The causal profiler runs a series of experiments. In each one it picks a cost center and a speedup between 0 and `maxConsideredSpeedUp` percent. It cannot make code faster, so it does the opposite: on every tick, for each fiber running inside the selected cost center, the profiler adds a delay that all other fibers owe. Each of them pays it by sleeping at its next synchronous step. Slowing everything else by 25% has the same effect on the ratio as speeding up the selected part by 25%.

Each experiment counts how often your [progress points](../reference/causal-profiler.md#progress-and-latency-points) were reached. Comparing the counts of experiments with different speedups for the same cost center shows whether a faster cost center would raise throughput. A rise means the part limits the program. A flat line means it does not.

A fiber pays its delay in two places: just before it runs a synchronous step, and when it ends without being interrupted. A fiber that blocks for a long time inside one step is therefore delayed only at its next synchronous step or when it ends. A fiber that was suspended on an asynchronous result is credited for the delay that built up meanwhile when it resumes, and is not delayed for it again.

### Limits

- ZIO Profiling reports CPU use of ZIO programs on the JVM. For heap profiling, use another tool such as async-profiler or VisualVM.
- Only tagged code gets its own name. Untagged code is attributed to the nearest enclosing tag, or to the root.
- The causal profiler considers only tagged cost centers as candidates.
- The profilers add overhead that grows as `samplingPeriod` shrinks.

### Related

- [Which profiler do I need?](which-profiler.md)
- [Sampling profiler reference](../reference/sampling-profiler.md) and [causal profiler reference](../reference/causal-profiler.md)

---

## Which Profiler Do I Need?

ZIO Profiling ships two profilers in the `zio-profiling` module, plus a JMH integration. They answer different questions.

### Where does my program spend its time?

Use the [sampling profiler](../reference/sampling-profiler.md). It records, at a fixed interval, which cost center each running fiber is in, and the result renders as a flamegraph. It is cheap, it stops when your program finishes, and it works on any program. Start with the [tutorial](../tutorials/first-flamegraph.md).

### Which part should I speed up?

Use the [causal profiler](../reference/causal-profiler.md). Time spent is not the same as time that matters: a part of a program that runs in parallel with a slower part can be made faster without changing the result at all. The causal profiler estimates how much the whole program would speed up if one part became faster. It needs a program that runs in a loop, and a progress point that marks one unit of work. Start with [Find a bottleneck with the causal profiler](../how-to/find-bottleneck-causal.md).

### How fast is my benchmark, and where does it spend its time?

Use the [JMH profiler](../reference/jmh-profiler.md), which runs the sampling profiler inside a JMH run. See [Profile JMH benchmarks](../how-to/profile-jmh-benchmarks.md).

### Related

- [How ZIO Profiling works](how-it-works.md) explains cost centers and what each profiler measures.

---

## Getting Started with ZIO Profiling

This page takes you from an empty build to your first profile in a few minutes. For a slower walk-through that also draws a flamegraph, see the [tutorial](tutorials/first-flamegraph.md).

### Add the dependencies

Add the library and the tagging compiler plugin to the module you want to profile. The artifacts, platforms and supported Scala versions are listed in [Installation](index.md#installation) and [Modules](index.md#modules).

The plugin is what gives the profile useful names. Without it, every sample lands in one unnamed entry.

### Profile your first program

The program below runs two effects at the same time. `SamplingProfiler().profile` runs it and returns a `ProfilingResult`: the number of samples taken in each cost center. A cost center is a name for a part of your program, such as `fast` or `slow` below.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.CostCenter
import zio.profiling.sampling._

val fast: UIO[Unit] = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("fast")(ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(200)))

val slow: UIO[Unit] = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("slow")(ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(600)))

val profile: Task[Unit] =
  SamplingProfiler()
    .profile(fast <&> slow)
    .flatMap(result => ZIO.foreach(result.stackCollapse)(Console.printLine(_)).unit)
```

Here `CostCenter.withChildCostCenter` names the two effects by hand. With the compiler plugin enabled, every `def` and `val` of type `ZIO` or `ZStream` gets such a name automatically, so you can leave the wrapping out. Running `profile` prints one line per cost center, such as `fast 20` and `slow 60`: the path of names, a space, and the sample count. The `slow` line has about three times as many samples as `fast`, because it runs three times as long.

### Next steps

- Draw a flamegraph from the output: [Profile a program and read the flamegraph](tutorials/first-flamegraph.md).
- Decide which profiler fits your question: [Which profiler do I need?](concepts/which-profiler.md).
- Find the part of a program that limits throughput: [Find a bottleneck with the causal profiler](how-to/find-bottleneck-causal.md).

---

## Find a Bottleneck with the Causal Profiler

Use the causal profiler when you want to know which part of your program is worth optimizing. A sampling profile shows where time is spent. A causal profile estimates how much the whole program would speed up if one part became faster. A part that takes a lot of time is not always the part that limits throughput.

This guide shows how to:

- mark the progress of your program with a progress point
- run the causal profiler on a program that runs in a loop
- write the result so you can open it in the Coz visualizer

It assumes that the effects you want to rank are tagged by the [compiler plugin](setup-tagging-plugin.md) (or by hand, see [Tag effects by hand](tag-effects-by-hand.md)). The profiler only ranks cost centers, so without tags there is nothing to rank.

### Step 1: Mark progress with a progress point

The profiler measures speed as the number of times a progress point is reached per unit of time. Put `CausalProfiler.progressPoint` where one unit of your work is done. For a request handler, that is the end of each request. For a loop, it is the end of each iteration.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.causal._

val fast: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(40))

val slow1: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(20))

val slow2: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(60))

val iteration: UIO[Unit] =
  (fast <&> (slow1 <&> slow2)) *> CausalProfiler.progressPoint("iteration done")
```

### Step 2: Run the profiler on an endless program

The profiler runs experiments until it has finished `iterations` of them, then interrupts your program itself. So the program you pass in must run forever. Use `forever`, which gives an effect of type `ZIO[R, E, Nothing]`, and `CausalProfiler.profile` only accepts that type.

The defaults are chosen for real programs, and they make a run slow. The profiler waits 30 seconds before its first experiment, runs each experiment for at least 1 second, and waits 2 seconds between experiments. For a quick first run, shorten those values:

```scala
val profiler = CausalProfiler(
  iterations = 10,
  warmUpPeriod = 0.seconds,
  coolOffPeriod = 0.seconds
)

profiler
  .profile(iteration.forever)
  .flatMap(_.renderToFile("profile.coz"))
```

Once you know the program works, raise `iterations` and keep the default timings. Each experiment picks a part of the program and slows down the other code that runs at the same time. Slowing everything else by the same amount is the same as speeding up the selected part. A larger number of iterations gives a more reliable ranking.

### Step 3: Read the result

`renderToFile` writes one block of text per experiment. Upload the file to the [Coz visualizer](https://plasma-umass.org/coz/) to see the result as a chart. Each experiment gives the cost center it selected and the speedup it applied. The chart shows how the program's throughput changed for each selected part.

Read the chart like this:

- A part where throughput rises with the speedup is a good place to optimize. Making it faster makes the whole program faster.
- A flat line means the part does not limit the program. Making it faster changes nothing.

For the program in Step 1, you should expect `slow2` to be the limiting part. Each iteration takes as long as its slowest parallel branch, which is `slow2` at 60 ms. A speedup of `slow1` or `fast` gives no gain, because `slow2` still takes the same time.

:::warning[Only cost centers are ranked]
The profiler considers only effects that run inside a cost center. Untagged code is ignored. If the chart lists no parts you expected, check that the module is compiled with the compiler plugin.
:::

### Step 4: Narrow the candidates (optional)

If you know which parts to test, pass `candidateSelector`. It receives the name of the last location of a cost center and returns `true` for the ones to consider:

```scala
CausalProfiler(
  iterations = 10,
  warmUpPeriod = 0.seconds,
  coolOffPeriod = 0.seconds,
  candidateSelector = _.contains("slow")
)
```

The selector only restricts which parts the profiler experiments with. It does not change how the program runs.

### Related

- [Causal profiler reference](../reference/causal-profiler.md) lists every option and the output format.
- [Set up the tagging compiler plugin](setup-tagging-plugin.md) makes the parts visible to the profiler.

## Fix Empty or Unnamed Profiles

This guide lists the usual reasons a profile has no useful content, and the fix for each.

### The profile has one line with no name

A line such as ` 123` means all samples landed in the root cost center. Nothing in the profiled code is tagged.

- Enable the [tagging compiler plugin](setup-tagging-plugin.md) in the module that contains the code, and run `sbt clean compile`.
- Or tag the effects yourself. See [Tag effects by hand](tag-effects-by-hand.md).

### The profile is missing a part of the program

The sampler counts only fibers that are running. Time spent waiting on an asynchronous result, for example `ZIO.sleep` or a queue `take`, is not counted. Only effects that run with the profiler attached are sampled: those inside `profile`, inside `.supervised(supervisor)`, or on the `supervisedRuntime`.

### The causal profiler dies with "Program completed before profiler could collect sufficient data"

The program ended before the profiler finished its experiments. Pass an effect that never ends, such as `iteration.forever`, or use `profileIterations`. If the iterations are slow, lower `iterations`, `warmUpPeriod` and `minExperimentDuration`.

### The causal profiler never finishes

The profiler experiments only with tagged cost centers that are running and not the root. If no part of the program is tagged, or `candidateSelector` rejects every name, no experiment ever starts. Tag the code, and check the selector. See [Find a bottleneck with the causal profiler](find-bottleneck-causal.md).

### The causal profile has no throughput lines

The program never reached a progress point during an experiment. Call `CausalProfiler.progressPoint` where one unit of work completes.

### JMH writes no `profile.folded`

The JMH profiler starts in the first warm-up iteration. Run with at least one warm-up iteration (`-wi 1` or more). See the [JMH profiler reference](../reference/jmh-profiler.md).

### Related

- [How ZIO Profiling works](../concepts/how-it-works.md) explains what each profiler counts.

## Profile JMH Benchmarks

The [Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH)](https://github.com/openjdk/jmh) measures how fast a piece of code runs. ZIO Profiling can attach a sampling profiler to a JMH run, so each benchmark also produces a profile of the ZIO effects it runs. This guide shows how to set up a benchmark, run it with the profiler, and find the profile file.

### Step 1: Tag the code you benchmark

Put the effects you want to profile in code that the compiler plugin tags, so that they have names in the profile. See [Set up the tagging compiler plugin](setup-tagging-plugin.md). The benchmark module needs the plugin too, because the effects you measure are usually defined there.

### Step 2: Add the JMH integration

Add the `zio-profiling-jmh` module to the project that holds your benchmarks:

```sbt
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling-jmh" % "0.3.5"
```

The module provides `zio.profiling.jmh.BenchmarkUtils`, which runs ZIO effects on the runtime that the profiler uses. Run your effects through `BenchmarkUtils.unsafeRun` rather than through `Unsafe` yourself, so that they are profiled.

### Step 3: Write a benchmark that runs ZIO effects

The benchmark below sums the doubled values of a list with ZIO. The effect is defined in a `def`, so the plugin tags it. It is a self-contained file: it needs only the `zio-profiling-jmh` dependency and the JMH annotations. The import `zio.{Scope => _, _}` hides ZIO's `Scope`, which would otherwise clash with JMH's `@State(Scope.Thread)`.

```scala
package bench

import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations._
import zio.{Scope => _, _}
import zio.profiling.jmh.BenchmarkUtils

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit

@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Array(Mode.Throughput))
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)
@Measurement(iterations = 5)
@Warmup(iterations = 3)
@Fork(1)
class SumBenchmarks {

  private val numbers: List[Int] = (1 to 1000).toList

  private def doubledSum: UIO[Int] =
    ZIO.foreach(numbers)(n => ZIO.succeed(n * 2)).map(_.sum)

  @Benchmark
  def sumWithZio(): Int = BenchmarkUtils.unsafeRun(doubledSum)
}
```

Keep each benchmark method to one call to `BenchmarkUtils.unsafeRun`. Put the effect itself in a `def` or `val` outside the method, so the compiler plugin can name it.

### Step 4: Run the benchmark with the profiler

With sbt-jmh, pass the profiler class to the `-prof` option. The argument is the fully qualified name of the benchmark method:

```sbt
Jmh/run -i 3 -wi 3 -f1 -t1 -prof zio.profiling.jmh.JmhZioProfiler bench.SumBenchmarks.sumWithZio
```

The options `-i`, `-wi`, `-f` and `-t` set the number of measurement iterations, warm-up iterations, forks and threads. Use the same values you use for the benchmark otherwise.

### Step 5: Find the profile

The profiler starts sampling during the first warm-up iteration and resets its counts when the measurement iterations start. Only the samples from the measurement iterations are written. After the last measurement iteration, it writes a `profile.folded` file into a directory named after the benchmark and its mode, inside the directory the JVM was started from.

For the benchmark above, which runs in throughput mode, the file is `<project directory>/bench.SumBenchmarks.sumWithZio-Throughput/profile.folded`. Turn it into a flamegraph as described in the [tutorial](../tutorials/first-flamegraph.md):

```bash
flamegraph.pl "bench.SumBenchmarks.sumWithZio-Throughput/profile.folded" > sum.svg
```

:::note[What the profile covers]
The profile records only the ZIO effects that run during the measurement iterations. Time spent in JMH itself, or in code that is not run through `BenchmarkUtils`, is not included. If the benchmark code is not tagged by the compiler plugin, the file has a single line with no name, as in the [tutorial](../tutorials/first-flamegraph.md).
:::

### Related

- [Profile a running application](profile-running-application.md) explains the runtime that the JMH profiler creates internally.

---

## Profile Part of a Program with a Supervisor

`SamplingProfiler().profile` and `CausalProfiler.profile` wrap the whole effect you pass in. When you want to profile only one part, for example one request handler in a larger application, attach the profiler as a supervisor to just that part. This guide shows how, for both profilers.

### Profile part of a program with the sampling profiler

`makeSupervisor` starts the sampler in the current scope and returns the supervisor that stores the samples. The sampler only sees effects that run with `.supervised(supervisor)`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.sampling._

val handleRequest: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(100))

val profiled: Task[ProfilingResult] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    SamplingProfiler().makeSupervisor.flatMap { supervisor =>
      handleRequest.supervised(supervisor) *> supervisor.value
    }
  }
```

Sampling stops when the scope closes. Read the samples before that, with `supervisor.value`.

### Profile part of a program with the causal profiler

`CausalProfiler.supervisor` creates the profiler as a supervisor. Reading its `value` waits until the profile is complete, so run the program on a separate fiber. The profiled effect needs OpSupervision enabled and must run forever:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.causal._

val iteration: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(20)) *> CausalProfiler.progressPoint("iteration")

val profile: Task[ProfilingResult] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    CausalProfiler(iterations = 10, warmUpPeriod = 0.seconds, coolOffPeriod = 0.seconds).supervisor.flatMap {
      supervisor =>
        iteration.forever
          .withRuntimeFlags(RuntimeFlags.enable(RuntimeFlag.OpSupervision))
          .supervised(supervisor)
          .fork
          .flatMap(fiber => supervisor.value <* fiber.interrupt)
    }
  }
```

`CausalProfiler.profile` does the same steps for you, and also fails with `Program completed before profiler could collect sufficient data` when the program ends early.

### Related

- [Profile a running application](profile-running-application.md) attaches the sampler to a whole runtime.
- [Sampling profiler reference](../reference/sampling-profiler.md) and [causal profiler reference](../reference/causal-profiler.md) describe the methods used here.

---

## Profile a Running Application

`SamplingProfiler().profile` profiles one effect and stops when that effect finishes. Sometimes you want a profiler that keeps collecting samples for as long as the application runs, for example in a long-running service or in a benchmark harness. This guide shows how to build a runtime that is profiled from the start, read its samples at any time, and shut it down.

### How it works

`SamplingProfiler().supervisedRuntime` creates a ZIO `Runtime` with the sampling profiler attached as a supervisor. Every effect you run with that runtime is observed. A background fiber takes a sample every `samplingPeriod`. The samples are kept in a `SamplingProfilerSupervisor`, which you get from the runtime's environment.

Creating the runtime needs an implicit `Unsafe` value, which is why it is wrapped in `Unsafe.unsafe`. Running effects through the runtime also uses the unsafe API.

### Step 1: Create the runtime

Create the runtime once, at startup. Creating it starts the sampling fiber.

### Step 2: Run your effects through the runtime

Use the runtime's unsafe API to run effects. Only effects run through this runtime are profiled.

### Step 3: Read the samples

Get the supervisor from the runtime's environment and ask it for the samples collected so far. `unsafeValue()` returns a `ProfilingResult` without waiting for anything, so you can call it while the application keeps running. `stackCollapseToFile` returns a `Task[Unit]`, so run it as an effect in your application.

### Step 4: Reset and shut down

To start a new measurement window, clear the samples with `reset()`. To stop profiling, shut the runtime down, which also stops the sampling fiber.

:::warning[Shut down the runtime]
A profiled runtime keeps a sampling fiber running until it is shut down. Shut it down when you are done, or the background sampling continues for the life of the process.
:::

### The complete sequence

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.sampling._

// Step 1: create the runtime
val profiledRuntime: Runtime.Scoped[SamplingProfilerSupervisor] =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    SamplingProfiler().supervisedRuntime
  }

// Step 2: run effects through the runtime
val work: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(500))

Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  profiledRuntime.unsafe.run(work)
}

// Step 3: read the samples
val supervisor = profiledRuntime.environment.get[SamplingProfilerSupervisor]

val snapshot: ProfilingResult = supervisor.unsafeValue()

snapshot.stackCollapseToFile("profile.folded")

// Step 4: reset and shut down
supervisor.reset()

Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  profiledRuntime.unsafe.shutdown()
}
```

### Choose a sampling period

The default sampling period is 10 ms. A shorter period gives more samples and more overhead. A longer period gives fewer samples and less overhead. Pass the period to the constructor:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.sampling._

val lowOverhead = SamplingProfiler(samplingPeriod = 50.millis)
```

### Related

- [Sampling profiler reference](../reference/sampling-profiler.md) describes every method used here.
- [Profile JMH benchmarks](profile-jmh-benchmarks.md) uses this runtime for benchmarks.

## Set Up the Tagging Compiler Plugin

The tagging compiler plugin gives each ZIO effect a name made from its place in your source code. Both profilers use those names. This guide shows how to turn the plugin on for a module, and what it changes in your code.

### Step 1: Add the plugin to the module you want to profile

The plugin must be enabled in the module that contains the code you want to profile. The rewritten code calls `CostCenter` from the `zio-profiling` library, so that dependency is needed in the same module:

```sbt
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling" % "0.3.5"
libraryDependencies += compilerPlugin("dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling-tagging-plugin" % "0.3.5")
```

In a multi-module build, add the `compilerPlugin` line only to the modules that contain effects you want named. The plugin is published for Scala 2.12, Scala 2.13 and Scala 3. Use the same `%%` form on every version; sbt picks the matching artifact.

### Step 2: Know what the plugin rewrites

The plugin looks at each `def` and `val` with a right-hand side whose type is a ZIO effect (`ZIO[R, E, A]`) or a stream (`ZStream[R, E, A]`). It wraps the right-hand side in a call to `CostCenter.withChildCostCenter` (or `withChildCostCenterStream` for streams). The name it passes is the fully qualified name of the definition, followed by the file name and line number.

Your code stays the same. The rewrite happens during compilation:

```text
val testEffect = ZIO.unit

// is compiled as if it were

val testEffect = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("foo.Foo.testEffect(Foo.scala:12)")(ZIO.unit)
```

Because the name holds the line number, it changes when you move code. That is expected: the name always points at the definition that was tagged.

### Step 3: Check that the plugin runs

Run `sbt clean compile` once after you add the plugin, so that every source file is compiled again with the rewrite. Then run a profile. With the plugin active, the names in the output look like the one above. Without it, the output contains a single entry with no name, because every sample lands in the root cost center.

:::note[Definitions that are not tagged]
Only `def` and `val` definitions are rewritten. Effects created inline, such as `ZIO.succeed(...)` passed straight into a call, are part of the enclosing definition and get that name. To give such an effect its own name, wrap it with `CostCenter.withChildCostCenter`. See [Tag effects by hand](tag-effects-by-hand.md).
:::

### Related

- [Tag effects by hand](tag-effects-by-hand.md) gives you the same names without the plugin.
- [CostCenter reference](../reference/cost-center.md) lists the methods on cost centers.

---

## Tag Effects by Hand

The compiler plugin names effects for you. Sometimes you want a name it does not give: a block inside a large `def`, a part of a stream, or a project that cannot use the plugin. Then you can wrap the effect yourself with `CostCenter`. This guide shows how.

### Wrap an effect in a cost center

`CostCenter.withChildCostCenter(name)(effect)` runs `effect` inside a new child cost center called `name`. The child is nested under whatever cost center is active when the call runs, so calls can be nested to build a path:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.CostCenter

val parse: UIO[Int] = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("parse")(ZIO.succeed(21))

val render: UIO[String] = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("render")(ZIO.succeed("done"))

val handle: UIO[String] = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("handle") {
  for {
    n <- parse
    s <- render
  } yield s"$s $n"
}
```

When `handle` runs, the time spent in `parse` is attributed to the path `handle;parse`, and the time in `render` to `handle;render`. The effect's result, errors and interruption behave as they would without the wrapper.

### Wrap a stream

For a `ZStream`, use `CostCenter.withChildCostCenterStream`. It has the same shape:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.profiling.CostCenter

val numbers: ZStream[Any, Nothing, Int] =
  CostCenter.withChildCostCenterStream("numbers")(ZStream.range(1, 1000))
```

### Choose names that you can search for

The name is the only part of the path you choose, so pick names that make the flamegraph readable:

- Use the name of the operation, such as `"parse"` or `"write-response"`, rather than a log message.
- Keep the names stable. Renaming a cost center splits its samples from older profiles, which makes comparisons harder.
- Do not add the line number or a counter. The profiler groups samples by name, so a name that changes on every run is treated as a new cost center each time.

### Use the current cost center

`CostCenter.getCurrent` returns the cost center the running fiber is in. It is useful when you want to log which part of the program produced a result:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.CostCenter

val whereAmI: UIO[CostCenter] = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("check")(CostCenter.getCurrent)
```

### Related

- [Set up the tagging compiler plugin](setup-tagging-plugin.md) does this automatically for every `def` and `val`.
- [CostCenter reference](../reference/cost-center.md) lists every method.

## Introduction to ZIO Profiling

ZIO Profiling is a collection of different profilers for better understanding the runtime behavior of ZIO programs.

[![Concept](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Concept-orange.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-profiling/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-profiling_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-profiling_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-profiling_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-profiling_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-profiling_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-profiling_2.13) [![ZIO Profiling](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-profiling?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-profiling)

### Introduction

Normal cpu profilers cannot really be used to profile code using an effect system. Profilers operating on a thread level will only see that threads are spending time in the evaluation loop of the effect system, producing profiles that are not useful for application developers.

Instead, profiling a program written using an effect system requires a profiler that is aware of the effect system and can report where the effects were constructed / which user code the effect system is spending time on. ZIO profiling aims to be that library for the ZIO effect system.

The library focuses exclusively on cpu profiling. For heap profiling please consider using other tools such as async-profiler or VisualVM.

ZIO Profiling ships a [sampling profiler](reference/sampling-profiler.md) that shows where your program spends its time, and a [causal profiler](reference/causal-profiler.md) that shows which part is worth optimizing. To choose between them, see [Which profiler do I need?](concepts/which-profiler.md).

### Installation

All modules are published for Scala 2.12, Scala 2.13 and Scala 3, on the JVM only, and depend on ZIO 2.

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Both profilers, CostCenter and the profiling results (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling" % "0.3.5"
)
```

### Modules

#### Tagging compiler plugin

The plugin names each ZIO effect and stream in your code after its source location. Both profilers report per name, so you almost always want it. See [Set up the tagging compiler plugin](how-to/setup-tagging-plugin.md) and the [plugin reference](reference/tagging-plugin.md).

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Compiler plugin that tags effects with their source location (JVM)
  compilerPlugin("dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling-tagging-plugin" % "0.3.5")
)
```

#### JMH integration

The module attaches the sampling profiler to JMH benchmarks. See [Profile JMH benchmarks](how-to/profile-jmh-benchmarks.md) and the [JMH profiler reference](reference/jmh-profiler.md).

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // JMH profiler that writes a flamegraph input file per benchmark (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling-jmh" % "0.3.5"
)
```

### Where to go next

New to the library? Follow [Getting Started](getting-started.md), then the [tutorial](tutorials/first-flamegraph.md).

## Causal Profiler Reference

The causal profiler lives in package `zio.profiling.causal`. It is experimental. It is inspired by [Coz](https://github.com/plasma-umass/coz): it selects a cost center, makes the rest of the program run relatively slower for a while, and counts how many progress points are reached. From that it estimates how much the program would speed up if the selected part were faster. For a how-to guide, see [Find a bottleneck with the causal profiler](../how-to/find-bottleneck-causal.md).

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.causal._
```

### CausalProfiler

```text
final case class CausalProfiler(
  iterations: Int = 100,
  candidateSelector: String => Boolean = _ => true,
  samplingPeriod: Duration = 20.millis,
  minExperimentDuration: Duration = 1.second,
  experimentTargetSamples: Int = 30,
  warmUpPeriod: Duration = 30.seconds,
  coolOffPeriod: Duration = 2.seconds,
  zeroSpeedupWeight: Int = 10,
  maxConsideredSpeedUp: Int = 100,
  sleepPrecision: Duration = 10.millis
)
```

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `iterations` | `100` | Number of experiments to run before the profile is complete. |
| `candidateSelector` | `_ => true` | Called with the last location of a candidate cost center. Only cost centers for which it returns `true` are selected for experiments. Cost centers that are the root are never selected. |
| `samplingPeriod` | `20.millis` | How often the profiler looks at where fibers are. Lower values increase overhead. |
| `minExperimentDuration` | `1.second` | Shortest length of an experiment. |
| `experimentTargetSamples` | `30` | Number of times each progress point should be reached during an experiment. The profiler lengthens or shortens the next experiment to get close to this number. |
| `warmUpPeriod` | `30.seconds` | Time to wait after the profile starts before the first experiment. |
| `coolOffPeriod` | `2.seconds` | Time to wait between two experiments. |
| `zeroSpeedupWeight` | `10` | On average, one experiment in every `zeroSpeedupWeight` applies no speedup at all, which gives a baseline to compare against. |
| `maxConsideredSpeedUp` | `100` | Largest speedup, as a percentage, that an experiment can apply. Values above 100 have no practical use. |
| `sleepPrecision` | `10.millis` | Estimated accuracy of `Thread.sleep`. Within this distance of the target time, the profiler busy-waits for accuracy. |

With the defaults, a profile takes at least `warmUpPeriod + iterations * minExperimentDuration + (iterations - 1) * coolOffPeriod`, which is a little over 5 minutes (328 seconds). There is no cool-off after the last experiment. For tests and first runs, lower `warmUpPeriod`, `coolOffPeriod` and `iterations`.

```scala
CausalProfiler(iterations = 10, warmUpPeriod = 0.seconds).iterations
// res0: Int = 10
```

### Methods

| Method | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `profile` | `[R, E](zio: ZIO[R, E, Nothing]): ZIO[R, E, ProfilingResult]` | Runs `zio` until the profile is complete, then interrupts it and returns the result. `zio` must never end on its own: use `forever`. If `zio` finishes before enough data is collected, the profile dies with the message `Program completed before profiler could collect sufficient data`. |
| `profileIterations` | `[R, E](zio: ZIO[R, E, Any]): ZIO[R, E, ProfilingResult]` | Runs `zio` in a loop and adds a progress point named `iteration done` after each run. Use it when one run of `zio` is one unit of work. |
| `supervisor` | `ZIO[Scope, Nothing, Supervisor[ProfilingResult]]` | Creates the profiler as a supervisor, for use with `zio.supervised`. Reading its `value` waits until the profile is complete. The profiled effects must have OpSupervision enabled. |

### Progress and latency points

The companion object `CausalProfiler` has the functions that mark progress in your program. They do nothing when no profile is running.

| Function | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `progressPoint(name)` | `UIO[Unit]` | Counts one unit of progress under `name`. The profiler measures throughput as the rate of these counts. |
| `enterLatencyPoint(name)` | `UIO[Unit]` | Marks the start of a unit of work whose latency you want to track. |
| `exitLatencyPoint(name)` | `UIO[Unit]` | Marks the end of a unit of work started with `enterLatencyPoint`. |
| `latencyPointScoped(name)` | `URIO[Scope, Unit]` | Calls `enterLatencyPoint` now and `exitLatencyPoint` when the scope closes. |

```scala
val request: UIO[Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped(CausalProfiler.latencyPointScoped("request") *> ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(10)))
```

Latency points count arrivals and departures during each experiment. `difference` in the output is arrivals minus departures: the number of units that entered during the experiment and had not left by its end.

### ProfilingResult

```text
final case class ProfilingResult(experiments: List[ExperimentResult])
```

| Member | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `experiments` | `List[ExperimentResult]` | One entry per completed experiment. |
| `render` | `String` | The experiments in the text format read by the Coz visualizer. |
| `renderToFile(path)` | `Task[Unit]` | Writes `render` to `path`, creating parent directories if needed. |

#### ExperimentResult

```text
final case class ExperimentResult(
  selected: CostCenter,
  speedup: Float,
  duration: Long,
  effectiveDuration: Long,
  selectedSamples: Long,
  throughputData: List[ThroughputData],
  latencyData: List[LatencyData]
)
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `selected` | The cost center that was sped up in this experiment. |
| `speedup` | Fraction of speedup applied, from `0` to `1`. `0.25` means the selected part was made 25% faster, by slowing everything else. |
| `duration` | Planned length of the experiment, in nanoseconds. |
| `effectiveDuration` | `duration` minus the total delay that was added to the other code during the experiment, in nanoseconds. This is the time the selected code effectively had to itself. |
| `selectedSamples` | Number of delay steps counted during the experiment: one for each running fiber in the selected cost center, or in a cost center nested under it, at each sampling tick. Despite its name, this counts delay steps, not sampled time. |
| `throughputData` | How often each progress point was reached during the experiment. |
| `latencyData` | Arrivals and departures for each latency point. |

`render` writes one block per experiment. The first line starts with `experiment` and has the form:

```text
experiment	selected=<cost center>	speedup=<speedup>	duration=<effective duration>	selected-samples=<samples>
```

Each following line is a `throughput-point` line (`name`, `delta`) or a `latency-point` line (`name`, `arrivals`, `departures`, `difference`), one for each progress point and latency point. The fields are separated by tabs.

#### ThroughputData and LatencyData

```text
final case class ThroughputData(name: String, delta: Int)
final case class LatencyData(name: String, arrivals: Int, departures: Int)
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `ThroughputData.name` | The name passed to `progressPoint`. |
| `ThroughputData.delta` | How many times that progress point was reached during the experiment. |
| `LatencyData.name` | The name passed to `enterLatencyPoint`, `exitLatencyPoint` or `latencyPointScoped`. |
| `LatencyData.arrivals` | How many times `enterLatencyPoint` ran during the experiment. |
| `LatencyData.departures` | How many times `exitLatencyPoint` ran during the experiment. |

Each has a `render` method that produces its line in the output below.

### Logging

The profiler logs at the `Info` level when it starts warming up, when each experiment starts and when profiling is done. An experiment line contains the experiment number, the selected cost center, the speedup and the planned duration in nanoseconds. Use these lines to follow the progress of a long run.

### Output

Load the file written by `renderToFile` into the [Coz visualizer](https://plasma-umass.org/coz/) to see the experiments as a chart. Each selected cost center is shown with the throughput change it caused at each speedup.

### Related

- [Find a bottleneck with the causal profiler](../how-to/find-bottleneck-causal.md) walks through a run.
- [CostCenter reference](cost-center.md) explains the names that experiments select.

---

## CostCenter Reference

A `CostCenter` is a named location in your program: a path of names from the outermost tagged effect down to the innermost one. Both profilers record their results per cost center. The compiler plugin creates cost centers for you, and you can create them yourself with the functions below. The type lives in package `zio.profiling`.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.CostCenter
```

### The type

```text
final case class CostCenter(locations: Chunk[String])
```

A cost center is a list of location names. The empty list is the root cost center, which is where code runs when no tag is active.

| Member | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `render` | `String` | The names joined with `;`. The root renders as the empty string. |
| `isRoot` | `Boolean` | `true` when there are no names. |
| `/(location)` | `CostCenter` | A child cost center, nested under this one, with `location` as its last name. |
| `location` | `Option[String]` | The last name, or `None` for the root. |
| `isChildOf(other)` | `Boolean` | `true` when `other`'s names are a prefix of this cost center's names. |
| `hasParent(name)` | `Boolean` | `true` when `name` is one of the names in the path, at any depth. |
| `hasParentMatching(regex)` | `Boolean` | `true` when some name in the path matches `regex` somewhere. |

Build a path with `/`, starting from `Root`:

```scala
val path = CostCenter.Root / "foo" / "bar"
// path: CostCenter = CostCenter(locations = IndexedSeq("foo", "bar"))

path.render
// res0: String = "foo;bar"

path.location
// res1: Option[String] = Some(value = "bar")

path.isChildOf(CostCenter.Root / "foo")
// res2: Boolean = true

path.hasParent("foo")
// res3: Boolean = true

path.hasParentMatching("^ba".r)
// res4: Boolean = true
```

`hasParent` compares whole names. `hasParentMatching` takes a regular expression and checks whether any name in the path contains a match, so `"^ba"` matches `bar`.

### Companion object

| Member | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `Root` | `CostCenter` | The root cost center, with no names. |
| `withChildCostCenter(name)(zio)` | `(name: String)(zio: ZIO[R, E, A]): ZIO[R, E, A]` | Runs `zio` in a child cost center named `name`, nested under the active one. |
| `withChildCostCenterStream(name)(stream)` | `(name: String)(stream: ZStream[R, E, A]): ZStream[R, E, A]` | The same, for a `ZStream`. |
| `getCurrent` | `UIO[CostCenter]` | The cost center that the running fiber is in. |
| `getCurrentUnsafe(fiber)` | `(implicit unsafe) => CostCenter` | The cost center of a given fiber, read without an effect. The sampling profiler uses it. |

The how-to guide [Tag effects by hand](../how-to/tag-effects-by-hand.md) shows the wrapping functions in use. The compiler plugin rewrites each tagged definition into a call to `withChildCostCenter` with a name of the form `fullName(File.scala:line)`.

```scala
val parse: UIO[Int] = CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("parse")(ZIO.succeed(21))
```

### Fibers

The active cost center is stored in a `FiberRef`. A fiber that is forked starts in the cost center of its parent. When the fiber is joined, the parent keeps its own cost center, so tags set inside a child fiber never leak back out.

### Naming

Names are compared exactly, so `"parse"` and `"Parse"` are different cost centers. Keep names stable between runs. A profile compares samples per cost center, and a name that changes on each run produces a new cost center each time.

### Related

- [Sampling profiler reference](sampling-profiler.md) reports samples per cost center.
- [Causal profiler reference](causal-profiler.md) selects cost centers for experiments. `candidateSelector` receives the last name of each one.

## JMH Profiler Reference

The `zio-profiling-jmh` module attaches the [sampling profiler](sampling-profiler.md) to a JMH run. It lives in package `zio.profiling.jmh`. For the steps to run a benchmark with it, see [Profile JMH benchmarks](../how-to/profile-jmh-benchmarks.md).

### Artifact

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling-jmh" % "0.3.5"
)
```

### JmhZioProfiler

`JmhZioProfiler` is a JMH `InternalProfiler`. Pass its fully qualified name to JMH with `-prof`:

```text
-prof zio.profiling.jmh.JmhZioProfiler
```

It has a no-argument constructor and a constructor that takes the profiler option string, which it ignores, so it accepts no options.

| Phase | What the profiler does |
|-------|------------------------|
| First warm-up iteration | Creates a runtime with a [`SamplingProfiler`](sampling-profiler.md) at the default sampling period. |
| First measurement iteration | Resets the collected samples, so warm-up is not included. |
| After the last measurement iteration | Writes `profile.folded` and shuts the runtime down. |

The profiler starts only in a warm-up iteration. Run with at least one warm-up iteration (`-wi 1` or more), or no profile is written.

JMH prints `zio-profiler results:` followed by the path of the file. The file is `profile.folded` in a directory named after the benchmark id, inside the working directory of the JVM, in the folded-stack format described in the [sampling profiler reference](sampling-profiler.md#profilingresult).

### BenchmarkUtils

`BenchmarkUtils` gives benchmark code access to the profiled runtime. Without the profiler attached, it uses `Runtime.default`.

| Method | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `unsafeRun(zio)` | `[E, A](zio: ZIO[Any, E, A]): A` | Runs `zio` on the profiled runtime and returns its value. If `zio` fails, throws a `FiberFailure` that wraps the failure. |
| `getRuntime()` | `Runtime[Any]` | The profiled runtime while a profile is running, otherwise `Runtime.default`. |
| `getSupervisor()` | `Supervisor[Any]` | The sampling supervisor while a profile is running, otherwise `Supervisor.none`. |

Only effects that run on the runtime from `getRuntime()` are profiled.

### Related

- [Profile a running application](../how-to/profile-running-application.md) shows the runtime that the profiler creates.
