## Sampling Profiler Reference

The sampling profiler lives in package `zio.profiling.sampling`. It records, at a fixed interval, which cost center each running fiber is in. The result shows how much time each cost center accounts for. For a step-by-step walk-through, see the [tutorial](../tutorials/first-flamegraph.md).

```scala
import zio.profiling.sampling._
```

### SamplingProfiler

```text
final case class SamplingProfiler(samplingPeriod: Duration = 10.millis)
```

| Parameter        | Default   | Meaning                                                                                  |
|------------------|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `samplingPeriod` | `10.millis` | Time between two samples. A shorter period gives more samples and more overhead.         |

`SamplingProfiler` is a case class with no companion `profile` method. Create an instance first: `SamplingProfiler().profile(...)`.

```scala
SamplingProfiler()
// res0: SamplingProfiler = SamplingProfiler(samplingPeriod = PT0.01S)
```

#### Methods

| Method | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `profile` | `[R, E](zio: ZIO[R, E, Any]): ZIO[R, E, ProfilingResult]` | Runs `zio` with a sampler attached, then returns the samples. The sampler stops when `zio` finishes. The value of `zio` is discarded; the result is the profile. If `zio` fails, so does the profile. |
| `makeSupervisor` | `URIO[Scope, SamplingProfilerSupervisor]` | Starts a sampler in the current scope and returns the supervisor that holds its samples. Sampling continues until the scope closes. Only effects run with `.supervised(supervisor)` are sampled. |
| `supervisedRuntime` | `(implicit unsafe: Unsafe): Runtime.Scoped[SamplingProfilerSupervisor]` | Creates a runtime with a sampler attached, so every effect run with it is sampled. Get the supervisor with `runtime.environment.get[SamplingProfilerSupervisor]`. Shut the runtime down when you are done. |

The how-to guide [Profile a running application](../how-to/profile-running-application.md) shows `supervisedRuntime` in use.

### What a sample counts

On every tick, the sampler looks at each fiber that is currently running and adds one to the count of that fiber's cost center. A fiber counts as running from when it starts or resumes until it suspends or ends. Work that waits for an asynchronous result is therefore not counted, while `ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(...))` is counted, because the fiber is running while it sleeps.

Because every running fiber is counted on every tick, the total number of samples can be larger than the wall-clock time when fibers run in parallel. Compare cost centers with each other, not with the run time.

### ProfilingResult

```text
final case class ProfilingResult(entries: List[ProfilingResult.Entry])

object ProfilingResult {
  final case class Entry(costCenter: CostCenter, samples: Long)
}
```

| Member | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `entries` | `List[Entry]` | One entry per cost center that was sampled, in no particular order. |
| `stackCollapse` | `List[String]` | One line per entry, in folded-stack format: the cost center path joined with `;`, a space, and the sample count. |
| `stackCollapseToFile(path)` | `Task[Unit]` | Writes `stackCollapse` to `path`, one line per entry, creating parent directories if needed. |

A cost center with no name (the root) renders as an empty path. Lines for it start with a space.

The output of `stackCollapse` for a hand-written result:

```scala
import zio.profiling.CostCenter

val example = ProfilingResult(
  List(
    ProfilingResult.Entry(CostCenter.Root / "outer" / "fast", 40),
    ProfilingResult.Entry(CostCenter.Root / "outer" / "slow", 60)
  )
)
```

```scala
example.stackCollapse
// res1: List[String] = List("outer;fast 40", "outer;slow 60")
```

The file format is the input of [FlameGraph](https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph): `flamegraph.pl profile.folded > profile.svg`.

### SamplingProfilerSupervisor

`SamplingProfilerSupervisor` is the supervisor that collects samples. You get one from `makeSupervisor` or from the environment of a `supervisedRuntime`.

| Method | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `value` | `UIO[ProfilingResult]` | The samples collected so far, as an effect. |
| `unsafeValue()` | `ProfilingResult` | The samples collected so far, read immediately. |
| `sample()` | `Unit` | Takes one sample by hand. The sampler calls this on every tick, so you rarely need it. |
| `reset()` | `Unit` | Clears all samples. The next profile starts from zero. |

### Related

- [CostCenter reference](cost-center.md) describes the names in each entry.
- [Causal profiler reference](causal-profiler.md) ranks parts of a program by their effect on throughput.

## Tagging Compiler Plugin Reference

The tagging plugin is a compiler plugin that wraps ZIO effects and streams in a [`CostCenter`](cost-center.md) at compile time. It has no options and no runtime API. This page describes what it rewrites. For the steps to enable it, see [Set up the tagging compiler plugin](../how-to/setup-tagging-plugin.md).

### Artifact

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  compilerPlugin("dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling-tagging-plugin" % "0.3.5")
)
```

The artifact is published for Scala 2.12, Scala 2.13 and Scala 3. The code it generates calls `zio.profiling.CostCenter`, so the module that uses the plugin must also depend on `zio-profiling`.

### What the plugin tags

The plugin visits every `def` and `val` that has a right-hand side, and tags it when its declared or inferred type, after resolving type aliases, is one of:

| Type | Rewritten to |
|------|--------------|
| `ZIO[R, E, A]` | `CostCenter.withChildCostCenter(name)(rhs)` |
| `ZStream[R, E, A]` | `CostCenter.withChildCostCenterStream(name)(rhs)` |

Other types are left alone, including `ZLayer`, `ZSink` and `ZPipeline`.

### Names

The name is the fully qualified name of the definition, followed by the file name and the line number in parentheses:

```text
zio.profiling.ProfilerExamples.slow(ProfilerExamples.scala:9)
```

Because the name holds the line number, it changes when you move the definition.

### Phases

On Scala 2 the plugin is named `zio-profiling-tagging` and runs after `typer` and before `patmat`. On Scala 3 the phase has the same name and runs after `Pickler` and before `Staging`.

### Related

- [Set up the tagging compiler plugin](../how-to/setup-tagging-plugin.md)
- [Tag effects by hand](../how-to/tag-effects-by-hand.md) for effects the plugin does not name.

## Profile a Producer-Consumer Program with the Causal Profiler

In this tutorial you will run the causal profiler on a program with producers and consumers that share a bounded queue, and read what it reports. A causal profile tells you how much faster the whole program would become if one part were faster. By the end you will know how to run an experiment, and how to read its lines.

You need an sbt project with ZIO 2 and the `zio-profiling` dependency from [Getting Started](../getting-started.md). A similar program is in the repository as `CausalProfilerProducerConsumerExample` in the `examples` module. It relies on the compiler plugin for names and uses the default warm-up.

### Step 1: Write the program

The program moves 10,000 items through a queue of size 10. Four producers offer items and twenty consumers take them. Each unit of work is the moment all producers and consumers have finished, and we mark it with a progress point.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.CostCenter
import zio.profiling.causal._

val items         = 10000
val queueSize     = 10
val producerCount = 4
val consumerCount = 20

val program: Task[Unit] =
  Queue.bounded[Unit](queueSize).flatMap { queue =>
    val producer: UIO[Unit] =
      CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("produce")(queue.offer(()).repeatN(items / producerCount - 1).unit)

    val consumer: UIO[Unit] =
      CostCenter.withChildCostCenter("consume")(queue.take.repeatN(items / consumerCount - 1).unit)

    for {
      producers <- ZIO.forkAll(List.fill(producerCount)(producer))
      consumers <- ZIO.forkAll(List.fill(consumerCount)(consumer))
      _         <- producers.join *> consumers.join
      _         <- CausalProfiler.progressPoint("iteration")
    } yield ()
  }
```

`CostCenter.withChildCostCenter` gives `produce` and `consume` their names by hand. With the [compiler plugin](../how-to/setup-tagging-plugin.md) you would not need it, but the names would then be source locations. The profiler only experiments with named parts.

### Step 2: Run the profiler

`profile` needs a program that never ends, so we add `forever`. The defaults wait 30 seconds before the first experiment, so we shorten them for this run.

```scala
val run: Task[Unit] =
  CausalProfiler(iterations = 30, experimentTargetSamples = 5, warmUpPeriod = 5.seconds, coolOffPeriod = 0.seconds)
    .profile(program.forever)
    .flatMap(_.renderToFile("profile.coz"))
```

The profiler logs a line when each experiment starts. When 30 experiments are done, it interrupts the program and writes `profile.coz`.

### Step 3: Read the output

Each experiment is a block of tab-separated lines. This is an invented example of the shape:

```scala
import zio.profiling.causal.{ExperimentResult, LatencyData, ThroughputData}

val result = ProfilingResult(
  List(
    ExperimentResult(
      selected = CostCenter.Root / "consume",
      speedup = 0.25f,
      duration = 1000000000L,
      effectiveDuration = 900000000L,
      selectedSamples = 100L,
      throughputData = List(ThroughputData("iteration", 12)),
      latencyData = List(LatencyData("request", 20, 18))
    )
  )
)
```

```scala
result.render
// res1: String = """experiment	selected=consume	speedup=0.25	duration=900000000	selected-samples=100
// throughput-point	name=iteration	delta=12
// latency-point	name=request	arrivals=20	departures=18	difference=2"""
```

The first line says: with `consume` made 25% faster, the experiment effectively lasted 900,000,000 ns. The `throughput-point` line says `iteration` was reached 12 times in it. To judge a cost center, compare experiments with different speedups for it. If the count rises as the speedup rises, speeding that part up speeds up the program.

### Step 4: Change the program and profile again

Raise `queueSize` to 1000, run the profiler again, and compare the two files. A larger queue means producers wait less. If the counts for `produce` and `consume` move differently, you have found out which side limits this program.

### What you learned

- The causal profiler needs named parts, a progress point and a program that runs forever.
- Each experiment reports the throughput of the progress points for one selected part at one speedup.
- You compare experiments to find the part that limits the program.

### Next steps

- [Find a bottleneck with the causal profiler](../how-to/find-bottleneck-causal.md) shows the same workflow for a loop.
- [Causal profiler reference](../reference/causal-profiler.md) lists every option and the output format.

## Profile a Program and Read the Flamegraph

In this tutorial you will profile a small ZIO program with the sampling profiler, write the result to a file, and turn that file into a flamegraph. A flamegraph shows which parts of your program used the most time. By the end you will know how to read one.

You need:

- an sbt project that uses Scala 2.12, Scala 2.13 or Scala 3 and ZIO 2
- the [FlameGraph](https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph) scripts, in particular `flamegraph.pl`, on your `PATH`

### Step 1: Add ZIO Profiling to your build

Add the library and the compiler plugin to your `build.sbt`:

```sbt
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling" % "0.3.5"
libraryDependencies += compilerPlugin("dev.zio" %% "zio-profiling-tagging-plugin" % "0.3.5")
```

The compiler plugin is not optional for this tutorial. It tags each effect with the place in your source code where it was defined. Without it, every sample lands in one unnamed entry and the flamegraph tells you nothing. You will see this in Step 5.

### Step 2: Write a program with two parts

Our program has two parts that run at the same time. `fast` takes 400 ms, and `slow` takes 600 ms. Both are built with `ZIO.succeed`, which runs the `Thread.sleep` call when the effect executes. `<&>` runs the two effects in parallel, so the program takes about 600 ms.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.profiling.sampling._

val fast: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(400))

val slow: UIO[Unit] = ZIO.succeed(Thread.sleep(600))

val program: UIO[Unit] = fast <&> slow
```

### Step 3: Profile the program

`SamplingProfiler()` creates a profiler with the default sampling period of 10 ms. Call `profile` with the effect you want to measure. Once the effect finishes, `profile` gives you a `ProfilingResult`. `stackCollapseToFile` writes that result in the folded-stack format that `flamegraph.pl` reads.

```scala
SamplingProfiler()
  .profile(program)
  .flatMap(_.stackCollapseToFile("profile.folded"))
```

The profiler takes samples only while the program runs. It does not change how the program runs, so the profiled effect keeps its normal result.

### Step 4: Understand the folded format

Each line of `profile.folded` is one cost center followed by a space and a sample count. A cost center is a path of names, joined with `;`, that describes where the time was spent. Here is a hand-written `ProfilingResult` so you can see the format without running a profile:

```scala
import zio.profiling.CostCenter

val example = ProfilingResult(
  List(
    ProfilingResult.Entry(CostCenter.Root / "outer" / "fast", 40),
    ProfilingResult.Entry(CostCenter.Root / "outer" / "slow", 60)
  )
)
```

```scala
example.stackCollapse.foreach(println)
// outer;fast 40
// outer;slow 60
```

The first line says that 40 samples were taken while the `fast` effect ran inside `outer`. The second line says that 60 samples were taken in `slow`. The sample counts are the numbers the flamegraph uses for the width of each bar.

### Step 5: Render the flamegraph

Turn the folded file into an SVG:

```bash
flamegraph.pl profile.folded > profile.svg
```

Open `profile.svg` in a browser. Each box is a cost center. Its width is proportional to its share of the samples, and a box sits on top of the cost center that contains it. In our program, `slow` should be wider than `fast`, because it runs for 600 ms and `fast` runs for 400 ms.

If you skipped the compiler plugin, the file contains one line with an empty name, for example ` 123`. All the time is in the root cost center, so there is nothing to compare. Add the plugin from Step 1 and profile again.

:::tip[Names come from your source]
With the plugin, each name looks like `fullName(File.scala:line)`, for example `zio.profiling.ProfilerExamples.slow(ProfilerExamples.scala:9)`. The exact text depends on your package, object and file names. The line number points to the definition that the plugin tagged.
:::

### What you learned

- The sampling profiler counts, every few milliseconds, which cost center each running fiber is in.
- `stackCollapseToFile` writes those counts as folded stacks, and `flamegraph.pl` draws them.
- The compiler plugin is what makes cost centers meaningful. Without it there is nothing to see.

### Next steps

- To tell which part of a program is worth optimizing, not just where the time goes, use the [causal profiler](../how-to/find-bottleneck-causal.md).
- To learn what each option of the sampling profiler does, read the [sampling profiler reference](../reference/sampling-profiler.md).

---

## Aspects(Zio-query)

An aspect changes how a query or a data source behaves without changing the code that defines it. ZIO Query has two kinds:

- A `DataSourceAspect` transforms a [data source](./creating-data-sources.md) into another data source. Use it to run code around every call to a data source, for example to record metrics or to limit the size of a batch.
- A `QueryAspect` transforms a `ZQuery` into another `ZQuery`. Use it to apply a `DataSourceAspect` to every data source used by a query, or to run code around a whole query.

Aspects are values, so they can be defined once and applied to many queries or data sources. This page shows how to create them, how to apply them with `@@`, and how to use `Described`, which many aspects and data source combinators need.

### Setting Up an Example

The examples on this page use one request type and one data source that records the calls it receives, so that we can see what each aspect changes:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.query._

final case class GetUserName(id: Int) extends Request[Nothing, String]

val log: Ref[Chunk[String]] =
  Unsafe.unsafe(implicit unsafe => Ref.unsafe.make(Chunk.empty[String]))

val userDataSource: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.make[Any, GetUserName]("UserDataSource") { requests =>
    log.update(_ :+ s"UserDataSource: ${requests.map(_.map(_.id).mkString("[", ", ", "]")).mkString(" ")}") *>
      ZIO.succeed(
        CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(requests.flatten)(r => r, r => Exit.succeed(s"user-${r.id}"))
      )
  }

def userName(id: Int): ZQuery[Any, Nothing, String] =
  ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(id))(userDataSource)

def show[A](query: ZQuery[Any, Nothing, A]): Unit = {
  val (result, calls) = Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(query.run <*> log.getAndSet(Chunk.empty)).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
  println(s"result: $result")
  calls.foreach(println)
}
```

In the output, each pair of square brackets is one batch of requests that the data source receives. See [How Batching, Pipelining, and Parallelism Work](./how-batching-works.md) for how batches are formed.

### Describing Values with `Described`

Aspects and data source combinators often take a function or an effect together with a description of it. `Described[A]` pairs a value with a `String` description:

```scala
final case class Described[+A](value: A, description: String)
```

The description is used to build the identifier of the data source that the combinator returns. Two data sources are equal when their identifiers are equal, and ZIO Query uses that equality to decide which requests belong to the same data source (and so can be batched together). For this reason, values that are equal should have the same description, and values that are not equal should have different descriptions.

The `?` syntax from `Described` adds a description to any value:

```scala
import zio.query.Described._

val logBefore: Described[UIO[Unit]] =
  log.update(_ :+ "before") ? "log before"

val logAfter: Described[Unit => UIO[Unit]] =
  ((_: Unit) => log.update(_ :+ "after")) ? "log after"
```

`Described` is also required by `DataSource#contramap`, `DataSource#contramapZIO`, `DataSource#eitherWith`, `DataSource#provideEnvironment` and `ZQuery#provideEnvironment`. For example, `provideEnvironment` removes the environment requirement of a data source by supplying a value for it, and the description of that value becomes part of the new data source's identifier:

```scala
val envDataSource: DataSource[Int, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.make[Int, GetUserName]("EnvUserDataSource") { requests =>
    ZIO.serviceWith[Int] { offset =>
      CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(requests.flatten)(r => r, r => Exit.succeed(s"user-${r.id + offset}"))
    }
  }

val providedDataSource: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  envDataSource.provideEnvironment(ZEnvironment(100) ? "offset 100")
```

```scala
providedDataSource.identifier
// res0: String = "EnvUserDataSource.provideSomeEnvironment(_ => offset 100)"
```

:::warning
`DataSource#contramap`, `contramapZIO` and `eitherWith` pass the results of the converted requests through unchanged. The query looks up the result of the original request, so these combinators work only when the converted request is equal to the original one. Otherwise the query dies with a `QueryFailure`.
:::

### Data Source Aspects

#### Running Code Around a Data Source

`DataSourceAspect.around` runs an effect before and an effect after every call to the data source's `runAll`. The result of the first effect is passed to the second one. Both are `Described`, and neither can fail. The effects are run with `ZIO.acquireReleaseWith`, so the second one runs even if the call is interrupted:

```scala
def around[R, A](
  before: Described[ZIO[R, Nothing, A]]
)(after: Described[A => ZIO[R, Nothing, Any]]): DataSourceAspect[R]
```

An aspect is applied to a data source with `DataSource#@@`:

```scala
val loggedDataSource: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  userDataSource @@ DataSourceAspect.around(logBefore)(logAfter)
```

The effects run once per call to the data source, not once per request. A query that fetches three users in parallel sends one call:

```scala
show(ZQuery.foreachPar(List(1, 2, 3))(id => ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(id))(loggedDataSource)))
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3)
// before
// UserDataSource: [1, 2, 3]
// after
```

The aspect also changes the identifier of the data source. The new identifier is the old one followed by `@@ around(`, the description of the first effect, `)(`, the description of the second effect and `)`:

```scala
loggedDataSource.identifier
// res2: String = "UserDataSource @@ around(log before)(log after)"
```

Because the identifier is different, requests sent to `loggedDataSource` are not batched together with requests sent to `userDataSource`.

#### Limiting the Batch Size

`DataSourceAspect.maxBatchSize(n)` splits every batch the data source receives into batches of at most `n` requests. It is the aspect form of `DataSource#batchN`:

```scala
val smallBatches: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  userDataSource @@ DataSourceAspect.maxBatchSize(2)
```

A data source that is limited to two requests receives five parallel requests as three batches, in one call to `runAll`:

```scala
show(ZQuery.foreachPar(List(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))(id => ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(id))(smallBatches)))
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3, user-4, user-5)
// UserDataSource: [1, 2] [3, 4] [5]
```

The smaller batches are the sequential batches of the outer `Chunk` described in [Creating Data Sources](./creating-data-sources.md), so a data source that executes them one after another never has more than `n` requests in flight at a time. If `n` is less than 1, the data source dies with an `IllegalArgumentException` when it runs.

#### Composing Data Source Aspects

`DataSourceAspect#>>>` (or `andThen`) combines two aspects into one that applies the left aspect first and the right aspect to the result. In the following data source, the batches are split first, and then the log effects wrap the call:

```scala
val limitedAndLogged: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  userDataSource @@ (DataSourceAspect.maxBatchSize(2) >>> DataSourceAspect.around(logBefore)(logAfter))
```

```scala
show(ZQuery.foreachPar(List(1, 2, 3))(id => ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(id))(limitedAndLogged)))
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3)
// before
// UserDataSource: [1, 2] [3]
// after
```

`DataSourceAspect[R]` is a trait with a single method, `apply[R1 <: R, A](dataSource: DataSource[R1, A]): DataSource[R1, A]`, so you can also implement your own aspect.

### Query Aspects

A `QueryAspect` is applied to a query with `ZQuery#@@`. The ready-made aspects in `QueryAspect` come in two groups: aspects that apply a data source aspect to all data sources in a query, and one that runs code around the query itself.

#### Applying Data Source Aspects to a Query

Data sources are usually created in one place and used from many queries, so it is often easier to apply an aspect to a query than to every data source. `QueryAspect.fromDataSourceAspect` turns a `DataSourceAspect` into a `QueryAspect`. It is implemented with `ZQuery#mapDataSources`, which you can also call directly. The aspect is applied to every data source that the query uses:

```scala
val query: ZQuery[Any, Nothing, List[String]] =
  ZQuery.foreachPar(List(1, 2, 3))(userName)
```

```scala
show(query @@ QueryAspect.fromDataSourceAspect(DataSourceAspect.maxBatchSize(2)))
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3)
// UserDataSource: [1, 2] [3]
```

`QueryAspect` also has shortcuts for the two data source aspects from the previous section:

| Query aspect                         | Equivalent                                                           |
| ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `QueryAspect.maxBatchSize(n)`        | `QueryAspect.fromDataSourceAspect(DataSourceAspect.maxBatchSize(n))` |
| `QueryAspect.aroundDataSource(b)(a)` | `QueryAspect.fromDataSourceAspect(DataSourceAspect.around(b)(a))`    |

```scala
show(query @@ QueryAspect.maxBatchSize(2))
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3)
// UserDataSource: [1, 2] [3]
```

```scala
show(query @@ QueryAspect.aroundDataSource(logBefore)(logAfter))
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3)
// before
// UserDataSource: [1, 2, 3]
// after
```

#### Running Code Around a Query

`QueryAspect.around` runs an effect before the query and an effect after it, using `ZQuery.acquireReleaseWith`. Unlike `aroundDataSource`, it wraps the query as a whole, not the calls to data sources, and its arguments are plain effects that do not need a description:

```scala
val logQuery: QueryAspect[Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any, Nothing, Any] =
  QueryAspect.around(log.update(_ :+ "query started"))(_ => log.update(_ :+ "query finished"))
```

```scala
show(query @@ logQuery)
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3)
// query started
// UserDataSource: [1, 2, 3]
// query finished
```

#### Composing Query Aspects

Like data source aspects, query aspects are composed with `>>>` (or `andThen`), and the left aspect is applied first:

```scala
show(query @@ (logQuery >>> QueryAspect.maxBatchSize(2)))
// result: List(user-1, user-2, user-3)
// query started
// UserDataSource: [1, 2] [3]
// query finished
```

### Summary

| To...                                      | Use                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Run code around calls to a data source     | `DataSourceAspect.around`, applied with `DataSource#@@`                                                                   |
| Limit the batch size of a data source      | `DataSourceAspect.maxBatchSize` or `DataSource#batchN`                                                                    |
| Apply these to all data sources in a query | `QueryAspect.aroundDataSource`, `QueryAspect.maxBatchSize`, `QueryAspect.fromDataSourceAspect` or `ZQuery#mapDataSources` |
| Run code around a whole query              | `QueryAspect.around`, applied with `ZQuery#@@`                                                                            |
| Combine aspects                            | `>>>` or `andThen`                                                                                                        |

---

## CompletedRequestMap

A `CompletedRequestMap` is what a [data source](./creating-data-sources.md) returns from `runAll`: a mapping from each request it executed to the result of that request, an `Exit[E, A]`. This page explains how to build one, how to look results up in it, which methods are deprecated, and how `ZQuery.fromRequests` submits several requests to a data source at once.

### Setting Up an Example

The examples on this page use the following request types:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.query._

final case class GetUserName(id: Int) extends Request[String, String]
final case class GetOrderCount(id: Int) extends Request[Nothing, Int]
```

### How a Query Reads the Map

A `CompletedRequestMap` is keyed by requests, and the type of each entry is tied to its request: a `Request[E, A]` is always mapped to an `Exit[E, A]`. This lets one data source answer requests of different result types.

After `runAll` returns, the query looks up the result of each request it submitted, using request equality. If the map has no entry for a request, the query dies with a `QueryFailure` that names the data source and the request. Make sure that the map has an entry for every request the data source received, and that each key is equal to the request the query submitted. Because requests are compared with `equals`, define them as case classes (or case objects).

You can read a map with:

| Method                      | Returns                                                           |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `lookup(request)`           | `Option[Exit[E, A]]`, the result of the request if there is one   |
| `contains(request)`         | `Boolean`, whether the map has a result for the request           |
| `requests`                  | `Set[Request[_, _]]`, all requests in the map                     |
| `isEmpty`                   | `Boolean`, whether the map has no entries                         |

### Creating a Map

All constructors are in the `CompletedRequestMap` companion object.

#### From a Single Result or Several Results

`single` creates a map with one entry, `empty` creates a map with none, and `apply` takes entries as `(request, exit)` pairs:

```scala
val one: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.single(GetUserName(1), Exit.succeed("Ann"))

val several: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap(
    GetUserName(1) -> Exit.succeed("Ann"),
    GetUserName(2) -> Exit.fail("no such user")
  )
```

```scala
several.lookup(GetUserName(1))
// res0: Option[Exit[String, String]] = Some(value = Success(value = "Ann"))
several.lookup(GetUserName(2))
// res1: Option[Exit[String, String]] = Some(
//   value = Failure(
//     cause = Fail(
//       value = "no such user",
//       trace = StackTrace(fiberId = None, stackTrace = IndexedSeq())
//     )
//   )
// )
several.lookup(GetUserName(3))
// res2: Option[Exit[String, String]] = None
several.contains(GetUserName(3))
// res3: Boolean = false
```

All entries given to `apply` must have the same error and result types. Use `combine` (see below) to put results of requests with different types in one map.

#### From a Collection

Data sources usually get their results from a database or a remote service as a collection. The following constructors build a map from a collection in one pass:

| Constructor                                           | Use when                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fromIterable(iterable)`                              | you already have `(request, exit)` pairs                                                      |
| `fromIterableWith(iterable)(toRequest, toExit)`       | you have your own values and functions that convert each of them to a request and to an `Exit` |
| `fromIterableOption(iterable)`                        | each result is an `Exit[E, Option[A]]` and `None` means that the entry does not exist         |

`fromIterableWith` avoids creating an intermediate collection of pairs. For example, a database query that returns rows of `(id, name)` can be turned into a map directly:

```scala
val rows: List[(Int, String)] = List(1 -> "Ann", 2 -> "Bob")

val fromRows: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(rows)(
    row => GetUserName(row._1),
    row => Exit.succeed(row._2)
  )
```

`fromIterableOption` is for lookups that may find nothing. A pair whose result is `Exit.succeed(Some(a))` is stored as a success with `a`, a failure is stored as a failure, and a pair with `Exit.succeed(None)` is left out of the map. A request that is left out is not completed, so the query dies with a `QueryFailure` for it, unless another map that you combine with this one has a result for it:

```scala
val withMissing: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableOption(
    List(
      GetOrderCount(1) -> Exit.succeed(Some(10)),
      GetOrderCount(2) -> Exit.succeed(None)
    )
  )
```

```scala
withMissing.lookup(GetOrderCount(1))
// res4: Option[Exit[Nothing, Int]] = Some(value = Success(value = 10))
withMissing.contains(GetOrderCount(2))
// res5: Boolean = false
```

#### Failing Several Requests at Once

When a whole call fails, use `fail`, `failCause` or `die` to complete all requests of a batch with the same failure. Each takes a `Chunk` of requests and the error, the `Cause` or the `Throwable`:

```scala
val requests: Chunk[GetUserName] = Chunk(GetUserName(1), GetUserName(2))

val failed: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.fail(requests, "database is down")

val failedWithCause: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.failCause(requests, Cause.fail("database is down"))

val died: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.die(requests, new RuntimeException("bug"))
```

See [Error Handling](./error-handling.md) for what each kind of failure means for the query.

#### Combining Maps

`combine` merges an `Iterable` of maps into one. If several maps have an entry for the same request, the entry from the last map wins:

```scala
val combined: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.combine(
    List(
      CompletedRequestMap.single(GetUserName(1), Exit.succeed("Ann")),
      CompletedRequestMap.single(GetOrderCount(1), Exit.succeed(10)),
      CompletedRequestMap.single(GetUserName(1), Exit.succeed("Anna"))
    )
  )
```

```scala
combined.lookup(GetUserName(1))
// res6: Option[Exit[String, String]] = Some(value = Success(value = "Anna"))
combined.lookup(GetOrderCount(1))
// res7: Option[Exit[Nothing, Int]] = Some(value = Success(value = 10))
```

#### From Parallel Collections of Requests and Results

`CompletedRequestMap.unsafe` has constructors that take a `Chunk` of requests and a `Chunk` of results in the same order, which is the shape many batch APIs return. They skip the creation of intermediate pairs, which can improve performance:

| Method                                                | Builds a map from                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `unsafe.fromExits(requests, responses)`               | a `Chunk` of requests and a `Chunk` of `Exit`s                             |
| `unsafe.fromSuccesses(requests, responses)`           | a `Chunk` of requests and a `Chunk` of successful values                   |
| `unsafe.fromWith(requests, responses)(toRequest, toExit)` | two `Chunk`s of any element types and functions that convert them      |

```scala
val fromChunks: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.unsafe.fromSuccesses(
    Chunk(GetUserName(1), GetUserName(2)),
    Chunk("Ann", "Bob")
  )
```

These methods are called unsafe because they do not check that the two collections have the same size. They pair the elements by position and stop at the end of the shorter one. It is up to you to make sure that the nth result belongs to the nth request.

### Deprecated Methods

`++`, `insert` and `insertOption` are deprecated since version 0.7.0. A `CompletedRequestMap` created by the constructors above is built by filling one mutable map, which is fast. These three methods can't change that map without exposing the mutation, so each call copies all entries into a new immutable map. Code that builds a map by folding with `insert` or `++` over many requests does not benefit from the faster constructors, and each step costs time that grows with the size of the map.

Replace them as follows:

| Deprecated                                    | Replacement                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `map.insert(request, exit)`                   | `CompletedRequestMap.single(request, exit)`, or `fromIterable` for many entries, then `combine`          |
| `map.insertOption(request, exit)`             | `CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableOption`                                                                 |
| `map1 ++ map2`                                | `CompletedRequestMap.combine(List(map1, map2))`                                                          |
| `list.foldLeft(empty)(_.insert(k, v))`        | `CompletedRequestMap.fromIterable` or `fromIterableWith`                                                 |

The following two maps are equal in content. The second one is built in a single pass:

```scala
@scala.annotation.nowarn("cat=deprecation")
val slow: CompletedRequestMap =
  rows.foldLeft(CompletedRequestMap.empty) { case (map, (id, name)) =>
    map.insert(GetUserName(id), Exit.succeed(name))
  }

val fast: CompletedRequestMap =
  CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(rows)(row => GetUserName(row._1), row => Exit.succeed(row._2))
```

### Submitting Several Requests at Once

`ZQuery.fromRequest` submits one request to a data source. When you have many requests for the same data source, `ZQuery.fromRequests` takes a `Chunk` or a `List` of requests and returns a query for all their results, in the same collection type and in the same order as the requests:

```scala
def fromRequests[R, E, A, B](requests: Chunk[A])(dataSource: DataSource[R, A]): ZQuery[R, E, Chunk[B]]
def fromRequests[R, E, A, B](requests: List[A])(dataSource: DataSource[R, A]): ZQuery[R, E, List[B]]
```

`fromRequestsWith` also takes a function that converts each element of the collection into a request, so you don't have to build the requests first:

```scala
def fromRequestsWith[R, E, In, A, B](as: Chunk[In], f: In => A)(dataSource: DataSource[R, A]): ZQuery[R, E, Chunk[B]]
def fromRequestsWith[R, E, In, A, B](as: List[In], f: In => A)(dataSource: DataSource[R, A]): ZQuery[R, E, List[B]]
```

The requests are submitted as one batch, as with `ZQuery#zipBatched`, so the data source receives them together in one call. [How Batching, Pipelining, and Parallelism Work](./how-batching-works.md) explains what that means for the data source. To try them, the following data source answers `GetUserName` requests from a map and records the batches it receives:

```scala
val calls: Ref[Chunk[String]] =
  Unsafe.unsafe(implicit unsafe => Ref.unsafe.make(Chunk.empty[String]))

val userDataSource: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.make[Any, GetUserName]("UserDataSource") { requests =>
    calls.update(_ :+ requests.map(_.map(_.id).mkString("[", ", ", "]")).mkString(" ")) *>
      ZIO.succeed(
        CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(requests.flatten)(
          request => request,
          request => if (request.id > 0) Exit.succeed(s"user-${request.id}") else Exit.fail("invalid id")
        )
      )
  }

def show[E, A](query: ZQuery[Any, E, A]): Unit = {
  val (result, received) = Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(query.run.exit <*> calls.getAndSet(Chunk.empty)).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
  println(s"result: $result")
  println(s"calls: ${received.mkString(", ")}")
}
```

```scala
show(ZQuery.fromRequests(List(GetUserName(1), GetUserName(2), GetUserName(3)))(userDataSource))
// result: Success(List(user-1, user-2, user-3))
// calls: [1, 2, 3]
```

```scala
show(ZQuery.fromRequestsWith(Chunk(3, 2, 1), GetUserName(_))(userDataSource))
// result: Success(Chunk(user-3,user-2,user-1))
// calls: [3, 2, 1]
```

If one of the requests fails, so does the query:

```scala
show(ZQuery.fromRequests(List(GetUserName(1), GetUserName(0)))(userDataSource))
// result: Failure(Fail(invalid id,StackTrace.none))
// calls: [1, 0]
```

#### Skipping the Cache

Like `ZQuery.fromRequest`, `fromRequests` and `fromRequestsWith` use the query cache. `ZQuery.fromRequestUncached` is a variant of `ZQuery.fromRequest` that does not. A repeated request is sent to the data source again, instead of reusing the earlier result. In the output below, the first query sends the request to the data source twice and the second sends it once:

```scala
show(ZQuery.fromRequestUncached(GetUserName(1))(userDataSource) *> ZQuery.fromRequestUncached(GetUserName(1))(userDataSource))
// result: Success(user-1)
// calls: [1] [1]
```

```scala
show(ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(1))(userDataSource) *> ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(1))(userDataSource))
// result: Success(user-1)
// calls: [1]
```

---

## Creating Data Sources

To construct a `ZQuery` that executes a request, you first need to create a `DataSource`. A `DataSource[R, A]` requires an environment `R` and is capable of executing requests of type `A`. It is defined in terms of:

- an `identifier` that uniquely identifies the data source
- an effectual function `runAll` from a `Chunk[Chunk[A]]` of requests to a `CompletedRequestMap` of requests and results

The outer `Chunk` represents batches of requests that must be performed sequentially. The inner `Chunk` represents a batch of requests that can be performed in parallel. This allows data sources to introspect on all the requests being executed and optimize the query. [How Batching, Pipelining, and Parallelism Work](./how-batching-works.md) shows which queries produce which batches.

Let's consider `getUserNameById` from the previous example.

We need to define a corresponding request type that extends `Request` for a given response type:

```scala
case class GetUserName(id: Int) extends Request[Throwable, String]
```

Now let's build the corresponding `DataSource`. We will create a `Batched` data source that executes requests that can be performed in parallel in batches but does not further optimize batches of requests that must be performed sequentially. We need to implement the following functions:

```scala
lazy val UserDataSource = new DataSource.Batched[Any, GetUserName] {
  val identifier: String = ???
  def run(requests: Chunk[GetUserName])(implicit trace: Trace): ZIO[Any, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap] = ???
}
```

We will use "UserDataSource" as our identifier. This name should not be reused for other data sources.

```scala
val identifier: String = "UserDataSource"
```

We will define two different behaviors depending on whether we receive a single request or multiple requests at once. For each request, we need to insert into the result map a value of type `Exit` (`fail` for an error and `succeed` for a success).

```scala
def run(requests: Chunk[GetUserName]): ZIO[Any, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap] =
  requests.toList match {
    case request :: Nil =>
      // get user by ID e.g. SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = $id
      val result: Task[String] = ???
      result.exit.map(CompletedRequestMap.single(request, _))
    case batch =>
      // get multiple users at once e.g. SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id IN ($ids)
      val result: Task[List[(Int, String)]] = ???
      result.foldCause(
        CompletedRequestMap.failCause(requests, _),
        CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(_)(kv => GetUserName(kv._1), kv => Exit.succeed(kv._2))
      )
  }
```

Now to build a `ZQuery`, we can use `ZQuery.fromRequest` and just pass the request and the data source:

```scala
def getUserNameById(id: Int): ZQuery[Any, Throwable, String] =
  ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(id))(UserDataSource)
```

To run a `ZQuery`, use `ZQuery#run`, which returns a `ZIO[R, E, A]`. [Running Queries and Caching](./running_queries.md) explains how results are cached and how to share a cache between runs.

For the other ways to build a data source from a function, and for the combinators that transform one, see the [DataSource Reference](./data-source-reference.md).

To run code around every call to a data source, or to limit its batch size, without changing its implementation, use [aspects](./aspects.md). The same page explains `Described`, which `DataSource#provideEnvironment` and other combinators require.

---

## Creating Queries

There are several ways to create a `ZQuery`. We've seen `ZQuery.fromRequest`, but you can also:

- create a query from a pure value with `ZQuery.succeed`
- create a query from an effect with `ZQuery.fromZIO`
- combine multiple queries with `ZQuery.collectAllPar` and `ZQuery.foreachPar` and their sequential equivalents `ZQuery.collectAll` and `ZQuery.foreach`

The choice between the parallel and the sequential combinators changes how requests are sent to data sources. See [How Batching, Pipelining, and Parallelism Work](./how-batching-works.md) for details.

If you have a `ZQuery`, you can use:

- `map` and `mapError` to modify the result or error type
- `flatMap`, `zipWith`, or `zipWithPar` to combine it with other queries
- `provide` and `provideSome` to eliminate some or all of its environmental requirements

To execute a query, see [Running Queries and Caching](./running_queries.md).

To recover from failures, convert errors to defects, or limit how long a query may run, see [Error Handling](./error-handling.md).

---

## DataSource Reference

A `DataSource[R, A]` is the component of ZIO Query that talks to the outside world: it receives requests of type `A`, may use an environment `R`, and returns a `CompletedRequestMap` with one result per request. [Creating Data Sources](./creating-data-sources.md) walks through writing one by hand. This page lists every constructor and combinator, so you can pick the shortest one for your case. For how the requests of a query end up in batches, see [How Batching, Pipelining, and Parallelism Work](./how-batching-works.md).

The shape of the type is:

```scala
trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  val identifier: String
  def runAll(requests: Chunk[Chunk[A]])(implicit trace: Trace): ZIO[R, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap]
}
```

The outer `Chunk` holds batches that must run one after another, and each inner `Chunk` holds requests that can run in parallel. A data source must return a result for every request it receives, otherwise the query dies with a `QueryFailure`. Most code does not implement `runAll` directly: the constructors below build the data source from a plain function.

### Usage

The following block defines a request type and a data source with `DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedZIO`, then queries it with four parallel lookups. The data source prints the size of each batch it receives, so we can see that the four lookups reach it as one call, and that the duplicate request is deduplicated:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.query._

case class GetUserName(id: Int) extends Request[Nothing, String]

val users: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedZIO[Any, Nothing, GetUserName, String]("users") { requests =>
    Console.printLine(s"users received ${requests.size} requests").orDie.as(requests.map(r => s"user-${r.id}"))
  }

def runSync[A](query: ZQuery[Any, Nothing, A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(query.run).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

Now we query the data source with ids `1`, `2`, `2` and `3`:

```scala
runSync(ZQuery.foreachPar(List(1, 2, 2, 3))(id => ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(id))(users)))
// res1: List[String] = List("user-1", "user-2", "user-2", "user-3")
```

The data source received three requests, not four: identical requests (compared with `equals`, so use case classes) are sent once per query run, because the results are cached by default.

### Choosing a Constructor

All constructors take a `name` first. The name becomes the data source's `DataSource#identifier`, and it must be unique per data source, see [Identifier and Equality](#identifier-and-equality). The following table lists the constructors by what the function you provide receives and returns:

| Constructor                                        | Your function                                 | Effectful | Can skip a request |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------------ |
| `DataSource.fromFunction`                          | `A => B`                                      | No        | No                 |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionZIO`                       | `A => ZIO[R, E, B]`                           | Yes       | No                 |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionOption`                    | `A => Option[B]`                              | No        | Yes                |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionOptionZIO`                 | `A => ZIO[R, E, Option[B]]`                   | Yes       | Yes                |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionBatched`                   | `Chunk[A] => Chunk[B]`                        | No        | No                 |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedZIO`                | `Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, E, Chunk[B]]`             | Yes       | No                 |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedOption`             | `Chunk[A] => Chunk[Option[B]]`                | No        | Yes                |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedOptionZIO`          | `Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, E, Chunk[Option[B]]]`     | Yes       | Yes                |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedWith`               | `Chunk[A] => Chunk[B]` and `B => Request`     | No        | No                 |
| `DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedWithZIO`            | `Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, E, Chunk[B]]` and `B => Request` | Yes | No                 |
| `DataSource.Batched.make`                          | `Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap]` | Yes  | Yes                |
| `DataSource.make`                                  | `Chunk[Chunk[A]] => ZIO[R, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap]` | Yes | Yes         |

Use the single-request functions (`DataSource.fromFunction`, `DataSource.fromFunctionZIO`, `DataSource.fromFunctionOption`, `DataSource.fromFunctionOptionZIO`) for tests and for backends that have no bulk operation. Use the batched functions when the backend can answer many requests in one call, which is the case ZIO Query exists to optimize. Use `DataSource.Batched.make` or `DataSource.make` when you need to build the `CompletedRequestMap` yourself.

In the signatures below, `A` is the request type and `B` is the result type. The implicit evidence `A <:< Request[E, B]` ties them together, so the type parameters are normally spelled out on the constructor, as in the examples.

### Creating Data Sources

The constructors are grouped by how they receive requests: one at a time, as a batch, or as raw batches of batches.

#### Functions of One Request

`DataSource.fromFunction`, `DataSource.fromFunctionZIO`, `DataSource.fromFunctionOption` and `DataSource.fromFunctionOptionZIO` call your function once per request. The effectful variants run the calls with `ZIO.foreachPar`, so the requests of one batch are processed in parallel. The `Option` variants model lookups that may find nothing:

```scala
object DataSource {
  def fromFunction[A, B](name: String)(f: A => B)(implicit ev: A <:< Request[Nothing, B]): DataSource[Any, A]
  def fromFunctionZIO[R, E, A, B](name: String)(f: A => ZIO[R, E, B])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): DataSource[R, A]
  def fromFunctionOption[A, B](name: String)(f: A => Option[B])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[Nothing, B]): DataSource[Any, A]
  def fromFunctionOptionZIO[R, E, A, B](name: String)(f: A => ZIO[R, E, Option[B]])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): DataSource[R, A]
}
```

A failing effect fails only its own request: the error becomes that request's result, and the other requests in the batch still succeed. A `None` leaves the request without a result, and a query that needs it dies with a `QueryFailure`, so use the `Option` variants only when a missing entry is a bug in the data source. The following block builds a pure data source and an effectful one that can fail:

```scala
case class User(id: Int, name: String)
case class GetUser(id: Int) extends Request[String, User]

val pure: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.fromFunction[GetUserName, String]("pure")(request => s"user-${request.id}")

val effectful: DataSource[Any, GetUser] =
  DataSource.fromFunctionZIO[Any, String, GetUser, User]("effectful") { request =>
    if (request.id > 0) ZIO.succeed(User(request.id, s"user-${request.id}"))
    else ZIO.fail(s"invalid id ${request.id}")
  }
```

Pick `DataSource.fromFunction` for tests and stubs: it needs no environment and no effects. Pick `DataSource.fromFunctionZIO` when each request needs a call to a service, for example an HTTP endpoint with no bulk variant. These constructors do not combine requests, so a database lookup per request still costs one round trip per request.

#### Functions of a Batch of Requests

`DataSource.fromFunctionBatched` and its variants hand your function the whole batch as a `Chunk[A]` and expect a result for every request. Results are matched to requests by position, so your function must return a chunk of the same size and in the same order. If the result is shorter, the requests without a result die with a `QueryFailure`. The four variants differ in whether the function is effectful and whether it may return `None` for a request:

```scala
object DataSource {
  def fromFunctionBatched[A, B](name: String)(f: Chunk[A] => Chunk[B])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[Nothing, B]): DataSource[Any, A]
  def fromFunctionBatchedZIO[R, E, A, B](name: String)(f: Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, E, Chunk[B]])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): DataSource[R, A]
  def fromFunctionBatchedOption[A, B](name: String)(f: Chunk[A] => Chunk[Option[B]])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[Nothing, B]): DataSource[Any, A]
  def fromFunctionBatchedOptionZIO[R, E, A, B](name: String)(f: Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, E, Chunk[Option[B]]])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): DataSource[R, A]
}
```

If the effect of an effectful variant fails, every request in that batch fails with the same cause. The next block shows the typical use: one bulk query for all ids, with the result for an unknown id left out:

```scala
val knownUsers: Map[Int, String] = Map(1 -> "Ada", 2 -> "Grace")

val bulk: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedOption[GetUserName, String]("bulk") { requests =>
    requests.map(request => knownUsers.get(request.id))
  }
```

Pick these constructors when the backend has a bulk operation such as `SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...)` and returns results in request order. For the SQL case, where rows come back in arbitrary order, use the `With` variants below.

#### Functions That Return Results in Any Order

`DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedWith` and `DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedWithZIO` take a second function that maps each result back to the request it answers. Your batch function may then return results in any order, and no longer has to return one per request:

```scala
object DataSource {
  def fromFunctionBatchedWith[A, B](name: String)(f: Chunk[A] => Chunk[B], g: B => Request[Nothing, B])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[Nothing, B]): DataSource[Any, A]
  def fromFunctionBatchedWithZIO[R, E, A, B](name: String)(f: Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, E, Chunk[B]], g: B => Request[E, B])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): DataSource[R, A]
}
```

Here `g` takes a result of type `B` and returns the request that produced it. The following block answers `FindUser` requests with a list of users in reverse order, and `g` rebuilds each request from the user's id:

```scala
case class FindUser(id: Int) extends Request[Nothing, User]

val unordered: DataSource[Any, FindUser] =
  DataSource.fromFunctionBatchedWith[FindUser, User]("unordered")(
    requests => requests.map(request => User(request.id, s"user-${request.id}")).reverse,
    user => FindUser(user.id)
  )
```

Pick the `With` variants when the backend returns rows keyed by id rather than in request order. The effectful variant fails every request of the batch if the effect fails.

#### Building a Batched Data Source by Hand

`DataSource.Batched` is a trait for data sources that process each batch of parallel requests in one call, and `DataSource.Batched.make` builds one from a function. Your function returns a `CompletedRequestMap` (see [CompletedRequestMap](./completed-request-map.md) for how to build one), so it controls the result of every request, including failures and omissions. You rarely need the trait directly: prefer the `fromFunction*` constructors, and fall back to `Batched.make` when they do not fit, for example when only some requests in a batch fail:

```scala
object DataSource {
  trait Batched[-R, -A] extends DataSource[R, A] {
    def run(requests: Chunk[A])(implicit trace: Trace): ZIO[R, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap]
    final def runAll(requests: Chunk[Chunk[A]])(implicit trace: Trace): ZIO[R, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap]
  }

  object Batched {
    def make[R, A](name: String)(f: Chunk[A] => ZIO[R, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap]): DataSource[R, A]
  }
}
```

`Batched` implements `runAll` for you: it calls `run` once per inner batch, in order, and skips requests that an earlier batch already completed. The next block builds a data source with `Batched.make` that answers known ids and fails the rest:

```scala
val manual: DataSource[Any, GetUser] =
  DataSource.Batched.make[Any, GetUser]("manual") { requests =>
    ZIO.succeed(
      CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(requests)(
        request => request,
        request =>
          knownUsers.get(request.id) match {
            case Some(name) => Exit.succeed(User(request.id, name))
            case None       => Exit.fail(s"unknown user ${request.id}")
          }
      )
    )
  }
```

#### Introspecting Sequential Batches

`DataSource.make` builds a data source from `runAll` itself. The function receives the `Chunk[Chunk[A]]` described above, so it sees the batches that must run sequentially and can optimize across them, for example by sending one query for all of them. Because it must produce the `CompletedRequestMap` itself, use it only when you need that view; `Batched` is enough otherwise:

```scala
object DataSource {
  def make[R, A](name: String)(f: Chunk[Chunk[A]] => ZIO[R, Nothing, CompletedRequestMap]): DataSource[R, A]
}
```

The following block flattens all batches into a single call:

```scala
val flattened: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.make[Any, GetUserName]("flattened") { batches =>
    ZIO.succeed(
      CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(batches.flatten)(
        request => request,
        request => Exit.succeed(s"user-${request.id}")
      )
    )
  }
```

#### A Data Source That Never Answers

`DataSource.never` is a `DataSource[Any, Any]` whose `runAll` never completes. Because of the contravariant type parameter, it can be used for any request type. It is useful in tests of timeouts, races and interruption:

```scala
object DataSource {
  val never: DataSource[Any, Any]
}
```

The next block queries it with a request, so the query never completes unless it is timed out or raced:

```scala
val hanging: ZQuery[Any, Nothing, String] =
  ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(1))(DataSource.never)
```

### Transforming Data Sources

The following methods on `DataSource` return a new data source. Each one derives the new `DataSource#identifier` from the original, so data sources built with the same combinators and the same descriptions are equal. Functions passed to `contramap`, `contramapZIO`, `eitherWith` and `provideSomeEnvironment` are wrapped in `Described`, a pair of a value and a string description that ZIO Query uses to build the identifier (see [Aspects](./aspects.md#describing-values-with-described)). Wrap a function with `Described(f, "description")`, or with `f ? "description"` after `import zio.query.Described._`. Equal functions need the same description, and different functions need different ones.

#### Limiting the Batch Size

`batchN(n)` splits each batch into groups of at most `n` requests, which the underlying data source then receives one group after another. Use it when the backend limits the number of items per call, for example an SQL `IN` clause or an API that accepts up to 100 ids. A value of `n` below `1` makes the data source die with an `IllegalArgumentException` when it runs:

```scala
trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  def batchN(n: Int): DataSource[R, A]
}
```

To cap the data source at two requests per call:

```scala
val capped: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] = users.batchN(2)
```

#### Changing the Request Type

`contramap` and `contramapZIO` return a data source for requests of type `B`, by converting each `B` request into an `A` request first. `contramapZIO` takes an effectful conversion that cannot fail, and runs the conversions of a batch in parallel:

```scala
trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  final def contramap[B](f: Described[B => A]): DataSource[R, B]
  final def contramapZIO[R1 <: R, B](f: Described[B => ZIO[R1, Nothing, A]]): DataSource[R1, B]
}
```

:::warning[The Result Is Keyed by the Converted Request]
The new data source returns the `CompletedRequestMap` of the original data source as is. A query looks up its result with the request it submitted, so the converted request must be equal to the submitted one, otherwise the query dies with a `QueryFailure`. Use `contramap` to normalize or enrich a request in a way that keeps it equal, for example to fill in a field.
:::

The following block shows the `?` syntax with a conversion that returns an equal request:

```scala
import zio.query.Described._

val same: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  users.contramap(((request: GetUserName) => request) ? "same")
```

#### Routing Requests to Two Data Sources

`eitherWith` combines two data sources into one for a request type `C`. The function sorts every request into `Left` for this data source or `Right` for the other one, and each side receives its own requests in parallel. The results of both are merged:

```scala
trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  final def eitherWith[R1 <: R, B, C](that: DataSource[R1, B])(f: Described[C => Either[A, B]]): DataSource[R1, C]
}
```

Use it to route one request hierarchy to two backends. As with `contramap`, the request returned by `f` must equal the request it came from, which holds when `A` and `B` are subtypes of `C`. The following block routes the requests of a sealed hierarchy to separate data sources:

```scala
sealed trait UserRequest                  extends Request[Nothing, String]
case class ByCache(id: Int)               extends UserRequest
case class ByDatabase(id: Int)            extends UserRequest

val cache: DataSource[Any, ByCache] =
  DataSource.fromFunction[ByCache, String]("cache")(request => s"cached-${request.id}")

val database: DataSource[Any, ByDatabase] =
  DataSource.fromFunction[ByDatabase, String]("database")(request => s"stored-${request.id}")

val routed: DataSource[Any, UserRequest] =
  cache.eitherWith(database)(Described[UserRequest => Either[ByCache, ByDatabase]]({
    case request: ByCache    => Left(request)
    case request: ByDatabase => Right(request)
  }, "byType"))
```

#### Racing Two Data Sources

`race` sends the same requests to both data sources and returns the results of the first one that completes, interrupting the other safely. Use it for hedging between a fast and a slow replica:

```scala
trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  final def race[R1 <: R, A1 <: A](that: DataSource[R1, A1]): DataSource[R1, A1]
}
```

The next block races a data source against `DataSource.never`, which always loses:

```scala
val raced: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] = users.race(DataSource.never)
```

#### Providing the Environment

`provideEnvironment` removes the whole environment requirement of a data source, and `provideSomeEnvironment` replaces it with a smaller one by mapping the new environment to the original. The environment is passed as a `Described` value, in the same way as the functions above:

```scala
trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  final def provideEnvironment(r: Described[ZEnvironment[R]]): DataSource[Any, A]
  final def provideSomeEnvironment[R0](f: Described[ZEnvironment[R0] => ZEnvironment[R]]): DataSource[R0, A]
}
```

The following block defines a data source that needs a `Prefix` service and provides it, so the result needs no environment:

```scala
case class Prefix(value: String)

val prefixed: DataSource[Prefix, GetUserName] =
  DataSource.fromFunctionZIO[Prefix, Nothing, GetUserName, String]("prefixed") { request =>
    ZIO.serviceWith[Prefix](prefix => s"${prefix.value}${request.id}")
  }

val ready: DataSource[Any, GetUserName] =
  prefixed.provideEnvironment(Described(ZEnvironment(Prefix("user-")), "Prefix(user-)"))
```

#### Identifier and Equality

`DataSource#identifier` is the name given to the constructor, and two data sources are equal when their identifiers are equal. `ZQuery` uses this equality to group requests: requests to equal data sources are batched together, so use one unique identifier per logical data source and do not reuse it for another one. `toString` returns the identifier.

### Submitting Requests

A `DataSource` is used through `ZQuery`. The constructors on `ZQuery` return a query that sends requests to the data source, and the optimizations of ZIO Query apply only to queries built with them.

#### Single Requests

`ZQuery.fromRequest` takes a request and a data source, both by name, and returns a query for the result. `DataSource#query` does the same from the data source side. The request is looked up in the cache first, so a repeated request within one run reaches the data source only once. `ZQuery.fromRequestUncached` skips the cache, so every occurrence reaches the data source:

```scala
object ZQuery {
  def fromRequest[R, E, A, B](request: => A)(dataSource: => DataSource[R, A])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, B]
  def fromRequestUncached[R, E, A, B](request: => A)(dataSource: => DataSource[R, A])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, B]
}

trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  final def query[E, A1 <: A, B](request: A1)(implicit ev: A1 <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, B]
}
```

To submit a request in the three ways:

```scala
val viaFromRequest: ZQuery[Any, Nothing, String] = ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUserName(1))(users)
val viaQuery: ZQuery[Any, Nothing, String]       = users.query(GetUserName(1))
val viaUncached: ZQuery[Any, Nothing, String]    = ZQuery.fromRequestUncached(GetUserName(1))(users)
```

Use `ZQuery.fromRequestUncached` for requests whose answer may change during a run, such as reading a counter. Requests that are not cached are also not deduplicated.

#### Many Requests at Once

`ZQuery.fromRequests` submits a `Chunk` or a `List` of requests, and `DataSource#queryAll` does the same for a `Chunk`. The results come back in the order of the requests. All the requests are submitted together, so they reach the data source in one batch, without the cost of one query per element. `ZQuery.fromRequestsWith` takes values and a function that turns each value into a request, which saves building the intermediate collection:

```scala
object ZQuery {
  def fromRequests[R, E, A, B](requests: Chunk[A])(dataSource: DataSource[R, A])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, Chunk[B]]
  def fromRequests[R, E, A, B](requests: List[A])(dataSource: DataSource[R, A])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, List[B]]
  def fromRequestsWith[R, E, In, A, B](as: Chunk[In], f: In => A)(dataSource: DataSource[R, A])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, Chunk[B]]
  def fromRequestsWith[R, E, In, A, B](as: List[In], f: In => A)(dataSource: DataSource[R, A])(implicit ev: A <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, List[B]]
}

trait DataSource[-R, -A] {
  final def queryAll[E, A1 <: A, B](requests: Chunk[A1])(implicit ev: A1 <:< Request[E, B]): ZQuery[R, E, Chunk[B]]
}
```

The following block fetches the names for a list of ids in one query:

```scala
runSync(ZQuery.fromRequestsWith(List(1, 2, 3), GetUserName(_))(users))
// res3: List[String] = List("user-1", "user-2", "user-3")
```

When you already have all the requests, prefer `ZQuery.fromRequests` and `ZQuery.fromRequestsWith` to combining one `ZQuery.fromRequest` query per element with `ZQuery.foreachPar`, because they avoid building a query per request.

---

## Error Handling(Zio-query)

A `ZQuery[R, E, A]` can fail with a typed error `E`, die with a defect, or be interrupted, just like a `ZIO` effect. This page shows where those failures come from when a query talks to a data source, what happens to the other requests in the same batch, and which `ZQuery` operators recover from each kind of failure, convert between them, or bound the time a query may take.

### How Errors Flow

Every request type declares its own error type, as in `Request[E, A]`. When a data source completes a request, it stores an `Exit[E, A]` for that request in the `CompletedRequestMap`, so each request succeeds or fails on its own. `ZQuery.fromRequest` turns that `Exit` into the result of the query, which is why the error type of a request becomes the error type of the query.

The effect returned by `DataSource#runAll` has the error type `Nothing`: a data source reports problems for individual requests through the `CompletedRequestMap`, not by failing as a whole. Three situations can therefore make a query fail:

| Situation                                              | Result in the query                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| The data source stores `Exit.fail(e)` for a request    | A failure of type `E`                    |
| The data source stores `Exit.die(t)` for a request     | A defect                                 |
| The data source returns no result for a request        | A defect: a [`QueryFailure`](#queryfailure-a-request-without-a-result) |

### Setting Up an Example

The examples on this page use one request type and three data sources. The request type fails with a `String` error. The first data source answers ids `1` and `2`, fails id `3` with a typed error, and fails id `4` with a defect. The second data source forgets to answer id `99`. The third counts how many times it is called.

```scala
import zio._
import zio.query._

final case class GetUser(id: Int) extends Request[String, String]

val userDataSource: DataSource[Any, GetUser] =
  DataSource.make[Any, GetUser]("UserDataSource") { requests =>
    ZIO.succeed(
      CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(requests.flatten)(
        r => r,
        r =>
          r.id match {
            case 3     => Exit.fail("user 3 not found")
            case 4     => Exit.die(new RuntimeException("connection reset"))
            case other => Exit.succeed(s"user-$other")
          }
      )
    )
  }

val forgetfulDataSource: DataSource[Any, GetUser] =
  DataSource.make[Any, GetUser]("ForgetfulDataSource") { requests =>
    ZIO.succeed(
      CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(requests.flatten.filter(_.id != 99))(r => r, r => Exit.succeed(s"user-${r.id}"))
    )
  }

val calls: Ref[Int] = Unsafe.unsafe(implicit unsafe => Ref.unsafe.make(0))

val countingDataSource: DataSource[Any, GetUser] =
  DataSource.make[Any, GetUser]("CountingDataSource") { requests =>
    calls.update(_ + 1) *> ZIO.succeed(
      CompletedRequestMap.fromIterableWith(requests.flatten)(r => r, _ => Exit.fail("service unavailable"))
    )
  }

def user(id: Int): ZQuery[Any, String, String] =
  ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUser(id))(userDataSource)

def run[E, A](query: ZQuery[Any, E, A]): Exit[E, A] =
  Unsafe.unsafe(implicit unsafe => Runtime.default.unsafe.run(query.run.exit).getOrThrowFiberFailure())

def describe[E, A](query: ZQuery[Any, E, A]): String =
  run(query) match {
    case Exit.Success(a) => s"success: $a"
    case Exit.Failure(c) =>
      c.failureOption
        .map(e => s"failure: $e")
        .orElse(c.dieOption.map(t => s"defect: ${t.getClass.getSimpleName}: ${t.getMessage}"))
        .getOrElse("interrupted")
  }
```

The `describe` helper runs a query and renders its outcome in one line, so that the output below stays short.

### Typed Errors and Defects

A request that the data source answers with `Exit.fail` fails the query with that error, and `Exit.die` makes the query die:

```scala
describe(user(1))
// res0: String = "success: user-1"
describe(user(3))
// res1: String = "failure: user 3 not found"
describe(user(4))
// res2: String = "defect: RuntimeException: connection reset"
```

#### A Failing Request Does Not Fail Its Batch

The requests in a batch are completed one by one, so a failing request does not change the results of the other requests in the same batch. To see this, we combine three requests with `ZQuery.foreachPar`, which sends them to the data source in one batch, and turn each result into an `Either` with `either`:

```scala
describe(ZQuery.foreachPar(List(1, 2, 3))(id => user(id).either))
// res3: String = "success: List(Right(user-1), Right(user-2), Left(user 3 not found))"
```

Each request has its own result: ids `1` and `2` succeeded and id `3` failed. Without `either`, the first failure fails the whole `foreachPar` query:

```scala
describe(ZQuery.foreachPar(List(1, 2, 3))(user))
// res4: String = "failure: user 3 not found"
```

### QueryFailure: A Request Without a Result

A data source must provide a result for every request it receives. If it leaves a request out of the `CompletedRequestMap`, the query dies with a `QueryFailure`. The defect carries the data source and the request that was not completed, and its message names both:

```scala
val forgotten = ZQuery.fromRequest(GetUser(99))(forgetfulDataSource)
// forgotten: ZQuery[Any, String, String] = zio.query.ZQuery@3c73b6c5

describe(forgotten)
// res5: String = "defect: QueryFailure: Data source ForgetfulDataSource did not complete request GetUser(99)."
```

A `QueryFailure` is a defect, not a typed error, so it does not appear in the error type of the query and `catchAll` does not recover from it. It signals a bug in the data source, not a condition that a caller is expected to handle.

The only operator that is aware of `QueryFailure` is `optional`. It converts a query to one that returns `Some` if the data sources returned results for all requests and `None` otherwise. Typed errors and other defects still fail the query:

```scala
describe(forgotten.optional)
// res6: String = "success: None"
describe(user(1).optional)
// res7: String = "success: Some(user-1)"
describe(user(3).optional)
// res8: String = "failure: user 3 not found"
```

:::note
`DataSource.fromFunctionOption` and `DataSource.fromFunctionOptionZIO` construct data sources that may not provide results for all requests. Use `optional` on queries built from them.
:::

### Recovering from Errors

The operators below follow the naming of `ZIO`. They differ in what they recover from: the `catchAll` family and the `fold`/`foldQuery`/`foldZIO` family handle typed errors only, while the `*Cause` variants also see defects.

| Operator                                  | Handles                  | Recovers with                  |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| `catchAll`                                | Typed errors             | A `ZQuery`                     |
| `catchAllZIO`                             | Typed errors             | A `ZIO` effect                 |
| `catchAllCause`                           | The whole `Cause`        | A `ZQuery`                     |
| `catchAllCauseZIO`                        | The whole `Cause`        | A `ZIO` effect                 |
| `fold`                                    | Typed errors and success | A pure value                   |
| `foldQuery`                               | Typed errors and success | A `ZQuery`                     |
| `foldZIO`                                 | Typed errors and success | A `ZIO` effect                 |
| `foldCauseQuery`                          | The whole `Cause` and success | A `ZQuery`                |
| `foldCauseZIO`                            | The whole `Cause` and success | A `ZIO` effect            |
| `either`                                  | Typed errors and success | `Either[E, A]`, cannot fail    |
| `optional`                                | `QueryFailure`           | `Option[A]`                    |

#### Recovering with a Fallback Query

`catchAll` takes a function from the error to a new query. The fallback query is a full query: it can issue requests of its own, and those requests are batched with the rest of the query:

```scala
describe(user(3).catchAll(_ => user(1)))
// res9: String = "success: user-1"
```

`catchAll` handles only typed errors. A defect passes through unchanged:

```scala
describe(user(4).catchAll(_ => user(1)))
// res10: String = "defect: RuntimeException: connection reset"
```

`catchAllCause` receives the whole `Cause`, so it can also recover from defects:

```scala
describe(user(4).catchAllCause(_ => user(1)))
// res11: String = "success: user-1"
```

To recover with an effect instead of a query, use `catchAllZIO` or `catchAllCauseZIO`:

```scala
describe(user(3).catchAllZIO(error => ZIO.succeed(s"fallback after: $error")))
// res12: String = "success: fallback after: user 3 not found"
```

#### Handling Both Outcomes

`fold` handles failure and success in one step and produces a query that cannot fail. `foldQuery` and `foldZIO` do the same with a query or an effect, and `foldCauseQuery` and `foldCauseZIO` receive the whole `Cause` for the failure case:

```scala
describe(user(3).fold(error => s"failed: $error", name => s"found: $name"))
// res13: String = "success: failed: user 3 not found"
describe(user(4).foldCauseQuery(cause => ZQuery.succeed(s"died: ${cause.isDie}"), name => ZQuery.succeed(name)))
// res14: String = "success: died: true"
```

`either` is the shortest way to make a failure visible as a value, as in the batch example above.

### Working with the Full Cause

`sandbox` moves the whole `Cause` into the error channel, so that typed errors and defects can be handled in one place with the ordinary operators. `unsandbox` is the inverse:

```scala
val sandboxed: ZQuery[Any, Cause[String], String] = user(4).sandbox
// sandboxed: ZQuery[Any, Cause[String], String] = zio.query.ZQuery@192c64cb

describe(sandboxed.mapError(cause => s"was a defect: ${cause.isDie}"))
// res15: String = "failure: was a defect: true"
describe(ZQuery.unsandbox(sandboxed))
// res16: String = "defect: RuntimeException: connection reset"
```

`sandboxWith` applies a function to the sandboxed query and unsandboxes the result. It is useful for partial recovery from both errors and defects at once:

```scala
describe(user(4).sandboxWith[Any, String, String](_.catchAll(_ => ZQuery.succeed("recovered"))))
// res17: String = "success: recovered"
```

### Converting Between Errors and Defects

`mapError` and `mapErrorCause` transform the error or the whole `Cause` without changing success values. They do not prevent batching of the requests in the query.

`orDie` turns a typed error into a defect. It requires the error type to be a `Throwable`; `orDieWith` takes a function that converts the error:

```scala
describe(user(3).orDieWith(message => new IllegalStateException(message)))
// res18: String = "defect: IllegalStateException: user 3 not found"
```

`refineOrDie` keeps only the errors matched by a partial function and turns all others into defects. `refineOrDieWith` takes a function that converts the unmatched error to a `Throwable`:

```scala
val refined: ZQuery[Any, Int, String] =
```
