```scala
  query[Person].filter(_.name == "John").delete.ifCond(_.age == 10)
}
ctx.run(q2)
// DELETE FROM Person WHERE name = 'John' IF age = 10
```

#### delete column
```scala
val q = quote {
  query[Person].map(p => p.age).delete
}
ctx.run(q)
// DELETE p.age FROM Person
```

#### list.contains / set.contains
requires `allowFiltering`
```scala
val q = quote {
  query[Book].filter(p => p.pages.contains(25)).allowFiltering
}
ctx.run(q)
// SELECT id, notes, pages, history FROM Book WHERE pages CONTAINS 25 ALLOW FILTERING
```

#### map.contains
requires `allowFiltering`
```scala
val q = quote {
  query[Book].filter(p => p.history.contains(12)).allowFiltering
}
ctx.run(q)
// SELECT id, notes, pages, history FROM book WHERE history CONTAINS 12 ALLOW FILTERING
```

#### map.containsValue
requires `allowFiltering`
```scala
val q = quote {
  query[Book].filter(p => p.history.containsValue(true)).allowFiltering
}
ctx.run(q)
// SELECT id, notes, pages, history FROM book WHERE history CONTAINS true ALLOW FILTERING
```

### Dynamic queries

Quill's default operation mode is compile-time, but there are queries that have their structure defined only at runtime. Quill automatically falls back to runtime normalization and query generation if the query's structure is not static. Example:

```scala
val ctx = new SqlMirrorContext(MirrorSqlDialect, Literal)

import ctx._

sealed trait QueryType
case object Minor extends QueryType
case object Senior extends QueryType

def people(t: QueryType): Quoted[Query[Person]] =
  t match {
    case Minor => quote {
      query[Person].filter(p => p.age < 18)
    }
    case Senior => quote {
      query[Person].filter(p => p.age > 65)
    }
  }

ctx.run(people(Minor))
// SELECT p.id, p.name, p.age FROM Person p WHERE p.age < 18

ctx.run(people(Senior))
// SELECT p.id, p.name, p.age FROM Person p WHERE p.age > 65
```

#### Dynamic query API

Additionally, Quill provides a separate query API to facilitate the creation of dynamic queries. This API allows users to easily manipulate quoted values instead of working only with quoted transformations.

**Important**: A few of the dynamic query methods accept runtime string values. It's important to keep in mind that these methods could be a vector for SQL injection.

Let's use the `filter` transformation as an example. In the regular API, this method has no implementation since it's an abstract member of a trait:

```
def filter(f: T => Boolean): EntityQuery[T]
```

In the dynamic API, `filter` is has a different signature and a body that is executed at runtime:

```
def filter(f: Quoted[T] => Quoted[Boolean]): DynamicQuery[T] =
  transform(f, Filter)
```

It takes a `Quoted[T]` as input and produces a `Quoted[Boolean]`. The user is free to use regular scala code within the transformation:

```scala
def people(onlyMinors: Boolean) =
  dynamicQuery[Person].filter(p => if(onlyMinors) quote(p.age < 18) else quote(true))
```

In order to create a dynamic query, use one of the following methods:

```scala
dynamicQuery[Person]
dynamicQuerySchema[Person]("people", alias(_.name, "pname"))
```

It's also possible to transform a `Quoted` into a dynamic query:

```scala
val q = quote {
  query[Person]
}
q.dynamic.filter(p => quote(p.name == "John"))
```

The dynamic query API is very similar to the regular API but has a few differences:

**Queries**
```scala
// schema queries use `alias` instead of tuples
dynamicQuerySchema[Person]("people", alias(_.name, "pname"))

// this allows users to use a dynamic list of aliases
val aliases = List(alias[Person](_.name, "pname"), alias[Person](_.age, "page"))
dynamicQuerySchema[Person]("people", aliases:_*)

// a few methods have an overload with the `Opt` suffix,
// which apply the transformation only if the option is defined:

def people(minAge: Option[Int]) =
  dynamicQuery[Person].filterOpt(minAge)((person, minAge) => quote(person.age >= minAge))

def people(maxRecords: Option[Int]) =
  dynamicQuery[Person].takeOpt(maxRecords)

def people(dropFirst: Option[Int]) =
  dynamicQuery[Person].dropOpt(dropFirst)

// method with `If` suffix, for better chaining
def people(userIds: Seq[Int]) =
  dynamicQuery[Person].filterIf(userIds.nonEmpty)(person => quote(liftQuery(userIds).contains(person.id)))
```

**Actions**
```scala
// actions use `set`
dynamicQuery[Person].filter(_.id == 1).update(set(_.name, quote("John")))

// or `setValue` if the value is not quoted
dynamicQuery[Person].insert(setValue(_.name, "John"))

// or `setOpt` that will be applied only the option is defined
dynamicQuery[Person].insert(setOpt(_.name, Some("John")))

// it's also possible to use a runtime string value as the column name
dynamicQuery[Person].filter(_.id == 1).update(set("name", quote("John")))

// to insert or update a case class instance, use `insertValue`/`updateValue`
val p = Person(0, "John", 21)
dynamicQuery[Person].insertValue(p)
dynamicQuery[Person].filter(_.id == 1).updateValue(p)
```

#### Dynamic query normalization cache

Quill is super fast for static queries (almost zero runtime overhead compared to directly sql executing).

But there is significant impact for dynamic queries.

Normalization caching was introduced to improve the situation, which will speedup dynamic queries significantly. It is enabled by default.

To disable dynamic normalization caching, pass following property to sbt during compile time

```
sbt -Dquill.query.cacheDynamic=false
```

---

## AsyncRedis

`AsyncRedis` exposes the same commands as `Redis`, but each command returns as soon as it has been queued. This lets a program send many commands before it waits for any reply.

### Return Types

A command on `Redis` has type `IO[RedisError, A]`. The same command on `AsyncRedis` has type `UIO[IO[RedisError, A]]`. The outer effect queues the command and never fails. The inner effect waits for the reply:

```scala
type Redis      = GenRedis[GenRedis.Sync]
type AsyncRedis = GenRedis[GenRedis.Async]
```

`Redis.local`, `Redis.singleNode` produce both services in one layer. `Redis.cluster` produces only `Redis`.

### Pipelining Commands

To send several commands and then wait for all the replies, see [How to Pipeline Commands](../how-to/pipeline-commands.md).

---

## Cluster

Redis Cluster spreads keys over several nodes by hashing each key to one of 16384 slots. ZIO Redis supports it through the `Redis.cluster` layer, which gives the same `Redis` service as a single node while routing every command to the node that owns its slot.

### Building the Cluster Layer

`Redis.cluster` requires a `CodecSupplier` and a `RedisClusterConfig`. The config lists one or more startup nodes as `RedisUri` values. The client contacts them in order, asks the first reachable node for the slot map with `CLUSTER SLOTS`, and then opens a connection to every master. To connect to a three-master cluster:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val clusterConfig: ULayer[RedisClusterConfig] =
  ZLayer.succeed(
    RedisClusterConfig(
      Chunk(
        RedisUri("localhost", 7000),
        RedisUri("localhost", 7001),
        RedisUri("localhost", 7002)
      )
    )
  )

val redis: ZLayer[Any, RedisError, Redis] =
  ZLayer.make[Redis](
    clusterConfig,
    ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8),
    Redis.cluster
  )
```

Listing several startup nodes is only about availability at start-up. If none of them can be reached, the layer fails with a `RedisError.IOError`. Once running, the client learns the other nodes from the cluster itself.

### RedisClusterConfig

`RedisClusterConfig` is a case class with the following fields:

| Field              | Type                       | Default                  | Meaning                                         |
| ------------------ | -------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `addresses`        | `Chunk[RedisUri]`          | none                     | Startup nodes used to discover the cluster      |
| `retry`            | `RetryClusterConfig`       | `RetryClusterConfig.Default` | Backoff used when a command has to be retried |
| `requestQueueSize` | `Int`                      | `16`                     | Request queue size of each node connection      |
| `auth`             | `Option[RedisConfig.Auth]` | `None`                   | Credentials used for every node                 |

`RetryClusterConfig` has three fields: `base: Duration`, `factor: Double` and `maxRecurs: Int`. The default is `RetryClusterConfig(100.millis, 1.5, 5)`, which means an exponential backoff that starts at 100 milliseconds, grows by a factor of 1.5 and gives up after five retries. To use a faster and shorter policy together with authentication:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val config: RedisClusterConfig =
  RedisClusterConfig(
    addresses = Chunk(RedisUri("redis-1.example.com:6379")),
    retry = RetryClusterConfig(base = 50.millis, factor = 2.0, maxRecurs = 3),
    auth = Some(RedisConfig.Auth("secret"))
  )
```

### RedisUri

`RedisUri` names a node by host and port, with optional `ssl`, `sni` and `verifyCertificate` settings. It is described in [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md). A TLS node is written as follows:

```scala
import zio.redis._

val secureNode: RedisUri = RedisUri("redis.example.com", 6380, ssl = true)
```

### Redirections

A cluster may answer a command with a redirection. `RedisError.Moved(slot, address)` means the slot now lives on another node, and `RedisError.Ask(slot, address)` means the slot is being migrated and this one command should be sent to the target node. Application code does not need to handle either error, because the cluster executor behind `Redis.cluster` does it:

| Situation                        | What the executor does                                                              |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Normal command                   | Hashes the first key with CRC16, picks the owning node and sends the command there  |
| `Ask`                            | Sends `ASKING` followed by the command to the node named in the error               |
| `Moved`                          | Reloads the slot map from the cluster, closes the old connections and resends       |
| `IOError` or any cluster error   | Retries the whole attempt with the exponential backoff from `RetryClusterConfig`    |

A command is retried at most `maxRecurs` times, and if it still fails the last error is returned to the caller. Commands without a key, such as `PING`, are sent to the node that owns slot 1.

### CrossSlot Errors

A command that touches several keys works only if all the keys hash to the same slot. Otherwise the cluster replies with `RedisError.CrossSlot`, which `Redis` surfaces as a failure. The executor routes by the first key only, so it cannot fix this for you. To force related keys into one slot, wrap a common part of each name in braces, which is called a hash tag. To write two keys that always share a slot:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def copyProfile(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.sAdd("{user:1}:friends", "ada") *> redis.sAdd("{user:1}:groups", "admins")
```

Only the text between the braces is hashed, so both keys land in the same slot.

### Cluster Commands

The commands below are methods on `Redis`, from the `Cluster` API trait. They are mostly useful for tooling and tests, since the executor already issues `ASKING` and `CLUSTER SLOTS` itself:

| Method                    | Redis command           | Returns            |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------ |
| `Redis#slots`             | `CLUSTER SLOTS`         | `Chunk[Partition]` |
| `Redis#asking`            | `ASKING`                | `Unit`             |
| `Redis#setSlotImporting`  | `CLUSTER SETSLOT ... IMPORTING` | `Unit`     |
| `Redis#setSlotMigrating`  | `CLUSTER SETSLOT ... MIGRATING` | `Unit`     |
| `Redis#setSlotNode`       | `CLUSTER SETSLOT ... NODE`      | `Unit`     |
| `Redis#setSlotStable`     | `CLUSTER SETSLOT ... STABLE`    | `Unit`     |

`Slot`, `Partition`, `Node` and `SlotRange` live in `zio.redis.options.Cluster`. A `Partition` has a `slotRange`, a `master` node and its `slaves`, and each `Node` has an `id` and an `address`. To list the master of every slot range:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def masters(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Chunk[String]] =
  redis.slots.map(_.map(p => s"${p.slotRange.start}-${p.slotRange.end} -> ${p.master.address}"))
```

The integration test `ClusterSpec` calls `Redis#slots` against a six-node Docker cluster in the same way.

### Limitations

Pub/Sub is not available through `Redis.cluster`; `RedisSubscription` connects to a single node, as described in [Pub/Sub](./pub-sub.md). Every command is routed by its first key, so transactions and scripts that span slots must use hash tags.

---

## Codecs

Every key, field and value that crosses the wire is encoded to bytes by a `BinaryCodec` from ZIO Schema. A `CodecSupplier` tells ZIO Redis which codec to use for a given `Schema`, and the `Redis` layers require one.

### CodecSupplier

`CodecSupplier` is a trait with a single method that returns a codec for any type that has a `Schema`:

```scala
trait CodecSupplier {
  def get[A: Schema]: BinaryCodec[A]
}
```

Two options are available: the built-in UTF-8 supplier and any ZIO Schema codec such as Protobuf.

### The UTF-8 Supplier

`CodecSupplier.utf8` writes primitives as their plain text form, which is what other Redis clients and `redis-cli` expect. It supports primitive types only. Decoding converts `Int`, `Long` and `Double` numerically and returns every other primitive as a `String`. Encoding a case class fails with a `RedisError.CodecError`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val supplier: ULayer[CodecSupplier] =
  ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8)
```

### Protobuf and Other Codecs

To store case classes, implement `CodecSupplier` with a ZIO Schema codec. This supplier uses Protobuf, from the `zio-schema-protobuf` dependency listed in [Getting Started](../getting-started.md):

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.schema.codec.{BinaryCodec, ProtobufCodec}

object ProtobufCodecSupplier extends CodecSupplier {
  def get[A: Schema]: BinaryCodec[A] = ProtobufCodec.protobufCodec
}
```

Any other ZIO Schema codec, such as JSON or Avro, plugs in the same way.

### Storing Your Own Types

With a structural codec in place, a case class only needs a `Schema`. To write and read a case class:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}

final case class User(id: Long, name: String)

object User {
  implicit val schema: Schema[User] = DeriveSchema.gen[User]
}

def saveAndLoad(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Option[User]] =
  for {
    _    <- redis.set("user:1", User(1L, "Ada"))
    user <- redis.get("user:1").returning[User]
  } yield user
```

Keys use the codec too, so `redis.set("user:1", ...)` encodes the key `"user:1"` with the supplier. The same supplier must be used for writes and reads. Values written by one codec cannot be read by another.

---

## Error Handling(Concepts)

Every command fails with a `RedisError`. This page lists its cases and shows how to recover from them.

### The RedisError Hierarchy

`RedisError` is a sealed trait, so pattern matches over it are checked for exhaustiveness. Its cases are:

| Case                                  | Meaning                                                               |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ProtocolError(message)`              | The server sent a reply the client cannot interpret                   |
| `CodecError(message)`                 | A value could not be encoded or decoded                               |
| `WrongType(message)`                  | A command ran against a key holding another type                      |
| `BusyGroup(message)`                  | A stream consumer group already exists                                |
| `NoGroup(message)`                    | A stream consumer group does not exist                                |
| `NoScript(message)`                   | A script SHA is not in the script cache                               |
| `NotBusy(message)`                    | `scriptKill` ran while no script was executing                        |
| `IOError(exception)`                  | The connection failed                                                 |
| `CommandNameNotFound(message)`        | The command is unknown to the client                                  |
| `CrossSlot(message)`                  | A cluster command touched keys in different slots                     |
| `Moved(slot, address)`                | A cluster slot lives on another node                                  |
| `Ask(slot, address)`                  | A cluster slot is being migrated to another node                      |
| `InvalidPubSubCommand(command)`       | A command is not valid on a subscription connection                   |
| `SubscriptionStreamAlreadyClosed(key)`| A subscription stream was used after it closed                        |

`Moved` and `Ask` extend `ClusterRedisError`. The cluster executor handles them itself; see [Cluster](./cluster.md). The last two cases extend `PubSubError`; see [Pub/Sub](./pub-sub.md).

### Recovering From Errors

Because the error channel is a plain ZIO error, the usual combinators apply. To treat a type clash as a missing value:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def safeGet(redis: Redis, key: String): IO[RedisError, Option[String]] =
  redis.get(key).returning[String].catchSome {
    case RedisError.WrongType(_) => ZIO.none
  }
```

To retry connection failures with a backoff:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def resilientGet(redis: Redis, key: String): IO[RedisError, Option[String]] =
  redis.get(key).returning[String].retry(
    Schedule.exponential(100.millis) && Schedule.recurs(3) && Schedule.recurWhile[RedisError] {
      case _: RedisError.IOError => true
      case _                     => false
    }
  )
```

---

## Pub/Sub

Redis Pub/Sub lets clients publish messages to named channels and lets other clients receive them as they arrive. ZIO Redis splits the feature in two: publishing is a command on `Redis`, and subscribing lives on a separate service, `RedisSubscription`.

### Why Two Services

A Redis connection that has issued `SUBSCRIBE` or `PSUBSCRIBE` is in subscription mode and may no longer be used for ordinary commands. For that reason `RedisSubscription` opens its own connection, built by its own layer, and `Redis` stays free for everything else. A program that both publishes and subscribes needs both layers:

| Service             | Layer                           | Requires                          | Provides                                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `Redis`             | `Redis.singleNode`              | `CodecSupplier` and `RedisConfig` | `publish` and the `pubSub*` introspection |
| `RedisSubscription` | `RedisSubscription.singleNode`  | `CodecSupplier` and `RedisConfig` | `subscribe`, `pSubscribe` and friends     |

`RedisSubscription.local` is the counterpart of `Redis.local` and connects to `localhost:6379`. There is no cluster variant of `RedisSubscription`. To build both services against one server:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val layers: ZLayer[Any, RedisError.IOError, Redis with RedisSubscription] =
  ZLayer.make[Redis with RedisSubscription](
    ZLayer.succeed(RedisConfig.Local),
    ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8),
    Redis.singleNode,
    RedisSubscription.singleNode
  )
```

See [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md) for `RedisConfig` and [Codecs](./codecs.md) for `CodecSupplier`.

### Publishing

`Redis#publish` posts a message to a channel and returns the number of clients that received it. The message can be any type with a `Schema`, and it is encoded with the `CodecSupplier`. To publish a string:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def announce(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.publish("news", "hello")
```

### Subscribing

Every subscribe method returns a result builder. Calling `returning[R]` on it produces a `Stream[RedisError, ...]` of decoded messages, and the subscription starts when the stream is run. The following methods are available on `RedisSubscription`:

| Method                             | Emits                               | Subscribes to           |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `RedisSubscription#subscribeSingle` | `R`                                 | one channel             |
| `RedisSubscription#subscribe`       | `(String, R)`, keyed by channel     | one or more channels    |
| `RedisSubscription#pSubscribe`      | `(String, R)`, keyed by channel     | one or more patterns    |

The `*With` variants (`subscribeSingleWith`, `subscribeWith`, `pSubscribeWith`) additionally take `onSubscribe` and `onUnsubscribe` callbacks, described below. To receive the first three messages from a single channel:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def firstThree(subscription: RedisSubscription): IO[RedisError, Chunk[String]] =
  subscription.subscribeSingle("news").returning[String].take(3).runCollect
```

To listen to several channels at once and learn which channel each message came from:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val printAll: ZIO[RedisSubscription, RedisError, Unit] =
  ZIO.serviceWithZIO[RedisSubscription] { subscription =>
    subscription
      .subscribe("news", "weather")
      .returning[String]
      .foreach { case (channel, message) => ZIO.debug(s"$channel: $message") }
  }
```

### Pattern Subscriptions

`RedisSubscription#pSubscribe` takes glob-style patterns, such as `news.*`, and emits every message published to a matching channel. The first element of each pair is the name of the channel the message was published to, not the pattern. To log every message under the `news.` prefix:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def watchNews(subscription: RedisSubscription): IO[RedisError, Unit] =
  subscription
    .pSubscribe("news.*")
    .returning[String]
    .foreach { case (channel, message) => ZIO.debug(s"$channel: $message") }
```

### Callbacks and Synchronization

Publishing right after forking a subscriber is racy, because the subscription may not be active yet. The `*With` methods accept callbacks of type `PubSubCallback`, an alias for `(String, Long) => UIO[Unit]`. The callback receives the channel (or pattern) name and the number of subscriptions the connection now holds. Completing a `Promise` in `onSubscribe` is the way to wait for the subscription before publishing:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def publishAfterSubscribed(redis: Redis, subscription: RedisSubscription): IO[RedisError, Option[String]] =
  for {
    ready <- Promise.make[Nothing, Unit]
    fiber <- subscription
               .subscribeSingleWith("news")(onSubscribe = (_, _) => ready.succeed(()).unit)
               .returning[String]
               .runHead
               .fork
    _     <- ready.await
    _     <- redis.publish("news", "hello")
    msg   <- fiber.join
  } yield msg
```

The same pattern is used by the integration tests in `PubSubSpec`. Both callbacks default to a no-op.

### Unsubscribing

`RedisSubscription#unsubscribe` and `RedisSubscription#pUnsubscribe` take channel names or patterns, and with no arguments they remove every subscription of that kind. The streams of the removed subscriptions then end. To stop a listener from outside:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def stopListening(subscription: RedisSubscription): IO[RedisError, Unit] =
  subscription.unsubscribe("news") *> subscription.pUnsubscribe()
```

Interrupting a stream, for example with `take` or `interruptWhen`, also ends the consumer. Use `onUnsubscribe` to be notified when Redis confirms the removal.

### Inspecting Pub/Sub State

`Redis` offers the `PUBSUB` introspection commands. They run on the normal connection:

| Method                  | Returns                                           |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `Redis#pubSubChannels`  | `Chunk[String]` of active channels matching a pattern |
| `Redis#pubSubNumSub`    | `Map[String, Long]` of subscriber counts per channel  |
| `Redis#pubSubNumPat`    | `Long`, the number of active pattern subscriptions    |

To print the number of subscribers of two channels:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def countSubscribers(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Map[String, Long]] =
  redis.pubSubNumSub("news", "weather")
```

### Errors

Besides the usual `RedisError` cases, subscription streams can fail with `RedisError.InvalidPubSubCommand` and `RedisError.SubscriptionStreamAlreadyClosed`, both subtypes of `RedisError.PubSubError`. See [Error Handling](./error-handling.md) for the full list.

---

## Getting Started(Zio-redis)

ZIO Redis exposes every Redis command as a method on the `Redis` service. This page shows how to build the `Redis` layer, run a first program, and read results back with `returning`.

### Installation

`zio-redis` is added to your build as shown in [Installation](./index.md#installation). Examples that store case classes also use the Protobuf codec from ZIO Schema:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Protobuf codec for ZIO Schema (JVM, Scala 2.12, 2.13, 3)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-protobuf" % "1.9.1"
)
```

### The Redis Service

The library defines two service types, both built from the same layers:

| Type         | Command return type      | Use it to                      |
| ------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| `Redis`      | `IO[RedisError, A]`      | Run commands one after another |
| `AsyncRedis` | `UIO[IO[RedisError, A]]` | Send commands without waiting  |

Most programs only need `Redis`. See [AsyncRedis](./concepts/async-redis.md) for the second one.

### Building the Layer

A `Redis` layer needs a [`CodecSupplier`](./concepts/codecs.md) and a connection. The following layers create it:

| Layer              | Requires                                 | Connects to                                            |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Redis.local`      | `CodecSupplier`                          | `localhost:6379`                                       |
| `Redis.singleNode` | `CodecSupplier` and `RedisConfig`        | The single server described by the config              |
| `Redis.cluster`    | `CodecSupplier` and `RedisClusterConfig` | A Redis Cluster (see [Cluster](./concepts/cluster.md)) |

To use the built-in UTF-8 codec supplier against a local server:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val layer: ZLayer[Any, RedisError.IOError, Redis] =
  ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8) >>> Redis.local
```

### Running a First Program

The program below stores a value with an expiry and reads it back. Commands such as `Redis#set` and `Redis#get` are methods on the service, so we obtain it with `ZIO.service`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

object FirstProgram extends ZIOAppDefault {
  val program: ZIO[Redis, RedisError, Unit] =
    for {
      redis <- ZIO.service[Redis]
      _     <- redis.set("greeting", "hello", Some(1.minute))
      value <- redis.get("greeting").returning[String]
      _     <- ZIO.debug(s"greeting = $value")
    } yield ()

  def run =
    program.provide(Redis.local, ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8))
}
```

### Choosing the Return Type

Redis stores bytes, so ZIO Redis cannot know which type a value should decode to. Commands that return user data therefore return a builder, and we finish the call with `returning[A]`, where `A` has a ZIO Schema `Schema`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def readCounter(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Option[Long]] =
  redis.get("counter").returning[Long]
```

Calling `redis.get("counter")` without `returning` does not compile. The compiler reports "Use `returning[A]` to specify method's return type".

Keys, field names and values are all encoded with the `CodecSupplier`, so the same codec must be used to write and to read a value.

### Next Steps

- [Configuration](./reference/configuration.md) explains `RedisConfig`, `RedisUri`, authentication and TLS.
- [Codecs](./concepts/codecs.md) explains how values are encoded.
- [Error Handling](./concepts/error-handling.md) lists every `RedisError`.

---

## How to Cache Values With a Time to Live

This guide shows how to use Redis as a cache that expires entries automatically, and how to load a missing entry on demand. It assumes a `Redis` layer as described in [Getting Started](../getting-started.md).

### Store a Value With an Expiry

To store a value that Redis deletes after one minute, pass an expiry to `Redis#set`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def cachePage(redis: Redis, url: String, html: String): IO[RedisError, Boolean] =
  redis.set(s"page:$url", html, Some(1.minute))
```

The result is `true` when Redis stored the value. `Redis#setEx` is an equivalent command with the key, the expiry and the value as positional arguments.

### Read the Remaining Lifetime

To see how long an entry has left, call `Redis#ttl`. It returns a `Duration`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def remaining(redis: Redis, url: String): IO[RedisError, Duration] =
  redis.ttl(s"page:$url")
```

### Load on a Cache Miss

To return the cached value when it exists and otherwise compute and store it, combine `Redis#get` with `Redis#set`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def cached[E](redis: Redis, key: String, ttl: Duration)(
  load: => IO[E, String]
): IO[Either[RedisError, E], String] =
  redis.get(key).returning[String].mapError(Left(_)).flatMap {
    case Some(hit) => ZIO.succeed(hit)
    case None      =>
      for {
        value <- load.mapError(Right(_))
        _     <- redis.set(key, value, Some(ttl)).mapError(Left(_))
      } yield value
  }
```

Two callers that miss at the same time both run `load`. To prevent that, guard the load with a lock as shown in [How to Build a Distributed Lock](../how-to/distributed-lock.md).

### Invalidate an Entry

To remove an entry before it expires, delete its key with `Redis#del`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def invalidate(redis: Redis, url: String): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.del(s"page:$url")
```

`Redis#del` returns the number of keys that existed.

## How to Connect to a Redis Cluster

This guide shows how to build a `Redis` layer for a Redis Cluster and how to keep related keys on one node. It assumes you know the basics from [Getting Started](../getting-started.md).

### Build the Layer

List a few startup nodes in a `RedisClusterConfig` and provide `Redis.cluster`. The client learns the remaining nodes from the cluster itself:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val redis: ZLayer[Any, RedisError, Redis] =
  ZLayer.make[Redis](
    ZLayer.succeed(
      RedisClusterConfig(Chunk(RedisUri("redis-1.example.com:6379"), RedisUri("redis-2.example.com:6379")))
    ),
    ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8),
    Redis.cluster
  )
```

The layer provides `Redis` only. `AsyncRedis` and `RedisSubscription` have no cluster variant.

### Use Hash Tags for Multi-Key Commands

A command that touches several keys must target one slot, otherwise it fails with `RedisError.CrossSlot`. Redis hashes only the part of a key between `{` and `}`, so keys that share a tag share a slot:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def addToBoth(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  for {
    _     <- redis.sAdd("{user:1}:roles", "admin")
    _     <- redis.sAdd("{user:1}:teams", "core")
    union <- redis.sUnionStore("{user:1}:all", "{user:1}:roles", "{user:1}:teams")
  } yield union
```

### Next Steps

For authentication, TLS nodes, retry settings and limitations, see [Cluster](../concepts/cluster.md).

## How to Connect With TLS and Authentication

This guide shows how to connect to a managed Redis service that requires a password and TLS, reading the settings from environment variables. All fields are described in [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

### Read the Settings From the Environment

Build the `RedisConfig` with `ZLayer.fromZIO`, so the settings are read when the layer is built. A missing host or port falls back to a default, and a missing password or user leaves `auth` unset:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

val config: ZLayer[Any, SecurityException, RedisConfig] =
  ZLayer.fromZIO {
    for {
      host     <- System.envOrElse("REDIS_HOST", "localhost")
      port     <- System.envOrElse("REDIS_PORT", "6379").map(_.toInt)
      password <- System.env("REDIS_PASSWORD")
      username <- System.env("REDIS_USER")
    } yield RedisConfig(
      host = host,
      port = port,
      ssl = true,
      auth = password.map(RedisConfig.Auth(_, username))
    )
  }
```

### Provide the Redis Layer

Wire the config into `Redis.singleNode`. The library authenticates every connection it opens:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def redisLayer(config: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, RedisConfig]): ZLayer[Any, Throwable, Redis] =
  ZLayer.make[Redis](
    config,
    ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8),
    Redis.singleNode
  )
```

### Set the Server Name When Needed

When the server certificate is issued for a different name than the host you connect to, set `sni` to that name. Keep `verifyCertificate = true` in production and turn it off only for local servers with self-signed certificates:

```scala
import zio.redis._

val behindProxy: RedisConfig =
  RedisConfig(host = "10.0.0.5", port = 6380, ssl = true, sni = Some("redis.example.com"))
```

## How to Build a Distributed Lock

This guide builds a lock that several processes can use to take turns on a shared resource. It uses `Redis#set` with the "only if absent" option to acquire the lock and a Lua script to release it safely.

### Acquire the Lock

To take the lock, set a key only when it does not exist yet, and give it an expiry so that a crashed holder cannot block everyone forever. `Update.SetNew` maps to the `NX` option:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def acquire(redis: Redis, name: String, owner: String, ttl: Duration): IO[RedisError, Boolean] =
  redis.set(s"lock:$name", owner, Some(ttl), Some(Update.SetNew))
```

The result is `true` for the one caller that got the lock and `false` for everyone else. The `owner` value must be unique per holder, for example a random UUID.

### Release the Lock

A holder must delete the key only if it is still the owner. If the lock expired and another process took it, a plain `Redis#del` would release the other process's lock. A Lua script performs the check and the delete atomically. `Redis#eval` needs an `Input` instance for the keys and arguments and an `Output` instance for the result, and the library does not provide implicit ones, so we declare an implicit `Input[String]` from `Input.StringInput` and an implicit `Output[Long]` from `Output.LongOutput`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._
import zio.redis.Input._
import zio.redis.Output._

implicit val stringInput: Input[String] = StringInput
implicit val longOutput: Output[Long]   = LongOutput

val releaseScript: String =
  """if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    |  return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
    |else
    |  return 0
    |end""".stripMargin

def release(redis: Redis, name: String, owner: String): IO[RedisError, Boolean] =
  redis
    .eval(releaseScript, Chunk(s"lock:$name"), Chunk(owner))
    .returning[Long]
    .map(_ == 1L)
```

See [Scripting](../reference/commands/scripting.md) for the full set of script commands.

### Run an Effect Under the Lock

To make sure the lock is always released, wrap the protected effect in `ZIO.acquireReleaseWith`. This version returns `None` when the lock is already held:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._
import zio.redis.Input._
import zio.redis.Output._

def withLock[R, A](redis: Redis, name: String, ttl: Duration)(
  effect: ZIO[R, RedisError, A]
): ZIO[R, RedisError, Option[A]] = {
  implicit val stringInput: Input[String] = StringInput
  implicit val longOutput: Output[Long]   = LongOutput

  val release =
    """if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end"""

  ZIO.randomWith(_.nextUUID).flatMap { token =>
    val owner = token.toString
    ZIO.acquireReleaseWith(
      redis.set(s"lock:$name", owner, Some(ttl), Some(Update.SetNew))
    )(acquired =>
      ZIO
        .when(acquired)(redis.eval(release, Chunk(s"lock:$name"), Chunk(owner)).returning[Long])
        .ignore
    ) {
      case true  => effect.map(Some(_))
      case false => ZIO.none
    }
  }
}
```

Choose `ttl` longer than the longest the protected effect can run. A lock that expires early can be held by two processes at once, so this lock suits efficiency use cases such as avoiding duplicate work, not strict correctness guarantees.

---

## How to Pipeline Commands

This guide shows how to send many commands without waiting for each reply, which cuts the cost of network round trips for bulk work. The difference between `Redis` and `AsyncRedis` is explained in [AsyncRedis](../concepts/async-redis.md).

### Get the Async Service

`Redis.local` and `Redis.singleNode` provide `AsyncRedis` next to `Redis`; `Redis.cluster` does not, so pipelining is available on single nodes only. Build the layers as described in [Redis](../reference/redis.md#layers).

### Queue a Batch and Await the Replies

Every `AsyncRedis` command returns an `UIO` whose result is the effect that waits for the reply. Queue all commands first, then await the inner effects together:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def writeAll(redis: AsyncRedis, entries: Chunk[(String, Long)]): IO[RedisError, Unit] =
  for {
    pending <- ZIO.foreach(entries) { case (key, value) => redis.set(key, value) }
    _       <- ZIO.collectAllDiscard(pending)
  } yield ()
```

The first `foreach` puts every command on the wire. The second step waits for the replies, so the batch pays for one round trip rather than one per command.

### Handle Errors

Queuing never fails. A failure of one command shows up when its inner effect is awaited, so call `.either` on each inner effect when one bad command must not hide the other results:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def readAll(redis: AsyncRedis, keys: Chunk[String]): UIO[Chunk[Either[RedisError, Option[Long]]]] =
  for {
    pending <- ZIO.foreach(keys)(key => redis.get(key).returning[Long])
    results <- ZIO.foreach(pending)(_.either)
  } yield results
```

---

## How to Publish and Subscribe to Typed Events

This guide shows how to publish case classes to Redis channels and consume them with a pattern subscription. The plain-string basics, callbacks and unsubscribing are covered in [Pub/Sub](../concepts/pub-sub.md).

### Define the Event and a Codec

Case classes need a structural codec, because `CodecSupplier.utf8` encodes primitives only. The publisher and the subscriber must use the same supplier. This guide uses Protobuf from `zio-schema-protobuf`; see [Codecs](../concepts/codecs.md):

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.schema.codec.{BinaryCodec, ProtobufCodec}

final case class OrderPlaced(orderId: Long, total: Double)

object OrderPlaced {
  implicit val schema: Schema[OrderPlaced] = DeriveSchema.gen[OrderPlaced]
}

object ProtobufSupplier extends CodecSupplier {
  def get[A: Schema]: BinaryCodec[A] = ProtobufCodec.protobufCodec
}
```

### Provide Both Layers

Publishing uses `Redis`; listening uses `RedisSubscription`, which owns its own connection. Both layers are described in [Pub/Sub](../concepts/pub-sub.md):

```scala
val layers: ZLayer[Any, RedisError.IOError, Redis & RedisSubscription] =
  ZLayer.make[Redis & RedisSubscription](
    ZLayer.succeed(RedisConfig.Local),
    ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](ProtobufSupplier),
    Redis.singleNode,
    RedisSubscription.singleNode
  )
```

### Publish an Event

Use one channel per event kind, for example `orders.placed`. `Redis#publish` returns how many clients received the message:

```scala
def placeOrder(redis: Redis, event: OrderPlaced): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.publish("orders.placed", event)
```

### Consume Every Order Event

Subscribe to the pattern `orders.*` to receive events from all order channels. Each element is a pair of the channel the message was published to and the decoded event:

```scala
val consume: ZIO[RedisSubscription, RedisError, Unit] =
  ZIO.serviceWithZIO[RedisSubscription] { subscription =>
    subscription
      .pSubscribe("orders.*")
      .returning[OrderPlaced]
      .foreach { case (channel, event) => ZIO.debug(s"$channel: ${event.orderId}") }
  }
```

Pub/Sub does not store messages. A subscriber that is not connected when an event is published never sees it. When events must not be lost, use [Streams](../reference/commands/streams.md) instead.

---

## How to Test With Embedded Redis

Tests that talk to Redis need a server. The `zio-redis-embedded` module starts a real Redis process for the duration of a test and shuts it down afterwards, so specs run without Docker or a pre-installed server.

### Prerequisites

Add `zio-redis-embedded` to your test dependencies, as shown in [Modules](../index.md#modules).

### Starting the Embedded Server

`EmbeddedRedis.layer` starts a Redis server on a free port and produces a `RedisConfig` for it. See [EmbeddedRedis](../reference/embedded-redis.md#layer) for the type and lifecycle.

### Writing a Spec

The spec below builds a `Redis` service on top of the embedded server and exercises it. The layer is provided with `provideShared`, so one server is started for the whole suite:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._
import zio.redis.embedded.EmbeddedRedis
import zio.test._

object EmbeddedRedisSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec: Spec[Any, Any] =
    suite("EmbeddedRedis")(
      test("stores and reads back a value") {
        for {
          redis <- ZIO.service[Redis]
          _     <- redis.set("greeting", "hello")
          value <- redis.get("greeting").returning[String]
        } yield assertTrue(value.contains("hello"))
      },
      test("counts with incr") {
        for {
          redis <- ZIO.service[Redis]
          one   <- redis.incr("counter")
          two   <- redis.incr("counter")
        } yield assertTrue(one == 1L, two == 2L)
      }
    ).provideShared(
      EmbeddedRedis.layer,
      ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8),
      Redis.singleNode
    ) @@ TestAspect.sequential
}
```

`CodecSupplier.utf8` is enough for primitive values. To store case classes, supply a structural codec instead, as shown in [Codecs](../concepts/codecs.md).

### Keeping Tests Independent

All tests in a suite share one server, so data written by one test is visible to the next. There are two ways to avoid interference:

- Use unique keys per test, for example by prefixing them with a random UUID from `Random.nextUUID`.
- Call `Redis#flushall` at the start of each test, and run the suite with `TestAspect.sequential`.

To clear the database before each test:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._
import zio.redis.embedded.EmbeddedRedis
import zio.test._

object CleanSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec: Spec[Any, Any] =
    (suite("clean database")(
      test("sees only its own key") {
        for {
          redis <- ZIO.service[Redis]
          _     <- redis.set("key", "value")
          keys  <- redis.keys("*").returning[String]
        } yield assertTrue(keys.size == 1)
      }
    ) @@ TestAspect.before(ZIO.serviceWithZIO[Redis](_.flushall(sync = true))) @@ TestAspect.sequential).provideShared(
      EmbeddedRedis.layer,
      ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8),
      Redis.singleNode
    )
}
```

### Testing Pub/Sub

`RedisSubscription.singleNode` accepts the same `RedisConfig`, so the embedded server also works for subscription tests. Provide both layers from one `EmbeddedRedis.layer`, which `provideShared` shares between them. See [Pub/Sub](../concepts/pub-sub.md) for the services.

### Limitations

The embedded server is a single node. Tests of [Cluster](../concepts/cluster.md) behavior need a real cluster, which the library's own integration tests start with Docker Compose. The Redis version is whatever the embedded library ships, so it can differ from your production version.

## Introduction to ZIO Redis

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-redis/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-redis_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-redis_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-redis_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-redis_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-redis_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-redis_2.13) [![ZIO Redis](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-redis?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-redis)

### Introduction

[ZIO Redis](https://github.com/zio/zio-redis) is a ZIO-native Redis client.
It aims to provide a **type-safe** and **performant** API for accessing Redis
instances.

### Installation

ZIO Redis is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3 on the JVM (Java 17 or later). Add it to your `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // ZIO Redis client (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-redis" % "1.3.3"
)
```

Values are encoded and decoded by a `CodecSupplier`. The built-in `CodecSupplier.utf8` handles strings and numbers; to store case classes, add a ZIO Schema codec as described in [Codecs](./concepts/codecs.md).

### Modules

#### Testing

`zio-redis-embedded` starts a real Redis process for the duration of a test, so specs run without Docker or a pre-installed server. Use the same version as `zio-redis`. See [How to Test With Embedded Redis](./how-to/test-with-embedded-redis.md).

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Embedded Redis server for tests (JVM)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-redis-embedded" % "1.3.3" % Test
)
```

### Features

- **Type-safe commands.** Results are decoded to any type with a ZIO Schema `Schema`; see [Codecs](./concepts/codecs.md).
- **All major command groups.** Strings, keys, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, geo, HyperLogLog and scripting; see the [command reference](./reference/commands/strings.md) pages.
- **Pub/Sub.** Subscriptions are exposed as ZIO streams; see [Pub/Sub](./concepts/pub-sub.md).
- **Pipelining.** `AsyncRedis` sends commands without waiting for replies; see [AsyncRedis](./concepts/async-redis.md).
- **Cluster support.** `Redis.cluster` follows slot redirections; see [Cluster](./concepts/cluster.md).
- **Embedded server for tests.** See [How to Test With Embedded Redis](./how-to/test-with-embedded-redis.md).

### Quick Example

To run an effect that uses Redis, provide the `Redis` layer. It needs a `CodecSupplier` and, for a local server, nothing else. See [Getting Started](./getting-started.md) for the details:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

object QuickExample extends ZIOAppDefault {
  val myApp: ZIO[Redis, RedisError, Unit] =
    for {
      redis <- ZIO.service[Redis]
      _     <- redis.set("myKey", 8L, Some(1.minute))
      v     <- redis.get("myKey").returning[Long]
      _     <- ZIO.debug(s"Value of myKey: $v")
      _     <- redis.hSet("myHash", ("k1", 6), ("k2", 2))
      _     <- redis.rPush("myList", 1, 2, 3, 4)
      _     <- redis.sAdd("mySet", "a", "b", "a", "c")
    } yield ()

  def run =
    myApp.provide(Redis.local, ZLayer.succeed[CodecSupplier](CodecSupplier.utf8))
}
```

## Connection

Connection commands act on the connection that the `Redis` service uses, rather than on data. This page covers the six commands on `Redis` for authenticating, selecting a database, naming the connection and checking that the server is alive.

### Authentication

`Redis#auth` authenticates the connection. With one argument it sends a password, and with two it sends a username and password for the Redis ACL system. Both return `Unit` on success and fail with a `RedisError` when the credentials are wrong:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def login(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Unit] =
  redis.auth("app-user", "secret")
```

Most programs do not call `Redis#auth` themselves. When a `RedisConfig` has credentials, the library authenticates every connection it opens, including after a reconnect. See [Configuration](../configuration.md) for how to set them.

### Choosing a Database

`Redis#select` switches the connection to the database with the given zero-based index. New connections start on database `0`. The selected database belongs to the connection, so it is lost if the connection is replaced after a failure:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def useDatabaseOne(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Unit] =
  redis.select(1L)
```

### Naming the Connection

A connection name makes the connection easy to find in `CLIENT LIST` output on the server. The following table lists the related commands:

| Command               | Returns          | Purpose                                              |
| --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Redis#clientSetName` | `Unit`           | Assigns a name to the connection                     |
| `Redis#clientGetName` | `Option[String]` | Returns the name, or `None` if none was set          |
| `Redis#clientId`      | `Long`           | Returns the connection ID, which never repeats       |

The ID increases with each new connection, so a larger ID means a later connection. The following example names the connection and reads both values back:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def describe(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, (Option[String], Long)] =
  for {
    _    <- redis.clientSetName("billing-service")
    name <- redis.clientGetName
    id   <- redis.clientId
  } yield (name, id)
```

### Checking the Server

`Redis#ping` returns `"PONG"` when called without a message, and echoes the message back when given one. The parameter has a default of `None`, so `redis.ping()` needs the parentheses:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def healthCheck(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Boolean] =
  redis.ping().map(_ == "PONG")

def echo(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, String] =
  redis.ping(Some("hello"))
```

### Option Types

The only type in `options/Connection.scala` is `Address`, a case class with an `ip: InetAddress` and a `port: Int`. No command in this group takes or returns it, so application code does not use it.

### Related Pages

- [Configuration](../configuration.md) explains credentials, TLS and the connection settings.
- [Error Handling](../../concepts/error-handling.md) lists the errors raised, such as authentication failures.
- [Keys](./keys.md) covers commands that act on data in the selected database.

## Geo

The geo commands store longitude and latitude pairs in a sorted set and answer distance and radius queries over them. This page documents the eight geo commands and the option types they accept.

All commands are methods on the `Redis` service. Keys and members are encoded with the configured [`CodecSupplier`](../../concepts/codecs.md). See [Getting Started](../../getting-started.md) for how to build the layer.

### Commands

The commands are grouped below by purpose:

| Group     | Method                         | Redis Command                   | Result                |
| --------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Add       | `Redis#geoAdd`                 | `GEOADD`                        | `Long`                |
| Inspect   | `Redis#geoDist`                | `GEODIST`                       | `Option[Double]`      |
| Inspect   | `Redis#geoHash`                | `GEOHASH`                       | `Chunk[Option[String]]` |
| Inspect   | `Redis#geoPos`                 | `GEOPOS`                        | `Chunk[Option[LongLat]]` |
| Search    | `Redis#geoRadius`              | `GEOSEARCH` (`FROMLONLAT`)      | `Chunk[GeoView]`      |
| Search    | `Redis#geoRadiusByMember`      | `GEOSEARCH` (`FROMMEMBER`)      | `Chunk[GeoView]`      |
| Store     | `Redis#geoRadiusStore`         | `GEOSEARCHSTORE` (`FROMLONLAT`) | `Long`                |
| Store     | `Redis#geoRadiusByMemberStore` | `GEOSEARCHSTORE` (`FROMMEMBER`) | `Long`                |

The search commands are sent as `GEOSEARCH` and `GEOSEARCHSTORE`, so they require Redis 6.2 or later. None of the commands uses `returning`, because the member name is always read back as a `String`.

### Option Types

The following types are available after `import zio.redis._`:

| Type                  | Shape                                                                          | Used by                                  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| `LongLat`             | `LongLat(longitude: Double, latitude: Double)`                                 | `geoAdd`, `geoPos`, `geoRadius` and more |
| `RadiusUnit`          | `Meters`, `Kilometers`, `Feet` or `Miles`                                      | `geoDist` and every radius command       |
| `WithCoord`           | Singleton `WithCoord`, adds the position to each result                        | `geoRadius`, `geoRadiusByMember`         |
| `WithDist`            | Singleton `WithDist`, adds the distance from the center to each result         | `geoRadius`, `geoRadiusByMember`         |
| `WithHash`            | Singleton `WithHash`, adds the raw geohash integer to each result              | `geoRadius`, `geoRadiusByMember`         |
| `Count`               | `Count(count: Long)`                                                           | Radius commands                          |
| `Order`               | `Order.Ascending` or `Order.Descending`                                        | Radius commands                          |
| `Store`               | `Store(key: String)`, the destination key                                      | `StoreResults`, `StoreBoth`              |
| `StoreDist`           | `StoreDist(key: String)`                                                       | `StoreDistances`, `StoreBoth`            |
| `StoreOptions`        | `StoreResults`, `StoreDistances` or `StoreBoth`                                | `geoRadiusStore`, `geoRadiusByMemberStore` |
| `GeoView`             | `GeoView(member, dist, hash, longLat)` where the last three are `Option`s      | Result of the search commands            |

A `GeoView` only has the optional fields that were requested with `WithDist`, `WithHash` and `WithCoord`. The others are `None`.

### Adding Members

`Redis#geoAdd` takes a key and at least one pair of a `LongLat` and a member. It returns the number of new members added. The `LongLat` is built with the longitude first, then the latitude:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def addCities(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.geoAdd(
    "cities",
    (LongLat(13.361389, 38.115556), "Palermo"),
    (LongLat(15.087269, 37.502669), "Catania")
  )
```

### Inspecting Members

`Redis#geoDist` returns the distance between two members, or `None` if either one is missing. The unit defaults to meters when `radiusUnit` is `None`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def distance(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Option[Double]] =
  redis.geoDist("cities", "Palermo", "Catania", Some(RadiusUnit.Kilometers))
```

`Redis#geoPos` and `Redis#geoHash` return one entry per requested member, with `None` for members that do not exist:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def positions(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, (Chunk[Option[LongLat]], Chunk[Option[String]])] =
  for {
    pos    <- redis.geoPos("cities", "Palermo", "Catania")
    hashes <- redis.geoHash("cities", "Palermo", "Catania")
  } yield (pos, hashes)
```

### Searching by Radius

`Redis#geoRadius` finds members within a radius of a coordinate, and `Redis#geoRadiusByMember` does the same around an existing member. Both accept the optional `withCoord`, `withDist`, `withHash`, `count` and `order` parameters, and return a `Chunk[GeoView]`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def nearby(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Chunk[GeoView]] =
  redis.geoRadius(
    "cities",
    LongLat(15.0, 37.0),
    200.0,
    RadiusUnit.Kilometers,
    withDist = Some(WithDist),
    count = Some(Count(5)),
    order = Some(Order.Ascending)
  )
```

To search around a member that is already in the key, pass the member instead of a coordinate. Here the position is also returned:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def aroundPalermo(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Chunk[(String, Option[LongLat])]] =
  redis
    .geoRadiusByMember("cities", "Palermo", 200.0, RadiusUnit.Kilometers, withCoord = Some(WithCoord))
    .map(_.map(view => (view.member, view.longLat)))
```

### Storing Search Results

`Redis#geoRadiusStore` and `Redis#geoRadiusByMemberStore` write the matches into another key and return how many members were stored. They take a `StoreOptions` value instead of the `with*` flags. Use `StoreResults` to store the matching members:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def storeNearby(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.geoRadiusStore(
    "cities",
    LongLat(15.0, 37.0),
    200.0,
    RadiusUnit.Kilometers,
    StoreResults(Store("cities:nearby")),
    count = Some(Count(10))
  )
```

The `StoreDistances` variant stores the distances in a second key with `STOREDIST`, and `StoreBoth` stores the members and the distances in two keys. To store both, pass a `Store` and a `StoreDist`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def storeNearbyWithDistances(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.geoRadiusStore(
    "cities",
    LongLat(15.0, 37.0),
    200.0,
    RadiusUnit.Kilometers,
    StoreBoth(Store("cities:nearby"), StoreDist("cities:distances")),
    count = Some(Count(10))
  )
```

### Next Steps

- [Sorted Sets](./sorted-sets.md) explains the structure that geo members are stored in, so commands such as `Redis#zRem` and `Redis#zCard` work on geo keys.
- [Keys](./keys.md) covers expiry and deletion.

## Hashes

A Redis hash maps field names to values under a single key, which makes it a good fit for objects and counters grouped by an owner. This page lists every hash command on `Redis` and shows how to call it.

Keys, fields and values are encoded with the configured [`CodecSupplier`](../../concepts/codecs.md). Commands that return user data end with `returning[A]`, as described in [Getting Started](../../getting-started.md).

### Command Overview

| Purpose              | Commands                                                       |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Write fields         | `Redis#hSet`, `Redis#hSetNx`                                   |
| Read fields          | `Redis#hGet`, `Redis#hmGet`, `Redis#hGetAll`                   |
| Inspect a hash       | `Redis#hExists`, `Redis#hLen`, `Redis#hStrLen`                 |
| List names or values | `Redis#hKeys`, `Redis#hVals`                                   |
| Remove fields        | `Redis#hDel`                                                   |
| Update numbers       | `Redis#hIncrBy`, `Redis#hIncrByFloat`                          |
| Sample and iterate   | `Redis#hRandField`, `Redis#hScan`                              |

### Writing Fields

`Redis#hSet` takes one or more `(field, value)` pairs and returns the number of fields that were added. `Redis#hSetNx` sets a single field only when it does not exist yet and returns `true` if it wrote the value:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def writeUser(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Boolean] =
  for {
    _     <- redis.hSet("user:1", "name" -> "Ada", "city" -> "London")
    added <- redis.hSetNx("user:1", "name", "Grace")
  } yield added
```

Here `added` is `false` because `name` already exists.

### Reading Fields

`Redis#hGet` returns an `Option` for one field, and `Redis#hmGet` returns a `Chunk[Option[V]]` with one entry per requested field, in order. `Redis#hGetAll` returns every pair as a `Map`, so `returning` takes two type parameters, the field type and the value type:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def readUser(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Map[String, String]] =
  for {
    name  <- redis.hGet("user:1", "name").returning[String]
    some  <- redis.hmGet("user:1", "name", "email").returning[String]
    all   <- redis.hGetAll("user:1").returning[String, String]
    _     <- ZIO.debug(s"name = $name, requested = $some")
  } yield all
```

### Inspecting a Hash

These commands answer questions about a hash without returning its data:

| Method                       | Returns   | Meaning                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Redis#hExists(key, field)`  | `Boolean` | Whether the field exists                                 |
| `Redis#hLen(key)`            | `Long`    | Number of fields                                         |
| `Redis#hStrLen(key, field)`  | `Long`    | String length of the value, or zero if field or key is missing |

To list the names or the values of a hash, use `Redis#hKeys` and `Redis#hVals`. Both return a `Chunk`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def describe(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, (Chunk[String], Chunk[String])] =
  for {
    names  <- redis.hKeys("user:1").returning[String]
    values <- redis.hVals("user:1").returning[String]
  } yield (names, values)
```

### Removing Fields

`Redis#hDel` removes one or more fields and returns how many were actually removed:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def dropFields(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  redis.hDel("user:1", "city", "email")
```

### Updating Numbers

`Redis#hIncrBy` adds a `Long` and `Redis#hIncrByFloat` adds a `Double` to a field. A missing field starts from zero, and the command returns the new value. Redis returns an error if the field holds a value of the wrong kind:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def countVisit(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, (Long, Double)] =
  for {
    visits <- redis.hIncrBy("stats", "visits", 1L)
    score  <- redis.hIncrByFloat("stats", "score", 0.5)
  } yield (visits, score)
```

### Sampling Random Fields

`Redis#hRandField` has two overloads. The first returns one random field as an `Option`. The second takes a `count` and a `withValues` flag and returns a `Chunk`:

| Overload                                          | Result type    |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| `hRandField(key)`                                 | `Option[V]`    |
| `hRandField(key, count, withValues = false)`      | `Chunk[V]`     |

A positive `count` returns at most that many distinct fields. A negative `count` returns exactly `abs(count)` fields and may repeat them. When `withValues` is `true`, fields and values are interleaved in the returned chunk, so both must decode to the same type `V`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def sample(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, (Option[String], Chunk[String])] =
  for {
    one  <- redis.hRandField("user:1").returning[String]
    many <- redis.hRandField("user:1", 2L, withValues = true).returning[String]
  } yield (one, many)
```

### Scanning

`Redis#hScan` iterates a hash with a cursor. Start with cursor `0` and pass the returned cursor into the next call until Redis returns `0` again. The optional `pattern` filters fields with a glob-style pattern, and `count` is a hint of type `Count` for how many entries to examine per call:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def scanAll(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Chunk[(String, String)]] = {
  def loop(cursor: Long, acc: Chunk[(String, String)]): IO[RedisError, Chunk[(String, String)]] =
    redis.hScan("user:1", cursor, Some("n*"), Some(Count(100L))).returning[String, String].flatMap {
      case (0L, items)   => ZIO.succeed(acc ++ items)
      case (next, items) => loop(next, acc ++ items)
    }

  loop(0L, Chunk.empty)
}
```

### Next Steps

- [Strings](./strings.md) covers plain values and counters.
- [Keys](./keys.md) covers expiry and deletion of the whole hash.
- [Sets](./sets.md) covers unordered collections of unique members.

## HyperLogLog

A HyperLogLog is a probabilistic structure that estimates how many distinct elements it has seen, using a small and fixed amount of memory. This page documents the three commands that ZIO Redis exposes for it.

All commands are methods on the `Redis` service. Keys and elements are encoded with the configured [`CodecSupplier`](../../concepts/codecs.md), so any type with a ZIO Schema `Schema` can be used for both. See [Getting Started](../../getting-started.md) for how to build the layer.

### Commands

The commands are grouped below by purpose:

| Method           | Redis Command | Result            | Purpose                                              |
| ---------------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Redis#pfAdd`    | `PFADD`       | `Boolean`         | Adds elements to a HyperLogLog                       |
| `Redis#pfCount`  | `PFCOUNT`     | `Long`            | Estimates the number of distinct elements            |
| `Redis#pfMerge`  | `PFMERGE`     | `Unit`            | Merges several HyperLogLogs into a destination key   |

None of these commands needs `returning`, because their results do not depend on a user type.

### Adding Elements

`Redis#pfAdd` takes a key and at least one element. It returns `true` if the internal registers of the HyperLogLog changed, and `false` otherwise:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def trackVisitors(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Boolean] =
  redis.pfAdd("visitors:today", "alice", "bob", "carol")
```

Adding an element that was already counted usually leaves the registers unchanged, so the result is `false` in that case.

### Counting Elements

`Redis#pfCount` returns the approximate number of distinct elements added to the key. When more than one key is given, it returns the approximate size of the union of all of them:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def countVisitors(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, (Long, Long)] =
  for {
    today <- redis.pfCount("visitors:today")
    both  <- redis.pfCount("visitors:today", "visitors:yesterday")
  } yield (today, both)
```

A key that does not exist counts as an empty HyperLogLog.

### Merging HyperLogLogs

`Redis#pfMerge` takes a destination key followed by at least one source key. It stores the union of the sources in the destination, and the sources are left untouched:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.redis._

def mergeVisitors(redis: Redis): IO[RedisError, Long] =
  for {
    _     <- redis.pfMerge("visitors:week", "visitors:today", "visitors:yesterday")
    count <- redis.pfCount("visitors:week")
  } yield count
```

### Next Steps

- [Sets](./sets.md) store exact members when an approximation is not acceptable.
- [Keys](./keys.md) covers expiry and deletion, which also apply to HyperLogLog keys.
