## Tutorial: Building a User Store

In this tutorial we build a small store that keeps users and their credit balances in RocksDB. We start with the data type and its encoding, then open a database with a column family, add and read users, move credits between two users atomically, and finally list all users. Each step builds on the previous one, and the last section assembles the application.

We assume that you have read [Getting Started](./getting-started.md).

### Step 1: Model the Data

A user has a name and a number of credits:

```scala
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8
import java.nio.file.Files
import org.rocksdb.{ ColumnFamilyDescriptor, ColumnFamilyHandle, Options }
import zio._
import zio.rocksdb._
import zio.stream.ZStream

case class User(name: String, credits: Long)
```

RocksDB stores bytes, so we need a `Serde[Any, User]`. The encoder writes the name with a length prefix, followed by the credits. The decoder reads them back in the same order. [Serialization](./serialization.md) explains each combinator:

```scala
val nameSerializer: Serializer[Any, String] =
  Serializer[Any, String] { s =>
    for {
      body   <- Serializer.string(s)
      length <- Serializer.int(body.length)
    } yield length ++ body
  }

val nameDeserializer: Deserializer[Any, String] =
  Deserializer.int.flatMap { length =>
    Deserializer[Any, Bytes] { bytes =>
      val (head, tail) = bytes.splitAt(length)
      if (head.length < length) ZIO.fail(DeserializeError.TooShort(bytes.length, length))
      else ZIO.succeed(Result(head, tail))
    }.map(body => new String(body.toArray, UTF_8))
  }

val userSerde: Serde[Any, User] =
  Serde(
    nameSerializer.divide(Serializer.long).contramap(u => (u.name, u.credits)),
    nameDeserializer.zip(Deserializer.long).map { case (name, credits) => User(name, credits) }
  )

val idSerde: Serde[Any, Long] = Serde(Serializer.long, Deserializer.long)
```

Two small helpers convert between a typed value and the `Array[Byte]` that the database expects. A decoding failure becomes a `Throwable`, so that it fits the `Task` of the database operations:

```scala
def encode[A](serde: Serde[Any, A], value: A): UIO[Array[Byte]] =
  serde(value).map(_.toArray)

def decode[A](serde: Serde[Any, A], bytes: Array[Byte]): Task[A] =
  serde.decode(Chunk.fromArray(bytes)).mapBoth(error => new RuntimeException(error.message), _.value)
```

### Step 2: Open the Database

Credit transfers need a transaction, so we open a `TransactionDB`. It extends `RocksDB`, so everything we do with a plain database works on it too. Each run gets a fresh temporary directory, which keeps the tutorial repeatable:

```scala
val database: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, TransactionDB] =
  ZLayer.scoped {
    for {
      path <- ZIO.attempt(Files.createTempDirectory("zio-rocksdb-tutorial").toString)
      db   <- TransactionDB.Live.open(new Options().setCreateIfMissing(true), path)
    } yield db
  }
```

We keep the users in their own column family, so that other data can share the database without key collisions. Creating the family returns its handle, which every later call receives:

```scala
val usersFamily: ZIO[TransactionDB, Throwable, ColumnFamilyHandle] =
  TransactionDB.createColumnFamily(new ColumnFamilyDescriptor("users".getBytes(UTF_8)))
```

### Step 3: Add and Read Users

Both functions encode the id and the user, then call the per-family overloads of `TransactionDB.put` and `TransactionDB.get`:

```scala
def addUser(users: ColumnFamilyHandle, id: Long, user: User): ZIO[TransactionDB, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    key   <- encode(idSerde, id)
    value <- encode(userSerde, user)
    _     <- TransactionDB.put(users, key, value)
  } yield ()

def findUser(users: ColumnFamilyHandle, id: Long): ZIO[TransactionDB, Throwable, Option[User]] =
  for {
    key   <- encode(idSerde, id)
    found <- TransactionDB.get(users, key)
    user  <- ZIO.foreach(found)(decode(userSerde, _))
  } yield user
```

### Step 4: Transfer Credits Atomically

Moving credits changes two keys, and a failure in between must not lose credits. `TransactionDB.atomically` runs the whole function in one transaction. `Transaction.getForUpdate` locks each user until the transaction ends, so two concurrent transfers cannot overwrite each other. If the sender has too few credits, the function fails and nothing is written:

```scala
def loadForUpdate(users: ColumnFamilyHandle, id: Long): ZIO[Transaction, Throwable, User] =
  for {
    key   <- encode(idSerde, id)
    found <- Transaction.getForUpdate(users, key, exclusive = true)
    bytes <- ZIO.fromOption(found).orElseFail(new NoSuchElementException(s"no user with id $id"))
    user  <- decode(userSerde, bytes)
  } yield user

def save(users: ColumnFamilyHandle, id: Long, user: User): ZIO[Transaction, Throwable, Unit] =
  for {
    key   <- encode(idSerde, id)
    value <- encode(userSerde, user)
    _     <- Transaction.put(users, key, value)
  } yield ()

def transfer(users: ColumnFamilyHandle, from: Long, to: Long, credits: Long): ZIO[TransactionDB, Throwable, Unit] =
  TransactionDB.atomically[Throwable, Unit] {
    for {
      sender   <- loadForUpdate(users, from)
      receiver <- loadForUpdate(users, to)
      _        <- ZIO.fail(new IllegalStateException("not enough credits")).when(sender.credits < credits)
      _        <- save(users, from, sender.copy(credits = sender.credits - credits))
      _        <- save(users, to, receiver.copy(credits = receiver.credits + credits))
    } yield ()
  }
```

See [Transactions](./transactions.md) for the locking rules and [How to Retry on a Lock Timeout](./how-to-retry-on-lock-timeout.md) for conflicts under load.

### Step 5: List All Users

`TransactionDB.newIterator` with a handle scans one column family as a stream. We decode every key and value as they arrive:

```scala
def allUsers(users: ColumnFamilyHandle): ZStream[TransactionDB, Throwable, (Long, User)] =
  TransactionDB.newIterator(users).mapZIO { case (key, value) =>
    decode(idSerde, key).zip(decode(userSerde, value))
  }
```

Keys are non-negative big-endian `Long` values here, so the scan returns the users in id order.

### The Complete Application

To assemble the steps into a runnable application, we create the family, add two users, transfer credits and print every user:

```scala
object UserStore extends ZIOAppDefault {
  val program: ZIO[TransactionDB, Throwable, Unit] =
    for {
      users <- usersFamily
      _     <- addUser(users, 1L, User("Ada", 100L))
      _     <- addUser(users, 2L, User("Grace", 50L))
      _     <- transfer(users, from = 1L, to = 2L, credits = 30L)
      _     <- allUsers(users).runForeach(Console.printLine(_))
    } yield ()

  def run = program.provide(database)
}
```

Running it prints `(1,User(Ada,70))` and `(2,User(Grace,80))`.

### Where to Go Next

- [How to Scan a Prefix](./how-to-scan-a-prefix.md) shows how to read only the entries whose key starts with a given prefix.
- [How to Test with a Temporary Database](./how-to-test-with-a-temporary-database.md) shows how to run tests against a real database in a temporary directory.
- The [reference pages](./reference-rocksdb.md) list every operation used here.

## Write Batches

A `WriteBatch` collects several writes and hands them to RocksDB in one call, so that they are applied atomically: after a crash, either all of them are visible or none are. In this guide we build a batch, write it to the database, and then look at the `RocksDB#flush` and `RocksDB#flushWal` operations that control when data reaches disk.

A batch is lighter than a [transaction](./transactions.md): it takes no locks and cannot read, so it fits writes whose values are already known. When a write depends on a value read earlier, use a transaction instead.

### The Problem

With plain `RocksDB.put`, every key is written separately. An application that stores a record under two keys, such as a user and an index entry that points to the user, has a window between the two calls in which a crash leaves a user without an index entry or an index entry without a user. Each `RocksDB.put` call is atomic on its own, but the pair is not.

### Writing a Batch

`WriteBatch.open` creates a batch inside a `Scope`, and the native batch is released when the scope ends. `WriteBatch#put` adds a key-value pair to the batch without touching the database. `RocksDB#write` applies the whole batch with the given `WriteOptions`. The `RocksDB` companion object has no accessor for `write`, so the call goes through the service:

```scala
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8
import org.rocksdb.WriteOptions
import zio._
import zio.rocksdb.{ RocksDB, WriteBatch }

val storeUser: ZIO[RocksDB, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      batch <- WriteBatch.open
      _     <- batch.put("user:42".getBytes(UTF_8), "Ada".getBytes(UTF_8))
      _     <- batch.put("index:name:Ada".getBytes(UTF_8), "42".getBytes(UTF_8))
      _     <- ZIO.serviceWithZIO[RocksDB](_.write(new WriteOptions(), batch))
    } yield ()
  }
```

After the call, both keys are readable, and a crash during the write cannot leave only one of them.

`WriteBatch.open(reservedBytes)` reserves buffer space up front for large batches, and `WriteBatch.open(serialized)` rebuilds a batch from the bytes of an earlier one.

### Writing to a Column Family

Each key can go to a different column family: `WriteBatch#put(cfHandle, key, value)` takes a `ColumnFamilyHandle` as its first argument, so a single batch can span families:

```scala
import org.rocksdb.{ ColumnFamilyHandle, WriteOptions }
import zio._
import zio.rocksdb.{ RocksDB, WriteBatch }

def storeInBoth(first: ColumnFamilyHandle, second: ColumnFamilyHandle): ZIO[RocksDB, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.scoped {
    for {
      batch <- WriteBatch.open
      _     <- batch.put(first, "k".getBytes("UTF-8"), "1".getBytes("UTF-8"))
      _     <- batch.put(second, "k".getBytes("UTF-8"), "2".getBytes("UTF-8"))
      _     <- ZIO.serviceWithZIO[RocksDB](_.write(new WriteOptions(), batch))
    } yield ()
  }
```

:::note
`WriteBatch` currently exposes only `WriteBatch#put`. To delete keys atomically together with writes, use a [transaction](./transactions.md).
:::

### Controlling Durability

RocksDB first buffers writes in memory and in a write-ahead log (WAL). `RocksDB#flush` writes the in-memory tables to disk, and `RocksDB#flushWal` moves the buffered write-ahead log to its file, syncing it when `sync` is `true`. Neither has a companion accessor, so call them on the service:

```scala
import org.rocksdb.FlushOptions
import zio._
import zio.rocksdb.RocksDB

val persist: ZIO[RocksDB, Throwable, Unit] =
  ZIO.serviceWithZIO[RocksDB] { db =>
    db.flush(new FlushOptions().setWaitForFlush(true)) *> db.flushWal(sync = true)
  }
```

`RocksDB#flush` also has variants that take one `ColumnFamilyHandle` or a list of them. To make a single write durable without a flush, pass `WriteOptions` with `setSync(true)` to `RocksDB#write` or to the transaction functions.

## Connect to MinIO or Another S3-Compatible Store

ZIO S3 works with any server that speaks the S3 API, such as MinIO for local development, or a hosted provider that is not AWS. To connect to such a server, pass its address as the endpoint when you build the layer. The endpoint overrides the AWS address that the client would otherwise use.

### Connect to MinIO

To connect to a local MinIO server, pass the server address as `uriEndpoint` and set `forcePathStyle` to `Some(true)`. MinIO expects the bucket name in the path, not in the host name:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

import java.net.URI

val minio: Layer[S3Exception, S3] =
  live(
    Region.US_EAST_1,
    AwsBasicCredentials.create("TESTKEY", "TESTSECRET"),
    Some(URI.create("http://localhost:9000")),
    forcePathStyle = Some(true)
  )
```

The repository's `docker-compose.yml` starts a MinIO server on port 9000 with the credentials `TESTKEY` and `TESTSECRET`, and it creates a bucket named `bucket-1`. Any region works with MinIO, so `Region.US_EAST_1` is a valid choice.

### Connect to Another Provider

To connect to a hosted S3-compatible service, pass its HTTPS address as `uriEndpoint`. Use a region that the provider documents for signing requests, and set `forcePathStyle` only if the provider requires path-style addressing:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

import java.net.URI

val provider: Layer[S3Exception, S3] =
  live(
    Region.EU_CENTRAL_1,
    AwsBasicCredentials.create("access-key", "secret-key"),
    Some(URI.create("https://s3.provider.example.com")),
    forcePathStyle = None
  )
```

The address `s3.provider.example.com` is a placeholder. Use the endpoint from your provider's documentation.

### Know the Region Limits

The `live` and `liveZIO` functions accept only regions from the AWS SDK's list, such as `Region.US_EAST_1`. A region name that the SDK does not know makes the layer fail with `InvalidSettings`, so pick the closest SDK region for the provider's signing name. The `live` layer built from `S3Settings` has no endpoint parameter, so it cannot connect to a custom endpoint. Use `live` or `liveZIO` with an endpoint instead, or the next section when the region name is not in the SDK's list.

### Use a Region the AWS SDK Does Not Know

To connect to a provider whose region name is not in the AWS SDK's list, build the region with `S3Region.unsafeFromString`, which skips the check, and connect with `Live.connect`, which takes the region, a credentials provider and the endpoint:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.s3._

import java.net.URI

val custom: ZLayer[Any, Throwable, S3] =
  ZLayer.scoped(
    Live.connect[Any](
      S3Region.unsafeFromString("custom-region-1"),
      providers.basic("access-key", "secret-key"),
      Some(URI.create("https://s3.provider.example.com")),
      forcePathStyle = Some(true)
    )
  )
```

The name is not checked, so a wrong region name fails later, when the client makes its first request.

### Verify the Connection

To check that the endpoint answers, list the buckets with the layer you built. A wrong address fails the effect with `SdkError`, wrong credentials fail it with an `S3Exception` from the server, and a credentials provider or client that cannot be built fails it with `ConnectionError`, as described in the [errors reference](./errors.md):

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

import java.net.URI

val check: ZIO[Any, S3Exception, Unit] =
  listBuckets
    .provideLayer(
      live(
        Region.US_EAST_1,
        AwsBasicCredentials.create("TESTKEY", "TESTSECRET"),
        Some(URI.create("http://localhost:9000")),
        forcePathStyle = Some(true)
      )
    )
    .unit
```

---

## Configure Credentials and Region(Zio-s3)

ZIO S3 builds its S3 client from a region and an AWS credentials source. The `live` and `liveZIO` functions take the region as a `software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region`, and the credentials either as a value or as a provider. This page shows how to choose each source, and the [settings reference](./settings.md) lists every parameter.

### Use Static Credentials

To pass an access key and secret key directly, use `live` with `AwsBasicCredentials`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

val s3Layer: Layer[S3Exception, S3] =
  live(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, AwsBasicCredentials.create("key", "secret"))
```

For temporary credentials, such as those issued by AWS STS, use `AwsSessionCredentials` in place of `AwsBasicCredentials`, or the `providers.session` provider.

### Use a Credentials Provider

To resolve credentials lazily, pass a provider from `zio.s3.providers` to `liveZIO`. Each provider is an effect that builds an AWS `AwsCredentialsProvider`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.s3.providers._

// environment variables
val fromEnv: ZLayer[Any, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, env)

// Java system properties
val fromSystem: ZLayer[Any, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, system)

// the EC2 instance profile
val fromInstance: ZLayer[Scope, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, instanceProfile)

// web identity token, used by workloads such as EKS service accounts
val fromWebIdentity: ZLayer[Scope, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, webIdentity)

// the AWS SDK default chain, which tries several sources in order
val fromDefaultChain: ZLayer[Scope, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, default)
```

The providers `env` and `system` need no scope, so their layers have type `ZLayer[Any, S3Exception, S3]`. The providers `instanceProfile`, `webIdentity`, `default`, `profile`, and `container` need a `Scope`, because they hold resources that the scope closes.

To pass a fixed key pair through a provider, use `providers.basic`, or `providers.session` for temporary credentials. These need no scope:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.s3.providers._

val fromKeys: ZLayer[Any, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, basic("key", "secret"))

val fromTemporaryKeys: ZLayer[Any, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, session("key", "secret", "token"))
```

To read the credentials that Amazon ECS or EKS inject into a container, use `container`. It needs a `Scope`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.s3.providers._

val fromContainer: ZLayer[Scope, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, container)
```

To read a named profile from `~/.aws/credentials`, use `profile` with `Some(name)`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.s3.providers._

val fromProfile: ZLayer[Scope, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, profile(Some("dev")))
```

### Use Custom Credential Logic

To fetch credentials from your own source, such as a secret store, build an effect that returns `AwsCredentials`, pass it to `settings`, and feed the result into the `live` layer that takes `S3Settings`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.{ AwsBasicCredentials, AwsCredentials }
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

// replace with a call to your secret store
val fetchCredentials: ZIO[Any, S3Exception, AwsCredentials] =
  ZIO.succeed(AwsBasicCredentials.create("key", "secret"))

val s3Layer: ZLayer[Any, S3Exception, S3] =
  settings(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, fetchCredentials) >>> live
```

### Handle Credential Failures

When a provider cannot resolve credentials, building the layer fails. The provider in `zio.s3.providers` reports `InvalidCredentials`, but `Live.connect` wraps that failure in `ConnectionError` when it builds the client, so the layer's error is `ConnectionError`, which extends `S3Exception`. Handle it where you build the layer:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.s3.errors.ConnectionError
import zio.s3.providers._

val s3Layer: ZLayer[Scope, S3Exception, S3] =
  liveZIO(Region.AF_SOUTH_1, instanceProfile)

val checked: ZIO[Scope, S3Exception, Boolean] =
  s3Layer.build.as(true).catchSome { case _: ConnectionError => ZIO.succeed(false) }
```

See the [errors reference](./errors.md) for the full error hierarchy.

### Choose the Region

Every layer takes a `Region` from `software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region`, such as `Region.CA_CENTRAL_1`. For S3-compatible storage that uses a region name the AWS SDK does not know, see [S3-compatible endpoints](./connect-to-an-s3-compatible-store.md).

---

## Download an Object

`getObject` returns the bytes of an object as a `Stream`, so a large object is never loaded into memory at once. This page shows how to write an object to a local file, how to read it as text, and how to read it line by line. The [operations reference](./s3-operations.md#object-operations) lists the signatures.

### Save an Object to a File

To write an object to a local file, run the byte stream into a file sink. The sink creates the file and closes it when the stream ends:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZSink

import java.nio.file.Paths

val save: ZIO[S3, Throwable, Long] =
  getObject("bucket-1", "upload/myfile.zip")
    .run(ZSink.fromPath(Paths.get("/my/path/to/download.zip")))
```

The effect returns the number of bytes written. When the key does not exist, `getObject` fails with an `S3Exception`, and the [handle errors how-to](./handle-errors.md) shows how to recover.

### Read an Object as Text

To read a small text object into a `String`, decode the bytes as UTF-8 and collect the chunks:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZPipeline

val text: ZIO[S3, Throwable, String] =
  getObject("bucket-1", "notes.txt")
    .via(ZPipeline.utf8Decode)
    .runCollect
    .map(_.mkString)
```

### Read an Object Line by Line

To process a large text object one line at a time, use `streamLines`. It decodes the bytes as UTF-8 and splits them into lines, so only the current line is held in memory:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

val firstTen: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Chunk[String]] =
  streamLines("bucket-1", "logs/app.log").take(10).runCollect
```

When the object is not valid UTF-8, `streamLines` fails with `DecodingException`. For binary objects, use `getObject` and process the bytes directly.

---

## Errors(Zio-s3)

Most ZIO S3 operations fail with `S3Exception`, the error type of the AWS S3 Java client. ZIO S3 adds its own subtypes of `S3Exception` for the failures that it detects itself, and it passes through the subtypes that the AWS SDK raises for S3 responses, such as `NoSuchKeyException`. This page lists each type and when the library raises it.

### Error Types

Each type below extends `S3Exception`, so a handler for `S3Exception` catches all of them:

- `InvalidCredentials(message: String)` is raised by the providers in `zio.s3.providers` when the AWS SDK cannot resolve credentials from that source.
- `InvalidSettings(message: String)` is raised when `S3Region.from` or `S3Settings.from` receives a region that the AWS SDK does not know.
- `ConnectionError(message: String, cause: Throwable)` is raised when the client cannot be built. Building the client wraps a failed credentials provider in this error, so a layer built from a provider fails with `ConnectionError`.
- `DecodingException(cause: CharacterCodingException)` is raised by `streamLines` when the object is not valid UTF-8.
- `SdkError(error: SdkException)` is raised by `execute` when the AWS SDK fails without an S3 response, such as a network error.
- `InvalidPartSize(message: String, size: Int)` is defined in the library, but no code path raises it today. An invalid part size or parallelism stops the effect with a defect instead, as the [multipart upload how-to](./upload-a-large-file-in-parts.md) describes.

The AWS SDK raises further subtypes of `S3Exception` for S3 responses, such as `NoSuchKeyException` when an object does not exist and `NoSuchBucketException` when a bucket does not exist. `execute` and the operations that call it directly, such as `getObjectMetadata` and `isBucketExists`, pass these through unchanged. `getObject`, `streamLines` and the part uploads of `multipartUpload` rewrap them into a plain `S3Exception` that keeps the status code, message and cause, so match `statusCode` there.

### Handle Errors

The [handle errors how-to](./handle-errors.md) shows how to recover from a missing object, from a failed connection, and from the failures that are defects rather than `S3Exception`.

---

## Getting Started(Zio-s3)

This page runs a first ZIO S3 program: it creates a bucket, stores a JSON object in it, and reads the object back. We use a local MinIO server, an object storage server compatible with the S3 API, so we need no AWS account. Add the dependency from the [installation section](./index.md#installation) first.

### Start a Local S3 Server

To start MinIO with the credentials that this page uses, run:

```bash
docker run -p 9000:9000 -e MINIO_ROOT_USER=MyKey -e MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD=MySecret minio/minio server --compat /data
```

### Write the Program

The program calls `createBucket`, `putObject` and `getObject`. Each call needs an `S3` service, which `live` builds from a region, credentials and the server address. MinIO requires path-style requests, so we set `forcePathStyle` to `Some(true)`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.{ ZPipeline, ZStream }

import java.net.URI

object ZIOS3Example extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val json: Chunk[Byte] = Chunk.fromArray("""{  "id" : 1 , "name" : "A1" }""".getBytes)

  val myApp: ZIO[S3, Throwable, Unit] = for {
    _ <- createBucket("docs")
    _ <- putObject(
           bucketName = "docs",
           key = "doc1",
           contentLength = json.length.toLong,
           content = ZStream.fromChunk(json),
           options = UploadOptions.fromContentType("application/json")
         )
    _ <- getObject("docs", "doc1")
           .via(ZPipeline.utf8Decode)
           .foreach(Console.printLine(_))
  } yield ()

  def run =
    myApp.provide(
      live(
        Region.CA_CENTRAL_1,
        AwsBasicCredentials.create("MyKey", "MySecret"),
        Some(URI.create("http://localhost:9000")),
        forcePathStyle = Some(true) // MinIO requires path-style requests
      )
    )
}
```

When the program runs, it prints the JSON text that it stored.

### Next Steps

- To learn the operations step by step without a server, follow the [tutorial](./tutorial.md).
- To use AWS instead of MinIO, see [credentials and region](./credentials.md).
- To look up every operation, see the [operations reference](./s3-operations.md).
- To upload large files, see [upload a large file in parts](./upload-a-large-file-in-parts.md). To read objects, see [download an object](./download-an-object.md).

---

## Handle Errors

Most ZIO S3 operations fail with `S3Exception`, so one handler can catch every failure. The [errors reference](./errors.md) lists the subtypes that the library raises. This page shows how to recover from the common failures.

### Handle a Missing Object

To handle a missing object, match an `S3Exception` with status code 404 in `ZIO#catchSome`. `getObject` rewraps the AWS SDK's `NoSuchKeyException` into a plain `S3Exception` that keeps the status code, so matching `NoSuchKeyException` never succeeds. Any other `S3Exception` continues to fail:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZPipeline

val readOrEmpty: ZIO[S3, Exception, String] =
  getObject("docs", "missing.txt")
    .via(ZPipeline.utf8Decode)
    .runCollect
    .map(_.mkString)
    .catchSome { case e: S3Exception if e.statusCode == 404 => ZIO.succeed("") }
```

### Handle Connection Failures

To handle a failure while building the layer, match `ConnectionError`. The error message comes from the AWS SDK, so log it or show it to the user rather than matching its text:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.s3.errors.ConnectionError

import java.net.URI

val connected: ZIO[Any, S3Exception, Unit] =
  listBuckets
    .provideLayer(
      live(
        Region.US_EAST_1,
        AwsBasicCredentials.create("TESTKEY", "TESTSECRET"),
        Some(URI.create("http://localhost:9000")),
        forcePathStyle = Some(true)
      )
    )
    .unit
    .catchSome { case e: ConnectionError => Console.printLine(s"cannot connect: ${e.getMessage}").orDie }
```

The `ConnectionError` type appears in the signature of the `live` value that takes `S3Settings`, and it appears in the error of the layer for a failed provider. Use `ZIO#catchSome` on the layer, as [configure credentials](./credentials.md#handle-credential-failures) shows, to recover from it.

### Know Which Failures Are Defects

Some failures stop the effect with a defect, not a typed `S3Exception`, so `ZIO#catchSome` on `S3Exception` does not see them. A defect is an unrecoverable error that ZIO reports through `Cause.Die`. Two cases produce one: `multipartUpload` with a part size below `PartSize.Min`, or a parallelism of 0 or less, so validate these values where you build them; and the stub, for several cases that a real server reports as errors, as the [testing how-to](./testing.md) lists.

---

## Introduction to ZIO S3

[ZIO S3](https://github.com/zio/zio-s3) is a thin wrapper over the AWS S3 async client for ZIO.

[![Production Ready](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Production%20Ready-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-s3/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-s3_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-s3_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-s3_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-s3_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-s3_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-s3_2.13) [![ZIO S3](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-s3?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-s3)

### Introduction

ZIO S3 exposes the main operations of the AWS S3 Java client as ZIO effects and ZIO Streams. Each operation needs an `S3` service, which we provide with a layer built from a region and credentials:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream

val s3Layer: Layer[S3Exception, S3] =
  live(Region.US_EAST_1, AwsBasicCredentials.create("accessKeyId", "secretAccessKey"))

// list all buckets available
val buckets: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  listBuckets.unit

// list all objects of all buckets
val allObjects: ZStream[S3, S3Exception, String] =
  ZStream
    .fromIterableZIO(listBuckets)
    .flatMap(bucket => listAllObjects(bucket.name).map(obj => obj.bucketName + "/" + obj.key))
```

All operations live in the package object `zio.s3`, so a single `import zio.s3._` brings them into scope. To run a first program end to end, follow [Getting Started](./getting-started.md). For a guided walk-through, see the [tutorial](./tutorial.md).

### Installation

Add ZIO S3 to your `build.sbt`. The library is published for the JVM only, for Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3:

```sbt
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // ZIO S3 client for the JVM, built on the AWS SDK v2 async client
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-s3" % "0.4.5"
)
```

## List Objects Page by Page

S3 returns at most `maxKeys` objects per request and gives a continuation token when more objects remain. ZIO S3 hides that paging for most uses: `listAllObjects` returns one stream of every object in a bucket. When you need one page at a time, you can call `listObjects` and `getNextObjects` yourself. The options that control a listing are in the [options reference](./options.md#listobjectoptions).

### Stream All Objects

To read every object in a bucket, call `listAllObjects`. It requests pages as the stream is consumed, so you can stop early without loading the whole bucket:

```scala
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception

val allKeys: ZStream[S3, S3Exception, String] =
  listAllObjects("docs").map(_.key)
```

### Limit a Listing by Prefix and Page Size

To list only the objects whose keys start with a prefix, and to request 500 objects per page, build the options with `ListObjectOptions.from`:

```scala
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception

val logKeys: ZStream[S3, S3Exception, String] =
  listAllObjects("docs", ListObjectOptions.from("logs/", 500)).map(_.key)
```

`ListObjectOptions.fromMaxKeys` sets only the page size, and `ListObjectOptions.fromStartAfter` starts the listing after a given key. For a combination of settings, call the `ListObjectOptions` constructor directly.

### Fetch One Page at a Time

To read a single page, call `listObjects`. The returned `S3ObjectListing` holds the objects of that page and a `nextContinuationToken` when more remain. Pass the listing to `getNextObjects` to fetch the following page:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception

val secondPage: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, S3ObjectListing] =
  for {
    first  <- listObjects("docs", ListObjectOptions.fromMaxKeys(100))
    second <- getNextObjects(first)
  } yield second
```

When `nextContinuationToken` is `None`, the listing is the last page, and `getNextObjects` returns an empty listing.

### Stream Pages

To stream whole pages instead of single objects, pass the first listing to `paginate`. It emits the first page, then each following page, and stops after the last one:

```scala
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception

val pageSizes: ZStream[S3, S3Exception, Int] =
  ZStream
    .fromZIO(listObjects("docs", ListObjectOptions.fromMaxKeys(100)))
    .flatMap(paginate)
    .map(_.objectSummaries.size)
```

### Know the Limits of Paging

`getNextObjects` requests each page after the first with the bucket name, the prefix, and the continuation token. It does not send the `delimiter`, `maxKeys` or `starAfter` options again. Two things follow: later pages use the default size of 1000 objects, not the `maxKeys` of the first request, and when you list with a delimiter, later pages can include keys that the first page grouped. Avoid a delimiter when you need every page to be consistent, or list the prefixes you need one at a time.

The stub does not return correct pages, as described in the [testing how-to](./testing.md). Check paging behavior against a MinIO server.

---

## Manage Buckets

A bucket is the container that holds objects. ZIO S3 can create, check, list and delete buckets. The [operations reference](./s3-operations.md#bucket-operations) lists the signatures.

### Create a Bucket If It Does Not Exist

To create a bucket only when it is missing, check it first with `isBucketExists`. `createBucket` on a bucket that already exists fails on a real server, so the check keeps the program safe to run twice:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

def ensureBucket(name: String): ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  isBucketExists(name).flatMap(exists => createBucket(name).unless(exists)).unit
```

### List the Buckets

To list the buckets of the account, call `listBuckets`. It returns a `Chunk` of `S3Bucket` values with a name and a creation date:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

val names: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Chunk[String]] =
  listBuckets.map(_.map(_.name))
```

### Delete a Bucket

To delete a bucket, call `deleteBucket`. S3 refuses to delete a bucket that still holds objects, so empty it first. This example deletes every object, then the bucket:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

def deleteWithContents(name: String): ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  listAllObjects(name).mapZIOPar(8)(obj => deleteObject(name, obj.key)).runDrain *>
    deleteBucket(name)
```

`deleteObject` succeeds when the key is already gone, so the cleanup is safe to repeat. The stub stops with a defect, not an `S3Exception`, when a bucket is missing or not empty, as the [testing how-to](./testing.md) describes.

---

## Model Types(Zio-s3)

The operations return values of a few model types. Each type is a case class that holds the fields of an S3 response, converted to Scala types. The [operations reference](./s3-operations.md) lists the operation that returns each type.

### S3Bucket

`S3Bucket` describes one bucket returned by `listBuckets`:

```scala
final case class S3Bucket(name: String, creationDate: Instant)

object S3Bucket {
  type S3BucketListing = Chunk[S3Bucket]
}
```

The `name` field is the bucket name, and `creationDate` is the time the bucket was created. The alias `S3BucketListing` is the type that `listBuckets` returns, a `Chunk` of buckets.

### S3ObjectListing

`S3ObjectListing` describes one page of a listing from `listObjects` or `getNextObjects`:

```scala
final case class S3ObjectListing(
  bucketName: String,
  delimiter: Option[String],
  starAfter: Option[String],
  objectSummaries: Chunk[S3ObjectSummary],
  nextContinuationToken: Option[String],
  prefix: Option[String]
)
```

The `objectSummaries` field holds the objects of the page. A `nextContinuationToken` of `None` means the page is the last one. The [list and paginate objects how-to](./list-objects-page-by-page.md) shows how to use the token.

### S3ObjectSummary

`S3ObjectSummary` describes one object in a listing:

```scala
final case class S3ObjectSummary(bucketName: String, key: String, lastModified: Instant, size: Long)
```

The `key` field is the full key of the object, including any slashes, and `size` is the object's length in bytes.

### Build Models from AWS Responses

Each model has a helper that converts the AWS SDK type: `S3Bucket.fromBucket` and `S3Bucket.fromBuckets`, `S3ObjectListing.fromResponse` for a `ListObjectsV2Response`, and `ObjectMetadata.fromResponse` for a `HeadObjectResponse`. Use them to convert the result of a call that you make with [`execute`](./run-s3-calls-with-the-raw-client.md). `S3ObjectListing.from` builds an empty listing for a bucket and a continuation token.

### ObjectMetadata

`ObjectMetadata` describes one object as returned by `getObjectMetadata`:

```scala
final case class ObjectMetadata(
  metadata: Map[String, String],
  contentType: String,
  contentLength: Long,
  eTag: String
)
```

The `metadata` field holds the user-defined metadata without the `x-amz-meta-` prefix, and `eTag` holds the ETag without the surrounding quotes. The [object metadata how-to](./set-and-read-object-metadata.md) shows how to read these fields.

---

## Options(Zio-s3)

The options types control how ZIO S3 lists objects and uploads them. Each type has a `default` value and helper constructors. The [operations reference](./s3-operations.md) shows which operations take each type.

### ListObjectOptions

`ListObjectOptions` controls a listing of objects in a bucket:

```scala
final case class ListObjectOptions(
  prefix: Option[String],
  maxKeys: Long,
  delimiter: Option[String],
  starAfter: Option[String]
)
```

The fields have these meanings:

- `prefix` keeps only the objects whose keys start with the prefix.
- `maxKeys` sets the number of objects per request. The default is `MaxKeys.Max`, which is 1000.
- `delimiter` is sent to S3 as the listing delimiter. S3 then groups the keys below the delimiter into common prefixes, but `S3ObjectListing` has no field for common prefixes, so those keys are left out of the listing and the prefixes are not returned. Later pages do not reapply it, as [list objects page by page](./list-objects-page-by-page.md#know-the-limits-of-paging) describes.
- `starAfter` starts the listing after the given key.

The companion object provides these constructors:

```scala
object ListObjectOptions {
  val default: ListObjectOptions
  def from(prefix: String, maxKeys: Long): ListObjectOptions
  def fromMaxKeys(maxKeys: Long): ListObjectOptions
  def fromStartAfter(startAfter: String): ListObjectOptions
}
```

`ListObjectOptions.default` has no prefix, no delimiter, no start key, and a page size of 1000.

### UploadOptions

`UploadOptions` controls the metadata and access settings of an uploaded object:

```scala
final case class UploadOptions(
  metadata: Map[String, String],
  cannedAcl: ObjectCannedACL,
  contentType: Option[String]
)
```

The fields have these meanings:

- `metadata` holds your own key-value pairs. ZIO S3 adds the `x-amz-meta-` prefix when it sends them.
- `cannedAcl` sets the access control list for the object. The default is `ObjectCannedACL.PRIVATE`.
- `contentType` sets the `Content-Type` header. When it is `None`, S3 applies its default.

The companion object provides these constructors:

```scala
object UploadOptions {
  val default: UploadOptions
  def from(metadata: Map[String, String], contentType: String): UploadOptions
  def fromContentType(contentType: String): UploadOptions
  def fromMetadata(metadata: Map[String, String]): UploadOptions
}
```

`UploadOptions.default` uses a private ACL, no metadata, and no content type. The stub uses `application/octet-stream` as its content type for `putObject` when none is given, and `binary/octet-stream` for `multipartUpload`, so the two differ in the stub.

### MultipartUploadOptions

`MultipartUploadOptions` adds the part size to the upload settings for `multipartUpload`:

```scala
final case class MultipartUploadOptions(
  uploadOptions: UploadOptions,
  partSize: Int
)
```

The `uploadOptions` field holds the metadata, ACL, and content type. The `partSize` field is the size of each part in bytes, and it must be at least `PartSize.Min`:

```scala
object MultipartUploadOptions {
  val default: MultipartUploadOptions
  def fromUploadOptions(options: UploadOptions): MultipartUploadOptions
  def fromPartSize(partSize: Int): MultipartUploadOptions
}
```

`MultipartUploadOptions.default` uses `UploadOptions.default` and the minimum part size.

### PartSize

`PartSize` holds the byte sizes that help build part sizes:

```scala
object PartSize {
  final val Kilo: Int = 1024
  final val Mega: Int = 1024 * Kilo
  final val Giga: Int = 1024 * Mega
  final val Min: Int = 5 * Mega
}
```

`PartSize.Min` is 5 MB, the smallest part that S3 accepts for every part except the last one. Multiply a constant by a count, as in `10 * PartSize.Mega`, to set a part size. The part size is an `Int`, so it cannot exceed 2 GiB minus one byte, and `2 * PartSize.Giga` overflows. S3 accepts at most 10,000 parts per upload, so the part size times 10,000 is the largest object that `multipartUpload` can store.

### MaxKeys

`MaxKeys` holds the default page size for listings:

```scala
object MaxKeys {
  val Max: Long = 1000L
}
```

`ListObjectOptions.default` uses `MaxKeys.Max`.

---

## Run S3 Calls with the Raw Client

ZIO S3 wraps the common S3 operations. For an operation it does not wrap, such as copying an object, call `execute`. It takes a function from the AWS `S3AsyncClient` to a `CompletableFuture`, and returns the result as a ZIO effect that fails with `S3Exception`.

### Copy an Object

To copy an object inside S3 without downloading it, build a `CopyObjectRequest` and run it with `execute`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.{ CopyObjectRequest, S3Exception }
import zio._
import zio.s3._

val copy: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  execute(
    _.copyObject(
      CopyObjectRequest
        .builder()
        .sourceBucket("docs")
        .sourceKey("people.csv")
        .destinationBucket("backups")
        .destinationKey("people-copy.csv")
        .build()
    )
  ).unit
```

### Check a Bucket Directly

To call any other operation, pass its request to the matching client method. This example sends a `HeadBucketRequest`:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.{ HeadBucketRequest, S3Exception }
import zio._
import zio.s3._

val bucketExists: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Boolean] =
  execute(_.headBucket(HeadBucketRequest.builder().bucket("docs").build())).as(true)
```

### Know How Failures Are Reported

`execute` fails with the `S3Exception` that the AWS SDK raises for an S3 response, such as `NoSuchBucketException`. When the SDK fails without an S3 response, for example on a network error, `execute` fails with `SdkError`. The [errors reference](./errors.md) lists both. The stub does not support `execute` and stops with a defect, so use a `live` layer in tests that call it.

---

## S3 Operations

The `S3` trait defines every operation that ZIO S3 supports. The package object `zio.s3` exposes each operation as a function that requires `S3` in the environment, so you call `createBucket("docs")` directly, not `s3.createBucket("docs")`. Every operation returns a ZIO effect or a ZIO Stream, and the failure type is `S3Exception`. The [settings reference](./settings.md) describes how to build the `S3` layer.

### Bucket Operations

Bucket operations create, delete, check, and list buckets. A bucket name must follow the S3 naming rules, and the stub maps each bucket to a directory:

```scala
trait S3 {
  def createBucket(bucketName: String): IO[S3Exception, Unit]
  def deleteBucket(bucketName: String): IO[S3Exception, Unit]
  def isBucketExists(bucketName: String): IO[S3Exception, Boolean]
  val listBuckets: IO[S3Exception, S3BucketListing]
}
```

`isBucketExists` returns `false` when the bucket is missing, and fails for other errors. `listBuckets` returns a `Chunk` of [`S3Bucket`](./models.md#s3bucket) values.

### Object Operations

Object operations read, write, inspect, and delete the objects inside a bucket. The key identifies an object, and a slash in the key does not create a folder on real S3:

```scala
trait S3 {
  def getObject(bucketName: String, key: String): Stream[S3Exception, Byte]
  def getObjectMetadata(bucketName: String, key: String): IO[S3Exception, ObjectMetadata]
  def putObject[R](
    bucketName: String,
    key: String,
    contentLength: Long,
    content: ZStream[R, Throwable, Byte],
    options: UploadOptions = UploadOptions.default,
    contentMD5: Option[String] = None
  ): ZIO[R, S3Exception, Unit]
  def deleteObject(bucketName: String, key: String): IO[S3Exception, Unit]
  def streamLines(bucketName: String, key: String): Stream[S3Exception, String]
}
```

`getObject` fails with `S3Exception` when the key does not exist. `putObject` takes the `contentLength` in bytes, which must match the number of bytes that the stream produces. `streamLines` decodes the object as UTF-8 and splits it into lines, and it fails with `DecodingException`, listed in the [errors reference](./errors.md#error-types), when the bytes are not valid UTF-8.

### Multipart Upload

The multipart operation uploads a stream in parts, as described in [stream large files with multipart upload](./upload-a-large-file-in-parts.md):

```scala
trait S3 {
  def multipartUpload[R](
    bucketName: String,
    key: String,
    content: ZStream[R, Throwable, Byte],
    options: MultipartUploadOptions = MultipartUploadOptions.default
  )(parallelism: Int): ZIO[R, S3Exception, Unit]
}
```

The `parallelism` argument must be greater than 0. The `options` argument holds the part size, which must be at least `PartSize.Min`, and a violation stops the effect with a defect.

### Listing Operations

Listing operations return one page of objects, the next page, or a stream of every object. The default page size is 1000 objects, as described in [list and paginate objects](./list-objects-page-by-page.md):

```scala
trait S3 {
  def listObjects(bucketName: String): IO[S3Exception, S3ObjectListing]
  def listObjects(bucketName: String, options: ListObjectOptions): IO[S3Exception, S3ObjectListing]
  def getNextObjects(listing: S3ObjectListing): IO[S3Exception, S3ObjectListing]
  def listAllObjects(bucketName: String): Stream[S3Exception, S3ObjectSummary]
  def listAllObjects(bucketName: String, options: ListObjectOptions): Stream[S3Exception, S3ObjectSummary]
  def paginate(initialListing: S3ObjectListing): Stream[S3Exception, S3ObjectListing]
}
```

`getNextObjects` returns an empty listing when the given listing has no continuation token. The stub differs and stops with a defect, as the [testing how-to](./testing.md) describes. `paginate` emits the initial listing first and then each following page.

### Escape Hatch

The `execute` operation runs a request on the underlying AWS `S3AsyncClient`, for operations that the library does not wrap:

```scala
trait S3 {
  def execute[T](f: S3AsyncClient => CompletableFuture[T]): IO[S3Exception, T]
}
```

The stub does not support `execute`, and the stub stops with a defect when you call it.

### Types Used by These Operations

The operations use the types from the [options reference](./options.md) for their settings, and the [models reference](./models.md) for their results. Every error is a subtype of `S3Exception`, as listed in the [errors reference](./errors.md).

---

## Set and Read Object Metadata

Each S3 object carries a content type, a size, an ETag, and a set of user-defined metadata entries. ZIO S3 lets you set these when you upload, and read them without downloading the object. The [models reference](./models.md#objectmetadata) describes the `ObjectMetadata` type, and the [options reference](./options.md#uploadoptions) describes the upload settings.

### Set Metadata and Content Type on Upload

To store user metadata and a content type with an object, pass an `UploadOptions` value to `putObject`. The metadata map holds your own keys, and ZIO S3 adds the `x-amz-meta-` prefix for you:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.{ ObjectCannedACL, S3Exception }
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream

val bytes: Chunk[Byte] = Chunk.fromArray("name,age\nJohn,42".getBytes)

val upload: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  putObject(
    bucketName = "docs",
    key = "people.csv",
    contentLength = bytes.length.toLong,
    content = ZStream.fromChunk(bytes),
    options = UploadOptions(
      metadata = Map("source" -> "crm-export"),
      cannedAcl = ObjectCannedACL.PRIVATE,
      contentType = Some("text/csv")
    )
  )
```

`UploadOptions.default` uses a private canned ACL and no content type, and `UploadOptions.from` sets both the metadata and the content type in one call.

### Read Metadata Without Downloading

To read an object's metadata, call `getObjectMetadata`. S3 answers with the headers only, so the object's bytes are not transferred:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

val info: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, String] =
  getObjectMetadata("docs", "people.csv").map { meta =>
    s"type=${meta.contentType} length=${meta.contentLength} etag=${meta.eTag} source=${meta.metadata.get("source").getOrElse("unknown")}"
  }
```

The `eTag` field has no surrounding quotes, because ZIO S3 removes them when it reads the response. S3 can return metadata keys in a different letter case from the one you wrote, so compare keys in lowercase, as the test suite does.

### Check the Content MD5

S3 can verify an upload against an MD5 checksum that you send with the request. Pass the checksum, encoded as Base64, in the `contentMD5` argument of `putObject`. Object locking on a bucket requires this checksum, and S3 rejects the upload without it:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import software.amazon.awssdk.utils.Md5Utils
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream

val data: Chunk[Byte] = Chunk.fromArray("name,age\nJohn,42".getBytes)
val checksum: String = Md5Utils.md5AsBase64(data.toArray)

val verified: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  putObject(
    bucketName = "docs",
    key = "people.csv",
    contentLength = data.length.toLong,
    content = ZStream.fromChunk(data),
    options = UploadOptions.default,
    contentMD5 = Some(checksum)
  )
```

S3 compares the checksum with the bytes it receives and rejects the request when they differ.

### Delete an Object

To remove an object, call `deleteObject`. S3 treats a missing key as already deleted, so the call succeeds when the key does not exist:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._

val remove: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] = deleteObject("docs", "people.csv")
```

### Know the Stub's Metadata Limits

The stub keeps content type and user metadata in memory, as described in the [testing how-to](./testing.md). Files that were not written through `putObject` report an empty content type and no metadata.

---

## Settings and Layers

The `S3` service is built as a ZIO layer. ZIO S3 provides several functions that build it, and a settings type, `S3Settings`, that holds a region and credentials. This page lists each function and its parameters. The [configure credentials how-to](./credentials.md) shows how to choose between them.

### Layer Functions

The table lists each function that builds an `S3` layer, and the errors that building it can produce:

| Function                                                          | Result                                    | Builds the client from                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `live(region, credentials, uriEndpoint?, forcePathStyle?)`        | `Layer[S3Exception, S3]`                  | A fixed `AwsCredentials` value                  |
| `liveZIO(region, provider, uriEndpoint?, forcePathStyle?)`        | `ZLayer[R, S3Exception, S3]`              | An `AwsCredentialsProvider` effect              |
| `live`                                                            | `ZLayer[S3Settings, ConnectionError, S3]` | An `S3Settings` value in the environment        |
| `settings(region, cred)`                                          | `ZLayer[R, S3Exception, S3Settings]`      | An `AwsCredentials` effect, as `S3Settings`     |
| `stub(path)`                                                      | `ZLayer[Any, Nothing, S3]`                | A local directory, for tests                    |

The optional parameters, `uriEndpoint` and `forcePathStyle`, default to `None`. With `None`, the AWS SDK uses its standard endpoint and addressing style. Set `uriEndpoint` to a `java.net.URI` to connect to another server, and set `forcePathStyle` to `Some(true)` to address buckets in the path, as [S3-compatible endpoints](./connect-to-an-s3-compatible-store.md) describes.

The `live` function that takes a region and credentials rejects any region that the AWS SDK does not know, and the layer fails with `InvalidSettings`. The `live` value that takes `S3Settings` does not accept an endpoint.

### S3Settings

`S3Settings` is a case class that holds the region and the credentials that the `live` value uses:

```scala
final case class S3Settings(s3Region: S3Region, credentials: AwsCredentials)

object S3Settings {
  def from(region: Region, credentials: AwsCredentials): IO[InvalidSettings, S3Settings]
}
```

`S3Settings.from` checks the region with `S3Region.from`, and fails with `InvalidSettings` when the region is not known to the AWS SDK.

### S3Region

`S3Region` wraps a `Region` that ZIO S3 has checked:

```scala
sealed abstract class S3Region(val region: Region)

object S3Region {
  def from(region: Region): Either[InvalidSettings, S3Region]
  def unsafeFromString(r: String): S3Region
}
```

`S3Region.from` accepts only the regions listed by `Region.regions()`. `S3Region.unsafeFromString` skips that check, so an unknown name is accepted and only fails later, when the client makes a request. Use it only with a server that accepts that name, and pass the result to `S3Settings` for the `live` value that takes `S3Settings`, or to `Live.connect` when you need an endpoint.

### Live

`Live` is the class behind every `live` layer. Its `connect` functions build the `S3` service as a scoped effect, and they are public, so you can build the client yourself:

```scala
object Live {
  def connect[R](
    region: S3Region,
    provider: RIO[R with Scope, AwsCredentialsProvider],
    uriEndpoint: Option[URI],
    forcePathStyle: Option[Boolean] = None
  ): ZIO[R with Scope, ConnectionError, S3]

  def connect[R](builder: S3AsyncClientBuilder): ZIO[R with Scope, ConnectionError, S3]
}
```

The first overload is what `liveZIO` uses. The second takes a configured AWS `S3AsyncClientBuilder`, for settings that the layer functions do not expose, such as a custom HTTP client or a proxy. Both fail with `ConnectionError` when the credentials or the client cannot be built.

### S3Stream

The package object defines `type S3Stream[A] = ZStream[S3, S3Exception, A]`, the type of the streaming operations such as `listAllObjects` and `streamLines`.

### Credential Providers

The `zio.s3.providers` object contains the providers that `liveZIO` accepts. The table lists each provider, its type, and whether it needs a `Scope`:

| Provider                 | Type                                                                    | Needs `Scope` |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `const(credentials)`     | `UIO[AwsCredentialsProvider]`                                           | No            |
| `basic(key, secret)`     | `UIO[AwsCredentialsProvider]`                                           | No            |
| `session(key, secret, token)` | `UIO[AwsCredentialsProvider]`                                      | No            |
| `system`                 | `IO[InvalidCredentials, SystemPropertyCredentialsProvider]`             | No            |
| `env`                    | `IO[InvalidCredentials, EnvironmentVariableCredentialsProvider]`        | No            |
| `profile(name?)`         | `ZIO[Scope, InvalidCredentials, ProfileCredentialsProvider]`            | Yes           |
| `container`              | `ZIO[Scope, InvalidCredentials, ContainerCredentialsProvider]`          | Yes           |
| `instanceProfile`        | `ZIO[Scope, InvalidCredentials, InstanceProfileCredentialsProvider]`    | Yes           |
| `webIdentity`            | `ZIO[Scope, InvalidCredentials, WebIdentityTokenFileCredentialsProvider]` | Yes         |
| `default`                | `ZIO[Scope, InvalidCredentials, AwsCredentialsProvider]`                | Yes           |

The providers that check the credentials when they are built fail with `InvalidCredentials`. The `webIdentity` provider needs the `sts` module of the AWS SDK on the classpath, which ZIO S3 already depends on.

---

## Test Without a Real S3

ZIO S3 includes a stub implementation of the `S3` service for tests. The stub stores each bucket as a directory under a root path on the local disk, so tests run without a network connection or an S3 server. To build the stub layer, call `stub` with the root path:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.nio.file.{ Path => ZPath }
import zio.s3._

val stubS3: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, S3] = stub(ZPath("/tmp/s3-data"))
```

The root directory must exist before the stub creates a bucket. Each bucket is a subdirectory, and each object is a file inside it, so the layout matches what you would see on disk after a sequence of `createBucket` and `putObject` calls.

### Run Effects Against the Stub

To use the stub in a test, provide the layer to the effect under test with `provideLayer`. The stub keeps its buckets on disk under the root path, so give each test suite its own root directory, and delete it when the suite ends, to keep the buckets of one suite out of another:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.nio.file.{ Path => ZPath }
import zio.s3._

val bucketsAfterCreate: ZIO[Any, Throwable, Boolean] =
  (for {
    _       <- createBucket("tests-bucket")
    buckets <- listBuckets
  } yield buckets.map(_.name).contains("tests-bucket"))
    .provideLayer(stub(ZPath("/tmp/s3-data")))
```

The check for the bucket name runs inside the same effect as the create call, so it reads the bucket that the create call made. Pass the result to the assertion library that your test framework provides.

### Give Each Test a Fresh Root Directory

To keep tests apart, create a temporary directory for each test and build the stub on it. The scoped directory is deleted when the scope closes:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.nio.file.Files
import zio.s3._

val isolated: ZIO[Scope, Throwable, Boolean] =
  for {
    root    <- Files.createTempDirectoryScoped(Some("s3-stub"), Seq.empty)
    buckets <- (createBucket("tests-bucket") *> listBuckets).provide(stub(root))
  } yield buckets.exists(_.name == "tests-bucket")
```

The same effect works inside a test of any framework, such as ZIO Test: run it with `ZIO.scoped` or provide the `Scope`, and assert on the result.

### Know Where the Stub Differs from AWS

The stub follows the `S3` API for common operations, but a few behaviors differ from a real server, and tests that depend on them can pass against the stub and fail against S3:

- Errors: `createBucket` on an existing name, `deleteBucket` on a missing or non-empty bucket, and `listObjects` on a missing bucket stop with a defect, not a typed `S3Exception`, so `catchSome` on `S3Exception` does not catch them. Test those cases against a real server.
- Metadata: the content type and user metadata that `putObject` stores live in memory. They are lost when the JVM exits, and files that were written outside `putObject`, such as the files already in the root directory, report an empty content type and no metadata.
- Pagination: the stub does not return correct pages when a listing has a `maxKeys` limit and more objects than that limit. `getNextObjects` ignores the continuation token and lists the bucket again with a page size of 100, and it stops with a defect when the listing has no token, where a real server returns an empty listing. Do not test pagination against the stub. Use a MinIO server as shown in [list and paginate objects](./list-objects-page-by-page.md).
- ETag: the stub computes the ETag from the file text decoded as UTF-8, so for binary content it differs from the MD5 that S3 reports.
- Multipart upload: the stub validates the part size and parallelism with the same defects as the live service, then writes the stream in one piece, so `parallelism` has no effect.
- Raw client: `execute` is not supported and stops with a defect, so code that calls `execute` needs a live layer in tests.

For tests that need the real behavior, run a MinIO server as shown in the [introduction](./index.md) and build a `live` layer with `forcePathStyle = Some(true)`.

---

## Tutorial: Upload, List and Download Files

In this tutorial, we build a small program that creates a bucket, uploads a text file, lists the objects in the bucket, and downloads the file again. We use the local stub from the [testing how-to](./testing.md), so we do not need a running S3 server or AWS account. The same code works against AWS or MinIO once we swap the layer, as [S3-compatible endpoints](./connect-to-an-s3-compatible-store.md) describes.

### Add the Dependency

Add ZIO S3 to your project as the [installation section](./index.md#installation) shows.

### Create an S3 Layer

Every ZIO S3 operation requires an `S3` service. The `stub` function builds one that stores buckets as directories under a root path on the local disk:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.nio.file.{ Path => ZPath }
import zio.s3._

val root: ZPath = ZPath("/tmp/zio-s3-tutorial")

val s3Layer: ZLayer[Any, Nothing, S3] = stub(root)
```

The root directory must exist before we create a bucket, so we create it in the first step of the program.

### Create a Bucket and Upload a File

To create a bucket and upload a text file, we call `createBucket` and `putObject`. The `contentLength` argument is the size of the data in bytes, and `UploadOptions.fromContentType` sets the `Content-Type` of the object:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception

val content: Chunk[Byte] = Chunk.fromArray("hello from zio-s3".getBytes)

val upload: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  for {
    _ <- createBucket("tutorial")
    _ <- putObject(
           bucketName = "tutorial",
           key = "greetings/hello.txt",
           contentLength = content.length.toLong,
           content = ZStream.fromChunk(content),
           options = UploadOptions.fromContentType("text/plain")
         )
  } yield ()
```

The key `greetings/hello.txt` contains a slash, so the stub stores the file in a `greetings` subdirectory. Real S3 treats the slash as part of the name, and the listing in the next step shows the full key.

### List the Objects in a Bucket

To list every object in a bucket, we call `listAllObjects`. It returns a stream of `S3ObjectSummary` values, and each summary holds the bucket name, the key, the last-modified time, and the size:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception

val printKeys: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  listAllObjects("tutorial")
    .runForeach(summary => Console.printLine(summary.key).orDie)
```

For a bucket with more than one page of results, see [list and paginate objects](./list-objects-page-by-page.md).

### Download a File

To read an object back, we call `getObject`, which returns a stream of bytes. We decode the bytes as UTF-8 text with `ZPipeline.utf8Decode`, then collect the text:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZPipeline

val download: ZIO[S3, Throwable, String] =
  getObject("tutorial", "greetings/hello.txt")
    .via(ZPipeline.utf8Decode)
    .runCollect
    .map(_.mkString)
```

`getObject` fails with `S3Exception` when the key does not exist. We handle that case in the [errors reference](./errors.md).

### Put It Together

The following program runs all the steps in order and prints the results. We run it with `sbt run`, and it creates files under `/tmp/zio-s3-tutorial`:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.nio.file.{ Files, Path => ZPath }
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.{ ZPipeline, ZStream }

object S3Tutorial extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val root: ZPath = ZPath("/tmp/zio-s3-tutorial")

  val content: Chunk[Byte] = Chunk.fromArray("hello from zio-s3".getBytes)

  val program: ZIO[S3, Throwable, Unit] =
    for {
      _       <- Files.createDirectories(root)
      _       <- createBucket("tutorial")
      _       <- putObject(
                   bucketName = "tutorial",
                   key = "greetings/hello.txt",
                   contentLength = content.length.toLong,
                   content = ZStream.fromChunk(content),
                   options = UploadOptions.fromContentType("text/plain")
                 )
      objects <- listAllObjects("tutorial").runCollect
      _       <- ZIO.foreachDiscard(objects)(summary => Console.printLine(s"object: ${summary.key}"))
      text    <- getObject("tutorial", "greetings/hello.txt").via(ZPipeline.utf8Decode).runCollect.map(_.mkString)
      _       <- Console.printLine(s"content: $text")
    } yield ()

  def run = program.provide(stub(root))
}
```

When the program runs, it prints the key `greetings/hello.txt` and the text `hello from zio-s3`. To try the same steps against a real server, replace `stub(root)` with a `live` layer, as shown in the [introduction](./index.md).

---

## Upload a Large File in Parts

S3 accepts a single `putObject` request for data of any size, but a large object is safer to send in parts: each part is a separate request, the parts can be sent in parallel, and a failed part can be retried without resending the whole file. ZIO S3 splits a stream into parts for you with `multipartUpload`, so a file never has to fit in memory.

### Upload a File in Parts

To upload a file as a multipart upload, pass a stream of bytes, the upload options, and the number of parts to send in parallel. In this example, each part is 10 MB, and four parts upload at the same time:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream
import java.nio.file.Paths

val upload: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  multipartUpload(
    "backups",
    "2026/archive.tar",
    ZStream.fromPath(Paths.get("/data/archive.tar")),
    MultipartUploadOptions(
      uploadOptions = UploadOptions.fromContentType("application/x-tar"),
      partSize = 10 * PartSize.Mega
    )
  )(4)
```

The second parameter list holds `parallelism`, the number of parts uploaded at the same time. The part size is set in `MultipartUploadOptions.partSize`, and the [options reference](./options.md#multipartuploadoptions) lists the other fields.

### Choose a Part Size

Every part except the last must be at least 5 MB, which is the minimum that S3 accepts. The constant `PartSize.Min` holds that value. Build the options from a part size with `MultipartUploadOptions.fromPartSize`, or from upload options with `MultipartUploadOptions.fromUploadOptions`, which uses the 5 MB minimum:

```scala
import zio.s3._

val defaultParts: MultipartUploadOptions = MultipartUploadOptions.fromUploadOptions(UploadOptions.default)

val tenMegabyteParts: MultipartUploadOptions = MultipartUploadOptions.fromPartSize(10 * PartSize.Mega)
```

A part size below 5 MB, or a parallelism of 0 or less, stops the effect with a defect, which is an unrecoverable error rather than an `S3Exception`. Check both values in the code that builds the options.

### Know What Happens on Failure

When a part fails to upload, `multipartUpload` stops and does not complete the upload. It also does not abort the upload, so the parts that already reached S3 can remain in the bucket and count toward storage. Until the library aborts uploads on failure, remove leftover uploads with the S3 API, through `execute`, or with a lifecycle rule that expires incomplete multipart uploads on the bucket.

### Upload an Empty Stream

When the stream holds no bytes, `multipartUpload` still completes the upload and creates an object of length 0. This is useful when a job must always create a marker object:

```scala
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception
import zio._
import zio.s3._
import zio.stream.ZStream

val marker: ZIO[S3, S3Exception, Unit] =
  multipartUpload("backups", "2026/_done", ZStream.empty)(1)
```

---

## Generated Files Are Owned by the Build

The CI plugin writes workflow files, so the question is who owns a file: the plugin or the developer. ZIO SBT gives two different answers, depending on the file.

### Files the Build Owns

`ci.yml`, `auto-approve.yml`, `auto-merge.yml` and the other generated workflows belong to `build.sbt`. Every one starts with an "autogenerated" header and is rewritten by `ciGenerateGithubWorkflow`. A hand edit is lost at the next generation, and `ciCheckGithubWorkflow` fails until the file matches what the build would write. This is deliberate: the build is the single source of truth, and a pull request that changes a workflow shows the change in `build.sbt` too.

The same applies to `.github/dependabot.yml`. When a feature is switched off, the plugin deletes only a file that carries its header, never a hand-written one.

### Files That Are Scaffolded Once

Two files are configuration of another tool and are expected to be edited by hand: `.github/release-drafter.yml` and `.scala-steward.conf`. The plugin writes them only the first time, when they do not exist. It never rewrites or deletes them afterward, and the drift check does not cover them.

### Why a Check Exists

A bot can change something that a generated file depends on, for example a Scala Steward bump of `zio-sbt-ci` itself. The committed files then no longer match what the build would write, and the `lint` job fails. The `regenerate-workflows.yml` workflow exists to fix exactly this on bot pull requests.

To keep the files in sync yourself, see [Keep the Generated Workflow in Sync](../how-to-guides/keep-the-workflow-in-sync.md).

---

## How the Plugins Fit Together

ZIO SBT splits the build of a ZIO library into three sbt plugins that each own one concern, and two modules that support them.

### One Plugin per Concern

The ecosystem plugin owns how the code is compiled and checked. It decides the Scala versions, the compiler options and the `fmt`, `lint` and `prepare` commands, so every ZIO library builds the same way.

The website plugin owns the documentation. It compiles the Markdown in `docs/` with mdoc, so every Scala example is type-checked, and wraps the result in a Docusaurus website. It also generates the `README.md` from `docs/index.md`, so the README and the first page of the website never disagree.

The CI plugin owns the GitHub workflows. It describes the whole pipeline in Scala, using the model of `zio-sbt-githubactions`, and writes the YAML files that GitHub runs. The workflow calls back into the other plugins: the `lint` job runs the `lint` command of the ecosystem plugin, and the `build` job runs the website build.

### How Documentation Reaches zio.dev

A documentation change travels through four stages:

1. `compileDocs` runs mdoc over `docs/` and writes the compiled pages to `website/docs`.
2. On a release, the `release-docs` job publishes `website/docs` to npm as the package `@zio.dev/<project>`.
3. The `notify-docs-release` job tells the `zio/zio` repository that a new version of the package exists.
4. The ZIO website, built from `zio/zio`, picks up the new package version and shows the pages under `zio.dev/<project>/`.

The first stage runs on a laptop, which is why `previewWebsite` can show the same pages locally. The other three run in CI.

### Source Embedding

`zio-sbt-source` is not a plugin. It is a library on the classpath of the docs project, so mdoc can load its `mdoc:embed` modifier. Embedding examples from real source files keeps the documentation compiling against the code it describes.

---

## Concepts(Zio-sbt)

These pages explain how the parts of ZIO SBT fit together and why the plugins work the way they do. They contain no recipes. For the exact names and defaults of settings, see the [Reference](../reference/index.md).

- [How the Plugins Fit Together](./how-the-plugins-fit-together.md) explains what each plugin owns and how the documentation travels from `docs/` to zio.dev.
- [Generated Files Are Owned by the Build](./generated-files.md) explains which files the CI plugin writes, which it only scaffolds, and why `build.sbt` stays the single source of truth.
