## Ordering Derivation

The Scala standard library provides a type class called `Ordering[A]` that compares values of type `A`. Every schema has a `Schema#ordering` method that builds an `Ordering[A]` from the structure the schema describes, so a type with a derived schema gets an ordering without a hand-written instance:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def ordering: Ordering[A]
}
```

The following example uses the derived ordering to sort a list of `Person` values:

```scala
import zio.schema._

case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}
```

Records compare field by field, so the people are sorted by `name` first:

```scala
List(
  Person("John", 42),
  Person("Jane", 34),
  Person("Jane", 20)
).sorted(Person.schema.ordering)
// res0: List[Person] = List(
//   Person(name = "Jane", age = 20),
//   Person(name = "Jane", age = 34),
//   Person(name = "John", age = 42)
// )
```

### How Values Compare

The ordering follows the structure of the schema:

- Primitives use the `compare` method of their standard type, such as numeric order for numbers and lexicographic order for strings.
- Records compare field by field, in declaration order. The first field that differs decides the result.
- Enums (sealed traits) compare by case first, in the order the cases are declared. Two values of the same case compare by their contents.
- `Option` values put `None` before any `Some`, and `Either` values put any `Left` before any `Right`.
- Tuples compare by their first element, then their second.
- Sequences such as `List`, `Vector`, and `Chunk` compare element by element, and a shorter sequence comes before a longer one that starts with it.

Each comparison converts both values to [`DynamicValue`](../operations/dynamic-data-representation.md) first, so a derived ordering is slower than a hand-written one. For sorting large collections in a hot path, a hand-written `Ordering` is faster.

:::caution
`Schema#ordering` returns 0 (equal) for any two `Set`, `Map`, `NonEmptyChunk`, `NonEmptyMap`, or `Fallback` values, whatever their contents. A record that contains such a field ignores that field when comparing. A binary primitive (`StandardType.BinaryType`) compares by the sum of its bytes, so two different byte chunks with the same sum are equal. To order by one of these types, write the `Ordering` yourself. For a `Set`, one way is to sort its elements and compare them as a `List`:

```scala
import zio.schema._

val setOrdering: Ordering[Set[Int]] =
  Schema[List[Int]].ordering.on[Set[Int]](_.toList.sorted)
```
:::

---

## Derivation of ZIO Test Generators

### Introduction

ZIO Test supports property-based testing with the `Gen` type. A `Gen[R, A]` is a random generator of values of type `A`, and a property test checks that a property holds for many values that the generator produces. The `zio-schema-zio-test` module provides a way to derive a `Gen[R, A]` from a `Schema[A]`, so we do not have to write a generator for each type by hand.

### Installation

To derive a generator from a schema, we add the following dependency to our `build.sbt` file:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-zio-test" % "1.9.2" % Test
```

### DeriveGen

The `DeriveGen` object in the `zio.schema` package provides the `DeriveGen.gen` operator. It takes a `Schema[A]` implicitly and returns a `Gen[Sized, A]`:

```scala
object DeriveGen {
  def gen[A](implicit schema: Schema[A]): Gen[Sized, A]
}
```

The `Sized` environment lets ZIO Test control the size of generated strings and sets. Sequences (`List`, `Vector`, `Chunk`) and maps do not follow it: each generated sequence or map is either empty or has exactly two elements.

### Example

To generate `Person` values, we first derive the schema, then derive the generator from it. We keep both in the companion object:

```scala
import zio.schema.{DeriveGen, DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.test.{Gen, Sized}

case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen
  val gen: Gen[Sized, Person]         = DeriveGen.gen
}
```

Next, we write a property test that checks a round trip through the schema's dynamic representation. Every generated `Person` must survive the conversion unchanged:

```scala
import zio.test._

object PersonRoundTripSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec: Spec[Sized, Nothing] =
    test("a generated Person survives a DynamicValue round trip") {
      check(Person.gen) { p =>
        assertTrue(Person.schema.fromDynamic(Person.schema.toDynamic(p)) == Right(p))
      }
    }
}
```

The `check` operator runs the property with many generated values. If any value fails the assertion, ZIO Test reports the smallest failing input it finds. [How to Property-Test Codecs with DeriveGen](../how-to/property-test-codecs.md) applies the same pattern to round trips through JSON and Protobuf, and shows how to generate values that pass validation.

### Limitations

The derived generator follows the structure of the schema, not its rules, so a few kinds of schema need extra care:

- Generated values ignore `@validate` rules. Filter them with `Gen#filter` and `Schema.validate` when a property needs valid values.
- A `Transform` schema generates a value of the underlying type and then applies the transformation. When the transformation fails, that sample is dropped instead of reported, so a transformation that rejects most inputs can leave `check` with few or no samples.
- Sequences and maps have zero or two elements, as described above. Write a generator by hand when a property depends on larger collections.
- A `Schema.Fail` schema generates no values at all.

:::caution
`DeriveGen.gen` throws an exception with the message "Missing handler for generating value of schema ..." when the schema is, or contains, a `NonEmptyChunk`, a `NonEmptyMap`, or a `Fallback`. For a type that contains one of these, write its generator by hand and derive generators for the other parts. For example, `Gen.chunkOf1(DeriveGen.gen[Int])` generates `NonEmptyChunk[Int]` values.
:::

---

## Combining Different Encoders

Because every codec is derived from the same `Schema`, one data model can move between formats without any conversion code. This example takes a value on a round trip through JSON and back, then through Protobuf and back, first for a single value and then for a stream of values. It also shows how to convert JSON input straight into Protobuf bytes.

### Prerequisites

The example uses the JSON and Protobuf modules:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json"     % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-protobuf" % "1.9.2"
)
```

### Define the Model and the Codecs

We start with a case class, derive its schema once, and derive a JSON codec and a Protobuf codec from that schema:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.schema.codec.{BinaryCodec, DecodeError, JsonCodec, ProtobufCodec}
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.stream.ZStream

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}

val jsonCodec: BinaryCodec[Person]     = JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[Person]
val protobufCodec: BinaryCodec[Person] = ProtobufCodec.protobufCodec[Person]
```

Both codecs have the same type, `BinaryCodec[Person]`, so code that works with one works with the other.

### Round-Trip a Single Value

`BinaryCodec#encode` returns bytes, and `BinaryCodec#decode` returns an `Either[DecodeError, Person]`, so the two round trips chain in a for-comprehension:

```scala
val michelle = Person("Michelle", 32)
// michelle: Person = Person(name = "Michelle", age = 32)

val roundTrip: Either[DecodeError, Person] =
  for {
    fromJson     <- jsonCodec.decode(jsonCodec.encode(michelle))
    fromProtobuf <- protobufCodec.decode(protobufCodec.encode(fromJson))
  } yield fromProtobuf
// roundTrip: Either[DecodeError, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "Michelle", age = 32)
// )

roundTrip == Right(michelle)
// res0: Boolean = true
```

### Convert JSON to Protobuf

The same chaining converts data between formats. To turn a JSON payload into Protobuf bytes, decode it with the JSON codec and encode the result with the Protobuf codec:

```scala
def jsonToProtobuf(json: Chunk[Byte]): Either[DecodeError, Chunk[Byte]] =
  jsonCodec.decode(json).map(protobufCodec.encode)

val incoming: Chunk[Byte] = Chunk.fromArray("""{"name":"Michelle","age":32}""".getBytes("UTF-8"))
```

Decoding the converted bytes with the Protobuf codec gives the person back:

```scala
jsonToProtobuf(incoming).flatMap(protobufCodec.decode)
// res1: Either[DecodeError, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "Michelle", age = 32)
// )
```

### Round-Trip a Stream

For a stream of values, the JSON codec's `BinaryCodec#streamEncoder` and `BinaryCodec#streamDecoder` pipelines keep the values apart. The Protobuf codec's stream decoder reads each chunk as one message, so the stream encodes and decodes each value on its own with `ZStream#map` and `ZStream#mapZIO`. The following program prints each step and checks that the people survive both round trips:

```scala
object CombiningExample extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val people: Chunk[Person] = Chunk(Person("Michelle", 32), Person("John", 42))

  def run: ZIO[Any, DecodeError, Unit] =
    for {
      result <- ZStream
                  .fromChunk(people)
                  .tap(person => ZIO.debug(s"input object is: $person"))
                  .via(jsonCodec.streamEncoder)
                  .via(jsonCodec.streamDecoder)
                  .tap(person => ZIO.debug(s"object after json roundtrip: $person"))
                  .map(protobufCodec.encode)
                  .mapZIO(bytes => ZIO.fromEither(protobufCodec.decode(bytes)))
                  .tap(person => ZIO.debug(s"person after protobuf roundtrip: $person"))
                  .runCollect
      _      <- ZIO.debug(s"are the old people the new people? ${result == people}")
    } yield ()
}
```

The [How to Encode and Decode Streams](../integration-with-zio-streams.md) guide explains why the Protobuf step works per value, and shows a framing scheme for sending many Protobuf values over a plain byte stream.

---

## How to Map a DTO to a Domain Object

In this guide, we read a `Person` from JSON that arrives in the shape of a `PersonDTO`, a data transfer object (DTO) with different fields. We describe `Person` as a transformation of the `PersonDTO` schema once, and then use that one schema to decode DTO-shaped JSON straight into `Person`, to encode a `Person` back into the DTO shape, and to convert `PersonDTO` values that are already in memory.

### The Problem

Layered applications keep the types they send over the network apart from the types their business logic uses. A service might receive people as JSON in the shape of `PersonDTO`, with the name split into two fields and the birthday as a tuple, while its domain type `Person` holds one name and a `LocalDate`. Converting between the two takes a pair of hand-written functions:

```scala
import java.time.LocalDate

final case class PersonDTO(firstName: String, lastName: String, birthday: (Int, Int, Int))
final case class Person(name: String, birthdate: LocalDate)

def toPerson(dto: PersonDTO): Person = {
  val (year, month, day) = dto.birthday
  Person(s"${dto.firstName} ${dto.lastName}", LocalDate.of(year, month, day))
}

def toDTO(person: Person): PersonDTO = {
  val names = person.name.split(" ")
  PersonDTO(
    names.head,
    names.last,
    (person.birthdate.getYear, person.birthdate.getMonthValue, person.birthdate.getDayOfMonth)
  )
}
```

Every place that reads a person then needs two steps: decode a `PersonDTO` with a codec for the DTO, and remember to call `toPerson`. A codec derived for `Person` itself cannot help, because it expects the fields `name` and `birthdate`, not the fields of the DTO.

With ZIO Schema, the conversion becomes part of a schema for `Person`. Any codec built from that schema reads and writes the DTO shape and hands us a `Person` directly.

### Prerequisites

The examples use the JSON codec, which also brings in schema derivation:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"      % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json" % "1.9.2"
)
```

On Scala 2, schema derivation also needs `scala-reflect` at compile time, as the [Installation](../index.md#installation) section shows.

### Defining the DTO and the Domain Type

Both types get a derived schema in their companion objects:

```scala
import java.time.LocalDate

import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec

final case class PersonDTO(firstName: String, lastName: String, birthday: (Int, Int, Int))

object PersonDTO {
  implicit val schema: Schema[PersonDTO] = DeriveSchema.gen[PersonDTO]
}

final case class Person(name: String, birthdate: LocalDate)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}
```

### Describing Person in Terms of PersonDTO

`Schema#transform` turns a schema for one type into a schema for another, given a function in each direction. Applied to the schema of `PersonDTO`, it gives a schema for `Person` that has the structure of the DTO:

```scala
val personFromDTO: Schema[Person] =
  PersonDTO.schema.transform(
    dto => {
      val (year, month, day) = dto.birthday
      Person(s"${dto.firstName} ${dto.lastName}", LocalDate.of(year, month, day))
    },
    (person: Person) => {
      val names = person.name.split(" ")
      PersonDTO(
        names.head,
        names.last,
        (person.birthdate.getYear, person.birthdate.getMonthValue, person.birthdate.getDayOfMonth)
      )
    }
  )
```

We keep `personFromDTO` as a plain value rather than an implicit one, so the derived `Person.schema` stays the default schema for `Person`, and we pass `personFromDTO` explicitly wherever the DTO shape is needed. The reverse function splits the name at spaces, so a name without a space becomes both the first and the last name. [Transforming Schemas](../operations/transforming-schemas.md) covers `Schema#transform` and `Schema#transformOrFail`, which lets a conversion fail with an error message.

### Decoding DTO-Shaped JSON into Person

In the JSON shape of `PersonDTO`, the three-element tuple appears as nested arrays, `[[year, month], day]`:

```scala
val json: String =
  """{"firstName":"John","lastName":"Doe","birthday":[[1981,7],13]}"""
```

A JSON codec built from `personFromDTO` decodes this JSON straight into a `Person`:

```scala
JsonCodec.jsonCodec(personFromDTO).decodeJson(json)
// res1: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "John Doe", birthdate = 1981-07-13)
// )
```

The codec derived from `Person.schema` expects the fields of `Person`, so it rejects the same input:

```scala
JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Person.schema).decodeJson(json)
// res2: Either[String, Person] = Left(value = ".name(missing)")
```

### Encoding Person in the DTO Shape

The same schema works in the other direction. Encoding a `Person` with it applies the reverse function and writes the fields of the DTO:

```scala
println(
  JsonCodec.jsonCodec(personFromDTO).encodeJson(Person("Jane Roe", LocalDate.of(1990, 1, 2)), None)
)
// {"firstName":"Jane","lastName":"Roe","birthday":[[1990,1],2]}
```

### Converting DTO Values in Memory

When a `PersonDTO` value is already in memory, for example because another layer of the application passes it in, no codec is involved. `Schema#migrate` builds a conversion function from one schema to another. It returns a `Left` with an error message when the structures of the two schemas cannot be reconciled, and otherwise a function that converts each value:

```scala
val dtoToPerson: Either[String, PersonDTO => Either[String, Person]] =
  PersonDTO.schema.migrate(personFromDTO)
```

Both schemas describe the same record structure, so the migration step changes nothing, and `personFromDTO` performs the mapping when it reads the result:

```scala
dtoToPerson.flatMap(convert => convert(PersonDTO("John", "Doe", (1981, 7, 13))))
// res4: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "John Doe", birthdate = 1981-07-13)
// )
```

[Schema Migration](../operations/schema-migration.md) explains how migrations handle schemas whose structures differ, such as an older version of a DTO.

### Going Further

- [Transforming Schemas](../operations/transforming-schemas.md) describes `Schema#transform`, `Schema#transformOrFail`, and related operations.
- [JSON Codecs](../derivations/codecs/json.md) covers the JSON codec and its configuration.
- [Combining Different Encoders](combining-different-encoders.md) uses the same schema with several codecs.

## Getting Started(Zio-schema)

On this page we install ZIO Schema and write a first program. We describe a `Person` case class with a schema, then use that one schema to encode and decode JSON, to validate values, and to look at a value without knowing its type. Each step builds on the one before it, so read them in order.

### Add the Dependencies

The first program needs the core module and the JSON codec module. We add both to `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"      % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json" % "1.9.2"
)
```

The JSON module depends on `zio-schema-derivation`, which provides `DeriveSchema`, so we do not add it separately. On Scala 2, the derivation macros also need `scala-reflect` at compile time. On Scala 3, the project must use Scala 3.9 or later. The [Installation](index.md#installation) section shows how to add `scala-reflect`, and [Modules](index.md#modules) lists the other modules with the platforms they support, ready to copy, with `%%%` for Scala.js and Scala Native.

### 1. Define a Case Class and Derive Its Schema

A `Schema[A]` is a value that describes the structure of `A`: its name, its fields, and the types of those fields. We rarely write one by hand. Instead, we let the compiler derive it from the case class. The syntax depends on the Scala version:

  

**Scala 2**

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Person(
  @validate(Validation.minLength(1)) name: String,
  @validate(Validation.between(0, 150)) age: Int
)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}
```

  
  

**Scala 3**

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Person(
  @validate(Validation.minLength(1)) name: String,
  @validate(Validation.between(0, 150)) age: Int
) derives Schema
```

  

On Scala 2, the `implicit val` in the companion object makes the schema available wherever a `Schema[Person]` is needed, without an import. On Scala 3, the `derives Schema` clause does the same thing. The `@validate` annotations attach rules to the fields; step 4 uses them.

### 2. Encode a Value as JSON

The `zio-schema-json` module turns any schema into a JSON codec. `JsonCodec.jsonCodec` returns a ZIO JSON `JsonCodec`, which can both encode and decode. We build the codec once and keep it:

```scala
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec

val personCodec = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Person.schema)
```

Encoding a `Person` produces its JSON text. The field names come from the case class:

```scala
val alice = Person("Alice", 30)
// alice: Person = Person(name = "Alice", age = 30)

println(personCodec.encodeJson(alice, None).toString)
// {"name":"Alice","age":30}
```

### 3. Decode JSON into a Value

The same codec reads JSON back. `JsonCodec#decodeJson` does not throw: it returns a `Right` with the value, or a `Left` with an error message:

```scala
personCodec.decodeJson("""{"name":"Bob","age":25}""")
// res1: Either[String, Person] = Right(value = Person(name = "Bob", age = 25))

personCodec.decodeJson("""{"name":"Bob"}""")
// res2: Either[String, Person] = Left(value = ".age(missing)")
```

The second input has no `age` field, so decoding fails. Some fields may be left out: a missing `Option` field decodes as `None`, a missing collection as an empty one, and a missing field that has a default value in the case class takes that default. [Automatic Schema Derivation](automatic-schema-derivation.md) shows the default values.

### 4. Validate Values

Decoding checks the shape of the input, not the `@validate` rules. This input has the right shape, so it decodes, even though the name is empty and the age is out of range:

```scala
val decoded = personCodec.decodeJson("""{"name":"","age":200}""")
// decoded: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "", age = 200)
// )
```

To check the rules, we call `Schema.validate` on the value. It returns one `ValidationError` per broken rule, and an empty `Chunk` when the value is valid:

```scala
decoded.map(person => Schema.validate(person).map(_.message))
// res3: Either[String, zio.Chunk[String]] = Right(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     "Expected the length of  to be at least 1 characters but was 0 characters.",
//     "200 should be equal to 150",
//     "200 should be less than 150"
//   )
// )

Schema.validate(alice).isEmpty
// res4: Boolean = true
```

In a real program, we decode first and validate second, and reject the input when either step fails.

### 5. Convert a Value to `DynamicValue`

A `DynamicValue` holds any value in a generic form: records, enums, sequences, and primitives, with no Scala type attached. Code that does not know about `Person`, such as a generic logger or a migration tool, can still read it. `Schema#toDynamic` converts a value to this form:

```scala
val dynamic: DynamicValue = Person.schema.toDynamic(alice)
```

A record becomes a `DynamicValue.Record` that maps each field name to a `DynamicValue`. We can list the field names without referring to `Person`, and `Schema#fromDynamic` turns the generic value back into a typed one:

```scala
dynamic match {
  case DynamicValue.Record(_, values) => values.keys.toList
  case _                              => Nil
}
// res5: List[String] = List("name", "age")

Person.schema.fromDynamic(dynamic)
// res6: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "Alice", age = 30)
// )
```

### Next Steps

You now have one schema that drives JSON encoding, validation, and dynamic values. To go further:

- [Your First Schema](tutorial/first-schema.md) is a longer tutorial that also covers binary codecs and diffing and patching values.
- [Automatic Schema Derivation](automatic-schema-derivation.md) explains what `DeriveSchema` produces, and [Schema Derivation on Scala 2 and Scala 3](derivations/derivation-scala-versions.md) covers `derives Schema`, Scala 3 enums, and union types.
- [Schema Annotations](schema-annotations.md) lists the annotations that rename fields, set defaults, and change the encoding.
- [JSON Codecs](derivations/codecs/json.md) describes the JSON configuration options, and [Codecs](derivations/codecs/index.md) lists the other formats.
- [Validating Types](operations/validating-types.md) and [Dynamic Data Representation](operations/dynamic-data-representation.md) cover steps 4 and 5 in depth.
- [Schema Methods](reference/schema-methods.md) lists everything a schema can do.

## Write a Custom Codec

The format modules cover JSON, Protobuf, Avro, and other common formats. When you need a different format, such as one line of text per record, you can implement the `Codec` trait yourself. A codec has four methods: `Codec#encode`, `Codec#decode`, `Codec#streamEncoder`, and `Codec#streamDecoder`. The [Codec Core Types](../reference/codec-core.md) page describes each trait.

This guide writes a codec that stores a `Person` as one line, `name,age`, and reads it back.

### Prerequisites

The `Codec` trait lives in the core module, and `DeriveSchema` in the derivation module:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"            % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-derivation" % "1.9.2"
)
```

### Define the Model

The model is an ordinary case class with a schema, so the rest of the library can use it:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.codec.{Codec, DecodeError}

case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}
```

### Implement the Codec

The codec extends `Codec[String, String, Person]`. The first type parameter is the whole output, a `String`. The second is the element type of a stream, which is also a `String`, one line per element. The third is the value type, `Person`.

The following class encodes a person by joining its fields with a comma, and decodes a line by splitting it:

```scala
final class PersonLineCodec extends Codec[String, String, Person] {

  override def encode(person: Person): String =
    s"${person.name},${person.age}"

  override def decode(line: String): Either[DecodeError, Person] =
    line.split(",", 2).toList match {
      case name :: age :: Nil if age.nonEmpty && age.forall(_.isDigit) =>
        Right(Person(name, age.toInt))
      case _ =>
        Left(DecodeError.MalformedField(Schema[Person], s"expected name,age but got: $line"))
    }

  override def streamEncoder: ZPipeline[Any, Nothing, Person, String] =
    ZPipeline.map(encode)

  override def streamDecoder: ZPipeline[Any, DecodeError, String, Person] =
    ZPipeline.mapZIO(line => ZIO.fromEither(decode(line)))
}
```

The `PersonLineCodec#decode` method returns a `Left` for input that does not match the format, so the caller decides how to report the error. The stream methods reuse the single-value methods: `ZPipeline.map` applies `PersonLineCodec#encode` to each element, and `ZPipeline.mapZIO` applies `PersonLineCodec#decode` and turns a `Left` into a failure of the stream.

This codec writes its own format and does not read the schema. Use it when the format is fixed by another system. For a format that should follow the model automatically, use one of the built-in codecs instead.

### Use the Codec

We create an instance of the codec:

```scala
val lineCodec = new PersonLineCodec
```

Encoding a person joins the name and the age with a comma:

```scala
lineCodec.encode(Person("John", 42))
// res0: String = "John,42"
```

Decoding a valid line gives the person back:

```scala
lineCodec.decode("John,42")
// res1: Either[DecodeError, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "John", age = 42)
// )
```

A line that does not match the format gives a `Left`:

```scala
lineCodec.decode("John").left.map(_.getMessage)
// res2: Either[String, Person] = Left(
//   value = "expected name,age but got: John"
// )
```

To process a stream of people, the streaming methods build a pipeline. The following program encodes two people, decodes the lines back, and collects the result:

```scala
val roundTrip: ZIO[Any, DecodeError, Chunk[Person]] =
  ZStream(Person("John", 42), Person("Jane", 34))
    .via(lineCodec.streamEncoder)
    .via(lineCodec.streamDecoder)
    .runCollect
```

Running the program with `Unsafe`, so that the page can print its result, gives both people back:

```scala
Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
  Runtime.default.unsafe.run(roundTrip).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
}
// res3: Chunk[Person] = IndexedSeq(
//   Person(name = "John", age = 42),
//   Person(name = "Jane", age = 34)
// )
```

### Where to Go Next

- [Codec Core Types](../reference/codec-core.md) describes the traits this guide implements.
- [How to Encode and Decode Streams](../integration-with-zio-streams.md) shows how to stream values with the built-in codecs.
- [Write a Custom Deriver](./custom-deriver.md) shows how to derive your own type class from a schema.

## Write a Custom Deriver

In this guide, we write a `Deriver` for a type class that counts the primitive values inside a type, so that every type with a schema gets an instance without a hand-written one. A `Person` with a name and an age has two. We implement one method for each kind of schema, derive instances for nested types, replace the derived instance with a hand-written one where needed, cache instances, and call the deriver from generic code.

### The Problem

A type class needs an instance for every type that uses it. Written by hand, each instance repeats knowledge that the type definition already holds, and every new field means another edit:

```scala
trait LeafCount[A] {
  def count: Int
}

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)
final case class Team(members: List[Person], lead: Option[Person])

object LeafCount {
  def apply[A](n: Int): LeafCount[A] = new LeafCount[A] {
    def count: Int = n
  }

  // name and age
  implicit val person: LeafCount[Person] = LeafCount(2)

  // the members and the lead each count as one Person
  implicit val team: LeafCount[Team] = LeafCount(person.count + person.count)
}
```

Nothing checks these numbers. Adding an `email` field to `Person` leaves both instances silently wrong, and with dozens of types the instances drift out of date one by one.

A schema already describes the structure of each type. A `Deriver` builds the instances from that description: `DeriveSchema.gen` goes from a type to its schema, and a deriver goes one step further, from the schema to an instance of your type class, such as a pretty-printer, a validator, or a count of fields. You write one method for each kind of schema, and the `Derive.derive` macro walks the structure of the type and calls those methods. `DeriveSchema.gen` itself is a separate macro and does not use `Deriver`.

### Prerequisites

`Deriver`, `Derive`, and `Factory` live in the `zio-schema-derivation` module:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"            % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-derivation" % "1.9.2"
)
```

On Scala 2, the derivation macros also need `scala-reflect` at compile time, as the [Installation](../index.md#installation) section shows. The guide assumes you know how to derive a schema with `DeriveSchema.gen`, as [Automatic Schema Derivation](../automatic-schema-derivation.md) explains.

### Define the Type Class

The type class is an ordinary trait with one type parameter. It has a single method, `count`:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.Deriver.WrappedF

trait LeafCount[A] {
  def count: Int
}

def known[A](n: Int): LeafCount[A] = new LeafCount[A] {
  def count: Int = n
}
```

The `known` helper builds an instance from a number. The deriver uses it for every kind of schema.

### Implement the Deriver

A `Deriver[F]` is parameterized by the type class `F`. The seven methods below are abstract, so every custom deriver must implement them. Each receives the nested instances for the parts of the type it contains:

- `derivePrimitive` handles a standard type, such as `String` or `Int`. A primitive has one value, so it counts as 1.
- `deriveRecord` handles a case class. Its `fields` are the instances for each field, and the count is their sum.
- `deriveEnum` handles a sealed trait. The count is the largest count of its cases.
- `deriveOption` and `deriveSequence` handle `Option` and collections. They count the same values as the element type.
- `deriveMap` handles a map. It counts the keys and the values.
- `deriveTransformedRecord` handles a case class with more than 22 fields. Its schema is a `GenericRecord` (a map from field names to values) wrapped in a transformation to the case class, so the method receives both. It counts the fields of the record.

The `summoned` argument is an instance of the type class that the compiler finds at the `Derive.derive` call site (an implicit value in scope or in a companion object), if there is one. The deriver decides whether to use it. Each method below returns it when present, so a hand-written instance replaces the derived one. The [Use Hand-Written Instances](#use-hand-written-instances) section shows when the compiler looks for one:

```scala
val leafCounter: Deriver[LeafCount] = new Deriver[LeafCount] {

  override def derivePrimitive[A](st: StandardType[A], summoned: => Option[LeafCount[A]]): LeafCount[A] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(1))

  override def deriveRecord[A](
    record: Schema.Record[A],
    fields: => Chunk[WrappedF[LeafCount, _]],
    summoned: => Option[LeafCount[A]]
  ): LeafCount[A] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(fields.map(_.unwrap.count).sum))

  override def deriveEnum[A](
    `enum`: Schema.Enum[A],
    cases: => Chunk[WrappedF[LeafCount, _]],
    summoned: => Option[LeafCount[A]]
  ): LeafCount[A] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(cases.map(_.unwrap.count).foldLeft(0)(math.max)))

  override def deriveOption[A](
    option: Schema.Optional[A],
    inner: => LeafCount[A],
    summoned: => Option[LeafCount[Option[A]]]
  ): LeafCount[Option[A]] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(inner.count))

  override def deriveSequence[C[_], A](
    sequence: Schema.Sequence[C[A], A, _],
    inner: => LeafCount[A],
    summoned: => Option[LeafCount[C[A]]]
  ): LeafCount[C[A]] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(inner.count))

  override def deriveMap[K, V](
    map: Schema.Map[K, V],
    key: => LeafCount[K],
    value: => LeafCount[V],
    summoned: => Option[LeafCount[Map[K, V]]]
  ): LeafCount[Map[K, V]] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(key.count + value.count))

  override def deriveTransformedRecord[A, B](
    record: Schema.Record[A],
    transform: Schema.Transform[A, B, _],
    fields: => Chunk[WrappedF[LeafCount, _]],
    summoned: => Option[LeafCount[B]]
  ): LeafCount[B] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(fields.map(_.unwrap.count).sum))
}
```

The `fields` and `cases` arguments are lazy, so the deriver reads them only when it needs them. Each `unwrap` call gives the instance for one field or case.

### Derive an Instance

The `Derive.derive` method applies a deriver to a type. It needs the type's schema in scope, which the companion object provides. We define two models, one of which contains a list and an option:

```scala
case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}

case class Team(members: List[Person], lead: Option[Person])

object Team {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Team] = DeriveSchema.gen[Team]
}
```

Next, we derive the instances and read their counts:

```scala
Derive.derive[LeafCount, Person](leafCounter).count
// res1: Int = 2

Derive.derive[LeafCount, Team](leafCounter).count
// res2: Int = 4
```

A `Person` has two primitive values. A `Team` has the members, which are a list of persons, plus the lead, which is an optional person. The list counts its element type, so the members contribute 2, and the lead contributes 2. The total is 4.

`Derive.derive` follows the Scala type and expects the schema in scope to have the shape that `DeriveSchema.gen` produces for it. A type it does not recognize, such as a plain class with a hand-written schema, needs a summoned instance; without one, `Deriver#deriveUnknown` throws an `IllegalArgumentException` at runtime.

On Scala 3, a deriver also has a `Deriver#derive` method, so `leafCounter.derive[Person]` is the same as `Derive.derive[LeafCount, Person](leafCounter)`. [How to Use ZIO Schema with Scala 3](scala-3.md#derive-your-own-type-class-with-derives) shows how to let a type write `derives LeafCount`.

### Override the Optional Methods

Besides the seven abstract methods, a few methods have default implementations that you can override when a kind of schema needs special handling:

- `deriveEither` handles `Either`. By default, it treats it as an enum with two cases and calls `deriveEnum`.
- `deriveSet` handles `Set`. By default, it calls `deriveSequence`.
- `deriveTupleN` handles tuples. By default, it treats the tuple as a record and calls `deriveRecord`.
- `derivePrimitiveAlias` handles a Scala 3 opaque type whose underlying type is a primitive. By default, it returns the summoned instance and throws an `IllegalArgumentException` when there is none.
- `deriveUnknown` handles a type that `Derive.derive` does not recognize. By default, it returns the summoned instance and throws an `IllegalArgumentException` when there is none.

### Use Hand-Written Instances

The compiler looks for a summoned instance for every type nested inside the derived type, but never for the top-level type passed to `Derive.derive`. That top-level instance is usually the one being defined, so looking it up would find the definition itself.

To see the difference, we give `Secret` a hand-written instance that counts nothing, so secrets do not show up in the count:

```scala
case class Secret(value: String, hint: String)

object Secret {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Secret]       = DeriveSchema.gen[Secret]
  implicit val leafCount: LeafCount[Secret] = known(0)
}

case class Account(owner: String, password: Secret)

object Account {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Account] = DeriveSchema.gen[Account]
}
```

Inside `Account`, the deriver receives the hand-written instance for `password` and returns it. When `Secret` is the top-level type, `summoned` is `None`, so the deriver counts its two fields:

```scala
Derive.derive[LeafCount, Account](leafCounter).count
// res3: Int = 1

Derive.derive[LeafCount, Secret](leafCounter).count
// res4: Int = 2
```

Our deriver checks `summoned` in every method. A deriver that should always prefer a hand-written instance can skip that check and call `Deriver#autoAcceptSummoned` instead. It returns a deriver that uses the summoned instance whenever there is one, and calls the original methods only when there is none:

```scala
val acceptingCounter: Deriver[LeafCount] = leafCounter.autoAcceptSummoned
```

### Reuse Instances with `Deriver#cached`

Each `Derive.derive` call derives every nested instance again. `Deriver#cached` returns a deriver that stores each instance it builds and returns the stored one the next time the same type comes up, across all calls that use it. Because `Deriver#cached` is a `lazy val`, calling it twice on the same deriver returns the same cache:

```scala
val cachedCounter: Deriver[LeafCount] = leafCounter.cached
```

Deriving `Team` after `Person` reuses the `Person` instance from the first call:

```scala
Derive.derive[LeafCount, Person](cachedCounter).count
// res5: Int = 2

Derive.derive[LeafCount, Team](cachedCounter).count
// res6: Int = 4
```

:::caution
The cache identifies a case class or sealed trait by its `TypeId`, which does not include type arguments. A cached deriver therefore returns the same instance for `Box[Int]` and `Box[String]`, whichever it derived first. Use an uncached deriver for generic types.
:::

### Write Generic Methods with `Factory`

`Derive.derive` is a macro, so it needs the concrete type at the place where it is called. A generic method such as `def leafCountOf[A]` cannot call it with its own type parameter `A`. The `Factory` type class moves that macro call to the caller: a `Factory[A]` is derived automatically wherever `A` is a concrete type, and `Factory#derive` applies a deriver to `A`.

We add a `Factory` context bound next to the `Schema` bound:

```scala
def leafCountOf[A: Factory: Schema]: LeafCount[A] =
  implicitly[Factory[A]].derive[LeafCount](leafCounter)
```

The caller passes a concrete type, and the compiler derives its `Factory`:

```scala
leafCountOf[Team].count
// res7: Int = 4
```

On Scala 2, the code that the `Factory` macro generates refers to `Factory`, `Deriver`, `Schema`, and `Derive` by their short names, so the code that calls a method like `leafCountOf` needs `import zio.schema._`.

### Where to Go Next

- [Automatic Schema Derivation](../automatic-schema-derivation.md) describes the built-in derivation of schemas.
- [How to Use ZIO Schema with Scala 3](scala-3.md) derives `LeafCount` with a `derives` clause and handles opaque types in a deriver.
- [Write a Custom Codec](./custom-codec.md) shows the other common extension point.
- [Schema Methods](../reference/schema-methods.md) lists what a derived schema can do.

## How to Work with Schemaless Data

In this guide, we handle data whose shape we do not know at compile time: webhook events from a third-party service, where every event type carries a different `data` object. We decode the JSON into a `DynamicValue`, read and redact fields in it, turn parts of it into a case class when we know their type, and store the whole event in a binary format.

`DynamicValue` is ZIO Schema's format-neutral value tree. Records keep their field names, sequences keep their elements, and every leaf keeps its standard type, so the same tree can come from JSON and go out as MessagePack, or become a typed value through a schema.

### The Problem

A service that receives arbitrary JSON usually parses it into the JSON library's own syntax tree and digs through it by hand. For example, reading the plan of a customer event with the ZIO JSON tree looks like this:

```scala
import zio.json.ast.Json

val raw = """{"id":"evt_1","type":"customer.created","data":{"email":"ana@example.com","plan":"pro"}}"""

val plan: Option[String] =
  Json.decoder.decodeJson(raw).toOption.flatMap {
    case Json.Obj(fields) =>
      fields.collectFirst { case ("data", Json.Obj(data)) => data }.flatMap { data =>
        data.collectFirst { case ("plan", Json.Str(plan)) => plan }
      }
    case _                => None
  }
```

That tree belongs to one format. Turning the payload into a case class, or writing it to a binary store, means another hand-written conversion for every target. With `DynamicValue`, the JSON codec builds the tree, and the same schemas and codecs that serve typed data take it from there.

### Prerequisites

The examples use the core module with the JSON and MessagePack codecs:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"          % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json"     % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-msg-pack" % "1.9.2"
)
```

The [DynamicValue](../operations/dynamic-data-representation.md) reference lists every case of the tree, and [Dynamic Data Representation](../operations/dynamic-data-representation.md) explains the idea behind it.

### Decode Unknown JSON into a DynamicValue

`Schema.dynamicValue` is the schema of a `DynamicValue`. By default, codecs write it in a self-describing form that records the name of every case, which is not what a third-party service sends. The `directDynamicMapping` annotation switches the JSON codec to plain JSON: objects become records, arrays become sequences, and `null` becomes `NoneValue`. We build that schema and its codec once:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.directDynamicMapping
import zio.schema.codec.{JsonCodec, MessagePackCodec}

val anyJson: Schema[DynamicValue] = Schema.dynamicValue.annotate(directDynamicMapping())

val anyJsonCodec = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(anyJson)

val raw: String =
  """{"id":"evt_1","type":"customer.created","data":{"email":"ana@example.com","plan":"pro","seats":3,"tags":["beta"]}}"""
```

Decoding the event gives a tree of records, sequences, and primitives:

```scala
val decoded: Either[String, DynamicValue] = anyJsonCodec.decodeJson(raw)
// decoded: Either[String, DynamicValue] = Right(
//   value = Record(
//     id = Structural,
//     values = ListMap(
//       "id" -> Primitive(value = "evt_1", standardType = string),
//       "type" -> Primitive(value = "customer.created", standardType = string),
//       "data" -> Record(
//         id = Structural,
//         values = ListMap(
//           "email" -> Primitive(value = "ana@example.com", standardType = string),
//           "plan" -> Primitive(value = "pro", standardType = string),
//           "seats" -> Primitive(value = 3, standardType = bigDecimal),
//           "tags" -> Sequence(
//             values = IndexedSeq(
//               Primitive(value = "beta", standardType = string)
//             )
//           )
//         )
//       )
//     )
//   )
// )
```

JSON has no field types, so every object becomes a `Record` with the `TypeId.Structural` id, every string a `String` primitive, every boolean a `Boolean` primitive, and every number a `java.math.BigDecimal` primitive. We keep the decoded event for the next sections:

```scala
val event: DynamicValue = decoded.getOrElse(DynamicValue.NoneValue)
```

Without `directDynamicMapping`, the same codec expects the self-describing form. It wraps each value in an object named after its case:

```scala
println(JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Schema.dynamicValue).encodeJson(DynamicValue("pro"), None))
// {"String":"pro"}
```

Use the plain `Schema.dynamicValue` when both sides use ZIO Schema and the tree must keep every detail. Use the annotated schema for JSON that other systems produce or read.

### Read Fields from the Tree

`DynamicValue` is a sealed trait, so reading it is pattern matching. The following helper follows a path of field names through nested records, and a second one reads a string leaf:

```scala
def field(value: DynamicValue, path: String*): Option[DynamicValue] =
  path.foldLeft(Option(value)) {
    case (Some(DynamicValue.Record(_, fields)), name) => fields.get(name)
    case _                                            => None
  }

def text(value: DynamicValue): Option[String] =
  value match {
    case DynamicValue.Primitive(s: String, _) => Some(s)
    case _                                    => None
  }
```

With these helpers, a service can route an event by its type and read the fields it cares about, without a class for each event type:

```scala
field(event, "type").flatMap(text)
// res2: Option[String] = Some(value = "customer.created")
field(event, "data", "plan").flatMap(text)
// res3: Option[String] = Some(value = "pro")
field(event, "data", "seats")
// res4: Option[DynamicValue] = Some(
//   value = Primitive(value = 3, standardType = bigDecimal)
// )
field(event, "data", "missing")
// res5: Option[DynamicValue] = None
```

### Change Values in the Tree

A `DynamicValue` is immutable, so a change builds a new tree. The following function masks every field whose name is in a set, at any depth, before the event goes to a log:

```scala
def redact(value: DynamicValue, secret: Set[String]): DynamicValue =
  value match {
    case DynamicValue.Record(id, fields) =>
      DynamicValue.Record(
        id,
        fields.map { case (name, fieldValue) =>
          val updated: DynamicValue =
            if (secret.contains(name)) DynamicValue.Primitive("***", StandardType.StringType)
            else redact(fieldValue, secret)
          name -> updated
        }
      )
    case DynamicValue.Sequence(values)   => DynamicValue.Sequence(values.map(redact(_, secret)))
    case DynamicValue.SomeValue(inner)   => DynamicValue.SomeValue(redact(inner, secret))
    case other                           => other
  }

val redacted: DynamicValue = redact(event, Set("email"))
```

The same codec writes the changed tree back as plain JSON, with the fields in their original order:

```scala
println(anyJsonCodec.encodeJson(redacted, None))
// {"id":"evt_1","type":"customer.created","data":{"email":"***","plan":"pro","seats":3,"tags":["beta"]}}
```

Plain JSON has no place for some kinds of node, so in direct mode the JSON encoder throws for them; [Schema.Dynamic](../operations/dynamic-data-representation.md#schemadynamic) lists which. A tree decoded from JSON never contains them. A tree built from a typed value can, for example from a sealed trait or a `Map`; encode such a tree with the plain `Schema.dynamicValue` instead.

### Convert Between Typed and Dynamic Values

When we do know the type, `Schema#toDynamic` turns a value into a tree and `Schema#fromDynamic` turns it back. The tree works with the same helpers as the JSON one, so the redaction above also applies to typed values:

```scala
final case class Customer(email: String, plan: String, seats: Int)

object Customer {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Customer] = DeriveSchema.gen[Customer]
}

val customerTree: DynamicValue = Customer.schema.toDynamic(Customer("ana@example.com", "pro", 3))
```

Redacting the tree and converting it back gives a typed value with the masked field:

```scala
Customer.schema.fromDynamic(redact(customerTree, Set("email")))
// res7: Either[String, Customer] = Right(
//   value = Customer(email = "***", plan = "pro", seats = 3)
// )
```

:::caution[Types That Do Not Convert Back]
For most types, `schema.fromDynamic(schema.toDynamic(x))` returns `Right(x)`. It returns a `Left` for `NonEmptyChunk`, ZIO Prelude's `NonEmptySet` and `NonEmptyMap`, and `Fallback`, including when they appear as fields of a case class. Keep such fields out of data that passes through `DynamicValue`, or model them as `Chunk`, `Set`, `Map`, or `Either` there and convert at the edges. [Round-Trip Limits](../operations/dynamic-data-representation.md#round-trip-limits) shows the failure.
:::

### Bind Dynamic JSON to a Case Class

Once a service knows which event type it has, it often wants the `data` object as a case class. `Schema#fromDynamic` requires each primitive to have exactly the standard type of the target field, and the JSON tree stores every number as a `BigDecimal`, so binding it directly fails on the `seats` field:

```scala
field(event, "data").map(data => Customer.schema.fromDynamic(data))
// res8: Option[Either[String, Customer]] = Some(
//   value = Left(
//     value = "Failed to cast Primitive(3,bigDecimal) to schema Primitive(int,Chunk())"
//   )
// )
```

The reliable route goes through JSON once more: encode the subtree with the direct codec, and decode the text with the codec of the target type. The typed JSON decoder parses numbers as the field types require and ignores fields the case class does not have, such as `tags`:

```scala
def bind[A](value: DynamicValue)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Either[String, A] =
  JsonCodec.jsonCodec(schema).decodeJson(anyJsonCodec.encodeJson(value, None))
```

The same `data` object now binds to a `Customer`:

```scala
field(event, "data").map(data => bind[Customer](data))
// res9: Option[Either[String, Customer]] = Some(
//   value = Right(
//     value = Customer(email = "ana@example.com", plan = "pro", seats = 3)
//   )
// )
```

Use `Schema#fromDynamic` directly for trees that came from `Schema#toDynamic`, where the standard types already match, and the JSON route for trees that came from JSON.

### Store the Tree in a Binary Format

The plain `Schema.dynamicValue` works with every codec, so a `DynamicValue` can move to a binary format without knowing its shape. The following codec stores the event as MessagePack in the self-describing form:

```scala
val storedCodec = MessagePackCodec.messagePackCodec(Schema.dynamicValue)

val stored = storedCodec.encode(event)
```

Decoding the bytes gives back the same tree, which the direct JSON codec can write as JSON again:

```scala
storedCodec.decode(stored) == Right(event)
// res10: Boolean = true

storedCodec.decode(stored).foreach(tree => println(anyJsonCodec.encodeJson(tree, None)))
// {"id":"evt_1","type":"customer.created","data":{"email":"ana@example.com","plan":"pro","seats":3,"tags":["beta"]}}
```

:::caution[Byte Values in the Self-Describing Form]
The self-describing form, which every codec uses for the plain `Schema.dynamicValue`, has no case for a `Primitive` that holds a `Byte`. The value is lost: the JSON codec, for example, writes it as `{}`. A tree decoded from JSON never holds a `Byte`, but one built with `Schema#toDynamic` from a type with a `Byte` field does. Convert such fields to `Short` or `Int` before storing the tree, or, for JSON, use the annotated schema from the start of this guide, which writes a `Byte` as a number that reads back as a `BigDecimal`.
:::

### Going Further

- [DynamicValue](../operations/dynamic-data-representation.md) lists every case of the tree and the round-trip limits.
- [Schema Migration](../operations/schema-migration.md) changes a `DynamicValue` from one schema version to another with migration steps.
- [How to Send a Schema over the Wire](send-schema-over-the-wire.md) sends the structure of a type along with the data, so the receiver can decode it without the class.
- [JSON Codecs](../derivations/codecs/json.md) and [MessagePack Codecs](../derivations/codecs/message-pack.md) describe the codecs used here.

## How to Write a Schema-Driven Codec

In this guide, we write a codec for a simple `key=value` text format, one entry per line, that works for any type with a schema. We write it once, by pattern matching on the cases of `Schema`, and then use it for an order with nested records, a list, an optional field, and a sealed trait, and for an unrelated configuration type, without writing anything per type.

This is how the built-in codecs work: each one walks the schema of a type and reads or writes the matching shape. The [Write a Custom Codec](custom-codec.md) guide writes a codec for one fixed type instead, and [Write a Custom Deriver](custom-deriver.md) shows a macro-based alternative that builds a type class instance for each type at compile time.

### The Problem

A hand-written codec knows one type. Writing the `key=value` format for an order by hand looks like this:

```scala
final case class LineItem(sku: String, quantity: Int)
final case class Order(id: Long, customer: String, items: List[LineItem], note: Option[String])

def encodeOrder(order: Order): String = {
  val itemLines = order.items.zipWithIndex.flatMap { case (item, i) =>
    List(s"items.$i.sku=${item.sku}", s"items.$i.quantity=${item.quantity}")
  }
  val noteLines = order.note.map(note => s"note=$note").toList

  (List(s"id=${order.id}", s"customer=${order.customer}") ++ itemLines ++ noteLines).mkString("\n")
}
```

Every new type needs another such function and its decoder, and every new field means editing both. The decoder side repeats the same field names as strings, so a renamed field breaks the format without a compile error.

A `Schema` already describes the fields, cases, and element types of a value. A codec that reads the schema instead of the type handles every type that has one.

### Prerequisites

The examples only use the core module:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema" % "1.9.2"
```

The examples derive schemas with `DeriveSchema`, from `zio-schema-derivation`, which on Scala 2 also needs `scala-reflect` at compile time. The [Installation](../index.md#installation) section shows both lines. The [Schema Data Types](../basic-building-blocks.md) page lists every case of `Schema` that the codec matches on.

### Define the Model

We use an order whose fields cover the common shapes: primitives, a list of records, an optional field, and a sealed trait with a case class and a case object:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.codec.{Codec, DecodeError}

final case class LineItem(sku: String, quantity: Int)

object LineItem {
  implicit val schema: Schema[LineItem] = DeriveSchema.gen[LineItem]
}

sealed trait Delivery

object Delivery {
  final case class Courier(street: String, city: String) extends Delivery
  case object Pickup                                     extends Delivery

  implicit val schema: Schema[Delivery] = DeriveSchema.gen[Delivery]
}

final case class Order(id: Long, customer: String, items: List[LineItem], note: Option[String], delivery: Delivery)

object Order {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Order] = DeriveSchema.gen[Order]
}

val order: Order =
  Order(1001L, "ana", List(LineItem("TEA-01", 2), LineItem("MUG-07", 1)), Some("leave at door"), Delivery.Courier("Main St 1", "Oslo"))
```

### Design the Format

Each line holds one primitive value. Its key is the path from the root to the value, with the parts joined by dots: a record field adds its name, and a list element adds its index. An optional field writes nothing when it is empty. A sealed trait writes the name of its case under the `type` key, followed by the fields of the case. The order above becomes:

```text
id=1001
customer=ana
items.0.sku=TEA-01
items.0.quantity=2
items.1.sku=MUG-07
items.1.quantity=1
note=leave at door
delivery.type=Courier
delivery.street=Main St 1
delivery.city=Oslo
```

One helper builds a key from a path and a name, so the root has no leading dot:

```scala
def key(path: String, name: String): String =
  if (path.isEmpty) name else s"$path.$name"
```

### Write the Encoder

The encoder takes a schema and a value and returns the entries for that value. It matches on the kind of schema, and for every kind that contains other values, it calls itself with the inner schema and the inner value.

Inside a generic function, the type of the value is unknown, so the function takes the schema as `Schema[_]` and the value as `Any`. Each branch casts the schema to a version with `Any` type parameters, which is safe because the value always comes from the same schema:

```scala
def entries(path: String, schema: Schema[_], value: Any): Chunk[(String, String)] =
  schema match {
    case lazySchema: Schema.Lazy[_] =>
      entries(path, lazySchema.schema, value)

    case Schema.Primitive(_, _) =>
      Chunk(path -> value.toString)

    case Schema.Optional(inner, _) =>
      value match {
        case Some(present) => entries(path, inner, present)
        case _             => Chunk.empty
      }

    case Schema.Transform(inner, _, g, _, _) =>
      g.asInstanceOf[Any => Either[String, Any]](value) match {
        case Right(underlying) => entries(path, inner, underlying)
        case Left(_)           => Chunk.empty
      }

    case sequence: Schema.Sequence[_, _, _] =>
      val seq = sequence.asInstanceOf[Schema.Sequence[Any, Any, Any]]
      seq.toChunk(value).zipWithIndex.flatMap { case (element, index) =>
        entries(key(path, index.toString), seq.elementSchema, element)
      }

    case record: Schema.Record[_] =>
      record.asInstanceOf[Schema.Record[Any]].fields.flatMap { field =>
        entries(key(path, field.fieldName), field.schema, field.get(value))
      }

    case enumSchema: Schema.Enum[_] =>
      enumSchema.asInstanceOf[Schema.Enum[Any]].cases.find(_.isCase(value)) match {
        case Some(matching) =>
          Chunk(key(path, "type") -> matching.caseName) ++ entries(path, matching.schema, matching.deconstruct(value))
        case None           => Chunk.empty
      }

    case _ =>
      Chunk(path -> value.toString)
  }

def encode[A](value: A)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): String =
  entries("", schema, value).map { case (k, v) => s"$k=$v" }.mkString("\n")
```

Each branch handles one kind of schema:

- `Schema.Lazy` wraps a schema that is built on first use. Derived schemas put one around most field schemas, and recursive types need it, so the encoder unwraps one layer and continues.
- `Schema.Primitive` is a leaf, so the encoder writes the value as text.
- `Schema.Optional` writes the inner value when there is one.
- `Schema.Transform` wraps a type that is stored as another type, such as a newtype around a `String`. Its `g` function turns the value into the underlying type, which the encoder then writes.
- `Schema.Sequence` covers `List`, `Vector`, `Chunk`, and other sequences. Its `toChunk` function lists the elements.
- `Schema.Record` covers case classes. Each field has a name, a schema, and a getter. `Field#fieldName` honours a `@fieldName` annotation.
- `Schema.Enum` covers sealed traits. `Case#isCase` finds the case of the value, and `Case#deconstruct` gives the value as that case.

Every other kind of schema, such as a `Map`, a `Set`, an `Either`, or a tuple, falls back to the value's `toString`. A complete codec gives each of them a branch of its own.

The encoder now writes the order in the format we designed:

```scala
println(encode(order))
// id=1001
// customer=ana
// items.0.sku=TEA-01
// items.0.quantity=2
// items.1.sku=MUG-07
// items.1.quantity=1
// note=leave at door
// delivery.type=Courier
// delivery.street=Main St 1
// delivery.city=Oslo
```

### Write the Decoder

The decoder walks the same schema, but builds values instead of taking them apart. It reads from a map of all the entries and returns a `Left` with a message when an entry is missing or cannot be parsed.

First, two helpers: one parses the text into a map, and one checks whether any entry exists at or below a path, which tells an optional field or a list element whether it is present:

```scala
def parse(text: String): Map[String, String] =
  text.linesIterator
    .filter(_.contains('='))
    .map { line =>
      val (k, v) = line.span(_ != '=')
      k -> v.drop(1)
    }
    .toMap

def present(path: String, props: Map[String, String]): Boolean =
  props.keys.exists(k => k == path || k.startsWith(path + "."))
```

Primitives are the only place where the decoder reads text. This version supports the standard types that the examples use and rejects the rest:

```scala
def readPrimitive(path: String, standardType: StandardType[_], text: String): Either[String, Any] = {
  val parsed: Option[Any] = standardType match {
    case StandardType.StringType => Some(text)
    case StandardType.IntType    => text.toIntOption
    case StandardType.LongType   => text.toLongOption
    case StandardType.DoubleType => text.toDoubleOption
    case StandardType.BoolType   => text.toBooleanOption
    case _                       => None
  }
  parsed.toRight(s"cannot read $path=$text as $standardType")
}
```

A last helper runs a step for each item of a chunk and stops at the first `Left`:

```scala
def collectAll[A](items: Chunk[A])(step: A => Either[String, Any]): Either[String, Chunk[Any]] =
  items.foldLeft[Either[String, Chunk[Any]]](Right(Chunk.empty)) { (acc, item) =>
    for {
      done <- acc
      next <- step(item)
    } yield done :+ next
  }
```

The decoder itself mirrors the encoder branch for branch:

```scala
def read(path: String, schema: Schema[_], props: Map[String, String]): Either[String, Any] =
  schema match {
    case lazySchema: Schema.Lazy[_] =>
      read(path, lazySchema.schema, props)

    case Schema.Primitive(standardType, _) =>
      props.get(path).toRight(s"missing key $path").flatMap(readPrimitive(path, standardType, _))

    case Schema.Optional(inner, _) =>
      if (present(path, props)) read(path, inner, props).map(Some(_)) else Right(None)

    case Schema.Transform(inner, f, _, _, _) =>
      read(path, inner, props).flatMap(f.asInstanceOf[Any => Either[String, Any]])

    case sequence: Schema.Sequence[_, _, _] =>
      val seq  = sequence.asInstanceOf[Schema.Sequence[Any, Any, Any]]
      val size = Iterator.from(0).takeWhile(index => present(key(path, index.toString), props)).size
      collectAll(Chunk.fromIterable(0 until size))(index => read(key(path, index.toString), seq.elementSchema, props))
        .map(seq.fromChunk)

    case record: Schema.Record[_] =>
      collectAll(record.fields)(field => read(key(path, field.fieldName), field.schema, props))
        .flatMap(values => Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe => record.construct(values) })

    case enumSchema: Schema.Enum[_] =>
      val typeKey = key(path, "type")
      for {
        name     <- props.get(typeKey).toRight(s"missing key $typeKey")
        matching <- enumSchema.caseOf(name).toRight(s"unknown case $name at $typeKey")
        value    <- read(path, matching.schema, props)
      } yield matching.asInstanceOf[Schema.Case[Any, Any]].construct(value)

    case other =>
      Left(s"unsupported schema at $path: ${other.getClass.getSimpleName}")
  }

def decode[A](text: String)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Either[String, A] =
  read("", schema, parse(text)).map(_.asInstanceOf[A])
```

The new calls are the constructors on the schema: `Schema.Sequence#fromChunk` builds the collection from its elements, `Schema.Record#construct` builds a case class from its field values in field order, and `Schema.Case#construct` turns a case value into the sealed trait. `Schema.Record#construct` takes an implicit `Unsafe`, because it receives the field values untyped, as a `Chunk[Any]`; the decoder makes sure each value has the right type by reading each field with the field's own schema. `Schema.Enum#caseOf` finds a case by the name the encoder wrote.

The decoder reads the encoded order back:

```scala
decode[Order](encode(order)) == Right(order)
// res2: Boolean = true
```

A missing entry or a value of the wrong type gives a `Left` that names the key:

```scala
decode[LineItem]("sku=TEA-01")
// res3: Either[String, LineItem] = Left(value = "missing key quantity")
decode[LineItem]("sku=TEA-01\nquantity=two")
// res4: Either[String, LineItem] = Left(
//   value = "cannot read quantity=two as int"
// )
```

### Use It for Any Type

The codec contains no reference to `Order`. Any type with a schema works, such as a configuration class written long after the codec:

```scala
final case class ServerConfig(host: String, port: Int, debug: Boolean, tags: Vector[String])

object ServerConfig {
  implicit val schema: Schema[ServerConfig] = DeriveSchema.gen[ServerConfig]
}

val config: ServerConfig = ServerConfig("localhost", 8080, debug = true, Vector("blue", "eu"))
```

The same two functions encode and decode it:

```scala
println(encode(config))
// host=localhost
// port=8080
// debug=true
// tags.0=blue
// tags.1=eu

decode[ServerConfig](encode(config)) == Right(config)
// res6: Boolean = true
```

The case object of `Delivery` also round-trips, since its schema is a record with no fields:

```scala
decode[Order](encode(order.copy(note = None, delivery = Delivery.Pickup)))
// res7: Either[String, Order] = Right(
//   value = Order(
//     id = 1001L,
//     customer = "ana",
//     items = List(
//       LineItem(sku = "TEA-01", quantity = 2),
//       LineItem(sku = "MUG-07", quantity = 1)
//     ),
//     note = None,
//     delivery = Pickup
//   )
// )
```

### Package It as a Codec

To plug the format into code that expects ZIO Schema's `Codec` interface, we wrap the two functions in a class that takes the schema implicitly. The stream methods treat each element as one whole encoded value, like the hand-written codec in [Write a Custom Codec](custom-codec.md):

```scala
final class KeyValueCodec[A](implicit schema: Schema[A]) extends Codec[String, String, A] {

  override def encode(value: A): String =
    entries("", schema, value).map { case (k, v) => s"$k=$v" }.mkString("\n")

  override def decode(text: String): Either[DecodeError, A] =
    read("", schema, parse(text))
      .map(_.asInstanceOf[A])
      .left
      .map(message => DecodeError.ReadError(Cause.empty, message))

  override def streamEncoder: ZPipeline[Any, Nothing, A, String] =
    ZPipeline.map(encode)

  override def streamDecoder: ZPipeline[Any, DecodeError, String, A] =
    ZPipeline.mapZIO(text => ZIO.fromEither(decode(text)))
}
```

One class now serves every type:

```scala
new KeyValueCodec[ServerConfig].decode("host=example.org\nport=443\ndebug=false")
// res8: Either[DecodeError, ServerConfig] = Right(
//   value = ServerConfig(
//     host = "example.org",
//     port = 443,
//     debug = false,
//     tags = Vector()
//   )
// )
```

### Choose Between Schema and DynamicValue

Instead of walking the schema and the value together, an encoder can first turn the value into a `DynamicValue` with `Schema#toDynamic` and walk that tree. The tree already holds the field names, case names, and elements, so the encoder needs no casts:

```scala
def dynamicEntries(path: String, value: DynamicValue): Chunk[(String, String)] =
  value match {
    case DynamicValue.Primitive(v, _)               => Chunk(path -> v.toString)
    case DynamicValue.SomeValue(inner)              => dynamicEntries(path, inner)
    case DynamicValue.NoneValue                     => Chunk.empty
    case DynamicValue.Sequence(values)              =>
      values.zipWithIndex.flatMap { case (v, index) => dynamicEntries(key(path, index.toString), v) }
    case DynamicValue.Record(_, fields)             =>
      Chunk.fromIterable(fields).flatMap { case (name, v) => dynamicEntries(key(path, name), v) }
    case DynamicValue.Enumeration(_, (caseName, v)) =>
      Chunk(key(path, "type") -> caseName) ++ dynamicEntries(path, v)
    case other                                      => Chunk(path -> other.toString)
  }
```

It produces the same entries for the order:

```scala
dynamicEntries("", Order.schema.toDynamic(order)) == entries("", Order.schema, order)
// res9: Boolean = true
```

The `DynamicValue` route is shorter and fine for tools, logs, and debugging output. Walking the schema directly avoids building the intermediate tree for every value, which matters in a codec on a hot path. A decoder follows the schema in either case, because it starts from text and has no value to convert: only the schema says which primitive type each entry holds.

### Where to Go Next

- [Schema Data Types](../basic-building-blocks.md) documents every case of `Schema` with its fields, including the ones this codec leaves to the fallback branch.
- [How to Define Schemas for Recursive Types](recursive-schemas.md) explains the `Schema.Lazy` nodes that the codec unwraps.
- [Codec Core Types](../reference/codec-core.md) describes the `Codec`, `Encoder`, and `Decoder` traits.
- [Write a Custom Deriver](custom-deriver.md) builds a type class instance per type at compile time instead of interpreting the schema at runtime.
