## How to Build a JSON HTTP API with ZIO HTTP

In this guide, we build a small user API with [ZIO HTTP](https://ziohttp.com) whose request and response bodies are JSON. ZIO Schema describes every model once; ZIO HTTP's `Endpoint` API reads those schemas to decode requests, encode responses, check validation rules, and report bad input. By the end, you have a server with two endpoints, `POST /users` and `GET /users/{id}`, that rejects invalid bodies with a structured error.

We work in this order:

- Define the request, response, and error models with their schemas and rules.
- Check the JSON wire format and the validation rules without starting a server.
- Describe the endpoints and implement them.
- Shape the error response that ZIO HTTP sends for a body it cannot accept.
- Put everything together in one runnable server.

The ZIO HTTP code in this guide targets **ZIO HTTP 3.11.6**. The documentation build does not compile ZIO HTTP, so the blocks that use it are shown without compile checks; the blocks that only use ZIO Schema are compiled.

### The Problem

An HTTP API reads bytes from a request, turns them into a value, checks the value, and writes another value back as bytes. Written by hand, each endpoint repeats that work for its own types. The JSON format, the field names, and the validation messages are spread over the handlers, and a field added to a model has to be added to every place that reads or writes it.

For example, a hand-written version of the create-user endpoint needs its own encoder and its own checks:

```scala
final case class CreateUser(name: String, email: String, age: Int)

def toJson(user: CreateUser): String =
  s"""{"name":"${user.name}","email":"${user.email}","age":${user.age}}"""

def check(user: CreateUser): List[String] =
  List(
    if (user.name.isEmpty) Some("name must not be empty") else None,
    if (!user.email.contains("@")) Some("email is invalid") else None,
    if (user.age < 18) Some("age must be at least 18") else None
  ).flatten
```

The encoder does not escape quotes in the name, the decoder is still missing, and nothing ties `check` to the endpoint, so a handler can forget to call it. In this guide, the schema of each model drives all of it: ZIO HTTP derives the JSON codecs from the schema and runs the schema's validation rules on every request body.

### Prerequisites

ZIO HTTP provides the server and the `Endpoint` API. ZIO Schema provides the schemas; its JSON module also brings in `zio-schema-derivation`, which provides `DeriveSchema.gen`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-http"        % "3.11.6",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"      % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json" % "1.9.2"
)
```

ZIO HTTP depends on ZIO Schema itself, so sbt keeps the newer of the two ZIO Schema versions. On Scala 2, schema derivation also needs `scala-reflect` at compile time, as the [Installation](../index.md#installation) section shows. We assume you know how to derive a schema and how ZIO effects compose.

### Define the Models

Each body type is a case class with a derived schema in its companion object. ZIO HTTP finds the schema there, so no import or extra wiring is needed. The request model, `CreateUser`, carries `@validate` rules on its fields; the response model, `User`, and the error model, `UserNotFound`, are plain:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec
import zio.schema.validation.{Validation, ValidationError}

final case class CreateUser(
  @validate(Validation.minLength(1) && Validation.maxLength(50)) name: String,
  @validate(Validation.email) email: String,
  @validate(Validation.greaterThan(17)) age: Int
)

object CreateUser {
  implicit val schema: Schema[CreateUser] = DeriveSchema.gen[CreateUser]
}

final case class User(id: Int, name: String, email: String, age: Int)

object User {
  implicit val schema: Schema[User] = DeriveSchema.gen[User]
}

final case class UserNotFound(id: Int, message: String)

object UserNotFound {
  implicit val schema: Schema[UserNotFound] = DeriveSchema.gen[UserNotFound]
}
```

The rules use ready-made validators: `Validation.email` checks the address format, and `Validation.greaterThan(17)` requires an adult. [How to Validate Untrusted Input](validate-input.md) covers the rules in more depth.

### Check the Wire Format Without a Server

ZIO HTTP encodes and decodes JSON bodies with the schema-based codec of `zio-schema-json`, so we can see what clients receive before writing any HTTP code. ZIO HTTP configures that codec with its own `CodecConfig`, whose settings for `null` values, empty collections, and field-name formats are described in the [Endpoint reference](https://ziohttp.com/reference/endpoint). Our models have no optional fields or collections, and the default field-name format keeps names as written. A `User` response body looks like this:

```scala
println(JsonCodec.jsonCodec(User.schema).encodeJson(User(1, "Ada", "ada@example.com", 36), None))
// {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com","age":36}
```

For a request body, ZIO HTTP decodes the bytes and then calls `Schema.validate` on the result, failing the request when either step fails. The following helper performs the same two steps, which lets a unit test check a model's rules without starting a server:

```scala
def decodeBody[A](body: String)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Either[String, A] =
  JsonCodec.jsonDecoder(schema).decodeJson(body) match {
    case Left(error) => Left(s"malformed body: $error")
    case Right(value) =>
      val errors = Schema.validate(value)
      if (errors.isEmpty) Right(value)
      else Left(s"failed validation: ${errors.map(_.message).mkString("; ")}")
  }
```

We try a valid body, a body that lacks the email address, and a body whose values break the rules:

```scala
decodeBody[CreateUser]("""{"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com","age":36}""")
// res2: Either[String, CreateUser] = Right(
//   value = CreateUser(name = "Ada", email = "ada@example.com", age = 36)
// )

decodeBody[CreateUser]("""{"name":"Ada","age":36}""")
// res3: Either[String, CreateUser] = Left(
//   value = "malformed body: .email(missing)"
// )

decodeBody[CreateUser]("""{"name":"","email":"ada@example.com","age":12}""")
// res4: Either[String, CreateUser] = Left(
//   value = "failed validation: Expected the length of  to be at least 1 characters but was 0 characters.; 12 should be greater than 17"
// )
```

The third body is well-formed JSON, so the decoder alone accepts it. Only the validation step rejects it.

### Describe the Endpoints

An `Endpoint` describes a route, its inputs, and its outputs as data. `Endpoint#in` declares the request body type, `Endpoint#out` the success body type, and `Endpoint#outError` an error body type with its status code. Each of them needs a codec for the type, and ZIO HTTP builds one from the implicit `Schema`. The following definitions describe our two endpoints:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.http._
import zio.http.codec._
import zio.http.endpoint._

val createUser =
  Endpoint(RoutePattern.POST / "users")
    .in[CreateUser]
    .out[User](Status.Created)

val getUser =
  Endpoint(RoutePattern.GET / "users" / PathCodec.int("id"))
    .out[User]
    .outError[UserNotFound](Status.NotFound)
```

`createUser` reads a `CreateUser` from the request body and answers `201 Created` with a `User`. `getUser` reads the `id` path segment as an `Int` and answers either `200 OK` with a `User` or `404 Not Found` with a `UserNotFound`.

### Implement the Endpoints

`Endpoint#implement` turns an endpoint into a `Route` by supplying a function from the endpoint's input to a ZIO effect that produces its output or fails with its error type. The handlers only see values that have already been decoded and validated. We keep the users in a `Ref`:

```scala
def routes(users: Ref[Map[Int, User]]) =
  Routes(
    createUser.implement { request =>
      users.modify { current =>
        val user = User(current.size + 1, request.name, request.email, request.age)
        (user, current + (user.id -> user))
      }
    },
    getUser.implement { id =>
      users.get.flatMap { current =>
        ZIO.fromOption(current.get(id)).orElseFail(UserNotFound(id, s"No user with id $id"))
      }
    }
  )
```

The handler of `createUser` cannot fail, so its error type is `ZNothing`. The handler of `getUser` fails with `UserNotFound`, which `Endpoint#outError` encodes as a JSON body with status 404.

### Return Decode and Validation Errors

When a request body does not decode, or decodes into a value that breaks a `@validate` rule, ZIO HTTP does not call the handler. It answers `400 Bad Request` with a body that has two fields, `name` and `message`, as JSON or HTML depending on the request's `Accept` header. A body that fails validation is reported as a `MalformedBody` error whose message includes the message of each `ValidationError`.

To send a request with `curl`, set the `Content-Type` header, so that ZIO HTTP picks its JSON codec for the body:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"","email":"ada@example.com","age":12}'
```

The default body suits debugging, but clients usually want a fixed format. We describe that format with a case class, `ApiProblem`, and a function that turns a chunk of `ValidationError`s into one:

```scala
final case class ApiProblem(error: String, details: List[String])

object ApiProblem {
  implicit val schema: Schema[ApiProblem] = DeriveSchema.gen[ApiProblem]

  def fromValidationErrors(errors: Chunk[ValidationError]): ApiProblem =
    ApiProblem(
      "validation_failed",
      errors.map {
        // the default RegexMatch message prints the whole regular expression
        case ValidationError.RegexMatch(value, _) => s"'$value' has an invalid format"
        case other                                => other.message
      }.toList
    )
}
```

For the third body of the previous section, the client would receive this JSON:

```scala
val problem = ApiProblem.fromValidationErrors(Schema.validate(CreateUser("", "ada@example.com", 12)))
// problem: ApiProblem = ApiProblem(
//   error = "validation_failed",
//   details = List(
//     "Expected the length of  to be at least 1 characters but was 0 characters.",
//     "12 should be greater than 17"
//   )
// )

println(JsonCodec.jsonCodec(ApiProblem.schema).encodeJson(problem, None))
// {"error":"validation_failed","details":["Expected the length of  to be at least 1 characters but was 0 characters.","12 should be greater than 17"]}
```

ZIO HTTP reports every decoding problem as an `HttpCodecError`. `Endpoint#outCodecError` adds a codec for those errors that ZIO HTTP prefers over its default one. The schema below converts an `HttpCodecError` to an `ApiProblem` with `Schema#transformOrFail`. A body that fails validation arrives as `HttpCodecError.MalformedBody` whose cause is an `HttpCodecError.InvalidEntity`, which holds the `ValidationError`s; other inputs, such as query parameters, report `InvalidEntity` directly:

```scala
import zio.http._
import zio.http.codec._
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec

val problemSchema: Schema[HttpCodecError] =
  Schema[ApiProblem].transformOrFail[HttpCodecError](
    problem => Right(HttpCodecError.CustomError(problem.error, problem.details.mkString("\n"))),
    {
      case HttpCodecError.MalformedBody(_, Some(HttpCodecError.InvalidEntity(_, errors))) =>
        Right(ApiProblem.fromValidationErrors(errors))
      case HttpCodecError.InvalidEntity(_, errors) =>
        Right(ApiProblem.fromValidationErrors(errors))
      case other =>
        Right(ApiProblem(other.productPrefix, List(other.getMessage())))
    }
  )

val problemContentCodec: HttpContentCodec[HttpCodecError] =
  HttpContentCodec.from(
    MediaType.application.json -> BinaryCodecWithSchema(
      JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec(problemSchema),
      problemSchema
    )
  )

val problemCodec: HttpCodec[HttpCodecType.ResponseType, HttpCodecError] =
  ContentCodec.content(problemContentCodec) ++ StatusCodec.BadRequest
```

The second function of `Schema#transformOrFail` runs when the server writes an error; the first one runs only when a ZIO HTTP client reads it back. Attaching the codec to an endpoint makes it the format for every decoding error of that endpoint:

```scala
val createUserChecked = createUser.outCodecError(problemCodec)
```

To hide the details of decoding errors from clients instead, call `Endpoint#emptyErrorResponse`, which answers `400 Bad Request` with an empty body.

:::caution[Limits of Schema Validation Apply]
ZIO HTTP runs `Schema.validate` on the body, so the same limits apply as anywhere else: a rule added with `Schema#validation` is not checked, and on Scala 2 the `@validate` annotations of a case class with more than 22 fields are dropped. [Rules That Are Silently Skipped](validate-input.md#rules-that-are-silently-skipped) explains each case and its workaround.
:::

### Putting It Together

The complete server combines the models, the endpoints with the custom error format, and the routes. Run it and send requests with `curl` as shown above:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.http._
import zio.http.codec._
import zio.http.endpoint._
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec
import zio.schema.validation.{Validation, ValidationError}

final case class CreateUser(
  @validate(Validation.minLength(1) && Validation.maxLength(50)) name: String,
  @validate(Validation.email) email: String,
  @validate(Validation.greaterThan(17)) age: Int
)

object CreateUser {
  implicit val schema: Schema[CreateUser] = DeriveSchema.gen[CreateUser]
}

final case class User(id: Int, name: String, email: String, age: Int)

object User {
  implicit val schema: Schema[User] = DeriveSchema.gen[User]
}

final case class UserNotFound(id: Int, message: String)

object UserNotFound {
  implicit val schema: Schema[UserNotFound] = DeriveSchema.gen[UserNotFound]
}

final case class ApiProblem(error: String, details: List[String])

object ApiProblem {
  implicit val schema: Schema[ApiProblem] = DeriveSchema.gen[ApiProblem]

  def fromValidationErrors(errors: Chunk[ValidationError]): ApiProblem =
    ApiProblem(
      "validation_failed",
      errors.map {
        // the default RegexMatch message prints the whole regular expression
        case ValidationError.RegexMatch(value, _) => s"'$value' has an invalid format"
        case other                                => other.message
      }.toList
    )
}

object UserApi extends ZIOAppDefault {

  val problemSchema: Schema[HttpCodecError] =
    Schema[ApiProblem].transformOrFail[HttpCodecError](
      problem => Right(HttpCodecError.CustomError(problem.error, problem.details.mkString("\n"))),
      {
        case HttpCodecError.MalformedBody(_, Some(HttpCodecError.InvalidEntity(_, errors))) =>
          Right(ApiProblem.fromValidationErrors(errors))
        case HttpCodecError.InvalidEntity(_, errors) =>
          Right(ApiProblem.fromValidationErrors(errors))
        case other =>
          Right(ApiProblem(other.productPrefix, List(other.getMessage())))
      }
    )

  val problemContentCodec: HttpContentCodec[HttpCodecError] =
    HttpContentCodec.from(
      MediaType.application.json -> BinaryCodecWithSchema(
        JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec(problemSchema),
        problemSchema
      )
    )

  val problemCodec: HttpCodec[HttpCodecType.ResponseType, HttpCodecError] =
    ContentCodec.content(problemContentCodec) ++ StatusCodec.BadRequest

  val createUser =
    Endpoint(RoutePattern.POST / "users")
      .in[CreateUser]
      .out[User](Status.Created)
      .outCodecError(problemCodec)

  val getUser =
    Endpoint(RoutePattern.GET / "users" / PathCodec.int("id"))
      .out[User]
      .outError[UserNotFound](Status.NotFound)
      .outCodecError(problemCodec)

  def routes(users: Ref[Map[Int, User]]) =
    Routes(
      createUser.implement { request =>
        users.modify { current =>
          val user = User(current.size + 1, request.name, request.email, request.age)
          (user, current + (user.id -> user))
        }
      },
      getUser.implement { id =>
        users.get.flatMap { current =>
          ZIO.fromOption(current.get(id)).orElseFail(UserNotFound(id, s"No user with id $id"))
        }
      }
    )

  override def run =
    Ref.make(Map.empty[Int, User]).flatMap { users =>
      Server.serve(routes(users)).provide(Server.default)
    }
}
```

`Server.default` listens on port 8080.

### Going Further

The ZIO HTTP [Endpoint reference](https://ziohttp.com/reference/endpoint) covers query parameters, headers, multiple error types, authentication, and OpenAPI generation, which also reads your schemas. On the ZIO Schema side, [How to Validate Untrusted Input](validate-input.md) goes deeper into rules and error reporting, [JSON Codecs](../derivations/codecs/json.md) describes `JsonCodec.Configuration`, and [Schema Annotations](../schema-annotations.md) shows how `@fieldName` and similar annotations change the JSON that clients see.

## How to Property-Test Codecs with DeriveGen

In this guide, we write a ZIO Test spec that encodes and decodes every model of a small order system with the JSON and Protobuf codecs, using random values that `DeriveGen.gen` generates from each model's schema. By the end, you have a spec where covering a new model takes one line, plus hand-written generators for the cases where the derived ones are not enough.

We start from the models and their schemas, write one reusable round-trip check, run it over every model, and then replace the derived generators where a property needs valid values or where `DeriveGen.gen` cannot generate a type at all.

### The Problem

A codec round trip, `decode(encode(value)) == Right(value)`, is the cheapest test that catches a broken codec: a renamed field, a sealed-trait case that encodes but does not decode, or an `Option` that comes back as a different value. To be useful, it needs many different values of every model, including empty collections, `None`, and every case of every sealed trait.

Writing those values by hand means one generator per type, and each one repeats the structure of its case class:

```scala
import java.util.UUID

import zio.test.{Gen, Sized}

final case class Customer(id: UUID, name: String, email: Option[String])
final case class LineItem(sku: String, quantity: Int, priceCents: Long)
final case class Order(id: Long, customer: Customer, items: List[LineItem])

val customerGen: Gen[Sized, Customer] =
  for {
    id    <- Gen.uuid
    name  <- Gen.string
    email <- Gen.option(Gen.string)
  } yield Customer(id, name, email)

val lineItemGen: Gen[Sized, LineItem] =
  for {
    sku        <- Gen.string
    quantity   <- Gen.int
    priceCents <- Gen.long
  } yield LineItem(sku, quantity, priceCents)

val orderGen: Gen[Sized, Order] =
  for {
    id       <- Gen.long
    customer <- customerGen
    items    <- Gen.listOf(lineItemGen)
  } yield Order(id, customer, items)
```

Every new field means editing a generator, and a generator that falls behind its case class still compiles when the new field has a default value, so the new field is never tested. A sealed trait needs one more generator per case, and forgetting a case leaves it untested without any warning.

The models already have schemas, and a schema describes the same structure. `DeriveGen.gen` turns a `Schema[A]` into a `Gen[Sized, A]`, so the generators stay in step with the models.

### Prerequisites

We need the derivation module, the two codecs under test, and `zio-schema-zio-test`, which provides `DeriveGen` and brings in ZIO Test. ZIO Test's sbt runner, `zio-test-sbt`, runs the specs:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-derivation" % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json"       % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-protobuf"   % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-zio-test"   % "1.9.2" % Test,
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-test-sbt"          % zioVersion  % Test
)
```

Here `zioVersion` is the ZIO version your project already uses. The guide assumes you know how `DeriveGen.gen` works on a single type; [Derivation of ZIO Test Generators](../derivations/zio-test-gen-derivation.md) introduces it.

### Defining the Models

The order system has four models: a `Customer` with an optional email, a `LineItem` whose quantity must be positive, a `Payment` sealed trait with two cases, and an `Order` that nests the others together with a list and a map. Each one keeps its derived schema in its companion object, where `DeriveGen.gen` and the codecs find it:

```scala
import java.util.UUID

import zio.schema.{DeriveGen, DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.validation.Validation
import zio.test.{Gen, Sized}

final case class Customer(id: UUID, name: String, email: Option[String])

object Customer {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Customer] = DeriveSchema.gen[Customer]
}

final case class LineItem(
  sku: String,
  @validate(Validation.greaterThan(0)) quantity: Int,
  priceCents: Long
)

object LineItem {
  implicit val schema: Schema[LineItem] = DeriveSchema.gen[LineItem]
}

sealed trait Payment

object Payment {
  final case class Card(last4: String, expiryMonth: Int) extends Payment
  final case class Invoice(dueInDays: Int)              extends Payment

  implicit val schema: Schema[Payment] = DeriveSchema.gen[Payment]
}

final case class Order(
  id: Long,
  customer: Customer,
  items: List[LineItem],
  tags: Map[String, String],
  payment: Payment
)

object Order {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Order] = DeriveSchema.gen[Order]
}
```

The `@validate` rule on `LineItem#quantity` does not matter for the round trip, but it matters later, when a property needs valid orders.

### Writing One Round-Trip Check

The check itself does not depend on the model or the format. It takes a `BinaryCodec[A]` and a generator, and asserts that every generated value survives `BinaryCodec#encode` and then `BinaryCodec#decode`. A second helper builds one suite per model, with one test per codec:

```scala
import zio.ZIO
import zio.schema.codec.{BinaryCodec, JsonCodec, ProtobufCodec}
import zio.test._

def roundTrip[A](codec: BinaryCodec[A], gen: Gen[Sized, A]): ZIO[Sized, Nothing, TestResult] =
  check(gen) { value =>
    assertTrue(codec.decode(codec.encode(value)) == Right(value))
  }

def roundTrips[A](label: String, gen: Gen[Sized, A])(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Spec[Sized, Nothing] = {
  val json: BinaryCodec[A]     = JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[A]
  val protobuf: BinaryCodec[A] = ProtobufCodec.protobufCodec[A]

  suite(label)(
    test("JSON")(roundTrip(json, gen)),
    test("Protobuf")(roundTrip(protobuf, gen))
  )
}
```

`roundTrips` takes the generator as an argument instead of deriving it, so the same helper works later with hand-written generators. Both codecs are built from the implicit `Schema[A]`, the same schema `DeriveGen.gen` reads. To test another format, such as MessagePack or Avro, we add one more `test` line to `roundTrips`.

### Round-Tripping Every Model

With the helper in place, the spec lists each model once and passes `DeriveGen.gen` for its generator:

```scala
import zio.Scope

object CodecRoundTripSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    suite("codec round trips")(
      roundTrips("Customer", DeriveGen.gen[Customer]),
      roundTrips("LineItem", DeriveGen.gen[LineItem]),
      roundTrips("Payment", DeriveGen.gen[Payment]),
      roundTrips("Order", DeriveGen.gen[Order])
    )
}
```

Each `check` runs the property with many generated values, 200 by default. The `Payment` generator picks a case at random for every sample, so the samples include both `Card` and `Invoice`, and the `Order` generator reuses the generators of the nested models. When a value fails, ZIO Test shrinks it and reports the smallest failing input it finds, which usually points at the single field the codec mishandles.

Testing the nested models on their own as well as inside `Order` keeps failures readable: a broken `Payment` encoding fails the small `Payment` suite with a small counterexample, not only the `Order` suite with a large one.

### Generating Values That Pass Validation

A derived generator follows the shape of the schema, not its `@validate` rules, so `DeriveGen.gen[LineItem]` produces zero and negative quantities. That is fine for a round trip, because the codecs read and write invalid values too, but a property about business logic usually needs valid input.

`DeriveGen` has no hook to override the generator of one field, so we write a generator for the type that needs different values, and build the enclosing type with a `for` comprehension that uses derived generators for everything else:

```scala
val validLineItem: Gen[Sized, LineItem] =
  for {
    sku        <- Gen.alphaNumericStringBounded(3, 12)
    quantity   <- Gen.int(1, 100)
    priceCents <- Gen.long(0L, 1000000L)
  } yield LineItem(sku, quantity, priceCents)

val validOrder: Gen[Sized, Order] =
  for {
    id       <- Gen.long
    customer <- DeriveGen.gen[Customer]
    items    <- Gen.listOfBounded(1, 20)(validLineItem)
    tags     <- DeriveGen.gen[Map[String, String]]
    payment  <- DeriveGen.gen[Payment]
  } yield Order(id, customer, items, tags, payment)
```

`validOrder` also fixes the collection sizes: `Gen.listOfBounded` generates between 1 and 20 line items, while the derived generator only ever produces zero or two.

When the rules reject only a small share of the values, a shorter option is to keep the derived generator and drop the invalid samples with `Gen#filter` and `Schema.validate`, which returns the failed checks as a `Chunk[ValidationError]`:

```scala
val filteredOrder: Gen[Sized, Order] =
  DeriveGen.gen[Order].filter(order => Schema.validate(order).isEmpty)
```

Both generators plug into properties the same way the derived ones do. The following spec checks a business rule that holds only for valid orders, and reuses `roundTrips` with the custom generator:

```scala
import zio.Scope

def totalUnits(order: Order): Long =
  order.items.map(_.quantity.toLong).sum

object OrderRulesSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    suite("orders")(
      test("every line item contributes at least one unit") {
        check(validOrder) { order =>
          assertTrue(totalUnits(order) >= order.items.size.toLong)
        }
      },
      test("filtered orders pass validation") {
        check(filteredOrder) { order =>
          assertTrue(Schema.validate(order).isEmpty)
        }
      },
      roundTrips("valid Order", validOrder)
    )
}
```

With `DeriveGen.gen[Order]` instead of `validOrder`, the first test fails as soon as a sample contains a line item with a quantity below one.

:::tip
Prefer a hand-written generator over `Gen#filter` when most random values break a rule, such as a string that must match a regular expression. A filter discards every rejected sample and draws again, so a strict rule makes the property slow.
:::

### Covering Types DeriveGen Cannot Generate

`DeriveGen.gen` has no generator for non-empty collections, so a model with a `NonEmptyChunk` field needs a hand-written generator. `Gen.chunkOf1` generates `NonEmptyChunk` values, and the remaining fields can still come from `DeriveGen.gen`:

```scala
import zio.NonEmptyChunk

final case class Shipment(orderIds: NonEmptyChunk[Long], carrier: String)

object Shipment {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Shipment] = DeriveSchema.gen[Shipment]
}

val shipmentGen: Gen[Sized, Shipment] =
  for {
    orderIds <- Gen.chunkOf1(Gen.long)
    carrier  <- DeriveGen.gen[String]
  } yield Shipment(orderIds, carrier)
```

The round trip then uses `roundTrip` directly with the codec and the hand-written generator:

```scala
import zio.Scope

object ShipmentRoundTripSpec extends ZIOSpecDefault {
  val json: BinaryCodec[Shipment] = JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[Shipment]

  def spec: Spec[TestEnvironment with Scope, Any] =
    test("Shipment survives a JSON round trip")(roundTrip(json, shipmentGen))
}
```

Passing `DeriveGen.gen[Shipment]` instead makes the test fail with an exception as soon as `check` samples the generator, as the next section describes.

### Knowing What the Derived Generator Covers

A passing round trip only covers the values the generator produces. The [Limitations](../derivations/zio-test-gen-derivation.md#limitations) section of the `DeriveGen` page lists the gaps of the derived generator. This guide already works around two of them: `validLineItem` replaces the derived generator because it ignores `@validate` rules, and `Gen.listOfBounded` replaces the derived sequences and maps, which always have zero or two elements whatever the `Sized` setting. Two more gaps decide whether a spec runs at all:

:::caution
`DeriveGen.gen` throws an exception with the message "Missing handler for generating value of schema ..." for a schema that is, or contains, a `NonEmptyChunk`, a `NonEmptyMap`, or a `Fallback`. For a field of one of these types, the exception comes when `check` samples the generator, so the test fails instead of running. Write the generator for that type by hand, as `shipmentGen` does.

A `Transform` schema, such as one built with `Schema#transformOrFail`, generates a value of the underlying type and then applies the transformation, and a sample whose transformation fails is dropped. A transformation that rejects most inputs makes the property slow, and one that rejects every input leaves `check` without a single sample: ZIO Test logs a warning that the generator did not produce any test cases, and the test may hang. Give such types a hand-written generator that produces only accepted values.
:::

### Going Further

The [Derivation of ZIO Test Generators](../derivations/zio-test-gen-derivation.md) page describes `DeriveGen.gen` on its own, and [Validating Types](../operations/validating-types.md) covers the `@validate` rules and `Schema.validate`. The [JSON](../derivations/codecs/json.md) and [Protobuf](../derivations/codecs/protobuf.md) codec pages describe how each format encodes options, sealed traits, and maps, which helps when a round trip fails on one format and passes on the other.

## How to Define Schemas for Recursive Types

In this guide, we give schemas to types that refer to themselves: a comment thread whose replies are comments, an expression tree whose nodes hold other expressions, and a menu whose items can open another menu. By the end, each type has a working `Schema` and round-trips through the JSON codec.

We start with `DeriveSchema.gen`, which handles recursion for us, then write a recursive schema by hand with `Schema.defer`, and finish with two types that refer to each other.

### The Problem

A recursive type needs a schema that contains itself. A comment has a list of replies, each reply is a comment, so the schema of the `replies` field is "a list of the schema we are defining right now".

Written as an ordinary value, that definition reads its own name before the name has a value. With a strict `val`, the inner reference sees `null`, because the field is not assigned until the whole right-hand side finishes. With a `lazy val`, the inner reference starts the initialization again from the beginning, and on Scala 2 this repeats until the stack overflows. Neither fails at compile time, so the mistake shows up only when the schema is first used.

ZIO Schema solves this with `Schema.Lazy`, a schema that builds its inner schema only when a codec or operation first asks for it. `Schema.defer` creates one, and `DeriveSchema.gen` uses it automatically.

### Prerequisites

The examples use the core module and the JSON codec, which brings in `DeriveSchema`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"      % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json" % "1.9.2"
)
```

On Scala 2, `DeriveSchema` also needs `scala-reflect` at compile time; the [Installation](../index.md#installation) section shows the line to add. The [Schema Data Types](../basic-building-blocks.md) page describes `Schema.Lazy` and the other schema cases this guide builds by hand.

### Derive a Schema for a Tree

`DeriveSchema.gen` detects the recursion and wraps every reference back to the type in `Schema.defer`, so a recursive case class needs nothing special. We still declare the schema as an `implicit lazy val`, the safe default for any schema in a cycle: unlike a strict `val`, it is never read as `null`, whatever order the objects that hold the schemas initialize in:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec

final case class Comment(author: String, text: String, replies: List[Comment])

object Comment {
  implicit lazy val schema: Schema[Comment] = DeriveSchema.gen[Comment]
}

val thread: Comment =
  Comment(
    "ana",
    "Ship it?",
    List(Comment("ben", "Tests first.", List(Comment("ana", "They pass.", Nil))))
  )

val commentCodec = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Comment.schema)
```

The JSON codec follows the recursion to any depth:

```scala
println(commentCodec.encodeJson(thread, None))
// {"author":"ana","text":"Ship it?","replies":[{"author":"ben","text":"Tests first.","replies":[{"author":"ana","text":"They pass.","replies":[]}]}]}
```

Decoding the same text gives the thread back:

```scala
commentCodec.decodeJson(commentCodec.encodeJson(thread, None)) == Right(thread)
// res1: Boolean = true
```

Derivation also works for a recursive sealed trait and for a generic type such as `Tree[A]`. Write the schema by hand only when you cannot derive it, for example when the type is not a case class or sealed trait, or when you build schemas at runtime.

### Write a Recursive Schema by Hand

When we write the schema ourselves, the rule is: declare every schema in the cycle as a `lazy val`, and wrap every reference back into the cycle in `Schema.defer`. `Schema.defer` takes its argument by name and returns a `Schema.Lazy`, so the reference is read only after every `lazy val` has a value.

The following expression tree has two cases: a number, and the sum of two expressions. The `Add` schema refers back to `Expr.schema` through `Schema.defer`, and `Expr.schema` refers to the `Add` schema the same way:

```scala
sealed trait Expr

object Expr {
  final case class Num(value: Int)              extends Expr
  final case class Add(left: Expr, right: Expr) extends Expr

  lazy val numSchema: Schema[Num] =
    Schema.CaseClass1[Int, Num](
      id0 = TypeId.parse("example.Expr.Num"),
      field0 = Schema.Field[Num, Int]("value", Schema[Int], get0 = _.value, set0 = (num, value) => num.copy(value = value)),
      defaultConstruct0 = Num(_)
    )

  lazy val addSchema: Schema[Add] =
    Schema.CaseClass2[Expr, Expr, Add](
      id0 = TypeId.parse("example.Expr.Add"),
      field01 = Schema.Field[Add, Expr]("left", Schema.defer(schema), get0 = _.left, set0 = (add, left) => add.copy(left = left)),
      field02 = Schema.Field[Add, Expr]("right", Schema.defer(schema), get0 = _.right, set0 = (add, right) => add.copy(right = right)),
      construct0 = Add(_, _)
    )

  implicit lazy val schema: Schema[Expr] =
    Schema.Enum2[Num, Add, Expr](
      id = TypeId.parse("example.Expr"),
      case1 = Schema.Case[Expr, Num](
        id = "Num",
        schema = numSchema,
        unsafeDeconstruct = _.asInstanceOf[Num],
        construct = num => num,
        isCase = _.isInstanceOf[Num]
      ),
      case2 = Schema.Case[Expr, Add](
        id = "Add",
        schema = Schema.defer(addSchema),
        unsafeDeconstruct = _.asInstanceOf[Add],
        construct = add => add,
        isCase = _.isInstanceOf[Add]
      )
    )
}

val sum: Expr = Expr.Add(Expr.Num(1), Expr.Add(Expr.Num(2), Expr.Num(3)))

val exprCodec = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Expr.schema)
```

The hand-written schema encodes a nested expression like a derived one, with each case wrapped in an object named after the case:

```scala
println(exprCodec.encodeJson(sum, None))
// {"Add":{"left":{"Num":{"value":1}},"right":{"Add":{"left":{"Num":{"value":2}},"right":{"Num":{"value":3}}}}}}

exprCodec.decodeJson(exprCodec.encodeJson(sum, None)) == Right(sum)
// res3: Boolean = true
```

`Num` takes no part in the cycle, so `numSchema` needs no `Schema.defer`. Adding one would do no harm: `Schema.defer` costs one extra layer, and codecs and operations look through it.

:::warning
Do not drop `Schema.defer` and rely on `lazy val` alone. A `lazy val` whose right-hand side reads the same `lazy val` again, directly or through another schema, keeps restarting its own initialization. Wrapping the back-reference in `Schema.defer` is what breaks the loop.
:::

### Handle Types That Refer to Each Other

Two types are mutually recursive when each one contains the other. A `Menu` has items, and one kind of item, `Submenu`, holds another `Menu`. We give each type its own derived schema in its companion object:

```scala
final case class Menu(title: String, items: List[MenuItem])

object Menu {
  implicit lazy val schema: Schema[Menu] = DeriveSchema.gen[Menu]
}

sealed trait MenuItem

object MenuItem {
  final case class Link(label: String, url: String) extends MenuItem
  final case class Submenu(menu: Menu)              extends MenuItem

  implicit lazy val schema: Schema[MenuItem] = DeriveSchema.gen[MenuItem]
}

val mainMenu: Menu =
  Menu(
    "Main",
    List(
      MenuItem.Link("Home", "/"),
      MenuItem.Submenu(Menu("Help", List(MenuItem.Link("FAQ", "/faq"))))
    )
  )

val menuCodec = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Menu.schema)
```

`DeriveSchema.gen[Menu]` finds the implicit `MenuItem.schema` and wraps it in `Schema.defer`, and `DeriveSchema.gen[MenuItem]` does the same with `Menu.schema`, so neither `lazy val` reads the other while it initializes. Encoding goes through both schemas in turn:

```scala
println(menuCodec.encodeJson(mainMenu, None))
// {"title":"Main","items":[{"Link":{"label":"Home","url":"/"}},{"Submenu":{"menu":{"title":"Help","items":[{"Link":{"label":"FAQ","url":"/faq"}}]}}}]}

menuCodec.decodeJson(menuCodec.encodeJson(mainMenu, None)) == Right(mainMenu)
// res5: Boolean = true
```

A hand-written pair follows the same rule as the expression tree: both schemas are `lazy val`s, and each reference to the other goes through `Schema.defer`. The `Expr` example above is already such a pair, since `Expr.schema` and `Expr.addSchema` refer to each other.

### Inspect a Recursive Schema

Code that pattern matches on a schema, such as a custom codec, meets `Schema.Lazy` nodes. A derived schema puts one around every field schema that comes from an implicit, such as the `Schema[String]` of `Comment#author`, not only around recursive references. `Schema.force` removes the `Lazy` layers from the outside of a schema, so a match sees the real case:

```scala
val authorSchema: Schema[_] = Comment.schema match {
  case record: Schema.Record[_] => record.fields.head.schema
  case other                    => other
}
// authorSchema: Schema[_] = Lazy(schema0 = <function0>)

authorSchema.isInstanceOf[Schema.Lazy[_]]
// res6: Boolean = true
Schema.force(authorSchema)
// res7: Schema[_] = Primitive(
//   standardType = string,
//   annotations = IndexedSeq()
// )
```

Only unwrap a `Lazy` when you are about to use the schema inside it. A function that forces every nested schema up front, instead of one level at a time, loops forever on a recursive type. The [How to Write a Schema-Driven Codec](generic-codec.md) guide shows a codec that unwraps one level at a time.

### Going Further

- [Schema Data Types](../basic-building-blocks.md) documents `Schema.Lazy`, `Schema.defer`, and `Schema.force` with every other schema case.
- [Manual Schema Construction](../manual-schema-construction.md) covers the record and enum constructors used in the hand-written example.
- [MetaSchema](../operations/serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md) explains how a recursive schema is kept when it is turned into data: the repeated part becomes a reference to the earlier node.
- [How to Send a Schema over the Wire](send-schema-over-the-wire.md) sends such a schema to another service.

## How to Use ZIO Schema with Scala 3

In this guide, we model a small domain in idiomatic Scala 3 and give every type a schema: case classes with `derives Schema`, an `enum` for a closed set of states, a union type for a field that holds one of several types, and an opaque type for an identifier. We then turn Scaladoc comments into schema descriptions and derive a type class of our own with a `derives` clause. Each section adds one Scala 3 feature, so you can jump to the one you need.

### The Problem

Most ZIO Schema examples use the Scala 2 idiom: an `implicit val schema = DeriveSchema.gen[A]` in a hand-written companion object for every type. That still compiles on Scala 3, but a Scala 3 code base usually looks different. Its types say `derives` instead of declaring companions, closed sets of values are `enum`s rather than sealed traits, identifiers are opaque types, and some fields are union types such as `Int | String`. Each of these behaves differently under derivation: some derive with no extra code, some need a hand-written schema, and one Scala 3 feature, Scaladoc, silently changes what the derived schema contains. This guide shows what to write for each.

### Prerequisites

Schema derivation lives in the `zio-schema-derivation` module, and the JSON module, used here to show encoded output, already depends on it:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"      % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json" % "1.9.2"
)
```

Scala 3 needs no `scala-reflect` dependency, because derivation uses inline methods and quoted macros instead of Scala 2 macros. Every example imports `zio.schema._`, which brings `Schema`, `DeriveSchema`, and the `Schema.derived` extension method into scope. The documentation build compiles its snippets with Scala 2.13, so the Scala 3 snippets on this page are plain code blocks.

:::note
The Scala 3 artifacts of ZIO Schema are compiled with Scala 3.9, so your project needs Scala 3.9 or later. An older Scala 3 compiler cannot read them and reports errors such as `Not found: type Schema`.
:::

### Derive a Schema with `derives Schema`

The shortest way to give a case class a schema is a `derives Schema` clause. The compiler calls `Schema.derived[Person]` and stores the result as a `given` in the companion object of `Person`, so every `Schema[Person]` lookup finds it without an import:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int) derives Schema

val json = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Schema[Person]).encodeJson(Person("Ada", 36), None)
```

`Schema.derived[A]` is an extension method on the `Schema` companion object that calls `DeriveSchema.gen[A]`. It is also the method to call when you write the `given` yourself, for example for a type from another library whose definition you cannot change:

```scala
import zio.schema._

// Defined in a library, so it cannot have a derives clause
final case class Money(amount: BigDecimal, currency: String)

object schemas {
  given Schema[Money] = Schema.derived[Money]
}

import schemas.given
```

`derives Schema`, `Schema.derived`, and `DeriveSchema.gen` all produce the same schema. Pick `derives Schema` for types you own and `Schema.derived` for the rest.

If the same sources also compile on Scala 2, keep the Scala 2 form instead, because Scala 2 has neither `derives` nor `given`. An implicit value in the companion object compiles on both versions:

```scala
import zio.schema._

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}
```

### Model Closed Sets of Values with Enums

A Scala 3 `enum` derives like a sealed trait: each case becomes a case of the schema. When no case has fields and the enum has no parameters, derivation also adds the `simpleEnum` annotation, so the JSON codec writes each case as a plain string, such as `"Active"`. Annotations on the cases work as on sealed-trait cases; here `@caseName` changes the name that codecs read and write:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.caseName

enum Status derives Schema {
  case Active
  case Suspended
  case Closed
}

enum Priority derives Schema {
  @caseName("low") case Low
  @caseName("high") case High
}
```

An enum whose cases carry data derives one record per case, and it gets no `simpleEnum` annotation. Neither does an enum with constructor parameters, such as `enum Colour(val rgb: Int)`, even when its cases have no fields of their own:

```scala
import zio.schema._

enum Shape derives Schema {
  case Circle(radius: Double)
  case Rectangle(width: Double, height: Double)
}
```

### Accept One of Several Types with a Union Type

A union type such as `Int | String` derives as an enum with one case per member. The cases are named `"1"`, `"2"`, and so on, in the order the members are written, the `TypeId` of the schema is named `|`, and the schema carries the `noDiscriminator` annotation. A union can be derived on its own or appear as the type of a field:

```scala
import zio.schema._

val keySchema: Schema[Int | String] = DeriveSchema.gen

final case class Lookup(key: Int | String) derives Schema
```

To encode a value, the schema picks the first member whose runtime type test (`isInstanceOf`) succeeds. Choose members that such a test can tell apart: `List[Int] | List[String]` cannot work, because both members erase to `List` and every list matches the first case.

### Give an Opaque Type a Schema

Derivation cannot see through an opaque type, so `DeriveSchema.gen` fails on one with the compile error "Deriving schema for ... is not supported". Define the schema yourself in the opaque type's companion object. Inside the scope that defines the opaque type, the type equals its underlying type, so the schema of the underlying type can be used as it is. Derivation of an enclosing case class then finds that `given`:

```scala
import zio.schema._

object ids {
  opaque type UserId = String

  object UserId {
    def apply(value: String): UserId = value

    given Schema[UserId] = Schema[String]
  }
}

import ids.UserId

final case class Account(id: UserId, owner: String) derives Schema
```

An opaque type often exists to guarantee an invariant, such as a well-formed email address. In that case, build the schema with `Schema#transformOrFail`, so decoding rejects a value that the smart constructor rejects:

```scala
import zio.schema._

object emails {
  opaque type Email = String

  object Email {
    def make(value: String): Either[String, Email] =
      if (value.contains("@")) Right(value) else Left(s"invalid email: $value")

    extension (email: Email) def value: String = email

    given Schema[Email] = Schema[String].transformOrFail(make, email => Right(email.value))
  }
}
```

### Turn Scaladoc into Descriptions

On Scala 3, derivation copies the Scaladoc comment of a type into a `description` annotation of its schema. This applies to case classes, objects, and enums. Comments on fields are not read. Comments on enum cases are not kept per case: every case without fields receives the comments of all the enum's cases, and a case with fields receives none. Give a case whose description matters an explicit `@description` annotation. The annotation holds the comment exactly as written, including the `/**` and `*/` delimiters:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.description

/** A customer who placed at least one order. */
final case class Customer(name: String) derives Schema

val doc: Option[String] =
  Schema[Customer].annotations.collectFirst { case d: description => d.text }
```

Here `doc` is `Some("/** A customer who placed at least one order. */")`. Strip the delimiters before showing the text to people, for example with `doc.map(_.stripPrefix("/**").stripSuffix("*/").trim)`.

An explicit `@description` annotation comes before the one taken from Scaladoc, so code that reads the first description sees yours. Scala 2 derivation never reads Scaladoc. In a project that builds for both versions, schemas therefore differ between the two builds; use explicit `@description` annotations when the description must be the same on both.

### Derive Your Own Type Class with `derives`

A `Deriver` builds instances of your own type class from a schema; [Write a Custom Deriver](custom-deriver.md) shows how to write one. The examples below use the `LeafCount` type class and the `leafCounter` deriver from that guide.

On Scala 3, every deriver has a `Deriver#derive` method, the same as `Derive.derive[LeafCount, A](leafCounter)`. It needs a `Schema[A]` in scope:

```scala
import zio.schema._

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int) derives Schema

object Person {
  given LeafCount[Person] = leafCounter.derive[Person]
}
```

To let a type write `derives LeafCount`, give the type class companion an inline `LeafCount.derived` method that takes the schema as a `using` parameter and calls the deriver. The `derives` clause must list `Schema` too, so that a schema is in scope when `LeafCount.derived` runs:

```scala
import zio.schema._

trait LeafCount[A] {
  def count: Int
}

object LeafCount {
  inline def derived[A](using schema: Schema[A]): LeafCount[A] = leafCounter.derive[A]
}

final case class Team(members: List[Person], lead: Option[Person]) derives Schema, LeafCount
```

The method must be `inline`, because the derivation macro has to see the concrete type, `Team`, at the place where the instance is created.

An opaque type whose underlying type is a primitive, such as `UserId`, reaches the deriver through `Deriver#derivePrimitiveAlias`. Its default implementation returns the summoned instance and throws at runtime when there is none, so a deriver used with opaque types should override it. The method receives the `StandardType` of the underlying type, and the macro needs a `ClassTag` for the opaque type:

```scala
import scala.reflect.ClassTag
import zio.schema._

val leafCounter: Deriver[LeafCount] = new Deriver[LeafCount] {
  // derivePrimitive, deriveRecord, and the other methods as in Write a Custom Deriver

  override def derivePrimitiveAlias[A: ClassTag, U](
    st: StandardType[U],
    summoned: => Option[LeafCount[A]]
  ): LeafCount[A] =
    summoned.getOrElse(known(1))
}
```

The opaque type still needs its own `Schema` in scope, as shown in [Give an Opaque Type a Schema](#give-an-opaque-type-a-schema).

### Going Further

[Schema Derivation on Scala 2 and Scala 3](../derivations/derivation-scala-versions.md) compares the two derivation mechanisms side by side, and [Automatic Schema Derivation](../automatic-schema-derivation.md) lists the shapes that derivation supports on both versions. One more difference matters for validation: on Scala 3, `@validate` annotations are kept on case classes with more than 22 fields, while Scala 2 drops them; [How to Validate Untrusted Input](validate-input.md) covers validation in general. For the annotations used above, such as `@caseName` and `@description`, see [Schema Annotations](../schema-annotations.md).

## How to Send a Schema over the Wire

In this guide, we send the structure of a type from one service to another, so the receiver can read data of that type without having its class on its classpath. The sender turns its `Schema` into a `MetaSchema` and encodes it as JSON. The receiver decodes the `MetaSchema`, rebuilds a schema from it, and uses that schema to decode the data into a `DynamicValue`.

This is the pattern behind a schema registry, a generic consumer that indexes every topic it reads, or an admin tool that displays records of any type.

### The Problem

A generic service, such as an indexer that receives orders, invoices, and shipments from different producers, cannot depend on every producer's case classes. Without the structure of the data, it can only treat each message as raw bytes or as untyped JSON, and it cannot check that a message has the fields the producer promised.

A `Schema[A]` describes that structure, but it cannot be serialized as it is: it contains the constructors, getters, and transformation functions of the type, and functions cannot travel over the network. ZIO Schema separates the two parts. `Schema#ast` returns a `MetaSchema`, a plain tree that keeps only the structure, and `MetaSchema` has its own schema, so any codec can encode it.

### Prerequisites

The examples use the core module and the JSON codec:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"      % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json" % "1.9.2"
)
```

The [MetaSchema](../operations/serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md) reference describes every node of the tree, and [DynamicValue](../operations/dynamic-data-representation.md) describes the values the receiver works with.

### Define the Sender's Model

The sender owns an `Order` type with a nested record, a list, and an optional field:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.directDynamicMapping
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec
import zio.schema.meta.MetaSchema

final case class LineItem(sku: String, quantity: Int)

object LineItem {
  implicit val schema: Schema[LineItem] = DeriveSchema.gen[LineItem]
}

final case class Order(id: String, items: List[LineItem], note: Option[String])

object Order {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Order] = DeriveSchema.gen[Order]
}
```

### Turn the Schema into Data

`Schema#ast` converts the schema into a `MetaSchema`. Its `toString` renders the tree compactly, so we can see what the receiver will get:

```scala
println(Order.schema.ast)
// product
// |--id: string
// items: list
// |--item: record
// |----sku: string
// |----quantity: int
// |--note: ?string
```

The rendering shows the field names, the primitive types, and a `?` on optional fields; the tree also keeps the type id of every record. It does not contain any Scala function.

### Encode the Schema as JSON

`MetaSchema.schema` is the schema of `MetaSchema` itself, so the JSON codec derives an encoder for it like for any other type. The sender encodes both the schema and an order:

```scala
val metaSchemaCodec = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(MetaSchema.schema)

val schemaMessage: String = metaSchemaCodec.encodeJson(Order.schema.ast, None).toString

val orderMessage: String =
  JsonCodec
    .jsonCodec(Order.schema)
    .encodeJson(Order("o-1", List(LineItem("TEA-01", 2), LineItem("MUG-07", 1)), Some("leave at door")), None)
    .toString
```

The schema message is ordinary JSON, which can go through HTTP, a message broker, or a database column:

```scala
println(schemaMessage)
// {"Product":{"id":"repl.MdocSession.MdocApp.Order","path":[],"fields":[["id",{"Value":{"valueType":"string","path":["id"],"optional":false}}],["items",{"ListNode":{"item":{"Product":{"id":"repl.MdocSession.MdocApp.LineItem","path":["items","item"],"fields":[["sku",{"Value":{"valueType":"string","path":["items","item","sku"],"optional":false}}],["quantity",{"Value":{"valueType":"int","path":["items","item","quantity"],"optional":false}}]],"optional":false}},"path":["items"],"optional":false}}],["note",{"Value":{"valueType":"string","path":["note"],"optional":true}}]],"optional":false}}
```

The type ids in this page start with `repl.MdocSession.MdocApp`, the object that the documentation tool wraps the examples in; in your code, they start with your package name. A real system sends the schema once, for example when a producer registers a topic, and then sends many data messages that refer to it.

:::caution[Do not use Schema#serializable]
`Schema#serializable` looks like a shortcut for this step, but it does not produce a usable schema of schemas: for a primitive such as `Schema[Int]` it encodes a meaningless value, and for a case class it throws a `ClassCastException`. Use `Schema#ast` with `MetaSchema.schema` as shown here.
:::

### Rebuild the Schema on the Receiver

The receiver has no `Order` class. It decodes the message into a `MetaSchema` with the same codec and calls `MetaSchema#toSchema` to get a working schema back. The Scala type is unknown on this side, so the result is a `Schema[_]`:

```scala
val receivedSchema: Either[String, Schema[_]] =
  metaSchemaCodec.decodeJson(schemaMessage).map(_.toSchema)
```

The rebuilt schema has the same structure as `Order.schema`, but it works on generic values: each record becomes a `GenericRecord` over a `ListMap[String, _]` keyed by field name, and each list becomes a `Chunk`.

### Decode Data with the Received Schema

A codec built from the rebuilt schema reads the JSON that the sender wrote with the original schema. The following helper decodes the text and turns the result into a `DynamicValue`, so the rest of the receiver can work with it without knowing its type:

```scala
def readWith[A](schema: Schema[A], json: String): Either[String, DynamicValue] =
  JsonCodec.jsonCodec(schema).decodeJson(json).map(schema.toDynamic)

val receivedOrder: Either[String, DynamicValue] =
  receivedSchema.flatMap(schema => readWith(schema, orderMessage))
```

The decoded order is a tree of records that keeps the field names, the list, and the optional note:

```scala
receivedOrder.foreach(println)
// Record(Nominal(Chunk(repl),Chunk(MdocSession,MdocApp),Order),ListMap(id -> Primitive(o-1,string), items -> Sequence(Chunk(Record(Nominal(Chunk(repl),Chunk(MdocSession,MdocApp),LineItem),ListMap(sku -> Primitive(TEA-01,string), quantity -> Primitive(2,int))),Record(Nominal(Chunk(repl),Chunk(MdocSession,MdocApp),LineItem),ListMap(sku -> Primitive(MUG-07,string), quantity -> Primitive(1,int))))), note -> SomeValue(Primitive(leave at door,string))))
```

The received schema also checks the structure of incoming data. A message whose line item has no `quantity` fails to decode, while the optional `note` may be absent:

```scala
receivedSchema.flatMap(schema => readWith(schema, """{"id":"o-2","items":[{"sku":"TEA-01"}]}"""))
// res3: Either[String, DynamicValue] = Left(
//   value = ".items[0].quantity(missing)"
// )
```

### Use the Decoded Data

The receiver handles the `DynamicValue` like any other dynamic data. A generic indexer, for example, writes it as plain JSON for a search engine, using the JSON codec in `directDynamicMapping` mode:

```scala
val plainJson = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(Schema.dynamicValue.annotate(directDynamicMapping()))
```

The plain JSON has the same shape as the order the sender encoded:

```scala
receivedOrder.foreach(order => println(plainJson.encodeJson(order, None)))
// {"id":"o-1","items":[{"sku":"TEA-01","quantity":2},{"sku":"MUG-07","quantity":1}],"note":"leave at door"}
```

The [How to Work with Schemaless Data](dynamic-data.md) guide shows how to read fields from the tree, change it, and bind parts of it to a case class.

### Know What the Schema Leaves Behind

A `MetaSchema` describes structure only. Everything in the original schema that is code or metadata stays with the sender: the functions of `Schema#transform` and `Schema#transformOrFail`, every annotation, and every field validation. [What the Round Trip Loses](../operations/serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md#what-the-round-trip-loses) lists each part and what the receiver gets instead.

The receiver therefore accepts any value of the underlying type: an `Email` that the sender builds with `Schema#transformOrFail` and a validating function arrives as a plain string, and the receiver does not run the check. Codec behaviour that comes from annotations, such as a case renamed with `@caseName`, is not applied on the receiving side either, so a receiver may fail to read data written with such annotations. Keep the types you send this way free of annotations that change the encoded form, or apply the same settings on the receiver.

### Going Further

- [MetaSchema](../operations/serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md) documents every node of the tree, `NodePath`, and how to extend the built-in types.
- [Serialization of the Schema Itself](../operations/serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md) explains why a schema is worth serializing.
- [Schema Migration](../operations/schema-migration.md) compares two `MetaSchema` values to move data between versions of a type.
- [How to Work with Schemaless Data](dynamic-data.md) continues with the `DynamicValue` the receiver decodes.

## How to Update Nested Data with Derived Optics

In this guide, we update fields deep inside an immutable `Order`: the city of the customer's address, the details of a card payment, and the quantity of every line item. Instead of writing optics by hand, we derive them from the schemas we already have with `Schema#makeAccessors` and `ZioOpticsBuilder`, and then compose them into one optic per path.

We start with one lens per field, compose lenses to reach into nested case classes, use prisms to work with one case of a sealed trait, and finish with a traversal that updates every element of a list. The [Optics Derivation](../derivations/optics-derivation.md) page explains how `Schema#makeAccessors` and `AccessorBuilder` work; this guide focuses on putting the derived optics to work.

### The Problem

Case classes are immutable, so changing one nested field means copying every level above it. With three levels, a one-field change already takes a nested `copy` chain:

```scala
final case class Address(street: String, city: String)
final case class Customer(name: String, address: Address)
final case class LineItem(sku: String, quantity: Int)
final case class Order(id: String, customer: Customer, items: List[LineItem])

def moveCustomer(order: Order, city: String): Order =
  order.copy(
    customer = order.customer.copy(
      address = order.customer.address.copy(city = city)
    )
  )

def doubleQuantities(order: Order): Order =
  order.copy(items = order.items.map(item => item.copy(quantity = item.quantity * 2)))
```

Every function that touches the address repeats the same path, and none of these paths is a value we can name, pass around, or combine with another one. Optics turn each path into a value, but writing a lens by hand for every field is the same boilerplate in a different place.

A schema already lists the fields of a case class and the cases of a sealed trait, so ZIO Schema can derive one optic for each of them.

### Prerequisites

The `zio-schema-optics` module provides `ZioOpticsBuilder` and brings in [ZIO Optics](https://zio.dev/zio-optics), whose `Optic` type the derived optics use. We also need the derivation module for `DeriveSchema.gen`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-derivation" % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-optics"     % "1.9.2"
)
```

### Deriving the Accessors

For each type, we derive its schema in the companion object and call `Schema#makeAccessors` with `ZioOpticsBuilder`. A case class schema returns one lens per field, in declaration order, and a sealed trait schema returns one prism per case. Destructuring the tuple gives each optic a name:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.optics._
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.schema.optics.ZioOpticsBuilder

final case class Address(street: String, city: String)

object Address {
  implicit val schema: Schema.CaseClass2[String, String, Address] =
    DeriveSchema.gen[Address]

  val (street, city) = schema.makeAccessors(ZioOpticsBuilder)
}

final case class Customer(name: String, address: Address)

object Customer {
  implicit val schema: Schema.CaseClass2[String, Address, Customer] =
    DeriveSchema.gen[Customer]

  val (name, address) = schema.makeAccessors(ZioOpticsBuilder)
}

final case class LineItem(sku: String, quantity: Int)

object LineItem {
  implicit val schema: Schema.CaseClass2[String, Int, LineItem] =
    DeriveSchema.gen[LineItem]

  val (sku, quantity) = schema.makeAccessors(ZioOpticsBuilder)
}

sealed trait Payment

object Payment {
  final case class Card(last4: String, expiry: String) extends Payment
  final case class Invoice(dueInDays: Int)            extends Payment

  implicit val schema: Schema.Enum2[Card, Invoice, Payment] =
    DeriveSchema.gen[Payment]

  val (card, invoice) = schema.makeAccessors(ZioOpticsBuilder)
}

final case class Order(id: String, customer: Customer, items: List[LineItem], payment: Payment)

object Order {
  implicit val schema: Schema.CaseClass4[String, Customer, List[LineItem], Payment, Order] =
    DeriveSchema.gen[Order]

  val (id, customer, items, payment) = schema.makeAccessors(ZioOpticsBuilder)
}
```

The precise schema types matter. `DeriveSchema.gen` returns a `Schema.CaseClass2[String, String, Address]`, and that type tells `Schema#makeAccessors` to return a pair of lenses. Declared as a plain `Schema[Address]`, the same value only promises an abstract `Accessors` type, and the tuple cannot be destructured.

The rest of the guide works on one sample order:

```scala
val order: Order =
  Order(
    id = "A-1001",
    customer = Customer("Ada Lovelace", Address("12 St James's Square", "London")),
    items = List(LineItem("SKU-1", 1), LineItem("SKU-2", 3)),
    payment = Payment.Card("4242", "08/27")
  )
```

### Reading and Writing One Field

Each lens reads its field with `Optic#get` and replaces it with `Optic#set`, which takes the new value first and the whole value second. Both return an `Either`, because the optics that `ZioOpticsBuilder` derives report failures as an `OpticFailure` instead of throwing:

```scala
Order.id.get(order)
// res1: package.OpticResult[OpticFailure, String] = Right(value = "A-1001")

Order.id.set("A-1002")(order).map(_.id)
// res2: Either[OpticFailure, String] = Right(value = "A-1002")
```

`Optic#update` combines the two: it reads the field, applies a function, and writes the result back. It takes the whole value first and the function second:

```scala
Customer.name.update(order.customer)(_.toUpperCase)
// res3: package.OpticResult[OpticFailure, Customer] = Right(
//   value = Customer(
//     name = "ADA LOVELACE",
//     address = Address(street = "12 St James's Square", city = "London")
//   )
// )
```

### Composing Lenses Across Nested Case Classes

The `Optic#>>>` operator composes two optics: the left one focuses on a part, and the right one focuses on a part of that part. Composing the `Order.customer`, `Customer.address`, and `Address.city` lenses gives one lens from an `Order` straight to the city:

```scala
val orderCity = Order.customer >>> Customer.address >>> Address.city
```

The composed lens has the same `Optic#get`, `Optic#set`, and `Optic#update` operations as the lenses it is built from:

```scala
orderCity.get(order)
// res4: package.OpticResult[OpticFailure, String] = Right(value = "London")

orderCity.set("Paris")(order).map(_.customer)
// res5: Either[OpticFailure, Customer] = Right(
//   value = Customer(
//     name = "Ada Lovelace",
//     address = Address(street = "12 St James's Square", city = "Paris")
//   )
// )

orderCity.update(order)(_.toUpperCase).map(_.customer.address)
// res6: Either[OpticFailure, Address] = Right(
//   value = Address(street = "12 St James's Square", city = "LONDON")
// )
```

`orderCity` replaces the nested `copy` chain of `moveCustomer`. Because it is a value, we define it once and reuse it wherever the code needs the customer's city.

### Working with One Case of a Sealed Trait

A prism focuses on one case of a sealed trait. `Optic#get` returns the case when the value matches it, and an `OpticFailure` otherwise:

```scala
Payment.card.get(order.payment)
// res7: package.OpticResult[OpticFailure, Payment.Card] = Right(
//   value = Card(last4 = "4242", expiry = "08/27")
// )

Payment.card.get(Payment.Invoice(dueInDays = 30))
// res8: package.OpticResult[OpticFailure, Payment.Card] = Left(
//   value = OpticFailure(message = "Cannot deconstruct to term Card")
// )
```

A lens and a prism compose through the `Either` that `Optic#get` returns. Reading the card of an order takes the `Order.payment` lens and then the `Payment.card` prism:

```scala
Order.payment.get(order).flatMap(payment => Payment.card.get(payment))
// res9: Either[OpticFailure, Payment.Card] = Right(
//   value = Card(last4 = "4242", expiry = "08/27")
// )
```

To change a card only when the order is paid by card, we update the field through the `Order.payment` lens and use the prism inside the update function. A payment of any other case passes through unchanged:

```scala
def renewCard(order: Order, expiry: String): Either[OpticFailure, Order] =
  Order.payment.update(order) { payment =>
    Payment.card.get(payment).map(_.copy(expiry = expiry)).getOrElse(payment)
  }
```

The same call renews the card of a card order and leaves an invoice order as it is:

```scala
renewCard(order, "08/30").map(_.payment)
// res10: Either[OpticFailure, Payment] = Right(
//   value = Card(last4 = "4242", expiry = "08/30")
// )

renewCard(order.copy(payment = Payment.Invoice(30)), "08/30").map(_.payment)
// res11: Either[OpticFailure, Payment] = Right(
//   value = Invoice(dueInDays = 30)
// )
```

### Updating Every Element of a Collection

A traversal focuses on all elements of a collection at once. `Schema#makeAccessors` derives one from a sequence schema, but `Schema.list` is typed as a plain `Schema[List[A]]`, which hides the sequence type that `Schema#makeAccessors` needs. Building the `Schema.Sequence` for `List[LineItem]` explicitly keeps that type, and `Schema#makeAccessors` then returns a traversal:

```scala
val lineItems: ZioOpticsBuilder.Traversal[List[LineItem], LineItem] =
  Schema
    .Sequence[List[LineItem], LineItem, String](
      elementSchema = LineItem.schema,
      fromChunk = _.toList,
      toChunk = items => Chunk.fromIterable(items),
      annotations = Chunk.empty,
      identity = "List"
    )
    .makeAccessors(ZioOpticsBuilder)
```

A traversal reads and writes the elements as a `Chunk`. Composing the `Order.items` lens with it gives an optic from an `Order` to all of its line items:

```scala
val orderItems = Order.items >>> lineItems
```

With `Optic#update`, the function receives every line item and returns the new ones. The following call doubles every quantity:

```scala
orderItems.update(order)(_.map(item => item.copy(quantity = item.quantity * 2))).map(_.items)
// res12: Either[OpticFailure, List[LineItem]] = Right(
//   value = List(
//     LineItem(sku = "SKU-1", quantity = 2),
//     LineItem(sku = "SKU-2", quantity = 6)
//   )
// )
```

:::warning
A traversal replaces existing elements; it never adds or removes them. The traversals that `ZioOpticsBuilder` derives for sequences write the new chunk position by position: extra elements in the new chunk are dropped, and when the new chunk is shorter, the remaining original elements stay in place. The traversals for maps and sets merge the new elements into the existing ones, so they can add entries but never remove any.
:::

Appending through the traversal leaves the order unchanged, because the new chunk has more elements than the list:

```scala
orderItems.update(order)(_ :+ LineItem("SKU-3", 1)).map(_.items)
// res13: Either[OpticFailure, List[LineItem]] = Right(
//   value = List(
//     LineItem(sku = "SKU-1", quantity = 1),
//     LineItem(sku = "SKU-2", quantity = 3)
//   )
// )
```

To change the length of the list, we update the whole list through the `Order.items` lens instead:

```scala
Order.items.update(order)(_ :+ LineItem("SKU-3", 1)).map(_.items)
// res14: Either[OpticFailure, List[LineItem]] = Right(
//   value = List(
//     LineItem(sku = "SKU-1", quantity = 1),
//     LineItem(sku = "SKU-2", quantity = 3),
//     LineItem(sku = "SKU-3", quantity = 1)
//   )
// )
```

:::note
`ZioOpticsBuilder` implements every lens get and set by converting the whole value to a `DynamicValue` and back, so a derived lens, and every optic composed from one, is much slower than the equivalent `copy` call. Use derived optics where the convenience of a reusable path matters more than speed, not in tight loops.
:::

### Going Further

The [Optics Derivation](../derivations/optics-derivation.md) page shows how `AccessorBuilder` defines the three kinds of optics and how `ZioOpticsBuilder` implements them. The [ZIO Optics](https://zio.dev/zio-optics) documentation covers the `Optic` type itself, including `Optic#zip` for setting two fields at once and the other operators that the derived optics support.
