## How to Validate Untrusted Input

In this guide, we accept a sign-up request as JSON, reject it when it breaks the rules of our model, and answer with an error response that lists every problem by field. The rules live on the case class as `@validate` annotations, so the same rules apply wherever the model is decoded. We start by declaring the rules, then decode and validate, group the errors by field, and finally render them as a JSON error body. The last section lists the cases where a rule is silently skipped, and what to do instead.

### The Problem

Data that arrives from outside, such as an HTTP request body, a message from a queue, or a row from a CSV file, can hold any value its type allows. A `String` username can be empty, and an `Int` age can be negative. Decoding only proves that the input has the right shape; it says nothing about whether the values make sense.

Without a library, every model gets a hand-written check that repeats the rules and the error messages:

```scala
final case class Signup(username: String, email: String, age: Int)

def checkSignup(signup: Signup): List[String] = {
  val usernameErrors =
    if (signup.username.length < 3) List("username: must be at least 3 characters")
    else if (signup.username.length > 20) List("username: must be at most 20 characters")
    else Nil
  val emailErrors =
    if (!signup.email.contains("@")) List("email: has an invalid format") else Nil
  val ageErrors =
    if (signup.age <= 17) List("age: must be greater than 17") else Nil
  usernameErrors ++ emailErrors ++ ageErrors
}
```

The check sits apart from the model, so adding a field without updating the check goes unnoticed, and every nested type needs its own check wired in by hand. With ZIO Schema, the rules sit on the fields themselves, and one call checks a value and everything nested inside it.

### Prerequisites

We need the core module for `Schema` and validation, and the JSON module for decoding. The JSON module already depends on `zio-schema-derivation`, which provides `DeriveSchema.gen`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"      % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json" % "1.9.2"
)
```

On Scala 2, schema derivation also needs `scala-reflect` at compile time, as the [Installation](../index.md#installation) section shows. This guide assumes you know how to derive a schema; the [Validation](../operations/validating-types.md) reference describes every rule and error type in detail.

### Declare the Rules on the Model

A rule is a `Validation[A]` value, and the `@validate` annotation attaches it to a field. When `DeriveSchema.gen` builds the schema, it stores the rule of each field in the schema. Several annotations on one field, or rules combined with `&&`, must all pass.

Our sign-up request has a username with a length limit, an email address, a minimum age, an optional US phone number, and a nested postal address. `Validation.email` and `PhoneNumberValidation.phoneNumberUS` are predefined validators, and `Validation#optional` lifts a rule for `String` to a rule for `Option[String]` that accepts `None`:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec
import zio.schema.validation._

final case class Address(
  @validate(Validation.minLength(1)) street: String,
  @validate(Validation.minLength(1)) city: String
)

object Address {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Address] = DeriveSchema.gen[Address]
}

final case class Signup(
  @validate(Validation.minLength(3) && Validation.maxLength(20)) username: String,
  @validate(Validation.email) email: String,
  @validate(Validation.greaterThan(17)) age: Int,
  @validate(PhoneNumberValidation.phoneNumberUS.optional()) phone: Option[String],
  address: Address
)

object Signup {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Signup] = DeriveSchema.gen[Signup]
}
```

`Address` has its own rules. `Signup` does not repeat them; checking a `Signup` also checks its address. The [Predefined Validators](../operations/validating-types.md#predefined-validators) section lists the other ready-made rules, such as `Validation.uuidV4`, `Validation.ipV4`, and `Validation.time`.

### Decode, Then Validate

Decoding and validating are two separate steps. First we decode a request whose username is too short, whose age is too low, and whose street is empty:

```scala
val json =
  """{"username":"jd","email":"jd@example.com","age":15,"address":{"street":"","city":"Springfield"}}"""
// json: String = "{\"username\":\"jd\",\"email\":\"jd@example.com\",\"age\":15,\"address\":{\"street\":\"\",\"city\":\"Springfield\"}}"

val decoded = JsonCodec.jsonDecoder(Signup.schema).decodeJson(json)
// decoded: Either[String, Signup] = Right(
//   value = Signup(
//     username = "jd",
//     email = "jd@example.com",
//     age = 15,
//     phone = None,
//     address = Address(street = "", city = "Springfield")
//   )
// )
```

The decoder returns `Right` even though three fields break their rules.

:::caution[Codecs Do Not Validate]
No codec in ZIO Schema runs validation rules when it decodes. A value that breaks its `@validate` rules decodes successfully. Always call `Schema.validate` on the decoded value before you trust it.
:::

`Schema.validate` walks the value with its schema and returns every failed check as a `ValidationError`. An empty `Chunk` means the value is valid:

```scala
decoded.map(signup => Schema.validate(signup).map(_.message))
// res1: Either[String, Chunk[String]] = Right(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     "Expected the length of  to be at least 1 characters but was 0 characters.",
//     "Expected the length of jd to be at least 3 characters but was 2 characters.",
//     "15 should be greater than 17"
//   )
// )
```

The walk descends into nested records, the elements of collections, and the content of `Option` and `Either`, so the empty street of the nested `Address` shows up without extra code.

`Schema.validate(value)` and its method form, `Schema#validate`, both check with the implicit `Schema[A]` in scope. When you hold a schema that is not the implicit one, pass it explicitly: `Schema.validate(value)(otherSchema)`.

### Group Errors by Field

A `ValidationError` describes what failed, such as a string that is too short, but it does not say which field it came from. A client needs the field name to show the error next to the right input. The schema knows the fields, so we can walk them ourselves: for each field of the record, `Schema.Field#get` reads the value, `Schema.Field#validation` checks the field's own rule, and `Schema.validate` with `Schema.Field#schema` checks everything nested inside the field:

```scala
def checkField[R, A](field: Schema.Field[R, A], record: R): Chunk[ValidationError] = {
  val value = field.get(record)
  val own   = field.validation.validate(value).swap.getOrElse(Chunk.empty)
  own ++ Schema.validate(value)(field.schema)
}

def fieldErrors[A](value: A)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Map[String, Chunk[ValidationError]] =
  schema match {
    case record: Schema.Record[A] =>
      record.fields
        .map(field => field.fieldName -> checkField(field, value))
        .filter(_._2.nonEmpty)
        .toMap
    case _ =>
      val errors = Schema.validate(value)
      if (errors.isEmpty) Map.empty else Map("value" -> errors)
  }
```

`Schema.Field#fieldName` is the name the codecs use, so it honours a `@fieldName` annotation. Applied to our decoded request, the errors now carry their field names:

```scala
decoded.map(fieldErrors(_))
// res2: Either[String, Map[String, Chunk[ValidationError]]] = Right(
//   value = Map(
//     "username" -> IndexedSeq(MinLength(minLength = 3, actualLength = 2, string = "jd")),
//     "age" -> IndexedSeq(GreaterThan(value = 15, expected = 17)),
//     "address" -> IndexedSeq(MinLength(minLength = 1, actualLength = 0, string = ""))
//   )
// )
```

An error inside the nested address is reported under `address`, the top-level field that contains it. To report `address.street` instead, call `fieldErrors` again on the nested value.

### Turn Errors into an Error Response

The client should get a stable, readable error body, not the raw `ValidationError` values. We translate each error into a short message by matching on the error cases, and describe the response itself with a case class, so its schema gives us a JSON encoder for free:

```scala
def describe(error: ValidationError): String =
  error match {
    case ValidationError.MinLength(min, _, _)     => s"must be at least $min characters"
    case ValidationError.MaxLength(max, _, _)     => s"must be at most $max characters"
    case ValidationError.GreaterThan(_, expected) => s"must be greater than $expected"
    case ValidationError.LessThan(_, expected)    => s"must be less than $expected"
    case ValidationError.RegexMatch(_, _)         => "has an invalid format"
    case other                                    => other.message
  }

final case class ErrorResponse(error: String, fields: Map[String, List[String]])

object ErrorResponse {
  implicit val schema: Schema[ErrorResponse] = DeriveSchema.gen[ErrorResponse]
}

val errorCodec = JsonCodec.jsonCodec(ErrorResponse.schema)
```

The `RegexMatch` case matters for rules built from a regular expression, such as `Validation.email`: its own message prints the whole regular expression, which a client cannot use.

Next, one function decodes the body, validates the result, and picks the response. A body that does not decode becomes a `malformed_body` error, and a body that decodes but breaks a rule becomes a `validation_failed` error:

```scala
def parseSignup(body: String): Either[ErrorResponse, Signup] =
  JsonCodec.jsonDecoder(Signup.schema).decodeJson(body) match {
    case Left(message) =>
      Left(ErrorResponse("malformed_body", Map("body" -> List(message))))
    case Right(signup) =>
      val errors = fieldErrors(signup)
      if (errors.isEmpty) Right(signup)
      else
        Left(
          ErrorResponse(
            "validation_failed",
            errors.map { case (name, problems) => name -> problems.map(describe).toList }
          )
        )
  }

def respond(body: String): String =
  parseSignup(body) match {
    case Left(response) => s"400 ${errorCodec.encodeJson(response, None)}"
    case Right(signup)  => s"201 created ${signup.username}"
  }
```

The `respond` function stands in for an HTTP handler. We send it our invalid request, a request that lacks required fields, and a valid request:

```scala
println(respond(json))
// 400 {"error":"validation_failed","fields":{"username":["must be at least 3 characters"],"age":["must be greater than 17"],"address":["must be at least 1 characters"]}}

println(respond("""{"username":"jane"}"""))
// 400 {"error":"malformed_body","fields":{"body":[".email(missing)"]}}

println(respond("""{"username":"jane_doe","email":"jane@example.com","age":30,"address":{"street":"1 Main St","city":"Springfield"}}"""))
// 201 created jane_doe
```

The same `ErrorResponse` type works for any model, because `fieldErrors` only needs a schema. If you build an HTTP API with ZIO HTTP, its `Endpoint` API runs `Schema.validate` on request bodies for you; [How to Build a JSON HTTP API with ZIO HTTP](json-http-api.md) shows how to shape its error responses.

### Rules That Are Silently Skipped

Validation fails open in a few cases: the rule exists, but `Schema.validate` reports no error. Each case below has a working alternative, and the [Validation](../operations/validating-types.md) reference shows each one with a runnable example.

#### Rules Added with `Schema#validation`

`Schema#validation(v)` stores the rule `v` as an annotation on the schema, but `Schema.validate` only reads the rules of record fields, so it never checks this one. [Rules on a Whole Schema](../operations/validating-types.md#rules-on-a-whole-schema) shows a value that breaks such a rule and still passes.

:::caution[`Schema#validation` Is Not Checked]
`Schema.validate` ignores a rule added with `Schema#validation`. Put the rule on a record field with `@validate` (or the `validation0` parameter of `Schema.Field.apply` in a hand-written schema), or call `Validation#validate` on the value directly.
:::

#### Rules That Fail Without an Error

`Validation.fail` always fails, but it fails with an empty list of errors. `Schema.validate` turns that empty list into "no errors", so a field annotated with `@validate(Validation.fail[Int])` passes. The same happens with the default `onLeft` of `Validation#right` and the default `onRight` of `Validation#left`, which are `Validation.fail`. [Constant Rules](../operations/validating-types.md#constant-rules) shows the effect.

:::caution[A Rule That Fails with No Error Reports Nothing]
Through `@validate`, a rule that fails without an error is reported as valid. Check such a rule with `Validation#validate` and test for `Left`, instead of relying on an empty `Schema.validate` result.
:::

#### Case Classes with More Than 22 Fields on Scala 2

On Scala 2, `DeriveSchema.gen` represents a case class with more than 22 fields as a `GenericRecord` and drops every `@validate` annotation of that class. Scala 3 derivation keeps them.

:::caution[Scala 2 Drops `@validate` Above 22 Fields]
On Scala 2, `Schema.validate` reports no errors for the fields of a case class with more than 22 fields. Move the validated fields into a nested case class with 22 fields or fewer, whose rules `Schema.validate` checks as part of the parent, or call `Validation#validate` on those field values directly.
:::

### Going Further

The [Validation](../operations/validating-types.md) reference covers every rule constructor, the boolean combinators, the regular-expression DSL, and all `ValidationError` cases. [Validating Types](../operations/validating-types.md) gives a shorter overview of validation, and [Schema Annotations](../schema-annotations.md) lists the other annotations that shape decoding, such as `@fieldName` and `@fieldDefaultValue`. On Scala 3, [How to Use ZIO Schema with Scala 3](scala-3.md) shows how to derive the same schemas with `derives Schema`.

## Introduction to ZIO Schema

[ZIO Schema](https://github.com/zio/zio-schema) is a [ZIO](https://zio.dev)-based library for modeling the schema of data structures as first-class values.

[![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project%20Stage-Development-green.svg)](https://github.com/zio/zio/wiki/Project-Stages) ![CI Badge](https://github.com/zio/zio-schema/workflows/CI/badge.svg) [![Sonatype Releases](https://img.shields.io/maven-central/v/dev.zio/zio-schema_2.13.svg?label=Sonatype%20Release)](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/dev.zio/zio-schema_2.13) [![Sonatype Snapshots](https://img.shields.io/maven-metadata/v?metadataUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fcentral.sonatype.com%2Frepository%2Fmaven-snapshots%2Fdev%2Fzio%2Fzio-schema_2.13%2Fmaven-metadata.xml&label=Sonatype%20Snapshot)](https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/dev/zio/zio-schema_2.13/) [![javadoc](https://javadoc.io/badge2/dev.zio/zio-schema_2.13/javadoc.svg)](https://javadoc.io/doc/dev.zio/zio-schema_2.13) [![ZIO Schema](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zio/zio-schema?style=social)](https://github.com/zio/zio-schema)

### Introduction

ZIO Schema helps us solve some of the most common problems in distributed computing, such as serialization, deserialization, and data migration.

It turns a compile-time construct (the type of a data structure) into a runtime construct (a value that can be read, manipulated, and composed at runtime). A schema is a structure of a data type. ZIO Schema reifies the concept of structure for data types. It makes a high-level description of any data type and makes them first-class values.

Creating a schema for a data type helps us to write codecs for that data type. ZIO Schema ships codecs for JSON, Protobuf, Avro, BSON, MessagePack, Thrift, and XML, and the same schema drives all of them.

### What Problems Does ZIO Schema Solve?

With schema descriptions that can be automatically derived for case classes and sealed traits, _ZIO Schema_ provides powerful features for free:

1. Generic programming without writing macros yourself. The derivation macros inspect your types once, and everything else works on the resulting schema value:
    1. Creating serialization and deserialization codecs for any supported protocol (JSON, Protobuf, etc.)
    2. Deriving an `Ordering` from the structure of the data, and deriving your own type classes with a `Deriver`
    3. Default values for data types
2. Automate ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipelines
    1. Diffing: diffing between two values of the same type
    2. Patching: applying a diff to a value to update it
    3. Migration: migrating values from one type to another
3. Computations as data: Not only can we turn types into values, but we can also turn computations into values. This opens up a whole new world of possibilities concerning distributed computing.

When our data structures need to be serialized, deserialized, persisted, or transported across the wire, then _ZIO Schema_ lets us focus on data modeling and automatically tackle all the low-level, messy details for us.

A growing number of ZIO libraries build on _ZIO Schema_, including [ZIO Flow](https://zio.dev/zio-flow), [ZIO Redis](https://zio.dev/zio-redis), [ZIO SQL](https://zio.dev/zio-sql) and [ZIO DynamoDB](https://zio.dev/zio-dynamodb).

### Installation

Every project needs two modules: `zio-schema`, which holds `Schema` itself, and `zio-schema-derivation`, which derives schemas for case classes and sealed traits. On the JVM, add them to `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // Schema, DynamicValue, diff and patch, migration, validation (JVM, Scala.js, Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema"            % "1.9.2",

  // DeriveSchema.gen and the Deriver API for your own type classes (JVM, Scala.js, Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-derivation" % "1.9.2"
)
```

In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use the `%%%` operator instead:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-schema"            % "1.9.2",

  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-schema-derivation" % "1.9.2"
)
```

On Scala 2, schema derivation uses macros that need `scala-reflect` at compile time. Scala 3 has no `scala-reflect` artifact, so a build that cross-compiles adds it only for Scala 2:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= {
  CrossVersion.partialVersion(scalaVersion.value) match {
    case Some((2, _)) => Seq("org.scala-lang" % "scala-reflect" % scalaVersion.value % Provided)
    case _            => Seq.empty
  }
}
```

ZIO Schema is published for Scala 2.12, 2.13, and 3.

:::caution[Scala 3 Projects Need Scala 3.9 or Later]
The Scala 3 artifacts are compiled with Scala 3.9, so a Scala 3 project must use Scala 3.9 or later to depend on them.
:::

[Getting Started](getting-started.md) walks through a first program: deriving a schema, encoding JSON, and validating values. The [Modules](#modules) section below lists the optional modules for codecs, optics, and testing.

### Modules

Every other feature lives in its own optional module, and we add only the modules we use. All modules share the core module's version, and each one already depends on `zio-schema` and `zio-schema-derivation`.

#### Codecs

A codec module encodes and decodes values in one data format, using their schemas. On the JVM, every codec is available. Copy the block and delete the lines you don't need:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // JSON codec (JVM, Scala.js, Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json"     % "1.9.2",

  // Protocol Buffers codec (JVM, Scala.js, Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-protobuf" % "1.9.2",

  // XML codec (JVM, Scala.js, Native)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-xml"      % "1.9.2",

  // Apache Avro codec (JVM only)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-avro"     % "1.9.2",

  // BSON codec for MongoDB (JVM only)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-bson"     % "1.9.2",

  // MessagePack codec (JVM only)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-msg-pack" % "1.9.2",

  // Apache Thrift codec (JVM only)
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-thrift"   % "1.9.2"
)
```

In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, only the JSON, Protocol Buffers, and XML codecs are available. The Avro, BSON, MessagePack, and Thrift codecs have no Scala.js or Scala Native artifacts:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  // JSON codec
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-schema-json"     % "1.9.2",

  // Protocol Buffers codec
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-schema-protobuf" % "1.9.2",

  // XML codec
  "dev.zio" %%% "zio-schema-xml"      % "1.9.2"
)
```

Each codec has its own page: [JSON](derivations/codecs/json.md), [Protocol Buffers](derivations/codecs/protobuf.md), [XML](derivations/codecs/xml.md), [Apache Avro](derivations/codecs/avro.md), [BSON](derivations/codecs/bson.md), [MessagePack](derivations/codecs/message-pack.md), and [Apache Thrift](derivations/codecs/thrift.md).

#### Optics

The optics module derives lenses, prisms, and traversals from a schema, for reading and updating nested data (JVM, Scala.js, Native):

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-optics" % "1.9.2"
```

In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use `%%%` instead of `%%`. [Optics Derivation](derivations/optics-derivation.md) describes the module.

#### Testing

The ZIO Test module derives ZIO Test generators (`Gen`) from a schema, for property-based tests (JVM, Scala.js, Native). Tests are its only users, so it goes in the `Test` configuration:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-zio-test" % "1.9.2" % Test
```

In a Scala.js or Scala Native project, use `%%%` instead of `%%`. [Derivation of ZIO Test Generators](derivations/zio-test-gen-derivation.md) describes the module.

#### Internal Modules

The build also publishes `zio-schema-macros`, an internal helper that the other modules pull in, so you never add it yourself.

### Example

In this example, we derive a schema for `Person` and then encode a `Person` value as a stream of Protocol Buffers bytes. The example needs the `zio-schema-protobuf` module:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.stream._
import zio.schema.codec.{BinaryCodec, ProtobufCodec}
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}

import java.io.IOException

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person]    = DeriveSchema.gen
  val protobufCodec: BinaryCodec[Person] = ProtobufCodec.protobufCodec
}

object Main extends ZIOAppDefault {
  def run: ZIO[Any, IOException, Unit] =
    ZStream
      .succeed(Person("John", 43))
      .via(Person.protobufCodec.streamEncoder)
      .runCollect
      .flatMap(x =>
        Console.printLine(s"Encoded data with protobuf codec: ${toHex(x)}")
      )

  def toHex(chunk: Chunk[Byte]): String =
    chunk.map("%02X".format(_)).mkString
}
```

Here is the output of running the above program:

```text
Encoded data with protobuf codec: 0A044A6F686E102B
```

## How to Encode and Decode Streams

This guide shows how to turn a `ZStream` of values into a stream of bytes and back with ZIO Schema codecs, for example to write records to a file, a socket, or a message queue. It covers the JSON codec, which streams directly, and the binary codecs, which need the messages kept apart.

Every `BinaryCodec[A]` has two stream methods besides `BinaryCodec#encode` and `BinaryCodec#decode`. `BinaryCodec#streamEncoder` is a `ZPipeline[Any, Nothing, A, Byte]` that turns values into bytes, and `BinaryCodec#streamDecoder` is a `ZPipeline[Any, DecodeError, Byte, A]` that turns bytes back into values. A `ZPipeline` is a reusable stream transformer that we attach to a stream with `ZStream#via`. The [Codec Core Types](reference/codec-core.md) page describes the traits.

### Choose a Strategy for Your Codec

A stream of bytes has no built-in boundaries between values: the bytes of two values can arrive in one chunk, and the bytes of one value can be split across chunks. A stream decoder must find where each value ends, which is called framing. The codecs differ in how they handle it:

| Codec               | `BinaryCodec#streamEncoder` output              | `BinaryCodec#streamDecoder` input       | How to stream                               |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| JSON                | One value per line, or one JSON array           | Any chunking for newline-delimited JSON | Use the pipelines directly                  |
| Protobuf, Avro, XML | Encodings concatenated with no separator        | Exactly one value per chunk             | Encode per message, or add your own framing |
| MessagePack, Thrift | Cumulative: element `n` repeats elements 1..`n` | Exactly one value per chunk             | Encode per message, or add your own framing |
| BSON                | No stream pipelines                             | No stream pipelines                     | Use zio-bson or the MongoDB driver          |

Only the JSON codec streams several values reliably through its pipelines. For the binary formats, the sections below show two patterns that work with every codec.

### Prerequisites

The examples use the JSON and Protobuf modules, which bring ZIO Streams with them:

```scala
libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-json"     % "1.9.2",
  "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-protobuf" % "1.9.2"
)
```

For other formats, add their modules as listed on the [Introduction to ZIO Schema Codecs](derivations/codecs/index.md#available-codecs) page.

### Stream JSON Values

The JSON codec writes newline-delimited JSON by default: each value on its own line. Its decoder tracks brackets and strings to find where each value ends, so the bytes can arrive in chunks of any size.

To set up the examples, we define a model, derive a JSON codec, and add a helper that runs an effect and returns its result:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.schema.codec.{BinaryCodec, DecodeError, JsonCodec}
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}
import zio.stream._

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}

val people: Chunk[Person] = Chunk(Person("John", 42), Person("Jane", 34))

val jsonCodec: BinaryCodec[Person] = JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[Person]

def runNow[E, A](effect: ZIO[Any, E, A]): A =
  Unsafe.unsafe { implicit unsafe =>
    Runtime.default.unsafe.run(effect).getOrThrowFiberFailure()
  }
```

To encode, we run the stream of people through the encoder pipeline and collect the bytes:

```scala
val jsonBytes: Chunk[Byte] =
  runNow(ZStream.fromChunk(people).via(jsonCodec.streamEncoder).runCollect)
```

The bytes hold one JSON document per line:

```scala
println(new String(jsonBytes.toArray, "UTF-8"))
// {"name":"John","age":42}
// {"name":"Jane","age":34}
```

To decode, we feed the bytes back in chunks of 5 bytes, so that every value is split across several chunks, and the decoder still returns both people:

```scala
runNow(ZStream.fromChunk(jsonBytes).rechunk(5).via(jsonCodec.streamDecoder).runCollect)
// res1: Chunk[Person] = IndexedSeq(
//   Person(name = "John", age = 42),
//   Person(name = "Jane", age = 34)
// )
```

### Stream a JSON Array

Some consumers expect one JSON array instead of one value per line. Setting `treatStreamsAsArrays = true` in `JsonCodec.Configuration` makes the encoder write a single array, and the decoder read the elements of one:

```scala
val arrayCodec: BinaryCodec[Person] =
  JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[Person](JsonCodec.Configuration(treatStreamsAsArrays = true))

val arrayBytes: Chunk[Byte] =
  runNow(ZStream.fromChunk(people).via(arrayCodec.streamEncoder).runCollect)
```

The output is one array, and decoding it gives the people back:

```scala
println(new String(arrayBytes.toArray, "UTF-8"))
// [{"name":"John","age":42},{"name":"Jane","age":34}]

runNow(ZStream.fromChunk(arrayBytes).via(arrayCodec.streamDecoder).runCollect)
// res3: Chunk[Person] = IndexedSeq(
//   Person(name = "John", age = 42),
//   Person(name = "Jane", age = 34)
// )
```

:::caution
With `treatStreamsAsArrays = true`, the stream decoder dies with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when the array arrives split across chunks of more than one byte, as it usually does when read from a socket or a file. Unless the whole array arrives in one chunk, collect the bytes first (for example with `ZStream#runCollect`) and decode them as one chunk, or use the default newline-delimited format, whose decoder handles any chunking.
:::

### Stream Values of a Binary Format

The stream decoders of the Protobuf, Avro, MessagePack, Thrift, and XML codecs decode each upstream chunk as exactly one message, and their encoders write no length or separator between messages.

:::caution
Do not connect `BinaryCodec#streamEncoder` to `BinaryCodec#streamDecoder` for these codecs when the stream has more than one value. The decoder reads the whole chunk as one message, so values are merged, dropped, or fail to decode. The MessagePack and Thrift stream encoders also repeat every earlier element in each element's output. Use one of the patterns below instead.
:::

To see the problem, we derive a Protobuf codec:

```scala
import zio.schema.codec.ProtobufCodec

val protobufCodec: BinaryCodec[Person] = ProtobufCodec.protobufCodec[Person]
```

Sending two people through its stream pipelines shows what goes wrong:

```scala
runNow(
  ZStream.fromChunk(people).via(protobufCodec.streamEncoder).via(protobufCodec.streamDecoder).runCollect.either
)
// res4: Either[DecodeError, Chunk[Person]] = Right(
//   value = IndexedSeq(Person(name = "Jane", age = 34))
// )
```

Two people go in, but the decoder treats the two encodings as one message, so they do not come back as two values.

#### One Value per Message

When the transport already keeps messages apart, such as Kafka records, WebSocket frames, or rows in a table, encode each value into its own `Chunk[Byte]` with `BinaryCodec#encode`, and decode each message with `BinaryCodec#decode`:

```scala
val messages: Chunk[Chunk[Byte]] =
  runNow(ZStream.fromChunk(people).map(protobufCodec.encode).runCollect)
```

Each message decodes on its own, so both people come back:

```scala
runNow(ZStream.fromChunk(messages).mapZIO(message => ZIO.fromEither(protobufCodec.decode(message))).runCollect)
// res5: Chunk[Person] = IndexedSeq(
//   Person(name = "John", age = 42),
//   Person(name = "Jane", age = 34)
// )
```

This works for every binary codec, including MessagePack and Thrift, because `BinaryCodec#encode` starts from an empty buffer for each value.

#### Length-Prefixed Framing

When the transport is a plain byte stream, such as a file or a TCP socket, add the framing yourself. A common scheme writes the length of each message as a 4-byte integer in front of it. The following helpers write and read that format for any `BinaryCodec`:

```scala
import java.nio.ByteBuffer

def writeFramed[A](codec: BinaryCodec[A]): ZPipeline[Any, Nothing, A, Byte] =
  ZPipeline.mapChunks[A, Byte](_.flatMap { value =>
    val message = codec.encode(value)
    Chunk.fromArray(ByteBuffer.allocate(4).putInt(message.size).array()) ++ message
  })

def splitFrames(buffer: Chunk[Byte], frames: Chunk[Chunk[Byte]]): (Chunk[Byte], Chunk[Chunk[Byte]]) =
  if (buffer.size < 4) (buffer, frames)
  else {
    val size = ByteBuffer.wrap(buffer.take(4).toArray).getInt
    if (buffer.size < 4 + size) (buffer, frames)
    else splitFrames(buffer.drop(4 + size), frames :+ buffer.slice(4, 4 + size))
  }

def readFramed[A](codec: BinaryCodec[A], bytes: ZStream[Any, Nothing, Byte]): ZStream[Any, DecodeError, A] =
  bytes.chunks
    .mapAccum(Chunk.empty[Byte])((buffer, chunk) => splitFrames(buffer ++ chunk, Chunk.empty))
    .flattenChunks
    .mapZIO(message => ZIO.fromEither(codec.decode(message)))
```

`writeFramed` encodes each value on its own and puts its length in front of it. `readFramed` keeps the bytes that do not yet form a whole message in a buffer, emits each complete message, and decodes it. Bytes left over at the end of the stream, from a truncated last message, are dropped.

With framing in place, we encode the people into one byte stream:

```scala
val framedBytes: Chunk[Byte] =
  runNow(ZStream.fromChunk(people).via(writeFramed(protobufCodec)).runCollect)
```

Reading the bytes back in chunks of 3 bytes still gives both people, because the decoder waits for each whole message:

```scala
runNow(readFramed(protobufCodec, ZStream.fromChunk(framedBytes).rechunk(3)).runCollect)
// res6: Chunk[Person] = IndexedSeq(
//   Person(name = "John", age = 42),
//   Person(name = "Jane", age = 34)
// )
```

The same helpers work with the Avro, MessagePack, Thrift, and XML codecs, because they call only `BinaryCodec#encode` and `BinaryCodec#decode`.

- [Introduction to ZIO Schema Codecs](derivations/codecs/index.md) compares the codecs and the annotations they support.
- [JSON Codecs](derivations/codecs/json.md) describes `treatStreamsAsArrays` and the other configuration fields.
- [Write a Custom Codec](how-to/custom-codec.md) shows how to implement `Codec#streamEncoder` and `Codec#streamDecoder` for your own format.

## Manual Schema Construction

`DeriveSchema.gen` writes schemas for us, but we can also build them by hand from the case classes described in [Basic Building Blocks](basic-building-blocks.md), with every constructor listed in the [Schema Data Types](basic-building-blocks.md) reference. Hand-written schemas are useful when a type cannot be derived or when we want full control over names and identifiers. This page builds schemas for the following domain models:

```scala
object Domain {
  final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

  sealed trait PaymentMethod

  object PaymentMethod {
    final case class CreditCard(number: String, expirationMonth: Int, expirationYear: Int) extends PaymentMethod
    final case class WireTransfer(accountNumber: String, bankCode: String) extends PaymentMethod
  }

  final case class Customer(person: Person, paymentMethod: PaymentMethod)
  
}
```

Let's begin by creating a schema for the `Person` data type with `Schema.CaseClass2`:

```scala
import zio.schema._

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] =
    Schema.CaseClass2[String, Int, Person](
      id0 = TypeId.fromTypeName("Person"),
      field01 = Schema.Field(name0 = "name", schema0 = Schema[String], get0 = _.name, set0 = (p, x) => p.copy(name = x)),
      field02 = Schema.Field(name0 = "age", schema0 = Schema[Int], get0 = _.age, set0 = (person, age) => person.copy(age = age)),
      construct0 = (name, age) => Person(name, age),
    )
}
```

The next step is writing a schema for the `PaymentMethod` sealed trait with `Schema.Enum2`, which needs one `Schema.Case` per subtype:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.schema._

sealed trait PaymentMethod

object PaymentMethod {
  implicit val schema: Schema[PaymentMethod] =
    Schema.Enum2[CreditCard, WireTransfer, PaymentMethod](
      id = TypeId.fromTypeName("PaymentMethod"),
      case1 = Schema.Case[PaymentMethod, CreditCard](
        id = "CreditCard",
        schema = CreditCard.schema,
        unsafeDeconstruct = pm => pm.asInstanceOf[PaymentMethod.CreditCard],
        construct = cc => cc.asInstanceOf[PaymentMethod],
        isCase = _.isInstanceOf[PaymentMethod.CreditCard],
        annotations = Chunk.empty
      ),
      case2 = Schema.Case[PaymentMethod, WireTransfer](
        id = "WireTransfer",
        schema = WireTransfer.schema,
        unsafeDeconstruct = pm => pm.asInstanceOf[PaymentMethod.WireTransfer],
        construct = wt => wt.asInstanceOf[PaymentMethod],
        isCase = _.isInstanceOf[PaymentMethod.WireTransfer],
        annotations = Chunk.empty
      )
    )

  final case class CreditCard(
      number: String,
      expirationMonth: Int,
      expirationYear: Int
  ) extends PaymentMethod

  object CreditCard {
    implicit val schema: Schema[CreditCard] =
      Schema.CaseClass3[String, Int, Int, CreditCard](
        id0 = TypeId.fromTypeName("CreditCard"),
        field01 = Schema.Field[CreditCard, String](
          name0 = "number",
          schema0 = Schema.primitive[String],
          get0 = _.number,
          set0 = (cc, n) => cc.copy(number = n)
        ),
        field02 = Schema.Field[CreditCard, Int](
          name0 = "expirationMonth",
          schema0 = Schema.primitive[Int],
          get0 = _.expirationMonth,
          set0 = (cc, em) => cc.copy(expirationMonth = em)
        ),
        field03 = Schema.Field[CreditCard, Int](
          name0 = "expirationYear",
          schema0 = Schema.primitive[Int],
          get0 = _.expirationYear,
          set0 = (cc, ey) => cc.copy(expirationYear = ey)
        ),
        construct0 = (n, em, ey) => CreditCard(n, em, ey)
      )
  }

  final case class WireTransfer(accountNumber: String, bankCode: String)
      extends PaymentMethod

  object WireTransfer {
    implicit val schema: Schema[WireTransfer] =
      Schema.CaseClass2[String, String, WireTransfer](
        id0 = TypeId.fromTypeName("WireTransfer"),
        field01 = Schema.Field[WireTransfer, String](
          name0 = "accountNumber",
          schema0 = Schema.primitive[String],
          get0 = _.accountNumber,
          set0 = (wt, an) => wt.copy(accountNumber = an)
        ),
        field02 = Schema.Field[WireTransfer, String](
          name0 = "bankCode",
          schema0 = Schema.primitive[String],
          get0 = _.bankCode,
          set0 = (wt, bc) => wt.copy(bankCode = bc)
        ),
        construct0 = (ac, bc) => WireTransfer(ac, bc)
      )
  }
}
```

And finally, we need to define the schema for the `Customer` data type:

```scala
import zio._
import zio.schema._

final case class Customer(person: Person, paymentMethod: PaymentMethod)

object Customer {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Customer] =
    Schema.CaseClass2[Person, PaymentMethod, Customer](
      id0 = TypeId.fromTypeName("Customer"),
      field01 = Schema.Field[Customer, Person](
        name0 = "person",
        schema0 = Person.schema,
        get0 = _.person,
        set0 = (c, p) => c.copy(person = p)
      ),
      field02 = Schema.Field[Customer, PaymentMethod](
        name0 = "paymentMethod",
        schema0 = Schema[PaymentMethod],
        get0 = _.paymentMethod,
        set0 = (c, pm) => c.copy(paymentMethod = pm)
      ),
      construct0 = (p, pm) => Customer(p, pm)
    )
}
```

Now that we have written all the required schemas, we can create encoders and decoders (codecs) for each of our domain models.

Let's start with Protobuf codecs. We need to add the following line to our `build.sbt`:

```scala
libraryDependencies += "dev.zio" %% "zio-schema-protobuf" % "1.9.2"
```

The following round trip encodes a `Customer` with the Protobuf codec and decodes it back to the same value:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.codec._

// Create a customer instance
val customer =
  Customer(
    person = Person("John Doe", 42),
    paymentMethod = PaymentMethod.CreditCard("1000100010001000", 6, 2024)
  )

// Create binary codec from customer 
val customerCodec: BinaryCodec[Customer] =
  ProtobufCodec.protobufCodec[Customer]

// Encode the customer object
val encodedCustomer: Chunk[Byte] = customerCodec.encode(customer)

// Decode the bytes back to a customer instance
val decodedCustomer: Either[DecodeError, Customer] =
  customerCodec.decode(encodedCustomer)

assert(Right(customer) == decodedCustomer)
```

## The Motivation Behind ZIO Schema

ZIO Schema is a library used in many ZIO projects such as _ZIO Flow_, _ZIO Redis_, _ZIO SQL_ and _ZIO DynamoDB_. It is all about reification of our types. Reification means turning something abstract, such as a side effect, a field access, or the structure of a type, into something "real": a value.

### Reification: Functional Effects

In functional effects, we reify by turning side-effects into values. For example, we might have a simple statement like this:

```scala
println("Hello")
println("World")
```

In ZIO, we reify these statements into values:

```scala
import zio._

val effect1 = ZIO.attempt(println("Hello"))
val effect2 = ZIO.attempt(println("World"))
```

Because the effects are values, we can combine them with operators, for example to run both in parallel and retry them on failure:

```scala
import zio._

val both = (ZIO.attempt(println("Hello")) zipPar ZIO.attempt(println("World"))).retryN(100)
```

### Reification: Optics

In Scala, we have product types like this case class of a `Person`:

```scala
final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)
```

This case class has two fields: `name` of type `String` and `age` of type `Int`.

The Scala language provides special support to access the fields inside case classes using the dot syntax:

```scala
val person = Person("Michelle", 32)
val name = person.name
val age  = person.age
```

However, field access is a special language feature. It is not a value, unlike the reified effects in the previous section (`println(...)` vs. `ZIO.attempt(println(...))`).

Because field access is not a value, we cannot pass it around or build operators on it. For example, we cannot combine two field accesses into one that reaches a field inside a nested structure.

The solution to this kind of problem is called an "optic". Optics provide a way to access the fields of a case class and nested structures. There are three main types of optics:

- `Lens`: A lens focuses on one field of a product type, such as a case class.
- `Prism`: A prism focuses on one case of a sum type, such as one subtype of a sealed trait.
- `Traversal`: A traversal focuses on all the elements of a collection.

Optics take something that is not a first-class **concept**, drilling down into a field of a case class or into a nested structure, and turn it into a first-class **value**.

Once we have a value, we can compose optics to solve hard problems in functional programming, such as updating a field deep inside nested case classes without a chain of `copy` calls, or updating every element of a collection inside a nested structure.

For more information on optics, refer to the [ZIO Optics](https://zio.dev/zio-optics/) documentation. ZIO Schema can derive these optics from a schema, as [Optics Derivation](derivations/optics-derivation.md) shows.

### Reification: Schema

The previous sections reify side effects into values (ZIO), and reify accessing and modifying fields inside case classes or arbitrary structures into values as well (optics).

**ZIO Schema** is now about how to **describe entire data structures using values**.

The built-in way to describe data structures in Scala is case classes and classes.

For example, assume we have the `Person` data type, like this:

```scala
final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)
```

It has the following information:

- Name of the structure: `Person`
- Fields: `name` and `age`
- Type of the fields: `String` and `Int`
- Type of the structure: `Person`

ZIO Schema reifies the structure of data types by turning this information into values. It does so not only for case classes, but also for other types such as collections, tuples, and enumerations. [Automatic Schema Derivation](automatic-schema-derivation.md) shows how to get such a value for your own types.

---

## Diffing and Patching

A schema can compute the difference between two values of its type and apply that difference to a value later. `Schema#diff` and `Schema#patch` provide these two operations:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def diff(thisValue: A, thatValue: A): Patch[A]

  def patch(oldValue: A, diff: Patch[A]): scala.util.Either[String, A]
}
```

`Schema#diff` takes two values of the same type `A` and returns a `Patch[A]` value that describes the differences between the two values. Conversely, `Schema#patch` takes a value of type `A` and a `Patch[A]` value and returns a new value of type `A` that is the result of applying the patch to the original value. The [Patch and Differ](../reference/patch-and-differ.md) reference page describes the `Patch` and `Differ` types in detail.

### Diffing Two Records

The following example computes the difference between two versions of a person and applies it to the older version:

```scala
import zio.schema._

case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}

val oldValue = Person("John", 42)
val newValue = Person("John", 43)

val personPatch: Patch[Person] = Person.schema.diff(oldValue, newValue)
```

Applying the patch to the old value gives the new value:

```scala
Person.schema.patch(oldValue, personPatch) == Right(newValue)
// res0: Boolean = true
```

A record patch holds one entry for every field, and the entry for an unchanged field is an identical patch. Applying the patch converts the whole record through `DynamicValue`, so the cost grows with the size of the record, not with the number of changed fields.

The `zio.schema.syntax` object adds the same operations as methods on any value that has an implicit schema. `DiffOps#diffEach` is an alias of `DiffOps#diff` that does not clash with `Seq#diff` from the Scala collections:

```scala
import zio.schema.syntax._

oldValue.runPatch(oldValue.diffEach(newValue))
// res1: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "John", age = 43)
// )
```

### Changes That Produce a Failing Patch

Some pairs of values cannot be described as a change of one into the other. For these pairs, `Schema#diff` returns a patch whose `Patch#isComparable` method is `false`, and applying that patch always returns `Left`. This happens when:

- Two values of a sealed trait or enumeration are different cases.
- One `Either` is a `Left` and the other is a `Right`.
- The values are `DynamicValue`s, which are never compared.
- A `Schema#transformOrFail` schema cannot convert one of the values back to its underlying type.

When such a pair appears inside a record, for example as one field of a case class, the record patch contains the failing entry, so applying the whole patch fails. The following sealed trait shows the first case:

```scala
sealed trait Shape

object Shape {
  final case class Circle(radius: Double) extends Shape
  final case class Square(side: Double)   extends Shape

  implicit val schema: Schema[Shape] = DeriveSchema.gen[Shape]
}

val circle: Shape = Shape.Circle(1.0)
val square: Shape = Shape.Square(2.0)

val shapePatch: Patch[Shape] = Shape.schema.diff(circle, square)
```

The patch is not comparable, and applying it fails:

```scala
shapePatch.isComparable
// res2: Boolean = false

Shape.schema.patch(circle, shapePatch)
// res3: Either[String, Shape] = Left(
//   value = "Non-comparable diff cannot be applied"
// )
```

Check `Patch#isComparable` before you store or send a patch. When it is `false`, keep the new value itself instead of the patch.

### Optional Values

A change between `Some` and `None`, in either direction, produces a patch that replaces the whole value. Applying it always gives the new value, whatever the input:

```scala
val optionPatch = Schema[Option[Int]].diff(Some(1), None)
// optionPatch: Patch[Option[Int]] = Total(value = None)

Schema[Option[Int]].patch(Some(5), optionPatch)
// res4: Either[String, Option[Int]] = Right(value = None)
```

A change between two `Some` values diffs the inner values as usual. Inverting a `Some`-to-`None` patch does not restore the old value, as [Patches That Cannot Be Inverted](../reference/patch-and-differ.md#patches-that-cannot-be-inverted) explains.

---

## Dynamic Data Representation

`DynamicValue` is a **self-describing value tree** that can hold any value a `Schema` can describe, without the Scala type that the value came from. Each node records both the data and its shape: a record keeps its field names, an enum keeps the name of its case, and a primitive keeps its `StandardType`. Code that does not know the type at compile time can therefore inspect, rewrite, and migrate the value, and a schema turns it back into a typed value later.

`DynamicValue` has no type parameter. The type information that a typed value carries in its Scala type is stored in the tree itself, so one `DynamicValue` type covers every value. The two conversions are `Schema#toDynamic`, which erases the type, and `Schema#fromDynamic` (or `DynamicValue#toTypedValue`), which restores it.

This differs from the relational database model, where the database schema holds the structure of the data and the data itself lives in a separate location. Document formats such as JSON or XML store the data and its structure together: a JSON document can carry type information next to the data, so there is no need for a separate schema. `DynamicValue` brings the same self-describing model to any value that has a `Schema`.

### Usage

A typed value becomes a `DynamicValue` through its schema. We define a `Person` and convert one value:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.meta.{Migration, NodePath}

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}

final case class Employee(name: String, age: Int)

object Employee {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Employee] = DeriveSchema.gen[Employee]
}

val alice: DynamicValue = DynamicValue(Person("Alice", 42))
```

Printing the dynamic value shows the mixture of the data and its structure:

```scala
println(alice)
// Record(Nominal(Chunk(repl),Chunk(MdocSession,MdocApp),Person),ListMap(name -> Primitive(Alice,string), age -> Primitive(42,int)))
```

The record keeps the `TypeId` of `Person`, and each field keeps its value together with its standard type. Decoding matches record fields by name and ignores the `TypeId`, so the dynamic form decodes into `Employee`, a different case class with the same fields, as well as into `Person`. A migration step can also change the value before it is decoded:

```scala
alice.toTypedValue[Person]
// res1: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "Alice", age = 42)
// )
alice.toTypedValue[Employee]
// res2: Either[String, Employee] = Right(
//   value = Employee(name = "Alice", age = 42)
// )
alice.transform(Chunk(Migration.DeleteNode(NodePath.root / "age")))
// res3: Either[String, DynamicValue] = Right(
//   value = Record(
//     id = Nominal(
//       packageName = IndexedSeq("repl"),
//       objectNames = IndexedSeq("MdocSession", "MdocApp"),
//       typeName = "Person"
//     ),
//     values = ListMap(
//       "name" -> Primitive(value = "Alice", standardType = string)
//     )
//   )
// )
```

Rewriting a value's structure this way, for example removing a field or making it optional, is dynamic value migration. [Applying Migrations](#applying-migrations) describes `DynamicValue#transform`, and [Schema Migration](schema-migration.md) shows how ZIO Schema computes the steps between two versions of a schema.

### Cases

`DynamicValue` is a sealed trait with one case per kind of schema node:

```scala
sealed trait DynamicValue

object DynamicValue {
  final case class Record(id: TypeId, values: ListMap[String, DynamicValue]) extends DynamicValue
  final case class Enumeration(id: TypeId, value: (String, DynamicValue))   extends DynamicValue
  final case class Sequence(values: Chunk[DynamicValue])                     extends DynamicValue
  final case class Dictionary(entries: Chunk[(DynamicValue, DynamicValue)])  extends DynamicValue
  final case class SetValue(values: Set[DynamicValue])                       extends DynamicValue
  sealed case class Primitive[A](value: A, standardType: StandardType[A])    extends DynamicValue
  sealed case class Singleton[A](instance: A)                                extends DynamicValue
  final case class SomeValue(value: DynamicValue)                            extends DynamicValue
  case object NoneValue                                                      extends DynamicValue
  sealed case class Tuple(left: DynamicValue, right: DynamicValue)           extends DynamicValue
  final case class LeftValue(value: DynamicValue)                            extends DynamicValue
  final case class RightValue(value: DynamicValue)                           extends DynamicValue
  final case class BothValue(left: DynamicValue, right: DynamicValue)        extends DynamicValue
  final case class DynamicAst(ast: MetaSchema)                               extends DynamicValue
  final case class Error(message: String)                                    extends DynamicValue
}
```

The table lists which schemas produce each case when `Schema#toDynamic` converts a value:

| Case          | Produced by `Schema#toDynamic` for                                                     |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Record`      | Case classes and `GenericRecord`; transient fields are left out                        |
| `Enumeration` | Sealed traits and other `Schema.Enum`s; the pair is the case name and the case's value |
| `Sequence`    | `List`, `Vector`, `Chunk`, and non-empty sequences such as `NonEmptyChunk`             |
| `Dictionary`  | `Map` and `NonEmptyMap`                                                                |
| `SetValue`    | `Set`                                                                                  |
| `Primitive`   | Every standard type, such as `Int`, `String`, `UUID`, and the `java.time` types        |
| `SomeValue`   | `Some`                                                                                 |
| `NoneValue`   | `None`                                                                                 |
| `Tuple`       | Pairs; larger tuples become nested pairs                                               |
| `LeftValue`   | `Left` of an `Either`, and `Fallback.Left`                                             |
| `RightValue`  | `Right` of an `Either`, and `Fallback.Right`                                           |
| `BothValue`   | `Fallback.Both`                                                                        |
| `Error`       | A `Schema.Fail`, or a `Schema#transformOrFail` whose reverse function returns `Left`   |
| `Singleton`   | Nothing; build it by hand                                                              |
| `DynamicAst`  | Nothing; build it by hand to carry a schema as data                                    |

A case object of a sealed trait becomes an `Enumeration` whose value is a `Record` with no fields. `DynamicAst` holds a [MetaSchema](serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md), the serializable description of a schema. When no other decoding rule matches the schema, a `Tuple` whose right side is a `DynamicAst` decodes into a pair of the left value and the schema rebuilt from the `MetaSchema`.

Code that processes a `DynamicValue` usually matches on these cases. The following function renders any tree as text:

```scala
def render(value: DynamicValue): String =
  value match {
    case DynamicValue.Record(_, fields)            =>
      fields.map { case (name, v) => s"$name = ${render(v)}" }.mkString("{", ", ", "}")
    case DynamicValue.Enumeration(_, (caseName, v)) => s"$caseName${render(v)}"
    case DynamicValue.Sequence(values)              => values.map(render).mkString("[", ", ", "]")
    case DynamicValue.SetValue(values)              => values.map(render).mkString("Set(", ", ", ")")
    case DynamicValue.Dictionary(entries)           =>
      entries.map { case (k, v) => s"${render(k)} -> ${render(v)}" }.mkString("Map(", ", ", ")")
    case DynamicValue.Primitive(v, _)               => v.toString
    case DynamicValue.Singleton(instance)           => instance.toString
    case DynamicValue.SomeValue(v)                  => render(v)
    case DynamicValue.NoneValue                     => "null"
    case DynamicValue.Tuple(l, r)                   => s"(${render(l)}, ${render(r)})"
    case DynamicValue.LeftValue(v)                  => s"Left(${render(v)})"
    case DynamicValue.RightValue(v)                 => s"Right(${render(v)})"
    case DynamicValue.BothValue(l, r)               => s"Both(${render(l)}, ${render(r)})"
    case DynamicValue.DynamicAst(_)                 => "<schema>"
    case DynamicValue.Error(message)                => s"<error: $message>"
  }
```

The same function handles a record, a map of lists, and an optional pair:

```scala
println(render(alice))
// {name = Alice, age = 42}
println(render(DynamicValue(Map("scores" -> List(1, 2)))))
// Map(scores -> [1, 2])
println(render(DynamicValue(Option(("x", 1)))))
// (x, 1)
```

### Creating Values

A `DynamicValue` comes either from a typed value and its schema, or from the case constructors directly.

#### From a Typed Value

The usual way to get a `DynamicValue` is to let a schema convert a typed value. Every entry point below calls the same conversion, so they all give the same result:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def toDynamic(value: A): DynamicValue
}

object Schema {
  def toDynamic[A](a: A)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): DynamicValue
}

object DynamicValue {
  def apply[A](a: A)(implicit ev: Schema[A]): DynamicValue
  def fromSchemaAndValue[A](schema: Schema[A], value: A): DynamicValue
}
```

`Schema#toDynamic` and `DynamicValue.fromSchemaAndValue` take the schema explicitly, while `DynamicValue.apply` and `Schema.toDynamic` find it implicitly. The conversion works for any schema, including collections and options:

```scala
Person.schema.toDynamic(Person("Bob", 30)) == DynamicValue(Person("Bob", 30))
// res7: Boolean = true

DynamicValue.fromSchemaAndValue(Schema[Option[Int]], Some(1))
// res8: DynamicValue = SomeValue(
//   value = Primitive(value = 1, standardType = int)
// )

Schema.toDynamic(List("a", "b"))
// res9: DynamicValue = Sequence(
//   values = IndexedSeq(
//     Primitive(value = "a", standardType = string),
//     Primitive(value = "b", standardType = string)
//   )
// )
```

The `zio.schema.syntax` object adds a `dynamic` extension method to any value that has an implicit schema:

```scala
import zio.schema.syntax._

Person("Carol", 25).dynamic
// res10: DynamicValue = Record(
//   id = Nominal(
//     packageName = IndexedSeq("repl"),
//     objectNames = IndexedSeq("MdocSession", "MdocApp"),
//     typeName = "Person"
//   ),
//   values = ListMap(
//     "name" -> Primitive(value = "Carol", standardType = string),
//     "age" -> Primitive(value = 25, standardType = int)
//   )
// )
```

#### By Hand

Every case is a public case class, so we can also build a tree directly. This is how code that reads an untyped source, such as a configuration file or a message from another service, produces a value for a schema to decode. The following tree has the same shape as a `Person`:

```scala
import scala.collection.immutable.ListMap

def int(i: Int): DynamicValue       = DynamicValue.Primitive(i, StandardType.IntType)
def str(s: String): DynamicValue    = DynamicValue.Primitive(s, StandardType.StringType)

val handMade: DynamicValue =
  DynamicValue.Record(
    TypeId.parse("example.Person"),
    ListMap("name" -> str("Dave"), "age" -> int(51))
  )
```

Because decoding ignores the `TypeId`, the hand-made record decodes as a `Person`:

```scala
handMade.toTypedValue[Person]
// res11: Either[String, Person] = Right(
//   value = Person(name = "Dave", age = 51)
// )
```

The other cases follow the shape of their schema. A sequence decodes into any sequence schema, `NoneValue` into an option, `RightValue` into an `Either`, and a `Dictionary` of key and value pairs into a `Map`:

```scala
Schema[List[Int]].fromDynamic(DynamicValue.Sequence(Chunk(int(1), int(2))))
// res12: Either[String, List[Int]] = Right(value = List(1, 2))

Schema[Option[String]].fromDynamic(DynamicValue.NoneValue)
// res13: Either[String, Option[String]] = Right(value = None)

Schema[Either[String, Int]].fromDynamic(DynamicValue.RightValue(int(7)))
// res14: Either[String, Either[String, Int]] = Right(value = Right(value = 7))

Schema[Map[String, Int]].fromDynamic(DynamicValue.Dictionary(Chunk(str("a") -> int(1))))
// res15: Either[String, Map[String, Int]] = Right(value = Map("a" -> 1))
```

### Core Operations

The operations on a `DynamicValue` either decode it back into a typed value or rewrite it with migration steps.

#### Converting to Typed Values

Four methods decode a `DynamicValue` with a schema. They differ only in how they report a failure: `DynamicValue#toTypedValue` and `Schema#fromDynamic` return the error message as a `String`, `DynamicValue#toValue` returns the full `DecodeError`, and `DynamicValue#toTypedValueOption` drops the error:

```scala
sealed trait DynamicValue {
  def toTypedValue[A](implicit schema: Schema[A]): Either[String, A]
  def toValue[A](implicit schema: Schema[A]): Either[DecodeError, A]
  def toTypedValueOption[A](implicit schema: Schema[A]): Option[A]
}

sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def fromDynamic(value: DynamicValue): Either[String, A]
}
```

A string primitive cannot become an `Int`, so each method reports the failure in its own way:

```scala
val notAnInt = DynamicValue.Primitive("forty-two", StandardType.StringType)
// notAnInt: DynamicValue.Primitive[String] = Primitive(
//   value = "forty-two",
//   standardType = string
// )

notAnInt.toTypedValue[Int]
// res16: Either[String, Int] = Left(
//   value = "Failed to cast Primitive(forty-two,string) to schema Primitive(int,Chunk())"
// )
notAnInt.toValue[Int]
// res17: Either[codec.DecodeError, Int] = Left(
//   value = CastError(
//     value = Primitive(value = "forty-two", standardType = string),
//     schema = Primitive(standardType = int, annotations = IndexedSeq())
//   )
// )
notAnInt.toTypedValueOption[Int]
// res18: Option[Int] = None
```

`DynamicValue#toValue` reports failures with `DecodeError`, the same error type the codecs use; the [Codec Core Types](../reference/codec-core.md) page describes its cases. A record fails with `DecodeError.IncompatibleShape` when it has a field that the target schema does not know, so a case class that stores the same data under another field name cannot decode the dynamic form of a `Person`:

```scala
case class Customer(fullName: String, age: Int)

object Customer {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Customer] = DeriveSchema.gen[Customer]
}

alice.toTypedValue[Customer].isLeft
// res19: Boolean = true
```

The decoder walks the schema and the tree together. A primitive must have the same `StandardType` as the schema, a record decodes field by field, an enumeration looks up its case by name, and a `Schema.Transform` decodes the underlying value and then applies the transformation's forward function. A `DynamicValue.Error` always fails with its message.

`DynamicValue.decodeStructure` is the record step on its own. It decodes a map of field values against a list of `Schema.Field`s and returns the decoded fields in a `ListMap`:

```scala
object DynamicValue {
  def decodeStructure(
    values: ListMap[String, DynamicValue],
    structure: Chunk[Schema.Field[_, _]]
  ): Either[DecodeError, ListMap[String, _]]
}
```

#### Applying Migrations

`DynamicValue#transform` applies a `Chunk` of `Migration` steps to the value and stops at the first step that fails:

```scala
sealed trait DynamicValue {
  def transform(transforms: Chunk[Migration]): Either[String, DynamicValue]
}
```

A migration step names the node it changes with a `NodePath`. The following steps make the `age` field optional, then try two orders of `Optional` and `Require` on the same field:

```scala
val age = NodePath.root / "age"
// age: NodePath = IndexedSeq("age")

alice.transform(Chunk(Migration.Optional(age)))
// res20: Either[String, DynamicValue] = Right(
//   value = Record(
//     id = Nominal(
//       packageName = IndexedSeq("repl"),
//       objectNames = IndexedSeq("MdocSession", "MdocApp"),
//       typeName = "Person"
//     ),
//     values = ListMap(
//       "name" -> Primitive(value = "Alice", standardType = string),
//       "age" -> SomeValue(value = Primitive(value = 42, standardType = int))
//     )
//   )
// )

alice.transform(Chunk(Migration.Optional(age), Migration.Require(age)))
// res21: Either[String, DynamicValue] = Left(
//   value = "Failed to require leaf at path age: Expected optional value at lead"
// )

alice.transform(Chunk(Migration.Require(age), Migration.Optional(age)))
// res22: Either[String, DynamicValue] = Right(
//   value = Record(
//     id = Nominal(
//       packageName = IndexedSeq("repl"),
//       objectNames = IndexedSeq("MdocSession", "MdocApp"),
//       typeName = "Person"
//     ),
//     values = ListMap(
//       "name" -> Primitive(value = "Alice", standardType = string),
//       "age" -> Primitive(value = 42, standardType = int)
//     )
//   )
// )
```

:::caution[Steps run from last to first]
`DynamicValue#transform` folds the chunk from the right, so the last step in the chunk runs first. In the example above, `Chunk(Optional, Require)` fails because `Require` runs first on a field that is not optional yet, while `Chunk(Require, Optional)` succeeds. List the steps in reverse order of how they should apply.
:::

The [Migration Operations](../reference/migration-operations.md) page describes each `Migration` case, and [Schema Migration](schema-migration.md) shows how `Migration.derive` computes the steps between two schemas.

### Schemas for DynamicValue

A `DynamicValue` can itself be a field of a typed value, and codecs can encode it. Two schemas describe it, and they serve different purposes.

#### Schema.Dynamic

`Schema.Dynamic` is the schema of a value whose shape is not known in advance. The implicit `Schema.dynamicValue` is an instance of it, so `Schema[DynamicValue]` resolves to `Schema.Dynamic`:

```scala
object Schema {
  implicit val dynamicValue: Schema[DynamicValue] = Schema.Dynamic()

  final case class Dynamic(annotations: Chunk[Any] = Chunk.empty) extends Schema[DynamicValue]
}
```

With this schema, `Schema#toDynamic` returns the value unchanged and `Schema#fromDynamic` accepts any tree except an `Error`. Its default value is `DynamicValue.NoneValue`. A case class can therefore carry a field of free-form data:

```scala
final case class Event(kind: String, payload: DynamicValue)

object Event {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Event] = DeriveSchema.gen[Event]
}

val signup = Event("signup", alice)
```

The payload survives the round trip through the dynamic representation unchanged:

```scala
Event.schema.fromDynamic(Event.schema.toDynamic(signup)) == Right(signup)
// res23: Boolean = true
```

By default, codecs encode a `Schema.Dynamic` value through `DynamicValue.schema`, described next, so the output records every case name. The JSON codec can instead map the tree to plain JSON when the schema carries the `directDynamicMapping` annotation from `zio.schema.annotation`. Records become JSON objects, sequences and sets become arrays, and `NoneValue` becomes `null`. When decoding, objects become records with `TypeId.Structural`, and numbers become `java.math.BigDecimal` primitives:

```scala
import zio.schema.annotation.directDynamicMapping
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec

val plainJson: Schema[DynamicValue] = Schema.dynamicValue.annotate(directDynamicMapping())
// plainJson: Schema[DynamicValue] = Dynamic(
//   annotations = IndexedSeq(directDynamicMapping())
// )

println(JsonCodec.jsonCodec(plainJson).encodeJson(alice, None))
// {"name":"Alice","age":42}

JsonCodec.jsonCodec(plainJson).decodeJson("""{"name":"Bob","tags":["a","b"]}""")
// res25: Either[String, DynamicValue] = Right(
//   value = Record(
//     id = Structural,
//     values = ListMap(
//       "name" -> Primitive(value = "Bob", standardType = string),
//       "tags" -> Sequence(
//         values = IndexedSeq(
//           Primitive(value = "a", standardType = string),
//           Primitive(value = "b", standardType = string)
//         )
//       )
//     )
//   )
// )
```

In direct mode, the JSON encoder throws for `Enumeration`, `Dictionary`, `Tuple`, `LeftValue`, `RightValue`, and `DynamicAst`, because plain JSON has no place to record them. An `Error` also throws, with its message. The [JSON Codecs](../derivations/codecs/json.md) page covers the codec itself.

#### DynamicValue.schema

`DynamicValue.schema` is an explicit enum schema that describes the structure of `DynamicValue` itself, with one case per `DynamicValue` case except `BothValue`, and one case per standard type of `Primitive` except `Byte`. Codecs use it to write a `DynamicValue` in a self-describing form. `DynamicValue.typeId` is the `TypeId` of that enum:

```scala
object DynamicValue {
  lazy val schema: Schema[DynamicValue]
  lazy val typeId: TypeId
}
```

:::caution[Values that DynamicValue.schema cannot encode]
`DynamicValue.schema` has no case for a `Primitive` that holds a `Byte`, and no case for `BothValue`. A codec that goes through this schema cannot write those values: the JSON codec, for example, writes a `Byte` primitive as `{}`, which no longer holds the value. This also applies to a `Schema.Dynamic` field encoded without `directDynamicMapping`. Convert such values before encoding, for example a `Byte` to a `Short`. The `Singleton` case is encoded without its `instance`, which decodes as `()`.
:::

The `DynamicValue` companion also defines implicit `StandardType` instances for `Instant`, `LocalDate`, `LocalTime`, `LocalDateTime`, `OffsetTime`, `OffsetDateTime`, and `ZonedDateTime`, which point to the matching `StandardType` objects.

### Round-Trip Limits

For most schemas, `schema.fromDynamic(schema.toDynamic(x))` returns `Right(x)`. A few schema kinds have a dynamic form but no decoding rule, so the round trip fails:

```scala
import zio.NonEmptyChunk

val nonEmptySchema = Schema[NonEmptyChunk[Int]]
// nonEmptySchema: Schema[NonEmptyChunk[Int]] = NonEmptySequence(
//   elementSchema = Primitive(standardType = int, annotations = IndexedSeq()),
//   fromChunkOption = zio.schema.Schema$$$Lambda$25231/0x00007d2db3a7ecf0@36dc3e1e,
//   toChunk = zio.schema.Schema$$$Lambda$25232/0x00007d2db3a7f850@26c30d14,
//   annotations = IndexedSeq(),
//   identity = "NonEmptyChunk"
// )

nonEmptySchema.fromDynamic(nonEmptySchema.toDynamic(NonEmptyChunk(1, 2)))
// res26: Either[String, NonEmptyChunk[Int]] = Left(
//   value = "Failed to cast Sequence(Chunk(Primitive(1,int),Primitive(2,int))) to schema NonEmptySequence(Primitive(int,Chunk()), NonEmptyChunk)"
// )
```

:::caution[Schemas that do not round-trip]
`Schema#fromDynamic` cannot decode values of non-empty collections (`NonEmptyChunk`, `NonEmptySet`), `NonEmptyMap`, or `Fallback`, even though `Schema#toDynamic` converts them: the round trip returns `Left` with a cast error. The same failure appears in every operation built on the round trip, such as `Schema#migrate`, `Schema#coerce`, and applying a record patch, when a value contains one of these types. Keep such fields out of data that must pass through `DynamicValue`, or convert them to `Chunk`, `Map`, or `Either` first. To keep a non-empty collection that round-trips, describe it as a transformed `Chunk`, for example `Schema[Chunk[Int]].transformOrFail(c => NonEmptyChunk.fromChunk(c).toRight("empty chunk"), nec => Right(nec.toChunk))`.
:::

### Integration

`DynamicValue` is the common currency of several ZIO Schema features:

- [Schema Migration](schema-migration.md) converts values between schema versions by turning them into `DynamicValue`s and applying `Migration` steps.
- [Migration Operations](../reference/migration-operations.md) lists the steps that `DynamicValue#transform` applies.
- [MetaSchema](serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md) describes the structure of a schema as data, and `DynamicValue.DynamicAst` carries one inside a value.

---

## ZIO Schema Operations

Once we define our schemas, we can use them to perform a variety of operations. Every operation is a method on `Schema[A]`, so it works the same way for any type that has a schema. The pages in this section cover the most common operations:

- [Getting The Default Value](the-default-value.md) describes `Schema#defaultValue` and `Schema#default`.
- [Transforming Schemas](transforming-schemas.md) describes `Schema#transform` and `Schema#transformOrFail`.
- [Validation](validating-types.md) describes `Schema#validate` and the `Validation` rules.
- [Diffing and Patching](diffing-and-patching.md) describes `Schema#diff` and `Schema#patch`.
- [Dynamic Data Representation](dynamic-data-representation.md) describes `Schema#toDynamic` and `Schema#fromDynamic`.
- [Schema Migration](schema-migration.md) describes `Schema#migrate` and `Schema#coerce`.
- [Serialization of the Schema Itself](serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md) describes `Schema#ast` and `Schema#serializable`.

The [Schema Methods](../reference/schema-methods.md) reference page shows each method with a short example.

### Method Overview

The following simplified listing shows the signatures of the operations on `Schema[A]`, grouped by purpose:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  type Accessors[Lens[_, _, _], Prism[_, _, _], Traversal[_, _]]

  // Building new schemas
  def ? : Schema[Option[A]]
  def optional: Schema[Option[A]]
  def <*>[B](that: Schema[B]): Schema[(A, B)]
  def zip[B](that: Schema[B]): Schema[(A, B)]
  def <+>[B](that: Schema[B]): Schema[scala.util.Either[A, B]]
  def orElseEither[B](that: Schema[B]): Schema[scala.util.Either[A, B]]
  def repeated: Schema[Chunk[A]]
  def transform[B](f: A => B, g: B => A)(implicit loc: SourceLocation): Schema[B]
  def transformOrFail[B](
    f: A => scala.util.Either[String, B],
    g: B => scala.util.Either[String, A]
  )(implicit loc: SourceLocation): Schema[B]

  // Defaults and annotations
  def defaultValue: scala.util.Either[String, A]
  def default(value: A): Schema[A]
  def annotations: Chunk[Any]
  def annotate(annotation: Any): Schema[A]

  // Validation
  def validate(value: A)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Chunk[ValidationError]
  def validation(validation: Validation[A]): Schema[A]

  // Dynamic values, diffing, and migration
  def toDynamic(value: A): DynamicValue
  def fromDynamic(value: DynamicValue): scala.util.Either[String, A]
  def diff(thisValue: A, thatValue: A): Patch[A]
  def patch(oldValue: A, diff: Patch[A]): scala.util.Either[String, A]
  def migrate[B](newSchema: Schema[B]): Either[String, A => scala.util.Either[String, B]]
  def coerce[B](newSchema: Schema[B]): Either[String, Schema[B]]

  // Structure
  def ast: MetaSchema
  def serializable: Schema[Schema[A]]
  def ordering: Ordering[A]
  def makeAccessors(b: AccessorBuilder): Accessors[b.Lens, b.Prism, b.Traversal]
}
```

---

## Schema Migration

### Automatic Migration

With ZIO Schema, we can automatically migrate data from one version of a schema to another. As software evolves, we often need to add, change or remove old fields. `Schema#migrate` and `Schema#coerce` help migrate data from the old schema to the new one:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def migrate[B](newSchema: Schema[B]): Either[String, A => scala.util.Either[String, B]]

  def coerce[B](newSchema: Schema[B]): Either[String, Schema[B]]
}
```

The `Schema#migrate` method compares the structure of the two schemas and derives the migration steps between them. When the two structures can be matched, it returns a `Right` with a function that converts values of the old type into values of the new type. It returns a `Left` only when a part of the old structure cannot be mapped to the new one at all, for example a record that becomes a primitive. `Schema#coerce` calls `Schema#migrate` in both directions and returns a schema for the new type that reads and writes through the old one.

The conversion function turns the old value into a [`DynamicValue`](dynamic-data-representation.md), applies the steps, and reads the result with the new schema. The following example removes a field and makes another field optional:

```scala
import zio.schema._

case class UserV1(name: String, age: Int, email: String)

object UserV1 {
  implicit val schema: Schema[UserV1] = DeriveSchema.gen[UserV1]
}

case class UserV2(name: String, age: Option[Int])

object UserV2 {
  implicit val schema: Schema[UserV2] = DeriveSchema.gen[UserV2]
}
```

Migrating a `UserV1` drops `email` and wraps `age` in `Some`:

```scala
UserV1.schema.migrate(UserV2.schema).map(migrateUser => migrateUser(UserV1("John", 42, "john@example.com")))
// res0: Either[String, Either[String, UserV2]] = Right(
//   value = Right(value = UserV2(name = "John", age = Some(value = 42)))
// )
```

The `zio.schema.syntax` object also provides `MigrationOps#migrate` as a method on any value that has an implicit schema, as in `UserV1("John", 42, "john@example.com").migrate[UserV2]`.

:::caution
`Schema#migrate` and `Schema#coerce` return `Right` even for changes that the library cannot apply to values. Adding a field, or changing the type of a primitive field (for example from `Int` to `Double`), produces a step that fails on every value, so the returned function always returns `Left`. The following migration adds a `role` field:

```scala
case class UserV3(name: String, age: Option[Int], role: String)

object UserV3 {
  implicit val schema: Schema[UserV3] = DeriveSchema.gen[UserV3]
}

UserV2.schema.migrate(UserV3.schema).map(migrateUser => migrateUser(UserV2("John", Some(42))))
// res1: Either[String, Either[String, UserV3]] = Right(
//   value = Left(
//     value = "Cannot add node at path role: No default value is available"
//   )
// )
```

The outer `Right` says that the migration was derived, and the inner `Left` says that applying it failed. The [Migration Operations](../reference/migration-operations.md) page lists which steps apply to values and which always fail. For an added field, give the field a default value in the new case class, for example `role: String = "member"`, and decode the old data with a codec, which fills in the default, or write the conversion by hand.
:::

### Manual Migration

Because a `DynamicValue` carries its type information inside the data, we can migrate it by applying a sequence of migration steps with `DynamicValue#transform`:

```scala
sealed trait DynamicValue {
  def transform(transforms: Chunk[Migration]): Either[String, DynamicValue]
}
```

[Running Several Steps](../reference/migration-operations.md#running-several-steps) describes the order in which `DynamicValue#transform` applies the steps and how it handles a failing step.

The `Migration` is a sealed trait with several subtypes. The [Migration Operations](../reference/migration-operations.md) page describes each of them:

```scala
sealed trait Migration
object Migration {
  final case class AddNode(override val path: NodePath, node: MetaSchema) extends Migration

  final case class DeleteNode(override val path: NodePath) extends Migration

  final case class AddCase(override val path: NodePath, node: MetaSchema) extends Migration

  // ...
}
```

With the `Migration` steps we describe the change and then apply it to a `DynamicValue`. The following example deletes the `age` field from a `Person1` value and reads the result as a `Person2`:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.schema.meta.Migration.DeleteNode
import zio.schema.meta.{Migration, NodePath}
import zio.schema.{DeriveSchema, Schema}

case class Person1(name: String, age: Int)

object Person1 {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person1] = DeriveSchema.gen
}

case class Person2(name: String)

object Person2 {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person2] = DeriveSchema.gen
}

val person1: Person1 = Person1("John Doe", 42)

val migrations: Chunk[Migration] = Chunk(DeleteNode(NodePath.root / "age"))

val person2 = DeriveSchema
```
