```scala
  .gen[Person1]
  .toDynamic(person1)
  .transform(migrations)
  .flatMap(_.toTypedValue[Person2])
  
assert(person2 == Right(Person2("John Doe")))
```

### Deriving Migrations

ZIO Schema provides a way to derive migrations automatically using the `Migration.derive` operation, which is what `Schema#migrate` uses:

```scala
object Migration {
  def derive(from: MetaSchema, to: MetaSchema): Either[String, Chunk[Migration]]
}
```

It takes two `MetaSchema` values, the old and the new schema, and returns a `Chunk[Migration]` that describes the migration steps. The following example derives the steps between two versions of a `Person` model and prints them:

```scala
import zio.schema.meta._

case class Person1(name: String, age: Int, language: String, height: Int)

object Person1 {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person1] = DeriveSchema.gen
}

case class Person2(
    name: String,
    role: String,
    language: Set[String],
    height: Double
)

object Person2 {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person2] = DeriveSchema.gen
}

val migrations = Migration.derive(
  MetaSchema.fromSchema(Person1.schema),
  MetaSchema.fromSchema(Person2.schema)
)
// migrations: Either[String, zio.Chunk[Migration]] = Right(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     IncrementDimensions(path = IndexedSeq("language", "item"), n = 1),
//     ChangeType(path = IndexedSeq("height"), value = double),
//     AddNode(
//       path = IndexedSeq("role"),
//       node = Value(
//         valueType = string,
//         path = IndexedSeq("role"),
//         optional = false
//       )
//     ),
//     DeleteNode(path = IndexedSeq("age"))
//   )
// )

println(migrations)
// Right(Chunk(IncrementDimensions(Chunk(language,item),1),ChangeType(Chunk(height),double),AddNode(Chunk(role),string),DeleteNode(Chunk(age))))
```

The output lists the steps that turn the old structure into the new one. Here, `language` changes from a `String` to a `Set[String]`, so the migration adds a dimension to it. The `height` field changes type, `role` is added, and `age` is removed. Deriving these steps succeeds, but applying them to a `Person1` value fails, because the `ChangeType` step for `height` and the `AddNode` step for `role` cannot be applied, as described in the caution above.

---

## Serialization of the Schema Itself

In distributed systems, we often move computation to the data instead of moving data to the computation. Large data sets are expensive to send over a slow network, so a receiver that already holds a function can be sent the data instead, or the other way around. To do that, both sides need to agree on the structure of the data. ZIO Schema makes the structure of a type a value, so the structure can be sent over the wire like any other data.

### Turning a Schema into Data

A `Schema[A]` holds constructors, getters, and transformation functions, and functions cannot be serialized, so a schema cannot be sent over the network or stored in a database as it is. The `Schema#ast` method returns a `MetaSchema` instead: a **schema described as plain data**, a tree of case classes that records the structure of the schema (its records, fields, enum cases, collections, and primitive types) without any Scala functions. `MetaSchema` has its own schema, `MetaSchema.schema`, so any codec can encode it, and the receiving side rebuilds a working schema with the same structure from it. [Schema Migration](schema-migration.md) also compares two `MetaSchema` values to compute the steps between schema versions.

### Sending a Schema over the Wire

The sender calls `Schema#ast` and encodes the result with a codec for `MetaSchema.schema`. The following example uses the JSON codec:

```scala
import zio.Chunk
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.codec.{BinaryCodec, DecodeError, JsonCodec}
import zio.schema.meta.MetaSchema

final case class Person(name: String, age: Int, email: Option[String])

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}

val personAst: MetaSchema = Person.schema.ast

val astCodec: BinaryCodec[MetaSchema] = JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[MetaSchema](MetaSchema.schema)

val sentAst: Chunk[Byte] = astCodec.encode(personAst)
```

The bytes on the wire are the JSON form of the tree:

```scala
println(new String(sentAst.toArray, java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
// {"Product":{"id":"repl.MdocSession.MdocApp.Person","path":[],"fields":[["name",{"Value":{"valueType":"string","path":["name"],"optional":false}}],["age",{"Value":{"valueType":"int","path":["age"],"optional":false}}],["email",{"Value":{"valueType":"string","path":["email"],"optional":true}}]],"optional":false}}
```

The receiver decodes the bytes back into a `MetaSchema` with the same codec:

```scala
val receivedAst: Either[DecodeError, MetaSchema] = astCodec.decode(sentAst)
```

The decoded tree is equal to the tree the sender encoded:

```scala
receivedAst == Right(personAst)
// res1: Boolean = true
```

### Rebuilding a Schema on the Receiver

`ExtensibleMetaSchema#toSchema` turns the tree back into a schema. The receiver does not have the `Person` class, so the rebuilt schema describes the same structure with generic types: a record becomes a `GenericRecord` whose values are `ListMap[String, _]`, and every sequence becomes a `Chunk`. The result has the type `Schema[_]`, because the Scala type is not known on the receiving side.

The rebuilt schema can read data that the sender encodes with the original schema. The following helper decodes JSON with any schema and returns the value as a `DynamicValue`:

```scala
def decodeAsDynamic[A](schema: Schema[A], json: Chunk[Byte]): Either[DecodeError, DynamicValue] =
  JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[A](schema).decode(json).map(schema.toDynamic)

val sentPerson: Chunk[Byte] =
  JsonCodec.schemaBasedBinaryCodec[Person].encode(Person("John", 42, Some("john@example.com")))
```

Next, the receiver rebuilds the schema from the tree and decodes the person with it:

```scala
receivedAst.map(ast => decodeAsDynamic(ast.toSchema, sentPerson)).foreach(println)
// Right(Record(Nominal(Chunk(repl),Chunk(MdocSession,MdocApp),Person),ListMap(name -> Primitive(John,string), age -> Primitive(42,int), email -> SomeValue(Primitive(john@example.com,string)))))
```

The same idea works with any other codec, such as Protobuf, because `MetaSchema.schema` is an ordinary schema.

### The `Schema#serializable` Method

`Schema#serializable` is meant to return a `Schema[Schema[A]]` that converts a schema to and from data in one step:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def serializable: Schema[Schema[A]]
}
```

:::caution
`Schema#serializable` does not work in the current version. It builds the schema of the *values* of `A` and treats it as the schema of a `Schema`. For a primitive schema such as `Schema[Int]`, encoding with the result, or calling `Schema#toDynamic` on it, produces a meaningless value, and for a case class it throws a `ClassCastException`. Use `Schema#ast` with `MetaSchema.schema` (or the implicit `Schema[Schema[A]]` described in [Serializing](#serializing)), and `ExtensibleMetaSchema#toSchema` on the receiving side, as shown above.
:::

### MetaSchema Nodes

`MetaSchema` is a type alias for `ExtensibleMetaSchema[DynamicValue :: End]`. The `BuiltIn` type parameter of `ExtensibleMetaSchema` is a type-level list of types whose schemas both sides already know; `MetaSchema` uses a list with only `DynamicValue` in it. Every node records its position in the tree as a [`NodePath`](#nodepath) and whether it is optional:

```scala
package object meta {
  type MetaSchema = ExtensibleMetaSchema[DynamicValue :: End]
  type NodePath   = NodePath.Type
}

sealed trait ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn <: TypeList] {
  def builtInInstances: SchemaInstances[BuiltIn]
  def path: NodePath
  def optional: Boolean
  def toSchema: Schema[_]
}

object ExtensibleMetaSchema {
  // Every case also takes (implicit builtInInstances: SchemaInstances[BuiltIn])
  final case class Value[BuiltIn <: TypeList](valueType: StandardType[_], path: NodePath = NodePath.root, optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Product[BuiltIn <: TypeList](id: TypeId, path: NodePath, fields: Chunk[Labelled[BuiltIn]] = Chunk.empty, optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Sum[BuiltIn <: TypeList](id: TypeId, path: NodePath, cases: Chunk[Labelled[BuiltIn]] = Chunk.empty, optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Tuple[BuiltIn <: TypeList](path: NodePath, left: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], right: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Either[BuiltIn <: TypeList](path: NodePath, left: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], right: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Fallback[BuiltIn <: TypeList](path: NodePath, left: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], right: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class ListNode[BuiltIn <: TypeList](item: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], path: NodePath, optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Dictionary[BuiltIn <: TypeList](keys: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], values: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn], path: NodePath, optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class FailNode[BuiltIn <: TypeList](message: String, path: NodePath, optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Ref[BuiltIn <: TypeList](refPath: NodePath, path: NodePath, optional: Boolean = false)
  final case class Known[BuiltIn <: TypeList](typeId: TypeId, path: NodePath, optional: Boolean = false)

  final case class Labelled[BuiltIn <: TypeList](label: String, schema: ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn])
}
```

### Creating Values

A `MetaSchema` usually comes from an existing schema, but its cases are public case classes that can also be built directly.

#### From a Schema

`Schema#ast` and `MetaSchema.fromSchema` both convert a schema into its `MetaSchema`. `ExtensibleMetaSchema.fromSchema` does the same for a custom list of built-in types, described in [Extending the Built-In Types](#extending-the-built-in-types):

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def ast: MetaSchema
}

object MetaSchema {
  def fromSchema[A](schema: Schema[A]): MetaSchema
}

object ExtensibleMetaSchema {
  def fromSchema[A, BuiltIn <: TypeList](schema: Schema[A])(implicit builtInInstances: SchemaInstances[BuiltIn]): ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn]
}
```

`Schema#ast` is shorthand for `MetaSchema.fromSchema`, so the two give equal results:

```scala
MetaSchema.fromSchema(Person.schema) == Person.schema.ast
// res3: Boolean = true
```

A recursive schema does not loop forever. When the conversion meets a record or enum it is already inside, it writes a `Ref` node that points to the path of the earlier node instead of expanding it again.

#### By Hand

Each case takes an implicit `SchemaInstances[BuiltIn]` in a second parameter list. For `MetaSchema`, the compiler derives it from the implicit `Schema[DynamicValue]`, so building a node only needs the `TypeList` syntax in scope:

```scala
import zio.constraintless.TypeList._
import zio.schema.meta.ExtensibleMetaSchema

val intNode: MetaSchema = ExtensibleMetaSchema.Value[DynamicValue :: End](StandardType.IntType)
// intNode: MetaSchema = Value(
//   valueType = int,
//   path = IndexedSeq(),
//   optional = false
// )

MetaSchema.fromSchema(Schema[Int]) == intNode
// res4: Boolean = true
```

Equality of nodes compares the fields of the first parameter list only. `ExtensibleMetaSchema.equals` also provides a ZIO Prelude `Equal[MetaSchema]` instance.

### Core Operations

Once we have a `MetaSchema`, we can inspect its nodes, serialize it, and turn it back into a schema.

#### Inspecting the Tree

`ExtensibleMetaSchema#toString` renders the tree in a compact text form. A top-level record shows as `product` and a nested one as `record`, enums show as `enum`, sequences as `list`, maps as `map`, and a `?` marks an optional node:

```scala
println(personAst)
// product
// |--name: string
// |--age: int
// |--email: ?string
```

Every node also exposes `ExtensibleMetaSchema#path`, its position from the root, and `ExtensibleMetaSchema#optional`, which is `true` when the schema wrapped the node in `Option`. A `Labelled` pairs a field or case name with the node for it. The fields of a record and the paths of their nodes are read like this:

```scala
personAst match {
  case ExtensibleMetaSchema.Product(_, _, fields, _) =>
    fields.map(field => (field.label, field.schema.path.render, field.schema.optional))
  case _                                             => Chunk.empty
}
// res6: Chunk[(String, String, Boolean)] = IndexedSeq(
//   ("name", "name", false),
//   ("age", "age", false),
//   ("email", "email", true)
// )
```

#### Serializing

`MetaSchema.schema` is the `Schema[MetaSchema]` that every codec uses to encode and decode a `MetaSchema`, as in [Sending a Schema over the Wire](#sending-a-schema-over-the-wire). `ExtensibleMetaSchema.schema` builds the same schema for any list of built-in types, and `MetaSchema.Labelled` is the `Labelled` type for `MetaSchema`:

```scala
object MetaSchema {
  type Labelled = ExtensibleMetaSchema.Labelled[DynamicValue :: End]

  val schema: Schema[MetaSchema]
}

object ExtensibleMetaSchema {
  implicit def schema[BuiltIn <: TypeList](implicit builtInInstances: SchemaInstances[BuiltIn]): Schema[ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn]]
}
```

The schema is also available implicitly, so `Schema[MetaSchema]` finds it. The implicit `Schema[Schema[A]]` that the `Schema` companion provides is built on it: it encodes a schema through its `MetaSchema` and decodes by calling `ExtensibleMetaSchema#toSchema`. The decoded value is typed `Schema[A]`, but it has the rebuilt structure described below, not the original schema:

```scala
object Schema {
  implicit def schemaSchema[A]: Schema[Schema[A]]
}
```

#### Rebuilding a Schema

`ExtensibleMetaSchema#toSchema` is the method the receiver calls in [Rebuilding a Schema on the Receiver](#rebuilding-a-schema-on-the-receiver):

```scala
sealed trait ExtensibleMetaSchema[BuiltIn <: TypeList] {
  def toSchema: Schema[_]
}
```

The values of a rebuilt record are `ListMap` instances keyed by field name. The following example converts a `Person` value, in its dynamic form, with the rebuilt schema:

```scala
val rebuilt: Schema[_] = personAst.toSchema

val asListMap: Either[String, Any] =
  rebuilt.fromDynamic(Person.schema.toDynamic(Person("Alice", 42, None)))
```

The result holds the same data as a `ListMap`:

```scala
asListMap
// res7: Either[String, Any] = Right(
//   value = ListMap("name" -> "Alice", "age" -> 42, "email" -> None)
// )
```

Each node becomes one schema:

| Node         | Rebuilt schema                                                                               |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Value`      | `Schema.Primitive` of the same `StandardType`                                                |
| `Product`    | `Schema.GenericRecord` with the same `TypeId` and field names, over `ListMap[String, _]`     |
| `Sum`        | An enum schema with the same `TypeId` and case names; its cases use identity constructors    |
| `Tuple`      | `Schema.Tuple2`                                                                              |
| `Either`     | `Schema.Either`                                                                              |
| `Fallback`   | `Schema.Fallback`                                                                            |
| `ListNode`   | `Schema[Chunk[_]]`                                                                           |
| `Dictionary` | `Schema.Map`                                                                                 |
| `FailNode`   | `Schema.Fail` with the same message                                                          |
| `Ref`        | A lazy schema (`Schema.defer`) that points to the rebuilt node at `refPath`                  |
| `Known`      | The built-in schema with the same `TypeId`, or `Schema.Fail` when no built-in schema matches |

When `ExtensibleMetaSchema#optional` is `true` for a node, `ExtensibleMetaSchema#toSchema` wraps the rebuilt schema in `Schema#optional`.

### What the Round Trip Loses

A `MetaSchema` describes only structure. Converting a schema with `Schema#ast` and rebuilding it with `ExtensibleMetaSchema#toSchema` keeps the shape of the data, including the `TypeId`, field names, and case names of records and enums, while everything that is code or metadata is gone:

| Part of the original schema                                             | What remains after the round trip                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Schema#transform`, `Schema#transformOrFail`, and schemas built on them | Only the underlying schema; the functions and the target type are gone                      |
| Annotations on schemas, fields, and cases                               | None, so `@fieldName`, `@caseName`, `@transientField`, default values, and similar are lost |
| Field validations and `@validate`                                       | None                                                                                        |
| Case class types                                                        | A `GenericRecord` over `ListMap[String, _]`                                                 |
| Sealed trait cases                                                      | Enum cases whose values are generic records                                                 |
| `Set`, `NonEmptyChunk`, `NonEmptySet`                                   | A `Chunk`                                                                                   |
| `NonEmptyMap`                                                           | A `Map`                                                                                     |
| `Fallback` below the top level                                          | An `Either`                                                                                 |
| `Schema.Dynamic` with annotations                                       | The full structure of `DynamicValue.schema` instead of `Schema.Dynamic`                     |

A field that the original schema built with `Schema#transform` therefore comes back as its underlying type, the way a newtype such as `Schema[BigDecimal]` arrives as its underlying primitive. For example, a schema for an `Email` wrapper rebuilds as a plain string schema:

```scala
final case class Email(value: String)

val emailSchema: Schema[Email] = Schema[String].transform(Email(_), _.value)
// emailSchema: Schema[Email] = Transform(
//   schema = Primitive(standardType = string, annotations = IndexedSeq()),
//   f = zio.schema.Schema$$Lambda$24422/0x00007d2db38e7070@757e6abd,
//   g = zio.schema.Schema$$Lambda$24423/0x00007d2db38e7440@6122dd37,
//   annotations = IndexedSeq(),
//   identity = SourceLocation(
//     path = "serialization-of-the-schema-itself.md",
//     line = 131,
//     col = 58
//   )
// )

println(emailSchema.ast)
// string
emailSchema.ast.toSchema
// res9: Schema[_] = Primitive(
//   standardType = string,
//   annotations = IndexedSeq()
// )
```

Annotations disappear in the same way, so codec settings that depend on them do not travel with the `MetaSchema`:

```scala
val annotated: Schema[Int] = Schema[Int].annotate("a note")
// annotated: Schema[Int] = Primitive(
//   standardType = int,
//   annotations = IndexedSeq("a note")
// )

annotated.annotations
// res10: Chunk[Any] = IndexedSeq("a note")
annotated.ast.toSchema.annotations
// res11: Chunk[Any] = IndexedSeq()
```

A `Fallback` at the top level of a schema keeps its own `Fallback` node, but `MetaSchema.schema` has no case for that node, so serialize such a schema inside a record or another container.

### NodePath

A `NodePath` is the path from the root of a schema to one of its nodes, as a sequence of labels. Record fields and enum cases use their names as labels, and the other nodes use fixed labels: `item` for the element of a sequence, `keys` and `values` for a map, and `left` and `right` for tuples and `Either`. `NodePath` is a ZIO Prelude subtype of `Chunk[String]`, so it supports every `Chunk` operation, and [Migration Operations](../reference/migration-operations.md) uses it to address the node each step changes.

The `NodePath` companion provides the root path and the operations for building and comparing paths:

```scala
object NodePath {
  val root: NodePath
  val empty: NodePath

  implicit class NodePathSyntax(self: NodePath) {
    def /(label: String): NodePath
    def /(subpath: NodePath): NodePath
    def relativeTo(path: NodePath): NodePath
    def isSubpathOf(path: NodePath): Boolean
    def partitionLeaf: (NodePath, Option[String])
    def render: String
  }
}
```

`NodePath.root` and `NodePath.empty` are both the empty path. `NodePathSyntax#/` appends a label or a whole path. `NodePathSyntax#relativeTo` removes a prefix, and returns the path unchanged when the prefix does not match. `NodePathSyntax#isSubpathOf` checks for a prefix, `NodePathSyntax#partitionLeaf` splits off the last label, and `NodePathSyntax#render` joins the labels with `/`, rendering the empty path as `ROOT`:

```scala
import zio.schema.meta.NodePath

val address = NodePath.root / "address"
// address: NodePath = IndexedSeq("address")
val street  = address / "street"
// street: NodePath = IndexedSeq("address", "street")

street.render
// res12: String = "address/street"
street.relativeTo(address)
// res13: NodePath = IndexedSeq("street")
street.isSubpathOf(address)
// res14: Boolean = true
street.partitionLeaf
// res15: (NodePath, Option[String]) = (
//   IndexedSeq("address"),
//   Some(value = "street")
// )
address / (NodePath.root / "city" / "zip")
// res16: NodePath = IndexedSeq("address", "city", "zip")
NodePath.root.render
// res17: String = "ROOT"
```

`ExtensibleMetaSchema.nodePathSchema` is the implicit `Schema[NodePath]`, which encodes a path as a sequence of strings.

### Extending the Built-In Types

Sometimes both sides of a connection already share some schemas, for example a common library of domain types. Listing those types in the `BuiltIn` parameter of `ExtensibleMetaSchema` keeps them out of the serialized description: `ExtensibleMetaSchema.fromSchema` writes a `Known` node holding only the type's `TypeId`, and `ExtensibleMetaSchema#toSchema` returns the shared schema instance itself, with its transforms and annotations intact.

The type list is built from `zio.constraintless.TypeList`, and the compiler needs an implicit `Schema` for each type in it to derive the `SchemaInstances[BuiltIn]`:

```scala
trait SchemaInstances[As <: TypeList] {
  def withInstance[B, D](use: Schema[B] => D)(implicit ev: B IsElementOf As): D
  def all: List[Schema[_]]
}
```

The following example adds a `Pet` enum to the built-in list:

```scala
import zio.constraintless.TypeList._
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.meta.ExtensibleMetaSchema

sealed trait Pet

object Pet {
  case object Rock                  extends Pet
  final case class Dog(name: String) extends Pet

  implicit lazy val schema: Schema[Pet] = DeriveSchema.gen[Pet]
}

type PetMetaSchema = ExtensibleMetaSchema[DynamicValue :: Pet :: End]

val petMetaSchemaSchema: Schema[PetMetaSchema] = ExtensibleMetaSchema.schema[DynamicValue :: Pet :: End]

val petMeta: PetMetaSchema = ExtensibleMetaSchema.fromSchema[Pet, DynamicValue :: Pet :: End](Pet.schema)
```

The schema of `Pet` becomes a single `Known` node, and rebuilding it returns the very same schema instance:

```scala
petMeta.isInstanceOf[ExtensibleMetaSchema.Known[_]]
// res19: Boolean = true
petMeta.toSchema eq Pet.schema
// res20: Boolean = true
```

Both sides must use the same type list, and the receiver decodes with `petMetaSchemaSchema` rather than `MetaSchema.schema`. Only record, enum, and `Schema.Dynamic` instances in the list become `Known` nodes, and the lookup compares schemas with `==`, so pass the same schema instance that the list holds.

### Integration

`MetaSchema` connects the structure of a schema to the rest of ZIO Schema:

- [DynamicValue](dynamic-data-representation.md) is the data counterpart of `MetaSchema`, and its `DynamicAst` case carries a `MetaSchema` inside a value.
- [Schema Migration](schema-migration.md) shows how `Migration.derive` compares two `MetaSchema` values to compute migration steps.
- [Migration Operations](../reference/migration-operations.md) lists the steps, several of which take a `NodePath` or a `MetaSchema`.
- [How to Send a Schema over the Wire](../how-to/send-schema-over-the-wire.md) walks through a complete sender and receiver.

---

## Getting The Default Value

Some tools need a sample value for a type, for example to fill a form, to build a test fixture, or to show a placeholder. The `defaultValue` method of a schema returns such a value. It has this signature:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def defaultValue: scala.util.Either[String, A]
}
```

The method returns `Right` with a value when the schema can produce one, and `Left` with an error message when it cannot.

### Standard Types

Every standard type has a default value. For example, `String` defaults to the empty string, and `Int` defaults to `0`:

```scala
import zio.schema._

Schema[String].defaultValue
// res0: Either[String, String] = Right(value = "")
Schema[Int].defaultValue
// res1: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 0)
```

Some standard defaults are not constant. `UUID` produces a new random value on each call. `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `OffsetTime`, `OffsetDateTime`, `ZonedDateTime`, `Year`, and `YearMonth` use the current clock. `ZoneId` uses the system time zone, `DayOfWeek` uses the first day of the week for the default locale, and `Currency` uses the currency of the default locale, so it returns `Left` when that locale has no country. The platform support for each type is listed in the [Standard Type Reference](../standard-type-reference.md).

### Default Values by Schema Kind

Each kind of schema computes its default in its own way. The following table lists the rule for each kind:

| Schema kind                              | `defaultValue`                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Primitive`                              | The value set with `Schema#default`, otherwise the default of the standard type |
| `Record` (case classes, `GenericRecord`) | Built from the default of each field; `Left` if any field has none              |
| `Enum` (sealed traits)                   | The default of the first case                                                   |
| `Optional`                               | `Right(None)`                                                                   |
| `Sequence`, `Set`, `Map`                 | An empty collection                                                             |
| `NonEmptySequence`, `NonEmptyMap`        | `Left`, because an empty value is not allowed                                   |
| `Tuple2`                                 | A pair of the two defaults; `Left` if either side has none                      |
| `Either`                                 | `Left` of the left default, otherwise `Right` of the right default              |
| `Fallback`                               | `Both` when both sides have a default, otherwise the side that has one          |
| `Transform`                              | The default of the underlying schema, passed through the forward function       |
| `Lazy`                                   | The default of the wrapped schema                                               |
| `Fail`                                   | `Left` with the failure message                                                 |
| `Dynamic`                                | `Right(DynamicValue.NoneValue)`                                                 |

A `Transform` is how schemas such as `Schema[BigDecimal]` and `Schema[java.net.URI]` are built, so their default is the default of the underlying primitive mapped to the new type.

### Overriding a Primitive Default with `default`

The `Schema#default` method returns a copy of a primitive schema that uses the value you pass as its default:

```scala
val retries: Schema[Int] = Schema[Int].default(3)
// retries: Schema[Int] = Primitive(
//   standardType = int,
//   annotations = IndexedSeq(fieldDefaultValue(value = 3))
// )

retries.defaultValue
// res2: Either[String, Int] = Right(value = 3)
```

The original `Schema[Int]` keeps its own default, so the override affects only the new schema.

:::caution
`Schema#default` stores the value as a `fieldDefaultValue` annotation on the schema, and only `Primitive` schemas (and a `Lazy` that wraps one) read it. Every other kind of schema ignores it: records, enumerations, `Transform` schemas, optionals, and collections keep computing their default with the rules above. For example, `Schema[BigDecimal]` is a `Transform`, so the override has no effect:

```scala
Schema[BigDecimal].default(BigDecimal(5)).defaultValue
// res3: Either[String, BigDecimal] = Right(value = 0)
```

To give a case class field a default, use a Scala default parameter or the `fieldDefaultValue` annotation on the field, as described in the next section.
:::

### Records and Enumerations

A record builds its default from the default value of each field. For each field, it first looks for a `fieldDefaultValue` annotation on the field, and otherwise it uses the default of the field's schema. If any field has no default, the record has none. The following case class uses only standard types, so every field has one:

```scala
case class Settings(host: String, port: Int)

object Settings {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Settings] = DeriveSchema.gen[Settings]
}
```

The default record holds the default of each field's type:

```scala
Settings.schema.defaultValue
// res4: Either[String, Settings] = Right(
//   value = Settings(host = "", port = 0)
// )
```

When a case class declares Scala default parameters, `DeriveSchema.gen` turns each one into a `fieldDefaultValue` annotation on its field. The record default then uses those values instead of the defaults of the field types:

```scala
case class Server(host: String = "localhost", port: Int = 8080)

object Server {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Server] = DeriveSchema.gen[Server]
}
```

The default `Server` uses the declared parameter values:

```scala
Server.schema.defaultValue
// res5: Either[String, Server] = Right(
//   value = Server(host = "localhost", port = 8080)
// )
```

The same `fieldDefaultValue` annotation also makes the field optional when decoding, so codecs such as the JSON codec fill in the declared value when the field is missing. The [Schema Annotations](../schema-annotations.md) page shows the annotation applied by hand.

An enumeration uses the default value of its first case, in the order the cases appear in the schema.

---

## Transforming Schemas

Using the `Schema#transform` method, we can transform a `Schema[A]` into a `Schema[B]` by supplying two functions that convert between `A` and `B`. In normal Scala code this would be the equivalent of `map`, but the conversion has to work in both directions, because a schema both produces and consumes values. When a conversion can fail, `Schema#transformOrFail` takes two functions that return an `Either` instead:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def transform[B](f: A => B, g: B => A)(implicit loc: SourceLocation): Schema[B]

  def transformOrFail[B](
    f: A => Either[String, B],
    g: B => Either[String, A]
  )(implicit loc: SourceLocation): Schema[B]
}
```

Therefore, if we have a schema for `A`, and a pair of conversions between `A` and `B`, we can derive a schema for `B` in terms of `Schema[A]`. The compiler fills in the implicit `SourceLocation` parameter with the place in the source code where the method is called.

:::note
In type theory, isomorphism refers to a relationship between two types that have a bijective correspondence or mapping between their elements. More specifically, if two types, let's say Type `A` and Type `B`, are isomorphic, it means that there exists a pair of functions—one going from A to B (often called the forward function) and another going from B to A (often called the backward function)—that satisfy certain properties.
:::

### The `Transform` Schema

Both methods return a `Schema.Transform`, a case class that stores the underlying schema and the two conversions:

```scala
object Schema {
  final case class Transform[A, B, I](
    schema: Schema[A],
    f: A => Either[String, B],
    g: B => Either[String, A],
    annotations: Chunk[Any],
    identity: I
  ) extends Schema[B]
}
```

`Schema#transform` wraps its plain functions so that they always succeed. The `annotations` start as a copy of the annotations of the underlying schema, and `identity` holds the `SourceLocation` of the call. Two transforms created at different places in the code are therefore different schemas, even when they wrap the same underlying schema.

### Transforming with Validation

`Schema#transformOrFail` is the right choice when only some values of `A` form a valid `B`. The forward function returns `Left` with a message for a value it rejects, and codecs report that message as a decoding error.

For example, assume we have a wrapper class `Age` that wraps an `Int` value, and the age must be between 0 and 120. We can define a `Schema[Age]` with `Schema#transformOrFail`:

```scala
import zio.schema._

case class Age(i: Int)

object Age {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Age] =
    Schema[Int].transformOrFail(
      (i: Int) =>
        if (i >= 0 && i <= 120)
          Right(Age(i))
        else
          Left("Age must be between 0 and 120"),
      (age: Age) => Right(age.i)
    )
}
```

Converting a value through `DynamicValue` runs the forward function, so an out-of-range age is rejected:

```scala
Age.schema.fromDynamic(Schema[Int].toDynamic(30))
// res0: Either[String, Age] = Right(value = Age(i = 30))
Age.schema.fromDynamic(Schema[Int].toDynamic(130))
// res1: Either[String, Age] = Left(value = "Age must be between 0 and 120")
```

### How Other Operations See a Transform

Most operations work on the underlying schema and convert with the two functions:

- `Schema#defaultValue` takes the default of the underlying schema and passes it through the forward function, so `Age.schema.defaultValue` is `Right(Age(0))`.
- `Schema#toDynamic` stores the underlying value, so a `DynamicValue` for an `Age` is a plain integer.
- `Schema#ast` describes only the underlying schema. The conversion functions cannot be serialized, so a receiver of the tree sees an `Int`.
- `Schema#validate` converts the value with the backward function and checks the underlying value.

---

## Validation(Operations)

Validation rules describe which values of a type are acceptable, such as a non-empty name or an age between 0 and 120. In ZIO Schema such a rule is a `Validation[A]`: a **composable rule** that decides whether a value of type `A` is acceptable, and explains why when it is not. Rules attach to the fields of a schema, so every program that holds the schema can check values the same way. The type parameter `A` is the type of value the rule checks; it is invariant. The fundamental operations are `Validation#validate`, which runs the rule, and the boolean operators `&&`, `||` and `!`, which combine rules.

`Validation` has these properties:

- Data, not code. A rule is a tree of predicates, so it can be inspected and combined before it runs.
- Error accumulation. A failed rule returns every failed check, not only the first.
- Pure. Validating never changes the value; the caller decides what to do with the errors.

A `Validation` wraps a boolean tree of predicates:

```scala
final case class Validation[A](bool: Bool[Predicate[A]]) {
  def &&(that: Validation[A]): Validation[A]
  def ||(that: Validation[A]): Validation[A]
  def unary_! : Validation[A]
  def validate(value: A): Either[Chunk[ValidationError], Unit]
}

object Validation extends Regexs with Time
```

All types on this page live in the `zio.schema.validation` package, except the `@validate` annotation, which lives in `zio.schema.annotation`. The [Usage](#usage) section shows the common path; the sections after it cover the full API.

### Usage

The simplest way to add a rule is the `@validate` annotation on a case class field. The rule becomes part of the derived schema:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Person(
    @validate(Validation.minLength(1)) name: String,
    @validate(Validation.between(0, 120)) age: Int
)

object Person {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Person] = DeriveSchema.gen[Person]
}
```

The `Validation.minLength(1)` rule rejects an empty name, and the `Validation.between(0, 120)` rule keeps the age in range; both bounds are inclusive. `Schema#validate` checks a value and returns the failed checks as a `Chunk[ValidationError]`. A valid value gives an empty chunk:

```scala
Person.schema.validate(Person("John", 42)).isEmpty
// res0: Boolean = true
```

An invalid value gives one entry per failed check. The following person breaks both rules:

```scala
val problems = Person.schema.validate(Person("", 130))
// problems: zio.Chunk[validation.ValidationError] = IndexedSeq(
//   MinLength(minLength = 1, actualLength = 0, string = ""),
//   EqualTo(value = 130, expected = 120),
//   LessThan(value = 130, expected = 120)
// )

problems.size
// res1: Int = 3
```

To print the individual failures, we iterate over the result:

```scala
problems.foreach(problem => println(problem))
// MinLength(1,0,)
// EqualTo(130,120)
// LessThan(130,120)
```

Each printed entry names the failed check and the values it compared. For example, `MinLength(1,0,)` means the name needs at least one character and had none. The result has three entries for two broken rules, because `Validation.between(lower, upper)` is built as `(greaterThan(lower) || equalTo(lower)) && (lessThan(upper) || equalTo(upper))`. An age of 130 fails both the less-than check and the equal-to check of the upper bound, so it reports two entries.

The codecs do not run these rules, so we call `Schema#validate` after decoding untrusted input, as [Validating After Decoding](#validating-after-decoding) shows. A rule can also run on its own with `Validation#validate`; see [Checking a Single Value](#checking-a-single-value).

### Attaching Rules to a Schema

A rule takes effect in `Schema.validate` only when it sits on a record field. ZIO Schema offers two ways to put it there: the `@validate` annotation for derived schemas, and the `validation0` parameter for schemas written by hand.

#### The `@validate` Annotation

`@validate` is a static annotation that holds one rule:

```scala
final case class validate[A](validation: Validation[A]) extends scala.annotation.StaticAnnotation
```

When `DeriveSchema.gen` builds a record schema, it reads the `@validate` annotations on each constructor parameter and stores their rule in `Schema.Field#validation` for that field. A field with several `@validate` annotations gets all of them, combined with `&&`. A field without one gets `Validation.succeed`. In this example, `name` carries two annotations and `price` carries one:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Product(
  @validate(Validation.minLength(1)) @validate(Validation.maxLength(50)) name: String,
  @validate(Validation.greaterThan(BigDecimal(0))) price: BigDecimal
)

object Product {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Product] = DeriveSchema.gen[Product]
}

Schema.validate(Product("", BigDecimal(-1))).map(_.message)
// res4: zio.Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq(
//   "Expected the length of  to be at least 1 characters but was 0 characters.",
//   "-1 should be greater than 0"
// )
```

:::caution[Scala 2 and Case Classes With More Than 22 Fields]
On Scala 2, `DeriveSchema.gen` represents a case class with more than 22 fields as a `GenericRecord`, and it drops every `@validate` annotation on such a class. `Schema.validate` then reports no errors for it. Scala 3 derivation keeps the annotations. On Scala 2, call `Validation#validate` on the field values directly.
:::

#### Field Rules in Hand-Written Schemas

`Schema.Field.apply` takes the rule through its `validation0` parameter, which defaults to `Validation.succeed`. See [Schema Data Types](../basic-building-blocks.md) for the other parameters. The following schema rejects temperatures below absolute zero:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Temperature(celsius: Double)

object Temperature {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Temperature] =
    Schema.CaseClass1[Double, Temperature](
      id0 = TypeId.parse("Temperature"),
      field0 = Schema.Field[Temperature, Double](
        name0 = "celsius",
        schema0 = Schema[Double],
        validation0 = Validation.greaterThan(-273.15),
        get0 = _.celsius,
        set0 = (t, c) => t.copy(celsius = c)
      ),
      defaultConstruct0 = c => Temperature(c)
    )
}

Schema.validate(Temperature(-300.0)).map(_.message)
// res6: zio.Chunk[String] = IndexedSeq(
//   "-300.0 should be greater than -273.15"
// )
```

#### Rules on a Whole Schema

`Schema#validation` returns a copy of the schema with the rule stored as a `@validate` annotation:

```scala
sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def validation(validation: Validation[A]): Schema[A]
}
```

`Schema.validate` does not read schema annotations. It only reads `Schema.Field#validation` of record fields, so the rule added below is never checked:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

val smallInt: Schema[Int] = Schema[Int].validation(Validation.lessThan(10))
// smallInt: Schema[Int] = Primitive(
//   standardType = int,
//   annotations = IndexedSeq(
//     validate(
//       validation = Validation(
//         bool = Leaf(value = LessThan(numType = IntType, value = 10))
//       )
//     )
//   )
// )

Schema.validate(100)(smallInt)
// res8: zio.Chunk[validation.ValidationError] = IndexedSeq()

Validation.lessThan(10).validate(100)
// res9: Either[zio.Chunk[validation.ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(LessThan(value = 100, expected = 10))
// )
```

:::caution[`Schema#validation` Is Not Checked by `Schema#validate`]
`Schema#validation(v)` adds a rule that `Schema#validate` never checks. To enforce a rule, put it on a field with `@validate` (or `validation0`), or call `v.validate(value)` directly.
:::

### Running Rules

Rules run either one at a time, through `Validation#validate`, or for a whole value, through `Schema.validate`, which visits every field rule in the value.

#### Checking a Single Value

`Validation#validate` returns `Right(())` when the value passes, and `Left` with the failed checks otherwise:

```scala
final case class Validation[A](bool: Bool[Predicate[A]]) {
  def validate(value: A): Either[Chunk[ValidationError], Unit]
}
```

A rule built with `&&` collects the errors of both sides. A rule built with `||` passes when either side passes, and reports the errors of both sides when both fail:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

val shortCode: Validation[String] = Validation.minLength(2) && Validation.maxLength(4)
// shortCode: Validation[String] = Validation(
//   bool = And(
//     left = Leaf(value = MinLength(n = 2)),
//     right = Leaf(value = MaxLength(n = 4))
//   )
// )

shortCode.validate("abc")
// res11: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Right(value = ())

shortCode.validate("abcdef")
// res12: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     MaxLength(maxLength = 4, actualLength = 6, string = "abcdef")
//   )
// )

(Validation.equalTo(0) || Validation.greaterThan(100)).validate(50)
// res13: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     EqualTo(value = 50, expected = 0),
//     GreaterThan(value = 50, expected = 100)
//   )
// )
```

#### Checking a Whole Value With a Schema

`Schema.validate` walks a value with its schema and runs the rule of every record field it meets. `Schema#validate` is the method form of the same operation:

```scala
object Schema {
  def validate[A](value: A)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Chunk[ValidationError]
}

sealed trait Schema[A] {
  def validate(value: A)(implicit schema: Schema[A]): Chunk[ValidationError]
}
```

`Schema#validate` checks with the implicit `Schema[A]` in scope, not with the schema that receives the call. In the common case, where the schema is the implicit value in the companion object, the two are the same. When you hold a schema that is not the implicit one, call `Schema.validate(value)(schema)` instead.

The walk follows the structure of the value. It descends into nested records, the active case of an enum, the elements of sequences, sets and maps (keys and values), the content of `Some`, `Left`, `Right` and `Fallback`, both sides of a tuple, and lazy schemas. For a transformed schema, it converts the value back to the underlying type and validates that. Primitive, dynamic and failing schemas add no checks. Nested rules work without extra code:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Tag(@validate(Validation.minLength(1)) label: String)

object Tag {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Tag] = DeriveSchema.gen[Tag]
}

final case class Post(title: String, tags: List[Tag])

object Post {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Post] = DeriveSchema.gen[Post]
}

Schema.validate(Post("Hello", List(Tag("scala"), Tag(""))))
// res15: zio.Chunk[validation.ValidationError] = IndexedSeq(
//   MinLength(minLength = 1, actualLength = 0, string = "")
// )
```

Besides the errors of the field rules, the walk can report two structural errors. A record that has no value for a field (for example a `GenericRecord` whose `ListMap` lacks a key) reports `ValidationError.MissingField`. A transformed schema whose reverse function fails reports `ValidationError.Generic` with the failure message.

#### Validating After Decoding

To reject invalid input, we decode first and then call `Schema.validate` on the result:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.codec.JsonCodec
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Account(@validate(Validation.minLength(3)) handle: String)

object Account {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Account] = DeriveSchema.gen[Account]
}

val decoded = JsonCodec.jsonDecoder(Account.schema).decodeJson("""{"handle":"x"}""")
// decoded: Either[String, Account] = Right(value = Account(handle = "x"))

decoded.map(Schema.validate(_))
// res17: Either[String, zio.Chunk[validation.ValidationError]] = Right(
//   value = IndexedSeq(MinLength(minLength = 3, actualLength = 1, string = "x"))
// )
```

:::caution[Codecs Do Not Validate]
The codecs do not validate when decoding: a value that breaks its `@validate` rules decodes successfully. Call `Schema.validate` after decoding.
:::

### Creating Rules

The `Validation` companion object has constructors for string and numeric checks, constant rules, and rules built from a collection of rules.

#### String Rules

`Validation.minLength` and `Validation.maxLength` bound the length of a string; both bounds are inclusive. `Validation.regex` requires the whole string to match a pattern built with the [Regex DSL](#the-regex-dsl):

```scala
object Validation {
  def minLength(n: Int): Validation[String]
  def maxLength(n: Int): Validation[String]
  def regex(r: Regex): Validation[String]
}
```

The following rules check a length and a digits-only pattern:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

Validation.minLength(2).validate("a")
// res19: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(MinLength(minLength = 2, actualLength = 1, string = "a"))
// )

Validation.maxLength(5).validate("hello")
// res20: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Right(value = ())

Validation.regex(Regex.digit.atLeast(1)).validate("2024")
// res21: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Right(value = ())
```

#### Numeric Rules

`Validation.greaterThan`, `Validation.lessThan` and `Validation.equalTo` compare a number with a fixed value; `Validation.greaterThan` and `Validation.lessThan` are strict. `Validation.between` accepts values from `lower` to `upper`, both included. Each constructor needs an implicit `NumType[A]`:

```scala
object Validation {
  def greaterThan[A](value: A)(implicit numType: NumType[A]): Validation[A]
  def lessThan[A](value: A)(implicit numType: NumType[A]): Validation[A]
  def equalTo[A](value: A)(implicit numType: NumType[A]): Validation[A]
  def between[A](lower: A, upper: A)(implicit numType: NumType[A]): Validation[A]
}
```

`NumType` has instances for `Int`, `Long`, `Short`, `Float`, `Double`, `BigDecimal` and `BigInt`. The same constructors work across these types:

```scala
Validation.greaterThan(0L).validate(5L)
// res22: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Right(value = ())

Validation.lessThan(1.5).validate(2.0)
// res23: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(LessThan(value = 2.0, expected = 1.5))
// )

Validation.equalTo(BigInt(42)).validate(BigInt(41))
// res24: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(EqualTo(value = 41, expected = 42))
// )

Validation.between(1, 10).validate(11)
// res25: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     LessThan(value = 11, expected = 10),
//     EqualTo(value = 11, expected = 10)
//   )
// )
```

`NumType` has no instance for `Byte` or `Char`. For such a type, we adapt an `Int` rule with `Validation#contramap`:

```scala
val positiveByte: Validation[Byte] = Validation.greaterThan(0).contramap[Byte](_.toInt)
// positiveByte: Validation[Byte] = Validation(
//   bool = Leaf(
//     value = Contramap(
//       pred = Leaf(value = GreaterThan(numType = IntType, value = 0)),
//       f = <function1>
//     )
//   )
// )

positiveByte.validate((-1).toByte)
// res26: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(GreaterThan(value = -1, expected = 0))
// )
```

#### Constant Rules

`Validation.succeed` accepts every value, and `Validation.fail` rejects every value. They are the neutral starting points for building rules in a loop:

```scala
object Validation {
  def succeed[A]: Validation[A]
  def fail[A]: Validation[A]
}
```

`Validation.fail` rejects the value without describing why, so its error chunk is empty:

```scala
Validation.succeed[Int].validate(1)
// res27: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Right(value = ())

Validation.fail[Int].validate(1)
// res28: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(value = IndexedSeq())
```

The empty chunk matters for `Schema.validate`, which reports field errors by collecting the error chunks of the failed rules. A rule that fails with an empty chunk adds nothing:

```scala
import zio.schema._
import zio.schema.annotation.validate
import zio.schema.validation.Validation

final case class Locked(@validate(Validation.fail[Int]) value: Int)

object Locked {
  implicit val schema: Schema[Locked] = DeriveSchema.gen[Locked]
}

Schema.validate(Locked(1))
// res30: zio.Chunk[validation.ValidationError] = IndexedSeq()
```

:::caution[Rules That Fail With No Errors Are Invisible to `@validate`]
`Validation.fail`, and any negation that fails with an empty error chunk, report no error through `@validate`: `Schema.validate` returns an empty chunk even though the rule failed. This affects a negated `Validation.succeed` and the negation of a passing `Validation#optional`, `Validation#contramap` or `Validation.either` rule (see [Boolean Operators](#boolean-operators)), as well as `Validation#right` and `Validation#left` with their default argument. To detect these failures, call `Validation#validate` and check for `Left`.
:::

#### Rules From a Collection of Rules

`Validation.allOf` requires every rule to pass, and `Validation.anyOf` requires at least one. Each has a varargs overload and an `Iterable` overload:

```scala
object Validation {
  def allOf[A](vs: Validation[A]*): Validation[A]
  def allOf[A](vl: Iterable[Validation[A]]): Validation[A]
  def anyOf[A](vs: Validation[A]*): Validation[A]
  def anyOf[A](vl: Iterable[Validation[A]]): Validation[A]
}
```

`Validation.allOf` folds the rules with `&&`, starting from `Validation.succeed`, and `Validation.anyOf` folds them with `||`, starting from `Validation.fail`. An empty `Validation.allOf` therefore accepts every value, and an empty `Validation.anyOf` rejects every value:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

val forbidden = List("admin", "root").map(name => !Validation.regex(Regex.literal(name)))
// forbidden: List[Validation[String]] = List(
//   Validation(
//     bool = Not(value = Leaf(value = Matches(r = Literal(str = "admin"))))
//   ),
//   Validation(
//     bool = Not(value = Leaf(value = Matches(r = Literal(str = "root"))))
//   )
// )

Validation.allOf(forbidden).validate("root").isLeft
// res32: Boolean = true

Validation.anyOf(Validation.equalTo(1), Validation.equalTo(2)).validate(2)
// res33: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Right(value = ())

Validation.anyOf(List.empty[Validation[Int]]).validate(5).isLeft
// res34: Boolean = true
```

### Combining and Adapting Rules

Combinators build larger rules from smaller ones. The boolean operators combine rules of the same type, and the adapters move a rule to a different input type.

#### Boolean Operators

`&&` passes when both rules pass, `||` passes when either passes, and `!` (written as a prefix) passes when the rule fails:

```scala
final case class Validation[A](bool: Bool[Predicate[A]]) {
  def &&(that: Validation[A]): Validation[A]
  def ||(that: Validation[A]): Validation[A]
  def unary_! : Validation[A]
}
```

A negated rule still explains its failures. Every predicate records an error for the opposite outcome, and negation reports that error:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

(!Validation.minLength(3)).validate("hello")
// res36: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     MaxLength(maxLength = 3, actualLength = 5, string = "hello")
//   )
// )

(!Validation.equalTo(0)).validate(0)
// res37: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(NotEqualTo(value = 0, expected = 0))
// )
```

The following table lists the error each constructor reports when the rule fails, and when its negation fails:

| Constructor                                                                  | Error when the rule fails           | Error when the negation fails   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `Validation.minLength(n)`                                                    | `MinLength(n, actual, string)`      | `MaxLength(n, actual, string)`  |
| `Validation.maxLength(n)`                                                    | `MaxLength(n, actual, string)`      | `MinLength(n, actual, string)`  |
| `Validation.regex(r)`                                                        | `RegexMatch(string, r)`             | `NotRegexMatch(string, r)`      |
| `Validation.greaterThan(x)`                                                  | `GreaterThan(value, x)`             | `LessThan(value, x)`            |
| `Validation.lessThan(x)`                                                     | `LessThan(value, x)`                | `GreaterThan(value, x)`         |
| `Validation.equalTo(x)`                                                      | `EqualTo(value, x)`                 | `NotEqualTo(value, x)`          |
| `Validation.succeed`                                                         | never fails                         | empty chunk                     |
| `Validation#optional` on `None`                                              | `EqualToNone()` (when not accepted) | `EqualToNone()` (when accepted) |
| `Validation#optional` on `Some`, `Validation#contramap`, `Validation.either` | errors of the inner rule            | empty chunk                     |

#### Adapting the Input Type

`Validation#contramap` runs a rule on a value derived from the input. `Validation#optional` lifts a rule to `Option`; its `validNone` parameter decides whether `None` passes. `Validation.either` builds a rule for `Either` from one rule per side. `Validation#right` and `Validation#left` lift a rule to one side of an `Either` and take a rule for the other side, which defaults to `Validation.fail`:

```scala
final case class Validation[A](bool: Bool[Predicate[A]]) {
  def contramap[B](f: B => A): Validation[B]
  def optional(validNone: Boolean = true): Validation[Option[A]]
  def right[B](onLeft: Validation[B] = Validation.fail[B]): Validation[Either[B, A]]
  def left[B](onRight: Validation[B] = Validation.fail[B]): Validation[Either[A, B]]
}

object Validation {
  def either[L, R](left: Validation[L], right: Validation[R]): Validation[Either[L, R]]
}
```

We adapt a string rule to a wrapper type, to optional values, and to both sides of an `Either`:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

final case class Username(value: String)

val usernameRule: Validation[Username] = Validation.minLength(3).contramap[Username](_.value)
// usernameRule: Validation[Username] = Validation(
//   bool = Leaf(
//     value = Contramap(pred = Leaf(value = MinLength(n = 3)), f = <function1>)
//   )
// )
usernameRule.validate(Username("jo"))
// res39: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(MinLength(minLength = 3, actualLength = 2, string = "jo"))
// )

val nickname: Validation[Option[String]] = Validation.minLength(2).optional()
// nickname: Validation[Option[String]] = Validation(
//   bool = Leaf(
//     value = Optional(pred = Leaf(value = MinLength(n = 2)), validNone = true)
//   )
// )
nickname.validate(None)
// res40: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Right(value = ())
nickname.validate(Some("x"))
// res41: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(MinLength(minLength = 2, actualLength = 1, string = "x"))
// )

val required: Validation[Option[String]] = Validation.minLength(2).optional(validNone = false)
// required: Validation[Option[String]] = Validation(
//   bool = Leaf(
//     value = Optional(pred = Leaf(value = MinLength(n = 2)), validNone = false)
//   )
// )
required.validate(None)
// res42: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(EqualToNone())
// )

val idOrName: Validation[Either[Int, String]] =
  Validation.either(Validation.greaterThan(0), Validation.minLength(1))
// idOrName: Validation[Either[Int, String]] = Validation(
//   bool = Leaf(
//     value = Either(
//       left = Leaf(value = GreaterThan(numType = IntType, value = 0)),
//       right = Leaf(value = MinLength(n = 1))
//     )
//   )
// )
idOrName.validate(Left(-5))
// res43: Either[zio.Chunk[ValidationError], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(GreaterThan(value = -5, expected = 0))
// )

Validation.minLength(1).right[Int]().validate(Left(1)).isLeft
// res44: Boolean = true
```

### Predefined Validators

The `Validation` object mixes in the `Regexs` and `Time` traits, so ready-made validators for common string formats are members of `Validation`. Phone number validators live in a separate object, `PhoneNumberValidation`.

#### Identifiers, Emails, and Network Addresses

These validators are values of type `Validation[String]`:

| Validator               | Accepts                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Validation.identifier` | One or more ASCII letters, digits or underscores                                                                     |
| `Validation.email`      | An email address with a domain name, a bracketed IPv4 address or a bracketed `IPv6:` address; at most 254 characters |
| `Validation.ipV4`       | A dotted IPv4 address with each part from 0 to 255; leading zeros are allowed                                        |
| `Validation.ipV6`       | An IPv6 address, including `::` shortening and an embedded IPv4 tail                                                 |
| `Validation.uuidV4`     | A version 4 UUID in the 8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal form                                                                  |

Each validator checks the whole string:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

Validation.identifier.validate("user_1").isRight
// res46: Boolean = true

Validation.email.validate("bob+and-alice@gmail.com").isRight
// res47: Boolean = true
Validation.email.validate("a@@a.com").isRight
// res48: Boolean = false

Validation.ipV4.validate("192.168.1.255").isRight
// res49: Boolean = true
Validation.ipV4.validate("10.0.0.256").isRight
// res50: Boolean = false

Validation.ipV6.validate("2001:cdba::3257:9652").isRight
// res51: Boolean = true

Validation.uuidV4.validate(java.util.UUID.randomUUID().toString).isRight
// res52: Boolean = true
Validation.uuidV4.validate("1e3118de-ddb6-11ec-8653-93e6961d46be").isRight
// res53: Boolean = false
```

The last UUID is a version 1 UUID, so `Validation.uuidV4` rejects it.

#### Durations and Times

`Validation.duration` accepts ISO-8601 durations such as `P1D` or `PT1H30M`, the form that `java.time.Duration#toString` produces. `Validation.time` builds a validator from a time format:

```scala
object Validation {
  lazy val duration: Validation[String]
  def time(format: String): Validation[String]
}
```

The format of `Validation.time` is close to the one of `java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter`. Each letter may appear once; a letter written twice requires two digits, and a letter written once accepts one or two digits:

| Letter | Meaning                                        | Allowed repetitions |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `H`    | Hour of day (`HH` accepts `00` to `24`)        | 1 or 2              |
| `h`    | Hour of the clock, `0` to `12`                 | 1 or 2              |
| `m`    | Minute, `0` to `59`                            | 1 or 2              |
| `s`    | Second, `0` to `59`                            | 1 or 2              |
| `S`    | Fraction of a second, exactly that many digits | 1 to 9              |
| `a`    | `AM` or `PM`                                   | 1                   |

Every other character is copied literally, except other letters, which are reserved. `Validation.time` throws `IllegalArgumentException` when the format repeats a letter, writes it too many times, uses a reserved letter, or contains no time field. These validators check durations and clock times:

```scala
Validation.duration.validate("PT1H30M").isRight
// res54: Boolean = true
Validation.duration.validate("1 hour").isRight
// res55: Boolean = false

Validation.time("HH:mm").validate("09:30").isRight
// res56: Boolean = true
Validation.time("HH:mm").validate("9:30").isRight
// res57: Boolean = false

Validation.time("h:mm a").validate("7:05 PM").isRight
// res58: Boolean = true
```

#### Phone Numbers

`PhoneNumberValidation` holds one validator per country, named `phoneNumber` followed by the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, such as `PhoneNumberValidation.phoneNumberUS`, `PhoneNumberValidation.phoneNumberDE` or `PhoneNumberValidation.phoneNumberJP`. Each validator accepts a number that starts either with an international prefix (`+`, `00`, or a country-specific one such as `011`) followed by the country calling code, or, for countries that have one, with the national trunk prefix. Digits may be separated by a space or a hyphen:

```scala
object PhoneNumberValidation extends PhoneNumberValidation

trait PhoneNumberValidation {
  lazy val phoneNumberUS: Validation[String]
  lazy val phoneNumberDE: Validation[String]
  // ... one `phoneNumberXX` for each of 253 country and territory codes
}
```

The trait also exposes the `Regex` pieces it builds the validators from: `optionalSpace`, `optionalSeparator`, `twoDigits`, `threeDigits`, `plus`, `doubleZero`, `internationalPrefix`, `nationalPrefixZero`, `nationalPrefixOne`, `nationalPrefixEight` and `digitsWithSeparator`. A US number dialled with the `011` prefix passes:

```scala
PhoneNumberValidation.phoneNumberUS.validate("011 1 447142964").isRight
// res59: Boolean = true
```

### The Regex DSL

`Regex` is a sealed trait that describes a regular expression as data. `Validation.regex` turns a `Regex` into a rule, and the predefined validators are built from it. A `Regex` always matches the whole input.

#### Building Blocks

The `Regex` companion object provides the atoms of a pattern:

```scala
object Regex {
  def literal(str: String): Regex
  def oneOf(chars: Char*): Regex
  def between(minChar: Char, maxChar: Char): Regex
  def filter(f: Char => Boolean): Regex

  val digit: Regex
  val digitNonZero: Regex
  val letter: Regex
  val digitOrLetter: Regex
  val hexDigit: Regex
  val hexDigitNonZero: Regex
}
```

`Regex.literal` matches an exact string. `Regex.oneOf` matches one of the given characters, and `Regex.between` matches one character in an inclusive range. `Regex.filter` matches one character for which the predicate holds; it tests every `Char` value up front, so build such a pattern once and reuse it. `Regex.letter` matches an ASCII letter, and `Regex.hexDigit` matches a digit or a letter from `a` to `f` in either case. The `NonZero` variants exclude `0`.

These constructors produce the case classes and objects of `Regex`, which a codec or a tool can inspect:

| Case                                                       | Built by                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `Literal(str: String)`                                     | `Regex.literal`               |
| `CharacterSet(set: Set[Char])`                             | `Regex.oneOf`, `Regex.filter` |
| `Between(start: Char, end: Char)`                          | `Regex.between`               |
| `Repeat(regex: Regex, min: Option[Int], max: Option[Int])` | the repetition operators      |
| `Sequence(first: Regex, second: Regex)`                    | `Regex#~`                     |
| `Alternate(left: Regex, right: Regex)`                     | `Regex#\|`                    |
| `Letter`, `Digit`                                          | `Regex.letter`, `Regex.digit` |
| `Empty`                                                    | matches the empty string      |

#### Repetition and Composition

Methods on `Regex` repeat a pattern and join patterns together. `Regex#~` matches one pattern followed by another, and `Regex#|` matches either pattern. The repetition methods take inclusive bounds:

```scala
sealed trait Regex {
  def atLeast(n: Int): Regex
  def atMost(n: Int): Regex
  def between(min: Int, max: Int): Regex
  def exactly(n: Int): Regex
  def + : Regex
  def * : Regex
  def ? : Regex
  def ~(that: Regex): Regex
  def |(that: Regex): Regex
}
```

`+` is `atLeast(1)`, `*` is `atLeast(0)` and `?` is `atMost(1)`. Unlike `Regex.between` on the companion, which takes two characters, `Regex#between` takes two repetition counts. We combine these into a pattern for hex colours such as `#a0b1c2`:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

val hexColor: Regex = Regex.literal("#") ~ Regex.hexDigit.exactly(6)

val semver: Regex =
  Regex.digit.+ ~ Regex.oneOf('.') ~ Regex.digit.+ ~ Regex.oneOf('.') ~ Regex.digit.+ ~
    (Regex.oneOf('-') ~ Regex.digitOrLetter.+).?
```

#### Testing and Rendering

`Regex#test` checks a string against the pattern, and `Regex.toRegexString` renders the pattern in `java.util.regex` syntax, escaping special characters:

```scala
sealed trait Regex {
  def test(string: String): Boolean
}

object Regex {
  def toRegexString(regex: Regex): String
}
```

The patterns from the previous section test and render as follows:

```scala
hexColor.test("#a0b1c2")
// res61: Boolean = true
hexColor.test("a0b1c2")
// res62: Boolean = false

semver.test("1.10.0-rc1")
// res63: Boolean = true

Regex.toRegexString(hexColor)
// res64: String = "(#)(((((\\d)|([a-f])))|([A-F]))){6}"
```

`Regex#test` compiles the pattern on every call. `Regex.toRegexString` throws `IllegalArgumentException` for a `Repeat` with neither a minimum nor a maximum, which the DSL methods never build.

### Validation Errors

`ValidationError` is a sealed trait; `ValidationError#message` gives a human-readable description. `Validation#validate` and `Schema.validate` return these cases:

| Case                                                           | Reported when                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `MinLength(minLength: Int, actualLength: Int, string: String)` | A string is shorter than the minimum length                         |
| `MaxLength(maxLength: Int, actualLength: Int, string: String)` | A string is longer than the maximum length                          |
| `GreaterThan[A](value: A, expected: A)`                        | `value` is not greater than `expected`                              |
| `LessThan[A](value: A, expected: A)`                           | `value` is not less than `expected`                                 |
| `EqualTo[A](value: A, expected: A)`                            | `value` is not equal to `expected`                                  |
| `NotEqualTo[A](value: A, expected: A)`                         | `value` is equal to `expected` under a negated `Validation.equalTo` |
| `EqualToNone()`                                                | An `Option` rule meets `None`                                       |
| `RegexMatch(str: String, expected: Regex)`                     | `str` does not match `expected`                                     |
| `NotRegexMatch(str: String, expected: Regex)`                  | `str` matches `expected` under a negated `Validation.regex`         |
| `MissingField(field: Schema.Field[_, _])`                      | A record value has no value for `field`                             |
| `Generic(message: String)`                                     | A transformed schema cannot convert the value back                  |
| `EqualToLeft[A](value: A)`, `EqualToRight[A](value: A)`        | Defined for `Either` checks; no built-in rule reports them          |

We print the messages of a failed rule with `ValidationError#message`:

```scala
import zio.schema.validation._

Validation.maxLength(3).validate("abcd").left.map(_.map(_.message))
// res66: Either[zio.Chunk[String], Unit] = Left(
//   value = IndexedSeq(
//     "Expected the length of abcd to be at most 3 characters but was 4 characters."
//   )
// )
```

`DecodeError` also has a separate `DecodeError.ValidationError` case, which carries the `Validation`, the `Schema.Field` and a message. The built-in codecs never report it, because they do not run rules while decoding. See [Codec Core Types](../reference/codec-core.md) for decode errors.

:::caution[`RegexMatch` Messages Print the Whole Pattern]
`ValidationError.RegexMatch#message` includes the complete `Regex` tree of the rule. For a predefined validator such as `Validation.email`, that message is very long and means nothing to an end user. Match on `ValidationError.RegexMatch` and write your own message; [How to Validate Untrusted Input](../how-to/validate-input.md) shows one way.
:::

### Low-Level Building Blocks

You rarely use these types directly; the constructors and combinators above build them for you. They matter when you inspect a rule, for example to translate it into a JSON Schema or a database constraint.

`Validation` wraps a `Bool[Predicate[A]]`. `Bool` is a boolean expression tree, `Predicate` is a single check, and `NumType` supplies the ordering for numeric checks:

```scala
sealed trait Bool[A] {
  def &&(that: Bool[A]): Bool[A]
  def ||(that: Bool[A]): Bool[A]
  def unary_! : Bool[A]
  def map[B](f: A => B): Bool[B]
}

object Bool {
  final case class And[A](left: Bool[A], right: Bool[A]) extends Bool[A]
  final case class Or[A](left: Bool[A], right: Bool[A])  extends Bool[A]
  final case class Leaf[A](value: A)                     extends Bool[A]
  final case class Not[A](value: Bool[A])                extends Bool[A]
}

sealed trait Predicate[A] {
  def validate(value: A): Either[Chunk[ValidationError], Chunk[ValidationError]]
  def contramap[B](f: B => A): Predicate[B]
}

sealed trait NumType[A] {
  def numeric: Numeric[A]
}
```

`Predicate#validate` returns `Left` with the errors of a failure, and `Right` with the errors to report if the predicate is negated. The `Predicate` cases are `Str.MinLength`, `Str.MaxLength`, `Str.Matches`, `Num.GreaterThan`, `Num.LessThan`, `Num.EqualTo`, `True`, `Optional`, `Contramap` and `Either`. The `NumType` instances are `IntType`, `LongType`, `ShortType`, `FloatType`, `DoubleType`, `BigDecimalType` and `BigIntType`. Reading the tree of a rule shows how it is built:

```scala
Validation.minLength(3).bool
// res67: Bool[Predicate[String]] = Leaf(value = MinLength(n = 3))

(Validation.minLength(3) && !Validation.maxLength(1)).bool
// res68: Bool[Predicate[String]] = And(
//   left = Leaf(value = MinLength(n = 3)),
//   right = Not(value = Leaf(value = MaxLength(n = 1)))
// )
```

### Integration

Rules reach the rest of ZIO Schema through record fields. `Schema.Field#validation` holds the rule of a field; see [Schema Data Types](../basic-building-blocks.md) for `Schema.Field` and the other schema cases, and [Basic Building Blocks](../basic-building-blocks.md) for how fields are declared in a schema. [Schema Methods](../reference/schema-methods.md) covers `Schema#validate` alongside the other methods of `Schema`, and [Schema Annotations](../schema-annotations.md) covers the other annotations that derivation reads. The [Standard Type Reference](../standard-type-reference.md) lists the types that the rules apply to. For a task-oriented walkthrough of checking request data, see [How to Validate Untrusted Input](../how-to/validate-input.md).
